Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.

Vinayapiṭake

In the Vinaya Piṭaka

Sāratthadīpanī-ṭīkā (dutiyo bhāgo)

Sāratthadīpanī-ṭīkā (Second Part)

1. Pārājikakaṇḍaṃ

1. The Pārājika Section

1. Paṭhamapārājikaṃ

1. The First Pārājika

Sudinnabhāṇavāravaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Sudinna Recitation Section

24. Anupadavaṇṇananti [M 2.0001][V 2.0001] padaṃ padaṃ paṭivaṇṇanaṃ, padānukkamena vaṇṇanaṃ vā. Bhaṇḍappayojanauddhārasāraṇādinā kiccenāti ettha vikkāyikabhaṇḍassa vikkiṇanaṃ bhaṇḍappayojanaṃ, dātuṃ [V 2.0002] saṅketite divase gantvā gahaṇaṃ uddhāro, “asukasmiṃ divase dātabba”nti satuppādanaṃ sāraṇaṃ. Catubbidhāyāti khattiyabrāhmaṇagahapatisamaṇānaṃ vasena catubbidhāya, bhikkhubhikkhunīupāsakaupāsikānaṃ vasena vā. Disvānassa etadahosīti hetuattho ayaṃ disvāna-saddo asamānakattuko yathā “ghataṃ pivitvā balaṃ hoti, sīhaṃ disvā bhayaṃ hotī”ti. Dassanakāraṇā hi evaṃ parivitakkanaṃ ahosi. Kiñcāpi ettha “bhabbakulaputtassā”ti vuttaṃ, tathāpi upanissayasampannassapi ajātasattuno viya antarāyo bhavissatīti imassa therassapi katapāpakammamūlavippaṭisāravasena adhigamantarāyo ahosīti vadanti.

24. `Anupadavaṇṇanā` means an explanation word by word, or an explanation in sequential order of the words. In the phrase `Bhaṇḍappayojanauddhārasāraṇādinā kiccena`, `bhaṇḍappayojanaṃ` is the selling of merchandise; `uddhāro` is going and taking it on the appointed day; and `sāraṇaṃ` is causing the thought to arise, 'It should be given on such-and-such a day.' `Catubbidhāya` means fourfold, either by way of khattiyas, brahmins, householders, and ascetics, or by way of monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen. In `Disvānassa etadahosīti`, this word `disvāna` is in the sense of cause and has a different agent, as in 'Having drunk ghee, there is strength,' and 'Having seen a lion, there is fear.' For, because of the reason of seeing, such a reflection occurred. Although here it is said, 'of a worthy clansman,' still, even for one endowed with supporting conditions, like Ajātasattu, an obstacle could arise. They say that for this elder too, due to remorse rooted in a past evil deed, there was an obstacle to attainment.

Kiṃ pana yesaṃ maggaphalānaṃ upanissayo atthi, buddhānaṃ sammukhībhāvepi tesaṃ antarāyo hotīti? Āma hoti, na pana buddhe paṭicca. Buddhā hi paresaṃ [M 2.0002] maggaphalādhigamāya ussāhajātā tattha nirantaraṃ yuttapayuttā eva honti, tasmā te paṭicca tesaṃ antarāyo na hoti, atha kho kiriyāparihāniyā vā pāpamittatāya vā hoti, kiriyāparihāni ca desakassa tasseva vā puggalassa tajjapayogābhāvato veditabbā, desakavasena panettha parihāni sāvakānaṃ vaseneva veditabbā, na buddhānaṃ vasena. Tathā hi sace dhammasenāpati dhanañjāniyassa brāhmaṇassa āsayaṃ ñatvā dhammaṃ desayissa, brāhmaṇo sotāpanno abhavissa. Evaṃ tāva desakassa vasena kiriyāparihāniyā antarāyo hoti. Sace pesso hatthārohaputto bhagavato sammukhā dhammaṃ suṇanto muhuttaṃ nisīdeyya, yāva tassa bhagavā attantapādike cattāro puggale vitthārena vibhajitvā deseti, sotāpattiphalena saṃyutto abhavissa. Evaṃ puggalassa vasena kiriyāparihāniyā antarāyo hoti nāma. Imassa hi upāsakassa kiriyāparihāni jātā apariniṭṭhitāya desanāya uṭṭhahitvā pakkantattā. Sace ajātasattu devadattassa vacanaṃ gahetvā pitughātakammaṃ nākarissa, sāmaññaphalasuttakathitadivase sotāpanno abhavissa, tassa vacanaṃ gahetvā pitughātakammassa katattā pana nāhosi. Evaṃ pāpamittatāya antarāyo hoti. Sudinnassapi pāpamittavasena antarāyo ahosīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yadi hi tena mātāpitūnaṃ vacanaṃ gahetvā purāṇadutiyikāya methunadhammo paṭisevito nābhavissa, na taṃmūlavippaṭisāravasena adhigamantarāyo abhavissa.

But is it that for those who have the supporting conditions for the paths and fruits, an obstacle arises even in the presence of the Buddhas? Yes, it does, but not on account of the Buddhas. For the Buddhas are zealous for others' attainment of the paths and fruits, and are constantly and diligently engaged therein. Therefore, an obstacle does not arise for them on account of the Buddhas, but rather from a decline in practice or from association with bad friends. A decline in practice should be understood as arising from a lack of suitable effort on the part of the teacher or of that very individual. Herein, a decline on the part of the teacher should be understood only with respect to the disciples, not with respect to the Buddhas. For if the General of the Dhamma, having known the disposition of the brahmin Dhanañjāni, had taught him the Dhamma, the brahmin would have become a stream-enterer. Thus, an obstacle arises from a decline in practice on the part of the teacher. If Pessa, the elephant-trainer's son, while listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Blessed One, had sat for a moment while the Blessed One analyzed and taught in detail the four kinds of individuals beginning with the one who torments himself, he would have become endowed with the fruit of stream-entry. Thus, an obstacle arises from a decline in practice on the part of the individual. For this lay follower, a decline in practice occurred because he got up and left when the teaching was unfinished. If Ajātasattu had not taken Devadatta's word and committed patricide, he would have become a stream-enterer on the day the Sāmaññaphala Sutta was spoken; but because he took his word and committed patricide, he did not. Thus, an obstacle arises from association with a bad friend. It should be seen that for Sudinna too, an obstacle arose due to a bad friend. For if he had not, having taken his parents' word, engaged in sexual intercourse with his former wife, the obstacle to attainment due to remorse rooted in that would not have arisen.

Yannūnāti parivitakkanatthe nipātoti āha “parivitakkadassanameta”nti. “Dhammaṃ suṇeyya”nti kiriyāpadena vuccamāno eva hi attho “yannūnā”ti nipātapadena jotīyati. Ahaṃ yannūna dhammaṃ suṇeyyanti yojanā. Yannūnāti ca yadi panāti attho. Yadi panāti idampi hi tena samānatthameva. Yaṃ dhammaṃ suṇātīti sambandho. Uḷāruḷārajanāti khattiyamahāsālādiuḷāruḷārajanākiṇṇā[V 2.0003]. Sace ayampi paṭhamaṃ āgaccheyya, bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā nisīdituṃ araharūpoti āha “pacchā āgatenā”ti. Sikkhattayūpasaṃhitanti adhisīlaadhicittaadhipaññāsaṅkhātasikkhattayayuttaṃ. Thokaṃ dhammakathaṃ sutvā ahosīti sambandho. Idhāpi sutvā-saddo hetuatthoti daṭṭhabbo, savanakāraṇā etadahosīti vuttaṃ [M 2.0003] hoti. Yadi evaṃ atha kasmā “ekamantaṃ nisinnassa…pe… etadahosī”ti vuttanti āha “taṃ panassa yasmā”tiādi. Tattha tanti parivitakkanaṃ.

Regarding `Yannūna`, it is a particle in the sense of reflection; thus, he said, `parivitakkadassanametaṃ` (this is an expression of reflection). The meaning expressed by the verb `Dhammaṃ suṇeyya` is indeed illuminated by the particle `yannūna`. The construction is `Ahaṃ yannūna dhammaṃ suṇeyya`. And `yannūna` has the meaning `yadi pana` (if perhaps). Indeed, this `yadi pana` has the same meaning as that. The connection is with `Yaṃ dhammaṃ suṇāti`. `Uḷāruḷārajana` means crowded with great and noble people, such as khattiya mahāsālas. 'If this one too had come first, he would have been fit to approach the Blessed One and sit down'; thus, he said `pacchā āgatena`. `Sikkhattayūpasaṃhitaṃ` means connected with the threefold training, designated as higher virtue, higher mind, and higher wisdom. The connection is with `Thokaṃ dhammakathaṃ sutvā ahosi` (Having heard a short Dhamma talk, it occurred). Here too, the word `sutvā` should be understood as being in the sense of cause; it is said that because of hearing, this occurred. If so, then why was it said, 'To him, having sat down to one side... this occurred'? He said, `taṃ panassa yasmā`, etc. Therein, `taṃ` is the reflection.

Saṅkhepakathāti visuṃ visuṃ paduddhāraṃ akatvā samāsato atthavaṇṇanā. Yena yena ākārenāti yena yena pakārena. Tena tena me upaparikkhatoti “kāmā nāmete aniccā dukkhā vipariṇāmadhammā aṭṭhikaṅkalūpamā”ti (ma. ni. 1.234; 2.42; pāci. 417; mahāni. 3; cūḷani. khaggavisāṇasuttaniddesa 147) ca ādinā yena yena ākārena kāmesu ādīnavaṃ okāraṃ saṃkilesaṃ, tabbipariyāyato nekkhamme ānisaṃsaṃ guṇaṃ pakāsentaṃ bhagavatā dhammaṃ desitaṃ ājānāmi avabujjhāmi, tena tena pakārena upaparikkhato vīmaṃsantassa mayhaṃ evaṃ hoti evaṃ upaṭṭhāti. Sikkhattayabrahmacariyanti adhisīlasikkhādisikkhattayasaṅgahaṃ seṭṭhacariyaṃ. Ekampi divasanti ekadivasamattampi. Akhaṇḍaṃ katvāti dukkaṭamattassapi anāpajjanena akhaṇḍitaṃ katvā, akhaṇḍaacchiddādibhāvāpādanena vā. Akhaṇḍalakkhaṇavacanañhetaṃ. Carimakacittanti cuticittaṃ. Kiñcipi ekadesaṃ asesetvā ekanteneva paripūretabbatāya ekantaparipuṇṇaṃ. Kilesamalena amalīnaṃ katvāti taṇhāsaṃkilesādinā asaṃkiliṭṭhaṃ katvā, cittuppādamattampi saṃkilesamalaṃ anuppādetvā. Accantameva visuddhaṃ katvā pariharitabbatāya ekantaparisuddhaṃ. Tato eva saṅkhaṃ viya likhitanti saṅkhalikhitaṃ. Tenāha “likhitasaṅkhasadisa”nti. Pariyodātaṭṭhena nimmalabhāvena saṅkhaṃ viya likhitaṃ dhotanti saṅkhalikhitanti āha “dhotasaṅkhasappaṭibhāga”nti. “Ajjhāvasatā”ti padappayogena agāranti bhummatthe upayogavacananti āha “agāramajjhe”ti. Dāṭhikāpi massuggahaṇeneva gahetvā “massu”tveva vuttaṃ, uttarādharamassunti attho. Kasāyena rattānīti kāsāyānīti āha “kasāyarasapītatāyā”ti. Paridahitvāti nivāsetvā ceva pārupitvā ca. Agārassa hitanti agāravāso agāraṃ uttarapadalopena, tassa vaḍḍhiāvahaṃ agārassa hitaṃ.

A brief explanation means describing the meaning concisely without separately extracting each word. 'In whatever way' means by whatever manner. 'By that, I examine thoroughly' means: in whatever way the Blessed One has taught the Dhamma—revealing the dangers, faults, and defilements of sensual pleasures and, in contrast, the benefits and virtues of renunciation—such as by stating, 'These sensual pleasures are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, like a skeleton' (MN 1.234; 2.42; Pāc. 417; Mahāni. 3; Cūḷani. Khaggavisāṇasutta Niddesa 147), I understand and comprehend it. By that manner, as I investigate and examine, thus it is for me, thus it appears to me. 'The holy life of the threefold training' means the supreme practice comprised of the threefold training beginning with the higher virtue. 'Even a single day' means even for just one day. 'Having made it unbroken' means having made it unbroken by not incurring even a dukkaṭa offense, or by not bringing it to a state of being broken, perforated, and so on. This is a statement of the characteristic of being unbroken. 'The final consciousness' means the death-consciousness. Because it must be fulfilled entirely, without leaving even a part remaining, it is 'entirely complete'. 'Having made it unstained by the stain of defilements' means having made it undefiled by craving, defilements, and so on, not allowing even a moment of consciousness with the stain of defilement to arise. Because it should be maintained as absolutely pure, it is 'entirely pure'. From that, 'scraped like a conch' is 'saṅkhalikhitaṃ'. Therefore, he said, 'like a scraped conch'. In the sense of being pure, due to its stainless state, it is 'scraped and washed like a conch', thus it is 'saṅkhalikhitaṃ'. He said, 'resembling a washed conch'. By the use of the word 'ajjhāvasatā', the word 'agāraṃ' is a term used in the locative sense; therefore, he said 'agāramajjhe' (in the middle of the house). Even 'dāṭhikā' (beard) is included by the term 'massu' and is thus called 'massu'; the meaning is hair on the upper and lower lip. 'Dyed with an astringent' is 'kāsāyāni'; therefore, he said, 'due to being tinged with the color of an astringent juice'. 'Having put on' means having worn the lower robe and having draped the upper robe. 'Beneficial to the household' (agārassa hitaṃ): 'agāravāso' (household life) becomes 'agāraṃ' by the elision of the latter word; that which brings growth to it is 'beneficial to the household'.

25. Ñātisālohitātiādīsu “ayaṃ ajjhattiko”ti jānanti, ñāyanti vāti ñātī, lohitena sambandhāti sālohitā. Pitupakkhikā ñātī, mātupakkhikā sālohitā. Mātupakkhikā pitupakkhikā vā ñātī[M 2.0004], sassusasurapakkhikā sālohitā. Mittāyantīti mittā, [V 2.0004] minanti vā sabbaguyhesu anto pakkhipantīti mittā. Kiccakaraṇīyesu sahabhāvaṭṭhena amā hontīti amaccā. Mamāyatīti mātā, piyāyatīti pitā. Sarīrakiccalesenāti uccārapassāvādisarīrakiccalesena. Ananuññātaṃ puttaṃ na pabbājetīti “mātāpitūnaṃ lokiyamahājanassa ca cittaññathattaṃ mā hotū”ti na pabbājeti. Tatoyeva ca suddhodanamahārājassa tathā varo dinno.

25. Regarding 'relatives and blood relations' and so on: they know, 'This one is internal,' or are known as such, thus they are 'relatives' (ñāti). They are connected by blood, thus they are 'blood relations' (sālohitā). The father's side are relatives; the mother's side are blood relations. Or, the mother's side and the father's side are relatives; the side of the father-in-law and mother-in-law are blood relations. They are affectionate, thus they are 'friends' (mittā). Or, they measure; they place one inside all secrets, thus they are friends. In the sense of being together in duties to be done, they are 'amā', thus they are 'ministers' (amaccā). She regards as 'mine', thus she is 'mother' (mātā). He is dear, thus he is 'father' (pitā). 'By the pretext of bodily functions' means by the pretext of bodily functions such as feces and urine. 'He does not ordain a son who has not been given permission' means he does not ordain him, thinking, 'Let there not be an alteration of mind for his mother and father and for the worldly populace.' For this very reason, a boon was given in that way to King Suddhodana.

26. Dhuranikkhepenāti bhaṇḍappayojanādīsu dhuranikkhepena. Tenāha “na hī”tiādi. Piyāyitabboti piyoti āha “pītijananako”ti. Manassa appāyanato manāpoti āha “manavaḍḍhanako”ti. Sukhedhito taruṇadārakakāle, tato parañca sappikhīrādisādurasamanuññabhojanādiāhārasampattiyā sukhaparihato. Atha vā daḷhabhattikadhātijanādiparijanasampattiyā ceva paricchedasampattiyā ca uḷārapaṇītasukhapaccayūpahārehi ca sukhedhito, akiccheneva dukkhapaccayavinodanena sukhaparihato. Ajjhattikaṅgasampattiyā vā sukhedhito, bāhiraṅgasampattiyā sukhaparihato.

26. 'By laying down the burden' means by laying down the burden in matters of goods and so on. Therefore, he said, 'For not...' and so on. He should be held dear, thus he is 'dear' (piyo); therefore, he said, 'joy-producing'. Because he enhances the mind, he is 'pleasing' (manāpo); therefore, he said, 'mind-enhancing'. He was nourished in comfort in the time of being a young boy, and after that, he was maintained in comfort through the abundance of food such as agreeable meals with the delicious taste of ghee, milk, and so on. Or, he was nourished in comfort through the abundance of a retinue of loyal servants, nurses, and so on, through the abundance of requisites, and through the provision of excellent and exquisite supports for comfort; he was maintained in comfort by dispelling the causes of suffering without difficulty. Or, he was nourished in comfort through the perfection of internal bodily features; he was maintained in comfort through the perfection of external features.

Kiñcīti etassa vivaraṇaṃ “appamattakampi kalabhāga”nti. Yadā jānāti-saddo bodhanattho na hoti, tadā tassa payoge “sappino jānāti, madhuno jānātī”tiādīsu viya karaṇatthe sāmivacanaṃ saddatthavidū icchantīti āha “kiñci dukkhena nānubhosī”ti. Tenāha “karaṇatthe sāmivacanaṃ, anubhavanatthe ca jānanā”ti. Ettha ca kiñci dukkhena nānubhosīti kenaci dukkhena karaṇabhūtena visayaṃ nānubhosīti evamattho veditabbo. “Kiñcī”ti etthāpi hi karaṇatthe sāmivacanassa lopo kato. Teneva ca vakkhati “vikappadvayepi purimapadassa uttarapadena samānavibhattilopo daṭṭhabbo”ti. Yadā pana jānāti-saddo saraṇattho hoti, tadā saraṇatthānaṃ dhātusaddānaṃ payoge “mātu sarati, pitu sarati, bhātu jānātī”tiādīsu viya upayogatthe sāmivacanaṃ saddasatthavidū vadantīti āha “atha vā kiñci dukkhaṃ nassarasīti attho”ti, kassaci dukkhassa ananubhūtattā attanā anubhūtaṃ appamattakampi dukkhaṃ pariyesamānopi abhāvatoyeva nassarasīti attho[M 2.0005]. Vikappadvayepīti anubhavanasaraṇatthavasena vutte dutiyatatiyavikappadvaye. Purimapadassāti “kiñcī”ti padassa. Uttarapadenāti “dukkhassā”ti padena. Samānavibhattilopoti uttarapadena samānassa sāmivacanassa lopo. “Kassaci dukkhassā”ti vattabbe vikappadvayepi purimapade sāmivacanassa lopaṃ katvā “kiñci dukkhassā”ti niddeso kato. Anicchakāti anicchantā. Evaṃ santeti nanu mayaṃ sudinna sāmādīsu kenacipi upāyena appaṭisādhanena appaṭikārena maraṇenapi tayā akāmakāpi [V 2.0005] vinā bhavissāma, evaṃ sati. Yenāti yena kāraṇena. Kiṃ panāti ettha kinti karaṇatthe paccattavacananti dassento āha “kena pana kāraṇenā”ti.

The explanation of `Kiñci` is: 'even a small amount, a sixteenth part.' When the word `jānāti` does not have the meaning of understanding, then in its usage, as in 'one knows of ghee, one knows of honey,' and so on, those skilled in grammar desire the genitive case in the instrumental sense; thus, it is said: 'you did not experience any suffering.' Therefore, it is said: 'the genitive case in the instrumental sense, and `jānāti` in the sense of experiencing.' And here, 'you did not experience any suffering' means 'you did not experience the object by means of any suffering which has become the instrument'—this is the meaning to be understood. Indeed, in `Kiñci` here too, the elision of the genitive case in the instrumental sense has been made. For this very reason, it will be said: 'In both alternatives, the elision of the case ending of the former word, which is the same as that of the latter word, should be seen.' But when the word `jānāti` has the meaning of remembering, then in the usage of verbal roots having the meaning of remembering, as in 'one remembers one's mother, one remembers one's father, one knows one's brother,' and so on, those skilled in grammar say that the genitive case is used in the sense of the object. Thus, it is said: 'Or else, the meaning is, "you do not remember any suffering."' Because no suffering whatsoever has been experienced before, even when searching for even a small amount of suffering experienced by oneself, one does not remember it precisely because of its non-existence—this is the meaning. 'In both alternatives' refers to the second and third alternatives stated in the sense of experiencing and remembering. 'Of the former word' refers to the word `kiñci`. 'By the latter word' refers to the word `dukkhassa`. 'The elision of the same case ending' means the elision of the genitive case, which is the same as that of the latter word. Although it should be stated as `kassaci dukkhassa`, in both alternatives, by eliding the genitive case of the former word, the indication is made as `kiñci dukkhassa`. `Anicchakā` means not desiring. `Evaṃ sante` means: 'Indeed, Sudinna, if this is so, shall we not, by some means such as conciliation, by some irremediable and uncorrectable means, even by death, be separated from you, though we are unwilling?' `Yena` means by what reason. In `Kiṃ pana`, showing that `kiṃ` is a singular form in the instrumental sense, it is said: 'But by what reason?'

28. Gandhabbanaṭanāṭakādīnīti ettha gandhabbā nāma gāyanakā, naṭā nāma raṅganaṭā, nāṭakā laṅghanakādayo. Paricārehīti ettha parito tattha tattha yathāsakaṃ visayesu cārehīti atthoti āha “indriyāni cārehī”tiādi. Paricārehīti vā sukhūpakaraṇehi attānaṃ paricārehi attano paricaraṇaṃ kārehi. Tathābhūto ca yasmā laḷanto kīḷanto nāma hoti, tasmā “laḷā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Bhuñjitabbato paribhuñjitabbato visesato pañca kāmaguṇā bhogā nāmāti āha “bhoge bhuñjanto”ti. Dānappadānānīti ettha niccadānaṃ dānaṃ nāma, uposathadivasādīsu dātabbaṃ atirekadānaṃ padānaṃ nāma. Paveṇīrakkhaṇavasena vā dīyamānaṃ dānaṃ nāma, attanāva paṭṭhapetvā dīyamānaṃ padānaṃ nāma. Pacurajanasādhāraṇaṃ vā nātiuḷāraṃ dānaṃ nāma, anaññasādhāraṇaṃ atiuḷāraṃ padānaṃ nāma. Ādi-saddena sīlādīni saṅgaṇhāti. Natthi etassa vacanappaṭivacanasaṅkhāto ālāpasallāpoti nirālāpasallāpo.

28. Here, in `gandhabbanaṭanāṭakādīni`, `gandhabbā` are singers, `naṭā` are stage-dancers, and `nāṭakā` are acrobats and the like. Here, `paricārehi` means 'let your senses roam all around, here and there, in their respective objects'; thus, it is said, 'let the senses roam,' etc. Alternatively, `paricārehi` means 'attend to yourself with means of comfort,' or 'cause your own attendance to be done.' And because one who is thus is called one who is playing and sporting, therefore `laḷā` and so on are stated. Because they are to be enjoyed and to be consumed, the five strands of sensual pleasure are especially called `bhogā` (enjoyments); thus it is said, 'enjoying enjoyments.' In `dānappadānāni`, regular giving is called `dāna`, while extra giving on occasions like the Uposatha days is called `padāna`. Or, what is given in the manner of maintaining a tradition is called `dāna`, while what is given after having established it oneself is called `padāna`. Or, what is common to many people and not excessively grand is called `dāna`, while what is not common to others and is exceedingly grand is called `padāna`. By the word `ādi` (etc.), virtue and the like are included. There is no conversation or exchange of speech, reckoned as speech and counter-speech, for him; hence, he is `nirālāpasallāpo` (one without conversation or exchange of speech).

30. Balaṃ gāhetvāti ettha balaggahaṇaṃ nāma kāyabalassa uppādanamevāti āha “kāyabalaṃ janetvā”ti. Assumukhanti assūni mukhe etassāti assumukho, taṃ assumukhaṃ, assukilinnamukhanti attho. Gāmoyeva gāmantasenāsanaṃ gāmapariyāpannattā gāmantasenāsanassa. Atirekalābhapaṭikkhepenāti “piṇḍiyālopabhojanaṃ nissāyā”ti (mahāva. 128) evaṃ vuttabhikkhāhāralābhato adhikalābho saṅghabhattādiatirekalābho, tassa paṭikkhepenāti attho. Tenāha “cuddasa [M 2.0006] bhattāni paṭikkhipitvā”ti. Saṅghabhattaṃ uddesabhattaṃ nimantanabhattaṃ salākabhattaṃ pakkhikaṃ uposathikaṃ pāṭipadikaṃ āgantukabhattaṃ gamikabhattaṃ gilānabhattaṃ gilānupaṭṭhākabhattaṃ vihārabhattaṃ dhurabhattaṃ vārabhattanti imāni cuddasa bhattāni. Tattha sakalassa saṅghassa dātabbaṃ bhattaṃ saṅghabhattaṃ. Katipaye bhikkhū uddisitvā dātabbaṃ bhattaṃ uddesabhattaṃ. Ekasmiṃ pakkhe ekadivasaṃ dātabbaṃ bhattaṃ pakkhikaṃ. Uposathe dātabbaṃ bhattaṃ uposathikaṃ. Pāṭipadadivase dātabbaṃ bhattaṃ pāṭipadikaṃ. Vihāraṃ uddissa dātabbaṃ bhattaṃ vihārabhattaṃ. Dhurageheyeva ṭhapetvā dātabbaṃ bhattaṃ dhurabhattaṃ. Gāmavāsīādīhi vārena dātabbaṃ bhattaṃ vārabhattaṃ.

30. Here, in `balaṃ gāhetvā`, 'taking strength' means simply the production of bodily strength, as stated: 'having generated bodily strength.' `Assumukhaṃ` means 'one who has tears on his face is `assumukho` (tearful-faced)'; that is, a face wet with tears. The village itself is the lodging on the village periphery, because the lodging on the village periphery is included within the village. 'By rejecting excessive gains' means the rejection of gains exceeding the almsfood gain mentioned in the phrase 'depending on almsfood,' such as a meal for the Sangha and other surplus gains; that is the meaning. Therefore, it is said: 'having rejected the fourteen meals.' These fourteen meals are: a meal for the Sangha, a designated meal, an invitation meal, a lottery meal, a fortnightly meal, an Uposatha meal, a first-day meal, a guest meal, a traveler's meal, a sick person's meal, a meal for an attendant of the sick, a monastery meal, a duty meal, and a rotation meal. Therein, the meal to be given to the entire Sangha is a meal for the Sangha. The meal to be given after designating a few monks is a designated meal. The meal to be given one day in a fortnight is a fortnightly meal. The meal to be given on the Uposatha day is an Uposatha meal. The meal to be given on the first day of the lunar fortnight is a first-day meal. The meal to be given intending the monastery is a monastery meal. The meal to be given, having been placed in the duty-residence, is a duty meal. The meal to be given by rotation by the village residents and others is a rotation meal.

Atha “gahapaticīvaraṃ paṭikkhipitvā”ti kasmā vuttaṃ. Gahaṇe hi sati paṭikkhepo yujjeyya, na ca paṭhamabodhiyaṃ gahapaticīvarassa paṭiggahaṇaṃ anuññātaṃ parato jīvakavatthusmiṃ anuññātattā. Teneva vakkhati jīvakavatthusmiṃ (mahāva. aṭṭha. 337) “bhagavato hi buddhabhāvappattito [V 2.0006] paṭṭhāya yāva idaṃ vatthaṃ, etthantare vīsati vassāni na koci gahapaticīvaraṃ sādiyi, sabbe paṃsukūlikāva ahesu”nti. Sudinno ca paṭhamabodhiyaṃyeva pabbajito. Teneva vakkhati “sudinno hi bhagavato dvādasame vasse pabbajito, vīsatime vasse ñātikulaṃ piṇḍāya paviṭṭho, sayaṃ pabbajjāya aṭṭhavassiko hutvā”ti. Tasmā “gahapaticīvaraṃ paṭikkhipitvā”ti kasmā vuttanti? Vuccate – ananuññātepi gahapaticīvare paṃsukūlikaṅgasamādānavasena gahapaticīvaraṃ paṭikkhittaṃ nāma hotīti katvā vuttaṃ “gahapaticīvaraṃ paṭikkhipitvā”ti.

Then, why was it said, "having rejected a householder's robe"? For if there were acceptance, rejection would be fitting, but in the first period of awakening, the acceptance of a householder's robe was not permitted, because it was allowed later in the case of Jīvaka. Therefore, it will be said in the Jīvaka passage (Mahāva. Aṭṭha. 337): "From the time the Blessed One attained Buddhahood until this matter, for twenty years no one accepted a householder's robe; all were wearers of discarded rags." And Sudinna went forth in the very first period of awakening. Therefore, it will be said: "For Sudinna went forth in the twelfth year of the Blessed One, entered his relatives' clan for alms in the twentieth year, having been ordained for eight years." Therefore, why was it said, "having rejected a householder's robe"? It is said: Even though a householder's robe was not permitted, by way of undertaking the ascetic practice of wearing discarded rags, a householder's robe is said to have been rejected. Therefore, it was said, "having rejected a householder's robe."

Loluppacāraṃ paṭikkhipitvāti kusalabhaṇḍassa bhusaṃ vilumpanaṭṭhena loluppaṃ vuccati taṇhā, loluppena caraṇaṃ loluppacāro, taṇhāvasena gharapaṭipāṭiṃ atikkamitvā bhikkhāya caraṇaṃ, taṃ paṭikkhipitvāti attho. Tenāha “gharapaṭipāṭiyā bhikkhāya pavisatī”ti. Ettha ca āraññikaṅgādipadhānaṅgavasena sesadhutaṅgānipi gahitāneva hontīti veditabbaṃ. Vajjīnanti rājāno apekkhitvā sāmivacanaṃ kataṃ, vajjīrājūnanti attho. Janapada-saddassa taṃnivāsīsupi pavattanato “vajjīsū”ti janapadāpekkhaṃ bhummavacanaṃ, vajjināmake janapadeti attho.

"Having rejected greedy conduct"—craving is called 'loluppa' because of its meaning of strongly plundering wholesome things. Conduct by means of 'loluppa' is 'loluppacāra,' which is going for alms by transgressing the order of houses due to craving. Rejecting that is the meaning. Therefore, it is said, "he enters for alms according to the order of houses." And here, it should be understood that the remaining ascetic practices are also taken by way of the principal ascetic practices such as the forest-dwelling practice. "Vajjīnaṃ"—referring to the kings, the genitive case is used; the meaning is "of the Vajjī kings." Since the word 'janapada' also applies to its inhabitants, "Vajjīsu" is a locative case referring to the country, meaning 'in the country named Vajjī.'

Upabhogaparibhogūpakaraṇamahantatāyāti [M 2.0007] pañcakāmaguṇasaṅkhātānaṃ upabhogānañceva hatthiassarathaitthiyādiupabhogūpakaraṇānañca mahantatāya. Upabhogūpakaraṇāneva hi idha paribhogūpakaraṇasaddena vuttāni. Tenevāha “ye hi tesaṃ upabhogā, yāni ca upabhogūpakaraṇāni, tāni mahantānī”ti. “Upabhogā hatthiassarathaitthīādayo, upabhogūpakaraṇāni tesameva suvaṇṇādiupakaraṇānī”tipi vadanti. Sārakānīti sārabhūtāni. Nidhetvāti nidahitvā, nidhānaṃ katvāti attho. Divasaparibbayasaṅkhātabhogamahantatāyāti divase divase paribhuñjitabbasaṅkhātabhogānaṃ mahantatāya. Jātarūparajatasseva pahūtatāyāti piṇḍapiṇḍavasena ceva suvaṇṇamāsakarajatamāsakādivasena ca jātarūparajatasseva pahūtatāya. Vittīti tuṭṭhi, vittiyā upakaraṇaṃ vittūpakaraṇaṃ, pahūtaṃ nānāvidhālaṅkārabhūtaṃ vittūpakaraṇametesanti pahūtavittūpakaraṇā. Tenāha “alaṅkārabhūtassā”tiādi. Vohāravasenāti vaṇijjāvasena vaḍḍhikatādivasena. Dhanadhaññassa pahūtatāyāti sattaratanasaṅkhātassa dhanassa sabbapubbaṇṇāparaṇṇasaṅgahitassa dhaññassa ca pahūtatāyāti attho. Tattha “suvaṇṇarajatamaṇimuttāveḷuriyavajirapavāḷāni satta ratanānī”ti vadanti. Sālivīhiādi pubbaṇṇaṃ purakkhataṃ sassaphalanti katvā, tabbipariyāyato muggamāsādi [V 2.0007] aparaṇṇanti veditabbaṃ. Ukkaṭṭhapiṇḍapātikattāti sesadhutaṅgaparivāritena ukkaṭṭhapiṇḍapātadhutaṅgena samannāgatattā. Tenāha “sapadānacāraṃ caritukāmo”ti.

"By the greatness of enjoyments and means of enjoyment" refers to the greatness of the enjoyments, reckoned as the five strands of sensual pleasure, and also of the means of enjoyment such as elephants, horses, chariots, women, and so on. Indeed, here the means of enjoyment are referred to by the term "means of partaking" (paribhogūpakaraṇa). Hence it is said, "For them, those enjoyments and the means of enjoyment are great." Some say, "The enjoyments are elephants, horses, chariots, women, and the like, while the means of enjoyment are their very own appurtenances such as gold." "Sārakāni" means essential. "Having stored" means having deposited, having made a treasure; that is the meaning. "By the greatness of wealth reckoned as daily enjoyment" refers to the greatness of wealth reckoned as that to be enjoyed day by day. "By the abundance of gold and silver itself" refers to the abundance of gold and silver itself, both by way of lumps and by way of gold māsakas, silver māsakas, and so on. "Vitti" means satisfaction. The means of satisfaction are 'vittūpakaraṇa'. They possess abundant means of satisfaction, which are various ornaments; hence they are 'pahūtavittūpakaraṇā' (possessing abundant means of satisfaction). Therefore it is said, "of what serves as an ornament" and so on. "By way of transaction" means by way of trade, by way of lending at interest, and so on. "By the abundance of wealth and grain" refers to the abundance of wealth, reckoned as the seven treasures, and of grain, which includes all early and late crops; that is the meaning. Herein, it is said, "Gold, silver, gems, pearls, beryl, diamonds, and coral are the seven treasures." "Early crops" are understood as grain and fruit such as Sāli rice and Vīhi rice, considered primary; conversely, beans, lentils, and so on should be understood as "late crops." "By being a foremost almsfood-gatherer" means by being endowed with the foremost almsfood-gathering ascetic practice, accompanied by the remaining ascetic practices. Hence it is said, "desiring to practice the continuous almsround."

31. Antojātatāya vā ñātisadisī dāsīti ñātidāsī. Pūtibhāveneva lakkhitabbadoso vā ābhidosiko, abhidosaṃ vā paccūsakālaṃ gato patto atikkantoti ābhidosiko. Tenāha “ekarattātikkantassa vā”tiādi. Pūtibhūtabhāvena paribhogaṃ nārahatīti aparibhogāraho. Chaḍḍanīyasabhāve nicchitepi pucchākāle sandehavohāravaseneva pucchituṃ yuttanti āha “sace”ti. Ariyavohārenāti ariyasamudācārena. Ariyā hi mātugāmaṃ bhaginivādena samudācaranti. Nissaṭṭhapariggahanti pariccattālayaṃ.

31. Or, due to being born within the household, a female slave resembling a relative is a 'ñātidāsī' (relative-slave). Or, 'ābhidosiko' is one whose fault is to be recognized by its putrid state; or 'ābhidosiko' is one who has gone to, reached, or passed the dawn time. Hence it is said, "or of that which has passed one night," etc. It is 'aparibhogāraho' (unfit for use) because it is not suitable for use due to being in a putrid state. Even when its nature as something to be discarded has been determined, it is proper to ask at the time of questioning only by way of doubtful speech; thus it is said, 'sace' (if). "By noble speech" means by noble custom. For the noble ones address a woman with the term "sister." "Nissaṭṭhapariggahaṃ" means 'one whose attachment has been relinquished.'

“Ākirā”ti vuttattā “viññatti vā”ti vuttaṃ, “sace taṃ chaḍḍanīyadhamma”nti pariyāyaṃ amuñcitvā vuttattā “payuttavācā vā”ti vuttaṃ, paccayapaṭisaṃyuttā vācā payuttavācā. Vattuṃ vaṭṭatīti nirapekkhabhāvato vuttaṃ[M 2.0008], idha pana visesato aparibhogārahattāva vatthuno. Aggaariyavaṃsikoti ariyavaṃsapaṭipattipūrakānaṃ aggo uttamo. Nimīyati saññāyatīti nimittaṃ, yathāsallakkhito ākāroti āha “gihikāle sallakkhitapubbaṃ ākāra”nti. Hatthapiṭṭhiādīni olokayamānā “sāmiputtassa me sudinnassa viya suvaṇṇakacchapapiṭṭhisadisā imā hatthapādapiṭṭhiyo, haritālavaṭṭiyo viya suvaṭṭitā aṅguliyo, madhuro saro”ti gihikāle sallakkhitapubbaṃ ākāraṃ aggahesi sañjāni sallakkhesi. Kasmā pana sā ñātidāsī disvāva na sañjānīti āha “sudinno hī”tiādi. Pabbajjupagatenāti pabbajjaṃ upagatena, pabbajitenāti attho. Gharaṃ pavisitvāti gehasāminiyā nisīditabbaṭṭhānabhūtaṃ antogehaṃ pavisitvā. Yaggheti imassa ārocayāmīti ayamatthoti āha “ārocanatthe nipāto”ti. “Yagghe jāneyyāsīti suṭṭhu jāneyyāsī”tipi atthaṃ vadanti. Ālapaneti dāsijanassa ālapane. Tenāha “evañhī”tiādi.

Because it is said, ‘Ākirāti’ (he scatters), it is stated, ‘or a declaration.’ And because it is stated, ‘if that is a thing to be discarded,’ without abandoning the implication, it is stated, ‘or connected speech’; speech connected with conditions is connected speech. ‘It is fitting to speak’ is said with reference to a state of indifference, but here, specifically, it is due to the object being unfit for use. ‘Aggaariyavaṃsika’ means the foremost, the highest, among those who fulfill the practice of the noble lineages. ‘Nimīyati saññāyati’ (it is perceived, it is recognized) is therefore called a sign (nimitta). The phrase ‘yathāsallakkhito ākāro’ (a characteristic as it was discerned) is explained as: ‘a characteristic previously discerned in the household life.’ Observing the backs of his hands and so on, she grasped, knew, and discerned the characteristic previously observed in the household life, thinking: ‘These backs of his hands and feet are like the back of my master's son Sudinna's golden tortoise; his fingers are well-rounded like green palmyra fruits; his voice is sweet.’ But why did that kinswoman slave not recognize him upon seeing him? It is said: ‘For Sudinna…’ and so on. ‘Pabbajjupagatenāti’ means by one who has gone to the going forth (pabbajjaṃ upagatena); the meaning is ‘by one who has gone forth’ (pabbajitena). ‘Gharaṃ pavisitvāti’ means having entered the inner house, which is the place where the mistress of the house is to sit. Regarding ‘yagghe,’ the meaning is ‘I will inform.’ Thus, it is said: ‘The particle is in the sense of informing.’ Some also say the meaning is: ‘“Yagghe jāneyyāsi” means “may you know thoroughly.”’ ‘Ālapaneti’ means in addressing a servant. Therefore, it is said: ‘For thus…’ and so on.

32. Gharesu sālā hontīti gharesu ekamante bhojanasālā honti pākāraparikkhittā susaṃvihitadvārabandhā susammaṭṭhavālikaṅgaṇā. Udakakañjiyanti udakañca kañjiyañca. Kasmā pana īdisāyameva sālāya aññataraṃ kuṭṭamūlanti ayamattho vuttoti āha “na hi pabbajitā”tiādi. Asāruppe ṭhāneti bhikkhūnaṃ ananucchavike padese. Atthi nu khoti nu-saddo pucchanatthe, kho-saddo vacanasiliṭṭhatāya vutto. Nukhoti vā nipātasamudāyo pucchanattho. Tena nāma-saddassa pucchanatthataṃ dasseti. Yesaṃ no tvanti yesaṃ no putto tvaṃ. Īdise ṭhāneti kiñcāpi [V 2.0008] taṃ ṭhānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ ananurūpaṃ na hoti, tathāpi mādisānaṃ mahābhogakulānaṃ puttassa parakule āsanasālāyaṃ nisīditvā bhojanaṃ nāma ayuttarūpanti maññamāno āha. Tenevāha “nanu nāma, tāta sudinna, sakaṃ gehaṃ gantabba”nti. Aññenapi pakārena nāmasaddassa pucchanatthatameva dassento āha “tathā atthi nu kho tātā”tiādi. Tathāti samuccayattho. Idāni nāmasaddassa maññanatthataṃ dassento āha “tathā atthi maññe”tiādi.

32. ‘Gharesu sālā hontīti’ means that in the houses, on one side, there are dining halls, enclosed by walls, with well-arranged door frames, and with well-swept sandy courtyards. ‘Udakakañjiyanti’ means both water and gruel. But why is this meaning, ‘a certain wall-base in such a hall,’ stated? It is said: ‘For renunciants do not…’ and so on. ‘Asāruppe ṭhāneti’ means in a place unbecoming to monks. In ‘Atthi nu kho,’ the word ‘nu’ is used in the sense of questioning, and the word ‘kho’ is stated for the elegance of speech. Or, the combination of particles ‘nu kho’ has the sense of questioning. By this, it shows the interrogative sense of the word ‘nāma.’ ‘Yesaṃ no tvanti’ means ‘you who are our son.’ Regarding ‘Īdise ṭhāne,’ although that place is not unsuitable for monks, yet, thinking, ‘for a son of those like us from families of great wealth, to sit and eat in an assembly hall in another's family is indeed an improper thing,’ he says this. Therefore, he says: ‘Surely, dear Sudinna, you should go to your own house.’ Demonstrating the interrogative sense of the word ‘nāma’ in another way, he says: ‘Similarly, “is there indeed, dear one?”’ and so on. ‘Tathāti’ has the sense of conjunction. Now, demonstrating the sense of supposition of the word ‘nāma,’ he says: ‘Similarly, “I suppose there is,”’ and so on.

Dukkhābhitunnatāyāti mānasikena dukkhena abhipīḷitattā. Etamatthanti “atthi nu kho, tāta sudinna, amhākaṃ dhana”ntiādinā yathāvuttamatthaṃ. Anokappanāmarisanatthavasenāti [M 2.0009] ettha anokappanaṃ asaddahanaṃ. Amarisanaṃ asahanaṃ. Anāgatavacanaṃ anāgatasaddappayogo, attho pana vattamānakālikova. Tenāha “paccakkhampī”ti. Na marisayāmīti na visahāmi. Taṃ na sundaranti “tadāya”nti pāṭhaṃ sandhāyāha. Alaṃ, gahapati, kataṃ me ajja bhattakiccanti thero ukkaṭṭhaekāsanikatāya paṭikkhipanto evamāha. Ukkaṭṭhaekāsanikatāyāti ca idaṃ bhūtakathanavasena vuttaṃ therassa tathābhāvadīpanatthaṃ. Mudukassapi hi ekāsanikassa yāya nisajjāya kiñcimattampi bhojanaṃ bhuttaṃ, vattasīsenapi tato vuṭṭhitassa puna bhuñjituṃ na vaṭṭati. Tenāha tipiṭakacūḷābhayatthero “āsanaṃ vā rakkheyya bhojanaṃ vā”ti. Ukkaṭṭhapiṇḍapātikopi samānoti nidassanamattamidaṃ, thero sapadānacārikesupi ukkaṭṭhoyeva. Ukkaṭṭhasapadānacārikopi hi purato ca pacchato ca āhaṭabhikkhampi aggahetvāva gharadvāre ṭhatvā pattavissajjanameva karoti, tasmā thero ukkaṭṭhasapadānacārikattāpi svātanāya bhikkhaṃ nādhivāseti. Atha kasmā “adhivāsesī”ti āha “sace ekabhattampi na gahessāmī”tiādi. Paṇḍitā hi mātāpitūnaṃ ācariyupajjhāyānaṃ vā kātabbaṃ anuggahaṃ ajjhupekkhitvā dhutaṅgavisuddhikā na bhavanti.

‘Dukkhābhitunnatāyāti’ means by being afflicted by mental suffering. ‘Etamatthanti’ refers to the aforesaid meaning, beginning with ‘Dear Sudinna, do we indeed have wealth?’ Regarding ‘Anokappanāmarisanatthavasenāti,’ here ‘anokappanaṃ’ is disbelief, and ‘amarisanaṃ’ is inability to endure. ‘Anāgatavacanaṃ’ is the use of a future-tense word, but the meaning is indeed present-tense. Therefore, it is said: ‘even manifestly.’ ‘Na marisayāmīti’ means ‘I cannot bear.’ Regarding ‘Taṃ na sundaraṃ,’ it is said with reference to the reading ‘tadāya.’ Regarding ‘Alaṃ, gahapati, kataṃ me ajja bhattakiccanti,’ the Elder said this, refusing on account of his strict one-session practice. And this, ‘ukkaṭṭhaekāsanikatāyāti,’ is stated by way of recounting a fact, in order to illustrate the Elder's nature. For even for a moderate one-session practitioner, if even a small amount of food has been eaten in a sitting, it is not permissible to eat again after having risen from that, even on account of the observance. Therefore, the Tipiṭaka Cūḷābhaya Thera said: ‘One should guard either the seat or the food.’ ‘Ukkaṭṭhapiṇḍapātikopi samānoti’—this is for the sake of illustration; the Elder was strict even among those who practice the systematic alms-round. For a strict systematic alms-gatherer, not accepting alms-food brought from before or after, stands at the house door and only has the bowl put away. Therefore, the Elder, also due to being a strict systematic alms-gatherer, did not consent to alms-food for the next day. Then why does it say, ‘he consented’? It is said: ‘If I do not accept even a single meal…’ and so on. For the wise do not become pure in the ascetic practices by neglecting the support that should be given to parents, teachers, or preceptors.

33. Majjhimappamāṇoti catuhattho puriso majjhimappamāṇo. “Chahattho”tipi keci. Tiro karonti etāyāti tirokaraṇīti sāṇipākāravacano ayaṃ tirokaraṇī-saddoti āha “tirokaraṇiyanti karaṇatthe bhumma”nti. “Tirokaraṇiyā”ti vattabbe “tirokaraṇiya”nti karaṇatthe bhummaṃ vuttaṃ. Tirokaraṇīya-saddo vā ayaṃ sāṇipākārapariyāyoti dassento āha “atha vā”tiādi. Taṃ parikkhipitvāti taṃ samantato khipitvā, parito bandhitvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tenāha “samantato katvā”ti. Vibhattipatirūpakopi nipāto hotīti āha “tenāti ayampi vā”tiādi.

33. ‘Majjhimappamāṇoti’ means a person four cubits tall is of medium size. Some also say ‘six cubits.’ ‘Tiro karonti etāyāti tirokaraṇī’ means ‘they conceal with this, therefore it is a screen.’ This word ‘tirokaraṇī’ is a term for a curtain or a rampart. Thus, it is said that in ‘tirokaraṇiyaṃ,’ the locative case is used in the sense of the instrumental; that is, when ‘tirokaraṇiyā’ should be stated, ‘tirokaraṇiyaṃ’ is stated instead. Or, demonstrating that this word ‘tirokaraṇīya’ is a synonym for a curtain or a rampart, it is said: ‘Or else…’ and so on. ‘Taṃ parikkhipitvāti’ means having cast it all around; that is, it is said to mean having bound it from the outside. Therefore, it is said: ‘having made it all around.’ A particle can also be a form-imitative of a case-ending. Thus, it is said: ‘“tenāti,” this also, or…’ and so on.

34. “Atha [V 2.0009] kho āyasmato sudinnassa pitā sake nivesane paṇītaṃ khādanīyaṃ bhojanīyaṃ paṭiyādāpetvā āyasmato sudinnassa kālaṃ ārocesi – ‘kālo, tāta sudinna, niṭṭhitaṃ bhatta’nti” evaṃ kālārocanassa pāḷiyaṃ anāruḷhattā āha – “kiñcāpi pāḷiyaṃ kālārocanaṃ [M 2.0010] na vutta”nti. Ārociteyeva kāleti “kālo, tāta sudinna, niṭṭhitaṃ bhatta”nti kāle ārociteyeva. Dve puñjeti kahāpaṇapuñjañca suvaṇṇapuñjañca.

34. As the announcement of the time, “Then Venerable Sudinna's father had fine food and drink prepared in his own house and announced the time to Venerable Sudinna: ‘It is time, dear Sudinna, the meal is ready,’” is not included in the Pāli text, it is said: “Even though the announcement of the time is not stated in the Pāli text.” “Ārociteyeva kāle” (only when the time is announced) means only when the time is announced, “It is time, dear Sudinna, the meal is ready.” “Dve puñje” (two heaps) means a heap of kahāpaṇas and a heap of gold.

Pettikanti pitito āgataṃ pettikaṃ. Nihitanti bhūmigataṃ. Payuttanti vaḍḍhivasena payojitaṃ. Taddhitalopaṃ katvā veditabbanti yathā aññatthāpi “pitāmahaṃ dhanaṃ laddhā, sukhaṃ jīvati sañjayo”ti vuttaṃ, evaṃ taddhitalopaṃ katvā vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Pitāmahato āgataṃ, pitāmahassa vā idaṃ petāmahaṃ. Pabbajitaliṅganti samaṇavesaṃ. Na rājabhītoti aparādhakāraṇā na rājakulā bhīto. Yesaṃ santakaṃ dhanaṃ gahitaṃ, te iṇāyikā. Palibuddho pīḷito.

“Pettikaṃ” (paternal) means what has come from the father. “Nihitaṃ” (deposited) means gone into the ground. “Payuttaṃ” (invested) means employed by way of interest. It should be understood that it is stated by making an elision of the taddhita suffix, just as elsewhere it is said: “Having obtained the grandfather's wealth, Sañjaya lives happily.” What has come from the grandfather, or what belongs to the grandfather, is “petāmahaṃ.” “Pabbajitaliṅgaṃ” (the sign of a renunciant) means the guise of a recluse. “Na rājabhīto” (not fearing the king) means not afraid of the royal family due to a cause of offense. Those whose wealth was taken, they are the creditors. “Palibuddho” (hindered) means oppressed.

Vibhattipatirūpakoti “tenā”ti padaṃ sandhāyāha. Taṃnidānanti taṃ dhanaṃ nidānaṃ kāraṇamassāti taṃnidānaṃ. Assāti paccattavacanassa, padassa vā. Bhayanti cittassa utrastākārena pavattabhayaṃ adhippetaṃ, na ñāṇabhayaṃ, nāpi “bhāyati etasmā”ti evaṃ vuttaṃ ārammaṇabhayanti āha “cittutrāsoti attho”ti. Chambhitattanti teneva cittutrāsabhayena sakalasarīrassa chambhitabhāvo. Visesato pana hadayamaṃsacalananti āha “kāyakampo hadayamaṃsacalana”nti. Lomahaṃsoti tena bhayena tena chambhitattena sakalasarīralomānaṃ haṭṭhabhāvo, so pana nesaṃ bhittiyaṃ nāgadantānaṃ viya uddhaṃmukhatāti āha “lomānaṃ haṃsanaṃ uddhaggabhāvo”ti.

“Vibhattipatirūpako” (a pseudo-case ending) is said with reference to the word “tena.” “Taṃnidānaṃ” (having that as its cause) means that wealth is its cause, its reason. “Assa” (of it) refers to the reflexive pronoun, or to the word itself. “Bhayaṃ” (fear) is intended to mean the fear that arises in the mind in a terrified manner, not the fear of knowledge, nor the fear related to an object, which is expressed as, “one fears on account of this.” Thus, it is said: “The meaning is mental terror.” “Chambhitattaṃ” (stiffness) means the state of stiffness of the entire body due to that very mental terror. Specifically, it is said: “Kāyakampo (bodily trembling) is the shaking of the heart's flesh.” “Lomahaṃso” (bristling of hairs) means the state of all body hairs standing on end due to that fear and that stiffness; and that is their standing upright like ivory pegs on a wall. Thus, it is said: “The bristling of hairs is their standing on end.”

35. Attanāti paccatte karaṇavacanaṃ, sayanti attho. Devaccharānanti anaccantiyo sandhāyāha. Devanāṭakānanti naccantiyo, pariyāyavacanaṃ vā etaṃ devakaññānaṃ. Samuppannabalavasokā hutvāti ayaṃ loko nāma attānaṃva cinteti, tasmā sāpi “idāni ahaṃ anāthā jātā”ti attānaṃva cintayamānā “ayaṃ ajja āgamissati, ajja āgamissatī”ti aṭṭha vassāni bahi na nikkhantā etaṃ nissāya mayā dārakopi na laddho, yassa ānubhāvena jīveyyāmi, ito cāmhi parihīnā aññato cāti samuppannabalavasokā hutvā. Kularukkhapatiṭṭhāpane bījasadisattā kulavaṃsappatiṭṭhāpako putto idha bījakoti adhippetoti āha “kulavaṃsabījakaṃ [M 2.0011] ekaṃ putta”nti. Saṃ nāma dhanaṃ, tassa patīti saṃpati, dhanavā [V 2.0010] vibhavasampanno. Diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikahitāvahattā tassa hitanti sāpateyyaṃ, tadeva dhanaṃ vibhavoti āha – “imaṃ sāpateyyaṃ evaṃ mahantaṃ amhākaṃ vibhava”nti.

35. “Attanā” (by oneself) is an instrumental word in the sense of self, meaning “oneself.” “Devaccharānaṃ” (of celestial nymphs) is said with reference to those who do not dance. “Devanāṭakānanti” (of celestial dancers) means those who dance, or this is a synonym for celestial maidens. “Samuppannabalavasokā hutvā” (having become overwhelmed by strong grief): this world, indeed, thinks only of itself. Therefore, she too, thinking only of herself, “Now I have become helpless,” and for eight years she did not go outside, thinking, “He will come today, he will come today.” “Because of relying on him, I did not get a child by whose power I might live; and I am deprived here and elsewhere.” Thus, she became overwhelmed by strong grief. In establishing the family tree, a son is like a seed; therefore, a son who establishes the family lineage is here intended as “bījaka” (seed). Thus, it is said: “one son, the seed of the family lineage.” “Saṃ” is a name for wealth; its lord is “saṃpati,” a wealthy person, one endowed with prosperity. Because it brings benefit in this life and the next, it is “his benefit” (tassa hitaṃ), hence “sāpateyyaṃ” (property). That very wealth is “vibhava” (prosperity). Thus, it is said: “This property, such great prosperity, is ours.”

36. Itthīnaṃ kumārībhāvappattito paṭṭhāya pacchimavayato oraṃ asati vibandhe aṭṭhame aṭṭhame sattāhe gabbhāsayasaññite tatiye āvatte katipayā lohitapīḷakā saṇṭhahitvā aggahitapubbā eva bhijjanti, tato lohitaṃ paggharati, tattha utusamaññā pupphasamaññā cāti āha – “pupphanti utukāle uppannalohitassa nāma”nti. Gabbhapatiṭṭhānaṭṭhāneti yasmiṃ okāse dārako nibbattati, tasmiṃ padese. Saṇṭhahitvāti nibbattitvā. Bhijjantīti aggahitapubbā eva bhijjanti. Ayañhi tāsaṃ sabhāvo. Dosenāti lohitamalena. Suddhe vatthumhīti paggharitalohitattā anāmayattā ca nahānato paraṃ catutthadivasato paṭṭhāya suddhe gabbhāsaye. Suddhe pana vatthumhi mātāpitūsu ekavāraṃ sannipatitesu yāva satta divasāni khettameva hoti gabbhasaṇṭhahanassa parittassa lohitalepassa vijjamānattā. Keci pana “aḍḍhamāsamattampi khettamevā”ti vadanti. Bāhāyanti adhikaraṇe bhummanti āha “purāṇadutiyikāya yā bāhā, tatra naṃ gahetvā”ti. Upayogatthe bhummavacanampi yujjatiyeva yathā “sudinnassa pādesu gahetvā”ti.

36. From the time a woman reaches maidenhood until the end of her youth, if there is no obstruction, in the third cycle, which is called the womb, in every eighth week, several blood clots form and break apart without having been previously held together. Then blood flows. At that time, it is called “season” and “flower.” Thus, it is said: “‘Flowering’ refers to the blood that arises during the menstrual season.” “Gabbhapatiṭṭhānaṭṭhāne” (in the place of conception) means in the place where a child is born, in that region. “Saṇṭhahitvā” (having formed) means having arisen. “Bhijjanti” (they break apart) means they break apart without having been previously held together. This is indeed their nature. “Dosena” (by impurity) means by the impurity of blood. “Suddhe vatthumhi” (in a pure receptacle) means in a pure womb, from the fourth day after bathing, due to the flowing of blood and being free from illness. But when the receptacle is pure, and the parents have come together once, for up to seven days, it is indeed a field for conception, due to the presence of a small residue of blood. Some, however, say: “Even up to half a month, it is indeed a field.” “Bāhāyaṃ” (by the arm) is in the locative case with the sense of location. Thus, it is said: “Taking him by the arm, which was the arm of the former second wife.” The locative case word is also appropriate in the sense of usage, as in “taking Sudinna by the feet.”

Pubbepi paññattasikkhāpadānaṃ sabbhāvato apaññatte sikkhāpadeti pārājikaṃ sandhāya vuttanti āha – “paṭhamapārājikasikkhāpade aṭṭhapite”ti. Vuttamevatthaṃ vibhāvento āha – “bhagavato kira paṭhamabodhiya”ntiādi. Evarūpanti pārājikapaññattiyā anurūpaṃ. Nidassanamattañcetaṃ, saṅghādisesapaññattiyā anurūpampi ajjhācāraṃ nākaṃsuyeva. Tenevāha – “avasese pañca khuddakāpattikkhandhe eva paññapesī”ti. Idañca thullaccayādīnaṃ pañcannaṃ lahukāpattikkhandhānaṃ sabbhāvamattaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, na pañcāpattikkhandhānaṃ anavasesato paññattattāva. Paṭhamabodhiyaṃ pañcannaṃ lahukāpattīnaṃ sabbhāvavacaneneva dhammasenāpatissa sikkhāpadapaññattiyācanā visesato garukāpattipaññattiyā pātimokkhuddesassa ca hetubhūtāti daṭṭhabbā. Keci [M 2.0012] pana “tasmiṃ tasmiṃ pana vatthusmiṃ avasesapañcakhuddakāpattikkhandhe eva paññapesīti idaṃ dvādasame vasse verañjāyaṃ vutthavassena bhagavatā tato paṭṭhāya aṭṭhavassabbhantare paññattasikkhāpadaṃ sandhāya vutta”nti vadanti, taṃ na sundaraṃ tato pubbepi sikkhāpadapaññattiyā sabbhāvato. Teneva verañjakaṇḍe “ekabhikkhunāpi ratticchedo vā pacchimikāya tattha vassaṃ upagacchāmāti vassacchedo vā na kato”ti ca “sāmampi pacanaṃ samaṇasāruppaṃ na hoti, na ca vaṭṭatī”ti ca vuttaṃ. Ārādhayiṃsūti cittaṃ gaṇhiṃsu, ajjhāsayaṃ [V 2.0011] pūrayiṃsu, hadayagāhiniṃ paṭipattiṃ paṭipajjiṃsūti attho. Ekaṃ samayanti ekasmiṃ samaye, paṭhamabodhiyanti attho.

Even before the training rules were laid down, the inherent nature of offenses was present, even in the absence of such rules. This refers to the pārājika offense, as stated: “at the establishment of the first pārājika training rule.” Clarifying the meaning already stated, he says: “at the Blessed One’s first awakening,” and so on. 'Of such a form' means in accordance with the laying down of the pārājika. This is merely an illustration; even behavior resembling the laying down of a saṅghādisesa offense was certainly not committed. Hence it is said: “He laid down only the remaining five minor categories of offenses.” This refers to the mere existence of the five minor categories of offenses, from thullaccaya downwards, not that all five categories were fully established at once. At the first awakening, the mere mention of the existence of the five minor offenses should be seen as the cause for the request for training rules by the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta), especially for the laying down of serious offenses and the recitation of the Pātimokkha. Some, however, claim: “The statement ‘the remaining five minor categories of offenses were established only in specific cases’ refers to the training rules laid down by the Blessed One after he had completed the rains retreat in Verañjā in the twelfth year, and within the next eight years.” This is not well-founded, as the inherent nature of training rules existed even before that. Thus, in the Verañjā section, it is said: “Not even a single bhikkhu broke the rains residence by a single night’s absence, or by saying, ‘I will go to that place for the latter part of the rains residence,’ thereby breaking the rains residence,” and “Even cooking for oneself is not proper for an ascetic, nor is it allowable.” ‘They pleased him’ means they grasped his intention, fulfilled his aspiration, and undertook a heart-capturing practice. ‘At one time’ means on a certain occasion; the meaning is ‘at the time of the first awakening.’”

Yaṃ ādīnavanti sambandho. Sikkhāpadaṃ paññapentoti paṭhamapārājikasikkhāpadaṃ paññapento. Ādīnavaṃ dassessatīti “varaṃ te, moghapurisa, āsīvisassa ghoravisassa mukhe aṅgajātaṃ pakkhittaṃ, na tveva mātugāmassa aṅgajāte aṅgajātaṃ pakkhitta”ntiādinā yaṃ ādīnavaṃ dassessati. Abhiviññāpesīti imassa “pavattesī”ti ayamattho kathaṃ laddhoti āha “pavattanāpi hī”tiādi. Kāyaviññatticopanatoti kāyaviññattivasena pavattacalanato. Kasmā panesa methunadhammena anatthikopi samāno tikkhattuṃ abhiviññāpesīti āha – “tikkhattuṃ abhiviññāpanañcesā”tiādi. Tattha tikkhattuṃ abhiviññāpananti muttipāpanavasena tīsu vāresu methunadhammassa pavattanaṃ.

The connection is with ‘what danger...’ When laying down the training rule, this means laying down the first pārājika training rule. He will show the danger: “Better for you, foolish man, that your male organ be placed in the mouth of a deadly venomous snake than that your male organ be placed in a woman’s female organ”—thus he will show the danger. Regarding ‘caused it to proceed’ (abhiviññāpesī), how is the meaning ‘caused to proceed’ (pavattesī) obtained? He says: “For causing to proceed is also…” ‘By bodily intimation’ means because of the movement proceeding by way of bodily intimation. But why did he, even though he had no need for the act of intercourse, cause it to proceed three times? He says: “And this threefold causing to proceed…” Here, ‘threefold causing to proceed’ means the proceeding of the act of intercourse on three occasions by way of causing emission.

Sabbesampi padānaṃ avadhāraṇaphalattā vināpi evakāraṃ avadhāraṇattho viññāyatīti āha “teneva ajjhācārenā”ti. Aṭṭha hi gabbhakāraṇāni. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Because all words have the result of determination, the sense of determination is understood even without the particle ‘eva’; therefore he said, ‘by that very transgression.’ For there are eight causes for conception. As it was said:—

“Methunacoḷaggahaṇaṃ, tanusaṃsaggo ca nābhiāmasanaṃ;

Pānaṃ dassanasavanaṃ, ghāyanamiti gabbhahetavo aṭṭhā”ti.

“Intercourse, taking hold of a cloth, bodily contact, and touching the navel; drinking, seeing, hearing, and smelling—these eight are causes for conception.”

Idāni avadhāraṇena nivattitamatthaṃ dassetukāmo āha – “kiṃ pana aññathāpi gabbhaggahaṇaṃ hotī”tiādi. Nanu ca nābhiparāmasanampi kāyasaṃsaggoyeva, kasmā naṃ visuṃ vuttanti? Ubhayesaṃ chandarāgavasena kāyasaṃsaggo vutto, itthiyā chandarāgavasena nābhiparāmasanaṃ, vatthuvasena vā taṃ visuṃ vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kathaṃ pana kāyasaṃsaggena gabbhaggahaṇaṃ hoti, kathañca tattha sukkasoṇitassa sambhavoti āha “itthiyo hī”tiādi[M 2.0013]. Chandarāguppattivasena itthiyā sukkakoṭṭhāso calito hoti, sopi gabbhasaṇṭhānassa paccayo hotīti adhippāyo. Itthisantānepi hi rasādisattadhātuyo labbhantiyeva. Tenāha – “aṅgapaccaṅgaparāmasanaṃ sādiyantiyopi gabbhaṃ gaṇhantī”ti. Gaṇṭhipadesu pana “kāyasaṃsaggādinā sattappakārena gabbhaggahaṇe pitu sukkakoṭṭhāsaṃ vinā chandarāgavasena mātu vikārappattaṃ lohitameva gabbhasaṇṭhānassa paccayo hotī”ti vuttaṃ. “Yassa aṅgapaccaṅgaparāmasanaṃ sādiyitvā mātā puttaṃ paṭilabhati, sace so aparena samayena paripuṇṇindriyo hutvā tādisaṃ pitaraṃ manussajātikaṃ jīvitā voropeti, pitughātakova hotī”ti vadanti.

Now, wishing to show the meaning excluded by the determination, he says: “But does conception also occur otherwise?” and so on. Is not touching the navel also just bodily contact? Why is it stated separately? Bodily contact is spoken of as being by way of the desire and lust of both; touching the navel is by way of the woman's desire and lust, or it should be understood as being stated separately by way of the object. But how does conception occur through bodily contact, and how do semen and blood arise there? He says: “For women…” and so on. By way of the arising of desire and lust, the woman’s portion of semen is agitated, and that too becomes a condition for the formation of the embryo—this is the intended meaning. For in a woman's constitution, the seven elements beginning with nutriment are indeed found. Therefore, it is said: “Even while consenting to the touching of limbs and members, they conceive.” In the knot-passages, however, it is said: “In the seven ways of conception, such as bodily contact, without the father’s portion of semen, the mother’s blood, transformed due to desire and lust, alone becomes the condition for the formation of the embryo.” They say: “If a mother obtains a son after consenting to the touching of limbs and members by someone, and if that son at a later time, having mature faculties, deprives such a human father of life, he is indeed a patricide.”

Taṃ [V 2.0012] asuciṃ ekadesaṃ mukhena aggahesīti purāṇacīvaraṃ dhovantī tattha yaṃ asuciṃ addasa, taṃ asuciṃ ekadesaṃ pivi. “Vaṭṭati tumhākaṃ methunadhammo”ti puṭṭho “kappatu vā mā vā kappatu, mayaṃ tena anatthikā”ti dassento āha “anatthikā mayaṃ etenā”ti. Kiñcāpi nābhiparāmasane methunarāgo natthi, tathāpi nābhiparāmasanakāle phassasādiyanavasena assādamattaṃ tassā ahosīti gahetabbaṃ, aññathā gabbhasaṇṭhahanaṃ na siyā. Diṭṭhamaṅgalikāya nābhiparāmasanena maṇḍabyassa nibbatti ahosi, caṇḍapajjotamātu nābhiyaṃ vicchikā pharitvā gatā, tena caṇḍapajjotassa nibbatti ahosīti āha “eteneva nayenā”tiādi. Purisaṃ upanijjhāyatīti vātapānādinā disvā vā diṭṭhapubbaṃ vā purisaṃ upanijjhāyati. Rājorodhā viyāti sīhaḷadīpe kira ekissā itthiyā tathā ahosi, tasmā evaṃ vuttaṃ.

She took a portion of that impurity with her mouth: while washing the old robe, she saw some impurity there and drank a portion of it. When asked, “Is the act of sexual intercourse permissible for you?” he replied, indicating, “We have no need for that,” by saying, “Whether it is permissible or not, we have no need of this.” Although there was no sexual lust in the touching of the navel, still, at the time of touching the navel, a mere taste of pleasure arose for her by way of enjoying the contact; this should be understood, otherwise the establishment of a fetus would not have occurred. Maṇḍabya was conceived through the touching of the navel by Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā. A scorpion, having crawled on Caṇḍapajjota’s mother’s navel, went away, and due to that Caṇḍapajjota was conceived; hence it is said, “By this very method,” and so on. She contemplates a man: either having seen a man through a window, etc., or she contemplates a man seen before. Like the royal harem: it is said that in the island of Sīhaḷa, it was so for a certain woman, which is why it was stated thus.

Idhāti imasmiṃ vatthusmiṃ. Ayanti sudinnassa purāṇadutiyikā. Yaṃ sandhāyāti yaṃ ajjhācāraṃ sandhāya. Sukkaṃ sandhāya “mātāpitaro ca sannipatitā hontī”ti vuttaṃ, mātā ca utunī hotīti lohitaṃ sandhāya. Tattha sannipatitā hontīti asaddhammavasena ekasmiṃ ṭhāne samāgatā saṅgatā honti. Mātā ca utunī hotīti idaṃ utusamayaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, na lokasamaññākarajassa lagganadivasamattaṃ. Gandhabboti tatrūpagasatto, gantabboti vuttaṃ hoti. Ta-kārassa dha-kāro katoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Atha vā gandhanato uppajjanagatiyā nimittupaṭṭhānena sūcanato [M 2.0014] dīpanato gandhoti laddhanāmena bhavagāmikammunā abbati pavattatīti gandhabbo, tattha uppajjanakasatto. Paccupaṭṭhito hotīti upagato hoti. Ettha ca na mātāpitūnaṃ sannipātaṃ olokayamāno samīpe ṭhito nāma hoti, kammayantayantito pana eko satto tasmiṃ okāse nibbattanako purimajātiyaṃ ṭhitoyeva gatinimittādiārammaṇakaraṇavasena upapattābhimukho hotīti adhippāyo.

‘Here’ means in this story. ‘This one’ refers to Sudinna’s former wife. ‘Referring to what’ means referring to what transgression. Referring to the semen, it is said, ‘and the mother and father are assembled’; the statement that ‘the mother is in season’ refers to the blood. There, ‘are assembled’ means they have come together and united in one place by way of an unrighteous act. ‘And the mother is in season’ refers to the time of fertility, not merely the day of attachment of the bodily fluid according to worldly convention. ‘Gandhabba’ means a being who has arrived there; it is said to mean ‘one who is to be gone to.’ The letter ‘ta’ should be seen as having been made into ‘dha.’ Alternatively, from ‘gandh’ (to indicate), because it indicates or illuminates by the presentation of a sign of the destiny to be born, it gets the name ‘gandha.’ By means of karma that leads to a new existence, it proceeds (abbati/pavattati), and is thus called ‘gandhabba’—the being to be born there. ‘Is present’ means has arrived. And here, it is not that he is one who stands nearby watching the union of the mother and father. But rather, impelled by the mechanism of kamma, a certain being, who is to be reborn in that opportunity, while still existing in the previous life, becomes oriented toward rebirth by way of taking as object the sign of destiny, and so on—this is the intended meaning.

Sannipātāti samodhānena samāgamena. Gabbhassāti gabbhe nibbattanakasattassa. Gabbhe nibbattanakasattopi hi gabbhoti vuccati. Yathāha – “yathā kho panānanda, aññā itthikā nava vā dasa vā māse gabbhaṃ kucchinā pariharitvā vijāyantī”ti (ma. ni. 3.205). Katthaci pana gabbhoti mātukucchi vutto. Yathāha –

‘Assembly’ (sannipātā) means by coming together, by gathering. ‘Of the womb’ (gabbhassa) refers to the being to be born in the womb. Indeed, even a being to be born in the womb is also called ‘womb’ (gabbha). As it is said: “Just as, Ānanda, some women carry a fetus in the womb for nine or ten months and then give birth.” In some places, however, ‘gabbha’ is used to refer to the mother’s womb. As it is said:

“Yamekarattiṃ paṭhamaṃ, gabbhe vasati māṇavo;

Abbhuṭṭhitova so yāti, sa gacchaṃ na nivattatī”ti. (jā. 1.15.363); –

“The first one night that the young man dwells in the womb; having arisen, he goes; going, he does not return.”

Ettha [V 2.0013] ca gabbhati attabhāvabhāvena pavattatīti gabbho, kalalādiavattho dhammappabandho, taṃnissitattā pana sattasantāno “gabbho”ti vutto yathā “mañcā ukkuṭṭhiṃ karontī”ti. Taṃnissayabhāvato mātukucchi “gabbho”ti veditabbo. Gabbho viyāti vā. Yathā hi nivāsaṭṭhānatāya sattānaṃ ovarako “gabbho”ti vuccati, evaṃ gabbhaseyyakānaṃ sattānaṃ yāva abhijāti nivāsaṭṭhānatāya mātukucchi “gabbho”ti vuttoti veditabbo. Avakkanti hotīti nibbatti hoti.

And here, that which proceeds as an individual existence is called ‘gabbha’; it is a continuum of phenomena in the state beginning with the kalala. But because the continuum of a being is dependent on it, it is called ‘gabbha,’ just as it is said, ‘the beds are making a noise.’ Because it is its support, the mother’s womb should be known as ‘gabbha.’ Or, it is like a ‘gabbha’ (chamber). Just as a private room, being a dwelling place for beings, is called a ‘gabbha,’ so too, because it is the dwelling place for beings lying in the womb up until birth, the mother’s womb is called ‘gabbha’—this should be understood. ‘Descent occurs’ means arising occurs.

Ārakkhadevatāti tassa ārakkhatthāya ṭhitā devatā. Assa taṃ ajjhācāranti sambandho. Tathā nicchāresunti tathā mahantaṃ saddaṃ katvā nicchāresuṃ. Kiñcāpi idha pāḷiyaṃ ākāsaṭṭhadevatā visuṃ na āgatā, tathāpi saddassa anussāvane ayamanukkamoti dassetuṃ cātumahārājikadevatāyo dvidhā katvā ākāsaṭṭhadevatā visuṃ vuttā. Tenettha ākāsaṭṭhakānaṃ visuṃ gahitattā cātumahārājikāti paribhaṇḍapabbataṭṭhakā veditabbā. Itihāti nipātasamudāyo evaṃsaddassa atthe daṭṭhabboti āha “eva”nti. Khaṇena muhuttenāti padadvayaṃ vevacanabhāvato samānatthamevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ekakolāhalamahosīti devabrahmalokesu [M 2.0015] ekakolāhalamahosi. Kiñcāpi hi so saddo yāva brahmalokā abbhuggacchi, tathāpi na so manussānaṃ visayo tesaṃ rūpaṃ viya, teneva bhikkhū pucchiṃsu – “kacci no tvaṃ, āvuso sudinna, anabhirato”ti.

‘Guardian deities’ are the deities stationed for his protection. The connection should be made with ‘his transgression.’ ‘Thus they cried out’ means they made a great sound and cried out. Although here in the Pāḷi the sky-dwelling deities are not mentioned separately, nevertheless, to show that this is the sequence in the proclamation of the sound, the deities of the Four Great Kings are divided in two and the sky-dwelling deities are mentioned separately. Therefore, since the sky-dwellers are taken separately here, by ‘Cātumahārājikā’ should be understood those dwelling on Mount Paribhaṇḍa. `Iti ha` is a collection of particles to be understood in the sense of the word `evaṃ` (thus); therefore, it is said `evaṃ`. The two words ‘khaṇena’ and ‘muhuttena,’ being synonyms, should be seen as having the same meaning. ‘There was a single uproar’ means there was a single uproar in the worlds of devas and brahmās. For although that sound went up as far as the brahmā world, it was not an object for humans, just like their form. For that very reason, the monks asked, “Friend Sudinna, are you perhaps discontented?”

37. “Evaṃ mātāputtānaṃ pabbajjā saphalā ahosi, pitā pana vippaṭisārābhibhūto vihāsī”ti vacanato sudinnassa tasmiṃ attabhāve arahattādhigamo nāhosīti viññāyati. Keci pana “pubbekatapuññatāya codiyamānassa bhabbakulaputtassāti vuttattā sudinno taṃ kukkuccaṃ vinodetvā arahattaṃ sacchākāsi, teneva pabbajjā anuññātā”ti vadanti. Taṃ pāḷiyā aṭṭhakathāya ca na sameti. Pubbekatapuññatā ca appamāṇaṃ tādisassapi antarākatapāpakammassa vasena ajātasattuno viya adhigamantarāyadassanato. Katākatānusocanalakkhaṇaṃ kukkuccaṃ idhādhippetanti āha “ajjhācārahetuko pacchānutāpo”ti. Kataṃ ajjhācāraṃ paṭicca anusocanavasena virūpaṃ saraṇaṃ cintanaṃ vippaṭisāroti āha “vippaṭisārotipi tasseva nāma”nti. Kucchitaṃ kataṃ kiriyāti kukataṃ, kukatameva kukkuccanti āha “kucchitakiriyābhāvato kukkucca”nti. Pariyādinnamaṃsalohitattāti parikkhīṇamaṃsalohitattā. Avipphārikoti uddesādīsu byāpārarahito, abyāvaṭoti attho. Vahacchinnoti [V 2.0014] chinnavaho, bhāravahanena chinnakkhandhoti vuttaṃ hoti. Taṃ taṃ cintayīti “yadi ahaṃ taṃ pāpaṃ na karissaṃ, ime bhikkhū viya paripuṇṇasīlo assa”ntiādinā taṃ taṃ cintayi.

37. “Thus, the going forth of the mother and son was fruitful, but the father, overwhelmed by remorse, lived on.” From this, it is understood that Sudinna did not attain arahantship in that existence. Some, however, say: “Because it was said, ‘of a capable clansman being urged by past merit,’ Sudinna dispelled that worry and realized arahantship; for that very reason, the going forth was permitted.” That does not accord with the Pāḷi and the commentary. Moreover, past merit is not a determining factor, for even in such a person, an obstacle to attainment is seen due to an intervening evil deed, as in the case of Ajātasattu. Here, worry (kukkucca) is intended as having the characteristic of sorrowing over what was done and not done; thus he said: “Regret due to transgression.” Remorse (vippaṭisāra) is unseemly remembering and thinking by way of sorrowing in dependence on a transgression that was done; thus he said: “Vippaṭisāra is also a name for that very thing.” A contemptible, done action is a misdeed (kukata); a misdeed itself is worry (kukkucca), thus he said: “It is worry (kukkucca) from its nature as a contemptible action.” “Because his flesh and blood were consumed” means because his flesh and blood were exhausted. “Unenergetic” means without activity in recitation and so on; the meaning is “unoccupied.” “With carrying cut off” means with his carrying cut; it is said to mean “with shoulder broken” from carrying a burden. “He thought of this and that” means he thought of this and that in various ways, such as: “If I had not done that evil deed, I would be of complete virtue like these monks.”

38. Evaṃbhūtanti kisalūkhādibhāvappattaṃ. Gaṇasaṅgaṇikāpapañcenāti gaṇe janasamāgame sannipatanaṃ gaṇasaṅgaṇikā, gaṇasaṅgaṇikāyeva papañco gaṇasaṅgaṇikāpapañco, tena. Yassāti ye assa. Kathāphāsukāti vissāsikabhāveneva kathākaraṇe phāsukā, sukhena vattuṃ sakkuṇeyyā, sukhasambhāsāti attho. Pasādassa pamāṇato ūnādhikattaṃ sabbadā sabbesaṃ natthīti āha “pasādapatiṭṭhānokāsassa sampuṇṇattā”ti. Dānīti imasmiṃ atthe etarahi-saddo atthīti āha “dānīti nipāto”ti. No-saddopi nu-saddo viya pucchanatthoti āha “kacci [M 2.0016] nu tva”nti. Tameva anabhiratinti tehi bhikkhūhi pucchitaṃ tameva gihibhāvapatthanākāraṃ anabhiratiṃ. “Tamevā”ti avadhāraṇena nivattitamatthaṃ dassento āha “adhikusalāna”ntiādi. Adhikusalā dhammā samathavipassanādayo. Atthīti visayabhāvena citte parivattanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, na pāpassa vattamānataṃ sandhāya, atthi visayabhāvena citte parivattatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Tenāha – “niccakālaṃ abhimukhaṃ viya me tiṭṭhatī”ti.

38. “In such a state” means having reached a state of being thin, rough, and so on. “Through the proliferation of socializing”: assembling in a group, a gathering of people, is socializing (gaṇasaṅgaṇikā); the proliferation of that very socializing is the proliferation of socializing (gaṇasaṅgaṇikāpapañco); by that. “Of whom” means of those who were his. “Easy to converse with” means they were comfortable in conversation due to familiarity, they could speak with ease; the meaning is that they were pleasant to converse with. That there is not for everyone at all times a deficiency or excess in the measure of faith, he said: “because of the completeness of the opportunity for establishing faith.” “Now” (dāni): because in this sense the word ‘etarahi’ is present, he said: “‘dāni’ is a particle.” The word ‘no’ is also in the sense of a question, like the word ‘nu’; thus he said: “Kacci nu tvaṃ.” “That very discontent”: that very discontent which was the state of longing for the household life, about which he was asked by those monks. Showing the meaning that was averted by the emphatic word “that very,” he said: “of higher wholesome states,” and so on. Higher wholesome states are serenity, insight, and so on. “There is” is said with reference to its revolving in the mind as an object, not with reference to the present existence of the evil; it is said to mean: “it exists and revolves in the mind as an object.” Therefore he said: “It stands before me constantly, as if face to face.”

Yaṃ tvanti ettha yanti hetuatthe nipāto, karaṇatthe vā paccattavacananti āha “yena pāpenā”ti. Anekapariyāyenāti ettha pariyāya-saddo kāraṇavacanoti āha “anekakāraṇenā”ti. Virāgatthāyāti bhavabhogesu virajjanatthāya. No rāgena rajjanatthāyāti bhavabhogesuyeva rāgena arañjanatthāya. Tenāha “bhagavatā hī”tiādi. Esa nayo sabbapadesūti adhippāyikamattaṃ sabbapadesu atidissati. Idaṃ panettha pariyāyavacanamattanti “visaṃyogāyā”tiādīsu sabbapadesu “kilesehi visaṃyujjanatthāyā”tiādinā padatthavibhāvanavasena vuttapariyāyavacanaṃ sandhāya vadati. Na saṃyujjanatthāyāti kilesehi na saṃyujjanatthāya. Aggahaṇatthāyāti kilese aggahaṇatthāya, bhavabhoge vā taṇhādiṭṭhivasena aggahaṇatthāya. Na saṅgahaṇatthāyāti etthāpi imināva nayena attho veditabbo.

Here in `yaṃ tvaṃ`, `yaṃ` is a particle in the sense of cause, or it is a case-ending in the instrumental sense; thus he said: “by which evil.” Here in `anekapariyāyena`, the word `pariyāya` expresses ‘reason’; thus he said: “for many reasons.” “For the sake of dispassion” means for the purpose of becoming dispassionate towards existence and enjoyments. “Not for being impassioned by passion” means for the purpose of not being impassioned by passion precisely in existence and enjoyments. Therefore he said: “For by the Blessed One,” and so on. “This is the method in all passages” means the intended meaning is indicated in all passages. But this here is just a synonymous expression. With reference to the synonymous expression stated by way of analyzing the word-meaning in all passages such as “for disunion,” etc., by way of “for the purpose of becoming disunited from the defilements,” etc., he speaks. “Not for the purpose of being united” means for the purpose of not being united with the defilements. “For the purpose of not grasping” means for the purpose of not grasping the defilements, or for the purpose of not grasping existence and enjoyments by way of craving and views. “For the purpose of not accumulating”: here too the meaning should be understood by this same method.

Nibbattitalokuttaranibbānamevāti saṅkhārehi nikkhantaṃ vivittaṃ, tatoyeva lokato uttiṇṇattā lokuttaraṃ nibbānaṃ. Madanimmadanāyāti vāti ettha avuttasamuccayatthena vā-saddena ādiatthena iti-saddena vā “pipāsavinayāyā”tiādi sabbaṃ saṅgahitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Nibbānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā pavattamānena ariyamaggena pahīyamānā rāgamānamadādayo taṃ patvā pahīyanti nāmāti āha “yasmā pana taṃ āgammā”tiādi. Tattha taṃ āgammāti nibbānaṃ āgamma paṭicca [V 2.0015] ariyamaggassa ārammaṇapaccayabhāvahetu. Mānamadapurisamadādayoti ettha jātiādiṃ nissāya seyyassa “seyyohamasmī”tiādinā uppajjanakamānoyeva madajananaṭṭhena madoti mānamado. Purisamado vuccati purisamāno, “ahaṃ puriso”ti uppajjanakamāno. “Asaddhammasevanasamatthataṃ nissāya pavatto māno, rāgo eva vā purisamado”ti keci. Ādi-saddena balamadayobbanamadādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti[M 2.0017]. Mahāgaṇṭhipade pana majjhimagaṇṭhipade ca “purisamado nāma sambhavo”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ idha yuttaṃ viya na dissati. Na hi “bhagavatā sambhavassa vināsāya dhammo desito”ti vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Nimmadāti vigatamadabhāvā. Imameva hi atthaṃ dassetuṃ “amadā”ti vuttaṃ. Madā nimmadīyanti ettha amadabhāvaṃ vināsaṃ gacchantīti madanimmadano. Esa nayo sesapadesupi.

“The produced world-transcending Nibbāna itself” means: Nibbāna is departed from formations, secluded; for that very reason, because of having crossed over from the world, it is world-transcending. In `Madanimmadanāya vā` (“for the subduing of intoxication, or...”), it should be seen that by the word `vā` in the sense of an unstated collection, or by the word `iti` in the sense of “and so on,” everything beginning with “for the removal of thirst” is included. Lust, conceit, intoxication, and so on, which are to be abandoned by the noble path that proceeds having made Nibbāna its object, are indeed abandoned upon reaching it; thus he said: “For since, having approached it,” and so on. Therein, “having approached it” means having approached Nibbāna, having depended on it, because it is the cause of the object-condition for the noble path. In “conceit-intoxication, man-intoxication, and so on,” the conceit that arises in a superior person depending on birth and so on, by way of “I am superior,” etc., is itself conceit-intoxication (mānamado) in the sense of generating intoxication. Man-intoxication (purisamado) is called man-conceit (purisamāno), the conceit that arises as “I am a man.” Some say: “Man-intoxication is the conceit that proceeds depending on the ability to engage in wrong principles, or it is just lust.” By the word “and so on” (`ādi`), he includes intoxication from strength, intoxication from youth, and so on. But in the Mahāgaṇṭhipada and the Majjhimagaṇṭhipada it is said: “Man-intoxication is called prosperity (sambhava).” That does not seem fitting here. For it is not right to say: “The Dhamma was taught by the Blessed One for the destruction of prosperity.” “Without intoxication” means because of the state of departed intoxication. Indeed, to show this very meaning, “free from intoxication” was said. Herein, intoxications are subdued (`madā nimmadīyanti`), that is, they go to a state free from intoxication, to destruction; hence the term `madanimmadano`, the subduing of intoxication. This is the method in the remaining passages as well.

Kāmapipāsāti kāmānaṃ pātukamyatā, kāmataṇhāti attho. Ālīyanti abhiramitabbaṭṭhena sevīyantīti ālayā, pañca kāmaguṇāti āha “pañca kāmaguṇālayā”ti. Pañcasu hi kāmaguṇesu chandarāgappahāneneva pañca kāmaguṇāpi pahīnā nāma honti, teneva “yo, bhikkhave, rūpesu chandarāgo”tiādi (saṃ. ni. 3.323) vuttaṃ. Pañcakāmaguṇesu vā ālayā pañcakāmaguṇālayā. Ālīyanti allīyanti abhiramanavasena sevantīti ālayāti hi taṇhāvicaritānaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tebhūmakavaṭṭanti tīsu bhūmīsu kammakilesavipākā vaṭṭanaṭṭhena vaṭṭaṃ. Virajjatīti palujjati. “Virajjatīti kāmavināso vutto, nirujjhatīti ekappahārena vināso”ti gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Virāgo nirodhoti sāmaññacodanāyapi “taṇhākkhayo”ti adhikatattā taṇhāya eva virajjanaṃ nirujjhanañca vuttaṃ.

Kāmapipāsā means the desire for the manifestation of sensual pleasures; it means sensual craving. Ālīyanti: they are to be delighted in, they are indulged in—thus they are ālayā (abodes). The five strands of sensual pleasure, thus it is said, are 'the five abodes of sensual pleasure.' For by abandoning desire and lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure, the five strands of sensual pleasure are indeed abandoned. Therefore, it is said: 'Monks, whatever desire and lust there is for forms,' etc. (Saṃ. Ni. 3.323). Or, the ālayā (abodes) in the five strands of sensual pleasure are pañcakāmaguṇālayā. Ālīyanti: they adhere, they indulge in delight—thus they are ālayā. Indeed, this is a designation for the wanderings of craving. Tebhūmakavaṭṭa means the round in the three realms by way of action, defilements, and results, in the sense of revolving. Virajjati means it perishes. In the Gaṇṭhipadas, it is stated: 'Virajjati refers to the destruction of sensual desire, while nirujjhati refers to complete destruction at once.' Even though 'dispassion and cessation' is a general statement, because 'the destruction of craving' is the intended meaning, it is specifically the dispassion for and cessation of craving that is spoken of.

Catasso yoniyoti ettha yonīti khandhakoṭṭhāsassapi kāraṇassapi passāvamaggassapi nāmaṃ. “Catasso nāgayoniyo (saṃ. ni. 3.342-343) catasso supaṇṇayoniyo”ti ettha hi khandhakoṭṭhāso yoni nāma. “Yoni hesā bhūmija phalassa adhigamāyā”ti (ma. ni. 3.226) ettha kāraṇaṃ. “Na cāhaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ brūmi, yonijaṃ mattisambhava”nti (ma. ni. 2.457; dha. pa. 396) ettha passāvamaggo. Idha pana khandhakoṭṭhāso “yonī”ti adhippeto. Yavanti tāya sattā amissitāpi samānajātitāya missitā hontīti yoni. Sā pana atthato aṇḍādiuppattiṭṭhānavisiṭṭho khandhānaṃ bhāgaso pavattiviseso, sā ca aṇḍajajalābujasaṃsedajaopapātikavasena catubbidhā. Vuttañhetaṃ “catasso kho imā, sāriputta, yoniyo. Katamā catasso? Aṇḍajā yoni jalābujā yoni saṃsedajā yoni opapātikā yonī”ti (ma. ni. 1.152).

Catasso yoniyo (four origins): here, the word yonī is a name for a division of the aggregates, a cause, or the birth canal. For example, in 'There are four origins of nāgas (Saṃ. Ni. 3.342-343), four origins of supaṇṇas,' here a division of the aggregates is called yonī. In 'This, Bhūmija, is the origin for attaining the fruit' (Ma. Ni. 3.226), cause is meant. In 'Nor do I call one a brahmin merely by birth or being born of a womb' (Ma. Ni. 2.457; Dhp. 396), the birth canal is referred to. Here, however, a division of the aggregates is intended by 'yonī'. Beings are mixed (yavanti) by it; though they may be unmixed, by being of the same species they become mixed; thus, it is called yoni. In meaning, it is a particular place of origin, such as from an egg, and a particular mode of occurrence of the aggregates by way of division. It is fourfold: egg-born, womb-born, moisture-born, and spontaneously born. For this is said: 'There are, Sāriputta, these four origins. Which four? The egg-born origin, the womb-born origin, the moisture-born origin, and the spontaneously born origin' (Ma. Ni. 1.152).
