Tattha [M 2.0018][V 2.0016] aṇḍe jātā aṇḍajā. Jalābumhi jātā jalābujā. Saṃsede jātā saṃsedajā. Vinā etehi kāraṇehi uppatitvā viya nibbattāti opapātikā. Ettha ca petaloke tiracchāne manussesu ca aṇḍajādayo catassopi yoniyo sambhavanti, manussesu panettha kecideva opapātikā honti mahāpadumakumārādayo viya. Aṇḍajāpi kontaputtā dvebhātiyatherā viya, saṃsedajāpi padumagabbhe nibbattapokkharasātibrāhmaṇapadumavatīdevīādayo viya kecideva honti, yebhuyyena pana manussā jalābujāva. Petesupi nijjhāmataṇhikapetānaṃ niccadukkhāturatāya kāmasevanā natthi, tasmā te gabbhaseyyakā na honti. Jālāvantatāya na tāsaṃ kucchiyaṃ gabbho saṇṭhāti, tasmā te opapātikāyeva saṃsedajatāyapi asambhavato, avasesapetā pana catuyonikāpi honti. Yathā ca te, evaṃ yakkhāpi sabbacatuppadapakkhijātidīghajātiādayopi sabbe catuyonikāyeva. Sabbe nerayikā ca catumahārājikato paṭṭhāya uparidevā ca opapātikāyeva, bhummadevā pana catuyonikāva honti. Tattha devamanussesu saṃsedajaopapātikānaṃ ayaṃ viseso – saṃsedajā mandā daharā hutvā nibbattanti, opapātikā soḷasavassuddesikā hutvā.

Among them, those born from an egg are aṇḍajā (egg-born). Those born from a womb are jalābujā (womb-born). Those born from moisture are saṃsedajā (moisture-born). Those who arise without these causes, as if having flown up, are opapātikā (spontaneously born). Here, in the realm of petas, among animals, and among humans, all four origins beginning with the egg-born are possible. Among humans, however, only some are opapātikā (spontaneously born), like the great prince Paduma and others. Egg-born humans also exist, like the two brother elders, the sons of Koṇṭa; and moisture-born humans also exist, like the brahmin Pokkharasāti who arose in a lotus womb, Queen Padumavatī, and others—only some exist. But for the most part, humans are womb-born. Among petas, the nijjhāmataṇhika petas have no indulgence in sensual pleasures due to being afflicted by constant suffering; therefore, they are not those who lie in a womb. Due to their flaming nature, a fetus does not form in their bellies; therefore, they are only spontaneously arisen, because of the impossibility of moisture-born existence as well. The remaining petas, however, can be of the four origins. And just as they are, so too are yakkhas, and all quadrupeds, species of birds, long-bodied species, and others; all are of the four origins. All hell-beings, and the devas from the realm of the Four Great Kings upwards, are only spontaneously arisen. Earth-devas, however, are of the four origins. Among them, this is the difference between the moisture-born and spontaneously arisen among devas and humans: the moisture-born arise weak and young; the spontaneously arisen arise as if sixteen years of age.

Pañca gatiyoti ettha sukatadukkaṭakammavasena gantabbā upapajjitabbāti gatiyo. Yathā hi kammabhavo paramatthato asatipi kārake paccayasāmaggiyā siddho, taṃsamaṅginā santānalakkhaṇena sattena katoti voharīyati, evaṃ upapattibhavalakkhaṇagatiyo paramatthato asatipi gamake taṃtaṃkammavasena yesaṃ tāni kammāni tehi gantabbāti voharīyanti. Apica gatigati nibbattigati ajjhāsayagati vibhavagati nipphattigatīti bahuvidhā gati nāma. Tattha “taṃ gatiṃ pecca gacchāmī”ti (a. ni. 4.184) ca “yassa gatiṃ na jānanti, devā gandhabbamānusā”ti (dha. pa. 420; su. ni. 649) ca ayaṃ gatigati nāma. “Imesaṃ kho panāhaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ sīlavantānaṃ neva jānāmi āgatiṃ vā gatiṃ vā”ti (ma. ni. 1.508) ayaṃ nibbattigati nāma. “Evampi kho te ahaṃ brahme gatiñca pajānāmi cutiñca pajānāmī”ti (ma. ni. 1.503) ayaṃ ajjhāsayagati nāma. “Vibhavo gati dhammānaṃ, nibbānaṃ arahato [M 2.0019] gatī”ti (pari. 339) ayaṃ vibhavagati nāma. “Dveyeva gatiyo sambhavanti anaññā”ti (dī. ni. 1.258; 2.34; 3.200) ayaṃ nipphattigati nāma. Tāsu idha gatigati adhippetā, sā pana nirayatiracchānayonipettivisayamanaussadevānaṃ vasena pañcavidhā hoti. Vuttañhetaṃ – “pañca kho imā, sāriputta, gatiyo. Katamā pañca? Nirayo tiracchānayoni pettivisayo manussā devā”ti (ma. ni. 1.153).

Pañca gatiyo (five destinies): here, they are called 'destinies' (gatiyo) because they are to be gone to, to be reborn into, by way of well-done and ill-done kamma. For just as kamma-existence, although in an ultimate sense there is no doer, is established by a conjunction of conditions and is conventionally spoken of as 'done' by a being characterized by continuity who is endowed with that conjunction; so too, destinies characterized by rebirth-existence, although in an ultimate sense there is no goer, are conventionally spoken of as 'to be gone to' by those whose kamma it is, according to that respective kamma. Furthermore, the term 'gati' has many meanings: destination of going (gatigati), destination of arising (nibbattigati), destination of inclination (ajjhāsayagati), destination of dissolution (vibhavagati), and destination of accomplishment (nipphattigati). Among these, 'destination of going' (gatigati) is exemplified by: 'After death, I go to that destination' (Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.184) and 'Whose destination neither devas nor gandhabbas nor humans know' (Dhammapada 420; Sutta Nipāta 649). 'Destination of arising' (nibbattigati) is exemplified by: 'Of these virtuous monks, I know neither their coming nor their going' (Majjhima Nikāya 1.508). 'Destination of inclination' (ajjhāsayagati) is exemplified by: 'Thus, O Brahmā, I know your destination and your passing away' (Majjhima Nikāya 1.503). 'Destination of dissolution' (vibhavagati) is exemplified by: 'Dissolution is the destination of phenomena; Nibbāna is the destination of the Arahant' (Parivāra 339). 'Destination of accomplishment' (nipphattigati) is exemplified by: 'Only two destinations are possible, no others' (Dīgha Nikāya 1.258; 2.34; 3.200). Among these, 'destination of going' (gatigati) is intended here. And that destination is fivefold by way of hell, the animal realm, the sphere of petas, humans, and devas. As it is said: 'These, Sāriputta, are the five destinies. Which five? Hell, the animal realm, the sphere of petas, humans, and devas' (Majjhima Nikāya 1.153).

Tattha [V 2.0017] yassa uppajjati, taṃ brūhentoyeva uppajjatīti ayo, sukhaṃ. Natthi ettha ayoti nirayo, tato eva ramitabbaṃ assādetabbaṃ tattha natthīti niratiatthena nirassādaṭṭhena ca nirayoti vuccati. Tiriyaṃ añcitāti tiracchānā, devamanussādayo viya uddhaṃ dīghā ahutvā tiriyaṃ dīghāti attho. Pakaṭṭhato sukhato ayanaṃ apagamo peccabhāvo, taṃ peccabhāvaṃ pattānaṃ visayoti pettivisayo, petayoni. Manassa ussannatāya manussā, satisūrabhāvabrahmacariyayogyatādiguṇavasena upacitamānasatāya ukkaṭṭhaguṇacittatāya manussāti vuttaṃ hoti, ayaṃ panattho nippariyāyato jambudīpavāsīvasena veditabbo. Yathāha – “tīhi, bhikkhave, ṭhānehi jambudīpakā manussā uttarakuruke ca manusse adhiggaṇhanti deve ca tāvatiṃse. Katamehi tīhi? Sūrā satimanto idha brahmacariyavāso”ti (a. ni. 9.21). Tathā hi buddhā ca bhagavanto paccekabuddhā aggasāvakā mahāsāvakā cakkavattino aññe ca mahānubhāvā sattā tattheva uppajjanti, tehi samānarūpāditāya pana saddhiṃ parittadīpavāsīhi itaramahādīpavāsinopi manussātveva paññāyiṃsu.

Therein, 'ayo' means well-being (sukhaṃ), that which arises with growth. 'Nirayo' (hell) is so called because 'there is no ayo here.' Furthermore, it is called niraya in the sense of having no delight (nirati) and no enjoyment (nirassāda), because there is nothing there to delight in or enjoy. 'Tiracchānā' (animals) are so called because they are 'bent horizontally' (tiriyaṃ añcitā), meaning they are long horizontally, not being tall and upright like devas and humans. 'Pettivisayo' (the realm of ghosts) is the sphere of those who have attained the state of 'having departed' (peccabhāva), which is a departure, a going away from excellent happiness; it is the ghost realm (petayoni). 'Manussā' (humans) are so called because of the eminence of their minds (manassa ussannatāya). It is said that they are humans because their minds are cultivated and possess excellent qualities, by virtue of such qualities as mindfulness, courage, and suitability for the holy life. This meaning, however, should be understood directly as referring to the inhabitants of Jambudīpa. As it is said: 'Monks, the humans of Jambudīpa surpass the humans of Uttarakuru and the devas of Tāvatiṃsa in three respects. What three? They are courageous, mindful, and here the holy life is lived.' Indeed, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, Paccekabuddhas, chief disciples, great disciples, wheel-turning monarchs, and other beings of great power arise only there. However, because of their similarity in form and other aspects, the inhabitants of the other great continents, along with those of the minor continents, are also designated as humans.

Apare pana bhaṇanti “lobhādīhi alobhādīhi ca sahitassa manassa ussannatāya manussā. Ye hi sattā manussajātikā, tesu visesato lobhādayo alobhādayo ca ussannā. Te lobhādiussannatāya apāyamaggaṃ, alobhādiussannatāya sugatimaggaṃ nibbānagāmimaggañca paripūrenti, tasmā lobhādīhi alobhādīhi ca sahitassa manassa ussannatāya parittadīpavāsīhi saddhiṃ catumahādīpavāsino sattavisesā manussāti vuccantī”ti. Lokiyā pana “manuno [M 2.0020] apaccabhāvena manussā”ti vadanti. Manu nāma paṭhamakappiko lokamariyādāya ādibhūto sattānaṃ hitāhitavidhāyako kattabbākattabbatāvasena pituṭṭhāniyo, yo sāsane mahāsammatoti vuccati amhākaṃ bodhisatto, paccakkhato paramparāya ca tassa ovādānusāsaniyaṃ ṭhitā sattā puttasadisatāya “manussā, mānusā”ti ca vuccanti. Tato eva hi te “mānavā manujā”ti ca voharīyanti.

Others, however, say: 'Human beings (manussā) are so called because of the predominance of a mind associated with both greed, etc., and non-greed, etc. For among beings of human birth, greed and its associated states, and non-greed and its associated states, are especially predominant. Through the predominance of greed and its associated states, they fulfill the path to the woeful states; and through the predominance of non-greed and its associated states, they fulfill the path to a good destination and the path leading to Nibbāna. Therefore, the distinguished beings who dwell in the four great continents, along with those in the minor continents, are called 'human' because of the predominance of a mind associated with both greed, etc., and non-greed, etc.' Worldly people, however, say: 'Human beings are so called because they are the offspring of Manu.' Manu was a being of the first aeon, the founder of worldly conventions, who determined what is beneficial and harmful for beings, establishing what should and should not be done, thus standing in the place of a father. In the Dispensation, he is called Mahāsammata, our Bodhisatta. Because beings abide in his instruction and admonition, either directly or through lineage, they are called 'humans' (manussā, mānusā) due to their likeness to sons. For this very reason, they are also referred to as 'mānavā' and 'manujā'.

Pañcahi kāmaguṇehi attano attano devānubhāvasaṅkhātehi iddhivisesehi ca dibbanti kīḷanti laḷanti jotantīti devā. Tattha kāmadevā kāmaguṇehi ceva iddhivisesehi ca, itare iddhiviseseheva dibbantīti veditabbā. Saraṇanti vā gamiyanti abhitthavīyantīti vā devā. Ettha ca nirayagatidevagatimanussagatīhi saddhiṃ okāsena khandhā vuttā. Tiracchānayonipettivisayaggahaṇena khandhānaṃ eva gahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ tesaṃ tādisassa paricchinnassa okāsassa abhāvato. Yattha yattha vā te araññasamuddapabbatapādādike nibaddhavāsaṃ vasanti, tādisassa ṭhānassa [V 2.0018] vasena okāsopi gahetabbo. Satta viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo nava sattāvāsā ca heṭṭhā saṃvaṇṇitanayā eva. Aparāparabhāvāyāti aparāparaṃ yoniādito yoniādibhāvāya. Ābandhanaṃ gaṇṭhikaraṇaṃ, saṃsibbanaṃ tunnakaraṇaṃ. Taṇhāya nikkhantaṃ tattha tassā sabbaso abhāvato, nikkhamanañcassa taṇhāya visaṃyogo evāti āha “visaṃyutta”nti.

They are called 'devas' because they sport (dibbanti)—that is, they play (kīḷanti), delight (laḷanti), and shine (jotanti)—with the five strands of sensual pleasure and with their respective special powers known as divine might. Herein, it should be understood that the sensual-realm devas (kāmadevā) sport with both the strands of sensual pleasure and special powers, while the others sport only with special powers. Or, they are called devas because they are gone to for refuge or are praised. Here, with regard to the destinies of hell, devas, and humans, the aggregates are spoken of along with their location. By the mention of the animal realm and the realm of ghosts, only the taking of the aggregates should be understood, because of the absence of such a defined location for them. Or, wherever they dwell in a fixed abode—in a forest, ocean, at the foot of a mountain, and so on—such a place should also be taken as their location. The seven stations of consciousness and the nine abodes of beings are as explained previously. 'For successive states of being' (aparāparabhāvāya) means from one state of origin, such as a womb, to another successive state of origin. 'Binding' (ābandhanaṃ) is the making of a knot; 'stitching' (saṃsibbanaṃ) is the act of sewing. It is 'departed from craving' (taṇhāya nikkhantaṃ) because of the complete absence of craving there; and this departure is precisely the disconnection (visaṃyoga) from craving. Therefore, it is said to be 'disconnected' (visaṃyutta).

Kāmānaṃ pahānanti ettha kāmaggahaṇena kāmīyatīti kāmo, kāmetīti kāmoti duvidhassapi kāmassa saṅgaho katoti āha “vatthukāmānaṃ kilesakāmānañca pahāna”nti. Vatthukāmappahānañcettha tesu chandarāgappahānenāti veditabbaṃ. Kāmasaññānanti kāmesu, kāmasahagatānaṃ vā saññānaṃ. Pariññāti tividhāpi pariññā idhādhippetāti āha “ñātatīraṇapahānavasena tividhā pariññā”ti. Tattha katamā ñātapariññā? Sabbaṃ tebhūmakaṃ nāmarūpaṃ “idaṃ rūpaṃ, ettakaṃ rūpaṃ, na ito bhiyyo, idaṃ nāmaṃ, ettakaṃ nāmaṃ, na ito bhiyyo”ti bhūtupādāyabhedaṃ rūpaṃ phassādibhedaṃ nāmañca lakkhaṇarasapaccupaṭṭhānapadaṭṭhānato vavatthapeti, kammāvijjādikañcassa paccayaṃ pariggaṇhāti, ayaṃ ñātapariññā.

Regarding 'the abandonment of sensual desires' (kāmānaṃ pahānaṃ): here, by the term 'sensual desires,' both that which is desired (kāmīyatīti kāmo) and that which desires (kāmetīti kāmo) are included. Thus, it is stated as 'the abandonment of object-based sensual desires (vatthukāma) and defilement-based sensual desires (kilesakāma).' Here, the abandonment of object-based sensual desires should be understood as the abandonment of desire and lust for them. 'The perception of sensual pleasures' (kāmasaññānaṃ) refers to perceptions relating to sensual pleasures, or those associated with sensual pleasures. 'Full understanding' (pariññā): the threefold full understanding is intended here, as stated: 'threefold full understanding in terms of understanding by knowing (ñātapariññā), understanding by scrutinizing (tīraṇapariññā), and understanding by abandoning (pahānapariññā).' Herein, what is understanding by knowing? It is when one determines all name-and-form in the three realms—'this is form, this much form, no more than this; this is name, this much name, no more than this'—distinguishing form by its elements and derived form, and name by its divisions such as contact, etc., and determining its characteristic, function, manifestation, and proximate cause, as well as grasping its conditions such as kamma and ignorance. This is understanding by knowing.

Katamā [M 2.0021] tīraṇapariññā? Evaṃ ñātaṃ katvā taṃ sabbaṃ tīreti aniccato dukkhato rogatoti dvācattālīsāya ākārehi, ayaṃ tīraṇapariññā nāma. Katamā pahānapariññā? Evaṃ tīrayitvā aggamaggena sabbasmiṃ chandarāgaṃ pajahati, ayaṃ pahānapariññā. Diṭṭhivisuddhikaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhiyo vā ñātapariññā, maggāmaggapaṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhiādayo, kalāpasammasanādianulomapariyosānā vā paññā tīraṇapariññā, ariyamagge ñāṇaṃ nippariyāyena pahānapariññā. Idha pana kāmasaññānaṃ sabhāvalakkhaṇapaṭivedhavasena aniccādisāmaññalakkhaṇavasena ca pavattamānānaṃ ñātatīraṇapariññānampi kiccanipphattiyā maggeneva ijjhanato maggakkhaṇaṃyeva sandhāya tividhāpi pariññā vuttā. Teneva “imesu pañcasu ṭhānesu kilesakkhayakaro lokuttaramaggova kathito”ti vuttaṃ.

What is understanding by scrutinizing? Having thus known it, one scrutinizes all of that as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, in forty-two ways. This is called understanding by scrutinizing. What is understanding by abandoning? Having thus scrutinized, one abandons all desire and lust through the supreme path. This is understanding by abandoning. Alternatively, the purification of view and the purification by overcoming doubt are understanding by knowing. The purification of knowledge and vision of the path and non-path, etc., or the wisdom beginning with comprehension by groups and ending with conformity knowledge, is understanding by scrutinizing. The knowledge in the noble path is, in a non-figurative sense, understanding by abandoning. Here, however, because the accomplishment of the function of both understanding by knowing and understanding by scrutinizing—which proceed by way of penetrating the own-nature characteristic of perceptions of sensual pleasures and by way of their general characteristics such as impermanence—is achieved only by the path, all three kinds of full understanding are spoken of with reference to the path-moment itself. Therefore it is said: 'In these five instances, only the supramundane path that destroys the defilements is described.'

Kāmesu, kāme vā pātumicchā kāmapipāsāti āha – “kāmesu pātabyatānaṃ, kāme vā pātumicchāna”nti. Imesu pañcasu ṭhānesūti “kāmānaṃ pahānaṃ akkhāta”ntiādinā vuttesu pañcasu ṭhānesu. Tīsu ṭhānesūti “virāgāya dhammo desito, no sarāgāya, visaṃyogāya dhammo desito, no saṃyogāya, anupādānāya dhammo desito, no saupādānāyā”ti evaṃ vuttesu ṭhānesu. Vippaṭisāraṃ karotīti evaṃ taṃ pāpaṃ vippaṭisāraṃ uppādeti. Kīdisaṃ vippaṭisāraṃ karotīti āha “īdisepi nāmā”tiādi.

Regarding 'thirst for sensual pleasures' (kāmapipāsā): it is the desire to drink in sensual pleasures, or the desire for sensual pleasures. Thus, he says: 'of those who are to be drunk in by sensual pleasures, or of those who desire to drink in sensual pleasures.' 'In these five instances' refers to the five instances stated in the passage beginning, 'the abandonment of sensual pleasures has been declared.' 'In three instances' refers to the instances stated thus: 'the Dhamma is taught for dispassion, not for passion; the Dhamma is taught for disjunction, not for conjunction; the Dhamma is taught for non-clinging, not for clinging.' 'He feels remorse' means that such an evil deed causes remorse to arise. As to 'What kind of remorse does he feel?' he says, 'Even such a thing,' etc.

39. Neva [V 2.0019] piyakamyatāyāti attani satthu neva piyabhāvakāmatāya. Na bhedapurekkhāratāyāti na satthu tena bhikkhunā bhedanādhippāyapurekkhāratāya. Na kalisāsanāropanatthāyāti na dosāropanatthāya. Kalīti kodhassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ, tassa sāsanaṃ kalisāsanaṃ, kodhavasena vuccamāno garahadoso. Velanti sikkhāpadavelaṃ. Mariyādanti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Sikkhāpadañhi anatikkamanīyaṭṭhena “velā, mariyādā”ti ca vuccati.

39. 'Not out of a desire for affection' means not out of a desire to be dear to the Teacher. 'Not with a preference for creating division' means not with the primary intention of causing a division between the Teacher and that monk. 'Not for the purpose of making an accusation' means not for the purpose of imputing a fault. 'Kali' is a term for anger; its instruction is 'kalisāsana,' which is a fault of censure spoken by way of anger. 'Vela' means the boundary of the training rule. 'Mariyādā' is a synonym for that very thing. For the training rule, because of its meaning of 'not to be transgressed,' is also called 'velā' and 'mariyādā.'

Ajjhācāravītikkamoti methunavasena pavattaajjhācārasaṅkhāto vītikkamo. Pakaraṇeti ettha pa-saddo ārambhavacanoti āha “kattuṃ ārabhatī”ti. Katthaci upasaggo dhātuatthameva vadati, na visesatthajotakoti āha “karotiyeva vā”ti. Jātiyāti [M 2.0022] khattiyādijātiyā. Gottenāti gotamakassapādigottena. Kolaputtiyenāti khattiyādijātīsuyeva sakkakulasotthiyakulādivisiṭṭhakulānaṃ puttabhāvena. Yasassīti mahāparivāro. Pesalanti piyasīlaṃ. Avikampamānenāti paṭighānunayehi akampamānena. Yassa tasmiṃ attabhāve uppajjanārahānaṃ maggaphalānaṃ upanissayo natthi, taṃ buddhā “moghapurisā”ti vadanti ariṭṭhalāḷudāyīādike viya. Upanissaye satipi tasmiṃ khaṇe magge vā phale vā asati “moghapurisā”ti vadantiyeva dhaniyaupasenattherādike viya. Sudinnassa pana tasmiṃ attabhāve maggaphalānaṃ upanissayo samucchinnoyeva, tena naṃ “moghapurisā”ti āha.

'The transgression of improper conduct' means the transgression designated as improper conduct that occurs by way of sexual intercourse. Here, in the word 'pakaraṇeti,' the prefix 'pa-' has the meaning of 'beginning'; thus, he says, 'he begins to do.' In some cases, a prefix expresses only the meaning of the root and does not indicate a special meaning; thus, he says, 'or he simply does.' 'By birth' means by a khattiya birth and so on. 'By clan' means by the Gotama, Kassapa clan, and so on. 'By being a son of a good family' means by being a son of distinguished families such as the Sakya clan, the Sotthiya clan, etc., even among the khattiya and other births. 'Famous' means having a large retinue. 'Amiable' means of pleasing conduct. 'Unwavering' means not wavering due to aversion and attachment. He for whom in that existence there is no supporting condition for the path and fruition which are fit to arise, him the Buddhas call a 'foolish man,' like Ariṭṭha, Lāḷudāyī, and others. Even when the supporting condition exists, if at that moment the path or fruition is absent, they still call them 'foolish men,' like Dhaniya, the elder Upasena, and others. But for Sudinna, in that existence, the supporting condition for the path and fruition was completely cut off; therefore, he was called a 'foolish man.'

Samaṇakaraṇānaṃ dhammānanti hirottappādīnaṃ. Maggaphalanibbānaggahaṇena paṭivedhasāsanassa gahitattā sāsanānanti paṭipattipariyattisāsanānaṃ gahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Chavinti tesaṃ pabhassarakaraṇaṃ chaviṃ. Kiṃ tanti āha “chāya”nti, tesaṃ pakāsakaṃ obhāsanti attho. Kiṃ tanti āha “sundarabhāva”nti. Chavimanugataṃ anucchavikaṃ. Patirūpantiādīsupi “tesa”nti ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ. Samaṇānaṃ kammaṃ sāmaṇakaṃ, na sāmaṇakaṃ assāmaṇakaṃ. Kathaṃ-saddayogena “na sakkhissasī”ti anāgatavacanaṃ kataṃ. “Nāma-saddayogenā”ti ca vadanti.

'Of the qualities that make one an ascetic' means of modesty, fear of wrongdoing, and so on. Since the teaching of penetration is included by the taking up of path, fruition, and Nibbāna, by 'of the teachings' should be understood the taking up of the teachings of practice and of learning. 'Complexion' (chavi) means that which makes them radiant. What is that? He says 'luster' (chāya); the meaning is their illuminator, their radiance. What is that? He says 'beauty' (sundarabhāva). 'Suitable' (anucchavika) is that which conforms to the complexion. In 'appropriate' (patirūpa) and so on, 'their' (tesaṃ) should also be brought in and connected. The conduct of ascetics is 'ascetic-like' (sāmaṇaka); what is not ascetic-like is 'unascetic-like' (assāmaṇaka). By connection with the word 'kathaṃ,' 'na sakkhissasi' ('you will not be able) is made a future tense statement. And some say, 'by connection with the word nāma.'

Dayālukenāti anukampāya sahitena. Paribhāsantoti garahanto. Niruttinayena āsīvisa-saddassa atthaṃ dassento āha “āsu sīgha”ntiādi. Etassāti āsīvisassa. Āgacchatīti yo tena daṭṭho, taṃ patiāgacchati. Āsittavisotipi āsīviso, sakalakāye āsiñcitvā viya ṭhapitaviso parassa ca sarīre āsiñcanavisoti attho. Asitavisotipi āsīviso. Yaṃ yañhi etena asitaṃ hoti paribhuttaṃ, taṃ visameva sampajjati, tasmā asitaṃ visaṃ etassāti asitavisoti vattabbe “āsīviso”ti niruttinayena [V 2.0020] vuttaṃ. Asisadisavisotipi āsīviso, asi viya tikhiṇaṃ parassa mammacchedanasamatthaṃ visaṃ etassāti āsīvisoti vuttaṃ hoti. Āsīti vā dāṭhā vuccati, tattha sannihitavisoti āsīviso. Sesasappehi kaṇhasappassa mahāvisattā āsīvisassānantaraṃ kaṇhasappo vutto. Sappamukhampi [M 2.0023] aṅgārakāsu viya bhayāvahattā akusaluppattiyā ṭhānaṃ na hotīti akusalakammato nivāraṇādhippāyena sīlabhedatopi suddhasīle ṭhitassa maraṇameva varataranti dassetuṃ “āsīvisassa kaṇhasappassa mukhe aṅgajātaṃ pakkhittaṃ vara”nti vuttaṃ. Pabbajitena hi katapāpakammaṃ bhagavato āṇātikkamanato vatthumahantatāya mahāsāvajjaṃ. Kāsunti āvāṭopi vuccati rāsipi.

By one endowed with compassion (`dayālukena`): that is, endowed with compassion (`anukampāya sahitena`). Censuring (`paribhāsanto`): that is, reproaching (`garahanto`). Explaining the meaning of the word `āsīvisa` according to etymology, he said, “`āsu` (swift),” and so on. Of this (`etassa`): of the `āsīvisa`. It returns (`āgacchati`): it returns to the one who has been bitten by it. One with poured poison (`āsittavisa`) is also an `āsīvisa`; the meaning is that its poison is as if poured and kept throughout its whole body, and it is a poison that is poured into another’s body. One with eaten poison (`asitavisa`) is also an `āsīvisa`. For whatever is eaten and consumed by it becomes poison itself. Therefore, although it should be said `asitavisa`—meaning, “for this one, what is eaten is poison”—it is called `āsīvisa` by way of etymology. One with poison like a sword (`asisadisavisa`) is also an `āsīvisa`; it is said to be an `āsīvisa` because its poison is sharp like a sword (`asi`), capable of cutting another’s vital points. Or, `āsī` is said to be a fang; thus, `āsīvisa` is one with poison deposited therein. Among other snakes, the black snake is mentioned immediately after the `āsīvisa` due to its great venomousness. Since even the mouth of a snake is terrifying like a pit of embers, it is not a place for the arising of the unwholesome. To show the intention of preventing unwholesome deeds, and that for one established in pure virtue, death is more excellent than a breach of virtue, it is said: “It is better to have placed the male organ in the mouth of an `āsīvisa`, a black snake.” Indeed, an evil deed committed by one who has gone forth is a grave offense due to the greatness of the object and because it transgresses the Blessed One’s command. `Kāsu`: it is called a pit and also a heap.

“Kinnu santaramānova, kāsuṃ khaṇasi sārathi;

Puṭṭho me samma akkhāhi, kiṃ kāsuyā karissasī”ti. (jā. 2.22.3) –

“Why, hurrying, do you dig a pit, O charioteer? Asked by me, dear friend, explain: what will you do with the pit?” (Jā. 2.22.3)

Ettha hi āvāṭo kāsu nāma.

Here, indeed, a pit is called `kāsu`.

“Aṅgārakāsuṃ apare phuṇanti, narā rudantā paridaḍḍhagattā”ti (jā. 2.22.462) –

“Others stir up a heap of embers, men weeping with scorched limbs.” (Jā. 2.22.462)

Ettha rāsi. Idha pana ubhayampi adhippetanti āha “aṅgārapuṇṇakūpe aṅgārarāsimhi vā”ti. Kassati khaṇīyatīti kāsu, āvāṭo. Kasīyati cīyatīti kāsu, rāsi. Padittāyāti dippamānāya. Saṃ-saddo ettha samantapariyāyoti āha “samantato pajjalitāyā”ti.

Here, it means a heap. Here, however, both are intended, thus he said: “in a pit full of embers or in a heap of embers.” It is dug (`kassati`), thus it is a `kāsu`, a pit. It is heaped up (`kasīyati`), thus it is a `kāsu`, a heap. Blazing (`padittāya`): that is, flaming (`dippamānāya`). Here, the prefix `saṃ-` is a synonym for `samanta` (all around), thus he said: “blazing all around (`samantato pajjalitāya`).”

Idaṃ mātugāmassa aṅgajāte aṅgajātapakkhipanaṃ nidānaṃ kāraṇamassa nirayupapajjanassāti itonidānaṃ, bhāvanapuṃsakañcetaṃ. Paccattavacanassa to-ādeso kato, tassa ca samāsepi alopo. Tattha nāma tvanti ettha tvaṃ-saddo “samāpajjissasī”ti iminā sambandhamupagacchamāno atthīti āha “tvanti taṃsaddassa vevacana”nti. “Yaṃ tanti pana pāṭho yuttarūpo”ti gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Yaṃ tanti nāyaṃ uddesaniddeso, yathā loke yaṃ vā taṃ vāti avaññātavacanaṃ, evaṃ daṭṭhabbanti āha – “yaṃ vā taṃ vā hīḷitaṃ avaññātanti vuttaṃ hotī”ti. Nīcajanānanti nihīnaguṇānaṃ sattānaṃ. Gāmadhammanti ettha gāma-saddena gāmavāsino vuttā abhedūpacārenāti āha “gāmavāsikamanussāna”nti. Kilesapaggharaṇakaṃ dhammanti rāgādikilesavissandanakadhammaṃ[V 2.0021]. Methunadhammo hi rāgaṃ paggharati. Methunadhammassa mahāsāvajjatāya oḷārikattā vuttaṃ “asukhuma”nti. Anipuṇanti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Udake bhavaṃ odakaṃ. Kiṃ taṃ? Udakakiccanti āha – “udakakiccaṃ antikaṃ avasānaṃ assā”ti. Samāpajjissatīti anāgatavacanaṃ nāma-saddayogena katanti āha – “samāpajjissatīti…pe… nāma-saddena [M 2.0024] yojetabba”nti. Loke methunadhammassa ādikattā koci paṭhamakappiko, na panāyanti āha – “sāsanaṃ sandhāya vadatī”ti. Bahūnanti puggalāpekkhaṃ, na pana akusalāpekkhanti āha “bahūnaṃ puggalāna”nti.

This insertion of the male organ into the female organ is the source (`nidānaṃ`), the reason (`kāraṇaṃ`), for his rebirth in hell; thus, `itonidānaṃ`. And this is a neuter noun of state (`bhāvanapuṃsaka`). The substitution of `-to` for the case ending (`paccattavacana`) is made, and there is no elision of its `a` even in a compound. There, in `nāma tvaṃ`, the word `tvaṃ` is connected with `samāpajjissasi`; thus, he said, “`tvaṃ` is a synonym for `taṃ`.” However, in the glossaries (`gaṇṭhipada`) it is said, “The reading `yaṃ taṃ` is more suitable.” This `yaṃ taṃ` is not a specific designation; just as in the world “whatever this or that” is a term of contempt, so it should be understood. Thus, it is said: “`yaṃ vā taṃ vā` means despised, disregarded.” Of lowly people (`nīcajanānaṃ`): of beings with inferior qualities. The village-practice (`gāmadhamma`): here, by the word `gāma` (village), village-dwellers are meant by way of figurative non-distinction; thus, he said, “of people dwelling in villages.” A practice that causes defilements to flow forth (`kilesapaggharaṇakaṃ dhammaṃ`): a practice that causes defilements such as lust to stream forth. For the practice of sexual intercourse (`methunadhammo`) indeed causes lust to flow forth. Due to the great blameworthiness and grossness of the practice of sexual intercourse, it is called “not subtle” (`asukhuma`). Not skillful (`anipuṇa`) is a synonym for that. Arising in water (`odaka`). What is that? It is a water-duty (`udakakicca`); thus, he said: “that for which the water-duty is near its end.” `Samāpajjissasi` is a future tense formed by connection with the particle `nāma`; thus, he said: “`samāpajjissasi`… should be connected with the particle `nāma`.” In the world, there is no one who is the originator of the practice of sexual intercourse, like some primeval being at the beginning of the aeon; thus, he said: “he speaks with reference to the Dispensation.” Of many (`bahūnaṃ`): this refers to persons, not to unwholesome states; thus, he said, “of many persons.”

Yaṃ asaṃvaraṃ paṭicca dubbharatādupposatādi hoti, so asaṃvaro dubbharatādi-saddena vutto kāraṇe phalūpacārenāti āha – “dubbharatādīnaṃ vatthubhūtassa asaṃvarassā”ti. Vatthubhūtassāti kāraṇabhūtassa. Vasati ettha phalaṃ tadāyattavuttitāyāti hi kāraṇaṃ vatthu. Attāti cittaṃ sarīrañca, cittameva vā. Dubbharatañceva dupposatañca āpajjatīti attanā paccayadāyakehi ca dukkhena bharitabbataṃ posetabbatañca āpajjati. Asaṃvare ṭhito hi ekacco attanopi dubbharo hoti dupposo, ekacco upaṭṭhākānampi. Kathaṃ? Yo hi ambilādīni laddhā anambilādīni pariyesati, aññassa ghare laddhaṃ aññassa ghare chaḍḍento sabbaṃ gāmaṃ caritvā rittapattova vihāraṃ pavisitvā nipajjati, ayaṃ attano dubbharo. Yo pana sālimaṃsodanādīnaṃ patte pūretvā dinnepi dummukhabhāvaṃ anattamanabhāvameva dasseti, tesaṃ vā sammukhāva taṃ piṇḍapātaṃ “kiṃ tumhehi dinna”nti apasādento sāmaṇeragahaṭṭhādīnaṃ deti, ayaṃ upaṭṭhākānaṃ dubbharo. Etaṃ disvā manussā dūratova parivajjenti “dubbharo bhikkhu na sakkā posetu”nti.

That lack of restraint (`asaṃvara`) on account of which there is difficulty in supporting (`dubbharatā`), difficulty in maintaining (`dupposatā`), and so on, is itself called by the term “difficulty in supporting, etc.” This is a figurative use of the effect for the cause. Thus, he said: “of the lack of restraint that is the basis (`vatthu`) for the difficulty in supporting, etc.” That which has become the basis (`vatthubhūtassa`): that is, that which has become the cause (`kāraṇabhūtassa`). For the cause is the basis (`vatthu`) because the effect dwells (`vasati`) therein, its existence depending on that. Self (`attā`): mind and body, or just the mind. He falls into a state of being difficult to support and difficult to maintain: that is, he becomes difficult to be supported and maintained by himself and by the providers of requisites. Indeed, one who is established in non-restraint may be difficult to support and maintain for himself, and another for his attendants. How so? One who, having received sour food, seeks non-sour food, or having received something at one house, discards it at another, and after wandering the entire village, enters the monastery with an empty bowl and lies down—this one is difficult to support for himself. Another, even when given a bowl filled with fine rice, meat, and other foods, shows only a sullen face and displeasure; or, right in front of the donors, disparaging the almsfood by saying, “What is this you have given?” he gives it to novices, laypeople, and others—this one is difficult to support for his attendants. Seeing such a monk, people avoid him from afar, thinking, “This monk is difficult to support; it is not possible to maintain him.”

Mahicchatanti ettha mahantāni vatthūni icchati, mahatī vā panassa icchāti mahiccho, tassa bhāvo mahicchatā, santaguṇavibhāvanatā paṭiggahaṇe amattaññutā ca. Mahiccho hi icchācāre ṭhatvā attani vijjamānasīladhutadhammādiguṇe vibhāveti, tādisassa paṭiggahaṇe amattaññutāpi hoti. Yaṃ sandhāya vadanti “santaguṇasambhāvanatā paṭiggahaṇe ca amattaññutā, etaṃ mahicchatālakkhaṇa”nti. Sā panesā mahicchatā “idhekacco saddho samāno ‘saddhoti maṃ jano jānātū’ti icchati, sīlavā samāno ‘sīlavāti maṃ jano jānātū’ti” iminā nayena āgatāyeva, tāya samannāgato puggalo dussantappiyo hoti, vijātamātāpissa cittaṃ gahetuṃ na sakkoti. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

Mahicchatā (great desire): here, one desires great things, or one has great desire, hence “mahiccho”; the state of such a one is “mahicchatā,” which is the displaying of one’s existing virtues and immoderation in acceptance. Indeed, one with great desire, standing in the sphere of desire, makes manifest the virtues present in oneself—such as morality and the ascetic practices—and such a one also has immoderation in acceptance. Regarding this, it is said: “The displaying of one’s existing virtues and immoderation in acceptance—this is the characteristic of great desire.” This great desire is what is shown by the method beginning: “Here, a certain person, being faithful, desires, ‘May people know me as faithful!’ Being virtuous, he desires, ‘May people know me as virtuous!’” A person endowed with this becomes difficult to satisfy, and even his own birth mother cannot grasp his mind. Therefore, it is said—

“Aggikkhandho [V 2.0022] samuddo ca, mahiccho cāpi puggalo;

Sakaṭena paccayaṃ dentu, tayopete atappiyā”ti. (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.252; a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.63; vibha. aṭṭha. 850; udā. aṭṭha. 31; mahāni. aṭṭha. 85);

“A mass of fire, the ocean, and a person of great desire; though they are given requisites by the cartload, these three are insatiable.”

Sattehi [M 2.0025] kilesehi ca saṅgaṇanaṃ samodhānaṃ saṅgaṇikāti āha – “gaṇasaṅgaṇikāya ceva kilesasaṅgaṇikāya cā”ti. Kosajjānugato ca hotīti kusītabhāvena anugato hoti, kusītassa bhāvo kosajjaṃ. Aṭṭhakusītavatthupāripūriyāti ettha kucchitaṃ sīdatīti kusīto da-kārassa ta-kāraṃ katvā. Yassa dhammassa vasena puggalo “kusīto”ti vuccati, so kusītabhāvo idha kusīta-saddena vutto. Vināpi hi bhāvajotanasaddaṃ bhāvattho viññāyati yathā “paṭassa sukka”nti, tasmā kusītabhāvavatthūnīti attho, kosajjakāraṇānīti vuttaṃ hoti. Tathā hi –

Saṅgaṇikā (gregariousness) is association and combination with beings and with defilements. Thus it is said: “by gregariousness with a group and by gregariousness with defilements.” And he is accompanied by sloth: that is, he is accompanied by the state of being slothful; the state of a slothful person is sloth (kosajja). Regarding the complete fulfillment of the eight grounds for sloth: here, “kusīta” (slothful) is derived from “kucchitaṃ sīdati” (one sinks in what is despicable), by changing the ‘da’ to a ‘ta.’ The quality by means of which a person is called “slothful” is here expressed by the word “kusīta.” For even without a word indicating a state, the meaning of a state is understood, as in “the whiteness of a cloth.” Therefore, the meaning should be understood as “the grounds for the state of sloth”; that is, the causes of sloth are being stated. Thus—

“Kammaṃ kho me kattabbaṃ bhavissati, kammaṃ kho pana me karontassa kāyo kilamissati, handāhaṃ nipajjāmīti so nipajjati, na vīriyaṃ ārabhati appattassa pattiyā anadhigatassa adhigamāya asacchikatassa sacchikiriyāya, idaṃ paṭhamaṃ kusītavatthu. Ahaṃ kho kammaṃ akāsiṃ, kammaṃ kho pana me karontassa kāyo kilanto, handāhaṃ nipajjāmi…pe… maggo kho me gantabbo bhavissati, maggaṃ kho pana me gacchantassa kāyo kilamissati, handāhaṃ nipajjāmi…pe… ahaṃ kho maggaṃ agamāsiṃ, maggaṃ kho pana me gacchantassa kāyo kilanto, handāhaṃ nipajjāmi…pe… ahaṃ kho gāmaṃ vā nigamaṃ vā piṇḍāya caranto nālatthaṃ lūkhassa vā paṇītassa vā bhojanassa yāvadatthaṃ pāripūriṃ, tassa me kāyo kilanto akammañño, handāhaṃ nipajjāmi…pe… ahaṃ kho gāmaṃ vā nigamaṃ vā piṇḍāya caranto alatthaṃ lūkhassa vā paṇītassa vā bhojanassa yāvadatthaṃ pāripūriṃ, tassa me kāyo garuko akammañño māsācitaṃ maññe, handāhaṃ nipajjāmi…pe… uppanno kho me ayaṃ appamattako ābādho, atthi kappo nipajjituṃ, handāhaṃ nipajjāmi…pe… ahaṃ kho gilānā vuṭṭhito aciravuṭṭhito gelaññā, tassa me kāyo dubbalo akammañño, handāhaṃ nipajjāmīti so nipajjati, na vīriyaṃ ārabhati appattassa pattiyā anadhigatassa adhigamāya asacchikatassa sacchikiriyāya. Idaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ kusītavatthu”nti (dī. ni. 3.334; a. ni. 8.80) –

“‘I will have work to do, but while I am working, my body will become tired. Come now, I will lie down.’ So he lies down; he does not arouse energy for the attainment of the un-attained, for the achievement of the un-achieved, for the realization of the un-realized. This is the first ground for sloth. ‘I have done work, and while I was working, my body became tired. Come now, I will lie down.’ …pe… ‘I will have to travel a road, but while I am traveling, my body will become tired. Come now, I will lie down.’ …pe… ‘I have traveled a road, and while I was traveling, my body became tired. Come now, I will lie down.’ …pe… ‘While wandering for alms in a village or town, I did not get enough coarse or fine food to my fill. My body is tired and unfit for work. Come now, I will lie down.’ …pe… ‘While wandering for alms in a village or town, I got enough coarse or fine food to my fill. My body is heavy and unfit for work, as if stuffed with beans, I think. Come now, I will lie down.’ …pe… ‘A slight illness has arisen in me. It is a suitable time to lie down. Come now, I will lie down.’ …pe… ‘I have recovered from illness, but I have not recovered for long. My body is weak and unfit for work. Come now, I will lie down.’ So he lies down; he does not arouse energy for the attainment of the un-attained, for the achievement of the un-achieved, for the realization of the un-realized. This is the eighth ground for sloth.”

Evamāgatāni [M 2.0026][V 2.0023] “handāhaṃ nipajjāmī”ti evaṃ pavattaosīdanāni uparūpari kosajjakāraṇattā aṭṭha kusītavatthūni nāma, tesaṃ pāripūriyā saṃvattatīti attho.

Thus, these instances of sinking down that occur with the thought, “Come now, I will lie down,” being successive causes of sloth, are called the eight grounds for sloth. The meaning is that this leads to their fulfillment.

Subharo hoti suposoti attano upaṭṭhākehi ca sukhena bharitabbo posetabboti attho. Saṃvare ṭhito hi ekacco attanopi subharo hoti suposo, ekacco upaṭṭhākānampi. Kathaṃ? Yo hi yaṃ kiñci lūkhaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vā laddhā tuṭṭhacittova bhuñjitvā vihāraṃ gantvā attano kammaṃ karoti, ayaṃ attano subharo. Yo pana paresampi appaṃ vā bahuṃ vā lūkhaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vā dānaṃ ahīḷetvā attamano vippasannamukho hutvā etesaṃ sammukhāva paribhuñjitvā yāti, ayaṃ upaṭṭhākānaṃ subharo. Etaṃ disvā manussā ativiya vissatthā honti, “amhākaṃ bhadanto subharo, thokathokenapi tussati, mayameva naṃ posessāmā”ti paṭiññaṃ katvā posenti. Appicchatanti icchāvirahitattaṃ. Ettha hi byañjanaṃ sāvasesaṃ viya, attho pana niravaseso. Appa-saddo hettha abhāvatthoti sakkā viññātuṃ “appābādhatañca sañjānāmī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.225) viya. Tenevāha “nittaṇhabhāva”nti.

He is easy to support and easy to nourish, meaning he is to be supported and nourished with ease for himself and by his attendants. For one who is established in restraint, a certain person is easy to support and nourish for himself, and another is easy to support and nourish for his attendants. How so? One who, having received anything, whether coarse or fine, eats it with a contented mind, goes to the monastery, and does his own work—this one is easy to support for himself. But one who, not disdaining the gift of others, whether little or much, coarse or fine, with a pleased mind and a serene face, having eaten right in front of them, departs—this one is easy to support for his attendants. Seeing this, people become exceedingly confident and, making a promise, “Our venerable sir is easy to support; he is satisfied even with a little. We ourselves will nourish him,” they nourish him. Fewness of wishes means the state of being without desire. Here, indeed, the expression is as if with a remainder, but the meaning is without remainder. Here, the word ‘appa’ (few) can be understood to have the meaning of absence, as in such phrases as, “I am aware of being free from illness.” Therefore, he said, “the state of being without craving.”

Tippabhedāya santuṭṭhiyāti yathālābhādisantosasāmaññena vuttaṃ, catūsu pana paccayesu tayo tayo santosāti dvādasavidho hoti santoso. Kathaṃ? Cīvare yathālābhasantoso yathābalasantoso yathāsāruppasantosoti tividho hoti santoso. Evaṃ piṇḍapātādīsu. Tassāyaṃ pabhedasaṃvaṇṇanā (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.252; saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 2.2.144; a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.65) – idha bhikkhu cīvaraṃ labhati sundaraṃ vā asundaraṃ vā, so teneva yāpeti aññaṃ na pattheti, labhantopi na gaṇhāti. Ayamassa cīvare yathālābhasantoso. Atha pana pakatidubbalo vā hoti ābādhajarābhibhūto vā, garucīvaraṃ pārupanto kilamati, so sabhāgena bhikkhunā saddhiṃ taṃ parivattetvā lahukena yāpentopi santuṭṭhoyeva hoti. Ayamassa cīvare yathābalasantoso. Pakatidubbalādīnañhi garucīvarāni na phāsubhāvāvahāni sarīrakhedāvahāni ca hontīti payojanavasena anatricchatādivasena tāni parivattetvā lahukacīvaraparibhogo na santosavirodhīti. Aparo [M 2.0027] paṇītapaccayalābhī hoti, so paṭṭacīvarādīnaṃ aññataraṃ mahagghacīvaraṃ bahūni vā pana cīvarāni labhitvā “idaṃ therānaṃ cirapabbajitānaṃ, idaṃ bahussutānaṃ anurūpaṃ, idaṃ gilānānaṃ, idaṃ appalābhānaṃ hotū”ti datvā tesaṃ purāṇacīvaraṃ vā saṅkārakūṭādito vā nantakāni uccinitvā tehi saṅghāṭiṃ katvā dhārentopi santuṭṭhova hoti. Ayamassa cīvare yathāsāruppasantoso. Mahagghañhi cīvaraṃ bahūni vā [V 2.0024] cīvarāni labhitvāpi tāni vissajjetvā tadaññassa gahaṇaṃ yathāsāruppanaye ṭhitattā na santosavirodhīti.

The phrase 'contentment with its threefold division' is spoken of in a general sense as contentment with whatever is obtained, and so on. However, regarding the four requisites, there are three types of contentment for each, thus contentment is of twelve kinds. How so? Regarding robes, contentment is of three kinds: contentment with whatever is obtained, contentment according to one’s strength, and contentment with what is suitable. The same applies to almsfood and the other requisites. This is the detailed explanation of its divisions: Here, a monk obtains a robe, whether fine or coarse. He maintains himself with just that and does not long for another; even when obtaining one, he does not accept it. This is his contentment with whatever is obtained regarding robes. Furthermore, a monk may be naturally weak or overcome by illness and old age; wearing a heavy robe, he becomes tired. He, having exchanged it with a fellow monk, remains content even while maintaining himself with a light one. This is his contentment according to his strength regarding robes. Indeed, for those who are naturally weak and so on, heavy robes are not conducive to comfort and bring about bodily fatigue. Thus, due to this reason and due to not having excessive desire, exchanging them and using a light robe is not contrary to contentment. Another monk is a recipient of fine requisites. He, having obtained a valuable robe, such as one made of silk, or many robes, gives them away, thinking, 'Let this be for the elders, for those long ordained; this is suitable for the learned; this is for the sick; let this be for those who receive little.' Then, having collected their old robes, or rags from a rubbish heap, and having made a patchwork robe from them, he remains content even while wearing it. This is his contentment with what is suitable regarding robes. Indeed, even having obtained a valuable robe or many robes, giving them up and taking another, because it stands in accordance with what is suitable, is not contrary to contentment.

Idha pana bhikkhu piṇḍapātaṃ labhati lūkhaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vā, so teneva yāpeti aññaṃ na pattheti, labhantopi na gaṇhāti. Ayamassa piṇḍapāte yathālābhasantoso. Yo pana attano pakativiruddhaṃ vā byādhiviruddhaṃ vā piṇḍapātaṃ labhati, yenassa paribhuttena aphāsu hoti, so sabhāgassa bhikkhuno taṃ datvā tassa hatthato sappāyabhojanaṃ bhuñjitvā samaṇadhammaṃ karontopi santuṭṭhova hoti. Ayamassa piṇḍapāte yathābalasantoso. Aparo bahuṃ paṇītaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ labhati, so taṃ cīvaraṃ viya cirapabbajitabahussutaappalābhagilānānaṃ datvā tesaṃ vā sesakaṃ piṇḍāya vā caritvā missakāhāraṃ bhuñjantopi santuṭṭhova hoti. Ayamassa piṇḍapāte yathāsāruppasantoso.

Here, a monk receives almsfood, whether coarse or refined. He maintains himself with just that and does not long for another; even when receiving one, he does not accept it. This is his contentment with whatever is obtained regarding almsfood. But a monk who receives almsfood that is contrary to his constitution or contrary to his illness, by eating which, there is discomfort for him, he, having given it to a fellow monk, and having eaten suitable food from his hand, remains content even while practicing the ascetic's duties. This is his contentment according to his strength regarding almsfood. Another receives much refined almsfood. He, having given it, like the robes, to those long ordained, the learned, those who receive little, and the sick, and even while eating their leftovers, or having gone for alms and eating mixed food, he remains content. This is his contentment with what is suitable regarding almsfood.

Idha pana bhikkhu senāsanaṃ labhati manāpaṃ vā amanāpaṃ vā, so tena neva somanassaṃ, na paṭighaṃ uppādeti, antamaso tiṇasantharakenapi yathāladdheneva tussati. Ayamassa senāsane yathālābhasantoso. Yo pana attano pakativiruddhaṃ vā byādhiviruddhaṃ vā senāsanaṃ labhati, yatthassa vasato aphāsu hoti, so taṃ sabhāgassa bhikkhuno datvā tassa santake sappāyasenāsane vasantopi santuṭṭhova hoti. Ayamassa senāsane yathābalasantoso. Aparo mahāpuñño leṇamaṇḍapakūṭāgārādīni bahūni paṇītasenāsanāni labhati, so tāni cīvarādīni viya cirapabbajitabahussutaappalābhagilānānaṃ datvā yattha katthaci vasantopi santuṭṭhova hoti. Ayamassa senāsane yathāsāruppasantoso. Yopi “uttamasenāsanaṃ nāma pamādaṭṭhānaṃ, tattha nisinnassa thinamiddhaṃ okkamati, niddābhibhūtassa puna paṭibujjhato pāpavitakkā pātubhavantī”ti paṭisañcikkhitvā tādisaṃ senāsanaṃ [M 2.0028] pattampi na sampaṭicchati, so taṃ paṭikkhipitvā abbhokāsarukkhamūlādīsu vasantopi santuṭṭhova hoti. Ayampissa senāsane yathāsāruppasantoso.

Here, a monk obtains a lodging, whether pleasant or unpleasant. He does not produce either joy or aversion on account of it; he is satisfied with whatever is obtained, even if it is just a grass mat. This is his contentment with whatever is obtained regarding lodgings. But a monk who obtains a lodging that is contrary to his constitution or contrary to his illness, where living causes him discomfort, he, having given it to a fellow monk, remains content even while living in a suitable lodging in his possession. This is his contentment according to his strength regarding lodgings. Another of great merit obtains many fine lodgings—caves, pavilions, gabled houses, and the like. He, having given them, like robes and so on, to those long ordained, the learned, those who receive little, and the sick, remains content even while living anywhere. This is his contentment with what is suitable regarding lodgings. And one who, having reflected, 'An excellent lodging is a basis for negligence. For one sitting there, sloth and torpor descend. For one overcome by sleep, upon reawakening, evil thoughts arise,' does not accept such a lodging even when obtained. He, having rejected it, remains content even while living in the open air, at the foot of a tree, and so on. This too is his contentment with what is suitable regarding lodgings.

Idha pana bhikkhu bhesajjaṃ labhati lūkhaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vā, so yaṃ labhati, teneva tussati aññaṃ na pattheti, labhantopi na gaṇhāti. Ayamassa gilānapaccaye yathālābhasantoso. Yo pana telena atthiko phāṇitaṃ labhati, so taṃ sabhāgassa bhikkhuno datvā tassa hatthato telaṃ gahetvā aññadeva vā pariyesitvā bhesajjaṃ karontopi santuṭṭhova hoti. Ayamassa gilānapaccaye yathābalasantoso. Aparo mahāpuñño bahuṃ telamadhuphāṇitādipaṇītabhesajjaṃ [V 2.0025] labhati, so taṃ cīvaraṃ viya cirapabbajitabahussutaappalābhagilānānaṃ datvā tesaṃ ābhatena yena kenaci yāpentopi santuṭṭhova hoti. Yo pana ekasmiṃ bhājane muttaharītakaṃ ṭhapetvā ekasmiṃ catumadhuraṃ “gaṇha, bhante, yadicchasī”ti vuccamāno sacassa tesu aññatarenapi rogo vūpasammati, atha “muttaharītakaṃ nāma buddhādīhi vaṇṇita”nti catumadhuraṃ paṭikkhipitvā muttaharītakeneva bhesajjaṃ karonto paramasantuṭṭhova hoti. Ayamassa gilānapaccaye yathāsāruppasantoso. Evaṃ yathālābhādivasena tippabhedo santoso catunnaṃ paccayānaṃ vasena dvādasavidho hotīti veditabbo.

Here, a bhikkhu obtains medicine, whether coarse or fine. Whatever he obtains, he is content with that and does not long for anything else; even when obtaining more, he does not accept it. This is his contentment with what is obtained in regard to requisites for the sick. But if one who needs oil obtains molasses, he gives it to a fellow bhikkhu, takes oil from his hand, or seeks another and prepares medicine, and is still content. This is his contentment according to ability in regard to requisites for the sick. Another, of great merit, obtains much fine medicine such as oil, honey, and molasses. He gives it, as one would a robe, to those who are long-ordained, learned, receive little, and are sick, and while sustaining himself with whatever is brought by them, he is still content. But if, when myrobalan steeped in cow's urine is placed in one bowl and the four sweets in another, he is told, 'Take, venerable sir, what you wish,' and if his illness subsides with either of them, then thinking, 'Myrobalan was praised by the Buddha and others,' he rejects the four sweets and, making medicine with only myrobalan steeped in cow's urine, is supremely content. This is his contentment as is suitable in regard to requisites for the sick. Thus, contentment, which is of three kinds by way of contentment with what is obtained and so on, becomes of twelve kinds by way of the four requisites; this should be understood.

Kāmavitakkabyāpādavitakkavihiṃsāvitakkānaṃ vasena akusalavitakkattayaṃ. Nekkhammavitakkaabyāpādavitakkaavihiṃ sāvitakkānaṃ vasena kusalavitakkattayaṃ. Sabbakilesāpacayabhūtāya vivaṭṭāyāti rāgādisabbakilesānaṃ apacayahetubhūtāya nibbānadhātuyā. Aṭṭhavīriyārambhavatthupāripūriyāti aṭṭhannaṃ vīriyārambhakāraṇānaṃ pāripūriyā. Yathā tathā paṭhamaṃ pavattaabbhussahanañhi upari vīriyārambhassa kāraṇaṃ hoti. Anurūpapaccavekkhaṇāsahitāni hi abbhussahanāni tammūlakāni vā paccavekkhaṇāni aṭṭha vīriyārambhavatthūnīti veditabbāni. Tathā hi –

By way of sensual thought, thought of ill will, and thought of harm, there is the triad of unwholesome thoughts. By way of thought of renunciation, thought of non-ill will, and thought of non-harm, there is the triad of wholesome thoughts. 'For the turning away which is the destruction of all defilements' means: for the Nibbāna-element, which is the cause for the destruction of all defilements such as lust. 'For the fulfillment of the eight grounds for arousing energy' means: for the fulfillment of the eight causes for arousing energy. For the initial exertion that has arisen in this or that way becomes a cause for the subsequent arousal of energy. Indeed, exertions accompanied by suitable reflection, or reflections rooted in them, should be understood as the eight grounds for arousing energy. Thus:

“Kammaṃ kho me kattabbaṃ bhavissati, kammaṃ kho pana me karontena na sukaraṃ buddhānaṃ sāsanaṃ manasi kātuṃ, handāhaṃ vīriyaṃ ārabhāmi appattassa pattiyā anadhigatassa adhigamāya asacchikatassa sacchikiriyāya. Ahaṃ kho kammaṃ akāsiṃ, kammaṃ kho panāhaṃ karonto [M 2.0029] nāsakkhiṃ buddhānaṃ sāsanaṃ manasi kātuṃ, handāhaṃ vīriyaṃ ārabhāmi…pe… maggo kho me gantabbo bhavissati, maggaṃ kho pana me gacchantena na sukaraṃ buddhānaṃ sāsanaṃ manasi kātuṃ, handāhaṃ vīriyaṃ ārabhāmi…pe… ahaṃ kho maggaṃ agamāsiṃ, maggaṃ kho panāhaṃ gacchanto nāsakkhiṃ buddhānaṃ sāsanaṃ manasi kātuṃ, handāhaṃ vīriyaṃ ārabhāmi…pe… ahaṃ kho gāmaṃ vā nigamaṃ vā piṇḍāya caranto nālatthaṃ lūkhassa vā paṇītassa vā bhojanassa yāvadatthaṃ pāripūriṃ, tassa me kāyo lahuko kammañño, handāhaṃ vīriyaṃ ārabhāmi…pe… ahaṃ kho gāmaṃ vā nigamaṃ vā piṇḍāya caranto alatthaṃ lūkhassa vā paṇītassa vā bhojanassa yāvadatthaṃ pāripūriṃ, tassa me kāyo balavā kammañño, handāhaṃ vīriyaṃ ārabhāmi…pe… uppanno kho me ayaṃ appamattako ābādho, ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ vijjati, yaṃ me ābādho pavaḍḍheyya, handāhaṃ vīriyaṃ ārabhāmi…pe… ahaṃ kho gilānā vuṭṭhito aciravuṭṭhito gelaññā, ṭhānaṃ [V 2.0026] kho panetaṃ vijjati, yaṃ me ābādho paccudāvatteyya, handāhaṃ vīriyaṃ ārabhāmi appattassa pattiyā anadhigatassa adhigamāya asacchikatassa sacchikiriyāyā”ti (dī. ni. 3.335; a. ni. 8.80) –

“I will have work to do, but while I am working, it will not be easy to keep the Buddhas’ teaching in mind. Come now, let me arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, the achievement of the unachieved, the realization of the unrealized. I have done work, but while I was working, I was unable to keep the Buddhas’ teaching in mind. Come now, let me arouse energy… A journey will have to be made, but while I am traveling, it will not be easy to keep the Buddhas’ teaching in mind. Come now, let me arouse energy… I have made a journey, but while I was traveling, I was unable to keep the Buddhas’ teaching in mind. Come now, let me arouse energy… While wandering for alms in a village or town, I did not obtain enough coarse or choice food to satisfy my needs; my body is light and fit for work. Come now, let me arouse energy… While wandering for alms in a village or town, I obtained enough coarse or choice food to satisfy my needs; my body is strong and fit for work. Come now, let me arouse energy… A slight illness has arisen in me. It is possible that this illness might worsen. Come now, let me arouse energy… I have risen from sickness, having recently recovered from illness. It is possible that this illness might recur. Come now, let me arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, the achievement of the unachieved, the realization of the unrealized.”

Evaṃ pavattaanurūpapaccavekkhaṇāsahitāni abbhussahanāni tammūlakāni vā paccavekkhaṇāni aṭṭha vīriyārambhavatthūni nāma.

Thus, the exertions accompanied by appropriate reflection on what has transpired, or reflections rooted therein, are called the eight grounds for arousing energy.

Tadanucchavikaṃ tadanulomikanti ettha ta-saddo vakkhamānāpekkho ca atītāpekkho ca hotīti āha “yaṃ idāni sikkhāpadaṃ paññapessatī”tiādi. Sabbanāmāni hi vakkhamānavacanānipi honti pakkantavacanānipi. Saṃvarappahānapaṭisaṃyuttanti pañcasaṃvarehi ceva pañcapahānehi ca paṭisaṃyuttaṃ. Pañcavidho hi saṃvaro sīlasaṃvaro satisaṃvaro ñāṇasaṃvaro khantisaṃvaro vīriyasaṃvaroti. Pahānampi pañcavidhaṃ tadaṅgappahānaṃ vikkhambhanappahānaṃ samucchedappahānaṃ paṭippassaddhippahānaṃ nissaraṇappahānanti.

Regarding 'It is suitable to that, it is in conformity with that': here, the word 'that' (ta) refers both to what will be stated and to what has been stated, as he said: 'Whatever training rule will now be laid down,' and so on. For all pronouns can refer to what will be said as well as to what has been said. 'Connected with restraint and abandonment' means: connected with the five restraints and the five abandonments. For restraint is fivefold: restraint by virtue, restraint by mindfulness, restraint by knowledge, restraint by forbearance, and restraint by energy. Abandonment is also fivefold: abandonment by substitution of opposites, abandonment by suppression, abandonment by cutting off, abandonment by tranquillization, and abandonment by escape.

Tattha “iminā pātimokkhasaṃvarena upeto hoti samupeto”ti (vibha. 511) evamāgato pātimokkhasaṃvaro sīlasaṃvaro nāma, so ca atthato [M 2.0030] kāyikavācasiko avītikkamo. “Rakkhati cakkhundriyaṃ, cakkhundriye saṃvaraṃ āpajjatī”ti (dī. ni. 1.213; ma. ni. 1.295; saṃ. ni. 4.239; a. ni. 3.16) evamāgatā indriyārakkhā satisaṃvaro, sā ca atthato tathāpavattā sati eva. “Sotānaṃ saṃvaraṃ brūmi, paññāyete pidhīyare”ti (su. ni. 1041; netti. 11) evamāgato ñāṇasaṃvaro. Ettha hi “sotānaṃ saṃvaraṃ brūmī”ti vatvā “paññāyete pidhīyare”ti vacanato sotasaṅkhātānaṃ taṇhādiṭṭhiduccaritaavijjādikilesānaṃ samucchedakañāṇaṃ pidahanaṭṭhena saṃvaroti vuttaṃ. “Khamo hoti sītassa uṇhassā”tievamāgatā (ma. ni. 1.24; ma. ni. 3.159; a. ni. 4.114) adhivāsanā khantisaṃvaro, sā ca atthato tathāpavattā khandhā adoso vā. Paññāti eke, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ. “Uppannaṃ kāmavitakkaṃ nādhivāsetī”ti (ma. ni. 1.26) evamāgataṃ kāmavitakkādīnaṃ vinodanavasena pavattaṃ vīriyameva vīriyasaṃvaro. Sabbo cāyaṃ saṃvaro yathāsakaṃ saṃvaritabbānaṃ dussīlyasaṅkhātānaṃ kāyavacīduccaritānaṃ muṭṭhassaccasaṅkhātassa pamādassa abhijjhādīnaṃ vā akkhanti aññāṇakosajjānañca saṃvaraṇato pidahanato chādanato “saṃvaro”ti vuccati. Saṃvaratīti saṃvaro, pidahati nivāreti pavattituṃ na [V 2.0027] detīti attho. Paccayasamavāye uppajjanārahānaṃ kāyaduccaritādīnaṃ tathā tathā anuppādanameva hi idha saṃvaraṇaṃ nāma. Evaṃ tāva pañcavidho saṃvaro veditabbo.

Herein, the Pātimokkha restraint, which is mentioned thus, “one is endowed with this Pātimokkha restraint,” is called the restraint of morality; and in essence, it is non-transgression by way of body and speech. The guarding of the sense faculties, which is mentioned thus, “one guards the eye faculty, one undertakes restraint in the eye faculty,” is called the restraint of mindfulness; and in essence, it is mindfulness itself occurring in such a way. The restraint of knowledge, which is mentioned thus, “I speak of the restraint of the streams; by wisdom they are shut.” For herein, having said, “I speak of the restraint of the streams,” because it is then stated, “by wisdom they are shut,” the knowledge that eradicates the defilements—such as craving, wrong view, misconduct, and ignorance, which are designated as ‘streams’—is called ‘restraint’ in the sense of shutting them off. Endurance, which is mentioned thus, “one is patient with cold and heat,” is called the restraint of patience; and in essence, it is patience occurring in such a way, or it is non-aversion. Some say it is wisdom, but that should not be accepted. Energy, which is mentioned thus, “one does not tolerate an arisen sensual thought,” and which proceeds by way of dispelling sensual thoughts and the like, is itself the restraint of energy. And all this restraint is called ‘restraint’ because it restrains, shuts off, and covers what should be respectively restrained: bodily and verbal misconduct designated as immorality; heedlessness designated as forgetfulness of the truths; or covetousness and the like; and impatience, ignorance, and laziness. ‘It restrains’ (saṃvarati), hence it is ‘restraint’ (saṃvaro); the meaning is that it shuts off, prevents, and does not allow to arise. For herein, restraint is indeed the very non-arising, in one way or another, of bodily misconduct and so on, which are liable to arise when there is a conjunction of causes. Thus, in the first place, the fivefold restraint should be understood.

Tena tena guṇaṅgena tassa tassa aguṇaṅgassa pahānaṃ tadaṅgappahānaṃ. Nāmarūpaparicchedādīsu hi vipassanāñāṇesu paṭipakkhabhāvato dīpālokeneva tamassa nāmarūpavavatthānena sakkāyadiṭṭhiyā, paccayapariggahena ahetuvisamahetudiṭṭhīnaṃ, tasseva aparabhāge uppannena kaṅkhāvitaraṇena kathaṃkathībhāvassa, kalāpasammasanena “ahaṃ mamā”ti gāhassa, maggāmaggavavatthānena amagge maggasaññāya, udayadassanena ucchedadiṭṭhiyā, vayadassanena sassatadiṭṭhiyā, bhayadassanena sabhaye abhayasaññāyātiādinā nayena tena tena vipassanāñāṇena tassa tassa aguṇaṅgassa pahānaṃ tadaṅgappahānanti veditabbaṃ. Yaṃ pana upacārappanābhedena samādhinā pavattinivāraṇato ghaṭappahāreneva udakapiṭṭhe sevālassa tesaṃ tesaṃ nīvaraṇādidhammānaṃ pahānaṃ, etaṃ vikkhambhanappahānaṃ nāma. Vikkhambhanameva pahānaṃ vikkhambhanappahānaṃ. Yaṃ catunnaṃ ariyamaggānaṃ bhāvitattā taṃtaṃmaggavato [M 2.0031] attano santāne “diṭṭhigatānaṃ pahānāyā”tiādinā (dha. sa. 277) nayena vuttassa samudayapakkhiyassa kilesagaṇassa accantaṃ appavattibhāvena pahānaṃ, idaṃ samucchedappahānaṃ nāma. Yaṃ pana phalakkhaṇe paṭippassaddhattaṃ vūpasantatā kilesānaṃ, etaṃ paṭippassaddhippahānaṃ nāma. Yaṃ sabbasaṅkhatanissaṭattā pahīnasabbasaṅkhataṃ nibbānaṃ, etaṃ nissaraṇappahānaṃ nāma. Sabbampi cetaṃ cāgaṭṭhena pahānanti vuccati. Evamimehi yathāvuttasaṃvarehi ceva pahānehi ca paṭisaṃyuttā dhammadesanā “saṃvarappahānapaṭisaṃyuttā”ti veditabbā.

The abandoning of each particular factor of non-virtue by each particular factor of virtue is the abandoning by substitution of opposites. For in the insight knowledges, beginning with the discernment of mind and matter, by their oppositional nature—just as the light of a lamp dispels darkness—the determination of mind and matter abandons identity view; the comprehension of conditions abandons the views of causelessness and wrong cause; the subsequent knowledge of overcoming doubt abandons the state of uncertainty; the contemplation of groups abandons the grasping of “I” and “mine”; the determination of path and non-path abandons the perception of non-path as path; the seeing of arising abandons the annihilation view; the seeing of passing away abandons the eternalist view; and the seeing of fearfulness abandons the perception of safety in what is fearful. In this way, it should be understood that the abandoning of each particular factor of non-virtue by each particular insight knowledge is the abandoning by substitution of opposites. Furthermore, the abandoning of the hindrances and other such states through concentration, distinguished as access and absorption, which prevents their occurrence like the parting of moss on the surface of water by a pot, is called the abandoning by suppression. The abandoning by suppression is the suppression itself as abandoning. The abandoning of the host of defilements belonging to the side of origination—spoken of in the manner of “for the abandoning of wrong views,” and so on—through its complete non-occurrence in one’s own continuum due to the development of the four noble paths, is called the abandoning by eradication. The pacification and calming of defilements at the moment of fruition is called the abandoning by pacification. Nibbāna, which is the escape from all conditioned things and has abandoned all conditioned things, is called the abandoning by escape. And all of this is called ‘abandoning’ in the sense of relinquishment. Thus, a discourse connected with these restraints and abandonings as described should be understood as one ‘connected with restraint and abandoning.’

Asuttantavinibaddhanti suttantesu anibaddhaṃ, pāḷianāruḷhanti attho. Pakiṇṇakadhammadesanā hi saṅgahaṃ na ārohati. Vuttamevatthaṃ pakāsento āha “pāḷivinimutta”nti. Atha vā asuttantavinibaddhanti suttābhidhammapāḷiṃ anāruḷhabhāvaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, pāḷivinimuttanti vinayapāḷiṃ anāruḷhabhāvaṃ sandhāya. Okkantikadhammadesanā nāma ñāṇena anupavisitvā antarā kathiyamānā dhammadesanā, paṭikkhipanādhippāyā bhaddālittherasadisā. Samparetabbato pecca gantabbato samparāyo, paraloko. Tattha bhavaṃ samparāyikaṃ. Vaṭṭabhayena tajjentoti “evaṃ dussīlā nirayādīsu dukkhaṃ pāpuṇantī”ti tajjento. Dīghanikāyappamāṇampi majjhimanikāyappamāṇampi dhammadesanaṃ karotīti “tena khaṇena tena muhuttena kathaṃ bhagavā tāvamahantaṃ dhammadesanaṃ karotī”ti na vattabbaṃ. Yāvatā hi lokiyamahājanā ekaṃ padaṃ kathenti, tāva ānandatthero aṭṭha padāni katheti. Ānandatthere pana ekaṃ [V 2.0028] padaṃ kathenteyeva bhagavā soḷasa padāni katheti. Iminā nayena lokiyajanassa ekapaduccāraṇakkhaṇe bhagavā aṭṭhavīsasataṃ padāni katheti. Kasmā? Bhagavato hi jivhā mudu, dantāvaraṇaṃ suphusitaṃ, vacanaṃ agaḷitaṃ, bhavaṅgaparivāso lahuko, tasmā sace eko bhikkhu kāyānupassanaṃ pucchati, añño vedanānupassanaṃ, añño cittānupassanaṃ, añño dhammānupassanaṃ, “iminā puṭṭhe ahaṃ pucchissāmī”ti eko ekaṃ na oloketi, evaṃ santepi tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ “ayaṃ paṭhamaṃ pucchi, ayaṃ dutiya”ntiādinā pucchanavāro tādisassa paññavato paññāyati sukhumassa antarassa labbhanato. Buddhānaṃ pana desanāvāro aññesaṃ na paññāyateva [M 2.0032] accharāsaṅghātamatte khaṇe anekakoṭisahassacittappavattisambhavato. Daḷhadhammena dhanuggahena khittasarassa vidatthicaturaṅgulaṃ tālacchāyaṃ atikkamanato puretaraṃyeva bhagavā cuddasavidhena kāyānupassanaṃ, navavidhena vedanānupassanaṃ, soḷasavidhena cittānupassanaṃ, pañcavidhena dhammānupassanaṃ katheti. Tiṭṭhantu vā ete cattāro, sace hi aññe cattāro sammappadhānesu, aññe iddhipādesu, aññe pañcindriyesu, aññe pañcabalesu, aññe sattabojjhaṅgesu, aññe aṭṭhamaggaṅgesu pañhe puccheyyuṃ, tampi bhagavā katheyya. Tiṭṭhantu vā ete aṭṭha, sace aññe sattatiṃsa janā bodhipakkhiyesu pañhe puccheyyuṃ, tampi bhagavā tāvadeva katheyya.

“Asuttantavinibaddha” means “not bound in the suttas,” that is, “not included in the Pāḷi.” For a teaching of miscellaneous Dhamma does not ascend to a compilation. Clarifying this very meaning, he says, “free from the Pāḷi.” Alternatively, “asuttantavinibaddha” is said referring to the state of not being included in the Sutta and Abhidhamma Pāḷi, while “pāḷivinimutta” is said referring to the state of not being included in the Vinaya Pāḷi. “Okkantikadhammadesanā” is a Dhamma teaching given intermittently, after having entered into it with knowledge; those with the intention of rebuking are like the Elder Bhaddāli. “Samparāya” is the other world because it is to be gone to in the future, to be gone to after death. That which exists there is “samparāyika.” “Threatening with the fear of the round of rebirth” means threatening thus: “In this way, the immoral reach suffering in hell and so on.” Regarding “He delivers a teaching as extensive as the Dīgha Nikāya or the Majjhima Nikāya”—one should not say, “How could the Blessed One give such an extensive teaching in that moment, in that instant?” For, in the time it takes worldly people to utter one word, the Elder Ānanda utters eight words. And when the Elder Ānanda utters one word, the Blessed One utters sixteen words. By this method, in the moment a worldly person utters one word, the Blessed One utters one hundred and twenty-eight words. Why? For the Blessed One’s tongue is soft, his gums are well-formed, his speech is unimpeded, and his life-continuum is light. Therefore, if one monk asks about contemplation of the body, another about contemplation of feeling, another about contemplation of mind, and another about contemplation of dhammas, one monk does not look at another, thinking, “After this one has asked, I will ask.” Even so, for those monks, the sequence of questions—“this one asked first, this one second,” and so on—is discernible to such a wise person because a subtle interval is obtainable. But the teaching sequence of the Buddhas is not discernible to others at all, because of the possibility of the arising of many thousands of crores of thought-moments in a moment as brief as a finger-snap. Even before an arrow shot by a strong archer passes through a palm-leaf target of one span and four fingers, the Blessed One teaches contemplation of the body in fourteen ways, contemplation of feeling in nine ways, contemplation of mind in sixteen ways, and contemplation of dhammas in five ways. Let these four stand. For if others were to ask questions on the four right strivings, others on the bases of psychic power, others on the five faculties, others on the five powers, others on the seven factors of enlightenment, and others on the eight path factors, the Blessed One would answer that too. Let these eight stand. If thirty-seven others were to ask questions on the factors pertaining to enlightenment, the Blessed One would answer that too in that very moment.

Mūlaṃ nissayo patiṭṭhāti pacchimaṃ pacchimaṃ paṭhamassa paṭhamassa vevacananti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tattha patiṭṭhāti sampayogavasena upanissayavasena ca okāsabhāvo. Sikkhāsaṅkhātānañhi avasesakusaladhammānaṃ methunaviratisampayogavasena vā patiṭṭhā siyā upanissayabhāvena vā. Tenevāha “methunasaṃvaro hī”tiādi. Vuttatthavasenāti patiṭṭhāadhigamūpāyavasena. Sikkhāpadavibhaṅge niddiṭṭhaviraticetanā taṃsampayuttadhammā ca sikkhāpadanti dassetukāmo āha – “ayañca attho sikkhāpadavibhaṅge vuttanayena veditabbo”ti. Sikkhāpadavibhaṅge hi viratiādayo dhammā nippariyāyato pariyāyato ca “sikkhāpada”nti vuttā. Vuttañhetaṃ –

“Root, support, foundation”—it should be seen that each latter word is a synonym for each former word. Therein, “foundation” is the condition by way of association and by way of decisive support. For, of the remaining wholesome states designated as “training,” abstinence from sexual intercourse is the foundation either by way of association or by way of being a decisive support. Therefore, he said, “For restraint from sexual intercourse…” and so on. “By way of the meaning stated” means by way of the means for attaining the foundation. Wishing to show that the volition of abstinence indicated in the Analysis of the Training Rules and the states associated with it are the “training rule,” he said: “And this meaning should be understood according to the method stated in the Analysis of the Training Rules.” For in the Analysis of the Training Rules, the states beginning with abstinence are called “training rule” both directly and indirectly. And this has been said:

“Tattha [V 2.0029] katamaṃ kāmesumicchācārā veramaṇī sikkhāpadaṃ? Yasmiṃ samaye kāmāvacaraṃ kusalaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ hoti somanassasahagataṃ ñāṇasampayuttaṃ kāmesumicchācārā viramantassa, yā tasmiṃ samaye kāmesumicchācārā ārati virati paṭivirati veramaṇī akiriyā akaraṇaṃ anajjhāpatti velānatikkamo setughāto, idaṃ vuccati kāmesumicchācārā veramaṇī sikkhāpadaṃ. Avasesā dhammā veramaṇiyā sampayuttā.

“Herein, what is the training rule of abstinence from sexual misconduct? At the time when a wholesome sense-sphere mind arises, accompanied by joy and associated with knowledge, for one abstaining from sexual misconduct, whatever at that time is the distaste, refraining, abstinence, abstention, non-action, non-doing, non-offense, non-transgression of the boundary, the breaking of the bridge—this is called the training rule of abstinence from sexual misconduct. The remaining states are associated with the abstention.”

“Tattha katamaṃ kāmesumicchācārā veramaṇī sikkhāpadaṃ? Yasmiṃ samaye kāmāvacaraṃ kusalaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ hoti somanassasahagataṃ ñāṇasampayuttaṃ kāmesumicchācārā viramantassa, yā tasmiṃ [M 2.0033] samaye cetanā sañcetanā cetayitattaṃ, idaṃ vuccati kāmesumicchācārā veramaṇī sikkhāpadaṃ. Avasesā dhammā cetanāya sampayuttā.

“Herein, what is the training rule of abstinence from sexual misconduct? At the time when a wholesome sense-sphere mind arises, accompanied by joy and associated with knowledge, for one abstaining from sexual misconduct, whatever at that time is the volition, intention, and state of having intended—this is called the training rule of abstinence from sexual misconduct. The remaining states are associated with the volition.”

“Tattha katamaṃ kāmesumicchācārā veramaṇī sikkhāpadaṃ? Yasmiṃ samaye kāmāvacaraṃ kusalaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ hoti somanassasahagataṃ ñāṇasampayuttaṃ kāmesumicchācārā viramantassa, yo tasmiṃ samaye phasso…pe… paggāho avikkhepo, idaṃ vuccati kāmesumicchācārā veramaṇī sikkhāpada”nti (vibha. 706).

“Herein, what is the training rule of abstinence from sexual misconduct? At the time when a wholesome sense-sphere mind arises, accompanied by joy and associated with knowledge, for one abstaining from sexual misconduct, whatever at that time is the contact… exertion… non-distraction—this is called the training rule of abstinence from sexual misconduct.” (Vibhaṅga 706).

Ettha hi yasmā na kevalaṃ viratiyeva sikkhāpadaṃ, cetanāpi sikkhāpadameva, tasmā taṃ dassetuṃ dutiyanayo vutto. Yasmā ca na kevalaṃ eteyeva dve dhammā sikkhāpadaṃ, cetanāsampayuttā pana paropaṇṇāsa dhammāpi sikkhitabbakoṭṭhāsato sikkhāpadameva, tasmā tatiyanayo dassito. Duvidhañhi sikkhāpadaṃ nippariyāyasikkhāpadaṃ pariyāyasikkhāpadanti. Tattha virati nippariyāyasikkhāpadaṃ. Sā hi “pāṇātipātā veramaṇī”ti pāḷiyaṃ āgatā, no cetanā. Viramanto ca tāya eva tato tato viramati, na cetanāya, cetanampi pana āharitvā dasseti, tathā sesacetanāsampayuttadhamme. Tasmā cetanā ceva avasesasampayuttadhammā ca pariyāyasikkhāpadanti veditabbaṃ.

Here, because not only abstinence but also intention is a training rule, the second method is stated to show that. And because not only these two things are the training rule, but also the fifty-five mental states associated with intention are the training rule by way of being a part that should be trained in, the third method is shown. For the training rule is twofold: the training rule in the direct sense and the training rule in the indirect sense. Therein, abstinence is the training rule in the direct sense. For it comes in the Pāḷi text as 'abstinence from killing living beings,' not intention. And one who abstains does so from this or that by that very abstinence, not by intention; yet intention is also introduced and shown, and likewise the remaining mental states associated with intention. Therefore, both intention and the remaining associated states should be understood as the training rule in the indirect sense.

Idāni na kevalaṃ idha viratiādayo dhammāva sikkhāpadaṃ, atha kho tadatthajotikā paññattipīti dassento āha “apicā”tiādi. “Yo tattha nāmakāyo padakāyoti idaṃ mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vutta”nti vadanti. Nāmakāyoti nāmasamūho nāmapaṇṇattiyeva. Padaniruttibyañjanāni nāmavevacanāneva “nāmaṃ nāmakammaṃ nāmaniruttī”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 1313-1315) viya. Sikkhākoṭṭhāsoti viratiādayova vuttā, tadatthajotakaṃ vacanampi sikkhāpadanti idampi ettha labbhateva.

Now, not only are the states beginning with abstinence the training rule here, but indeed the designation that illuminates their meaning is also a training rule; showing this, he said, 'Moreover,' etc. They say, 'It is stated in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā: "Whatever there is the name-body, the phrase-body..."' 'Name-body' means a collection of names, just the designation of a name. Phrases, expressions, and syllables are just synonyms for 'name,' just as in passages such as 'name, naming, expression of a name,' etc. (Dhammasaṅgaṇī 1313–1315). As 'the part of the training,' only abstinence and so on were stated; that the word which illuminates its meaning is also a training rule—this too is indeed obtained here.

Atthavaseti vuddhivisese ānisaṃsavisese. Tesaṃ pana sikkhāpadapaññattikāraṇattā āha “dasa kāraṇavase”ti, dasa kāraṇaviseseti attho. Tenāha “hitavisese”ti. Atthoyeva vā atthavaso, dasa atthe dasa kāraṇānīti vuttaṃ hoti. Atha vā attho [M 2.0034] phalaṃ tadadhīnavuttitāya vaso [V 2.0030] etassāti atthavaso, hetūti evampettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Suṭṭhu devāti idaṃ rājantepurappavesanasikkhāpade (pāci. 494 ādayo) vuttaṃ. “Ye mama sotabbaṃ saddahātabbaṃ maññissanti, tesaṃ taṃ assa dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāyā”ti vuttattā “yo ca tathāgatassa vacanaṃ sampaṭicchati, tassa taṃ dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāya hotī”ti vuttaṃ. Asampaṭicchane ādīnavanti bhaddālisutte (ma. ni. 2.134 ādayo) viya asampaṭicchane ādīnavaṃ dassetvā. Sukhavihārābhāve sahajīvamānassa abhāvato sahajīvitāpi sukhavihārova vutto. Sukhavihāro nāma catunnaṃ iriyāpathavihārānaṃ phāsutā.

By 'reason of benefit' is meant special growth, special advantages. But regarding these, because they are the reason for the laying down of the training rule, he said 'by way of ten reasons,' the meaning of which is 'ten special reasons.' Therefore he said 'for special welfare.' Or, the benefit itself is the 'reason by way of benefit'; 'ten benefits' means 'ten reasons' is what is said. Alternatively, the benefit is the fruit; because its occurrence is dependent on that, it is a 'reason by way of benefit' (atthavaso). Thus, the meaning here should be understood as 'cause' (hetu). 'Well said, deva'—this was said in the training rule on entering the royal inner quarters (Pācittiya 494, etc.). Because it is said, 'For those who will think, "This should be listened to and believed by me," it will be for their long-term welfare and happiness,' it is also said, 'And whoever accepts the word of the Tathāgata, for them it is for long-term welfare and happiness.' As for 'the danger in not accepting,' just as in the Bhaddāli Sutta (MN 65), having shown the danger in not accepting. Due to the absence of pleasant abiding when there is no living together, living together is also called 'pleasant abiding.' 'Pleasant abiding' means the comfort of the four postures.

Maṅkutanti nittejabhāvaṃ. Dhammenātiādīsu dhammoti bhūtaṃ vatthu. Vinayoti codanā ceva sāraṇā ca. Satthusāsananti ñattisampadā ceva anussāvanasampadā ca. Piyasīlānanti sikkhākāmānaṃ. Tesañhi sīlaṃ piyaṃ hoti. Tenevāha “sikkhattayapāripūriyā ghaṭamānā”ti. Sandiṭṭhamānāti saṃsayaṃ āpajjamānā. Ubbāḷhā hontīti pīḷitā honti. Saṅghakammānīti satipi uposathapavāraṇānaṃ saṅghakammabhāve gobalibaddañāyena uposathaṃ pavāraṇañca ṭhapetvā upasampadādisesasaṅghakammānaṃ gahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Samaggānaṃ bhāvo sāmaggī.

'Being dispirited' means the state of being without splendor. In 'by the Dhamma,' etc., 'Dhamma' means a true matter. 'Vinaya' means both accusation and reminding. 'The Teacher's instruction' means both the accomplishment of the motion and the accomplishment of the proclamation. 'Those for whom virtue is dear' means for those who desire the training. For them, virtue is dear. Therefore he said, 'striving for the fulfillment of the threefold training.' 'Being uncertain' means falling into doubt. 'Being troubled' means they are afflicted. As for 'Saṅgha acts,' even though Uposatha and Pavāraṇā are Saṅgha acts, by the ox-and-bull maxim, having set aside Uposatha and Pavāraṇā, the taking of the remaining Saṅgha acts beginning with higher ordination should be understood. The state of being united is harmony.

“Na vo ahaṃ, cunda, diṭṭhadhammikānaṃyeva āsavānaṃ saṃvarāya dhammaṃ desemī”ti (dī. ni. 3.182) ettha vivādamūlabhūtā kilesā āsavāti āgatā.

In the passage, 'I do not teach the Dhamma to you, Cunda, only for the restraint of the taints pertaining to the present life' (DN 3.182), the defilements that are the root of disputes are referred to as 'taints'.

“Yena devūpapatyassa, gandhabbo vā vihaṅgamo;

Yakkhattaṃ yena gaccheyyaṃ, manussattañca abbaje;

Te mayhaṃ āsavā khīṇā, viddhastā vinaḷīkatā”ti. (a. ni. 4.36) –

By which one might be reborn as a deva, or a gandhabba or a bird; by which I might go to the state of a yakkha, and attain a human state—those taints of mine are destroyed, scattered, uprooted.
