Ettha tebhūmakaṃ kammaṃ avasesā ca akusalā dhammā. Idha pana parūpavādavippaṭisāravadhabandhādayo ceva apāyadukkhabhūtā ca nānappakārā upaddavā āsavāti āha – “asaṃvare ṭhitena tasmiṃyeva attabhāve pattabbā”tiādi. Yadi hi bhagavā sikkhāpadaṃ na paññapeyya, tato asaddhammapaṭisevanaadinnādānapāṇātipātādihetu ye uppajjeyyuṃ parūpavādādayo diṭṭhadhammikā nānappakārā anatthā, ye ca taṃnimittameva nirayādīsu [M 2.0035] nibbattassa pañcavidhabandhanakammakāraṇādivasena mahādukkhānubhavananānappakārā anatthā, te sandhāya idaṃ vuttaṃ “diṭṭhadhammikānaṃ āsavānaṃ saṃvarāya samparāyikānaṃ āsavānaṃ paṭighātāyā”ti. Diṭṭhadhammo vuccati paccakkho attabhāvo[V 2.0031], tattha bhavā diṭṭhadhammikā. Tena vuttaṃ “tasmiṃyeva attabhāve pattabbā”ti. Sammukhā garahaṇaṃ akitti, parammukhā garahaṇaṃ ayaso. Atha vā sammukhā parammukhā ca garahaṇaṃ akitti, parivārahāni ayasoti veditabbaṃ. Āgamanamaggathakanāyāti āgamanadvārapidahanatthāya. Samparetabbato pecca gantabbato samparāyo, paralokoti āha “samparāye narakādīsū”ti. Methunādīni rajjanaṭṭhānāni, pāṇātipātādīni dussanaṭṭhānāni.

Here, kamma of the three planes and the remaining unwholesome states are called 'taints' (āsavā). But here, various kinds of troubles—such as blame from others, remorse, execution, and imprisonment, as well as those which are the suffering of the lower realms—are called 'taints' (āsavā), he says: '[these are] to be attained in this very existence by one who dwells unrestrained,' etc. For if the Blessed One had not laid down the training rule, then due to the cause of engaging in wrong practice, taking what is not given, killing living beings, etc., various harms pertaining to the present life, such as blame from others, would arise; and due to that very same cause, various harms—such as the experiencing of great suffering by way of the five kinds of bondage, instruments of punishment, etc., for one reborn in hell and other such states—would arise. With reference to these, this was said: 'for the restraint of the taints pertaining to the present life and for the warding off of the taints pertaining to the future life.' The 'presently visible state' is called the directly perceived existence; those that occur therein are 'pertaining to the present life.' Therefore it was said, 'to be attained in this very existence.' Blame to one's face is ill-repute (akitti); blame behind one's back is disgrace (ayaso). Alternatively, blame both to one's face and behind one's back is ill-repute; loss of retinue should be understood as disgrace. 'For blocking the path of approach' means for the purpose of closing the door of approach. Because it is to be gone to after death, it is the 'future life' (samparāyo); it is the next world, he says: 'in the future life, in hell, etc.' Sexual intercourse and the like are grounds for lust; killing living beings and the like are grounds for hatred.

Cuddasa khandhakavattāni nāma vattakkhandhake vuttāni āgantukavattaṃ āvāsikagamikaanumodanabhattaggapiṇḍacārikaāraññikasenāsanajantāgharavaccakuṭiupajjhāyasaddhivihārikaācariyaantevāsikavattanti imāni cuddasa vattāni. Tato aññāni pana kadāci tajjanīyakammakatādikāleyeva caritabbāni dveasīti mahāvattāni, na sabbāsu avatthāsu caritabbāni, tasmā cuddasakhandhakavattesu agaṇitāni, tāni pana “pārivāsikānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ vattaṃ paññapessāmī”ti (cūḷava. 75 ādayo) ārabhitvā “na upasampādetabbaṃ…pe… na chamāyaṃ caṅkamante caṅkame caṅkamitabba”nti (cūḷava. 76) vuttāvasānāni chasaṭṭhi, tato paraṃ “na, bhikkhave, pārivāsikena bhikkhunā pārivāsikavuḍḍhatarena bhikkhunā saddhiṃ, mūlāyapaṭikassanārahena, mānattārahena, mānattacārikena, abbhānārahena bhikkhunā saddhiṃ ekacchanne āvāse vatthabba”ntiādinā (cūḷava. 82) vuttavattāni pakatattacaritabbehi anaññattā visuṃ agaṇetvā pārivāsikavuḍḍhatarādīsu puggalantaresu caritabbattā tesaṃ vasena sampiṇḍetvā ekekaṃ katvā gaṇitāni pañcāti ekasattati vattāni, ukkhepanīyakammakatavattesu vuttaṃ “na pakatattassa bhikkhuno abhivādanaṃ paccuṭṭhānaṃ…pe… nahāne piṭṭhiparikammaṃ sāditabba”nti (cūḷava. 75) idaṃ abhivādanādīnaṃ asādiyanaṃ ekaṃ, “na pakatatto bhikkhu sīlavipattiyā anuddhaṃsetabbo”tiādīni (cūḷava. 51) dasāti evametāni dvāsīti vattāni. Etesveva pana kānici tajjanīyakammādivattāāni, kānici pārivāsikādivattānīti aggahitaggahaṇena dvāsīti eva, aññattha pana aṭṭhakathāpadese appakaṃ [M 2.0036] ūnamadhikaṃ vā gaṇanūpagaṃ na hotīti “asīti khandhakavattānī”ti vuttaṃ.

The fourteen duties of the sections (khandhakavattas) are stated in the chapter on duties: the duty for incoming monks, the duty for resident monks, the duty for those departing, the duty of expressing appreciation, the duty in the refectory, the duty for those on alms-round, the duty for forest-dwellers, the duty for lodgings, the duty for the steam-bath, the duty for the latrine, the duty towards a preceptor, the duty towards a co-resident, the duty towards a teacher, and the duty towards a pupil—these are the fourteen duties. Other duties, however, the eighty-two great duties, are to be observed only on certain occasions, such as when an act of censure has been carried out; they are not to be observed in all circumstances. Therefore, they are not counted among the fourteen duties of the sections. Of these, there are sixty-six duties beginning with, “I will prescribe the duties for monks on probation…” (Cūḷavagga 75, etc.), and ending with what was said, “One should not give the higher ordination… one should not walk on a walking path that is on the ground” (Cūḷavagga 76). Furthermore, the duties stated beginning with, “O bhikkhus, a monk on probation should not dwell under the same roof with a monk senior in probation, with one deserving of being sent back to the beginning, with one deserving of the mānatta penance, with one undergoing the mānatta penance, or with one deserving of rehabilitation…” (Cūḷavagga 82), are not counted separately because they are not different from the duties to be observed by an ordinary monk; but because they are to be observed in relation to other individuals such as one who is senior in probation, they are grouped together according to those individuals, and, making each one, are counted as five. Thus, there are seventy-one duties. In the duties for one who has undergone an act of suspension, what was said, “An ordinary monk should not accept salutation, rising up… a back-rub while bathing” (Cūḷavagga 75)—this non-acceptance of salutation and so forth is one duty. The ten duties beginning with, “An ordinary monk should not be reproached for a lapse in virtue…” (Cūḷavagga 51). Thus, these are the eighty-two duties. Among these, some are duties related to the act of censure and so on, and some are duties related to probation and so on. Thus, by including what was not previously included, there are indeed eighty-two. Elsewhere, however, in a section of the commentary, a slight deficiency or excess is not considered significant in the count, and so it is said, “eighty duties of the sections.”

Saṃvaravinayoti sīlasaṃvaro satisaṃvaro ñāṇasaṃvaro khantisaṃvaro vīriyasaṃvaroti pañcavidhopi saṃvaro yathāsakaṃ saṃvaritabbānaṃ vinetabbānañca kāyaduccaritādīnaṃ saṃvaraṇato saṃvaro, vinayanato vinayoti vuccati. Pahānavinayoti tadaṅgappahānaṃ vikkhambhanappahānaṃ samucchedappahānaṃ paṭippassaddhippahānaṃ nissaraṇappahānanti pañcavidhampi pahānaṃ yasmā cāgaṭṭhena pahānaṃ[V 2.0032], vinayanaṭṭhena vinayo, tasmā pahānavinayoti vuccati. Samathavinayoti satta adhikaraṇasamathā. Paññattivinayoti sikkhāpadameva. Sikkhāpadapaññattiyā hi vijjamānāya eva sikkhāpadasambhavato paññattivinayopi sikkhāpadapaññattiyā anuggahito hoti.

The Vinaya of Restraint: The five-fold restraint—restraint by virtue, restraint by mindfulness, restraint by knowledge, restraint by patience, and restraint by effort—is called ‘restraint’ (saṃvara) because it restrains bodily misconduct and so forth, which should be restrained and disciplined according to each case, and it is called ‘discipline’ (vinaya) because it disciplines. The Vinaya of Abandonment: The five-fold abandonment—abandonment by substitution of opposites, abandonment by suppression, abandonment by eradication, abandonment by tranquillization, and abandonment by escape—is so called because ‘abandonment’ (pahāna) is in the sense of relinquishing, and ‘discipline’ (vinaya) is in the sense of disciplining. The Vinaya of Settlement is the seven ways of settling legal questions. The Vinaya of Prescription is the training rule itself. For, since a training rule comes to be only when there is a prescription of a training rule, the Vinaya of Prescription is also supported by the prescription of training rules.

Idāni –

Now:

“Yaṃ saṅghasuṭṭhu, taṃ saṅghaphāsu, yaṃ saṅghaphāsu, taṃ dummaṅkūnaṃ puggalānaṃ niggahāya, yaṃ dummaṅkūnaṃ puggalānaṃ niggahāya, taṃ pesalānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ phāsuvihārāya, yaṃ pesalānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ phāsuvihārāya, taṃ diṭṭhadhammikānaṃ āsavānaṃ saṃvarāya, yaṃ diṭṭhadhammikānaṃ āsavānaṃ saṃvarāya, taṃ samparāyikānaṃ āsavānaṃ paṭighātāya, yaṃ samparāyikānaṃ āsavānaṃ paṭighātāya, taṃ appasannānaṃ pasādāya, yaṃ appasannānaṃ pasādāya, taṃ pasannānaṃ bhiyyobhāvāya, yaṃ pasannānaṃ bhiyyobhāvāya, taṃ saddhammaṭṭhitiyā, yaṃ saddhammaṭṭhitiyā, taṃ vinayānuggahāya.

“What is for the good order of the Saṅgha is for the comfort of the Saṅgha. What is for the comfort of the Saṅgha is for the disciplining of unruly individuals. What is for the disciplining of unruly individuals is for the comfortable dwelling of virtuous bhikkhus. What is for the comfortable dwelling of virtuous bhikkhus is for the restraint of defilements in this present life. What is for the restraint of defilements in this present life is for the warding off of defilements in future lives. What is for the warding off of defilements in future lives is for inspiring confidence in the unconfident. What is for inspiring confidence in the unconfident is for the increase of the confident. What is for the increase of the confident is for the endurance of the true Dhamma. What is for the endurance of the true Dhamma is for the support of the Vinaya.”

“Yaṃ saṅghasuṭṭhu, taṃ saṅghaphāsu, yaṃ saṅghasuṭṭhu, taṃ dummaṅkūnaṃ puggalānaṃ niggahāya, yaṃ saṅghasuṭṭhu, taṃ pesalānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ phāsuvihārāya, yaṃ saṅghasuṭṭhu, taṃ diṭṭhadhammikānaṃ āsavānaṃ saṃvarāya, yaṃ saṅghasuṭṭhu, taṃ samparāyikānaṃ āsavānaṃ paṭighātāya, yaṃ saṅghasuṭṭhu, taṃ appasannānaṃ pasādāya, yaṃ saṅghasuṭṭhu, taṃ pasannānaṃ bhiyyobhāvāya, yaṃ saṅghasuṭṭhu, taṃ saddhammaṭṭhitiyā, yaṃ saṅghasuṭṭhu, taṃ vinayānuggahāya.

“What is for the good order of the Saṅgha is for the comfort of the Saṅgha. What is for the good order of the Saṅgha is for the disciplining of unruly individuals. What is for the good order of the Saṅgha is for the comfortable dwelling of virtuous bhikkhus. What is for the good order of the Saṅgha is for the restraint of defilements in this present life. What is for the good order of the Saṅgha is for the warding off of defilements in future lives. What is for the good order of the Saṅgha is for inspiring confidence in the unconfident. What is for the good order of the Saṅgha is for the increase of the confident. What is for the good order of the Saṅgha is for the endurance of the true Dhamma. What is for the good order of the Saṅgha is for the support of the Vinaya.”

“Yaṃ [M 2.0037] saṅghaphāsu, taṃ dummaṅkūnaṃ puggalānaṃ niggahāya, yaṃ saṅghaphāsu, taṃ pesalānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ phāsuvihārāya, yaṃ saṅghaphāsu, taṃ diṭṭhadhammikānaṃ āsavānaṃ saṃvarāya, yaṃ saṅghaphāsu, taṃ samparāyikānaṃ āsavānaṃ paṭighātāya, yaṃ saṅghaphāsu, taṃ appasannānaṃ pasādāya, yaṃ saṅghaphāsu, taṃ pasannānaṃ bhiyyobhāvāya, yaṃ saṅghaphāsu, taṃ saddhammaṭṭhitiyā, yaṃ saṅghaphāsu, taṃ vinayānuggahāya, yaṃ saṅghaphāsu, taṃ saṅghasuṭṭhutāya.

“What is for the comfort of the Saṅgha is for the disciplining of unruly individuals. What is for the comfort of the Saṅgha is for the comfortable dwelling of virtuous bhikkhus. What is for the comfort of the Saṅgha is for the restraint of defilements in this present life. What is for the comfort of the Saṅgha is for the warding off of defilements in future lives. What is for the comfort of the Saṅgha is for inspiring confidence in the unconfident. What is for the comfort of the Saṅgha is for the increase of the confident. What is for the comfort of the Saṅgha is for the endurance of the true Dhamma. What is for the comfort of the Saṅgha is for the support of the Vinaya. What is for the comfort of the Saṅgha is for the good order of the Saṅgha.”

“Yaṃ dummaṅkūnaṃ puggalānaṃ niggahāya…pe… yaṃ pesalānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ phāsuvihārāya…pe… yaṃ diṭṭhadhammikānaṃ āsavānaṃ saṃvarāya…pe… yaṃ samparāyikānaṃ āsavānaṃ paṭighātāya…pe… yaṃ appasannānaṃ pasādāya…pe… yaṃ pasannānaṃ bhiyyobhāvāya…pe… yaṃ saddhammaṭṭhitiyā…pe… yaṃ vinayānuggahāya, taṃ saṅghasuṭṭhutāya[V 2.0033], yaṃ vinayānuggahāya, taṃ saṅghaphāsutāya, yaṃ vinayānuggahāya, taṃ dummaṅkūnaṃ puggalānaṃ niggahāya, yaṃ vinayānuggahāya, taṃ pesalānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ phāsuvihārāya, yaṃ vinayānuggahāya, taṃ diṭṭhadhammikānaṃ āsavānaṃ saṃvarāya, yaṃ vinayānuggahāya, taṃ samparāyikānaṃ āsavānaṃ paṭighātāya, yaṃ vinayānuggahāya, taṃ appasannānaṃ pasādāya, yaṃ vinayānuggahāya, taṃ pasannānaṃ bhiyyobhāvāya, yaṃ vinayānuggahāya, taṃ saddhammaṭṭhitiyā (pari. 334).

“What is for the disciplining of unruly individuals…pe… What is for the comfortable dwelling of virtuous bhikkhus…pe… What is for the restraint of defilements in this present life…pe… What is for the warding off of defilements in future lives…pe… What is for the inspiring of confidence in the unconfident…pe… What is for the increase of the confident…pe… What is for the endurance of the true Dhamma…pe… What is for the support of the Vinaya, that is for the good order of the Saṅgha. What is for the support of the Vinaya, that is for the comfort of the Saṅgha. What is for the support of the Vinaya, that is for the disciplining of unruly individuals. What is for the support of the Vinaya, that is for the comfortable dwelling of virtuous bhikkhus. What is for the support of the Vinaya, that is for the restraint of defilements in this present life. What is for the support of the Vinaya, that is for the warding off of defilements in future lives. What is for the support of the Vinaya, that is for the inspiring of confidence in the unconfident. What is for the support of the Vinaya, that is for the increase of the confident. What is for the support of the Vinaya, that is for the endurance of the true Dhamma.” (Pari. 334)

“Atthasataṃ dhammasataṃ, dve ca niruttisatāni;

Cattāri ñāṇasatāni, atthavase pakaraṇe”ti (pari. 334) –

“One hundred results, one hundred causes, and two hundred expressions; Four hundred knowledges in the exposition according to the result.” (Pari. 334)

Yaṃ vuttaṃ parivāre, taṃ dassento “apicetthā”tiādimāha.

Wishing to show what was stated in the Parivāra, he said, 'apicettha' and so forth.

Tattha “yaṃ saṅghasuṭṭhu, taṃ saṅghaphāsu, yaṃ saṅghaphāsu, taṃ dummaṅkūnaṃ puggalānaṃ niggahāyā”ti iminā anukkamena yaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ sandhāya āsannāsannapadānaṃ uparūparipadehi saddhiṃ yojitattā saṅkhalikabandhanasadisattā “saṅkhalikanaya”nti vuttaṃ. Saṅkhalikanayaṃ katvāti sambandho. “Yaṃ saṅghasuṭṭhu, taṃ saṅghaphāsu, yaṃ saṅghasuṭṭhu, taṃ dummaṅkūnaṃ puggalānaṃ niggahāyā”ti evamādinā dasasu padesu ekamekaṃ padaṃ tadavasesehi navanavapadehi yojetvā yaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ sandhāya “ekekapadamūlikaṃ dasakkhattuṃ yojanaṃ katvā”ti vuttaṃ.

Therein, with reference to what was stated in the sequence, 'What is for the good order of the Saṅgha is for the comfort of the Saṅgha; what is for the comfort of the Saṅgha is for the disciplining of unruly individuals,' it is called the 'chain method' (saṅkhalikanaya) because the proximate terms are connected with the subsequent terms, similar to a chain-link. The connection should be understood as 'having applied the chain method.' With reference to what was stated by connecting each single term among the ten terms with the remaining nine terms—such as, 'What is for the good order of the Saṅgha is for the comfort of the Saṅgha; what is for the good order of the Saṅgha is for the disciplining of unruly individuals'—it is said, 'having made the connection with each term as the root ten times'.

Atthasatantiādīsu [M 2.0038] saṅkhalikanaye tāva purimapurimapadānaṃ vasena dhammasataṃ veditabbaṃ, pacchimapacchimānaṃ vasena atthasataṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kathaṃ? Kiñcāpi parivāre “yaṃ saṅghasuṭṭhu, taṃ saṅghaphāsū”tiādinā saṅkhalikanaye khaṇḍacakkameva vuttaṃ, tathāpi teneva nayena baddhacakkassapi nayo dinno, tasmā “yaṃ saṅghasuṭṭhu, taṃ saṅghaphāsū”tiādiṃ vatvā “yaṃ vinayānuggahāya, taṃ saṅghasuṭṭhū”ti yojetvā baddhacakkaṃ kātabbaṃ. Evaṃ “yaṃ saṅghaphāsu, taṃ dummaṅkūnaṃ puggalānaṃ niggahāyā”tiādiṃ vatvāpi “yaṃ vinayānuggahāya, taṃ saṅghasuṭṭhu, yaṃ saṅghasuṭṭhu, taṃ saṅghaphāsū”ti yojetvā baddhacakkaṃ kātabbaṃ. Iminā anukkamena sesapadesupi yojitesu saṅkhalikanayena dasa baddhacakkāni honti. Tesu ekekasmiṃ cakke purimapurimapadānaṃ vasena dasa dasa dhammā, pacchimapacchimapadānaṃ vasena dasa dasa atthāti saṅkhalikanaye atthasataṃ dhammasatañca sampajjati. Ekamūlakanaye pana “yaṃ saṅghasuṭṭhu, taṃ saṅghaphāsu, yaṃ saṅghasuṭṭhu, taṃ dummaṅkūnaṃ puggalānaṃ niggahāyā”ti evamādinā ekameva padaṃ sesehi navahi padehi yojitanti purimapadassa [V 2.0034] ekattā ekameva dhammapadaṃ naveva atthapadāni honti, tasmā ekamūlakanaye dasasu padesu ekamekaṃ mūlaṃ katvā dasakkhattuṃ yojanāya katāya dhammapadānaṃ vasena dhammapadāni dasa, atthapadāni navutīti atthasataṃ dhammasatañca na sampajjati, tasmā ekamūlakanaye saṅkhalikanaye vuttanayena atthasataṃ dhammasatañca aggahetvā yaṃ tattha dasadhammapadānaṃ navutiatthapadānañca vasena padasataṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ dhammasatanti gahetvā tadatthajotanavasena aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttāni saṅghasuṭṭhubhāvādīni atthapadāni atthasatanti evaṃ gahite atthasataṃ dhammasatañca sampajjati. Evaṃ tāva atthasataṃ dhammasatañca veditabbaṃ. Dve ca niruttisatānīti ettha pana atthajotikānaṃ niruttīnaṃ vasena niruttisataṃ, dhammabhūtānaṃ niruttīnaṃ vasena niruttisatanti dve niruttisatāni ca veditabbāni. Cattāri ñāṇasatānīti atthasate ñāṇasataṃ, dhammasate ñāṇasataṃ, dvīsu niruttisatesu dve ñāṇasatānīti cattāri ñāṇasatāni.

Regarding 'one hundred results,' etc.: first, in the chain method, one hundred causes should be understood by way of the preceding terms, and one hundred results should be seen by way of the subsequent terms. How? Although in the Parivāra, in the chain method beginning with 'What is for the good order of the Saṅgha is for the comfort of the Saṅgha,' only a partial wheel (khaṇḍacakka) is stated, nevertheless, by that same method, the way of the complete wheel (baddhacakka) is also given. Therefore, after stating the passage beginning 'What is for the good order of the Saṅgha is for the comfort of the Saṅgha,' the complete wheel should be formed by connecting it as 'What is for the support of the Vinaya is for the good order of the Saṅgha.' Similarly, after stating the passage beginning 'What is for the comfort of the Saṅgha is for the disciplining of unruly individuals,' the complete wheel should be formed by connecting it as 'What is for the support of the Vinaya is for the good order of the Saṅgha; what is for the good order of the Saṅgha is for the comfort of the Saṅgha.' When the remaining terms are connected in this sequence, there are ten complete wheels in the chain method. In each of those wheels, by way of the preceding terms, there are ten causes each, and by way of the subsequent terms, there are ten results each. Thus, in the chain method, one hundred results and one hundred causes are accomplished. In the single-root method, however, by the method beginning 'What is for the good order of the Saṅgha is for the comfort of the Saṅgha; what is for the good order of the Saṅgha is for the disciplining of unruly individuals,' only one term is connected with the remaining nine terms. Thus, because the preceding term is single, there is only one cause-term and nine result-terms. Therefore, in the single-root method, by making each of the ten terms a root and connecting them ten times, there are ten cause-terms and ninety result-terms. Thus, one hundred results and one hundred causes are not accomplished. Therefore, in the single-root method, without taking the one hundred results and one hundred causes in the way stated for the chain method, all the one hundred terms mentioned there—the ten cause-terms and ninety result-terms—should be taken as 'one hundred causes.' Then, the result-terms stated in the commentary, such as 'the state of being for the good order of the Saṅgha,' which illuminate that meaning, should be taken as 'one hundred results.' When taken in this way, one hundred results and one hundred causes are accomplished. Thus, first, the one hundred results and one hundred causes should be understood. As for 'and two hundred expressions,' here, one hundred expressions should be understood by way of the expressions that illuminate the result, and one hundred expressions by way of the expressions that are the causes themselves; thus, two hundred expressions should be known. As for 'four hundred knowledges': there are one hundred knowledges on the one hundred results, one hundred knowledges on the one hundred causes, and two hundred knowledges on the two hundred expressions; thus, four hundred knowledges.

Evañca pana, bhikkhaveti ettha ca-saddo bhinnakkamena yojetabboti āha “uddiseyyātha cā”ti. Kathaṃ panettha “uddiseyyāthā”ti vutte pariyāpuṇeyyāthātiādi atthasambhavoti āha “atirekānayanattho hi ettha ca-saddo”ti. Vuttatthato atirekassa atthassa ānayanaṃ atirekānayanaṃ, so attho etassāti atirekānayanattho, avuttasamuccayatthoti [M 2.0039] vuttaṃ hoti. “Asaṃvāso”ti vuttattā “daḷhaṃ katvā”ti vuttaṃ.

In 'Evañca pana, bhikkhave' ('And thus, O bhikkhus'), the particle 'ca' should be connected with a different sequence; thus, he said, 'uddiseyyātha ca' ('And you should recite'). How, when 'uddiseyyātha' ('you should recite') is said, is the meaning 'pariyāpuṇeyyātha' ('you should learn thoroughly'), etc., possible? He said, 'For here, the particle "ca" has the meaning of bringing an additional meaning' (atirekānayanattho). Bringing an additional meaning beyond the one already stated is atirekānayana. It has that meaning, therefore it is atirekānayanattho; this means it has the meaning of including what has not been said (avuttasamuccayattho). Because 'non-communion' (asaṃvāso) was stated, 'having made firm' (daḷhaṃ katvā) was said.

Iti samantapāsādikāya vinayaṭṭhakathāya sāratthadīpaniyaṃ

Thus, in the Sāratthadīpanī, a sub-commentary on the Vinaya Commentary, the Samantapāsādikā,

Paṭhamapaññattikathā niṭṭhitā.

the Discourse on the First Enactment is concluded.

Sudinnabhāṇavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Sudinna Recitation Section is concluded.

Makkaṭivatthukathāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Story of the Female Monkey.

40. Anuttānapadavaṇṇanāti uttānaṃ vuccati pākaṭaṃ, tappaṭipakkhena anuttānaṃ apākaṭaṃ appacuraṃ duviññeyyañca, anuttānānaṃ padānaṃ vaṇṇanā anuttānapadavaṇṇanā. Uttānapadavaṇṇanāya payojanābhāvato anuttānaggahaṇaṃ. Pacurapaṭisevano hotīti bahulapaṭisevano hoti, divase divase nirantaraṃ paṭisevatīti attho. Pacuratthe hi vattamānavacananti sabbadā paṭisevanābhāvepi “iha [V 2.0035] mallā yujjhantī”tiādīsu viya bāhullavuttiṃ upādāya vattamānavacanaṃ. Āhiṇḍantāti vicarantā. Aññesupīti aññesupi bhikkhūsu.

40. The explanation of obscure words: 'uttāna' is said to be clear; by its opposite, 'anuttāna' is unclear, scarce, and difficult to understand. The explanation of obscure words is 'anuttānapadavaṇṇanā.' Because there is no purpose in explaining clear words, the term 'anuttāna' is taken up. 'Pacurapaṭisevano hoti' means one who frequently associates; the meaning is, one associates continuously day after day. For the present tense is used in the sense of abundance; thus, even when there is no constant association, the present tense is used by taking up the sense of abundance, as in such phrases as 'here the Mallas fight.' 'Āhiṇḍantā' means wandering about. 'Aññesupi' means among other monks as well.

41. Sahoḍḍhaggahitoti saha bhaṇḍena gahito. Attano micchāgāhena lesaoḍḍanena vā paripuṇṇatthampi paṭhamapaññattiṃ aññathā karonto “tañca kho manussitthiyā, no tiracchānagatāyā”ti āha. Dassananti sānurāgadassanaṃ. Gahaṇanti anurāgavaseneva hatthena gahaṇaṃ. Āmasanaṃ attano sarīrena tassā sarīrassa upari āmasanamattaṃ, phusanaṃ tato daḷhataraṃ katvā saṃphusanaṃ, ghaṭṭanaṃ tatopi daḷhataraṃ katvā sarīrena sarīrassa ghaṭṭanaṃ. Taṃ sabbampīti dassanādi sabbampi.

41. 'Sahoḍḍhaggahito' means taken along with the goods. By his own wrong grasp or by way of pretext, while distorting the complete meaning of the first regulation, he says, 'And that is for a human woman, not for an animal.' 'Dassana' means seeing with lust. 'Gahaṇa' means grasping with the hand out of lust. 'Āmasana' is the mere stroking of her body with his own body; 'phusana' is touching; 'saṃphusana' is a thorough touching, done more firmly than that; 'ghaṭṭana' is the rubbing of body against body, done even more firmly than that. 'Taṃ sabbaṃpi' means all of it: everything beginning with seeing.

42. Daḷhataraṃ sikkhāpadamakāsīti imasmiṃ adhikāre anupaññattiyā sikkhāpadassa daḷhīkaraṇaṃ sithilakaraṇañca pasaṅgato āpannaṃ vibhajitvā dassetukāmo “duvidhañhi sikkhāpada”ntiādimāha. Tattha yassa sacittakassa sikkhāpadassa cittaṃ akusalameva hoti, taṃ lokavajjaṃ. Yassa sacittakācittakapakkhasahitassa acittakassa ca sacittakapakkhe cittaṃ akusalameva [M 2.0040] hoti, tampi surāpānādi lokavajjanti imamatthaṃ sampiṇḍetvā dassetuṃ “yassa sacittakapakkhe cittaṃ akusalameva hoti, taṃ lokavajjaṃ nāmā”ti vuttaṃ. “Sacittakapakkhe”ti hi idaṃ vacanaṃ acittakaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Na hi ekaṃsato sacittakassa “sacittakapakkhe”ti visesane payojanaṃ atthi. Sacittakapakkheti ca vatthuvītikkamavijānanacittena “sacittakapakkhe”ti gahetabbaṃ, na paṇṇattivijānanacittena. Yadi hi “na vaṭṭatī”ti paṇṇattivijānanacittenapi yassa sikkhāpadassa sacittakapakkhe cittaṃ akusalameva, tampi lokavajjanti vadeyya, sabbesaṃ paṇṇattivajjasikkhāpadānampi lokavajjatā āpajjeyya paṇṇattivajjānampi “na vaṭṭatī”ti jānitvā vītikkame akusalacittasseva sambhavato. Na hi bhagavato āṇaṃ jānitvā maddantassa kusalacittaṃ uppajjati anādariyavasena paṭighacittasseva uppajjanato.

42. Regarding the statement 'He made the training rule more stringent': in this context, wishing to explain by analyzing the strengthening and loosening of the training rule, which arise by way of implication from the subsequent enactments, he says, 'For the training rule is twofold,' and so on. Herein, that training rule involving intention, whose intention is only unwholesome, is a worldly offense. And that which, in the case of a training rule without intention that includes an aspect with intention, has an intention that is only unwholesome in that aspect with intention—that too, like drinking alcohol, is a worldly offense. To summarize and show this meaning, it is said, 'That in which, in the aspect with intention, the intention is only unwholesome, is called a worldly offense.' For indeed, this phrase 'in the aspect with intention' is said with reference to that which is without intention. For there is no purpose in qualifying a training rule that is entirely with intention with 'in the aspect with intention.' And 'in the aspect with intention' should be understood by the mind that knows the transgression of the object, not by the mind that knows the precept. For if one were to say that even in the case of a training rule where, in the aspect with intention, the intention is only unwholesome, even by the mind that knows the precept as 'it is not allowed,' that too is a worldly offense, then the state of being a worldly offense would apply to all training rules that are offenses by designation, since even in transgressing offenses by designation, knowing them as 'it is not allowed,' only an unwholesome mind arises. For in one who knowingly violates the Blessed One's command, a wholesome mind does not arise, because only a mind of aversion arises due to disrespect.

Apicettha “sacittakapakkhe cittaṃ akusalamevā”ti vacanato acittakassa vatthuajānanavasena acittakapakkhe cittaṃ akusalamevāti ayaṃ niyamo natthīti viññāyati. Yadi hi acittakassa acittakapakkhepi cittaṃ akusalameva siyā, “sacittakapakkhe”ti idaṃ visesanaṃ niratthakaṃ siyā. “Yassa cittaṃ akusalameva hoti, taṃ lokavajja”nti ettake vutte surāti ajānitvā pivantassa gandhavaṇṇakādibhāvaṃ ajānitvā tāni limpantīnaṃ bhikkhunīnañca [V 2.0036] vināpi akusalacittena āpattisambhavato ekantākusalaṃ sacittakasikkhāpadaṃ ṭhapetvā surāpānādiacittakasikkhāpadānaṃ lokavajjatā na siyāti tesampi saṅgaṇhatthaṃ “yassa sacittakapakkhe cittaṃ akusalameva hoti, taṃ lokavajja”nti vuttaṃ. Teneva cūḷagaṇṭhipade majjhimagaṇṭhipade ca vuttaṃ “etaṃ sattaṃ māressāmīti tasmiṃyeva padese nipannaṃ aññaṃ mārentassa pāṇasāmaññassa atthitāya yathā pāṇātipāto hoti, evaṃ etaṃ majjaṃ pivissāmīti aññaṃ majjaṃ pivantassa majjasāmaññassa atthitāya akusalameva hoti. Yathā pana kaṭṭhasaññāya sappaṃ ghātentassa pāṇātipāto na hoti, evaṃ nāḷikerapānasaññāya majjaṃ pivantassa akusalaṃ na hotī”ti.

Moreover, here, from the statement 'in the aspect with intention, the intention is only unwholesome,' it is understood that there is no such fixed rule that for a training rule without intention, due to ignorance of the object, the intention in the aspect without intention is only unwholesome. For if, in the case of a training rule without intention, even in the aspect without intention, the intention were only unwholesome, then this qualifier 'in the aspect with intention' would be meaningless. If it were simply said, 'That whose intention is only unwholesome is a worldly offense,' then—because for one who drinks alcohol without knowing it to be alcohol, and for nuns who smear themselves with it without knowing its nature of smell, color, etc., an offense can arise even without an unwholesome mind—setting aside the training rule with intention which is entirely unwholesome, the state of being a worldly offense would not apply to training rules without intention, such as drinking alcohol. Therefore, to include them also, it is said, 'That in which, in the aspect with intention, the intention is only unwholesome, is a worldly offense.' For the same reason, in the Cūḷagaṇṭhipada and the Majjhimagaṇṭhipada, it is stated: 'Just as when one thinks, "I will kill this being," and then kills another being lying in that very place, because there is the commonality of a living being, it is an act of killing a living being; similarly, when one thinks, "I will drink this intoxicant," and then drinks another intoxicant, because there is the commonality of intoxicants, it is only unwholesome. But just as one who kills a snake, perceiving it as a stick, does not commit the act of killing a living being, so too for one who drinks an intoxicant, perceiving it as coconut water, the act is not unwholesome.'

Keci pana vadanti “sāmaṇerassa surāti ajānitvā pivantassa pārājiko natthi, akusalaṃ pana hotī”ti, taṃ tesaṃ matimattaṃ. “Bhikkhuno ajānitvāpi bījato paṭṭhāya majjaṃ pivantassa pācittiyaṃ, sāmaṇero jānitvā [M 2.0041] pivanto sīlabhedaṃ āpajjati, na ajānitvā”ti ettakameva hi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ, “akusalaṃ pana hotī”ti na vuttanti. Aparampi vadanti “ajānitvā pivantassapi sotāpannassa mukhaṃ surā na pavisati kammapathappattaakusalacitteneva pātabbato”ti, tampi na sundaraṃ. Bodhisatte kucchigate bodhisattamātu sīlaṃ viya hi idampi ariyasāvakānaṃ dhammatāsiddhanti veditabbaṃ. Teneva dīghanikāye kūṭadantasuttaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.352) vuttaṃ –

Some, however, say, 'For a novice who unknowingly drinks alcohol, there is no pārājika offense, but it is unwholesome.' That is merely their opinion. Indeed, only this much is stated in the commentary: 'In the case of a bhikkhu, even if he unknowingly drinks an intoxicant originating from seeds, it is a pācittiya offense. A novice who knowingly drinks incurs a breach of virtue; not so if unknowingly.' It is not stated, 'but it is unwholesome.' Others further say, 'Even for a stream-enterer who drinks unknowingly, alcohol does not enter his mouth because it must be drunk only with an unwholesome mind that has reached the course of action.' That, too, is not sound. For just as the virtue of the Bodhisatta's mother is inviolable when the Bodhisatta is in the womb, so too should this be understood as established by the nature of things for noble disciples. Therefore, in the Dīghanikāya commentary on the Kūṭadanta Sutta, it is said—

“Bhavantarepi hi ariyasāvako jīvitahetupi neva pāṇaṃ hanati, na suraṃ pivati. Sacepissa surañca khīrañca missetvā mukhe pakkhipanti, khīrameva pavisati, na surā. Yathā kiṃ? Yathā koñcasakuṇānaṃ khīramissake udake khīrameva pavisati, na udakaṃ. Idaṃ yonisiddhanti ce? Idampi dhammatāsiddhanti veditabba”nti.

Indeed, even in another existence, a noble disciple does not kill a living being even for the sake of life, nor does he drink alcohol. If they mix alcohol and milk and put it in his mouth, only the milk enters, not the alcohol. What is that like? Just as for cranes, in water mixed with milk, only the milk enters, not the water. If one were to say, 'This is accomplished by its origin,' it should be understood, 'This too is accomplished by the nature of things.'

Yadi evaṃ surāpānasikkhāpadaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (pāci. aṭṭha. 329) “vatthuajānanatāya cettha acittakatā veditabbā, akusaleneva pātabbatāya lokavajjatā”ti kasmā vuttaṃ? Nāyaṃ doso. Ayañhettha adhippāyo – sacittakapakkhe akusalacitteneva pātabbatāya lokavajjatāti. Imināyeva hi adhippāyena aññesupi lokavajjesu acittakasikkhāpadesu akusalacittatāyeva vuttā, na pana sacittakatā. Teneva bhikkhunīvibhaṅgaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (pāci. aṭṭha. 1227) vuttaṃ –

If so, why is it said in the commentary on the training rule regarding drinking alcohol: 'Herein, the state of being without intention should be understood as due to not knowing the object; it is a worldly fault because it is to be drunk only with an unwholesome mind'? This is not a fault. For this is the intention here: in the case where there is intention, it is a worldly fault because it is to be drunk only with an unwholesome mind. Indeed, with this very intention, in other training rules without intention that are worldly faults, only the state of having an unwholesome mind is stated, not the state of having intention. Therefore, it is said in the commentary on the Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga—

“Giraggasamajjaṃ [V 2.0037] cittāgārasikkhāpadaṃ saṅghāṇi itthālaṅkāro gandhakavaṇṇako vāsitakapiññāko bhikkhunīādīhi ummaddanaparimaddanāti imāni dasa sikkhāpadāni acittakāni lokavajjāni akusalacittānī”ti,

'The hilltop festival; the training rule concerning a picture gallery; a saṅghāṇi garment; a woman's ornament; scented dye; perfumed oil-cake; massaging and rubbing by nuns and others—these ten training rules are without intention, are worldly faults, and involve unwholesome minds.'

Ayaṃ panettha adhippāyo – vināpi cittena āpajjitabbattā acittakāni, citte pana sati akusaleneva āpajjitabbattā lokavajjāni ceva akusalacittāni cāti. Tasmā bhikkhuvibhaṅge āgatāni surāpānauyyuttauyyodhikasikkhāpadāni tīṇi, bhikkhunīvibhaṅge āgatāni giraggasamajjādīni dasāti imesaṃ terasannaṃ acittakasikkhāpadānaṃ lokavajjatādassanatthaṃ “sacittakapakkhe”ti idaṃ visesanaṃ katanti niṭṭhamettha gantabbaṃ. Yasmā [M 2.0042] pana paṇṇattivajjassa vatthuvītikkamavijānanacittena sacittakapakkhe cittaṃ siyā kusalaṃ, siyā akusalaṃ, siyā abyākataṃ, tasmā tassa sacittakapakkhe cittaṃ akusalamevāti ayaṃ niyamo natthīti sesaṃ paṇṇattivajjanti vuttaṃ.

Herein, this is the intention: they are without intention because an offense can be incurred even without intention; but when intention is present, they are both worldly faults and involve unwholesome minds because the offense must be incurred only with an unwholesome mind. Therefore, to show the nature of being a worldly fault for these thirteen training rules without intention—the three training rules found in the Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga on drinking alcohol, military displays, and mock battles, and the ten beginning with the hilltop festival found in the Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga—this qualifier 'in the case of intention' has been made. This is the conclusion to be reached here. However, since for a fault by designation, with a mind that knows the object and the transgression, the mind in the intentional case might be wholesome, might be unwholesome, or might be indeterminate, there is no fixed rule that its mind in the intentional case is only unwholesome. Therefore, the remainder is said to be a fault by designation.

Rundhantīti vītikkamaṃ rundhantī. Dvāraṃ pidahantīti vītikkamalesassa dvāraṃ pidahantī. Sotaṃ pacchindamānāti uparūpari vītikkamasotaṃ pacchindamānā. Atha vā rundhantīti anāpattilesaṃ rundhantī. Dvāraṃ pidahantīti anāpattilesassa dvāraṃ pidahantī. Sotaṃ pacchindamānāti anāpattisotaṃ pacchindamānā, āpattimeva kurumānāti vuttaṃ hoti. Nanu ca lokavajje kāci anupaññatti uppajjamānā sithilaṃ karontī uppajjati, tasmā “lokavajje anupaññatti uppajjamānā…pe… gāḷhataraṃ karontī uppajjatī”ti idaṃ kasmā vuttanti āha “aññatra adhimānā aññatra supinantā”tiādi. “Aññatra adhimānā”ti imissā anupaññattiyā “vītikkamābhāvā”ti kāraṇaṃ vuttaṃ, “aññatra supinantā”ti imissā “abbohārikattā”ti kāraṇaṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha vītikkamābhāvāti pāpiccho icchāpakatotiādivītikkamābhāvā. Uttarimanussadhamme hi “pāpiccho icchāpakato uttarimanussadhammaṃ ullapatī”ti (mahāva. 129) vacanato visaṃvādanādhippāyena musā bhaṇanto pārājiko hoti. Ayaṃ pana adhimānena adhigatasaññī hutvā ullapati, na sikkhāpadaṃ vītikkamitukāmo, tasmā “aññatra adhimānā”ti ayaṃ anupaññatti uppajjamānā vītikkamābhāvā anāpattikarā jātā. Abbohārikattāti supinante vijjamānāyapi cetanāya vītikkamicchāya ca abbohārikattā. Kiñcāpi hi supinante mocanassādacetanā saṃvijjati, kadāci upakkamanampi hoti, tathāpi thinamiddhena abhibhūtattā taṃ cittaṃ abbohārikaṃ, cittassa abbohārikattā upakkamakiriyāsaṃvattanikāpi cetanā abbohārikā. Teneva [V 2.0038] “atthesā bhikkhave cetanā, sā ca kho abbohārikā”ti (pārā. 235) bhagavatā vuttā, tasmā “aññatra supinantā”ti ayaṃ anupaññatti abbohārikattā anāpattikarā jātā.

‘Obstructing’ means obstructing transgression. ‘Closing the door’ means closing the door to any pretext for transgression. ‘Cutting off the stream’ means repeatedly cutting off the stream of transgression. Alternatively, ‘obstructing’ means obstructing any pretext for non-offense. ‘Closing the door’ means closing the door to any pretext for non-offense. ‘Cutting off the stream’ means cutting off the stream of non-offense, which is to say, making it an offense. Now then, in the case of a worldly fault, some supplementary ruling arises making it lax. Therefore, why was it said, ‘In the case of a worldly fault, when a supplementary ruling arises… it arises making it stricter’? He said, ‘Except through overestimation, except in a dream,’ and so on. For this supplementary ruling ‘Except through overestimation,’ the reason given is ‘the absence of transgression.’ For this one, ‘except in a dream,’ the reason given is ‘its inoperativeness.’ Therein, ‘absence of transgression’ means the absence of a transgression such as having evil desires and being overcome by such desires. For regarding a superhuman state, according to the text, ‘One with evil desires, overcome by such desires, boasts of a superhuman state,’ one who speaks falsely with the intention to deceive is subject to a Pārājika offense. This one, however, boasts through overestimation, having the perception of having attained it, not with the desire to transgress the training rule. Therefore, this supplementary ruling, ‘except through overestimation,’ when it arises, makes for no offense due to the absence of transgression. ‘Due to being inoperative’ means that in a dream, even though there is intention and a desire to transgress, it is inoperative. For although in a dream the intention for the pleasure of emission exists, and sometimes an attempt even occurs, nevertheless, because one is overcome by sloth and torpor, that mind is inoperative. Due to the mind’s being inoperative, the intention that brings about the action of the attempt is also inoperative. For that very reason, it was said by the Blessed One, ‘Monks, there is that intention, but it is inoperative.’ Therefore, this supplementary ruling, ‘except in a dream,’ makes for no offense due to its inoperativeness.

Akate vītikkameti “kukkuccāyantā na bhuñjiṃsū”tiādīsu viya vītikkame akate. Sithilaṃ karontīti paṭhamaṃ sāmaññato baddhasikkhāpadaṃ mocetvā [M 2.0043] attano attano visaye anāpattikaraṇavasena sithilaṃ karontī. Dvāraṃ dadamānāti anāpattiyā dvāraṃ dadamānā. Tenevāha “aparāparampi anāpattiṃ kurumānā”ti. Nanu ca sañcarittasikkhāpade “antamaso taṅkhaṇikāyapī”ti anupaññatti uppajjamānā āpattimeva karontī uppannā, atha kasmā “anāpattiṃ kurumānā uppajjatī”ti vuttanti āha “antamaso taṅkhaṇikāyapī”tiādi. Udāyinā bhikkhunā taṅkhaṇikāya sañcarittaṃ āpannavatthusmiṃ paññattattā “kate vītikkame”ti vuttaṃ. Paññattigatikāva hotīti mūlapaññattiyaṃyeva antogadhā hoti.

Regarding 'when a transgression is not committed': this is like in the cases of 'being scrupulous, they did not eat,' and so on, where a transgression was not committed. 'Making it lax' means that, having first released the generally established training rule, they make it lax in their respective spheres by way of making it no offense. 'Giving an opening' means giving an opening for no offense. For that reason, he said, 'making it no offense again and again.' Now then, in the training rule on acting as a go-between, the supplementary ruling 'even for a moment' arose, making it an offense. So why was it said, 'it arises making it no offense'? He said, 'even for a moment,' and so on. Because it was laid down concerning the case where the monk Udāyin committed the offense of acting as a go-between for a moment, it was said, 'when a transgression is committed.' 'It follows the course of the ruling' means it is included within the original ruling itself.

Makkaṭivatthukathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Story of the Monkey is concluded.

Santhatabhāṇavāro

The Recitation Section on Furnishings

Vajjiputtakavatthuvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Story of the Vajjiputtaka Monks

43. Vesālī nivāso etesanti vesālikāti āha “vesālivāsino”ti. Vajjīsu janapade vasantā vajjino, vajjīnaṃ puttakā vajjiputtakāti āha “vajjiraṭṭhe vesāliyaṃ kulānaṃ puttā”ti. Ñātīnaṃ byasananti ñātīnaṃ vināso. So pana ñātīnaṃ vināso rājadaṇḍādikāraṇena hotīti āha “rājadaṇḍabyādhimaraṇavippavāsanimittenā”ti. Bhogānaṃ byasanaṃ vināso bhogabyasanaṃ. Tañca hiraññasuvaṇṇadāsidāsādīnaṃ upabhogaparibhogavatthūnaṃ rājadaṇḍādinā vināsoti āha “esa nayo dutiyapadepī”ti. Na buddhaṃ garahāmāti “asabbaññu buddho”tiādinā buddhaṃ na garahāma. Na dhammagarahinoti “aniyyāniko dhammo”tiādinā dhammaṃ na garahāma. Na saṅghagarahinoti “duppaṭipanno saṅgho”tiādinā saṅghaṃ na garahāma. Aṭṭhatiṃsārammaṇesūti dasa kasiṇā dasa asubhā dasānussatiyo cattāro brahmavihārā cattāro āruppā catudhātuvavatthānaṃ āhāre paṭikūlasaññāti imesu cattālīsakammaṭṭhānesu pāḷiyaṃ anāgatattā ālokākāsakasiṇadvayaṃ ṭhapetvā avasesāni gahetvā vuttaṃ. Vibhattā kusalā [V 2.0039] dhammāti “imasmiṃ ārammaṇe idaṃ hotī”ti evaṃ vibhattā upacārajjhānena saddhiṃ paṭhamajjhānādayo mahaggatakusalā dhammā[M 2.0044]. Teva dhammeti te eva kusale dhamme. Majjhimayāmo bhikkhūnaṃ niddākilamathavinodanokāsattā na gahitoti āha “paṭhamayāmañca pacchimayāmañcā”ti. Saccāni bujjhati paṭivijjhatīti bodhi, arahattamaggañāṇaṃ. Upakārakattena tassa pakkhe bhavā bodhipakkhiyāti āha “bodhissa pakkhe bhavānaṃ, arahattamaggañāṇassa upakārakāna”nti. Cattāro satipaṭṭhānā, cattāro sammappadhānā, cattāro iddhipādā, pañcindriyāni, pañca balāni, satta bojjhaṅgā, ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggoti ime sattatiṃsa bodhipakkhiyadhammā. “Gihipalibodhaṃ āvāsapalibodhañca pahāyā”ti imesaṃyeva dvinnaṃ palibodhānaṃ upacchedassa sudukkarabhāvato vuttaṃ. Yuttapayuttāti sammadeva yuttā.

43. Vesālī is their residence, thus they are called Vesālikā; therefore, it is said, “residents of Vesālī.” Dwelling in the Vajjian countries, they are Vajjis; the sons of the Vajjis are Vajjiputtakas; therefore, it is said, “sons of families in Vesālī in the Vajjian country.” The ruin of relatives means the destruction of relatives. That destruction of relatives occurs due to royal punishment and other causes; therefore, it is said, “due to reasons such as royal punishment, disease, death, and separation.” The ruin of wealth is the destruction of wealth, which is the destruction of items of enjoyment and use, such as gold, silver, female and male slaves, and so on, by royal punishment and the like; therefore, it is said, “this is the method in the second case as well.” We do not revile the Buddha means we do not revile the Buddha by saying, “the Buddha is not omniscient,” and so on. We are not revilers of the Dhamma means we do not revile the Dhamma by saying, “the Dhamma does not lead to liberation,” and so on. We are not revilers of the Saṅgha means we do not revile the Saṅgha by saying, “the Saṅgha is of wrong practice,” and so on. Regarding “among the thirty-eight meditation objects”: in the context of these forty meditation subjects—ten kasiṇas, ten impurities, ten recollections, four divine abidings, four formless states, the analysis of the four elements, and the perception of repulsiveness in food—it is stated by taking the remaining ones after setting aside the light and space kasiṇas, as they are not found in the Pāḷi text. “Analyzed wholesome states” refers to the sublime wholesome states, such as the first jhāna and so on, along with access concentration, which are analyzed thus: “in this meditation object, this arises.” “Those very states” means those very wholesome states. The middle watch was not included because it is an opportunity for monks to dispel sleepiness and fatigue; therefore, it is said, “the first watch and the last watch.” One understands and penetrates the truths, thus it is enlightenment (bodhi), which is the knowledge of the path to Arahantship. Because they are helpful, they exist on the side of that, thus they are factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyā); therefore, it is said, “those that are on the side of enlightenment, being helpful to the knowledge of the path to Arahantship.” The four foundations of mindfulness, the four right strivings, the four bases of spiritual power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the Noble Eightfold Path—these are the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. It is said, “having abandoned the encumbrance of a householder and the encumbrance of a residence,” because of the great difficulty in cutting off just these two encumbrances. “Properly applied” means rightly applied.

Āsayanti ajjhāsayaṃ. Sikkhaṃ appaccakkhāya bhikkhubhāve ṭhatvā paṭisevitamethunānaṃ tesaṃ vajjiputtakānaṃ upasampadaṃ anujānanto bhagavā “pārājiko hoti asaṃvāso”ti evaṃ paññattasikkhāpadaṃ samūhanati nāmāti āha – “yadi hi bhagavā…pe… paññattaṃ samūhaneyyā”ti. “Yo pana bhikkhū”ti vuttattā pana sikkhaṃ paccakkhāya paṭisevitamethunassa upasampadaṃ anujānanto na samūhanati nāma. Na hi so bhikkhu hutvā paṭisevati. “So āgato na upasampādetabbo”ti vacanato sāmaṇerabhūmi anuññātāti āha “sāmaṇerabhūmiyaṃ pana ṭhito”tiādi. Uttamatthanti arahattaṃ nibbānameva vā.

“Inclination” (āsayanti) means intention (ajjhāsayaṃ). The Blessed One, by permitting the higher ordination of those Vajjiputtaka monks who had engaged in sexual intercourse while remaining in the state of a monk without having renounced the training, is said to abolish the training rule that was laid down thus: “He is subject to a pārājika offense, he is not in communion.” Therefore, it is said: “If the Blessed One… and so on… were to abolish the laid-down rule.” However, because of the statement, “Whatever monk…,” one who permits the higher ordination for a person who engaged in sexual intercourse after having renounced the training is not said to abolish the rule. For that person does not engage in it after having become a monk. Because of the ruling, “Having returned, he is not to be given higher ordination,” the stage of a novice is permitted. Therefore, it is said, “But while standing at the stage of a novice,” and so on. “The ultimate goal” means either Arahantship or Nibbāna itself.

Vajjiputtakavatthuvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Story of the Vajjiputtaka Monks is concluded.

Catubbidhavinayakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Fourfold Vinaya Discourse

45. Nīharitvāti sāsanato nīharitvā. Tathā hi “pañcahupāli aṅgehi samannāgatena bhikkhunā nānuyuñjitabbaṃ. Katamehi pañcahi? Suttaṃ na jānāti, suttānulomaṃ na jānātī”ti (pari. 442) evamādipariyattisāsanato suttaṃ suttānulomañca nīharitvā pakāsesuṃ, “anāpatti evaṃ amhākaṃ ācariyānaṃ uggaho paripucchāti gaṇhātī”ti evamādipariyattisāsanato ācariyavādaṃ nīharitvā pakāsesuṃ, bhārukacchakavatthusmiṃ (pārā. 78) “āyasmā [M 2.0045] upāli evamāha anāpatti āvuso supinantenā”ti evamādipariyattisāsanato eva attanomatiṃ nīharitvā pakāsesuṃ. Tāya hi attanomatiyā thero etadaggaṭṭhānaṃ labhi.

45. “Nīharitvā” means having extracted from the teaching. Indeed, it is said: “Upāli, a monk endowed with five qualities should not be questioned. With which five? He does not know the Sutta; he does not know what is in accordance with the Sutta” (Pari. 442). From scriptural teachings such as this, they extracted the Sutta and what is in accordance with the Sutta and declared them. From scriptural teachings such as, “There is no offense; this is the learning and inquiry of our teachers, this is what is grasped,” they extracted the teachers' doctrine and declared it. In the case of Bhārukaccha (Pārā. 78), from scriptural teachings such as, “Venerable Upāli said thus: ‘Friend, there is no offense in a dream,’” they extracted their own opinion and declared it. Indeed, by that very opinion of his, the elder obtained the foremost position.

Vuttanti [V 2.0040] nāgasenattherena vuttaṃ. Pajjate anena atthoti padaṃ, bhagavatā kaṇṭhādivaṇṇappavattiṭṭhānaṃ āhacca visesetvā bhāsitaṃ padaṃ āhaccapadaṃ, bhagavatoyeva vacanaṃ. Tenāha “āhaccapadanti suttaṃ adhippeta”nti. “Idaṃ kappati, idaṃ na kappatī”ti evaṃ avisesetvā “yaṃ, bhikkhave, mayā ‘idaṃ na kappatī’ti appaṭikkhittaṃ, tañce akappiyaṃ anulometi, kappiyaṃ paṭibāhati, taṃ vo na kappatī”tiādinā (mahāva. 305) vuttaṃ sāmaññalakkhaṇaṃ idha “raso”ti adhippetanti āha “rasoti suttānuloma”nti. Dhammasaṅgāhakappabhutiācariyaparamparato ānītā aṭṭhakathātanti idha “ācariyavaṃso”ti adhippetāti āha “ācariyavaṃsoti ācariyavādo”ti.

It is said by the elder Nāgasena. A 'pada' is that by which meaning is known. An 'āhaccapada' is a word spoken by the Blessed One, having touched and specified the place of origin of sounds; it is the very word of the Blessed One. Therefore, he said: “By 'āhaccapada' a sutta is intended.” Without specifying, “This is allowable, this is not allowable,” the general characteristic spoken of in the passage beginning, “Monks, whatever I have not rejected as ‘this is not allowable,’ if it accords with what is unallowable and rejects what is allowable, that is not allowable for you” (Mahāva. 305), is here intended as 'rasa' (flavor). Thus, he said: “'Rasa' means what is in accordance with the Sutta.” The commentary tradition, handed down from the lineage of teachers beginning with the compilers of the Dhamma, is here intended as 'the lineage of teachers.' Thus, he said: “'The lineage of teachers' means the teachers' doctrine.”

Idha vinayavinicchayassa adhikatattā tadanucchavikameva suttaṃ dassento āha – “suttaṃ nāma sakale vinayapiṭake pāḷī”ti. Mahāpadesāti mahāokāsā, mahantāni vinayassa patiṭṭhāpanaṭṭhānāni yesu patiṭṭhāpito vinayo vinicchayati asandehato. Mahantāni vā kāraṇāni mahāpadesā, mahantāni vinayavinicchayakāraṇānīti vuttaṃ hoti. “Atthato pana ‘yaṃ, bhikkhave’tiādinā vuttā sādhippāyā pāḷiyeva mahāpadesā”ti vadanti. Tenevāha “ye bhagavatā evaṃ vuttā”tiādi. Ime ca mahāpadesā khandhake āgatā, tasmā tesaṃ vinicchayakathā tattheva āvi bhavissatīti idha na vuccati. Yadipi tattha tattha bhagavatā pavattitā pakiṇṇakadesanāva aṭṭhakathā, sā pana dhammasaṅgāhakehi paṭhamaṃ tīṇi piṭakāni saṅgāyitvā tassa atthavaṇṇanānurūpeneva vācanāmaggaṃ āropitattā “ācariyavādo”ti vuccati ācariyā vadanti saṃvaṇṇenti pāḷiṃ etenāti katvā. Tenāha – “ācariyavādo nāma…pe… aṭṭhakathātantī”ti. Tisso saṅgītiyo āruḷhoyeva ca buddhavacanassa atthasaṃvaṇṇanābhūto kathāmaggo mahāmahindattherena tambapaṇṇidīpaṃ ābhato, pacchā tambapaṇṇiyehi mahātherehi sīhaḷabhāsāya ṭhapito nikāyantaraladdhisaṅkarapariharaṇatthaṃ. Kiñcāpi attanomati suttādīhi saṃsanditvāva parikappīyati, tathāpi sā na suttādīsu visesato [M 2.0046] niddiṭṭhāti āha “suttasuttānulomaācariyavāde muñcitvā”ti. Anubuddhiyāti suttādīniyeva anugatabuddhiyā. Nayaggāhenāti suttādito labbhamānanayaggahaṇena.

Here, because the analysis of the Vinaya is the main subject, showing a sutta that is suitable for it, he says: "'Sutta' means the Pāḷi in the entire Vinaya Piṭaka." 'Mahāpadesā' means great authorities, the great foundations of the Vinaya, wherein the established Vinaya is decided without doubt. Or, great reasons are 'mahāpadesā'; it means they are the great reasons for the analysis of the Vinaya. But regarding the meaning, they say: "The Pāḷi itself, with its intention, spoken in the passage beginning, 'Monks, whatever...,' is the Mahāpadesā." For that reason, he said: "Those things that were spoken thus by the Blessed One," and so on. These Mahāpadesas are found in the Khandhakas; therefore, the discussion of their analysis will become clear there and is not stated here. Although the scattered teachings given by the Blessed One here and there are themselves the commentary, because the compilers of the Dhamma first recited the three Piṭakas and then established the path of recitation in accordance with the explanation of its meaning, it is called 'Ācariyavāda' (the teachers' doctrine), on the basis that by this the teachers explain and elucidate the Pāḷi. For that reason, he said: "'Ācariyavāda' means... the commentary tradition." And the path of discourse, which is the explanation of the meaning of the Buddha's word and which had ascended the three Councils, was brought to the island of Tambapaṇṇi by the great elder Mahinda. Later, it was established in the Sinhalese language by the great elders of Tambapaṇṇi in order to avoid mixture with the doctrines of other schools. Although one's own opinion is conjectured only after comparing it with the Suttas and so on, it is nevertheless not specifically pointed out in the Suttas and so on. Thus, he said: "apart from the Sutta, what is in accordance with the Sutta, and the teachers' doctrine." 'Anubuddhiyā' means by the wisdom that follows the Suttas and so on. 'Nayaggāhena' means by grasping the method obtainable from the Suttas and so on.

Attanomatiṃ sāmaññato paṭhamaṃ dassetvā idāni tameva visesetvā dassento “apicā”tiādimāha. Idāni tattha paṭipajjitabbākāraṃ dassento āha – “taṃ pana attanomatiṃ gahetvā kathentenā”tiādi. Atthenāti attanā sallakkhitena atthena. Ācariyavāde otāretabbāti ācariyavāde ñāṇena anuppavesetabbā. Sabbadubbalāti puggalassa sayaṃ [V 2.0041] paṭibhānabhāvato. Pamādapāṭhavasena ācariyavādassa kadāci suttānulomena asaṃsandanāpi siyā, so na gahetabboti dassento āha – “ācariyavādopi…pe… samento eva gahetabbo”ti. Samentameva gahetabbanti yathā suttena saṃsandati, evaṃ mahāpadesato atthā uddharitabbāti dasseti. Suttānulomassa suttekadesattepi sutte viya “idaṃ kappati, idaṃ na kappatī”ti paricchinditvā āhaccabhāsitaṃ kiñci natthīti āha – “suttānulomato hi suttameva balavatara”nti. Appaṭivattiyanti appaṭibāhiyaṃ. Kārakasaṅghasadisanti pamāṇattā saṅgītikārakasaṅghasadisaṃ. Buddhānaṃ ṭhitakālasadisanti iminā buddheheva kathitattā dharamānabuddhasadisanti vuttaṃ hoti. Sutte hi paṭibāhite buddhova paṭibāhito hoti. Sakavādī suttaṃ gahetvā kathetīti sakavādī attano suttaṃ gahetvā voharati. Paravādī suttānulomanti aññanikāyavādī attano nikāye suttānulomaṃ gahetvā katheti. Khepaṃ vā garahaṃ vā akatvāti “kiṃ iminā”ti khepaṃ vā “kimesa bālo vadatī”ti garahaṃ vā akatvā. Suttānulomanti paravādinā vuttaṃ aññanikāye suttānulomaṃ. Sutte otāretabbanti sakavādinā attano sutte otāretabbaṃ. Suttasmiṃyeva ṭhātabbanti attano sutteyeva ṭhātabbaṃ. Evaṃ sesavāresupi atthayojanā kātabbā. Ayanti sakavādī. Paroti aññanikāyavādī. Evaṃ sesesupi.

Having first shown self-opinion generally, now, showing that very thing by distinguishing it, he says 'apicā' and so on. Now, showing the manner in which one should proceed therein, he says: 'But one who speaks having taken up that self-opinion,' and so on. 'Atthena' means with a meaning well-marked by oneself. 'Ācariyavāde otāretabbā' means it should be properly introduced into the teacher’s doctrine with knowledge. 'Sabbadubbalā' is said because it is a matter of the individual's own intelligence. By way of a negligent text, the teacher’s doctrine may sometimes not correspond with what is in accordance with the Sutta; that should not be taken up. Showing this, he says: 'Even the teacher’s doctrine...pe... should be taken up only if it accords.' 'Should be taken up only if it accords' shows that just as it corresponds with the Sutta, so should the meanings be extracted by means of the great authorities. Although what is in accordance with the Sutta is a part of the Sutta, just as in a Sutta, there is nothing spoken specifically, having demarcated it by saying 'this is allowable, this is not allowable.' Thus, he says: 'For, compared to what is in accordance with the Sutta, the Sutta itself is more powerful.' 'Appaṭivattiyanti' means unrefutable. 'Kārakasaṅghasadisanti' means, because of its authority, it is like the Sangha of compilers of the council. 'Buddhānaṃ ṭhitakālasadisanti' means by this, because it was spoken by the Buddhas themselves, it is said to be like the living Buddha. For if the Sutta is refuted, the Buddha himself is refuted. 'A proponent of his own doctrine speaks having taken up the Sutta' means a proponent of his own doctrine speaks, having taken up his own Sutta. 'A proponent of another doctrine's suttānuloma' means a proponent of another Nikāya speaks, having taken up what is in accordance with the Sutta in his own Nikāya. 'Without making blame or censure' means without making blame, saying 'What of this?', or censure, saying 'What is this fool saying?'. 'Suttānulomanti' means what is in accordance with the Sutta in another Nikāya spoken by the opponent. 'Sutte otāretabbaṃ' means it should be brought into line with his own Sutta by the proponent of his own doctrine. 'Suttasmiṃyeva ṭhātabbaṃ' means one should stand firm in one’s own Sutta. Thus, the application of the meaning should be made in the remaining cases as well. 'Ayaṃ' is the proponent of his own doctrine. 'Para' is the proponent of another Nikāya. Thus it should be known in the remaining cases as well.

Nanu ca “suttānulomato suttameva balavatara”nti heṭṭhā vuttaṃ, idha pana “suttānulome suttaṃ otāretabba”ntiādi kasmā vuttanti? Nāyaṃ virodho. “Suttānulomato suttameva balavatara”nti hi idaṃ [M 2.0047] sakamateyeva suttaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tattha hi sakamatipariyāpannameva suttādiṃ sandhāya “attanomati sabbadubbalā, attanomatito ācariyavādo balavataro, ācariyavādato suttānulomaṃ balavataraṃ, suttānulomato suttameva balavatara”nti ca vuttaṃ. Idha pana paravādinā ānītaṃ aññanikāye suttaṃ sandhāya “suttānulome suttaṃ otāretabba”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tasmā paravādinā ānītaṃ suttādiṃ attano suttānulomaācariyavādaattanomatīsu otāretvā samentaṃyeva gahetabbaṃ, itaraṃ na gahetabbanti ayaṃ nayo idha vuccatīti na koci pubbāparavirodho.

Is it not so that it was stated previously, 'Compared to what is in accordance with the Sutta, the Sutta itself is more powerful'? But here, why is it said, 'The Sutta should be brought into line with what is in accordance with the Sutta,' and so on? This is not a contradiction. For the statement, 'Compared to what is in accordance with the Sutta, the Sutta itself is more powerful,' was said referring to a Sutta within one's own view. There, referring to the Sutta, etc., that are included only within one's own view, it was said: 'Self-opinion is the weakest of all; more powerful than self-opinion is the teacher's doctrine; more powerful than the teacher's doctrine is what is in accordance with the Sutta; and compared to what is in accordance with the Sutta, the Sutta itself is the most powerful.' But here, the statement, 'The Sutta should be brought into line with what is in accordance with the Sutta,' and so on, was said referring to a Sutta in another Nikāya brought by an opponent. Therefore, having brought into line a Sutta, etc., brought by an opponent with one's own suttānuloma, teacher's doctrine, and self-opinion, only that which accords should be taken up; the other should not be taken up. This is the method spoken of here, so there is no contradiction whatsoever between the former and the latter.

Bāhirakasuttanti tisso saṅgītiyo anāruḷhaguḷhavessantarādīni mahāsaṅghikanikāyavāsīnaṃ suttāni. Vedallādīnanti ādi-saddena guḷhaummaggādiggahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ, itaraṃ gārayhasuttaṃ na gahetabbaṃ. Attanomatiyameva ṭhātabbanti iminā aññanikāyato ānītasuttatopi sakanikāye attanomatiyeva balavatarāti dasseti. Sakavādī suttaṃ gahetvā katheti, paravādīpi suttamevātievamādinā [V 2.0042] samānajātikānaṃ vasena vāro na vutto, suttassa sutteyeva otāraṇaṃ bhinnaṃ viya hutvā na paññāyati, vuttanayeneva ca sakkā yojetunti.

'Bāhirakasutta' means the suttas of those dwelling in the Mahāsaṅghika Nikāya, such as the Guḷha and Vessantara, which were not included in the three Saṅgītis. By the word 'ādi' in 'Vedallādīni,' the inclusion of the Guḷha, Ummagga, and so on should be known; the other reprehensible sutta should not be taken up. By the statement 'One should stand firm only in one's own opinion,' it is shown that compared even to a sutta brought from another Nikāya, one's own opinion in one's own Nikāya is more powerful. By such statements as, 'A proponent of his own doctrine speaks having taken up a sutta, and an opponent also speaks having taken up only a sutta,' a turn is not stated by way of them being of the same kind. The application of a sutta to a sutta itself, having become as if separate, is not apparent. And it is possible to apply it only by the method that was stated.

Idāni sakavādīparavādīnaṃ kappiyākappiyādibhāvaṃ sandhāya vivāde uppanne tattha paṭipajjitabbavidhiṃ dassento āha – “atha panāyaṃ kappiyanti gahetvā kathetī”tiādi. Tattha sutte ca suttānulome ca otāretabbanti sakavādinā attanoyeva sutte ca suttānulome ca otāretabbaṃ. Paro kāraṇaṃ na vindatīti paravādī kāraṇaṃ na labhati. Suttato bahuṃ kāraṇañca vinicchayañca dassetīti paravādī attano suttato bahuṃ kāraṇaṃ vinicchayañca āharitvā dasseti. Sādhūti sampaṭicchitvā akappiyeva ṭhātabbanti iminā attano nikāye suttādīni alabhantena sakavādinā paravādīvacaneyeva ṭhātabbanti vadati. Dvinnampi kāraṇacchāyā dissatīti sakavādīparavādīnaṃ ubhinnampi kappiyākappiyabhāvasādhakaṃ kāraṇapatirūpakaṃ dissati. Yadi dvinnampi kāraṇacchāyā dissati, kasmā “akappiyeva ṭhātabba”nti āha “vinayañhi patvā”tiādi. “Vinayaṃ patvā”ti vuttamevatthaṃ pākaṭataraṃ katvā dassento āha “kappiyākappiyavicāraṇamāgammā”ti. Rundhitabbantiādīsu [M 2.0048] dubbiññeyyavinicchaye kappiyākappiyabhāve sati kappiyanti gahaṇaṃ rundhitabbaṃ, akappiyanti gahaṇaṃ gāḷhaṃ kātabbaṃ. Aparāparaṃ pavattakappiyagahaṇasotaṃ pacchinditabbaṃ, garukabhāvasaṅkhāte akappiyabhāveyeva ṭhātabbanti attho.

Now, showing the method to be practiced when a dispute has arisen concerning the state of what is allowable, unallowable, and so forth, for the proponent of his own doctrine and the opponent, he says: 'But if this one speaks, having taken up the view, "This is allowable,"' and so on. Therein, 'it should be brought into line with the sutta and the suttānuloma' means it should be brought into line with his own sutta and suttānuloma by the proponent of his own doctrine. 'The other does not find a reason' means the opponent does not obtain a reason. 'He shows much reason and decision from the sutta' means the opponent, having brought forth much reason and decision from his own sutta, shows it. By the statement, 'Having accepted it, saying "Good," one should stand firm only on the unallowable,' he says that the proponent of his own doctrine, not finding the suttas and so forth in his own Nikāya, should stand firm only in the opponent's statement. 'A semblance of a reason is seen for both' means a semblance of a reason that establishes the state of allowable or unallowable is seen for both the proponent of his own doctrine and the opponent. If a semblance of a reason is seen for both, why did he say, 'One should stand firm only on the unallowable'? He said, 'For, with respect to the Vinaya,' and so on. Showing the meaning of the statement 'with respect to the Vinaya' by making it clearer, he says, 'having come to the investigation of the allowable and unallowable.' In 'It should be obstructed,' and so on, when there is a state of allowable and unallowable in a decision that is difficult to discern, the taking up of 'allowable' should be obstructed; the taking up of 'unallowable' should be made firm. The stream of taking up the allowable that occurs again and again should be cut off; one should stand firm only in the state of the unallowable, which is designated as a grave matter—this is the meaning.

Bahūhi suttavinicchayakāraṇehīti bahūhi suttehi ceva tato ānītavinicchayakāraṇehi ca. Attano gahaṇaṃ na vissajjetabbanti sakavādinā attano akappiyanti gahaṇaṃ na vissajjetabbaṃ. Idāni vuttamevatthaṃ nigamento “eva”ntiādimāha. Tattha yoti sakavādīparavādīsu yo koci. Keci pana “sakavādīsuyeva yo koci idhādhippeto”ti vadanti, evaṃ sante “atha panāyaṃ kappiyanti gahetvā kathetī”tiādīsu sabbattha ubhopi sakavādinoyeva siyuṃ heṭṭhā vuttasseva nigamanavasena “eva”ntiādīnaṃ vuttattā, tasmā taṃ na gahetabbaṃ. Atirekakāraṇaṃ labhatīti ettha suttādīsu purimaṃ purimaṃ atirekakāraṇaṃ nāma, yo vā suttādīsu catūsu bahutaraṃ kāraṇaṃ labhati, so atirekakāraṇaṃ labhati nāma.

‘By many reasons for deciding on the Suttas’ means by many Suttas and by the reasons for decision brought from them. ‘One should not relinquish one’s own position’ means that a proponent of his own doctrine should not give up his own position that 'it is unallowable.' Now, summarizing the meaning already stated, he says ‘thus’ and so on. Here, ‘whoever’ refers to anyone among proponents of their own doctrine or opponents. However, some say, ‘Here, only whoever among proponents of their own doctrine is intended.’ If so, then in all cases like ‘but now this one, having taken what is proper, speaks,’ and so on, both would only be proponents of their own doctrine, because ‘thus’ and so on are stated as a summary of what was said before; therefore, that statement should not be accepted. ‘Gains the superior reason’ here means that among the suttas and so forth, each preceding one is called the superior reason. Or, whoever among the four—suttas and so forth—obtains a greater number of reasons, that person is said to gain the superior reason.

Suṭṭhu pavatti etassāti suppavatti, suṭṭhu pavattati sīlenāti vā suppavatti. Tenāha “suppavattīti suṭṭhu pavatta”nti. Vācāya uggataṃ vācuggataṃ, vacasā suggahitanti vuttaṃ hoti. Suttatoti imassa vivaraṇaṃ “pāḷito”ti. Ettha ca “suttaṃ nāma sakalaṃ vinayapiṭaka”nti vuttattā [V 2.0043] pāḷitoti tadatthadīpikā aññāyeva pāḷi veditabbā. Anubyañjanasoti imassa vivaraṇaṃ “paripucchato ca aṭṭhakathāto cā”ti. Pāḷiṃ anugantvā atthassa byañjanato pakāsanato anubyañjananti hi paripucchā aṭṭhakathā ca vuccati. Ettha ca aṭṭhakathāya visuṃ gahitattā paripucchāti theravādo vutto. Saṅghabhedassa pubbabhāge pavattakalahassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ saṅgharājīti. Kukkuccakoti aṇumattesupi vajjesu bhayadassanavasena kukkuccaṃ uppādento. Tantiṃ avisaṃvādetvāti pāḷiṃ aññathā akatvā. Avokkamantoti anatikkamanto.

‘Suppavatti’ (of good conduct) means that for this person there is a good proceeding, or that one proceeds well through virtue. Therefore it is said, ‘suppavatti means well-proceeded.’ ‘Vācuggata’ (elevated by speech) means well-grasped by speech. The explanation of ‘from the Sutta’ (suttato) is ‘from the Pāḷi’ (pāḷito). And here, since it is said that ‘sutta means the entire Vinayapiṭaka,’ by ‘pāḷito’ another Pāḷi text which illuminates its meaning should be understood. The explanation of ‘anubyañjanaso’ (in detail) is ‘from questioning and from the commentary.’ Indeed, because they follow the Pāḷi and clarify the meaning through detailed explanation and manifestation, both questioning and commentary are called ‘anubyañjana.’ And here, because the commentary is taken separately, by ‘questioning’ (paripucchā) the Theravāda is meant. ‘Saṅgharājī’ (a crack in the Saṅgha) is a designation for the quarrel that occurs in the preliminary stage of a schism of the Saṅgha. ‘Kukkuccaka’ (scrupulous) refers to one who arouses scrupulousness by seeing danger even in minor faults. ‘Not distorting the Tanti’ means not altering the Pāḷi. ‘Avokkamanto’ (not transgressing) means not overstepping.

Vitthunatīti atthaṃ adisvā nitthunati. Vipphandatīti kampati. Santiṭṭhituṃ na sakkotīti ekasmiṃyeva atthe patiṭṭhātuṃ na sakkoti. Tenāha “yaṃ [M 2.0049] yaṃ parena vuccati, taṃ taṃ anujānātī”ti. Paravādaṃ gaṇhātīti “ucchumhi kasaṭaṃ yāvajīvikaṃ, raso sattāhakāliko, tadubhayavinimutto ca ucchu nāma visuṃ natthi, tasmā ucchupi vikāle vaṭṭatī”ti paravādinā vutte tampi gaṇhāti. Ekekalomanti palitaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Yamhīti yasmiṃ puggale. Parikkhayaṃ pariyādānanti atthato ekaṃ.

‘He laments’ (vitthunati) means, not seeing the meaning, he laments. ‘He struggles’ (vipphandati) means he trembles. ‘He is unable to settle’ (santiṭṭhituṃ na sakkoti) means he cannot be established in any single meaning. Therefore, it is said: ‘Whatever is said by another, that he agrees with.’ ‘He accepts the view of others’ (paravādaṃ gaṇhāti) means when an opponent says, ‘In sugarcane, the pulp is for life, the juice is for seven days, and there is no separate thing called sugarcane apart from these two; therefore, sugarcane is also permissible at the wrong time,’ he accepts that too. ‘Each single hair’ (ekekalomaṃ)—this is said referring to gray hair. ‘In whom’ (yamhi) means in which person. ‘Exhaustion and depletion’ (parikkhayaṃ pariyādānaṃ)—these are one in meaning.

Ācariyaparamparā kho panassa suggahitā hotīti ettha ācariyaparamparāti ācariyānaṃ vinicchayaparamparā. Teneva vakkhati “yathā ācariyo ca ācariyācariyo ca pāḷiñca paripucchañca vadanti, tathā ñātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Pubbāparānusandhitoti “idaṃ pubbavacanaṃ, idaṃ paravacanaṃ, ayamanusandhī”ti evaṃ pubbāparānusandhito. Ācariyaparamparanti imasseva vevacanaṃ theravādaṅganti, therapaṭipāṭinti attho. Dve tayo parivaṭṭāti dve tisso paramparā.

‘The succession of teachers is well grasped by him.’ Here, ‘succession of teachers’ (ācariyaparamparā) means the succession of the teachers’ decisions. Therefore, it will be said: ‘As the teacher and the teacher’s teacher speak on the Pāḷi text and the questioning, so it is proper to understand.’ ‘From the connection of the former and the latter’ (pubbāparānusandhito) means: ‘This is the earlier statement, this is the later statement, this is the connection’—thus from the connection of the former and the latter. ‘The succession of teachers’ (ācariyaparamparā) is another term for this very thing, that is, a constituent of the Theravāda tradition (theravādaṅga); the meaning is ‘the succession of the elders’ (therapaṭipāṭi). ‘Two or three cycles’ (dve tayo parivaṭṭā) means two or three successions.

Imehi ca pana tīhi lakkhaṇehīti “suttamassa svāgataṃ hotī”tiādinā heṭṭhā vuttehi tīhi lakkhaṇehi. Ettha ca paṭhamena lakkhaṇena vinayassa suṭṭhu uggahitabhāvo vutto, dutiyena uggahitena acalatā suppatiṭṭhitatā vuttā, tatiyena yaṃ pāḷiyā aṭṭhakathāya ca natthi, tampi ācariyavacanena vinicchinituṃ samatthatā vuttā. Otiṇṇe vatthusminti codanāsaṅkhāte vītikkamasaṅkhāte vā vatthusmiṃ saṅghamajjhe otiṇṇe, osaṭeti attho. Vuttameva vibhāvento “codakena ca cuditakena ca vutte vattabbe”ti āha. Keci pana “codakena otiṇṇe vatthusmiṃ cuditakena ca vutte vattabbe”ti evaṃ yojenti. Apare pana “codakena ca cuditakena ca vutte vinayadharena ca vattabbe”ti evampi yojenti. “Codakena ca cuditakena ca vutte vattabbe”ti ayameva pana yojanā sundaratarāti veditabbā. Vatthu oloketabbanti tassa tassa sikkhāpadassa vatthu oloketabbaṃ. “Tiṇena vā paṇṇena vā…pe… yo āgaccheyya, āpatti [V 2.0044] dukkaṭassā”ti (pārā. 517) hi idaṃ nissaggiye aññātakaviññattisikkhāpadassa vatthusmiṃ paññattaṃ, thullaccayadubbhāsitāpattīnaṃ mātikāya anāgatattā “pañcannaṃ āpattīnaṃ aññatara”nti vuttaṃ. Aññataraṃ vā āpattinti “kāle vikālasaññī āpatti dukkaṭassa, kāle vematiko āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti [M 2.0050] evamādinā (pāci. 250) āgataṃ dukkaṭaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Sikkhāpadantaresūti vinītavatthuṃ antokatvā ekekasmiṃ sikkhāpadantare.

‘And by these three characteristics’ refers to the three characteristics mentioned below, beginning with ‘the sutta is well-received by him.’ And here, by the first characteristic, the state of having thoroughly mastered the Discipline is stated; by the second, unwaveringness and being well-established in what has been mastered are stated; and by the third, the ability to decide even that which is not in the Pāḷi or the commentary by means of the teachers' words is stated. ‘When a matter has arisen’ (otiṇṇe vatthusmiṃ) means when a matter—whether designated as an accusation or a transgression—has descended into the midst of the Saṅgha; the meaning is it has come down. Clarifying what was already said, he stated, ‘When both the accuser and the accused have spoken, what should be said must be said.’ Some, however, connect it thus: ‘When the accuser has brought the matter and the accused has spoken, what should be said must be said.’ Still others connect it thus: ‘When both the accuser and the accused have spoken, the Vinaya expert also should speak.’ But it should be known that this very connection, ‘When both the accuser and the accused have spoken, what should be said must be said,’ is the most suitable. ‘The basis should be examined’ means the basis of each respective training rule should be investigated. Indeed, this statement in the Nissaggiya section, in the basis of the training rule on requesting from an unrelated person, is prescribed: ‘With grass or with a leaf…pe… whoever should come, there is an offense of wrong conduct.’ Because the offenses of grave transgression and wrong speech had not yet come in the mātikā, it is said, ‘one of the five offenses.’ ‘Or another offense’ is said referring to the offense of wrong conduct that comes in passages such as, ‘At the right time, perceiving it as the wrong time, there is an offense of wrong conduct; at the right time, being uncertain, there is an offense of wrong conduct.’ ‘Among other training rules’ means including the settled cases within each respective training rule.

Sukhumāti attanopi duviññeyyasabhāvassa lahuparivattino cittassa sīghaparivattitāya vuttaṃ. Tenāha “cittalahukā”ti. Cittaṃ lahu sīghaparivatti etesanti cittalahukā. Teti te vītikkame. Taṃvatthukanti te adinnādānamanussaviggahavītikkamā vatthu adhiṭṭhānaṃ kāraṇametassāti taṃvatthukaṃ. Sīlāni sodhetvāti yaṃvatthukaṃ kukkuccaṃ uppannaṃ, taṃ amanasikaritvā avasesasīlāni sodhetvā. Pākaṭabhāvato sukhavaḷañjanatāya ca “dvattiṃsākāraṃ tāva manasi karohī”ti vuttaṃ. Aññasmiṃ pana kammaṭṭhāne kataparicayena tadeva manasi kātabbaṃ. Kammaṭṭhānaṃ ghaṭayatīti antarantarā khaṇḍaṃ adassetvā cittena saddhiṃ ālambanabhāvena cirakālaṃ ghaṭayati. Saṅkhārā pākaṭā hutvā upaṭṭhahantīti vipassanākammaṭṭhāniko ce, tassa saṅkhārā pākaṭā hutvā upaṭṭhahanti. Sace katapārājikavītikkamo bhaveyya, tassa satipi asaritukāmatāya vippaṭisāravatthuvasena punappunaṃ taṃ upaṭṭhahatīti cittekaggataṃ na vindati. Tena vuttaṃ “kammaṭṭhānaṃ na ghaṭayatī”tiādi. Attanā jānātīti sayameva jānāti. Paccatte cetaṃ karaṇavacanaṃ, attā jānātīti vuttaṃ hoti. Aññā ca devatā jānantīti ārakkhadevatāhi aññā paracittaviduniyo devatā ca jānanti.

‘Subtle’ is said because of the swift changing of the mind, which has a nature difficult to know and is quick to transform. Therefore, it is said, ‘of light mind.’ Their mind is light, swiftly changing; thus, they are called ‘of light mind.’ ‘They’ refers to those transgressions. ‘Based on that’ means that those transgressions of taking what is not given and sexual intercourse are its object, basis, and cause; therefore, it is called ‘based on that.’ ‘Having purified the virtues’ means disregarding whatever object of remorse has arisen and purifying the remaining virtues. Because of its evident nature and its ease of practice, it is said, ‘First, bring to mind the thirty-two aspects.’ But when one is familiar with another meditation subject, that very one should be brought to mind. ‘He applies himself to the meditation subject’ means he applies himself for a long time, without showing any interval, with the mind together with its object. ‘Formations, having become evident, appear’ means that if he is a meditator of insight, for him, the formations, having become evident, appear. If he has committed a pārājika transgression, then, even when not wishing to remember it, that transgression repeatedly arises as an object of remorse, and thus he does not attain one-pointedness of mind. Therefore, it is said, ‘he does not apply himself to the meditation subject,’ and so on. ‘He knows by himself’ means he himself knows. In this context, this is an instrumental expression used in the sense of the agent; it means ‘the self knows.’ ‘And other deities know’ means that other deities apart from the guardian deities, those who know the minds of others, also know.

Niṭṭhitā catubbidhavinayakathāvaṇṇanā

The commentary on the fourfold Vinaya discussion is completed.

Vinayadharassa ca lakkhaṇādikathāvaṇṇanā.

And the commentary on the discussion of the characteristics, etc., of a Vinaya master.

Bhikkhupadabhājanīyavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Bhikkhu Rules.

Tasmāti yasmā pana-saddaṃ apanetvā aniyamena puggaladīpakaṃ yo-saddameva āha, tasmā. Etthāti imasmiṃ yo-sadde. Pana-saddassa nipātamattattā yo-saddasseva atthaṃ pakāsento “yo kocīti vuttaṃ hotī”ti āha. Yo koci nāmāti yo vā so vā yo kocīti vutto. Vāsadhurayutto vāti vipassanādhurayutto vā. Sīlesūti pakatīsu.

‘Therefore’ means: because, having removed the word `pana`, it states only the word `yo`, which indicates a person indefinitely, therefore... ‘Here’ means in this word `yo`. Because the word `pana` is merely a particle, clarifying the meaning of only the word `yo`, it is said, ‘whoever is meant.’ ‘Whoever by name’ means: whoever there is, he is called ‘whoever.’ ‘Or one yoked to the burden of residence’ means or one yoked to the burden of insight. ‘In virtues’ means in natural states.

Bhikkhatīti [M 2.0051][V 2.0045] yācati. Labhanto vā alabhanto vāti yo koci bhikkhati bhikkhaṃ esati gavesati, so taṃ labhatu vā mā vā, tathāpi bhikkhatīti bhikkhūti ayamettha adhippāyo. Ariyāya yācanāyāti “uddissa ariyā tiṭṭhanti, esā ariyāna yācanā”ti evaṃ vuttāya ariyayācanāya, na kapaṇaddhikavaṇibbakayācakānaṃ viya “dehi dehī”ti evaṃ pavattayācanāya. Bhikkhācariyanti uñchācariyaṃ. Ajjhupagatattāti anuṭṭhitattā. Kājabhattanti kājehi ānītaṃ bhattaṃ. Agghaphassavaṇṇabhedenāti agghādīnaṃ purimapakativijahena. Purimapakativijahanañhettha bhedoti adhippetaṃ. Dhovitvā apanetuṃ asakkuṇeyyasabhāvaṃ malaṃ, tathā apanetuṃ sakkuṇeyyasabhāvā jallikā. Bhinnapaṭadharoti nibbacanaṃ bhinnapaṭadhare bhikkhu-saddassa niruḷhattā kataṃ.

‘He begs’ means he asks. Whether receiving or not: whoever begs, seeks alms, searches for them—whether he receives them or not, he still begs; therefore, he is called a bhikkhu.
