This is the intention here. ‘By the noble asking’ means by the noble asking spoken of thus: “The noble ones stand with a purpose; this is the asking of the noble ones.” It is not by the kind of asking that proceeds as “Give, give!” like that of miserable, wretched, and common beggars. ‘The practice of alms-gathering’ means the practice of gleaning. ‘Because of having undertaken it’ means because of having approached and stood by it. ‘Food brought by crows’ means food brought by crows. ‘By the breaking of value, touch, and appearance’ means by the abandoning of the former natural state of value, and so on. Here, ‘breaking’ is intended to mean the abandoning of the former natural state. `Mala` is dirt of a nature that cannot be removed by washing; `jallikā` is scum of a nature that can be removed. ‘Wearer of torn cloths’: the etymology is given because the word `bhikkhu` is established in the meaning of ‘wearer of torn cloths’.

Upanissayasampannanti pubbe aṭṭhaparikkhāradānūpanissayasampannaṃ. Yo hi cīvarādike aṭṭha parikkhāre pattacīvarameva vā sotāpannādiariyassa puthujjanasseva vā sīlasampannassa datvā “idaṃ parikkhāradānaṃ anāgate ehibhikkhubhāvāya paccayo hotū”ti patthanaṃ paṭṭhapesi, tassa taṃ sati adhikārasampattiyaṃ buddhānaṃ sammukhībhāve iddhimayaparikkhāralābhāya saṃvattatīti veditabbaṃ. Brahmaghosanti uttamaghosaṃ, brahmuno ghosasadisaṃ vā ghosaṃ. Brahmacariyanti sāsanabrahmacariyaṃ maggabrahmacariyañca. Dukkhassa sammā antakiriyāyāti yojetabbaṃ. Bhaṇḍūti muṇḍo. Vāsīti dantakaṭṭhacchedanavāsi. Bandhananti kāyabandhanaṃ. Yutto bhāvanānuyogo assāti yuttayogo, tassa yuttayogassa, bhāvanānuyogamanuyuttassāti vuttaṃ hoti. Iriyāpathasampannatāvibhāvanatthaṃ “saṭṭhivassikatthero viyā”ti vuttaṃ. Buddhova pabbajjācariyo upasampadācariyo ca assāti buddhācariyako. Paṭhamabodhiyampi paṭhamakāleyeva sesaupasampadānaṃ abhāvoti āha “paṭhamabodhiyaṃ ekasmiṃ kāle”ti. Pañca pañcavaggiyattherāti pañcavaggiyattherā pañca. Tīṇi satanti tīṇi satāni, gāthābandhasukhatthaṃ vacanavipallāso kato. Eko ca theroti aṅgulimālattheraṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Na vuttāti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ na vuttā. Tatthāti vinayapāḷiyaṃ.

‘Endowed with a supporting condition’ means endowed with the supporting condition of having previously given the eight requisites. For whoever, having given the eight requisites such as robes, or just a bowl and robes, to a noble one such as a stream-enterer or to a virtuous ordinary person, established the aspiration, “May this gift of requisites be a condition for the state of an ehi-bhikkhu in the future,” for him, when the attainment of eligibility is present, it should be known that this leads to the gain of requisites made by psychic power in the presence of the Buddhas. ‘Brahmaghosa’ means the supreme voice, or a voice like the voice of Brahmā. ‘The holy life’ means the holy life of the teaching and the holy life of the path; it should be connected with “for the complete ending of suffering.” ‘Bhaṇḍu’ means shaven-headed. ‘Vāsi’ means an adze for cutting tooth-wood. ‘Bandhana’ means a girdle. ‘One applied to the practice’ means one for whom there is application to the practice of meditation; it is said of one who is devoted to the practice of meditation. To illustrate the perfection of deportment, it is said, “like an elder of sixty years.” ‘One with the Buddha as teacher’ means one for whom the Buddha himself is the going-forth preceptor and the higher-ordination preceptor. Regarding the first awakening, because there was an absence of other higher ordinations at the very first time, it says “at the first awakening, at one time.” ‘The five elders of the group of five’ means the five elders of the group of five. ‘Three hundred’ means three hundreds; for the ease of constructing the verse, a grammatical inversion was made. ‘And one elder’ is said in reference to the elder Aṅgulimāla. ‘Not said’ means not said in the commentary. ‘There’ means in the Vinaya Pāḷi.

Veḷuvanamahāvihāre [M 2.0052] gandhakuṭiyaṃ nisinnoyeva bhagavā mahākassapattherassa attānaṃ uddissa pabbajitabhāvaṃ viditvā tassa paccuggamanaṃ karonto tigāvutaṃ maggaṃ ekakova gantvā bahuputtanigrodhamūle pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā nisinno attano santikaṃ āgantvā paramanipaccakāraṃ dassetvā “satthā me bhante bhagavā, sāvakohamasmi, satthā me bhante bhagavā, sāvakohamasmī”ti tikkhattuṃ attano sāvakattaṃ sāvetvā ṭhitassa mahākassapattherassa nipaccakāramahattataṃ [V 2.0046] attano ca mahānubhāvataṃ dīpetuṃ yassa aññassa ajānaṃyeva “jānāmī”ti paṭiññassa bāhirakassa satthuno evaṃ sabbacetasā samannāgato pasannacitto sāvako evarūpaṃ paramanipaccakāraṃ kareyya, tassa vaṇṭacchinnatālapakkaṃ viya gīvato muddhāpi vipateyya, sattadhā vā phaleyyāti dassento “yo kho, kassapa, evaṃ sabbacetasā samannāgataṃ sāvakaṃ ajānaṃyeva vadeyya ‘jānāmī’ti, apassaṃyeva vadeyya ‘passāmī’ti, muddhāpi tassa vipateyya, sattadhā vā phaleyya, ahaṃ kho, kassapa, jānaṃyeva vadāmi ‘jānāmī’ti, passaṃyeva vadāmi ‘passāmī’” (saṃ. ni. 2.154) ti vatvā jātimadamānamadarūpamadappahānatthaṃ tīhi ovādehi mahākassapattheraṃ ovadanto “tasmātiha te kassapā”tiādimāha.

At the Veḷuvana Mahāvihāra, while seated in the fragrant chamber, the Blessed One, knowing that the Elder Mahākassapa had gone forth for His sake, went out to meet him. He walked alone for three gāvutas and sat cross-legged at the foot of the Bahuputta banyan tree. When Mahākassapa arrived and showed the highest reverence, declaring three times, “Venerable Sir, the Blessed One is my Teacher; I am a disciple. Venerable Sir, the Blessed One is my Teacher; I am a disciple,” the Buddha, in order to reveal the greatness of such reverence and His own great power, showed that if a disciple, endowed with such a complete mind and a confident heart, were to perform such supreme reverence to any other outside teacher who, not knowing, would profess, ‘I know,’ that teacher’s head would fall from his neck like a ripe palm fruit cut from its stalk, or would split into seven pieces. He then said: “Whoever, Kassapa, not knowing a disciple endowed with such a complete mind, were to say, ‘I know,’ or not seeing, were to say, ‘I see,’ his head would fall or would split into seven pieces. But I, Kassapa, knowing, say, ‘I know,’ and seeing, say, ‘I see.’” (Cf. SN 16.11) Having spoken thus, and in order to advise the Elder Mahākassapa with three exhortations for the abandonment of pride of birth, pride of conceit, and pride of form, He began with, “Therefore, Kassapa…”

Tattha (saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 2.2.154) tasmātihāti tasmā icceva vuttaṃ hoti, yasmā ahaṃ jānantova “jānāmī”ti passanto eva ca “passāmī”ti vadāmi, tasmāti attho. Ti-kāra ha-kārā nipātā. Ihāti vā imasmiṃ sāsane, ta-kāro padasandhivasena āgato. Evaṃ sikkhitabbanti idāni vuccamānākārena sikkhitabbaṃ. Tibbanti bahalaṃ mahantaṃ. Hirottappañcāti hirī ca ottappañca. Paccupaṭṭhitaṃ bhavissatīti upasaṅkamanato paṭhamatarameva upaṭṭhitaṃ bhavissati. Tathā hi sati tesaṃ purato assa sagāravasappatissavatā saṇṭhāti. Yo ca therādīsu hirottappaṃ upaṭṭhapetvā upasaṅkamati, therādayopi taṃ sahirikā saottappā ca hutvā upasaṅkamantīti ayamettha ānisaṃso. Kusalūpasaṃhitanti kusalanissitaṃ, anavajjadhammanissitanti attho. Aṭṭhiṃ katvāti attānaṃ tena dhammena aṭṭhikaṃ katvā, taṃ vā dhammaṃ “esa mayhaṃ dhammo”ti aṭṭhiṃ katvā. Manasi katvāti citte ṭhapetvā. Sabbacetasā samannāharitvāti cittassa thokampi bahi gantuṃ adento [M 2.0053] sabbena samannāhāracittena samannāharitvā. Ohitasototi ṭhapitasoto, dhamme nihitasototi attho. Evañhi te sikkhitabbanti ñāṇasotañca pasādasotañca odahitvā “mayā desitaṃ dhammaṃ sakkaccameva suṇissāmī”ti evañhi te sikkhitabbaṃ. Sātasahagatā ca me kāyagatāsatīti asubhesu ceva ānāpāne ca paṭhamajjhānavasena sukhasampayuttā kāyagatāsati. Yo ca panāyaṃ tividho ovādo, therassa ayameva pabbajjā ca upasampadā ca ahosi.

Herein, `tasmātihāti` means 'therefore, here' (`tasmā idha`). Because I, knowing, say, 'I know,' and seeing, say, 'I see,' therefore—this is the meaning. The syllables `ti` and `ha` are particles. `iha` means 'in this dispensation,' and the syllable `ta` has come about through euphonic combination. `evaṃ sikkhitabbaṃ` means one should train in the manner now being explained. `tibbaṃ` means intense, abundant, great. `hirottappaṃ` means moral shame and moral dread. `paccupaṭṭhitaṃ bhavissati` means it will be present even before approaching. For when this is so, reverence and deference are established in their presence. And whoever, having established moral shame and dread towards elders and so on, approaches them, the elders too, having moral shame and dread, approach them—this is the benefit herein. `kusalūpasaṃhitaṃ` means based on the wholesome, that is, based on blameless qualities. `aṭṭhiṃ katvā` means making oneself desirous of that Dhamma, or making that Dhamma the essence, thinking, 'This is my Dhamma.' `manasi katvā` means having placed it in the mind. `sabbacetasā samannāharitvā` means having brought the mind to bear completely, not allowing even a little of it to go outside. `ohitasoto` means one with an applied ear, that is, one with an ear directed to the Dhamma. `evaṃ hi te sikkhitabbaṃ` means you should train thus: having inclined the ear of wisdom and the ear of confidence, thinking, 'I will listen carefully to the Dhamma taught by me.' `sātasahagatā ca me kāyagatāsati` means mindfulness directed to the body, conjoined with pleasure by way of the first jhāna, in regard to the foul and to breathing. And this threefold instruction was indeed the Elder’s going forth and higher ordination.

Kasiṇārammaṇaṃ rūpāvacarajjhānaṃ rūpasaññā. Saññāsīsena hettha jhānaṃ vuttaṃ, tadeva ca uddhumātakapaṭibhāgārammaṇattā “uddhumātakasaññā”ti vuttaṃ. Sopākasāmaṇero bhagavatā puṭṭho “ete dve rūpāvacarabhāvena ekatthā, byañjanameva nāna”nti āha. Āraddhacittoti ārādhitacitto. Garudhammapaṭiggahaṇādiupasampadā upari vitthārato sayameva āvi bhavissati.

The form-sphere jhāna which has a kasiṇa as its object is the perception of form. Herein, jhāna is spoken of under the heading of perception, and that very jhāna, because it has the counterpart sign of a bloated corpse as its object, is called 'the perception of a bloated corpse.' The novice Sopāka, when asked by the Blessed One, said, “These two are one in meaning through their nature as form-sphere states; only the expression is different.” `āraddhacittoti` means one with a pleased mind. The higher ordination, beginning with the acceptance of the weighty principles, will become clear in detail later on.

Kalyāṇaputhujjanādayoti [V 2.0047] ettha bahūnaṃ nānappakārānaṃ sakkāyadiṭṭhiādīnaṃ avihatattā janeti, tāhi vā janitoti puthujjano, kalyāṇo ca so puthujjano cāti kalyāṇaputhujjano, so ādi yesaṃ sotāpannādīnaṃ te kalyāṇaputhujjanādayo. Kalyāṇaggahaṇena cettha andhaputhujjanaṃ nivatteti. Dvidhā hi puthujjanā andhaputhujjano kalyāṇaputhujjanoti. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Regarding `kalyāṇaputhujjanādayo` (good worldlings and others): herein, because one has not destroyed the many various kinds of personality view and so on, one generates them, or is generated by them; thus, one is a `puthujjano` (worldling). And that worldling is good, thus a `kalyāṇaputhujjano` (good worldling). He is the beginning of those such as stream-enterers; thus, they are the good worldlings and others. Herein, by the inclusion of 'good', the blind worldling is excluded. For worldlings are twofold: the blind worldling and the good worldling. As it is said:

“Duve puthujjanā vuttā, buddhenādiccabandhunā;

Andho puthujjano eko, kalyāṇeko puthujjano”ti. (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.7; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.2; saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 2.2.61; a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.51);

“Two worldlings are spoken of by the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun: one is a blind worldling, and one is a good worldling.”

Bhadrāya paññāya bhadrāya vimuttiyāti yojetabbaṃ. Sīlenātiādīsu sīlanti catupārisuddhisīlaṃ. Samādhīti vipassanāpādakā aṭṭha samāpattiyo. Paññāti lokiyalokuttarañāṇaṃ. Vimuttīti ariyaphalavimutti. Vimuttiñāṇadassananti ekūnavīsatividhaṃ paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ. Yathāsambhavena cettha yojanā veditabbā. Kalyāṇaputhujjanassa hi sīlādayo tayo eva sambhavanti, ariyānaṃ pana sabbepi sīlādayo. Sāro bhikkhūtipi kalyāṇaputhujjanādayova vuttāti āha “tehiyeva sīlasārādīhī”tiādi. Atha vā nippariyāyato khīṇāsavova sāro [M 2.0054] bhikkhu nāmāti āha “vigatakilesapheggubhāvato vā”tiādi.

It should be connected as “with excellent wisdom, with excellent liberation.” In the phrases beginning with “by virtue,” `sīla` is the fourfold purity of virtue. `samādhi` is the eight attainments that are the basis for insight. `paññā` is mundane and supramundane knowledge. `vimutti` is the liberation of the noble fruition. `vimuttiñāṇadassana` is the nineteenfold reviewing knowledge. Herein, the connection should be understood as is appropriate. For a good worldling, only the first three, beginning with virtue, are possible; but for the noble ones, all those beginning with virtue are possible. When it is said, “a monk who is the essence,” this refers to the good worldlings and others, as stated: “by those very essences of virtue, and so on.” Alternatively, in the direct sense, only one whose cankers are destroyed is called a monk who is the essence, as stated: “or because of being devoid of the worthlessness of defilements, etc.”

Yopi kalyāṇaputhujjano anulomapaṭipadāya paripūrakārī sīlasampanno indriyesu guttadvāro bhojane mattaññū jāgariyānuyogamanuyutto pubbarattāpararattaṃ bodhipakkhiyānaṃ dhammānaṃ bhāvanānuyogamanuyutto viharati “ajja vā sve vā aññataraṃ sāmaññaphalaṃ adhigamissāmī”ti, sopi vuccati sikkhatīti sekhoti āha “puthujjanakalyāṇakena saddhi”nti. Satta ariyāti cattāro maggaṭṭhā, heṭṭhimā ca tayo phalaṭṭhāti ime satta ariyā. Tisso sikkhāti adhisīlādikā tisso sikkhā. Sikkhāsu jātoti vā sekho. Ariyapuggalo hi ariyāya jātiyā jāyamāno sikkhāsu jāyati, na yoniyaṃ. Sikkhanasīloti vā sekho, puggalādhiṭṭhānāya vā kathāya sekhassa ayanti anaññasādhāraṇā maggaphalattayadhammā sekhapariyāyena vuttā. Asekhoti ca yattha sekhabhāvāsaṅkā atthi, tatthāyaṃ paṭisedhoti lokiyanibbānesu asekhabhāvānāpatti daṭṭhabbā. Sīlasamādhipaññāsaṅkhātā hi sikkhā attano paṭipakkhakilesehi vimuttattā parisuddhā, upakkilesānaṃ ārammaṇabhāvampi anupagamanato [V 2.0048] etā sikkhāti vattuṃ yuttā, aṭṭhasupi maggaphalesu vijjanti, tasmā catumaggaheṭṭhimaphalattayasamaṅgino viya arahattaphalasamaṅgīpi tāsu sikkhāsu jātoti taṃsamaṅgino arahato itaresaṃ viya sekhatte sati sekhassa ayanti, sikkhā sīlaṃ etassāti ca sekhoti vattabbo siyāti taṃ nivattanatthaṃ “asekho”ti yathāvuttasekhabhāvapaṭisedho kato. Arahattaphalehi pavattamānā sikkhā pariniṭṭhitasikkhākiccattā na sikkhākiccaṃ karonti, kevalaṃ sikkhāphalabhāveneva pavattanti, tasmā tā na sikkhāvacanaṃ arahanti, nāpi taṃsamaṅgī sekhavacanaṃ, na ca sikkhanasīlo, sikkhāsu jātoti ca vattabbataṃ arahati, heṭṭhimaphalesu pana sikkhā sakadāgāmimaggavipassanādīnaṃ upanissayabhāvato sikkhākiccaṃ karontīti sikkhāvacanaṃ arahanti, taṃsamaṅgino ca sekhavacanaṃ sikkhanasīlā, sikkhāsu jātāti ca vattabbataṃ arahanti “sikkhantīti sekhā”ti apariyositasikkhānaṃ dassitattā, “na sikkhatīti asekho”ti iminā pariyositasikkho dassito, na sikkhāya rahitoti āha – “sekkhadhamme atikkamma [M 2.0055] …pe… khīṇāsavo asekhoti vuccatī”ti. Vuddhippattasikkho vā asekhoti etasmiṃ atthe sekhadhammesu eva ṭhitassa kassaci ariyassa asekhabhāvāpattīti arahattamaggadhammā vuddhippattā ca yathāvuttehi atthehi sekhāti katvā taṃsamaṅgino aggamaggaṭṭhassa asekhabhāvo āpannoti? Na, taṃsadisesu tabbohārato. Arahattamaggato hi ninnānākaraṇaṃ arahattaphalaṃ ṭhapetvā pariññākiccakaraṇaṃ vipākabhāvañca, tasmā te eva sekhā aggaphaladhammabhāvaṃ āpannāti sakkā vattuṃ. Kusalasukhato ca vipākasukhaṃ santataratāya paṇītataranti vuddhippattā ca te dhammā hontīti taṃsamaṅgī asekhoti vuccatīti.

Even a good worldling who, following the conforming practice, is a fulfiller, is endowed with virtue, has guarded doors in the sense faculties, knows the measure in food, is devoted to the practice of wakefulness, and dwells devoted to the development of the factors of enlightenment in the early and late watches of the night, thinking, 'Today or tomorrow I will attain one or another fruit of recluseship'—he too is said to be one who trains, hence a learner (sekho); thus it is said, 'together with a good worldling.' The seven noble ones are the four established in the path and the three lower ones established in the fruit; these are the seven noble ones. The three trainings are the three trainings beginning with higher virtue. Or, one is a learner because one is 'born in the trainings' (sikkhāsu jāto). For a noble person, being born by a noble birth, is born in the trainings, not in a womb. Or, one is a learner because one's 'nature is to train' (sikkhanasīlo). Or, in a discourse based on the person, the dhammas of the three paths and fruits, which are not common to others, are called 'sekha' by way of designation for a learner. And 'non-learner' (asekho) is a negation where there is a doubt about the state of being a learner; thus, the non-attainment of the state of a non-learner in the mundane and Nibbāna should be understood. For the trainings, designated as virtue, concentration, and wisdom, are pure because they are liberated from their opposing defilements, and it is fitting to call them 'trainings' because they do not even approach the state of being an object for the corruptions. They are found in all eight paths and fruits. Therefore, just as one endowed with the four paths and the three lower fruits, so too one endowed with the fruit of Arahantship is 'born in those trainings'. Thus, for that one endowed, the Arahant, if he were a learner like the others, it could be said 'this is of the learner' and 'training is his nature', and he could be called a 'learner'. To prevent this, the negation of the state of being a learner as stated, 'non-learner', is made. The trainings that proceed by means of the fruit of Arahantship, because the task of training is completed, do not perform the function of training; they proceed only as the result of training. Therefore, they are not worthy of the term 'training', nor is one endowed with them worthy of the term 'learner', nor is it right to say of him that his 'nature is to train' or he is 'born in the trainings'. In the lower fruits, however, the trainings, because they are a basis for the path of the once-returner, insight, and so on, do perform the function of training, and thus are worthy of the term 'training'. And those endowed with them are worthy of the term 'learner' and of being called 'one whose nature is to train' and 'born in the trainings', because 'they train (sikkhanti), thus they are learners (sekhā)' shows those with incomplete training, while 'he does not train (na sikkhati), thus he is a non-learner (asekho)' shows one with completed training. It is not that he is without training; thus it is said: 'Having gone beyond the dhammas of a learner... the one whose cankers are destroyed is called a non-learner'. Or, a non-learner is one whose training has reached growth. In this sense, for some noble one established in the very dhammas of a learner, there is the attainment of the state of a non-learner. And since the dhammas of the Arahant path have reached growth and are 'trainings' according to the meanings stated, has the state of a non-learner been attained by one endowed with them, one on the highest path? No, because of that designation for those similar to him. For, setting aside the fruit of Arahantship from the path of Arahantship, the performance of the function of full understanding and the state of being a result are different causes. Therefore, it cannot be said that those very learners have attained the state of the dhammas of the highest fruit. And because resultant happiness is more peaceful and more sublime than wholesome happiness, and those dhammas have reached growth, one endowed with them is called a non-learner.

Sabbantimena pariyāyenāti sabbantimena paricchedena. Upasampadākammassa adhikārattā “pañcavaggakaraṇīye”ti vuttaṃ. Pañcannaṃ vaggo samūhoti pañcavaggo, pañcaparimāṇayutto vā vaggo pañcavaggo, tena kattabbaṃ kammaṃ pañcavaggakaraṇīyaṃ. Yāvatikā bhikkhūti yattakā bhikkhū. Kammappattāti kammārahā pārājikaṃ anāpannā anukkhittā ca. Upasampadākammassa pañcavaggakaraṇīyattā pañceva bhikkhū kammappattā ettakehipi kammasiddhito, itare chandārahā. Ñatticatutthenāti ettha kiñcāpi ñatti sabbapaṭhamaṃ vuccati, tissannaṃ pana anussāvanānaṃ atthabyañjanabhedābhāvato atthabyañjanabhinnā ñatti tāsaṃ catutthāti katvā “ñatticatuttha”nti vuccati. Byañjanānurūpameva aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “tīhi anussāvanāhi ekāya ca ñattiyā”ti vuttaṃ, atthappavattikkamena pana “ekāya ñattiyā tīhi anussāvanāhī”ti vattabbaṃ. Vatthuñattianaussāvanasīmāparisasampattisampannattāti ettha vatthūti upasampadāpekkho puggalo, so ṭhapetvā ūnavīsativassaṃ [V 2.0049] antimavatthuṃ ajjhāpannapubbaṃ paṇḍakādayo ca ekādasa abhabbapuggale veditabbo. Ūnavīsativassādayo hi terasa puggalā upasampadāya avatthu, ime pana ṭhapetvā aññasmiṃ upasampadāpekkhe sati upasampadākammaṃ vatthusampattisampannaṃ nāma hoti.

“By the very last designation” means by the very last definition. Because it is the authority for the act of higher ordination, it is called “to be done by a group of five.” A collection of five is a five-group; or a group endowed with the measure of five is a five-group. The act to be done by it is “to be done by a five-group.” “As many monks” means however many monks. “Qualified for the act” means worthy of the act: those who have not fallen into a pārājika offense and have not been suspended. Because the act of higher ordination is to be done by a group of five, only five monks are qualified for the act. With just this many the act is accomplished; the others are worthy of giving consent. Regarding “with the motion as the fourth”: here, although the motion is stated first, because the three announcements have no difference in meaning and phrasing, the motion, which is different in meaning and phrasing, is made the fourth of them, and thus it is called “with the motion as the fourth.” Corresponding to the phrasing, it is said in the commentary, “with three announcements and one motion”; but according to the sequence of how the meaning proceeds, it should be said, “with one motion and three announcements.” Regarding “because it is endowed with the accomplishment of the individual, motion, announcements, boundary, and assembly”: here, “individual” (vatthu) means the person aspiring to higher ordination. He is to be understood by excluding one under twenty years of age, one who has previously committed an extreme offense, a eunuch, and so on—the eleven unsuitable persons. Indeed, those under twenty years of age and so on—thirteen persons—are non-individuals (avatthu) for higher ordination. But excluding these, when there is another person aspiring to higher ordination, the act of higher ordination is called “endowed with the accomplishment of the individual.”

Vatthusaṅghapuggalañattīnaṃ aparāmasanāni pacchā ñattiṭṭhapanañcāti ime tāva pañca ñattidosā. Tattha “ayaṃ itthannāmo”ti upasampadāpekkhassa akittanaṃ vatthuaparāmasanaṃ nāma. “Suṇātu me, bhante, saṅgho”ti ettha “suṇātu me, bhante”ti vatvā “saṅgho”ti abhaṇanaṃ saṅghaaparāmasanaṃ nāma. “Itthannāmassa upasampadāpekkho”ti upajjhāyassa akittanaṃ puggalaaparāmasanaṃ [M 2.0056] nāma. Sabbena sabbaṃ ñattiyā anuccāraṇaṃ ñattiaparāmasanaṃ nāma. Paṭhamaṃ kammavācaṃ niṭṭhāpetvā “esā ñattī”ti vatvā “khamati saṅghassā”ti evaṃ ñattikittanaṃ pacchā ñattiṭṭhapanaṃ nāma. Iti imehi dosehi vimuttāya ñattiyā sampannaṃ ñattisampattisampannaṃ nāma.

These, firstly, are the five faults of a motion: the non-mentioning of the candidate (vatthu), the Sangha, the preceptor (puggala), and the motion itself, and placing the motion afterwards. Therein, not stating of the one seeking higher ordination, “This is so-and-so,” is called non-mentioning of the candidate. In the phrase, “May the Sangha hear me, venerable sirs,” having said, “May it hear me, venerable sirs,” and not saying, “the Sangha,” is called non-mentioning of the Sangha. Not stating of the preceptor, “[the candidate] is the aspirant for higher ordination of so-and-so,” is called non-mentioning of the preceptor. The non-reciting of the motion in its entirety is called non-mentioning of the motion. Having first completed the announcements and then stating the motion—for instance by saying, “This is the motion… it is agreeable to the Sangha”—is called placing the motion afterwards. Thus, being endowed with a motion that is free from these faults is called being endowed with the accomplishment of the motion.

Vatthusaṅghapuggalānaṃ aparāmasanāni sāvanāya hāpanaṃ akāle sāvananti ime pañca anussāvanadosā. Tattha vatthādīnaṃ aparāmasanāni ñattiyaṃ vuttasadisāneva. Tīsu pana anussāvanāsu yattha katthaci etesaṃ aparāmasanaṃ aparāmasanameva, sabbena sabbaṃ pana kammavācaṃ avatvā catukkhattuṃ ñattikittanameva. Atha vā pana kammavācabbhantare akkharassa vā padassa vā anuccāraṇaṃ vā duruccāraṇaṃ vā sāvanāya hāpanaṃ nāma. Sāvanāya anokāse paṭhamaṃ ñattiṃ aṭṭhapetvā anussāvanakaraṇaṃ akāle sāvanaṃ nāma. Iti imehi dosehi vimuttāya anussāvanāya sampannaṃ anussāvanasampattisampannaṃ nāma.

These five are the faults of an announcement: the non-mentioning of the candidate, the Sangha, and the preceptor; omission from the announcement; and an untimely announcement. Therein, the non-mentioning of the candidate and so on are just as stated in the case of the motion. But in the three announcements, the non-mentioning of these anywhere is simply non-mentioning. Furthermore, not reciting the announcement text in its entirety but only stating the motion four times; or else, within the announcement text, the non-reciting or mispronouncing of a syllable or a word, is called omission from the announcement. Making the announcement on an unsuitable occasion, without having first established the motion, is called an untimely announcement. Thus, being endowed with an announcement that is free from these faults is called being endowed with the accomplishment of the announcement.

Vipattisīmālakkhaṇaṃ samatikkantāya pana sīmāya kataṃ sīmāsampattisampannaṃ nāma. Yāvatikā bhikkhū kammappattā, tesaṃ anāgamanaṃ, chandārahānaṃ chandassa anāharaṇaṃ, sammukhībhūtānaṃ paṭikkosananti ime pana tayo parisadosā, tehi vimuttāya parisāya kataṃ parisasampattisampannaṃ nāma.

Furthermore, what is done in a boundary that has overcome the characteristics of a faulty boundary is called being endowed with the accomplishment of the boundary. These three are the faults of the assembly: the non-arrival of as many monks as are eligible for the act, the not bringing of the consent of those who are entitled to give consent, and the protest of those who are present. What is done by an assembly that is free from these faults is called being endowed with the accomplishment of the assembly.

Upasampadākammavācāsaṅkhātaṃ bhagavato vacanaṃ upasampadākammakaraṇassa kāraṇattā ṭhānaṃ, yathā ca taṃ kattabbanti bhagavatā anusiṭṭhaṃ, tathā katattā tadanucchavikaṃ yathāvuttaṃ anūnaṃ ñattianussāvanaṃ uppaṭipāṭiyā ca avuttaṃ ṭhānārahaṃ. Yathā kattabbanti hi bhagavatā vuttaṃ, tathā akate upasampadākammassa kāraṇaṃ na hotīti na taṃ ṭhānārahaṃ. Tenāha “kāraṇārahena satthusāsanārahenā”ti. Iminā ñattianussāvanasampatti kathitāti veditabbā. “Samaggena saṅghenā”ti [V 2.0050] iminā pana parisasampatti kathitāva. “Akuppenā”ti iminā pārisesato vatthusīmāsampattiyo kathitāti veditabbā. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana akuppalakkhaṇaṃ ekattha sampiṇḍetvā dassetuṃ akuppenāti imassa “vatthuñattianussāvanasīmāparisasampattisampannattā akopetabbataṃ appaṭikkositabbataṃ upagatenā”ti attho vutto. Keci pana “ṭhānārahenātiettha ‘na hatthacchinno pabbājetabbo’tiādi (mahāva. 119) satthusāsanaṃ ṭhāna”nti vadanti.

The Blessed One's word, designated as the formal act of higher ordination, is a basis, since it is the cause for performing the act of higher ordination. And as it has been instructed by the Blessed One how it should be done, because it is done so, the motion and announcements—being suitable, as stated, without deficiency, and not stated out of sequence—are worthy of being a basis. For it has been said by the Blessed One, “It should be done thus”; if it is not done so, it is not a cause for the act of higher ordination, and thus it is not worthy of being a basis. Therefore, he said, “by what is worthy of being a cause, worthy of the Teacher’s instruction.” By this, it should be known that the accomplishment of the motion and announcements is stated. But by this, “By a united Sangha,” the accomplishment of the assembly is indeed stated. By this, “By what is unshakeable,” it should be known that the accomplishments of the candidate and the boundary are stated by implication. In the commentary, however, to show the characteristic of “unshakeable” by summarizing it in one place, the meaning of “by what is unshakeable” is given as: “because it is endowed with the accomplishment of the candidate, motion, announcements, boundary, and assembly, it has attained a state that cannot be shaken and cannot be protested against.” Some, however, say that here, in “worthy of being a basis,” the Teacher’s instruction, such as “one whose hand is cut off should not be given the going forth,” etc., is the basis.

“Ñatticatutthena [M 2.0057] kammenā”ti imasmiṃ adhikāre pasaṅgato āharitvā yaṃ kammalakkhaṇaṃ sabbaaṭṭhakathāsu papañcitaṃ, taṃ yathāāgataṭṭhāneyeva dassetukāmo idha tassa avacane tattha vacane ca payojanaṃ dassetuṃ “imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne ṭhatvā”tiādimāha.

In this section on “by a formal act with the motion as fourth,” having brought up in this connection the characteristic of the formal act which is elaborated in all the commentaries, and wishing to present it only in its proper place, and to show the purpose for its not being stated here but being stated there, the author said, “But standing in this place,” and so on.

Aṭṭhasu upasampadāsu ehibhikkhūpasampadā saraṇagamanūpasampadā ovādapaṭiggahaṇūpasampadā pañhabyākaraṇūpasampadāti imāhi upasampadāhi upasampannānaṃ lokavajjasikkhāpadavītikkame abhabbattā garudhammapaṭiggahaṇūpasampadā dūtenūpasampadā aṭṭhavācikūpasampadāti imāsañca tissannaṃ upasampadānaṃ bhikkhunīnaṃyeva anuññātattā ñatticatuttheneva kammena upasampanno gahitoti veditabbo. Tathā hi ehibhikkhūpasampadā antimabhavikānaṃyeva, saraṇagamanūpasampadā parisuddhānaṃ, ovādapaṭiggahaṇapañhabyākaraṇūpasampadā mahākassapasopākānaṃ, na ca te bhabbā pārājikādilokavajjaṃ āpajjituṃ, garudhammapaṭiggahaṇādayo ca bhikkhunīnaṃyeva anuññātā, ayañca bhikkhu, tasmā ettha ñatticatutthena upasampannova gahitoti veditabbo.

Among the eight kinds of higher ordination, because those ordained by these higher ordinations—the ehi-bhikkhu higher ordination, the higher ordination by taking refuge, the higher ordination by acceptance of the exhortation, and the higher ordination by answering a question—are incapable of transgressing training rules that are worldly faults; and because these three higher ordinations—the higher ordination by acceptance of the weighty rules, the higher ordination by a messenger, and the higher ordination by eight statements—are permitted only for bhikkhunīs, it should be understood that one ordained by a formal act with a motion and three announcements is meant. For indeed, the ehi-bhikkhu higher ordination is only for those in their final existence; the higher ordination by taking refuge is for the purified; the higher ordinations by acceptance of the exhortation and by answering a question are for Mahākassapa and Sopāka, and they are not capable of falling into worldly faults such as a pārājika offense. The acceptance of the weighty rules and so on are permitted only for bhikkhunīs, and this is a bhikkhu. Therefore, it should be understood that here one ordained by a formal act with a motion and three announcements is meant.

Paṇṇattivajjesu pana sikkhāpadesu aññepi ehibhikkhūpasampadāya upasampannādayo saṅgahaṃ gacchanti. Tepi hi sahaseyyādipaṇṇattivajjaṃ āpattiṃ āpajjantiyeva. Yadi evaṃ paṇṇattivajjesupi sikkhāpadesu “ayaṃ imasmiṃ atthe adhippeto bhikkhū”ti ñatticatuttheneva kammena upasampanno kasmā vuttoti? Sabbasikkhāpadavītikkamārahattā sabbakālikattā ca. Ehibhikkhūpasampadādayo hi na sabbasikkhāpadavītikkamārahā asabbakālikā ca. Tathā hi aṭṭhasu upasampadāsu ñatticatutthakammūpasampadā dūtenūpasampadā aṭṭhavācikūpasampadāti imā tissoyeva thāvarā, sesā buddhe dharamāneyeva ahesuṃ. Teneva ca bhikkhunīvibhaṅgepi (pāci. 658) “tatra yāyaṃ bhikkhunī samaggena ubhatosaṅghena ñatticatutthena kammena akuppena ṭhānārahena upasampannā, ayaṃ imasmiṃ atthe adhippetā bhikkhunī”ti dūtenūpasampadāya aṭṭhavācikūpasampadāya ca upasampannaṃ antokatvā ubhatosaṅghena ñatticatuttheneva kammena upasampannā bhikkhunī vuttā, na garudhammapaṭiggahaṇūpasampadāya upasampannā tassā upasampadāya pāṭipuggalikabhāvato [V 2.0051] asabbakālikattā. Garudhammapaṭiggahaṇūpasampadā hi mahāpajāpatiyā eva anuññātattā pāṭipuggalikāti, tasmā sabbasikkhāpadavītikkamārahaṃ [M 2.0058] sabbakālikāya ñatticatutthakammūpasampadāya upasampannameva gahetvā sabbasikkhāpadāni paññattānīti gahetabbaṃ. Yadi evaṃ paṇṇattivajjesu sikkhāpadesu ca ehibhikkhūpasampannādīnampi saṅgaho kathaṃ viññāyatīti? Atthato āpannattā. Tathā hi “dve puggalā abhabbā āpattiṃ āpajjituṃ buddhā ca paccekabuddhā ca, dve puggalā bhabbā āpattiṃ āpajjituṃ bhikkhū ca bhikkhuniyo cā”ti (pari. 322) sāmaññato vuttattā ehibhikkhūpasampannādayopi asañcicca assatiyā acittakaṃ paṇṇattivajjaṃ sahaseyyādiāpattiṃ āpajjantīti atthato āpannanti ayamettha sāro. Yaṃ panettha ito aññathā kenaci papañcitaṃ, na taṃ sārato paccetabbaṃ.

However, in the training rules concerning offenses of designation, others such as those ordained by the ehi-bhikkhu ordination are also included. For they too indeed commit offenses of designation, such as lying down together. If so, why is it said in the training rules concerning offenses of designation, “This bhikkhu is intended in this matter,” only for one ordained by a formal act with a motion and three announcements? Because they are fit to transgress all the training rules and are for all time. For the ehi-bhikkhu ordination and the others are not fit to transgress all the training rules and are not for all time. Indeed, among the eight kinds of higher ordination, only three are stable: ordination by a formal act with a motion and three announcements, ordination by means of a messenger, and ordination by the eight statements. The rest existed only while the Buddha was alive. Therefore, in the Bhikkhunī-vibhaṅga as well, it is said, “Herein, that bhikkhunī who has been ordained by a formal act with a motion and three announcements by a complete dual Saṅgha, unalterable and fit for her status—this bhikkhunī is intended in this matter.” This means that, including those ordained by means of a messenger and by the eight statements, a bhikkhunī ordained by a formal act with a motion and three announcements by a complete dual Saṅgha is spoken of, not one ordained by acceptance of the weighty rules, because that ordination is individual and not for all time. For the ordination by acceptance of the weighty rules is individual because it was permitted only for Mahāpajāpatī. Therefore, it should be understood that all the training rules are laid down taking into account only one who is ordained by a formal act with a motion and three announcements, which is fit for transgressing all the training rules and is for all time. If so, how is the inclusion of those ordained by the ehi-bhikkhu ordination and the others understood in the training rules concerning offenses of designation? Because they fall under it by way of meaning. For it is said in general, “Two persons are incapable of committing an offense: Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas. Two persons are capable of committing an offense: bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs.” Thus, those ordained by the ehi-bhikkhu ordination and the others also, unintentionally, unmindfully, without intention, commit an offense of designation, such as lying down together—they fall under it by way of meaning. This is the essence here. Whatever has been elaborated here otherwise by anyone, that should not be accepted as the essence.

Niruttivasenāti nibbacanavasena. Abhilāpavasenāti vohāravasena. Anuppannāya kammavācāyāti anuppannāya ñatticatutthakammavācāya. Guṇavasenāti sīlāditaṃtaṃguṇayogato. Ettha ca bhindati pāpake akusale dhammeti bhikkhūti nibbacanaṃ veditabbaṃ.

By way of etymology means by way of derivation. By way of expression means by way of conventional usage. “Anuppannāya kammavācāya” means by a formal act with a motion and three announcements that has not yet arisen. “By way of qualities” means by way of association with those various qualities such as morality and so forth. And here, the derivation “He breaks up evil, unwholesome states, thus he is a bhikkhu” should be understood.

Bhikkhupadabhājanīyavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Analysis of the Word 'Bhikkhu' is concluded.

Sikkhāsājīvapadabhājanīyavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Analysis of the Terms 'Training' and 'Livelihood'

Sikkhitabbāti āsevitabbā. Uttamanti visiṭṭhaṃ. Adhisīlādīsu vijjamānesu sīlādīhipi bhavitabbaṃ. Yathā hi omakatarappamāṇaṃ chattaṃ vā dhajaṃ vā upādāya atirekappamāṇaṃ “atichattaṃ atidhajo”ti vuccati, evamihāpi “anukkaṭṭhasīlaṃ upādāya adhisīlena bhavitabbaṃ, tathā anukkaṭṭhaṃ cittaṃ paññañca upādāya adhicittena adhipaññāya ca bhavitabba”nti manasi katvā sīlādiṃ sarūpato vibhāvetukāmo “katamaṃ panettha sīla”ntiādimāha. Aṭṭhaṅgasīlaṃ dasaṅgasīlesveva antogadhattā visuṃ aggahetvā “pañcaṅgadasaṅgasīla”nti ettakameva vuttaṃ. Pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlanti cārittavārittavasena duvidhaṃ vinayapiṭakapariyāpannaṃ sikkhāpadasīlaṃ. Tañhi yo naṃ pāti rakkhati, taṃ mokkheti moceti āpāyikādīhi dukkhehīti pātimokkhanti vuccati. Saṃvaraṇaṃ saṃvaro[M 2.0059], kāyavācāhi avītikkamo. Pātimokkhameva saṃvaro pātimokkhasaṃvaro. So eva sīlanaṭṭhena sīlanti pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlaṃ.

“Should be trained” means should be cultivated. “Supreme” means distinguished. When there are such things as higher morality, there must also be morality and so forth as their basis. For just as, with reference to an umbrella or a banner of an inferior measure, an excessive measure is called “an over-umbrella” or “an over-banner,” so too here, having considered that “with reference to non-excellent morality, there must be higher morality, and similarly, with reference to non-excellent mind and wisdom, there must be higher mind and higher wisdom,” and wishing to explain morality and so forth according to its own nature, he said, “What, here, is morality?” and so on. Since the eight-precept morality is included within the ten-precept morality, not taking it separately, only “the five-precept and ten-precept morality” is mentioned. The Pātimokkha-restraint morality is the two-fold training-rule morality included in the Vinaya Piṭaka, by way of conduct to be followed and conduct to be avoided. For it protects one who guards it, and it liberates, it frees from sufferings such as those of the woeful states; therefore, it is called Pātimokkha. Restraining is restraint: non-transgression with body and speech. The Pātimokkha itself is restraint, thus Pātimokkha-restraint. That very thing, in the sense of being a foundation, is morality, thus it is Pātimokkha-restraint morality.

Aparo [V 2.0052] nayo (udā. aṭṭha. 31; itivu. aṭṭha. 97) – kilesānaṃ balavabhāvato pāpakiriyāya sukarabhāvato puññakiriyāya ca dukkarabhāvato bahukkhattuṃ apāyesu patanasīloti pātī, puthujjano. Aniccatāya vā bhavābhavādīsu kammavegakkhitto ghaṭiyantaṃ viya anavaṭṭhānena paribbhamanato gamanasīloti pātī, maraṇavasena vā tamhi tamhi sattanikāye attabhāvassa patanasīloti pātī, sattasantāno, cittameva vā. Taṃ pātinaṃ saṃsāradukkhato mokkhetīti pātimokkhaṃ. Cittassa hi vimokkhena satto vimuttoti vuccati. Vuttañhi “cittavodānā visujjhantī”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.100), “anupādāya āsavehi cittaṃ vimutta”nti (mahāva. 28) ca.

Another explanation: because of the strength of the defilements, the ease of doing evil, and the difficulty of doing good, the worldling is called “pāti,” as he has the nature to fall into the woeful states frequently. Or, because of impermanence, being tossed by the force of kamma in various states of existence, wandering unstably like a potter's wheel, he is called “pāti” because he has the nature to go. Or, by way of death, the continuity of a being, or even the mind itself, is called “pāti” because it has the nature to fall into an individual existence in each and every group of beings. It liberates that “pāti” (one who falls) from the suffering of saṃsāra, thus it is Pātimokkha. For by the liberation of the mind, a being is said to be liberated. For it is said: “they are purified by the purification of the mind,” and “the mind is liberated from the taints through non-clinging.”

Atha vā avijjādinā hetunā saṃsāre patati gacchati pavattatīti pāti. “Avijjānīvaraṇānaṃ sattānaṃ taṇhāsaṃyojanānaṃ sandhāvataṃ saṃsarata”nti (saṃ. ni. 2.124) hi vuttaṃ. Tassa pātino sattassa taṇhādisaṃkilesattayato mokkho etenāti pātimokkho. “Kaṇṭhekāḷo”tiādīnaṃ viyassa samāsasiddhi veditabbā.

Alternatively, because of causes such as ignorance, one falls, goes, or proceeds in saṃsāra, thus one is a “pāti.” For it is said: “For beings hindered by ignorance, fettered by craving, running on, wandering on…” By this, there is liberation for that “pāti” being from the three defilements starting with craving, thus it is Pātimokkha. The formation of this compound should be understood like that of “Kaṇṭhekāḷo” and so on.

Atha vā pāteti vinipāteti dukkhehīti pāti, cittaṃ. Vuttañhi “cittena nīyati loko, cittena parikassatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.62). Tassa pātino mokkho etenāti pātimokkho. Patati vā etena apāyadukkhe saṃsāradukkhe cāti pāti, taṇhāsaṃkileso. Vuttañhi “taṇhā janeti purisaṃ (saṃ. ni. 1.55-57), taṇhādutiyo puriso”ti (a. ni. 4.9; itivu. 15, 105) ca ādi. Tato pātito mokkhoti pātimokkho.

Or, because it causes one to fall, causes downfall through sufferings, it is called “pāti”—the mind. For it has been said: 'The world is led by the mind, by the mind it is dragged around.' By this, there is liberation from that which causes one to fall, thus it is Pātimokkha. Or, because by this one falls into the suffering of the woeful states and the suffering of saṃsāra, it is called “pāti”—the defilement of craving. For it has been said: 'Craving generates a person,' and 'a person has craving as a companion,' and so on. Liberation from that which causes one to fall is Pātimokkha.

Atha vā patati etthāti pāti, cha ajjhattikabāhirāni āyatanāni. Vuttañhi “chasu loko samuppanno, chasu kubbati santhava”nti (saṃ. ni. 1.70; su. ni. 171). Tato chaajjhattikabāhirāyatanasaṅkhātato pātito mokkhoti pātimokkho.

Or, because one falls herein, it is called “pāti”—the six internal and external sense bases. For it has been said: 'The world arises in the six, in the six it makes acquaintance.' Liberation from that place of falling, designated as the six internal and external sense bases, is Pātimokkha.

Atha [M 2.0060] vā pāto vinipāto assa atthīti pātī, saṃsāro. Tato mokkhoti pātimokkho.

Or, because it has falling and downfall, it is called “pātī”—saṃsāra. Liberation from that is Pātimokkha.

Atha vā sabbalokādhipatibhāvato dhammissaro bhagavā patīti vuccati, muccati etenāti mokkho, patino mokkho tena paññattattāti patimokkho, patimokkho eva pātimokkho. Sabbaguṇānaṃ vā mūlabhāvato uttamaṭṭhena pati ca so yathāvuttena atthena mokkho cāti [V 2.0053] patimokkho, patimokkho eva pātimokkho. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “pātimokkhanti mukhametaṃ pamukhameta”nti (mahāva. 135) vitthāro.

Or, because of being the lord of the entire world, the Blessed One, the sovereign of the Dhamma, is called “pati.” That by which one is liberated is “mokkho.” It is the Lord’s (teaching of) liberation because it was laid down by him, thus it is Patimokkha; Patimokkha itself is Pātimokkha. Or, because it is the root of all virtues, it is “pati” in the sense of 'supreme'; and it is “mokkho” in the aforementioned sense; thus it is Patimokkho; Patimokkho itself is Pātimokkha. For so it has been said: 'This Pātimokkha is the beginning, this is the foremost,' in detail.

Atha vā pa-iti pakāre, atīti accantatthe nipāto, tasmā pakārehi accantaṃ mokkhetīti pātimokkho. Idañhi sīlaṃ sayaṃ tadaṅgavasena samādhisahitaṃ paññāsahitañca vikkhambhanavasena samucchedavasena ca accantaṃ mokkheti mocetīti pātimokkho.

Or, “pa-” is a particle in the sense of 'modes'; “ati-” is a particle in the sense of 'exceedingly'. Therefore, because it exceedingly liberates by various modes, it is Pātimokkha. For this virtue, itself through liberation by substitution, and when accompanied by concentration and wisdom, through suppression and eradication, exceedingly liberates and sets free; therefore, it is Pātimokkha.

Pati pati mokkhoti vā patimokkho, tamhā tamhā vītikkamadosato paccekaṃ mokkhetīti attho, patimokkho eva pātimokkho. Mokkho vā nibbānaṃ, tassa mokkhassa paṭibimbabhūtoti patimokkho. Sīlasaṃvaro hi sūriyassa aruṇuggamanaṃ viya nibbānassa udayabhūto tappaṭibhāgo ca yathārahaṃ kilesanibbāpanato, patimokkhoyeva pātimokkho. Pativattati mokkhābhimukhanti vā patimokkhaṃ, patimokkhameva pātimokkhanti evaṃ tāvettha pātimokkhasaddassa attho veditabbo.

Or, because it liberates in each respective case (“pati pati mokkho”), it is Patimokkho; the meaning is that it liberates individually from each respective fault of transgression. Patimokkho itself is Pātimokkha. Or, “mokkho” is Nibbāna; because this is a reflection of that liberation, it is Patimokkho. For restraint by morality is the arising of Nibbāna, like the dawn for the sun, and it is its counterpart because it appropriately extinguishes the defilements; Patimokkho itself is Pātimokkha. Or, because it proceeds facing liberation, it is Patimokkha; Patimokkha itself is Pātimokkha. In this way, then, the meaning of the word Pātimokkha is to be understood here.

Saṃvarati pidahati etenāti saṃvaro, pātimokkhameva saṃvaro pātimokkhasaṃvaro. So eva sīlaṃ pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlaṃ, atthato pana tato tato vītikkamitabbato viratiyo ceva cetanā ca.

Because by this one restrains and closes off, it is called “saṃvaro” (restraint). The Pātimokkha itself is restraint, thus Pātimokkha-restraint. That itself is virtue, thus the virtue of Pātimokkha-restraint. In terms of meaning, however, it is the abstinences and the volitions concerning those things to be transgressed in each respective case.

Adhisīlanti vuccatīti anavasesato kāyikavācasikasaṃvarabhāvato ca maggasīlassa padaṭṭhānabhāvato ca pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlaṃ adhikaṃ visiṭṭhaṃ sīlaṃ adhisīlanti vuccati. Pajjotānanti ālokānaṃ. Nanu ca paccekabuddhāpi dhammatāvasena pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlena samannāgatāva honti, evaṃ sati kasmā “buddhuppādeyeva pavattati, na vinā buddhuppādā”ti [M 2.0061] niyametvā vuttanti āha – “na hi taṃ paññattiṃ uddharitvā”tiādi. Kiñcāpi paccekabuddhā pātimokkhasaṃvarasampannāgatā honti, na pana tesaṃ vasena vitthāritaṃ hutvā pavattatīti adhippāyo. “Imasmiṃ vatthusmiṃ imasmiṃ vītikkame idaṃ nāma hotī”ti paññapanaṃ aññesaṃ avisayo, buddhānaṃyeva esa visayo, buddhānaṃ balanti āha – “buddhāyeva panā”tiādi. Lokiyasīlassa adhisīlabhāvo pariyāyenāti nippariyāyameva taṃ dassetuṃ “pātimokkhasaṃvaratopi ca maggaphalasampayuttameva sīlaṃ adhisīla”nti vuttaṃ. Na hi taṃ samāpanno bhikkhūti gahaṭṭhesu sotāpannānaṃ sadāravītikkamasambhavato vuttaṃ. Tathā hi te saputtadārā agāraṃ ajjhāvasanti.

It is called “adhisīla” (higher virtue) because the virtue of Pātimokkha-restraint is a superior and distinguished virtue, on account of its being the complete bodily and verbal restraint and because it is the basis for the virtue of the path. “Pajjotānaṃ” means 'of the lights'. Is it not that Paccekabuddhas are also endowed with the virtue of Pātimokkha-restraint by nature? If so, why is it stated with the restriction, 'It exists only in the dispensation of a Buddha; it does not exist without the arising of a Buddha'? To this, it is said: 'For they do not… that legislation,' etc. The intention is this: although Paccekabuddhas are endowed with Pātimokkha-restraint, it does not become widespread and established through them. The act of legislating, 'In this case, for this transgression, such-and-such is the result,' is not the domain of others; this is the domain of Buddhas alone. It is the power of the Buddhas. To this, it is said: 'But only the Buddhas…,' etc. The status of worldly virtue as higher virtue is stated figuratively. In order to show it literally, it is said: 'Even more so than the Pātimokkha-restraint, the virtue associated with the path and fruit is the higher virtue.' The phrase 'a bhikkhu who has attained that' is stated because for householder stream-enterers, the possibility of transgression with a wife exists. For indeed, they live at home with wife and children.

Samādāpanaṃ [V 2.0054] samādānañcāti aññesaṃ samādāpanaṃ sayaṃ samādānañca. Adhicittanti vuccatīti maggasamādhissa adhiṭṭhānabhāvato adhicittanti vuccati. Na vinā buddhuppādāti kiñcāpi paccekabuddhānaṃ vipassanāpādakaṃ aṭṭhasamāpatticittaṃ hotiyeva, na pana te tattha aññe samādāpetuṃ sakkontīti na tesaṃ vasena vitthāritaṃ hutvā pavattatīti adhippāyo. Vipassanāpaññāyapi adhipaññatāsādhane “na vinā buddhuppādā”ti vacanaṃ imināva adhippāyena vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Lokiyacittassa adhicittatā pariyāyenāti nippariyāyameva taṃ dassetuṃ “tatopi ca maggaphalacittameva adhicitta”nti āha. Taṃ pana idha anadhippetanti iminā aṭṭhakathāvacanena lokiyacittassa vasena adhicittasikkhāpi idha adhippetāti viññāyati. Na hi taṃ samāpanno bhikkhu methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevatīti ca iminā lokiyaadhicittaṃ samāpanno methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevatīti āpannaṃ. Adhipaññāniddese ca “tatopi ca maggaphalapaññāva adhipaññā”ti vatvā “sā pana idha anadhippetā. Na hi taṃ samāpanno bhikkhu methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevatī”ti vuttattā lokiyapaññāvasena adhipaññāsikkhāyapi idhādhippetabhāvo taṃ samāpannassa methunadhammapaṭisevanañca aṭṭhakathāyaṃ anuññātanti viññāyati. Idañca sabbaṃ “tatra yāyaṃ adhisīlasikkhā, ayaṃ imasmiṃ atthe adhippetā sikkhā”ti imāya pāḷiyā na sameti. Ayañhi pāḷi adhisīlasikkhāva idha adhippetā, na itarāti dīpeti, tasmā pāḷiyā aṭṭhakathāya ca evamadhippāyo veditabbo – lokiyaadhicittaadhipaññāsamāpannassa tathārūpapaccayaṃ paṭicca “methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevissāmī”ti citte uppanne tato adhicittato [M 2.0062] adhipaññato ca parihāni sambhavatīti taṃ dvayaṃ samāpannena na sakkā methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevitunti pāḷiyaṃ adhisīlasikkhāva vuttā. Adhisīlasikkhañhi yāva vītikkamaṃ na karoti, tāva samāpannova hoti. Na hi cittuppādamattena pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlaṃ bhinnaṃ nāma hotīti. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana lokiyaadhicittato adhipaññato ca parihāyitvāpi bhikkhuno methunadhammapaṭisevanaṃ kadāci bhaveyyāti taṃ dvayaṃ appaṭikkhipitvā maggaphaladhammānaṃ akuppasabhāvattā taṃ samāpannassa bhikkhuno tato parihāyitvā methunadhammapaṭisevanaṃ nāma na kadāci sambhavatīti lokuttarādhicittaadhipaññānaṃyeva paṭikkhepo katoti veditabbo.

Causing others to undertake and undertaking oneself: this means causing others to undertake and undertaking it oneself. It is called ‘higher mind’ because it is the foundation for the concentration of the path; thus it is called ‘higher mind’. ‘Not without the arising of a Buddha’: although Paccekabuddhas do possess the mind of the eight attainments which is the basis for insight, they are not able to cause others to undertake it. Therefore, the intention is that it does not become widespread and proceed by means of them. It should be understood that the statement ‘not without the arising of a Buddha’ in establishing the state of higher wisdom for insight-wisdom is also spoken with this same intention. The state of higher mind for a mundane consciousness is spoken of by way of interpretation. To show this directly, it is said, ‘Moreover, only the mind of the path and fruition is the higher mind’. However, by this commentary statement, 'But that is not intended here,' it is understood that the training in higher mind by way of mundane consciousness is also intended here. And by this statement, ‘For a monk who has attained that does not engage in the sexual act,’ it follows that one who has attained the mundane higher mind engages in the sexual act. And in the exposition on higher wisdom, after saying, ‘Moreover, only the wisdom of the path and fruition is higher wisdom,’ because it is said, ‘But that is not intended here. For a monk who has attained that does not engage in the sexual act,’ it is understood that the training in higher wisdom by way of mundane wisdom is also intended here, and that for one who has attained that, engaging in the sexual act is permitted in the commentary. And all this does not agree with this Pāḷi passage: ‘Therein, whichever is the training in higher virtue, this is the training intended in this context’. For this Pāḷi passage clarifies that only the training in higher virtue is intended here, not the others. Therefore, the intention of both the Pāḷi and the commentary should be understood thus: For one who has attained mundane higher mind and higher wisdom, when the thought ‘I will engage in the sexual act’ arises dependent on a suitable condition, a decline from that higher mind and from that higher wisdom is possible. Therefore, it is not possible for one who has attained those two to engage in the sexual act; thus, only the training in higher virtue is mentioned in the Pāḷi. For as long as one does not commit a transgression of the training in higher virtue, one remains in attainment. For the virtue of Pātimokkha restraint is not broken by the mere arising of a thought. In the commentary, however, it is said that even after declining from mundane higher mind and higher wisdom, a monk's engagement in the sexual act might sometimes occur. Therefore, without rejecting those two, because of the unshakeable nature of the states of the path and fruition, for a monk who has attained them, declining from them and engaging in the sexual act is never possible. Thus, it should be understood that the rejection is made only of the supramundane higher mind and higher wisdom.

Atthi dinnaṃ atthi yiṭṭhantiādinayappavattanti iminā –

By this [passage] which proceeds in the manner of, 'There is what is given, there is what is offered,' and so on—

“Tattha katamaṃ kammassakataññāṇaṃ? ‘Atthi dinnaṃ, atthi yiṭṭhaṃ, atthi hutaṃ, atthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko, atthi ayaṃ loko, atthi paro loko, atthi mātā, atthi pitā, atthi sattā opapātikā, atthi loke samaṇabrāhmaṇā sammaggatā sammā [V 2.0055] paṭipannā, ye imañca lokaṃ parañca lokaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā pavedentī’ti yā evarūpā paññā pajānanā…pe… amoho dhammavicayo sammādiṭṭhi, idaṃ vuccati kammassakataññāṇaṃ. Ṭhapetvā saccānulomikaṃ ñāṇaṃ sabbāpi sāsavā kusalā paññā kammassakataññāṇa”nti (vibha. 793) –

“Herein, what is the knowledge of ownership of kamma? ‘There is a result of what is given; there is a result of what is offered; there is a result of what is sacrificed; there is fruit and result of good and bad kamma; there is this world; there is the next world; there is mother; there is father; there are beings born spontaneously; there are in the world ascetics and brahmins who are rightly conducted and rightly practicing, who, having directly known and realized this world and the next by themselves, proclaim them’—such wisdom, understanding… non-delusion, investigation of the Dhamma, right view: this is called the knowledge of ownership of kamma. Excluding the knowledge that conforms to the truths, all tainted wholesome wisdom is the knowledge of ownership of kamma” (Vibhaṅga 793).

Imaṃ vibhaṅgapāḷiṃ saṅgaṇhāti.

He includes this Pāḷi text from the Vibhaṅga.

Tattha (vibha. aṭṭha. 793) atthi dinnantiādīsu dinnapaccayā phalaṃ atthīti iminā upāyena attho veditabbo. Dinnanti ca deyyadhammasīsena dānaṃ vuttaṃ. Yiṭṭhanti mahāyāgo, sabbasādhāraṇaṃ mahādānanti attho. Hutanti pahonakasakkāro adhippeto. Atthi mātā, atthi pitāti mātāpitūsu sammāpaṭipattimicchāpaṭipattiādīnaṃ phalasambhavo vutto. Idaṃ vuccatīti yaṃ ñāṇaṃ “idaṃ kammaṃ sakaṃ, idaṃ no saka”nti jānāti, idaṃ kammassakataññāṇaṃ nāma vuccatīti attho. Tattha tividhaṃ kāyaduccaritaṃ catubbidhaṃ vacīduccaritaṃ tividhaṃ manoduccaritanti idaṃ na sakakammaṃ nāma, tīsu dvāresu dasavidhampi sucaritaṃ sakakammaṃ nāma. Attano vāpi hotu parassa vā, sabbampi akusalaṃ na sakakammaṃ [M 2.0063] nāma. Kasmā? Atthabhañjanato anatthajananato ca. Attano vā hotu parassa vā, sabbampi kusalaṃ sakakammaṃ nāma. Kasmā? Anatthabhañjanato atthajananato ca. Evaṃ jānanasamatthe imasmiṃ kammassakataññāṇe ṭhatvā bahuṃ dānaṃ datvā sīlaṃ pūretvā uposathaṃ samādiyitvā sukhena sukhaṃ sampattiyā sampattiṃ anubhavitvā nibbānaṃ pattānaṃ sattānaṃ gaṇanaparicchedo natthi. Ṭhapetvā saccānulomikaṃ ñāṇanti maggasaccassa paramatthasaccassa ca anulomanato saccānulomikanti laddhanāmaṃ vipassanāñāṇaṃ ṭhapetvā avasesā sabbāpi sāsavā kusalā paññā kammassakataññāṇamevāti attho.

Therein (Vibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā 793), in 'There is what is given,' etc., the meaning should be understood by this method: there is a result from the condition of giving. And 'what is given' refers to giving, with the item to be given as the principal aspect. 'What is offered' is a great sacrifice; the meaning is a great gift common to all. 'What is sacrificed' is intended as hospitality offered to guests. 'There is mother, there is father' refers to the arising of results from right practice, wrong practice, etc., towards mother and father. The meaning of 'This is called' is: the knowledge that knows, 'This kamma is one's own, this is not one's own,' this is called the knowledge of ownership of kamma. Therein, the threefold bodily misconduct, the fourfold verbal misconduct, and the threefold mental misconduct—this is not called one's own kamma. The tenfold good conduct in the three doors is called one's own kamma. Whether it be one's own or another's, all unwholesome kamma is not called one's own kamma. Why? Because it destroys benefit and generates what is not beneficial. Whether it be one's own or another's, all wholesome kamma is called one's own kamma. Why? Because it destroys what is not beneficial and generates benefit. Standing in this knowledge of ownership of kamma, which is capable of knowing thus, having given much in charity, having fulfilled virtue, having undertaken the Uposatha, having experienced happiness from happiness and attainment from attainment, there is no counting or limit to the beings who have reached Nibbāna. The meaning of 'Excluding the knowledge that conforms to the truths' is: excluding the insight knowledge that has received the name 'in conformity with the truths' because of its conformity to the truth of the path and to the ultimate truth, all remaining tainted wholesome wisdom is indeed the knowledge of ownership of kamma.

Tilakkhaṇākāraparicchedakanti aniccādilakkhaṇattayassa hutvā abhāvādiākārapaacchindanakaṃ. Adhipaññāti vuccatīti maggapaññāya adhiṭṭhānabhāvato vipassanāñāṇaṃ adhipaññāti vuccati.

‘Discrimination of the aspects of the three characteristics’ means that which, with regard to the three characteristics such as impermanence, determines the aspects of non-existence and so on. It is called ‘higher wisdom’ because insight knowledge is called higher wisdom due to its serving as the basis for path wisdom.

“Kalyāṇakārī kalyāṇaṃ, pāpakārī ca pāpakaṃ;

Anubhoti dvayametaṃ, anubandhati kāraka”nti. (saṃ. ni. 1.256);

“The doer of good experiences good, and the doer of evil experiences evil. One experiences this pair. It befits the doer.”

Evaṃ [V 2.0056] atīte anāgate ca vaṭṭamūlakadukkhasallakkhaṇavasena saṃvegavatthutāya vimuttiākaṅkhāya paccayabhūtā kammassakatapaññā adhipaññātipi vadanti. Lokiyapaññāya adhipaññābhāvo pariyāyenāti nippariyāyameva taṃ dassetuṃ “tatopi ca maggaphalapaññāva adhipaññā”ti vuttaṃ.

Thus, regarding the past and the future, the wisdom concerning ownership of kamma, which is a cause for the aspiration for liberation due to its nature of prompting urgency through perceiving the characteristic of suffering as rooted in the cycle of existence, is also called higher wisdom. The status of higher wisdom for mundane wisdom is only figurative. To show that this is without figure of speech, it is said: ‘Moreover, only the wisdom of the path and its fruit is higher wisdom’.

Saha ājīvanti etthāti sājīvoti sabbasikkhāpadaṃ vuttanti āha – “sabbampi…pe… tasmā sājīvanti vuccatī”ti. Tattha sikkhāpadanti “nāmakāyo padakāyo niruttikāyo byañjanakāyo”ti vuttaṃ bhagavato vacanasaṅkhātaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ. Sabhāgavuttinoti samānavuttikā, sadisappavattikāti attho. Tasmiṃ sikkhatīti ettha ādheyyāpekkhattā adhikaraṇassa kimādheyyamapekkhitvā “tasmi”nti adhikaraṇaṃ niddiṭṭhanti āha – “taṃ sikkhāpadaṃ cittassa adhikaraṇaṃ katvā”ti, taṃ sājīvasaṅkhātaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ “yathāsikkhāpadaṃ nu kho sikkhāmi, na sikkhāmī”ti evaṃ pavattivasena sikkhāpadavisayattā tadādheyyabhūtassa cittassa adhikaraṇaṃ katvāti attho. Nanu ca “sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno”ti imassa padabhājanaṃ karontena “yaṃ sikkhaṃ sājīvañca samāpanno, tadubhayaṃ dassetvā tesu sikkhati, tena [M 2.0064] vuccati sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno”ti vattabbaṃ siyā, evamavatvā “tasmiṃ sikkhati, tena vuccati sājīvasamāpanno”ti ettakameva kasmā vuttanti antolīnacodanaṃ sandhāyāha “na kevalañcāyametasmi”ntiādi.

‘They live together here,’ thus it is called ‘sājīva’—all the training rules are spoken of thus: ‘All… therefore it is called sājīva’. Here, ‘training rule’ refers to ‘the collection of names, the collection of terms, the collection of expressions, the collection of syllables’—this is the training rule designated as the Blessed One’s speech. ‘Similar conduct’ means conduct that is alike, behavior that is similar—this is the meaning. ‘He trains in that’—here, due to the expectation of something to be based on, considering what is to be based upon in the matter, ‘in that’ refers to the matter as explained: ‘taking that training rule as the basis for the mind’. That training rule, designated as ‘sājīva,’ is considered in terms of whether one trains according to it or not—thus, because it is the domain of the training rule, it serves as the basis for the mind that is based on it. Now, when analyzing the phrase ‘one who has attained to training and shared livelihood,’ should it not be said: ‘Having shown both the training and the shared livelihood in which one has become established, one trains in them, therefore it is said, “one who has attained to training and shared livelihood”’? Instead, why is only ‘he trains in that, therefore it is called “one who has attained to shared livelihood”’ said? Referring to an implicit objection, he says: ‘Not only this…’ and so on.

Tassā ca sikkhāyāti tassā adhisīlasaṅkhātāya sikkhāya. Sikkhaṃ paripūrentoti

‘Of that training’ refers to that training reckoned as higher virtue. ‘Fulfilling the training’ means…

Sīlasaṃvaraṃ paripūrento, vārittasīlavasena viratisampayuttaṃ cetanaṃ cārittasīlavasena virativippayuttaṃ cetanañca attani pavattentoti attho. Tasmiñca sikkhāpade avītikkamanto sikkhatīti “nāmakāyo padakāyo niruttikāyo byañjanakāyo”ti evaṃ vuttaṃ bhagavato vacanasaṅkhātaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ avītikkamanto hutvā tasmiṃ yathāvuttasikkhāpade sikkhatīti attho. Sīlasaṃvarapūraṇaṃ sājīvānatikkamanañcāti idameva ca dvayaṃ idha sikkhanaṃ nāmāti adhippāyo. Tattha sājīvānatikkamo sikkhāpāripūriyā paccayo. Sājīvānatikkamato hi yāva maggā sikkhāpāripūrī hoti. Apicettha “sikkhaṃ paripūrento sikkhatī”ti iminā viraticetanāsaṅkhātassa sīlasaṃvarassa visesato santāne pavattanakālova gahito, “avītikkamanto sikkhatī”ti iminā pana appavattanakālopi. Sikkhañhi paripūraṇavasena attani pavattentopi niddādivasena appavattentopi vītikkamābhāvā “avītikkamanto sikkhatī”ti vuccatīti.

One fulfills the restraint of virtue by causing to arise in oneself the intention associated with abstinence through the aspect of avoidance, and the intention not associated with abstinence through the aspect of performance—this is the meaning. Moreover, by not transgressing that training rule, one trains—this refers to training in the training rule proclaimed by the Blessed One, which is reckoned as ‘body of names, body of words, body of expressions, and body of syllables,’ by not transgressing it. The fulfillment of virtue-restraint and the non-transgression of livelihood—these two alone are what is meant by training here. Of these, the non-transgression of livelihood is a condition for the complete fulfillment of the training. For the complete fulfillment of the training extends up to the path on account of non-transgression of livelihood. Furthermore, in the phrase ‘one trains by fulfilling the training,’ the time when the intention of abstinence, reckoned as virtue-restraint, is specifically caused to occur in the mental continuum is taken; but in the phrase ‘one trains by not transgressing,’ even the time when it does not occur is included. For whether one is causing the training to occur in oneself by way of fulfillment, or not causing it to occur due to sleep and the like, because there is no transgression, it is said, ‘one trains by not transgressing’.

Sikkhāsājīvapadabhājanīyavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition of the section on the analysis of ‘training and livelihood’ is finished.

Sikkhāpaccakkhānavibhaṅgavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Exposition of Renouncing the Training

“Appaccakkhāya [V 2.0057] appaccakkhātāyā”ti ubhayathāpi pāṭho tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu vutto. Dubbalye āvikatepīti “yaṃnūnāhaṃ buddhaṃ paccakkheyya”ntiādinā dubbalabhāve pakāsitepi. Sikkhāya pana paccakkhātāyāti “buddhaṃ paccakkhāmī”tiādinā sikkhāya paccakkhātāya. Yasmā dirattavacane gahite tena purimapacchimapadāni saṃsiliṭṭhāni honti, na tasmiṃ aggahite, tasmā dirattavacanena byañjanasiliṭṭhatāmattameva payojananti āha “byañjanasiliṭṭhatāyā”ti. Mukhāruḷhatāyāti yasmā evarūpaṃ vacanaṃ lokassa mukhamāruḷhaṃ, tasmāti attho.

“Appaccakkhāya appaccakkhātāyā”ti: The reading is stated in both ways in all three Gaṇṭhipadas. `Dubbalye āvikatepīti` means: even when the state of weakness is made manifest by such phrases as, “If only I could renounce the Buddha.” `Sikkhāya pana paccakkhātāyāti` means: but when the training has been renounced by such phrases as, “I renounce the Buddha.” Because, when the word `dhiratta` (shame!) is taken, the preceding and succeeding words become well-connected by it, but they are not when it is not taken, therefore, the purpose of the word `dhiratta` is merely the smoothness of the expression; thus, he says, `byañjanasiliṭṭhatāyā` (for the sake of the smoothness of the expression). `Mukhāruḷhatāyāti`: The meaning is that it is so called because such a statement has become current among the people.

Byañjanaṃ [M 2.0065] sampādetīti tassa visuṃ atthābhāvato vuttamevatthaṃ aññapadena dīpento byañjanaṃ sampādeti. Vuttamevatthaṃ kāraṇena vibhāvento āha “parivārakapadavirahitañhī”tiādi. Atthadīpakaṃ padaṃ atthapadaṃ.

`Byañjanaṃ sampādetīti`: Since it has no separate meaning, it completes the expression by elucidating the meaning already stated with another word. `Vuttamevatthaṃ kāraṇena vibhāvento āha “parivārakapadavirahitañhī”tiādi`: Analyzing the meaning already stated with a reason, he says, “For it is devoid of a qualifying word,” and so on. `Atthadīpakaṃ padaṃ atthapadaṃ`: A word that illuminates the meaning is a meaning-word.

Sikkhāpaccakkhānassāti “buddhaṃ paccakkhāmī”tiādisikkhāpaccakkhānavacanassa. “Buddhaṃ paccakkhāmī”tiādīsu “evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, dubbalyāvikammañceva hoti sikkhā ca paccakkhātā”ti vuttattā ubhayampi hotīti āha – “ekaccaṃ dubbalyāvikammaṃ attho hotī”ti. Kiñcāpi “buddhaṃ paccakkhāmī”tiādisikkhāpaccakkhānavacanassa dubbalyāvikammapadattho na hoti, tathāpi “buddhaṃ paccakkhāmī”ti vutte sikkhāparipūraṇe dubbalyāvibhāvassapi gamyamānattā “sikkhāpaccakkhānassa ekaccaṃ dubbalyāvikammaṃ attho hotī”ti vuttaṃ. Naṃ sandhāyāti naṃ atthabhūtaṃ dubbalyāvikammaṃ sandhāya.

`Sikkhāpaccakkhānassā`ti: This refers to the statement of renouncing the training, such as “I renounce the Buddha.” In such phrases as “I renounce the Buddha,” since it is said, “Thus, monks, there is both a manifestation of weakness and the training is renounced,” both occur. Thus, he says: “`ekaccaṃ dubbalyāvikammaṃ attho hotī`”ti (in some cases, the meaning is a manifestation of weakness). Although the statement of renouncing the training, such as “I renounce the Buddha,” does not have the explicit meaning of the term 'manifestation of weakness', nevertheless, when “I renounce the Buddha” is said, because the state of weakness in fulfilling the training is also understood, it is said, “Of the renunciation of the training, in some cases the meaning is a manifestation of weakness.” `Naṃ sandhāyā`ti: This refers to that manifestation of weakness which has become the meaning.

Visesāvisesanti ettha yena dubbalyāvikammameva hoti, na sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ, tattha sikkhāpaccakkhānadubbalyāvikammānaṃ atthi viseso. Yena pana sikkhāpaccakkhānañceva dubbalyāvikammañca hoti, tattha nevatthi visesoti veditabbaṃ. Kaṭhakicchajīvaneti dhātūsu paṭhitattā vuttaṃ “kicchajīvikappatto”ti. Ukkaṇṭhanaṃ ukkaṇṭhā, kicchajīvikā, taṃ ito pattoti ukkaṇṭhito. Itoti ito ṭhānato, ito vihārato vā. Etthāti gantumicchitaṃ padesaṃ vadati. Anabhiratiyā pīḷito vikkhittacitto hutvā sīsaṃ ukkhipitvā uddhaṃmukho ito cito ca olokento āhiṇḍatīti āha “uddhaṃ kaṇṭhaṃ katvā viharamāno”ti.

Visesāvisesanti: Here, by which statement there is only a manifestation of weakness and not a renunciation of the training, there is a difference between the renunciation of the training and the manifestation of weakness. But by which statement there is both a renunciation of the training and a manifestation of weakness, it should be understood that there is no difference. Kaṭhakicchajīvaneti: Because it is recited among the roots as `kaṭha` in the sense of `kicchajīvana` (difficult livelihood), it is said, “having attained a difficult livelihood.” Ukkaṇṭhanaṃ ukkaṇṭhā, kicchajīvikā, taṃ ito pattoti ukkaṇṭhito: `Ukkaṇṭhanaṃ` is `ukkaṇṭhā` (discontent), a difficult livelihood; `ukkaṇṭhito` means one who has attained that from this. Itoti: This means from this place, or from this monastery. Etthāti: This refers to the place one wishes to go. Anabhiratiyā pīḷito vikkhittacitto hutvā sīsaṃ ukkhipitvā uddhaṃmukho ito cito ca olokento āhiṇḍatīti āha “uddhaṃ kaṇṭhaṃ katvā viharamāno”ti: Because, oppressed by dissatisfaction, with a distracted mind, having raised his head, with face upwards, looking hither and thither, he wanders, he says, “dwelling with his neck held up.”

Aṭṭīyamānoti ettha aṭṭamiva attānamācarati aṭṭīyatīti aṭṭīyasaddassa antogadhaupamānabhūtakammattā [V 2.0058] upameyyabhūtena attanāva sakammakattaṃ, na bhikkhubhāvenāti āha “bhikkhubhāvanti bhikkhubhāvenā”ti. Na hi so bhikkhubhāvaṃ aṭṭamiva ācarati, kiñcarahi attānaṃ tasmā bhikkhubhāvena karaṇabhūtena attānaṃ aṭṭīyamānoti evamettha attho daṭṭhabboti āha “karaṇatthe upayogavacana”nti. Kaṇṭhe āsattena aṭṭīyeyyāti ettha pana karaṇattheyeva karaṇavacananti āha – “yathālakkhaṇaṃ karaṇavacaneneva vutta”nti. Kattuatthe vā upayogavacanaṃ daṭṭhabbanti āha – “tena vā bhikkhubhāvenā”tiādi, tena kattubhūtena bhikkhubhāvenāti attho. Imasmiṃ panatthe aṭṭaṃ karotīti aṭṭīyatīti [M 2.0066] aṭṭīya-saddaṃ nipphādetvā tato kammani māna-sadde kate “aṭṭīyamāno”ti padasiddhi veditabbā. Tenevāha – “aṭṭo kariyamāno pīḷiyamāno”ti. Jigucchamānoti iminā pana sambandhe kariyamāne bhikkhubhāvanti upayogatthe eva upayogavacananti āha – “asuciṃ viya taṃ jigucchanto”ti, taṃ bhikkhubhāvaṃ jigucchantoti attho. Sacāhanti sace ahaṃ.

Aṭṭīyamānoti: Here, `aṭṭīyati` is formed from the phrase `aṭṭam iva attānaṃ ācarati` (he acts towards himself as if he were afflicted). Because the object of the word `aṭṭīya` is implied within the simile, its transitivity is with `attā` (oneself), which is the subject of comparison, and not with `bhikkhubhāva` (the state of being a monk). Thus, he says, `bhikkhubhāvanti bhikkhubhāvenā` (the accusative `bhikkhubhāvaṃ` has the sense of the instrumental `bhikkhubhāvena`). For he does not act towards monkhood as if it were afflicted; rather, he acts thus towards himself. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as being afflicted towards himself by that monkhood as the instrumental cause. Thus, he says, `karaṇatthe upayogavacanaṃ` (the accusative case is in the sense of the instrument). But in the phrase `kaṇṭhe āsattena aṭṭīyeyya`, the instrumental case is indeed in the sense of the instrument. Thus, he says, `yathālakkhaṇaṃ karaṇavacaneneva vuttaṃ` (it is stated with the instrumental case itself, according to its characteristic). Or the accusative case should be seen in the sense of the agent. Thus he says, `tena vā bhikkhubhāvenā` etc., meaning, "by that monkhood which has become the agent." But in this meaning, having derived the word `aṭṭīyati` from `aṭṭaṃ karoti` (he causes affliction), and then having formed the word `-māna` in the passive sense, the formation of the word `aṭṭīyamāno` should be understood. For that very reason, he says, `aṭṭo kariyamāno pīḷiyamāno` (being afflicted, being oppressed). But when the connection is made with `jigucchamāno`, he says that `bhikkhubhāvaṃ` is in the accusative case in the objective sense, hence, `asuciṃ viya taṃ jigucchanto` (being disgusted with it as if it were impure), meaning, “being disgusted with that monkhood.” `Sacāhan`ti means `sace ahaṃ` (if I).

Paccakkhānākārena vuttānīti “paccakkheyyaṃ paccakkheyya”nti vuttattā paccakkhānākārasambandhena vuttāni. Bhāvavikappākārenāti “assaṃ assa”nti āgatattā yaṃ yaṃ bhavitukāmo, tassa tassa bhāvassa vikappākārena, bhikkhubhāvato aññabhāvavikappākārenāti adhippāyo.

Paccakkhānākārena vuttānīti: They are stated in the manner of renunciation because they are stated as, “I would renounce, I would renounce”; thus, they are stated in connection with the manner of renunciation. Bhāvavikappākārenāti: This means in the manner of conceptualizing states. Because it is given as, “I would be, I would be,” the intention is: in the manner of conceptualizing whatever state one wishes to become, that is, in the manner of conceptualizing a state other than that of a monk.

50. Na ussahāmīti attano tattha tattha ussahābhāvaṃ dasseti. Na visahāmīti ekabhattādīnaṃ asayhabhāvaṃ dasseti. Na ramāmīti “pabbajjāmūlakaṃ natthi me sukha”nti dasseti. Nābhiramāmīti pabbajjāya attano santosābhāvaṃ dasseti.

50. Na ussahāmīti: This shows one's lack of striving in this and that. Na visahāmīti: This shows one's inability to bear such things as the one-meal-a-day practice. Na ramāmīti: This shows, “There is no happiness for me rooted in the going-forth.” Nābhiramāmīti: This shows one's lack of contentment with the going-forth.

Idāni sikkhāpaccakkhānavāre ṭhatvā ayaṃ vinicchayo veditabbo – tattha “sāmaññā cavitukāmo”tiādīhi padehi cittaniyamaṃ dasseti. “Buddhaṃ dhamma”ntiādīhi padehi khettaniyamaṃ dasseti. Yathā hi loke sassānaṃ ruhanaṭṭhānaṃ “khetta”nti vuccati, evamidampi sikkhāpaccakkhānassa ruhanaṭṭhānattā “khetta”nti vuccati. “Paccakkhāmi dhārehī”ti etena kālaniyamaṃ dasseti. “Vadatī”ti iminā payoganiyamaṃ dasseti. “Alaṃ me buddhena, kinnu me buddhena, na mamattho buddhena, sumuttāhaṃ buddhenā”tiādīhi anāmaṭṭhakālavasenapi paccakkhānaṃ hotīti dasseti. “Viññāpetī”ti iminā vijānananiyamaṃ dasseti. “Ummattako sikkhaṃ paccakkhāti, ummattakassa santike sikkhaṃ paccakkhātī”tiādīhi puggalaniyamaṃ dasseti. “Ariyakena milakkhassa santike sikkhaṃ paccakkhāti, so ca nappaṭivijānāti, appaccakkhātā hoti sikkhā”tiādīhi puggalādiniyame satipi vijānananiyamāsambhavaṃ dasseti[V 2.0059]. “Davāya sikkhaṃ paccakkhāti, appaccakkhātā hoti sikkhā”tiādīhi khettādiniyame satipi cittaniyamābhāvena na ruhatīti dasseti. “Sāvetukāmo na sāveti, apaccakkhātā hoti sikkhā”ti iminā cittaniyamepi sati payoganiyamābhāvena na ruhatīti [M 2.0067] dasseti. “Aviññussa sāveti, viññussa na sāvetī”ti etehi cittakhettakālapayogapuggalavijānananiyamepi sati yaṃ puggalaṃ uddissa sāveti, tasseva savanena ruhati, na aññassāti dasseti. “Sabbaso vā pana na sāveti, appaccakkhātā hoti sikkhā”ti idaṃ pana cittādiniyameneva sikkhā paccakkhātā hoti, na aññathāti dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Tasmā cittakhettakālapayogapuggalavijānananiyamavasena sikkhāya paccakkhānaṃ ñatvā tadabhāvena appaccakkhānaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Now, standing in the section on renouncing the training, this determination should be understood. Therein, by the phrases beginning with 'desiring to fall away from the state of an ascetic,' he indicates the determination of intention. By the phrases beginning with 'the Buddha, the Dhamma,' he indicates the determination of the field. Just as in the world, a place for the growing of crops is called a 'field,' so too this is called a 'field' because it is the place for the renunciation of the training to arise. By this, 'I renounce, you should remember,' he indicates the determination of time. By this, 'he speaks,' he indicates the determination of application. By the phrases beginning with 'Enough for me is the Buddha, what have I to do with the Buddha, the Buddha is of no use to me, I am well freed from the Buddha,' he shows that renunciation occurs even by way of an unspecified time. By this, 'he informs,' he indicates the determination of understanding. By the phrases beginning with 'A madman renounces the training, one renounces the training in the presence of a madman,' he indicates the determination of the person. By the phrases beginning with 'An Aryan renounces the training in the presence of a barbarian, and the latter does not understand it, the training is not renounced,' he shows the impossibility of the determination of understanding even when the determination of the person and so on is present. By the phrases beginning with 'He renounces the training in jest, the training is not renounced,' he shows that it is not accomplished due to the absence of the determination of intention, even when the determination of the field and so on is present. By this, 'Desiring to make it heard, he does not make it heard, the training is not renounced,' he shows that it is not accomplished due to the absence of the determination of application, even when the determination of intention is present. By these, 'He makes it heard to one who does not understand, he does not make it heard to one who understands,' he shows that even when the determinations of intention, field, time, application, person, and understanding are present, it is accomplished only by the hearing of that very person for whom he makes it heard, not for another. But this, 'Or he does not make it heard at all, the training is not renounced,' is said to show that the training is renounced only through the determination of intention and so on, and not otherwise. Therefore, having known the renunciation of the training by way of the determination of intention, field, time, application, person, and understanding, non-renunciation should be understood by their absence.

Kathaṃ? Upasampannabhāvato cavitukāmatācitteneva hi sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ hoti, na davā vā ravā vā bhaṇantassa. Evaṃ cittavasena sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ hoti, na tadabhāvena.

How so? Indeed, the renunciation of the training occurs only through the intention of desiring to fall away from the state of one who is fully ordained, not for one who speaks in jest or heedlessly. Thus, the renunciation of the training occurs by way of intention, and not by its absence.
