Tathā “buddhaṃ paccakkhāmi, dhammaṃ paccakkhāmi, saṅghaṃ paccakkhāmi, sikkhaṃ, vinayaṃ, pātimokkhaṃ, uddesaṃ, upajjhāyaṃ, ācariyaṃ, saddhivihārikaṃ, antevāsikaṃ, samānupajjhāyakaṃ, samānācariyakaṃ, sabrahmacāriṃ paccakkhāmī”ti evaṃ vuttānaṃ buddhādīnaṃ catuddasannaṃ, “gihīti maṃ dhārehi, upāsako, ārāmiko, sāmaṇero, titthiyo, titthiyasāvako, assamaṇo, asakyaputtiyoti maṃ dhārehī”ti evaṃ vuttānaṃ gihiādīnaṃ aṭṭhannañcāti imesaṃ dvāvīsatiyā khettapadānaṃ yassa kassaci savevacanassa vasena tesu ca yaṃkiñci vattukāmassa yaṃkiñci vadatopi sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ hoti, na rukkhādīnaṃ aññatarassa nāmaṃ gahetvā sikkhaṃ paccakkhantassa. Evaṃ khettavasena sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ hoti, na tadabhāvena.

Likewise, of the fourteen terms beginning with the Buddha that are stated thus: 'I renounce the Buddha... I renounce my fellow in the holy life'; and of the eight terms beginning with 'layperson' that are stated thus: 'You should remember me as a layperson... you should remember me as not a son of the Sakyan'—with regard to these twenty-two field-terms, by way of any synonym, for one who wishes to say any one of them, even when saying any other one of them, the renunciation of the training occurs. It does not occur for one who renounces the training by taking the name of a tree or some other such thing. Thus, the renunciation of the training occurs by way of the field, and not by its absence.

Tattha yadetaṃ “paccakkhāmī”ti ca “maṃ dhārehī”ti ca vuttaṃ vattamānakālavacanaṃ, yāni ca “alaṃ me buddhena, kinnu me buddhena, na mamattho buddhena, sumuttāhaṃ buddhenā”tiādinā nayena ākhyātavasena kālaṃ anāmasitvā purimehi cuddasahi padehi saddhiṃ yojetvā vuttāni “alaṃ me”tiādīni cattāri padāni, tesaṃyeva ca savevacanānaṃ vasena paccakkhānaṃ hoti, na “paccakkhāsi”nti vā “paccakkhissa”nti vā “maṃ dhāresī”ti vā “dhāressasī”ti vā “yanūnāhaṃ paccakkheyya”nti vātiādīni atītānāgataparikappavacanāni bhaṇantassa. Evaṃ vattamānakālavasena ceva anāmaṭṭhakālavasena ca paccakkhānaṃ hoti, na tadabhāvena.

Therein, that which is stated as 'I renounce' and 'you should remember me' is a statement in the present tense. And there are those four phrases beginning with 'Enough for me,' which are stated by being combined with the preceding fourteen phrases, by way of verbs without specifying a time, in the manner of 'Enough for me is the Buddha... I am well freed from the Buddha.' The renunciation occurs by way of these very phrases and their synonyms. It does not occur for one who utters statements of the past, future, or optative, such as 'You renounced,' or 'You will renounce,' or 'You remembered me,' or 'You will remember me,' or 'Would that I might renounce.' Thus, renunciation occurs by way of the present tense and by way of unspecified time, and not by their absence.

Payogo [M 2.0068][V 2.0060] pana duvidho kāyiko vācasiko. Tattha “buddhaṃ paccakkhāmī”tiādinā nayena yāya kāyaci bhāsāya vacībhedaṃ katvā vācasikapayogeneva paccakkhānaṃ hoti, na akkharalikhanaṃ vā hatthamuddādidassanaṃ vā kāyapayogaṃ karontassa. Evaṃ vācasikapayogeneva paccakkhānaṃ hoti, na tadabhāvena.

Application, however, is twofold: bodily and verbal. Therein, renunciation occurs only through verbal application, by making an utterance in any language whatsoever in the manner of 'I renounce the Buddha,' and so on. It does not occur for one performing a bodily application, such as writing letters or showing hand gestures. Thus, renunciation occurs only through verbal application, and not by its absence.

Puggalo pana duvidho yo ca paccakkhāti, yassa ca paccakkhāti. Tattha yo paccakkhāti, so sace ummattakakhittacittavedanāṭṭānaṃ aññataro na hoti. Yassa pana paccakkhāti, so sace manussajātiko hoti, na ca ummattakādīnaṃ aññataro, sammukhībhūto ca sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ hoti. Na hi asammukhībhūtassa dūtena vā paṇṇena vā ārocanaṃ ruhati. Evaṃ yathāvuttapuggalavasena paccakkhānaṃ hoti, na tadabhāvena.

The person, however, is twofold: the one who renounces and the one to whom he renounces. Therein, regarding the one who renounces: if he is not one of these—a madman, one of distracted mind, or one overcome by pain. And regarding the one to whom he renounces: if he is of human birth, is not one of the madmen and so on, and is present in person, the renunciation of the training is effective. For an announcement made to one who is not present, whether by messenger or by letter, is not accomplished. Thus, renunciation occurs by way of the persons as described, and not by their absence.

Vijānanampi niyamitāniyamitavasena duvidhaṃ. Tattha yassa yesaṃ vā niyametvā “imassa imesaṃ vā ārocemī”ti vadati, sace te yathā pakatiyā loke manussā vacanaṃ sutvā āvajjanasamaye jānanti, evaṃ tassa vacanānantarameva tassa “ayaṃ ukkaṇṭhito”ti vā “gihibhāvaṃ patthayatī”ti vā yena kenaci ākārena sikkhāpaccakkhānabhāvaṃ jānanti, paccakkhātā hoti sikkhā. Atha aparabhāge “kiṃ iminā vutta”nti cintetvā jānanti, aññe vā jānanti, appaccakkhātāva hoti sikkhā. Aniyametvā ārocentassa pana sace vuttanayena yo koci manussajātiko vacanatthaṃ jānāti, paccakkhātāva hoti sikkhā. Evaṃ vijānanavasena paccakkhānaṃ hoti, na tadabhāvena. Iti imesaṃ vuttappakārānaṃ cittādīnaṃ vaseneva sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ hoti, na aññathāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Understanding, too, is twofold: by way of being specified and unspecified. Therein, when one, having specified, declares, “I will inform this one or these ones,” if those persons, upon hearing the speech as is normal for people in the world, understand at the moment of apprehension, and thus immediately after his speech they understand by some means the fact of his renunciation of the training—that “this one is discontented” or “desires the lay state”—the training is renounced. But if they understand at a later time, after reflecting, “What was said by this one?” or if others understand, the training is not renounced. However, for one who informs without specifying, if any human being understands the meaning of the speech in the manner stated, the training is renounced. Thus, renunciation occurs by means of understanding, not by its absence. Therefore, it should be understood that the renunciation of the training occurs only by means of these stated types of mind, etc., and not otherwise.

51. “Vadatī”ti vacībhedappayogaṃ dassetvā tadanantaraṃ “viññāpetī”ti vuttattā teneva vacībhedena adhippāyaviññāpanaṃ idhādhippetaṃ, na yena kenaci upāyenāti āha “teneva vacībhedenā”ti. Padapaccābhaṭṭhaṃ katvāti padaviparāvuttiṃ katvā. Idañca padappayogassa aniyamitattā vuttaṃ. Yathā hi loke “āhara pattaṃ, pattaṃ āharā”ti aniyamitena padappayogena tadatthaviññāpanaṃ diṭṭhaṃ, evamidhāpi “buddhaṃ paccakkhāmi, paccakkhāmi buddha”nti aniyamitena padappayogena tadatthaviññāpanaṃ hotiyevāti adhippāyo. Buddhaṃ paccakkhāmīti atthappadhāno ayaṃ [M 2.0069] niddeso, na saddappadhānoti āha “milakkhabhāsāsu vā aññatarabhāsāya tamatthaṃ vadeyyā”ti. Māgadhabhāsato avasiṭṭhā sabbāpi andhadamiḷādibhāsā milakkhabhāsāti veditabbā. Khettapadesu ekaṃ vattukāmo sacepi aññaṃ vadeyya, khettapadantogadhattā paccakkhātāva [V 2.0061] hoti sikkhāti dassento āha “buddhaṃ paccakkhāmīti vattukāmo”tiādi. Yadipi “buddhaṃ paccakkhāmī”ti vattuṃ anicchanto cittena taṃ paṭikkhipitvā aññaṃ vattukāmo puna virajjhitvā tameva vadeyya, tathāpi sāsanato cavitukāmatācitte sati khettapadasseva vuttattā aṅgapāripūrisambhavato hotveva sikkhāpaccakkhānanti veditabbaṃ. Khettameva otiṇṇanti sikkhāpaccakkhānassa ruhanaṭṭhānabhūtaṃ khettameva otiṇṇaṃ.

51. Because 'communicates' is said immediately after showing the use of verbal expression with 'speaks', the communication of intention by that very verbal expression is intended here, not by any means whatsoever; hence it is said, 'by that very verbal expression.' 'Having reversed the words' means having inverted the words. And this is said because the use of words is not fixed. For just as in the world the communication of that meaning is seen through the unfixed use of words, such as 'bring the bowl, the bowl bring,' so too here, the intention is that the communication of that meaning occurs through the unfixed use of words, such as 'I renounce the Buddha, the Buddha I renounce.' This statement, 'I renounce the Buddha,' is primary in meaning, not primary in sound; hence it is said, 'or if one were to state that meaning in one of the barbarian languages.' All remaining languages other than the Māgadha language, such as Andha and Damiḷa, should be known as barbarian languages. To show that if, within the domain of expression, one intending to say one thing were to say another, the training is still renounced because it is included within the domain of expression, it is said, 'intending to say “I renounce the Buddha,”' etc. Even if one, not wishing to say 'I renounce the Buddha,' having rejected it with the mind and intending to say something else, then makes a slip and says that very thing, still, if the mind has the desire to leave the Dispensation, because what was said is within the domain of expression and because the fulfillment of the factors is possible, the renunciation of the training indeed occurs—this should be known. 'The domain itself is entered' means: the domain which is the basis for the establishment of the renunciation of the training is entered.

“Paccakkhāmi dhārehī”ti vattamānakālassa padhānabhāvena vattumicchitattā atītānāgataparikappavacanehi nevatthi sikkhāpaccakkhānanti dassento āha “sace pana buddhaṃ paccakkhinti vā”tiādi. Vadati viññāpetīti ettha vadatīti iminā payogassa niyamitattā ekassa santike attano vacībhedappayogeneva sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ hoti, na dūtasāsanādippayogenāti dassento āha “dūtaṃ vā pahiṇātī”tiādi. Tattha “mama sikkhāpaccakkhānabhāvaṃ kathehī”ti mukhasāsanavasena “dūtaṃ vā pahiṇātī”ti vuttaṃ. Paṇṇe likhitvā pahiṇanavasena “sāsanaṃ vā pesetī”ti vuttaṃ. Rukkhādīsu akkharāni likhitvā dassanavasena “akkharaṃ vā chindatī”ti vuttaṃ. Hatthamuddāya vā tamatthaṃ ārocetīti hatthena adhippāyaviññāpanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Adhippāyaviññāpako hi hatthavikāro hatthamuddā. Hattha-saddo cettha tadekadesesu aṅgulīsu daṭṭhabbo “na sabbaṃ hatthaṃ mukhe pakkhipissāmī”tiādīsu (pāci. 618) viya. Tasmā adhippāyaviññāpakena aṅgulisaṅkocādinā hatthavikārena tamatthaṃ ārocetīti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

To show that there is no renunciation of the training by means of statements referring to the past or future—because it is wished to be spoken with the present tense as primary, as in 'I renounce, bear witness'—he said, 'But if “I renounced the Buddha,”...' etc. Herein, in 'speaks, communicates,' because the usage is specified by 'speaks,' the renunciation of the training occurs only by the use of one's own verbal expression in the presence of another, not by the use of a messenger, message, or the like; to show this, he said, 'or sends a messenger,' etc. Therein, 'or sends a messenger' is said by way of oral instruction, as in 'Tell of the fact of my renunciation of the training.' 'Or dispatches a message' is said by way of writing on a leaf and sending it. 'Or carves a letter' is said by way of writing letters on trees, etc., and showing them. 'Or communicates that meaning by a hand-seal' is said with reference to communicating the intention by hand. For a modification of the hand that communicates intention is a hand-seal. And the word 'hand' here should be understood as its parts, such as the fingers, as in 'I will not put the whole hand in my mouth' (Pāci. 618). Therefore, the meaning here should be understood thus: one communicates that meaning by a modification of the hand that communicates intention, such as the bending of a finger.

Cittasampayuttanti paccakkhātukāmatācittasampayuttaṃ. Idāni vijānanavasena sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ niyamitāniyamitavasena dvidhā veditabbanti dassento āha – “yadi ayameva jānātū”tiādi. Ayañca vibhāgo “vadati viññāpetīti ekavisayattā [M 2.0070] yassa vadati, tasseva vijānanaṃ adhippetaṃ, na aññassā”ti iminā nayena laddhoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Na hi yassa vadati, tato aññaṃ viññāpetīti ayamattho sambhavati. Soyeva jānātīti avadhāraṇena tasmiṃ avijānanteyeva aññassa jānanaṃ paṭikkhipati. Tenevāha – “atha so na jānāti, añño samīpe ṭhito jānāti, apaccakkhātā hoti sikkhā”ti. Tasmā “ayameva jānātū”ti ekaṃ niyametvā ārocite yadipi sopi jānāti aññopi, niyamitassa pana niyamitavasena vijānanasambhavato sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ hotiyevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ “añño mā jānātū”ti aniyamitattā. Dvinnampi niyametvāti idaṃ “dve vā jānantu eko vā, imesaṃyeva dvinnaṃ ārocemī”ti evaṃ niyametvā ārocanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tenevāha – “ekasmiṃ [V 2.0062] jānantepi dvīsu jānantesupī”ti. Tasmā “dveyeva jānantu, eko mā jānātū”ti evaṃ dvinnaṃ niyametvā ārocite dvīsuyeva jānantesu sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ hoti, na ekasmiṃ jānanteti vadanti.

Cittasampayutta means “associated with the mind that desires to renounce.” Now, showing that the renunciation of the training, in terms of understanding, should be understood as twofold—specified and unspecified—he said, “If only this one should know,” etc. And this distinction should be understood as derived from the principle: “When one speaks or communicates, because the object is singular, the understanding intended is that of the one to whom one speaks, not of another.” For it is not possible that one communicates to someone other than the one to whom one speaks. By the emphasis “only he knows,” it rejects the knowing of another when he himself does not know. Therefore, he said: “But if he does not know, and another standing nearby knows, the training is not renounced.” Therefore, when it is announced, having specified one, “Let only this one know,” even if he himself knows and another also knows, the renunciation of the training still occurs, since the specified one knows as specified; this is because it is unspecified, “Let another not know.” This phrase 'having specified two' was said in reference to announcing after having specified thus: 'Whether two may know or one may know, I am announcing only to these two.' Therefore, he said, “whether one knows or two know.” Therefore, if it is announced, having specified two, “Let only these two know, let one not know,” then the renunciation of the training occurs only when both know, not when only one knows—so they say.

Sabhāgeti vissāsike. Parisaṅkamānoti “sace te jāneyyuṃ, maṃ te vāressantī”ti āsaṅkamāno. Samayaññūti sāsanācārakusalo, idha pana tadadhippāyajānanamattenapi samayaññū nāma hoti. Teneva āha – “ukkaṇṭhito ayaṃ…pe… sāsanato cutoti jānātī”ti. Tasmā “buddhaṃ paccakkhāmī”ti imassa atthaṃ ñatvāpi sace “ayaṃ bhikkhubhāvato cavitukāmo, gihī vā hotukāmo”ti na jānāti, appaccakkhātāva hoti sikkhā. Sace pana “buddhaṃ paccakkhāmī”ti vacanassa atthaṃ ajānitvāpi “ukkaṇṭhito gihī hotukāmo”ti adhippāyaṃ jānāti, paccakkhātāva hoti sikkhā. Aññasmiṃ khaṇe sotaviññāṇavīthiyā saddaggahaṇaṃ, aññasmiṃyeva ca manoviññāṇavīthiyā tadatthavijānananti āha – “taṅkhaṇaññeva pana apubbaṃ acarimaṃ dujjāna”nti. Na hi ekasmiṃyeva khaṇe saddasavanaṃ tadatthavijānanañca sambhavati. Tathā hi “ghaṭo”ti vā “paṭo”ti vā kenaci vutte tattha gha-saddaṃ paccuppannaṃ gahetvā ekā sotaviññāṇavīthi uppajjitvā nirujjhati, tadanantaraṃ ekā manoviññāṇavīthi tameva atītaṃ gahetvā uppajjati. Evaṃ tena vuttavacane yattakāni akkharāni honti, tesu ekamekaṃ akkharaṃ paccuppannamatītañca gahetvā sotaviññāṇavīthiyā manoviññāṇavīthiyā ca uppajjitvā niruddhāya avasāne [M 2.0071] tāni akkharāni sampiṇḍetvā akkharasamūhaṃ gahetvā ekā manoviññāṇavīthi uppajjitvā nirujjhati. Tadanantaraṃ “ayamakkharasamūho etassa nāma”nti nāmapaññattiggahaṇavasena aparāya manoviññāṇavīthiyā uppajjitvā niruddhāya tadanantaraṃ uppannāya manoviññāṇavīthiyā “ayametassa attho”ti pakatiyā tadatthavijānanaṃ sambhavati.

Sabhāgeti means “with those in whom he confides.” Parisaṅkamāno means “being apprehensive, thinking, ‘If they knew, they would prevent me.’ ” Samayaññū means “skilled in the conduct of the Dispensation”; here, however, one is called a samayaññū even by merely knowing that intention. Therefore, he said, “He knows ‘This one is discontented... fallen from the Dispensation.’ ” Therefore, even if one understands the meaning of “I renounce the Buddha,” if one does not know that “this monk desires to fall from the state of a monk or desires to become a layperson,” the training is not renounced. But if, without understanding the meaning of the statement “I renounce the Buddha,” one knows the intention that “he is discontented and desires to become a layperson,” the training is indeed renounced. The grasping of the sound by the ear-consciousness process is in one moment, and the understanding of its meaning by the mind-consciousness process is in another; therefore, he said, “At that very moment, however, it is difficult to know simultaneously.” For it is not possible for both the hearing of the sound and the understanding of its meaning to occur in the very same moment. For example, when someone says “ghaṭo” or “paṭo,” an ear-consciousness process arises and ceases upon grasping the present sound “gha.” Immediately after that, a mind-consciousness process arises, grasping that very same past object. Thus, in that spoken utterance, for however many syllables there are, after the series of ear-consciousness and mind-consciousness processes grasping each single syllable as present and past has arisen and ceased, at the end, a mind-consciousness process arises and ceases, having combined those syllables and grasped the collection of syllables. Immediately afterward, after another mind-consciousness process has arisen and ceased, apprehending the concept of the name, thinking, “This collection of syllables is such-and-such a name,” then, by the mind-consciousness process that arises immediately afterward, the understanding of its meaning naturally occurs, thinking, “This is its meaning.”

Āvajjanasamayenāti bhummatthe karaṇavacanaṃ, atthābhogasamayeti attho. Idāni tameva āvajjanasamayaṃ vibhāvento āha – “yathā pakatiyā…pe… jānantī”ti. Teneva vacībhedena adhippāyaviññāpanassa idhādhippetattā aparabhāge “kiṃ iminā vutta”nti taṃ kaṅkhantassa cirena adhippāyavijānanaṃ aññenapi kenaci upāyantarena sambhavati, na kevalaṃ vacībhedamattenāti āha – “atha aparabhāge…pe… appaccakkhātā hoti sikkhā”ti. “Gihī bhavissāmī”ti vutte atthabhedo kālabhedo ca hotīti appaccakkhātā hoti sikkhā. “Dhārehī”ti hi imassa yo attho kālo ca, na so “bhavissāmī”ti etassa. “Gihī [V 2.0063] homī”ti vutte pana atthabhedoyeva, na kālabhedo “homī”ti vattamānakālasseva vuttattā. “Gihī jātomhi, gihīmhī”ti etthāpi atthassa ceva kālassa ca bhinnattā appaccakkhātā hoti sikkhā. “Ajja paṭṭhāyā”ti idaṃ tathā vuttepi dosabhāvato paripuṇṇaṃ katvā vuttaṃ. “Dhārehī”ti atthappadhānattā niddesassa pariyāyavacanehipi sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ hotiyevāti dassento āha “jānāhī”tiādi. Dhārehi jānāhi sañjānāhi manasi karohīti hi etāni padāni atthato kālato ca abhinnāni.

Āvajjanasamayena: the instrumental ending is in the sense of the locative; the meaning is “at the time of attending to the meaning.” Now, elaborating on that very time of attending, he said, “As naturally… they know.” Because the communication of intention by that very verbal expression is intended here, for one who later doubts, “What was said by this?” the understanding of the intention is possible only after a long time and by some other means, not merely by the verbal expression alone. Therefore, he said, “But later… the training is not renounced.” When “I will become a layperson” is said, because there is a difference in meaning and a difference in time, the training is not renounced. For whatever meaning and time this “Bear it” has, that is not the meaning and time of “I will become.” But when “I am a layperson” is said, there is only a difference in meaning, not a difference in time, because “I am” is spoken in the present tense. Here also, in the case of “I was born a layperson, I am a layperson,” because both the meaning and the time are different, the training is not renounced. This phrase “From today onwards,” even if said thus, is stated having made it complete because of the presence of a fault. Because “Bear it” is primary in meaning, showing that the renunciation of the training occurs even with synonymous expressions of the instruction, he said “Know,” etc. For these words—“Bear it,” “Know,” “Recognize,” “Take to heart”—are not different in meaning and in time.

52. Purimāneva cuddasāti buddhādisabrahmacārīpariyantāni. Hotu bhavatūti idampi paṭikkhepamattamevāti āha “hotu, pariyattanti attho”ti.

52. The former fourteen are those beginning with the Buddha and ending with his fellow celibates. “Let it be, let it be”—this is also merely a rejection; therefore, he said, “Let it be” means “enough.”

53. Vaṇṇapaṭṭhānanti mahāsaṅghikānaṃ buddhaguṇaparidīpakaṃ ekaṃ suttanti vadanti. Upāligāthāsūti (ma. ni. 2.76) –

53. Vaṇṇapaṭṭhāna: they say it is a sutta of the Mahāsaṅghikas that illuminates the virtues of the Buddha. In the Upāligāthā (MN 56):

“Dhīrassa [M 2.0072] vigatamohassa,

Pabhinnakhīlassa vijitavijayassa;

Anīghassa susamacittassa;

Vuddhasīlassa sādhupaññassa;

Vesamantarassa vimalassa;

Bhagavato tassa sāvakohamasmi.

“Of the steadfast one, free from delusion, who has destroyed the stake of defilement, who has conquered what is to be conquered; of the one without affliction, with a well-pacified mind; of the one with developed virtue, with excellent wisdom; of the one who has crossed over the uneven, the stainless one; of that Blessed One, I am a disciple.

“Akathaṃkathissa tusitassa;

Vantalokāmisassa muditassa;

Katasamaṇassa manujassa;

Antimasārīrassa narassa;

Anopamassa virajassa;

Bhagavato tassa sāvakohamasmi.

“Of the one without doubt, the contented one; who has relinquished worldly allurements, the joyful one; who has fulfilled the ascetic's task, the human being; who bears his final body, the noble man; of the incomparable one, the dustless one; of that Blessed One, I am a disciple.

“Asaṃsayassa kusalassa;

Venayikassa sārathivarassa;

Anuttarassa [V 2.0064] ruciradhammassa;

Nikkaṅkhassa pabhāsakassa;

Mānacchidassa vīrassa;

Bhagavato tassa sāvakohamasmi.

“Of the one free from doubt, the skillful one; the trainer, the supreme charioteer; the unsurpassed one, of delightful Dhamma; the one without uncertainty, the illuminator; the one who has cut off conceit, the hero; of that Blessed One, I am a disciple.

“Nisabhassa appameyyassa;

Gambhīrassa monappattassa;

Khemaṅkarassa vedassa;

Dhammaṭṭhassa saṃvutattassa;

Saṅgātigassa muttassa;

Bhagavato tassa sāvakohamasmi.

“Of the bull among men, the immeasurable one; the profound one, who has attained the sage's knowledge; the maker of security, the knower; the one established in Dhamma, the self-restrained one; who has overcome the battle, the liberated one; of that Blessed One, I am a disciple.

“Nāgassa pantasenassa;

Khīṇasaṃyojanassa muttassa;

Paṭimantakassa dhonassa;

Pannaddhajassa vītarāgassa;

Dantassa nippapañcassa;

Bhagavato tassa sāvakohamasmi.

“Of the great being, who dwells in remote lodgings; whose fetters are destroyed, the liberated one; the reflective one, the pure one; whose banner is lowered, free from lust; the tamed one, free from proliferation; of that Blessed One, I am a disciple.

“Isisattamassa [M 2.0073] akuhassa;

Tevijjassa brahmappattassa;

Nhātakassa padakassa;

Passaddhassa viditavedassa;

Purindadassa sakkassa;

Bhagavato tassa sāvakohamasmi.

“Of the seventh sage, the one free from deceit; possessing the three knowledges, who has attained the sublime state; the one who has washed away evil, the one who knows the path; the tranquil one, who has known what is to be known; the foremost giver, the able one; of that Blessed One, I am a disciple.

“Ariyassa bhāvitattassa;

Pattippattassa veyyākaraṇassa;

Satimato vipassissa;

Anabhinatassa no apanatassa;

Anejassa [V 2.0065] vasippattassa;

Bhagavato tassa sāvakohamasmi.

“Of the noble one, with a developed self; who has attained what is to be attained, the explainer; the mindful one, the discerning one; not leaning towards, not leaning away; the imperturbable one, who has attained mastery; of that Blessed One, I am a disciple.

“Samuggatassa jhāyissa;

Ananugatantarassa suddhassa;

Asitassa hitassa;

Pavivittassa aggappattassa;

Tiṇṇassa tārayantassa;

Bhagavato tassa sāvakohamasmi.

“Of the one who has risen up, the meditative one; with no inner defilement, the pure one; the unattached one, the beneficial one; the secluded one, who has reached the highest; who has crossed over, who helps others to cross; of that Blessed One, I am a disciple.

“Santassa bhūripaññassa;

Mahāpaññassa vītalobhassa;

Tathāgatassa sugatassa;

Appaṭipuggalassa asamassa;

Visāradassa nipuṇassa;

Bhagavato tassa sāvakohamasmi.

“Of the peaceful one, of abundant wisdom; of great wisdom, free from greed; the Tathāgata, the Well-Gone One; the one without a rival, the unequalled one; the fearless one, the skillful one; of that Blessed One, I am a disciple.

“Taṇhacchidassa [M 2.0074] buddhassa;

Vītadhūmassa anupalittassa;

Āhuneyyassa yakkhassa;

Uttamapuggalassa atulassa;

Mahato yasaggappattassa;

Bhagavato tassa sāvakohamasmī”ti. –

“Of the one who has cut off craving, the Buddha; the one free from smoke, the unsoiled one; the one worthy of offerings, the venerable being; the supreme person, the unequalled one; the great one, who has attained the summit of glory; of that Blessed One, I am a disciple.”

Evaṃ upāligahapatinā vuttāsu upālisutte āgatagāthāsu.

Thus in the verses that have come down in the Upāli Sutta, spoken by the householder Upāli.

Yathārutamevāti yathāvuttameva, pāḷiyaṃ āgatamevāti adhippāyo. Yasmā “sammāsambuddhaṃ anantabuddhiṃ anomabuddhiṃ bodhipaññāṇa”nti imāni vaṇṇapaṭṭhāne āgatanāmāni, “dhīra”ntiādīni pana upāligāthāsu āgatanāmāni. Tattha bodhi vuccati sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ, taṃ sañjānanahetuttā paññāṇaṃ etassāti bodhipaññāṇo, bhagavā. Dhiyā paññāya rāti gaṇhāti[V 2.0066], sevatīti vā dhīro. Samucchinnasabbacetokhīlattā pabhinnakhīlo. Sabbaputhujjane vijiniṃsu vijayanti vijinissanti cāti vijayā. Ke te? Maccumārakilesamāradevaputtamārā. Te vijitā vijayā etenāti vijitavijayo, bhagavā. Kilesamāramaccumāravijayeneva panettha abhisaṅkhārakkhandhamārāpi vijitāva hontīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

“Just as heard” means “just as spoken,” “just as it has come down in the Pāli text”—this is the intention. Because “Sammāsambuddha, Anantabuddhi, Anomabuddhi, Bodhipaññāṇa” are names that have come down in the section on praise, whereas “Dhīra,” and so on, are names that have come down in the verses of Upāli. Therein, “bodhi” is called the knowledge of omniscience. Because it is the cause of full and distinct knowing, that knowledge exists for him, thus he is “Bodhipaññāṇo,” the Blessed One. He takes up or resorts to with wisdom, thus he is “Dhīro.” Because all the stakes of the heart are completely cut off, he is “Pabhinnakhīlo.” They conquered, are conquering, and will conquer all worldlings, thus they are “vijayā” (conquerors). Who are they? The Māra of death, the Māra of defilements, and the Devaputta Māra. Because those conquerors were conquered by him, he is “Vijitavijayo,” the Blessed One. Here, by the very conquest of the Māra of defilements and the Māra of death, it should be understood that the Māra of formations and the Māra of the aggregates are also conquered.

Svākkhātantiādīsu (visuddhi. 1.147) sātthasabyañjanakevalaparipuṇṇaparisuddhabrahmacariyassa pakāsanato svākkhāto dhammo, atthavipallāsābhāvato vā suṭṭhu akkhātoti svākkhāto. Yathā hi aññatitthiyānaṃ dhammassa attho vipallāsaṃ āpajjati “antarāyikā”ti vuttadhammānaṃ antarāyikattābhāvato, “niyyānikā”ti ca vuttadhammānaṃ niyyānikattābhāvato, tena te aññatitthiyā durakkhātadhammāyeva honti, na tathā bhagavato dhammassa attho vipallāsaṃ āpajjati “ime dhammā antarāyikā niyyānikā”ti evaṃ vuttadhammānaṃ tathābhāvānatikkamanatoti. Evaṃ tāva pariyattidhammo svākkhāto dhammo.

In 'Svākkhāta,' and so on, the Dhamma is 'well-proclaimed' because it proclaims the holy life which is complete in every way, pure, with its meaning and phrasing; or, because there is no distortion of meaning, it is 'well-declared,' thus 'svākkhāto.' For just as the meaning of the Dhamma of other sectarians falls into distortion—because the dhammas said to be 'obstructive' are not obstructive, and the dhammas said to be 'leading out' do not lead out—for that reason, those other sectarians have a poorly proclaimed Dhamma. The meaning of the Blessed One's Dhamma does not fall into distortion in that way, because the dhammas spoken of as 'these dhammas are obstructive, these dhammas lead out' do not transgress that very nature. Thus, the scriptural Dhamma is the well-proclaimed Dhamma.

Lokuttaradhammo pana nibbānānurūpāya paṭipattiyā paṭipadānurūpassa ca nibbānassa akkhātattā svākkhāto. Yathāha –

The supramundane Dhamma, however, is 'well-proclaimed' because the practice conforming to Nibbāna and Nibbāna conforming to the path are declared. As it is said:

“Supaññattā [M 2.0075] kho pana tena bhagavatā sāvakānaṃ nibbānagāminī paṭipadā saṃsandati nibbānañca paṭipadā ca. Seyyathāpi nāma gaṅgodakaṃ yamunodakena saṃsandati sameti, evameva supaññattā tena bhagavatā sāvakānaṃ nibbānagāminī paṭipadā saṃsandati nibbānañca paṭipadā cā”ti (dī. ni. 2.296).

“‘Indeed, the path leading to Nibbāna has been well-proclaimed by that Blessed One for his disciples; the path and Nibbāna converge. Just as the water of the Ganges converges and meets with the water of the Yamunā, even so has the path leading to Nibbāna been well-proclaimed by that Blessed One for his disciples; the path and Nibbāna converge.’”

Ariyamaggo cettha antadvayaṃ anupagamma majjhimāpaṭipadābhūtova “majjhimā paṭipadā”ti akkhātattā svākkhāto. Sāmaññaphalāni paṭippassaddhakilesāneva “paṭippassaddhakilesānī”ti akkhātattā svākkhātāni. Nibbānaṃ sassatāmatatāṇaleṇādisabhāvameva sassatādisabhāvavasena akkhātattā svākkhātanti evaṃ lokuttaradhammopi svākkhāto.

And here, the Noble Path, not approaching the two extremes and being the middle way, is declared as 'the middle path'; thus it is 'well-proclaimed.' The fruits of recluseship, being the very pacification of defilements, are declared as 'the pacification of defilements'; thus they are 'well-proclaimed.' Nibbāna, being of the very nature of the eternal, deathless, refuge, shelter, and so on, is declared in terms of its nature as eternal, and so on; thus it is 'well-proclaimed.' In this way, the supramundane Dhamma is also 'well-proclaimed.'

Ariyamaggo attano santāne rāgādīnaṃ abhāvaṃ karontena ariyapuggalena sāmaṃ daṭṭhabbo “ariyamaggena mama rāgādayo pahīnā”ti sayaṃ attanā anaññaneyyena passitabboti sandiṭṭhi, sandiṭṭhi eva sandiṭṭhiko. Apica navavidho lokuttaradhammo yena yena adhigato hoti, tena tena ariyasāvakena parasaddhāya gantabbataṃ hitvā paccakkhañāṇena sayaṃ daṭṭhabboti sandiṭṭhiko. Atha vā pasatthā diṭṭhi sandiṭṭhi, sandiṭṭhiyā jayatīti sandiṭṭhiko. Tathā hettha ariyamaggo sampayuttāya, ariyaphalaṃ kāraṇabhūtāya, nibbānaṃ visayibhūtāya sandiṭṭhiyā kilese jayati, tasmā yathā rathena jayatīti rathiko, evaṃ navavidhopi lokuttaradhammo sandiṭṭhiyā jayatīti [V 2.0067] sandiṭṭhiko. Atha vā diṭṭhanti dassanaṃ vuccati, diṭṭhameva sandiṭṭhaṃ, sandassananti attho. Sandiṭṭhaṃ arahatīti sandiṭṭhiko. Lokuttaradhammo hi bhāvanābhisamayavasena sacchikiriyābhisamayavasena ca dissamānoyeva vaṭṭabhayaṃ nivatteti, tasmā yathā vatthamarahatīti vatthiko, evaṃ sandiṭṭhaṃ arahatīti sandiṭṭhiko.

The noble path is to be seen by the noble individual himself, who brings about the absence of lust and so forth in his own continuum, thinking, “By the noble path, my lusts and other defilements have been abandoned.” It is to be seen by oneself, by one's own self, not to be led by another; thus it is sandiṭṭhi. Sandiṭṭhi itself is sandiṭṭhiko. Moreover, the ninefold supramundane Dhamma, by whichever noble disciple it is attained, is to be seen by that noble disciple himself through direct knowledge, having abandoned going by faith in others; thus, it is sandiṭṭhiko. Alternatively, a praiseworthy view is sandiṭṭhi; because one conquers by sandiṭṭhi, it is sandiṭṭhiko. For here, the noble path conquers the defilements by means of the sandiṭṭhi that is associated with it, that is the cause of the noble fruit, and that has Nibbāna as its object. Therefore, just as one who conquers with a chariot is a charioteer (rathiko), so too the ninefold supramundane Dhamma conquers by sandiṭṭhi; thus, it is sandiṭṭhiko. Alternatively, diṭṭha is called seeing; diṭṭha itself is sandiṭṭha, meaning 'seeing well'. That which is worthy of being seen well is sandiṭṭhiko. For the supramundane Dhamma, being seen by way of the breakthrough of cultivation and the breakthrough of realization, turns away the danger of the round of existence. Therefore, just as one who is worthy of cloth is called vatthiko, so that which is worthy of being seen well is called sandiṭṭhiko.

Attano phaladānaṃ sandhāya nāssa āgametabbo kālo atthīti akālo. Yathā hi lokiyakusalassa upapajjaaparāpariyāyetiādinā phaladānaṃ pati āgametabbo kālo atthi, na evametassāti attho. Akāloyeva akāliko, na pañcāhasattāhādibhedaṃ kālaṃ khepetvā phalaṃ deti, attano pana pavattisamanantarameva phaladoti [M 2.0076] vuttaṃ hoti. Atha vā attano phalappadāne vippakaṭṭho dūro kālo patto upanīto assāti kāliko, kālantaraphaladāyī. Ko so? Lokiyo kusaladhammo. Ayaṃ pana samanantaraphaladāyakattā na kālikoti akāliko. Maggameva hi sandhāya “akāliko”ti idaṃ vuttaṃ.

Regarding the giving of its own fruit, there is no time to be awaited for it; thus, it is akālo. Just as for a worldly wholesome state there is a time to be awaited for the giving of its fruit—by way of ripening in this life, the next, or subsequent lives—it is not so for this; that is the meaning. Akālo itself is akāliko; it does not give its fruit after a lapse of time divided into five days, seven days, etc., but it is said to give its fruit immediately after its own occurrence. Alternatively, that for which, in the giving of its own fruit, a remote, distant time must be reached is kāliko (timely), a giver of fruit after an interval of time. What is that? The worldly wholesome Dhamma. But this, because it gives its fruit immediately, is not kāliko, hence akāliko. For it is with reference to the path itself that this term akāliko is used.

“Ehi passa imaṃ dhamma”nti evaṃ pavattaṃ ehipassavidhiṃ arahatīti ehipassiko. Kasmā panesa taṃ vidhiṃ arahatīti? Paramatthato vijjamānattā parisuddhattā ca. Rittamuṭṭhiyañhi hiraññaṃ vā suvaṇṇaṃ vā atthīti vatvāpi “ehi passa ima”nti na sakkā vattuṃ. Kasmā? Avijjamānattā. Vijjamānampi ca gūthaṃ vā muttaṃ vā manuññabhāvappakāsanena cittasampahaṃsanatthaṃ “ehi passa ima”nti na sakkā vattuṃ, apica kho naṃ tiṇehi vā paṇṇehi vā paṭicchādetabbameva hoti. Kasmā? Aparisuddhattā. Ayaṃ pana navavidhopi lokuttaradhammo sabhāvato ca vijjamāno vigatavalāhake ca ākāse sampuṇṇacandamaṇḍalaṃ viya paṇḍukambale nikkhittajātimaṇi viya ca parisuddho, tasmā vijjamānattā parisuddhattā ca ehipassavidhiṃ arahatīti ehipassiko.

“Come and see this Dhamma”—thus, it is worthy of the invitation “come and see” (ehipassavidhi), hence it is ehipassiko. But why is it worthy of that invitation? Because it exists in the ultimate sense and is utterly pure. For if one were to say of an empty fist, “There is silver or gold here,” one could not say, “Come and see this.” Why? Because it does not exist. Even if something exists, like feces or urine, one could not say, “Come and see this,” to gladden the mind by showing its pleasant nature; on the contrary, it should be covered with grass or leaves. Why? Because it is impure. But this ninefold supramundane Dhamma both exists by its own nature and is pure, like the full moon's orb in a cloudless sky or a high-quality gem placed on a white woolen blanket. Therefore, because it exists and is pure, it is worthy of the invitation “come and see,” hence it is ehipassiko.

Upanetabboti opaneyyiko. Ayaṃ panettha vinicchayo – upanayanaṃ upanayo, ādittaṃ celaṃ vā sīsaṃ vā ajjhupekkhitvāpi bhāvanāvasena attano citte upanayanaṃ uppādanaṃ arahatīti opaneyyiko. Idaṃ saṅkhate lokuttaradhamme yujjati, asaṅkhato pana attano citte ārammaṇabhāvena upanayanaṃ arahatīti opaneyyiko, sacchikiriyāvasena allīyanaṃ arahatīti attho[V 2.0068]. Atha vā nibbānaṃ upaneti ariyapuggalanti ariyamaggo upaneyyo, sacchikātabbataṃ upanetabboti phalanibbānadhammo upaneyyo, upaneyyo eva opaneyyiko.

It is to be led towards, hence it is 'opaneyyiko'. Herein is the determination: 'upanayana' is 'upanayo' (leading towards). Even disregarding one's burning cloth or head, it is worthy of being brought into or produced in one's own mind by means of cultivation; therefore, it is 'opaneyyiko'. This applies to the conditioned supramundane Dhamma. As for the unconditioned, however, it is 'opaneyyiko' because it is worthy of being brought into one's own mind as an object; the meaning is that it is worthy of being adhered to by means of realization. Alternatively, because the noble path leads noble individuals to Nibbāna, the noble path is 'upaneyyo' (to be led towards). Because it is to be led to the state of being realized, the fruit-and-Nibbāna Dhamma is 'upaneyyo'. 'Upaneyyo' itself is 'opaneyyiko'.

Sabbehi ugghaṭitaññūādīhi viññūhi “bhāvito me maggo, adhigataṃ phalaṃ, sacchikato nirodho”ti attani attani veditabboti paccattaṃ veditabbo viññūhi. Na hi upajjhāyena bhāvitena maggena saddhivihārikassa kilesā pahīyanti, na so tassa phalasamāpattiyā phāsu viharati, na tena sacchikataṃ nibbānaṃ sacchikaroti, tasmā na esa parassa sīse ābharaṇaṃ viya daṭṭhabbo, attano pana citteyeva daṭṭhabbo, anubhavitabbo viññūhīti vuttaṃ hoti.

It is to be known individually by all the wise, from those of quick understanding onwards, 'The path has been cultivated by me, the fruit has been attained, cessation has been realized.' Thus, it is 'to be known individually by the wise'. For the defilements of a disciple are not abandoned by the path cultivated by his preceptor; the disciple does not dwell comfortably through the preceptor's attainment of fruition, nor does he realize the Nibbāna realized by the preceptor. Therefore, this is not to be seen like an ornament on another's head, but is to be seen in one's own mind; it is to be experienced by the wise—thus it is said.

Asaṅkhatanti [M 2.0077] saṅgamma samāgamma paccayasamodhānalakkhaṇena saṅgamena sannipatitvā anurūpehi paccayehi akataṃ anibbattitanti asaṅkhataṃ. Natthi ettha matanti amataṃ, etasmiṃ vā adhigate natthi puggalassa mataṃ maraṇanti amataṃ. Kiñcāpi ettha “svākkhātaṃ dhammaṃ paccakkhāmī”tiādinā sabbattha dhamma-saddappayogo dassito, tathāpi dhamma-saddena ayojetvā vutte vevacane na paccakkhānaṃ nāma na hotīti “svākkhātaṃ paccakkhāmī”tiādinā vuttepi sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ hotiyevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Svākkhātaṃ dhamma”ntiādinā pana dhamma-saddappayogo svākkhātā-disaddānaṃ dhamma-visesanabhāvadassanatthaṃ katoti veditabbaṃ. Ekadhammakkhandhassapi nāmanti ettha “paṭhamadhammakkhandhaṃ dutiyadhammakkhandhaṃ pucchādhammakkhandhaṃ vissajjanādhammakkhandha”ntiādinā dhammakkhandhanāmāni veditabbāni.

'Asaṅkhata' (unconditioned) means that which is not made, not produced, by suitable conditions coming together, assembling, or uniting, characterized by the combination of causes. 'Amata' (deathless) means that there is no death here; or, when this is attained, there is no death or dying for that person, hence it is 'amata'. Although the use of the word 'dhamma' is shown everywhere in phrases such as 'I renounce the well-taught Dhamma', it should be understood that a renunciation does not fail to occur when a synonym is used without being connected to the word 'dhamma'; even when one says 'I renounce the well-taught', the renunciation of the training indeed occurs. The use of the word 'dhamma' in phrases like 'the well-taught Dhamma' is done to show that words like 'svākkhāta' serve to qualify the Dhamma. In the phrase 'the name of even one Dhamma aggregate', the names of the Dhamma aggregates should be understood by way of 'the first Dhamma aggregate, the second Dhamma aggregate, the question Dhamma aggregate, the answer Dhamma aggregate', and so on.

Suppaṭipannanti svākkhāte dhammavinaye yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipannattā suppaṭipannaṃ. Majjhimāya paṭipadāya antadvayaṃ anupagamma paṭipannattā kāyavacīmanovaṅkakuṭilajimhadosappahānāya paṭipannattā ca ujuppaṭipannaṃ. Ñāyo vuccati nibbānaṃ ariyamaggādīhi ñāyati paṭivijjhīyati sacchikarīyatīti katvā, tadatthāya paṭipannattā ñāyappaṭipannaṃ. Yathā paṭipannā guṇasambhāvanāya parehi kariyamānaṃ paccuṭṭhānādisāmīcikammaṃ arahanti, tathā paṭipannattā sāmīcippaṭipannaṃ.

Regarding 'well-practiced' (suppaṭipanna): because of practicing as instructed in the well-proclaimed Dhamma and Discipline, one is 'well-practiced.' Because of practicing by not approaching the two extremes by means of the middle way, and because of practicing for the abandoning of the faults of crookedness, perversion, and deviousness of body, speech, and mind, one is 'uprightly-practiced' (ujuppaṭipanna). Nibbāna is called the 'true way' (ñāya) because it is known, penetrated, and realized by the noble path and so on; because of practicing for the sake of that, one is 'practicing for the true way' (ñāyappaṭipanna). Because they practice in such a way that, due to the arising of their virtues, they are worthy of proper duties such as rising up to greet, etc., performed by others, they are 'properly-practiced' (sāmīcippaṭipanna).

Yugaḷavasena paṭhamamaggaṭṭho phalaṭṭhoti idamekaṃ yugaḷanti evaṃ cattāri purisayugāni honti. Ettha pana “catupurisayugaṃ saṅgha”nti vattabbe “cattārī”ti vibhattilopaṃ akatvā niddeso katoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Cattāri purisayugāni etthāti catupurisayugoti hi saṅgho vuccati. Aṭṭhapurisapuggalanti [V 2.0069] purisapuggalavasena eko paṭhamamaggaṭṭho, eko phalaṭṭhoti iminā nayena aṭṭheva purisapuggalā honti. Aṭṭha purisapuggalā etthāti aṭṭhapurisapuggalo, saṅgho. Ettha ca purisoti vā puggaloti vā ekatthānetāni padāni, veneyyavasena panetaṃ vuttaṃ.

By way of pairs, the one on the first path and the one on the fruit—this is one pair. In this way, there are four pairs of persons. Here, it should be understood that when it should be said, 'the Sangha is the four pairs of persons' (catupurisayugaṃ saṅghaṃ), the statement is made as 'cattāri' without eliding the case ending. For the Sangha is called 'catupurisayuga' because there are four pairs of persons therein. Regarding 'eight individual persons' (aṭṭhapurisapuggala): by way of individual persons, there is one on the first path and one on the fruit; in this manner, there are indeed eight individual persons. The Sangha is 'aṭṭhapurisapuggala' because there are eight individual persons therein. And here, the words 'purisa' and 'puggala' are synonymous; but this is stated for the sake of those to be trained.

Āhuneyyantiādīsu (visuddhi. 1.156) ānetvā hunitabbanti āhunaṃ, dūratopi ānetvā sīlavantesu dātabbānaṃ catunnaṃ paccayānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Taṃ āhunaṃ paṭiggahetuṃ yutto tassa mahapphalabhāvakaraṇatoti āhuneyyo, saṅgho. Atha vā dūratopi āgantvā sabbasāpateyyampi ettha hunitabbanti [M 2.0078] āhavanīyo, sakkādīnampi vā āhavanaṃ arahatīti āhavanīyo. Yo cāyaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ āhavanīyo aggi, yattha hutaṃ mahapphalanti tesaṃ laddhi. Sace hutassa mahapphalatāya āhavanīyo, saṅghova āhavanīyo. Saṅghe hutañhi mahapphalaṃ hoti. Yathāha –

Regarding 'worthy of offerings' (āhuneyya) and so on: 'āhuna' means 'what should be brought and offered.' This is a designation for the four requisites that should be brought even from afar and given to the virtuous. The Sangha is 'āhuneyya' because it is fit to receive that 'āhuna,' as it causes the fruit thereof to be great. Alternatively, one is 'āhavanīya' (worthy of sacrificial offerings) because all of one's property should be offered here, even coming from afar. Or, one is 'āhavanīya' because one is worthy of offerings even from Sakka and others. And that sacrificial fire of the brahmins, in which what is offered has great fruit—this is their doctrine. If something is 'āhavanīya' because what is offered therein has great fruit, then the Sangha alone is 'āhavanīya.' For what is offered to the Sangha has great fruit. As it is said:

“Yo ca vassasataṃ jantu, aggiṃ paricare vane;

Ekañca bhāvitattānaṃ, muhuttamapi pūjaye;

Sāyeva pūjanā seyyo, yañce vassasataṃ huta”nti. (dha. pa. 107);

“Should a person for a hundred years tend the fire in the forest, and should they for just a moment honor one who has developed themselves—that very honor is better than the sacrifice of a hundred years.”

Tadetaṃ nikāyantare “āhavanīyo”ti padaṃ idha “āhuneyyo”ti iminā padena atthato ekaṃ, byañjanato panettha kiñcimattameva nānaṃ.

This word 'āhavanīyo' in another collection is, in meaning, one with the word 'āhuneyyo' here; there is only some slight difference in the letters.

Pāhuneyyanti ettha pana pāhunaṃ vuccati disāvidisato āgatānaṃ piyamanāpānaṃ ñātimittānaṃ atthāya sakkārena paṭiyattaṃ āgantukadānaṃ. Tampi ṭhapetvā te tathārūpe piyamittādike pāhunake saṅghasseva dātuṃ yuttaṃ, saṅghova taṃ paṭiggahetuṃ yutto. Saṅghasadiso hi pāhunako natthi. Tathā hesa ekabuddhantare vītivatteyeva dissati, abbokiṇṇañca piyamanāpattakarehi sīlādidhammehi samannāgatoti evaṃ pāhunamassa dātuṃ yuttaṃ, pāhunañca paṭiggahetuṃ yuttoti pāhuneyyo.

Regarding 'worthy of hospitality' (pāhuneyya): here, 'pāhuna' is said to be a gift for guests, prepared with honor for the sake of dear and agreeable relatives and friends who have come from all directions. Setting aside even such guests as dear friends and the like, it is fitting to give that gift only to the Sangha; the Sangha alone is fit to receive it. For there is no guest like the Sangha. Indeed, this Sangha is seen even when an interval between Buddhas has passed, and it is endowed with uninterrupted virtues such as morality, which bring about what is dear and agreeable. Thus, it is fitting to give a guest-offering to it, and it is fit to receive a guest-offering; hence, it is 'pāhuneyya'.

Dakkhanti etāya sattā yathādhippetāhi sampattīhi vaḍḍhantīti dakkhiṇā, paralokaṃ saddahitvā dātabbadānaṃ. Taṃ dakkhiṇaṃ arahati, dakkhiṇāya vā hito yasmā naṃ mahapphalakaratāya visodhetīti dakkhiṇeyyo. Ubho hatthe sirasi patiṭṭhāpetvā sabbalokena kariyamānaṃ añjalikammaṃ arahatīti añjalikaraṇīyo. Anuttaraṃ puññakkhettanti sabbalokassa asadisaṃ puññaviruhanaṭṭhānaṃ[V 2.0070]. Yathā hi rañño vā amaccassa vā sālīnaṃ vā yavānaṃ vā viruhanaṭṭhānaṃ rañño sālikkhettaṃ yavakkhettanti vuccati, evaṃ saṅgho sabbalokassa puññānaṃ viruhanaṭṭhānaṃ. Saṅghaṃ nissāya hi lokassa nānappakārahitasukhasaṃvattanikāni puññāni viruhanti, tasmā saṅgho anuttaraṃ puññakkhettaṃ lokassa. Etthāpi “suppaṭipannaṃ saṅgha”ntiādinā sabbattha saṅgha-saddappayogo suppaṭipannā-disaddānaṃ saṅghavisesanabhāvadassanatthaṃ kato, tasmā “suppaṭipannaṃ paccakkhāmī”tiādinā vuttepi sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ hotiyevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

It is called ‘dakkhiṇā’ (a religious donation) because by this, beings see and increase with their desired attainments; it is a gift to be given with faith in the next world. One is ‘dakkhiṇeyya’ (worthy of donations) because one is worthy of that donation, or because one is beneficial to the donation, purifying it by making it of great fruit. One is ‘añjalikaraṇīya’ (worthy of reverential salutation) because one is worthy of the act of añjali performed by the whole world by placing both hands on the head. ‘Anuttaraṃ puññakkhettaṃ’ (an unsurpassed field of merit) means an incomparable place for the growth of merit for the whole world. For just as a place for the growth of rice or barley belonging to a king or a minister is called the king's rice field or barley field, so the Sangha is the place for the growth of merit for the whole world. For, dependent on the Sangha, merits that bring about various kinds of welfare and happiness for the world grow. Therefore, the Sangha is the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. Here too, the use of the word ‘Sangha’ everywhere in phrases like ‘the well-practiced Sangha’ is done to show that words like ‘well-practiced’ are qualifiers of the Sangha. Therefore, it should be understood that even when one says, ‘I renounce the well-practiced,’ it is indeed a renunciation of the training.

Sikkhāvevacanesu [M 2.0079] pana sikkhā-saddaṃ vinā kevalaṃ bhikkhu-saddo bhikkhunī-saddo ca sikkhāya adhivacanaṃ na hotīti “bhikkhusikkhaṃ bhikkhunīsikkha”nti vutteyeva sīsaṃ eti, adhisīlādayo pana sikkhā evāti “adhisīlaṃ paccakkhāmī”tiādinā vuttepi sīsaṃ eti. Paṭhamaṃ pārājikantiādinā sikkhāpadānaṃyeva gahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ, na āpattīnaṃ.

In the case of synonyms for training, however, the mere words ‘bhikkhu’ and ‘bhikkhunī’ without the word ‘sikkhā’ are not designations for the training. Thus, only when it is said ‘the bhikkhu's training’ or ‘the bhikkhunī's training’ does it take effect. But higher virtue and so on are indeed the training; thus, even when it is said ‘I renounce higher virtue’ and so on, it takes effect. By ‘the first pārājika’ and so on, the taking of the training rules themselves should be understood, not the taking of the offenses.

Upajjhāyavevacanesu upajjhāyo hutvā yo pabbājesi ceva upasampādesi ca, taṃ sandhāya “yo maṃ pabbājesī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Yassa mūlenāti yassa padhānabhāvena kāraṇabhāvena vā. Yassa mūlaṃ padhānabhāvo kāraṇabhāvo vā etissāti yassamūlikā, pabbajjā upasampadā ca. Mūla-saddassa sāpekkhabhāvepi niccasāpekkhatāya gamakattā taddhitavutti daṭṭhabbā.

In the case of synonyms for ‘preceptor,’ the phrase ‘the one who gave me the going forth’ and so on was said in reference to the one who, having become a preceptor, gave both the going forth and the higher ordination. ‘By whose root’ means by whose state as a principal ground or as a causal ground. ‘Yassamūlikā’ (rooted in whom) means ‘for which the root is his state as a principal ground or as a causal ground,’ referring to the going forth and the higher ordination. Even though the word ‘mūla’ (root) has a relative nature, the taddhita derivative formation should be understood as indicative of this due to its constant relativity.

Ācariyavevacanesu pana yo upajjhaṃ adatvā ācariyova hutvā pabbājesi, kammavācācariyo hutvā upasampādesi ca, taṃ sandhāya “yo maṃ pabbājesi, yo maṃ anusāvesī”ti vuttaṃ. Imehi dvīhi vacanehi pabbajjācariyo ca upasampadācariyo ca dassito. Yāhaṃ nissāya vasāmīti nissayācariyaṃ dasseti. Yāhaṃ uddisāpemītiādinā pana dhammācariyo vutto. Tattha uddisāpemīti pāṭhaṃ uddisāpemi. Paripucchāmīti uggahitapāṭhassa atthaṃ paripucchāmi. Saddhivihārikavevacanādīsu ca vuttānusāreneva attho veditabbo. Tassa mūleti ettha pana tassa santiketi attho daṭṭhabbo.

But regarding the synonyms for ‘teacher,’ with reference to one who, without providing a preceptor, himself became the teacher and gave the going forth, and who, having become the teacher of the formal act, conferred the higher ordination, it is said: ‘the one who gave me the going forth’ and ‘the one who instructed me.’ By these two statements, both the teacher of the going forth and the teacher of the higher ordination are indicated. The phrase ‘the one on whom I depend to live’ indicates the dependence teacher. By the phrase ‘the one from whom I have recitation made’ and so on, the Dhamma teacher is spoken of. Therein, ‘I have recitation made’ means ‘I have the text recited.’ ‘I question’ means ‘I question the meaning of the text that has been learned.’ In the synonyms for ‘co-resident’ (saddhivihārika) and so on, the meaning is to be understood according to the explanations given. As for ‘at his root’ (tassa mūle), here the meaning is to be understood as ‘in his presence’ (tassa santike).

Okallakoti khuppipāsādidukkhaparetānaṃ khīṇasukhānaṃ nahānādisarīrapaṭijagganarahitānaṃ kapaṇamanussānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Moḷibaddhoti sikhābaddho omukkamakuṭo vā. Kiñcāpi dvevāciko upāsako paṭhamabodhiyaṃyeva sambhavati, tathāpi tadā labbhamānanāmaṃ gahetvā vuttepi sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ hotiyevāti dassanatthaṃ “dvevāciko upāsako”ti vuttaṃ. “Dvevāciko”ti idameva [V 2.0071] panettha vevacananti daṭṭhabbaṃ, tasmā “dvevācikoti maṃ dhārehī”ti ettakepi vutte sīsaṃ eti. Evaṃ sesesupi.

‘Okallaka’ is a designation for miserable people afflicted by the pains of hunger, thirst, and so on, who are devoid of happiness, and who lack bodily care such as bathing. ‘Moḷibaddha’ means one whose hair is tied in a topknot or who wears a crown. Although a lay follower who declares himself with two utterances (dvevāciko upāsako) arises only at the first awakening, nevertheless, to show that even if it is said, having taken the name obtainable at that time, there is still a rejection of the training, the phrase ‘a lay follower who declares himself with two utterances’ is used. Here, ‘dvevācika’ alone is to be understood as the synonym. Therefore, even if one says only ‘Consider me as one who declares himself with two utterances,’ it takes effect. The same applies to the rest.

Kumārakoti [M 2.0080] kumārāvattho ativiya daharasāmaṇero. Cellakoti tato mahantataro khuddakasāmaṇero. Ceṭakoti majjhimo. Moḷigalloti mahāsāmaṇero. Samaṇuddesoti pana avisesato sāmaṇerādhivacanaṃ. Nigaṇṭhupaṭṭhākotiādīnipi titthiyasāvakavevacanānīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

‘Kumāraka’ refers to a very young novice (sāmaṇera) who is still in the state of a boy. ‘Cellaka’ is a slightly older, small novice. ‘Ceṭaka’ is a middle-aged novice. ‘Moḷigalla’ is a senior novice. ‘Samaṇuddesa,’ however, is a general designation for novices without distinction. ‘Nigaṇṭhupaṭṭhāka’ and similar terms are to be understood as synonyms for disciples of heretical teachers.

Dussīloti nissīlo sīlavirahito. Pāpadhammoti dussīlattā eva hīnajjhāsayatāya lāmakasabhāvo. Asucisaṅkassarasamācāroti aparisuddhakāyakammāditāya asuci hutvā saṅkāya saritabbasamācāro. Dussīlo hi kiñcideva asāruppaṃ disvā “idaṃ asukena kataṃ bhavissatī”ti paresaṃ āsaṅkanīyo hoti. Kenacideva karaṇīyena mantayante bhikkhū disvā “kacci nu kho ime mayā katakammaṃ jānitvā mantentī”ti attanoyeva saṅkāya saritabbasamācāro. Paṭicchannakammantoti lajjitabbatāya paṭicchādetabbakammanto. Assamaṇoti na samaṇo. Salākaggahaṇādīsu “ahampi samaṇo”ti micchāpaṭiññāya samaṇapaṭiñño, aseṭṭhacāritāya abrahmacārī, uposathādīsu “ahampi brahmacārī”ti micchāpaṭiññāya brahmacāripaṭiñño, pūtinā kammena sīlavipattiyā anto anupaviṭṭhattā antopūti, chahi dvārehi rāgādikilesānussavanena tintattā avassuto, sañjātarāgādikacavarattā sīlavantehi chaḍḍetabbattā ca kasambujāto. Koṇṭhoti dussīlādhivacanametaṃ.

‘Dussīla’ means one without virtue, devoid of virtue. ‘Pāpadhamma’ means one of bad character, of a base nature due to being immoral. ‘Asucisaṅkassarasamācāra’ means one of impure and suspicious behavior; being impure due to unpurified bodily actions and so on, his conduct should be regarded with suspicion. For an immoral person, upon seeing something improper, becomes a subject of suspicion for others, who think, ‘This must have been done by so-and-so.’ Seeing monks discussing some matter, his own conduct becomes worthy of suspicion, as he thinks, ‘Could they know about what I did and be discussing it?’ ‘Paṭicchannakammanta’ means one of concealed actions, whose actions should be hidden due to shame. ‘Assamaṇa’ means not an ascetic. In matters like taking lots, he falsely claims, ‘I too am an ascetic,’ thus he is one who claims to be an ascetic. ‘Abrahmacārī’ means not a celibate, due to ignoble conduct. Regarding observances like the Uposatha, he falsely declares, ‘I too am a celibate,’ thus he is one who claims to be a celibate. He is inwardly rotten (antopūti) because putrid deeds and moral failure have entered within. He is oozing (avassuto) due to being steeped in the outflow of defilements like lust through the six doors. He is born from filth (kasambujāta) due to the arising of the rubbish of defilements like lust and because he should be discarded by the virtuous. ‘Koṇṭha’ is a designation for an immoral person.

“Yāni vā panaññānipi atthi buddhavevacanāni vā”tiādinā yaṃ-saddaparāmaṭṭhānaṃ buddhādivevacanānaṃyeva taṃ-saddena parāmasanaṃ hotīti āha – “tehi ākārehi…pe… buddhādīnaṃ vevacanehī”ti. Kathaṃ pana tāni ākārādisaddehi voharīyantīti āha “vevacanāni hī”tiādi. Saṇṭhānavantānaṃ buddhādīnaṃ saṇṭhānadīpanaṃ tāva hotu, saṇṭhānarahitānaṃ pana dhammasikkhādīnaṃ kathanti āha “sikkhāpaccakkhānasaṇṭhānattā eva vā”ti. Sikkhāpaccakkhānarūpāni hi vevacanāni “sikkhāpaccakkhānasaṇṭhānānī”ti vuccanti. Evaṃ khoti ettha khoti avadhāraṇatthe nipātoti āha “evamevā”ti.

With the phrase, “Or whatever other synonyms there are for the Buddha,” etc., he states that the word ‘taṃ’ refers specifically to the synonyms of the Buddha and others, which are referred to by the word ‘yaṃ,’ thus: “By those characteristics… through the synonyms of the Buddha and others.” But how are those synonyms expressed by terms like ‘characteristics’ and so on? He explains: “Because they are synonyms…” etc. Let the indication of form first apply to those like the Buddha who possess form. But how does this apply to those without form, such as the Dhamma, the training, etc.? He says: “Or because they have the form of the rejection of the training.” For synonyms that take the form of the rejection of the training are called “having the form of the rejection of the training.” In the phrase ‘Evaṃ kho,’ he says that ‘kho’ is a particle used in the sense of emphasis, thus meaning: “just so.”

54. Mucchāparetoti [M 2.0081] mucchāya abhibhūto. Vacanatthavijānanasamatthaṃ tiracchānagataṃ dassetuṃ “nāgamāṇavakassā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tihetukapaṭisandhikāti yebhuyyavasena vuttaṃ. Na hi sabbāpi devatā [V 2.0072] tihetukapaṭisandhikāva honti dvihetukānampi sambhavato. Atikhippaṃ jānantīti devatānaṃ bhavaṅgaparivāsassa manussānaṃ viya adandhabhāvato vuttaṃ.

54. ‘Mucchāpareta’ means overwhelmed by infatuation. To illustrate an animal incapable of understanding the meaning of words, it is said, “of the young Nāga,” etc. ‘Tihetukapaṭisandhikā’ is stated as a general rule, for not all deities are reborn with three root-causes, as those with two may also arise. ‘Atikhippaṃ jānantī’ is said because the flow of the life-continuum of deities, unlike that of humans, is not slow.

Sabhāgassāti purisassa. Visabhāgassāti mātugāmassa. Anariyakoti māgadhavohārato añño. Davāti sahasā. Ravāti virajjhitvā. Aññaṃ bhaṇissāmīti aññaṃ bhaṇanto buddhaṃ paccakkhāmīti bhaṇatīti yojetabbaṃ. Akkharasamayānabhiññatāya vā karaṇasampattiyā abhāvato vā kathetabbaṃ kathetuṃ asakkonto hutvā aññaṃ kathento ravā bhaṇati nāma. Ubhayathāpi aññaṃ bhaṇitukāmassa aññabhaṇanaṃ samānanti āha “purimena ko viseso”ti.

‘Sabhāgassa’ refers to a man. ‘Visabhāgassa’ refers to a woman. ‘Anariyaka’ means other than the Magadhan dialect. ‘Davā’ means rashly. ‘Ravā’ means erringly. It should be connected thus: one who, intending to say one thing but saying another, says, “I reject the Buddha.” Alternatively, one who, being unable to say what should be said due to lack of familiarity with the conventions of letters or lack of competence in articulation, says something else, is said to be ‘speaking erringly.’ In either case, since for one intending to say one thing, the saying of another is the same, he says, “What is the difference from the former?”

Vācetīti pāḷiṃ kathento aññaṃ uggaṇhāpento vā vāceti. Paripucchatīti pāḷiyā atthaṃ paripucchanto pāḷiṃ paripucchati. Uggaṇhātīti aññassa santike pāḷiṃ uggaṇhāti. Sajjhāyaṃ karotīti uggahitapāḷiṃ sajjhāyati. Vaṇṇetīti pāḷiyā atthaṃ saṃvaṇṇento pāḷiṃ vaṇṇeti. Mahallakassa kiñci ajānanato aviditindriyatāya vā “potthakarūpasadisassā”ti vuttaṃ, mattikāya katarūpasadisassāti attho. Garumedhassāti ārammaṇesu lahuppavattiyā abhāvato dandhagatikatāya garupaññassa, mandapaññassāti vuttaṃ hoti. Sabbaso vāti iminā “idaṃ padaṃ sāvessāmi ‘sikkhaṃ paccakkhāmī’”ti evaṃ pavattacittuppādassa abhāvaṃ dasseti. Yasmā pana asati evarūpe cittuppāde kenaci pariyāyena tathāvidhaṃ vacībhedaṃ katvā sāvanaṃ nāma neva sambhavati, tasmā vuttaṃ “buddhaṃ paccakkhāmītiādīsu…pe… vacībhedaṃ katvā na sāvetī”ti.

‘Vāceti’ means: while speaking the Pāḷi or making another learn it, one recites. ‘Paripucchati’ means: while questioning the meaning of the Pāḷi, one questions the Pāḷi. ‘Uggaṇhāti’ means: one learns the Pāḷi in the presence of another. ‘Sajjhāyaṃ karoti’ means: one rehearses the Pāḷi that has been learned. ‘Vaṇṇeti’ means: while describing the meaning of the Pāḷi, one describes the Pāḷi. In the case of an elder, because of not knowing something or due to the state of having unpenetrated faculties, it is said, “like a figure made of plaster”—the meaning is, like a figure made with clay. ‘Garumedhassa’ means: for one of slow intellect, due to the state of being slow-moving because of the absence of quick engagement with objects; this is said to mean one of dull intellect. By ‘sabbaso vā,’ this indicates the absence of a thought-arising such as, “I will announce this statement: ‘I renounce the training.’” Moreover, since, when such a thought-arising is absent, an announcement by making such a verbal utterance in any way is not possible, therefore it is said, “In cases like ‘I renounce the Buddha,’ etc., … having made a verbal utterance, one does not announce.”

Sikkhāpaccakkhānavibhaṅgavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the analysis of giving up the training is concluded.

Mūlapaññattivaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Root Designations

55. Niddisitabbassāti [M 2.0082] vivaritabbassa pakāsetabbassa. Kilesehīti ahirikādīhi kilesehi. Ito paṭṭhāyāti duṭṭhulla-padato paṭṭhāya. Tassa kammassāti methunadhammapaṭisevanasaṅkhātassa kammassa. Dassanantiādi vuttanayameva. Assāti methunadhammassa.

‘To be pointed out’ means to be explained, to be made clear. ‘By defilements’ means by defilements such as shamelessness, etc. ‘From here onward’ means starting from the coarse word. ‘Of that action’ refers to the action designated as indulging in sexual intercourse. ‘Seeing,’ etc., is just as stated in the previously mentioned manner. ‘Of it’ means of the sexual act.

Dvīhi dvīhi samāpajjitabbā dvayaṃdvayasamāpattīti āha “dvayena dvayena samāpajjitabbato”ti. Rāgapariyuṭṭhānena sadisabhāvappattiyā mithunānaṃ idaṃ methunaṃ, methunameva dhammo methunadhammoti [V 2.0073] āha “ubhinnaṃ rattāna”ntiādi. Tattha rattānanti methunarāgena rattānaṃ. Sārattānanti teneva rāgena ativiya rattānaṃ. Avassutānanti lokassādamittasanthavavasena uppannamethunarāgena tintānaṃ. Pariyuṭṭhitānanti methunarāguppattiyā pariyonaddhacittānaṃ. Sadisānanti rattatādīhi sadisānaṃ.

‘Dvayaṃdvayasamāpatti’ is that which is to be entered into by two and two; therefore, it is said, “because it is to be entered into by two by two.” Through the obsession of lust and the attainment of a similar state, this act of a couple is methuna (sexual intercourse); the very nature of sexual intercourse is methunadhamma. Therefore, he said, “of the two being impassioned,” etc. Therein, ‘impassioned’ means those impassioned by lust for sexual intercourse. ‘Very impassioned’ means those exceedingly impassioned by that very lust. ‘Infatuated’ means those saturated by lust for sexual intercourse that has arisen by way of worldly pleasure, intimacy, and familiarity. ‘Overwhelmed’ means those whose minds are enveloped by the arising of lust for sexual intercourse. ‘Similar’ means those who are similar in being impassioned, etc.

Yasmā “paṭisevati nāmā”ti padaṃ mātikāya natthi, tasmā “paṭisevati nāmāti kasmā uddhaṭa”nti yo maññati, tassa kāraṇaṃ dassento “paṭiseveyyāti ettha…pe… mātikāpada”nti āha. Itthiyā nimittenāti idaṃ “maggena gacchatī”tiādi viya daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yathā hi “maggena gacchatī”ti vutte “maggaṃ gacchati, magge vā gacchatī”ti ayamattho labbhati, evaṃ “itthiyā nimittena pavesetī”ti vutte “itthiyā nimittaṃ paveseti, nimitte vā pavesetī”ti ayamattho labbhati. Idañca yebhuyyena purisapayogadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Nimittaṃ aṅgajātanti atthato ekaṃ. Pavesanaṃ nāma na bahi chupanamattanti āha “vātena asamphuṭṭhe allokāse”ti. Abbhantarañhi pavesento “pavesetī”ti vuccati, na bahi chupanto. Abbhantaranti ca pakatiyā sabbaso pihitassa nimittassa vātena asamphuṭṭhokāso vuccatīti.

55. Since the phrase “paṭisevati nāmā” is not in the mātikā, for one who might think, “Why is ‘paṭisevati nāmā’ extracted?”—showing the reason, he said, “Here, in ‘paṭiseveyya’… it is a mātikā phrase.” This phrase, “itthiyā nimittena,” should be understood like “maggena gacchatī,” etc. Just as indeed, when it is said, “maggena gacchatī,” the meaning obtained is “he goes along the path” or “he goes on the path,” so too when it is said, “itthiyā nimittena pavesetī,” the meaning obtained is “he inserts the woman’s organ” or “he inserts in the organ.” And this was said mostly for the purpose of showing the man’s action. ‘Nimitta’ and ‘aṅgajāta’ are, in meaning, one. The act of entering is not mere external touching; therefore, he said, “in a space untouched by the wind.” Indeed, one who inserts internally is said to “insert,” not one who touches externally. And “internally” is said to be the space untouched by wind of the organ that is naturally completely covered.

Idāni sabbathā lesokāsapidahanatthaṃ itthinimitte purisanimitte ca labbhamānaṃ pavesakāle aññamaññaṃ phassārahaṃ padesavisesaṃ vibhajitvā dassento “itthinimitte cattāri passānī”tiādimāha. Vātena hi asamphuṭṭhe allokāse yattha katthaci ekenapi padesena chupitvā pavesento “pavesetī”ti vuccati. Vemajjhanti yathā cattāri passāni asamphusanto paveseti, evaṃ katavivarassa itthinimittassa heṭṭhimatalaṃ vuccati[M 2.0083], purisanimitte pana majjhanti aggakoṭiṃ sandhāya vadati. Uparīti aggakoṭito uparibhāgappadeso. Idañca majjhena samiñjitvā pavesentassa majjhimapabbasamiñjitaṅguliṃ katthaci pavesentassa aṅguliyā majjhimapabbapiṭṭhisadisaṃ aṅgajātassa uparibhāgavemajjhaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Heṭṭhā pavesentoti itthinimittassa heṭṭhimabhāgena chupantaṃ pavesento. Majjhena pavesentoti abbhantaratalaṃ chupitvā majjhena pavesento. Katthaci acchupantaṃ pavesetvā nīharantassa hi natthi pārājikaṃ, dukkaṭaṃ pana hoti chinnasīsavatthusmiṃ vaṭṭakate mukhe acchupantaṃ pavesetvā nīharantassa viya. Majjheneva chupantaṃ pavesentoti aggakoṭiyā chupantaṃ pavesento. Majjhimapabbapiṭṭhiyā samiñjitaṅgulinti sambandho. Atha vā samiñjitaṅguliṃ majjhimapabbapiṭṭhiyā pavesento viyāti yojetabbaṃ. Saṅkocetvāti nimittamajjhena bhinditvā. Uparibhāgenāti saṅkocitassa uparibhāgakoṭiyā. Idāni purisanimittassa heṭṭhā vuttesu chasu ṭhānesu uparīti vuttaṭṭhānantarassa vasena visuṃ cattāri [V 2.0074] passāni gahetvā purisanimitte dasadhā ṭhānabhedaṃ dassento “tatthā”tiādimāha. Heṭṭhā pana visuṃ tāni aggahetvā “cattāri passānī”ti vacanasāmaññatopi visuṃ visuṃ labbhamānāni ekaccaṃ gahetvā cha ṭhānāni vuttāni. Tulādaṇḍasadisaṃ pavesentassāti ujukaṃ pavesentassa.

Now, for the purpose of completely closing off any loophole, dividing and showing the specific areas in the female and male organs that are susceptible to mutual contact during penetration, he says, “In the female organ, there are four sides,” and so on. For, in a moist space untouched by wind, one who enters by touching with even a single spot anywhere at all is said to “enter.” ‘Vemajjha’ (the middle) is said to be the lower surface of the female organ that has been opened, just as one enters without touching the four sides. But in the male organ, ‘the middle’ refers to the tip. ‘Above’ means the area of the upper part from the tip. And this is said with reference to the upper middle part of the genital organ—which is similar to the back of the middle joint of a finger when one inserts a finger with its middle joint contracted somewhere—for one who enters by contracting it in the middle. ‘Entering below’ means entering while touching with the lower part of the female organ. ‘Entering in the middle’ means entering in the middle by touching the inner surface. For one who inserts without touching anywhere and withdraws, there is no offense entailing expulsion, but there is a dukkaṭa offense, like one who inserts and withdraws without touching in the round opening of a severed head. ‘Entering while touching only with the middle’ means entering without touching with the tip. The connection is with the phrase ‘a finger contracted at the back of the middle joint.’ Alternatively, it should be construed as ‘like one who inserts a contracted finger by the back of its middle joint.’ ‘Having contracted’ means having bent the organ in the middle. ‘By the upper part’ means by the tip of the upper part of the contracted organ. Now, with regard to the six places mentioned below for the male organ, taking the four sides separately in relation to the place mentioned as “above,” showing the tenfold division of places in the male organ, he says, “therein,” and so on. Below, however, without taking those separately, from the general statement “four sides”—although they are obtained separately—by taking some of them, six places are mentioned. ‘For one who inserts it like a balance rod’ means for one who inserts it straight.

Nimitte jātanti attano nimitte jātaṃ. Cammakhīlanti nimitte uṭṭhitaṃ cammameva. “Uṇṇigaṇḍo”tipi vadanti. Nimitte jātampi cammakhīlādi nimittamevāti āha “āpatti pārājikassā”ti. “Upahatakāyappasāda”nti avatvā “naṭṭhakāyappasāda”nti vacanaṃ upādinnabhāvassa natthitādassanatthaṃ. Tenevāha – “matacammaṃ vā sukkhapīḷakaṃ vā”ti. Sati hi upādinnabhāve upahatepi kāyappasāde upahatindriyavatthusmiṃ viya pārājikāpattiyeva siyā, matacammaṃ pana sukkhapīḷakañca anupādinnakaṃ upādinnakeyeva ca pārājikāpatti. Tenevāha “āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti. Na ca evaṃ karontassa anāpatti sakkā vattunti dukkaṭaṃ vuttaṃ, itthinimittassa pana naṭṭhepi upādinnabhāve pārājikāpattiyeva. Mate akkhāyite yebhuyyena akkhāyite pārājikāpattivacanato methunassādenāti iminā kāyasaṃsaggarāgaṃ nivatteti. Sati hi kāyasaṃsaggarāge saṅghādisesova siyā, bījānipi nimittasaṅkhyaṃ na gacchantīti dukkaṭameva vuttaṃ. “Nimittena nimittaṃ pavesetī”ti hi vuttaṃ.

“Born on the organ” means born on one's own organ. “A skin tag” means just the skin that has arisen on the organ. They also call it a “wart.” Even if a skin tag or the like is born on the organ, it is just the organ itself; therefore, he said, “There is an offense of Pārājika.” Not saying “impaired bodily sensitivity,” the statement “destroyed bodily sensitivity” is used to show the absence of the state of being appropriated. For that very reason, he said: “dead skin or a dry blister.” For if there were the state of being appropriated, even if the bodily sensitivity were impaired, just as with an impaired sense-faculty basis, there would be an offense of Pārājika. But dead skin and a dry blister are unappropriated, and an offense of Pārājika occurs only with what is appropriated. Therefore, he said: “There is an offense of Dukkaṭa.” And it is not possible to say there is no offense for one who acts thus; therefore, Dukkaṭa is stated. But in the case of a woman's organ, even if the appropriated state is destroyed, there is an offense of Pārājika. From the statement that there is an offense of Pārājika in the case of a corpse that is not eaten, or mostly eaten, by this phrase 'with the pleasure of sexual intercourse,' he prevents lust for bodily contact. For if there were lust for bodily contact, it would be an offense of Saṅghādisesa. And since even testicles do not count as the organ, only Dukkaṭa is stated. For it is said: “He inserts an organ into an organ.”

Idāni [M 2.0084] imissā methunakathāya asabbhirūpattā “īdisaṃ ṭhānaṃ kathentehi suṇantehi ca evaṃ paṭipajjitabba”nti anusāsanto “ayañca methunakathā nāmā”tiādimāha. Methunakathāya rāgavuddhihetuttā hāsavisayattā ca tadubhayanivattanatthaṃ paṭikūlamanasikārādīsu niyojeti. Paṭikūlamanasikārena hi rāgo nivattati, samaṇasaññādīsu paccupaṭṭhitesu hāso nivattati. Sattānuddayāyāti sattānaṃ apāyadukkhādīhi anurakkhaṇatthaṃ. Lokānukampāyāti sattalokavisayāya anukampāya.

Now, because this talk on sexual intercourse is unsuitable for good people, while instructing, “When speaking of or listening to such a topic, one should conduct oneself thus,” he said the passage beginning, “And this is called the talk on sexual intercourse.” Because talk on sexual intercourse is a cause for the increase of lust and is a subject of amusement, for the purpose of counteracting both, he enjoins contemplation on repulsiveness and so on. For by contemplation on repulsiveness, lust is averted; when perceptions such as the perception of a recluse are established, amusement is averted. “Out of compassion for beings” means for the purpose of protecting beings from the suffering of the lower realms and so on. “Out of compassion for the world” means with compassion that has the world of beings as its object.

Mukhaṃ apidhāyāti mukhaṃ apidahitvā, yena kenaci pamādena kadāci mandahāso bhaveyya, tadā garuttaṃ kuppeyya, tasmā tādise kāle garubhāvassa avikopanatthaṃ bījakena mukhaṃ paṭicchādetvā nisīditabbanti adhippāyo. Atha vā mukhaṃ apidhāyāti mukhaṃ pidahitvāti attho. Bījakena mukhaṃ paṭicchādetvā hasamānena na nisīditabbanti ayamettha adhippāyo. Dantavidaṃsakanti dante dassetvā vivaritvā cāti attho. Gabbhitenāti saṅkocaṃ anāpajjantena, ussāhajātenāti attho. Yadi hi “īdisaṃ nāma asabbhiṃ kathemī”ti saṅkocaṃ [V 2.0075] āpajjeyya, atthavibhāvanaṃ na siyā, tasmā “tādisena sammāsambuddhenapi tāva īdisaṃ kathitaṃ, kimaṅgaṃ panāhaṃ kathemī”ti evaṃ ussāhajātena kathetabbanti adhippāyo. Satthupaṭibhāgenāti satthukappena, satthusadisenāti attho.

“Not covering the mouth” means having not covered the mouth. If, due to some carelessness, a slight smile should ever arise, then one's gravity would be disturbed. Therefore, on such an occasion, in order not to disturb one's state of gravity, one should sit having covered the mouth with a fan—this is the intended meaning. Alternatively, “not covering the mouth” means “having covered the mouth.” One should not sit laughing while covering the mouth with a fan—this is the intended meaning here. “Showing the teeth” means having shown and bared the teeth. “With pride” means without falling into hesitation, with energy arisen—this is the meaning. For if one were to fall into hesitation, thinking, “I am speaking such an unbecoming thing,” the explanation of the meaning would not be possible. Therefore, one should speak with energy arisen, thinking, “Even the Perfectly Enlightened One spoke of such a thing; why then should I not speak?”—this is the intended meaning. “As a counterpart to the Teacher” means in the manner of the Teacher, resembling the Teacher—this is the meaning.

Mūlapaññattivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Original Regulations is concluded.

Anupaññattivaṇṇanā

Commentary on Further Regulations

Tiracchānesu gatāyāti tiracchānesu uppannāya. Yasmā tiracchānagatā nāma atikhuddakāpi honti, yesaṃ maggesu tilaphalamattampi pavesanaṃ nappahoti, tasmā na sabbāva tiracchānagatitthiyo pārājikavatthubhūtāti pavesanappahonakavasena labbhamānakatiracchānagatitthiyo paricchinditvā dassento “pārājikavatthubhūtā eva cetthā”tiādimāha. Apadānaṃ ahimacchātiādigāthā pārājikavatthūnaṃ heṭṭhimaparicchedadassanatthaṃ porāṇehi ṭhapitā. Tattha ahīti jātiniddesena sabbāpi [M 2.0085] sappajāti saṅgahitāti āha – “ahiggahaṇena…pe… dīghajāti saṅgahitā”ti. Tattha gonasāti sappavisesā, yesaṃ piṭṭhīsu mahantāni maṇḍalāni sandissanti. Macchaggahaṇaṃ odakajātiyā upalakkhaṇapadanti āha – “macchaggahaṇena…pe… odakajāti saṅgahitā”ti. Teneva maṇḍūkakacchapānaṃ sapādakattepi odakajātikattā saṅgaho kato.

“Gone to animals” means “born among animals.” Because those called “animal females” are also extremely small, such that not even the size of a sesame seed can enter their passages, therefore not all animal females constitute a ground for pārājika. Thus, by delimiting and showing those animal females whose passages are capable of receiving penetration, it is said, “Only these here constitute a ground for pārājika,” and so forth. The verse beginning “the footless, the snake, the fish” was established by the ancients to show the lower limit of the grounds for pārājika. There, by “snake” (ahi), all snake species are included by way of indicating the genus—it is said: “By the term ‘snake’… the long-bodied species are included.” Among them, “gonasā” refers to a particular kind of snake, on whose backs large circular patterns appear. The term “fish” is an indicative term for water-born creatures—it is said: “By the term ‘fish’… the water-born species are included.” For that very reason, frogs and turtles, though having feet, are included because they are water-born.

Mukhasaṇṭhānanti oṭṭhacammasaṇṭhānaṃ. Vaṇasaṅkhepaṃ gacchatīti vaṇasaṅgahaṃ gacchati navasu vaṇamukhesu saṅgahitattāti adhippāyo. Vaṇe thullaccayañca “amaggena amaggaṃ paveseti, āpatti thullaccayassā”ti imassa vasena veditabbaṃ. Tasmiñhi sutte dvīsu sambhinnavaṇesu ekena vaṇena pavesetvā dutiyena nīharantassa thullaccayaṃ vuttaṃ. Vakkhati ca “imassa suttassa anulomavasena sabbattha vaṇasaṅkhepe thullaccayaṃ veditabba”nti (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.66). Kukkuṭiggahaṇampi sabbāya pakkhijātiyā upalakkhaṇapadanti āha – “kukkuṭiggahaṇena…pe… pakkhijāti saṅgahitā”ti. Majjāriggahaṇampi catuppadajātiyā upalakkhaṇapadanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tenāha – “majjāriggahaṇena…pe… catuppadajāti saṅgahitā”ti. Rukkhasunakhā nāma kalandakātipi vadanti. Maṅgusāti naṅgulā.

“The shape of the mouth” refers to the shape of the lip-skin. “It goes to the summary of wounds” means it reaches the collection of wounds, because it is included among the nine wound-openings—this is the intended meaning. Regarding wounds, a grave offense should be understood based on the statement: “He inserts into an improper path by an improper path; there is an offense of grave transgression.” In that discourse, it is stated that when two wounds are connected, inserting through one wound and extracting through the other incurs a grave offense. And it will be stated: “In accordance with this discourse, a grave offense should be understood in all cases of wound summaries.” The mention of “chicken” is also an indicative term for all bird species—it is said: “By the mention of ‘chicken’… the bird species is included.” Similarly, the mention of “cat” should be seen as an indicative term for the four-footed species. Hence it is said: “By the mention of ‘cat’… the four-footed species is included.” Some say that “tree-dogs” (rukkhasunakha) are what are called “kalandaka” (squirrels). “Maṅgusā” means “mongoose” (naṅgulā).

Parājita-saddo upasaggassa vuddhiṃ katvā ta-kārassa ca ka-kāraṃ katvā pārājikoti niddiṭṭhoti āha “pārājikoti parājito”ti. “Katthaci āpattīti ‘pārājikena dhammena anuddhaṃseyyā’tiādīsu [V 2.0076] (pārā. 384, 391), katthaci sikkhāpadanti idaṃ pana disvā jānitabba”nti gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Parājayatīti pārājikaṃ, pārājikāti ca kattusādhanena pārājika-saddena sikkhāpadaṃ āpatti ca vuccatīti dassento āha “yo taṃ atikkamatī”tiādi. Puggalo pana kammasādhanena pārājika-saddena vuccatīti dassento āha “puggalo yasmā parājito”tiādi.

The word `parājita` is explained as `pārājika` by strengthening the prefix and changing the letter `ta` to `ka`; thus, it is said, “`pārājika` means `parājito` (defeated).” “In some contexts, it refers to an offense, as in ‘should not revile with a pārājika offense,’ and in others, it refers to a training rule; this should be understood upon seeing it,” as stated in the Gaṇṭhipadas. That which defeats is `pārājika`; to show that by the agentive derivation the word `pārājika` refers to both the training rule and the offense, it is said, “whoever transgresses it,” and so forth. To show that a person, however, is referred to by the word `pārājika` with the objective derivation, it is said, “a person because he is defeated,” and so forth.

Etameva hi atthaṃ sandhāyāti “taṃ āpattiṃ āpanno puggalo parājito hoti parājayamāpanno”ti etamatthaṃ sandhāya. Cuto paraddhotiādinā hi taṃ āpattiṃ āpannapuggalo cuto hoti parājito parājayaṃ āpannoti ayamattho viññāyati, na pana puggalo pārājiko nāma hotīti etamatthaṃ sandhāyāti evamattho gahetabbo. Na hi parivārepi gāthā puggalavuttipārājikasaddanibbacanadassanatthaṃ vuttā [M 2.0086] āpattivuttīnaṃ pārājikā-disaddānaṃ nibbacanavibhāgappasaṅge vuttattā.
