Ayañhi parivāragāthāya attho (pari. aṭṭha. 339) – yadidaṃ puggalāpattisikkhāpadapārājikesu āpattipārājikaṃ nāma vuttaṃ, taṃ āpajjanto puggalo yasmā parājito parājayamāpanno saddhamā cuto paraddho bhaṭṭho niraṅkato ca hoti, anīhaṭe tasmiṃ puggale puna uposathapavāraṇādibhedo saṃvāso natthi, tenetaṃ iti vuccati tena kāraṇena etaṃ āpattipārājikaṃ iti vuccatīti. Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepattho – yasmā parājito hoti etena, tasmā etaṃ pārājikanti vuccatīti. Paribhaṭṭhoti sāsanato bhaṭṭho, parihīnoti attho. Chinnoti antarā khaṇḍito.

For this very meaning is intended: “That person who has committed that offense is defeated, having attained defeat”—this is the meaning intended. By “fallen, cast off,” and so forth, it is indeed understood that the person who has committed that offense is fallen, defeated, having attained defeat. However, the meaning to be taken is not that the person is called a `pārājika`. For the verse in the Parivāra is not spoken to show the derivation of the word `pārājika` as it refers to a person, since it was spoken on the occasion of analyzing the derivation of words like `pārājika` that refer to offenses. This is the meaning of the Parivāra verse: Regarding the pārājikas concerning the person, the offense, and the training rule, there is that which is called the “offense-pārājika.” Because a person who commits it is defeated, has attained defeat, has fallen from the good Dhamma, is cast off, ruined, and annulled, and because for that person, as long as they are not rehabilitated, there is no longer communion such as Uposatha, Pavāraṇā, and so forth, for that reason it is called thus; for that reason, this offense is called a pārājika. Herein, this is the concise meaning: Because one is defeated by this, therefore it is called `pārājika`. `Paribhaṭṭha` means fallen from the Dispensation; the meaning is “deprived.” `Chinna` means broken in the middle.

Saddhiṃ yojanāyāti padayojanāya saddhiṃ. Catubbidhaṃ saṅghakammanti apalokanādivasena catubbidhaṃ kammaṃ. Sīmāparicchinnehīti ekasīmāpariyāpannehi. Pakatattā nāma pārājikaṃ anāpannā anukkhittā ca. Pañcavidhopīti nidānuddesādivasena pañcavidhopi. Nahāpitapubbakānaṃ viya odhisaanuññātaṃ ṭhapetvā avasesaṃ sabbampi sikkhāpadaṃ sabbehipi lajjīpuggalehi anatikkamanīyattā vuttaṃ “sabbehipi lajjīpuggalehi samaṃ sikkhitabbabhāvato”ti. Samanti saddhiṃ, ekappahārena vā. Sikkhitabbabhāvatoti anatikkamanavasena uggahaparipucchādinā ca sikkhitabbabhāvato. Sāmaññasikkhāpadesu “idaṃ tayā na sikkhitabba”nti evaṃ abahikātabbato “na ekopi tato bahiddhā sandissatī”ti vuttaṃ. Yaṃ taṃ vuttanti sambandho.

“Together with the explanation” means together with the word-by-word explanation. “The fourfold Sangha act” refers to the fourfold act by way of announcement (apalokana), and so forth. “By those who have delimited a boundary” means “by those included within a single boundary.” “Those who are normal” refers to those who have not incurred a pārājika offense and have not been suspended. “Fivefold” also refers to the fivefold division by way of the introduction, recitation, and so forth. Except for what is specifically allowed, as for those who were formerly barbers, all the remaining training rules are untransgressable by all conscientious individuals; it is said, “because it is to be trained in equally by all conscientious individuals.” “Equally” means together, or at once. “Because it is to be trained in” means because it is to be trained in by way of non-transgression and by way of learning, questioning, and so forth. In the common training rules, because it is not to be excluded thus, “This is not to be trained in by you,” it is said, “not even one is seen outside of it.” “That which was stated” is the connection.

56. Na kevalaṃ itthiyā eva nimittaṃ pārājikavatthūti iminā kevalaṃ itthiyā eva nimittaṃ [V 2.0077] pārājikavatthu na hoti, atha kho ubhatobyañjanakapaṇḍakapurisānampi nimittaṃ pārājikavatthūti dasseti. Na ca manussitthiyā evāti iminā pana manussitthiyā eva nimittaṃ pārājikavatthu na hoti, amanussitthitiracchānagatitthiamanussubhatobyañjanakādīnampi nimittaṃ pārājikavatthūti dasseti. “Vatthumeva na hotīti amanussitthipasaṅgena āgataṃ suvaṇṇarajatādimayaṃ paṭikkhipatī”ti tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ, taṃ yuttaṃ viya na dissati. Na hi ito pubbe amanussitthiggahaṇaṃ kataṃ atthi, yena tappasaṅgo siyā. Idāneva hi “tisso itthiyo”tiādinā amanussitthiggahaṇaṃ kataṃ, na ca amanussitthiggahaṇena suvaṇṇarajatādimayānaṃ [M 2.0087] pasaṅgo yutto. Manussāmanussatiracchānajātivasena tividhā katvā pārājikavatthubhūtasattānaṃ niddesena suvaṇṇarajatādimayānaṃ pasaṅgassa nivattitattā. Tathā hi itthipurisādīsu manussāmanussādīsu vā kañci anāmasitvā avisesena “methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭiseveyyā”ti ettakameva mātikāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Tassa padabhājane ca “paṭisevati nāmā”ti mātikaṃ padaṃ uddharitvā “yo nimittena nimittaṃ aṅgajātena aṅgajātaṃ antamaso tilaphalamattampi paveseti, eso paṭisevati nāmā”ti paṭisevanākārova dassito, na pana pārājikavatthubhūtanimittanissayā manussāmanussatiracchānagatā itthipurisapaṇḍakaubhatobyañjanakā niyametvā dassitā, tasmā “itthiyā eva nu kho nimittaṃ pārājikavatthu, udāhu aññesampī”ti evamādi sandeho siyā, nimittavohāro ca suvaṇṇarajatādimayarūpakesu ca labbhatiyeva. Teneva vinītavatthūsu (pārā. 71) “lepacittassa nimittaṃ aṅgajātena chupi, dārudhītalikāya nimittaṃ aṅgajātena chupī”ti vuttaṃ, tasmā nimittasāmaññato “suvaṇṇarajatādimayānampi nimittaṃ pārājikavatthu hoti, na hotī”ti kassaci āsaṅkā siyā. Teneva “lepacittādivatthūsu tassa kukkuccaṃ ahosī”ti vuttaṃ. Tasmā tadāsaṅkānivattanatthaṃ pārājikavatthubhūtasattaniyamanatthañca jātivasena manussāmanussādito tidhā katvā pārājikavatthubhūte satte bhagavā vibhajitvā dasseti, tasmā “vatthumeva na hotī”ti nimittasāmaññato pasaṅgāgataṃ suvaṇṇarajatādimayānaṃ nimittaṃ paṭikkhipatīti vattabbaṃ.

56. By this statement, 'Not only the mark of a woman is a ground for a Pārājika offense,' it is shown that not only is the mark of a woman a ground for a Pārājika offense, but indeed, the mark of a hermaphrodite, a eunuch, and a male is also a ground for a Pārājika offense. And by this statement, 'And not only of a human woman,' it is shown that not only is the mark of a human woman a ground for a Pārājika offense, but the mark of a non-human female, an animal female, a non-human hermaphrodite, and so on, is also a ground for a Pārājika offense. The statement in all three glosses, 'By "It is not an object at all," it rejects that which is made of gold, silver, etc., which has arisen by implication from a non-human female,' does not seem correct. For before this, the mention of a non-human female has not been made, by which such an implication would arise. Only now, by 'three women,' etc., is the mention of a non-human female made. And the implication of things made of gold, silver, etc., from the mention of a non-human female is not suitable, because the implication of things made of gold, silver, etc., is precluded by the specification of beings who are the object of a Pārājika offense, having been classified threefold by way of species: human, non-human, and animal. For indeed, in the Mātikā, without specifying anyone among women, men, etc., or among humans, non-humans, etc., it is stated only this much, without distinction: 'should engage in sexual intercourse.' And in its word-analysis, having extracted the Mātikā term 'engages,' the manner of engagement is shown thus: 'Whoever inserts a mark into a mark, a sexual organ into a sexual organ, even to the extent of a sesame seed, this is called "engages."' But the human, non-human, and animal women, men, eunuchs, and hermaphrodites who are the basis for the object of a Pārājika offense are not specified and shown. Therefore, a doubt such as, 'Is the mark of a woman only a ground for a Pārājika offense, or of others as well?' might arise. And the term 'mark' is indeed found in reference to figures made of gold, silver, etc. For that very reason, in the Vinītavatthus it is said: 'He touched the mark of a painted figure with his sexual organ; he touched the mark of a wooden doll with his sexual organ.' Therefore, from the general sense of 'mark,' a certain person might have the doubt, 'Is the mark of things made of gold, silver, etc., a ground for a Pārājika offense or not?' For that very reason, it is said, 'Regarding the objects of painted figures, etc., he had remorse.' Therefore, to dispel that doubt and to define the beings who are the object of a Pārājika offense, the Blessed One, having classified them threefold by way of species—human, non-human, etc.—divides and shows the beings who are the object of a Pārājika offense. Therefore, it should be said that by the statement, 'It is not an object at all,' it rejects the mark of things made of gold, silver, etc., which has arisen by implication from the general sense of 'mark.'

Tayo maggeti bhummatthe upayogavacananti āha “tīsu maggesūti attho veditabbo”ti. Evaṃ sabbatthāti iminā “dve magge”ti etthāpi dvīsu maggesūti attho veditabboti atidissati.

Regarding 'tayo magge,' he said, 'The meaning should be understood as "in the three paths,"' because it is an accusative case expression used in the locative sense. By 'thus in all cases,' it is indicated that here in 'dve magge' as well, the meaning should be understood as 'in the two paths.'

Anupaññattivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on Further Regulations is concluded.

Paṭhamacatukkakathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the First Tetrad.

57. Assāti [V 2.0078] ākhyātikapadanti tassa atthaṃ dassento “hotī”ti āha. Gaṇṭhipadesu pana “assāti puggalaṃ parāmasitvā hotīti [M 2.0088] vacanaseso dassito”tipi atthavikappo dassito, na so sundarataro. Yadi hi vacanaseso adhippeto siyā, “hotī”ti vattabbaṃ, teneva aññasmiṃ atthavikappe hotīti vacanaseso kato.

57. As 'assā' is a finite verb, showing its meaning, he said 'hoti.' But in the glosses, an alternative meaning is also shown: 'The word "assā" refers to a person, and "hoti" is shown as the remainder of the statement.' That meaning is not superior. For if a remainder of the statement were intended, 'hoti' should have been stated. For that very reason, in another alternative meaning, 'hoti' is made the remainder of the statement.

58. Sādiyantassevāti ettha sādiyanaṃ nāma sevetukāmatācittassa upaṭṭhāpananti āha “paṭisevanacittasamaṅgissā”ti. “Paṭipakkhaṃ atthayantīti sikkhākāmānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ paṭipakkhaṃ dussīlabhāvaṃ atthayantī”ti gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Attano veripuggalassa pana paṭipakkhabhūtaṃ kañci amittaṃ atthayanti gavesantīti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Paccatthikā hi attano veriṃ nāsetukāmā tassa paṭipakkhabhūtaṃ kañci amittaṃ attano sahāyabhāvamupagacchantaṃ icchanti. Rājapaccatthikādīnaṃ upari vakkhamānattā tadanurūpavasena atthaṃ dassento “bhikkhū eva paccatthikā bhikkhupaccatthikā”ti āha. “Bhikkhussa paccatthikā bhikkhupaccatthikā”ti evaṃ pana vuccamāne bhikkhussa paccatthikā rājādayopi ettheva saṅgayhantīti rājapaccatthikādayo visuṃ na vattabbā siyuṃ, aññattha pana bhikkhussa paccatthikā bhikkhupaccatthikāti ayamattho labbhateva “sāsanapaccatthikā”ti yathā. Issāpakatāti paresaṃ lābhasakkārādiasahanalakkhaṇāya issāya abhibhūtā. Nipparipphandanti paripphandavirahitaṃ, yathā calituṃ parivattituṃ na sakkoti, tathā gahetvāti attho. Sampayojentīti vaccamaggena saddhiṃ yojenti.

58. Here in 'sādiyantassa eva,' consenting (sādiyanaṃ) means the arising of a mind with the desire to engage; therefore, he said, 'of one endowed with a mind for engagement.' In the glosses it is said: 'As for "paṭipakkhaṃ atthayantī," it means they desire the state of bad morality, which is contrary to monks who desire the training.' However, in the case of one's own enemy, the meaning here should be understood as they desire or seek some foe who is an opponent. For enemies, wishing to destroy their own foe, desire some foe who is an opponent to him to approach and become their ally. Because 'enemies of the king,' etc., will be spoken of later on, showing the meaning in a way that is suitable for that, he said, 'Monks themselves are the enemies; "bhikkhupaccatthikā."' But if it were said thus, 'The enemies of a monk are "bhikkhupaccatthikā,"' then the enemies of a monk, such as kings, would also be included right here, and 'enemies of the king,' etc., would not need to be stated separately. But elsewhere, this meaning, 'the enemies of a monk are "bhikkhupaccatthikā,"' is indeed obtained, as in 'enemies of the Dispensation.' 'Issāpakatā' means overwhelmed by envy, which has the characteristic of not being able to endure the gain, honor, etc., of others. 'Nipparipphandaṃ' means without movement; that is, having seized him so that he is not able to move or turn. 'Sampayojenti' means they join him with the passage for excrement.

Tasmiṃ khaṇeti tasmiṃ pavesanakkhaṇe, aggato yāva mūlā pavesanakālo “pavesanakkhaṇo”ti vuccati. Sādiyanaṃ nāma sevanacittassa uppādananti āha “sevanacittaṃ upaṭṭhāpetī”ti. Paviṭṭhakāleti aṅgajātassa yattakaṃ ṭhānaṃ pavesanārahaṃ, tattakaṃ anavasesato paviṭṭhakāle. Evaṃ paviṭṭhassa uddharaṇārambhato antarā ṭhitakālo ṭhitaṃ nāma. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana mātugāmassa sukkavissaṭṭhiṃ patvā sabbathā vāyamato oramitvā ṭhitakālaṃ sandhāya “sukkavissaṭṭhisamaye”ti vuttaṃ. Uddharaṇaṃ nāma yāva aggā nīharaṇakāloti āha – “nīharaṇakāle paṭisevanacittaṃ upaṭṭhāpetī”ti. Aṅgārakāsunti aṅgārarāsiṃ. Evarūpe kāle asādiyanaṃ nāma na sabbesaṃ visayoti āha “imañhi evarūpaṃ āraddhavipassaka”ntiādi[M 2.0089]. Ekādasahi aggīhīti rāgadosamohajātijarāmaraṇasokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsasaṅkhātehi ekādasahi aggīhi. Rāgādayo hi anuḍahanaṭṭhena “aggī”ti vuccanti. Te hi yassa santi[V 2.0079], taṃ niḍahanti, mahāpariḷāhā ca honti dunnibbāpayā ca. Bhagavatā ca dummaṅkūnaṃ puggalānaṃ niggaho icchitoyevāti āha – “paccatthikānañcassa manorathavighātaṃ karonto”ti. Assāti asādiyantassa yathāvuttaguṇasamaṅgissa.

'At that moment' means at the moment of entry. The period of entry from the tip to the root is called 'the moment of entry.' 'Acceptance' means the arising of the mind of enjoyment; thus he said, 'it establishes the mind of enjoyment.' 'At the time of having entered' means when the entire extent of the organ suitable for entry has entered without remainder. For one who has thus entered, the period of remaining stationary in the interval before the start of withdrawal is called 'the stationary state.' In the commentary, however, referring to the stationary state after a woman's emission of fluid and the man has completely ceased his exertion, it is said, 'at the time of fluid emission.' 'Withdrawal' means the period of drawing out up to the tip; thus he said, 'at the time of withdrawal, it establishes the mind of re-enjoyment.' 'Aṅgārakāsu' means a heap of embers. At such a time, 'non-acceptance' is not within the capacity of everyone; thus he said, 'for one like this, engaged in insight,' and so forth. 'By the eleven fires' means by the eleven fires designated as lust, hatred, delusion, birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, and despair. For lust, etc., are called 'fires' in the sense of burning. They indeed burn one in whom they exist, cause great suffering, and are hard to extinguish. And the Blessed One indeed desired the restraint of wicked individuals; thus he said, 'while frustrating the desires of his enemies.' 'Assa' means for one who does not accept, endowed with the qualities as described.

Paṭhamacatukkakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the First Tetrad is concluded.

Ekūnasattatidvisatacatukkakathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Discourses on the Tetrads from Sixty-Nine to Two Hundred

59-60. Akkhāyitanimittā akkhāyita-saddena vuttā uttarapadalopenāti āha “soṇasiṅgālādīhi akkhāyitanimitta”nti. Akkhāyitaṃ nimittaṃ yassā sā akkhāyitanimittā. “Jāgaranti”ntiādi visesanarahitattā “suddhikacatukkānī”ti vuttaṃ.

59-60. The term 'akkhāyitanimittā' is stated by the word 'akkhāyita' through the elision of the latter word; thus he said, “the sign uneaten by dogs, jackals, and so forth.” She whose sign is uneaten is 'akkhāyitanimittā.' The phrases beginning with 'jāgaranti,' being without specific qualifiers, are called “the pure tetrads.”

Samānācariyakā therāti ekācariyassa pāṭhakantevāsikā. Mahābhayeti brāhmaṇatissabhaye. Gaṅgāya aparabhāgo aparagaṅgaṃ. Vata reti garahatthe nipāto. Avissajjantena kiṃ kattabbanti āha “niccakālaṃ sotabba”ntiādi. Evaṃ vinayagarukānanti iminā upari tehi vuccamānavinicchayassa garukaraṇīyatāya kāraṇaṃ vuttaṃ. Sabbaṃ pariyādiyitvāti sabbaṃ pārājikakkhettaṃ anavasesato gahetvā. Sotaṃ chinditvāti pārājikakkhette vītikkamasotaṃ chinditvā. Apaññattabhāvato yuttiabhāvato ca “pārājikacchāyā panettha na dissatī”ti vuttaṃ. Keci pana “upaḍḍhakkhāyitabhāvassa dubbinicchayattā tattha pārājikaṃ na paññapesī”ti vadanti, taṃ akāraṇaṃ, na ca dubbinicchayatā apaññattikāraṇaṃ yebhuyyakkhāyitādīsupi dubbinicchayabhāvassa samānattā. Upaḍḍhakkhāyitato hi kiñcideva adhikaṃ ūnaṃ vā yadi khāyitaṃ siyā, tampi yebhuyyena khāyitaṃ akkhāyitanti saṅkhyaṃ gacchatīti upaḍḍhakkhāyitamiva yebhuyyakkhāyitādīnipi dubbinicchayāneva. Apica upaḍḍhakkhāyitaṃ yadi sabhāvato [M 2.0090] pārājikakkhettaṃ siyā, na tattha bhagavā dubbinicchayanti pārājikaṃ na paññapeti.

The elders of the same practice were the pupils of a single teacher. 'Great fear' refers to the fear of the brahmin Tissa. The other side of the Ganges is the farther bank of the Ganges. The phrase “vata re” is a particle used in the sense of censure. “What should be done by one not relinquishing?”—he said, “One should listen constantly,” and so on. Thus, by this phrase 'for those who revere the Vinaya,' the reason is stated for why the judgment spoken by them above should be taken seriously. “Having exhausted everything” means having taken the entire sphere of pārājika offenses without remainder. “Cutting off the stream” means severing the stream of transgression within the sphere of pārājika offenses. Due to the absence of an enactment and the lack of logical justification, it is said, “Here, not even the shadow of a pārājika offense is seen.” Some, however, say, “Because the state of being half-eaten is difficult to ascertain, the Buddha did not enact a pārājika offense in that case.” But this is groundless, for difficulty of ascertainment is not a reason for non-enactment, since a similar difficulty of ascertainment exists even in cases of 'mostly eaten' and the like. For if something is eaten slightly more or less than half, it would still be reckoned as 'mostly eaten' or 'not eaten'; thus, like 'half-eaten,' 'mostly eaten' and the like are also indeed difficult to ascertain. Moreover, if 'half-eaten' were by nature within the sphere of pārājika offenses, the Blessed One would not have refrained from enacting a pārājika offense there on the grounds that it was difficult to ascertain.

Idāni therena katavinicchayameva upatthambhetvā aparampi tattha kāraṇaṃ dassento “apicā”tiādimāha. Nimitte appamattikāpi maṃsarāji sace avasiṭṭhā hoti, taṃ yebhuyyakkhāyitameva hoti, tato paraṃ pana sabbaso khāyite nimitte dukkaṭamevāti dassento āha “tato paraṃ thullaccayaṃ natthī”ti. Atha vā yebhuyyena khāyitaṃ nāma vaccamaggapassāvamaggamukhānaṃ catūsu koṭṭhāsesu dve koṭṭhāse atikkamma yāva tatiyakoṭṭhāsassa pariyosānā [V 2.0080] khāditaṃ, tato paraṃ pana tatiyakoṭṭhāsaṃ atikkamma yāva catutthakoṭṭhāsassa pariyosānā khāditaṃ dukkaṭavatthūti veditabbaṃ. Matasarīrasmiṃyeva veditabbanti “mataṃ yebhuyyena akkhāyita”ntiādivacanato. “Yadipi nimittaṃ sabbaso khāyitantiādi sabbaṃ jīvamānakasarīrameva sandhāya vutta”nti mahāgaṇṭhipade vuttaṃ. Kenaci pana “taṃ vīmaṃsitvā gahetabba”nti likhitaṃ. Kimettha vīmaṃsitabbaṃ jīvamānakasarīrasseva adhikatattā matasarīre labbhamānassa vinicchayassa visuṃ vakkhamānattā ca. Teneva mātikāṭṭhakathāyampi (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. paṭhamapārājikavaṇṇanā) –

Now, having supported the decision already made by the elder, he further presents another reason there, saying, “Moreover.” If even a small trace of flesh remains on the sign, it is 'mostly eaten.' Beyond that, however, to show that when the sign is entirely eaten, it is only a dukkaṭa offense, he says, “Beyond that, there is no thullaccaya.” Alternatively, 'mostly eaten' means that in the four sections of the anal passage, the urinary passage, and the mouth, having passed two sections, it is eaten up to the end of the third section. Beyond that, however, passing the third section and being eaten up to the end of the fourth section is to be understood as the basis for a dukkaṭa offense. It should be understood only in the case of a dead body, from the statement, “a corpse is mostly uneaten.” “The entire passage beginning ‘Even if the sign is entirely eaten’ is all stated with reference to a living body,” as mentioned in the Mahāgaṇṭhipada. However, someone has written, “That should be investigated and then taken.” What is to be investigated here? Since the living body is the primary case, and the decision obtainable regarding a dead body will be separately stated. Therefore, even in the Mātikāṭṭhakathā (Kaṅkhā. Aṭṭha. First Pārājikavaṇṇanā)—

“Jīvamānakasarīrassa vuttappakāre magge sacepi tacādīni anavasesetvā sabbaso chinne nimittasaṇṭhānamattaṃ paññāyati, tattha antamaso aṅgajāte uṭṭhikaṃ anaṭṭhakāyappasādaṃ pīḷakaṃ vā cammakhīlaṃ vā pavesentassapi sevanacitte sati pārājikaṃ, naṭṭhakāyappasādaṃ sukkhapīḷakaṃ vā matacammaṃ vā lomaṃ vā pavesentassa dukkaṭaṃ. Sace nimittasaṇṭhānamattampi anavasesetvā sabbaso maggo uppāṭito, tattha upakkamato vaṇasaṅkhepavasena thullaccaya”nti –

“In the case of a living body, in the path of the aforesaid type, even if the skin and so forth are completely severed without remainder and only the mere shape of the sign is discernible, there, for one who inserts into the sexual organ even so much as a small growth, a boil that has not lost its sensory quality, or a skin tag, if there is an intention for intercourse, it is a pārājika offense. For one who inserts a boil that has lost its sensory quality, a dry boil, dead skin, or hair, it is a dukkaṭa offense. If the path is entirely uprooted, without even the mere shape of the sign remaining, there, from the attempt, by way of inclusion as a wound, it is a thullaccaya offense.”

Jīvamānakasarīrasmiṃyeva yathāvuttavinicchayo dassito.

Thus, the aforesaid decision is shown only in the case of a living body.

Sabbaso khāyitanti nimittappadese bahiṭṭhitaṃ chavicammaṃ sabbaso chinditvā soṇasiṅgālādīhi khāyitasadisaṃ kataṃ. Tenevāha “chavicammaṃ natthī”ti. Nimittamaṃsassa pana abbhantare chavicammassa ca vijjamānattā “nimittasaṇṭhānaṃ paññāyatī”ti vuttaṃ. Tenevāha “pavesanaṃ jāyatī”ti. Nimittasaṇṭhānaṃ pana [M 2.0091] anavasesetvāti nimittākārena ṭhitaṃ chavicammamaṃsādiṃ anavasesetvā. Jīvamānakasarīre labbhamānavisesaṃ dassetvā idāni matasarīre labbhamānavisesaṃ dassento āha “matasarīre panā”tiādi.

“Entirely eaten” means the outer skin in the region of the sexual organ is entirely cut away, making it similar to what has been eaten by dogs, jackals, and so on. For that very reason, he said, “there is no outer skin.” However, because the flesh of the sexual organ and the inner skin are present inside, it is said, “the form of the sexual organ is apparent.” For that very reason, he said, “penetration occurs.” “Without leaving the form of the sexual organ” means without leaving remaining the skin, flesh, etc., that exist in the shape of the sexual organ. Having shown the distinction that can be obtained in a living body, now, while showing the distinction that can be obtained in a dead body, he said, “But in a dead body,” and so on.

Manussānaṃ jīvamānakasarīretiādinā pana akkhiādayopi vaṇasaṅgahaṃ gacchantīti vaṇena ekaparicchedaṃ katvā akkhiādīsupi thullaccayaṃ vuttaṃ. Tesañca vaṇasaṅgaho “navadvāro mahāvaṇo”ti (mi. pa. 2.6.1) evamādisuttānusārena veditabbo. Tiracchānagatānaṃ akkhikaṇṇavaṇesu dukkaṭaṃ pana aṭṭhakathāppamāṇena gahetabbaṃ. Yathā hi manussāmanussatiracchānagatesu vaccamaggapassāvamaggamukhānaṃ pārājikavatthubhāve nānākaraṇaṃ natthi, evaṃ akkhiādīnampi thullaccayādivatthubhāve ninnānākaraṇena bhavitabbaṃ. Vaṇe thullaccayañca “amaggena [V 2.0081] amaggaṃ paveseti, āpatti thullaccayassā”ti (pārā. 66) sāmaññato vuttaṃ, na pana “manussāna”nti visesanaṃ atthi. Yadi ca tiracchānagatānaṃ vaṇesu thullaccayena na bhavitabbaṃ, pataṅgamukhamaṇḍūkassa mukhasaṇṭhāne vaṇasaṅkhepato thullaccayaṃ na vattabbaṃ, vuttañca, tasmā aṭṭhakathācariyā evettha pamāṇaṃ. Bhagavato adhippāyaññuno hi aṭṭhakathācariyā. Teneva vuttaṃ “buddhena dhammo vinayo ca vutto, yo tassa puttehi tatheva ñāto”tiādi (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.). Manussānanti itthipurisapaṇḍakaubhatobyañjanakānaṃ sāmaññato vuttaṃ. Vatthikosesūti vatthipuṭesu purisānaṃ aṅgajātakosesu. Matasarīraṃ yāva uddhumātakādibhāvena kuthitaṃ na hoti, tāva allasarīranti veditabbaṃ. Tenāha – “yadā pana sarīraṃ uddhumātakaṃ hotī”tiādi. Pārājikavatthuñca thullaccayavatthuñca vijahatīti ettha pārājikavatthubhāvaṃ thullaccayavatthubhāvañca vijahatīti attho veditabbo. Matānaṃ tiracchānagatānanti sambandho.

However, by “in the living body of humans,” and so on, the eyes and so on are also included in the category of a wound. Thus, having made a single demarcation with “wound,” a grave offense is stated also in the case of the eyes and so on. And their inclusion as a wound should be understood in accordance with the Sutta, such as, “the great wound with nine doors.” However, a dukkaṭa offense in the case of wounds in the eyes and ears of animals should be taken according to the authority of the commentary. Indeed, just as there is no distinction in the state of being a basis for a pārājika offense for the openings of the anus, urethra, and mouth in humans, non-humans, and animals, so too, in the state of being a basis for a grave offense and so on for the eyes and so on, it should be without distinction. And the grave offense in a wound is stated generally: “If one enters a non-path by a non-path, the offense is a thullaccaya,” but there is no specification “of humans.” And if there should not be a grave offense for wounds in animals, a grave offense should not be stated for the mouth-form of the Pataṅga frog, due to its inclusion as a wound; but it is stated. Therefore, the commentary teachers are the authority here. Indeed, the commentary teachers are those who know the intention of the Blessed One. For that very reason it is said: “The Dhamma and Vinaya were taught by the Buddha, and thus understood by his sons,” and so on. “Of humans” is stated generally for women, men, paṇḍakas, and those with both sexes. Vatthikosesu means in the scrotal sacs, in the sacs of the male sexual organ. As long as a dead body is not putrid by way of being bloated and so on, it should be known as a “moist body.” For that reason, he said: “But when the body becomes bloated…” and so on. Here, “it abandons the basis for a pārājika and the basis for a thullaccaya”—the meaning should be understood as “it abandons the state of being a basis for a pārājika and the state of being a basis for a thullaccaya.” The connection is “of dead animals.”

Methunarāgena vatthikosaṃ pavesentassa thullaccayaṃ vuttanti āha “patthikosaṃ appavesento”ti. Itthiyā appavesentoti itthiyā nimittaṃ appavesento. Appavesentoti ca pavesanādhippāyassa abhāvaṃ dasseti. Pavesanādhippāyena bahi chupantassa pana methunassa pubbapayogattā dukkaṭeneva bhavitabbaṃ. Nimittena nimittaṃ chupati, thullaccayanti idaṃ “na ca, bhikkhave, rattacittena aṅgajātaṃ chupitabbaṃ, yo chupeyya, āpatti thullaccayassā”ti [M 2.0092] (mahāva. 252) imassa suttassa vasena vuttaṃ. Tattha ca kesañci aññathāpi atthavikappassa vidhiṃ dassento “mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ panā”tiādimāha. Tattha kiñcāpi “katvā mahāaṭṭhakathaṃ sarīra”nti (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.ganthārambhakathā) vuttaṃ, tathāpi sesaaṭṭhakathāsu “methunarāgena mukhenā”ti vacanassa abhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ panā”ti vuttaṃ. “Aṅgajātenā”ti avuttattā “avisesenā”ti vuttaṃ.

Because a grave offense is stated for one who inserts into a scrotal sac with sexual lust, he said, “not inserting into the scrotal sac.” “Not inserting into a woman's” means not inserting into a woman's sexual organ. And “not inserting” shows the absence of the intention to insert. However, for one who touches externally with the intention to insert, because it is a preliminary act of sexual intercourse, it should be only a dukkaṭa offense. “Touching a sexual organ with a sexual organ is a grave offense”—this statement is said by way of this Sutta: “And, monks, the sexual organ should not be touched with a lustful mind. Whoever should touch it, the offense is a thullaccaya.” And there, while showing the method of an alternative interpretation of the meaning for some, he said, “But in the Great Commentary,” and so on. Although it is said there, “having made the Great Commentary the body,” nevertheless, “But in the Great Commentary” is said to show the absence of the phrase “with sexual lust, with the mouth” in the other commentaries. Because “with the sexual organ” is not stated, “without distinction” is stated.

Idāni mahāaṭṭhakathaṃ pāḷiyā saṃsanditvā dassento “yaṃ tāva mahāaṭṭhakathāya”ntiādimāha. Itarathā hi dukkaṭaṃ siyāti pakatimukhena chupantassa visāṇādiggahaṇe viya dukkaṭaṃ siyā. Evaṃ mahāaṭṭhakathaṃ pāḷiyā saṃsanditvā idāni tattha kesañci aññathā atthavikappaṃ dassento “keci panā”tiādimāha. Saṅghādisesoti kāyasaṃsaggasikkhāpadena saṅghādiseso. Vuttanayenevāti methunarāgeneva. “Nimittamukhenā”ti vuttattā tiracchānagatitthiyā passāvamaggaṃ methunarāgena pakatimukhena chupantassa dukkaṭanti veditabbaṃ. Kāyasaṃsaggarāgena dukkaṭanti nimittamukhena vā pakatimukhena vā kāyasaṃsaggarāgena chupantassa dukkaṭameva.

Now, while showing the Great Commentary by comparing it with the Pāḷi, he said, “As for what is in the Great Commentary,” and so on. As for “otherwise, it would be a dukkaṭa,” it means for one who touches with the natural mouth, like the grasping of a horn, etc., it would be a dukkaṭa. Thus, having compared the Great Commentary with the Pāḷi, now, while showing an alternative interpretation of the meaning by some there, he said, “But some,” and so on. Saṅghādisesa means a saṅghādisesa offense by the training rule on bodily contact. ‘By the method stated’ means ‘with sexual lust.’ Because it was stated, “with the sexual organ as the mouth,” it should be understood that it is a dukkaṭa for one who touches the urinary passage of a female animal with sexual lust using the natural mouth. “A dukkaṭa for lust for bodily contact” means that for one who touches with lust for bodily contact, whether with the sexual organ as the mouth or with the natural mouth, it is only a dukkaṭa.

Ekūnasattatidvisatacatukkakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the discourse on the sixty-ninth, two-hundredth, and fourfold topics is concluded.

Santhatacatukkabhedakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Fourfold Division of 'Santhatā'

61-2. Paṭipannakassāti [V 2.0082] āraddhavipassakassa. Upādinnakanti kāyindriyaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Upādinnakena phusatīti upādinnakena phusīyati ghaṭṭīyatīti evaṃ kammani ya-kāralopena attho veditabbo. Atha vā evaṃ karonto kiñci upādinnakaṃ upādinnakena na phusati na ghaṭṭetīti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Lesaṃ oḍḍessantīti lesaṃ samuṭṭhāpessanti, parikappessantīti vuttaṃ hoti. Santhatādibhedehi bhinditvāti santhatādivisesanehi visesetvā, santhatādīhi catūhi yojetvāti vuttaṃ hoti.

61-2. 'For one who is practicing' means for one who has undertaken insight meditation. 'Acquired' is said with reference to the bodily faculty. 'Touches with what is acquired' means it is touched or struck by what is acquired—thus, the meaning should be understood by the elision of the letter 'ya' in the passive construction. Alternatively, the meaning here should be understood thus: 'In doing so, one does not touch or strike anything acquired with what is acquired.' 'They will offer a pretext' means they will give rise to a pretext, they will contrive; this is what is said. 'Having divided by the distinctions such as "covered"' means having distinguished by the qualifiers such as 'covered,' having connected with the four beginning with 'covered'; this is what is said.

Santhatāyāti ekadese samudāyavohāro “paṭo daḍḍho”tiādīsu viya. Tathā hi paṭassa ekadesepi daḍḍhe “paṭo daḍḍho”ti voharanti[M 2.0093], evaṃ itthiyā vaccamaggādīsu kismiñci magge santhate itthī “santhatā”ti vuccati. Tenāha “santhatā nāmā”tiādi. Vatthādīni anto appavesetvā bahi ṭhapetvā bandhanaṃ sandhāya “paliveṭhetvā”ti vuttaṃ. Ekadese samudāyavohāravaseneva bhikkhupi “santhato”ti vuccatīti āha “santhato nāmā”tiādi. Yattake paviṭṭheti tilaphalamatte paviṭṭhe. Akkhiādimhi santhatepi yathāvatthukamevāti āha “thullaccayakkhette thullaccayaṃ, dukkaṭakkhette dukkaṭameva hotī”ti.

Regarding ‘covered’: this is a collective term applied to a part, as in such instances as ‘the cloth is burnt.’ For, even when a part of the cloth is burnt, they say, ‘the cloth is burnt.’ Similarly, when any passage of a woman, such as the passage for excrement, is covered, the woman is called ‘covered.’ Therefore, he said, ‘“Covered” means…,’ and so on. ‘Having wrapped around’ is said with reference to binding, having placed the cloth, etc., outside without inserting it inside. By way of a collective term for a part, a monk too is called ‘covered’; thus, he said, ‘“Covered” means…,’ and so on. ‘When inserted to whatever extent’ means when inserted to the extent of a sesame seed. Even when the eye-socket, etc., is covered, it is just according to the object; thus, he said, ‘in the sphere of a grave offense, it is a grave offense; in the sphere of a light offense, it is just a light offense.’

Khāṇuṃ ghaṭṭentassa dukkaṭanti itthinimittassa anto khāṇuṃ pavesetvā samatalaṃ atirittaṃ vā khāṇuṃ ghaṭṭentassa dukkaṭaṃ pavesābhāvato. Sace pana īsakaṃ anto pavisitvā ṭhitaṃ khāṇukameva aṅgajātena chupati, pārājikameva. Tassa talanti veḷunaḷādikassa antotalaṃ. Vinītavatthūsu “tena kho pana samayena aññataro bhikkhu sīvathikaṃ gantvā chinnasīsaṃ passitvā vaṭṭakate mukhe acchupantaṃ aṅgajātaṃ pavesesi. Tassa kukkuccaṃ ahosi…pe… anāpatti bhikkhu pārājikassa, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti vuttattā tassa suttassa anulomato “ākāsagatameva katvā pavesetvā nīharati, dukkaṭa”nti (pārā. 73) vuttaṃ. Bahiddhā khāṇuketi antopavesitaveṇupabbādikassa bahi nikkhantakhāṇuke. Methunarāgena indriyabaddhaānindriyabaddhasantānesu yattha katthaci upakkamantassa na sakkā anāpattiyā bhavitunti “dukkaṭamevā”ti vuttaṃ. Teneva vinītavatthumhi aṭṭhikesu upakkamantassa dukkaṭaṃ vuttaṃ.

‘For one striking a stump, there is a light offense’ means: for one who, having inserted a stump into the female organ, strikes the stump until it is level or in excess, there is a light offense because there is no further insertion. But if one touches with the sexual organ a small stump that has entered slightly and is stationary, it is a grave offense indeed. ‘Its surface’ means the inner surface of bamboo, reeds, and so on. In the Vinītavatthu, because it is said: ‘At that time, a certain monk went to a charnel ground, saw a severed head, and inserted his sexual organ into the mouth, which was like a bowl, without touching it. He felt remorse… There is no grave offense for the monk, but there is a light offense,’ in accordance with that rule, it is said, ‘Having made it as if gone into space, one inserts and withdraws it; there is a light offense.’ ‘The stump outside’ means on the stump protruding outside of an inserted bamboo joint, and so on. For one who, with sexual lust, makes an attempt anywhere on a continuum connected with a faculty or not connected with a faculty, it is not possible to be without an offense; thus it is said, ‘it is a light offense indeed.’ For that very reason, in the Vinītavatthu, for one who makes an attempt on bones, a light offense is stated.

Santhatacatukkabhedakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Fourfold Division of ‘Covered’ is concluded.

Rājapaccatthikādicatukkabhedakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Fourfold Division Beginning with Royal Enemies

65. Sāmaññajotanāya [V 2.0083] pakaraṇato visesavinicchayoti āha “dhuttāti methunupasaṃhitakhiḍḍāpasutā”tiādi. Idāni sāmaññatopi atthasambhavaṃ dassento “itthidhuttasurādhuttādayo vā”ti āha. Hadayanti hadayamaṃsaṃ.

65. For the purpose of general elucidation, the specific determination is from the context; thus he said, ‘“A rogue” means one addicted to play connected with sexual intercourse,’ and so on. Now, showing the possibility of meaning even from the general sense, he said, ‘or female rogues, liquor rogues, and others.’ ‘Heart’ means the flesh of the heart.

Sabbākārena catukkabhedakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Fourfold Division in All Respects is concluded.

Āpattānāpattivāravaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Section on Offenses and Non-Offenses

66. Paṭiññākaraṇaṃ [M 2.0094] natthīti pucchitabbābhāvato. Na hi dūsako “kena cittena vītikkamaṃ akāsi, jānitvā akāsi, udāhu ajānitvā”ti evaṃ pucchāya arahati. Tatthevāti vesāliyaṃ mahāvane eva. Sabbaṅgagatanti ṭhapetvā kesalomadantanakhānaṃ maṃsavinimuttaṭṭhānañceva thaddhasukkhacammañca udakamiva telabindu avasesasabbasarīraṃ byāpetvā ṭhitaṃ. Sarīrakampādīnīti ādi-saddena akkhīnaṃ pītavaṇṇādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Pittakosake ṭhitanti hadayapapphāsānaṃ antare yakanamaṃsaṃ nissāya patiṭṭhite mahākosātakīkosasadise pittakose ṭhitaṃ. Kupiteti pittakosato calitvā bahi nikkhante.

66. ‘There is no making a declaration’ means there is no need to question. For an accuser is not entitled to ask, ‘With what state of mind did you commit the transgression? Did you do it knowingly or unknowingly?’ ‘Right there’ means in the Great Forest at Vesālī itself. ‘Pervading the entire body’ means it pervades and is situated in the entire remaining body, like a drop of oil on water, excluding the hair of the head, body hair, teeth, nails, those places devoid of flesh, and the hardened, dry skin. ‘Trembling of the body, etc.’: by the word ‘etc.’ is included the yellow discoloration of the eyes, and so on. ‘Situated in the bile sac’ means situated in the bile sac, which is like a large sponge gourd, established resting on the flesh of the liver between the heart and lungs. ‘Agitated’ means having moved from the bile sac and come out.

Vissaṭṭhacittoti vissaṭṭhapakaticitto. Yakkhummattakoti yakkhā kira yassa cittaṃ khipitukāmā honti, tassa setamukhaṃ nīlodaraṃ surattahatthapādaṃ mahāsīsaṃ pajjalitanettaṃ bheravaṃ vā attabhāvaṃ nimminitvā dassenti, bheravaṃ vā saddaṃ sāventi, kathentasseva vā mukhena hatthaṃ pakkhipitvā hadayamaṃsaṃ maddanti, tena so satto ummattako hoti khittacitto. Tenevāha “bheravāni vā ārammaṇāni dassetvā”tiādi. Tattha bheravānīti dassanamatteneva sattānaṃ bhayaṃ chambhitattaṃ lomahaṃsaṃ uppādetuṃ samatthāni. Niccameva ummattako hotīti yassa pittakosato pittaṃ calitvā bahi nikkhantaṃ hoti, taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Yassa pana pittaṃ calitvā pittakoseyeva ṭhitaṃ hoti bahi anikkhantaṃ, so antarantarā saññaṃ paṭilabhati, na niccameva ummattako hotīti veditabbaṃ. Ñatvāti saññāpaṭilābhena jānitvā. Adhimattāyāti adhikappamāṇāya.

‘One whose mind is disturbed’ means one whose natural mind is disturbed. ‘One made mad by a yakkha’ refers to how yakkhas, it is said, wishing to agitate someone’s mind, manifest a terrifying form—white-faced, blue-bellied, with very red hands and feet, a huge head, and blazing eyes—and show it to him, or they make him hear a frightful sound, or, while he is speaking, they thrust their hand into his mouth and crush the flesh of his heart. By this, that being becomes insane, with a deranged mind. Therefore, he said, ‘by showing terrifying objects, etc.’ Therein, ‘terrifying’ refers to things that, merely by being seen, are capable of instilling fear, stupefaction, and horripilation in beings. ‘Is perpetually insane’ is said with reference to one from whose bile sac bile has moved and exited. But as for one whose bile, having moved, remains within the bile sac without exiting, he regains consciousness intermittently and should be understood as not being perpetually insane. ‘Having known’ means having known by regaining consciousness. ‘In excessive measure’ means in an excessive amount.

Āpattānāpattivāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Section on Offenses and Non-Offenses is concluded.

Padabhājanīyavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Word-by-Word Analysis is concluded.

Pakiṇṇakakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on Miscellaneous Topics

Pakiṇṇakanti [V 2.0084] vomissakanayaṃ. Samuṭṭhānanti uppattikāraṇaṃ. Kiriyātiādi nidassanamattaṃ, akiriyādīnampi saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Vedanāyāti sahayoge karaṇavacanaṃ, vedanāya saha kusalañcāti vuttaṃ hoti. Sabbasaṅgāhakavasenāti [M 2.0095] sabbesaṃ sikkhāpadānaṃ saṅgāhakavasena. Cha sikkhāpadasamuṭṭhānānīti kāyo vācā kāyavācā kāyacittaṃ vācācittaṃ kāyavācācittanti evaṃ vuttāni cha āpattisamuṭṭhānāni. Āpattiyeva hi sikkhāpadasīsena vuttā. Samuṭṭhānādayo hi āpattiyā honti, na sikkhāpadassa, imesu pana chasu samuṭṭhānesu purimāni tīṇi acittakāni, pacchimāni sacittakāni. Tesu ekena vā dvīhi vā tīhi vā catūhi vā chahi vā samuṭṭhānehi āpattiyo samuṭṭhahanti, pañcasamuṭṭhānā āpatti nāma natthi. Tattha ekasamuṭṭhānā catutthena ca pañcamena ca chaṭṭhena ca samuṭṭhānena samuṭṭhāti, na aññena. Dvisamuṭṭhānā paṭhamacatutthehi ca dutiyapañcamehi ca tatiyachaṭṭhehi ca catutthachaṭṭhehi ca pañcamachaṭṭhehi ca samuṭṭhānehi samuṭṭhāti, na aññehi. Tisamuṭṭhānā paṭhamehi ca tīhi, pacchimehi ca tīhi samuṭṭhānehi samuṭṭhāti, na aññehi. Catusamuṭṭhānā paṭhamatatiyacatutthachaṭṭhehi ca dutiyatatiyapañcamachaṭṭhehi ca samuṭṭhānehi samuṭṭhāti, na aññehi. Chasamuṭṭhānā chahipi samuṭṭhāti.

“Miscellaneous” means a mixed method. “Origin” means the cause of arising. “Action,” etc., is merely an illustration; the inclusion of non-action and the like should also be understood. “With feeling” is the instrumental case in the sense of accompaniment; it means “together with feeling, and wholesome.” “By way of comprehensive inclusion” means by way of including all training rules. The six origins of the training rules—namely, body, speech, body-and-speech, body-and-mind, speech-and-mind, and body-speech-and-mind—are thus said to be the six origins of offenses. For it is the offense itself that is spoken of under the heading of the training rule. The origins, etc., belong to the offense, not to the training rule. Among these six origins, the first three are non-mental, and the latter three are mental. Among them, offenses arise through one, two, three, four, or six origins; there is no such thing as an offense with five origins. Therein, an offense of one origin arises through the fourth, the fifth, or the sixth origin, not through another. An offense of two origins arises through the first and fourth, the second and fifth, the third and sixth, the fourth and sixth, or the fifth and sixth origins, not through others. An offense of three origins arises through the first three or through the latter three origins, not through others. An offense of four origins arises through the first, third, fourth, and sixth, or through the second, third, fifth, and sixth origins, not through others. An offense of six origins arises through all six.

Sikkhāpadaṃ nāma atthi chasamuṭṭhānanti etthāpi sikkhāpadasīsena āpatti vuttāti veditabbā. Teneva vakkhati “sabbañcetaṃ āpattiyaṃ yujjati, sikkhāpadasīsena pana sabbaaṭṭhakathāsu desanā āruḷhā”ti. Kāyādīhi chahi samuṭṭhānaṃ uppatti, cha vā samuṭṭhānāni etassāti chasamuṭṭhānaṃ. Atthi catusamuṭṭhānanti kāyo kāyavācā kāyacittaṃ kāyavācācittanti imāni cattāri, vācā kāyavācā vācācittaṃ kāyavācācittanti imāni vā cattāri samuṭṭhānāni etassāti catusamuṭṭhānaṃ. Atthi tisamuṭṭhānanti kāyo vācā kāyavācāti imāni tīṇi, kāyacittaṃ vācācittaṃ kāyavācācittanti imāni vā tīṇi samuṭṭhānāni etassāti tisamuṭṭhānaṃ. Dvisamuṭṭhānaṃ ekasamuṭṭhānañca samuṭṭhānasīsavasena dassento “atthi kathinasamuṭṭhāna”ntiādimāha. Terasa hi samuṭṭhānasīsāni paṭhamapārājikasamuṭṭhānaṃ adinnādānasamuṭṭhānaṃ sañcarittasamuṭṭhānaṃ samanubhāsanasamuṭṭhānaṃ kathinasamuṭṭhānaṃ eḷakalomasamuṭṭhānaṃ padasodhammasamuṭṭhānaṃ addhānasamuṭṭhānaṃ theyyasatthasamuṭṭhānaṃ dhammadesanāsamuṭṭhānaṃ bhūtārocanasamuṭṭhānaṃ corivuṭṭhāpanasamuṭṭhānaṃ ananuññātasamuṭṭhānanti.

Regarding 'There is a training rule with six origins,' here too it should be understood that the offense is spoken of under the heading of the training rule. Therefore, it will be said: “All this applies to the offense, but in all the commentaries, the exposition is presented under the heading of the training rule.” Its origin is an arising from the six, beginning with the body; or, it has six origins. Thus, it is called 'of six origins'. Regarding 'There is a fourfold origin': it has as its origins these four—body, body-and-speech, body-and-mind, and body-speech-and-mind; or these four—speech, body-and-speech, speech-and-mind, and body-speech-and-mind. Thus, it is called 'of four origins'. Regarding 'There is a threefold origin': it has as its origins these three—body, speech, and body-and-speech; or these three—body-and-mind, speech-and-mind, and body-speech-and-mind. Thus, it is called 'of three origins'. Showing the twofold origin and the single origin by way of the headings of the origins, he said, “There is the origin relating to kathina,” etc. Indeed, there are thirteen headings of the origins: the origin of the first pārājika, the origin of taking what is not given, the origin of acting as a go-between, the origin of formal admonition, the origin relating to kathina, the origin of sheep’s wool, the origin of foot-soiling, the origin of the journey, the origin of theft by a caravan, the origin of teaching the Dhamma, the origin of declaring a superhuman state, the origin of ordaining a thief, and the origin of unauthorized action.

Tattha [M 2.0096][V 2.0085] “atthi chasamuṭṭhāna”nti iminā sañcarittasamuṭṭhānaṃ vuttaṃ. “Atthi catusamuṭṭhāna”nti iminā pana addhānasamuṭṭhānaṃ ananuññātasamuṭṭhānañca saṅgahitaṃ. Yañhi paṭhamatatiyacatutthachaṭṭhehi samuṭṭhāti, idaṃ addhānasamuṭṭhānaṃ. Yaṃ pana dutiyatatiyapañcamachaṭṭhehi samuṭṭhāti, idaṃ ananuññātasamuṭṭhānaṃ. “Atthi tisamuṭṭhāna”nti iminā adinnādānasamuṭṭhānaṃ bhūtārocanasamuṭṭhānañca saṅgahitaṃ. Yañhi sacittakehi tīhi samuṭṭhānehi samuṭṭhāti, idaṃ adinnādānasamuṭṭhānaṃ. Yaṃ pana acittakehi tīhi samuṭṭhāti, idaṃ bhūtārocanasamuṭṭhānaṃ. “Atthi kathinasamuṭṭhāna”ntiādinā pana avasesasamuṭṭhānasīsena dvisamuṭṭhānaṃ ekasamuṭṭhānañca saṅgaṇhāti. Tathā hi yaṃ tatiyachaṭṭhehi samuṭṭhāti, idaṃ kathinasamuṭṭhānanti vuccati. Yaṃ paṭhamacatutthehi samuṭṭhāti, idaṃ eḷakalomasamuṭṭhānaṃ. Yaṃ chaṭṭheneva samuṭṭhāti, idaṃ dhuranikkhepasamuṭṭhānaṃ, samanubhāsanasamuṭṭhānantipi tasseva nāmaṃ. Ādi-saddasaṅgahitesu pana paṭhamapārājikasamuṭṭhānapadasodhammatheyyasatthadhammadesanācorivuṭṭhāpanasamuṭṭhānesu yaṃ kāyacittato samuṭṭhāti, idaṃ paṭhamapārājikasamuṭṭhānaṃ. Yaṃ dutiyapañcamehi samuṭṭhāti, idaṃ padasodhammasamuṭṭhānaṃ. Yaṃ catutthachaṭṭhehi samuṭṭhāti, idaṃ theyyasatthasamuṭṭhānaṃ. Yaṃ pañcameneva samuṭṭhāti, idaṃ dhammadesanāsamuṭṭhānaṃ. Yaṃ pañcamachaṭṭhehi samuṭṭhāti, idaṃ corivuṭṭhāpanasamuṭṭhānanti veditabbaṃ.

Therein, by “there is a sixfold origin,” the origin of acting as a go-between is stated. By “there is a fourfold origin,” the origin of the journey and the origin of unauthorized action are included. For that which arises from the first, third, fourth, and sixth is the origin of the journey. That which arises from the second, third, fifth, and sixth is the origin of unauthorized action. By “there is a threefold origin,” the origin of taking what is not given and the origin of declaring a superhuman state are included. For that which arises from the three origins with consciousness is the origin of taking what is not given. But that which arises from the three without consciousness is the origin of declaring a superhuman state. By “There is the origin relating to kathina,” etc., he includes the twofold origin and the single origin under the remaining headings of the origins. Thus, that which arises from the third and sixth is called the origin of the kathina. That which arises from the first and fourth is the origin of sheep’s wool. That which arises from the sixth alone is the origin of abandoning responsibility; 'the origin of formal admonition' is also a name for that very thing. But among those included by the word 'etc.'—in the origins of the first pārājika, foot-soiling, theft by a caravan, teaching the Dhamma, and ordaining a thief—that which arises from body and mind is the origin of the first pārājika. That which arises from the second and fifth is the origin of foot-soiling. That which arises from the fourth and sixth is the origin of theft by a caravan. That which arises from the fifth alone is the origin of teaching the Dhamma. That which arises from the fifth and sixth should be known as the origin of ordaining a thief.

Evaṃ samuṭṭhānasīsena sabbasikkhāpadāni terasadhā dassetvā idāni kiriyāvasena pañcadhā dassento “tatrāpi kiñci kiriyato samuṭṭhātī”tiādimāha. Tattha kiñcīti sikkhāpadasīsena āpattiṃ vadati. Tasmā yā kāyena vā vācāya vā pathavīkhaṇanādīsu viya vītikkamaṃ karontassa hoti, ayaṃ kiriyato samuṭṭhāti nāma. Yā kāyavācāya kattabbaṃ akarontassa hoti paṭhamakathināpatti viya, ayaṃ akiriyato samuṭṭhāti nāma. Yā karontassa ca akarontassa ca hoti aññātikāya bhikkhuniyā hatthato cīvarapaṭiggahaṇāpatti viya, ayaṃ kiriyākiriyato samuṭṭhāti nāma. Yā siyā karontassa ca siyā akarontassa ca hoti rūpiyapaṭiggahaṇāpatti viya, ayaṃ siyā kiriyato siyā akiriyato samuṭṭhāti nāma. Yā siyā karontassa ca siyā karontassa ca akarontassa ca hoti kuṭikārāpatti viya, ayaṃ siyā kiriyato siyā kiriyākiriyato samuṭṭhāti nāma.

Having shown all the training rules in thirteen ways by way of their origin-headings, now, showing them in five ways by way of action, he says, “Among these, something arises from action,” and so on. Herein, “something” refers to an offense by way of the heading of the training rule. Therefore, whichever offense occurs to one who transgresses with body or speech, as in digging the earth and so on, this is called “arising from action.” Whichever offense occurs to one not doing what should be done by body and speech, like the first kaṭhina offense, this is called “arising from inaction.” Whichever offense occurs to one who is doing and to one who is not doing, like the offense of accepting a robe from the hand of an unrelated bhikkhunī, this is called “arising from action-and-inaction.” Whichever offense might occur to one who is doing or might occur to one who is not doing, like the offense of accepting money, this is called “arising from possible action and possible inaction.” Whichever offense might occur to one who is doing, or might occur to one who is doing and not doing, like the offense regarding the construction of a hut, this is called “arising from possible action and possible action-and-inaction.”

Idāni [M 2.0097] sabbasikkhāpadāni saññāvasena dvidhā katvā dassento “tatrāpi atthi saññāvimokkha”ntiādimāha. Saññāya abhāvena vimokkho assāti saññāvimokkhanti majjhepadalopasamāso daṭṭhabbo. Yato hi vītikkamasaññāabhāvena muccati, idaṃ saññāvimokkhanti vuccati. Cittaṅgaṃ labhatiyevāti kāyacittādisacittakasamuṭṭhāneheva samuṭṭhahanato[V 2.0086]. “Labhatiyevā”ti avadhāraṇena no na labhatīti dasseti. Tasmā yaṃ cittaṅgaṃ labhati, na labhati ca, taṃ “itara”nti vuttaṃ itara-saddassa vuttapaṭiyogavisayattā.

Now, showing all the training rules divided into two by way of perception, he says, “Therein too, there is liberation by perception,” and so on. `Saññāvimokkha` (liberation by perception) should be understood as a compound with elision of the middle term, meaning: “liberation is due to the absence of perception.” For, because one is freed due to the absence of the perception of transgression, this is called `saññāvimokkha`. As for the phrase `cittaṅgaṃ labhatiyeva` (the mental factor is indeed obtained), this is because it arises only from origins accompanied by consciousness, such as those of body-and-mind, and so on. By the emphatic particle in `labhatiyevā`, it shows that it is not the case that it is not obtained. Therefore, that which obtains a mental factor and that which does not, is called “the other,” because the word “other” has as its object the counterpart of what was stated.

Puna sabbasikkhāpadāni cittavasena dvidhā dassento “puna atthi sacittaka”ntiādimāha. Yaṃ saheva cittena āpajjatīti yaṃ sacittakeneva samuṭṭhānena āpajjati, no acittakena. Vināpīti api-saddena sahāpi cittena āpajjatīti dasseti. Yañhi kadāci acittakena, kadāci sacittakena samuṭṭhānena samuṭṭhāti, taṃ acittakanti vuccati. Ettha ca saññādukaṃ anāpattimukhena, sacittakadukaṃ āpattimukhena vuttanti idametesaṃ nānākaraṇanti veditabbaṃ.

Again, showing all the training rules as twofold by way of consciousness, he says, “Again, there is that which is with consciousness,” and so on. “That which one commits together with consciousness” means that which one commits only by an origin accompanied by consciousness, not by one without consciousness. The phrase `vināpi` (even without) shows, by the particle `api`, that one also commits it together with consciousness. For that which arises sometimes from an origin without consciousness and sometimes from an origin with consciousness is called `acittaka` (without consciousness). And herein, the pair concerning perception is stated from the perspective of non-offense, while the pair concerning consciousness is stated from the perspective of offense—this should be understood as what makes them different.

Lokavajjadukassa heṭṭhā vuttalakkhaṇattā taṃ avibhajitvā idāni sabbasikkhāpadāni kammavasena duvidhāni, kusalādivasena vedanāvasena ca tividhāni hontīti dassento “kammakusalavedanāvasenā”tiādimāha. Ettha pana kiñcāpi aṭṭhakathāsu āgatanayena kāyakammaṃ vacīkammanti kammavasena dukaṃ vuttaṃ, tikameva pana dassetuṃ vaṭṭati. Sabbameva hi sikkhāpadaṃ kāyadvāre āpajjitabbato vacīdvāre āpajjitabbato kāyavacīdvāre āpajjitabbato ca tividhaṃ hoti. Teneva mātikāṭṭhakathāyaṃ (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. paṭhamapārājikavaṇṇanā) vuttaṃ “sabbāva kāyakammavacīkammatadubhayavasena tividhā honti. Tattha kāyadvāre āpajjitabbā kāyakammanti vuccati, vacīdvāre āpajjitabbā vacīkammanti vuccati, ubhayattha āpajjitabbā kāyakammavacīkamma”nti. Tatoyeva ca adinnādānasikkhāpadādīsu kāyakammavacīkammanti tadubhayavasena dassitaṃ.

Since the characteristics of the pair of worldly faults have been stated below, without analyzing that, he now shows that all training rules are twofold by way of action, and threefold by way of what is wholesome, etc., and by way of feeling, saying, “by way of action, wholesome, and feeling,” and so on. Herein, although in the commentaries a pair by way of action—bodily action and verbal action—is stated according to the transmitted method, it is nevertheless proper to show only a triad. For every single training rule is threefold, in that it is to be committed through the body-door, to be committed through the speech-door, or to be committed through both the body-and-speech-door. For that very reason, in the Mātikā Commentary it is said: “All are threefold by way of bodily action, verbal action, and both. Herein, what is to be committed through the body-door is called bodily action; what is to be committed through the speech-door is called verbal action; what is to be committed through both is called bodily-and-verbal action.” And for that very reason, in the training rules on taking what is not given, etc., that training rule is shown by way of both of them as ‘bodily-and-verbal action’.

Atthi pana sikkhāpadaṃ kusalantiādinā āpattiṃ āpajjanto kusalacittasamaṅgī vā āpajjati akusalacittasamaṅgī vā abyākatacittasamaṅgī vāti [M 2.0098] dasseti, na pana kusalāpi āpatti atthīti. Na hi kusalā āpatti nāma atthi “āpattādhikaraṇaṃ siyā akusalaṃ siyā abyākataṃ, natthi āpattādhikaraṇaṃ kusala”nti (pari. 303) vacanato. Dasa kāmāvacarakiriyacittānīti hasituppādavoṭṭhabbanehi saddhiṃ aṭṭha mahākiriyacittāni. Dvinnaṃ abhiññācittānaṃ āpattisamuṭṭhāpakattaṃ paññattiṃ ajānantassa iddhivikubbanādīsu daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yaṃ kusalacittena āpajjatīti yaṃ sikkhāpadasīsena gahitaṃ āpattiṃ kusalacittasamaṅgī āpajjati. Iminā pana vacanena taṃ kusalanti āpattiyā vuccamāno kusalabhāvo pariyāyatova, na paramatthatoti dasseti. Kusalacittena hi āpattiṃ āpajjanto saviññattikaṃ aviññattikaṃ [V 2.0087] vā sikkhāpadavītikkamākārappavattaṃ rūpakkhandhasaṅkhātaṃ abyākatāpattiṃ āpajjati. Itarehi itaranti itarehi akusalābyākatacittehi yaṃ āpajjati, taṃ itaraṃ, akusalaṃ abyākatañcāti attho. Idañca āpattiṃ āpajjanto akusalacittasamaṅgī vā āpajjati kusalābyākatacittasamaṅgī vāti dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Evaṃ santepi sabbasikkhāpadesu kiñci akusalacittameva kiñci kusalābyākatavasena dvicittaṃ, kiñci sabbesaṃ vasena ticittanti ayameva pabhedo labbhati, na aññoti veditabbaṃ.

By the text beginning, 'Is there, however, a wholesome training rule?', it is shown that one who commits an offense does so either with a mind associated with the wholesome, or with a mind associated with the unwholesome, or with a mind associated with the indeterminate, but not that a wholesome offense also exists. For there is no such thing as a wholesome offense, as it is stated: 'An offense can be unwholesome or indeterminate, but there is no offense that is wholesome' (Pari. 303). The ten sense-sphere functional consciousnesses are the eight great functional consciousnesses together with the smile-producing and determining consciousnesses. The role of the two consciousnesses of direct knowledge in giving rise to offenses should be seen in relation to displays of psychic power, transformations, etc., for one who does not know the regulation. 'That which is committed with a wholesome mind' refers to the offense, taken up under the heading of a training rule, committed by one whose mind is associated with the wholesome. By this statement, however, it is shown that when the offense is called 'wholesome,' its wholesome nature is only conventional, not ultimate. For one who commits an offense with a wholesome mind incurs an indeterminate offense consisting of the aggregate of form, arising in the manner of transgressing a training rule, whether accompanied by communicative or non-communicative action. As for 'by the others, the other,' this means that what is committed by other minds—the unwholesome or the indeterminate—is the other, that is, unwholesome or indeterminate. This is said to show that one who commits an offense does so either with a mind associated with the unwholesome or with the wholesome or indeterminate. Even so, regarding all the training rules, some involve only the unwholesome mind; some, by way of the wholesome and indeterminate, involve two kinds of mind; and some, by way of all, involve three kinds of mind. This is the only classification to be understood, and no other.

Tivedanaṃ dvivedanaṃ ekavedananti idañca yathāvuttavedanāvaseneva labbhati, nāññathāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Nipajjitvā nirodhaṃ samāpannassa sahaseyyavasena tadākārappavattarūpakkhandhasseva āpattibhāvato “atthi avedana”ntipi vattabbametaṃ, kadāci karahaci yadicchakaṃ sambhavatīti aggahetvā yebhuyyavasena labbhamānaṃyeva gahetvā vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

Regarding 'threefold feeling, twofold feeling, and one feeling,' it should be understood that this too is obtained only by way of the aforementioned feeling, and not otherwise. For one who, having lain down, has attained cessation, because the very form-aggregate that proceeds in that manner is in a state of offense by way of sharing a bed, it should also be said, 'There is non-feeling.' This occurs only sometimes, somewhere, spontaneously; not taking it thus, it should be known that this was stated having taken only that which is obtained in the majority of cases.

Idāni yathāvuttasamuṭṭhānādīni imasmiṃ saṃvaṇṇiyamānasikkhāpade vibhajitvā dassento “imaṃ pakiṇṇakaṃ viditvā”tiādimāha. Tattha viditvāti imassa “veditabba”nti iminā aparakālakiriyāvacanena sambandho veditabbo. Kiriyasamuṭṭhānanti idaṃ yebhuyyavasena vuttaṃ parūpakkame sati sādiyantassa akiriyasamuṭṭhānabhāvato. “Manodvāre āpatti nāma natthīti idampi bāhullavaseneva vutta”nti vadanti. Cittaṃ panettha aṅgamattaṃ hotīti paṭhamapārājikaṃ kāyacittato samuṭṭhātīti cittamettha āpattiyā aṅgameva hoti. Na tassa vasena kammabhāvo labbhatīti viññattijanakavasena [M 2.0099] kāyadvāre pavattattā tassa cittassa vasena imassa sikkhāpadassa manokammabhāvo na labbhatīti attho. Sikkhāpadassa heṭṭhā vuttanayena paññattibhāvato “sabbañcetaṃ āpattiyaṃ yujjatī”ti vuttaṃ. Na hi yathāvuttasamuṭṭhānādi paññattiyaṃ yujjati.

Now, while showing the aforementioned origins and so on by analyzing them in this training rule that is being commented upon, he said, 'Having known this miscellaneous section,' and so on. Therein, the connection of this 'viditvā' with 'veditabbaṃ', this word of a later action, should be known. This 'arising from action' is stated by way of the majority, because for one who consents when there is an assault by another, it is a state of arising from non-action. They say, 'This too, "There is no such thing as an offense at the mind-door," is stated only by way of the general case.' Herein, the mind is only a factor. Thus, the first pārājika arises from the body and mind; therefore, the mind here is only a factor of the offense. The state of being a kamma is not obtained by means of it. The meaning is: because it occurs at the body-door by way of generating communication, the state of being a mental kamma for this training rule is not obtained by means of that mind. Because it is a state of communication in the manner stated below this training rule, it was said, 'And all this is suitable in an offense.' For the aforementioned origins and so on are not suitable in a prescription.

Pakiṇṇakakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition of miscellaneous topics is completed.

Vinītavatthuvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Adjudicated Cases

Idaṃ kinti kathetukamyatāya pucchati. Vinītāni vinicchitāni vatthūni vinītavatthūni. Tāni hi “āpattiṃ tvaṃ bhikkhu āpanno pārājikaṃ. Anāpatti bhikkhu pārājikassa, āpatti saṅghādisesassa. Anāpatti bhikkhu asādiyantassā”tiādinā bhagavatāyeva vinicchitāni[V 2.0088]. Tenāha “bhagavatā sayaṃ vinicchitāna”nti. Uddānagāthāti uddesagāthā, saṅgahagāthāti vuttaṃ hoti. Vatthugāthāti “tena kho pana samayena aññataro bhikkhū”tiādikā nidānavatthudīpikā vinītavatthupāḷiyeva tesaṃ tesaṃ vatthūnaṃ ganthanato “vatthugāthā”ti vuttā, na chandovicitilakkhaṇena. Gāthānaṃ vatthu vatthugāthāti evaṃ vā ettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Etthāti vinītavatthūsu. Dutiyādīnanti dutiyapārājikādīnaṃ. Dutiyādīni vinicchinitabbānīti yojetabbaṃ. Sippikānanti cittakārādisippikānaṃ. Yaṃ passitvā passitvā cittakārādayo cittakammādīni uggaṇhantā karonti, taṃ “paṭicchannakarūpa”nti vuccati.

Why this? He asks out of a desire to speak. Cases that are disciplined and decided are Adjudicated Cases. For they were decided by the Blessed One himself, with statements such as: 'You, monk, have committed a Pārājika offense.' 'No Pārājika offense for the monk, but a Saṅghādisesa offense.' 'No offense for the monk who does not consent.' Therefore, he said, 'decided by the Blessed One himself.' `Uddānagāthā` means summary verses, compilation verses; this is what is meant. `Vatthugāthā`: the Pāḷi of the Adjudicated Cases itself, which is the elucidator of the origin-story, such as 'At that time, a certain monk...', is called 'case verses' because it strings together those various cases, not because of the characteristic of metrical analysis. Or, the meaning here should be seen thus: the case of the verses is `vatthugāthā`. 'Here' means in the Adjudicated Cases. 'Of the second, etc.' means of the second Pārājika, etc. It should be connected as 'the second, etc., are to be decided.' 'Of artisans' means of artisans such as painters, etc. That which painters and others, having seen again and again, learn and make, such as the work of painting, etc., is called a 'hidden-hand form'.

67. Purimāni dve vatthūnīti makkaṭivatthuṃ vajjiputtakavatthuñca. Tāni pana kiñcāpi anupaññattiyaṃ āgatāneva, tathāpi bhagavatā sayaṃ vinicchitavatthubhāvato adinnādānādīsu anupaññattiyaṃ āgatāni rajakādivatthūni viya puna vinītavatthūsu pakkhittāni. Yadi evaṃ “tassa kukkuccaṃ ahosī”ti idaṃ virujjheyya, anupaññattiyañhi aññe bhikkhū disvā taṃ bhikkhuṃ codesunti? Saccametaṃ, tehi pana bhikkhūhi anupaññattiyaṃ vuttanayena codetvā “nanu, āvuso, tatheva taṃ hotī”ti vutte tassa kukkuccaṃ ahosīti gahetabbaṃ. “Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesī”ti idañca tehi bhikkhūhi anupaññattiyaṃ vuttanayena bhagavato ārocite “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ bhikkhu makkaṭiyā methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevī”ti bhagavatā [M 2.0100] puṭṭho samāno “saccaṃ bhagavā”ti bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesīti gahetabbaṃ.

67. 'The first two cases' means the monkey case and the Vajjiputtaka case. But although those cases have indeed come in the supplementary regulation, nevertheless, because they are cases decided by the Blessed One himself, they were again placed in the Adjudicated Cases, like the cases of the washerman and others that have come in the supplementary regulation on theft and so on. If so, this statement, 'He had remorse,' would be contradicted; for in the supplementary regulation, other monks, having seen, accuse that monk. This is true. But it should be understood that he had remorse when, having been accused by those monks in the manner stated in the supplementary regulation, it was said, 'Surely, friend, it is just so?' And this, 'He reported this matter to the Blessed One,' should be understood thus: when the matter was reported to the Blessed One by those monks in the manner stated in the supplementary regulation, being asked by the Blessed One, 'Is it true, monk, that you engaged in sexual intercourse with a female monkey?', he reported this matter to the Blessed One, saying, 'It is true, Blessed One.'

Vajjiputtakavatthumhi pana sikkhaṃ appaccakkhāya dubbalyaṃ anāvikatvā methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevitvā vibbhamitvā ye ānandattheraṃ upasaṅkamitvā puna pabbajjaṃ upasampadañca yāciṃsu, te sandhāya “aṭṭhānametaṃ, ānanda, anavakāso, yaṃ tathāgato vajjīnaṃ vā vajjiputtakānaṃ vā kāraṇā sāvakānaṃ pārājikaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññattaṃ samūhaneyyā”tiādi anupaññattiyaṃ vuttaṃ. Ye pana avibbhamitvā saliṅge ṭhitāyeva uppannakukkuccā bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ, te sandhāya “āpattiṃ tumhe, bhikkhave, āpannā pārājika”nti idha vuttaṃ. Keci pana imaṃ adhippāyaṃ ajānantāva “aññameva makkaṭivatthu vajjiputtakavatthu ca vinītavatthūsu āgata”nti vadanti.

But in the Vajjiputtaka case, with reference to those who, without giving up the training and without revealing their weakness, engaged in sexual intercourse, disrobed, approached the Elder Ānanda, and again requested the going forth and higher ordination, it was said in the supplementary regulation: 'This is not the place, Ānanda, it is not the occasion, that the Tathāgata would remove a Pārājika training rule laid down for the disciples on account of the Vajjis or the Vajjiputtakas,' and so on. But with reference to those who, not having disrobed, while remaining in their own characteristic, with remorse having arisen, reported this matter to the Blessed One, it was said here: 'You, monks, have committed a Pārājika offense.' Some, however, not knowing this intention, say: 'It is another monkey case and another Vajjiputtaka case that have come in the Adjudicated Cases.'

Kuse ganthetvāti kusatiṇāni ganthetvā. Kesehīti manussakesehi. Taṃ rāganti kāyasaṃsaggarāgaṃ. Ñatvāti sayameva jānitvā. Yadi kāyasaṃsaggarāgena kataṃ, kāyasaṃsaggarāgasikkhāpadassa [V 2.0089] vinītavatthūsu avatvā idha kasmā vuttanti? Vuccate – kiñcāpi taṃ kāyasaṃsaggarāgena kataṃ, tassa pana bhikkhuno pārājikakkhette katupakkamattā “pārājikaṃ nu kho ahaṃ āpanno”ti pārājikavisayaṃ kukkuccaṃ ahosīti idha vuttaṃ. Tenevāha – “anāpatti bhikkhu pārājikassa, āpatti saṅghādisesassā”ti.

'Having bound with kusa' means having bound with kusa grass. 'With hair' means with human hair. 'That lust' means lust for bodily contact. 'Having known' means having known by oneself. If it was done with lust for bodily contact, why was it stated here, without being stated in the Adjudicated Cases of the training rule on bodily contact? It is said: although it was done with lust for bodily contact, it was stated here because that monk, due to his undertaking being made in the sphere of a Pārājika offense, had remorse concerning a Pārājika, thinking, 'Have I committed a Pārājika?' Therefore, He said: 'No Pārājika offense for the monk; there is a Saṅghādisesa offense.'

68. Atidassanīyāti divasampi passantānaṃ atittikaraṇato ativiya dassanayoggā. Vaṇṇapokkharatāyāti ettha pokkharatā vuccati sundarabhāvo, vaṇṇassa pokkharatā vaṇṇapokkharatā, tāya vaṇṇapokkharatāya, vaṇṇasampattiyāti attho. Porāṇā pana pokkharanti sarīraṃ vadanti, vaṇṇaṃ vaṇṇameva. Tesaṃ matena vaṇṇañca pokkharañca vaṇṇapokkharāni, tesaṃ bhāvo vaṇṇapokkharatā, tasmā vaṇṇapokkharatāyāti parisuddhena vaṇṇena ceva sarīrasaṇṭhānasampattiyā cāti attho. Atha vā vaṇṇasampannaṃ pokkharaṃ vaṇṇapokkharanti uttarapadalopo pubbapadassa daṭṭhabbo, tassa bhāvo vaṇṇapokkharatā, tāya vaṇṇapokkharatāya, vaṇṇasampannasarīratāyāti attho. Padhaṃsesīti abhibhavīti attho. Kathaṃ pana asādiyantī nisīdīti āha – “asaddhammādhippāyena…pe… khāṇukā viyā”ti.

68. “Exceedingly worthy of seeing” (atidassanīyā) means being extremely worthy of seeing because of causing non-satiation even for those who see her all day long. “By excellence of complexion” (vaṇṇapokkharatāya): Herein, pokkharatā is said to be a state of beauty; the state of beauty of the complexion is vaṇṇapokkharatā; by that excellence of complexion means by the perfection of complexion. The ancients, however, say pokkhara refers to the body, and vaṇṇa is simply complexion. According to their view, vaṇṇapokkharāni are complexion and body, and their state is vaṇṇapokkharatā. Therefore, “by excellence of complexion” means by a pure complexion and by the perfection of bodily form. Alternatively, vaṇṇapokkhara means a pokkhara endowed with complexion, where the elision of the latter word of the first member of the compound should be understood. Its state is vaṇṇapokkharatā; by that excellence of complexion means by the state of having a body endowed with complexion. “She dominates” (padhaṃsesi) means she overwhelms. But how does she sit without yielding? He said: “With an unrighteous intention… like a stake.”

Na [M 2.0101] limpatīti na allīyati. Kāmesūti vatthukāmakilesakāmesu. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā paduminipaṇṇe udakabindu na saṇṭhāti, yathā ca sūcimukhe sāsapo na santiṭṭhati, evameva yo abbhantare duvidhenapi kāmena na limpati, tasmiṃ kāmo na saṇṭhāti, tamahaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ vadāmīti.

“Does not cling” means does not adhere. “To sensual pleasures” means to both sensual pleasures as objects and sensual pleasures as defilements. This is said: just as a drop of water does not stand on a lotus leaf, and just as a mustard seed does not stay on the point of a needle, even so, one who is not stained internally by either kind of sensual pleasure—sensual pleasure does not stay in him. Such a one I call a brahmin.

69. Purisasaṇṭhānaṃ antarahitaṃ, itthisaṇṭhānaṃ uppannanti phalassa vināsuppādadassanena kāraṇassapi vināsuppādā vuttāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Purisindriye hi naṭṭhe purisasaṇṭhānaṃ antaradhāyati, itthindriye samuppanne itthisaṇṭhānaṃ pātubhavati. Tathā hi “yassa itthindriyaṃ uppajjati, tassa purisindriyaṃ uppajjatīti? No. Yassa vā pana purisindriyaṃ uppajjati, tassa itthindriyaṃ uppajjatīti? No”ti yamakapakaraṇe (yama. 3. indriyayamaka.188) vuttattā indriyadvayassa ekasmiṃ santāne sahapavattiyā asambhavato yasmiṃ khaṇe itthindriyaṃ pātubhavati, tato pubbe sattarasamacittato paṭṭhāya purisindriyaṃ nuppajjati. Tato pubbe uppannesu ca purisindriyesu sahajarūpehi saddhiṃ kamena niruddhesu tasmiṃ santāne itthindriyaṃ uppajjati. Tato purisasaṇṭhānākārena pavattesu kammajarūpesu sesarūpesu ca kañci kālaṃ pavattitvā niruddhesu itthisaṇṭhānākārena [V 2.0090] ca catujarūpasantatiyā pavattāya purisasaṇṭhānaṃ antarahitaṃ, itthisaṇṭhānaṃ pātubhūtanti vuccati. Itthiyā purisaliṅgapātubhāvepi ayameva nayo veditabbo.

69. By seeing the destruction and arising of the effect—namely, “the male form has disappeared, the female form has arisen”—it should be understood that the destruction and arising of the cause are also stated. For when the male faculty is destroyed, the male form disappears; when the female faculty arises, the female form manifests. Indeed, as it is stated in the Yamaka: “For whom the female faculty arises, does the male faculty arise? No. Or for whom the male faculty arises, does the female faculty arise? No.” Because the two faculties cannot coexist in the same continuum, at the moment the female faculty appears, the male faculty does not arise from the seventeenth mind-moment prior. And when the previously arisen male faculties have ceased in sequence along with their co-nascent material phenomena, the female faculty arises in that continuum. Thereafter, when the kamma-born and other material phenomena—which had proceeded for some time in the manner of the male form—have ceased, and when the continuity of the four kinds of material phenomena proceeds in the manner of the female form, it is said that the male form has disappeared and the female form has appeared. This same method should be understood also in the case of the manifestation of the male characteristic in a female.

Purisaliṅgaṃ uttamaṃ, itthiliṅgaṃ hīnanti iminā ca purisindriyassa uttamabhāvo, itthindriyassa ca hīnabhāvo vuttoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Na hi indriyassa hīnukkaṭṭhabhāvaṃ vinā tannissayassa liṅgassa hīnukkaṭṭhatā sambhavati. Purisaliṅgaṃ balavaakusalena antaradhāyatītiādināpi indriyasseva vināsuppādā vuttāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Indriye hi vinaṭṭhe uppanne ca tannissayassa liṅgassapi antaradhānaṃ patiṭṭhānañca sambhavati. Kathaṃ panettha purisaliṅgaṃ balavaakausalena antaradhāyati, itthiliṅgaṃ dubbalakusalena patiṭṭhātīti? Vuccate – paṭisandhiyaṃ tāva purisindriyuppādakaṃ anupahatasāmatthiyaṃ balavakusalakammaṃ yāvatāyukaṃ purisindriyameva uppādeti, antarā pana kenaci laddhapaccayena pāradārikattādinā balavaakusalakammena upahatasāmatthiyaṃ tadeva paṭisandhidāyakaṃ kusalakammaṃ dubbalībhūtaṃ purisindriyaṃ anuppādetvā attano sāmatthiyānurūpaṃ [M 2.0102] itthindriyaṃ pavatte uppādeti. Yadā pana paṭisandhidānakāleyeva kenaci laddhapaccayena pāradārikattādinā balavaakusalakammena purisindriyuppādanasāmatthiyaṃ upahataṃ hoti, tadā dubbalībhūtaṃ kusalakammaṃ purisindriyaṃ anuppādetvā paṭisandhiyaṃyeva itthindriyaṃ uppādeti. Tasmā “purisaliṅgaṃ balavaakusalena antaradhāyati, itthiliṅgaṃ dubbalakusalena patiṭṭhātī”ti vuccati.

The male characteristic is superior, the female characteristic is inferior—by this, it should be understood that the superior nature of the male faculty and the inferior nature of the female faculty are stated. For without the inferior or superior nature of the faculty, the inferiority or superiority of the characteristic that depends on it is not possible. By the statement beginning, “The male characteristic disappears due to strong unwholesome kamma,” it should also be understood that the destruction and arising of the faculty itself are stated. For when the faculty is destroyed or arises, the disappearance or establishment of the characteristic that depends on it also occurs. How, in this case, does the male characteristic disappear due to strong unwholesome kamma, while the female characteristic is established due to weak wholesome kamma? It is said: At rebirth-linking, a strong wholesome kamma capable of producing the male faculty, its capacity unimpaired, generates the male faculty for the entire lifespan. However, in the interim, its capacity having been impaired by some strong unwholesome kamma which has found a condition—such as adultery—that same wholesome kamma that gave rebirth, now weakened, fails to produce the male faculty and instead generates the female faculty during the course of life, in accordance with its own capacity. But if, at the very time of rebirth-linking, the capacity to produce the male faculty is impaired by some strong unwholesome kamma which has found a condition—such as adultery—then the weakened wholesome kamma fails to produce the male faculty and instead generates the female faculty right at rebirth. Therefore, it is said: “The male characteristic disappears due to strong unwholesome kamma, while the female characteristic is established due to weak wholesome kamma.”

Dubbalaakusalena antaradhāyatīti pāradārikattādibalavaakusalakammassa purisindriyuppādanavibandhakassa dubbalabhāve sati antaradhāyantaṃ itthiliṅgaṃ dubbalaakusalena antaradhāyatīti vuttaṃ. Tathā hi pāradārikattādinā balavaakusalakammena bāhitattā purisindriyuppādane asamatthaṃ paṭisandhiyaṃ itthiyā itthindriyuppādakaṃ dubbalakusalakammaṃ yadā pavattiyaṃ brahmacariyavāsamicchācārapaṭivirativasena purisattapatthanāvasena vā katupacitabalavakusalakammena āhitasāmatthiyaṃ purisindriyuppādane samatthaṃ itthindriyaṃ anuppādetvā attano sāmatthiyānurūpaṃ purisindriyaṃ uppādeti, tadā purisindriyuppādanavibandhakassa balavaakusalakammassa dubbalabhāve sati taṃ itthindriyaṃ antarahitanti “itthiliṅgaṃ antaradhāyantaṃ dubbalaakusalena antaradhāyatī”ti vuccati. Yathāvuttanayeneva balavatā kusalakammena purisindriyassa uppāditattā “purisaliṅgaṃ balavakusalena patiṭṭhātī”ti vuccati. Pubbe itthibhūtassa paṭisandhiyaṃ purisindriyuppādepi ayaṃ nayo veditabbo. Ubhayampi akusalena antaradhāyati, kusalena paṭilabbhatīti idaṃ sugatibhavaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, duggatiyaṃ pana ubhinnaṃ uppatti vināso ca akusalakammenevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

“It disappears through weak unwholesome kamma”: this is said because when the strong unwholesome kamma, such as adultery, which obstructs the arising of the male faculty, becomes weak, the disappearing female characteristic disappears through weak unwholesome kamma. For, at the time of rebirth-linking, the weak wholesome kamma that produces the female faculty in a woman is incapable of producing the male faculty, being suppressed by strong unwholesome kamma such as adultery. When, in the course of life, through strong wholesome kamma accumulated by living the holy life, abstaining from sexual misconduct, or by aspiring for manhood, it has acquired the capacity to produce the male faculty, it produces the male faculty in accordance with its own capacity, without producing the female faculty. At that time, when the strong unwholesome kamma that obstructs the arising of the male faculty has become weak, that female faculty has disappeared. Thus, it is said, “The disappearing female characteristic disappears through weak unwholesome kamma.” In the way just stated, because the male faculty has been produced by strong wholesome kamma, it is said, “The male characteristic is established by strong wholesome kamma.” This method should also be understood for one who was previously female, even regarding the production of the male faculty at rebirth-linking. This saying, “Both disappear through unwholesome kamma and are regained through wholesome kamma,” is said with reference to a fortunate existence. But in an unfortunate existence, it should be understood that the arising and destruction of both are solely through unwholesome kamma.

Ubhinnampi [V 2.0091] sahaseyyāpatti hotīti “yo pana bhikkhu mātugāmena sahaseyyaṃ kappeyya, pācittiyaṃ. Yā pana bhikkhunī purisena sahaseyyaṃ kappeyya, pācittiya”nti vuttattā ubhinnampi sahaseyyavasena pācittiyāpatti hoti. Dukkhīti cetodukkhasamaṅgitāya dukkhī. Dummanoti dosena duṭṭhamano, virūpamano vā domanassābhibhūtatāya. “Samassāsetabbo”ti vatvā samassāsetabbavidhiṃ dassento “hotu mā cintayitthā”tiādimāha. Anāvaṭoti avārito. Dhammoti pariyattipaṭipattipaṭivedhasaṅkhāto tividhopi saddhammo. Saggo ca maggo ca saggamaggo, saggassa [M 2.0103] vā maggo saggamaggo, saggūpapattisādhikā paṭipatti.
