Bhikkhuniyā saddhiṃ saṃvidhāya addhānagamane āpatti pariharitabbāti dassento “saṃvidahanaṃ parimocetvā”ti āha. “Mayaṃ asukaṃ nāma ṭhānaṃ gacchāmā”ti vatvā “ehi saddhiṃ gamissāmā”tiādinā asaṃvidahitattā anāpatti.

“For both, there is a pācittiya offense for lying down together.” Because it is said, “Whatever bhikkhu should lie down together with a woman, it is a pācittiya offense. Whatever bhikkhunī should lie down together with a man, it is a pācittiya offense,” for both there is a pācittiya offense by way of lying down together. “Distressed” (dukkhī) means distressed due to being endowed with mental suffering. “Displeased” (dummano) means having a mind corrupted by aversion, or a distorted mind due to being overwhelmed by displeasure. Having said, “He should be consoled” (samassāsetabbo), the commentary shows the method of consolation by saying, “Let it be, do not worry,” and so on. “Unobstructed” (anāvaṭo) means unprevented. “Dhamma” refers to the threefold true Dhamma: learning, practice, and penetration. “The path to heaven” (saggamaggo) means heaven and path; or the path for heaven; it is the practice conducive to rebirth in heaven. To show that the offense when traveling after making an arrangement with a bhikkhunī should be avoided, it is said, “Having rescinded the agreement” (saṃvidahanaṃ parimocetvā). Because, having said, “We are going to such and such a place,” one did not make an arrangement with words such as, “Come, let us go together,” there is no offense.

Bahigāmeti attano vasanagāmato bahi. Gāmantaranadīpārarattivippavāsagaṇaohīyanāpattīhi anāpattīti “dutiyikā bhikkhunī pakkantā vā hotī”tiādinā (pāci. 693) vuttaanāpattilakkhaṇehi saṃsandanato vuttaṃ. Ārādhikāti cittārādhane samatthā. Tā kopetvāti tā pariccajitvā. Lajjiniyo…pe… labbhatīti “saṅgahe asati ukkaṇṭhitvā vibbhameyyāpī”ti saṅgahavaseneva vuttaṃ. Alajjiniyo…pe… labbhatīti alajjibhāvato asantapakkhaṃ bhajantīti vuttaṃ. Aññātikā…pe… vaṭṭatīti idaṃ pana imissā āveṇikaṃ katvā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ anuññātanti vadanti. Bhikkhubhāvepīti bhikkhukālepi. Parisāvacaroti upajjhāyo ca ācariyo ca hutvā parisupaṭṭhāko. Aññassa santike nissayo gahetabboti tassa santike upasampannehi saddhivihārikehi aññassa ācariyassa santike nissayo gahetabbo. Taṃ nissāya vasantehipīti antevāsike sandhāya vadati. Upajjhā gahetabbāti upasampadatthaṃ upajjhā gahetabbā, aññassa santike upasampajjitabbanti vuttaṃ hoti.

“Outside the village” (bahigāme) means outside of one's own dwelling village. The ruling of “no offense” is stated by comparison with the characteristics of non-offenses mentioned in such passages as “the second bhikkhunī has departed or...” (Pāc. 693), which refer to cases of going between villages, crossing rivers, staying overnight, and being left behind by the group. “Capable of pleasing” (ārādhikā) means able to satisfy the mind. “Having angered them” (tā kopetvā) means having abandoned them. “The modest ones... it is obtained” (lajjiniyo…pe… labbhatīti)—this is said with reference to the benefit of support, as in “when there is no support, they may become discontented and wander about.” “The shameless ones... it is obtained” (alajjiniyo…pe… labbhatīti)—this means they associate with the unrestrained side because of their shamelessness. “For an unrelated one... it is permissible” (aññātikā…pe… vaṭṭatīti)—this, however, they say, is permitted in the commentary specifically for her. “Even in the state of a bhikkhu” (bhikkhubhāvepi) means even during the time as a bhikkhu. “One who attends the assembly” (parisāvacaro) means being a preceptor and teacher, and attending to the community. “Support should be sought from another” (aññassa santike nissayo gahetabbo)—this means that the co-residents ordained in his presence should seek support from another teacher. “Even by those dwelling in dependence on him” (taṃ nissāya vasantehipi)—this refers to the pupils. “A preceptor should be taken” (upajjhā gahetabbā)—this means a preceptor should be taken for the purpose of ordination; one should be ordained in the presence of another, is what is meant.

Vinayakammanti vikappanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Puna kātabbanti puna vikappetabbaṃ. Puna paṭiggahetvā sattāhaṃ vaṭṭatīti “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, bhikkhunīnaṃ sannidhi bhikkhūhi, bhikkhūnaṃ sannidhi bhikkhunīhi paṭiggāhāpetvā paribhuñjitu”nti (cūḷava. 421) vacanato puna paṭiggahitaṃ tadahu sāmisampi vaṭṭatīti dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Sattame divaseti idaṃ tañca nissaggiyaṃ anāpajjitvāva punapi sattāhaṃ paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭatīti dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Yasmā pana bhikkhuniyā nissaggiyaṃ bhikkhussa vaṭṭati, bhikkhussa nissaggiyaṃ bhikkhuniyā vaṭṭati, tasmā aṭṭhamepi divase liṅgaparivatte sati anissajjitvāva antosattāhe paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭatīti [V 2.0092] vadanti. Taṃ pakatatto rakkhatīti aparivattaliṅgo taṃ paṭiggahaṇavijahanato rakkhati, avibhattatāya paṭiggahaṇaṃ na vijahatīti adhippāyo. Sāmaṃ gahetvāna nikkhipeyyāti paṭiggahetvā sayaṃ nikkhipeyya. Paribhuñjantassa [M 2.0104] āpattīti liṅgaparivatte sati paṭiggahaṇavijahanato puna paṭiggahetvā paribhuñjantassa āpatti.

The term “vinayakamma” is said with reference to the act of assignment (vikappana). “It should be done again” means it should be assigned again. “Having received it again, it is permissible for seven days”—this is said to show that what has been received again, even if it is food for that day, is permissible, in accordance with the statement, “Monks, I allow bhikkhunīs to have things received from bhikkhus, and bhikkhus from bhikkhunīs, and to consume them” (Cūḷava. 421). “On the seventh day”—this is said to show that without incurring that offense of forfeiture (nissaggiya), it is permissible to consume it again for seven days. Moreover, since what is subject to forfeiture for a bhikkhunī is permissible for a bhikkhu, and what is subject to forfeiture for a bhikkhu is permissible for a bhikkhunī, some say that even on the eighth day, if a change of gender has occurred, it is permissible to consume it within seven days without having forfeited it. “One who remains in the original state protects it” (taṃ pakatatto rakkhati) means that one whose gender has not changed protects it from the relinquishment of the acceptance; the meaning is that the acceptance is not relinquished due to its undivided nature. “One should take it oneself and put it away” (sāmaṃ gahetvāna nikkhipeyyā) means one should receive it and then put it away oneself. “There is an offense for one who consumes it” (paribhuñjantassa āpatti) refers to an offense for one who, after a change of gender, consumes it after receiving it again due to the relinquishment of the prior acceptance.

“Hīnāyāvattanenāti pārājikaṃ āpannassa gihibhāvūpagamanenā”ti tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ, taṃ suvuttaṃ. Na hi pārājikaṃ anāpannassa sikkhaṃ appaccakkhāya “vibbhamissāmī”ti gihiliṅgaggahaṇamattena bhikkhubhāvo vinassati. Pārājikaṃ āpanno ca bhikkhuliṅge ṭhito yāva na paṭijānāti, tāva attheva tassa bhikkhubhāvo, na so anupasampannasaṅkhyaṃ gacchati. Tathā hi so saṃvāsaṃ sādiyantopi theyyasaṃvāsako na hoti, sahaseyyādiāpattiṃ na janeti, omasavāde pācittiyañca janeti. Teneva “asuddho hoti puggalo aññataraṃ pārājikaṃ dhammaṃ ajjhāpanno, tañce suddhadiṭṭhi samāno okāsaṃ kārāpetvā akkosādhippāyo vadeti, āpatti omasavādassā”ti (pārā. 389) omasavāde pācittiyaṃ vuttaṃ. Asati hi bhikkhubhāve dukkaṭaṃ bhaveyya, sati ca bhikkhubhāve paṭiggahitassa paṭiggahaṇavijahanaṃ nāma ayuttaṃ, tasmā sabbaso bhikkhubhāvassa abhāvato pārājikaṃ āpajjitvā gihiliṅgaggahaṇena gihibhāvūpagamanaṃ idha “hīnāyāvattana”nti adhippetaṃ, na pana pakatattassa gihiliṅgaggahaṇamattaṃ. Teneva katthaci sikkhāpaccakkhānena samānagatikattā hīnāyāvattanaṃ visuṃ na gaṇhanti. Sikkhāpaccakkhānena paṭiggahaṇavijahane vutte pārājikaṃ āpannassa gihibhāvūpagamanena sabbaso bhikkhubhāvassa abhāvato vattabbameva natthīti. Tathā hi buddhadattācariyena attano vinayavinicchaye –

“‘By reverting to a lower state’ means, as stated in all three knot-sections, ‘through one who has committed a pārājika offense adopting the state of a householder,’” and this is well said. For the state of a bhikkhu is not lost merely by adopting the appearance of a householder without renouncing the training and declaring, “I will disrobe,” by one who has not committed a pārājika offense. And one who has committed a pārājika offense, but remains in the appearance of a bhikkhu, retains his state as a bhikkhu until he confesses it; he does not fall into the category of one not ordained. Indeed, even if such a person consents to communion, he is not a fraudulent communicant, does not incur an offense for sharing a bed, etc., but does incur a pācittiya offense for abusive speech. Therefore, in the rule on abusive speech, a pācittiya offense is stated: “If a person who has committed any one of the pārājika offenses is impure, and one of pure view, having made an opportunity, speaks with the intention of abuse, there is an offense of abusive speech.” For if the state of a bhikkhu were absent, it would be a wrong-doing; but if the state of a bhikkhu exists, it is inappropriate to speak of relinquishing what has been accepted. Hence, here, ‘reverting to a lower state’ is intended to mean one who has committed a pārājika offense and then adopts the appearance of a householder, thereby completely losing the state of a bhikkhu—not merely adopting the appearance of a householder while still in his natural state. Therefore, in some cases, because it has the same outcome as renouncing the training, ‘reverting to a lower state’ is not treated separately. When the relinquishment of acceptance is mentioned through renouncing the training, there is nothing further to be said, since for one who has committed a pārājika offense, adopting the state of a householder means the complete absence of the state of a bhikkhu. Indeed, as the teacher Buddhadatta states in his Vinayavinicchaya:

“Acchedagāhanirapekkhanisaggato ca,

Sikkhāppahānamaraṇehi ca liṅgabhedā;

Dānena tassa ca parassa abhikkhukassa,

Sabbaṃ paṭiggahaṇameti vināsameva”nti. –

“By taking through force and by abandonment without regard,

And by abandoning the training, by death, and by change of gender;

And by giving to him and to another who is not a bhikkhu,

All acceptance comes to utter destruction.”

Ettakameva vuttaṃ. Tathā dhammasirittherenapi –

Only this much was said. Likewise, by the Elder Dhammasiri:

“Sikkhāmaraṇaliṅgehi, anapekkhavisaggato;

Acchedānupasampanna-dānā gāhopasammatī”ti. –

“By abandoning the training, by death, and by change of gender,

By abandonment without regard;

By taking through force, by giving to one not ordained, and by taking through trust, acceptance is stilled.”

Vuttaṃ[M 2.0105][V 2.0093]. Yadi ca pakatattassa gihiliṅgaggahaṇamattenapi paṭiggahaṇaṃ vijaheyya, tepi ācariyā visuṃ tampi vadeyyuṃ, na vuttañca, tato viññāyati “pakatattassa gihiliṅgaggahaṇamattaṃ idha hīnāyāvattananti nādhippeta”nti. Bhikkhuniyā pana sikkhāpaccakkhānassa abhāvato gihiliṅgaggahaṇamattenapi paṭiggahaṇaṃ vijahati.

It has been said. And if, by merely adopting the appearance of a householder, one in his natural state were to relinquish acceptance, those teachers would have stated that separately. And it was not stated. From that, it is understood that ‘the mere adopting of the appearance of a householder by one in his natural state is not intended here as reverting to a lower state.’ For a bhikkhunī, however, on account of the absence of renouncing the training, she relinquishes acceptance even by merely adopting the appearance of a householder.

Anapekkhavissajjanenāti aññassa adatvāva anatthikatāya “natthi iminā kammaṃ, na idāni naṃ paribhuñjissāmī”ti vatthūsu vā “puna paṭiggahetvā paribhuñjissāmī”ti paṭiggahaṇe vā anapekkhavissajjanena. Acchinditvā gāhenāti corādīhi acchinditvā gahaṇena.

‘By abandoning without regard’ means abandoning an object without giving it to another, due to not needing it, thinking, ‘There is no use for this; I will not use it now’; or abandoning the acceptance without any thought of accepting it again to use. ‘By taking after snatching’ means by its being taken after being snatched by thieves and so on.

Etthāti bhikkhuvihāre. Uparopakāti tena ropitā rukkhagacchā. Terasasu sammutīsūti bhattuddesakasenāsanapaññāpakabhaṇḍāgārikacīvarapaṭiggāhakacīvarabhājakayāgubhājakaphalabhājakakhajjabhājakaappamattakavissajjakasāṭiyaggāhāpakapattaggāhāpakaārāmikapesakasāmaṇerapesakasammutisaṅkhātāsu terasasu sammutīsu. Kāmaṃ purimikāya pacchimikāya ca senāsanaggāho paṭippassambhatiyeva, purimikāya pana senāsanaggāhe paṭippassaddhe pacchimikāya aññattha upagantuṃ sakkāti purimikāya senāsanaggāhapaṭippassaddhiṃ visuṃ dassetvā pacchimikāya senāsanaggāhe paṭippassaddhe na sakkā aññattha upagantunti tattha bhikkhūhi kattabbasaṅgahaṃ dassento “sace pacchimikāya senāsane gahite”tiādimāha.

‘Here’ means in the Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga. ‘Planted above’ refers to trees and bushes planted by him. ‘Among the thirteen appointments’ means among the thirteen appointments designated as: the meal distributor, the lodging assigner, the storeroom keeper, the robe receiver, the robe distributor, the gruel distributor, the fruit distributor, the snack distributor, the dispenser of trifles, the cloth-collecting officer, the bowl-collecting officer, the monastery attendant-directing officer, and the novice-directing officer. Indeed, the taking of a lodging for both the earlier and later periods is certainly relinquished. However, when the taking of a lodging for the earlier period is relinquished, it is possible to go elsewhere for the later period. Therefore, having shown the relinquishment of the taking of a lodging for the earlier period separately, he states that when the taking of a lodging for the later period is relinquished, it is not possible to go elsewhere. Therefore, showing the summary of what should be done by the bhikkhus there, he said, ‘If, in the later period, the lodging is taken,’ and so on.

Pakkhamānattameva dātabbanti bhikkhunīnaṃ paṭicchannāyapi āpattiyā mānattacārasseva anuññātattā. Puna pakkhamānattameva dātabbanti bhikkhukāle ciṇṇamānattābhāvato. Bhikkhunīhi abbhānakammaṃ kātabbanti bhikkhukāle ciṇṇamānattatāya bhikkhunīkālepi ciṇṇamānattā icceva saṅkhyaṃ gacchatīti katvā vuttaṃ. Sace akusalavipāke…pe… chārattaṃ mānattameva dātabbanti mānattaṃ carantassa liṅgaparivattādhikārattā vuttaṃ. Sace pana bhikkhukāle paṭicchannāya sādhāraṇāpattiyā parivasantassa asamādiṇṇaparivāsassa vā liṅgaṃ parivattati, tassa bhikkhunīkāle pakkhamānattaṃ carantassa akusalavipāke parikkhīṇe puna liṅge parivattite parivāsaṃ datvā parivutthaparivāsassa chārattaṃ mānattaṃ dātabbanti vadanti.

The half-month mānatta should be given, because for bhikkhunīs, even for a concealed offense, only the conduct of mānatta is permitted. Again, the half-month mānatta should be given, on account of mānatta not having been practiced during the time as a bhikkhu. The act of rehabilitation should be done by the bhikkhunīs: this is said having considered that because mānatta was practiced during the time as a bhikkhu, it is counted as having been practiced also during the time as a bhikkhunī. ‘If, as a result of unwholesome kamma… the six-night mānatta should be given’: this is said because it is a case of a change of gender for one practicing mānatta. But if, during the time as a bhikkhu, while undergoing probation for a concealed common offense—or for one whose probation was not undertaken—the gender changes, for that one, while practicing the half-month mānatta during the time as a bhikkhunī, when the result of unwholesome kamma is exhausted and the gender changes again, having given probation, for the one who has completed probation, the six-night mānatta should be given—so they say.

Sañcarittāpattīti [M 2.0106] sādhāraṇāpattidassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Parivāsadānaṃ natthīti bhikkhukāle appaṭicchannabhāvato. Bhikkhunīkāle pana ārocitāpi sādhāraṇāpatti sace bhikkhukāle anārocitā, paṭicchannāva hotīti vadanti. Bhikkhūhi mānatte adinneti aciṇṇamānattāya liṅgaparivatte [V 2.0094] sati. Bhikkhunībhāve ṭhitāyapi tā suppaṭippassaddhā evāti sambandho. Yā āpattiyo pubbe paṭippassaddhāti yā asādhāraṇāpattiyo pubbe bhikkhubhāve paṭippassaddhā. “Pārājikaṃ āpannassa liṅgaparivatte sati santānassa ekattā na puna so upasampadaṃ labhati, tathā vibbhantāpi bhikkhunī liṅgaparivatte sati puna upasampadaṃ na labhatī”ti vadanti.

The term 'offense of acting as a go-between' is stated to show a common offense. There is no granting of probation because it was not concealed during the time as a monk. However, they say that even if a common offense is confessed during the time as a nun, if it was not confessed during the time as a monk, it is indeed considered concealed. 'Mānatta is not given by the monks' means due to mānatta not having been practiced when the gender changed. Even when she is established as a nun, those offenses are fully calmed—this is the connection. 'The offenses that were previously settled' means those uncommon offenses that were settled in the previous state as a monk. They say, 'For one who has committed a pārājika, when the gender changes, due to the oneness of the continuity, he does not receive ordination again; likewise, a nun who has gone astray, when the gender changes, does not receive ordination again.'

71. “Anupādinnakesūti adhikārattā upādinnakepi eseva nayoti vutta”nti cūḷagaṇṭhipade majjhimagaṇṭhipade ca vuttaṃ, taṃ duvuttaṃ. Na hi upādinnakesu nimitte upakkamantassa dukkaṭaṃ dissati. Tathā hi upādinnakesu nimitte appavesetvā bahi upakkamantassa thullaccayaṃ vuttaṃ “na ca, bhikkhave, rattacittena aṅgajātaṃ chupitabbaṃ, yo chupeyya, āpatti thullaccayassā”ti (mahāva. 252) vuttattā. Ettha ca yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pubbe vicāritameva. Dukkaṭamevāti mocanarāgassa abhāvato. Tathevāti muccatu vā mā vāti imamatthaṃ atidissati.

71. It is stated in the Cūḷagaṇṭhipada and the Majjhimagaṇṭhipada, 'Regarding non-appropriated things, because it is the topic, this same method applies also to appropriated things'; but that statement is poorly stated. Indeed, for one who makes an attempt on the sign in appropriated things, an offense of wrong-doing is not seen. For it is stated that for one who makes an attempt externally without inserting it into the sign in appropriated things, there is a grave offense: 'Monks, one with a lustful mind should not touch the sexual organ; whoever should touch it, there is a grave offense' (Mahāvagga 252). And here, whatever should be said has all been previously considered in the commentary. 'It is only an offense of wrong-doing' is due to the absence of the lust for emission. 'Similarly' overlooks this meaning: 'whether it is emitted or not'.

Avisayoti asādiyanaṃ nāma evarūpe ṭhāne dukkaranti katvā vuttaṃ. Mātugāmassa vacanaṃ gahetvāti “ahaṃ vāyamissāmi, tvaṃ mā vāyamī”tiādinā vuttavacanaṃ gahetvā. Ubhayavāyāmeneva āpattīti saññāya “tvaṃ mā vāyamī”ti vuttaṃ.

‘Not the domain’ is stated having considered that non-consent in such a situation is difficult. ‘Having taken the woman’s word’ means having taken the word spoken, such as, ‘I will make an effort, you do not make an effort.’ With the perception that the offense occurs only through the effort of both, it was said, ‘You do not make an effort.’

73. Vaṭṭakateti imassa atthaṃ dassento “vivaṭe”ti āha. “Pārājikabhayena ākāsagatameva katvā pavesanādīni karontassa sahasā tālukaṃ vā passaṃ vā aṅgajātaṃ phusati ce, dukkaṭameva methunarāgassa abhāvato”ti vadanti, upaparikkhitvā gahetabbo. Suphusitāti suṭṭhu pihitā. Antomukhe okāso natthīti dantānaṃ supihitabhāvato antomukhe pavesetuṃ okāso natthi. Uppāṭite pana oṭṭhamaṃse dantesuyeva upakkamantassa thullaccayanti pataṅgamukhamaṇḍūkassa mukhasaṇṭhāne [M 2.0107] viya vaṇasaṅkhepavasena thullaccayaṃ. “Methunarāgena itthiyā appavesento nimittena nimittaṃ chupati, thullaccaya”nti iminā vā lakkhaṇena samānattā idha thullaccayaṃ vuttaṃ. Bahi nikkhantadantajivhāsupi eseva nayo.

73. To explain the meaning of this term 'vaṭṭakate', he said 'vivaṭe'. They say, 'For one who, out of fear of a pārājika, having treated it as just being in space, is performing actions such as insertion, if the sexual organ suddenly touches the palate or the side, it is only an offense of wrong-doing, because of the absence of sexual lust.' This should be understood after examination. 'Suphusitā' means well closed. 'There is no space inside the mouth' means that because the teeth are well closed, there is no space to insert inside the mouth. However, if the flesh of the lip is torn open and one makes an attempt on the teeth themselves, it is a grave offense. Like the shape of the mouth of a grasshopper-mouthed frog, by way of a summary of the wound, it is a grave offense. Because of being similar to this characteristic: 'One with sexual lust, not inserting into a woman, touches sign with sign, it is a grave offense,' a grave offense is stated here. This same method applies also to teeth and a tongue that are protruding outside.

Amuccante thullaccayanti “ceteti upakkamati na muccati, āpatti thullaccayassā”ti (pārā. 262) vacanato. Nijjhāmataṇhikādīti ādi-saddena khuppipāsikādipetīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Allīyitumpi na sakkāti nijjhāmataṇhikānaṃ lomakūpehi samuṭṭhitaaggijālāhi niccaṃ pajjalitasarīratāya khuppipāsikādīnaṃ ativiya paṭikūlavirūpabībhacchaaṭṭhicammāvasiṭṭhaniccāturasarīratāya [V 2.0095] āmasitumpi na sakkā. Devatā viya sampattiṃ anubhontīti ettha yāsanti sāmivacanaṃ yāti paccattavacanena vipariṇāmetvā yojetabbaṃ “yā devatā viya sampattiṃ anubhontī”ti. Dassanādīsu dassanaṃ nāma bhikkhunā tāsaṃ dassanaṃ, gahaṇampi bhikkhunāva tāsaṃ aṅgapaccaṅgagahaṇaṃ. Āmasanādīni pana tāsaṃ kiccāni. Tattha āmasanaṃ nāma attano sarīrena bhikkhuno sarīrassa upari āmasanamattaṃ, phusanaṃ tato daḷhataraṃ katvā samphusanaṃ, ghaṭṭanaṃ tatopi daḷhataraṃ katvā sarīrena sarīrassa ghaṭṭanaṃ. Visaññaṃ katvāti yathā so katampi upakkamanaṃ na jānāti, evaṃ katvā. Yadipi āmasanādi tassā kiccaṃ, tathāpi teneva anāpattiṃ avatvā “taṃ puggalaṃ visaññaṃ katvā”ti vacanato akatavisañño jānitvā sādiyati ce, pārājikameva. Bhikkhuno pana dassanagahaṇesu sati asādiyanaṃ nāma na hotīti dassanagahaṇesu paññāyamānesu anāpatti na vuttā. Yadi pana paṭhamaṃ dassanagahaṇesu sati pacchā taṃ puggalaṃ visaññaṃ katvā āmasanādīni karontī attano manorathaṃ pūretvā gacchati, natthi pārājikaṃ.

‘When there is no emission, a grave offense’ is in accordance with the text: ‘He intends, he makes an effort, there is no emission; it is a grave offense.’ Regarding 'nijjhāmataṇhikādi', by the word 'ādi', the inclusion of hungry ghosts such as the 'khuppipāsikā' should be understood. ‘It is not possible even to cling to them’ means that because the bodies of the 'nijjhāmataṇhikā' are constantly blazing with flames of fire arisen from their hair-pores, and because the bodies of the 'khuppipāsikā' and others are extremely repulsive, ugly, disgusting, reduced to bone and skin, and perpetually sick, it is not possible even to touch them. Regarding ‘enjoying attainments like a deity,’ here the genitive plural 'yāsaṃ' should be transformed into the nominative singular 'yā' and connected as ‘she who enjoys attainments like a deity.’ Among ‘seeing, etc.,’ ‘seeing’ means the monk's seeing of them, and ‘grasping’ is the monk's grasping of their limbs. ‘Stroking, etc.,’ however, are their actions. Therein, ‘stroking’ means merely touching the monk's body with one's own body; ‘contact’ is making contact more firmly than that; and ‘rubbing’ is rubbing body against body, having done it even more firmly than that. ‘Having made unconscious’ means having done it in such a way that he does not know the attempt even when it is made. Even though stroking, etc., is her action, nevertheless, without stating ‘no offense’ on that account, in accordance with ‘having made that person unconscious,’ if one who has not been made unconscious knowingly consents, it is a pārājika indeed. For a monk, however, when there is seeing and grasping, there is no such thing as non-consent; therefore, when seeing and grasping are apparent, ‘no offense’ is not stated. If, however, there is first seeing and grasping, and afterwards, having made that person unconscious, she performs stroking, etc., fulfills her desire, and leaves, there is no pārājika.

Upahatakāyappasādoti anaṭṭhepi kāyappasāde kāyaviññāṇuppādane asamatthatāpādanavasena vātapittādīhi upahatakāyappasādo. Sevanacittavasena āpattīti yathā santhatanimittavasena upādinnaphassaṃ avindantassapi sevanacittavasena āpatti, evamidhāpi pittavātādinā upahatakāyappasādattā avediyantassapi sevanacittavasena āpatti.

'Impaired body sensitivity' means that even though the body sensitivity is not destroyed, it is impaired by wind, bile, etc., by way of bringing about the inability to produce body-consciousness. 'An offense occurs by way of the thought of indulgence' means: just as for one who does not experience appropriated contact by way of a prepared sign, there is an offense by way of the thought of indulgence, so too here, for one who does not feel it due to the body sensitivity being impaired by bile, wind, etc., there is an offense by way of the thought of indulgence.

Nanu [M 2.0108] ca chupitamattavatthusmiṃ “methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevissāmīti chupitamatte vippaṭisārī ahosī”ti vuttattā methunassa pubbapayoge dukkaṭena bhavitabbaṃ, atha kasmā “āpatti saṅghādisesassā”ti vuttanti imaṃ antolīnacodanaṃ manasikatvā taṃ pariharituṃ “yo methuna”ntiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha sīsanti maggena maggapaṭipādanaṃ. Tañhi payogānaṃ matthakasadisattā “sīsa”nti vuttaṃ tato paraṃ payogābhāvato. Dukkaṭe tiṭṭhantīti dukkaṭaṃ janenti. Dukkaṭañhi janentā hatthaggāhādayo payogā “dukkaṭe tiṭṭhantī”ti vuttā aññissā āpattiyā janakavasena appavattanato.

Should it not be that, in the matter of mere touching, since it was said, 'Thinking, "I will engage in sexual intercourse," he became remorseful upon the mere touch,' there should be a dukkaṭa offense in the preliminary effort of sexual intercourse? Then why was it said, 'It is an offense of saṅghādisesa'? Having considered this implied objection, in order to refute it, the passage beginning 'Whatever [monk engages in] sexual intercourse...' was introduced. Therein, 'head' (sīsa) means, by 'path', the accomplishment of the path. For it is called 'head' because it is like the head of the efforts, as there is no further effort beyond that. 'They stand in dukkaṭa' means they produce a dukkaṭa offense. Indeed, the efforts such as grasping the hand, etc., which produce a dukkaṭa offense, are said 'to stand in dukkaṭa' because they do not proceed by way of being a generator of another offense.

74. Jātipupphagumbānanti jātisumanagumbānaṃ. Ussannatāyāti bāhullatāya. Upacāreti āsannappadese. Tena vātupatthambhenāti “aṅgamaṅgāni vātupatthaddhāni hontī”ti evaṃ vuttavātupatthambhena. Iminā niddokkamanassa kāraṇaṃ vuttaṃ. Ekarasanti āvajjanādivīthicittehi abbokiṇṇaṃ.

74. 'Jātipupphagumbānaṃ' means thickets of jātisumana flowers. 'Ussannatāya' means due to profusion. 'Upacāre' means in a nearby place. By 'tena vātupatthambhena' is meant by the wind-stiffening thus stated: 'The major and minor limbs become stiffened by wind.' By this, the cause of falling asleep is stated. 'Ekarasa' means uninterrupted by the process-cognitions such as adverting and so on.

76. Saṅgāmasīsayodho [V 2.0096] bhikkhūti yasmā kilesārīhi anabhibhūto hutvā te parājesi, tasmā saṅgāmamukhe yodhasadiso bhikkhu.

76. 'Saṅgāmasīsayodho bhikkhu' (the monk who is a warrior at the head of the battle) means: because, being unconquered by the enemies which are the defilements, he vanquished them, therefore he is a monk like a warrior at the front of the battle.

77. Uppanne vatthusminti methunavatthusmiṃ uppanne. Parivattakadvāramevāti saṃvaraṇavivaraṇavasena ito cito ca parivattanayoggadvārameva. Rukkhasūcikaṇṭakadvāranti rukkhasūcidvāraṃ kaṇṭakadvārañca. “Rukkhasūcidvāraṃ kaṇṭakadvāra”micceva vā pāṭho. Yaṃ ubhosu passesu rukkhathambhe nikhaṇitvā tattha vijjhitvā majjhe dve tisso rukkhasūciyo pavesetvā karonti, taṃ rukkhasūcidvāraṃ. Yaṃ pavesananikkhamanakāle apanetvā thakanayoggaṃ, ekāya bahūhi vā kaṇṭakasākhāhi kataṃ, taṃ kaṇṭakadvāraṃ. Cakkalakayuttadvāranti heṭṭhā etaṃ cakkaṃ yojetvā kataṃ mahādvāraṃ, yaṃ na sakkā ekena saṃvarituṃ vivarituñca. Gopphetvāti rajjūhi ganthetvā. Ekaṃ dussasāṇidvāramevāti ettha kilañjasāṇidvārampi saṅgahaṃ gacchati.

77. 'Uppanne vatthusmiṃ' means when the matter of sexual intercourse has arisen. 'Parivattakadvārameva' is just a door suitable for turning from one side to the other by means of closing and opening. 'Rukkhasūcikaṇṭakadvāraṃ' means the wooden-bolt door and the thorn door. Or the reading is just 'rukkhasūcidvāraṃ kaṇṭakadvāraṃ'. The door which they make by setting up wooden posts on both sides, piercing them, and inserting two or three wooden bolts in the middle, that is the wooden-bolt door. The door which is made with one or many thorny branches, suitable for blocking and removed at the time of entering and exiting, that is the thorn door. 'Cakkalakayuttadvāraṃ' is a great door made by fitting a wheel below, which cannot be closed and opened by one person. 'Gopphetvā' means having tied with ropes. In 'a single door of cloth or hemp' (dussasāṇidvārameva), a door of matting or hemp (kilañjasāṇidvāra) is also included.

Yattha dvāraṃ saṃvaritvā nipajjituṃ na sakkā hoti, tattha kattabbavidhiṃ dassetuṃ “sace bahūnaṃ vaḷañjanaṭṭhānaṃ hotī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Bahūnaṃ avaḷañjanaṭṭhānepi ekaṃ āpucchitvā nipajjituṃ vaṭṭatiyeva. Atha bhikkhū…pe… nisinnā hontīti idaṃ tattha bhikkhūnaṃ sannihitabhāvasandassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. “Nisinno [M 2.0109] vā pana hotu nipanno vā, yena kenaci iriyāpathena samannāgato sace tattha sannihito hoti, ābhogaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Keci pana “nisinnā hontīti vacanato sace nipannā honti, ābhogaṃ kātuṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti, taṃ na sundaraṃ. Yadi hi “nisinnā hontī”ti vacanato nipanne ābhogaṃ kātuṃ na vaṭṭati, ṭhitepi caṅkamantepi ābhogaṃ kātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Na hi nisinnavacanaṃ nipannaṃyeva nivatteti, tasmā “nisinnā hontī”ti idaṃ tattha tesaṃ atthitāmattasandassanatthaṃ, na sesairiyāpathasamaṅgitānivattanatthaṃ. Evaṃ santepi nipajjitvā niddāyanto asantapakkhe ṭhitattā ābhogāraho na hotīti amhākaṃ khanti. Asantapakkhe ṭhitattāyeva hi raho nisajjāya nipajjitvā niddāyanto anāpattiṃ na karotīti vuttaṃ. Dvārasaṃvaraṇaṃ nāma bhikkhunīādīnaṃ pavesananivāraṇatthanti āha – “bhikkhuniṃ vā mātugāmaṃ vā āpucchituṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti. “Itthiubhatobyañjanakaṃ itthipaṇḍakañca āpucchituṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti. Mātugāmassa antogabbhe ṭhitabhāvaṃ jānitvāpi dvāre yathāvuttavidhiṃ katvā nipajjantassa anāpatti. Nisseṇiṃ āropetvāti uparitalaṃ āropetvā visaṅkharitvā bhūmiyaṃ pātetvā chinditvā vā nipajjitumpi vaṭṭati. Dvepi dvārāni jaggitabbānīti ettha sace ekasmiṃ dvāre kavāṭaṃ vā natthi, heṭṭhā vuttanayena saṃvarituṃ vā na sakkā, itaraṃ dvāraṃ asaṃvaritvāpi nipajjituṃ vaṭṭati.

Where it is not possible to lie down after having secured the door, to show the procedure to be followed there, the passage beginning, 'If it is a place of use for many...' was stated. Even in a place not used by many, it is indeed proper to lie down after having informed one person. Then, the statement 'the monks... are seated' was stated to show the fact of the monks' presence there. 'Whether one is seated or lying down, or endowed with any posture, if one is present there, it is proper to make an intimation'—this is stated in all three key passages. Some, however, say, 'Because of the phrase "are seated," if they are lying down, it is not proper to make an intimation'; that is not sound. For if, because of the phrase 'are seated,' it is not proper to make an intimation to one who is lying down, then it would not be proper to make an intimation to one who is standing or walking either. The word 'seated' does not exclude only 'lying down'; therefore, the phrase 'are seated' is merely to show their presence there, not to exclude those endowed with other postures. Even so, it is our opinion that one who lies down and is sleeping, being in the category of the unaware, is not fit for an intimation. Indeed, it is because he is in the category of the unaware that it is said that one who lies down and sleeps during a private meeting commits an offense. Securing the door is for the purpose of preventing the entry of nuns and others; thus he said: 'It is not proper to inform a nun or a woman.' They say: 'It is not proper to inform a female hermaphrodite or a female paṇḍaka.' Even knowing that a woman is inside the inner chamber, for one who lies down after having followed the aforesaid procedure at the door, there is no offense. 'Nisseṇiṃ āropetvā' (having placed the ladder): having placed it up to the upper floor, dismantled it, and dropped it to the ground, or having broken it, it is also proper to lie down. 'Both doors are to be guarded': in this regard, if one door has no panel, or it is not possible to secure it in the way stated below, it is proper to lie down even without securing the other door.

Bhikkhācārā [V 2.0097] paṭikkammāti bhikkhācārato nivattitvā. Dvārapālassāti dvārakoṭṭhake mahādvāre nisseṇimūle vā ṭhatvā dvārarakkhaṇakassa. Pacchimānaṃ bhāroti ekānubandhavasena āgacchante sandhāya vuttaṃ. Asaṃvutadvāre antogabbhe vāti yojetabbaṃ. Bahi vāti gabbhato bahi. Nipajjanakālepi…pe… vaṭṭatiyevāti ettha “dvārajagganakassa tadadhīnattā tadā tassa tattha sannihitāsannihitabhāvaṃ anupadhāretvāpi ābhogaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatiyevā”ti vadanti.

'Bhikkhācārā paṭikkamma' means having returned from the alms-round. 'Dvārapālassa' refers to the doorkeeper who guards the door, standing at the gate-tower, the great gate, or the foot of the ladder. 'The burden of the last ones' is said in reference to those coming in a continuous file. It should be connected as: 'inside the inner chamber with an unsecured door.' 'Bahi vā' means 'or outside the chamber.' Here, regarding 'Even at the time of lying down... it is indeed proper,' they say: 'Because the guarding of the door is his responsibility, it is indeed proper at that time to make an intimation even without investigating his presence or absence there.'

Yena kenaci parikkhitteti pākārena vā vatiyā vā yena kenaci parikkhitte. “Parikkhepassa uccato pamāṇaṃ sahaseyyappahonake vuttanayena veditabba”nti vadanti. Yadi pana ekasmiṃ padese parikkhepo vuttappamāṇato nīcataro hoti, vaṭṭati. Mahāpariveṇaṃ hotīti mahantaṃ [M 2.0110] aṅgaṇaṃ hoti. Mahābodhiyaṅgaṇalohapāsādayaṅgaṇasadisanti bahusañcāradassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ, na mahāparicchedadassanatthaṃ. Aruṇe uggate uṭṭhahati, anāpattīti suddhacittena nipannassa niddāyantasseva aruṇe uggateyeva niddāvaseneva anāpatti. Pabujjhitvā puna supati, āpattīti aruṇe uggate pabujjhitvā aruṇuggamanaṃ ajānitvāpi anuṭṭhahitvāva sayitasantānena sayantassa āpatti, purāruṇe pabujjhitvāpi ajānitvā sayitasantānena sayantassapi aruṇe uggate āpattiyeva. Yathāparicchedameva vuṭṭhātīti aruṇe uggateyeva uṭṭhahati. Tassa āpattīti asuddhacitteneva nipannattā niddāyantassapi aruṇe uggate divāpaṭisallānamūlikā āpatti. “Evaṃ nipajjanto anādariyadukkaṭāpi na muccatī”ti vuttattā asuddhacittena nipajjanto aruṇuggamanato puretaraṃ uṭṭhahantopi anuṭṭhahantopi nipajjanakāleyeva anādariyadukkaṭaṃ āpajjati, divāpaṭisallānamūlikaṃ pana dukkaṭaṃ aruṇe uggateyeva āpajjati.

“Enclosed by any means” means enclosed by any means, whether by a wall or a fence. They say, “The height of the enclosure should be understood according to the method stated in the case of what is sufficient for co-sleeping.” However, if in one place the enclosure is lower than the stated measure, it is permissible. “A great surrounding area” means a large courtyard. It is said to be like the courtyards of the Great Bodhi Tree and the Lohapāsāda to show a place of much traffic, not to indicate a large enclosure. “When dawn arises, one rises—there is no offense.” This means that for one who lies down with a pure mind, while he is sleeping, if dawn arises, by the power of sleep itself, there is no offense. “If one awakens and then sleeps again, there is an offense.” This means that when dawn arises, for one who awakens, even without knowing that dawn has arisen, and without getting up, continues to sleep with a continuity of sleep, there is an offense. Even for one who awakens before dawn, and without knowing it, continues to sleep with a continuity of sleep, when dawn arises, there is indeed an offense. “One gets up just at the boundary” means one gets up just as dawn arises. “There is an offense for him” means that because he lay down with an impure mind, even for one who is sleeping when dawn arises, there is an offense rooted in daytime seclusion. Because it is said, “Lying down in this way, one is not freed from the dukkaṭa offense of disrespect,” one who lies down with an impure mind incurs the dukkaṭa offense of disrespect at the very time of lying down, whether he gets up before dawn or does not get up. But the dukkaṭa offense rooted in daytime seclusion is incurred only when dawn arises.

Yaṃ panettha tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ “rattiṃ dvāraṃ saṃvaritvā nipanno sace aruṇuggamanavelāyaṃ dvāre vivaṭepi nipajjati, tassa āpatti akhette saṃvaritvā nipannattā. Aruṇuggamanavelāyaṃ vivaṭepi dvāre “nipajjissāmī”ti rattiṃ dvāraṃ saṃvaritvāpi nipannassa akhette pihitattā nipajjanakāle anādariyadukkaṭaṃ, aruṇe uggate nipajjanamūladukkaṭañca hoti. Rattiṃ pihitepi apihitepi dvāre nipannassa aruṇuggamanakkhaṇeyeva apihitadvāre pihite pihitadvāre ca puna vivaritvā pihite khette pihitattā anāpattī”ti, taṃ aṭṭhakathāya na sameti. Rattiṃ dvāraṃ asaṃvaritvā nipannasseva hi aruṇuggamane āpatti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ dassitā, tasmā khette vā pihitaṃ hotu akhette vā, saṃvaraṇamevettha pamāṇanti amhākaṃ khanti.

As for what is said here in all three knot-passages: “If one who has lain down after closing the door at night lies down even if the door is open at the time of dawn, there is an offense for him because he lay down having closed it in a non-region. For one who has lain down having also closed the door at night with the thought, ‘I will lie down,’ even if the door is open at the time of dawn, because it was closed in a non-region, there is a dukkaṭa of disrespect at the time of lying down, and when dawn arises, there is also a dukkaṭa rooted in lying down. For one who lies down at night with the door either closed or not closed, if at the very moment of dawn an unclosed door is closed, or a closed door is opened and then closed again, because it is closed in a region, there is no offense”—that statement does not agree with the commentary. Indeed, in the commentary, an offense at dawn is shown only for one who has lain down without closing the door at night. Therefore, whether it is closed in a region or in a non-region, the closing itself is the standard here—this is our preference.

Niddāvasena nipajjatīti niddābhibhūtatāya ekapassena nipajjati, evaṃ pana nipanno nipanno [V 2.0098] nāma na hotīti anāpatti vuttā. Apassāya supantassāti kaṭiyā piṭṭhivemajjhassa ca antare appamattakampi padesaṃ bhūmiṃ aphusāpetvā thambhādiṃ apassāya supantassa. Sahasāva vuṭṭhātīti pakkhalitvā patito viya sahasā vuṭṭhāti. Tattheva sayati na vuṭṭhātīti niddābhibhūtatāya [M 2.0111] supanto na vuṭṭhāti, na mucchāpareto. Teneva “avisayattā āpatti na dissatī”ti na vuttaṃ.

“He lies down by the power of sleep” means he lies down on one side because he is overcome by sleep. But one who has lain down in this way is not called “one who has lain down,” hence “no offense” is stated. “For one sleeping while leaning” means for one sleeping leaning on a pillar or the like, without letting even a small spot between the hip and the middle of the back touch the ground. “He gets up suddenly” means he gets up suddenly, as if having slipped and fallen. “He sleeps right there and does not get up” means, being overcome by sleep, he sleeps and does not get up; he is not overcome by a faint. For that very reason, it was not said, “Because it is beyond the range of control, an offense is not seen.”

Ekabhaṅgenāti ekassa passassa bhañjanena, heṭṭhā vuttanayena pāde bhūmito amocetvāva ekaṃ passaṃ bhañjitvā nāmetvā nipannoti vuttaṃ hoti. Mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana mahāpadumattherena vuttanti sambandho. Mucchitvā patitattā therena “avisayattā āpatti na dissatī”ti vuttaṃ. Ācariyā pana yathā yakkhagahitako bandhitvā nipajjāpito ca paravaso hoti, evaṃ aparavasattā mucchitvā patito kañci kālaṃ jānitvāpi nipajjatīti anāpattiṃ na vadanti. Yo ca yakkhagahitako, yo ca bandhitvā nipajjāpitoti imassa mahāaṭṭhakathāvādassa pacchimattā soyeva pamāṇato gahetabbo. Tathā ca vakkhati “sabbattha yo yo aṭṭhakathāvādo vā theravādo vā pacchā vuccati, sova pamāṇato daṭṭhabbo”ti (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.92). Yakkhagahitaggahaṇeneva cettha visaññībhūtopi saṅgahitoti veditabbaṃ. Ekabhaṅgena nipanno pana atthato anipannattā muccatiyevāti mahāaṭṭhakathāvādena so appaṭikkhittova hotīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Divā saṃvaritvā nipannassa kenaci vivaṭepi dvāre anāpatti nipajjanakāle saṃvaritvā nipannattā. Sace divā saṃvaritvā dvārasamīpe nipanno pacchā sayameva dvāraṃ vivarati, evampi vaṭṭati. Acittakā cāyaṃ āpatti kiriyā ca akiriyā ca.

“By one bend” means by the bending of one side; it means that, according to the method stated previously, without releasing the feet from the ground, having bent and inclined one side, he has lain down. But in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, it is connected with what was said by the Elder Mahāpaduma. Because he had fainted and fallen, it was said by the Elder, “Because it is beyond the range of control, an offense is not seen.” The teachers, however, do not state “no offense,” saying that just as one possessed by a yakkha or one who is bound and made to lie down is under another's control, so one who has fainted and fallen, not being under another's control, lies down even while being aware for some time. Both “one possessed by a yakkha” and “one who is bound and made to lie down”—because this is the latter part of this Mahā-aṭṭhakathā view, that very view should be taken as the standard. And so it will be said: “In all cases, whichever commentary view or Elders' view is stated later, that should be regarded as the standard.” It should be known that here, by the taking of “one possessed by a yakkha,” one who has become unconscious is also included. But one who has lain down with one bend is indeed freed because in reality he has not lain down. Thus it should be seen that this view is not rejected by the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā view. For one who has lain down having closed the door during the day, even if the door is opened by someone, there is no offense, because he lay down having closed it at the time of lying down. If, having closed it during the day, one lies down near the door and afterwards opens the door himself, even this is allowable. And this offense is unintentional, and it is both an action and a non-action.

78. “Apade padaṃ karonto viyā”ti vatvā puna tamevatthaṃ āvikaronto “ākāse padaṃ dassento viyā”ti āha. Etadagganti eso aggo. Yadidanti yo ayaṃ. Sesamettha uttānatthameva.

78. Having said, “As if making a track where there is no track,” then, making that same meaning clear, he said, “as if showing a track in the sky.” “This is the chief” means this is the chief. “Namely, this” means “which is this.” The rest here has an obvious meaning.

Vinītavatthuvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Vinītavatthu is concluded.

Tatridantiādi heṭṭhā vuttatthameva.

The passage beginning “Therein, this…” has the same meaning as was stated previously.

Iti samantapāsādikāya vinayaṭṭhakathāya sāratthadīpaniyaṃ

Thus, in the Sāratthadīpanī, the sub-commentary to the Vinaya Commentary, the Samantapāsādikā—

Paṭhamapārājikavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the first Pārājika is concluded.

2. Dutiyapārājikaṃ

2. The Second Pārājika

Adutiyena [M 2.0112][V 2.0099] jinena yaṃ dutiyaṃ pārājikaṃ pakāsitaṃ, tassa idāni yasmā saṃvaṇṇanākkamo patto, tasmā yaṃ suviññeyyaṃ, yañca pubbe pakāsitaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ vajjayitvā assa dutiyassa ayaṃ saṃvaṇṇanā hotīti sambandho.

The second pārājika, which was declared by the Peerless Conqueror—now, since the turn for its explanation has arrived, therefore, setting aside all that is easily understood and what was previously declared, this explanation is of this second one—such is the connection to be understood.

Dhaniyavatthuvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Account of Dhaniya

84. Rājagaheti ettha duggajanapadaṭṭhānavisesasampadādiyogato padhānabhāvena rājūhi gahitaṃ pariggahitanti rājagahanti āha “mandhātu…pe… vuccatī”ti. Tattha mahāgovindena mahāsattena pariggahitaṃ reṇunā pariggahitameva hotīti mahāgovindaggahaṇaṃ. Mahāgovindapaaggahitatākittanañhi tadā reṇunā magadharājena pariggahitabhāvūpalakkhaṇaṃ. Tassa hi so purohito. “Mahāgovindoti mahānubhāvo purātano eko magadharājā”ti keci. Pariggahitattāti rājadhānībhāvena pariggahitattā. Gayhatīti gaho, rājūnaṃ gahoti rājagahaṃ, nagarasaddāpekkhāya napuṃsakaniddeso. Aññepettha pakāreti “nagaramāpanena raññā kāritasabbagahattā rājagahaṃ, gijjhakūṭādīhi parikkhittattā pabbatarājehi parikkhittagehasadisantipi rājagahaṃ, sampannabhavanatāya rājamānaṃ gehantipi rājagahaṃ, suvihitārakkhatāya anatthāvahabhāvena upagatānaṃ paṭirājūnaṃ gahaṃ gehabhūtantipi rājagahaṃ, rājūhi disvā sammā patiṭṭhāpitattā tesaṃ gahaṃ gehabhūtantipi rājagahaṃ. Ārāmarāmaṇeyyakādīhi rājate, nivāsasukhatādinā sattehi mamattavasena gayhati pariggayhatīti vā rājagaha”nti edise pakāre. So padeso ṭhānavisesabhāvena uḷārasattaparibhogoti āha “taṃ paneta”ntiādi. Tattha buddhakāle cakkavattikāle cāti idaṃ yebhuyyavasena vuttaṃ. Tesanti yakkhānaṃ. Vasanavananti āpānabhūmibhūtaṃ upavanaṃ. Gijjhā ettha santīti gijjhaṃ, kūṭaṃ. Taṃ etassāti gijjhakūṭo. Gijjho viyāti vā gijjhaṃ, kūṭaṃ. Taṃ etassāti gijjhakūṭo, pabbato. Gijjhasadisakūṭoti gijjhakūṭoti [V 2.0100] vā majjhepadalopīsamāso yathā “sākapatthavo”ti, tasmiṃ gijjhakūṭe. Tenāha “gijjhā”tiādi.

84. Here, ‘Rājagaha’ is so called because it was seized and taken possession of primarily by kings due to its connection with the special quality of being a place in a region difficult to access, as it is said: ‘Mandhātu… etc. …is called.’ There, its being taken possession of by the Great Being Mahāgovinda means it was taken possession of by Reṇu; thus, the seizure by Mahāgovinda is mentioned. For the mention of its being taken possession of by Mahāgovinda is an indication of its being taken possession of by King Reṇu of Magadha at that time, for Mahāgovinda was his chaplain. Some say: ‘Mahāgovinda was a powerful ancient king of Magadha.’ ‘Taken possession of’ means taken possession of as a royal capital. ‘Is seized’ is ‘gaha’; ‘the seizure of kings’ is Rājagaha. The neuter gender is used with reference to the word ‘nagara’ (city). Other explanations are also given here: ‘It is called Rājagaha because all the houses were built by the king when laying out the city; also Rājagaha because, being surrounded by mountains like Gijjhakūṭa, it resembled a house encircled by mountain kings; also Rājagaha because, due to its splendid buildings, it was a residence esteemed by kings; also Rājagaha because, due to its excellent defenses, for rival kings who approached bringing harm, it became a place of seizure, like a prison; also Rājagaha because kings, upon seeing it, properly established it as their dwelling, and thus it became their possession, like a house.’ Or, ‘It is called Rājagaha because it shines (rājate) with its parks, groves, and so on, or because beings, due to the comfort of dwelling there, seize (gayhati) and take possession of (pariggayhati) it with a sense of attachment.’ Such are the explanations. That region, being a special place, is enjoyed by eminent beings, as it is said: ‘But that…’ etc. There, ‘during the time of the Buddha and the wheel-turning monarchs’—this is said generally. ‘Their’ refers to the yakkhas. ‘Vasanavana’ (dwelling forest) means a pleasure grove that serves as a drinking ground. Gijjhakūṭa is so called because vultures (gijjhā) are there (santi) on its peak (kūṭa). Or, its peak is like a vulture (gijjho viya), hence Gijjhakūṭa, the mountain. Or, it is a compound with the middle term elided from gijjhasadisakūṭo (a peak resembling a vulture), like ‘sākapatthavo.’ On that Gijjhakūṭa. Therefore, it is said: ‘Vultures…’ etc.

Tato [M 2.0113] paraṃ saṅghoti tiṇṇaṃ janānaṃ upari saṅgho catuvaggakaraṇīyādikammappattattā. Tasmiṃ pabbate sannipatitvā samāpattiyā vītināmentīti yathāphāsukaṭṭhāne piṇḍāya caritvā katabhattakiccā āgantvā cetiyagabbhe yamakamahādvāraṃ vivarantā viya taṃ pabbataṃ dvidhā katvā anto pavisitvā rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānāni māpetvā tattha samāpattiyā vītināmenti.

Then, ‘the Sangha’ means a Sangha of more than three individuals, having attained the qualification for acts requiring a quorum of four and so on. ‘Having assembled on that mountain, they spent their time in meditative attainment’ means that after going for alms in a comfortable location and completing their meal-duty, they returned and, as if opening the great twin door of a cetiya chamber, they split that mountain in two, entered inside, created places for staying during the night and day, and there they spent their time in meditative attainment.

Kadā panete tattha vasiṃsu? Atīte kira anuppanne tathāgate bārāṇasiṃ upanissāya ekasmiṃ gāmake ekā kuladhītā khettaṃ rakkhati, tassā khettakuṭiyā vīhayo bhajjantiyā tattha mahākarañjapupphappamāṇā mahantamahantā manoharā pañcasatamattā lājā jāyiṃsu. Sā te gahetvā mahati paduminipatte ṭhapesi. Tasmiñca samaye eko paccekasambuddho tassā anuggahatthaṃ avidūre khettapāḷiyā gacchati. Sā taṃ disvā pasannamānasā supupphitaṃ mahantaṃ ekaṃ padumaṃ gahetvā tattha lāje pakkhipitvā paccekabuddhaṃ upasaṅkamitvā pañcahi lājasatehi saddhiṃ taṃ padumapupphaṃ datvā pañcapatiṭṭhitena vanditvā “imassa, bhante, puññassa ānubhāvena ānubhāvasampanne pañcasataputte labheyya”nti pañca puttasatāni patthesi. Tasmiṃyeva khaṇe pañcasatā migaluddakā sambhatasambhārā paripakkapaccekabodhiñāṇā tasseva paccekabuddhassa madhuramaṃsaṃ datvā “etissā puttā bhaveyyāmā”ti patthayiṃsu. Atītāsu anekāsu jātīsu tassā puttabhāvena āgatattā tathā tesaṃ ahosi. Sā yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā devaloke nibbatti, tato cutā jātassare padumagabbhe nibbatti. Tameko tāpaso disvā paṭijaggi. Tassā padasā vicarantiyā paduddhāre paduddhāre bhūmito padumāni uṭṭhahanti. Eko vanacarako disvā bārāṇasirañño ārocesi. Rājā taṃ ānetvā aggamahesiṃ akāsi, tassā gabbho saṇṭhāti. Mahāpadumakumāro mātukucchiyaṃ vasi, sesā bahi nikkhantaṃ gabbhamalaṃ nissāya saṃsedajabhāvena nibbattā. “Opapātikabhāvenā”ti keci. Te vayappattā uyyāne padumassare kīḷantā ekekasmiṃ padume nisīditvā khayavayaṃ paṭṭhapetvā paccekabodhiñāṇaṃ nibbattayiṃsu. Ayaṃ tesaṃ byākaraṇagāthā ahosi –

But when did they live there? In the past, it is said, before the Tathāgata had arisen, near Bārāṇasī in a certain village, a daughter of a family was guarding a field. In her field hut, as rice grains were being parched, there appeared five hundred large, delightful grains of popped rice, each the size of a large karañja flower. She took them and placed them on a large lotus leaf. At that time, a Paccekabuddha, out of compassion for her, was passing by the edge of the field not far away. Seeing him, with a devout mind, she took a large, fully bloomed lotus, placed the popped rice inside it, approached the Paccekabuddha, and offered him the lotus flower along with the five hundred grains of popped rice. She paid homage with the five-point prostration and made this aspiration: ‘Venerable sir, by the power of this merit, may I obtain five hundred sons endowed with power and influence.’ She wished for five hundred sons. At that very moment, five hundred hunters, who had accumulated the necessary conditions and whose knowledge for Paccekabodhi was ripe, offered sweet meat to that same Paccekabuddha and made the aspiration: ‘May we be her sons.’ Because they had been her sons in many past lives, it happened just so for them. She lived out her lifespan and was reborn in the heavenly realm. After passing away from there, she was reborn in a lotus womb in the Jātassara lake. A certain ascetic saw her and looked after her. As she walked, lotuses sprang up from the ground at every lifting of her foot. A forest dweller saw this and reported it to the king of Bārāṇasī. The king brought her and made her his chief queen. She conceived. The Mahāpaduma prince dwelt in his mother's womb, while the others were born by way of moisture-birth, depending on the impurity of the womb that was expelled. Some say it was by way of spontaneous generation. When they came of age, while playing in a lotus lake in a park, each sat on a lotus, established contemplation on decay and vanishing, and brought forth the knowledge of Paccekabodhi. This was their verse of declaration:

“Saroruhaṃ [M 2.0114] padumapalāsamatrajaṃ, supupphitaṃ bhamaragaṇānuciṇṇaṃ;

Aniccatāyaṃ vayataṃ viditvā, eko care khaggavisāṇakappo”ti. –

‘A lotus sprung from the lake, with tender, dust-free petals, beautifully blooming, frequented by swarms of bees; having known this to be impermanent and subject to decay, one should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn.’

Tasmiṃ [V 2.0101] kāle te tattha vasiṃsu. Tadā cassa pabbatassa “isigilī”ti samaññā udapādi. Ime isayoti ime paccekabuddhaisī. Samā ñāyati etāyāti samaññā, nāmanti attho.

At that time, they lived there. Then the designation ‘Isigili’ arose for that mountain. ‘These are seers’ means these are Paccekabuddha seers. ‘Designation’ (samaññā) means ‘it is known by this,’ that is, a name.

Tiṇacchadanā kuṭiyo majjhepadalopīsamāsaṃ katvā, ekadese vā samudāyavohāravasena “tiṇakuṭiyo”ti vuttā. “Vassaṃ upagacchiṃsū”ti vacanato vassūpagamanārahā sadvārabandhā eva veditabbāti āha “tiṇacchadanā sadvārabandhā kuṭiyo”ti. Vassaṃ upagacchantenāti vassāvāsaṃ upagacchantena. Nālakapaṭipadanti “moneyyaṃ te upaññissa”ntiādinā (su. ni. 721) satthārā nālakattherassa desitaṃ puthujjanakālato pabhuti kilesacittaṃ anuppādetvā paṭipajjitabbaṃ moneyyapaṭipadaṃ. Taṃ pana paṭipadaṃ sutvā nālakatthero tīsu ṭhānesu appiccho ahosi dassane savane pucchāyāti. So hi desanāpariyosāne pasannacitto bhagavantaṃ vanditvā vanaṃ paviṭṭho. Puna “aho vatāhaṃ bhagavantaṃ passeyya”nti lolabhāvaṃ na janesi, ayamassa dassane appicchatā. Tathā “aho vatāhaṃ puna dhammadesanaṃ suṇeyya”nti lolabhāvaṃ na janesi, ayamassa savane appicchatā. Tathā “aho vatāhaṃ puna moneyyapaṭipadaṃ puccheyya”nti lolabhāvaṃ na janesi, ayamassa pucchāya appicchatā.

The huts with grass roofs, having formed a compound with the middle term omitted, are called “grass huts” in some places by way of collective designation. From the statement “they undertook the rains residence,” it should be understood that only those with secured doors are suitable for undertaking the rains residence. Thus it is said: “grass-roofed huts with secured doors.” By ‘entering the rains’ is meant undertaking the rains residence. The practice of Nālaka refers to the path of sagacity taught by the Teacher to the Elder Nālaka with the words, “I will teach you sagacity,” etc. (Snp 721), a path of sagacity to be practiced from the time of being an ordinary person without arousing a defiled mind. Having heard that practice, the Elder Nālaka became one of few desires in three respects: regarding seeing, hearing, and questioning. For at the end of the teaching, with a confident mind, he paid homage to the Blessed One and entered the forest. He did not again give rise to longing with the thought, “Oh, if only I could see the Blessed One again”—this was his having few desires regarding seeing. Similarly, he did not give rise to longing with the thought, “Oh, if only I could hear a Dhamma teaching again”—this was his having few desires regarding hearing. Likewise, he did not give rise to longing with the thought, “Oh, if only I could ask about the practice of sagacity again”—this was his having few desires regarding questioning.

So evaṃ appiccho samāno pabbatapādaṃ pavisitvā ekavanasaṇḍe dve divasāni na vasi, ekarukkhamūle dve divasāni na nisīdi, ekasmiṃ gāme dve divasāni piṇḍāya na pāvisi. Iti vanato vanaṃ, rukkhato rukkhaṃ, gāmato gāmaṃ āhiṇḍanto anurūpapaṭipadaṃ paṭipajjitvā aggaphale patiṭṭhāsi. Ekassa bhagavato kāle ekoyeva naṃ pūreti. Imañhi moneyyapaṭipadaṃ ukkaṭṭhaṃ katvā pūrento bhikkhu satteva māsāni jīvati, majjhimaṃ katvā pūrento satta vassāni, mudukaṃ katvā pūrento soḷasa vassāni. Ayaṃ pana thero ukkaṭṭhaṃ katvā pūresi, tasmā satta māse ṭhatvā attano [M 2.0115] āyusaṅkhārassa parikkhayaṃ ñatvā nahāyitvā nivāsetvā kāyabandhanaṃ bandhitvā diguṇaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ pārupitvā dasabalābhimukho pañcapatiṭṭhitena taṃ vanditvā añjaliṃ paggahetvā hiṅgulakapabbataṃ nissāya ṭhitakova anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbāyi. Tassa parinibbutabhāvaṃ ñatvā bhagavā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ tattha gantvā sarīrakiccaṃ katvā dhātuyo gāhāpetvā cetiyaṃ patiṭṭhāpetvā agamāsi. Evarūpaṃ paṭipadaṃ paṭipannenapi vassaṃ upagacchantena channe sadvārabandheyeva ṭhāne upagantabbaṃ. Appicchataṃ nissāyapi sikkhāpadassa anatikkamanīyattaṃ dassetuṃ “nālakapaṭipadaṃ paṭipannenapī”ti vuttaṃ.

Thus, being one of few desires, he entered the foot of a mountain. He did not stay for two days in a single forest grove, nor sit for two days at the foot of a single tree, nor enter the same village for alms for two days. Wandering thus from forest to forest, from tree to tree, and from village to village, he practiced a suitable practice and was established in the highest fruit. In the time of one Blessed One, only one person fulfills it. For a bhikkhu who fulfills this practice of sagacity, if he fulfills it in the highest degree, he lives for only seven months; if in the medium degree, seven years; if in the gentle degree, sixteen years. This elder, however, fulfilled it in the highest degree. Therefore, having stayed for seven months, knowing the exhaustion of his life-formation, he bathed, put on his lower robe, fastened his waistband, draped his double outer robe, and facing the Ten-Powered One, paid homage with the five-point prostration. Raising his joined palms, leaning against the Hiṅgulaka Mountain, while still standing he attained final Nibbāna with the Nibbāna-element without remainder. Knowing that he had attained final Nibbāna, the Blessed One went there with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, performed the funeral rites, had the relics collected, had a cetiya established, and then departed. Even by one practicing such a practice, the rains residence must be undertaken in a covered place with secured doors. To show that the training rule should not be transgressed even on account of having few desires, it was said, “even by one practicing the Nālaka path…”

Pañcannaṃ chadanānanti tiṇapaṇṇaiṭṭhakasilāsudhāsaṅkhātānaṃ pañcannaṃ chadanānaṃ. “Na, bhikkhave, asenāsanikena vassaṃ [V 2.0102] upagantabbanti (mahāva. 204) vacībhedaṃ katvā vassūpagamanaṃ sandhāyeva paṭikkhepo, na ālayakaraṇavasena upagamanaṃ sandhāyā”ti vadanti. Pāḷiyaṃ pana avisesattā aṭṭhakathāyañca “nālakapaṭipadaṃ paṭipannenapī”tiādinā aviseseneva daḷhaṃ katvā vuttattā asenāsanikassa nāvādiṃ vinā aññattha ālayo na vaṭṭatīti amhākaṃ khanti. Nāvāsatthavajesuyeva hi “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, nāvāyaṃ vassaṃ upagantu”ntiādinā (mahāva. 203) sati asati vā senāsane vassūpagamanassa visuṃ anuññātattā “na, bhikkhave, asenāsanikena vassaṃ upagantabba”nti ayaṃ paṭikkhepo tattha na labbhatīti asati senāsane ālayavasenapi nāvādīsu upagamanaṃ vuttaṃ. Anudhammatāti vattaṃ. Rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānādīnīti ādi-saddena vaccakuṭipassāvaṭṭhānādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti.

‘Of the five kinds of coverings’ refers to the five coverings reckoned as grass, leaves, bricks, stone, and plaster. Some say that the prohibition, “Bhikkhus, the rains residence should not be undertaken by one without a lodging” (Vin-m 2.204), by making a verbal distinction, refers only to undertaking the rains residence, not to taking up residence for the sake of shelter. However, because there is no distinction in the Pāḷi, and because it is stated firmly and without distinction in the commentary with the words, “even by one practicing the Nālaka path,” etc., our view is that for one without a lodging, a dwelling elsewhere, apart from a boat or the like, is not allowable. For only in the case of boats, caravans, and cowherds’ settlements is undertaking the rains residence separately permitted with the words, “I allow, bhikkhus, to undertake the rains residence in a boat,” etc. (Vin-m 2.203), whether there is a lodging or not. Therefore, this prohibition, “Bhikkhus, the rains residence should not be undertaken by one without a lodging,” does not apply there. Thus, when there is no lodging, undertaking residence in a boat or the like, even for the sake of shelter, is stated. ‘Conformity to the Dhamma’ is the practice. In ‘places for the night, places for the day, etc.,’ the word ‘etc.’ includes latrines, urinals, and the like.

Katikavattāni ca khandhakavattāni ca adhiṭṭhāyāti pariyattidhammo nāma tividhampi saddhammaṃ patiṭṭhāpeti, tasmā sakkaccaṃ uddisatha uddisāpetha, sajjhāyaṃ karotha, padhānaghare vasantānaṃ saṅghaṭṭanaṃ akatvā antovihāre nisīditvā uddisatha uddisāpetha, sajjhāyaṃ karotha, dhammassavanaṃ samiddhaṃ karotha, pabbājentā sodhetvā pabbājetha, sodhetvā upasampādetha, sodhetvā nissayaṃ detha. Ekopi hi kulaputto pabbajjañca upasampadañca labhitvā sakalaṃ sāsanaṃ patiṭṭhāpeti. Attano thāmena yattakāni sakkotha, tattakāni dhutaṅgāni samādiyatha, antovassaṃ nāmetaṃ sakaladivasaṃ rattiyā ca paṭhamapacchimayāmesu appamattehi bhavitabbaṃ, vīriyaṃ ārabhitabbaṃ[M 2.0116]. Porāṇakamahaātherāpi sabbapalibodhe chinditvā antovasse ekacariyavattaṃ pūrayiṃsu. Bhasse mattaṃ jānitvā dasavatthukakathaṃ dasaasubhadasānussatiaṭṭhatiṃsārammaṇakathaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Āgantukānaṃ vattaṃ kātuṃ, sattāhakaraṇīyena gatānaṃ apaloketvā dātuṃ vaṭṭati. Viggāhikapisuṇapharusavacanāni mā vadatha, divase divase sīlāni āvajjentā caturārakkhaṃ ahāpentā manasikārabahulā viharatha, cetiyaṃ vā bodhiṃ vā vandantena gandhamālaṃ vā pūjentena pattaṃ vā thavikāya pakkhipantena na kathetabbaṃ, antogāme manussehi saddhiṃ paccayasaṃyuttakathā vā visabhāgakathā vā na kathetabbā, rakkhitindriyehi bhavitabbaṃ, khandhakavattañca sekhiyavattañca pūretabbanti evamādinā katikavattāni khandhakavattāni ca adhiṭṭhahitvā.

Having undertaken the Katikavattas and the Khandhakavattas, it is said that the Dhamma of study, indeed, establishes the threefold Saddhamma. Therefore, recite carefully, have others recite, and engage in recitation. Those dwelling in the meditation hall should not cause disturbance; sitting inside the monastery, recite, have others recite, and engage in recitation. Make listening to the Dhamma peaceful. When giving the going-forth, having first investigated, give the going-forth. Having first investigated, give the higher ordination. Having first investigated, give dependence. For even a single clansman, having obtained both the going-forth and the higher ordination, can establish the entire Dispensation. According to your strength, undertake as many ascetic practices as you can. During the rains-residence, indeed, one should be diligent the entire day, and during the first and last watches of the night. Energy should be aroused. Even the ancient great elders, having cut off all hindrances, fulfilled the practice of solitary conduct during the rains-residence. Knowing the measure in speech, it is proper to engage in talk on the ten topics for discussion, the ten kinds of foulness, the ten recollections, and the thirty-eight meditation objects. It is proper to perform the duties for visitors and to give permission to those who go away on seven-day duties after having informed the community. Do not speak quarrelsome, slanderous, or harsh words. Day by day, reflecting on the precepts, not diminishing the four protections, dwell with frequent mindfulness. When paying respects to a shrine or a Bodhi tree, or offering incense or flowers, or placing a bowl in a bag, one should not converse. Inside the village, talk connected with requisites or unsuitable talk should not be engaged in with people. One should be guarded in one’s senses. The Khandhakavattas and the Sekhiyavattas should be fulfilled. Thus, having undertaken the Katikavattas and the Khandhakavattas in this manner…

“Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, vassaṃvuṭṭhānaṃ tīhi ṭhānehi pavāretu”nti (mahāva. 209) vuṭṭhavassānaṃ pavāraṇāya anuññātattā imassa suttassa vasena pavāraṇādivasassa aruṇuggamanato paṭṭhāya appavāritāpi “vuṭṭhavassā”ti vuccanti. Kiñcāpi “imaṃ temāsaṃ vassaṃ upemī”ti (mahāva. aṭṭha. 184) vacanato pavāraṇādivasassa temāsantogadhattā taṃ divasaṃ yāva na pavārenti[V 2.0103], tāva vassaṃ vasantā nāma honti, tathāpi ekadesena avuṭṭhampi taṃ divasaṃ vuṭṭhabhāgāpekkhāya vuṭṭhameva hotīti katvā evaṃ vuttaṃ katākatabhāgāpekkhāya samudāye pavattakatākatavohāro viya. Vippakatañhi yaṃ kiñci “katākata”nti vuccati. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, vassaṃvuṭṭhānaṃ kathinaṃ attharitu”nti (mahāva. 306) imassa pana suttassa vasena nippariyāyato mahāpavāraṇāya pavāritā pāṭipadadivasato paṭṭhāya “vuṭṭhavassā”ti vuccantīti dassetuṃ “mahāpavāraṇāya pavāritā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Pāṭipadadivasato paṭṭhāya hi vassānassa pacchime māse kathinatthāro anuññāto parivāre “kathinassa atthāramāso jānitabboti vassānassa pacchimo māso jānitabbo”ti (pari. 412) vuttattā. “Mahāpavāraṇāya pavāritā”ti idañca purimikāya vassūpagatānaṃ sabhāvadassanamattaṃ, kenaci antarāyena appavāritāpi “vuṭṭhavassā”icceva vuccanti.

“I allow, bhikkhus, those who have completed the rains-residence to invite criticism on three occasions.” Because those who have completed the rains-residence are permitted to hold the Pavāraṇā, from the dawn of the Pavāraṇā day onwards, even those who have not performed the Pavāraṇā are called “those who have completed the rains-residence” by the authority of this discourse. Although, based on the statement “I will spend these three months in rains-residence,” since the Pavāraṇā day is included within the three months, until they perform the Pavāraṇā, they are still considered to be observing the rains-residence. Nevertheless, even if it is not fully completed in one respect, that day is regarded as completed in anticipation of the completed portion; hence it is spoken of in this way, just as in a collective, the usage of “done and undone” prevails in anticipation of the done and undone portion. For anything incomplete is indeed called “done and undone.” “I allow, bhikkhus, those who have completed the rains-residence to spread the Kathina cloth.” By the authority of this discourse, those who have performed the Mahāpavāraṇā are unequivocally called “those who have completed the rains-residence” from the first day after Pavāraṇā onward. To indicate this, the phrase “those who have performed the Mahāpavāraṇā” and so on is stated. From the first day after Pavāraṇā onward, the spreading of the Kathina cloth is permitted in the last month of the rains season, as it is said in the Parivāra: “The month for spreading the Kathina cloth should be understood as the last month of the rains season.” And this phrase, “those who have performed the Mahāpavāraṇā,” merely reflects the actual state of those who entered the earlier rains-residence. Even if they have not performed the Pavāraṇā due to some obstacle, they are still called “those who have completed the rains-residence.”

“Āpucchitabbā”ti vatvā idāni āpucchanavidhiṃ dassento “sace imaṃ kuṭi”ntiādimāha. Paṭijagganakaṃ vā na labhatīti vihārapaccante kate [M 2.0117] paṭijagganakaṃ na labhati. Te pana bhikkhū janapadacārikaṃ pakkamiṃsūti sambandho. Addhānagamane cārikāvohāro sāsane niruḷho. Kiñcāpi ayaṃ cārikā nāma mahājanasaṅgahatthaṃ buddhānaṃyeva labbhati, buddhe upādāya pana ruḷhīsaddavasena sāvakānampi vuccati kilañjādīhi katabījanīnampi tālavaṇṭavohāro viya. Saṅgopetvāti ekasmiṃ padese rāsiṃ katvā. Idāni tameva saṅgopanavidhiṃ dassento “yathā ca ṭhapita”ntiādimāha. Na ovassīyatīti anovassakaṃ, kammani aka-saddo daṭṭhabbo. Yathā ca ṭhapitaṃ na ovassīyati na temīyatīti attho.

Having said, “One should ask for leave,” he now shows the method of asking for leave by saying, “If this hut,” and so on. “Or, he does not obtain a caretaker” means that if a dwelling is on the outskirts of the monastery, he does not obtain a caretaker. “But those bhikkhus set out on a wandering tour through the countryside”—this is the connection. The usage of “wandering tour” for traveling long distances is established in the Dispensation. Although this wandering tour, for the purpose of gathering the great populace, is indeed available only to the Buddhas, by extension from the Buddha, due to conventional usage, it is also said of disciples—just as the usage of “palm-leaf fan” applies even to fans made of reeds and the like. “Having stored away” means having made a pile in one place. Now, showing that very method of storing, he says, “And as it was placed,” and so on. “It is not rained upon” means a place not rained upon; the suffix `aka` should be understood in the sense of the object. The meaning is: and as it was placed, it is not rained upon, it is not moistened.

Anavayoti ettha vayoti hāni “āyavayo”tiādīsu viya. Natthi etassa attano sippe vayo ūnatāti avayoti āha “anūno paripuṇṇasippo”ti. Ācariyassa kammaṃ ācariyakanti āha “ācariyakamme”ti. Piṭṭhasaṅghāṭo dvārabāhā, kaṭṭhakammaṃ thambhādi. Telatambamattikāyāti telamissatambamattikāya.

Here, in `anavayo`, `vayo` means loss, as in `āyavayo` and similar terms. “There is no loss or deficiency for him in his own craft”; therefore, he said `avayo`, meaning “not deficient, fully skilled.” The teacher’s work is `ācariyakaṃ`; therefore, he said `ācariyakamme`. `Piṭṭhasaṅghāṭo` is a lintel; `dvārabāhā` is a door-frame; `kaṭṭhakammaṃ` is woodwork, such as pillars and so on. `Telatambamattikāyā` means with reddish clay mixed with oil.

85. Kuṭikāya karaṇabhāvanti kuṭiyā katabhāvaṃ. Saddasatthavidūhi kiṃ-saddayoge anāgatavacanassa icchitattā vuttaṃ “tassa lakkhaṇaṃ saddasatthato pariyesitabba”nti. Mettāpubbabhāganti mettājhānassa pubbabhāgabhūtaṃ sabbasattesu hitapharaṇamattaṃ. Kasmā panetaṃ vuttaṃ, nanu anuddayā-saddo karuṇāya pavattatīti? Saccametaṃ, ayaṃ pana anuddayāsaddo anurakkhaṇamatthaṃ antonītaṃ katvā pavattamāno mettāya karuṇāya ca pavattatīti idha mettāya pavattamāno [V 2.0104] vutto, tasmā suvuttametaṃ “etena mettāpubbabhāgaṃ dassetī”ti. Karuṇāpubbabhāganti karuṇājhānassa pubbabhāgabhūtaṃ sattesu anukampamattaṃ. Cikkhallaṃ mattikā, tassa maddanaṃ udakaṃ āsiñcitvā hatthādīhi parimaddanaṃ. Mettākaruṇānanti appanāppattamettākaruṇānaṃ. Kiñcāpi therena sañcicca khuddānukhuddakā pāṇā maraṇādhippāyena na byābādhitā, tathāpi karuṇāya abhāvena “evaṃ kate ime pāṇā vinassissantī”ti anupaparikkhitvā katattā theraṃ vigarahi. Janānaṃ samūho janatāti āha “pacchimo janasamūho”ti. Pātabyabhāvanti vināsetabbataṃ. Pāṇātipātaṃ karontānanti therena akatepi pāṇātipāte parehi sallakkhaṇākāraṃ dasseti. Imassa diṭṭhānugatinti imassa diṭṭhiyā anugamanaṃ. Ghaṃsitabbeti ghaṭṭayitabbe, vināsitabbeti attho. Evaṃ maññīti yathā therena kataṃ, evaṃ mā maññi. “Mā pacchimā [M 2.0118] janatā pāṇesu pātabyataṃ āpajjī”ti vacanato yo bhikkhu iṭṭhakapacanapattapacanakuṭikaraṇavihārakārāpanavihārasammajjanapaṭaggidānakūpapokkharaṇīkhaṇāpanādīsu yattha “khuddānukhuddakānaṃ pāṇānaṃ vihiṃsā bhavissatī”ti jānāti, tena tādise padese kappiyavacanaṃ vatvāpi na taṃ kammaṃ kāretabbanti dasseti.

85. “Kuṭikāya karaṇabhāvaṃ” means the state of a hut having been made. It is said by those skilled in grammar that because the future tense is desired in connection with the word 'kiṃ', “its characteristic should be sought from grammar.” “Mettāpubbabhāga” means the preliminary part of loving-kindness jhāna, which is merely the spreading of welfare to all beings. Why is this said? Does not the word 'anuddayā' apply to compassion? This is true. However, this word 'anuddayā', when used with the meaning of 'protection' included within it, applies to both loving-kindness and compassion. Here, it is said as applying to loving-kindness. Therefore, it is well said: “by this, it shows the preliminary part of loving-kindness.” “Karuṇāpubbabhāga” means the preliminary part of compassion jhāna, which is merely sympathy for beings. “Cikkhallaṃ” is clay; its kneading is the sprinkling of water and mixing it with hands and so on. “Mettākaruṇānaṃ” refers to loving-kindness and compassion that have reached absorption. Although the elder did not intentionally harm tiny creatures with the intent to kill, he was rebuked because he acted out of an absence of compassion, without considering, “If this is done, these creatures will perish.” A group of people is 'janatā', thus he said, “the later group of people.” “Pātabyabhāvaṃ” means the state of being destroyable. “Pāṇātipātaṃ karontānaṃ” shows a characteristic to be noted by others, even though the elder did not commit the destruction of life. “Imassa diṭṭhānugati” means following the view of this one. “Ghaṃsitabbe” means to be struck, that is, to be destroyed. “Evaṃ maññī” means: do not think as the elder did. Because of the statement, “May the later generation not fall into destructiveness towards beings,” it is shown that if a bhikkhu knows that in such activities as baking bricks, baking bowls, making a hut, causing a monastery to be made, sweeping a monastery, giving a firebrand, or causing wells and ponds to be dug, there will be harm to tiny creatures, he should not have that work done in such a place, even after speaking the words that make it allowable.

Tattha tattha vuttameva āpattinti pathavīkhaṇanabhūtagāmapātabyatādīsu vuttapācittiyādiāpattiṃ. Ādikammikattā anāpattīti kuṭikaraṇapaccayā anāpatti. Sikkhāpadaṃ atikkamitvāti “na ca, bhikkhave, sabbamattikāmayā kuṭikā kātabbā, yo kareyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti vuttasikkhāpadaṃ atikkamitvā. Yadi aññena kataṃ labhitvā vasantassa anāpatti siyā, na bhagavā taṃ kuṭikaṃ bhindāpeyyāti āha – “kataṃ labhitvā tattha vasantānampi dukkaṭamevā”ti. Yathā vā tathā vā missā hotūti heṭṭhā mattikā upari dabbasambhārātiādinā yena kenaci ākārena missā hotu. Giñjakāvasathasaṅkhepenāti ettha giñjakā vuccanti iṭṭhakā, giñjakāhi eva kato āvasatho giñjakāvasatho. Iṭṭhakāmayassa āvasathassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Taṃ kira āvasathaṃ yathā sudhāparikammena payojanaṃ natthi, evaṃ iṭṭhakāhi eva cinitvā chādetvā karonti, tulādaṇḍakavāṭaphalakāni pana dārumayāneva. Vikirantāti cuṇṇavicuṇṇaṃ karontā.

As for 'the offense already mentioned in various places', this refers to the pācittiya and other offenses stated in connection with digging the earth, destroying plant life, and so on. As for 'no offense for the first doer', this means there is no offense on account of making the hut. 'Having transgressed the training rule' refers to transgressing the training rule that states: “Bhikkhus, a hut should not be made entirely of clay. Whoever does so commits an offense of wrong-doing.” If there were no offense for one dwelling in a hut made by another after having received it, the Blessed One would not have had that hut demolished. Thus it is said: “Even for those dwelling there after receiving it when made, it is still an offense of wrong-doing.” 'Let it be mixed in one way or another' means let it be mixed in whatever manner, for example, with clay below and wood materials above. As for the summary regarding the 'giñjaka' dwelling: here, 'giñjaka' are called bricks. A dwelling made only of bricks is a 'giñjakāvasatha'. This is a term for a dwelling made of brick. It seems they make that dwelling by just stacking and covering with bricks, such that there is no need for plasterwork; but the beams, door leaves, and planks are made of wood. 'They scatter' means they reduce it to powder.

Kissāti kena kāraṇena. Vayakammampi atthīti dvārakavāṭādiabhisaṅkharaṇādīsu katavayakammampi atthi. Bhikkhūnaṃ akappiyattā eva titthiyavatānurūpattā titthiyadhajo. Mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttakāraṇesu attano adhippetakāraṇadvayaṃ patiṭṭhāpetvā aparānipi tattha vuttakāraṇāni dassento āha – “aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana aññānipi kāraṇāni vuttānī”tiādi. Tattha [V 2.0105] sattānuddayāyāti tādisāya kuṭikāya karaṇapaccayā vinassamānasattesu anuddayāya. Yasmā sabbamattikāmayā kuṭi sukarā bhindituṃ, tasmā tattha ṭhapitaṃ pattacīvarādi aguttaṃ hoti, corādīhi avaharituṃ sakkā. Tena vuttaṃ “pattacīvaraguttatthāyā”ti. Senāsanabāhullapaṭisedhanatthāyāti senāsanānaṃ bahubhāvanisedhanatthāya, tādisassa vā senāsanassa abhisaṅkharaṇe bhikkhūnaṃ uddesaparipucchādīni sesakammāni pariccajitvā niccabyāvaṭatānisedhanatthaṃ. Anupavajjoti dosaṃ āropetvā na vattabbo.

‘Kissa’ means ‘for what reason?’ ‘There is also work done’ means there is also work done in the construction of door leaves and so on. It is a ‘banner of sectarians’ because it is unsuitable for bhikkhus and resembles the practice of sectarians. Among the reasons given in the Great Commentary, having established two reasons of his own, and showing the other reasons mentioned there, he says: ‘Moreover, in the commentary, other reasons are given,’ and so on. Therein, ‘out of compassion for beings’ means out of compassion for beings who are being destroyed on account of the construction of such a hut. Because a hut made entirely of clay is easy to break into, bowls, robes, and so on, placed there are unguarded and can be stolen by thieves and others. For that reason, it is said, ‘for the protection of bowls and robes.’ ‘For the purpose of preventing a proliferation of lodgings’ means for the purpose of preventing lodgings from becoming many, or for preventing bhikkhus from being constantly busy with the construction of such a lodging, having abandoned their other duties like recitation and inquiry. ‘Not to be censured’ means one should not be spoken of after imputing a fault.

Pāḷimuttakavinicchayavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Pāḷimuttakavinicchaya

Pāḷimuttakavinicchayesu [M 2.0119] tañca kho…pe… na vaṇṇamaṭṭhatthāyāti idaṃ chattadaṇḍaggāhakasalākapañjaravinandhanaṃ sandhāyāti vadanti. Sabbatthāti chattadaṇḍe sabbattha. Āraggenāti nikhādanamukhena. Ghaṭakampi vāḷarūpampi bhinditvā dhāretabbanti sace tādisaṃ akappiyachattaṃ labhati, ghaṭakampi vāḷarūpampi bhinditvā tacchetvā dhāretabbaṃ. Suttakena vā daṇḍo veṭhetabboti yathā chattadaṇḍe lekhā na paññāyati, tathā veṭhetabbo. Daṇḍabundeti daṇḍamūle, chattadaṇḍassa heṭṭhimataleti attho. Chattamaṇḍalikanti chattassa anto khuddakamaṇḍalaṃ. Ukkiritvāti uṭṭhapetvā. Sā vaṭṭatīti yadipi rajjukehi na bandhanti, bandhituṃ pana yuttaṭṭhānattā vaṭṭati.

In the Pāḷimuttakavinicchayas, they say that the phrase ‘and that… not for the sake of mere adornment’ refers to the binding of the cage-like support that holds the umbrella staff. ‘Everywhere’ means everywhere on the umbrella staff. ‘With the tip’ means with the piercing end. ‘The joint and the animal figure should be broken off and carried’ means if one obtains such an unallowable umbrella, the joint and the animal figure should be broken off, trimmed, and carried. ‘Or the staff should be wrapped with a cord’ means it should be wrapped in such a way that the markings on the umbrella staff are not visible. ‘At the base of the staff’ means at the root of the staff, that is, the lower surface of the umbrella staff. ‘The small circle of the umbrella’ means the small circle inside the umbrella. ‘Having raised’ means having lifted up. ‘It is allowable’ means even if they do not tie it with cords, it is allowable because it is a suitable place for tying.

Nānāsuttakehīti nānāvaṇṇehi suttehi. Idañca tathā karontānaṃ karaṇappakāradassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ, ekavaṇṇasuttakenapi vuttappakārena sibbituṃ na vaṭṭatiyeva. Paṭṭamukheti paṭṭakoṭiyaṃ. Dvinnaṃ paṭṭānaṃ saṅghaṭṭitaṭṭhānaṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Pariyanteti cīvarapariyante. Cīvaraanuvātaṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Veṇinti varakasīsākārena sibbanaṃ. Saṅkhalikanti biḷālabandhanākārena sibbanaṃ. “Veṇiṃ saṅkhalika”nti cettha upayogavacanaṃ “karontī”ti karaṇakiriyāpekkhaṃ.
