Agghiyagayamuggarādīnīti ettha agghiyaṃ nāma cetiyasaṇṭhānena sibbanaṃ, mūle tanukaṃ agge mahantaṃ katvā gadākārena sibbanaṃ gayā, mūle ca agge ca ekasadisaṃ katvā muggarākārena sibbanaṃ muggaro. Kakkaṭakkhīni ukkirantīti gaṇṭhikapaṭṭapāsakapaṭṭānaṃ ante pāḷibaddhaṃ katvā kakkaṭakānaṃ akkhisaṇṭhānaṃ uṭṭhapenti, karontīti attho. “Koṇasuttapiḷakāti gaṇṭhikapāsakapaṭṭānaṃ koṇehi nīhaṭasuttānaṃ koṭiyo”ti tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Kathaṃ pana tā piḷakā duviññeyyarūpā kātabbāti? Koṇehi nīhaṭasuttānaṃ antesu ekavāraṃ gaṇṭhikakaraṇena vā puna [V 2.0106] nivattetvā sibbanena vā duviññeyyasabhāvaṃ katvā suttakoṭiyo rassaṃ katvā chinditabbā. Dhammasirittherena pana –

‘With various threads’ means with threads of different colors. This is said to show the manner of doing for those who act accordingly; even with a single-colored thread, it is not at all allowable to sew in the manner described. ‘At the mouth of the cloth’ means at the edge of the cloth. This is said with reference to the place where two edges of the cloth meet. ‘Along the border’ means along the edge of the robe. This is said with reference to the robe’s border. ‘Braiding’ means sewing in the shape of a varaka head. ‘Chain-stitching’ means sewing in the manner of a cat’s binding. In the phrase ‘veṇiṃ saṅkhalikaṃ’, this is the accusative case, used in relation to the action verb ‘karonti’ (they make). ‘Agghiya, gaya, and muggaro’ etc.: here, ‘agghiya’ refers to sewing in the shape of a cetiya; ‘gaya’ means sewing thin at the base and large at the top, in the shape of a club; and ‘muggaro’ means sewing evenly at both the base and top, in the shape of a mallet. ‘Making crab’s eyes’ means: having made a border-binding at the ends of the knotted cloths and looped cloths, they raise up the shape of a crab’s eye; this is the meaning of ‘they make’. ‘Corner-thread patches’ refers to the ends of the threads drawn from the corners of the knotted cloths and looped cloths. This is mentioned in all three knot locations. But how should those patches be made difficult to discern? By making a single knot at the ends of the threads drawn from the corners, or by turning back and sewing again, making their nature difficult to discern, then cutting the thread ends short. However, by the Elder Dhammasiri—

“Koṇasuttā ca piḷakā, duviññeyyāva kappare”ti –

‘Corner threads and patches should be made difficult to discern.’

Vuttaṃ. Tathā ācariyabuddhadattattherenapi –

It was said. Likewise, by the Elder Ācariya Buddhadatta too—

“Suttā ca piḷakā tattha, duviññeyyāva dīpitā”ti –

‘Threads and patches there are indeed explained as being difficult to discern.’

Vuttaṃ[M 2.0120]. Tasmā tesaṃ matena koṇasuttā ca piḷakā ca koṇasuttapiḷakāti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

It was said. Therefore, according to their opinion, the meaning here should be understood as ‘corner threads and patches’ (koṇasuttapiḷakā).

Maṇināti masāragallādipāsāṇena. Na ghaṭṭetabbanti na ghaṃsitabbaṃ, aṃsabaddhakakāyabandhanāni pana saṅkhādīhi ghaṃsituṃ vaṭṭati. Pāsakaṃ katvā bandhitabbanti rajanakāle bandhitabbaṃ, sesakāle mocetvā ṭhapetabbaṃ. Gaṇṭhiketi dantamayādigaṇṭhike. Piḷakāti binduṃ binduṃ katvā uṭṭhāpetabbapiḷakā.

‘With a gem’ means with a stone such as masāragalla. ‘Should not be rubbed’ means it should not be polished. However, it is allowable to polish shoulder straps and waistbands with shells and the like. ‘Having made a loop, it should be tied’ means it should be tied at the time of dyeing; at other times, it should be untied and put aside. ‘A knot’ refers to a knot made of ivory, etc. ‘A spot’ refers to a spot that should be raised up by making it dot by dot.

“Telavaṇṇoti samaṇasāruppavaṇṇaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, maṇivaṇṇaṃ pana pattaṃ aññena kataṃ labhitvā paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti. Pattamaṇḍaleti tipusīsādimaye pattamaṇḍale. “Na, bhikkhave, citrāni pattamaṇḍalāni dhāretabbāni rūpakākiṇṇāni bhittikammakatānī”ti (cūḷava. 253) vuttattā “bhittikammaṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, makaradantakaṃ chinditu”nti vacanato “makaradantakaṃ pana vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ.

‘Oil-colored’ is said with reference to a color suitable for an ascetic; but they say that if a bowl of gem color is obtained, made by another, it is allowable to use it. ‘Bowl stands’ refers to bowl stands made of tin, lead, and so on. Because it is said, ‘Bhikkhus, decorated bowl stands should not be used, those filled with figures or made with wall-painting work’ (Cūḷavagga 253), it is said, ‘wall-painting work is not allowable.’ From the statement, ‘I allow, bhikkhus, the cutting of a makaradantaka,’ it is said, ‘but a makaradantaka is allowable.’

Makaramukhanti makaramukhasaṇṭhānaṃ. Deḍḍhubhasīsanti udakasappasīsasaṇṭhānaṃ. Acchīnīti kuñjaracchisaṇṭhānāni. Rajjukakāyabandhanaṃ ekameva vaṭṭatīti rajjukaṃ bandhantena ekaguṇameva katvā bandhituṃ vaṭṭati, majjhe bhinditvā diguṇaṃ katvā bandhituṃ na vaṭṭati, diguṇaṃ pana akatvā ekarajjukameva satavārampi punappunaṃ āvijjitvā bandhituṃ vaṭṭati. Ekampi na vaṭṭatīti ekaguṇampi katvā bandhituṃ na vaṭṭati. Bahurajjuke…pe... vaṭṭatīti idaṃ kāyabandhanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, na dasā sandhāya. Īdisañhi kāyabandhanaṃ bandhituṃ vaṭṭati. Teneva ācariyabuddhadattattherena vuttaṃ –

‘Makara-face’ means shaped like a makara’s face. ‘Deḍḍhubha-head’ means shaped like a water snake’s head. ‘Eyes’ means shaped like an elephant’s eyes. ‘Only a single-rope waistband is allowable’ means: when tying the rope, it is allowable to tie it having made it single-ply; it is not allowable to tie it having made it double-ply by folding it in the middle. However, without making it double-ply, it is allowable to tie a single rope by twisting it again and again, even a hundred times. ‘Not even one is allowable’ means it is not allowable to tie it, even if made single-ply. ‘Many-roped… is allowable’—this is said with reference to the waistband, not with reference to the fringes. For it is allowable to wear such a waistband. Therefore it was said by the Elder Ācariya Buddhadatta:

“Ekarajjumayaṃ [V 2.0107] vuttaṃ, muninā kāyabandhanaṃ;

Pañcapāmaṅgasaṇṭhānaṃ, ekampi ca na vaṭṭati.

‘A waistband made of a single rope was declared by the Sage; shaped like a chisel handle, even one is not allowable.’

“Rajjuke ekato katvā, bahū ekāya rajjuyā;

Nirantarañhi veṭhetvā, kataṃ vaṭṭati bandhitu”nti.

‘Having gathered many ropes together, and having wrapped them continuously with a single rope, it is allowable to tie one so made.’

Murajaṃ pana kāyabandhanaṃ na vaṭṭati “na, bhikkhave, uccāvacāni kāyabandhanāni dhāretabbāni kalābukaṃ deḍḍhubhakaṃ murajaṃ maddavīṇaṃ, yo dhāreyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 278) vuttattā. Kiṃ pana bahurajjuke ekato katvā [M 2.0121] ekena nirantaraṃ veṭhetvā kataṃ murajasaṅkhyaṃ na gacchatīti? Āma na gacchati. Murajañhi nāma nānāvaṇṇehi suttehi murajavaṭṭisaṇṭhānaṃ veṭhetvā kataṃ. Keci pana “murajanti bahurajjuke ekato saṅkaḍḍhitvā ekāya rajjuyā paliveṭhetvā katarajjū”ti vadanti, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ. Yadi cetaṃ murajaṃ siyā, “bahurajjuke ekato katvā ekena nirantaraṃ veṭhetvā kataṃ bahurajjuka”nti na vattabbaṃ, “taṃ vaṭṭatī”ti idaṃ virujjheyya. Murajaṃ pana pāmaṅgasaṇṭhānañca dasāsu vaṭṭati “kāyabandhanassa dasā jīranti. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, murajaṃ maddavīṇa”nti (cūḷava. 278) vuttattā. Teneva vakkhati “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, murajaṃ maddavīṇanti idaṃ dasāsuyeva anuññāta”nti.

However, a muraja waistband is not permissible, for it is said (Cūḷavagga 278): 'Bhikkhus, various kinds of waistbands should not be worn: a kalābuka, a deḍḍhubhaka, a muraja, a maddavīṇā. Whoever wears one commits an offense of wrong-doing.' But does not one made by gathering many strands together and continuously wrapping them with one strand count as a muraja? Indeed, it does not. For a muraja is made by wrapping with threads of various colors into the shape of a drum-hoop. Some, however, say, 'A muraja refers to a multi-stranded cord gathered together and wrapped around with a single strand,' but this should not be accepted. If this were a muraja, the statement 'a many-roped one is made by gathering many ropes together and wrapping them continuously with one' should not have been said, and the statement 'that is allowable' would be contradicted. But a muraja and one shaped like a chisel handle are permissible for fringes, for it is said (Cūḷavagga 278): 'The fringes of a waistband wear out. I allow, bhikkhus, a muraja and a maddavīṇā.' Therefore, it will be said: 'The statement "I allow, bhikkhus, a muraja and a maddavīṇā" is a permission only for fringes.'

Kāyabandhanavidheti “kāyabandhanassa pavananto jīrati. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, vidha”nti vuttattā kāyabandhanassa pāsante dasāmūle tassa thirabhāvatthaṃ kattabbe dantavisāṇādimaye vidhe. “Aṭṭha maṅgalāni nāma saṅkho cakkaṃ puṇṇakumbho gayā sirīvaccho aṅkuso dhajaṃ sovatthika”nti vadanti. Paricchedalekhāmattanti ubhosu koṭīsu kātabbaparicchedarājimattaṃ. “Ujukamevā”ti vuttattā caturassādivaṅkagatikaṃ na vaṭṭati. “Chattadaṇḍadhammakaraṇaañjananāḷikā nānāvaṇṇalekhāpaakammakatā na vaṭṭantī”ti vadanti.

Concerning the vidha for a waistband: Since it is said, 'The hanging end of a waistband wears out. I allow, monks, a vidha,' a vidha made of ivory, horn, etc., should be made at the root of the waistband's fringe to ensure its firmness. They say, 'The eight auspicious symbols are: the conch, the wheel, the full pot, an elephant's forehead ornament, the śrīvatsa, the goad, the flag, and the swastika.' 'A mere defining line' means merely a defining line to be made at both ends. Since it is said, 'only straight,' anything crooked, such as a square, is not permissible. They say that umbrella handles, staffs, water strainers, ointment tubes, and those made with various colored drawings or elaborate work are not permissible.

Ārakaṇṭaketi potthakādiabhisaṅkharaṇatthaṃ kate dīghamukhasatthake. Vaṭṭamaṇikanti vaṭṭaṃ katvā aggakoṭiyaṃ uṭṭhāpetabbapubbuḷaṃ. Aññaṃ vā vaṇṇamaṭṭhanti iminā piḷakādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Maṇikanti ekāvaṭṭamaṇi. Piḷakanti sāsapamattikā muttarājisadisā bahuvaṭṭalekhā. “Imasmiṃ adhikāre avuttattā lekhaniyaṃ yaṃ kiñci vaṇṇamaṭṭhaṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti. Valitakanti majjhe valiṃ uṭṭhāpetvā. Maṇḍalaṃ hotīti uttarāraṇiyā pavesanatthaṃ āhaṭamaṇḍalaṃ hoti.

Ārakaṇṭaka means a long-mouthed knife made for embellishing palm-leaf manuscripts and so on. Vaṭṭamaṇika means a round protuberance to be raised at the tip after making it round. Or, by 'other vaṇṇamaṭṭha', it includes piḷaka and so on. Maṇika means a single round gem. Piḷaka means something the size of a mustard seed, resembling a line of urine, with many circular lines. They say, 'Since it is not stated in this context, any incised decoration is permissible.' Valitaka means having raised a crease in the middle. 'It becomes a circle' means it becomes a circle made for the purpose of inserting the upper fire-stick.

Kiñcāpi [V 2.0108] ettha dantakaṭṭhacchedanavāsiyeva vuttā, mahāvāsiyampi pana na vaṭṭatiyeva. Ujukameva bandhitunti sambandho. “Ubhosu vā passesu ekapassevā”ti vacanaseso. Kattarayaṭṭhikoṭiyaṃ kataayovalayānipi vaṭṭanti, yesaṃ aññamaññasaṅghaṭṭanena saddo niccharati.

Although here only an adze for cutting tooth-sticks is mentioned, even a large adze is not permissible. The connection is 'it should be tied straight only.' The remainder of the statement is 'on both sides or on one side.' Iron rings made at the tip of a knife-handle are also permissible, from whose mutual striking a sound is produced.

Āmaṇḍasāraketi [M 2.0122] āmalakehi katabhājane. Bhūmattharaṇeti cittakaṭasārakacittattharaṇādike parikammakatāya bhūmiyā attharitabbaattharaṇe. Pānīyaghaṭeti iminā kuṇḍikasarakepi saṅgaṇhāti. Bījaneti caturassabījane. Sabbaṃ…pe… vaṭṭatīti yathāvuttesu mañcapīṭhādīsu itthirūpaṃ vinā sabbaṃ mālākammalatākammādi vaṇṇamaṭṭhaṃ bhikkhuno vaṭṭati. Senāsane kiñci paṭisedhetabbaṃ natthi aññatra viruddhasenāsanāti etthāyamadhippāyo – senāsanaparikkhāresu paṭisedhetabbaṃ nāma kiñci natthi, viruddhasenāsanaṃ pana sayameva paṭikkhipitabbanti. Aññesanti sīmasāmino vuttā. Rājavallabhā paranikāyikāpi ekanikāyikāpi uposathapavāraṇānaṃ antarāyakarā alajjino rājakulūpagā vuccanti. Tesaṃ lajjiparisāti tesaṃ sīmasāmikānaṃ pakkhā hutvā anubalaṃ dātuṃ samatthā lajjiparisā. Sukatamevāti aññesaṃ santakepi attano sīmāya antovuttavidhinā kataṃ sukatameva.

Āmaṇḍasāraka means a vessel made of āmalaka fruit. Bhūmattharaṇa means a spread to be laid on a prepared ground, such as a decorated mat, a decorated spread, and so on. By 'water pitcher', it includes even small pitchers and pots. Bījana means a four-cornered fan. 'Everything... (etc.)... is permissible' means that in the aforementioned beds, benches, etc., everything except female figures, such as garland work, creeper designs, and other decorations, is permissible for a monk. 'There is nothing to reject regarding a dwelling except an incompatible dwelling.' Here, the intended meaning is this: regarding the requisites of a dwelling, there is nothing to reject, but an incompatible dwelling must be refused by oneself. By 'others' are meant the owners of the boundary. The king's favorites, whether from other sects or the same sect, who cause obstacles to the Uposatha and Pavāraṇa ceremonies, are shameless and are called 'those who frequent royal families.' 'Their modest assembly' means a modest assembly capable of lending support by siding with those boundary owners. 'It is well-done indeed' means that even if it belongs to others, what has been done according to the stated method within one's own boundary is indeed well-done.

Pāḷimuttakavinicchayavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Pāḷimuttaka-vinicchaya is completed.

86. Devena gahitadārūnīti raññā pariggahitadārūni, rañño santakānīti vuttaṃ hoti. Khaṇḍākhaṇḍaṃ karontoti khuddakaṃ mahantañca khaṇḍaṃ karonto.

86. 'Timber taken by a god' means timber appropriated by the king; that is to say, it is said to be the king's property. 'Cutting into pieces' means cutting into small and large pieces.

87. Kulabhogaissariyādīhi mahatī mattā pamāṇaṃ etassāti mahāmatto. Tenāha – “mahatiyā issariyamattāya samannāgato”ti.

87. 'Mahāmatta' means one for whom there is a great measure or standard in terms of family, wealth, lordship, and so on. Therefore it is said: 'endowed with a great measure of lordship.'

88. Avajjhāyantīti heṭṭhā katvā olokenti, cintenti vā. Tenāha “avajānantā”tiādi. Lāmakato vā cintentīti nihīnato cintenti. Kathentīti “kiṃ nāmetaṃ kiṃ nāmeta”nti aññamaññaṃ kathenti.

88. 'Avajjhāyanti' means they look down upon, or they think. Therefore it is said, 'disdaining,' and so on. Or 'they think of it as inferior' means they think of it as debased. 'They discuss' means they say to each other, 'What is this? What is this?'

Kathaṃ panettha “dārūnī”ti bahuvacanaṃ “adinna”nti ekavacanena saddhiṃ sambandhamupagacchatīti āha – “adinnaṃ ādiyissatīti ayaṃ ujjhāyanattho”tiādi. Ujjhāyanassa adinnādānavisayattā adinnādānaṃ ujjhāyanatthoti vuttaṃ. Satipi panettha gopakena dinnadārūnaṃ [V 2.0109] gahaṇe ujukaṃ avatvā lesena gahitattā thero “adinnaṃ ādiyī”ti veditabbo. Vacanabhedeti ekavacanabahuvacanānaṃ bhede.

How then does the plural 'logs' here relate to the singular 'what is not given'? It is said: 'He will take what is not given'—this is the meaning of censure, and so on. Because censure concerns the act of taking what is not given, it is said that taking what is not given is the meaning of censure. Moreover, in this case, even though the logs were given by the guard, because he did not speak straightforwardly but took them by a hint, the elder should be understood as 'he took what was not given.' 'Difference in number' means the difference between singular and plural forms.

Sabbāvantaṃ [M 2.0123] parisanti bhikkhubhikkhunīādisabbāvayavavantaṃ parisaṃ. Sabbā catuparisasaṅkhaātā pajā ettha atthīti sabbāvantā, parisā. Senā etassa atthīti seniko, seniko eva seniyo. Bimbisāroti tassa nāmanti ettha bimbīti suvaṇṇaṃ, tasmā sārasuvaṇṇasadisavaṇṇatāya bimbisāroti vuccatīti veditabbo. Catuttho bhāgo pādoti veditabboti imināva sabbajanapadesu kahāpaṇassa vīsatimo bhāgo māsakoti idañca vuttameva hotīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Porāṇasatthānurūpaṃ lakkhaṇasampannā uppāditā nīlakahāpaṇāti veditabbā. Rudradāmena uppādito rudradāmako. So kira nīlakahāpaṇassa tibhāgaṃ agghati. Yasmiṃ padese nīlakahāpaṇā na santi, tatthāpi nīlakahāpaṇānaṃ vaḷañjanaṭṭhāne ca avaḷañjanaṭṭhāne ca samānaagghavasena pavattamānaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ gahetvā nīlakahāpaṇavaseneva paricchedo kātabboti vadanti.

'Sabbāvantaṃ parisā' means an assembly possessing all its components, such as monks, nuns, and so on. Since all the people, counted as the fourfold assembly, are present here, it is 'sabbāvantā parisā.' 'Seniko' means one who has an army; 'seniyo' is just 'seniko.' 'Bimbisāro' is his name. Here, 'bimba' means golden color; therefore, he is called Bimbisāro because of having a complexion similar to the color of pure gold—this should be understood. 'The fourth part is to be known as a pāda'—by this, it should be understood that it is also stated that in all regions, the twentieth part of a kahāpaṇa is a māsaka. Nīlakahāpaṇā are to be understood as those produced in accordance with ancient treatises and possessing the required characteristics. Rudradāmako was issued by Rudradāma. It is said that it was worth a third of a nīlakahāpaṇa. They say that in places where nīlakahāpaṇā are not available, even there, whether in a place where nīlakahāpaṇā are used or not used, taking goods that are circulating at an equivalent value, the determination should be made in terms of nīlakahāpaṇā.

Dhaniyavatthuvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Story of Dhaniya is finished.

Tassattho…pe… vuttanayeneva veditabboti iminā “bhagavatā bhikkhūnaṃ idaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ evaṃ paññattaṃ hoti ca, idañca aññaṃ vatthu udapādī”ti evaṃ paṭhamapārājikavaṇṇanāyaṃ (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.39) vuttanayena tassattho veditabbo. “Idāni yaṃ taṃ aññaṃ vatthu uppannaṃ, taṃ dassetuṃ ‘tena kho pana samayenā’tiādimāhā”ti evaṃ anupaññattisambandho ca tattha vuttanayeneva veditabboti dasseti.

By the phrase, 'Its meaning... (etc.)... should be understood in the same way as stated,' it is shown that its meaning should be understood in the manner stated in the commentary on the first Pārājika (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 1.39), as in: 'The Blessed One established this training rule for the monks in this way, and this other case arose.' And it shows that the connection to the supplementary rule should also be understood in the same way as stated there, as in: 'Now, to show that other case that arose, it begins with “At that particular time…” and so on.'

90-91. Rajakā attharanti etthāti rajakattharaṇaṃ, rajakattharaṇanti rajakatitthaṃ vuccatīti āha “rajakatitthaṃ gantvā”ti. Vuttamevatthaṃ vibhāvento āha “tañhī”tiādi.

90-91. Because washermen spread cloths there, it is a washermen’s spreading place; the washermen’s spreading place is called a washermen’s ford. Thus it is said, “having gone to the washermen’s ford.” Explaining the meaning already stated, it is said, “for indeed,” and so forth.

Padabhājanīyavaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Word-by-Word Analysis

92. “Abhinavaniviṭṭho ekakuṭikādigāmo yāva manussā pavisitvā vāsaṃ na kappenti, tāva gāmasaṅkhyaṃ na gacchatī”ti vadanti, tasmā tattha gāmappavesanāpucchādikiccampi natthi. Yakkhapariggahabhūtoti saupaddavavasena vuttaṃ, yakkhanagarādiṃ vā saṅgaṇhāti. Yakkhanagarampi āpaṇādīsu dissamānesu gāmasaṅkhyaṃ [M 2.0124] gacchati, adissamānesu na gacchati, tasmā [V 2.0110] yakkhanagarampi pavisantena āpaṇādīsu dissamānesu sabbaṃ gāmappavesanavattaṃ kātabbaṃ, adissamānesu na kātabbanti vadanti. Punapi āgantukāmāti iminā tesaṃ tattha sāpekkhabhāvaṃ dasseti. Yato pana nirapekkhāva hutvā pakkamanti, so gāmasaṅkhyaṃ na gacchati, tasmā tattha gāmappavesanāpucchādikiccampi natthi.

92. “A newly established village with just one hut and so forth does not count as a village until people enter and take up residence,” they say. Therefore, there is no duty of asking for permission to enter such a place and so forth. The phrase “possessed by spirits” is used to indicate a place fraught with dangers, or it may refer to a city of spirits and so forth. Even a city of spirits is considered a village if shops and so forth are visible, but not if they are not visible. Therefore, when entering a city of spirits, if shops and so forth are visible, all the customary duties of village entry must be performed, but if they are not visible, they need not be performed—so they say. Furthermore, by the phrase 'desiring to come again,' their attachment to that place is shown. But when they depart without any attachment, it does not count as a village. Therefore, in such cases, there is no duty of asking for permission to enter the place and so forth either.

Nanu ca “gāmā vā araññā vā”ti ettakameva mātikāyaṃ vuttaṃ, tasmā gāmalakkhaṇaṃ dassetvā araññameva dassetabbaṃ siyā, gāmūpacāro nāmātiādi pana kasmā vuttanti āha – “gāmūpacārotiādi araññaparicchedadassanatthaṃ vutta”nti. Gāmūpacāre hi dassite ṭhapetvā gāmañca gāmūpacārañca avasesaṃ araññaṃ nāmāti araññaparicchedo sakkā dassetuṃ, idañca gāmagāmūpacāre asaṅkarato dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Mātikāyaṃ pana gāmaggahaṇeneva gāmūpacāropi saṅgahitoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Gāmūpacāro hi loke gāmasaṅkhyameva gacchati. Evañca katvā mātikāya anavasesaavaharaṇaṭṭhānapariggaho siddho hoti. Indakhīleti ummāre. Araññasaṅkhepaṃ gacchatīti “nikkhamitvā bahi indakhīlā sabbametaṃ arañña”nti (vibha. 529) abhidhamme vuttattā. Vemajjhameva indakhīloti vuccatīti indakhīlaṭṭhāniyattā asatipi indakhīle vemajjhameva tathā vuccati. Yattha pana dvārabāhāpi natthi, tattha ubhosu passesu vatiyā vā pākārassa vā koṭivemajjhameva indakhīlaṭṭhāniyattā “indakhīlo”ti gahetabbaṃ. Uḍḍāpentoti palāpento. Luṭhitvāti parivattetvā.

But is it not said in the matrix only “from a village or from the wilderness”? Therefore, having shown the characteristics of a village, only the wilderness should be shown. So why is “the vicinity of a village, namely,” and so forth mentioned? To this it is said: “'The vicinity of a village,' and so forth is stated in order to show the delimitation of the wilderness.” For when the vicinity of a village is shown, by excluding the village and the vicinity of the village, the remainder is called wilderness—thus, the delimitation of the wilderness can be shown. And this is stated in order to show the village and the vicinity of the village without confusion. In the matrix, however, it should be understood that by mentioning the village alone, the vicinity of the village is also included. For in the world, the vicinity of a village goes by the very designation of “village.” And when that is done, the matrix achieves its purpose of comprehensively including all locations of theft without anything left over. “Indakhīla” means at the threshold. Because it is included in the definition of the wilderness, “having gone out beyond the Indakhīla, all this is wilderness” is stated in the Abhidhamma (Vibhaṅga 529). Because it is the location of an indakhīla, the very middle is so called, even when there is no actual indakhīla. But where even a doorpost does not exist, there on both sides the exact middle of the end of a fence or wall should be taken as “indakhīla” because it is the location of an indakhīla. “Uḍḍāpento” means “driving away.” “Luṭhitvā” means “having rolled over.”

Majjhimassa purisassāti thāmamajjhimassa purisassa. Iminā pana vacanena suppamusalapātopi baladassanavaseneva katoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kurundaṭṭhakathāyaṃ mahāpaccariyañca gharūpacāro gāmoti adhippāyena “gharūpacāre ṭhitassa leḍḍupāto gāmūpacāro”ti vuttaṃ. Dvāreti nibbakosassa udakapatanaṭṭhānato abbhantaraṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Antogeheti ca pamukhassa abbhantarameva sandhāya vuttaṃ. Kataparikkhepoti imināva gharassa samantato tattako paricchedo gharūpacāro nāmāti vuttaṃ hoti. Yassa pana gharassa samantato gorūpānaṃ pavesananivāraṇatthaṃ pākāravatiādīhi parikkhepo kato hoti, tattha sova parikkhepo gharūpacāro, suppapātādiparicchedo pana aparikkhittagharaṃ sandhāya vuttoti daṭṭhabbaṃ[M 2.0125]. Idamettha pamāṇanti vikālagāmappavesanādīsu gāmagāmūpacārānaṃ asaṅkarato vinicchayassa veditabbattā. Kurundīādīsu vuttanayena hi gharūpacārassa gāmoti āpannattā gharagharūpacāragāmagāmūpacārānaṃ saṅkaro siyā. Evaṃ sabbatthāti iminā ito pubbepi pacchimasseva vādassa pamāṇabhāvaṃ dasseti[V 2.0111]. Keci pana “ito paṭṭhāya vakkhamānavādaṃ sandhāya vutta”nti vadanti, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ.

Of a man of medium size: this refers to a man of medium strength. By this statement, it should be understood that even a throw with a winnowing basket or a pestle is done as a demonstration of strength. In the Kurunda commentary and the Mahāpaccariya, with the intention that the vicinity of a house is a village, it is said, “For one standing in the vicinity of a house, a clod-throw is the vicinity of the village.” The doorway refers to the area inside from the place where water falls from the eaves. “Inside the house” refers specifically to the interior of the entrance. “With a defined boundary”: by this very phrase, it is stated that such an extent all around the house is called the vicinity of the house. However, for a house where a boundary is made all around with walls, fences, and so forth, to prevent the entry of cattle, that boundary itself is the vicinity of the house. But the delimitation by the fall of a winnowing basket and so forth refers to a house without such an enclosure, it should be understood. This is the measure here: because in cases like entering a village at an improper time and so forth, the decision must be known without confusion regarding the village and village-vicinity. For according to the method stated in the Kurundī and so forth, since it is accepted that the vicinity of a house is a village, there would be confusion between house, house-vicinity, village, and village-vicinity. Thus in all cases: this indicates that even before this, the later opinion holds as the standard. Some, however, say, “This refers to the opinion to be explained from now on,” but that should not be accepted.

Sesampīti gāmūpacāralakkhaṇaṃ sandhāya vadati. Tatrāti tasmiṃ gāmūpacāraggahaṇe. Tassa gāmaparicchedadassanatthanti tassa aparicchedassa gāmassa gāmaparicchedaṃ dassetunti attho. Yadi evaṃ “gāmo nāmā”ti padaṃ uddharitvā “aparikkhittassa gāmassa gharūpacāre ṭhitassa majjhimassa purisassa leḍḍupāto”ti kasmā na vuttanti? “Gāmo nāmāti idha avuttampi adhikāravasena labbhatiyevā”ti vadanti. Apare pana bhaṇanti “gāmūpacāro nāmāti imināva gāmassa ca gāmūpacārassa ca saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Kathaṃ? ‘Gāmassa upacāro gāmūpacāro’ti evaṃ viggahe kariyamāne ‘parikkhittassa gāmassa indakhīle ṭhitassa majjhimassa purisassa leḍḍupāto’ti iminā parikkhittassa gāmassa gāmūpacāralakkhaṇaṃ dassitaṃ hoti, ‘gāmasaṅkhāto upacāro gāmūpacāro’ti evaṃ pana gayhamāne ‘aparikkhittassa gāmassa gharūpacāre ṭhitassa majjhimassa purisassa leḍḍupāto’ti iminā aparikkhittassa gāmassa gāmaparicchedo dassitoti sakkā viññātu”nti. “Gharūpacāre ṭhitassa majjhimassa purisassa leḍḍupāto”ti iminā parikkhittassapi gāmassa sace leḍḍupātato dūre parikkhepo hoti, leḍḍupātoyeva gāmaparicchedoti gahetabbanti vadanti. Pubbe vuttanayenevāti parikkhittagāme vuttanayeneva.

The phrase 'Sesampi' is said in reference to the characteristics of the vicinity of a village. 'Tatra' means in that acceptance of the village’s vicinity. 'Tassa gāmaparicchedadassanatthaṃ' means 'to show the boundary of that unenclosed village'; this is the meaning. If so, why was it not stated by extracting the phrase 'gāmo nāma' and saying, 'For an unenclosed village, it is the clod-throw of a medium-sized man standing in the vicinity of a house'? They say, 'Even if "gāmo nāma" is not mentioned here, it is obtained by way of the topic.' Others, however, say: 'By this "gāmūpacāro nāma" itself, the inclusion of both the village and the village vicinity should be understood. How? When the analysis is made as "the vicinity of the village is gāmūpacāro," then by this "for an enclosed village, it is the clod-throw of a medium-sized man standing at the threshold post," the characteristic of the vicinity of an enclosed village is shown. But when it is taken as "the vicinity designated as a village is gāmūpacāro," then by this "for an unenclosed village, it is the clod-throw of a medium-sized man standing in the vicinity of a house," the boundary of an unenclosed village is shown; thus it can be known.' By this 'the clod-throw of a medium-sized man standing in the vicinity of a house,' they say that even for an enclosed village, if the enclosure is farther than a clod-throw, the clod-throw itself should be taken as the village boundary. 'Pubbe vuttanayeneva' means in the same way as stated previously for an enclosed village.

Saṅkarīyatīti missīyati. Etthāti gharagharūpacāragāmagāmūpacāresu. “Vikāle gāmappavesane parikkhittassa gāmassa parikkhepaṃ atikkamantassa āpatti pācittiyassa, aparikkhittassa gāmassa upacāraṃ okkamantassa āpatti pācittiyassā”ti (pāci. 513) vuttattā gāmagāmūpacārānaṃ asaṅkaratā icchitabbāti āha – “asaṅkarato cettha vinicchayo veditabbo vikāle gāmappavesanādīsū”ti. Ettha ca “parikkhittassa gāmassa parikkhepaṃ, aparikkhittassa [M 2.0126] parikkhepārahaṭṭhānaṃ atikkamantassa vikālagāmappavesanāpatti hotī”ti keci vadanti, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ padabhājaniyaṃ pana “parikkhittassa gāmassa parikkhepaṃ atikkamantassa āpatti pācittiyassa, aparikkhittassa gāmassa upacāraṃ okkamantassa āpatti pācittiyassā”ti (pāci. 513) vuttattā. Aparikkhittassa gāmassa gharūpacārato paṭṭhāya dutiyaleḍḍupātasaṅkhātassa gāmūpacārassa okkamane āpatti veditabbā. Teneva vikālagāmappavesanasikkhāpadaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (pāci. aṭṭha. 512) “aparikkhittassa gāmassa upacāro adinnādāne vuttanayeneva veditabbo”ti vuttaṃ. Mātikāṭṭhakathāyampi (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. dutiyapārājikavaṇṇanā) vuttaṃ “yvāyaṃ aparikkhittassa gāmassa upacāro dassito, tassa vasena [V 2.0112] vikālagāmappavesanādīsu āpatti paricchinditabbā”ti. Yadi evaṃ “vikāle gāmaṃ paviseyyā”ti iminā virujjhatīti? Na virujjhati gāmūpacārassapi gāmaggahaṇena gahitattā. Tasmā parikkhittassa gāmassa parikkhepaṃ atikkamantassa, aparikkhittassa upacāraṃ okkamantassa vikālagāmappavesanāpatti hotīti niṭṭhamettha gantabbaṃ. Vikāle gāmappavesanādīsūti ādi-saddena gharagharūpacārādīsu ṭhitānaṃ uppannalābhabhājanādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti.

'Saṅkarīyati' means it is mixed. 'Ettha' means in these: the house, the house vicinity, the village, and the village vicinity. Because it is said, 'When entering a village at the wrong time, for an enclosed village, for one who crosses the enclosure, there is an offense of expiation; for an unenclosed village, for one who enters the vicinity, there is an offense of expiation' (Pāci. 513), the non-confusion of the village and the village vicinity is to be desired. Thus he said, 'And here the decision should be understood as being without confusion in regard to entering a village at the wrong time, etc.' And here, some say, 'For an enclosed village, the offense of entering a village at the wrong time occurs for one who crosses its enclosure; for an unenclosed village, for one who crosses the place suitable for an enclosure.' That should not be accepted. But since it is said in the word-analysis, 'For an enclosed village, for one who crosses the enclosure, there is an offense of expiation; for an unenclosed village, for one who enters the vicinity, there is an offense of expiation' (Pāci. 513), for an unenclosed village, the offense should be understood as occurring upon entering the village vicinity, which is reckoned as the second clod-throw starting from the house vicinity. For that very reason, in the commentary on the training rule for entering a village at the wrong time (Pāci. Aṭṭha. 512), it is said: 'The vicinity of an unenclosed village should be understood in the same way as stated in the section on taking what is not given.' In the commentary on the Mātikā (Kaṅkhā. Aṭṭha. Dutiyapārājikavaṇṇanā) also, it is stated: 'By means of this which has been shown as the vicinity of an unenclosed village, the offenses in cases such as entering a village at the wrong time should be determined.' If so, does this contradict 'one might enter a village at the wrong time'? It does not contradict, because the village vicinity is also included by the term 'village'. Therefore, the conclusion should be reached here that the offense of entering a village at the wrong time occurs for one who crosses the enclosure of an enclosed village, or for one who enters the vicinity of an unenclosed village. In 'entering a village at the wrong time, etc.,' the word 'etc.' includes such things as the sharing of gains that have arisen for those staying in a house, a house vicinity, and so on.

Nikkhamitvā bahi indakhīlāti indakhīlato bahi nikkhamitvāti attho. Ettha ca vinayapariyāyena tāva “ṭhapetvā gāmañca gāmūpacārañca avasesaṃ arañña”nti (pārā. 92) āgataṃ, suttantapariyāyena āraññikaṃ bhikkhuṃ sandhāya “āraññakaṃ nāma senāsanaṃ pañcadhanusatikaṃ pacchima”nti (pārā. 654) āgataṃ. Vinayasuttantā ubhopi pariyāyadesanā nāma, abhidhammo pana nippariyāyadesanā. Nippariyāyato ca gāmavinimuttaṃ ṭhānaṃ araññameva hotīti abhidhammapariyāyena araññaṃ dassetuṃ “nikkhamitvā bahi indakhīlā”ti (vibha. 529) vuttaṃ. “Ācariyadhanu nāma pakatihatthena navavidatthippamāṇaṃ, jiyāya pana āropitāya catuhatthappamāṇa”nti vadanti. Lesokāsanisedhanatthanti “mayā neva gāme, na araññe haṭaṃ, ghare vā gharūpacāresu vā gāmūpacāresu vā aññatarasmi”nti vattuṃ mā labhatūti vuttaṃ hoti.

'Nikkhamitvā bahi indakhīlā' means having gone out, away from the threshold post. And here, according to the Vinaya exposition, it is stated: 'Excluding the village and the village vicinity, the remainder is wilderness' (Pārā. 92). According to the Suttanta exposition, in reference to a forest-dwelling bhikkhu, it is stated: 'A so-called forest dwelling has a minimum distance of five hundred bow-lengths' (Pārā. 654). Both the Vinaya and Suttanta are called conventional teachings, whereas the Abhidhamma is the direct teaching. And according to the direct teaching, a place separate from the village is simply wilderness; thus, to show 'wilderness' according to the Abhidhamma exposition, it is said: 'having gone out, outside the threshold post' (Vibha. 529). They say: 'A teacher's bow is nine spans by a natural hand, but when the string is strung, it is four cubits.' 'Lesokāsanisedhanatthaṃ' means for the purpose of negating a loophole; that is to say, it is said so that one may not get the chance to say: 'I took it neither in the village nor in the wilderness, but in a house, or in a house vicinity, or in a village vicinity.'

Kappiyanti anurūpavasena vuttaṃ. Akappiyampi pana appaṭiggahitañce, adinnasaṅkhyameva gacchati. Pariccāgādimhi akate “idaṃ mayhaṃ santaka”nti aviditampi parapariggahitameva [M 2.0127] mātāpitūnaṃ accayena mandānaṃ uttānaseyyakānaṃ dārakānaṃ santakamiva.

'Kappiyaṃ' (allowable) is said in terms of suitability. But what is unallowable, if unaccepted, simply counts as 'not given'. Even if relinquishment, etc., has not been made, and even if it is not known to the owner that 'this is my property,' it is still considered possessed by another—like the belongings of foolish, helpless infants after the death of their parents.

Yassa vasena puriso thenoti vuccati, taṃ theyyanti āha “avaharaṇacittassetaṃ adhivacana”nti. Saṅkhā-saddo ñāṇakoṭṭhāsapaññattigaṇanādīsu dissati. “Saṅkhāyekaṃ paṭisevatī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.168) hi ñāṇe dissati. “Papañcasaññāsaṅkhā samudācarantī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.204) koṭṭhāse. “Tesaṃ tesaṃ dhammānaṃ saṅkhā samaññā”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 1313) paññattiyaṃ. “Na sukaraṃ saṅkhātu”ntiādīsu (dha. pa. 196; apa. thera. 1.10.2) gaṇanāyaṃ. Tattha koṭṭhāsavacanaṃ saṅkhā-saddaṃ sandhāyāha “saṅkhāsaṅkhātanti atthato eka”nti. Tenāha “koṭṭhāsassetaṃ adhivacana”nti. Papañcasaṅkhāti taṇhāmānadiṭṭhisaṅkhātā papañcakoṭṭhāsā. “Eko cittakoṭṭhāsoti yañca pubbabhāge avaharissāmīti pavattaṃ cittaṃ, yañca gamanādisādhakaṃ parāmasanādisādhakaṃ vā majjhe pavattaṃ, yañca [V 2.0113] ṭhānācāvanappayogasādhakaṃ, tesu ayameveko pacchimo cittakoṭṭhāso idhādhippeto”ti keci vadanti. Cūḷagaṇṭhipade pana “ūnamāsakamāsakaūnapañcamāsakapañcamāsakāvaharaṇacittesu eko cittakoṭṭhāso”ti vuttaṃ. “Anekappabhedattā cittassa eko cittakoṭṭhāsoti vutta”nti mahāgaṇṭhipade majjhimagaṇṭhipade ca vuttaṃ. Idamevettha sundarataraṃ “theyyacittasaṅkhāto eko cittakoṭṭhāso”ti vuttattā. Theyyasaṅkhātenāti theyyacittakoṭṭhāsena karaṇabhūtena, na vissāsatāvakālikādigāhavasappavattacittakoṭṭhāsenāti vuttaṃ hoti.

That by which a person is called a thief is theft; regarding this, it is said: 'This is a designation for the thought of stealing.' The word 'saṅkhā' is seen in contexts such as knowledge, divisions, designations, and counting. For instance, in 'saṅkhāyekaṃ paṭisevatī' (MN 2.168), it appears in the sense of knowledge. In 'papañcasaññāsaṅkhā samudācarantī' (MN 1.204), it refers to divisions. In 'tesaṃ tesaṃ dhammānaṃ saṅkhā samaññā' (Dhs 1313), it denotes designation. In 'na sukaraṃ saṅkhātu' (Dhp 196; Ap 1.10.2), it pertains to counting. There, referring to the word 'saṅkhā' in the sense of 'division', it is said: 'Saṅkhā and saṅkhāta are one in meaning.' Therefore, it is stated: 'This is a designation for a division.' 'Papañcasaṅkhā' means the divisions of proliferation designated as craving, conceit, and views. Some say: 'A single division of consciousness is that consciousness which arises in the preliminary stage with the thought, “I will steal”; that which arises in the middle, accomplishing the going, handling, etc.; and that which accomplishes the effort of moving it from its place. Among these, only this last division of consciousness is intended here.' In the Cūḷagaṇṭhipada, however, it is said: 'In the case of thoughts of stealing a thing worth less than a māsaka, a māsaka, less than five māsakas, or five māsakas, there is one division of consciousness.' In the Mahāgaṇṭhipada and Majjhimagaṇṭhipada, it is said: 'Because consciousness has many different kinds, it is called a single division of consciousness.' This here is the better explanation, because it is said: 'a single division of consciousness designated as the thought of theft.' 'By that which is designated as theft' means by the division of consciousness that is the thought of theft, which has become the instrument, not by the division of consciousness that has arisen due to taking something on trust, for a temporary period, and so on—this is what is said.

Abhiyogavasenāti aḍḍakaraṇavasena. Abhiyuñjatīti codeti, aḍḍaṃ karotīti attho. Parikappitaṭṭhānanti okāsaparikappanavasena parikappitappadesaṃ. Suṅkaghātanti ettha rājūnaṃ deyyabhāgassa etaṃ adhivacanaṃ suṅkoti, so ettha haññati adatvā gacchantehīti suṅkaghāto. “Ettha paviṭṭhehi suṅko dātabbo”ti rukkhapabbatādisaññāṇena niyamitappadesassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ.

`Abhiyogavasena` means by way of making a legal claim. `Abhiyuñjati` means to accuse; the meaning is to make a legal claim. `Parikappitaṭṭhānaṃ` means a place determined by way of assigning a location. `Suṅkaghāta` (toll-post): here, `suṅka` is a designation for the portion owed to kings; it is called `suṅkaghāta` because the toll is 'struck down' here by those who go without paying. This is a designation for a place defined by a sign such as a tree or a mountain, with the rule: 'Toll must be paid by those who have entered here.'

Pañcavīsatiavahārakathāvaṇṇanā

The Elucidation of the Account of the Twenty-Five Modes of Appropriation

Ākulāti [M 2.0128] saṅkulā. Luḷitāti viloḷitā. Katthacīti ekissāya aṭṭhakathāyaṃ. Ekaṃ pañcakaṃ dassitanti “parapariggahitañca hoti, parapariggahitasaññī ca, garuko ca hoti parikkhāro pañcamāsako vā atirekapañcamāsako vā, theyyacittañca paccupaṭṭhitaṃ hoti, āmasati, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Phandāpeti, āpatti thullaccayassa. Ṭhānā cāveti, āpatti pārājikassā”ti (pārā. 122) evaṃ vuttapañcaavahāraṅgāni ekaṃ pañcakanti dassitaṃ. Dve pañcakāni dassitānīti “chahākārehi adinnaṃ ādiyantassa āpatti pārājikassa. Na ca sakasaññī, na ca vissāsaggāhī, na ca tāvakālikaṃ, garuko ca hoti parikkhāro pañcamāsako vā atirekapañcamāsako vā, theyyacittañca paccupaṭṭhitaṃ hoti, āmasati, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Phandāpeti, āpatti thullaccayassa. Ṭhānā cāveti, āpatti pārājikassā”ti evaṃ vuttesu chasu padesu ekaṃ apanetvā avasesāni pañca padāni ekaṃ pañcakanti dassetvā heṭṭhā vuttapañcakañca gahetvā dve pañcakāni dassitāni. Ettha panāti “pañcahākārehi adinnaṃ ādiyantassā”tiādīsu. Sabbehipi padehīti “parapariggahitañca hotī”tiādīhi padehi. Labbhamānāniyeva pañcakānīti pañcavīsatiyā avahāresu labbhamānapañcakāni.

`Ākula` means `saṅkula` (confused). `Luḷita` means `viloḷita` (agitated). 'Somewhere' means in a certain commentary. One pentad is shown: 'It is possessed by another, and one perceives it as possessed by another, and the requisite is valuable—worth five māsakas or more—and the thought of theft is present; if one touches it, it is an offense of wrong-doing. If one causes it to shake, it is an offense of grave misconduct. If one moves it from its place, it is an offense entailing defeat.' (cf. Vin. iii. 56) Thus, these five factors of appropriation are shown as one pentad. Two pentads are shown: 'For one who takes what is not given in six ways, there is an offense entailing defeat: one does not perceive it as one's own, one does not take it on trust, one does not take it for a temporary period, the requisite is valuable—worth five māsakas or more—and the thought of theft is present; if one touches it, it is an offense of wrong-doing. If one causes it to shake, it is an offense of grave misconduct. If one moves it from its place, it is an offense entailing defeat.' Thus, after showing that among these six stated items, by removing one, the remaining five items constitute one pentad, and by including the previously mentioned pentad, two pentads are shown. 'Here, however' refers to passages such as 'In five ways, for one taking what is not given…'. 'By all the items' means by items such as 'it is possessed by another…'. 'The very pentads that are obtainable' means the pentads obtainable among the twenty-five modes of appropriation.

Pañcannaṃ avahārānaṃ samūho pañcakaṃ, sako hattho sahattho, tena nibbatto, tassa vā sambandhīti [V 2.0114] sāhatthiko, avahāro. Sāhatthikādi pañcakaṃ sāhatthikapañcakanti ādipadavasena nāmalābho daṭṭhabbo kusalādittikassa kusalattikavohāro viya. Imināva nayena pubbapayogādi pañcakaṃ pubbapayogapañcakaṃ, theyyāvahārādi pañcakaṃ theyyāvahārapañcakanti nāmalābho daṭṭhabboti. Tatiyapañcamesu pañcakesūti sāhatthikapañcakatheyyāvahārapañcakesu. Labbhamānapadavasenāti sāhatthikapañcake labbhamānassa nissaggiyāvahārapadassa vasena theyyāvahārapañcake labbhamānassa parikappāvahārapadassa ca vasena yojetabbanti attho.

A collection of five modes of appropriation is a pentad. One’s own hand is `sahattho`; an appropriation (`avahāro`) produced by it or related to it is `sāhatthiko`. The pentad beginning with `sāhatthika` is called the `sāhatthikapañcaka`; the acquisition of the name should be understood as being based on the initial term, like the designation 'the wholesome triad' for the triad beginning with 'wholesome'. By this same method, the acquisition of the names for the pentad beginning with 'prior effort' as the `pubbapayogapañcaka`, and the pentad beginning with 'appropriation by theft' as the `theyyāvahārapañcaka` should be understood. 'In the third and fifth pentads' means in the `sāhatthikapañcaka` and the `theyyāvahārapañcaka`. 'By means of the obtainable term' means that the connection should be made by means of the term 'appropriation by relinquishment' (`nissaggiyāvahāra`) which is obtainable in the `sāhatthikapañcaka`, and by means of the term 'appropriation by determination' (`parikappāvahāra`) which is obtainable in the `theyyāvahārapañcaka`. This is the meaning.

Āṇattiyā nibbatto avahāro āṇattiko. Nissajjanaṃ nissaggo, suṅkaghātaṭṭhāne parikappitokāse vā ṭhatvā bhaṇḍassa bahi pātanaṃ. Nissaggova nissaggiyo. Kiriyāsiddhito puretarameva pārājikāpattisaṅkhātaṃ [M 2.0129] atthaṃ sādhetīti atthasādhako. “Asukassa bhaṇḍaṃ yadā sakkosi, tadā avaharā”ti evarūpo hi āṇāpanapayogo parassa telakumbhiyā pādagghanakaṃ telaṃ avassaṃ pivanakānaṃ upāhanādīnaṃ nikkhepapayogo ca āṇattassa bhaṇḍaggahaṇato upāhanādīnaṃ telapātanato ca puretarameva pārājikāpattisaṅkhātaṃ atthaṃ sādheti. Sāhatthikapayogopi hi evarūpo atthasādhakoti vuccati. Vuttañhetaṃ mātikāṭṭhakathāyaṃ (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. dutiyapārājikavaṇṇanā) –

An appropriation produced from a command is `āṇattiko` (commanded). `Nissajjana` is `nissagga` (relinquishment), which is the act of dropping goods outside while standing in a toll-post or a determined place. `Nissagga` itself is `nissaggiya`. Because it accomplishes the purpose, designated as an offense entailing defeat, even before the completion of the act, it is an `atthasādhaka` (accomplisher of the purpose). For indeed, an application of a command of this sort, 'Appropriate the goods of so-and-so whenever you can,' and the application of placing into another’s oil pot sandals and so on, which will certainly absorb oil to the value of a `pāda`, accomplishes the purpose, designated as an offense entailing defeat, even before the commanded person takes the goods or the oil is absorbed by the sandals and so on. Indeed, even an application by one's own hand of this sort is called an `atthasādhaka`. This is stated in the Commentary on the Mātikā (Kankhāvitaraṇī, The Explanation of the Second Pārājika):

“Atthasādhako nāma ‘asukassa bhaṇḍaṃ yadā sakkosi, tadā taṃ avaharā’ti āṇāpeti. Tattha sace paro anantarāyiko hutvā taṃ avaharati, āṇāpakassa āṇattikkhaṇeyeva pārājikaṃ. Parassa vā pana telakumbhiyā pādagghanakaṃ telaṃ avassaṃ pivanakāni upāhanādīni pakkhipati, hatthato muttamatteyeva pārājika”nti.

“An `atthasādhaka` (one who accomplishes a purpose) is one who commands, ‘When you are able, appropriate the goods of so-and-so.’ In that case, if the other person, being without hindrance, appropriates it, the commander incurs an offense entailing defeat at the very moment of the command. Or, if one puts into another’s oil pot sandals and so forth, which will certainly absorb oil worth a `pāda`, an offense entailing defeat is incurred as soon as they are released from the hand.”

Dhurassa nikkhipanaṃ dhuranikkhepo. Ārāmābhiyuñjanādīsu attano ca parassa ca dānaggahaṇesu nirussāhabhāvāpajjanaṃ. Sahatthā avaharatīti sahatthena gaṇhāti. “Asukassa bhaṇḍaṃ avaharā”ti aññaṃ āṇāpetīti etthāpi āṇāpakassa āṇattikkhaṇeyeva āpatti daṭṭhabbā. Yadi evaṃ imassa, atthasādhakassa ca ko visesoti? Taṅkhaṇaññeva gahaṇe niyuñjanaṃ āṇattikapayogo, kālantarena gahaṇatthaṃ niyogo atthasādhakoti ayametesaṃ viseso. Tenevāha – “asukassa bhaṇḍaṃ yadā sakkosi, tadā avaharāti āṇāpetī”ti. Ettha ca āṇāpanapayogova atthasādhakoti dassito, sāhatthikavasenapi atthasādhakapayogo pana upari āvi bhavissati. Dhuranikkhepo pana upanikkhittabhaṇḍavasena veditabboti idaṃ nidassanamattaṃ. Ārāmābhiyuñjanādīsupi tāvakālikabhaṇḍadeyyānaṃ adānepi eseva nayo.

The laying down of a burden is `dhuranikkhepo` (abandonment of a burden). It is the state of becoming unenthusiastic in tasks such as attending to the monastery, and in giving and receiving for oneself and others. `Sahatthā avaharati` (one appropriates by one’s own hand) means one takes with one’s own hand. If one commands another, saying, “Appropriate the goods of so-and-so,” even here, an offense should be seen as occurring for the commander at the very moment of the command. If so, what is the difference between this and an `atthasādhaka`? Engaging someone to take something at that very moment is the application of a command (`āṇattikapayoga`), while the assignment to take something at a later time is `atthasādhaka`—this is the distinction between them. Therefore, it is said: “One commands, ‘When you are able, appropriate the goods of so-and-so.’” Here, the application of command itself is shown to be `atthasādhaka`, but the `atthasādhaka` application by way of one’s own hand will become clear later. The abandonment of a burden, however, should be understood by way of goods that have been entrusted—this is merely an illustration. Similarly, even in cases like attending to the monastery, if temporary goods that should be given are not given, the same principle applies.

“Āṇattivasena [V 2.0115] pubbapayogo veditabbo”ti vuttattā anantarāyena gaṇhantassa ‘asukassa bhaṇḍaṃ avaharā’ti āṇāpanaṃ bhaṇḍaggahaṇato pubbattā pubbapayogo, payogena saha vattamāno avahāro sahapayogo, “asukaṃ nāma bhaṇḍaṃ harissāmā”ti saṃvidahitvā [M 2.0130] sammantayitvā avaharaṇaṃ saṃvidāvahāro. Saṅketakammaṃ nāma pubbaṇhādikālaparicchedavasena sañjānanakammaṃ, nimittakammaṃ nāma saññuppādanatthaṃ akkhinikhaṇanādinimittakaraṇaṃ. Ṭhānācāvanavasena sahapayogoti idaṃ pana nidassanamattaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, khilasaṅkamanādīsupi asati ca ṭhānācāvane sahapayogo daṭṭhabbo. Vuttañhetaṃ mātikāṭṭhakathāyaṃ (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. dutiyapārājikavaṇṇanā) “ṭhānācāvanavasena khilādīni saṅkāmetvā khettādiggahaṇavasena ca sahapayogo veditabbo”ti.

Since it is said, “Prior effort should be understood by way of command,” the command ‘Appropriate the goods of so-and-so’ given to one who takes without hindrance, being prior to the taking of the goods, is `pubbapayoga` (prior effort). A mode of appropriation occurring together with the effort is `sahapayoga` (simultaneous effort). The appropriation by resolving and agreeing, thinking, ‘We will take such-and-such goods,’ is `saṃvidāvahāra` (prearranged appropriation). `Saṅketakamma` (act of signaling) is the act of recognition by determining the time, such as morning, etc. `Nimittakamma` (act of marking) is the making of signs like winking an eye, etc., for the purpose of producing a signal. Regarding `sahapayoga` by way of displacement from a place, this should be seen merely as an illustration. Even in cases like moving boundary markers, etc., where there is no displacement from a place, `sahapayoga` should be understood. For it is said in the Mātikāṭṭhakathā (Kankhāvitaraṇī, Commentary on the Second Pārājika): ‘`Sahapayoga` should be understood by way of displacement from a place, and also by way of moving boundary markers and so on, and by way of taking fields and so on.’

Theno vuccati coro, tassa bhāvo theyyaṃ, tena avaharaṇaṃ theyyāvahāro. Yo hi sandhicchedādīni katvā adissamāno avaharati, tulākūṭamānakūṭakūṭakahāpaṇādīhi vā vañcetvā gaṇhāti, tassevaṃ gaṇhato avahāro theyyāvahāro. Pasayha abhibhavitvā avaharaṇaṃ pasayhāvahāro. Yo hi pasayha balakkārena paresaṃ santakaṃ gaṇhāti gāmaghātakādayo viya, attano pattabalito vā vuttanayena adhikaṃ gaṇhāti rājabhaṭādayo viya, tassevaṃ gaṇhato avahāro pasayhāvahāro. Bhaṇḍavasena ca okāsavasena ca parikappetvā avaharaṇaṃ parikappāvahāro. Tiṇapaṇṇādīhi aṅgulimuddikādiṃ paṭicchādetvā pacchā tassa paṭicchannassa avaharaṇaṃ paṭicchannāvahāro. Kusaṃ saṅkāmetvā avaharaṇaṃ kusāvahāro.

`Thena` is called a thief. His state is `theyya` (theft). The appropriation by means of it is `theyyāvahāra` (appropriation by theft). Indeed, for one who, having committed house-breaking and so on, appropriates unseen, or deceives with false scales, false measures, counterfeit coins, and so on, and takes—the appropriation by such a one is `theyyāvahāra`. The appropriation by overpowering with force is `pasayhāvahāra` (forcible appropriation). Indeed, for one who takes the property of others by force, by violence, like village raiders and so on, or who takes more than what is due by one’s own acquired power, in the manner stated, like royal officials and so on—the appropriation by such a one is `pasayhāvahāra`. The appropriation by prearrangement regarding goods and by prearrangement regarding opportunity is `parikappāvahāra` (prearranged appropriation). The appropriation by concealing a finger-ring and so on with grass, leaves, and so on, and later appropriating that which was concealed, is `paṭicchannāvahāra` (concealed appropriation). The appropriation by moving a boundary marker (`kusa`) is `kusāvahāra` (appropriation by means of a `kusa` marker).

Tulayitvāti upaparikkhitvā. Sāmīcīti vattaṃ, āpatti pana natthīti adhippāyo. Mahājanasammaddoti mahājanasaṅkhobho. Bhaṭṭhe janakāyeti apagate janakāye. “Idañca kāsāvaṃ attano santakaṃ katvā etasseva bhikkhuno dehī”ti kiṃkāraṇā evamāha? Cīvarasāmikena yasmā dhuranikkhepo kato, tasmā tassa adinnaṃ gahetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Avahārakopi vippaṭisārassa uppannakālato paṭṭhāya cīvarasāmikaṃ pariyesanto vicarati “dassāmī”ti, cīvarasāmikena ca “mameta”nti vutte etenapi avahārakena ālayo pariccatto, tasmā evamāha. Yadi evaṃ cīvarasāmikoyeva “attano santakaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti kasmā na vuttoti? Ubhinnampi kukkuccavinodanatthaṃ. Kathaṃ? Avahārakassa “mayā sahatthena na dinnaṃ, bhaṇḍadeyyameta”nti kukkuccaṃ uppajjeyya, itarassa “mayā paṭhamaṃ dhuranikkhepaṃ katvā pacchā adinnaṃ gahita”nti kukkuccaṃ uppajjeyyāti.

‘Having weighed’ means ‘having examined’. ‘Proper’ means ‘the practice’; the intention is that there is no offense. ‘Disturbance of the great assembly’ means ‘commotion among the great assembly’. ‘When the crowd has dispersed’ means ‘when the gathering of people has departed’. Why did he say, ‘Make this robe your own and give it to this very monk’? Because the owner of the robe had relinquished his responsibility, it was not permissible for that monk to take what was not given. The appropriator too, from the time regret arose, wandered searching for the robe’s owner, thinking, ‘I will give it back.’ And when the robe’s owner said, ‘This is mine,’ this appropriator also abandoned his clinging. That is why he spoke thus. If so, why was it not said to the robe’s owner himself, ‘Take what is your own’? To dispel the scruples of both. How so? The appropriator might have had scruples, thinking, ‘I did not give it with my own hand; this is an item that should be given.’ The other might have had scruples, thinking, ‘First I relinquished responsibility, and then I took what was not given.’

Samagghanti [M 2.0131] appagghaṃ. Dāruatthaṃ pharatīti dārūhi kattabbakiccaṃ sādheti. Mayi santetiādi [V 2.0116] sabbaṃ raññā pasādena vuttaṃ, “therena pana ananucchavikaṃ kata”nti na maññitabbaṃ.

‘`Samaggha`’ means ‘of little value’. ‘It serves the purpose of wood’ means ‘it accomplishes the tasks to be done with wood’. ‘While I am here,’ and so on—all this was spoken by the king out of faith. One should not think, ‘But the Elder acted inappropriately.’

Ekadivasaṃ dantakaṭṭhacchedanādinā yā ayaṃ agghahāni vuttā, sā sabbā bhaṇḍasāminā

Whatever loss of value was mentioned as arising from the cutting of tooth-sticks and so on, on a certain day—all of this was said concerning the owner of the goods.

Kiṇitvā gahitameva sandhāya vuttā, sabbaṃ panetaṃ aṭṭhakathācariyappamāṇena gahetabbaṃ. Pāsāṇañca sakkharañca pāsāṇasakkharaṃ. Dhāreyyatthaṃ vicakkhaṇoti imasseva vivaraṇaṃ “āpattiṃ vā anāpattiṃ vā”tiādi.

It was said with reference to his having bought and taken it. But all this should be understood according to the authority of the commentary teachers. 'Stone and gravel' means 'stone-gravel'. The explanation of 'one who is discerning for the purpose of retaining' is this very phrase: 'whether it is an offense or not an offense,' and so on.

Pañcavīsatiavahārakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the twenty-five kinds of appropriation is concluded.

Akkhadassāti ettha akkha-saddena kira vinicchayasālā vuccati. Tattha nisīditvā vajjāvajjaṃ passantīti akkhadassā vuccanti dhammavinicchanakā. Haneyyunti ettha hananaṃ nāma hatthapādādīhi pothanañceva sīsādicchedanañca hotīti āha – “haneyyunti potheyyuñceva chindeyyuñcā”ti. Teneva padabhājaniyañca “hatthena vā pādena vā kasāya vā vettena vā aḍḍhadaṇḍakena vā chejjāya vā haneyyu”nti vuttaṃ. Tattha aḍḍhadaṇḍakenāti dvihatthappamāṇena rassamuggarena veḷupesikāya vā. Chejjāyāti hatthapādasīsādīnaṃ chedanena. Nīhareyyunti gāmanigamādito nīhareyyuṃ. Corosi…pe… thenosīti ettha “paribhāseyyu”nti padaṃ ajjhāharitvā attho veditabboti āha “corosīti evamādīni ca vatvā paribhāseyyu”nti.

Herein, by the word ‘akkha,’ it is said, a judgment hall is meant. Because they sit there and discern what is an offense and what is not an offense, the adjudicators of the Dhamma are called ‘akkhadassā’ (those who see the case). Herein, ‘hananaṃ’ (striking) is both striking with hands, feet, and so on, and the cutting off of the head, and so on. Thus, He said: ‘“They would strike” means they would both strike and cut off.’ For that same reason, in the word-analysis it is also said: ‘They would strike with a hand or a foot, with a whip or a cane, with a half-staff, or by cutting.’ Therein, ‘by a half-staff’ means with a short club of two cubits in length, or with a strip of bamboo. ‘By cutting’ means by the cutting off of hands, feet, head, and so on. ‘They would banish’ means they would banish from a village, a town, and so on. Herein, in ‘You are a thief… you are a robber,’ the meaning should be understood by supplying the word ‘they would revile.’ Thus, He said: ‘Having said, “You are a thief,” and so on, they would revile.’

93. Yaṃ taṃ bhaṇḍaṃ dassitanti sambandho. Yattha yattha ṭhitanti bhūmiādīsu yattha yattha ṭhitaṃ. Yathā yathā ādānaṃ gacchatīti bhūmiādīsu ṭhitaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ sabbaso aggahaṇepi yena yena ākārena gahaṇaṃ upagacchati.

93. The connection is to be made as: 'That merchandise which was shown.' 'Wherever it is placed' means wherever it is placed on the ground and so on. 'In whatever way it comes to be taken' means: the merchandise placed on the ground and so on, even without being grasped entirely, comes to be taken in whatever manner.

Bhūmaṭṭhakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Commentary on the Section on the Ground.

94. Phandāpeti, sabbattha dukkaṭamevāti ettha “uṭṭhahissāmī”ti phandāpetvā puna anuṭṭhahitvā tattheva sayantassapi aṅgapaccaṅgaṃ aphandāpetvā ekapayogena uṭṭhahantassapi dukkaṭamevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Aññasmiṃ vā gamanassa [M 2.0132] anupakāreti yathā dvārapidahane kumbhiṭṭhānagamanassa anupakārattā anāpatti, evaṃ aññasmiṃ vā gamanassa anupakāre kāyavacīkamme anāpatti. Vācāya vācāyāti ekekatthadīpikāya vācāya vācāya. Upaladdhoti ñāto. Puññāni ca karissāmāti ettha “musāvādaṃ katvā puññāni karissāmāti vadantassa dukkaṭamevā”ti [V 2.0117] tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ, taṃ imasmiṃyeva padese aṭṭhakathāvacanena virujjhati. Tathā hi “yaṃ yaṃ vacanaṃ musā, tattha tattha pācittiya”nti ca “na hi adinnādānassa pubbapayoge pācittiyaṭṭhāne dukkaṭaṃ nāma atthī”ti ca vakkhati. Evaṃ pana vutte na virujjhati “musāvādaṃ katvā puññāni ca karissāmāti vadantassa pācittiyena saddhiṃ dukkaṭa”nti. Tathā hi “akappiyapathaviṃ khaṇantānaṃ dukkaṭehi saddhiṃ pācittiyānīti mahāpaccariyaṃ vutta”nti ca “yathā ca idha, evaṃ sabbattha pācittiyaṭṭhāne dukkaṭā na muccatī”ti ca vakkhati. Sace pana kusalacitto “puññāni karissāmā”ti vadati, anāpatti “buddhapūjaṃ vā dhammapūjaṃ vā saṅghabhattaṃ vā karissāmāti kusalaṃ uppādeti, kusalacittena gamane anāpattī”ti ca “yathā ca idha, evaṃ sabbattha atheyyacittassa anāpattī”ti ca vakkhamānattā.

94. To cause movement: in all cases, it is only a dukkaṭa offense. Herein, it should be understood that it is only a dukkaṭa offense for one who, having caused movement with the thought, 'I will get up,' then does not get up but remains lying there; and also for one who gets up with a single effort without causing the major and minor limbs to move. Or, if it is not helpful for going elsewhere: just as there is no offense in closing a door when going to the place of the pot, because it is not helpful for that journey, so too, in the case of a bodily or verbal action that is not helpful for going elsewhere, there is no offense. 'By speech, by speech' means by each and every speech that clarifies a meaning. 'Understood' means known. 'And I will do meritorious deeds': Here, it is said in all three Gaṇṭhipada commentaries that for one who says, 'Having told a lie, I will do meritorious deeds,' there is only a dukkaṭa offense. That statement, however, contradicts the statement of the commentary in this very section. For it will be said, 'Whatever statement is false, in each case there is a pācittiya offense,' and, 'Indeed, in the preliminary act of taking what is not given, there is no such thing as a dukkaṭa offense in a case where a pācittiya is incurred.' But when it is stated in this way, it is not contradictory: 'For one who says, "Having told a lie, I will also do meritorious deeds," there is a dukkaṭa offense together with a pācittiya.' For it is said in the Mahāpaccarī, 'For those digging on unsuitable ground, there are pācittiya offenses together with dukkaṭa offenses,' and it will also be said, 'Just as here, so everywhere in a case where a pācittiya is incurred, one is not freed from a dukkaṭa.' If, however, one with a wholesome mind says, 'We will do meritorious deeds,' there is no offense. For it will be said: 'He generates a wholesome state by thinking, "I will make an offering to the Buddha, or an offering to the Dhamma, or provide a meal for the Saṅgha." For one with a wholesome mind, there is no offense in going,' and also, 'Just as here, so everywhere, for one with a mind free from the intention to steal, there is no offense.'

Pamādalikhitanti veditabbanti aparabhāge potthakāruḷhakāle pamajjitvā likhitanti veditabbaṃ. Pāḷiyaṃ sesaaṭṭhakathāsu ca “kudālaṃ vā piṭakaṃ vā”ti idameva dvayaṃ vatvā vāsipharasūnaṃ avuttattā tesampi saṅkhepaṭṭhakathādīsu āgatabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “saṅkhepaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana mahāpaccariyañcā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Theyyacittena katattā “dukkaṭehi saddhiṃ pācittiyānī”ti vuttaṃ. Tato paraṃ sabbakiriyāsūti bījaggahaṇato paraṃ kattabbakiriyāsu. Sabbaṃ purimanayenevāti yāva piṭakapariyosānā hatthavārapadavāresu dukkaṭaṃ.

'It should be understood as written through negligence' means it should be understood as written negligently in a later part, at the time of transcribing it into a book. In the Pāḷi and in the remaining commentaries, having stated only these two, 'a hoe or a basket,' and since the adze and the axe are not mentioned, in order to show their inclusion in the condensed commentaries and others, it is said: 'But in the condensed commentary and the Mahāpaccarī, etc.' Because it was done with a mind set on stealing, it is said, 'pācittiya offenses together with dukkaṭa offenses.' 'After that, in all actions' means: in the actions to be performed after the taking of the seed. 'Everything is in accordance with the previous method' means: up to the completion of the basket, for the turns of the hand and the turns of the foot, there is a dukkaṭa offense.

Therehi dassitanti pubbapayogasahapayogadukkaṭesu asammohatthaṃ samodhānetvā dhammasaṅgāhakattherehi dassitaṃ. “Sabbesampi dukkaṭānaṃ imesuyeva aṭṭhasu saṅgahetabbabhāvato itarehi sattahi dukkaṭehi vinimuttaṃ vinayadukkaṭeyeva saṅgahetabba”nti vadanti. Dasavidhaṃ ratananti “muttā maṇi veḷuriyo saṅkho silā pavāḷaṃ rajataṃ jātarūpaṃ lohitaṅgo masāragalla”nti evamāgataṃ dasavidhaṃ ratanaṃ.

'Shown by the elders' means: it was shown by the elder compilers of the Dhamma, who combined the dukkaṭa offenses of preliminary acts and concurrent acts for the sake of non-confusion. They say: 'Since all dukkaṭa offenses are to be included within these eight, that which is distinct from the other seven dukkaṭa offenses—the Vinaya-dukkaṭa—is alone to be included here.' 'The tenfold jewel' means the tenfold jewel that has come down as: 'pearl, gem, beryl, conch, crystal, coral, silver, gold, ruby, and cat's-eye.'

“Maṇi [M 2.0133] muttā veḷuriyo ca saṅkho,

Silā pavāḷaṃ rajatañca hemaṃ;

Salohitaṅgañca masāragallaṃ,

Daseti dhīro ratanāni jaññā”ti. –

“Gem, pearl, and beryl, and conch, crystal, coral, and silver and gold, and ruby and cat’s-eye—the wise should know these ten as the jewels.”

Hi vuttaṃ.

For it is said.

Sattavidhaṃ [V 2.0118] dhaññanti sāli vīhi yavo kaṅgu kudrūso varako godhumoti idaṃ sattavidhaṃ dhaññaṃ. Āvudhabhaṇḍādinti ādi-saddena tūriyabhaṇḍaitthirūpādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Anāmasitabbe vatthumhi dukkaṭaṃ anāmāsadukkaṭaṃ. Durupaciṇṇadukkaṭanti “na kattabba”nti vāritassa katattā duṭṭhu āciṇṇaṃ caritanti durupaciṇṇaṃ, tasmiṃ dukkaṭaṃ durupaciṇṇadukkaṭaṃ. Vinaye paññattaṃ dukkaṭaṃ vinayadukkaṭaṃ. “Saṅghabhedāya parakkamatī”ti sutvā taṃnivāraṇatthāya ñāte atthe avadantassa ñātadukkaṭaṃ. Ekādasa samanubhāsanā nāma bhikkhupātimokkhe cattāro yāvatatiyakā saṅghādisesā, ariṭṭhasikkhāpadanti pañca, bhikkhunīpātimokkhe ekaṃ yāvatatiyakaṃ pārājikaṃ, cattāro saṅghādisesā, caṇḍakāḷīsikkhāpadanti cha. Vassāvāsādiṃ paṭissuṇitvā na sampādentassa paṭissavanimittaṃ dukkaṭaṃ paṭissavadukkaṭaṃ.

The seven kinds of grain are: sāli rice, paddy, barley, millet, kudrūsa, varaka, and wheat; this is the sevenfold grain. Regarding 'weapons, implements, etc.': by the word 'etc.,' it includes musical instruments, images of women, and so forth. In the case of an object that should not be touched, the offense of wrong-doing is an anāmāsadukkaṭa, an offense concerning an untouchable object. The durupaciṇṇadukkaṭa (offense of wrong-doing through wrong practice): because of doing what was forbidden with the words, 'This should not be done,' a wrong practice has been performed; the offense of wrong-doing in that case is a durupaciṇṇadukkaṭa. An offense of wrong-doing prescribed in the Vinaya is a vinayadukkaṭa. Hearing, 'He is striving to create a schism in the Sangha,' and not speaking for the purpose of preventing it when the matter is known, is a ñātadukkaṭa, an offense of wrong-doing through knowing. The eleven formal acts of censure are: in the Bhikkhu Pātimokkha, the four Saṅghādisesa offenses that are concluded by a third announcement, and the Ariṭṭha training rule—making five; in the Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha, one Pārājika offense that is concluded by a third announcement, four Saṅghādisesa offenses, and the Caṇḍakāḷī training rule—making six. For one who, having promised the rains-residence or the like, does not fulfill it, the offense of wrong-doing on account of the promise is a paṭissavadukkaṭa, an offense of wrong-doing through promise.

Pubbasahapayoge ca, anāmāsadurupaciṇṇe;

Vinaye ceva ñāte ca, ñattiyā ca paṭissave;

Aṭṭhete dukkaṭā vuttā, vinaye vinayaññunā.

In preliminary and concurrent actions, and in what concerns an untouchable object and wrong practice; in the Vinaya and in what is known, in a formal motion and in a promise; these eight offenses of wrong-doing are declared in the Vinaya by one who knows the Vinaya.

Sahapayogato paṭṭhāya cettha purimā purimā āpattiyo paṭippassambhantīti āha “atha dhuranikkhepaṃ akatvā”tiādi. Tattha “dhuranikkhepaṃ akatvā”ti vuttattā dhuranikkhepaṃ katvā khaṇantassa purimāpattiyo na paṭippassambhantīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Viyūhanadukkaṭaṃ paṭippassambhati, uddharaṇadukkaṭe patiṭṭhātīti idaṃ pāḷiyaṃ āgatānukkamena dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Yadi pana paṃsuṃ uddharitvā saussāhova puna khaṇati, uddharaṇadukkaṭaṃ paṭippassambhati, khaṇanadukkaṭe patiṭṭhāti.

He said, 'Starting from the concurrent action, the preceding offenses here subside,' and so on, beginning with 'Then, without having abandoned the burden.' Therein, because it is said, 'without having abandoned the burden,' it should be understood that for one who digs after having abandoned the burden, the preceding offenses do not subside. 'The offense of wrong-doing for dismantling subsides, and one becomes established in the offense of wrong-doing for removing'—this is said to show the sequence as it has come down in the Pāḷi. If, however, having removed the soil, one digs again with zeal, the offense of wrong-doing for removing subsides, and one becomes established in the offense of wrong-doing for digging.

Kataṃ karaṇaṃ kiriyāti atthato ekanti āha “virūpā sā kiriyā”ti. Idāni vuttamevatthaṃ parivārapāḷiyā nidassento “vuttampi ceta”ntiādimāha. Tattha aparaddhaṃ viraddhaṃ khalitanti sabbametaṃ yañca dukkaṭanti ettha vuttassa dukkaṭassa pariyāyavacanaṃ. Yañhi duṭṭhu kataṃ, virūpaṃ vā kataṃ[M 2.0134], taṃ dukkaṭaṃ. Taṃ panetaṃ yathā satthārā vuttaṃ, evaṃ akatattā aparaddhaṃ, kusalaṃ virajjhitvā pavattattā viraddhaṃ, ariyavaṃsappaṭipadaṃ anāruḷhattā khalitaṃ. Yaṃ manusso kareti idaṃ panettha opammanidassanaṃ. Tassattho – yathā yaṃ loke manusso āvi vā yadi vā raho pāpaṃ karoti, taṃ dukkaṭanti pavedenti, evamidampi buddhapaṭikuṭṭhena lāmakabhāvena pāpaṃ, tasmā dukkaṭanti veditabbanti.

'An act, a doing, an action'—these are one in meaning; thus he said, 'that action is improper.' Now, illustrating this same meaning with the Pāḷi of the Parivāra, he said, 'And this has been said,' and so on. Therein, 'transgressed' (aparaddha), 'deviated' (viraddha), 'stumbled' (khalita)—all these are synonyms for the 'dukkaṭa' (wrongly done) spoken of here in 'and whatever is wrongly done.' For whatever is badly done, or done improperly, that is a 'dukkaṭa.' And this is 'transgressed' because it was not done as the Teacher taught; it is 'deviated' because it proceeded having deviated from what is wholesome; it is 'stumbled' because it did not ascend to the practice of the noble lineage. 'What a person does'—this here is an illustration by way of comparison. Its meaning is: just as in the world, whatever evil a person does, whether openly or in secret, people declare it to be 'wrongly done,' so too this is evil through its base nature which is despised by the Buddha; therefore, it should be understood as 'wrongly done.'

Yathā [V 2.0119] dukkhā, kucchitā vā gati dugatīti vattabbe “duggatī”ti vuttaṃ, yathā ca kaṭukaṃ phalametassāti kaṭukaphalanti vattabbe “kaṭukapphala”nti vuttaṃ, evamidhāpi thūlattā accayattā ca thūlaccayanti vattabbe “thullaccaya”nti vuttanti dassetuṃ “samparāye ca duggatī”tiādimāha. Saṃyoge pana kate saṃyogaparassa rassattaṃ siddhamevāti manasi katvā “saṃyogabhāvo veditabbo”ti ettakameva vuttaṃ. Ekassa mūleti ekassa santike. Accayo tena samo natthīti desanāgāmīsu accayesu tena samo thūlo accayo natthi. Tenetaṃ iti vuccatīti thūlattā accayassa etaṃ thullaccayanti vuccatīti attho.

Just as 'a painful or despised destination' (dukkhā, kucchitā vā gati), which should be expressed as dugati, is said as duggati; and just as 'that which has a bitter fruit' (kaṭukaṃ phalametassā), which should be expressed as kaṭukaphala, is said as kaṭukapphala; so too here, to show that what should be expressed as thūlaccaya—due to its being a gross (thūla) offense (accaya)—is said as thullaccaya, he stated, 'and a miserable destiny in the future,' and so on. Furthermore, having kept in mind that when a conjunction is made, the shortening of the vowel before the conjunct consonant is established, only this much was said: 'the state of conjunction should be understood.' 'At the root of one' means in the presence of one. 'There is no offense equal to it' means that among the offenses removable by confession, there is no gross offense equal to it. 'Therefore it is called this' means: because of the grossness of the offense, it is called a 'gross offense' (thullaccaya). This is the meaning.

“Sabbatthāpi āmasane dukkaṭaṃ phandāpane thullaccayañca visuṃ visuṃ theyyacittena āmasanaphandāpanapayogaṃ karontasseva hoti, ekapayogena gaṇhantassa pana uddhāre pārājikameva, na dukkaṭathullaccayānī”ti vadanti. Sahapayogaṃ pana akatvāti ettha “pubbapayoge āpannāpattīnaṃ paṭippassaddhiyā abhāvato sahapayogaṃ katvāpi lajjidhammaṃ okkantena pubbapayoge āpannāpattiyo desetabbā”ti tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāvacanaṃ pana kate sahapayoge pubbapayoge āpannāpattīnampi paṭippassaddhiṃ dīpeti, aññathā “sahapayogaṃ pana akatvā”ti idaṃ visesanameva niratthakaṃ siyā. Yañca heṭṭhā vuttaṃ “sace panassa tatthajātake tiṇarukkhalatādimhi chinnepi lajjidhammo okkamati, saṃvaro uppajjati, chedanapaccayā dukkaṭaṃ desetvā muccatī”ti, tampi sahapayoge kate pubbapayoge āpannāpattīnaṃ paṭippassaddhimeva dīpeti sahapayoge chedanapaccayā āpannadukkaṭasseva desanāya vuttattā. Sahapayogato paṭṭhāyevāti ca idaṃ sahapayogaṃ pattassa tato pubbe āpannānaṃ pubbapayogāpattīnampi paṭippassaddhiṃ dīpeti. Tena hi ayamattho viññāyati “yāva sahapayogaṃ na pāpuṇāti, tāva pubbe āpannāpattīnaṃ paṭippassaddhi na [M 2.0135] hoti, sahapayogaṃ pattakālato pana paṭṭhāya tāsampi paṭippassaddhi hotī”ti, tasmā suṭṭhu upaparikkhitvā yuttataraṃ gahetabbaṃ.

They say: 'In all cases, for touching there is an offense of wrong-doing, and for causing to move a gross offense; these occur only for one who performs the efforts of touching and causing to move separately and with a thieving mind. But for one who takes with a single effort, at the point of lifting it is only a Pārājika offense, not the offenses of wrong-doing and gross offense.' Regarding the phrase, 'But without having made a concurrent effort': here, it is stated in all three glosses, 'Because the offenses incurred in the preliminary effort have not subsided, even after making a concurrent effort, one who has entered a state of conscientiousness must confess the offenses incurred in the preliminary effort.' The word of the Commentary, however, indicates the subsidence of even those offenses incurred in the preliminary effort when a concurrent effort is made; otherwise, this qualification, 'But without having made a concurrent effort,' would be meaningless. And what was stated below—'But if, for him, even when grass, trees, creepers, etc., growing there are cut, a state of conscientiousness arises and restraint is born, he is freed after confessing the offense of wrong-doing incurred on account of cutting'—that too indicates the subsidence of offenses incurred in the preliminary effort when a concurrent effort is made, because the confession spoken of is only for the offense of wrong-doing incurred on account of cutting in the concurrent effort. And the phrase 'Starting from the concurrent effort' indicates the subsidence of even the offenses from the preliminary effort that were incurred before that by one who has reached the concurrent effort. Therefore, this meaning is understood: 'As long as one does not reach the concurrent effort, there is no subsidence of the offenses previously incurred. But starting from the time the concurrent effort is reached, there is subsidence of those offenses as well.' Therefore, having investigated thoroughly, the more suitable meaning should be accepted.

Bahukāpi āpattiyo hontu, ekameva desetvā muccatīti etthāyamadhippāyo – sace khaṇanaviyūhanuddharaṇesu dasa dasa katvā āpattiyo āpannā, tāsu uddharaṇe dasa āpattiyo desetvā muccati visabhāgakiriyaṃ patvā purimāpurimāpattīnaṃ paṭippassaddhattāti. Jātivasena pana samānakiriyāya āpannāpattiyo ekattena gahetvā “ekameva desetvā”ti vuttaṃ, tasmā imināpi kurundaṭṭhakathāvacanena paṭhamaṃ mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttapurimāpattipaṭippassaddhimeva samatthayati, na pana ubhinnaṃ aṭṭhakathānaṃ atthato nānākaraṇaṃ atthi. Aparampettha pakāraṃ vaṇṇayanti “samānakiriyāsupi purimapurimakhaṇanapaccayā āpannāpattiyo pacchimapacchimakhaṇanaṃ patvā paṭippassambhantīti [V 2.0120] iminā adhippāyena ‘paṃsukhaṇanādīsu ca lajjidhamme uppanne bahukāpi āpattiyo hontu, ekameva desetvā muccatīti kurundaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vutta’”nti. “Evañca sati ‘bahukāpi āpattiyo hontū’ti na vattabbaṃ bhaveyya, vuttañca, tasmā visabhāgakiriyameva patvā purimāpattīnaṃ paṭippassaddhiṃ icchanteneva bahukāsupi āpattīsu ekameva desetvā muccatīti imasmiṃ ṭhāne visuṃyeveko desanākkamo dassito”tipi vadanti. Ayametesaṃ adhippāyo – yathā idha purimāpattīnaṃ paṭippassaddhi aṭṭhakathācariyappamāṇena gahitā, evaṃ bahukāsupi āpattīsu ekameva desetvā muccatīti idampi idha aṭṭhakathācariyappamāṇatoyeva veditabbaṃ. Yathā ca pāḷiyaṃ pācittiyaṭṭhānepi dukkaṭameva hotīti idha āveṇikaṃ katvā āpattiviseso dassito, evaṃ purimāpattīnaṃ paṭippassaddhiviseso ca desanāviseso ca aṭṭhakathācariyehi dassitoti.

Even if there are many offenses, by confessing just one, one is freed—this is the intended meaning herein: if one has committed ten offenses each in digging, scattering, and removing, then among them, by confessing the ten offenses in removing, one is freed because, upon undertaking a dissimilar action, the preceding offenses have subsided. However, by way of type, the offenses committed through a similar action are taken as one; hence, it is said, 'by confessing just one.' Therefore, by this statement of the Kurundaṭṭhakathā as well, it supports only the subsiding of the preceding offense stated first in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, and there is no difference in meaning between the two commentaries. They explain another method herein: 'Even in similar actions, the offenses committed due to the preceding instances of digging subside upon reaching the succeeding instances of digging. With this intention, it is said in the Kurundaṭṭhakathā, "In digging earth and so on, when a matter for shame has arisen, even if there are many offenses, by confessing just one, one is freed."' They also say: 'And if this were so, the phrase "even if there are many offenses" should not be said, yet it is said. Therefore, by one who desires the subsiding of the preceding offenses only upon reaching a dissimilar action, a distinct sequence of confession is shown in this place, namely: "even in many offenses, one is freed by confessing just one."' This is their intended meaning: just as herein the subsiding of the preceding offenses is taken according to the authority of the commentary teachers, so too, this point that 'even in many offenses, by confessing just one, one is freed' should be understood herein only by the authority of the commentary teachers. And just as in the Pāḷi, 'even in a case for a pācittiya, it is only a dukkaṭa,' a special distinction of offense is shown herein by making it an exception, so too, a special distinction in the subsiding of preceding offenses and a special distinction in confession are shown by the commentary teachers.

Heṭṭhato osīdentoti “sāmikesu āgantvā apassitvā gatesu gaṇhissāmī”ti theyyacittena heṭṭhābhūmiyaṃ osīdento. Bundenāti kumbhiyā heṭṭhimatalena. Evaṃ ekaṭṭhāne ṭhitāya kumbhiyā ṭhānācāvanaṃ chahi ākārehi veditabbanti sambandho. Valayaṃ nīharati, pārājikanti ākāsagataṃ akatvā ghaṃsitvā nīharantassa chinnakoṭito nīhaṭamatte pārājikaṃ. Ito cito ca sāretīti ghaṃsantoyeva ākāsagataṃ akatvā sāreti.

As for 'sinking down from below': it means sinking it into the ground below with a thievish intention, thinking, 'When the owners have come, not seen, and gone, I will take it.' As for 'with the base': it means with the bottom surface of the pot. Thus, the displacement from its position of a pot standing in one place should be understood in six ways—this is the connection. As for 'He removes a bracelet, it is a pārājika': for one who removes it by scraping, without making it airborne, the moment it is removed from the severed end, it is a pārājika. As for 'He moves it from here and there': while scraping, without making it airborne, he moves it.

Chinnamatte [M 2.0136] pārājikanti avassaṃ ce patati, chinnamatte pārājikaṃ. Paricchedoti “pañcamāsakaṃ vā atirekapañcamāsakaṃ vā”ti vuttagaṇanaparicchedo. Apabyūhantoti “heṭṭhā ṭhitaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti hatthena dvidhā karonto. Upaḍḍhakumbhiyanti upaḍḍhapuṇṇāya kumbhiyā. Nanu ca aṭṭhakathācariyappamāṇena saṅkhepaṭṭhakathādīsu vuttampi kasmā na gahetabbanti āha – “vinayavinicchaye hi āgate garuke ṭhātabba”nti. Vinayadhammatāti vinayagarukānaṃ dhammatā. Vinayagarukā hi vinayavinicchaye āgate garuke tiṭṭhanti. Vinayagarukatābyāpanatthañhi vinayagarukoyevettha vinaya-saddena vutto, vinayassa vā esā dhammatā tesaṃ garugāravaṭṭhānassa vinayavisayattā.

As for 'The moment it is cut, it is a pārājika': if it certainly falls, the moment it is cut, it is a pārājika. As for 'demarcation': it is the demarcation of quantity stated as 'five māsakas or more than five māsakas.' As for 'pushing aside': it means dividing it in two with the hand, thinking, 'I will take what is placed below.' As for 'a half-pot': it means of a pot that is half-full. But surely, why should that which is stated in the summary commentaries and so on, by the authority of the commentary teachers, not be accepted?
