To this, he said: 'For when a Vinaya adjudication has arisen, one must stand by the weighty opinion.' 'The nature of the Vinaya' means the nature of those who respect the Vinaya. For those who respect the Vinaya, when a Vinaya adjudication has arisen, stand by the weighty opinion. Indeed, for the purpose of showing respect for the Vinaya, herein 'those who respect the Vinaya' themselves are spoken of by the word 'Vinaya'; or, this is the nature of the Vinaya, because the object of their high regard is a matter of the Vinaya.

Idāni saṅkhepaṭṭhakathādīsu vuttaṃ pāḷiyāpi na sametīti dassento āha “apicā”tiādi. Bhājananti pattādibhājanaṃ. Pattādiṃ apūretvā gaṇhantassa anuddhaṭepi mukhavaṭṭiparicchedo hoti, pūretvā gaṇhantassa pana uddharaṇakāle hotīti āha “mukhavaṭṭiparicchedena vā uddhārena vā”ti. Yadā pana telakumbhīādīsu telādīnaṃ abahubhāvato bhājanaṃ [V 2.0121] nimujjāpetvā gaṇhituṃ na sakkā hoti, tadā mukhavaṭṭiparicchedeneva hoti. Cikkananti thaddhaṃ. Ākaḍḍhanavikaḍḍhanayogganti ettha abhimukhaṃ kaḍḍhanaṃ ākaḍḍhanaṃ, parato kaḍḍhanaṃ vikaḍḍhanaṃ. Paṭinīharitunti attano bhājanato paṭinīharituṃ. Hatthato muttamatte pārājikanti theyyacittena parasantakaggahaṇapayogassa katattā. Mahāaṭṭhakathāyameva “sacepi mariyādaṃ dubbalaṃ katvā sukkhataḷākassa udakanibbahanaṭṭhānaṃ udakaniddhamanatumbaṃ vā pidahati, aññato ca gamanamagge vā pāḷiṃ bandhati, sukkhamātikaṃ vā ujuṃ karoti, pacchā deve vuṭṭhe udakaṃ āgantvā mariyādaṃ bhindati, sabbattha bhaṇḍadeyya”nti vuttattā “taṃ pana tattheva sukkhataḷāke sukkhamātikāya ujukaraṇavinicchayena virujjhatī”ti vuttaṃ.

Now, to show that what is stated in the summary commentaries and so on does not accord with the Pāḷi text, he says: 'Moreover,' and so on. 'Vessel' refers to a vessel such as a bowl. For one who takes without filling a bowl or other container, the demarcation is at the rim even without lifting it. But for one who takes after filling it, it occurs at the time of lifting. Hence, he says: 'either by the demarcation of the rim or by lifting.' However, when in vessels like oil pots, due to the small quantity of oil or other contents, it is not possible to take by submerging a vessel, then the demarcation is solely by the rim. 'Sticky' means stiff. As for 'fit for pulling and dragging': herein, pulling toward oneself is 'pulling,' and pulling away is 'dragging.' 'To withdraw' means to withdraw from one’s own vessel. As for 'Once released from the hand, it entails a pārājika': this is because the effort of taking what belongs to another has been made with a thievish intention. In the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā itself, it is stated: 'Even if one weakens a boundary and blocks the water outlet of a dried-up pond or a water drain, or builds an embankment on a path for passage elsewhere, or straightens a dried-up channel, and later, when rain falls, the water comes and breaks the boundary—in all such cases, compensation is due.' Because this is stated, it is said: 'But that is contradicted by the ruling on straightening a dried-up channel in that very dried-up pond.'

Avahāralakkhaṇanti pañcavīsatiyā avahāresu ekampi avahāralakkhaṇaṃ, ṭhānācāvanapayogo eva vā. Uddhāreti kumbhiyā phuṭṭhaṭṭhānato kesaggamattepi uddhaṭe. Yuttanti ṭhānācāvanapayogasabbhāvato yuttaṃ. Saṅgopanatthāyāti iminā suddhacittataṃ dasseti. Palibujjhissatīti nivāressati. Vuttanayeneva pārājikanti hatthato muttamatteyeva pārājikaṃ. Suddhacittova [M 2.0137] uddharatīti kumbhiyaṃ telassa ākiraṇato puretarameva suddhacitto nikkhipitvā pacchā suddhacittova uddharati. Neva avahāroti theyyacittena avaharaṇapayogassa akatattā. Attano bhājanattā pana “na gīvā”ti vuttaṃ, anāpattimattameva vuttaṃ, na pana evaṃ vicāritanti adhippāyo. Atha vā anāpattimattameva vuttanti imināpi tattha “gīvā”ti vacanābhāvato “na gīvā”ti pubbe vuttamahāaṭṭhakathāvādameva patiṭṭhāpeti, pacchā dassitena kurundivādenapi mahāaṭṭhakathāvādova samatthito. Attano bhaṇḍanti telākiraṇato puretarameva attano kumbhiyaṃ suddhacittena ṭhapitaṃ pītatelaṃ attano parikkhāraṃ. Sammohaṭṭhānanti āpattivinicchayavasena sammohaṭṭhānaṃ.

The characteristic of taking is any one of the twenty-five methods of taking, or simply the effort to move it from its place. He takes it: even if he lifts it just a hair’s breadth from where it was touching in the pot. Suitable: it is suitable because of the existence of an effort to move it from its place. For the purpose of concealing: this shows the purity of mind. He will obstruct: he will prevent. In the manner stated, it is a pārājika offense: it becomes a pārājika offense as soon as it is released from the hand. With a pure mind, he takes it: from the time of pouring the oil into the pot, having placed it beforehand with a pure mind, he later takes it out with a pure mind. It is not theft: because the effort of taking was not done with a thieving mind. But since it is his own vessel, it is said, “not the neck”—this is merely stated as non-offense, but the intention is not to consider it in this way. Alternatively, by this statement 'it is merely stated as non-offense': because there is no mention of “the neck” in that context, it establishes the view of the Great Commentary previously stated as “not the neck.” Later, even with the explanation given in the Kurundi, the position of the Great Commentary is supported. His own property: the yellow oil placed in his own pot with a pure mind before pouring in oil is his own requisite. A ground for delusion: a ground for delusion with regard to settling offenses.

Bahigataṃ nāma hotīti tato paṭṭhāya telassa aṭṭhānabhāvato adhomukhabhāvato ca bahigataṃ nāma hoti. Anto paṭṭhāya chidde kariyamāne telassa nikkhamitvā gatagataṭṭhānaṃ bhājanasaṅkhyameva gacchatīti āha – “bāhirantato pādagghanake gaḷite pārājika”nti. Yathā tathā vā katassāti bāhirantato abbhantarato vā paṭṭhāya katassa. Majjhe ṭhapetvā katachiddeti majjhe thokaṃ kapālaṃ ṭhapetvā pacchā taṃ chindantena katachidde. “Mariyādacchedane anto ṭhatvā bahimukho chindanto bahi antena kāretabbo, bahi ṭhatvā antomukho chindanto anto antena kāretabbo, anto ca bahi ca chinditvā majjhe ṭhapetvā taṃ chindanto majjhena kāretabbo”ti (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.108) vuttattā “taḷākassa ca mariyādabhedena sametī”ti vuttaṃ. Idamettha yuttanti [V 2.0122] anto ca bahi ca paṭṭhāya katachidde majjhena kāretabbo. Anto paṭṭhāya kate pana bāhirantena, bahi paṭṭhāya kate abbhantarena kāretabboti ayaṃ tippakāropi ettha vemaṭṭhachidde yutto. Udake katapayogassa abhāvato “ṭhānācāvanapayogassa abhāvā”ti vuttaṃ.

‘It is called 'gone outside'’: from that point onward, because of the oil's inability to stay and its downward-facing nature, it is called 'gone outside.' When a hole is being made starting from within, the oil, having flowed out, wherever it goes, goes only to what is reckoned as the vessel; thus it is said: 'If it spills from the foot-measure, from the outer boundary, it is a pārājika offense.' However it is done: of that which is done starting from the outer boundary or from the inner boundary. In a hole made by leaving something in the middle: in a hole made by one who, having left a small piece of the pot in the middle, later cuts it. 'Regarding cutting a boundary: if one stands inside and cuts facing outward, the offense should be reckoned by the outer boundary; if one stands outside and cuts facing inward, the offense should be reckoned by the inner boundary; if one cuts both inside and outside and, having left the middle, cuts that, the offense should be reckoned by the middle.' Because it is said thus, it is said, 'it is similar to breaking the boundary of a pond.' This is suitable here: in a hole made starting from both inside and outside, the offense should be reckoned by the middle. But in one made starting from the inside, it should be reckoned by the outer boundary; in one made starting from the outside, it should be reckoned by the inner boundary. This threefold distinction is also suitable here in the case of a hole in a Vemaṭṭha. Due to the absence of an effort made on the water, it is said, 'because of the absence of an effort of displacement.'

Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ tāva vuttanti mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Patthinnassa khādanaṃ itarassa pānañca sappiādīnaṃ paribhogoti āha – “akhāditabbaṃ vā apātabbaṃ vā karotī”ti. Kathaṃ pana tathā karotīti āha “uccāraṃ vā passāvaṃ vā”tiādi. Kasmā panettha dukkaṭaṃ vuttanti āha “ṭhānācāvanassa natthitāya dukkaṭa”nti. Purimadvayanti bhedanaṃ chaḍḍanañca. Kasmā na sametīti [M 2.0138] āha “tañhī”tiādi. Kumbhijajjarakaraṇenāti puṇṇakumbhiyā jajjarakaraṇena. Mātikāujaukaraṇenāti udakapuṇṇāya mātikāya ujukaraṇena. Ekalakkhaṇanti bhedanaṃ kumbhijajjarakaraṇena chaḍḍanaṃ mātikāya ujukaraṇena saddhiṃ ekasabhāvaṃ ṭhānācāvanapayogasabbhāvato. Pacchimaṃ pana dvayanti jhāpanaṃ aparibhogakaraṇañca.

In the commentary, it is first stated: it is stated in the Great Commentary. The eating of what is set aside, the drinking of the other, and the use of ghee and so on is meant; therefore, he says: 'he makes it uneatable or undrinkable.' But how does he do so? He says: 'excrement or urine,' and so on. Why is a dukkaṭa offense stated here? He says: 'because of the absence of displacement, it is a dukkaṭa offense.' The first pair: breaking and discarding. Why do they not accord? He says: 'That indeed...' and so on. By making the pot dilapidated: by making a full pot dilapidated. By straightening the water-channel: by straightening a water-channel full of water. A single characteristic: breaking by making the pot dilapidated and discarding by straightening the water-channel are of one nature, because of the existence of an effort of displacement. The latter pair, however, is burning and making unfit for use.

Ettha evaṃ vinicchayaṃ vadantīti ettha mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vutte eke ācariyā evaṃ vinicchayaṃ vadanti. Pacchimadvayaṃ sandhāya vuttanti ettha purimadvaye vinicchayo heṭṭhā vuttānusārena sakkā viññātunti tattha kiñci avatvā pacchimadvayaṃ sandhāya ṭhānācāvanassa natthitāya dukkaṭanti idaṃ vuttanti adhippāyo. Theyyacittenāti attano vā parassa vā kātukāmatāvasena uppannatheyyacittena. Vināsetukāmatāyāti hatthapādādiṃ chindanto viya kevalaṃ vināsetukāmatāya. Purimadvaye kiṃ hoti, kiṃ adhippāyena na kiñci vuttanti āha – “purimadvaye pana…pe… pārājika”nti. Tattha vuttanayena bhindantassa vā chaḍḍentassa vāti muggarena pothetvā bhindantassa udakaṃ vā vālikaṃ vā ākiritvā uttarāpentassāti attho. Ayuttanti ceti pāḷiyaṃ purimapadadvayepi dukkaṭasseva vuttattā “purimadvaye…pe… pārājikanti idaṃ ayutta”nti yadi tumhākaṃ siyāti attho. Nāti ayuttabhāvappasaṅgaṃ nisedhetvā tattha kāraṇamāha “aññathā gahetabbatthato”ti. Kathaṃ panettha attho gahetabboti āha “pāḷiyaṃ hī”tiādi. Nāsetukāmatāpakkhe heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva atthassa avirujjhanato “theyyacittapakkhe”ti vuttaṃ. “Evaṃ vinicchayaṃ vadantī”ti ito paṭṭhāya vuttassa sabbassapi ekasseva vacanattā “evameke vadantī”ti nigamanavasena vuttaṃ.

Here, some teachers explain the decision in this way: here, regarding what is said in the Great Commentary, some teachers explain the decision thus. It is said with reference to the latter pair: here, because the decision on the first pair can be known according to what was previously stated, without saying anything about that, it is said with reference to the latter pair, 'it is a dukkaṭa offense because of the absence of displacement'—this is the intention. 'With a thieving mind': with a thieving mind that has arisen through the desire to take for oneself or for another. 'With the intention to destroy': solely with the intention to destroy, like one cutting off hands, feet, and so on. What happens in the first two cases? With what intention is nothing said? He says: 'But in the first two cases... a pārājika offense.' There, according to the method stated, 'of one who breaks or of one who discards' means: of one who breaks by striking with a mallet, or of one who causes to overflow by scattering water or sand. This is the meaning. And as for 'It is unsuitable': because in the Pāḷi text only a dukkaṭa offense is stated for the first two cases, the meaning is, 'if it were your view that this statement, «in the first two cases... a pārājika offense», is unsuitable.' No: having denied the implication of unsuitability, he states the reason there: 'because the meaning is to be taken otherwise.' But how is the meaning to be taken here? He says: 'For in the Pāḷi...' and so on. In the case of the intention to destroy, because the meaning does not conflict with the method previously stated, it is said, 'in the case of a thieving mind.' 'Some explain the decision in this way': because all that has been said starting from this point is the single statement of one person, it is stated by way of conclusion, 'thus some say.'

Idāni yathāvuttavasena pāḷiyā atthe gayhamāne mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ catunnampi sāmaññato vuttassa pacchimadvayaṃ sandhāya vuttanti vacane visesābhāvato pāḷiyaṃ vuttesu catūsu padesu “chaḍḍeti [V 2.0123] vā aparibhogaṃ vā karotī”ti imesaṃ padānaṃ visesābhāvappasaṅgato ca sayaṃ aññathā pāḷiṃ aṭṭhakathañca saṃsanditvā atthaṃ dassetukāmo “ayaṃ panettha sāro”tiādimāha. Vinītavatthumhi “saṅghassa puñjakitaṃ tiṇaṃ theyyacitto jhāpesī”si (pārā. 156) vuttattā vinītavatthumhi tiṇajjhāpako viyāti imināva [M 2.0139] ṭhānā acāvetukāmovāti etthāpi theyyacittena ṭhānā acāvetukāmoti idaṃ vuttameva hotīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Achaḍḍetukāmoyevāti etthāpi theyyacittenāti sambandhitabbaṃ. Idañhi theyyacittapakkhaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ nāsetukāmatāpakkhassa vakkhamānattā. Tenevāha “nāsetukāmatāpakkhe panā”tiādi. Itarathāpi yujjatīti theyyacittābhāvā ṭhānā cāvetukāmassapi dukkaṭaṃ yujjatīti vuttaṃ hoti.

Now, when the meaning of the Pāḷi is being understood according to what has been stated, because there is no distinction in the statement in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā that it was said with reference to the latter two of the four generally mentioned cases, and because of the implication of no distinction between these terms, ‘discards’ or ‘renders unusable,’ among the four terms stated in the Pāḷi, he, wishing to show the meaning by reconciling the Pāḷi and the commentary himself in another way, said, ‘But this is the essence here,’ and so on. Because it is said in the Vinītavatthu, ‘With a thieving mind, he burned a pile of grass belonging to the Saṅgha,’ it should be understood that just as with the grass-burner in the Vinītavatthu, by this very statement, here too in the case of ‘intending to remove it from its place,’ this means ‘intending to remove it from its place with a thieving mind’ was indeed said. Here too, in the case of ‘intending only not to discard it,’ it should be connected with ‘with a thieving mind.’ For this was said with reference to the case of a thieving mind, since the case of intending to destroy is about to be stated. For that very reason, he said, ‘But in the case of intending to destroy,’ and so on. The statement ‘Even otherwise it is suitable’ means that because of the absence of a thieving mind, a dukkaṭa offense is suitable even for one who intends to remove it from its place.

Bhūmaṭṭhakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Bhūmaṭṭhakathā is concluded.

Ākāsaṭṭhakathāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Ākāsaṭṭhakathā

96. Ākāsaṭṭhakathāyaṃ mukhatuṇḍakenāti mukhaggena. Kalāpaggenāti piñchakalāpassa aggena. Pasāretīti gahaṇatthaṃ pasāreti. Aggahetvā vāti leḍḍuādīhi paharitvā nayanavasena aggahetvā vā. Ākāsaṭṭhavinicchaye vuccamānepi tappasaṅgena ākāsaṭṭhassa vehāsaṭṭhādibhāvamupagatepi asammohatthaṃ “yasmiṃ aṅge nilīyatī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Antovatthumhīti parikkhittavatthussa anto. Antogāmeti parikkhittassa gāmassa anto. Aparikkhitte pana vatthumhi, gāme vā ṭhitaṭṭhānameva ṭhānaṃ. Aṭavimukhaṃ karotīti araññābhimukhaṃ karoti. Rakkhatīti tena payogena tassa icchitaṭṭhānaṃ agatattā rakkhati. Bhūmiyā gacchantaṃ sandhāya “dutiyapadavāre vā”ti vuttaṃ. Gāmato nikkhantassāti parikkhittagāmato nikkhantassa. Kapiñjaro nāma ekā pakkhijāti.

96. In the Ākāsaṭṭhakathā, 'mukhatuṇḍakena' means with the tip of the beak. 'Kalāpaggena' means with the tip of the tail-feather bundle. 'Pasāreti' means one spreads it out for the purpose of grasping. 'Aggahetvā vā' means either having struck it with a clod and so on, or not having grasped it by way of directing it. Even though it is said in the determination of the sky-dweller that through that connection, the sky-dweller has attained the state of being a sky-dweller and so on, for the purpose of non-confusion, it is said, 'on which limb it hides,' and so on. 'Antovatthumhi' means inside an enclosed property. 'Antogāme' means inside an enclosed village. But in an unenclosed property or village, the very place where one stands is the 'place'. 'Aṭavimukhaṃ karoti' means one makes it face the forest. 'Rakkhati' means that by that effort, because it has not gone to its desired place, one guards it. With reference to one going on the ground, it was said, 'or in the section of the second term.' 'Gāmato nikkhantassa' means of one who has gone out from an enclosed village. Kapiñjara is the name of a certain species of bird.

Ākāsaṭṭhakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Ākāsaṭṭhakathā is concluded.

Vehāsaṭṭhakathāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Vehāsaṭṭhakathā

97. Vehāsaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana cīvaravaṃse ṭhapitassa cīvarassa ākaḍḍhane yathāvuttappadesātikkamo ekadvaṅgulamattākaḍḍhanena siyāti adhippāyena vuttaṃ “ekadvaṅgulamattākaḍḍhaneneva pārājika”nti. Idañca tādisaṃ nātimahantaṃ cīvaravaṃsadaṇḍakaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, mahante pana tato adhikamattākaḍḍhaneneva [M 2.0140] siyā. Rajjukena bandhitvāti ekāya rajjukoṭiyā cīvaraṃ bandhitvā [V 2.0124] aparāya koṭiyā cīvaravaṃsaṃ bandhitvā ṭhapitacīvaraṃ. Muttamatte aṭṭhatvā patanakasabhāvattā “mutte pārājika”nti vuttaṃ.

97. In the Vehāsaṭṭhakathā, however, regarding the pulling of a robe placed on a robe-pole, the statement, 'a pārājika is incurred by a pulling of the measure of just one or two finger-breadths,' was said with the intention that the transgression of the aforementioned place would occur by a pulling of one or two finger-breadths. And this was said with reference to such a robe-pole or rod that is not very large; with a large one, however, it would be only by a pulling of a measure greater than that. As for 'tied with a cord': it is a robe placed by tying the robe with one end of a cord and tying the robe-pole with the other end. Because it has the nature of falling, not staying, just upon being released, it is said, 'when released, it is a pārājika.'

Ekamekassa phuṭṭhokāsamatte atikkante pārājikanti bhittiṃ aphusāpetvā ṭhapitattā vuttaṃ. Bhittiṃ nissāya ṭhapitanti paṭipāṭiyā ṭhapitesu nāgadantādīsuyeva āropetvā bhittiṃ phusāpetvā ṭhapitaṃ. Paṇṇantaraṃ āropetvā ṭhapitāti aññehi ṭhapitaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ.

As for 'For each one, when the measure of the touched place is transgressed, it is a pārājika': this is said because it was placed without making it touch the wall. As for 'placed leaning against a wall': it is placed upon things like elephant-tusk pegs that are standing in sequence, making it touch the wall. As for 'having placed it by way of an inscription': this is said with reference to an inscription placed by others.

Vehāsaṭṭhakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Vehāsaṭṭhakathā is concluded.

Udakaṭṭhakathāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Udakaṭṭhakathā

98. Udakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ sandamānaudake nikkhittaṃ na tiṭṭhatīti āha “asandanake udake”ti. Anāpattīti hatthavārapadavāresu dukkaṭāpattiyā abhāvaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Kaḍḍhatīti heṭṭhato osāreti. Uppalādīsūti ādi-saddena padumapuṇḍarīkādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Rattaṃ padumaṃ, setaṃ puṇḍarīkaṃ. Setaṃ vā padumaṃ, rattaṃ puṇḍarīkaṃ. Atha vā rattaṃ vā hotu setaṃ vā satapattaṃ padumaṃ, ūnasatapattaṃ puṇḍarīkaṃ. Vatthu pūratīti pārājikavatthu pahoti. Tasmiṃ chinnamatte pārājikanti udakato accuggatassa udakavinimuttaṭṭhānato chedanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Yaṃ vatthuṃ pūretīti yaṃ pupphaṃ pārājikavatthuṃ pūreti. Dasahi pupphehi katakalāpo hatthako, mahantaṃ kalāpaṃ katvā baddhaṃ bhārabaddhaṃ. Rajjukesu tiṇāni santharitvāti ettha “dve rajjukāni udakapiṭṭhe ṭhapetvā tesaṃ upari tiriyato tiṇāni santharitvā tesaṃ upari bandhitvā vā abandhitvā vā tiriyatoyeva pupphāni ṭhapetvā heṭṭhato gatāni dve rajjukāni ukkhipitvā pupphamatthake ṭhapentī”ti vadanti.

98. In the Udakaṭṭhakathā, because an object placed in flowing water does not stay, he said, 'in non-flowing water.' As for 'no offense': this is said with reference to the absence of a dukkaṭa offense in the cases of hand-turns and foot-turns. 'He drags' means he moves it down from below. In 'water lilies, etc.', the word 'etc.' includes the paduma, puṇḍarīka, and so on. The red one is a paduma; the white one is a puṇḍarīka. Or, the white one is a paduma; the red one is a puṇḍarīka. Alternatively, whether it be red or white, that with a hundred petals is a paduma; that with less than a hundred petals is a puṇḍarīka. 'It fulfills the object' means the object for a pārājika is sufficient. 'Just upon that being cut, it is a pārājika' is said with reference to cutting that which has emerged high up from the water from a place free from water. 'Whatever object it fulfills' means whatever flower fulfills the object for a pārājika. A bunch made with ten flowers is a 'handful' (hatthako); a large bunch made and tied is a 'load' (bhārabaddhaṃ). Regarding 'having spread grass on ropes', in this connection they say: 'Having placed two ropes on the surface of the water, having spread grass crosswise on top of them, having placed the flowers on top of them either tied or untied, and having lifted the two ropes that went underneath from below, they place them on top of the flowers.'

Kesaggamattampi yathāṭhitaṭṭhānato cāvetīti pārimantena phuṭṭhokāsaṃ, orimantena kesaggamattaṃ cāveti. Sakalamudakanti daṇḍena phuṭṭhokāsagataṃ sakalamudakaṃ. Na udakaṃ ṭhānanti attanā kataṭṭhānassa aṭṭhānattā. Idaṃ ubhayanti ettha “bandhanaṃ amocetvā…pe… pārājika”nti idamevekaṃ, “paṭhamaṃ bandhanaṃ…pe… ṭhānaparicchedo”ti idaṃ dutiyaṃ. Paduminiyanti padumagacche. Uppāṭitāyāti parehi attano atthāya uppāṭitāya.

As for 'he displaces it even a hair's breadth from its original position': he displaces the touched place with the far end, and displaces it by a hair's breadth with the near end. As for 'all the water': it is all the water that has gone to the place touched by the stick. As for 'it is not the water's place': this is because a place made by oneself is not a proper place. As for 'this is both': here, 'without releasing the binding... a pārājika' is one; 'the first binding... the determination of the place' is the second. 'In a lotus pond' means in a lotus thicket. 'Having been uprooted' means having been uprooted by others for their own purpose.

Bahi [M 2.0141] ṭhapiteti udakato bahi ṭhapite. Hatthakavasena khuddakaṃ katvā

As for 'when placed outside': it means when placed outside of the water. Having made it small by way of a handful,

Baddhaṃ kalāpabaddhaṃ. Muḷālanti kandaṃ. Pattaṃ vā pupphaṃ vāti idaṃ kaddamassa anto pavisitvā ṭhitaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Sakalamudakanti [V 2.0125] vāpiādīsu pariyāpannaṃ sakalamudakaṃ. Niddhamanatumbanti vāpiyā udakassa nikkhamanamaggaṃ. Udakavāhakanti mahāmātikaṃ. Na avahāroti idaṃ pubbasadisaṃ na hotīti āha – “kasmā…pe… evarūpā hi tattha katikā”ti. Avahāro natthīti sabbasādhāraṇe apariggahaṭṭhāne gahitattā. Mātikaṃ āropetvāti khuddakamātikaṃ āropetvā. Maritvā…pe… tiṭṭhantīti ettha “matamacchānaṃyeva tesaṃ santakattā amate gaṇhantassa natthi avahāro”ti vadanti.

'Bound' means bound in a bunch. 'Lotus root' means the tuber. 'A leaf or a flower' is said with reference to that which has entered and remains inside the mud. 'All the water' means all the water included in reservoirs and so on. 'The draining gourd' means the exit path for the water of the reservoir. 'The water channel' means a large canal. As for 'there is no theft': this is not like the previous case, therefore he said, 'Why... for such is the agreement there.' 'There is no theft' is because it was taken in a place not owned, a place that is common to all. 'Having laid a channel' means having laid a small channel. Regarding 'having died... they remain', in this connection they say: 'Because only the dead fish are their property, for one who takes the living ones, there is no theft.'

Udakaṭṭhakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Commentary on Water is concluded.

Nāvaṭṭhakathāvaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Commentary on Boats

99. Nāvaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana yā bandhanā muttamatte ṭhānā na cavatīti iminā caṇḍasote baddhanāvaṃ paṭikkhipati. Tāva dukkaṭanti “bandhanaṃ moceti, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti evaṃ mocentassa paññattaṃ dukkaṭaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Thullaccayampi pārājikampi hotīti ettha paṭhamaṃ ṭhānā acāvetvā mutte thullaccayaṃ, paṭhamaṃ ṭhānā cāvetvā mutte pārājikanti veditabbaṃ.

99. However, in the Commentary on Boats, by the statement, 'which, when merely released from its mooring, does not move from its place,' it rejects the case of a boat tied in a swift current. As for 'a dukkaṭa offense,' this is stated in reference to the dukkaṭa offense prescribed for one who releases in this way: 'He releases the mooring; there is an offense of dukkaṭa.' Regarding the statement, 'There may also be a thullaccaya or a pārājika,' it should be understood that if it is released without first being moved from its place, it is a thullaccaya; if it is first moved from its place and then released, it is a pārājika.

“Pāse baddhasūkaro viyā”tiādinā vuttaṃ sandhāyāha “tattha yutti pubbe vuttā evā”ti. Vippanaṭṭhā nāvāti visamavātādīhi vināsaṃ patvā udake nimujjitvā heṭṭhā bhūmitalaṃ appatvā majjhe ṭhitaṃ sandhāya vadati. Teneva “adho vā opilāpentassa…pe… nāvātalena phuṭṭhokāsaṃ mukhavaṭṭiṃ atikkantamatte pārājika”nti vuttaṃ. Opilāpentassāti osīdāpentassa. Atikkantamatteti phuṭṭhokāsaṃ atikkantamatte. Eseva nayoti muttamatte pārājikanti dasseti.

With reference to what was said beginning with 'like a boar tied with a snare,' he says, 'the reasoning there is just as was stated before.' As for 'a lost boat,' this is said in reference to one that, having come to destruction through contrary winds and so on, has sunk in the water and is situated in the middle without having reached the bottom ground. For that very reason, it is said: 'Or for one causing it to sink below... (and so on)... a pārājika offense occurs as soon as the rim of the opening has passed beyond the place touched by the bottom of the boat.' 'For one causing it to sink' (opilāpentassa) means for one causing it to submerge. 'As soon as it has passed' (atikkantamatteti) means at the moment of passing beyond the place that was touched. This is the method; it shows that it is a pārājika offense as soon as it is released.

Nāvākaḍḍhanayoggamahāyottatāya yottakoṭito paṭṭhāya sakalampi “ṭhāna”nti vuttaṃ.

Because it is a great rope suitable for pulling a boat, everything from the end of the rope onwards is called the 'place'.

Asatipi vāte yathā vātaṃ gaṇhāti, tathā ṭhapitattā “vātaṃ gaṇhāpetī”ti vuttaṃ. Balavā ca vāto āgammāti iminā [M 2.0142] asati vāte ayaṃ payogo katoti dasseti. Teneva “puggalassa natthi avahāro”ti vuttaṃ. Sati pana vāte kato payogo ṭhānācāvanapayogoyevāti mātikāujukaraṇe viya attheva avahāroti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ṭhānācāvanapayogo na hotīti sukkhamātikāujukaraṇe viya asati vāte katapayogattā. Bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ pana hotīti nāvāsāmikassa bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ hoti.

Even when there is no wind, since it is placed in such a way as to catch the wind, it is said, 'it causes it to catch the wind.' And by the text 'a strong wind comes,' it is shown that this effort is made when there is no wind. Therefore, it is said, 'there is no theft for the person.' But when there is wind, the effort made is indeed the effort of moving from the place; thus, just as in the case of straightening a plumb line, it should be understood that there is indeed a theft. It is not an effort of moving from the place because, like straightening a dry plumb line, it is an effort made when there is no wind. As for 'compensation is due,' this means compensation is due to the boat-owner.

Nāvaṭṭhakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Commentary on Boats is concluded.

Yānaṭṭhakathāvaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Commentary on Vehicles

100. Yānaṭṭhakathāyaṃ [V 2.0126] dukayuttassāti dvīhi goṇehi yuttassa. Ayuttakanti goṇehi ayuttaṃ. Kappakatāti yathā dvīhi bhāgehi heṭṭhā patiṭṭhāti, evaṃ katā. Tīṇi vā cattāri vā ṭhānānīti akappakatāya upatthambhaniyā vasena tīṇi ṭhānāni, kappakatāya vasena cattāri ṭhānānīti. Tathā pathaviyaṃ ṭhapitassa tīṇi ṭhānānīti sambandho. Tanti phalakassa vā dārukassa vā upari ṭhapitaṃ pathaviyaṃ ṭhapitañca. Dvīhi akkhasīsehīti dvīhi akkhakoṭīhi. Dārūnaṃ upari ṭhapitassāti dvinnaṃ dārūnaṃ upari dvīhi akkhakoṭīhi olambetvā sakaṭasālāyaṃ ṭhapitassa. Heṭṭhimatalassāti sakaṭabāhāya bhūmiṃ phusitvā ṭhitassa heṭṭhimabhāgassa. Sesaṃ nāvāyaṃ vuttasadisanti iminā “yadi pana taṃ evaṃ gacchantaṃ pakatigamanaṃ upacchinditvā aññaṃ disābhāgaṃ neti, pārājikaṃ. Sayameva yaṃ kañci gāmaṃ sampattaṃ ṭhānā acāventova vikkiṇitvā gacchati, nevatthi avahāro, bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ pana hotī”ti imaṃ nayaṃ atidissati.

100. In the Commentary on Vehicles, 'of one yoked to a pair' (dukayuttassa) means of one yoked to two oxen. 'Unyoked' (ayuttakaṃ) means not yoked to oxen. 'Constructed' (kappakatā) means made in such a way that it stands on two parts below. 'Three or four places' means that for an unconstructed one, by means of props, there are three places; for a constructed one, there are four places. Similarly, the connection is: 'for one placed on the ground, there are three places.' 'That' (tanti) refers to that which is placed on top of a plank or a log, and that which is placed on the ground. 'With two axle-heads' (dvīhi akkhasīsehi) means with two axle-ends. 'Of that placed on top of wood' (dārūnaṃ upari ṭhapitassa) means of that placed in a cart-shed, suspended by its two axle-ends on top of two pieces of wood. 'Of the lower surface' (heṭṭhimatalassa) means of the lower part of the cart-pole that is situated touching the ground. 'The rest is similar to what was said for the boat'—by this, it points to the following method: 'But if one interrupts its natural course while it is going along and directs it to another direction, it is a pārājika offense. If it reaches some village by itself, and one sells it and departs without moving it from its place, there is no theft, but compensation is due.'

Yānaṭṭhakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Commentary on Vehicles is concluded.

Bhāraṭṭhakathāvaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Commentary on Burdens

101. Bhāraṭṭhakathāyaṃ purimagale galavāṭakoti purimagale uparimagalavāṭako. Uraparicchedamajjheti urapariyantassa majjhe. Anāṇattattāti “asukaṭṭhānaṃ nehī”ti anāṇattattā. Yo cāyaṃ sīsabhāre [M 2.0143] vuttoti yo cāyaṃ vinicchayo sīsabhāre vutto. Sīsādīhi vā gahito hotūti sambandho. Tādisanti tappaṭicchādanasamatthaṃ.

101. In the Commentary on Burdens, 'the knot of the front load' (purimagale galavāṭako) means the knot of the upper load at the front. 'Between the chest boundary' (uraparicchedamajjhe) means in the middle of the chest's extent. 'Because it is not commanded' (anāṇattattā) means because it is not ordered, 'take it to such a place.' 'And this is said in the head-load' (yo cāyaṃ sīsabhāre vutto) refers to the judgment stated regarding the head-load. 'Or let it be grasped by the head, etc.' is the connection. 'Such' (tādisaṃ) means capable of covering that.

Bhāraṭṭhakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Commentary on Burdens is concluded.

Ārāmaṭṭhakathāvaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Commentary on Monasteries

102. Ārāmaṭṭhakathāyaṃ bandhananti pupphānaṃ vaṇṭe patiṭṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ. Abhiyuñjatīti codeti aḍḍaṃ karoti. Adinnādānassa payogattāti sahapayogamāha vatthumhiyeva katapayogattā. Sahapayogavasena hetaṃ dukkaṭaṃ. Vinicchayappasutanti vinicchaye niyuttaṃ. Kakkhaḷoti dāruṇo. Dhuraṃ nikkhipatīti ussāhaṃ ṭhapeti, attano santakakaraṇe nirussāho hotīti attho. Kūṭaḍḍakārakopi [V 2.0127] sace dhuraṃ na nikkhipati, natthi avahāroti āha “sace sayampi katadhuranikkhepo hotī”ti. Sayampīti abhiyuñjakopi. Katadhuranikkhepoti “na dāni naṃ imassa dassāmī”ti evaṃ tassa dāne katadhuranikkhepo. Kiṅkārappaṭissāvibhāveti “kiṃ karomi kiṃ karomī”ti evaṃ kiṅkārameva paṭissuṇanto vicaratīti kiṅkārapaṭissāvī, tassa bhāvo kiṅkārapaṭissāvibhāvo, tasmiṃ, attano vasavattibhāveti vuttaṃ hoti.

102. In the Commentary on Monasteries, 'binding' (bandhanaṃ) refers to the place established on the stalks of flowers. 'Presses the claim' (abhiyuñjati) means accuses or makes a claim. 'Because it is an attempt at theft' (adinnādānassa payogattā)—this refers to a direct attempt, because the attempt is made on the object itself. By means of this direct attempt, it is a dukkaṭa offense. 'Engaged in judgment' (vinicchayappasutaṃ) means appointed to judgment. 'Harsh' (kakkhaḷo) means cruel. 'Lays down the burden' (dhuraṃ nikkhipati) means gives up effort; the meaning is that he becomes without effort in making it his own property. Even a false claimant, if he does not lay down the burden, there is no theft—thus it is said, 'if he himself has also laid down the burden.' 'He himself also' (sayampi) refers to the claimant as well. 'Having laid down the burden' (katadhuranikkhepo) means having laid down the burden with regard to giving it to him, thinking, 'I will not give it to him now.' In the state of one who responds with 'What shall I do?' (kiṅkārappaṭissāvibhāve): one who wanders about responding only with 'What shall I do? What shall I do?' is a kiṅkārapaṭissāvī. The state of being such is kiṅkārapaṭissāvibhāvo. In that state, it is said to be the state of being under one's own control.

Ukkocaṃ datvāti lañjaṃ datvā. Kūṭavinicchayikānanti kūṭavinicchaye niyuttānaṃ vinayadharānaṃ. “Gaṇhā”ti avatvā “asāmikassa sāmiko aya”ntiādinā pariyāyena vuttepi tassa santakabhāvaṃ paricchinditvā pavattavacanattā kūṭavinicchayaṃ karontānaṃ kūṭasakkhīnañca pārājikameva. Asatipi cettha ṭhānācāvane ubhinnaṃ dhuranikkhepoyeva ṭhānācāvanaṭṭhāne tiṭṭhati. Imasmiṃ dhuranikkhepe pārājike sāmikassa vimatuppādanapayoge kate thullaccayaṃ, tasseva dhuranikkhepapayoge nipphādite pārājikaṃ. Sayaṃ parājayaṃ pāpuṇātīti kūṭaḍḍakārako parājayaṃ pāpuṇāti.

'Having given a bribe' (ukkocaṃ datvā) means having given a bribe. 'Of false judges' (kūṭavinicchayikānaṃ) refers to Vinaya experts appointed to give false judgments. Even if not explicitly told 'take,' but through indirect statements like 'this is the owner of this ownerless thing,' because the statement proceeds after having defined its state of ownership, for those who make false judgments and for false witnesses, it is a pārājika offense indeed. Even if there is no moving from the place here, the laying down of the burden by both parties stands in the place of moving from the place. In this pārājika offense involving the laying down of the burden, if an attempt to create doubt in the owner is made, it is a thullaccaya offense; when that very attempt to lay down the burden is completed, it is a pārājika offense. 'He himself incurs defeat' (sayaṃ parājayaṃ pāpuṇāti)—the false claimant incurs defeat.

Ārāmaṭṭhakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Commentary on Monasteries is concluded.

Vihāraṭṭhakathāvaṇṇanā

Elucidation of the Commentary on the Monastery.

103. Vihāraṭṭhakathāyaṃ [M 2.0144] vihāropi pariveṇampi āvāsopi vihārotveva saṅkhaṃ gacchatīti āha “vihāraṃ vā”tiādi. Tattha vihāranti mahāvihāraṃ. Pariveṇanti mahāvihārassa abbhantare visuṃ visuṃ pākāraparicchinnaṭṭhānaṃ. Āvāsanti ekaṃ āvasathaṃ. Abhiyoge katepi avahārassa asijjhanato vuttaṃ “abhiyogo na ruhatī”ti. Gaṇasantake pana paricchinnasāmikattā sakkā dhuraṃ nikkhipāpetunti āha “dīghabhāṇakādibhedassa pana gaṇassā”ti. Idhāpi sace ekopi dhuraṃ na nikkhipati, rakkhatiyeva. Sabbesaṃ dhuranikkhepeneva hi pārājikaṃ.

103. In the Commentary on the Monastery, a monastery, a precinct, or a residence are all counted as a 'monastery'—thus it is said, 'a monastery or...' and so on. Therein, 'monastery' means a great monastery. 'Precinct' refers to separate places within the great monastery enclosed by walls. 'Residence' means a single lodging. Even if a claim is made, since the appropriation does not succeed, it is said, 'the claim does not hold.' However, regarding property belonging to a community, because it has defined owners, it is possible to have the burden relinquished; thus, it is said, 'for a community such as that divided into the Dīghabhāṇakas, etc.' Here too, if even one does not relinquish the burden, it remains protected. For it is only by the relinquishment of the burden by all that a pārājika offense occurs.

Vihāraṭṭhakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Elucidation of the Commentary on the Monastery is concluded.

Khettaṭṭhakathāvaṇṇanā

Elucidation of the Commentary on Fields.

104. Khettaṭṭhakathāyaṃ satta dhaññānīti sālivīhiyavakaṅgukudrūsavarakagodhumānaṃ vasena satta dhaññāni[V 2.0128]. Nirumbhitvā vātiādīsu “gaṇhantassā”ti paccekaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Tattha nirumbhitvā gahaṇaṃ nāma vīhisīsaṃ acchinditvā yathāṭhitameva hatthena gahetvā ākaḍḍhitvā bījamattasseva gahaṇaṃ. Ekamekanti ekamekaṃ vīhisīsaṃ. Uppāṭetvā vāti muggamāsādīni uddharitvā vā. Yasmiṃ bīje vātiādi nirumbhitvā gahaṇādīsu yathākkamaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Sālisīsādīni nirumbhitvā gaṇhantassa yasmiṃ bīje vatthu pūrati, ekamekaṃ hattheneva chinditvā gaṇhantassa yasmiṃ sīse vatthu pūrati, asitena lāyitvā gaṇhantassa yassaṃ muṭṭhiyaṃ vatthu pūrati, bahūni ekato uppāṭetvā gaṇhantassa yasmiṃ muggamāsādiphale vatthu pūratīti evamettha yathākkamo veditabbo. “Tasmiṃ bandhanā mocitamatte”ti vacanato tasmiṃ bījādimhi bandhanā mocite sati tato anapanītepi pārājikamevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Acchijjamānoti acchinno hutvā ṭhito. Jaṭitānīti chinditāni acchinnehi saddhiṃ jaṭitāni hontīti attho. Sabhusanti palālasahitaṃ. Abhusanti palālarahitaṃ.

104. In the Commentary on the Field, 'the seven grains' (satta dhaññāni) refers to the seven grains, namely: rice, paddy, barley, millet, kudrūsa, varaka, and wheat. In the phrases 'having plucked' (nirumbhitvā vā) and so on, 'for one who takes' should be applied to each case. Therein, 'taking by plucking' refers to not cutting off the ear of paddy, but taking it just as it is with the hand, pulling it, and taking only the seed. 'One by one' (ekamekaṃ) means one ear of paddy at a time. 'Having uprooted' (uppāṭetvā vā) means having pulled up mung beans, black lentils, or other pulses. The phrase 'in which seed' (yasmiṃ bīje vā) and so on should be applied in due order to the actions of plucking, taking, etc. For one who takes ears of rice by plucking, the offense is fulfilled with whichever seed; for one who cuts off each one by hand and takes it, the offense is fulfilled with whichever ear; for one who reaps with a sickle and takes, the offense is fulfilled with whichever handful; for one who uproots many at once and takes, the offense is fulfilled with whichever fruit of mung bean, black lentil, or the like—thus, the sequence here should be understood. From the statement 'at the very moment of being released from its stalk,' it should be understood that when that seed or other part is released from its stalk, even if it is not removed from that place, it is indeed a pārājika offense. 'Being uncut' (acchijjamāno) means remaining uncut. 'Entangled' (jaṭitāni) means that cut items become entangled with uncut items; this is the meaning. 'With chaff' (sabhusaṃ) means together with the straw. 'Without chaff' (abhusaṃ) means without the straw.

Khīlenāti [M 2.0145] khāṇukena. Ettha ca khīlasaṅkamanādīsu ubhayaṃ sambhavati sahapayogo dhuranikkhepo ca. Yadā hi parassa khettādīsu ekadesaṃ khīlasaṅkamanādivasena attano santakaṃ karoti, tadā satipi paṭhamataraṃ sāmikānaṃ dhuranikkhepe khīlasaṅkamanādisahapayogaṃ vinā na hotīti sahapayogeneva pārājikaṃ. Teneva mātikāṭṭhakathāyaṃ (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. dutiyapārājikavaṇṇanā) vuttaṃ “ṭhānācāvanavasena khīlādīni saṅkāmetvā khettādiggahaṇavasena ca sahapayogo veditabbo”ti. Yadā pana asati dhuranikkhepe khīlasaṅkamanādimattaṃ kataṃ, tadā vinā dhuranikkhepena na hotīti dhuranikkhepeneva pārājikaṃ. Tenevettha “tañca kho sāmikānaṃ dhuranikkhepenā”ti vuttaṃ. Evaṃ sabbatthāti yathāvuttamatthaṃ rajjusaṅkamanādīsupi atidisati.

'With a stake' means with a post. Here, in cases of moving a stake and so on, both are possible: a direct attempt and the relinquishment of the burden. For when one makes a part of another's field or the like one's own by means of moving a stake, etc., then even if there has been a prior relinquishment of the burden by the owners, it does not happen without the direct attempt of moving the stake or the like; thus, it is a pārājika offense only through the direct attempt. Therefore, in the Mātikāṭṭhakathā it is said: 'A direct attempt should be understood as moving stakes and the like by way of displacing them, and by way of taking possession of a field or the like.' But when only the moving of the stake or the like is done, and there is no relinquishment of the burden, then it does not happen without the relinquishment of the burden; thus, it is a pārājika offense only through the relinquishment of the burden. Therefore, here it is said: 'and that, with the relinquishment of the burden by the owners.' 'Thus everywhere' extends the aforesaid meaning also to cases of moving ropes and the like.

Yaṭṭhinti mānadaṇḍaṃ. Ekasmiṃ anāgate thullaccayaṃ, tasmiṃ āgate pārājikanti ettha sace dārūni nikhaṇitvā tattakeneva gaṇhitukāmo hoti, avasāne dārumhi pārājikaṃ. Sace tattha sākhāyopi katvā gahetukāmo hoti, avasānasākhāya pārājikanti veditabbaṃ. Tattakena asakkontoti dārūni nikhaṇitvā vatiṃ kātuṃ asakkonto. Khettamariyādanti vuttamevatthaṃ vibhāvetuṃ “kedārapāḷi”nti vuttaṃ. Vitthataṃ karotīti pubbe vijjamānameva mariyādaṃ vitthiṇṇaṃ karoti. Akataṃ vā pana patiṭṭhapetīti pubbe akataṃ vā mariyādaṃ ṭhapeti.

‘Yaṭṭhi’ means a measuring rod. 'When one part has not been reached, it is a grave offense; when it has been reached, it is a pārājika offense.' Here, if one intends to take possession by driving in posts, the pārājika offense occurs at the final post. If one intends to take possession by also making branches there, it should be understood that the pārājika offense occurs at the final branch. 'Being unable with that much' means being unable to make a fence after having driven in the posts. 'The boundary of the field'—to clarify the meaning already stated, 'the embankment of a rice-paddy' is said. 'He makes it extensive' means he extends a boundary that already existed before. 'Or he establishes one that was not made' means he sets up a boundary that was not made before.

Khettaṭṭhakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Elucidation of the Commentary on Fields is concluded.

Vatthuṭṭhakathāvaṇṇanā

Elucidation of the Commentary on Building Sites

105. Vatthuṭṭhakathāyaṃ [V 2.0129] tiṇṇaṃ pākārānanti iṭṭhakasilādārūnaṃ vasena tiṇṇaṃ pākārānaṃ. Eteneva nayenāti iminā “kevalaṃ bhūmiṃ sodhetvā…pe… aparikkhipitvā vā”ti vuttamatthaṃ nidasseti.

105. In the Commentary on Building Sites, 'of the three enclosures' means of the three enclosures by way of brick, stone, and wood. By this very method, it indicates the meaning stated as: 'merely having cleared the ground... or without having enclosed.'

Gāmaṭṭhakathāvaṇṇanā

Elucidation of the Commentary on the Village

106. Gāmaṭṭhakathāyaṃ gāmo nāmāti pāḷiyaṃ na vuttaṃ sabbaso gāmalakkhaṇassa pubbe vuttattā.

106. In the Commentary on the Village, as for 'what is called a village', it is not stated in the Pāḷi, because the characteristic of a village has been entirely stated previously.

Araññaṭṭhakathāvaṇṇanā

Elucidation of the Commentary on the Wilderness

107. Araññaṭṭhakathāyaṃ [M 2.0146] araññaṃ nāmāti idaṃ pana na kevalaṃ pubbe vuttaaraññalakkhaṇappattimattena araññaṃ idhādhippetaṃ, kintu yaṃ attano araññalakkhaṇena araññaṃ parapariggahitañca hoti, taṃ araññaṃ idhādhippetanti dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Tenāti puna araññavacanena. Na pariggahitabhāvo araññassa lakkhaṇanti yadi hi pariggahitabhāvo araññalakkhaṇaṃ siyā, “araññaṃ nāma yaṃ manussānaṃ pariggahita”nti ettakameva vadeyyāti adhippāyo. Yanti iminā pubbe vuttalakkhaṇameva araññaṃ parāmaṭṭhanti āha “yaṃ pana attano araññalakkhaṇena arañña”nti.

107. In the Commentary on the Wilderness, as for this 'what is called a wilderness', here a wilderness is not intended merely by its having attained the characteristic of a wilderness previously stated. Rather, it is stated to show that what is intended here is a wilderness that, being a wilderness by its own wilderness-characteristic, is also possessed by others. The state of being possessed is not the characteristic of a wilderness. For if being possessed were the characteristic of a wilderness, one would say only this much: 'What is called a wilderness is that which is possessed by humans.' This is the intention. By this word 'which' (yaṃ), he refers to the wilderness with the very characteristic stated previously, saying: 'but that which is a wilderness by its own wilderness-characteristic...'

Vinivijjhitvāti ujukameva vinivijjhitvā. Paṇṇaṃ vāti tālapaṇṇādi paṇṇaṃ vā. Addhagatopīti cirakālaṃ tattheva ṭhitopi. Na gahetabboti ettha pana yo parehi araññasāmikānaṃ hatthato kiṇitvā tacchetvā tattheva ṭhapito, so araññasāmikena anuññātopi na gahetabbo. Sāmikehi chaḍḍitoti gahetuṃ vaṭṭatīti paṃsukūlasaññāya gahaṇaṃ vuttaṃ. Lakkhaṇacchinnassāpīti araññasāmikānaṃ hatthato kiṇitvā gaṇhantehi katasaññāṇassa. Challiyā pariyonaddhaṃ hotīti iminā sāmikānaṃ nirapekkhataṃ dīpeti. Tena vuttaṃ “gahetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Yadi sāmikānaṃ sāpekkhatā atthi, na vaṭṭati. Tāni katāni ajjhāvutthāni ca hontīti tāni gehādīni katāni pariniṭṭhitāni manussehi ca ajjhāvutthāni honti. Dārūnipīti gehādīnaṃ katattā tato avasiṭṭhadārūnipi. Etesanti etesaṃ yathāvuttadārūnaṃ.

‘Having pierced through’ means having pierced straight through. ‘Or a leaf’ means a leaf such as a palm leaf. ‘Even if a long time has passed’ means even if it has remained there for a long time. ‘It should not be taken’—here, however, that which has been bought by others from the wilderness owners, cut, and left there, even if permitted by the wilderness owner, it should not be taken. ‘Discarded by the owners’ means it is permissible to take; this refers to taking with the perception of a dust-heap rag. ‘Even of that which is marked’—of a mark made by those who take it after buying from the wilderness owners. ‘It is covered with bark’—by this, it indicates the owners’ lack of concern. Therefore, it is said, 'it is permissible to take.' If the owners have concern, it is not permissible. ‘Those are made and inhabited’—those houses, etc., are made, finished, and inhabited by people. ‘Even pieces of wood’—even the pieces of wood leftover from making those houses, etc. ‘Of these’ means of these aforementioned pieces of wood.

Tesaṃ [V 2.0130] ārakkhaṭṭhānanti tesaṃ araññapālānaṃ ṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ. Dehīti vutte dātabbamevāti ettha “dehī”ti vutte “dassāmī”ti ābhogasabbhāvato “dehī”ti avutte adatvāpi gantuṃ vaṭṭatiyeva. Gantuṃ dethāti gamanaṃ detha. Adisvā gacchati, bhaṇḍadeyyanti parisuddhacittena gacchati, bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ. Yattha katthaci nītānampi dārūnaṃ araññasāmikānaṃyeva santakattā suddhacittena nikkhantopi puna theyyacittaṃ uppādetvā gacchati, pārājikamevāti vadanti.

‘Their guarding place’ means the standing place of those forest guards. In the phrase 'When "give" is said, it must be given': here, when 'give' is said, because of the existence of the mental advertence 'I will give', if 'give' is not said, it is indeed permissible to go even without giving. 'Allow to go' means allow the going. As for 'He goes without seeing, it is a thing to be given': this means if he goes with a pure mind, it is a thing to be given. Because the pieces of wood, even when taken anywhere, belong to the wilderness owners themselves, even though one has departed with a pure mind, if one then generates a thieving intention and goes, they say it is indeed a pārājika offense.

Araññaṭṭhakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Elucidation of the Commentary on the Wilderness is concluded.

Udakakathāvaṇṇanā

Elucidation of the Account of Water

108. Udakakathāyaṃ [M 2.0147] mahākucchikā udakacāṭi udakamaṇiko. “Samekhalā cāṭi udakamaṇiko”tipi vadanti. Tatthāti tesu bhājanesu. Nibbahanaudakanti “mahodakaṃ āgantvā taḷākamariyādaṃ mā chindī”ti taḷākarakkhaṇatthaṃ tassa ekapassena vissajjitaudakaṃ. Niddhamanatumbanti sassādīnaṃ atthāya udakanikkhamanamaggaṃ. Mariyādaṃ dubbalaṃ katvāti idaṃ avassaṃ chinnasabhāvadassanatthaṃ bhaṇḍadeyyavisayadassanatthañca vuttaṃ. Mariyādaṃ dubbalaṃ akatvāpi yathāvuttappayoge kate mariyādaṃ chinditvā nikkhantaudakagghānurūpena avahārena kāretabbameva.

108. In the Account of Water: a large-bellied vessel is a water pot or a water jar. They also say, “A water pot with a girdle is a water jar.” ‘Therein’ means among those containers. ‘Water for discharge’ means water released on one side for the purpose of protecting the pond, with the thought, “Lest a great flood come and break the pond’s boundary.” ‘A drainage trough’ means a path for water to flow out for the sake of crops and so on. “Having weakened the boundary”—this is said to show the nature of what is inevitably broken and to show the scope of what is liable for compensation. Even without weakening the boundary, if the stated application is made and it breaks the boundary, he must be made to compensate according to the value of the water that has flowed out.

Aniggateti anikkhamitvā taḷākasmiṃyeva udake ṭhite. Asampattevāti taḷākato nikkhamitvā mahāmātikāya eva ṭhite. Anikkhanteti taḷākato anikkhante udake. Subaddhāti bhaṇḍadeyyampi na hotīti adhippāyo. Tenāha “nikkhante baddhā bhaṇḍadeyya”nti, taḷākato nikkhamitvā paresaṃ khuddakamātikāmukhaṃ apāpuṇitvā mahāmātikāyaṃyeva ṭhite baddhā ce, bhaṇḍadeyyanti attho. “Anikkhante baddhā subaddhā, nikkhante baddhā bhaṇḍadeyya”nti hi idaṃ dvayaṃ heṭṭhā vuttavikappadvayassa yathākkamena vuttaṃ. Natthi avahāroti ettha “avahāro natthi, bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ pana hotī”ti keci vadanti, taḷākagataudakassa sabbasādhāraṇattā taṃ ayuttaṃ viya dissati, “anikkhante baddhā subaddhā”ti iminā ca aṭṭhakathāvacanena na sameti. Vatthuṃ…pe… na sametīti ettha taḷākagataudakassa sabbasādhāraṇattā apariggahitaṃ idha vatthunti adhippāyo.

‘Not having departed’ means when the water remains right in the pond without having exited. ‘Not having reached’ means when, having left the pond, it remains only in the main channel. ‘Not having exited’ means when the water has not exited from the pond. ‘Well-secured’ means that compensation is not required; this is the intention. Therefore, he said, ‘When it has exited, it is secured; compensation is required.’ This means: having exited from the pond but not having reached the opening of others’ small channels, if it remains only in the main channel and is secured, compensation is required. For these two—‘When not exited, it is secured, well-secured; when it has exited, it is secured, compensation is required’—are stated in order corresponding to the two alternatives mentioned below. Herein, regarding ‘There is no theft,’ some say, ‘There is no theft, but compensation is required.’ Yet because the water in the pond is common to all, that seems inappropriate, and it does not agree with this statement of the commentary: ‘When not exited, it is secured, well-secured.’ Herein, regarding ‘The object… does not agree,’ the intention is that because the water in the pond is common to all, the object here is said to be unappropriated.

Udakakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Account of Water is concluded.

Dantaponakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Account of the Tooth-Stick.

109. Dantakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ [V 2.0131] tato paṭṭhāya avahāro natthīti “yathāsukhaṃ bhikkhusaṅgho paribhuñjatū”ti yathāsukhaṃ paribhogatthāya ṭhapitattā vassaggena abhājetabbattā arakkhitabbattā sabbasādhāraṇattā ca aññaṃ saṅghikaṃ viya na hotīti theyyacittena gaṇhantassapi natthi avahāro[M 2.0148]. Vattanti dantakaṭṭhaggahaṇe vattaṃ. Idāni tadeva vattaṃ dassento “yo hī”tiādimāha. “Puna sāmaṇerā āharissantī”ti keci therā vadeyyunti yojetabbaṃ.

109. In the account of the tooth-stick: from that point onward, there is no theft because it is established for the purpose of use as one pleases—with the thought, “Let the community of monks use as they please”—and because it is not to be divided at the end of the rains retreat, not to be guarded, and is common to all, it is not like other property belonging to the Sangha. Thus, even for one who takes it with a thieving mind, there is no theft. The word 'observance' means the observance in taking a tooth-stick. Now, showing that very observance, he said, “Whoever,” and so forth. It should be construed that some elders might say, “The novices will bring more.”

Dantaponakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Account of the Tooth-Stick is finished.

Vanappatikathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on Forest Trees.

110. Vanappatikathāyaṃ “ujukameva tiṭṭhatīti rukkhabhārena kiñcideva bhassitvā ṭhitattā hotiyeva ṭhānācāvananti adhippāyena vutta”nti vadanti. Vātamukhaṃ sodhetīti yathā vāto āgantvā rukkhaṃ pāteti, evaṃ vātassa āgamanamaggaṃ rundhitvā ṭhitāni sākhāgumbādīni chinditvā apanento sodheti. “Maṇḍūkakaṇṭakaṃ vā visanti maṇḍūkānaṃ naṅguṭṭhe aggakoṭiyaṃ ṭhitakaṇṭaka”nti vadanti, “ekaṃ visamacchakaṇṭaka”ntipi vadanti.

110. In the discourse on forest trees, they say: 'It stands straight indeed'—this is said with the meaning that there is indeed a moving from its place, because it stands having slipped down somewhat due to the weight of the tree. 'He cleanses the wind's mouth'—just as the wind comes and fells a tree, so he cleanses by cutting and removing the branches, thickets, and so forth, that stand blocking the path of the wind's coming. They say, 'It is a frog's thorn,' meaning 'a thorn located at the very tip of a frog's tail.' They also say, 'It is a single poisonous fish-thorn.'

Vanappatikathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on Forest Trees is finished.

Haraṇakakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on Carrying Away.

111. Haraṇakakathāyaṃ haraṇakanti hariyamānaṃ. Abhimukhaṃ katvā kaḍḍhanaṃ ākaḍḍhanaṃ, sesadisākaḍḍhanaṃ vikaḍḍhanaṃ. Pādaṃ agghati, pārājikamevāti ettha antaṃ na gaṇhāmīti asallakkhitattā antassa ca gaṇhissāmīti sallakkhitasseva paṭassa ekadesattā pārājikaṃ vuttaṃ. Sahabhaṇḍahārakanti bhaṇḍahārakena saddhiṃ. Santajjetvāti dhanuādīhi santajjetvā.

111. In the discourse on carrying away, 'haraṇaka' means 'being carried away.' Drawing towards oneself is 'ākaḍḍhanaṃ'; drawing from other directions is 'vikaḍḍhanaṃ.' Regarding 'It is worth a pāda, it is indeed a pārājika,' here, a pārājika is stated because one did not consider, 'I will not take the end,' and because the end is part of the very cloth that was considered with the thought, 'I will take it.' 'Sahabhaṇḍahāraka' means 'together with the thief of goods.' 'Santajjetvā' means 'having threatened with a bow and so forth.'

Soti bhaṇḍahārako. Anajjhāvutthakanti apariggahitakaṃ, asāmikanti attho.

That one is the thief of goods. 'Anajjhāvutthaka' means 'unpossessed,' that is, 'ownerless' is the meaning.

Āharāpente dātabbanti ettha “chaḍḍetvā dhuraṃ nikkhipitvā gatānampi nirālayānaṃ puna āharāpanassa vuttattā bhikkhūnampi attano santake parikkhāre acchinditvā parehi gahite tattha [V 2.0132] dhuranikkhepaṃ katvāpi puna taṃ balakkārenapi āharāpetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti desavāsino ācariyā vadanti, sīhaḷadīpavāsino pana taṃ keci ācariyā na icchanti. Teneva [M 2.0149] mahāgaṇṭhipade majjhimagaṇṭhipade ca vuttaṃ “amhākaṃ pana taṃ na ruccatī”ti. Aññesūti mahāpaccariādīsu. Vicāraṇā eva natthīti tatthāpi paṭikkhepābhāvato ayamevatthoti vuttaṃ hoti.

Regarding 'it should be given when one makes them bring it back,' here, the local teachers say: 'Since it is stated that it is permissible to make even those who are without attachment bring things back again after they have abandoned them, relinquished the burden, and gone, it is also permissible for monks, when their own requisites have been seized and taken by others, to make them return those requisites even by force, after having relinquished the burden in that matter.' However, some teachers residing on the island of Sri Lanka do not agree with that. For that very reason, in the Mahāgaṇṭhipada and the Majjhimagaṇṭhipada it is stated: 'But for us, that is not approved.' 'In other texts' means in the Mahāpaccari and so forth. 'There is indeed no deliberation'—because there is no rejection there either, it is said that this is this very meaning.

Haraṇakakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on Carrying Away is finished.

Upanidhikathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on Deposits.

112. Upanidhikathāyaṃ “saṅgopanatthāya attano hatthe nikkhittassa bhaṇḍassa guttaṭṭhāne paṭisāmanapayogaṃ vinā aññasmiṃ payoge akatepi rajjasaṅkhobhādikāle ‘na dāni tassa dassāmi, na mayhaṃ dāni dassatī’ti ubhohipi sakasakaṭṭhāne nisīditvā dhuranikkhepe kate pārājikameva paṭisāmanapayogassa katattā”ti vadanti. Attano hatthe nikkhittattāti ettha attano hatthe saṅgopanatthāya nikkhittakālato paṭṭhāya tappaṭibaddhattā ārakkhāya bhaṇḍasāmikaṭṭhāne ṭhitattā ṭhānassa ca tadāyattatāya ṭhānācāvanassa alabbhanato natthi avahāroti adhippāyo.

112. In the discourse on deposits, they say: 'For goods placed in one's own hand for the purpose of safekeeping, even if no other effort is made, without the effort of storing it in a guarded place, at a time of disturbance of the kingdom and so forth, if, having sat in their respective places, both relinquish the burden, thinking, "Now I will not give it to him," and "Now he will not give it to me," it is indeed a pārājika, because the effort of safekeeping was undertaken.' Here, regarding the phrase 'because it was placed in one's own hand': from the time it was placed in one's own hand for safekeeping, because it is connected to that person, because one stands in the position of the owner of the goods for the purpose of protection, and because the place is dependent on that person, a moving from the place is not obtained; therefore, there is no misappropriation—this is the intention.

Dhammaṃ vācāpetvāti dhammaṃ kathāpetvā. Eseva nayoti uddhāreyeva pārājikaṃ. Kasmā? Aññehi asādhāraṇassa abhiññāṇassa vuttattā. “Aññaṃ tādisameva gaṇhante yujjatīti idaṃ saññāṇaṃ kathenteneva ‘asukasmiṃ ṭhāne’ti okāsassa ca niyamitattā tasmiṃ ṭhāne ṭhitaṃ pattaṃ apanetvā tasmiṃ okāse aññaṃ tādisameva pacchā ṭhapitaṃ pattaṃ sandhāya kathita”nti tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Corena sallakkhitapattassa gahaṇābhāvepi “idaṃ thenetvā gaṇhissāmī”ti tasmiṃ okāse ṭhite tādise vatthumatte tassa theyyacittasabbhāvato aññaṃ tādisameva gaṇhante yujjatīti corassa avahāro dassito. Padavārenāti therena nīharitvā dinnaṃ pattaṃ gahetvā gacchato corassa padavārena. Taṃ atādisameva gaṇhante yujjatīti “mamāyaṃ patto na hotī”ti vā “mayā kathito ayaṃ patto na hotī”ti vā jānitvā theyyacittena gaṇhantassa “idaṃ thenetvā gaṇhissāmī”ti vatthumatte theyyacittaṃ uppādetvā gaṇhantassa ca avahārasabbhāvato vuttaṃ.

‘Having had the Dhamma recited’ means ‘having had the Dhamma spoken.’ This is the method: it is a pārājika by the mere lifting. Why? Because an identifying mark not common to others is stated. Regarding ‘It is justified when taking another similar item,’ this sign is spoken by the one who says ‘in such a place,’ and because the location is specified, it is stated in all three Gaṇṭhipadas that this is spoken in reference to a similar bowl placed later in that very location, after having removed the bowl that was in that place. Even in the absence of taking the bowl marked by the thief, because of the existence of his thieving mind towards a mere object of that kind situated in that location, thinking ‘I will steal this and take it,’ it is justified when taking another similar item; thus the misappropriation by the thief is shown. ‘By the sequence of steps’ means by the sequence of steps of the thief who goes, having taken the bowl given by the elder who had brought it out. Regarding ‘It is justified when taking something that is not similar,’ it is stated because of the existence of misappropriation for one who takes it with a thieving mind, knowing ‘This bowl is not mine,’ or ‘This is not the bowl spoken of by me,’ and for one who takes it having aroused a thieving mind towards a mere object, thinking ‘I will steal this and take it.’

Gāmadvāranti [M 2.0150] samaṇasāruppaṃ vohāramattametaṃ, antogāmaṃ icceva vuttaṃ hoti. Vuttanayeneva therassa [V 2.0133] pārājikanti theyyacitteneva parasantakassa gahitattā uddhāreyeva therassa pārājikaṃ. Corassa dukkaṭanti asuddhacittena gahitattā gahitakāle corassa dukkaṭaṃ. Vuttanayeneva ubhinnampi dukkaṭanti corassa sāmikena dinnattā pārājikaṃ natthi, asuddhacittena gahitattā dukkaṭaṃ, therassa pana attano santakepi asuddhacittatāya dukkaṭanti.

'The village gate'—this is merely a conventional expression appropriate for a recluse; it is said to mean simply 'inside the village.' According to the method stated, it is a pārājika for the elder: because what belonged to another was taken with a thieving mind, it is a pārājika for the elder by the mere lifting. It is a dukkaṭa for the thief: because it was taken with an impure mind, it is a dukkaṭa for the thief at the time of taking. According to the method stated, it is a dukkaṭa for both: for the thief, there is no pārājika because it was given by the owner, but because it was taken with an impure mind, it is a dukkaṭa. As for the elder, even though it was his own property, because of the impure state of his mind, it is a dukkaṭa.

Āṇattiyā gahitattāti ettha “pattacīvaraṃ gaṇha, asukaṃ nāma gāmaṃ gantvā piṇḍāya carissāmā”ti evaṃ therena kataāṇattiyā vihārassa parabhāge upacārato paṭṭhāya yāva tassa gāmassa parato upacāro, tāva sabbaṃ khettameva jātanti adhippāyo. Maggato okkammāti ettha ubhinnaṃ sakaṭacakkamaggānaṃ antarāḷampi maggoyevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Aṭṭhatvā anisīditvāti ettha vihāraṃ pavisitvā sīsādīsu bhāraṃ bhūmiyaṃ anikkhipitvāva tiṭṭhanto nisīdanto vā vissamitvā theyyacitte vūpasante puna theyyacittaṃ uppādetvā gacchati ce, pāduddhārena kāretabbo. Sace bhūmiyaṃ nikkhipitvā puna taṃ gahetvā gacchati, uddhārena kāretabbo. Kasmā? Āṇāpakassa āṇattiyā yaṃ kattabbaṃ, tassa tāva pariniṭṭhitattā. Keci pana “purimasmiṃ theyyacitte avūpasantepi vuttanayeneva vissamitvā gacchato pāduddhārena uddhārena vā kāretabbo”ti vadanti, “asukaṃ nāma gāmanti aniyametvā ‘antogāmaṃ pavisissāmā’ti avisesena vutte vihārasāmantā sabbopi gocaragāmo khettamevā”tipi vadanti. Sesanti maggukkamanavihārābhimukhagamanādi sabbaṃ. Purimasadisamevāti anāṇattiyā gahitepi sāmikassa kathetvā gahitattā heṭṭhā vuttavihārūpacārādi sabbaṃ khettamevāti katvā vuttaṃ.

Regarding 'Because it was taken by command': here, the meaning is this: because of the command made by the elder, 'Take the bowl and robe; having gone to such-and-such a village, we will wander for alms,' starting from the vicinity in the outer part of the monastery, as far as the vicinity beyond that village extends, all that becomes a single field. Regarding 'stepping off the path': here, it should be understood that the space between the two cart-wheel tracks is also the path. Regarding 'without having stood and without having sat down': here, if one enters the monastery and, without placing the burden from one's head, etc., on the ground, rests while standing or sitting, and when the thievish thought has subsided, one arouses a thievish thought again and goes, one should be dealt with by foot-lifting. If, having placed it on the ground, one takes it again and goes, one should be dealt with by lifting. Why? Because that which was to be done by the command of the commander has, to that extent, been completed. Some, however, say: 'Even if the initial thievish thought has not subsided, one who rests in the manner described and then goes should be dealt with by foot-lifting or by lifting.' They also say: 'If, without specifying "such-and-such a village," one says generally, "We will enter the village," then the entire alms-resort village in the vicinity of the monastery is the field.' The rest—stepping off the path, going towards the monastery, and so on—is all just like the former case. 'It is just like the former' is said because, even though it was taken without a command, it was taken after telling the owner; therefore, the entire vicinity of the monastery, etc., previously mentioned is considered the field.

Eseva nayoti “antarāmagge theyyacittaṃ uppādetvā”tiādinā vuttanayaṃ atidisati. Nimitte vā kateti “cīvaraṃ me kiliṭṭhaṃ, ko nu kho rajitvā dassatī”tiādinā nimitte kate. Vuttanayenevāti anāṇattassa therena saddhiṃ pattacīvaraṃ gahetvā gamanavāre vuttanayeneva. Ekapasse vāti vihārassa mahantatāya attānaṃ adassetvā ekasmiṃ passe vasanto vā. Theyyacittena paribhuñjanto jīrāpetīti theyyacitte uppanne ṭhānācāvanaṃ akatvā nivatthapārutanīhāreneva paribhuñjanto [M 2.0151] jīrāpeti, ṭhānā cāventassa pana theyyacitte sati pārājikameva sīse bhāraṃ khandhe karaṇādīsu viya. Yathā tathā vā nassatīti aggiādinā vā upacikādīhi khāditaṃ vā nassati.

'This is the method' indicates the method stated beginning with 'having aroused a thievish thought on the path.' 'Or when a sign is made' means when a sign is made, such as, 'My robe is soiled. Who, I wonder, will dye it and give it to me?' 'By the method stated' means by the method stated in the case of going, having taken the bowl and robe together with the elder, without being commanded. 'Or on one side' means dwelling on one side without showing oneself, due to the large size of the monastery. 'Using it and wearing it out with a thievish thought' means: when a thievish thought has arisen, without causing a change of place, one uses it and wears it out merely by way of wearing it as a lower garment and an upper robe. But for one who causes a change of place while having a thievish thought, it is a pārājika offense, just as in the cases of placing a burden on the head or shoulder. 'Or it is lost in one way or another' means it is lost either by fire, etc., or is eaten by termites, etc.

Añño vā kocīti iminā pana yena ṭhapitaṃ, sopi saṅgahitoti veditabbaṃ. Tava thūlasāṭako laddhotiādinā musāvāde dukkaṭaṃ adinnādānapayogattā. Itaraṃ gaṇhato uddhāre pārājikanti [V 2.0134] ettha “pavisitvā tava sāṭakaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti imināva upanidhibhāvato muttattā sāmikassa itaraṃ gaṇhatopi attano sāṭake ālayassa sabbhāvato ca uddhāre pārājikaṃ vuttaṃ. Na jānantīti tena vuttaṃ vacanaṃ asuṇantā na jānanti. Eseva nayoti ettha sace jānitvāpi cittena na sampaṭicchanti, eseva nayoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Paṭikkhipantīti ettha cittena paṭikkhepopi saṅgahitovāti veditabbaṃ. Yācitā vā ayācitā vāti ettha yācitā yadi cittenapi sampaṭicchanti, naṭṭhe gīvā. Ayācitā pana yadipi cittena sampaṭicchanti, natthi gīvā.

By this 'Or someone else,' it should be understood that the one by whom it was placed is also included. In 'Your thick cloth has been obtained,' etc., there is a dukkaṭa offense for false speech, because it is an attempt at theft. Regarding 'For one who takes the other, there is a pārājika offense upon lifting': here, because one is freed from the state of it being a deposit by the very words, 'Enter and take your cloth,' and because, even when the owner takes the other one, there is still attachment to his own cloth, a pārājika offense upon lifting is stated. 'They do not know' means: not hearing the words spoken by him, they do not know. Regarding 'This is the method': here, it should be understood that if, even after knowing, they do not accept it with their mind, this is the method. Regarding 'They refuse': here, it should be understood that mental refusal is also included. Regarding 'Requested or unrequested': here, if requested, and they accept it even mentally, should it be lost, there is liability. But if unrequested, even if they accept it mentally, there is no liability.

Gahetvā ṭhapetīti ettha cāletvā tasmiṃyeva ṭhāne ṭhapitepi naṭṭhe gīvā. Upacāre vijjamāneti bhaṇḍāgārassa samīpe uccārapassāvaṭṭhāne vijjamāne. Mayi ca mate saṅghassa ca senāsane vinaṭṭheti ettha “kevalaṃ saṅghassa senāsanaṃ mā nassīti imināva adhippāyena vivaritumpi vaṭṭatiyevā”ti vadanti. Sahāyehi bhavitabbanti tehipi kiñci kiñci dātabbanti vuttaṃ hoti. Ayaṃ sāmīcīti bhaṇḍāgāre vasantānaṃ idaṃ vattaṃ.

Regarding 'having taken, one places it': here, even if one moves it and places it in that very same spot, should it be lost, there is liability. 'When available in the vicinity' means when a place for defecation and urination is available near the storeroom. Regarding 'And when I am dead, the Sangha's lodging will be lost': here, they say, 'It is fitting to open it with only this intention: "Let not the Sangha's lodging be lost."' 'One should have companions' means it is said that something or other should also be given by them. 'This is proper conduct' means this is the duty for those dwelling in the storeroom.

Lolamahātheroti mando momūho hasitakīḷitappasuto vā mahāthero. Attano attano vasanagabbhesu sabhāgabhikkhūnaṃ parikkhāraṃ ṭhapentīti yojetabbaṃ. Itarehīti tasmiṃyeva gabbhe vasantehi itarabhikkhūhi. Vihāravāre niyutto vihāravāriko, vāraṃ katvā vihārarakkhaṇako. Nivāpanti bhattavetanaṃ. Paṭipathaṃ gatesūti corānaṃ āgamanaṃ ñatvā “paṭhamataraṃyeva gantvā saddaṃ karissāmā”ti corānaṃ abhimukhaṃ gatesu. Nissitake jaggentīti attano attano nissitake sikkhācariyāya posentāpi nissitake vihāraṃ jaggāpenti. “Asahāyassa adutiyassā”ti pāṭho yutto, pacchimaṃ purimasseva vevacanaṃ. Asahāyassa vā attadutiyassa vāti imasmiṃ pana pāṭhe ekena ānītaṃ dvinnaṃ nappahotīti [M 2.0152] attadutiyassapi vāro nivāritoti vadanti, taṃ “yassa sabhāgo bhikkhu bhattaṃ ānetvā dātā natthī”ti iminā na sametīti vīmaṃsitabbaṃ. Upajīvantena ṭhātabbanti abbhokāsikena rukkhamūlikenapi pākavaṭṭaṃ upanissāya jīvantena pattacīvararakkhaṇatthāya vihāravāre sampatte ṭhātabbaṃ. Paripucchanti pucchitapañhavissajjanaṃ aṭṭhakathaṃ vā. Diguṇanti vassaggena pāpitaṃ vināva dve koṭṭhāseti vadanti. Pakkhavārenāti aḍḍhamāsavārena.

'The great elder Lola' means a great elder who is dull, deluded, or given to laughter and play. It should be construed that they place the requisites of like-minded monks in their respective dwelling cells. 'By others' means by other monks dwelling in that same cell. One appointed to monastery duty is a vihāravārika; having taken a turn, he is a guardian of the monastery. 'They provide' means the food-wage. 'When they had gone to meet them on the path' means: having learned of the arrival of thieves, they went to face the thieves, thinking, 'We will go first and make a noise.' 'They make their dependents keep watch' means: even while supporting their own dependents by the practice of alms-going, they have their dependents keep watch over the monastery. The reading 'of one without a companion, without a second' is correct; the latter word is a synonym for the former. But regarding this reading, 'of one without a companion or with oneself as a second,' some say that the turn is forbidden even for one with himself as a second because what is brought by one is not sufficient for two. That does not accord with the statement, 'one for whom there is no like-minded monk who is a giver, having brought food,' and should be investigated. 'One living in dependence must stand guard' means: even one who lives in the open or at the root of a tree, living in dependence on a cooked-food ration, must stand guard when his turn for monastery duty arrives, in order to protect the bowl and robes. 'They ask' means the answering of a question that was asked, or the commentary. 'Double' means two portions, without what is obtained from the best of the rains-residence, so they say. 'By fortnightly turn' means by a half-month turn.

Upanidhikathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the section concerning deposits is concluded.

Suṅkaghātakathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Section on the Toll Gate

113. Suṅkaghātakathāyaṃ [V 2.0135] tato hanantīti tato nīharantā hananti. Tanti suṅkaṭṭhānaṃ. Yatoti yato nīhariyamānabhaṇḍato. Rājakanti rājāyattaṃ. Tampi rājārahamevāti āha “ayamevattho”ti. Itoti ito bhaṇḍato. Dutiyaṃ pādaṃ atikkāmetīti ettha “paṭhamaṃ pādaṃ paricchedato bahi ṭhapetvā dutiye pāde uddhaṭamatte pārājika”nti vadanti uddharitvā bahi aṭṭhapitopi bahi ṭhitoyeva nāma hotīti katvā. Yattha yattha padavārena āpatti kāretabbā, tattha tattha sabbatthāpi eseva nayoti vadanti. Suṅkaghātato bahi bahisuṅkaghātaṃ. Avassaṃ patanakanti avassaṃ suṅkaghātato bahi patanakaṃ. Pubbe vuttanayenevāti avassaṃ patanake hatthato muttamatteti vuttaṃ hoti. Vaṭṭantaṃ puna anto pavisatīti mahāaṭṭhakathāvacanassa kurundisaṅkhepaṭṭhakathāhi adhippāyo pakāsito. Anto ṭhatvā bahi gacchantaṃ rakkhatīti bhikkhuno payogena gamanavegassa antoyeva vūpasantattā. Parivattetvā abbhantarimaṃ bahi ṭhapetīti abbhantare ṭhitaṃ puṭakaṃ parivattetvā bahi ṭhapeti. Ettha ca “abbhantarime puṭake bhūmito mocitamatte pārājika”nti vadanti.

113. In the Exposition on the Toll-Gate: 'From there they take' means those taking away from there, they take. 'Taṃ' refers to the toll-station. 'Yato' means from which goods are being taken away. 'Rājakaṃ' means belonging to the king. That too is indeed worthy of the king, hence it is said, 'This is the meaning.' 'Ito' means from these goods. Regarding 'he makes it cross the second step,' here they say, 'Having placed the first step outside the boundary, as soon as the second step is lifted, it is a pārājika offense.' This is because having lifted it, even if not placed outside, it is indeed called 'being outside.' Wherever an offense is to be determined by the measure of a step, in all such cases, this is the method, they say. 'Outside the toll-gate' means beyond the toll-gate. 'Inevitable falling' means inevitably falling outside the toll-gate. By the previously stated method—it is said that in the case of inevitable falling, it is as soon as it is released from the hand. As for 'that which has rolled re-enters inside,' the meaning of this statement from the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā is clarified by the Kurundi and Saṅkhepa commentaries. 'Standing inside, he guards that which is going outside'—this is because the momentum of movement has ceased right inside due to the bhikkhu's effort. 'Having turned it around and placing the inner one outside' means taking the inner bundle, turning it around, and placing it outside. And here, they say, 'As soon as the inner bundle is freed from the ground, it is a pārājika offense.'

“Gacchante yāne vā…pe… ṭhapetīti suṅkaghātaṃ apavisitvā bahiyeva ṭhapetī”ti tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ suṅkaṭṭhānassa bahi ṭhapitanti vakkhamānattā. Ācariyā pana “suṅkaṭṭhānassa bahi ṭhita”nti pāṭhaṃ vikappetvā “paṭhamaṃ antosuṅkaghātaṃ paviṭṭhesuyeva yānādīsu ṭhapitaṃ pacchā yānena saddhiṃ nīhaṭaṃ suṅkaghātassa bahi ṭhitaṃ, na ca tena nīta”nti [M 2.0153] atthaṃ vadanti. Ayaṃ pana tesaṃ adhippāyo – suṅkaṭṭhānassa anto paviṭṭhayānādīsu ṭhapitepi bhikkhussa payogaṃ vinā aññena nīhaṭattā nevatthi pārājikaṃ, “atra paviṭṭhassa suṅkaṃ gaṇhantū”ti vuttattā aññena nīhaṭassa bahi ṭhite bhaṇḍadeyyampi na hotīti. Ayameva ca nayo “vaṭṭitvā gamissatīti vā añño naṃ vaṭṭessatīti vā anto ṭhapitaṃ pacchā sayaṃ vā vaṭṭamānaṃ aññena vā vaṭṭitaṃ bahi gacchati, rakkhatiyevā”ti iminā vacanena sametīti yuttataro viya dissati. Suṅkaṭṭhānassa anto pavisitvā puna paccāgacchatopi tena passena paricchedaṃ atikkamantassa yadi tatopi gacchantānaṃ hatthato suṅkaṃ gaṇhanti, sīmātikkame pārājikameva.

'In a moving vehicle... he places it' means: not having entered the toll-gate, he places it right outside. This is stated in all three knot-points, because it will be said 'placed outside the toll-station.' The teachers, however, analyzing the reading 'situated outside the toll-station,' say the meaning is thus: 'First, something is placed in a vehicle, etc., that has already entered inside the toll-gate; later, taken out with the vehicle, it is situated outside the toll-gate, but it was not taken by him.' This, however, is their intention: even if it is placed in a vehicle, etc., that has entered inside the toll-station, because it was taken out by another without the bhikkhu's effort, there is no pārājika offense, for it was said, 'Let them take the toll of one who has entered here.' When it is taken out by another and is situated outside, there is also no liability for the goods. And this very method seems more fitting as it agrees with this statement: 'Thinking, "It will go, having been rolled," or "Another will roll it," something is placed inside; later, being rolled either by itself or by another, it goes outside; it is indeed guarded.' For one who, having entered inside the toll-station and then returning, crosses the boundary by that side, if they take the toll from the hands of those going from there, upon crossing the boundary, it is indeed a pārājika offense.

Hatthisuttādīsūti hatthisikkhādīsu. Imasmiṃ ṭhāneti yathāvuttayānādīhi vuttappakārena nīharaṇe. Anāpattīti tattha “sahatthā”ti vacanato aññena nīharāpentassa anāpatti. Idhāti imasmiṃ [V 2.0136] adinnādānasikkhāpade. Tatrāti tasmiṃ eḷakalomasikkhāpade. Hontīti ettha iti-saddo hetuattho, yasmā eḷakalomāni nissaggiyāni honti, tasmā pācittiyanti attho. Idha anāpattīti imasmiṃ sikkhāpade avahārābhāvā anāpatti. Upacāranti suṅkaghātaparicchedato bahi samantā dvinnaṃ leḍḍupātānaṃ abbhantaraṃ vatiāsannappadesasaṅkhātaṃ upacāraṃ. Tādisaṃ upacāraṃ okkamitvā pariharaṇe sādīnavattā dukkaṭaṃ vuttaṃ. Etthāti suṅkaghāte. “Dvīhi leḍḍupātehīti ayaṃ niyamo ācariyaparamparābhato”ti mahāgaṇṭhipade vuttaṃ.

'Regarding the elephant training rules, etc.' refers to the elephant training rules and similar matters. 'In this case' means in the removal in the manner stated with regard to the aforesaid vehicles, etc. 'No offense' means: there, because of the word 'by one's own hand,' there is no offense for one who has it removed by another. 'Here' refers to this training rule on taking what is not given. 'There' refers to that training rule on sheep's wool. Regarding 'are,' here the word `iti` has the meaning of cause; the meaning is: because sheep's wool is to be forfeited, therefore it is a pācittiya offense. 'Here, no offense' means in this training rule, there is no offense due to the absence of theft. `Upacāra` (vicinity) refers to the vicinity reckoned as the area near the fence, which is all around outside the toll-gate boundary, within two clod-throws. Having entered such a vicinity and carrying it around, a `dukkaṭa` offense is stated because of the faultiness of the act. 'Here' means at the toll-gate. 'By two clod-throws'—this rule has come down through the succession of teachers, so it is said in the Mahāgaṇṭhipada.

Suṅkaghātakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on the Toll-Gate is concluded.

Pāṇakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discourse on Living Beings

114. Pāṇakathāyaṃ tiracchānagatassa ekantena pādagghanakatā na sambhavatīti āha – “ekaṃsena avahārakappahonakapāṇaṃ dassento”ti. Bhujissaṃ harantassa avahāro natthīti parapariggahitābhāvato. Bhujissoti adāso. Āṭhapitoti mātāpitūhi iṇaṃ gaṇhantehi “yāva iṇadānā ayaṃ tumhākaṃ santike hotū”ti iṇadāyakānaṃ niyyātito. Yasmā mātāpitaro dāsānaṃ viya puttānaṃ na [M 2.0154] sāmino. Yesañca santike āṭhapito, tepi tassa hatthakamme sāmino, na tassāti āha “avahāro natthī”ti. Dhanaṃ pana gataṭṭhāne vaḍḍhatīti ettha “āṭhapetvā gahitadhanaṃ vaḍḍhiyā saha avahārakassa gīvā”ti tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ.

114. In the discourse on living beings, for an animal, the state of being made worth a quarter [of a kahāpaṇa] is not entirely possible; thus he said: 'showing a living being that is entirely suitable for theft.' For one carrying away a free person, there is no theft, because of the state of not being possessed by another. 'Bhujissa' means a non-slave. 'Āṭhapita' means one who, when his parents take a loan, is handed over to the creditors, with the words, 'Until the loan is repaid, let this one be in your possession.'
