Because parents are not owners of their children as they are of slaves, and those in whose presence he is placed are owners of his manual labor but not of him, he said, 'there is no theft.' But 'wealth increases in the place it has gone'; here, 'the wealth taken after having been pledged, together with interest, is the neck [i.e., responsibility] of the thief,' is said in all three knot-points.

Antojāta…pe… avahāro hotīti ettha padesacārittavasena attanāva attānaṃ niyyātetvā dāsabyaṃ upagataṃ avaharantassapi pārājikamevāti veditabbaṃ. Gehadāsiyā kucchimhi dāsassa jātoti evampi sambhavatīti sambhavantaṃ gahetvā vuttaṃ. Gehadāsiyā kucchismiṃ pana aññassa jātopi ettheva saṅgahito. Karamarānīto nāma bandhagāhagahito. Tenāha “paradesato paharitvā”tiādi. Tattha paradesato paharitvāti paradesaṃ vilumpakehi rājarājamahāmattādīhi mahācorehi paradesato paharitvā. Anāpatti pārājikassāti yadi tassa vacanena tato adhikaṃ vegaṃ na vaḍḍheti, anāpatti. Pariyāyenāti pariyāyavacanena. Manussaviggahe “maraṇavaṇṇaṃ vā saṃvaṇṇeyyā”ti vuttattā pariyāyakathāyapi na muccati, idha pana “adinnaṃ theyyasaṅkhātaṃ ādiyeyyā”ti ādānasseva vuttattā pariyāyakathāya muccati.

Here, in the passage beginning 'born inside...' and ending '...there is theft,' it should be understood that for one who abducts a person who has entered into slavery by handing himself over according to local custom, it is indeed a pārājika offense. 'Born to a slave in the womb of a household slave-woman'—this is stated by taking into account what is possible, as this too can occur. But one born of another in the womb of a household slave-woman is also included here. 'Brought as a captive of war' means one seized by capture. Therefore, he said, 'having plundered from another country,' and so on. There, 'having plundered from another country' means having been brought from another country by plunderers of other countries, such as kings, royal ministers, and great thieves. There is no offense of pārājika if, by his speech, one does not increase the momentum more than that which already exists. 'By an indirect expression' means by indirect speech. In the case of killing a human being, because it is said, 'one might praise the qualities of death,' one is not absolved even by indirect speech. But here, because it is said, 'one might take what is not given, designated as theft,' and only the taking itself is mentioned, one is absolved by indirect speech.

Pāṇakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on Living Beings is concluded.

Apadakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on Footless Beings

Apadakathāyaṃ [V 2.0137] nāmenāti sappanāmena vā sāmikena katanāmena vā. Karaṇḍapuṭanti peḷāya pidhānaṃ. Āhaccāti paharitvā.

In the discourse on footless beings, 'by name' means either by the name of the snake or by the name given by the owner. 'Karaṇḍapuṭa' means the lid of a basket. 'Āhacca' means having struck.

Catuppadakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on Quadrupeds

116. Catuppadakathāyaṃ bhiṅkacchāpanti bhiṅkabhiṅkāti saddāyanato evaṃladdhanāmaṃ hatthipotakaṃ. Antovatthumhīti parikkhitte antovatthumhi. Rājaṅgaṇeti parikkhitte nagare vatthudvārato bahirājaṅgaṇe. Hatthisālā ṭhānanti nibbakosato udakapātabbhantaraṃ ṭhānaṃ. Bahinagare ṭhitassāti [M 2.0155] parikkhittanagaraṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, aparikkhittanagare pana antonagare ṭhitassapi ṭhitaṭṭhānameva ṭhānaṃ. Khaṇḍadvāranti attanā khaṇḍitadvāraṃ. Sākhābhaṅganti bhañjitasākhaṃ. Nipannassa dveti bandhanena saddhiṃ dve. Ghātetīti ettha “theyyacittena vināsentassa sahapayogattā dukkaṭameva, na pācittiya”nti ācariyā vadanti.

116. In the discourse on quadrupeds, 'bhiṅkacchāpa' refers to a young elephant that has acquired its name from making the sound 'bhiṅkabhiṅka'. 'Antovatthumhi' means within an enclosed compound. 'Rājaṅgaṇa' means the royal courtyard outside the property gate within an enclosed city. 'Hatthisālā ṭhāna' means the place within the elephant stable, specifically the area from the husk-removal place to within the water trough. 'Standing outside the city' is said in reference to an enclosed city; but in an unenclosed city, even for one standing inside the city, the place where one stands is just the 'place'. 'Khaṇḍadvāra' means a door broken by oneself. 'Sākhābhaṅga' means a broken branch. 'Nipannassa dve' means two, together with the tether. Regarding 'Ghāteti' (he kills), here the teachers say: 'For one who destroys with a thieving mind, because it is a preliminary action, it is only a dukkaṭa offense, not a pācittiya.'

Catuppadakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on Quadrupeds is concluded.

Oṇirakkhakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on Goods Entrusted for Safekeeping

Oṇirakkhakathāyaṃ oṇinti oṇītaṃ, ānītanti attho. “Oṇirakkhassa santike ṭhapitaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ upanidhi viya saṅgopanatthāya anikkhipitvā muhuttaṃ olokanatthāya ṭhapitattā tassa ṭhānācāvanamattena pārājikaṃ janetī”ti vadanti.

In the discourse on goods entrusted for safekeeping, 'oṇi' means 'deposited'; the meaning is 'brought'. They say: 'Because goods placed near a guardian—like a formal deposit—were not entrusted for the purpose of safekeeping but were placed for a moment for the purpose of inspection, for that person, merely by moving it from its place, it does not generate a pārājika offense.'

Saṃvidāvahārakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on Theft by Agreement

Saṃvidāvahārakathāyaṃ “sambahulā saṃvidahitvā eko bhaṇḍaṃ avaharati, āpatti sabbesaṃ pārājikassā”ti pāḷiyaṃ avisesena vuttattā āṇāpakānaṃ āṇattikkhaṇe āpatti, avahārakassa uddhāreti yathāsambhavaṃ yojetvā attho gahetabbo āṇattikathāyaṃ “so taṃ bhaṇḍaṃ avaharati, āpatti sabbesaṃ pārājikassā”tiādīsu viya. Etthāpi hi āṇāpakassa āṇattikkhaṇeyeva āpatti vuttā. Tathā ca vakkhati “atha taṃ bhaṇḍaṃ avassaṃ hāriyaṃ hoti, yaṃ [V 2.0138] parato sabbesaṃ āpatti pārājikassāti vuttaṃ, tato imassa taṅkhaṇeyeva pārājikaṃ hotīti ayaṃ yutti sabbattha veditabbā”ti (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.121). Saṃvidāvahāre ca “āṇatti natthī”ti na vattabbā “antevāsikesu ekamekassa ekeko māsako sāhatthiko hoti, pañca āṇattikā”ti vacanato. Āṇattiyā ca sati āṇāpakassa āṇattikkhaṇeyeva āpatti icchitabbā, na uddhāre.

In the discourse on theft by agreement, since it is stated in the Pāḷi without distinction, 'Many conspire, and one steals an item; the pārājika offense is for all,' the meaning should be understood by applying it as is suitable: for the instigators, the offense is at the moment of the command; for the one who takes it away, it is at the removal. This is like in the discourse on command, in such passages as, 'He takes away that item... the pārājika offense is for all.' For here too, the offense for the instigator is said to be at the very moment of the command. And so it will be said: 'Then that item must certainly be taken away... it is said that thereafter the pārājika offense is for all. Therefore, for this one, the pārājika occurs at that very moment. This reasoning should be known everywhere.' And in theft by agreement, it should not be said, 'There is no command,' because it is stated: 'Among the resident pupils, for each one, one māsaka is by his own hand, five are by command.' And when there is a command, the offense for the instigator should be accepted as being at the very moment of the command, not at the removal.

Yadi evaṃ “tesu eko bhaṇḍaṃ avaharati, tassuddhāre sabbesaṃ pārājika”nti kasmā vuttanti? Nāyaṃ doso. Ettha hi sabbesaṃyeva āpattidassanatthaṃ [M 2.0156] avahārakassapi āpattisambhavaṭṭhānaṃ dassento “tassuddhāre sabbesaṃ pārājika”nti āha, na pana āṇāpakānampi uddhāreyeva āpattidassanatthanti evamattho gahetabbo. “Sambahulā ekaṃ āṇāpenti ‘gacchetaṃ āharā’ti, tassuddhāre sabbesaṃ pārājika”ntiādīsupi evameva attho gahetabbo. Atha vā saṃvidāvahāre āṇāpakānampi uddhāreyeva āpatti, na āṇattikkhaṇeti āveṇikamidaṃ lakkhaṇanti aṭṭhakathācariyappamāṇena gahetabbaṃ, ito vā aññena pakārena yathā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pubbenāparaṃ na virujjhati, tathā vīmaṃsitvā gahetabbaṃ.

If so, why is it said, 'Among them, one steals the goods; upon its removal, it is a pārājika for all'? This is not a fault. Here, in order to show the offense for all, while also indicating the place where the offense can arise for the one who takes it away, he said, 'upon its removal, it is a pārājika for all.' But he did not say this in order to show that for the instigators, too, the offense is only at the removal. This is how the meaning should be taken. In such cases as, 'Many command one, “Go, bring that,” upon its removal, it is a pārājika for all,' and so on, this very same meaning should be taken. Alternatively, in theft by agreement, the offense for the instigators, too, is at the very removal, not at the moment of the command—this is a unique characteristic, and it should be taken on the authority of the commentary teachers. Or, apart from this, by some other method, it should be investigated and taken in such a way that in the commentary a later statement does not contradict a former one.

Saṃvidhāyāti saṃvidahitvā. Tena nesaṃ dukkaṭāpattiyoti āṇattivasena pārājikāpattiyā asambhave sati vuttaṃ. Yadi hi te āṇattā avassaṃ taṃ haranti, pārājikāpattiyeva nesaṃ daṭṭhabbā, na dukkaṭāpatti. Sāhatthikaṃ vā āṇattikassa āṇattikaṃ vā sāhatthikassa aṅgaṃ na hotīti bhinnakālavisayattā aññamaññassa aṅgaṃ na hoti. Tathā hi sahatthā avaharantassa ṭhānācāvane āpatti, āṇattiyā pana āṇattikkhaṇeyevāti bhinnakālavisayā sāhatthikāṇattikehi āpajjitabbāpattiyo.

'Saṃvidhāya' means 'having conspired'. Therefore, 'for them it is a dukkaṭa offense' is said when there is an impossibility of a pārājika offense by way of command. For if they, having been commanded, certainly take that item, only a pārājika offense should be seen for them, not a dukkaṭa offense. An act by one's own hand is not a component of a commanded act, nor is a commanded act a component of an act by one's own hand. Because their time and domain are different, they are not components of each other. Indeed, for one who takes away with his own hand, the offense occurs at the removal from the place; but in the case of a command, it occurs at the very moment of the command. Thus, the offenses to be incurred by one's own hand and by command are different in time and domain.

Saṃvidāvahārakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on Theft by Agreement is concluded.

Saṅketakammakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on Action by Agreement.

119. Saṅketakammakathāyaṃ ocarake vuttanayenevāti “avassaṃ hāriye bhaṇḍe”tiādinā vuttanayena. Pāḷiyaṃ taṃ saṅketaṃ pure vā pacchā vāti ettha taṃ saṅketanti sāmiatthe upayogavacananti daṭṭhabbaṃ, tassa saṅketassāti attho. Atha vā taṃ saṅketaṃ asampatvā pure vā taṃ saṅketaṃ atikkamma pacchā vāti evamettha yojanā veditabbā. Tenevāha – “ajjāti niyāmitaṃ [V 2.0139] taṃ saṅketaṃ atikkammā”tiādi. Taṃ nimittaṃ pure vā pacchā vāti etthāpi imināva nayena attho veditabbo.

119. In the discourse on action by agreement, regarding the phrase 'in the manner stated in the Ocaraka,' it means by the method stated in 'Regarding goods that must be taken,' and so on. In the Pāḷi, herein the phrase 'that agreement, whether before or after,' the words 'that agreement' (taṃ saṅketaṃ) should be understood as the accusative case used in the sense of the genitive; the meaning is 'of that agreement.' Alternatively, the construction here should be understood thus: either before, not having reached that agreement, or after, having transgressed that agreement. Therefore, He said: 'Having transgressed that agreement fixed for today,' and so on. Herein also, regarding 'that sign, whether before or after,' the meaning should be understood by this same method.

Saṅketakammakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on Action by Agreement is concluded.

Nimittakammakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on Action by Sign

120. Nimittakammakathāyaṃ [M 2.0157] akkhinikhaṇādinimittakammaṃ pana lahukaṃ ittarakālaṃ, tasmā taṅkhaṇeyeva taṃ bhaṇḍaṃ avaharituṃ na sakkā. Tathā hi kiñci bhaṇḍaṃ dūre hoti kiñci bhāriyaṃ, taṃ gahetuṃ yāva gacchati, yāva ukkhipituṃ vāyamati, tāva nimittakammassa pacchā hoti. Evaṃ santepi nimittakammato paṭṭhāya gaṇhituṃ āraddhattā teneva nimittena avaharatīti vuccati. Yadi evaṃ “purebhattapayogova eso”ti vādo pamāṇabhāvaṃ āpajjatīti? Nāpajjati. Na hi saṅketakammaṃ viya nimittakammaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tattha hi kālaparicchedo atthi, idha natthi. Kālavasena hi saṅketakammaṃ vuttaṃ, kiriyāvasena nimittakammanti ayametesaṃ viseso. “Taṃ nimittaṃ pure vā pacchā vā taṃ bhaṇḍaṃ avaharati, mūlaṭṭhassa anāpattī”ti idaṃ pana tena nimittakamme kate gaṇhituṃ anārabhitvā sayameva gaṇhantassa vasena vuttaṃ.

120. In the discourse on action by sign, the action by sign, such as the winking of an eye, is slight and of a different moment; therefore, it is not possible to take the goods at that very moment. For some goods are far away, and some are heavy; while one goes to take them, while one strives to lift them, by then it is after the action by sign. Even so, because the taking was initiated starting from the action by sign, it is said that one takes by that very sign. If so, does the argument 'this is an application before the meal' attain the state of being a standard? It does not. For an action by sign should not be seen like an action by agreement. There, a time-limit exists; here, it does not. For action by agreement is spoken of in terms of time, whereas action by sign is in terms of action—this is their distinction. However, the statement, 'Whether before or after that sign one takes the goods, there is no offense for the originator,' is said with reference to one who, after that action by sign was done, takes it on his own accord, without having initiated the taking.

Nimittakammakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on Action by Sign is concluded.

Āṇattikathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on Commands

121. Āṇattikathāyaṃ asammohatthanti yasmā saṅketakammanimittakammāni karonto eko purebhattādīsu vā akkhinikhaṇanādīni vā disvā “gaṇhā”ti vadati, eko gahetabbabhaṇḍanissitaṃ katvā “purebhattaṃ evaṃvaṇṇasaṇṭhānaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ gaṇhā”ti vadati, eko “tvaṃ itthannāmassa pāvada, so aññassa pāvadatū”tiādinā puggalapaṭipāṭiyā ca āṇāpeti, tasmā kālavasena kiriyāvasena bhaṇḍavasena puggalavasena ca āṇatte visaṅketāvisaṅketavasena etesu saṅketakammanimittakammesu asammohatthaṃ. Nimittasaññaṃ katvāti “īdisaṃ nāma bhaṇḍa”nti vaṇṇasaṇṭhānādivasena gahaṇassa nimittabhūtaṃ saññāṇaṃ katvā.

121. In the discourse on commands, 'for the sake of non-confusion' is said because, when performing actions by agreement or actions by sign, one person, having seen times such as before the meal or signs such as the winking of an eye, says, 'Take it!'; another, making it dependent on the goods to be taken, says, 'Before the meal, take the goods of such color and shape!'; and another commands by a sequence of persons, saying, 'You tell so-and-so, let him tell another,' and so on. Therefore, it is for the sake of non-confusion in these actions by agreement and actions by sign, regarding a command given by way of time, action, goods, and person, through agreement and non-agreement. 'Having made a perception as a sign' means having made a mark which is a sign for taking, by way of color, shape, etc., thinking 'goods of such a kind.'

Yathādhippāyaṃ gacchatīti dutiyo tatiyassa, tatiyo catutthassāti evaṃ paṭipāṭiyā ce vadantīti vuttaṃ hoti. Sace pana dutiyo catutthassa āroceti, na yathādhippāyaṃ āṇatti gatāti [V 2.0140] nevatthi thullaccayaṃ, paṭhamaṃ vuttadukkaṭameva hoti. Tadeva hotīti bhaṇḍaggahaṇaṃ vinā kevalaṃ sāsanappaṭiggahaṇamattasseva siddhattā tadeva thullaccayaṃ hoti[M 2.0158], na dukkaṭaṃ nāpi pārājikanti attho. Sabbatthāti īdisesu sabbaṭṭhānesu.

The phrase 'it goes according to intention' means it is said thus: if the second tells the third, and the third tells the fourth, they speak in sequence. But if the second informs the fourth, the command has not gone according to intention, so there is no grave offense; there is only the previously stated minor offense. 'That alone occurs' means that because only the mere receiving of the message is accomplished, without the taking of the goods, that itself is a grave offense; it is not a minor offense, nor is it an offense entailing expulsion. 'In all cases' means in all such instances.

Tesampi dukkaṭanti ārocanapaccayā dukkaṭaṃ. Paṭiggahitamatteti ettha avassaṃ ce paṭiggaṇhāti, tato pubbeva ācariyassa thullaccayaṃ, na pana paṭiggahiteti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kasmā panassa thullaccayanti āha – “mahājano hi tena pāpe niyojito”ti.

'For them also a minor offense' means a minor offense on account of informing. Herein, regarding 'just upon it being received,' if he definitely receives it, a grave offense for the teacher should be understood as occurring even before that, and not, however, when it has been received. Why then is there a grave offense for him? He said: 'For a great number of people are instigated by him into that evil.'

Mūlaṭṭhasseva dukkaṭanti ayaṃ tāva aṭṭhakathānayo, ācariyā pana “visaṅketattā eva mūlaṭṭhassāti pāḷiyaṃ avuttattā paṭiggaṇhantasseva taṃ dukkaṭaṃ vuttaṃ, imināva heṭṭhā āgatavāresupi paṭiggaṇhantānaṃ paṭiggahaṇe dukkaṭaṃ veditabbaṃ, taṃ pana tattha okāsābhāvato avatvā idha vutta”nti vadanti.

'A minor offense for the originator only'—this, firstly, is the method of the commentary. The teachers, however, say: 'Because, on account of the non-agreement, it is not stated in the Pāḷi that the offense is for the originator only, that minor offense is stated for the one who accepts only. By this very reasoning, also in the cases that come below, a minor offense should be known for the acceptors at the point of acceptance. But that, not having been stated there for lack of opportunity, is stated here.'

Evaṃ puna āṇattiyāpi dukkaṭameva hotīti paṭhamaṃ atthasādhakattābhāvato vuttaṃ. Āṇattikkhaṇeyeva pārājikoti maggānantaraphalaṃ viya atthasādhikāṇatticetanākkhaṇeyeva pārājiko. Badhiratāyāti uccaṃ bhaṇanto badhiratāya vā na sāvetīti vuttaṃ hoti. “Āṇatto ahaṃ tayā”ti imasmiṃ vāre puna paṭikkhipitabbābhāvena atthasādhakattābhāvato mūlaṭṭhassa natthi pārājikaṃ. “Paṇṇe vā silāya vā yattha katthaci ‘coriyaṃ kātabba’nti likhitvā ṭhapite pārājikamevā”ti tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Taṃ pana yasmā adinnādānato pariyāyakathāya muccati, tasmā vīmaṃsitvā gahetabbaṃ. Yadi pana “asukasmiṃ nāma ṭhāne asukaṃ nāma bhaṇḍaṃ ṭhitaṃ, taṃ avaharā”ti paṇṇe likhitvā kassaci peseti, so ce taṃ bhaṇḍaṃ avaharati, āṇattiyā avahaṭaṃ nāma hotīti yuttaṃ āṇāpakassa pārājikaṃ.

'Thus, again, even with a command, it is only a minor offense'—this was said first because there is no accomplishment of the purpose. 'The pārājika offense occurs at the very moment of the command' means that, like the fruit immediately following the path, one becomes subject to pārājika at the very moment of the volition of command that accomplishes the purpose. 'Due to deafness' means that it is said that even if one speaks loudly, one does not make it heard due to deafness. In the case of 'I was commanded by you,' since there is no possibility of refusal and because there is no accomplishment of the purpose, there is no pārājika offense for the originator. 'If one writes on a leaf or a stone, “Stealing should be done,” and leaves it anywhere, it is a pārājika offense'—this is stated in all three sub-commentaries. But since that statement is distinguished from the section on taking what is not given by way of indirect speech, it should be considered after investigation. If, however, one writes on a leaf, 'In such-and-such a place, such-and-such goods are located; take them,' and sends it to someone, and if that person takes those goods, it is called 'taken by command'; thus it is proper that the one who gave the command incurs a pārājika offense.

Āṇattikathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on Commands is concluded.

Āpattibhedavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Kinds of Offenses

122. Tattha tatthāti bhūmaṭṭhathalaṭṭhādīsu. Aṅgañca dassentoti yojetabbaṃ. Vatthubhedenāti avaharitabbassa vatthussa garukalahukabhedena. Āpattibhedanti pārājikathullaccayadukkaṭānaṃ vasena āpattibhedaṃ. Manussabhūtena parena pariggahitaṃ parapariggahitaṃ.

122. Here, 'here and there' (tattha tattha) refers to places such as on the ground and in open spaces. And 'showing the limb' (aṅgañca dassento) should be construed. 'By the nature of the object' (vatthubhedena) means according to the distinction between heavy and light objects to be taken. 'Division of offenses' (āpattibhedaṃ) refers to the division of offenses by way of pārājika, thullaccaya, and dukkaṭa. That which is 'appropriated by another' (parapariggahitaṃ) means that which is appropriated by another human being.

125. Na [M 2.0159][V 2.0141] ca sakasaññīti iminā pana parapariggahitaṃ vatthu kathitaṃ. Na ca vissāsaggāhī, na ca tāvakālikanti iminā pana parapariggahitasaññā kathitā. Na vissāsaggāhitāti vissāsaggāhena aggahitabhāvo. Na tāvakālikatāti pacchā dātabbataṃ katvā aggahitabhāvo. Anajjhāvutthakanti “mameda”nti pariggahavasena anajjhāvutthakaṃ araññe dārutiṇapaṇṇādi. Chaḍḍitanti kaṭṭhahārādīhi atibhārāditāya anatthikabhāvena araññādīsu chaḍḍitaṃ. Chinnamūlakanti naṭṭhaṃ pariyesitvā ālayasaṅkhātassa mūlassa chinnattā chinnamūlaṃ. Asāmikanti anajjhāvutthakādīhi tīhi ākārehi dassitaṃ asāmikavatthu. Ubhayampīti yathāvuttalakkhaṇaṃ asāmikaṃ attano santakañca.

125. By 'not with the perception "it is one's own"' is stated an object appropriated by another. By 'not taken on trust, nor temporarily' is stated the perception of being appropriated by another. 'Not taken on trust' means the state of not being taken by way of trust. 'Not temporarily' means the state of not being taken after having made it a condition to give it back later. 'Not dwelt in' means wood, grass, leaves, and so forth in the forest that are not dwelt in by way of appropriation with the thought 'this is mine'. 'Discarded' means that which is discarded in the forest and so forth, being unwanted due to excessive weight and so forth, by wood-gatherers and so forth. 'Rootless' means that which is lost, its root, namely clinging, being severed after searching. 'Ownerless' is ownerless material shown in three ways: not dwelt in, discarded, and rootless. 'Both' refers to both ownerless things with the aforementioned characteristics and one's own property.

Āpattibhedavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Kinds of Offenses is concluded.

Anāpattibhedavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Kinds of Non-Offenses

131. Yāya seyyāya sayito kālaṃ karoti, sā anuṭṭhānaseyyā nāma. “Cittena pana adhivāsetī”ti vuttamatthaṃ vibhāvetuṃ “na kiñci vadatī”ti vuttaṃ. Pākatikaṃ kātunti yattakaṃ gahitaṃ paribhuttaṃ vā, tattakaṃ dātabbanti vuttaṃ hoti.

131. The bed on which one lies down and dies is called the 'bed of non-rising'. To clarify the meaning stated by 'but if he consents with his mind', it is said, 'he says nothing'. 'To make it ordinary' means that whatever was taken or used should be given back.

Paṭidassāmīti yaṃ gahitaṃ, tadeva vā aññaṃ vā tādisaṃ puna dassāmīti attho. Saṅghasantake saṅghaṃ anujānāpetumasakkuṇeyyattā kassaci vatthuno ananujānitabbato ca “saṅghasantakaṃ pana paṭidātumeva vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ.

'I will return it' means 'I will give back what was taken, or something else similar to it.' Since it is impossible to obtain permission from the Sangha regarding Sangha property, and also because no item is to be permitted, it is said, 'but it is indeed proper to return Sangha property'.

Tasmiṃyeva attabhāve nibbattāpīti tasmiṃyeva matasarīre uppannāpi. Vinītavatthūsu sāṭakataṇhāya tasmiṃyeva matasarīre nibbattapeto viyāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Rukkhādīsu laggitasāṭake vattabbameva natthīti manussehi apariggahitaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Sace pana taṃ ārakkhakehi pariggahitaṃ hoti, gahetuṃ na vaṭṭatīti.

'Even if reborn in that very existence' means even if arisen in that very dead body. It should be understood as a hungry ghost reborn in that very dead body due to craving for cloth, as in the Vinītavatthu. Regarding cloth hanging on trees and so forth, the statement 'there is nothing to be said' is made with reference to what is unappropriated by humans. However, if it is appropriated by guards, it is not proper to take it.

Anāpattibhedavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Kinds of Non-Offenses is concluded.

Padabhājanīyavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Analysis of Terms is concluded.

Pakiṇṇakakathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of Miscellaneous Topics

Dārukhaṇḍādīsu [M 2.0160][V 2.0142] “bhāriyamidaṃ, tvaṃ ekapassaṃ ukkhipāhi, ahaṃ ekapassaṃ ukkhipāmī”ti ubhayesaṃ payogena ekassa vatthuno ṭhānācāvanaṃ sandhāya “sāhatthikāṇattika”nti vuttaṃ. Idañca kāyavācānaṃ īdise ṭhāne aṅgabhāvamattadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Yāya pana cetanāya samuṭṭhāpito payogo sāhatthiko āṇattiko vā padhānabhāvena ṭhānācāvanaṃ sādheti, tassā vasena āpatti kāretabbā. Aññathā sāhatthikaṃ vā āṇattikassa aṅgaṃ na hoti, āṇattikaṃ vā sāhatthikassāti idaṃ virujjhati.

In the case of pieces of wood and so forth, the term 'personal and commanded' is used with reference to moving an object from its place through the combined effort of two people, as when they say, 'This is heavy; you lift one side, and I will lift the other side.' And this is stated merely to show the subordinate role of body and speech in such a situation. However, the offense should be determined based on the volition by which the effort is initiated, whether personal or commanded, which primarily accomplishes the act of moving the object from its place. Otherwise, this statement would be contradictory: that a personal action is not a factor of a commanded one, or that a commanded action is not a factor of a personal one.

Pakiṇṇakakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of Miscellaneous Topics is concluded.

Vinītavatthuvaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Decided Cases

132. Vinītavatthūsu sandhāvatīti suṭṭhu dhāvati. Vidhāvatīti vividhā nānappakārena dhāvati. Kāyavacīdvārabhedaṃ vināpīti kāyacopanaṃ vacībhedañca vinā. Paṭisaṅkhānabalenāti tathāvidhacittuppāde ādīnavapaccavekkhaṇabalena.

132. In the Decided Cases: 'sandhāvati' means it runs well. 'Vidhāvati' means it runs in various diverse ways. 'Kāyavacīdvārabhedaṃ vināpi' means without bodily agitation and verbal utterance. 'Paṭisaṅkhānabalena' means by the power of reflecting on the danger in the arising of such a state of mind.

135. Pucchāsabhāgenāti pucchānurūpena. Nirutti eva patho niruttipatho, tasmiṃ niruttipathe. Tenāha “vohāravacanamatte”ti.

135. 'Pucchāsabhāgena' means in accordance with the question. Nirutti is itself the path, hence 'niruttipatha'; in that path of expression. Therefore, it is said, 'merely a conventional expression.'

137. Yathākammaṃ gatoti iminā tassa matabhāvaṃ dasseti. Abbhuṇheti imināpi vuttameva pariyāyantarena vibhāvetuṃ “allasarīre”ti vuttaṃ. Visabhāgasarīreti itthisarīre. Visabhāgasarīrattā accāsannena na bhavitabbanti āha “sīse vā”tiādi. Vaṭṭatīti visabhāgasarīrepi attanāva vuttavidhiṃ kātuṃ sāṭakañca gahetuṃ vaṭṭati. Keci pana “kiñcāpi iminā sikkhāpadena anāpatti, itthirūpaṃ pana āmasantassa dukkaṭa”nti vadanti.

137. By 'gone according to his kamma,' his state of being dead is shown. By 'he should lift up' as well, 'a wet body' is stated in order to clarify what has already been said by means of another expression. 'A body of the opposite kind' means a woman's body. Because it is a body of the opposite kind, one should not be too close; thus it is said, 'on the head,' etc. 'It is fitting' means it is fitting to perform the prescribed method oneself and to take the robe, even with a body of the opposite kind. Some, however, say: 'Although there is no offense under this training rule, for one who touches a woman's form, there is a dukkaṭa offense.'

138. Kusaṃ saṅkāmetvāti kusaṃ parivattetvā. Kūṭamānakūṭakahāpaṇādīhīti ādi-saddena tulākūṭakaṃsakūṭavañcanādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Tattha [M 2.0161] kūṭamānaṃ hadayabhedasikhābhedarajjubhedavasena tividhaṃ hoti. Tattha hadayanti nāḷiādimānabhājanānaṃ abbhantaraṃ, tassa bhedo chiddakaraṇaṃ hadayabhedo, so sappitelādiminanakāle labbhati. Tāni hi gaṇhanto heṭṭhāchiddena mānena “saṇikaṃ āsiñcā”ti vatvā antobhājane bahuṃ paggharāpetvā gaṇhāti, dadanto chiddaṃ pidhāya sīghaṃ pūretvā [V 2.0143] deti. Sikhābhedo tilataṇḍulādiminanakāle labbhati. Tāni hi gaṇhanto saṇikaṃ sikhaṃ ussāpetvā gaṇhāti, dento vegena pūretvā sikhaṃ chindanto deti. Rajjubhedo khettavatthuminanakāle labbhati. Khettādiṃ minantā hi amahantampi mahantaṃ katvā minanti, mahantampi amahantaṃ. Kūṭakahāpaṇo pākaṭoyeva.

138. 'Kusaṃ saṅkāmetvā' means having changed the lot. By 'with false measures, false coins, etc.,' the word 'etc.' includes false scales, false bowls, deceit, and so on. Among these, a false measure is of three kinds: by breaking the interior, breaking the peak, or breaking the cord. Herein, 'the interior' refers to the inside of measuring vessels such as a nāḷi. Breaking it means making a hole; this is called 'breaking the interior.' It is found when measuring ghee, oil, and so on. For when receiving, one says, 'Pour slowly,' and using a measure with a hole at the bottom, causes a large amount to leak out and collects it; when giving, one covers the hole, fills it quickly, and gives it. 'Breaking the peak' is found when measuring sesame, rice, and so on. For when receiving, one slowly raises the peak to gather more; when giving, one fills it quickly and cuts off the peak while giving it. 'Breaking the cord' is found when measuring fields or land. For those measuring fields, etc., make what is not large into large, and what is large into not large. A false coin is self-evident.

Tulākūṭaṃ pana rūpakūṭaṃ aṅgakūṭaṃ gahaṇakūṭaṃ paṭicchannakūṭanti catubbidhaṃ hoti. Tattha rūpakūṭaṃ nāma dve tulā sarūpā katvā gaṇhanto mahatiyā gaṇhāti, dadanto khuddikāya deti. Aṅgakūṭaṃ nāma gaṇhanto pacchābhāge hatthena tulaṃ akkamati, dadanto pubbabhāge akkamati. Gahaṇakūṭaṃ nāma gaṇhanto mūle rajjuṃ gaṇhāti, dadanto agge. Paṭicchannakūṭaṃ nāma tulaṃ susiraṃ katvā anto ayacuṇṇaṃ pakkhipitvā gaṇhanto taṃ pacchābhāge karoti, dadanto aggabhāge.

A fraudulent scale, however, is of four kinds: form fraud, beam fraud, handling fraud, and concealed fraud. Herein, form fraud is when one makes two scales of the same form, but receives with the large one and gives with the small one. Beam fraud is when, while receiving, one presses down on the back part of the scale with one's hand, and while giving, one presses down on the front part. Handling fraud is when, while receiving, one holds the cord at the base, and while giving, holds it at the tip. Concealed fraud is when one makes the scale-beam hollow, puts iron powder inside, and while receiving, makes the powder go to the back part, and while giving, makes it go to the front part.

Kaṃso vuccati suvaṇṇapāti, tāya vañcanaṃ kaṃsakūṭaṃ. Kathaṃ? Ekaṃ suvaṇṇapātiṃ katvā aññā dve tisso lohapātiyo suvaṇṇavaṇṇā karonti, tato janapadaṃ gantvā kiñcideva aḍḍhaṃ kulaṃ pavisitvā “suvaṇṇabhājanāni kiṇathā”ti vatvā agghe pucchite samagghataraṃ dātukāmā honti. Tato tehi “kathaṃ imesaṃ suvaṇṇabhāvo jānitabbo”ti vutte “vīmaṃsitvā gaṇhathā”ti suvaṇṇapātiṃ pāsāṇe ghaṃsitvā sabbapātiyo datvā gacchanti.

A golden bowl is called a 'kaṃsa,' and deception using it is called 'kaṃsakūṭa.' How so? They make one golden bowl and two or three other metal bowls the color of gold. Then, going to a district, they enter some wealthy family and say, 'Buy these golden vessels.' When asked the price, they ask for a very high price. Then, when they are asked, 'How can we know these are truly golden?' they reply, 'Examine and then take them.' They rub the golden bowl on a touchstone, give all the bowls, and leave.

Vañcanaṃ nāma tehi tehi upāyehi paresaṃ vañcanaṃ. Tatridamekaṃ vatthu – eko kira luddako migañca migapotakañca gahetvā āgacchati. Tameko dhutto “kiṃ, bho, migo agghati, kiṃ migapotako”ti āha. “Migo dve kahāpaṇe, migapotako eka”nti ca vutte ekaṃ kahāpaṇaṃ datvā migapotakaṃ gahetvā thokaṃ gantvā nivatto “na me, bho, migapotakena attho, migaṃ me dehī”ti āha. Tena hi dve kahāpaṇe dehīti. So āha – “nanu, bho, mayā paṭhamaṃ eko kahāpaṇo [M 2.0162] dinno”ti? “Āma dinno”ti. “Imaṃ migapotakaṃ gaṇha, evaṃ so ca kahāpaṇo, ayañca kahāpaṇagghanako migapotakoti dve kahāpaṇā bhavissantī”ti. So “kāraṇaṃ vadatī”ti sallakkhetvā migapotakaṃ gahetvā migaṃ adāsīti.

Deception means deceiving others through various means. Here is one instance: A hunter, it seems, was coming along having caught a deer and a fawn. A rogue asked him, 'Sir, how much is the deer? How much is the fawn?' When he replied, 'The deer is two kahāpaṇas, the fawn is one,' the rogue gave one kahāpaṇa, took the fawn, went a little way, then turned back and said, 'Sir, I have no use for the fawn, give me the deer.' 'In that case, give me two kahāpaṇas.' He said, 'But sir, did I not already give you one kahāpaṇa?' 'Yes, you did.' 'Then take this fawn. That kahāpaṇa and this fawn, which is worth one kahāpaṇa, will make two kahāpaṇas.' Thinking, 'He speaks reason,' the hunter took the fawn and gave him the deer.

Balasāti balena. Panthaghāta-ggahaṇena himaviparāmosagumbaviparāmosāpi saṅgahitā. Tattha yaṃ himapātasamaye himena paṭicchannā hutvā maggappaṭipannaṃ janaṃ mūsanti, ayaṃ himaviparāmoso. Yaṃ gummādīhi paṭicchannā janaṃ mūsanti, ayaṃ gumbaviparāmoso.

'Balasā' means by force. By the inclusion of waylaying, plundering by concealment in snow and plundering by concealment in thickets are also included. Herein, plundering by concealment in snow is when, during a time of snowfall, they hide themselves with snow and plunder people traveling on the path. Plundering by concealment in thickets is when, hidden by thickets and so on, they plunder people.

Uddhāreyeva [V 2.0144] pārājikanti “sace sāṭako bhavissati, gaṇhissāmī”ti parikappassa pavattattā sāṭakassa ca tattha sabbhāvato. Padavārena kāretabboti bhūmiyaṃ anikkhipitvāva vīmaṃsitattā vuttaṃ. Pariyuṭṭhitoti anubaddho. Disvā haṭattā parikappāvahāro na dissatīti iminā parikappāvahārassa asambhavaṃ dassento mahāpaccariādīsu vuttassa ayuttabhāvaṃ vibhāveti. Mahāaṭṭhakathāyantiādinā pana parikappāvahārasambhavaṃ pāḷiyā saṃsandanabhāvañca vibhāvento mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttameva suvuttanti dīpeti. Teneva mātikāṭṭhakathāyampi mahāaṭṭhakathānayova dassito.

The Pārājika offense is only in the removal, because of the occurrence of the intention, 'If it is a robe, I will take it,' and because of the existence of the robe there. 'It should be done by way of steps' is said because it was investigated without placing it on the ground. 'Pariyuṭṭhito' means pursued. By this statement, 'because it was taken after seeing, removal with prior intention is not found,' showing the impossibility of removal with prior intention, he clarifies the inappropriateness of what was said in the Mahāpaccari and other texts. But by the text beginning 'In the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā,' while clarifying the possibility of removal with prior intention and its consistency with the Pāḷi, he shows that what was said in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā is indeed well-said. For that very reason, in the Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā too, the method of the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā is shown.

Kecīti mahāaṭṭhakathāyameva ekacce ācariyā. Mahāpaccariyaṃ panāti pana-saddo kecivādato mahāpaccarivādassa visesasandassanattho. Tena kecivādo mahāpaccarivādenapi na sametīti dasseti. Mahāaṭṭhakathānayo eva ca mahāpaccarivādenapi saṃsandanato yuttataroti vibhāveti.

'Keci' means certain teachers in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā itself. In 'Mahāpaccariyaṃ pana,' the word 'pana' is for the purpose of showing the distinction of the Mahāpaccari view from the 'keci' view. By that, it shows that the 'keci' view does not agree even with the Mahāpaccari view. And it clarifies that the method of the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā is more reasonable because it is consistent even with the Mahāpaccari view.

Alaṅkārabhaṇḍanti aṅgulimuddikādi alaṅkārabhaṇḍaṃ. Kusaṃ pātetvāti vilīvamayaṃ vā tālapaṇṇamayaṃ vā katasaññāṇaṃ yaṃ kiñci kusaṃ pātetvā. Samagghataranti appagghataraṃ. Parakoṭṭhāsato kuse uddhaṭepi na tāva kusassa parivattanaṃ jātanti vuttaṃ “uddhāre rakkhatī”ti. Siveyyakanti siviraṭṭhe jātaṃ.

'Alaṅkārabhaṇḍa' means ornamental goods such as finger-rings. 'Kusaṃ pātetvā' means having cast down any mat made as a sign, whether made of split bamboo or of palm leaf. 'Samagghataraṃ' means less valuable. Even when a mat is lifted from another's portion, because the transfer of the mat has not yet occurred, it is said, 'he protects it in the removal.' 'Siveyyaka' means produced in the Sivi country.

139. Jantāgharavatthusmiṃ yasmā ānandatthero tattha anāpattibhāvaṃ jānāti, tasmā “tassa kukkuccaṃ ahosī”ti na vuttaṃ. Yasmā ca sayaṃ bhagavato nārocesi, tasmā “ārocesī”ti ekavacanaṃ na vuttaṃ.

139. In the story of the steam-bath house, because the Elder Ānanda knew that there was a state of no-offense there, it was not said, 'he had remorse.' And because he himself did not inform the Blessed One, therefore the singular word 'ārocesi' was not used.

140. Vighāsanti [M 2.0163] khāditāvasesaṃ ucchiṭṭhaṃ vā. Kappiyaṃ kārāpetvāti pacāpetvā. Attaguttatthāyāti taṃnimittaupaddavato attānaṃ rakkhaṇatthāya. Jighacchābhibhūtā hi sīhādayo attanā khādiyamānaṃ gaṇhantānaṃ anatthampi kareyyuṃ. Parānuddayatāyāti sīhādīsu parasattesu anukampāya. Jighacchāvinodanatthañhi tehi khādiyamānaṃ te palāpetvā gaṇhato tesu anukampā nāma na bhavissati.

140. 'Vighāsa' means the remainder of what has been eaten, or leftovers. 'Having had it made allowable' means having had it cooked. 'For the sake of protecting oneself' means for the sake of protecting oneself from danger on account of that. For lions and others, overcome by hunger, might do harm to those who take what is being eaten by them. 'Out of compassion for others' means out of compassion for other beings such as lions. For, for one who takes what is being eaten by them for the sake of dispelling hunger, having chased them away, there will be no such thing as compassion for them.

141. Tekaṭulayāguvatthumhi viyāti musāvādasāmaññato vuttaṃ. Āṇattehīti sammatena āṇattehi. Āṇattenāti sāmikehi āṇattena. Aparassa bhāgaṃ dehīti asantaṃ puggalaṃ dassetvā [V 2.0145] gahitattā “bhaṇḍadeyya”nti vuttaṃ. Aññenāti yathāvuttehi sammatādīhi catūhi aññena. “Aparampi bhāgaṃ dehī”ti vuttepi saṅghasantakattā amūlakameva gahitanti “uddhāreyeva bhaṇḍagghena kāretabbo”ti vuttaṃ. Itarehi dīyamānanti sammatena, tena āṇattena vā dīyamānaṃ. Evaṃ gaṇhatoti “aparampi bhāgaṃ dehī”ti vatvā vā kūṭavassāni gaṇetvā vā gaṇhato. Sudinnanti heṭṭhā sāmikena, tena āṇattena vā dīyamānaṃ gihisantakaṃ “aparassa bhāgaṃ dehī”ti vatvā gaṇhato aparassa abhāvato sāmisantakameva hotīti bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ jātaṃ. Idha pana tehi evaṃ dīyamānaṃ “aparampi bhāgaṃ dehīti vatvā vā kūṭavassāni gaṇetvā vā gaṇhato dehī”ti vuttattā aññātakaviññattimattaṃ ṭhapetvā neva pārājikaṃ na bhaṇḍadeyyanti sudinnameva hoti.

141. In the story of the three-pot gruel, 'viya' is said from the general standpoint of false speech. 'Āṇattehi' means by one appointed by agreement. 'Āṇattena' means by one ordered by the owners. Because it was taken by indicating a non-existent person while saying, 'Give a portion to another,' it is called 'bhaṇḍadeyya' (goods to be returned). Even when it is said, 'Give another portion too,' since it belongs to the Sangha, it is taken without basis; hence it is said, 'restitution of the value of the goods should be made only upon removal.' 'Given by others' means given by the one appointed by agreement or by one ordered by him. 'Taking thus' refers to one who takes by either saying, 'Give another portion too,' or by counting false years. 'Well-given': previously, when householder's property given by the owner or by one ordered by him is taken by saying, 'Give a portion to another,' due to the absence of 'another,' it remains the owner's property and becomes 'bhaṇḍadeyya.' Here, however, because it was said 'give' to one who takes what is given by them in this way—either by saying 'Give another portion too' or by counting false years—setting aside the mere intimation to an unknown person, it is neither a Pārājika offense nor 'bhaṇḍadeyya,' but is simply well-given.

142-3. Parikkhāravatthūsu vuttaparikkhārassa heṭṭhā vuttabhaṇḍassa ca ko viseso? Yaṃ paribhogayoggaṃ ābharaṇādirūpaṃ akatvā yathāsabhāvato ṭhapitaṃ, taṃ bhaṇḍaṃ. Yaṃ pana tathā katvā paribhuñjituṃ anucchavikākārena ṭhapitaṃ ābharaṇādikaṃ, taṃ parikkhāranti veditabbaṃ.

What is the difference between the requisites (parikkhāra) mentioned in the stories on requisites and the goods (bhaṇḍa) mentioned below? That which is suitable for use, such as ornaments, kept in its natural state without being fashioned, is 'goods' (bhaṇḍa). But that which, having been fashioned thus, such as ornaments, is kept in a manner suitable for use, should be known as 'requisites' (parikkhāra).

144-146. Saṅkāmetvāti ṭhitaṭṭhānato apanetvā. Thavikanti upāhanatthavikādi yaṃkiñci thavikaṃ. Āharāpentesu bhaṇḍadeyyanti “gahite attamano hotī”ti (mahāva. 356) vacanato anattamanassa santakaṃ gahitampi [M 2.0164] puna dātabbamevāti vuttaṃ. “Sammukhībhūtehi bhājetabba”nti (mahāva. 379) vacanato bhājanīyabhaṇḍaṃ upacārasīmaṭṭhānaṃyeva pāpuṇātīti āha “upacārasīmāyaṃ ṭhitasseva gahetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti.

'Saṅkāmetvā' means having removed it from the place where it was. 'Thavika' means any kind of bag, such as a shoe-bag. Regarding 'bhaṇḍadeyya when having things brought,' it is said that because of the statement, 'One is pleased when it is taken,' even what is taken that belongs to someone who is displeased must be given back. Because of the statement, 'It should be distributed by those who are present,' distributable goods reach only those standing in the vicinity-boundary; therefore, he said, 'It is permissible for one standing within the vicinity-boundary to take it.'

148-9. “Bhaṇḍadeyyanti ubhinnaṃ sālayabhāve sati corassa vā sāmikassa vā sampattassa kassaci dātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti. Eseva nayoti paṃsukūlasaññāya gahite bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ, theyyacittena pārājikanti attho. Gāmesūti gāmikesu manussesu. Gāma-ggahaṇena hettha gāmaṭṭhā vuttā. Vuṭṭhahantesūti gāmaṃ chaḍḍetvā palāyantesu. Puna āvasante janapadeti jānapadikesu puna āgantvā vasantesu.

They say: 'Bhaṇḍadeyya means that when both have a claim, it is permissible to give it to whichever one—the thief or the owner—is present.' This is the method: if taken with the perception of it being refuse-rag, it is bhaṇḍadeyya; with a thievish thought, it is a Pārājika offense. This is the meaning. 'In villages' means among the village people. Here, by the term 'village,' village-dwellers are meant. 'Vuṭṭhahantesu' means among those fleeing after abandoning the village. 'Puna āvasante janapade' means among the country-folk who have returned and are dwelling there again.

Avisesena vuttanti “saussāhā vā nirussāhā vā”ti visesaṃ aparāmasitvā sāmaññato vuttaṃ. Na hi katipayānaṃ anussāhe sati saṅghikaṃ asaṅghikaṃ hotīti ayamettha adhippāyo. Saussāhamattameva pamāṇanti sāmikānaṃ paricchinnabhāvato vuttaṃ. Tatoti gaṇasantakato puggalasantakato vā. Senāsanatthāya niyamitanti idaṃ nidassanamattaṃ, catūsu paccayesu [V 2.0146] yassa kassaci atthāya niyamitepi vuttanayameva. Issaravatāyāti paraṃ āpucchitvā vā anāpucchitvā vā dātabbakiccaṃ natthi, ayamevettha pamāṇanti evaṃ attano issarabhāvena. Agghena kāretabboti agghānurūpaṃ dukkaṭena thullaccayena vā kāretabbo. Issaravatāya paribhuñjato gīvāti na kevalaṃ ettheva gīvā, heṭṭhā kulasaṅgahatthāya issaravatāya vā dinnepi gīvāyeva. Sukhāditamevāti antovihāre nisīditvā ghaṇṭippaharaṇādivuttavidhānassa katattā sukhāditaṃ. Saṅghikañhi vebhaṅgiyabhaṇḍaṃ antovihāre vā bahisīmāya vā hotu, bahisīmāyaṃ ṭhitehi apaloketvā bhājetuṃ na vaṭṭati, ubhayattha ṭhitampi pana antosīmāyaṃ ṭhitehi apaloketvā bhājetuṃ vaṭṭatiyeva. Teneva tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ “vihāreyeva nisīditvā evaṃ katattā sukhāditanti āhā”ti. Ayañca attho vassūpanāyikakkhandhakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ āvi bhavissati.

‘It is said without distinction’ means it is stated generally, without considering the distinction of ‘whether zealous or unzealous.’ For the intention here is that when a few are unzealous, that which is communal does not become non-communal. ‘Only zeal is the measure’ is said because the owners have defined it. ‘From that’ means whether from the community’s possession or an individual’s possession. ‘It is designated for the purpose of lodging’ is merely an illustration; the same principle applies even when any of the four requisites are designated for any purpose. ‘By authority’ means that there is no obligation to give, whether after asking others or without asking; this alone is the measure here, thus by one’s own authority. ‘One should be dealt with according to value’ means one should be dealt with by a minor offense (dukkaṭa) or a grave offense (thullaccaya) according to its value. ‘It is a fault for one who enjoys by authority’ means it is not only a fault here; even below, when given by authority for the sake of supporting lay devotees, it is still a fault. ‘It is well-eaten’ means it is well-eaten because the procedure of striking the bell, etc., as mentioned, was done while sitting inside the monastery. For communal divisible goods, whether they are inside the monastery or outside the boundary, it is not permissible for those standing outside the boundary to divide them after obtaining consent. But even if the goods are in both places, it is permissible for those inside the boundary to divide them after obtaining consent. Therefore, it is said in all three knotty passages: ‘He said, “Because it was done thus, sitting only inside the monastery, it is well-eaten.”’ And this meaning will become clear in the commentary on the Vassūpanāyikakkhandhaka.

150. Vuttavādakavatthūsu pāḷiyaṃ yugasāṭakanti sāṭakayugaṃ. Tulanti palasataṃ. Doṇanti soḷasanāḷimattaṃ. Paricchedaṃ pana katvāti yattakaṃ [M 2.0165] icchitaṃ, tattakaṃ agghavasena vā cīvarādipaccayavasena vā paricchedaṃ katvā. Upārambhāti “bhadantā aparicchedaṃ katvā vadantī”ti evaṃ dosāropanato.

150. In the aforementioned cases, in the Pāḷi, ‘yugasāṭaka’ means a pair of cloths. ‘Tula’ means a hundred palas. ‘Doṇa’ refers to a measure of sixteen nāḷis. ‘But having made a determination’ means having made a determination of as much as is desired, whether in terms of value or in terms of requisites such as robes, etc. ‘Upārambhā’ refers to the imputation of a fault, such as, ‘Venerable sirs, you speak without making a determination,’ thus laying blame.

153. Chātajjhattanti jighacchādukkhena pīḷitaattasantānaṃ. Dhanukanti khuddakadhanukaṃ. Baddho hotīti tiriyaṃ baddho hoti. Sunakhadaṭṭhanti sāmikehi vissajjitasunakhena gahitaṃ. Yaṭṭhiyā saha pātetīti sūkarassa āgamanato puretarameva tattha abajjhanatthāya pāteti. Maddanto gacchati, bhaṇḍadeyyanti ekasūkaragghanakaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ dātabbaṃ. Na hi tena maggena gacchantā sabbeva sūkarā tena pāsena bajjhanti, ekoyeva paṭhamataraṃ gacchanto bajjhati, tasmā ekasūkaragghanakaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ dātabbaṃ. Pacchā gacchatīti tena katapayogena agantvā pacchā sayameva gacchati. Heṭṭhā vuttesupi īdisesu ṭhānesu eseva nayo. Uddharitvā chaḍḍetīti puretarameva uddharitvā chaḍḍeti. Vihārabhūmiyanti vihārasāmantā araññappadese. Rakkhaṃ yācitvāti rājarājamahāmattādīnaṃ santikaṃ gantvā anuddissa rakkhaṃ yācitvā.

153. ‘Chātajjhatta’ means one whose personal continuity is afflicted by the suffering of hunger. ‘Dhanuka’ refers to a small bow. ‘It is bound’ means it is bound crosswise. ‘Bitten by a dog’ means seized by a dog released by its owners. ‘He makes it fall with a stick’ means he makes it fall beforehand, before the pig's arrival, so that it will not be caught there. Regarding ‘He goes crushing, it is a case where goods must be given,’ it means goods equivalent to the value of one pig must be given. For not all pigs going by that path are caught by that snare; only the one going first is caught. Therefore, goods equivalent to the value of one pig must be given. ‘It goes later’ means it goes later by itself, not having come by means of the effort made by him. In similar cases mentioned below, this is the same method. ‘Having lifted it up, he discards it’ means he lifts it up and discards it beforehand. ‘On monastery ground’ refers to a wilderness area in the vicinity of the monastery. ‘Having asked for protection’ means having gone to kings, royal ministers, etc., and having asked for unspecified protection.

Kumīnamukhanti kumīnassa anto macchānaṃ pavisanamukhaṃ. Gumbe khipati, bhaṇḍadeyyamevāti kumīnassa anto pavisitabbānaṃ macchānaṃ agghena bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ.

‘Mouth of the fish-trap’ means the entrance for fish to enter into the fish-trap. Regarding ‘He throws it in a bush, it is a case where goods must be given,’ it means it is a case where goods must be given, equivalent to the value of the fish that would have entered the fish-trap.

156. Vīsatiṃsādivasena paricchinnā bhikkhū etthāti paricchinnabhikkhukaṃ. Therānanti āgantukattherānaṃ[V 2.0147]. Tesampīti āvāsikabhikkhūnampi. Paribhogatthāyāti saṅghikaparibhogavasena paribhuñjanatthāya. Gahaṇeti pāṭhaseso daṭṭhabbo. Yatthāti yasmiṃ āvāse. Aññesaṃ atthibhāvanti aññesaṃ āgantukabhikkhūnaṃ atthibhāvaṃ. Tatthāti tādise āvāse. Bhājetvā khādantīti āgantukānampi sampattānaṃ bhājetvā khādantīti adhippāyo. Catūsu paccayesu sammā upanentīti ambaphalādīni vikkiṇitvā cīvarādīsu catūsu paccayesu sammā upanenti. Cīvaratthāya niyametvā dinnāti “imesaṃ rukkhānaṃ phalāni vikkiṇitvā cīvaresuyeva upanetabbāni, na bhājetvā khāditabbānī”ti evaṃ niyametvā dinnā. Tesupi āgantukā [M 2.0166] anissarāti paccayaparibhogatthāya niyametvā dinnattā bhājetvā khādituṃ anissarā.

156. ‘A place with a limited number of monks’ means a place where monks are limited by way of twenty, thirty, etc. ‘Of the elders’ refers to the visiting elders. ‘Of them also’ includes the resident monks as well. ‘For the purpose of use’ means for the purpose of using by way of communal use. ‘In taking’ is a textual remainder to be understood. ‘Where’ means in whichever monastery. ‘The presence of others’ means the presence of other visiting monks. ‘There’ means in such a monastery. ‘They divide and eat’: the intention is that they also divide it for the visiting monks who have arrived, and then they eat. ‘They properly apply to the four requisites’ means having sold fruits like mangoes, etc., they properly apply the proceeds to the four requisites, such as robes, etc. ‘Given, having designated for the purpose of robes’ means they were given with the stipulation: ‘The fruits of these trees must be sold and applied only to robes; they are not to be divided and eaten.’ ‘In these too, visiting monks are not in authority’ means they are not in authority to divide and eat, as the items were given having been designated for the purpose of using the requisites.

Na tesu…pe… ṭhātabbanti ettha āgantukehi heṭṭhā vuttanayena bhājetvā khāditabbanti adhippāyo. Tesaṃ katikāya ṭhātabbanti “bhājetvā na khāditabba”nti vā “ettakesu rukkhesu phalāni gaṇhissāmā”ti vā “ettakāni phalāni gaṇhissāmā”ti vā “ettakānaṃ divasānaṃ abbhantare gaṇhissāmā”ti vā “na kiñci gaṇhissāmā”ti vā evaṃ katāya āvāsikānaṃ katikāya āgantukehi ṭhātabbaṃ. Mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “anissarā”ti vacanena dīpitoyeva attho mahāpaccariyaṃ “catunnaṃ paccayāna”ntiādinā vitthāretvā dassito. Paribhogavasenevāti ettha eva-saddo aṭṭhānappayutto. Paribhogavasena tameva bhājetvāti yojetabbaṃ. Etthāti etasmiṃ vihāre raṭṭhe vā. Senāsanapaccayanti senāsanañca tadatthāya niyametvā ṭhapitañca.

‘Not in them…pe… should one abide’: here, the intention is that it should be divided and eaten by the visiting monks according to the method stated above. ‘Their agreement should be abided by’ means the visiting monks should abide by the agreement made by the residents, thus: “It should not be divided and eaten,” or “We will take fruits from this many trees,” or “We will take this many fruits,” or “We will take them within this many days,” or “We will not take anything.” The meaning explained by the word “anissarā” (not in authority) in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā is shown in detail in the Mahāpaccariya by “of the four requisites,” etc. In ‘paribhogavaseneva,’ here the word ‘eva’ is used in the wrong place. It should be construed as ‘paribhogavasena tam eva bhājetvā’ (having divided that very thing by way of use). ‘Here’ means in this monastery or country. ‘The lodging requisite’ means the lodging and that which has been set aside, having been designated for that purpose.

Lāmakakoṭiyāti lāmakaṃ ādiṃ katvā, lāmakasenāsanato paṭṭhāyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Senāsanepi tiṇādīni lāmakakoṭiyāva vissajjetabbāni, senāsanaparikkhārāpi lāmakakoṭiyāva vissajjetabbā. Mūlavatthucchedaṃ pana katvā na upanetabbanti iminā kiṃ vuttaṃ hotīti? Tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu tāva idaṃ vuttaṃ “sabbāni senāsanāni na vissajjetabbānīti vuttaṃ hotī”ti. Lāmakakoṭiyā vissajjentehipi senāsanabhūmiyo na vissajjetabbāti ayamattho vutto hotīti no khanti, vīmaṃsitvā yaṃ ruccati, taṃ gahetabbaṃ.

By ‘lāmakakoṭiyā’ (from the inferior end) it is said that one should take the inferior as the beginning, starting from an inferior lodging. Even in the case of lodgings, grass and so forth should be disposed of from the inferior end, and lodging requisites should also be disposed of from the inferior end. But what is meant by the statement, “Having destroyed the root-object, one should not apply it”? Indeed, in all three Gaṇṭhipadas, this is stated: “It is said that all lodgings should not be disposed of.” The meaning conveyed is that even when disposing of from the inferior end, the lodging grounds should not be disposed of. This is our preference; after investigating, one should accept what is agreeable.

Dhammasantakena buddhapūjaṃ kātuṃ, buddhasantakena vā dhammapūjaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati, na vaṭṭatīti? “Tathāgatassa kho etaṃ vāseṭṭha adhivacanaṃ dhammakāyo itipīti ca yo kho, vakkali, dhammaṃ passati, so maṃ passatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.87) ca vacanato vaṭṭatīti vadanti. Keci pana “evaṃ sante ‘yo, bhikkhave, maṃ upaṭṭhaheyya, so gilānaṃ upaṭṭhaheyyā’ti vacanato buddhasantakena gilānassapi bhesajjaṃ kātuṃ yuttanti āpajjeyya, tasmā na vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti, taṃ [V 2.0148] akāraṇaṃ. Na hi “yo, bhikkhave, maṃ upaṭṭhaheyya, so gilānaṃ upaṭṭhaheyyā”ti iminā attano ca gilānassa ca ekasadisatā tadupaṭṭhānassa vā [M 2.0167] samaphalatā vuttā. Ayañhettha attho “yo maṃ ovādānusāsanīkaraṇena upaṭṭhaheyya, so gilānaṃ upaṭṭhaheyya, mama ovādakaraṇena gilāno upaṭṭhātabbo”ti. Bhagavato ca gilānassa ca upaṭṭhānaṃ ekasadisanti evaṃ panettha attho na gahetabbo. Tasmā “yo vo, ānanda, mayā dhammo ca vinayo ca desito paññatto, so vo mamaccayena satthā”ti vacanato “ahañca panidāni eko ovadāmi anusāsāmi, mayi parinibbute imāni caturāsīti buddhasahassāni tumhe ovadissanti anusāsissantī”ti vuttattā ca bahussutaṃ bhikkhuṃ pasaṃsantena ca “yo bahussuto, na so tumhākaṃ sāvako nāma, buddho nāma esa cundā”ti vuttattā dhammagarukattā ca tathāgatassa pubbanayo eva pasatthataroti amhākaṃ khanti.

Is it proper to make an offering to the Buddha with what belongs to the Dhamma, or to make an offering to the Dhamma with what belongs to the Buddha, or is it not proper? Some say, “It is proper,” citing the words: “Vāseṭṭha, this is a designation for the Tathāgata: ‘The Dhamma-body,’ and ‘He who, Vakkali, sees the Dhamma, sees me’” (Saṃ. Ni. 3.87). Others, however, say: “If that were so, it would follow from the statement, ‘Whoever, monks, would attend to me should attend to the sick,’ that it is fitting to prepare medicine for the sick with what belongs to the Buddha. Therefore, it is not proper.” That is not a valid reason. For by the statement, “Whoever, monks, would attend to me should attend to the sick,” the equivalence of myself and the sick person, or the equal fruitfulness of attending to them, is not stated. This is the meaning here: “Whoever would attend to me by carrying out my advice and instruction, they should attend to the sick; the sick should be attended to by carrying out my advice.” The meaning here should not be taken as “attending to the Blessed One and attending to the sick are equivalent.” Therefore, based on the words, “Ānanda, the Dhamma and Vinaya that I have taught and laid down for you shall be your teacher after my passing,” and because it was said, “Now I alone advise and instruct, but after my final passing, these eighty-four thousand sections of the teachings will advise and instruct you,” and because, when praising a learned monk, it was said, “He who is learned is not your disciple, Cunda—he is a Buddha,” and because of the Tathāgata’s respect for the Dhamma, it is our preference that the former way is more praiseworthy.

Paṇṇaṃ āropetvāti “ettakeheva rukkhehi ettakameva gahetabba”nti paṇṇaṃ āropetvā, likhitvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Nimittasaññaṃ katvāti saṅketaṃ katvā. Dārakāti tesaṃ puttanattādayo dārakā. Aññepi ye keci gopakā honti, te sabbepi vuttā. Sabbatthāpi gihīnaṃ gopakadāne yattakaṃ gopakā denti, tattakaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Saṅghike pana yathāparicchedameva gahetabbanti dīpitattā “atthato eka”nti vuttaṃ.

By ‘paṇṇaṃ āropetvā’ (having placed on a leaf) is meant having written on a leaf, stipulating, ‘Only this much should be taken from this many trees.’ By ‘nimittasaññaṃ katvā’ (having made a sign) is meant having made a convention. By ‘dārakā’ (children) are meant their sons, grandsons, and so on. Also, whatever other caretakers there are, they are all included. In all cases, regarding a gift from a layperson's caretaker, whatever the caretaker gives, that much should be taken. But in the case of what belongs to the Sangha, it should be taken only according to the determined amount; because it is thus explained, it is said, ‘in meaning, it is one.’

Tatoti yathāvuttauposathāgārādikaraṇatthāya ṭhapitadārusambhārato. Āpucchitvāti kārakasaṅghaṃ āpucchitvā. Taṃ sabbampi āharitvāti anāpucchitvāpi tāvakālikaṃ āharitvā. Āharāpentoti ettha anāharāpentepi dātabbameva. Ayameva bhikkhu issaroti ekassa bhikkhuno pāpuṇanaṭṭhānaṃ, tatoyeva senāsanato tassa dātabbaṃ, na ca so tato uṭṭhāpetabboti vuttaṃ hoti.

By ‘tato’ (from that) is meant from the store of timber set aside for the purpose of constructing an Uposatha hall and so on, as previously mentioned. By ‘āpucchitvā’ (having asked) is meant having asked permission from the acting Saṅgha. By ‘taṃ sabbampi āharitvā’ (having brought all that) is meant having brought it temporarily, even without asking permission. By ‘āharāpento’ (having it brought), here, even if not having it brought, it must be given. By ‘ayameva bhikkhu issaro’ (this very bhikkhu is the master), it is said that it is a place obtained by a single bhikkhu; therefore, it should be given to him from that lodging, and he should not be made to get up from there.

“Udakapūjanti cetiyaṭṭhānesu siñcana”nti gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Vattasīsenāti kevalaṃ saddhāya, na vetanādiatthāya. Savatthukanti saha bhūmiyā. Tiṇamattaṃ pana dātabbanti kasmā vuttaṃ, kiṃ taṃ garubhaṇḍaṃ na hotīti? Na hoti. Arakkhitaagopitaṭṭhāne hi vinassakabhāvena ṭhitaṃ garubhaṇḍaṃ na hoti, tasmā tādisaṃ sandhāya “tiṇamattaṃ pana dātabba”nti vuttaṃ. Jaggitvāti saṃvacchare saṃvacchare jaggitvā.

In the Gaṇṭhipadas it is said: '`Udakapūjaṃ` means sprinkling at cetiya sites.' By `Vattasīsenā` is meant merely out of faith, not for the sake of payment or the like. By `savatthukaṃ` is meant together with the land. But why is it said, 'a mere blade of grass should be given'? Is that not a valuable item? It is not. Indeed, in an unprotected and unguarded place, an item that is of a perishable nature is not a valuable item. Therefore, with reference to such a thing, it is said, 'but a mere blade of grass should be given.' By `jaggitvā` is meant having taken care of year after year.

Kuṭṭanti [M 2.0168] gehabhittiṃ. Pākāranti parikkhepapākāraṃ. Tatoti chaḍḍitavihārato. Tato [V 2.0149] āharitvā senāsanaṃ kataṃ hotīti sāmantagāmavāsīhi bhikkhūhi chaḍḍitavihārato dārusambhārādiṃ āharitvā senāsanaṃ kataṃ hoti.

By `kuṭṭaṃ` is meant a house wall. By `pākāraṃ` is meant an enclosure wall. By `tato` is meant from a discarded dwelling. By 'Having brought from there, a lodging is made' is meant that a lodging is made by the bhikkhus dwelling in a nearby village, having brought timber, materials, and so forth from a discarded dwelling.

157. Catubhāgaudakasambhinneti catutthabhāgena udakena sambhinne. Odanabhājanīyavatthusminti “dehi aparassa bhāga”nti āgatavatthusmiṃ.

157. By `Catubhāgaudakasambhinne` is meant mixed with a fourth part of water. By `Odanabhājanīyavatthusmiṃ` is meant in the incident that has come down with the words, 'Give the other's share.'

159. Ayyā attanā kātuṃ yuttampi na karonti, ativiya thaddhāti pasādaṃ bhinditvā cittena kuppanti, tasmā “pasādānurakkhaṇatthāyā”ti vuttaṃ. Iddhiṃ paṭisaṃharīti iddhiṃ vissajjesi. Sakaṭṭhāneyeva aṭṭhāsīti iddhiyā vissajjitattā eva “pāsādo puna āgacchatū”ti anadhiṭṭhitepi sayameva āgantvā sakaṭṭhāneyeva aṭṭhāsi. “Yāva dārakā pāsādaṃ ārohanti, tāva pāsādo tesaṃ santike hotū”ti pubbe adhiṭṭhitattā eva ca kālaparicchedaṃ katvā adhiṭṭhitena tato paraṃ iddhi vissajjitā nāma hotīti katvā vuttaṃ “thero iddhiṃ paṭisaṃharī”ti. Yasmā te dārakā evaṃ gahetvā gatānaṃ santakā na honti, yasmā ca īdisena payogena therena te ānītā nāma na honti, tasmā thero evamakāsīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tenevāha “vohāravasenā”tiādi. Attano pakativaṇṇaṃ avijahitvā bahiddhā hatthiādidassanaṃ “ekopi hutvā bahudhā hotī”ti (dī. ni. 1.238; ma. ni. 1.147; saṃ. ni. 5.842) āgatañca adhiṭṭhānavasena nipphannattā adhiṭṭhāniddhi nāma. “So pakativaṇṇaṃ vijahitvā kumārakavaṇṇaṃ vā dasseti nāgavaṇṇaṃ vā…pe… vividhampi senābyūhaṃ dassetī”ti (paṭi. ma. 3.13) evaṃ āgatā iddhi pakativaṇṇavijahanavikāravasena pavattattā vikubbaniddhi nāma. Attānaṃ adassetvā bahiddhā hatthiādidassanampi ettheva saṅgahitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Pakativaṇṇavijahanañhi nāma attano pakatirūpassa aññesaṃ adassanaṃ, na sabbena sabbaṃ tassa nirodhanaṃ. Evañca katvā “attānaṃ adassetvā bahiddhā hatthiādidassanampi ettheva saṅgahita”nti idaṃ “pakativaṇṇaṃ vijahitvā”ti vuttamūlapadena na virujjhati.

159. They do not do what is proper for them to do themselves; being extremely stubborn, they break confidence and become agitated in mind. Therefore, it is said, 'for the sake of preserving confidence.' 'He withdrew the psychic power' means he released the psychic power. 'It stood in its very own place' means that because it had been released by psychic power, even though it was not willed, 'Let the palace return,' it came back by itself and stood in its original place. And because it had been previously willed, 'Let the palace remain near them until the children ascend it,' and because a time limit had been set by that act of willing, after which the psychic power is said to be released, it is therefore said, 'the elder withdrew the psychic power.' Since those children were not the property of those who had gone taking them, and since they were not in fact brought by the elder through such a device, it should be understood that the elder acted thus. Hence it is said, 'by way of convention,' etc. The external appearance of an elephant, etc., without abandoning one's natural form, as it appears in 'being one, he becomes many,' is called 'resolve-based psychic power' (adhiṭṭhāniddhi) because it is produced by the power of resolve. The psychic power that appears as 'abandoning his natural form, he displays the form of a boy or the form of a serpent... or even various military formations,' is called 'transformation-based psychic power' (vikubbaniddhi) because it operates by way of the transformation of abandoning one's natural form. It should be understood that even the external display of an elephant, etc., while making oneself invisible, is included here. For 'abandoning one's natural form' means making one's own natural form invisible to others, not its complete and utter annihilation. And so, the statement that 'even the external display of an elephant, etc., while making oneself invisible, is included here,' does not contradict the root statement, 'abandoning his natural form.'

Vinītavatthuvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Decided Cases is concluded.

Iti samantapāsādikāya vinayaṭṭhakathāya sāratthadīpaniyaṃ

Thus in the Sāratthadīpanī, a sub-commentary on the Samantapāsādikā, the Commentary on the Vinaya—

Dutiyapārājikavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Explanation of the Second Pārājika is complete.

Anusāsanīkathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discourse on Instruction

Parājitakilesenāti [M 2.0169][V 2.0150] santāne puna anuppattidhammatāpādanena catūhi maggañāṇehi saha vāsanāya samucchinnasabbakilesena. Idhāti imasmiṃ sāsane. Tena sikkhāpadena samaṃ aññaṃ anekanayavokiṇṇaṃ gambhīratthavinicchayaṃ kiñci sikkhāpadaṃ na vijjatīti yojetabbaṃ. Attho ca vinicchayo ca atthavinicchayā, gambhīrā atthavinicchayā assāti gambhīratthavinicchayaṃ. Vatthumhi otiṇṇeti codanāvatthumhi saṅghamajjhaṃ otiṇṇe, ekena ekasmiṃ codite, sayameva vā āgantvā attano katavītikkame ārociteti vuttaṃ hoti. Etthāti otiṇṇe vatthumhi.

“Pārājitakilesena” means by one whose defilements are defeated, that is, by whom all defilements, along with their latent tendencies, are utterly cut off through the four path-knowledges, by bringing about the characteristic of not arising again in the continuum. “Idha” means in this Dispensation. It should be connected thus: “No other training rule exists that is equal to that training rule, which is diverse in many ways and involves a profound determination of meaning.” “Atthavinicchayā” means meaning and determination; “gambhīratthavinicchayaṃ” means it has profound meaning-determination. “Vatthumhi otiṇṇe” means when one has entered into the midst of the Saṅgha concerning the matter of accusation, either being accused by someone, or having come oneself and declared one's own transgression—thus it is said. “Ettha” means in the matter that has been entered into.

Vinicchayaṃ karontena sahasā “pārājika”nti avatvā yaṃ kattabbaṃ, taṃ dassetuṃ “pāḷi”ntiādimāha. Vinicchayoti pārājikāpattivinicchayo. Avatvāvāti “tvaṃ pārājikaṃ āpanno”ti avatvāva. Kappiyepi ca vatthusminti avatvāpi gaṇhituṃ kappiye mātupitusantakepi vatthusmiṃ. Lahuvattinoti theyyacittuppādena lahuparivattino. Āsīvisanti sīghameva sakalasarīre pharaṇasamatthavisaṃ.

When making a determination, in order to show what should be done without hastily declaring “pārājika,” he said “pāḷi,” and so forth. “Vinicchayo” means the determination of a pārājika offense. “Avatvāvā” means without saying, “You have incurred a pārājika.” “Kappiyepi ca vatthusmin” means even in a permissible matter, that is, even in a matter concerning the possessions of one's mother or father, which it is permissible to take without asking. “Lahuvattino” means those who swiftly change their minds due to the arising of thieving thoughts. “Āsīvisa” means poison capable of spreading rapidly throughout the entire body.

Anusāsanīkathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on Instruction is completed.

Pārājikakaṇḍaṭṭhakathāya paṭhamabhāgavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the First Part of the Pārājika Section is completed.

3. Tatiyapārājikaṃ

3. The Third Pārājika

Tīhīti [V 2.0151] kāyavacīmanodvārehi. Vibhāvitanti pakāsitaṃ, desitaṃ paññattanti vuttaṃ hoti.

“By three” means by the doors of body, speech, and mind. “Vibhāvitaṃ” means made clear, taught, and designated—this is what is said.

Paṭhamapaññattinidānavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Origin of the First Designation

162. Tikkhattuṃ pākāraparikkhepavaḍḍhanenāti tikkhattuṃ pākāraparikkhepena nagarabhūmiyā vaḍḍhanena. Visālībhūtattāti gāvutantaraṃ gāvutantaraṃ puthubhūtattā. Bārāṇasirañño kira (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.146; khu. pā. aṭṭha. 6. ratanasuttavaṇṇanā) aggamahesiyā kucchimhi gabbho [M 2.0170] saṇṭhāsi, sā ñatvā rañño nivedesi, rājā gabbhaparihāraṃ adāsi. Sā sammā parihariyamānā gabbhaparipākakāle vijāyanagharaṃ pāvisi. Puññavantīnaṃ paccūsasamaye gabbhavuṭṭhānaṃ hoti, sā ca tāsaṃ aññatarā, tena paccūsasamaye alattakapaṭalabandhujīvakapupphasadisaṃ maṃsapesiṃ vijāyi. Tato “aññā deviyo suvaṇṇabimbasadise putte vijāyanti, aggamahesī maṃsapesinti rañño purato mama avaṇṇo uppajjeyyā”ti cintetvā tena avaṇṇabhayena taṃ maṃsapesiṃ ekasmiṃ bhājane pakkhipitvā paṭikujjitvā rājamuddikāya lañchetvā gaṅgāya sote pakkhipāpesi. Manussehi chaḍḍitamatte devatā ārakkhaṃ saṃvidahiṃsu. Suvaṇṇapaṭṭikañcettha jātihiṅgulakena “bārāṇasirañño aggamahesiyā pajā”ti likhitvā bandhiṃsu. Tato taṃ bhājanaṃ ūmibhayādīhi anupaddutaṃ gaṅgāsotena pāyāsi.

162. “By increasing the city's area three times with the construction of walls” means by expanding the city's land threefold with the enclosure of walls. “It became very spacious” means because it was broadened by a gāvuta at a time. It is said that in the womb of the chief queen of the King of Bārāṇasī, a fetus was conceived. Knowing this, she informed the king, who then provided care for her pregnancy. Being well-tended, she entered the delivery chamber when the time of birth arrived. For the meritorious, childbirth occurs at dawn, and she was one of them. Therefore, at dawn, she gave birth to a lump of flesh resembling a sheet of red lac and a bandhujīvaka flower. Thinking, “Other queens give birth to sons like golden images, but the chief queen bears a lump of flesh—this might bring me disgrace before the king,” she, fearing such disgrace, placed the lump of flesh in a vessel, covered it, sealed it with the royal signet, and had it cast into the Ganges' current. As soon as it was discarded by humans, the deities arranged for its protection. They also tied to it a golden plate, on which they wrote with genuine vermilion, “The offspring of the chief queen of the King of Bārāṇasī.” Then, the vessel, undisturbed by waves or other dangers, floated along the Ganges' current.

Tena ca samayena aññataro tāpaso gopālakakulaṃ nissāya gaṅgātīre viharati. So pātova gaṅgaṃ otiṇṇo taṃ bhājanaṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā paṃsukūlasaññāya aggahesi. Athettha taṃ akkharapaṭṭikaṃ rājamuddikālañchanañca disvā muñcitvā taṃ maṃsapesiṃ addasa. Disvānassa etadahosi “siyā gabbho, tathā hissa duggandhapūtibhāvo natthī”ti. Udakappavāhenāgatassapi hi usmā na vigacchati, usmā ca nāma īdisāya saviññāṇakatāya bhaveyyāti “siyā gabbho”ti [V 2.0152] cintesi. Puññavantatāya pana duggandhaṃ nāhosi sausumagatāya pūtibhāvo ca. Evaṃ pana cintetvā assamaṃ netvā naṃ suddhe okāse ṭhapesi. Atha aḍḍhamāsaccayena dve maṃsapesiyo ahesuṃ. Tāpaso disvā sādhukataraṃ ṭhapesi. Tato puna aḍḍhamāsaccayena ekamekissā pesiyā hatthapādasīsānamatthāya pañca pañca piḷakā uṭṭhahiṃsu. Atha tato aḍḍhamāsaccayena ekā maṃsapesi suvaṇṇabimbasadiso dārako, ekā dārikā ahosi. Tesu tāpasassa puttasineho uppajji, dārakānaṃ puññupanissayato aṅguṭṭhakato cassa khīraṃ nibbatti. Tato pabhuti ca khīrabhattaṃ alabhittha. Tāpaso bhattaṃ bhuñjitvā khīraṃ dārakānaṃ mukhe āsiñcati. Tesaṃ pana yaṃ yaṃ udaraṃ pavisati, taṃ sabbaṃ maṇibhājanagataṃ viya dissati. Carimabhave bodhisatte kucchigate bodhisattamātu viya udaracchaviyā [M 2.0171] acchavippasannatāya evaṃ te nicchavī ahesuṃ. Apare āhu “sibbitvā ṭhapitā viya nesaṃ aññamaññaṃ līnā chavi ahosī”ti. Evaṃ te nicchavitāya vā līnacchavitāya vā “licchavī”ti paññāyiṃsu.

At that time, a certain ascetic lived on the banks of the Ganges, relying on a family of cowherds. Early in the morning, he entered the Ganges and, seeing that vessel floating toward him, he took it, thinking it was discarded cloth. But upon noticing the inscribed plaque and the royal seal, he opened it and saw the lump of flesh inside. Seeing it, he thought, “This might be an embryo, for it does not have a foul or putrid smell.” Indeed, even when carried by the water’s flow, its warmth did not fade—and such warmth could only belong to something with consciousness. Thus, he concluded, “This must be an embryo.” Due to its merit, however, there was no foul smell, and due to its warmth, there was no putrefaction. Having reflected thus, he took it to his hermitage and placed it in a clean spot. After half a month, the lump of flesh split into two masses. The ascetic, seeing this, tended to them more carefully. Then, after another half-month, five protrusions—for the hands, feet, and head—appeared on each mass. Another half-month later, one mass became a boy like a golden image, and the other a girl. Affection for a son arose in the ascetic’s heart for them. Due to the children’s supporting merit, milk flowed from his thumb, and from then on, he obtained milk-rice. The ascetic would eat his meal and then pour milk into the children’s mouths. Whatever entered their bellies could be seen as if placed in a jeweled vessel. Just as when the Bodhisatta is in his mother's womb in his final existence, the skin of her abdomen is exceedingly clear, so too were these two without skin. Others say, “Their skins were so tightly joined that they appeared sewn together.” Thus, because they were either without skin or had adhering skin, they came to be known as the “Licchavis.”

Tāpaso dārake posento ussūre gāmaṃ bhikkhāya pavisati, atidivā paṭikkamati. Tassa taṃ byāpāraṃ ñatvā gopālakā āhaṃsu – “bhante, pabbajitānaṃ dārakaposanaṃ palibodho, amhākaṃ dārake detha, mayaṃ posessāma, tumhe attano kammaṃ karothā”ti. Tāpaso “sādhū”ti paṭissuṇi. Gopālakā dutiyadivase maggaṃ samaṃ katvā pupphehi okiritvā dhajapaṭākā ussāpetvā tūriyehi vajjamānehi assamaṃ āgatā. Tāpaso “mahāpuññā dārakā, appamādeneva vaḍḍhetha, vaḍḍhetvā aññamaññaṃ āvāhaṃ karotha, pañcagorasena rājānaṃ tosetvā bhūmibhāgaṃ gahetvā nagaraṃ māpetha, tattha kumāraṃ abhisiñcathā”ti vatvā dārake adāsi. Te “sādhū”ti paṭissuṇitvā dārake netvā posesuṃ. Dārakā vuḍḍhimanvāya kīḷantā vivādaṭṭhānesu aññe gopālakadārake hatthenapi pādenapi paharanti, te rodanti. “Kissa rodathā”ti ca mātāpitūhi vuttā “ime nimmātāpitikā tāpasapositā amhe atīva paharantī”ti vadanti. Tato nesaṃ posakamātāpitaropi “ime dārakā aññe dārake vihesenti dukkhāpenti, na ime saṅgahetabbā, vajjetabbā ime”ti āhaṃsu. Tato pabhuti kira so padeso “vajjī”ti vuccati yojanasataparimāṇena.

The ascetic, while raising the children, would enter the village for alms when the sun was high and return very late in the day. Knowing his routine, the cowherds said to him, “Venerable sir, raising children is a hindrance for ascetics. Give us the children; we will raise them, and you may attend to your own duties.” The ascetic agreed, saying, “Very well.” The next day, the cowherds leveled the path, scattered flowers, raised banners and flags, and came to the hermitage with music playing. The ascetic said, “These children are greatly meritorious. Raise them with diligence, and when grown, marry one another. Please the king with the five products of the cow, receive a portion of land, build a city, and consecrate a prince there.” Having spoken thus, he gave them the children. They agreed, saying, “Very well,” took the children, and raised them. As the children grew, while playing, they would strike other cowherd children with their hands and feet in places of dispute, making them cry. When asked by their parents why they were crying, they replied, “These motherless and fatherless ones, raised by the ascetic, strike us excessively.” Then their foster parents also said, “These children harass and cause distress to other children. They should not be kept; they should be avoided.” From then on, it is said, that region of a hundred yojanas in extent came to be called “Vajji.”

Atha taṃ padesaṃ gopālakā rājānaṃ tosetvā aggahesuṃ. Tattha ca nagaraṃ māpetvā soḷasavassuddesikaṃ kumāraṃ abhisiñcitvā rājānaṃ akaṃsu. Rajjasampattidāyakassa kammassa katattā asambhinne eva rājakule uppannattā ca rājakumārassa puññānubhāvasañcoditā devatādhiggahitā akaṃsūti keci. Dārakassa dārikāya saddhiṃ vāreyyaṃ katvā katikaṃ akaṃsu “bāhirato [V 2.0153] dārikā na ānetabbā, ito dārikā na kassaci dātabbā”ti. Tesaṃ paṭhamasaṃvāsena dve dārakā jātā dhītā ca putto ca. Evaṃ soḷasakkhattuṃ dve dve jātā. Tato tesaṃ dārakānaṃ yathākkamaṃ vaḍḍhantānaṃ ārāmuyyānanivāsaṭṭhānaparivārasampattiṃ gahetuṃ appahontaṃ nagaraṃ tikkhattuṃ gāvutantarena gāvutantarena parikkhipiṃsu. Tassa punappunaṃ visālīkatattā “vesālī”tveva [M 2.0172] nāmaṃ jātaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ – “tikkhattuṃ pākāraparikkhepavaḍḍhanena visālībhūtattā vesālīti vuccatī”ti.

Then the cowherds, having pleased the king, took possession of that region. There they built a city, consecrated a prince who was about sixteen years old, and made him king. Some say that deities, urged by the power of the prince's merit, took possession of him and made this happen, because a deed that yields royal prosperity had been performed and because he was born in an unbroken royal family. They arranged a marriage for the boy with the girl and made a pact: "No girls shall be brought from outside, nor shall any girl from here be given to anyone else." From their first union, two children were born—a daughter and a son. In this way, two children were born on sixteen occasions. Then, as their children grew in succession, the city being insufficient to accommodate the complement of monasteries, parks, dwelling places, and retinue, they expanded the city three times, by a gāvuta each time. Because it was repeatedly made vast, its name became "Vesālī." Hence it is said: "Because it became vast through being expanded three times by the addition of encircling walls, it is called Vesālī."

Idampi ca nagaranti na kevalaṃ rājagahasāvatthiyo yevāti dasseti. Tattha mahāvanaṃ nāmātiādi majjhimabhāṇakasaṃyuttabhāṇakānaṃ samānaṭṭhakathā. Majjhimaṭṭhakathāyañhi (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.146) saṃyuttaṭṭhakathāyañca (saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 3.5.984-985) imināva nayena vuttaṃ. Dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.359) pana “mahāvaneti bahinagare himavantena saddhiṃ ekābaddhaṃ hutvā ṭhitaṃ sayaṃjātaṃ vanaṃ atthi, yaṃ mahantabhāveneva mahāvananti vuccati, tasmiṃ mahāvane. Kūṭāgārasālāyanti tasmiṃ vanasaṇḍe saṅghārāmaṃ patiṭṭhāpesuṃ. Tattha kaṇṇikaṃ yojetvā thambhānaṃ upari kūṭāgārasālāsaṅkhepena devavimānasadisaṃ pāsādaṃ akaṃsu, taṃ upādāya sakalopi saṅghārāmo kūṭāgārasālāti paññāyitthā”ti vuttaṃ. Vanamajjhe katattā “vanaṃ nissāyā”ti vuttaṃ. Ārāmeti saṅghārāme. Haṃsavaṭṭakacchadanenāti haṃsavaṭṭakapaṭicchannena, haṃsamaṇḍalākārenāti attho.

"And this is a city" shows that it is not only Rājagaha and Sāvatthī. Here, the explanation of 'Mahāvana' and so on is a commentary common to the reciters of the Majjhima and Saṃyutta Nikāyas. For in the Majjhima commentary and the Saṃyutta commentary, it is stated in this very way. In the Dīgha Nikāya commentary, however, it is said: "'Mahāvana' refers to a naturally grown forest outside the city, standing contiguous with the Himalayas, which is called Mahāvana simply because of its vastness. In that great forest. 'In the Kūṭāgārasālā' means that in that forest grove, they established a monastery for the Saṅgha. There, having fitted a pinnacle, they built a palace-like structure resembling a celestial mansion above the pillars in the form of a gabled hall, and on account of that, the entire monastery came to be known as the Kūṭāgārasālā.' Thus it is said." Because it was made in the middle of the forest, it is called "adjoining the forest." "In the park" means in the monastery for the Saṅgha. "With a roof of haṃsavaṭṭaka" means covered with a haṃsavaṭṭaka; the meaning is, in the shape of a circle of haṃsas.

Anekapariyāyenāti ettha pariyāya-saddo kāraṇavacanoti āha “anekehi kāraṇehī”ti, ayaṃ kāyo aviññāṇakopi saviññāṇakopi evampi asubho evampi asubhoti nānāvidhehi kāraṇehīti attho. Asubhākārasandassanappavattanti kesādivasena tatthāpi vaṇṇādito asubhākārassa sabbaso dassanavasena pavattaṃ. Kāyavicchandaniyakathanti attano parassa ca karajakāye vicchandanuppādanakathaṃ. Muttaṃ vātiādinā byatirekamukhena kāyassa amanuññataṃ dasseti. Tattha ādito tīhi padehi adassanīyatāya asārakatāya majjhe catūhi duggandhatāya, ante ekena lesamattenapi manuññatābhāvamassa dasseti.
