Atha khotiādinā anvayato sarūpeneva amanuññatāya dassanaṃ. Chandoti dubbalarāgo. Rāgoti balavarāgo. “Kesā lomādī”ti saṅkhepato vuttamatthaṃ vibhāgena dassetuṃ “yepi hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Asubhāti āgantukena subhākārena virahitattā asubhā. Asucinoti attano sabhāveneva asucino. Paṭikūlāti nāgarikassa asucikaṭṭhānaṃ viya jigucchanīyattā paṭikūlā.

In the phrase "by many reasons," the word "reason" (pariyāya) has the meaning of cause; thus, he said, "by many causes." The meaning is: this body, whether without consciousness or with consciousness, is in this way foul and in that way foul—through various causes. "The arising of the perception of the foul aspect" means the arising through the perception in every way of the foul aspect in terms of color and so on, even in the case of hair and so on. "Talk that causes revulsion towards the body" is talk that generates revulsion toward one's own and others' bodies born of action. By means of "urine," and so on, it shows the unloveliness of the body by way of contrast. There, with the first three phrases, it shows its lack of loveliness due to its unsightliness and worthlessness; in the middle, with four, due to its foul smell; and at the end, with one, due to the absence of even the slightest degree of loveliness. Then, by "but indeed," and so on, is the showing of its unloveliness directly, by its very nature. "Desire" (chanda) is weak lust. "Lust" (rāga) is strong lust. To show in detail the meaning stated concisely as "hair, body hair, and so on," the passage beginning "for those which" was stated. "Foul" (asubha) because it is devoid of any adventitious beautiful appearance. "Impure" (asuci) because they are impure by their own nature. "Repulsive" (paṭikūla) because they are disgusting, like a filthy place for a city-dweller.

Kesā [M 2.0173][V 2.0154] nāmete vaṇṇatopi paṭikūlā, saṇṭhānatopi gandhatopi āsayatopi okāsatopi paṭikūlāti dassento “so ca nesaṃ…pe… pañcahi kāraṇehi veditabbo”ti āha. Manuññepi (visuddhi. 1.383; vibha. aṭṭha. 356) hi yāgupatte vā bhattapatte vā kesavaṇṇaṃ kiñci disvā “kesamissakamidaṃ, haratha na”nti jigucchanti, evaṃ kesā vaṇṇato paṭikūlā. Rattiṃ paribhuñjantāpi kesasaṇṭhānaṃ akkavākaṃ vā makacivākaṃ vā chupitvā tatheva jigucchanti, evaṃ saṇṭhānatopi paṭikūlā. Telamakkhanapupphadhūpādisaṅkhāravirahitānañca kesānaṃ gandho paramajeguccho hoti, tato jegucchataro aggimhi pakkhittānaṃ. Kesā hi vaṇṇasaṇṭhānato appaṭikūlāpi siyuṃ, gandhena pana paṭikūlāyeva. Yathā hi daharassa kumārakassa vaccaṃ vaṇṇato haliddivaṇṇaṃ, saṇṭhānatopi haliddipiṇḍasaṇṭhānaṃ, saṅkāraṭṭhāne chaḍḍitañca uddhumātakakāḷasunakhasarīraṃ vaṇṇato tālapakkavaṇṇaṃ, saṇṭhānato vaṭṭetvā vissaṭṭhamudiṅgasaṇṭhānaṃ, dāṭhāpissa sumanamakuḷasadisāti ubhayampi vaṇṇasaṇṭhānato siyā appaṭikūlaṃ, gandhena pana paṭikūlameva, evaṃ kesāpi siyuṃ vaṇṇasaṇṭhānato appaṭikūlā, gandhena pana paṭikūlāyevāti.

These, which are called hairs, are repulsive by way of color, by way of shape, by way of smell, by way of basis, and by way of location. To show this, he said: 'And this of them... (etc.) ...should be known by five reasons.' Indeed, even in what is agreeable, if one sees in a bowl of gruel or a bowl of rice something the color of a hair, they are disgusted, saying, 'This is mixed with hair, take it away!' Thus, hairs are repulsive by way of color. Even when eating at night, if they touch a calotropis fibre or a spider's web fibre, which has the shape of a hair, they are disgusted in the same way. Thus, they are repulsive by way of shape. And the smell of hairs that are without the preparations of applying oil, wearing flowers, and using incense is extremely disgusting; more disgusting than that is the smell of hairs thrown on a fire. Indeed, hairs might be not repulsive by way of color and shape, but by smell, they are surely repulsive. Just as a young boy’s excrement is the color of turmeric by way of color and has the shape of a lump of turmeric by way of shape; and the corpse of a bloated black dog discarded in a rubbish heap is the color of a ripe palmyra fruit by way of color and, having been rolled, has the shape of a discarded drum by way of shape, and its fangs, too, are like jasmine buds—thus both might be not repulsive by way of color and shape, but by smell, they would surely be repulsive. Similarly, hairs too might be not repulsive by way of color and shape, but by smell, they are surely repulsive.

Yathā pana asuciṭṭhāne gāmanissandena jātāni sūpeyyapaṇṇāni nāgarikamanussānaṃ jegucchāni honti aparibhogāni, evaṃ kesāpi pubbalohitamuttakarīsapittasemhādinissandena jātattā jegucchāti idaṃ tesaṃ āsayato pāṭikulyaṃ. Ime ca kesā nāma gūtharāsimhi uṭṭhitakaṇṇakaṃ viya ekatiṃsakoṭṭhāsarāsimhi jātā, te susānasaṅkāraṭṭhānādīsu jātasākaṃ viya parikhādīsu jātakamalakuvalayādipupphaṃ viya ca asuciṭṭhāne jātattā paramajegucchāti idaṃ tesaṃ okāsato pāṭikulyaṃ. Yathā ca kesānaṃ, evaṃ sabbakoṭṭhāsānañca vaṇṇasaṇṭhānagandhāsayokāsavasena pañcadhā paṭikūlatā veditabbāti āha “evaṃ lomādīna”nti. Pañcapañcappabhedenāti ettha bāhiratthasamāso daṭṭhabbo pañca pañca pabhedā etassāti pañcapañcappabhedoti.

Just as, for example, herbs for curry that have grown in an impure place from the village effluent are disgusting and unusable to city-dwellers, so too, head hairs, because of being born from the effluent of pus, blood, urine, feces, bile, phlegm, and so on, are disgusting. This is their repulsiveness by way of basis. And these things called head hairs are like a mushroom that has sprouted on a heap of dung, being born in the heap of thirty-one parts. They, like a vegetable grown in a cemetery, rubbish heap, and so on, and like a lotus, water lily, or other flower grown in a moat, and so on, because of being born in an impure place, are extremely disgusting. This is their repulsiveness by way of location. And just as for the head hairs, so too for all the parts, the repulsiveness should be known in five ways: by way of color, shape, smell, basis, and location. Thus he said: 'Thus for the body hairs, and so on.' Herein, in 'by fivefold and fivefold division,' a bahubbīhi compound should be seen: it has five and five divisions, thus it is 'of fivefold and fivefold division.'

Saṃvaṇṇentoti vitthārento. Asubhāyāti asubhamātikāya. Phātikammanti bahulīkāro. Pañcaṅgavippahīnaṃ pañcaṅgasamannāgatanti ettha kāmacchando byāpādo thinamiddhaṃ uddhaccakukkuccaṃ vicikicchāti imesaṃ pañcannaṃ nīvaraṇānaṃ [M 2.0174] pahānavasena pañcaṅgavippahīnatā veditabbā. Na hi etesu appahīnesu jhānaṃ uppajjati, tenassetāni pahānaṅgānīti vuccanti. Kiñcāpi hi jhānakkhaṇe aññepi akusalā dhammā pahīyanti, tathāpi etāneva visesena jhānantarāyakarāni. Kāmacchandena hi nānāvisayapalobhitaṃ cittaṃ na ekattārammaṇe samādhiyati, kāmacchandābhibhūtaṃ [V 2.0155] vā cittaṃ na kāmadhātuppahānāya paṭipadaṃ paṭipajjati, byāpādena ca ārammaṇe paṭihaññamānaṃ na nirantaraṃ pavattati, thinamiddhābhibhūtaṃ akammaññaṃ hoti, uddhaccakukkuccaparetaṃ avūpasantameva hutvā paribbhamati, vicikicchāya upahataṃ jhānādhigamasādhikaṃ paṭipadaṃ nārohati. Iti visesena jhānantarāyakarattā etāneva pahānaṅgānīti vuttāni.

'Explaining' means explaining in detail. 'Regarding the repulsive' means regarding the matrix of the repulsive. 'Development' means making abundant. Herein, in the phrase 'abandoned in five factors and possessed of five factors,' the state of being 'abandoned in five factors' should be known by way of the abandoning of these five hindrances: sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt. Indeed, when these have not been abandoned, jhāna does not arise; therefore, these are called 'the factors of abandoning.' And although at the moment of jhāna other unwholesome states are also abandoned, nevertheless, these alone are specifically obstructive to jhāna. For a mind enticed by various sense-objects through sensual desire is not concentrated on a single object; or a mind overwhelmed by sensual desire does not undertake the path for abandoning the sense-sphere. And through ill will, being struck against the object, it does not proceed uninterruptedly. Being overwhelmed by sloth and torpor, it becomes unworkable. Being overcome by restlessness and remorse, it wanders about, being simply unpacified. Being afflicted by doubt, it does not enter upon the practice that accomplishes the attainment of jhāna and so on. Thus, because they are specifically obstructive to jhāna, these alone are called 'the factors of abandoning.'

Yasmā pana vitakko ārammaṇe cittaṃ abhiniropeti, vicāro anuppabandhati, tehi avikkhepāya sampāditapayogassa cetaso payogasampattisambhavā pīti pīnanaṃ, sukhañca upabrūhanaṃ karoti, atha naṃ sasampayuttadhammaṃ etehi abhiniropanānubandhanapīnanaupabrūhanehi anuggahitā ekaggatā ekattārammaṇe samaṃ sammā ādhiyati, tasmā vitakko vicāro pīti sukhaṃ cittekaggatāti imesaṃ pañcannaṃ uppattivasena pañcaṅgasamannāgatatā veditabbā. Uppannesu hi etesu pañcasu jhānaṃ uppannaṃ nāma hoti, tenassa etāni pañca samannāgataṅgānīti vuccanti. Tasmā na etehi samannāgataṃ aññadeva jhānaṃ nāma atthīti gahetabbaṃ. Yathā pana aṅgamattavaseneva caturaṅginī senā, pañcaṅgikaṃ tūriyaṃ aṭṭhaṅgiko ca maggoti vuccati, evamidampi aṅgamattavaseneva “pañcaṅgika”nti vā “pañcaṅgasamannāgata”nti vā vuccatīti veditabbaṃ.

Since initial application places the mind upon the object and sustained application connects it—and because through them the perfection of effort is possible for a mind whose effort has been accomplished for the sake of non-distraction—rapture causes delighting and happiness causes strengthening. Then, one-pointedness, supported by these—placing, connecting, delighting, and strengthening—is, together with its associated states, evenly and rightly established on a single object. Therefore, the state of being 'possessed of five factors' should be known by way of the arising of these five: initial application, sustained application, rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind. For when these five have arisen, jhāna is said to have arisen. Therefore, these are called its five 'possessed factors.' Thus, it should be understood that there is no other thing called jhāna apart from that which is possessed of these factors. Just as, by way of the factors alone, an army is called 'four-factored,' a musical instrument 'five-factored,' and the path 'eight-factored,' so too this jhāna, by way of the factors alone, is called 'five-factored' or 'possessed of five factors.' Thus it should be known.

Etāni ca pañcaṅgāni kiñcāpi upacārakkhaṇepi atthi, atha kho upacāre pakaticittato balavatarāni, idha pana upacāratopi balavatarāni rūpāvacarakkhaṇappattāni. Ettha hi vitakko suvisadena ākārena ārammaṇe cittaṃ abhiniropayamāno uppajjati, vicāro ativiya ārammaṇaṃ anumajjamāno, pītisukhaṃ sabbāvantampi kāyaṃ pharamānaṃ. Teneva vuttaṃ “nāssa kiñci sabbāvato kāyassa vivekajena pītisukhena apphuṭaṃ hotī”ti. Cittekaggatāpi heṭṭhimamhi samuggapaṭale uparimaṃ samuggapaṭalaṃ viya ārammaṇe suphusitā hutvā uppajjati. Ayametesaṃ [M 2.0175] itarehi viseso, tasmā “pañcaṅgasamannāgata”nti appanājhānameva visesetvā vuttaṃ.

And although these five factors are present even in the access moment, at the access stage they are stronger than in an ordinary mind. Here, however, they are even stronger than at the access stage, having reached the moment of the fine-material sphere. For here, initial application arises, placing the mind upon the object in a very clear way; sustained application, thoroughly examining the object; and rapture and happiness, pervading the entire body. For that reason it is said: 'There is nothing of his entire body that is not pervaded by the rapture and happiness born of seclusion.' One-pointedness of mind also arises, well-established on the object, like the upper lid of a casket on the lower lid. This is their distinction from the others. Therefore, 'possessed of five factors' is said specifically with respect to absorption jhāna.

Tividhakalyāṇaṃ dasalakkhaṇasampannanti ettha pana jhānassa ādimajjhapariyosānavasena tividhakalyāṇatā, tesaṃyeva ādimajjhapariyosānānaṃ lakkhaṇavasena dasalakkhaṇasampannatā veditabbā. Vitthāranayaṃ panettha sayameva pakāsayissati. Kilesacorehi anabhibhavanīyattā jhānaṃ “cittamañjūsa”nti vuttaṃ. Nissāyāti pādakaṃ katvā.

Herein, regarding 'of threefold excellence, endowed with ten characteristics': the threefold excellence of jhāna should be understood by way of its beginning, middle, and end; its endowment with ten characteristics should be understood by way of the characteristics of these same beginning, middle, and end. The Teacher himself will set forth the detailed method here. Because it cannot be overcome by the thieves that are the defilements, jhāna is called 'the mind’s casket.' 'Nissāya' means 'having made it a basis.'

Dasalakkhaṇavibhāvaneneva [V 2.0156] tividhakalyāṇatāpi vibhāvitā hotīti dasalakkhaṇaṃ tāva dassento “tatrimānī”tiādimāha. Tattha pāripanthikato cittavisuddhītiādīnaṃ padānaṃ attho “tatrāyaṃ pāḷī”tiādinā vuttapāḷivaṇṇanāyameva āvi bhavissati. Tatrāti tasmiṃ dasalakkhaṇavibhāvane. Paṭipadāvisuddhīti paṭipajjati jhānaṃ etāyāti paṭipadā, gotrabhupariyosāno pubbabhāgiyo bhāvanānayo. Paripanthato visujjhanaṃ visuddhi, paṭipadāya visuddhi paṭipadāvisuddhi. Sā panāyaṃ yasmā jhānassa uppādakkhaṇe labbhati, tasmā vuttaṃ “paṭipadāvisuddhi ādī”ti. Upekkhānubrūhanāti visodhetabbatādīnaṃ abhāvato jhānapariyāpannāya tatramajjhattupekkhāya kiccanipphattiyā anubrūhanā. Sā panāyaṃ yasmā visesato jhānassa ṭhitikkhaṇe labbhati, tena vuttaṃ “upekkhānubrūhanā majjhe”ti. Sampahaṃsanāti tattha dhammānaṃ anativattanādisādhakassa ñāṇassa kiccanipphattivasena pariyodapanā. Sā pana yasmā jhānassa osānakkhaṇe pākaṭā hoti, tasmā vuttaṃ “sampahaṃsanā pariyosāna”nti. Imāni tīṇi lakkhaṇānīti paripanthato cittassa visujjhanākāro, majjhimassa samathanimittassa paṭipajjanākāro, tattha pakkhandanākāroti imāni tīṇi jhānassa ādito uppādakkhaṇe appanāppattilakkhaṇāni. Tehi ākārehi vinā appanāppattiyā abhāvato asati ca appanāyaṃ tadabhāvato ādikalyāṇañceva visuddhipaṭipadattā yathāvuttehi lakkhaṇehi samannāgatattā ca tilakkhaṇasampannañca. Iminā nayena majjhapariyosānalakkhaṇānañca yojanā veditabbā.

By the exposition of the ten characteristics, the threefold excellence is also explained. Therefore, first showing the ten characteristics, he says, 'Herein, these...' and so on. Therein, the meaning of terms such as 'purification of mind from obstacles' will become evident in the commentary on the Pāḷi text beginning, 'Herein, this is the Pāḷi...' 'Therein' means in that exposition of the ten characteristics. 'Purity of practice': 'practice' (paṭipadā) is that by which one attains jhāna; it is the method of development in the preliminary part, culminating in change-of-lineage. Purification from obstacles is 'purity' (visuddhi); the purity of the practice is 'purity of practice' (paṭipadāvisuddhi). Since this is obtained at the moment of the arising of jhāna, it is said, 'Purity of practice is the beginning.' 'Fostering by equanimity' means the strengthening by the accomplishment of the function of that neutral equanimity included in the jhāna, due to the absence of things to be purified. Since this is particularly obtained at the moment of the stability of jhāna, it is therefore said, 'Fostering by equanimity is in the middle.' 'Clarification' refers to the cleansing through the accomplishment of the function of knowledge that achieves the non-transgression of the states therein. Since this becomes evident at the moment of the culmination of jhāna, it is therefore said, 'Clarification is at the end.' These three characteristics are: the manner of purifying the mind from obstacles, the manner of practicing towards the intermediate sign of calm, and the manner of plunging into it. These three are the characteristics of attaining absorption at the moment of arising, from the beginning. Without these manners, there is no attainment of absorption; and when absorption is absent, they are absent. It is the initial excellence and is complete with the three characteristics, because it is a path of purification and is endowed with the aforesaid characteristics. In this way, the application of the middle and final characteristics should also be understood.

Keci [M 2.0176] pana “paṭipadāvisuddhi nāma sasambhāriko upacāro, upekkhānubrūhanā nāma appanā, sampahaṃsanā nāma paccavekkhaṇā”ti vaṇṇayanti, taṃ na yuttaṃ. Tathā hi sati ajhānadhammehi jhānassa guṇasaṃkittanaṃ nāma kataṃ hoti. Na hi bhūmantaraṃ bhūmantarapariyāpannaṃ hoti, pāḷiyā cetaṃ virujjhati. “Ekattagataṃ cittaṃ paṭipadāvisuddhipakkhandañceva hoti upekkhānubrūhitañca ñāṇena ca sampahaṃsita”nti (paṭi. ma. 1.158) hi pāḷiyaṃ vuttaṃ. Ettha hi ekattagataṃ cittanti indriyānaṃ ekarasabhāvena ekaggatāya ca sikhāppattiyā tadanuguṇaṃ ekattagataṃ sasampayuttaṃ appanāppattaṃ cittaṃ vuttaṃ, tasseva ca paṭipadāvisuddhipakkhandatādi anantaraṃ vuccate. Tasmā pāḷiyaṃ ekasmiṃyeva appanācittakkhaṇe paṭipadāvisuddhiādīnaṃ vuttattā antoappanāyameva parikammāgamanavasena paṭipadāvisuddhi, tatramajjhattupekkhāya kiccavasena upekkhānubrūhanā, dhammānaṃ anativattanādibhāvasādhanena pariyodāpakassa ñāṇassa kiccanipphattivasena sampahaṃsanā ca veditabbā.

Some, however, explain: 'Purity of practice is access concentration with effort; fostering by equanimity is absorption; and clarification is reviewing.' This is not appropriate. For in that case, the qualities of jhāna would be extolled by non-jhāna factors. For one plane is not included in another plane, and this contradicts the Pāḷi text. For in the Pāḷi it is said: 'The mind that has become one-pointed has plunged into purity of practice, is fostered by equanimity, and is clarified by knowledge' (Paṭis. I 158). Here, 'the mind that has become one-pointed' refers to the mind that has attained absorption, which has become one-pointed, associated with, and suitable for that, through the single function of the faculties and the culmination of one-pointedness. Immediately following this, its plunging into purity of practice, and so on, is stated. Therefore, since in the Pāḷi, purity of practice and so on are stated as existing in the single moment of the absorption consciousness itself, it should be understood that within absorption itself, purity of practice is by way of the arrival of the preliminary work; fostering of equanimity is by way of the function of that neutral equanimity; and clarification is by way of the accomplishment of the function of the knowledge that purifies by establishing the state of non-transgression of the states, and so on.

Kathaṃ? Yasmiṃ (paṭi. ma. aṭṭha. 2.1.158; visuddhi. 1.175) vāre appanā uppajjati[V 2.0157], tasmiṃ yo nīvaraṇasaṅkhāto kilesagaṇo tassa jhānassa paripantho, tato cittaṃ visujjhati, visuddhattā āvaraṇavirahitaṃ hutvā majjhimaṃ samathanimittaṃ paṭipajjati. Majjhimaṃ samathanimittaṃ nāma samappavatto appanāsamādhiyeva, līnuddhaccasaṅkhātānaṃ ubhinnaṃ antānaṃ anupagamanena majjhimo, savisesaṃ paccanīkadhammānaṃ vūpasamanato samatho, yogino sukhavisesānaṃ kāraṇabhāvato nimittanti katvā. Tassa pana appanācittassa anantarapaccayabhūtaṃ gotrabhucittaṃ satipi parittamahaggatabhāvabhede paccayapaccayuppannabhāvabhede ca ekissāyeva santatiyā pariṇāmūpagamanato ekasantatipariṇāmanayena tathattaṃ appanāsamādhivasena samāhitabhāvaṃ upagacchamānaṃ majjhimaṃ samathanimittaṃ paṭipajjati nāma. Evaṃ paṭipannattā tathattupagamanena tattha pakkhandati nāma. Yasmiñhi khaṇe tathattaṃ majjhimaṃ samathanimittaṃ paṭipajjati, tasmiṃyeva khaṇe tathattupagamanena appanāsamādhinā samāhitabhāvūpagamanena tattha pakkhandati nāma. Evaṃ tāva purimasmiṃ gotrabhucitte vijjamānā paripanthavisuddhimajjhimasamathappaṭipattipakkhandanākārā āgamanavasena nipphajjamānā paṭhamassa jhānassa uppādakkhaṇeyeva paṭipadāvisuddhīti veditabbā. Teyeva hi ākārā paccayavisesato jhānakkhaṇe nipphajjamānā paṭipadāvisuddhīti vuttā.

How? At the time when absorption arises, the mind is purified from the group of defilements called the hindrances, which is an obstacle to that jhāna. Because of being purified, being free from covering, it attains the middle sign of serenity. The middle sign of serenity is none other than the evenly proceeding absorption-concentration itself. It is 'middle' by not approaching the two extremes called sluggishness and restlessness. It is 'serenity' because it pacifies the opposing states with distinction. It is a 'sign' because it is the cause of the yogī's special happiness. Now, the change-of-lineage consciousness, which is the immediate condition for that absorption consciousness—even though there is a difference in the state of being limited and exalted, and a difference in the state of being cause and effect—is called 'attaining the middle sign of serenity' because, having undergone transformation within a single continuity, it approaches that very state of being composed by means of absorption-concentration, by the method of transforming a single continuity. Thus, because it has been attained, by reaching that very state, it is said to 'plunge' therein. For at the moment when it attains that very middle sign of serenity, at that very moment, by reaching that very state, by means of absorption-concentration, by reaching the state of being composed, it is said to 'plunge' therein. Thus, the modes of purity from obstacles, the practice of middle serenity, and plunging, which exist in the preceding change-of-lineage consciousness and are accomplished by way of approach, should be known as 'purity of practice' at the very arising-moment of the first jhāna. For these very modes, being accomplished at the moment of jhāna due to a special condition, are called 'purity of practice'.

Evaṃ [M 2.0177] visuddhassa pana tassa cittassa puna sodhetabbābhāvato visodhane byāpāraṃ akaronto visuddhaṃ cittaṃ ajjhupekkhati nāma. Samathabhāvūpagamanena samathappaṭipannassa puna samādhāne byāpāraṃ akaronto samathappaṭipannaṃ ajjhupekkhati nāma. Samathappaṭipannabhāvato eva cassa kilesasaṃsaggaṃ pahāya ekattena upaṭṭhitassa puna ekattupaṭṭhāne byāpāraṃ akaronto ekattupaṭṭhānaṃ ajjhupekkhati nāma. Evaṃ tatramajjhattupekkhāya kiccavasena upekkhānubrūhanā veditabbā.

Thus, for that purified mind, because there is no further state of needing to be purified, not making an effort in purifying, one is said to equanimously observe the purified mind. For one who has undertaken serenity by reaching the state of serenity, again not making an effort in concentration, one is said to equanimously observe that which has been undertaken as serenity. And for that one who, precisely because of the state of having undertaken serenity, has abandoned association with defilements and is established in oneness, again not making an effort in the establishment of oneness, one is said to equanimously observe the establishment of oneness. Thus, the fostering of equanimity should be known by way of the function of neutrality therein.

Ye panete evaṃ upekkhānubrūhite tasmiṃ jhānacitte jātā samādhipaññāsaṅkhātā yuganaddhadhammā aññamaññaṃ anativattamānā hutvā pavattā, yāni ca saddhādīni indriyāni nānākilesehi vimuttattā vimuttirasena ekarasāni hutvā pavattāni, yañcesa tadupagaṃ tesaṃ anativattanaekarasasabhāvānaṃ anucchavikaṃ vīriyaṃ vāhayati, yā cassa tasmiṃ khaṇe pavattā āsevanā, sabbepi te ākārā yasmā ñāṇena saṃkilesavodānesu taṃ taṃ ādīnavañca ānisaṃsañca disvā tathā tathā sampahaṃsitattā visodhitattā pariyodāpitattā nipphannā, tasmā dhammānaṃ anativattanādibhāvasādhanena pariyodāpakassa ñāṇassa kiccanipphattivasena sampahaṃsanā veditabbāti vuttaṃ.

Now, these states yoked in a pair, called concentration and wisdom, born in that jhāna-consciousness thus fostered by equanimity, proceed without transgressing one another. And the faculties such as faith, because of being liberated from various defilements, proceed having a single function with the taste of liberation. And the energy which suitably bears those states of a non-transgressing, single-taste nature, and the practice that proceeds for him at that moment—all those modes are accomplished because, by means of knowledge, having seen the respective danger and benefit in defilement and purification, they are accordingly gladdened, purified, and cleansed. Therefore, it is said that gladdening is to be known by way of the accomplishment of the function of knowledge, which is the purifier, by means of establishing the nature of non-transgression, etc., of the states.

Atha [V 2.0158] kasmā sampahaṃsanāva “pariyosāna”nti vuttā, na upekkhānubrūhanāti? Yasmā tasmiṃ bhāvanācitte upekkhāvasena ñāṇaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti, tasmā ñāṇakiccabhūtā sampahaṃsanā “pariyosāna”nti vuttā. Tathā hi appanākāle bhāvanāya samappavattiyā paṭipakkhassa ca suppahānato paggahādīsu byāpārassa akātabbato ajjhupekkhanāva hoti. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “samaye cittassa ajjhupekkhanā visuddhaṃ cittaṃ ajjhupekkhatī”ti ca ādi. Sā panāyaṃ ajjhupekkhanā ñāṇassa kiccasiddhiyā hoti visesato ñāṇasādhanattā appanābyāpārassa, tasmā ñāṇakiccabhūtā sampahaṃsanā “pariyosāna”nti vuttā. Evaṃ tividhāya paṭipadāvisuddhiyā laddhavisesāya tividhāya upekkhānubrūhanāya sātisayaṃ paññindriyassa adhimattabhāvena catubbidhāpi sampahaṃsanā sijjhatīti āgamanupekkhāñāṇakiccavasena dasapi ākārā jhāne eva veditabbā.

Now then, why is gladdening called the 'conclusion,' and not the fostering of equanimity? Because in that development-consciousness, knowledge becomes manifest by way of equanimity, therefore gladdening, which is the function of knowledge, is called the 'conclusion.' For at the time of absorption, because of the even proceeding of the development and the good abandoning of the opponent, and because there is no effort to be made in exertion, etc., there is only equanimous observation. In reference to which it is said, 'At that time, there is equanimous observation of the mind; one equanimously observes the purified mind,' and so forth. Now, this equanimous observation is for the accomplishment of the function of knowledge, especially because the effort of absorption is a means for knowledge. Therefore, gladdening, which is the function of knowledge, is called the 'conclusion.' Thus, by the threefold purity of practice, which has gained distinction, by the threefold fostering of equanimity, with excellence, due to the exceeding degree of the wisdom faculty, the fourfold gladdening is also accomplished. Thus, the ten modes—by way of the functions of approach, equanimity, and knowledge—should be known as pertaining only to jhāna.

Evaṃ [M 2.0178] tividhattagataṃ cittantiādīni tasseva cittassa thomanavacanāni. Tattha evaṃ tividhattagatanti evaṃ yathāvuttena vidhinā paṭipadāvisuddhipakkhandanaupekkhānubrūhanañāṇasampahaṃsanāvasena tividhabhāvaṃ gataṃ. Vitakkasampannanti kilesakkhobhavirahitattā vitakkena sundarabhāvamupagataṃ. Cittassa adhiṭṭhānasampannanti tasmiṃyeva ārammaṇe cittassa nirantarappavattisaṅkhātena adhiṭṭhānena sampannaṃ anūnaṃ. Yathā adhiṭṭhānavasiyaṃ adhiṭṭhānanti jhānappavatti, tathā idhāpi cittassa adhiṭṭhānanti cittekaggatāpi yujjati. Tena hi ekasmiṃyeva ārammaṇe cittaṃ adhiṭṭhāti, na ettha vikkhipatīti. Samādhisampannanti visuṃ vuttattā pana vuttanayeneva gahetabbo. Atha vā samādhisseva jhānaṅgasaṅgahitattā “cittassa adhiṭṭhānasampanna”nti jhānaṅgapañcakavasena vuttaṃ. Samādhisampannanti indriyasaṅgahitattā indriyapañcakavasena.

The phrases 'a mind gone to a threefold state,' etc., are words of praise for that very mind. Therein, 'gone to a threefold state' means gone to a threefold state by the aforesaid method, by way of the purity of practice, plunging, the fostering of equanimity, and the gladdening by knowledge. 'Endowed with initial application' means, because of being free from the agitation of defilements, it has reached a beautiful state through initial application. 'Endowed with the mind's determination' means endowed with the determination characterized as the uninterrupted proceeding of the mind on that very object, not deficient. Just as in the mastery of determination, 'determination' is the proceeding of jhāna, so too here, 'the mind's determination' is fittingly one-pointedness of mind. For by that, the mind determines upon a single object; it does not get distracted from it. Now, because 'endowed with concentration' is stated separately, it should be taken in the way already stated. Alternatively, because concentration itself is included in the jhāna factors, 'endowed with the mind's determination' is stated by way of the five jhāna factors. 'Endowed with concentration' is stated by way of the five faculties because it is included in the faculties.

Asubhasaññāparicitenāti sakalaṃ kāyaṃ asubhanti pavattāya saññāya sahagatattā jhānaṃ asubhasaññā, tena paricitena paribhāvitena. Cetasāti cittena. Bahulanti abhiṇhaṃ. Viharatoti viharantassa, asubhasamāpattibahulassāti attho. Methunadhammasamāpattiyāti methunadhammena samaṅgibhāvato. Paṭilīyatīti ekapassena nilīyati nilīnaṃ viya hoti. Paṭikuṭatīti saṅkucati. Paṭivattatīti nivattati. Na sampasārīyatīti na visarati, abhirativasena na pakkhandatīti attho. Atha vā paṭilīyatīti saṅkucati tattha paṭikūlatāya saṇṭhitattā. Paṭikuṭatīti apasakkati na upasakkati. Paṭivattatīti nivattati, tato eva na sampasārīyatīti. Nhārudaddulanti nhārukhaṇḍaṃ nhāruvilekhanaṃ vā.

By 'one familiar with the perception of foulness' (asubhasaññāparicitena), it is meant that the jhāna is the perception of foulness, because it is accompanied by the perception that arises as 'the whole body is foul'; by that, one is familiar and well-developed. By 'with the mind' (cetasā) means with the consciousness. By 'frequently' (bahulaṃ) means constantly. By 'dwells' (viharati) means for one dwelling, meaning for one who frequently attains the perception of foulness. By 'attainment of sexual intercourse' (methunadhammasamāpattiyā) means due to being endowed with sexual activity. By 'shrinks away' (paṭilīyati) means it draws back to one side, as if hiding. By 'recoils' (paṭikuṭati) means it contracts. By 'turns away' (paṭivattati) means it retreats. By 'does not extend' (na sampasārīyati) means it does not spread out; the meaning is it does not eagerly rush forward due to delight. Alternatively, 'shrinks away' means it contracts, being established there due to repulsiveness. 'Recoils' means it withdraws, it does not approach. 'Turns away' means it retreats, and from that very state, it does not extend. By 'a tendon fragment' (nhārudaddulaṃ) means a piece of tendon or a tendon scraping.

Addhamāsanti [V 2.0159] accantasaṃyoge upayogavacanaṃ. Paṭisallīyitunti yathāvuttakālaṃ paṭi paṭi divase divase samāpattiyaṃ dhammacintāya cittaṃ nilīyituṃ. Payuttavācanti paccayapaṭisaṃyuttavācaṃ, buddhā imesu divasesu piṇḍāya na caranti, vihāreyeva nisīdanti, tesaṃ dinnaṃ mahapphalaṃ hotīti ādivacanaṃ.

By 'half a month' (addhamāsaṃ) is a term used in the sense of continuous duration. By 'to withdraw into solitude' (paṭisallīyituṃ) means for the mind to withdraw into meditative attainment and reflection on the Dhamma, day by day, for the stated period. By 'engaged speech' (payuttavācaṃ) means speech connected with requisites, such as the statement: 'The Buddhas do not go for alms on these days; they remain seated in the monastery; what is given to them then is of great fruit,' and so forth.

Kalyāṇūpanissayavasenāti pabbajjāya upanissayavasena. Pare kirāti kira-saddo arucisūcanattho. Tenāha “idaṃ pana icchāmatta”nti, pavattiajānanaṃ ārocayitābhāvo ñāte nivāraṇañcāti idaṃ tesaṃ icchāmattaṃ[M 2.0179], na pana kāraṇanti attho. Apare pana vadanti “etasmiṃ kira aḍḍhamāse na koci buddhaveneyyo ahosi, atha satthā imaṃ aḍḍhamāsaṃ phalasamāpattisukhena vītināmessāmi, iti mayhañceva sukhavihāro bhavissati, anāgate ca pacchimā janatā ‘satthāpi gaṇaṃ pahāya ekako vihāsi, kimaṅgaṃ pana maya’nti diṭṭhānugatiṃ āpajjissati, tadassa bhavissati dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāyāti iminā kāraṇena evamāhā”ti. Neva koci bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamatīti ṭhapetvā piṇḍapātanīhārakaṃ añño koci neva bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamati, bhikkhusaṅgho pana satthu vacanaṃ sampaṭicchitvā ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ adāsi. So pātova gandhakuṭipariveṇasammajjanamukhodakadantakaṭṭhadānādīni sabbakiccāni tasmiṃ tasmiṃ khaṇe katvā apagacchati.

By 'by way of the basis of goodness' (kalyāṇūpanissayavasena) is meant by way of the basis for going forth. By 'others say' (pare kira), the word 'kira' indicates disapproval. Therefore, it is said, 'This is merely their wish.' The meaning is that this—the lack of an announcement to those who did not know the event and the prevention when it was known—is merely their wish, not a reason. Others, however, say, 'During this half-month, there was no one worthy of being trained by the Buddha. Therefore, the Teacher thought, “I will spend this half-month in the bliss of fruition attainment. This would be both a pleasant abiding for me and, in the future, the later generations will think, ‘Even the Teacher lived alone, having left the community—why should we not do so as well?’ and fall into imitative behavior. That will be for their long-term welfare and happiness.” For this reason, he spoke thus.' By 'no one approached the Blessed One' (neva koci bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamati) is meant that no one else approached the Blessed One except for the one who brought the alms-food. The community of monks, however, having accepted the Teacher’s instruction, assigned one monk. He, early in the morning, having performed all duties at their appropriate times—such as sweeping the fragrant hut’s enclosure and providing water for washing the face and tooth-sticks—then departed.

Anekakāraṇasammissoti ettha kāyassa asuciduggandhajegucchapaṭikūlatāva anekakāraṇaṃ. Maṇḍanakapakatikoti alaṅkārakasabhāvo. Koci taruṇopi yuvā na hoti, koci yuvāpi maṇḍanakajātiko na hoti yathā upasantasabhāvo ālasiyabyasanādīhi vā abhibhūto, idha pana daharo ceva yuvā ca maṇḍanakajātiko ca adhippeto. Paṭhamayobbanaṃ nāma pannarasavassato yāva dvattiṃsa saṃvaccharāni, soḷasavassato vā yāva tettiṃsa vassāni. Kuṇapanti matakaḷevaraṃ, ahissa kuṇapaṃ ahikuṇapaṃ. Evaṃ itarānipi. Atipaṭikūlajigucchanīyasabhāvato cettha imāneva tīṇi vuttānīti veditabbāni. Aññesañhi sasasūkarādīnaṃ kuṇapaṃ manussā kaṭukabhaṇḍādīhi abhisaṅkharitvā paribhuñjantipi, imesaṃ pana kuṇapaṃ abhinavampi jigucchantiyeva, ko pana vādo kālātikkamena pūtibhūte. Atipaṭikūlajigucchanīyatā ca nesaṃ ativiya duggandhatāya, sā ca ahīnaṃ tikhiṇakopatāya kukkuramanussānaṃ odanakummāsūpacayatāya ca sarīrassa hotīti vadanti.

By 'mixed with many causes' (anekakāraṇasammissoti) here, the body's impurity, foul smell, loathsomeness, and repulsiveness are the many causes. By 'adorned by nature' (maṇḍanakapakatiko) is meant having the nature of being adorned. Some who are young are not youthful, and some who are youthful are not of a nature to adorn themselves—such as those with a calm disposition or those overcome by laziness, misfortune, and so on. Here, however, the intended meaning is one who is young, youthful, and of a nature to adorn themselves. 'First youth' refers to the age from fifteen to thirty-two years, or from sixteen to thirty-three years. By 'carrion' (kuṇapaṃ) is meant a dead body; the carrion of a snake is snake-carrion. The same applies to others. It should be understood that due to their extremely repulsive and disgusting nature, only these three are mentioned here. For people consume the carrion of other animals like rabbits and pigs after preparing them with spices and the like, but they are disgusted even by the fresh carrion of these (snakes, dogs, and humans)—how much more so when it has rotted over time. And their extreme repulsiveness and disgust are due to their intensely foul smell, which, they say, arises in snakes from their fierce anger, and in the bodies of dogs and humans from an accumulation of rice and gruel.

Samaṇakuttakoti samaṇakiccako, kāsāvanivāsanādivasena samaṇakiccakārīti vuttaṃ hoti[V 2.0160]. Tenāha “samaṇavesadhārako”ti. Sabbamakaṃsūti puthujjanā sāvajjepi tattha anavajjasaññino hutvā karaṇakārāpanasamanuññatādibhedaṃ sabbamakaṃsu. Lohitakanti ettha “lohitagata”ntipi paṭhanti. Vaggūti matā vaggumatā. Puññasammatāti pujjabhavaphalanibbattanena [M 2.0180] sattānaṃ punanena visodhanena puññanti sammatā. Pavāhessāmīti gamayissāmi, visodhessāmīti attho.

By 'a corrupt ascetic' (samaṇakuttako) is meant one who performs the duties of an ascetic; that is to say, one who performs the duties of an ascetic by way of wearing ochre robes and so on. Therefore, it is said, 'one who wears the garb of an ascetic.' By 'they did everything' (sabbamakaṃsu) is meant that ordinary people, even when there was fault, perceiving no fault there, did everything, distinguished as doing it themselves, causing it to be done, consenting, and so on. Here, for 'Lohitaka' (lohitakaṃ), some also read 'lohitagataṃ'. By 'Vaggu' is meant Vaggumatā. By 'considered meritorious' (puññasammatā) is meant they are considered as merit (puñña) because they produce the fruit of a worthy existence and because they purify beings. By 'I shall drive them away' (pavāhessāmi), the meaning is 'I shall cause them to go; I shall purify them.'

163. Māradheyyaṃ vuccati tebhūmakā dhammā. Vacanatthato pana mārassa dheyyaṃ māradheyyaṃ. Dheyyanti ṭhānaṃ vatthu nivāso gocaro. Māro vā ettha dhiyati tiṭṭhati pavattatīti māradheyyaṃ, māroti cettha kilesamāro adhippeto, kilesamāravaseneva ca devaputtamārassa kāmabhave ādhipaccanti. Māravisayaṃ nātikkamissatīti cintetvāti evamayaṃ saṃvegaṃ paṭilabhitvā māravisayaṃ atikkameyyāpi, mayā pana evaṃ vutte uppannaṃ saṃvegaṃ paṭippassambhetvā māravisayaṃ nātikkamissatīti evaṃ cintetvā. Dvivacananti dvikkhattuṃ vacanaṃ, āmeḍitavacananti vuttaṃ hoti. Niyojentīti ettha ayaṃ andhabālā devatā evaṃ uppannasaṃvegamūlakaṃ samaṇadhammaṃ katvā “ayaṃ māravisayaṃ atikkameyyāpī”ti cintetvā attano aññāṇatāya “matā saṃsārato muccantī”ti evaṃladdhikāpi samānā attano laddhivasena matā bhikkhū saṃsārato muccantīti imamatthaṃ anupaparikkhitvā taṃ tattha niyojesīti veditabbaṃ.

163. The phenomena of the three planes are called Māradheyya. In terms of word-meaning, however, Māra's domain is Māradheyya. 'Dheyya' means place, ground, abode, or range. Or, because Māra is placed, stands, and proceeds here, it is Māradheyya. And here, by 'Māra' the Māra of defilements is intended; and it is through the power of the defilement-Māra that the deity Māra has sovereignty in the sensual realm of existence. Thinking, 'He will not transcend the domain of Māra': this means thinking as follows: 'This one, having gained a sense of urgency, might transcend the domain of Māra; but when I have spoken thus, he will calm the arisen sense of urgency and will not transcend the domain of Māra.' 'Twice-spoken' (dvivacanaṃ) means spoken two times; that is to say, a repeated utterance (āmeḍitavacanaṃ). Here, concerning 'urging' (niyojenti), it should be understood that this blind and foolish deity, thinking, 'This one, having undertaken the ascetic's practice rooted in this arisen sense of urgency, might transcend the domain of Māra,' and being, due to her own ignorance, one who held the view that 'the dead are freed from saṃsāra,' urged him in that direction without investigating this matter—that monks who die are freed from saṃsāra according to her own view.

Kiñcāpi asubhakathaṃ kathentena bhagavatā yathā tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ maraṇabhayaṃ na bhavissati, tathā desitattā bhikkhūnañca taṃ dhammakathaṃ sutvā asubhabhāvanānuyogena kāye vigatachandarāgatāya maraṇassa abhipatthitabhāvato bhayaṃ natthi, taṃ pana asihatthaṃ tathā vicarantaṃ disvā tadaññesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ uppajjanakabhayaṃ sandhāya “hotiyeva bhaya”ntiādi vuttanti vadanti. “Attanāpi attānaṃ jīvitā voropenti, aññamaññampi jīvitā voropentī”ti vuttattā “sabbānipi tāni pañca bhikkhusatāni jīvitā voropesī”ti idaṃ yebhuyyavasena vuttanti gahetabbaṃ. Appakañhi ūnamadhikaṃ vā gaṇanūpagaṃ na hotīti “pañcasatānī”ti vuttaṃ. Tasmā ye ca attanāva attānaṃ aññamaññañca jīvitā voropesuṃ, te ṭhapetvā avasese puthujjanabhikkhū sabbe ca ariye ayaṃ jīvitā voropesīti veditabbaṃ.

Although the Blessed One, in giving the discourse on unattractiveness, taught in such a way that those monks would have no fear of death—and indeed, for the monks, having heard that Dhamma talk, through devotion to the practice of contemplating unattractiveness, they became free of desire and lust for the body and, desiring death, thus had no fear—yet, they say that the words 'Fear indeed arises,' and so on, were spoken with reference to the fear that would arise in the other monks upon seeing that man with sword in hand moving about in such a way. Because it was said, 'They deprive themselves of life, and they deprive one another of life,' this statement, 'He deprived all those five hundred monks of life,' should be understood as spoken by way of generalization. For a small amount, whether less or more, is not included in the count; thus 'five hundred' was said. Therefore, it should be understood that, setting aside those who deprived themselves and one another of life, this man deprived the remaining ordinary monks and all the noble ones of life.

164. Paṭisallānā vuṭṭhitoti ettha paṭisallānanti tehi tehi sattasaṅkhārehi paṭinivattitvā apasakkitvā sallānaṃ nilīyanaṃ vivecanaṃ, kāyacittehi tato vivittatā ekībhāvoti vuttaṃ hoti. Tenāha “ekībhāvato”ti[M 2.0181], pavivekatoti attho. Ekībhāvoti hi [V 2.0161] kāyacittaviveko vutto. Vuṭṭhitoti tato duvidhavivekato bhavaṅguppattiyā rūpārammaṇādisaṅkhārasamāyogena gahaṭṭhapabbajitādisattasamāgamena ca apeto. Uddesaṃ paripucchaṃ gaṇhantīti attano attano ācariyānaṃ santike gaṇhanti. Kāmaṃ dasānussatiggahaṇeneva ānāpānassatipi gahitā, sā pana tattha sannipatitabhikkhūsu bahūnaṃ sappāyā sātthikā ca, tasmā puna gahitā. Tathā hi bhagavā tameva kammaṭṭhānaṃ tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ kathesi. Āhāre paṭikūlasaññā asubhakammaṭṭhānasadisā, cattāro pana āruppā ādikammikānaṃ ananurūpāti tesaṃ idha aggahaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

164. “Having emerged from seclusion” (paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito)—herein, “seclusion” (paṭisallānaṃ) means withdrawing from, turning away from those various formations related to beings; it is hiding, solitude. It is said to be seclusion from them in body and mind, a state of being alone. Hence it is said, “from being alone” (ekībhāvato)—the meaning is solitude (paviveka). For “being alone” refers to the seclusion of body and mind. “Having emerged” (vuṭṭhito) means being free from that twofold seclusion, from the arising of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), from association with formations such as visible forms, and from association with beings like householders and renunciants. “They take up the recitation and questioning” means they receive it in the presence of their respective teachers. Although mindfulness of breathing is included in the taking up of the ten recollections, it is taken up again here because it is suitable and beneficial for many of the monks gathered there. For the Blessed One taught that very meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) to those monks. The perception of the repulsiveness of food is similar to the meditation on foulness, but the four formless states are unsuitable for beginners—thus, their non-inclusion here should be understood.

Vesāliṃ upanissāyāti vesālīnagaraṃ gocaragāmaṃ katvā. Upaṭṭhānasālāyanti dhammasabhāyaṃ. Muhuttenevāti satthari saddhamme ca gāravena upagatabhikkhūnaṃ vacanasamanantarameva uṭṭhahiṃsūti katvā vuttaṃ. Buddhakāle kira bhikkhū bhagavato sandesaṃ sirasā sampaṭicchituṃ ohitasotā viharanti. Yassāti yassa kattabbassa. Kālanti desanākālaṃ sandhāya vadati.

“Relying on Vesālī” (Vesāliṃ upanissāya) means making the city of Vesālī one's alms-resort village. “In the attendance hall” (upaṭṭhānasālāyaṃ) means in the Dhamma assembly hall. “In a moment” (muhutteneva) is said because, out of reverence for the Teacher and the true Dhamma, the monks who had approached rose up immediately upon hearing his words. It is said that in the time of the Buddha, the monks dwelt with ears attentive to receive the Blessed One's message upon their heads. “Of which” (yassa) means of which task to be done. “Time” (kālaṃ) is said with reference to the time for the teaching.

Paṭhamapaññattinidānavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the origin of the first laying-down is finished.

Ānāpānassatisamādhikathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on Concentration through Mindfulness of Breathing

165. Arahattappattiyāti arahattappattiatthāya. Aññaṃ pariyāyanti arahattādhigamatthāya aññampi kāraṇaṃ. Ācikkhantoti pasaṃsāpubbakaṃ desento, pasaṃsā ca tattha abhirucijananena ussāhanatthā. Tañhi sutvā bhikkhū “bhagavā imaṃ samādhiṃ anekehi ākārehi pasaṃsati, santo kirāyaṃ samādhi paṇīto ca asecanako ca sukho ca vihāro, pāpadhamme ca ṭhānaso antaradhāpetī”ti sañjātābhirucino ussāhajātā sakkaccaṃ anuyuñjitabbaṃ paṭipajjitabbaṃ maññanti.

165. “For the attainment of arahantship” means for the purpose of attaining arahantship. “Another method” means another reason for the purpose of realizing arahantship. “He explains” means he teaches with praise beforehand, and the praise there is for the purpose of encouraging exertion by generating delight. For having heard that, the monks think: “The Blessed One praises this concentration in many ways. Indeed, this concentration is peaceful, sublime, satisfying, a pleasant abiding, and it causes evil, unwholesome states to disappear from their very cause.” Thus, with delight and exertion generated in them, they consider that it should be respectfully practiced and undertaken.

Atthayojanakkamanti atthañca yojanakkamañca. Bhagavā attano paccakkhabhūtaṃ samādhiṃ desanānubhāvena tesampi bhikkhūnaṃ āsannaṃ paccakkhañca karonto [M 2.0182] sampiṇḍanavasena “ayampi kho”tiādimāha. Assāsapassāsapariggāhikāti dīgharassādivisesehi saddhiṃ assāsapassāse paricchijja gāhikā, te ārabbha pavattāti attho.

“The sequence of meaning and application” means both the meaning and the sequence of application. The Blessed One, making that concentration, which was directly perceived by himself, also near and directly perceived for those monks through the power of his teaching, spoke by way of summary, saying, “This too,” and so on. “Taking hold of the in-breaths and out-breaths” means taking hold by discerning the in-breaths and out-breaths along with their distinctions of long and short, etc.; the meaning is that it arises in dependence on them.

Idāni yathāvuttamatthaṃ pāḷiyā vibhāvento āha “vuttañheta”ntiādi. Tattha no passāso [V 2.0162] no assāsoti so soyeva attho paṭisedhena visesetvā vutto. Assāsavasenāti assāsaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Passāsavasenāti etthāpi eseva nayo. Upaṭṭhānaṃ satīti asammussanatāya tameva assāsaṃ passāsañca upagantvā ṭhānaṃ sati nāmāti attho. Ettāvatā ānāpānesu sati ānāpānassatīti ayamattho vutto hoti. Idāni sativaseneva puggalaṃ niddisitukāmena “yo assasati, tassupaṭṭhāti, yo passasati, tassupaṭṭhātī”ti vuttaṃ. Yo assasati, tassa sati assāsaṃ upagantvā tiṭṭhati. Yo passasati, tassa sati passāsaṃ upagantvā tiṭṭhatīti attho.

Now, explaining the aforesaid meaning in terms of the Pāḷi, he says, “For it was said,” and so on. Therein, “no in-breath, no out-breath”—that very same meaning is stated, specified by way of negation. “By way of the out-breath” means it is said as “having made the out-breath the object.” “By way of the in-breath”—here too, this is the method. “Mindfulness is established”—the meaning is that mindfulness, due to non-forgetfulness, approaches and remains on that very out-breath and in-breath; this is what is called mindfulness. By this much, the meaning “mindfulness on the out-breaths and in-breaths is mindfulness of breathing” has been stated. Now, wishing to indicate the person by means of mindfulness itself, it is said, “For whomever breathes out, mindfulness is established for them; for whomever breathes in, mindfulness is established for them.” The meaning is: for whomever breathes out, their mindfulness approaches the out-breath and remains; for whomever breathes in, their mindfulness approaches the in-breath and remains.

Yuttoti sampayutto. Ānāpānassatiyanti ānāpānassatiyaṃ paccayabhūtāyanti attho. Purimasmiñhi atthe samādhissa satiyā sahajātādipaccayabhāvo vutto sampayuttavacanato, dutiyasmiṃ pana upanissayabhāvopi. Upacārajjhānasahagatā hi sati appanāsamādhissa upanissayo hotīti ubhayathāpi sahajātādīnaṃ sattannampi paccayānaṃ vasena paccayabhāvaṃ dasseti. “Puna caparaṃ, udāyi, akkhātā mayā sāvakānaṃ paṭipadā, yathāpaṭipannā me sāvakā cattāro satipaṭṭhāne bhāventī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.247) uppādanavaḍḍhanaṭṭhena bhāvanāti vuccatīti tadubhayavasena atthaṃ dassento “bhāvitoti uppādito vaḍḍhito cā”ti āha. Tattha bhāvaṃ vijjamānataṃ ito gatoti bhāvito, uppādito paṭiladdhamattoti attho. Uppanno pana laddhāsevano bhāvito, paguṇabhāvaṃ āpādito vaḍḍhitoti attho. Bahulīkatoti bahulaṃ pavattito. Tena āvajjanādivasībhāvappattimāha. Yo hi vasībhāvaṃ āpādito, so icchiticchitakkhaṇe samāpajjitabbato punappunaṃ pavattissati. Tena vuttaṃ “punappunaṃ kato”ti. Yathā “idheva, bhikkhave, samaṇo (ma. ni. 1.139; a. ni. 4.241) vivicceva kāmehī”ti (dī. ni. 1.226; saṃ. ni. 2.152) ca evamādīsu paṭhamapade vutto eva-saddo [M 2.0183] dutiyādīsupi vuttoyeva hoti, evamidhāpīti āha “ubhayattha eva-saddena niyamo veditabbo”ti.

“Connected” means associated. “With mindfulness of breathing” means that which serves as a condition for mindfulness of breathing. In the first sense, the conditionality of co-nascence and so forth of concentration with mindfulness was stated due to the word “associated”; in the second sense, however, the conditionality of decisive support is also stated. For the mindfulness accompanied by access concentration serves as a decisive support for absorption concentration. Thus, in both ways, it shows the conditionality by means of the seven types of conditions, such as the co-nascent condition. In passages such as, “Furthermore, Udāyī, I have declared to the disciples the path by which my disciples develop the four foundations of mindfulness,” “development” (bhāvanā) is said to be in the sense of production and growth. Showing the meaning in both these ways, he said, “Developed means produced and grown.” Therein, bhāvito (developed) is so called because it has “gone” (ito) to a “state of being” (bhāvaṃ); the meaning is “produced,” that is, merely obtained. But what has arisen, when one has gained familiarity with it, is “developed”; the meaning is that it is “grown,” brought to a state of proficiency. “Made much of” means frequently made to occur. By this, he indicates the attainment of mastery in adverting and so on. For that which has been brought to a state of mastery can be attained at any desired moment, so it will be made to occur again and again. Hence, it is said, “done again and again.” Just as in passages like, “Here, monks, a recluse,” and “quite secluded from sensual pleasures,” the word “eva” (indeed, quite) stated in the first phrase applies also to the second and subsequent phrases, so too here. Thus he says, “the restriction by the word ‘eva’ should be understood in both instances.”

Ubhayapadaniyamena laddhaguṇaṃ dassetuṃ “ayaṃ hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Asubhakammaṭṭhānanti asubhārammaṇaṃ jhānamāha. Tañhi asubhesu yogakammabhāvato yogino sukhavisesānaṃ kāraṇabhāvato ca “asubhakammaṭṭhāna”nti vuccati. Kevalanti iminā ārammaṇaṃ nivatteti. Paṭivedhavasenāti jhānapaṭivedhavasena. Jhānañhi bhāvanāvisesena ijjhantaṃ attano visayaṃ paṭivijjhantameva pavattati yathāsabhāvato paṭivijjhīyati cāti paṭivedhoti vuccati. Oḷārikārammaṇattāti bībhacchārammaṇattā. Paṭikūlārammaṇattāti jigucchitabbārammaṇattā. Pariyāyenāti [V 2.0163] kāraṇena lesantarena vā. Ārammaṇasantatāyapīti anukkamena vicetabbataṃ pattārammaṇassa paramasukhumataṃ sandhāyāha. Sante hi sannisinne ārammaṇe pavattamāno dhammo sayampi sannisinnova hoti. Tenāha – “santo vūpasanto nibbuto”ti, nibbutasabbapariḷāhoti attho. Ārammaṇasantatāya tadārammaṇānaṃ dhammānaṃ santatā lokuttaradhammārammaṇāhi paccavekkhaṇāhi dīpetabbā.

To show the quality obtained by the restriction of both phrases, 'This indeed...' and so on was said. 'Meditation subject of the unlovely' refers to the jhāna that has an unlovely object. Indeed, that jhāna is called 'meditation subject of the unlovely' because it is a practice connected with unlovely things and because it is a cause of special happiness for the yogi. By this word 'only,' he excludes the object. 'By way of penetration' means by way of the penetration of jhāna. Indeed, jhāna, being accomplished through special development, proceeds by penetrating its own object; and because it penetrates according to its true nature, it is called 'penetration.' 'Because of having a gross object' means because of having a disgusting object. 'Because of having a repulsive object' means because of having an object to be loathed. 'By a synonym' means by a reason or by a subtle hint. 'Because of the peacefulness of the object'—he says this referring to the supreme subtlety of the object that has attained seclusion in sequence. A state occurring in a peaceful, well-settled object is itself well-settled. Therefore he said, 'peaceful, calmed, extinguished'; the meaning is 'with all fevers extinguished.' Because of the peacefulness of the object, the peacefulness of the states having that object should be illuminated by the reviewing knowledges that have supramundane states as their object.

Nāssa santapaṇītabhāvāvahaṃ kiñci secananti asecanako, asecanakattā anāsittako, anāsittakattā eva abbokiṇṇo asammisso parikammādinā, tatoyeva pāṭiyekko, visuṃyeveko āveṇiko asādhāraṇo. Sabbametaṃ sarasato eva santabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ, parikammaṃ vā santabhāvanimittaṃ. Parikammanti ca kasiṇakaraṇādinimittuppādapariyosānaṃ, tādisaṃ idha natthīti adhippāyo. Tadā hi kammaṭṭhānaṃ nirassādattā asantaṃ appaṇītaṃ siyā. Upacārena vā natthi ettha santatāti yojanā. Yathā upacārakkhaṇe nīvaraṇavigamena aṅgapātubhāvena ca paresaṃ santatā hoti, na evamimassa. Ayaṃ pana ādimanasi…pe… paṇīto cāti yojanā. Kecīti uttaravihāravāsike sandhāyāha. Anāsittakoti upasecanena anāsittako. Tenāha “ojavanto”ti, ojavantasadisoti attho. Madhuroti iṭṭho. Cetasikasukhappaṭilābhasaṃvattanaṃ tikacatukkajjhānavasena upekkhāya vā santabhāvena sukhagatikattā sabbesampi vasena veditabbaṃ. Jhānasamuṭṭhānapaṇītarūpaphuṭasarīratāvasena pana kāyikasukhappaṭilābhasaṃvattanaṃ [M 2.0184] daṭṭhabbaṃ, tañca kho jhānato vuṭṭhitakāle. Imasmiṃ pakkhe appitappitakkhaṇeti idaṃ hetumhi bhummavacanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

There is nothing that brings about a state of peace and refinement for it to be sprinkled with; thus, it is called 'unsprinkled' (asecanaka). Being unsprinkled, it is unmoistened. Being unmoistened, it is unmixed, unadulterated by preparation and the like. Hence, it is singular, distinct, separate, unique, and not shared. All this is said to show its peaceful state by its very nature, or that preparation is a sign of a peaceful state. By 'preparation' is meant that which has as its end the arising of the sign, beginning with the making of a kasiṇa and so forth; the intention is that such a thing does not exist here. For then, the meditation subject might be unpeaceful and unrefined due to its lack of savor. Alternatively, the connection is that there is no peacefulness here by way of access concentration. Just as for others, in the moment of access concentration, there is peacefulness through the removal of the hindrances and the manifestation of the factors, it is not so for this one. This, however, is refined from the very beginning… and so on. 'Some'—he says this referring to the dwellers of the Uttaravihāra monastery. 'Unmoistened' means not moistened by sprinkling. Therefore, he says it is 'juicy,' meaning similar to something juicy. 'Sweet' means pleasant. It should be understood as conducive to the attainment of mental happiness by way of the third and fourth jhānas, or by way of equanimity, because its peaceful nature is a condition for happiness for all. Moreover, it should be seen as conducive to the attainment of bodily happiness by way of the body being pervaded by refined form born of jhāna—and that, indeed, is at the time of emerging from jhāna. In this view, this phrase 'at the moment of absorption and non-absorption' should be understood as a locative case in the sense of cause.

Avikkhambhiteti jhānena sakasantānato anīhaṭe appahīne. Akosallasambhūteti akosallaṃ vuccati avijjā, tato sambhūte. Avijjāpubbaṅgamā hi sabbe pāpadhammā. Khaṇenevāti attano pavattikkhaṇeneva. Antaradhāpetīti ettha antaradhāpanaṃ vināsanaṃ. Taṃ pana jhānakattukassa idhādhippetattā pariyuṭṭhānappahānaṃ hotīti āha “vikkhambhetī”ti. Vūpasametīti visesena upasameti. Visesena upasamanaṃ pana sammadeva upasamanaṃ hotīti āha “suṭṭhu upasametī”ti.

'Not suppressed' (avikkhambhita) by jhāna means not removed, not abandoned from one's own continuum. 'Born from unskillfulness' (akosallasambhūta) means unskillfulness (akosalla) is said to be ignorance (avijjā), born from that. For all evil states are preceded by ignorance. 'In a moment' (khaṇeneva) means in the very moment of its own occurrence. 'Causes to disappear' (antaradhāpeti) here means destruction. However, because the one who practices jhāna is intended here, it is the abandoning of the manifestation (of defilements) that occurs—hence he says, 'suppresses' (vikkhambheti). 'Calms' (vūpasameti) means it calms in a special way. And calming in a special way is indeed a right calming—hence he says, 'it calms well' (suṭṭhu upasameti).

Nanu ca aññopi samādhi attano pavattikkhaṇeneva paṭipakkhadhamme antaradhāpeti vūpasameti, atha kasmā ayameva samādhi evaṃ visesetvā vuttoti? Pubbabhāgato paṭṭhāya nānāvitakkavūpasamanasabbhāvato. Vuttañhetaṃ “ānāpānassati bhāvetabbā vitakkupacchedāyā”ti [V 2.0164] (a. ni. 9.1; udā. 31). Apica tikkhapaññassa ñāṇuttarassetaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ, ñāṇuttarassa ca kilesappahānaṃ itarehi sātisayaṃ yathā saddhādhimuttehi diṭṭhippattassa, tasmā imaṃ visesaṃ sandhāya “ṭhānaso antaradhāpeti vūpasametī”ti vuttaṃ. Atha vā nimittapātubhāve sati khaṇeneva aṅgapātubhāvasabbhāvato ayameva samādhi “ṭhānaso antaradhāpeti vūpasametī”ti vutto yathā taṃ mahato akālameghassa uṭṭhitassa dhārānipāte khaṇeneva pathaviyaṃ rajojallassa vūpasamo. Tenevāha “seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, mahā akālamegho uṭṭhito”tiādi. Sāsanikassa jhānabhāvanā yebhuyyena nibbedhabhāgiyāva hotīti āha “nibbedhabhāgiyattā”ti. Buddhānaṃ pana ekaṃsena nibbedhabhāgiyāva hoti. Imameva hi kammaṭṭhānaṃ bhāvetvā sabbepi sammāsambuddhā sammāsambodhiṃ adhigacchanti, ariyamaggassa pādakabhūto ayaṃ samādhi anukkamena vaḍḍhitvā ariyamaggabhāvaṃ upagato viya hotīti āha “anupubbena ariyamaggavuḍḍhippatto”ti. Ayaṃ panattho virāganirodhapaṭinissaggānupassanānaṃ vasena sammadeva yujjati.

Is it not so that any other concentration also causes opposing states to disappear and calms them at the very moment of its occurrence? So why is this concentration alone spoken of in such a distinguished way? Because, from the preliminary stage onward, it has the nature of calming various thoughts. For it is said: 'Mindfulness of breathing should be developed for the cutting off of thoughts.' Moreover, this meditation subject is for one with sharp wisdom and superior knowledge, and the abandoning of defilements by one with superior knowledge is superior to that of others—just as the one who has attained to vision is superior to those liberated by faith. Therefore, with this distinction in mind, it is said, 'It causes to disappear and calms on the spot.' Alternatively, because when the sign appears, this concentration itself has the nature of manifesting the factors in a moment, it is said to 'cause to disappear and calm on the spot'—just as when a great untimely cloud arises, the dust and mire on the ground are instantly calmed by the downpour of rain. Hence it is said: 'Just as, monks, a great untimely cloud arises,' etc. For one in the Dispensation, the development of jhāna for the most part partakes of penetration. Therefore, it is said, 'Because it partakes of penetration.' But for the Buddhas, it exclusively partakes of penetration. For it is by developing this very meditation subject that all the Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones attain perfect self-enlightenment. This concentration, serving as the foundation for the noble path, gradually grows and is as if it has reached the state of the noble path. Therefore, it is said, 'Having gradually attained the growth of the noble path.' This meaning, however, is properly suitable in terms of contemplating dispassion, cessation, and relinquishment.

Kathanti [M 2.0185] idaṃ pucchanākāravibhāvanapadaṃ, pucchā cettha kathetukamyatāvasena aññesaṃ asambhavato, sā ca upari desanaṃ āruḷhānaṃ sabbesaṃ pakāravisesānaṃ āmasanavasenāti imamatthaṃ dassento “kathanti…pe… vitthāretukamyatāpucchā”ti āha. Kathaṃ bahulīkatoti etthāpi ānāpānassatisamādhīti padaṃ ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ. Tattha kathanti ānāpānassatisamādhibahulīkāraṃ nānappakārato vitthāretukamyatāpucchā. Bahulīkato ānāpānassatisamādhīti tathā puṭṭhadhammanidassananti imamatthaṃ “eseva nayo”ti imināyeva atidissati. Heṭṭhā papañcavasena vuttamatthaṃ sukhaggahaṇatthaṃ saṅgahetvā dassento “ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepattho”ti āha, piṇḍatthoti vuttaṃ hoti.

The word 'How?' (kathaṃ) is a term that clarifies the mode of questioning. And here the question arises from a desire to speak, because of the impossibility for others to ask, and it does so by touching upon all the specific details that have arisen in the teaching above. To show this meaning, he says, 'The question 'How?'... is a question from a desire to elaborate.' Also in the phrase 'How is it made much of?' the term 'the concentration through mindfulness of breathing' should be brought in and connected. Therein, 'How?' is a question from a desire to elaborate in various ways on the making much of the concentration through mindfulness of breathing. The phrase 'The concentration through mindfulness of breathing is made much of' is an indication of the teaching asked about in that way. This meaning is pointed out by this very phrase 'This is the method.' Gathering the meaning stated previously in detail for the sake of easy comprehension, he shows it by saying, 'This is the brief meaning here,' which means the summarized meaning is stated.

Tamatthanti taṃ “kathaṃ bhāvito”tiādinā pucchāvasena saṅkhepato vuttamatthaṃ. “Idha tathāgato loke uppajjatī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.291; a. ni. 3.61) idha-saddo lokaṃ upādāya vutto. “Idheva tiṭṭhamānassā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.369) okāsaṃ. “Idhāhaṃ, bhikkhave, bhuttāvī assaṃ pavārito”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.30) padapūraṇamattaṃ. “Idha bhikkhu dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇātī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 5.73) pana sāsanaṃ. “Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhū”ti idhāpi sāsanamevāti dassento “bhikkhave, imasmiṃ sāsane bhikkhū”ti vatvā tamevatthaṃ pākaṭaṃ katvā dassetuṃ “ayaṃ hī”tiādimāha. Tattha sabbappakāraānāpānassatisamādhinibbattakassāti sabbappakāraggahaṇaṃ soḷasa pakāre sandhāya. Te hi [V 2.0165] imasmiṃyeva sāsane. Bāhirakā hi jānantā ādito catuppakārameva jānanti. Tenāha “aññasāsanassa tathābhāvappaṭisedhano”ti, yathāvuttassa puggalassa nissayabhāvappaṭisedhanoti attho. Etena “idha, bhikkhave”ti idaṃ antogadhaeva-saddanti dasseti. Santi hi ekapadānipi avadhāraṇāni yathā vāyubhakkhoti. Tenevāha “idheva, bhikkhave, samaṇo”tiādi. Paripuṇṇasamaṇakaraṇadhammo hi yo, so sabbappakāraānāpānassatisamādhinibbattako. Parappavādāti paresaṃ aññatitthiyānaṃ nānappakāravādā titthāyatanāni.

'That meaning' refers to the meaning briefly stated by way of the question, 'How is it developed?' etc. In phrases like 'Here, a Tathāgata arises in the world,' the word 'here' is used in reference to the world. In phrases like 'While standing right here,' it refers to a place. In phrases like 'Here, monks, I have eaten and am satisfied,' it is merely a sentence-filler. In phrases like 'Here, a monk masters the Dhamma,' however, it refers to the Dispensation. To show that in 'Here, monks, a monk,' it also refers solely to the Dispensation, having said, 'Monks, in this Dispensation, a monk,' and in order to make that very meaning clear, he stated, 'This is because...' etc. Therein, regarding 'the producer of concentration through mindfulness of breathing of all kinds,' the inclusion of 'all kinds' refers to the sixteen aspects. For these exist only within this Dispensation. Outsiders, even if they know, know only the first four aspects. Therefore, he said, 'It is a denial of such a state in other teachings,' meaning it is a denial of a state of support for such a person as described. By this, it is shown that the phrase 'Here, monks' implicitly contains the word 'only.' For there are single words that also denote exclusivity, like 'wind-eater.' For that very reason, he said, 'Here alone, monks, is the ascetic,' etc. For he who possesses the qualities that make a complete ascetic is one who produces concentration through mindfulness of breathing of all kinds. 'The doctrines of others' refers to the various doctrines of other sectarians, the bases of their views.

Araññādikasseva [M 2.0186] bhāvanānurūpasenāsanataṃ dassetuṃ “imassa hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Duddamo damathaṃ anupagato goṇo kūṭagoṇo. Yathā thanehi sabbaso khīraṃ na paggharati, evaṃ dohapaṭibandhinī kūṭadhenu. Assāti gopassa. Rūpasaddādike paṭicca uppajjanakaassādo rūpārammaṇādiraso. Pubbe āciṇṇārammaṇanti pabbajitato pubbe, anādimati vā saṃsāre paricitārammaṇaṃ. Upacāravasena upanisīdati, appanāvasena upanipajjatīti yojetabbaṃ.

To show the suitability of dwelling places like the forest for meditation, 'For this one,' etc., was said. A bull that is hard to tame and has not undergone taming is a rogue bull. Just as milk does not flow at all from the udders, so too a rogue cow obstructs milking. 'Assāti' means 'of the cowherd.' The pleasure arising dependent on forms, sounds, etc., is the relish consisting of form-objects, etc. 'Previously practiced object' means an object familiar before going forth, or in beginningless saṃsāra. It should be connected thus: 'approaches' by way of access concentration, and 'settles down' by way of absorption concentration.

Idhāti imasmiṃ sāsane. Nibandheyyāti bandheyya. Satiyāti sammadeva kammaṭṭhānasallakkhaṇavasappavattāya satiyā. Ārammaṇeti kammaṭṭhānārammaṇe. Daḷhanti thiraṃ, yathā satokārissa upacārappanābhedo samādhi ijjhati, tathā thāmagataṃ katvāti attho.

'Here' means in this Dispensation. 'He should bind' means he should bind. 'With mindfulness' means with mindfulness that proceeds correctly by way of observing the characteristics of the meditation subject. 'On the object' means on the meditation subject as object. 'Firmly' means steadfastly; the meaning is: having made it strong, so that concentration, distinguished as access and absorption, is accomplished for one who applies mindfulness.

Muddhabhūtanti santatādivisesaguṇavantatāya buddhādīhi ariyehi samāsevitabhāvato ca muddhasadisaṃ, uttamanti attho. Visesādhigamadiṭṭhadhammasukhavihārapadaṭṭhānanti sabbesaṃ buddhānaṃ ekaccānaṃ paccekabuddhānaṃ buddhasāvakānañca visesādhigamassa ceva aññakammaṭṭhānena adhigatavisesānaṃ diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārassa ca padaṭṭhānabhūtaṃ. Vatthuvijjācariyo viya bhagavā yogīnaṃ anurūpanivāsaṭṭhānupadissanato. Bhikkhu dīpisadiso araññe ekako viharitvā paṭipakkhanimmathanena icchitatthasādhanato. Phalamuttamanti sāmaññaphalamāha. Parakkamajavayoggabhūminti bhāvanussāhajavassa yoggakaraṇabhūmibhūtaṃ.

'Supreme' means like the head, because it is endowed with special qualities such as continuity, and because it is frequented by noble ones such as the Buddhas; the meaning is 'excellent.' 'The basis for attaining distinction and the blissful abiding in this very life' is the foundation for the attainment of distinction by all Buddhas, some Paccekabuddhas, and disciples of the Buddha, and also for the blissful abiding in this very life of those who have attained distinction through another meditation subject. Like a master of site-lore, the Blessed One points out suitable dwelling places for yogis. A monk is like a leopard, because he dwells alone in the forest and accomplishes his desired goal by crushing the opposing forces. 'The highest fruit' refers to the fruit of asceticism. 'The ground for swift striving' is the ground that makes one fit for the swiftness of zealous effort in meditation.

Evaṃ vuttalakkhaṇesūti abhidhammapariyāyena suttantapariyāyena vuttalakkhaṇesu. Rukkhasamīpanti “yāvatā majjhanhike kāle samantā chāyā pharati, nivāte paṇṇāni patanti, ettāvatā rukkhamūlanti vuccatī”ti evaṃ vuttaṃ rukkhassa samīpaṭṭhānaṃ. Avasesasattavidhasenāsananti pabbataṃ kandaraṃ giriguhaṃ susānaṃ vanappatthaṃ abbhokāsaṃ palālapuñjanti evaṃ vuttaṃ. Ututtayānukūlaṃ dhātucariyānukūlanti gimhādiututtayassa semhādidhātuttayassa mohādicaritattayassa [V 2.0166] ca anukūlaṃ. Tathā hi gimhakāle araññaṃ anukūlaṃ sommasītalabhāvato, hemante rukkhamūlaṃ himapātanivāraṇato, vassakāle suññāgāraṃ vassanivāraṇagehasambhavato. Semhadhātukassa semhapakatikassa araññaṃ anukūlaṃ dūraṃ gantvā bhikkhācaraṇena semhassa vūpasamanato, pittadhātukassa rukkhamūlaṃ anukūlaṃ sītavātasamphassasambhavato[M 2.0187], vātadhātukassa suññāgāraṃ anukūlaṃ vātanivāraṇato. Mohacaritassa araññaṃ anukūlaṃ. Mahāaraññe hi cittaṃ na saṅkucati vivaṭaṅgaṇabhāvato, dosacaritassa rukkhamūlaṃ anukūlaṃ pasādanīyabhāvato, rāgacaritassa suññāgāraṃ anukūlaṃ visabhāgārammaṇānaṃ pavesanivāraṇato. Alīnānuddhaccapakkhikanti asaṅkocāvikkhepapakkhikaṃ. Sayanañhi kosajjapakkhikaṃ, ṭhānacaṅkamanāni uddhaccapakkhikāni, na evaṃ nisajjā. Tato eva tassā santatā. Nisajjāya daḷhabhāvaṃ pallaṅkābhujanena, assāsapassāsānaṃ pavattanasukhataṃ uparimakāyassa ujukaṭṭhapanena, ārammaṇapariggahūpāyaṃ parimukhaṃ satiyā ṭhapanena dassento.

‘In the characteristics thus stated’ means in the characteristics stated by way of the Abhidhamma and by way of the Suttanta. The vicinity of a tree is the place near a tree thus stated: “As far as the shadow spreads all around at midday, and where leaves fall when there is no wind, that much is called ‘the root of a tree’.” The remaining seven kinds of dwelling places are those thus stated: a mountain, a ravine, a mountain cave, a charnel ground, a forest wilderness, an open space, and a heap of straw. ‘Suitable for the three seasons, and suitable for the humors and temperaments’ means suitable for the three seasons beginning with summer, for the three bodily humors beginning with phlegm, and for the three temperaments beginning with delusion. For so it is: in the hot season, the forest is suitable because of its pleasant coolness; in winter, the root of a tree because it prevents the falling of frost; in the rainy season, an empty house because it can be a shelter that wards off the rain. For one with a phlegmatic humor, the forest is suitable because phlegm is allayed by going far on alms-round; for one with a bilious humor, the root of a tree is suitable because of the possibility of contact with cool wind; for one with a windy humor, an empty house is suitable because it wards off the wind. For one of a deluded temperament, the forest is suitable, for in a great forest the mind does not shrink because of the open space; for one of a hateful temperament, the root of a tree is suitable because it is inspiring of serenity; for one of a lustful temperament, an empty house is suitable because it prevents the entry of unsuitable objects. ‘Belonging to the side of non-sloth and non-restlessness’ means belonging to the side of non-constriction and non-distraction. For lying down belongs to the side of laziness, and standing and walking belong to the side of restlessness, but sitting is not so. Therefore, it is continuous. The firmness of sitting is shown by the folding of the legs crosswise, the ease of the flow of the in-breaths and out-breaths by keeping the upper body straight, and the means of grasping the object by establishing mindfulness in front.

Ūrubaddhāsananti ūrūnamadhobandhanavasena nisajjā. Heṭṭhimakāyassa anujukaṃ ṭhapanaṃ nisajjāvacaneneva bodhitanti. Ujuṃ kāyanti ettha kāya-saddo uparimakāyavisayoti āha – “uparimaṃ sarīraṃ ujukaṃ ṭhapetvā”ti. Taṃ pana ujukaṭṭhapanaṃ sarūpato payojanato ca dassetuṃ “aṭṭhārasā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Na paṇamantīti na oṇamanti. Na paripatatīti na vigacchati vīthiṃ na vilaṅgheti, tato eva pubbenāparaṃ visesuppattiyā vuḍḍhiṃ phātiṃ upagacchati. Idha pari-saddo abhi-saddena samānatthoti āha “kammaṭṭhānābhimukha”nti, bahiddhā puthuttārammaṇato nivāretvā kammaṭṭhānaṃyeva purakkhatvāti attho. Parīti pariggahaṭṭho “pariṇāyikā”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 16, 20) viya. Niyyānaṭṭho paṭipakkhato niggamanaṭṭho, tasmā pariggahitaniyyānanti sabbathā gahitāsammosaṃ pariccattasammosaṃ satiṃ katvā, paramaṃ satinepakkaṃ upaṭṭhapetvāti attho. Satovāti satiyā samannāgato eva saranto eva assasati, nāssa kāci sativirahitā assāsappavatti hotīti attho. Sato passasatīti etthāpi satova passasatīti eva-saddo ānetvā vattabbo. Satokārīti sato eva hutvā satiyā eva vā kātabbassa kattā, karaṇasīlo vā.

The ‘posture with the thighs bound’ is sitting by way of binding the thighs from below. The placing of the lower body in a not-straight manner is indicated by the very term ‘sitting’. Regarding ‘straightening the body’, here the word ‘body’ refers to the upper part of the body, as stated: ‘having straightened the upper body.’ To show this straightening from its nature and its purpose, the phrase ‘eighteen’ and so on is stated. ‘Not bending’ means not leaning forward. ‘Not swaying’ means not deviating from the course, not transgressing the path; thereby, from the former to the latter, through the arising of distinctions, it attains growth and expansion. Here, the prefix ‘pari-’ has the same meaning as the prefix ‘abhi-’, as stated in ‘facing towards the meditation object’, meaning having averted from external, diverse objects and having placed only the meditation subject in front. ‘Pari-’ has the meaning of ‘encompassing’, as in terms like ‘guide’, etc. (Dhammasaṅgaṇi 16, 20). ‘Mukhaṃ’ has the meaning of ‘leading out’, meaning ‘emerging from what is opposite’. Therefore, ‘a fully grasped leading-out’ means having completely abandoned confusion, having established mindfulness, and having set up supreme mindfulness and discernment. ‘Mindful, he breathes in’ means being endowed with mindfulness, just remembering, he breathes in; for him, there is no occurrence of breathing in that is devoid of mindfulness. Regarding ‘mindful, he breathes out’, here too the word ‘just’ (eva) should be supplied and connected: ‘mindful, just he breathes out.’ ‘A doer with mindfulness’ means one who, being mindful, is a doer of what should be done with mindfulness, or one who is of the nature to do so.

Bāttiṃsāya ākārehīti catūsu catukkesu āgatāni dīgharassādīni soḷasa padāni assāsapassāsavasena dvidhā vibhajitvā vuttehi dīghamassāsaṃ ādiṃ katvā paṭinissaggānupassipassāsapariyantehi bāttiṃsākārehi. Yadi “satova assasati, sato passasatī”ti etassa vibhaṅge vuttaṃ, atha kasmā “assasati [M 2.0188] passasati”cceva avatvā “satokārī”ti [V 2.0167] vuttaṃ? Ekarasaṃ desanaṃ kātukāmatāya. Paṭhamacatukke padadvayameva hi vattamānakālavasena āgataṃ, itarāni anāgatakālavasena, tasmā ekarasaṃ desanaṃ kātukāmatāya sabbattha “satokāri”cceva vuttaṃ. Dīghaṃassāsavasenāti dīghaassāsavasena, vibhattialopaṃ katvā niddeso. Dīghanti vā bhagavatā vuttaassāsavasena. Cittassa ekaggataṃ avikkhepanti vikkhepassa paṭipakkhabhāvato avikkhepoti laddhanāmaṃ cittassa ekaggabhāvaṃ pajānato sati upaṭṭhitā ārammaṇaṃ upagantvā ṭhitā hoti. Tāya satiyā tena ñāṇenāti yathāvuttāya satiyā yathāvuttena ca ñāṇena. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – dīghaṃ assāsaṃ ārammaṇabhūtaṃ avikkhittacittassa asammohato vā sampajānantassa tattha sati upaṭṭhitāva hoti, taṃ sampajānantassa ārammaṇakaraṇavasena asammohavasena vā sampajaññaṃ, tadadhīnasatisampajaññena taṃsamaṅgī yogāvacaro satokārī nāma hotīti. Paṭinissaggānupassī assāsavasenāti paṭinissaggānupassī hutvā assasanassa vasena. “Paṭinissaggānupassiassāsavasenā”ti vā pāṭho, tassa paṭinissaggānupassino assāsā paṭinissaggānupassiassāsā, tesaṃ vasenāti attho.

By thirty-two modes: by dividing the sixteen terms, such as long and short, which come in the four tetrads, into two by way of in-breath and out-breath, thus by the thirty-two modes which are spoken of, beginning with the long in-breath and ending with the out-breath contemplating relinquishment. If it is said in the analysis of this, ‘He breathes in mindfully, he breathes out mindfully,’ then why, without saying ‘he breathes in and breathes out,’ is it stated as ‘acting mindfully’? It is because of the desire to make the teaching of a single flavor. In the first tetrad, only two terms are given in the present tense, while the others are in the future tense. Therefore, to make the teaching consistent in flavor, ‘acting mindfully’ is stated everywhere. ‘By way of the long in-breath’ means ‘by way of the long in-breath’; the exposition is made by eliding the inflectional ending. Or, ‘long’ refers to the in-breath spoken of by the Blessed One. ‘Unification of mind, non-distraction’: because it is the opposite of distraction, the mind's one-pointedness obtains the name ‘non-distraction’. For one who understands this, mindfulness is established; having approached the object, it remains fixed. ‘By that mindfulness and by that knowledge’ means by the mindfulness as described and by the knowledge as described. This is what is meant: For one whose mind is undistracted and who clearly comprehends the long in-breath as the object, or who clearly comprehends by way of non-confusion, mindfulness is indeed established there. For one who clearly comprehends that, clear comprehension arises either by way of making that the object or by way of non-confusion. The meditator who is endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension dependent on that is called ‘one who acts mindfully’. ‘By way of the in-breath of one contemplating relinquishment’ means by way of the breathing in of one who is contemplating relinquishment. Alternatively, the reading may be ‘by way of the in-breaths of one contemplating relinquishment’; the meaning is: the in-breaths of one who contemplates relinquishment are ‘in-breaths of relinquishment contemplation,’ and it is by way of these.

Anto uṭṭhitasasanaṃ assāso, bahi uṭṭhitasasanaṃ passāsoti āha – “assāsoti bahinikkhamanavāto”tiādi. Suttantaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana bahi uṭṭhahitvāpi anto sasanato assāso, anto uṭṭhahitvāpi bahi sasanato passāsoti katvā uppaṭipāṭiyā vuttaṃ. Atha vā mātukucchiyaṃ bahi nikkhamituṃ aladdhokāso nāsikāvāto mātukucchito nikkhantamatte paṭhamaṃ bahi nikkhamatīti vinayaṭṭhakathāyaṃ uppattikkamena “ādimhi sāso assāso”ti bahinikkhamanavāto vutto. Tenevāha “sabbesampi gabbhaseyyakāna”ntiādi. Suttantaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana pavattiyaṃ bhāvanārambhasamaye paṭhamaṃ nāsikāvātassa anto ākaḍḍhitvā pacchā bahi vissajjanato pavattikkamena “ādimhi sāso assāso”ti antopavisanavāto vutto. Suttantanayoyeva cettha “assāsādimajjhapariyosānaṃ satiyā anugacchato ajjhattaṃ vikkhepagatena cittena kāyopi cittampi sāraddhā ca honti iñjitā ca phanditā ca, passāsādimajjhapariyosānaṃ satiyā anugacchato bahiddhā [M 2.0189] vikkhepagatena cittena kāyopi cittampi sāraddhā ca honti iñjitā ca phanditā cā”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.157) imāya pāḷiyā sameti. “Bhāvanārambhe pavattikkamasseva icchitattā sundarataro”ti vadanti. Tāluṃ āhacca nibbāyatīti tāluṃ āhacca nirujjhati. Tena kira sampatijāto bāladārako khipitaṃ karoti. Evaṃ tāvātiādi yathāvuttassa atthassa nigamanaṃ. Keci “evaṃ tāvāti anena pavattikkamena assāso bahinikkhamanavātoti gahetabbanti adhippāyo”ti vadanti.

The breath rising internally is the in-breath (assāsa); the breath rising externally is the out-breath (passāsa). Thus it is said: 'The in-breath is the wind exiting outward,' and so on. However, in the Suttanta commentary, it is stated in reverse order: the breath that, having arisen outside, enters inside is the in-breath (assāsa); and the breath that, having arisen inside, goes outside is the out-breath (passāsa).
