Alternatively, in the Vinaya commentary, according to the order of origination, it is stated that 'initially, the breath is the in-breath,' referring to the outgoing wind, because in the mother's womb, the nasal wind has no opportunity to exit, but upon emerging from the womb, it first exits outward. Hence, it is said, 'For all beings in the womb,' and so on. But in the Suttanta commentary, in the course of practice, at the start of meditation, because the nasal wind is first drawn inward and afterward expelled outward, according to the order of occurrence, 'initially, the breath is the in-breath' is stated, referring to the incoming wind. Here, the method of the Suttanta alone accords with this Pali passage: 'For one who follows with mindfulness the beginning, middle, and end of the in-breath, with the mind internally scattered, both body and mind become agitated, stirred, and disturbed. For one who follows with mindfulness the beginning, middle, and end of the out-breath, with the mind externally scattered, both body and mind become agitated, stirred, and disturbed' (Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.157). They say, 'Because the order of occurrence at the start of meditation is desired, it is more excellent.' 'Having struck the palate, it is extinguished' means it ceases upon touching the palate. It is said that because of this, a newly born infant sneezes. 'Thus far' and so on is the conclusion of the meaning as stated above. Some say, 'The intention is that by "thus far," according to this order of occurrence, the in-breath should be taken as the wind exiting outward.'

Addhānavasenāti [V 2.0168] kāladdhānavasena. Ayañhi addhāna-saddo kālassa desassa ca vācakoti. Tattha desaddhānaṃ udāharaṇabhāvena dassetvā kāladdhānassa vasena assāsapassāsānaṃ dīgharassataṃ vibhāvetuṃ “yathā hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha okāsaddhānanti okāsabhūtaṃ addhānaṃ. Pharitvāti byāpetvā. Cuṇṇavicuṇṇāpi anekakalāpabhāvena, dīghamaddhānanti dīghaṃ padesaṃ. Tasmāti saṇikaṃ pavattiyā dīghasantānatāya dīghāti vuccanti. Ettha ca hatthiādisarīre sunakhādisarīre ca assāsapassāsānaṃ desaddhānavisiṭṭhena kāladdhānavaseneva dīgharassatā vuttāti veditabbā “saṇikaṃ pūretvā saṇikameva nikkhamanti, sīghaṃ pūretvā sīghameva nikkhamantī”ti vacanato. Manussesūti samānappamāṇesupi manussasarīresu. Dīghaṃ assasantīti dīghaṃ assāsappabandhaṃ pavattentīti attho. Passasantīti etthāpi eseva nayo. Sunakhasasādayo viya rassaṃ assasanti passasanti cāti yojanā. Idaṃ pana dīghaṃ rassañca assasanaṃ passasanañca tesaṃ sattānaṃ sarīrassa sabhāvoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tesanti tesaṃ sattānaṃ. Teti assāsapassāsā. Ittaramaddhānanti appakaṃ kālaṃ. Navahākārehīti bhāvanamanuyuñjantassa pubbenāparaṃ aladdhavisesassa kevalaṃ addhānavasena ādito vuttā tayo ākārā, te ca kho ekacco assāsaṃ suṭṭhu sallakkheti, ekacco passāsaṃ, ekacco tadubhayanti imesaṃ tiṇṇaṃ puggalānaṃ vasena. Keci pana “assasatipi passasatipīti ekajjhaṃ vacanaṃ bhāvanāya nirantaraṃ pavattidassanattha”nti vadanti. Chandavasena pubbe viya tayo, tathā pāmojjavasenāti imehi navahi ākārehi.

Addhānavasena means by way of time-addhāna. This word 'addhāna' indeed denotes both time and place. Therein, after illustrating place-addhāna by way of example, 'yathā hi' and so on is stated to make known the length and shortness of in-breaths and out-breaths by way of time-addhāna. Therein, 'okāsaddhāna' means addhāna that is a location. 'Pharitvā' means having pervaded. Even fine particles, by being many clusters, cover a long addhāna—meaning a long region. Therefore, because of their slow progression and long continuity, they are called 'long.' And here it should be understood that the length and shortness of in-breaths and out-breaths in the bodies of elephants, etc., and in the bodies of dogs, etc., are stated by way of time-addhāna, distinguished by place-addhāna, according to the statement: 'They fill slowly and exit slowly; they fill quickly and exit quickly.' 'Among humans' means even in human bodies of similar size. 'They breathe in long' means they cause a long series of in-breaths to proceed; this is the meaning. The same method applies also to 'they breathe out.' The connection is: like dogs, hares, and so on, they breathe in short and breathe out short. But this long and short in-breathing and out-breathing should be seen as the nature of the bodies of those beings. The word 'tesaṃ' means 'of those beings.' The word 'te' means 'those in-breaths and out-breaths.' 'Ittaramaddhāna' means a short time. 'By nine modes': for one applying themself to meditation who has not yet attained a subsequent distinction from a previous one, there are the three modes stated from the beginning solely by way of addhāna. And those are: one person carefully marks the in-breath, another the out-breath, and another both—this is by way of these three persons. Some, however, say that the phrase 'breathes in and breathes out' is a single statement for the purpose of showing the uninterrupted occurrence of the meditation. By way of desire, there are three as before; similarly, by way of joy, there are three—thus, by these nine modes.

Kāmañcettha ekassa puggalassa tayo eva ākārā labbhanti, tantivasena pana sabbesaṃ pāḷiāruḷhattā tesaṃ vasena parikammassa kātabbattā ca “tatrāyaṃ [M 2.0190] bhikkhu navahākārehī”ti vuttaṃ. Evaṃ pajānatoti evaṃ yathāvuttehi ākārehi assāsapassāse pajānato, tattha manasikāraṃ pavattentassa. Ekenākārenāti dīghaṃassāsādīsu catūsu ākāresu ekena ākārena, navasu tīsu vā ekena. Tathā hi vakkhati –

Although here only three modes are obtained for one individual, yet because all are included in the Pali by way of the textual lineage, and because the preliminary work ought to be done by means of them, it is said, 'Therein, this monk by nine modes.' 'Thus knowing' means for one who knows the in-breaths and out-breaths with the modes as stated, for one who causes attention to proceed therein. 'With one mode' means with one mode among the four modes beginning with the long in-breath, or with one among the nine or three. For thus he will say—

“Dīgho rasso ca assāso,

Passāsopi ca tādiso;

Cattāro vaṇṇā vattanti,

Nāsikaggeva bhikkhuno”ti. (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.165);

Long and short is the in-breath, and the out-breath is also such; four types occur for a monk, right at the nostril-tip.

Ayaṃ bhāvanā assāsapassāsakāyānupassanāti katvā vuttaṃ “kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānabhāvanā sampajjatī”ti.

Because this meditation is the contemplation of the body by way of in-breaths and out-breaths, it is said, 'The development of the foundation of mindfulness which is the contemplation of the body is accomplished.'

Idāni [V 2.0169] pāḷivaseneva te nava ākāre bhāvanāvidhiñca dassetuṃ “yathāhā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha “kathaṃ pajānātī”ti pajānanavidhiṃ kathetukamyatāya pucchati. Dīghaṃ assāsanti vuttalakkhaṇaṃ dīghaṃ assāsaṃ. Addhānasaṅkhāteti addhānanti saṅkhaṃ gate dīghe kāle, dīghaṃ khaṇanti attho. Koṭṭhāsapariyāyo vā saṅkhāta-saddo “theyyasaṅkhāta”ntiādīsu viya, tasmā addhānasaṅkhāteti addhānakoṭṭhāse desabhāgeti attho. Chando uppajjatīti bhāvanāya pubbenāparaṃ visesaṃ āvahantiyā laddhassādattā tattha sātisayo kattukāmatālakkhaṇo kusalacchando uppajjati. Chandavasenāti tathāpavattachandassa vasena visesabhāvanamanuyuñjantassa kammaṭṭhānaṃ vuḍḍhiṃ phātiṃ gamentassa. Tato sukhumataranti yathāvuttachandappavattiyā purimakato sukhumataraṃ. Bhāvanābalena hi paṭippassaddhadarathapariḷāhatāya kāyassa assāsapassāsā sukhumatarā hutvā pavattanti. Pāmojjaṃ uppajjatīti assāsapassāsānaṃ sukhumatarabhāvena ārammaṇassa santataratāya kammaṭṭhānassa ca vīthippaṭipannatāya bhāvanācittasahagato pamodo khuddikādibhedā taruṇapīti uppajjati. Cittaṃ vivattatīti anukkamena assāsapassāsānaṃ ativiya sukhumatarabhāvappattiyā anupaṭṭhahane vicetabbākārappattehi tehi [M 2.0191] cittaṃ vinivattatīti keci. Bhāvanābalena pana sukhumatarabhāvappattesu assāsapassāsesu tattha paṭibhāganimitte uppanne pakatiassāsapassāsato cittaṃ nivattati. Upekkhā saṇṭhātīti tasmiṃ paṭibhāganimitte upacārappanābhede samādhimhi uppanne puna jhānanibbattanatthaṃ byāpārābhāvato ajjhupekkhanaṃ hoti, sā panāyaṃ upekkhā tatramajjhattupekkhāti veditabbā.

Now, to show those nine modes and the method of meditation according to the Pāḷi text itself, 'yathāhā' and so on was begun. Therein, 'how does one know?' is asked out of a desire to state the method of knowing. 'Breathes in long' means a long in-breath with the stated characteristic. 'Addhānasaṅkhāte' means in a long time that has gone to the count of 'addhāna'; the meaning is 'a long moment.' Alternatively, the word 'saṅkhāta' has the sense of 'division,' as in 'theyyasaṅkhāta' and so on. Therefore, 'addhānasaṅkhāte' means in the division of addhāna, in the part of space; this is the meaning. 'Desire arises' means that because the meditation brings about a subsequent distinction from a previous one and delight has been obtained, an excellent wholesome desire, characterized by the wish to act, arises there. 'By way of desire' means for one who, by means of such arisen desire, applies oneself to the special meditation, causing the meditation subject to grow and flourish. 'More subtle than that' means subtler than the former, due to the aforementioned occurrence of desire. For, by the power of meditation, with the calming of bodily distress and agitation, the in-breaths and out-breaths become more subtle and proceed. 'Joy arises' means that because the in-breaths and out-breaths have become more subtle, the object has become more tranquil, and the meditation subject has entered the path, a joy accompanied by the meditation-mind arises—a young rapture of the kinds such as minor joy. 'The mind turns away'—some say that as the in-breaths and out-breaths gradually attain an extremely subtle state and cease to appear, the mind turns away from them when they have reached a state where they must be investigated. But by the power of meditation, when the in-breaths and out-breaths have reached a more subtle state and the counterpart sign arises there, the mind turns away from the natural in-breaths and out-breaths. 'Equanimity is established' means that when, in regard to that counterpart sign, concentration of the access and absorption kinds has arisen, because there is no further effort for the purpose of producing jhāna, there is an overlooking. And this equanimity should be understood as equanimity as neutrality there.

Imehi navahi ākārehīti imehi yathāvuttehi navahi pakārehi pavattā. Dīghaṃ assāsapassāsā kāyoti dīghākārā assāsapassāsā cuṇṇavicuṇṇāpi samūhaṭṭhena kāyo. Assāsapassāse nissāya uppannanimittampi ettha assāsapassāsasāmaññavasena vuttaṃ. Upaṭṭhānaṃ satīti taṃ ārammaṇaṃ upagantvā tiṭṭhatīti sati upaṭṭhānaṃ nāma. Anupassanā ñāṇanti samathavasena nimittassa anupassanā vipassanāvasena assāsapassāse tannissayañca kāyaṃ “rūpa”nti, cittaṃ taṃsampayuttadhamme ca “arūpa”nti vavatthapetvā nāmarūpassa anupassanā ca ñāṇaṃ tattha yathābhūtāvabodho. Kāyo upaṭṭhānanti so kāyo ārammaṇakaraṇavasena upagantvā sati ettha tiṭṭhatīti upaṭṭhānaṃ nāma. Ettha ca “kāyo upaṭṭhāna”nti iminā itarakāyassapi saṅgahoti tathā vuttaṃ sammasanacārassapi idha icchitattā. No satīti so kāyo sati nāma na hoti. Sati upaṭṭhānañceva sati ca saraṇaṭṭhena upaṭṭhānaṭṭhena ca. Tāya satiyāti yathāvuttāya satiyā. Tena ñāṇenāti yathāvutteneva ñāṇena. Taṃ kāyanti taṃ assāsapassāsakāyañceva tannissayarūpakāyañca. Anupassatīti jhānasampayuttañāṇena ceva vipassanāñāṇena [V 2.0170] ca anu anu passati. Tena vuccati kāye kāyānupassanā satipaṭṭhānabhāvanāti tena anupassanena yathāvutte kāye ayaṃ kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānabhāvanāti vuccati. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yā ayaṃ yathāvutte assāsapassāsakāye tassa nissayabhūte karajakāye ca kāyasseva anupassanā anudakabhūtāya marīciyā udakānupassanā viya na aniccādisabhāve kāye niccādibhāvānupassanā, atha kho yathārahaṃ aniccadukkhānattā subhabhāvasseva anupassanā. Atha vā kāye “ahanti vā, mamanti vā, itthīti vā, puriso”ti vā gahetabbassa kassaci abhāvato tādisaṃ ananupassitvā [M 2.0192] kāyamattasseva anupassanā kāyānupassanā, tāya kāyānupassanāya sampayuttā satiyeva upaṭṭhānaṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ, tassa bhāvanā vaḍḍhanā kāyānupassanā satipaṭṭhānabhāvanāti.

By these nine aspects: it proceeds by these nine modes as stated. ‘Long in-breaths and out-breaths, the body’: long in-breaths and out-breaths, even though they are minute particles, are called the body in the sense of an aggregate. The sign that arises dependent on in-breaths and out-breaths is also spoken of here by the general term ‘in-breaths and out-breaths’. ‘Establishment, mindfulness’: mindfulness is called ‘establishment’ because it approaches and remains fixed on that object. ‘Observation, knowledge’: the observation of the sign by way of serenity; and by way of insight, having defined the in-breaths and out-breaths and the body dependent on them as ‘form,’ and the mind and its associated states as ‘the immaterial,’ the observation of name-and-form is knowledge, which is the understanding of it as it truly is. ‘The body is the establishment’: the body is called ‘establishment’ because mindfulness approaches it as an object and remains there. And here, by ‘the body is the establishment,’ the other body is also included. It is said thus because the practice of comprehension is also intended here. ‘Not mindfulness’: that body is not called mindfulness. Mindfulness is establishment, and mindfulness is so called in the sense of remembering and in the sense of being established. ‘With that mindfulness’: with mindfulness as described. ‘With that knowledge’: with knowledge as described. ‘That body’: both the body of in-breaths and out-breaths and the material body dependent on it. ‘One observes’: one observes again and again with knowledge associated with absorption and with insight-knowledge. Therefore, it is called ‘the development of the establishment of mindfulness through the observation of the body in the body’: by that observation, in the body as described, this is called ‘the development of the establishment of mindfulness through the observation of the body’. This is what is meant: this observation of the body itself—in the body of in-breaths and out-breaths as described and in the material body that is its support—is not like the observation of water in a waterless mirage, that is, it is not the observation of a nature of permanence, etc., in a body that has the nature of impermanence, etc. But rather, it is the observation appropriately of impermanence, suffering, non-self, and the state of unattractiveness. Or alternatively, because in the body there is nothing whatsoever to be grasped as ‘I,’ ‘mine,’ ‘woman,’ or ‘man,’ not observing in such a way, the observation of the mere body itself is the observation of the body. The mindfulness associated with that observation of the body is the establishment of mindfulness, and its development and increase is the development of the establishment of mindfulness through the observation of the body.

Eseva nayoti “navahi ākārehī”tiādinā vuttavidhiṃ rassa-pade atidissati. Etthāti etasmiṃ yathādassite “kathaṃ dīghaṃ assasanto”tiādinā āgate pāḷinaye. Idhāti imasmiṃ rassapadavasena āgate pāḷinaye. Ayanti yogāvacaro. Addhānavasenāti dīghakālavasena. Ittaravasenāti parittakālavasena. Imehi ākārehīti imehi navahi ākārehi.

‘This is the method’: the method stated by ‘in nine ways,’ etc., is clearly indicated in the short expression. ‘Here’: in this Pāḷi method that has come as ‘how breathing in long,’ etc., as shown. ‘Here’: in this Pāḷi method that has come by way of the short expression. ‘This’: the meditator. ‘By duration’: by way of a long period of time. ‘By brevity’: by way of a short period of time. ‘By these aspects’: by these nine aspects.

Tādisoti dīgho rasso ca. Cattāro vaṇṇāti cattāro ākārā te ca dīghādayo eva. Nāsikaggeva bhikkhunoti gāthāsukhatthaṃ rassaṃ katvā vuttaṃ. Nāsikagge vāti vā-saddo aniyamattho, tena uttaroṭṭhaṃ saṅgaṇhāti.

‘Such’: both long and short. ‘Four forms’: four aspects, and they are indeed long, etc. ‘Nāsikaggeva bhikkhuno’ (at the tip of the nose, O bhikkhu): is stated in shortened form for the ease of the verse. ‘Nāsikagge vā’ (or at the tip of the nose): the word ‘vā’ has a non-restrictive meaning; thereby, it includes the upper lip.

Sabbakāyappaṭisaṃvedīti sabbassa kāyassa paṭi paṭi paccekaṃ sammadeva vedanasīlo jānanasīlo, tassa vā paṭi paṭi sammadeva vedo etassa atthi, taṃ vā paṭi paṭi sammadeva vedamānoti attho. Tattha tattha sabba-ggahaṇena assāsādikāyassa anavasesapariyādāne siddhepi anekakalāpasamudāyabhāvato tassa sabbesampi bhāgānaṃ saṃvedanadassanatthaṃ paṭi-saddaggahaṇaṃ, tattha sakkaccakāribhāvadassanatthaṃ saṃ-saddaggahaṇanti imamatthaṃ dassento “sakalassā”tiādimāha. Tattha yathā samānesupi assāsapassāsesu yogino paṭipattividhāne paccekaṃ sakkaccaṃyeva paṭipajjitabbanti dassetuṃ visuṃ desanā katā, evaṃ tamevatthaṃ dīpetuṃ satipi atthassa samānatāya “sakalassā”tiādinā padadvayassa visuṃ visuṃ atthavaṇṇanā katāti veditabbā. Pākaṭaṃ karontoti vibhūtaṃ karonto, sabbaso vibhāventoti attho. Pākaṭīkaraṇaṃ vibhāvanaṃ tattha asammuyhanañāṇeneva nesaṃ pavattanena hotīti dassento “evaṃ viditaṃ karonto”tiādimāha[V 2.0171]. Tattha tasmāti yasmā ñāṇasampayuttacitteneva assāsapassāse pavatteti, na vippayuttacittena, tasmā evaṃbhūto sabbakāyappaṭisaṃvedī assasissāmi passasissāmīti sikkhatīti vuccati buddhādīhīti yojanā. Cuṇṇavicuṇṇavisaṭeti anekakalāpatāya cuṇṇavicuṇṇabhāvena visaṭe. Ādi pākaṭo [M 2.0193] hoti satiyā ñāṇassa ca vasena katapubbābhisaṅkhārassa pavattattā. Tādisena bhavitabbanti catutthapuggalasadisena bhavitabbaṃ, pageva satiṃ ñāṇañca paccupaṭṭhapetvā tīsupi ṭhānesu ñāṇasampayuttameva cittaṃ pavattetabbanti adhippāyo.

‘Experiencing the whole body’: one who has the habit of feeling or knowing each and every part of the entire body quite well; or, for that person, there is the feeling of each and every part quite well; or, one who experiences it quite well—this is the meaning. There, although by the taking of ‘whole,’ the complete inclusion of the body of in-breaths, etc., is accomplished, because it is a collection of many aggregates, the prefix ‘paṭi-’ is taken to show the experiencing of all its parts. There, the prefix ‘saṃ-’ is taken to show the state of acting with care. Showing this meaning, he said ‘of the entire,’ etc. There, just as a separate teaching was given to show that in the method of practice, the meditator should practice each part with care even when the in-breaths and out-breaths are similar, so too, to illuminate that very meaning, it should be known that a separate explanation of the meaning of the two phrases beginning with ‘of the entire’ has been made, even though their meaning is similar. ‘Making it clear’: making it evident, making it fully manifest—this is the meaning. Making clear is clarification. Therein, it happens through their proceeding only with non-bewildered knowledge. Showing this, he said ‘knowing it thus,’ etc. There, ‘therefore’: because one causes the in-breaths and out-breaths to proceed only with a mind associated with knowledge, not with a mind dissociated from it, therefore such a one who trains thus, ‘I will breathe in experiencing the whole body, I will breathe out experiencing the whole body,’ is called so by the Buddhas and others—this is the connection. ‘Scattered like fine powder’: scattered in the manner of fine powder due to being a collection of many kalāpas. In the beginning, it becomes clear by the power of mindfulness and knowledge, due to the proceeding of the previously made formation. ‘One should become like that’: one should become like the fourth person. Having first established mindfulness and knowledge, one should cause the mind associated with knowledge to proceed in all three places—this is the intention.

Evanti vuttappakārena sabbakāyappaṭisaṃvedanavaseneva. Ghaṭatīti ussahati. Vāyamatīti vāyāmaṃ karoti, manasikāraṃ pavattetīti attho. Tathābhūtassāti ānāpānassatiṃ bhāventassa. Saṃvaroti sati vīriyampi vā. Tāya satiyāti yā sā ānāpāne ārabbha pavattā sati, tāya. Tena manasikārenāti yo so tattha satipubbaṅgamo bhāvanāmanasikāro, tena saddhinti adhippāyo. Āsevatīti “tisso sikkhāyo”ti vutte adhikusaladhamme āsevati. Tadāsevanañhettha sikkhananti adhippetaṃ. Purimanayeti purimasmiṃ bhāvanānaye, paṭhamavatthudvayeti adhippāyo. Tatthāpi kāmaṃ ñāṇuppādanaṃ labbhateva assāsapassāsānaṃ yāthāvato dīgharassabhāvāvabodhasabbhāvato, tathāpi taṃ na dukkaraṃ yathāpavattānaṃ tesaṃ gahaṇamattabhāvatoti tattha vattamānakālappayogo kato. Idaṃ pana dukkaraṃ purisassa khuradhārāyaṃ gamanasadisaṃ, tasmā sātisayenettha pubbābhisaṅkhārena bhavitabbanti dīpetuṃ anāgatakālappayogo katoti imamatthaṃ dassetuṃ “tattha yasmā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha ñāṇuppādanādīsūti ādi-saddena kāyasaṅkhārapassambhanapītipaṭisaṃvedanādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Keci panettha “saṃvarasamādānānaṃ saṅgaho”ti vadanti.

‘Thus’: in the manner explained, it is precisely by way of experiencing the whole body. ‘Strives’ means makes an effort. ‘Exerts’ means puts forth energy, the meaning being that one directs attention. ‘For one such as this’ refers to one who develops mindfulness of breathing. ‘Restraint’ refers to mindfulness or energy. ‘By that mindfulness’ means by that mindfulness which has arisen concerning the in-and-out breaths. ‘By that attention’ refers to that attention in development which is preceded by mindfulness; the intention is ‘together with that’. ‘Practices’ means one cultivates higher wholesome qualities, as stated in ‘the three trainings’. Here, it is intended that the practice of those qualities is the training. ‘In the previous way’ refers to the earlier method of development; the intention is in the first two subjects. There, indeed, the arising of knowledge can be achieved regarding the true nature of the in-and-out breaths—whether long or short—because of the possibility of discerning them correctly. Yet, it is not difficult because it is merely the grasping of their occurrence as they arise. Thus, the present tense is used there. But this is difficult, like a person walking on a razor’s edge. Therefore, to show that extraordinary preliminary effort must be made here, the future tense is used. To explain this meaning, it is said, ‘because therein,’ etc. ‘Therein, in the arising of knowledge, etc.’—the word ‘etc.’ includes the calming of bodily formations, the experiencing of joy, and so on. Some, however, say here that it refers to the inclusion of restraint and undertaking.

Kāyasaṅkhāranti assāsapassāsaṃ. So hi cittasamuṭṭhānopi samāno karajakāyapaṭibaddhavuttitāya tena saṅkharīyatīti kāyasaṅkhāroti vuccati. Yo pana “kāyasaṅkhāro vacīsaṅkhāro”ti (ma. ni. 1.102) evamāgato kāyasaṅkhāro cetanālakkhaṇo satipi dvārantaruppattiyaṃ yebhuyyavuttiyā tabbahulavuttiyā ca kāyadvārena lakkhito, so idha nādhippeto. Passambhentotiādīsu pacchimaṃ pacchimaṃ padaṃ purimassa purimassa atthavacanaṃ. Tasmā passambhanaṃ nāma vūpasamanaṃ, tañca tathāpayoge asati uppajjanārahassa oḷārikassa kāyasaṅkhārassa payogasampattiyā anuppādananti daṭṭhabbaṃ[M 2.0194]. Tatrāti “oḷārikaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ passambhento”ti ettha. Apariggahitakāleti kammaṭṭhānassa anāraddhakāle, tato eva kāyacittānampi apariggahitakāle. “Nisīdati pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāyā”ti hi iminā kāyapariggaho[V 2.0172], “parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā”ti iminā cittapariggaho vutto. Tenevāha – “kāyopi cittampi pariggahitā hontī”ti. Kāyoti karajakāyo. Sadarathāti sapariḷāhā. Sā ca nesaṃ sadarathatā garubhāvena viya oḷārikatāya avinābhāvinīti āha “oḷārikā”ti. Balavatarāti sabalā thūlā. Santā hontīti cittaṃ tāva bahiddhā vikkhepābhāvena ekaggaṃ hutvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ pariggahetvā pavattamānaṃ santaṃ hoti vūpasantaṃ, tato eva taṃsamuṭṭhānā rūpadhammā lahumudukammaññabhāvappattā, tadanuguṇatāya sesaṃ tisantatirūpanti evaṃ citte kāye ca vūpasante pavattamāne tannissitā assāsapassāsā santasabhāvā anukkamena sukhumasukhumatarasukhumatamā hutvā pavattanti. Tena vuttaṃ “yadā panassa kāyopī”tiādi. Passambhemīti paṭhamāvajjanā. Ābhujanaṃ ābhogo, sammā anu anu āharaṇaṃ samannāhāro, tasmiṃyeva atthe aparāparaṃ pavattaāvajjanā tasseva atthassa manasikaraṇaṃ citte ṭhapanaṃ manasikāro, vīmaṃsā paccavekkhaṇā.

‘Bodily formation’ means in-and-out breathing. Although it arises from the mind, because it occurs in connection with the physical body, it is conditioned by it; therefore, it is called ‘bodily formation’. However, the bodily formation mentioned as ‘bodily formation, verbal formation’ (MN 1.44), which is characterized by volition and, despite arising at other doors, is predominantly manifested at the body door due to its prevalence and frequency, is not intended here. In ‘calming,’ and so forth, each subsequent word explains the meaning of the preceding one. Therefore, ‘calming’ means pacification, and it should be understood as the non-arising—due to the successful application of effort—of the gross bodily formation which is liable to arise when such application is absent. Therein means: in this context of ‘calming the gross bodily formation’. ‘At the time when it is not grasped’ refers to the period when the meditation object has not yet been taken up, and therefore the body and mind are also not grasped. For by this phrase, ‘he sits down, folding his legs crosswise, setting his body upright,’ the grasping of the body is stated; and by this phrase, ‘establishing mindfulness at the forefront,’ the grasping of the mind is stated. Hence it is said, ‘both body and mind are grasped’. ‘Body’ refers to the physical body. ‘With distress’ means with affliction. And that state of distress is inseparable from grossness, as if due to heaviness; hence it is said, ‘gross’. ‘Stronger’ means powerful and coarse. ‘They become tranquil’: First, the mind, being free from external distraction, becomes unified, grasps the meditation object, and thus becomes tranquil and pacified. Then, the material phenomena arising from it attain a state of lightness, softness, and workability. Accordingly, the continuity of the remaining material phenomena is also of a similar quality. When the mind and body are thus pacified and functioning, the in-and-out breaths dependent on them, being tranquil by nature, gradually become subtler, more subtle, and most subtle. Therefore, it is said, ‘but when his body too…’. ‘I shall calm’ is the initial adverting. Bending is application; rightly bringing back again and again is sustained application; in the same sense, there is repeated adverting; fixing the mind on that object is attention; examination is reviewing.

Sāraddheti sadarathe sapariḷāhe. Adhimattanti balavaṃ oḷārikaṃ, liṅgavipallāsena vuttaṃ. Kāyasaṅkhāro hi adhippeto. “Adhimattaṃ hutvā pavattatī”ti kiriyāvisesanaṃ vā etaṃ. Sukhumanti etthāpi eseva nayo. Kāyamhīti ettha citte cāti ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ.

‘Agitated’ means in a state of distress, of feverishness. ‘Excessive’ means strong and gross; it is stated with a reversal of gender, for bodily formation is intended. Or this is an adverbial qualification, meaning ‘it occurs excessively’. ‘Subtle’—here too, the same method applies. In ‘in the body’—here, ‘and in the mind’ should also be brought in and connected.

Paṭhamajjhānato vuṭṭhāya kariyamānaṃ dutiyajjhānassa nānāvajjanaṃ parikammaṃ paṭhamajjhānaṃ viya dūrasamussāritapaṭipakkhanti katvā taṃsamuṭṭhāno kāyasaṅkhāro paṭhamajjhāne ca dutiyajjhānūpacāre ca oḷārikoti sadiso vutto. Esa nayo sesupacāradvayepi. Atha vā dutiyajjhānādīnaṃ adhigamāya paṭipajjato dukkhāpaṭipadādivasena kilamato yogino kāyakilamathacittupaghātādivasena vitakkādisaṅkhobhena saparipphandatāya ca cittappavattiyā dutiyajjhānādiupacāresu kāyasaṅkhārassa oḷārikatā veditabbā. Atisukhumoti aññattha labbhamāno kāyasaṅkhāro catutthajjhāne [M 2.0195] atikkantasukhumo. Sukhumabhāvopissa tattha natthi kuto oḷārikatā appavattanato. Tenāha “appavattimeva pāpuṇātī”ti.

The diverse adverting that is the preliminary work for the second jhāna, undertaken after emerging from the first jhāna, is like the first jhāna in that its adversary is cast far away. Therefore, the bodily formation arising from it is said to be coarse, similar to that in the first jhāna and in the access to the second jhāna. This same method applies to the remaining two access states as well. Alternatively, for a yogi undertaking the path to attain the second jhāna and so on, who is exhausted due to a painful practice and so forth—because of bodily fatigue, mental oppression, agitation due to thoughts and so on, and the agitated nature of the mind’s activity—the bodily formation is to be understood as coarse in the access to the second jhāna and so on. As for the bodily formation found elsewhere as ‘exceedingly subtle,’ in the fourth jhāna it is beyond subtle. Because of its non-occurrence there, it has no state of subtlety, let alone coarseness. Therefore, he said: ‘It attains to mere non-occurrence.’

Lābhissa sato anupubbasamāpattisamāpajjanavelaṃ ekāsaneneva vā sabbesaṃ jhānānaṃ paṭilābhaṃ sandhāya majjhimabhāṇakā heṭṭhimaheṭṭhimajjhānato uparūparijhānūpacārepi sukhumataraṃ icchanti. Tattha hi sopacārānaṃ jhānānaṃ uparūpari visesavantatā santatā ca sambhaveyya, ekāvajjanūpacāraṃ vā sandhāya evaṃ vuttaṃ. Evañhi heṭṭhā vuttavādena imassa vādassa avirodho siddho bhinnavisayattā. Sabbesaṃyevāti ubhayesampi. Yasmā te sabbepi vuccamānena vidhinā passaddhimicchantiyeva[V 2.0173]. Apariggahitakāle pavattakāyasaṅkhāro pariggahitakāle paṭippassambhatīti idaṃ sadisasantānatāya vuttaṃ. Na hi te eva oḷārikā assāsādayo sukhumā honti. Passambhanākāro pana tesaṃ heṭṭhā vuttoyeva.

The Majjhima reciters, referring to the time of successively entering the attainments for one who has gained them, or to the attainment of all jhānas in a single sitting, desire what is more subtle even in the access of the higher and higher jhānas than in the lower and lower jhānas. For in that case, the excellence and tranquility of the jhānas with their access could arise in higher and higher degrees. Or, it is said thus with reference to the access of a single adverting. For if it is said thus, the non-contradiction of this view with the view stated previously is established, because their objects are different. ‘Of all indeed’ means of both. Because all of them, by the method being explained, indeed desire tranquility. This statement, ‘the bodily formation that occurred at the ungrasped time is calmed at the grasped time,’ is said because of the similarity of continuity. For indeed, those very coarse in-breaths and so on do not become subtle. But the manner of their calming was indeed stated previously.

Mahābhūtapariggahe sukhumoti catudhātumukhena vipassanābhinivesaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Sakalarūpapariggahe sukhumo bhāvanāya uparūpari paṇītabhāvato. Tenevāha “rūpārūpapariggahe sukhumo”ti. Lakkhaṇārammaṇikavipassanāyāti kalāpasammasanamāha. Nibbidānupassanāto paṭṭhāya balavavipassanā, tato oraṃ dubbalavipassanā. Pubbe vuttanayenāti “apariggahitakāle”tiādinā samathanaye vuttanayena. “Apariggahe pavatto kāyasaṅkhāro mahābhūtapariggahe paṭippassambhatī”tiādinā vipassanānayepi paṭippassaddhi yojetabbāti vuttaṃ hoti.

‘Subtle in the grasping of the great elements’ is said with reference to the inclination towards insight by means of the four elements. It is subtle in the grasping of all form because of the progressively more refined state through development. For that very reason, he said, ‘subtle in the grasping of form and formless’. ‘In insight with characteristics as its object’ refers to the comprehension of groups. From the contemplation of disenchantment onwards, insight is strong; prior to that, it is weak insight. ‘By the method previously stated’ means by the method stated in the section on tranquility, beginning with ‘at the ungrasped time’. It is said that the calming should also be applied in the method of insight, as in, ‘The bodily formation that occurred in the ungrasped state is calmed in the grasping of the great elements,’ and so on.

Assāti imassa “passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāra”nti padassa. Codanāsodhanāhīti anuyogaparihārehi. Evanti idāni vuccamānākārena. Kathanti yaṃ idaṃ “passambhayaṃ…pe… sikkhatī”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ kathaṃ kena pakārena kāyasaṅkhārassa passambhanaṃ yogino ca sikkhanaṃ hotīti kathetukāmatāya pucchitvā kāyasaṅkhāre sarūpato oḷārikasukhumato vūpasamato anuyogaparihārato ca dassetuṃ “katame kāyasaṅkhārā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha kāyikāti rūpakāye bhavā. Kāyappaṭibaddhāti kāyasannissitā. Kāye sati honti, asati na honti, tato eva te akāyasamuṭṭhānāpi kāyena saṅkharīyantīti kāyasaṅkhārā. Passambhentoti oḷārikoḷārikaṃ passambhento.

Of this phrase 'calming the bodily formation.' As for 'codanāsodhanāhi,' it means by means of questioning and answering. As for 'evaṃ,' it means in the manner now being explained. As for 'kathaṃ': having asked, with the desire to explain regarding what was said, 'calming... trains,' 'How, in what manner, does the calming of the bodily formation and the training of the yogi occur?', the passage beginning 'What are the bodily formations?' was commenced in order to show the bodily formations in terms of their nature, in terms of coarseness and subtlety, in terms of pacification, and in terms of questioning and answering. Therein, as for 'kāyikā,' it means existing in the physical body. As for 'kāyappaṭibaddhā,' it means dependent on the body. When the body exists, they exist; when it does not exist, they do not. For that very reason, even those not originating from the body are conditioned by the body; therefore, they are 'bodily formations.' As for 'passambhento,' it means calming the coarsest of the coarse.

Sesapadadvayaṃ [M 2.0196] tasseva vevacanaṃ. Oḷārikañhi kāyasaṅkhāraṃ avūpasantasabhāvaṃ sannisīdāpento “passambhento”ti vuccati, anuppādanirodhaṃ pāpento “nirodhento”ti, suṭṭhu santasabhāvaṃ nayanto “vūpasamento”ti.

The remaining two words are synonyms of that very one. Indeed, one who causes the coarse bodily formation, which has an unpacified nature, to settle down is called 'one who is calming' (passambhento); one who causes it to reach non-arising and cessation is called 'one who is stopping' (nirodhento); one who leads it to a thoroughly tranquil nature is called 'one who is pacifying' (vūpasamento).

Yathārūpehīti yādisehi. Kāyasaṅkhārehīti oḷārikehi kāyasaṅkhārehi. Ānamanāti abhimukhena kāyassa namanā. Vinamanāti visuṃ visuṃ passato namanā. Sannamanāti sabbato, suṭṭhu vā namanā. Paṇamanāti pacchato namanā. Iñjanādīni ānamanādīnaṃ vevacanāni, adhimattāni vā abhimukhacalanādīni ānamanādayo, mandāni iñjanādayo. Passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāranti [V 2.0174] tathārūpaṃ ānamanādīnaṃ kāraṇabhūtaṃ oḷārikaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ paṭippassambhento. Tasmiñhi passambhite ānamanādayopi passambhitā eva honti.

As for 'of such a kind,' it means of whatever kind. As for 'by bodily formations,' it means by the coarse bodily formations. As for 'bending forward,' it is the bending of the body towards the front. As for 'bending sideways,' it is bending while looking in various directions. As for 'bending down,' it is bending from all sides, or bending well. As for 'bending back,' it is bending backwards. 'Trembling, etc.' are synonyms of 'bending forward, etc.'; or, 'bending forward, etc.' are excessive movements like moving towards the front, while 'trembling, etc.' are slight movements. 'Calming the bodily formation' means calming the coarse bodily formation of such a kind that is the cause of bending forward, etc. For when that is calmed, bending forward, etc., are also calmed indeed.

Santaṃ sukhumanti yathārūpehi kāyasaṅkhārehi kāyassa aparipphandanahetūhi ānamanādayo na honti, tathārūpaṃ darathābhāvato santaṃ, anoḷārikatāya sukhumaṃ. Passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāranti sāmaññato ekaṃ katvā vadati. Atha vā pubbe oḷārikoḷārikaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ paṭippassambhento anukkamena kāyassa aparipphandanahetubhūte sukhumasukhumatare uppādetvā tepi paṭippassambhetvā paramasukhumatāya koṭippattaṃ yaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ paṭippassambheti, taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “santaṃ sukhumaṃ passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāra”nti.

As for 'peaceful and subtle': the bodily formation of such a kind—by which, as they are causes for the body's non-trembling, bending forward and so on do not occur—is 'peaceful' due to the absence of agitation, and 'subtle' due to its non-coarseness. He speaks of 'calming the bodily formation' generally, making it one. Alternatively, having first calmed the coarsest bodily formation, and then having gradually produced subtler and more subtle ones which have become the cause for the body's non-trembling, and having calmed those too, it is with reference to the bodily formation that one calms, which has reached the peak of utmost subtlety, that it was said: 'calming the peaceful, subtle bodily formation'.

Itītiādi codakavacanaṃ. Tattha itīti pakāratthe nipāto, kirāti arucisūcane, evañceti attho. Ayañhettha adhippāyo “vuttappakārena yadi atisukhumampi kāyasaṅkhāraṃ passambhetī”ti. Evaṃ santeti evaṃ sati tayā vuttākāre labbhamāne. Vātūpaladdhiyāti vātassa upaladdhiyā. Ca-saddo samuccayattho, assāsādivātārammaṇassa cittassa pabhāvanā uppādanā pavattanā na hoti, te ca tena passambhetabbāti adhippāyo. Assāsapassāsānañca pabhāvanāti oḷārike assāsapassāse bhāvanāya paṭippassambhetvā sukhumānaṃ tesaṃ pabhāvanā ca na hoti ubhayesaṃ tesaṃ tena paṭippassambhetabbato. Ānāpānassatiyāti ānāpānārammaṇāya satiyā ca pavattanaṃ na hoti ānāpānānaṃ [M 2.0197] abhāvato. Tato eva taṃsampayuttassa ānāpānassatisamādhissa ca pabhāvanā uppādanāpi na hoti. Na hi kadāci ārammaṇena vinā sārammaṇā dhammā sambhavanti. Na ca naṃ tanti ettha nanti nipātamattaṃ. Taṃ vuttavidhānaṃ samāpattiṃ paṇḍitā paññavanto na ceva samāpajjantipi tato na vuṭṭhahantipīti yojanā. Evaṃ codako sabbena sabbaṃ abhāvūpanayanaṃ passambhananti adhippāyena codeti.

'Iti' and so forth is the questioner's statement. Herein, 'iti' is a particle indicating manner; 'kira' suggests disapproval; the meaning is 'just so.' The intention here is: 'If, in the manner stated, one calms even the subtlest bodily formation.' 'Evaṃ sante' means 'when it is so,' that is, when the condition stated by you is obtained. 'Vātūpaladdhiyā' means by the perception of wind. The particle 'ca' is conjunctive, meaning that the cultivation, arising, and continuation of the mind whose object is the in-and-out breath wind do not occur, and those too must be calmed by it—this is the intention. 'Assāsapassāsānañca pabhāvanā' means that after calming the coarse in-and-out breaths by cultivation, there is no cultivation of their subtle counterparts either, because both of them are to be calmed by it. 'Ānāpānassatiyā' means that the continuation of mindfulness whose object is the in-and-out breath does not occur due to the absence of the in-and-out breaths. Consequently, neither the cultivation nor the arising of the concentration of mindfulness of breathing associated with it takes place. For mental states with an object never arise without their object. In 'Na ca naṃ taṃ' (and not that), 'naṃ' is merely a particle. The wise and discerning do not enter into that attainment as described, nor do they emerge from it—this is the connection. Thus, the questioner asks with the intention that 'calming' means bringing about a state of non-existence in every way.

Puna iti kirātiādi yathāvuttāya codanāya vissajjanā. Tattha kirāti yadīti etassa atthe nipāto. Iti kira sikkhati, mayā vuttākārena yadi sikkhatīti attho. Evaṃ santeti evaṃ passambhane sati. Pabhāvanā hotīti yadipi oḷārikā kāyasaṅkhārā paṭippassambhanti, sukhumā pana atthevāti anukkamena paramasukhumabhāvappattassa vasena nimittuppattiyā ānāpānassatiyā ānāpānassatisamādhissa ca pabhāvanā ijjhatevāti adhippāyo.

Again, 'iti kira' and so forth is the answer to the aforementioned question. Herein, 'kira' is a particle in the sense of 'if.' 'Iti kira sikkhati' means 'if one trains in the manner I have described.' 'Evaṃ sante' means 'when there is such calming.' 'Pabhāvanā hoti' means that even though the coarse bodily formations are calmed, the subtle ones still exist. Thus, by way of one who has gradually reached a state of extreme subtlety, through the arising of the sign, the cultivation of mindfulness of breathing and of the concentration of mindfulness of breathing is indeed accomplished—this is the intended meaning.

Yathā [V 2.0175] kathaṃ viyāti yathāvuttavidhānaṃ taṃ kathaṃ viya daṭṭhabbaṃ, atthi kiñci tadatthasampaṭipādane opammanti adhippāyo. Idāni opammaṃ dassetuṃ “seyyathāpī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha seyyathāpīti opammatthe nipāto. Kaṃseti kaṃsabhājane. Nimittanti nimittassa, tesaṃ saddānaṃ pavattākārassāti attho. Sāmiatthe hi idaṃ upayogavacanaṃ. Suggahitattāti suṭṭhu gahitattā. Sumanasikatattāti suṭṭhu citte ṭhapitattā. Sūpadhāritattāti sammadeva upadhāritattā sallakkhitattā. Sukhumakā saddāti anurave āha, ye appakā. Appattho hi ayaṃ ka-saddo. Sukhumasaddanimittārammaṇatāpīti sukhumo saddova nimittaṃ sukhumasaddanimittaṃ, tadārammaṇatāyapīti vuttaṃ hoti. Kāmaṃ tadā sukhumāpi saddā niruddhā, saddanimittassa pana suggahitattā sukhumatarasaddanimittārammaṇabhāvenapi cittaṃ pavattati. Ādito paṭṭhāya hi tassa tassa niruddhassa saddassa nimittaṃ avikkhittena cittena upadhārentassa anukkamena pariyosāne atisukhumasaddanimittampi ārammaṇaṃ katvā cittaṃ pavattateva. Cittaṃ na vikkhepaṃ gacchati tasmiṃ yathāupaṭṭhite nimitte samādhānasabbhāvato.

'Yathā kathaṃ viya' means: How is that which has been described to be seen? The intention is: Is there any simile for accomplishing that meaning? Now, to present the simile, 'just as' and so forth is stated. Herein, 'seyyathāpi' is a particle in the sense of a simile. 'Kaṃseti' means in a bronze vessel. 'Nimittaṃ' means 'of the sign,' that is, 'of the mode of occurrence of those sounds.' Indeed, this is the accusative case used in the sense of the genitive (possessive). 'Suggahitattā' (because it is well-grasped) means because it is thoroughly grasped. 'Sumanasikatattā' (because it is well-attended to) means because it is thoroughly established in the mind. 'Sūpadhāritattā' (because it is well-retained) means because it is properly retained and carefully observed. 'Sukhumakā saddā' (subtle sounds) refers to the reverberation, which are slight. Indeed, this 'ka' suffix has the meaning of 'slight.' 'The state of having the subtle-sound-sign as its object' (sukhumasaddanimittārammaṇatāpi) means: the subtle sound itself is the sign, hence 'subtle-sound-sign'; 'the state of having that as its object' is what is said. Although at that time even the subtle sounds have ceased, because the sound-sign is well-grasped, the mind continues to operate by taking an even subtler sound-sign as its object. Indeed, for one who, from the very beginning, observes the sign of each ceased sound with an undistracted mind, gradually, in the end, the mind certainly operates by taking even an extremely subtle sound-sign as its object. The mind does not become scattered because of the existence of concentration on that sign as it has appeared.

Evaṃ santetiādi vuttassevatthassa nigamanavasena vuttaṃ. Tattha yassa suttapadassa saddhiṃ codanāsodhanāhi attho vutto, taṃ uddharitvā kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānāni vibhāgato dassetuṃ “passambhaya”ntiādi vuttaṃ[M 2.0198]. Tattha passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāranti vuttaassāsapassāsā kāyoti yojanā veditabbā. Atha vā passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāranti ettha assāsapassāsā kāyoti evamattho daṭṭhabbo. Mahāsatipaṭṭhānasutte (dī. ni. 2.372 ādayo; ma. ni. 1.105 ādayo) kāyānupassanaṃ kathentena paṭhamacatukkasseva vuttattā, ānāpānassatisuttepi “yasmiṃ samaye, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dīghaṃ vā assasanto dīghaṃ assasāmīti pajānāti…pe… passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ passasissāmīti sikkhati. Kāye kāyānupassī, bhikkhave, tasmiṃ samaye bhikkhu viharatī”ti (ma. ni. 2.149) vuttattā ca “kāyānupassanāvasena vuttassa paṭhamacatukkassā”ti vuttaṃ.

'Evaṃ sante' and so forth is stated by way of concluding the meaning of what has been said. Herein, having extracted the sutta passage whose meaning has been explained along with questions and answers, 'calming' and so forth is stated to show the foundations of mindfulness of the body-contemplation by way of its divisions. Herein, in the phrase 'calming the bodily formation,' the connection 'the aforementioned in-and-out breaths are the body' should be understood. Alternatively, here in 'calming the bodily formation,' the meaning 'the in-and-out breaths are the body' should be understood. And because in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta, when explaining body-contemplation, only the first tetrad is mentioned, and also because in the Ānāpānassati Sutta it is said: 'At such a time, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu breathing in long knows, "I breathe in long"... trains himself, "I shall breathe out calming the bodily formation." At that time, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body,' therefore it is said, 'of the first tetrad explained by way of body-contemplation'.

Ādikammikassa kammaṭṭhānavasenāti samathakammaṭṭhānaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, vipassanākammaṭṭhānaṃ pana itaracatukkesupi labbhateva. Etthāti paṭhamacatukke. Saha paṭisambhidāhīti nidassanamattametaṃ, puññavantānaṃ pana upanissayasampannānaṃ abhiññāpi sijjhatiyeva. Catubbidhanti pātimokkhasaṃvarādivasena catubbidhaṃ. Anāpajjananti sattannaṃ āpattikkhandhānaṃ aññatarassa anāpajjanaṃ. Āpannavuṭṭhānanti āpannasappaṭikammāpattito yathādhammaṃ paṭikammakaraṇena vuṭṭhānaṃ, desanāgāminito desanāya, vuṭṭhānagāminito parivāsādivinayakammakaraṇena vuṭṭhānanti vuttaṃ hoti[V 2.0176]. Desanāyapi hi āpannāpattito vuṭṭhānaṃ hotīti sāpi vuṭṭhāneneva saṅgahitā. Kilesehi ca appaṭipīḷananti kodho upanāho makkho palāso issā macchariyaṃ māyā sāṭheyyaṃ thambho sārambho māno atimāno mado pamādoti evamādīhi pāpadhammehi appaṭipīḷanaṃ, tesaṃ anuppādananti vuttaṃ hoti.

'By way of the beginner's meditation subject' is stated with reference to tranquility meditation; insight meditation, however, can indeed be found in the other tetrads. 'Here' means in the first tetrad. 'Together with the analytical knowledges' is merely an example; for the meritorious and for those endowed with supporting conditions, higher knowledge can indeed be achieved. 'Fourfold' means fourfold by way of restraint through the Pātimokkha, and so forth. 'Non-transgression' means the non-commission of any of the seven groups of offenses. 'Emerging from an offense' means emerging from an offense requiring prescribed redress by performing the appropriate disciplinary procedure in accordance with the Dhamma; from an offense requiring confession, by confession; and from an offense requiring reinstatement, by performing procedures of probation, and so forth—this is what is meant. Indeed, since there is emergence from an offense even through confession, that too is included under 'emerging.' And 'not being oppressed by defilements' means not being afflicted by such evil qualities as anger, resentment, contempt, spite, envy, stinginess, deceit, craftiness, stubbornness, rivalry, conceit, arrogance, intoxication, and negligence—that is, not producing them.

Yamidaṃ ābhisamācārikasīlaṃ vuccatīti sambandho. Dveasīti khandhakavattāni cuddasavidhaṃ mahāvattanti ettha mahāvattaṃ nāma vattakkhandhake vuttāni āgantukavattaṃ āvāsikagamikaanumodanabhattaggapiṇḍacārikaāraññikasenāsanajantāgharavaccakuṭiupajjhāyasaddhivihārikaācariyaantevāsikavattanti cuddasa vattāni. Tato aññāni pana kadāci tajjanīyakammakatādikāleyeva caritabbāni dvāsīti khandhakavattāni, na sabbāsu avatthāsu caritabbāni, tasmā mahāvattesu agaṇitāni. Tattha “pārivāsikānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ vattaṃ paññapessāmī”ti ārabhitvā “na upasampādetabbaṃ…pe… na chamāyaṃ caṅkamante caṅkame caṅkamitabba”nti (cūḷava. 76) vuttavattāni chasaṭṭhi, tato paraṃ [M 2.0199] “na, bhikkhave, pārivāsikena bhikkhunā pārivāsikavuḍḍhatarena bhikkhunā saddhiṃ mūlāyapaṭikassanārahena, mānattārahena, mānattacārikena, abbhānārahena bhikkhunā saddhiṃ ekacchanne āvāse vatthabba”ntiādinā (cūḷava. 82) vuttāni pakatatte caritabbehi anaññattā visuṃ tāni agaṇetvā pārivāsikavuḍḍhatarādīsu puggalantaresu caritabbattā tesaṃ vasena sampiṇḍetvā ekekaṃ katvā gaṇitāni pañcāti ekasattati vattāni, ukkhepanīyakammakatavattesu vattapaññāpanavasena vuttaṃ “na pakatattassa bhikkhuno abhivādanaṃ…pe… nahāne piṭṭhiparikammaṃ sāditabba”nti (cūḷava. 51) idaṃ abhivādanādīnaṃ asādiyanaṃ ekaṃ, “na pakatatto bhikkhu sīlavipattiyā anuddhaṃsetabbo”tiādīni (cūḷava. 51) ca dasāti evametāni dvāsīti. Etesveva pana kānici tajjanīyakammādivattāni kānici pārivāsikādivattānīti aggahitaggahaṇena dvāsīti eva. Aññattha pana aṭṭhakathāpadese appakaṃ ūnamadhikaṃ vā gaṇanūpagaṃ na hotīti asīti khandhakavattānīti vuccati. Ābhisamācārikasīlanti ettha abhisamācāroti uttamasamācāro, abhisamācārova ābhisamācārikaṃ, abhisamācāraṃ vā ārabbha paññattaṃ ābhisamācārikaṃ, tadeva sīlanti ābhisamācārikasīlaṃ. Khandhakavattapariyāpannassa sīlassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Ahaṃ sīlaṃ rakkhāmi, kiṃ ābhisamācārikenātiādīsu sīlanti ubhatovibhaṅgapariyāpannameva gahetabbaṃ khandhakavattapariyāpannassa ābhisamācārikaggahaṇena gahitattā. Paripūreti paripuṇṇe, paripūriteti vā attho.

This is the connection: “This is called the training in proper conduct.” There are eighty-two Khandhaka procedures and fourteen kinds of major procedures. Here, the major procedures refer to the fourteen procedures mentioned in the Vattakkhandhaka: the procedures for incoming monks, resident monks, departing monks, expressing appreciation, the refectory, alms-round, forest-dwelling, lodging, the steam-bath house, the latrine, the preceptor, the co-resident, the teacher, and the pupil. Other procedures, the eighty-two Khandhaka procedures, such as those for one subject to an act of censure, are to be followed only on certain occasions, not in all situations, and thus are not counted among the major procedures. Here, beginning with “I will prescribe the procedure for probationary monks,” up to “One should not walk on the ground… one should walk only on the walking path,” sixty-six procedures are mentioned. After that, “A probationary monk should not dwell under the same roof with a senior probationary monk, one deserving to be sent back to the root, one deserving mānatta, one observing mānatta, or one deserving rehabilitation,” and so on—these are to be followed by monks in good standing without distinction. Because they are to be observed by different individuals such as senior probationary monks and so forth, they are grouped together and counted as five, making seventy-one procedures. Regarding the procedures for those subject to an act of suspension, it is stated: “A monk in good standing should not be greeted… nor should he be given a back massage during bathing.” This refusal to accept greetings and so on counts as one. “A monk in good standing should not be reproached for a failure in virtue,” and so on—these make ten. Thus, these total eighty-two. Among these, some are procedures for the act of censure and so forth, and some are procedures for probationary monks and the like; thus, by including what was not previously included, the total is indeed eighty-two. Elsewhere in the commentaries, a slight variation in the count is not considered significant, so they are generally referred to as the eighty Khandhaka procedures. Here, abhisamācāra means superior conduct. Ābhisamācārika is simply abhisamācāra, or it is what is prescribed concerning abhisamācāra; that very thing is ābhisamācārikasīla. This is a designation for the virtue included in the Khandhaka procedures. In statements like “I observe the precepts—what is the training in proper conduct?” the word “precepts” should be understood as encompassing only what is included in both Vibhaṅgas, since what is included in the Khandhaka procedures is already covered by the term “training in proper conduct.” “Fulfills” means “is complete,” or “has been fulfilled.”

Tatoti [V 2.0177] yathāvuttasīlavisodhanato paraṃ. Āvāsoti āvāsapalibodho. Kulantiādīsupi eseva nayo. Tattha (visuddhi. 1.41) āvāsoti ekopi ovarako vuccati ekampi pariveṇaṃ sakalopi saṅghārāmo. Svāyaṃ na sabbasseva palibodho hoti, yo panettha navakammādiussukkaṃ vā āpajjati, bahubhaṇḍasannicayo vā hoti, yena kenaci vā kāraṇena apekkhavā paṭibaddhacitto, tasseva palibodho hoti, na itarassa.

Thereafter: that is, after the purification of virtue as stated. Dwelling: this means the impediment of a dwelling. The same principle applies to “family” and so forth. Therein (Vism. I, 41), “dwelling” is said to mean even a single cell, a single monastic building, or an entire monastery. This is not an impediment for everyone; it is an impediment only for one who is zealous about new construction and the like, or who accumulates many possessions, or whose mind is attached and bound for some reason or other. It is not an impediment for another.

Kulanti ñātikulaṃ vā upaṭṭhākakulaṃ vā. Ekaccassa hi upaṭṭhākakulampi “sukhite sukhito”tiādinā nayena saṃsaṭṭhassa viharato palibodho hoti, so kulamānusakehi vinā dhammassavanāya sāmantavihārampi na gacchati. Ekaccassa mātāpitaropi palibodhā na honti koraṇḍakavihāravāsittherassa bhāgineyyadaharabhikkhuno viya.

Family: this means a family of relatives or a family of supporters. For some, even a family of supporters becomes an impediment when one lives closely associated with them, in the manner of thinking, “If they are happy, I am happy,” and so forth; such a one does not even go to a neighboring monastery to hear the Dhamma without those family members. For others, even their parents are not an impediment, as in the case of the young nephew-monk of the elder who resided at Koraṇḍaka Monastery.

Lābhoti [M 2.0200] cattāro paccayā. Te kathaṃ palibodhā honti? Puññavantassa hi bhikkhuno gatagataṭṭhāne manussā mahāparivāre paccaye denti, so tesaṃ anumodento dhammaṃ desento samaṇadhammaṃ kātuṃ okāsaṃ na labhati, aruṇuggamanato yāva paṭhamayāmo, tāva manussasaṃsaggo na upacchijjati, puna balavapaccūseyeva bāhullikapiṇḍapātikā āgantvā “bhante, asuko upaṭṭhāko upāsako upāsikā amacco amaccadhītā tumhākaṃ dassanakāmā”ti vadanti, so “gaṇhāvuso pattacīvara”nti gamanasajjova hoti niccabyāvaṭo, tasseva te paccayā palibodhā honti. Tena gaṇaṃ pahāya yattha naṃ na jānanti, tattha ekakena caritabbaṃ. Evaṃ so palibodho upacchijjati.

Gain: this means the four requisites. How do they become an impediment? For a meritorious monk, people offer requisites in great abundance wherever he goes. While expressing his appreciation to them and teaching the Dhamma, he finds no opportunity to practice the ascetic’s duties. From dawn until the first watch of the night, his association with people does not cease. Then, very early in the morning, many supporters arrive saying, “Venerable sir, such-and-such a supporter, male or female lay follower, minister or minister’s daughter, wishes to see you.” He is always busy and ready to go, saying, “Take the bowl and robe, friend.” For such a one, these requisites become an impediment. Therefore, abandoning the group, he should wander alone where he is not known. In this way, that impediment is cut off.

Gaṇoti suttantikagaṇo vā ābhidhammikagaṇo vā. Yo tassa uddesaṃ vā paripucchaṃ vā dento samaṇadhammassa okāsaṃ na labhati, tassa gaṇo palibodho hoti. Tena so evaṃ upacchinditabbo – sace tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ bahu kataṃ hoti, appaṃ avasiṭṭhaṃ, taṃ niṭṭhapetvā araññaṃ pavisitabbaṃ. Sace appaṃ kataṃ, bahu avasiṭṭhaṃ, yojanato paraṃ agantvā antoyojanaparicchede aññaṃ gaṇavācakaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “ime āyasmā uddesādīhi saṅgaṇhatū”ti vattabbaṃ. Evampi alabhamānena “mayhaṃ, āvuso, ekaṃ kiccaṃ atthi, tumhe yathāphāsukaṭṭhānāni gacchathā”ti gaṇaṃ pahāya attano kammaṃ kātabbaṃ.

Group: this means a group studying the Suttanta or a group studying the Abhidhamma. For one who, while giving them instruction or answering their questions, does not find an opportunity for the ascetic’s duties, the group becomes an impediment. Therefore, it should be cut off thus: If much has been done for those monks and little remains, he should finish it and enter the forest. If little has been done and much remains, then without going beyond a yojana, within the boundary of a yojana, he should approach another teacher of a group and say, “May the venerable one take care of these monks with instruction and so on.” If unable to find such a person, he should say, “Friends, I have some business; you may go to places convenient for you,” and, abandoning the group, he should do his own work.

Kammenāti kammapalibodhena. “Kammañca pañcama”ntipi pāṭho. Tattha kammanti navakammaṃ. Taṃ karontena vaḍḍhakīādīhi laddhāladdhaṃ jānitabbaṃ, katākate ussukkaṃ āpajjitabbanti sabbathāpi [V 2.0178] palibodho hoti. Sopi evaṃ upacchinditabbo – sace appaṃ avasiṭṭhaṃ hoti, niṭṭhapetabbaṃ. Sace bahu, saṅghikaṃ ce, navakammaṃ saṅghassa vā bhārahārakabhikkhūnaṃ vā niyyātetabbaṃ. Attano santakaṃ ce, attano bhārahārakānaṃ niyyātetabbaṃ. Tādisaṃ alabhantena saṅghassa pariccajitvā gantabbaṃ.

“By work” means by the impediment of work. There is also a reading: “And work as the fifth.” Here, “work” means new construction. For one engaged in it, it is necessary to know what has been obtained or not obtained from carpenters and others, and to make an effort regarding what has been done or not done; in every way it becomes an impediment. That too should be severed thus: if little remains, it should be completed. If much, and it belongs to the Sangha, the new construction should be handed over to the Sangha or to the monks entrusted with the responsibility. If it is one’s own, it should be handed over to one’s own attendants responsible for it. If one is unable to find such a person, one should relinquish it to the Sangha and depart.

Addhānanti maggagamanaṃ. Yassa hi katthaci pabbajjāpekkho vā hoti, paccayajātaṃ vā kiñci laddhabbaṃ hoti. Sace taṃ alabhanto na sakkoti adhivāsetuṃ, araññaṃ pavisitvā samaṇadhammaṃ karontassapi gamikacittaṃ nāma duppaṭivinodayaṃ [M 2.0201] hoti, tasmā gantvā taṃ kiccaṃ tīretvāva samaṇadhamme ussukkaṃ kātabbaṃ.

“Journey” means traveling on a road. For one who has someone expecting ordination somewhere, or some requisite to be obtained, if, unable to obtain it, he cannot endure, then even when entering the forest and practicing the ascetic’s life, the thought of traveling is difficult to dispel. Therefore, one should go, complete that task, and only then make an effort in the ascetic’s life.

Ñātīti vihāre ācariyupajjhāyasaddhivihārikaantevāsikasamānupajjhāyakasamānācariyakā, ghare mātā pitā bhātāti evamādikā. Te gilānā imassa palibodhā honti. Tasmā so palibodho te upaṭṭhahitvā tesaṃ pākatikakaraṇena upacchinditabbo. Tattha upajjhāyo tāva gilāno sace lahuṃ na vuṭṭhāti, yāvajīvaṃ paṭijaggitabbo, tathā pabbajjācariyo upasampadācariyo saddhivihāriko upasampāditapabbājitaantevāsikasamānupajjhāyakā ca. Nissayācariyauddesācariyanissayantevāsikauddesantevāsikasamānācariyakā pana yāva nissayauddesā anupacchinnā, tāva paṭijaggitabbā. Pahontena tato uddhampi paṭijaggitabbā eva. Mātāpitūsu upajjhāye viya paṭijaggitabbaṃ. Sacepi hi te rajje ṭhitā honti, puttato ca upaṭṭhānaṃ paccāsīsanti, kātabbameva. Atha tesaṃ bhesajjaṃ natthi, attano santakaṃ dātabbaṃ. Asati, bhikkhācariyāya pariyesitvāpi dātabbameva. Bhātubhaginīnaṃ pana tesaṃ santakameva yojetvā dātabbaṃ. Sace natthi, attano santakaṃ tāvakālikaṃ datvā pacchā labhantena gaṇhitabbaṃ, alabhantena na codetabbā. Aññātakassa bhaginiyā sāmikassa bhesajjaṃ neva kātuṃ, na dātuṃ vaṭṭati, “tuyhaṃ sāmikassa dehī”ti vatvā pana bhaginiyā dātabbaṃ. Bhātu jāyāyapi eseva nayo, tesaṃ pana puttā imassa ñātakāyevāti tesaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati.

“Relatives” means, in the monastery, the teacher, preceptor, co-resident, pupil, those with the same preceptor, and those with the same teacher; at home, mother, father, brother, and so on. They, when sick, become an impediment for him. Therefore, that impediment should be severed by attending to them and restoring them to their normal condition. Herein, first, if the preceptor is sick and does not quickly recover, he should be cared for as long as he lives; so too the ordination teacher, the higher ordination teacher, the co-resident, the pupil one has ordained and given higher ordination, and those with the same preceptor. But the dependence teacher, the instructor, the dependence pupil, the instruction pupil, and those with the same teacher should be cared for as long as the dependence or instruction has not ceased. If capable, one should care for them even beyond that. Mother and father should be cared for like the preceptor. Even if they are established in a kingdom and expect attendance from their son, it must be done. If they have no medicine, one should give from one’s own possessions. If there is none, one should seek it even by going on alms-round and give it. For brothers and sisters, only their own possessions should be used to provide for them. If they have none, one should temporarily give from one’s own and take it back later when one obtains it; if one does not obtain it, they should not be reproached. For one's sister's husband, who is a non-relative, it is not proper to prepare or give medicine, but one may say, “Give this to your husband,” and give it to the sister. The same principle applies to the brother’s wife; but their sons are this one’s relatives, so it is proper to provide for them.

Ābādhoti yo koci rogo. So bādhayamāno palibodho hoti, tasmā bhesajjakaraṇena upacchinditabbo. Sace pana katipāhaṃ bhesajjaṃ karontassapi na vūpasammati, “nāhaṃ tuyhaṃ dāso, na bhatako, taṃyevamhi posento anamatagge saṃsāravaṭṭe dukkhappatto”ti attabhāvaṃ garahitvā samaṇadhammo kātabbo.

“Sickness” means any kind of disease. While it afflicts, it becomes an impediment; therefore, it should be severed by the use of medicine. But if, even after using medicine for some days, it does not subside, then, reproaching one's own body, one should practice the ascetic’s life, reflecting: “I am not your slave, nor your hired servant. It is by nourishing you that I have attained suffering in this beginningless round of existence.”

Ganthoti [V 2.0179] pariyattipariharaṇaṃ. Taṃ sajjhāyādīhi niccabyāvaṭasseva palibodho hoti, na itarassa.

“Study” means the learning and retaining of the scriptures. It becomes an impediment only for one constantly engaged in recitation and the like, not for another.

Iddhiyāti [M 2.0202] iddhipalibodhena. “Iddhīti te dasā”tipi pāṭho. Tattha iddhīti pothujjanikā iddhi. Sā hi uttānaseyyakadārako viya taruṇasassaṃ viya ca dupparihārā hoti, appamattakena ca bhijjati. Sā pana vipassanāya palibodho hoti, na samādhissa samādhiṃ patvā pattabbato, tasmā vipassanātthikena iddhipalibodho upacchinditabbo, itarena avasesāti. Kammaṭṭhānabhāvanaṃ paribundheti uparodheti pavattituṃ na detīti palibodho, ra-kārassa la-kāraṃ katvā vutto, paripanthoti attho. Upacchinditabboti samāpanena saṅgahaṇena uparundhitabbo, apalibodho kātabboti attho.

“By psychic power” means by the impediment of psychic power. There is also a reading: “Psychic powers are those ten.” Here, “psychic power” refers to the psychic power of an ordinary person. For just like an infant lying on its back or a tender crop, it is hard to maintain and is easily broken by even a slight cause. Moreover, it becomes an impediment to insight, not to concentration, because it is to be attained after having attained concentration. Therefore, one who desires insight should sever the impediment of psychic power; for another, it is not necessary. An impediment is what obstructs, hinders, and does not allow the development of a meditation subject to proceed. The word is spoken with an 'l' in place of an 'r'; the meaning is 'a hindrance.' “Should be severed” means it should be stopped by restraining and controlling it, making it non-obstructive—that is the meaning.

Kammaṭṭhāne niyutto kammaṭṭhāniko, bhāvanamanuyuñjanto. Tena kammaṭṭhānikena. Paricchinditvāti “imasmiṃ vihāre sabbepi bhikkhū”ti evaṃ paricchinditvā. Sahavāsīnanti sahavāsīnaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ. Muducittataṃ janetīti attani muducittataṃ uppādeti. Ayañca sahavāsīnaṃ cittamaddavajananādiattho “manussānaṃ piyo hotī”tiādinayappavattena mettānisaṃsasuttena (a. ni. 8.1) dīpetabbo.

A meditator is one engaged in a meditation subject, applying himself to development. By that meditator. “Having defined” means having defined thus: “All the monks in this monastery.” “Fellow residents” means the monks who are co-residents. “He generates tenderness of mind” means he produces tenderness of mind in himself. And this meaning of generating gentleness of mind in co-residents and so on should be explained by the Discourse on the Benefits of Loving-Kindness, which proceeds in the manner beginning, “He is dear to human beings.”

Anolīnavuttiko hotīti sammāpaṭipattiyaṃ olīnavuttiko hīnavīriyo na hoti, āraddhavīriyo hotīti attho. Dibbesupi ārammaṇesu, pageva itaresūti adhippāyo. Sabbatthāti sabbasmiṃ samaṇakaraṇīye, sabbasmiṃ vā kammaṭṭhānānuyoge. Atthayitabbanti pubbāsevanavasena atthayitabbaṃ. Yogassa bhāvanāya anuyuñjanaṃ yogānuyogo, tadeva karaṇīyaṭṭhena kammaṃ, tassa yogānuyogakammassa. Padaṭṭhānattāti nipphattihetuttā.

“He is one whose conduct is not sluggish” means that in right practice, he is not one whose conduct is sluggish or of deficient energy, but is of aroused energy—this is the meaning. Even in divine objects, how much more so in others—this is the intention. “In all” means in all of an ascetic’s duties, or in all application to the meditation subject. “It should be desired” means it should be desired through prior cultivation. Applying oneself to the development of the practice is 'application to the practice'; that very thing is 'work' in the sense of what should be done; of that work of application to the practice. “Because it is the foundation” means because it is the condition for arising.

Odātakasiṇe ālokakasiṇaṃ, kasiṇugghāṭimākāsakasiṇe paricchinnākāsakasiṇañca antogadhaṃ katvā pāḷiyaṃ pathavīkasiṇādīnaṃ rūpajjhānārammaṇānaṃ aṭṭhannaṃyeva kasiṇānaṃ sarūpato vuttattā ākāsakasiṇaṃ ālokakasiṇañca vajjetvā “aṭṭhatiṃsārammaṇesū”ti pāḷiyaṃ āgatanayeneva vuttaṃ. Aṭṭhakathānayena pana ākāsakasiṇe ālokakasiṇe ca visuṃ gahite cattālīsaṃyeva kammaṭṭhānāni. Tatrimāni cattālīsa kammaṭṭhānāni – dasa kasiṇā, dasa asubhā[M 2.0203], dasa anussatiyo, cattāro brahmavihārā, cattāro āruppā, ekā saññā, ekaṃ vavatthānanti. Tattha pathavīkasiṇaṃ āpokasiṇaṃ tejokasiṇaṃ vāyokasiṇaṃ nīlakasiṇaṃ pītakasiṇaṃ [V 2.0180] lohitakasiṇaṃ odātakasiṇaṃ ālokakasiṇaṃ paricchinnākāsakasiṇanti ime dasa kasiṇā. Uddhumātakaṃ vinīlakaṃ vipubbakaṃ vicchiddakaṃ vikkhāyitakaṃ vikkhittakaṃ hatavikkhittakaṃ lohitakaṃ puḷavakaṃ aṭṭhikanti ime dasa asubhā. Buddhānussati dhamma saṅgha sīla cāga devatānussati maraṇassati kāyagatāsati ānāpānassati upasamānussatīti imā dasa anussatiyo. Mettā karuṇā muditā upekkhāti ime cattāro brahmavihārā. Ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ nevasaññānāsaññāyatananti ime cattāro āruppā. Āhāre paṭikūlasaññā ekā saññā. Catudhātuvavatthānaṃ ekaṃ vavatthānanti.

The light kasiṇa is included within the white kasiṇa, and the limited-space kasiṇa within the space kasiṇa, which opens up the kasiṇa. Because in the Pāli, only eight kasiṇas, such as the earth kasiṇa, are mentioned in their own nature as objects for the rūpa jhānas, it is stated in the manner that has come down in the Pāli in the phrase “among the thirty-eight objects,” thereby excluding the space kasiṇa and the light kasiṇa. However, according to the commentary tradition, when the space kasiṇa and the light kasiṇa are taken separately, there are forty meditation subjects in total. These forty meditation subjects are: ten kasiṇas, ten foulnesses, ten recollections, four divine abidings, four formless states, one perception, and one analysis. Among them, the ten kasiṇas are: the earth kasiṇa, the water kasiṇa, the fire kasiṇa, the air kasiṇa, the blue kasiṇa, the yellow kasiṇa, the red kasiṇa, the white kasiṇa, the light kasiṇa, and the limited-space kasiṇa. The ten foulnesses are: a bloated corpse, a discolored corpse, a festering corpse, a split corpse, a gnawed corpse, a scattered corpse, a hacked and scattered corpse, a bloody corpse, a worm-infested corpse, and a skeleton. The ten recollections are: recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dhamma, recollection of the Saṅgha, recollection of virtue, recollection of generosity, recollection of deities, recollection of death, mindfulness of the body, mindfulness of breathing, and recollection of peace. The four divine abidings are: loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity. The four formless states are: the base of infinite space, the base of infinite consciousness, the base of nothingness, and the base of neither perception nor non-perception. The one perception is: the perception of the repulsiveness of food. The one analysis is: the analysis of the four elements.

Yaṃ yassa caritānukūlanti ettha rāgacaritassa tāva dasa asubhā kāyagatāsatīti ekādasa kammaṭṭhānāni anukūlāni, dosacaritassa cattāro brahmavihārā cattāri vaṇṇakasiṇānīti aṭṭha, mohacaritassa ca vitakkacaritassa ca ekaṃ ānāpānassatikammaṭṭhānameva, saddhācaritassa purimā cha anussatiyo, buddhicaritassa maraṇassati upasamānussati catudhātuvavatthānaṃ āhāre paṭikūlasaññāti cattāri, sesakasiṇāni cattāro ca āruppā sabbacaritānaṃ anukūlāni. Kasiṇesu ca yaṃ kiñci parittaṃ vitakkacaritassa, appamāṇaṃ mohacaritassa anukūlanti veditabbaṃ. Yathāvutteneva nayenāti “yogānuyogakammassa padaṭṭhānattā”ti imamatthaṃ atidisati.

Here, regarding what is suitable for which temperament: for the lustful temperament, the ten foulnesses and mindfulness of the body—these eleven meditation subjects—are suitable. For the hateful temperament, the four divine abidings and the four color kasiṇas—these eight—are suitable. For the deluded temperament and the discursive temperament, only the single meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing is suitable. For the faithful temperament, the first six recollections are suitable. For the intelligent temperament, mindfulness of death, recollection of peace, analysis of the four elements, and the perception of the repulsiveness of food—these four—are suitable. The remaining kasiṇas and the four formless attainments are suitable for all temperaments. Among the kasiṇas, it should be understood that whatever is limited is suitable for the discursive temperament, and the immeasurable is suitable for the deluded temperament. “In the manner thus stated” refers to this meaning: “because it is the foundation for the undertaking of meditative practice.”

Yaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetukāmo hoti, tasseva vasena catukkapañcakajjhānāni nibbattetvā jhānapadaṭṭhānaṃ vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā āsavakkhayappattassa khīṇāsavassa santike gahetabbanti āha – “imināva kammaṭṭhānena…pe… uggahetabba”nti. Arahantādayo hītiādi ekaccakhīṇāsavato bahussutova kammaṭṭhānadāne seyyoti dassanatthaṃ āraddhaṃ. Mahāhatthipathaṃ nīharanto viyāti kammaṭṭhānapathaviṃ mahāhatthipathaṃ katvā dassento viya. Sappāyāsappāyaṃ paricchinditvāti yassa kammaṭṭhānaṃ ācikkhati, tassa upakārānupakāraṃ yuttimagganena paricchinditvā.

One who wishes to take up a meditation subject should receive it from one whose taints are destroyed, who has attained the destruction of the taints after having generated the fourfold and fivefold jhānas based on that very subject and developed insight with jhāna as its foundation. Thus it is said: “By means of this very meditation subject… one should undertake.” The passage beginning “Arahants, etc.” is stated to show that a learned one is superior to some whose taints are destroyed in the giving of a meditation subject. “Like one leading out a great elephant track” means as if showing the ground of the meditation subject after having made it a great elephant track. “Having determined what is suitable and unsuitable” means having discerned by means of reasoned investigation what is beneficial or unbeneficial for the one to whom he teaches the meditation subject.

Idāni [M 2.0204] kammaṭṭhānadāyakassa santikaṃ gacchantena dhotamakkhitehi pādehi upāhanā āruhitvā chattaṃ gahetvā telanāḷimadhuphāṇitādīni gāhāpetvā antevāsikaparivutena na gantabbaṃ, gamikavattaṃ pana pūretvā attano pattacīvaraṃ sayameva gahetvā antarāmagge yaṃ yaṃ vihāraṃ pavisati, sabbattha paviṭṭhakāle āgantukavattaṃ, nikkhamanakāle gamikavattanti yathārahaṃ taṃ taṃ vattaṃ pūrentena sallahukaparikkhārena paramasallekhavuttinā hutvā gantabbanti imamatthaṃ saṅkhipitvā dassento “sallahukavuttinā vinayācārasampannenā”ti āha. Evaṃ pana gantvā taṃ vihāraṃ [V 2.0181] pavisantena antarāyeva dantakaṭṭhaṃ kappiyaṃ kārāpetvā gahetvā pavisitabbaṃ, na ca muhuttaṃ vissamitvā pādadhovanamakkhanādīni katvā ācariyassa santikaṃ gamissāmīti aññaṃ pariveṇaṃ pavisitabbaṃ. Kasmā? Sace hissa tatra ācariyassa visabhāgā bhikkhū bhaveyyuṃ, taṃ te āgamanakāraṇaṃ pucchitvā ācariyassa avaṇṇaṃ pakāsetvā “naṭṭhosi, sace tassa santikaṃ āgato”ti vippaṭisāraṃ uppādeyyuṃ, yena tatova paṭinivatteyya, tasmā ācariyassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ pucchitvā ujukaṃ tattheva gantabbaṃ.

Now, one going to the teacher who gives meditation subjects should not go with washed and anointed feet, wearing sandals, carrying an umbrella, having caused oil, honey, molasses, etc., to be taken, or surrounded by disciples. Instead, fulfilling the duties of a traveler, taking one’s own bowl and robe oneself, one should go. When entering any monastery along the way, one should observe the customs for visitors upon entering and the duties of a traveler when leaving. One must fulfill each appropriate duty accordingly, traveling lightly equipped and practicing utmost austerity. Summarizing this meaning, it is said: “One should go as one who practices simplicity, endowed with the conduct of the Vinaya.” Having gone thus, when entering that monastery, one should have a tooth-stick made allowable along the way and take it inside. And one should not enter another monastic cell to rest for a while, wash one’s feet, or anoint them, thinking, “I will go to the teacher’s presence afterward.” Why? If there are monks there who are disagreeable to the teacher, they might ask the reason for his coming, speak ill of the teacher, and say, “You are lost if you have come to him,” causing regret, so that he might turn back from there. Therefore, one should ask for the teacher’s dwelling place and go straight there.

Vuttappakāramācariyanti –

A teacher of the kind described is:

“Piyo garu bhāvanīyo, vattā ca vacanakkhamo;

Gambhīrañca kathaṃ kattā, no caṭṭhāne niyojako”ti. (a. ni. 7.37; netti. 113) –

“Beloved, revered, and to be esteemed; an admonisher, and patient with words; a speaker of profound discourse, and one who does not engage a pupil in what is inappropriate.”

Evamādinā vuttappakāraṃ saddhādiguṇasamannāgataṃ ekantahitesiṃ vuḍḍhipakkhe ṭhitaṃ kalyāṇamittaṃ ācariyaṃ. Vattapaṭipattiyā ārādhitacittassāti ettha sace ācariyo daharataro hoti, pattacīvarapaṭiggahaṇādīni na sāditabbāni. Sace vuḍḍhataro, gantvā ācariyaṃ vanditvā ṭhātabbaṃ. “Nikkhipāvuso, pattacīvara”nti vuttena nikkhipitabbaṃ. “Pānīyaṃ pivā”ti vuttena sace icchati, pātabbaṃ. “Pāde dhovā”ti vuttena na tāva dhovitabbā. Sace hi ācariyena ābhatamudakaṃ bhaveyya, na sāruppaṃ siyā. “Dhovāvuso, na mayā ābhataṃ, aññehi ābhata”nti vuttena pana yattha ācariyo na passati, evarūpe paṭicchanne vā okāse abbhokāsavihārassapi vā ekamante nisīditvā pādā dhovitabbā. Sace ācariyo telanāḷiṃ āharati, uṭṭhahitvā ubhohi hatthehi sakkaccaṃ [M 2.0205] gahetabbā. Sace hi na gaṇheyya, “ayaṃ bhikkhu ito eva paṭṭhāya sambhogaṃ kopetī”ti ācariyassa aññathattaṃ bhaveyya. Gahetvā pana na āditova pādā makkhetabbā. Sace hi taṃ ācariyassa gattabbhañjanatelaṃ bhaveyya, na sāruppaṃ siyā, tasmā paṭhamaṃ sīsaṃ makkhetvā khandhādīni makkhetabbāni. “Sabbapārihāriyatelamidaṃ, āvuso, pādepi makkhehī”ti vuttena pana pāde makkhetvā “imaṃ telanāḷiṃ ṭhapemi, bhante”ti vatvā ācariye gaṇhante dātabbā.

In this manner, a teacher of the kind described, endowed with qualities such as faith, solely benevolent, established in the side of growth, a spiritual friend. Here, regarding one whose mind is pleased by the practice of duties: if the teacher is younger, the receiving of the bowl and robe, and so on, should not be accepted. If the teacher is older, one should go, pay homage, and stand. If told, “Friend, put down the bowl and robe,” one should put them down. If told, “Drink the water,” and one wishes to, one should drink. If told, “Wash your feet,” one should not wash them at once. For if the water was brought by the teacher, it would not be proper. But if told, “Wash, friend, this was not brought by me—others brought it,” then in a concealed place where the teacher does not see, or in a solitary spot even in an open-air dwelling, one should sit aside and wash one's feet. If the teacher brings an oil-tube, one should rise and receive it carefully with both hands. For if one does not take it, the teacher might have a change of mind, thinking, “This monk, from this very moment, ruins communion.” Having received it, one should not anoint the feet first of all. For if it were the teacher’s body-anointing oil, it would not be proper. Therefore, one should first anoint the head, then the shoulders and so on. If told, “Friend, this oil is for all-round use, anoint your feet too,” then after anointing the feet, one should say, “Venerable sir, I shall put down this oil-tube,” and give it when the teacher takes it.

Gatadivasato paṭṭhāya “kammaṭṭhānaṃ me, bhante, kathetha”iccevaṃ na vattabbaṃ. Dutiyadivasato pana paṭṭhāya sace ācariyassa pakatiupaṭṭhāko atthi, taṃ yācitvā vattaṃ kātabbaṃ. Sace yācitopi [V 2.0182] na deti, okāse laddheyeva kātabbaṃ. Karontena ca khuddakamajjhimamahantāni tīṇi dantakaṭṭhāni upanāmetabbāni. Sītaṃ uṇhanti duvidhaṃ mukhadhovanudakañca nhānodakañca paṭiyādetabbaṃ. Tato yaṃ ācariyo tīṇi divasāni paribhuñjati, tādisameva niccaṃ upaṭṭhāpetabbaṃ, niyamaṃ akatvā yaṃ vā taṃ vā paribhuñjantassa yathāladdhaṃ upanāmetabbaṃ. Kiṃ bahunā vuttena, yaṃ taṃ bhagavatā “antevāsikena, bhikkhave, ācariyamhi sammā vattitabbaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ sammāvattanā – kālasseva vuṭṭhāya upāhanā omuñcitvā ekaṃsaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ karitvā dantakaṭṭhaṃ dātabbaṃ, mukhodakaṃ dātabbaṃ, āsanaṃ paññapetabbaṃ. Sace yāgu hoti, bhājanaṃ dhovitvā yāgu upanāmetabbā”tiādikaṃ (mahāva. 66) khandhake vattaṃ paññattaṃ, taṃ sabbampi kātabbaṃ. Iti iminā yathāvuttena nayena paṭipajjanto vattapaṭipattiyā cittaṃ ārādhetīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Starting from the day of arrival, one should not say, “Venerable sir, please explain the meditation subject to me.” However, starting from the second day, if the teacher has a regular attendant, one should request him and perform the duties. If, even when requested, he does not permit it, one should perform the duties only when the opportunity is obtained. And while performing them, three tooth-sticks—small, medium, and large—should be offered. Water for washing the face and bathing water of two kinds, cold and hot, should be prepared. Thereafter, whatever the teacher uses for three days, that same kind should always be provided. For a teacher who uses this or that without a fixed rule, whatever is obtained should be offered. What is the use of saying much? Whatever duty the Blessed One has prescribed in the Khandhaka—“Monks, a pupil should attend to the teacher properly. Herein, this is the proper way of attending: rising early, removing one's sandals, arranging the upper robe over one shoulder, giving a tooth-stick, giving water for the face, preparing a seat. If there is rice-gruel, one should wash the bowl and offer the rice-gruel,” and so on (Mahāvagga 66)—all of that should be done. Thus, it should be understood that one who practices according to this aforesaid method pleases the teacher's mind through the practice of duties.

Pañcasandhikanti pañcapabbaṃ, pañcabhāganti attho. Kammaṭṭhānassa uggaṇhananti kammaṭṭhānaganthassa uggaṇhanaṃ, tadatthaparipucchā kammaṭṭhānassa paripucchanā. Atha vā ganthato atthato ca kammaṭṭhānassa uggaṇhanaṃ uggaho, tattha saṃsayaparipucchanā paripucchā. Kammaṭṭhānassa upaṭṭhānanti nimittupaṭṭhānaṃ, evaṃ bhāvanamanuyuñjantassa “evamidaṃ nimittaṃ upaṭṭhātī”ti upadhāraṇaṃ, tathā kammaṭṭhānappanā “evaṃ jhānamappetī”ti.
