Kammaṭṭhānassa lakkhaṇanti gaṇanānubandhanāphusanānaṃ vasena bhāvanaṃ ussukkāpetvā ṭhapanāya sampatti, tato parampi vā sallakkhaṇādivasena matthakappattīti kammaṭṭhānasabhāvassa sallakkhaṇaṃ. Tenāha – “kammaṭṭhānasabhāvupadhāraṇanti vuttaṃ hotī”ti.

Pañcasandhika means five sections; five parts is the meaning. The 'learning of the meditation subject' means the learning of the text on the meditation subject, and the 'inquiring about the meditation subject' is the inquiry about its meaning. Alternatively, 'learning' (uggaho) is the learning of the meditation subject from the text and from its meaning, and 'inquiring' (paripucchā) is the inquiry about doubts therein. 'The appearing of the meditation subject' means the appearing of the sign (nimitta); for one who applies himself to meditation in this way, it is the ascertainment that 'this sign appears in this way.' Similarly, the 'application of the meditation subject' is 'thus it brings about jhāna.' 'The characteristic of the meditation subject' is the success in establishment by arousing diligence in the cultivation by means of counting, pursuing, and touching. Or, beyond that, it is the attainment of the summit by means of observation, etc., which is the discerning of the nature of the meditation subject. Therefore, it is said: 'It is called the ascertainment of the nature of the meditation subject.'

Attanāpi [M 2.0206] na kilamati odhiso kammaṭṭhānassa uggaṇhanato, tato eva ācariyampi na viheṭheti dhammādhikaraṇampi bhāvanāya matthakaṃ pāpanato. Tasmāti taṃnimittaṃ attanoakilamanaācariyāviheṭhanahetu. Thokanti thokaṃ thokaṃ. Tatthāti yattha ācariyo vasati, tattha. Sappāyaṃ hotīti āvāsasappāyādilābhena manasikāraphāsutā bhāvanānukūlatā hoti. Yojanaparamanti iminā gāvutaaḍḍhayojanānipi saṅgaṇhāti. Yasmā pana mandapañño gāvute aḍḍhayojane yojanamatte vā vasanto kammaṭṭhānassa kismiñcideva ṭhāne sandehe vā satisammose vā jāte kālasseva vihāre vattaṃ katvā antarāmagge piṇḍāya caritvā bhattakiccapariyosāneyeva ācariyassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā taṃ divasaṃ ācariyassa santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ sodhetvā dutiyadivase ācariyaṃ vanditvā nikkhamitvā antarāmagge piṇḍāya caritvā akilamantoyeva attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ āgantuṃ sakkhissati, tasmā vuttaṃ “mandapañño yojanaparamaṃ gantvā”ti. Sace tikkhapañño yojanaparame phāsukaṭṭhānaṃ na labhati, tena kammaṭṭhāne sabbaṃ gaṇṭhiṭṭhānaṃ chinditvā [V 2.0183] visuddhaṃ āvajjanapaṭibaddhaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ katvā yojanaparamato dūrampi gantuṃ vaṭṭatīti āha “tikkhapañño dūrampi gantvā”ti.

He does not tire himself by learning the meditation subject in a limited way, and for that very reason he does not trouble the teacher, by bringing the cultivation to its culmination. Therefore, that is the reason for not tiring oneself and not troubling the teacher. 'A little' means a little at a time. 'There' means where the teacher resides. 'It becomes suitable' means that by obtaining a suitable dwelling, etc., there is ease of attention and conduciveness to cultivation. By 'at most a yojana,' it includes a gāvuta and a half-yojana. For a person of dull wisdom, dwelling at a distance of a gāvuta, a half-yojana, or a yojana, if a doubt or confusion arises at any point in the meditation subject, he can, in the early morning, perform his duties in the monastery, go for alms on the way, and after finishing his meal, go to the teacher's dwelling place. That same day, having clarified the meditation subject in the teacher's presence, he can, on the next day, pay respects to the teacher, depart, go for alms on the way, and return to his own dwelling place without tiring himself. Therefore, it is said, 'A person of dull wisdom, having gone at most a yojana.' If a person of sharp wisdom does not find a suitable place within a yojana, he, having cut off all knotty points in the meditation subject and made the meditation subject pure and connected with reflection, may go even further than a yojana. Thus, it is said: 'A person of sharp wisdom, having gone even far.'

Aṭṭhārasasenāsanadosavivajjitanti mahattaṃ, navattaṃ, jiṇṇattaṃ, panthanissitattaṃ, soṇḍī, paṇṇaṃ, pupphaṃ, phalaṃ, patthanīyatā, nagarasannissitatā, dārusannissitatā, khettasannissitatā, visabhāgānaṃ puggalānaṃ atthitā, paṭṭanasannissitatā, paccantasannissitatā, rajjasīmasannissitatā, asappāyatā, kalyāṇamittānaṃ alābhoti imehi aṭṭhārasahi senāsanadosehi vivajjitaṃ. Imesañhi aṭṭhārasannaṃ dosānaṃ aññatarena samannāgataṃ senāsanaṃ bhāvanāya ananurūpaṃ.

It is devoid of the eighteen faults of a dwelling: largeness, newness, dilapidation, being on a road, proximity to a pond, a place with vegetables, a place with flowers, a place with fruit, being sought after, proximity to a city, proximity to a timber-lot, proximity to fields, the presence of incompatible persons, proximity to a port, proximity to a border region, proximity to a kingdom's boundary, unsuitability, and the lack of good friends. For a dwelling endowed with any one of these eighteen faults is unsuitable for cultivation.

Kasmā? Mahāvihāre (visuddhi. 1.52) tāva bahū nānāchandā sannipatanti, te aññamaññaṃ paṭiviruddhatāya vattaṃ na karonti, bodhiyaṅgaṇādīni asammaṭṭhāneva honti, anupaṭṭhāpitaṃ pānīyaṃ paribhojanīyaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ “gocaragāme piṇḍāya carissāmī”ti pattacīvaramādāya nikkhantopi sace passati vattaṃ akataṃ, pānīyaghaṭaṃ vā rittaṃ, athānena vattaṃ kātabbaṃ hoti, pānīyaṃ upaṭṭhāpetabbaṃ[M 2.0207], akaronto vattabhede dukkaṭaṃ āpajjati. Karontassa kālo atikkamati, atidivā paviṭṭho niṭṭhitāya bhikkhāya kiñci na labhati. Paṭisallānagatopi sāmaṇeradaharabhikkhūnaṃ uccāsaddena saṅghakammehi ca vikkhipati. Yattha pana sabbaṃ vattaṃ katameva hoti, avasesāpi ca ghaṭṭanā natthi, evarūpe mahāvihārepi vihātabbaṃ.

Why? In a large monastery, for instance, many of diverse inclinations gather. Due to mutual opposition, they do not perform their duties; the grounds of the Bodhi tree, etc., remain unswept; drinking water and water for use are not set out. There, a monk who has taken his bowl and robe and set out thinking, 'I will go for alms in the alms-resort village,' if he sees that the duties have not been done or that the water pot is empty, must then perform the duty and set out the water. If he does not do so, he incurs a dukkaṭa offense for breach of duty. While he is doing it, time passes; having entered the village late in the day, he gets nothing as the alms-gathering is over. Even when gone into seclusion, he is distracted by the loud voices of novices and young monks and by the formal acts of the Sangha. But in a large monastery where all duties are already done and there are no other disturbances, one may dwell there.

Navavihāre bahu navakammaṃ hoti, akarontaṃ ujjhāyanti. Yattha pana bhikkhū evaṃ vadanti “āyasmā yathāsukhaṃ samaṇadhammaṃ karotu, mayaṃ navakammaṃ karissāmā”ti, evarūpe vihātabbaṃ.

In a new monastery, there is much new construction work, and they criticize one who does not do it. But where the monks say, 'Let the venerable one practice the ascetic's duties at his ease; we will do the new construction work,' in such a monastery one may dwell.

Jiṇṇavihāre pana bahu paṭijaggitabbaṃ hoti, antamaso attano senāsanamattampi appaṭijaggantaṃ ujjhāyanti, paṭijaggantassa kammaṭṭhānaṃ parihāyati.

In a dilapidated monastery, however, much repair is needed. They criticize one who does not repair even so much as his own lodging. For one who is repairing it, the meditation subject deteriorates.

Panthanissite mahāpathavihāre rattindivaṃ āgantukā sannipatanti. Vikāle āgatānaṃ attano senāsanaṃ datvā rukkhamūle vā pāsāṇapiṭṭhe vā vasitabbaṃ hoti, punadivasepi evamevāti kammaṭṭhānassa okāso na hoti. Yattha pana evarūpo āgantukasambādho na hoti, tattha vihātabbaṃ.

In a monastery situated on a great highway, visitors gather day and night. Having given one's own lodging to those who arrive at the wrong time, one has to dwell at the foot of a tree or on a flat rock. Since it is the same on the next day, there is no opportunity for the meditation subject. But where there is no such crowding with visitors, one may dwell there.

Soṇḍī [V 2.0184] nāma pāsāṇapokkharaṇī hoti. Tattha pānīyatthaṃ mahājano samosarati, nagaravāsīnaṃ rājakulūpakattherānaṃ antevāsikā rajanakammatthāya āgacchanti, tesaṃ bhājanadārudoṇikādīni pucchantānaṃ “asuke ca asuke ca ṭhāne”ti dassetabbāni honti. Evaṃ sabbakālampi niccabyāvaṭo hoti.

A 'soṇḍī' is a stone pond. There, a great crowd of people assembles for water. The disciples of elders from the city who frequent the royal family come for the purpose of dyeing. When they ask for things like pots and wooden troughs, one has to show them, saying, 'They are in such and such a place.' Thus, one is constantly busy at all times.

Yattha nānāvidhaṃ sākapaṇṇaṃ hoti, tatthassa kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā divāvihāraṃ nisinnassapi santike sākahārikā gāyamānā paṇṇaṃ uccinantiyo visabhāgasaddasaṅghaṭṭanena kammaṭṭhānantarāyaṃ karonti.

Where there are various kinds of leafy vegetables, for a monk who has taken up his meditation subject and is sitting in daytime seclusion, women gathering vegetables nearby, singing as they gather, create an obstruction to his meditation subject by the impact of the discordant sound.

Yattha pana nānāvidhā mālāgacchā supupphitā honti, tatrāpi tādisoyeva upaddavo.

Where various kinds of flowering shrubs are in full bloom, there too, the same kind of trouble arises.

Yattha nānāvidhaṃ ambajambupanasādiphalaṃ hoti, tattha phalatthikā āgantvā yācanti, adentassa kujjhanti, balakkārena vā gaṇhanti, sāyanhasamaye vihāramajjhe caṅkamantena te disvā “kiṃ upāsakā evaṃ karothā”ti vuttā yathāruci akkosanti, avāsāyapissa parakkamanti.

Where various kinds of fruits such as mangoes, rose apples, and jackfruits abound, fruit-seekers come and beg. If not given, they grow angry or take them by force. In the evening, when a monk walking in the middle of the monastery sees them and says, 'Lay followers, why do you act thus?', they abuse him as they please and even attempt to drive him away.

Patthanīye [M 2.0208] pana lokasammate dakkhiṇagirihatthikucchicetiyagiricittalapabbatasadise vihāre viharantaṃ “ayaṃ arahā”ti sambhāvetvā vanditukāmā manussā samantā osaranti, tenassa na phāsu hoti. Yassa pana taṃ sappāyaṃ hoti, tena divā aññattha gantvā rattiṃ vasitabbaṃ.

But in a desirable and world-renowned monastery, like Dakkhiṇagiri, Hatthikucchi, Cetiyagiri, or Cittalapabbata, people think, “This is an arahant,” and gather from all around wanting to pay homage. This causes him discomfort. But if such a place is suitable for him, he should go elsewhere by day and dwell there at night.

Nagarasannissite visabhāgārammaṇāni āpāthamāgacchanti, kumbhadāsiyopi ghaṭehi nighaṃsantiyo gacchanti, okkamitvā maggaṃ na denti, issaramanussāpi vihāramajjhe sāṇiṃ parikkhipitvā nisīdanti.

In a dwelling near a city, disagreeable objects come into view. Even slave women carrying pots pass by jostling, and do not step aside to give way. Powerful men, too, sit spreading out cloths in the middle of the monastery.

Dārusannissaye pana yattha kaṭṭhāni ca dabbupakaraṇarukkhā ca santi, tattha kaṭṭhahārikā pubbe vuttasākapupphahārikā viya aphāsukaṃ karonti. Vihāre rukkhā santi, te “chinditvā gharāni karissāmā”ti manussā āgantvā chindanti. Sace sāyanhasamaye padhānagharā nikkhamitvā vihāramajjhe caṅkamanto te disvā “kiṃ upāsakā evaṃ karothā”ti vadati, yathāruci akkosanti, avāsāyapissa parakkamanti.

But in a dwelling near a timber-lot, where there are timber and trees for making implements, wood-gatherers, like the aforementioned vegetable and flower gatherers, cause discomfort. If there are trees in the monastery, people come and cut them, saying, “We will build houses.” If, emerging from the meditation hall in the evening and walking in the center of the monastery, one sees them and says, “Lay followers, why do you act thus?” they abuse him as they please and even attempt to drive him away.

Yo [V 2.0185] pana khettasannissito hoti samantā khettehi parivārito, tattha manussā vihāramajjheyeva khalaṃ katvā dhaññaṃ maddanti, pamukhesu sayanti, aññampi bahuṃ aphāsuṃ karonti. Yatrapi mahāsaṅghabhogo hoti, ārāmikakulānaṃ gāvo rundhanti, udakavāraṃ paṭisedhenti, manussā vīhisīsaṃ gahetvā “passatha tumhākaṃ ārāmikakulānaṃ kamma”nti saṅghassa dassenti. Tena tena kāraṇena rājarājamahāmattānaṃ gharadvāraṃ gantabbaṃ hoti, ayampi khettasannissiteneva saṅgahito.

But a monastery that is near fields, surrounded by fields on all sides, is a place where people make threshing floors right in the monastery's center, threshing grain, sleeping at the entrances, and causing much other discomfort. Even where there is abundant communal property of the Sangha, people confine the cattle of the monastery attendants' families, deny their turn for water, and take ears of rice, showing them to the Sangha and saying, “See the work of your monastery attendants' families!” For these reasons, one must go to the door of kings and high ministers—this too is included as a fault of being near fields.

Yattha aññamaññavisabhāgā verī bhikkhū viharanti, ye kalahaṃ karontā “mā, bhante, evaṃ karothā”ti vāriyamānā “etassa paṃsukūlikassa āgatakālato paṭṭhāya naṭṭhāmhā”ti vattāro bhavanti.

Where mutually hostile and quarrelsome monks dwell, who, when restrained from conflict with the words, “Venerables, do not act thus,” are ones to reply, “We have been ruined ever since this rag-robe wearer arrived.”

Yopi udakapaṭṭanaṃ vā thalapaṭṭanaṃ vā sannissito hoti, tattha abhiṇhaṃ nāvāhi ca satthehi ca āgatamanussā “okāsaṃ detha, pānīyaṃ detha, loṇaṃ dethā”ti ghaṭṭayantā aphāsuṃ karonti.

And one who dwells near a water port or a land port is frequently disturbed by people arriving in boats or caravans and pressing him, saying, “Give us space, give us water, give us salt!”

Paccantasannissite pana manussā buddhādīsu appasannā honti.

In a border region, however, the people are not devoted to the Buddha and so on.

Rajjasīmasannissite [M 2.0209] rājabhayaṃ hoti. Tañhi padesaṃ eko rājā “na mayhaṃ vase vattatī”ti paharati, itaropi “na mayhaṃ vase vattatī”ti. Tatrāyaṃ bhikkhu kadāci imassa rañño vijite vicarati, kadāci etassa, atha naṃ “carapuriso aya”nti maññamānā anayabyasanaṃ pāpenti.

In a place near the borders of kingdoms, there is the threat of kings. For one king may attack that territory, thinking, ‘This territory does not come under my control,’ while the other king also thinks, ‘This territory does not come under my control.’ A monk wandering there might sometimes live in the territory of one king and sometimes in that of the other. Then, thinking, ‘This is a spy,’ they inflict disaster and ruin upon him.

Asappāyatāti visabhāgarūpādiārammaṇasamosaraṇena vā amanussapariggahitatāya vā asappāyatā. Tatridaṃ vatthu – eko kira thero araññe vasati. Athassa ekā yakkhinī paṇṇasāladvāre ṭhatvā gāyi. So nikkhamitvā dvāre aṭṭhāsi, sā gantvā caṅkamanasīse gāyi. Thero caṅkamanasīsaṃ agamāsi, sā sataporise papāte ṭhatvā gāyi. Thero paṭinivatti, atha naṃ sā vegena gantvā gahetvā “mayā, bhante, na eko, na dve tumhādisā khāditā”ti āha.

‘Unsuitability’ means unsuitability either due to an environment where incompatible sights and other sense objects are encountered, or one haunted by non-human beings. Here is an instance: A certain elder, it seems, lived in the forest. A female yakkha stood at the door of his leaf hut and sang. He went out and stood at the door, but she went to the head of the walking path and sang. The elder went to the head of the walking path, but she stood at the edge of a precipice as deep as a hundred men and sang. The elder turned back, but she swiftly went and seized him, and said, ‘Venerable sir, I have devoured not one, not two like you.’

Yattha na sakkā hoti ācariyaṃ vā ācariyasamaṃ vā upajjhāyaṃ vā upajjhāyasamaṃ vā [V 2.0186] kalyāṇamittaṃ laddhuṃ, tattha so kalyāṇamittānaṃ alābho mahādosoyeva. Tasmā imesaṃ aṭṭhārasannaṃ dosānaṃ aññatarena samannāgataṃ senāsanaṃ bhāvanāya ananurūpanti veditabbaṃ. Vuttampi cetaṃ aṭṭhakathāsu –

Where one cannot find a teacher or one equal to a teacher, a preceptor or one equal to a preceptor, or a good friend, there the lack of good friends is a great fault indeed. Therefore, a dwelling possessed of any one of these eighteen faults should be understood as unsuitable for meditation. And this has also been stated in the commentaries:

“Mahāvāsaṃ navāvāsaṃ, jarāvāsañca panthaniṃ;

Soṇḍiṃ paṇṇañca pupphañca, phalaṃ patthitameva ca.

“A large dwelling, a new dwelling, and an old dwelling, one on a road; one near a tavern, leaves, flowers, fruit, and a desirable one.

“Nagaraṃ dārunā khettaṃ, visabhāgena paṭṭanaṃ;

Paccantasīmāsappāyaṃ, yattha mitto na labbhati.

“One near a city, timber, or a field; one with incompatible people, or near a port; a border region, a kingdom’s border, an unsuitable place, and where a friend is not found.

“Aṭṭhārasetāni ṭhānāni, iti viññāya paṇḍito;

Ārakā parivajjeyya, maggaṃ sappaṭibhayaṃ yathā”ti. (visuddhi. 1.52);

“These eighteen places the wise should recognize, and avoid from afar, as one avoids a perilous path.”

Pañcasenāsanaṅgasamannāgatanti gāmato nātidūranāccāsannatādīhi pañcahi senāsanaṅgehi samannāgataṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

‘Endowed with the five factors of a dwelling’ means possessing the five factors of a dwelling, such as not being too far from or too close to a village. For the Blessed One has said:

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, senāsanaṃ pañcaṅgasamannāgataṃ hoti? Idha, bhikkhave, senāsanaṃ nātidūraṃ hoti nāccāsannaṃ gamanāgamanasampannaṃ, divā appākiṇṇaṃ rattiṃ appasaddaṃ appanigghosaṃ, appaḍaṃsamakasavātātapasarīsapasamphassaṃ, tasmiṃ kho pana senāsane viharantassa [M 2.0210] appakasirena uppajjanti cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhārā, tasmiṃ kho pana senāsane therā bhikkhū viharanti bahussutā āgatāgamā dhammadharā vinayadharā mātikādharā, te kālena kālaṃ upasaṅkamitvā paripucchati paripañhati ‘idaṃ, bhante, kathaṃ, imassa ko attho’ti. Tassa te āyasmanto avivaṭañceva vivaranti, anuttānīkatañca uttāniṃ karonti, anekavihitesu ca kaṅkhāṭhāniyesu dhammesu kaṅkhaṃ paṭivinodenti. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, senāsanaṃ pañcaṅgasamannāgataṃ hotī”ti (a. ni. 10.11).

“And how, monks, is a lodging endowed with five factors? Here, monks, a lodging is neither too far nor too near, and is accessible for coming and going; it is uncrowded by day, and by night quiet, with little noise. There is little contact from gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things. And for one dwelling in that lodging, the robes, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites arise without difficulty. And in that lodging, elder monks dwell who are learned, versed in the scriptures, upholders of the Dhamma, upholders of the Vinaya, and upholders of the summaries. From time to time, one approaches them to ask and inquire: ‘Venerable sirs, how is this? What is the meaning of this?’ Those venerable ones reveal what is unrevealed, clarify what is obscure, and dispel doubt regarding the various points in the Dhamma that cause doubt. Thus, monks, a lodging is endowed with five factors.”

Ettha ca nātidūraṃ nāccāsannaṃ gamanāgamanasampannanti ekaṃ aṅgaṃ, divā appākiṇṇaṃ rattiṃ appasaddaṃ appanigghosanti ekaṃ, appaḍaṃsamakasavātātapasarīsapasamphassanti ekaṃ, tasmiṃ kho pana [V 2.0187] senāsane viharantassa…pe… parikkhārāti ekaṃ, tasmiṃ kho pana senāsane therā…pe… kaṅkhaṃ paṭivinodentīti ekaṃ. Evaṃ pañcaṅgāni veditabbāni.

Herein, ‘neither too far nor too near, and accessible for coming and going’ is one factor. ‘Uncrowded by day, and by night quiet with little noise’ is another. ‘Little contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things’ is another. ‘That one dwelling in that lodging obtains requisites… without difficulty’ is another. ‘That elder monks… who dispel doubt dwell in that lodging’ is another. Thus, the five factors should be understood.

Upacchinnakhuddakapalibodhenāti ettha pana khuddakapalibodhe upacchindantena dīghāni kesanakhalomāni chinditabbāni, jiṇṇacīvaresu aggaḷaanuvātaparibhaṇḍadānādinā daḷhīkammaṃ vā tantucchedādīsu tunnakammaṃ vā kātabbaṃ, kiliṭṭhāni vā rajitabbāni. Sace patte malaṃ hoti, patto pacitabbo, mañcapīṭhādīni sodhetabbāni. Bhattasammadaṃ paṭivinodetvāti bhojananimittaṃ parissamaṃ vinodetvā. Āhāre hi āsayaṃ paviṭṭhamatte tassa āgantukatāya yebhuyyena siyā sarīrassa koci parissamo, taṃ vūpasametvā. Tasmiñhi avūpasante sarīrakhedena cittaṃ ekaggataṃ na labheyyāti. Uggahetabbato uggaho, sabbopi kammaṭṭhānavidhi, na pubbe vuttauggahamattaṃ. Ācariyato uggaho ācariyuggaho, tato. Ekapadampīti ekakoṭṭhāsampi.

‘Having cut off minor obstacles’—here, one who is cutting off minor obstacles should cut long hair, nails, and body hair. For worn-out robes, strengthening work should be done by adding fastenings, reinforcing edges, and patching, or mending work should be done on broken threads and so on, or they should be dyed if they are soiled. If the bowl has grime, it should be baked. Beds and benches should be cleaned. ‘Having dispelled the fatigue from food’ means having removed the weariness on account of the meal. For when food has just entered the stomach, there is usually some bodily weariness due to its being new; one should calm that down. For if that is not calmed down, the mind cannot achieve one-pointedness due to bodily fatigue. ‘What should be learned’ (uggaha) is so-called because it should be learned; it is the entire method of the meditation subject, not just the ‘learning’ mentioned previously. ‘Learning from a teacher’ (ācariyuggaha) is learning from a teacher. ‘Even a single phrase’ (ekapadampi) means even a single part.

Anubandhanāti assāsapassāsānaṃ anugamanavasena satiyā nirantaraṃ anupavattanā. Phusanāti assāsapassāse gaṇentassa gaṇanaṃ paṭisaṃharitvā te satiyā anubandhantassa yathā appanā hoti, tathā cittaṃ ṭhapentassa ca nāsikaggādiṭṭhānassa nesaṃ phusanā. Yasmā pana gaṇanādivasena viya phusanādivasena visuṃ manasikāro natthi, phuṭṭhaphuṭṭhaṭṭhāneyeva [M 2.0211] gaṇanā kātabbāti dassetuṃ idha phusanāgahaṇanti dīpento “phusanāti phuṭṭhaṭṭhāna”nti āha. Ṭhapanāti samādhānaṃ. Tañhi sammadeva ārammaṇe cittassa ādhānaṃ ṭhapanaṃ hoti. Tathā hi samādhi “cittassa ṭhiti saṇṭhitī”ti niddiṭṭho. Samādhippadhānā pana appanāti āha “ṭhapanāti appanā”ti. Aniccatādīnaṃ saṃlakkhaṇato sallakkhaṇā vipassanā. Pavattato nimittato ca vinivaṭṭanato vinivaṭṭanā maggo. Sakalasaṃkilesapaṭippassaddhibhāvato sabbaso suddhīti pārisuddhi phalaṃ. Tesanti vivaṭṭanāpārisuddhīnaṃ. Paṭipassanāti pati pati dassanaṃ pekkhanaṃ. Tenāha “paccavekkhaṇā”ti.

Anubandhanā (connection) is the uninterrupted continuity of mindfulness by following the in-breaths and out-breaths. Phusanā (touching) is the touching of the in-breaths and out-breaths at the tip of the nose or other such locations when, after ceasing to count, one connects them with mindfulness, establishing the mind in such a way that absorption occurs. However, since there is no separate mental application by way of touching as there is by way of counting, and in order to show that counting itself should be done at the very place of contact, he explains the taking up of 'touching' here by saying, 'Phusanā is the place of contact.' Ṭhapanā (fixing) is concentration. For it is the proper placing and fixing of the mind on its object. Thus, concentration is defined as 'the steadiness and stability of the mind.' But absorption has concentration as its chief, so it is stated: 'Fixing is absorption.' Sallakkhaṇā (discernment) is insight, by discerning impermanence and so on by noting their characteristics. Vinivaṭṭanā (turning away) is the path, by turning away from the course of existence and from signs. Pārisuddhi (purity) is the fruit, by the complete pacification of all defilements, thus complete purity. 'Of these' (tesaṃ) means of turning away and purity. Paṭipassanā (reviewing) is the repeated seeing and observing. Hence it is said: 'Paccavekkhaṇā (reviewing).'

Khaṇḍanti ekaṃ tīṇi pañcāti evaṃ gaṇanāya khaṇḍanaṃ. Okāseti gaṇanāvidhiṃ sandhāyāha, gaṇanānissitova na kammaṭṭhānanissito. Sikhāppattaṃ nu khoti idaṃ cirataraṃ gaṇanāya manasikarontassa vasena vuttaṃ. So hi tathā laddhaṃ avikkhepamattaṃ nissāya evaṃ maññeyya. Assāsapassāsesu yo upaṭṭhāti, taṃ gahetvāti idaṃ assāsapassāsesu yassa ekova paṭhamaṃ upaṭṭhāti, taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Yassa pana ubhopi upaṭṭhahanti, tena ubhayampi gahetvā gaṇetabbaṃ[V 2.0188]. Yo upaṭṭhātīti iminā ca dvīsu nāsāpuṭavātesu yo pākaṭataro upaṭṭhāti, so gahetabboti ayampi attho dīpitoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Pavattamānaṃ pavattamānanti āmeḍitavacanena nirantaraṃ assāsapassāsānaṃ upalakkhaṇaṃ dasseti. Evanti vuttappakārena upalakkhetvāvāti attho. Paṭhamaṃ ekekasmiṃ upaṭṭhitepi upalakkhetvāva gaṇentassa kamena ubhopi pākaṭā hontīti āha – “assāsapassāsā pākaṭā hontī”ti. Tena “upalakkhetvāva gaṇetabba”nti imassa “tassevaṃ gaṇayato…pe… pākaṭā hontī”ti idaṃ kāraṇavacanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tattha pākaṭā hontīti gaṇanāvasena bahiddhā vikkhepābhāvato vibhūtā honti.

Khaṇḍa (breaking off) is the breaking off of the count thus: 'one, three, five.' He says 'okāseti' with reference to the method of counting; it is dependent on counting, not on the meditation subject. 'Has it reached the peak?' This is said with reference to one who gives attention by counting for a very long time. For he, relying on the mere non-distraction thus obtained, might think thus. 'Taking that which appears among the in- and out-breaths'—this is said with reference to one for whom only one appears first. But for one for whom both appear, both should be taken and counted. And by this 'whichever appears,' this meaning is also shown and should be understood: that of the two nostril-winds, whichever appears more clearly, that one should be taken. 'Occurring, occurring'—by this repeated phrase, he shows the continuous observation of the in- and out-breaths. 'Thus' means having observed in the manner described. Even if at first only one appears, for one who observes and counts, in due course both become clear; thus he said, 'the in-breaths and out-breaths become clear.' Therefore, for the statement 'one should count by observing,' this—'for one counting thus... they become clear'—should be seen as the reason. Therein, 'they become clear' means they become distinct by way of counting, due to the absence of external distraction.

Palighāya parivattanakaṃ yattha nikkhipanti, so palighatthambho. Tiyāmarattinti accantasaṃyoge upayogavacanaṃ. Purimanayenāti sīghagaṇanāya, gopālakagaṇanāyāti attho. Eko dve tīṇi cattāri pañcāti gaṇanāvidhidassanaṃ. Tasmā aṭṭhātiādīsupi ekato paṭṭhāyeva paccekaṃ aṭṭhādīni pāpetabbāni. “Sīghaṃ sīghaṃ gaṇetabbamevā”ti vatvā tattha [M 2.0212] kāraṇaṃ nidassanañca dasseti “gaṇanāpaṭibaddhe hī”tiādinā. Tattha arīyati tena nāvāti arittaṃ, pājanadaṇḍo. Arittena upatthambhanaṃ arittupatthambhanaṃ, tassa vasena.

The post where they place the turning bar of the gate is the `palighatthambho` (gate-post). The word `tiyāmarattinti` is an expression in the accusative case, signifying continuous connection. `Purimanayena` means by swift counting, that is, by the counting of a cowherd; this is the meaning. `Eko dve tīṇi cattāri pañcāti` is a demonstration of the counting method. Therefore, in cases like 'eight' and so on, each number should be reached individually, starting from one. Having said, 'It should be counted swiftly, swiftly,' he shows the reason and example for this with the phrase beginning, 'For it is connected with counting.' Therein, `arittaṃ` is that by which a boat is propelled, a steering oar. `Arittupatthambhanaṃ` is supporting with an oar, by means of that.

Nippariyāyato nirantarappavatti nāma ṭhapanāyamevāti āha “nirantarappavattaṃ viyā”ti. Anto pavisantaṃ manasikaronto anto cittaṃ paveseti nāma. Bahi cittanīharaṇepi eseva nayo. Vātabbhāhatanti abbhantaragatavātaṃ bahulaṃ manasikarontassa vātena taṃ ṭhānaṃ abbhāhataṃ viya medena pūritaṃ viya ca hoti, tathā upaṭṭhāti. Nīharatoti phuṭṭhokāsaṃ muñcitvā nīharato. Tathā pana nīharato vātassa gatisamanvesanamukhena nānārammaṇesu cittaṃ vidhāvatīti āha “puthuttārammaṇe cittaṃ vikkhipatī”ti.

He said, 'like uninterruptedly occurring,' because uninterrupted occurrence, in the absolute sense, is indeed establishment. By attending to the wind entering within, one is said to cause the mind to enter within. This same method applies also to the expelling of the mind outwards. `Vātabbhāhataṃ` (struck by wind) means that for one who frequently attends to the wind that has gone within, that place becomes as if struck by the wind and as if filled with fat, and thus it appears. `Nīharato` (expelling) means expelling by releasing the place that was touched. However, for one thus expelling, the mind runs about to various objects by way of investigating the movement of the wind; therefore, he said, 'the mind scatters among diverse objects.'

Etanti etaṃ assāsapassāsajātaṃ. Anugamananti pavattapavattānaṃ assāsapassāsānaṃ ārammaṇakaraṇavasena satiyā anu anu pavattanaṃ anugacchanaṃ. Tenevāha – “tañca kho ādimajjhapariyosānānugamanavasenā”ti. Nābhi ādi tattha paṭhamaṃ uppajjanato. Paṭhamuppattivasena hi idha ādicintā, na uppattimattavasena. Tathā hi te nābhito paṭṭhāya yāva nāsikaggā sabbattha uppajjanteva. Yattha yattha ca uppajjanti, tattha tattheva bhijjanti dhammānaṃ gamanābhāvato. Yathāpaccayaṃ pana desantarappattiyaṃ gatisamaññā. Hadayaṃ majjhanti hadayasamīpaṃ tassa uparibhāgo majjhaṃ. Nāsikaggaṃ pariyosānanti nāsikaṭṭhānaṃ tassa pariyosānaṃ assāsapassāsānaṃ samaññāya tadavadhibhāvato. Tathā hete cittasamuṭṭhānā vuttā, na ca bahiddhā cittasamuṭṭhānānaṃ [V 2.0189] sambhavo atthi. Tenāha “abbhantarapavisanavātassa nāsikaggaṃ ādī”ti. Pavisananikkhamanapariyāyo pana taṃsadisavaseneva vuttoti veditabbo. Vikkhepagatanti vikkhepaṃ upagataṃ, vikkhittaṃ asamāhitanti attho. Sāraddhāyāti sadarathabhāvāya. Iñjanāyāti kammaṭṭhānamanasikārassa calanāya. Vikkhepagatena cittenāti hetumhi karaṇavacanaṃ, itthambhūtalakkhaṇe vā. Sāraddhāti sadarathā. Iñjitāti iñjanakā calanakā, tathā phanditā.

This refers to the in-breaths and out-breaths that have arisen. 'Following' (anugamana) means the successive application of mindfulness by taking as an object the successively occurring in-breaths and out-breaths, following them again and again. For that reason, he said: 'and that, by way of following the beginning, middle, and end.' The navel is the beginning, because they first arise there. For here, the concept of 'beginning' is based on the first arising, not on mere arising. Indeed, these breaths arise everywhere, starting from the navel up to the tip of the nose. And wherever they arise, right there they cease, because of the non-movement of phenomena. The term 'movement,' however, is a convention for arising in another location according to conditions. The heart is the middle, meaning the upper part near the heart is the middle. The tip of the nose is the end, meaning the location of the nose is their end, by the convention of in-breaths and out-breaths, because that is their limit. For indeed, these are said to be mind-originated, and there is no possibility of mind-originated phenomena arising externally. Therefore, he said: 'For the wind entering internally, the tip of the nose is the beginning.' The account of entering and exiting, however, should be understood as being stated by way of similarity to that. 'Distracted' (vikkhepagataṃ) means gone to distraction, scattered, unconcentrated; this is the meaning. 'For agitation' (sāraddhāya) is for the state of agitation. 'For wavering' (iñjanāya) is for the wavering of the attention to the meditation subject. In 'with a distracted mind' (vikkhepagatena cittena), the instrumental case is used in the sense of cause, or to describe a state. 'Agitated' (sāraddhā) means agitated. 'Moving' (iñjitā) means moving, shaking, and likewise trembling.

Ādimajjhapariyosānavasenātiādimajjhapariyosānānugamanavasena na manasi kātabbanti sambandho. “Anubandhanāya manasikarontena phusanāvasena [M 2.0213] ṭhapanāvasena ca manasi kātabba”nti yena adhippāyena vuttaṃ, taṃ vivarituṃ “gaṇanānubandhanāvasena viyā”tiādimāha. Tattha visuṃ manasikāro natthīti gaṇanāya anubandhanāya ca vinā yathākkamaṃ kevalaṃ phusanāvasena ṭhapanāvasena ca kammaṭṭhānamanasikāro natthi. Nanu phusanāya vinā ṭhapanāya viya phusanāya vinā gaṇanāyapi manasikāro natthiyevāti? Yadipi natthi, gaṇanā pana yathā kammaṭṭhānamanasikārassa mūlabhāvato padhānabhāvena gahetabbā, evaṃ anubandhanā ṭhapanāya tāya vinā ṭhapanāya asambhavato. Tasmā satipi phusanāya nānantarikabhāve gaṇanānubandhanā eva mūlabhāvato padhānabhāvena gahetvā itarāsaṃ tadabhāvaṃ dassento āha – “gaṇanānubandhanāvasena viya hi phusanāṭhapanāvasena visuṃ manasikāro natthī”ti. Yadi evaṃ tā kasmā uddese visuṃ gahitāti āha “phuṭṭhaphuṭṭhaṭṭhāneyevā”tiādi. Tattha phuṭṭhaphuṭṭhaṭṭhāneyeva gaṇentoti iminā gaṇanāya phusanā aṅganti dasseti. Tenāha – “gaṇanāya ca phusanāya ca manasi karotī”ti. Tatthevāti phuṭṭhaphuṭṭhaṭṭhāneyeva. Teti assāsapassāse. Satiyā anubandhantoti gaṇanāvidhiṃ anugantvā satiyā nibandhanto, phuṭṭhokāseyeva te nirantaraṃ upadhārentoti attho. Appanāvasena cittaṃ ṭhapentoti yathā appanā hoti, evaṃ yathāupaṭṭhite nimitte cittaṃ ṭhapento samādahanto. Anubandhanāya cātiādīsu anubandhanāya ca phusanāya ca ṭhapanāya ca manasi karotīti vuccatīti yojanā. Svāyamatthoti yvāyaṃ “phuṭṭhaphuṭṭhaṭṭhāneyeva gaṇento tattheva gaṇanaṃ paṭisaṃharitvā te satiyā anubandhanto”ti vutto, so ayamattho. Yā accantāya na minoti na vinicchinati, sā mānassa samīpeti upamā yathā goṇo viya gavayoti.

The connection is that one should not attend by way of following the beginning, middle, and end. To explain the intention with which it was said, 'One who attends by way of following should attend by way of touching and by way of fixing,' he stated the passage beginning, 'as by way of counting and following.' Therein, 'there is no separate attention' means that without counting and following, there is no attention to the meditation subject, in sequence, merely by way of touching and by way of fixing. Is it not the case that, just as there is no fixing without touching, there is also no attention in counting without touching? Even if that is not the case, just as counting should be taken as primary because it is the foundation of attention to the meditation subject, so too is following for fixing, because fixing is impossible without it. Therefore, even though touching is not immediately subsequent, taking counting and following as primary because they are the foundation, and showing that the others lack this status, he said: 'For there is no separate attention by way of touching and fixing as there is by way of counting and following.' If so, why are they taken up separately in the exposition? To this, he replied with the passage beginning, 'Only at the place where each is touched.' Therein, by the words 'counting only at the place where each is touched,' he shows that touching is a component of counting. Therefore, he said: 'One attends by way of counting and by way of touching.' 'Right there' (tattheva) means only at the place where each is touched. 'Them' (te) means the in-breaths and out-breaths. 'Following with mindfulness' (satiyā anubandhanto) means, having followed the method of counting, one binds them with mindfulness, continuously focusing on them only at the place that is touched; this is the meaning. 'Placing the mind by way of absorption' (appanāvasena cittaṃ ṭhapento) means placing and concentrating the mind on the sign as it has appeared, so that absorption occurs. In the passage beginning 'by way of following...' (anubandhanāya ca...), the construction is that it is said: 'one attends by way of following, and by way of touching, and by way of fixing.' 'This is that meaning' (svāyamattho) refers to the meaning of what was said: 'counting only at the place where each is touched, having withdrawn the counting right there, and following them with mindfulness.' That which does not measure or discriminate absolutely, that is proximate to conceit; the simile is like a gavaya is to a bull.

Paṅguḷoti pīṭhasappī. Dolāti peṅkholo. Kīḷatanti kīḷantānaṃ. Mātāputtānanti attano bhariyāya puttassa ca. Ubho koṭiyoti āgacchantassa purimakoṭiṃ, gacchantassa pacchimakoṭinti dvepi koṭiyo. Majjhañcāti dolāphalakasseva majjhaṃ. Upanibandhanatthambho viyāti upanibandhanatthambho, nāsikaggaṃ mukhanimittaṃ vā, tassa mūle samīpe ṭhatvā. Kathaṃ ṭhatvā[V 2.0190]? Satiyā vasena. Satiñhi tattha sūpaṭṭhitaṃ karonto yogāvacaro tattha ṭhito nāma hoti avayavadhammena samudāyassa apadisitabbato[M 2.0214]. Nimitteti nāsikaggādinimitte. Satiyā nisinnoti sativasena nisīdanto. “Satiñhi tatthā”tiādinā ṭhāne viya vattabbaṃ. Tatthāti phuṭṭhaṭṭhāne. Teti nagarassa anto bahi ca gatā manussā tesaṃ saṅgahā ca hatthagatā. Ādito pabhutīti upameyyatthadassanato paṭṭhāya.

A cripple (paṅguḷa) is one who shuffles on a stool (pīṭhasappī). A swing (dolā) is a hammock (peṅkhola). 'Playing' refers to those who are playing. 'Mother and son' means one’s own wife and son. 'Both ends' refers to the front end for one coming and the back end for one going—thus, both ends. 'And the middle' means the middle of the swing’s plank. 'Like a post for tying' means a post for tying, or the tip of the nose or the mouth-sign, standing near its base. How does one stand? By means of mindfulness. For a meditator, by making mindfulness well-established there, is said to be 'standing there,' because the aggregate is to be designated by way of its constituent parts. 'In the sign' refers to the sign of the tip of the nose, etc. 'Sitting with mindfulness' means sitting by way of mindfulness. It should be stated as in the passage beginning with 'For mindfulness is established there.' 'There' means at the place of contact. 'They' refers to the people who have gone inside and outside the city and have come into their count. 'From the beginning onwards' means starting from the showing of the meaning of the subject of the comparison.

Gāthāyaṃ nimittanti upanibandhananimittaṃ. Anārammaṇamekacittassāti ekassa cittassa na ārammaṇaṃ, ārammaṇaṃ na hontīti attho. Ajānato ca tayo dhammeti nimittaṃ assāso passāsoti ime nimittādayo tayo dhamme ārammaṇakaraṇavasena avindantassa. Ca-saddo byatireke. Bhāvanāti ānāpānassatisamādhibhāvanā. Nupalabbhatīti na upalabbhati na sijjhatīti ayaṃ codanāgāthāya attho. Dutiyā pana parihāragāthā suviññeyyāva.

In the verse, 'the sign' is the binding sign. 'Not an object for a single mind' means it is not an object for a single mind; the meaning is that they do not become an object. 'And for one who does not know the three things' refers to one who does not obtain these three things beginning with the sign—the sign, in-breath, and out-breath—by way of making them an object. The word 'ca' is in the sense of exclusion. 'Development' is the development of concentration through mindfulness of breathing. 'Is not obtained' means it is not obtained, it is not accomplished—this is the meaning of the verse of censure. The second, the remedial verse, however, is easily understood.

Kathanti tāsaṃ codanāparihāragāthānaṃ atthaṃ vivarituṃ kathetukamyatāpucchā. Ime tayo dhammātiādīsu padayojanāya saddhiṃ ayamatthaniddeso – ime nimittādayo tayo dhammā ekacittassa kathaṃ ārammaṇaṃ na honti, asatipi ārammaṇabhāve na cime na ca ime tayo dhammā aviditā honti, kathañca na honti aviditā, tesañhi aviditatte cittañca kathaṃ vikkhepaṃ na gacchati, padhānañca bhāvanāya nipphādakaṃ vīriyañca kathaṃ paññāyati, nīvaraṇānaṃ vikkhambhakaṃ sammadeva samādhānāvahaṃ bhāvanānuyogasaṅkhātaṃ payogañca yogī kathaṃ sādheti, uparūpari lokiyalokuttarañca visesaṃ kathamadhigacchatīti.

“How?” is a question expressing the desire to speak in order to explain the meaning of those verses of censure and remedy. In the passage beginning with “these three things,” this is the explanation of the meaning together with the syntactical connection of the words: How are these three things beginning with the sign not an object for a single mind? Even when they are not in a state of being an object, it is not that these three things are unknown. And how are they not unknown? And if they are unknown, how does the mind not go to distraction? And how is the striving, the energy that accomplishes the development, known? And how does the yogi accomplish the practice, known as application to development, which suppresses the hindrances and rightly brings about concentration? And how does one attain, higher and higher, the mundane and supramundane distinction?

Idāni tamatthaṃ kakacopamāya sādhetuṃ “seyyathāpī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Bhūmibhāgassa visamatāya cañcale rukkhe chedanakiriyā na sukarā siyā, tathā ca sati kakacadantagati duviññeyyāti āha – “same bhūmibhāge”ti. Kakacenāti khuddakena kharapattena. Tenāha “puriso”ti. Phuṭṭhakakacadantānanti phuṭṭhaphuṭṭhakakacadantānaṃ vasena. Tena kakacadantehi phuṭṭhaphuṭṭhaṭṭhāneyeva purisassa satiyā upaṭṭhānaṃ dasseti. Tenāha – “na āgate vā gate vā kakacadante manasi karotī”ti.

Now, to establish that meaning with the simile of the saw, the passage beginning “Suppose…” was stated. The act of cutting a tree that is unsteady due to the unevenness of the ground would not be easy, and that being so, the movement of the saw’s teeth would be difficult to discern; therefore, he said, “on level ground.” “With a saw” means with a small, rough blade. Therefore, he said, “a person…” “Touched by the saw’s teeth” means by way of the saw’s teeth that have touched and touched again. Thus, it shows the establishment of the person’s mindfulness only at the place touched again and again by the saw’s teeth. Therefore, he said, “he does not attend to the saw’s teeth as they come or go.”

Kakacassa [M 2.0215] ākaḍḍhanakāle purisābhimukhaṃ pavattā āgatā, pellanakāle tato vigatā gatāti vuttā, na ca āgatā vā gatā vā kakacadantā aviditā honti sabbattha satiyā upaṭṭhitattā chinditabbaṭṭhānaṃ aphusitvā gacchantānaṃ āgacchantānañca kakacadantānaṃ abhāvato. Padhānanti [V 2.0191] rukkhassa chedanavīriyaṃ. Payoganti tasseva chedanakiriyaṃ. Upamāyaṃ “visesamadhigacchatī”ti padaṃ pāḷiyaṃ natthi, yojetvā pana dassetabbaṃ. Teneva visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.227) upamāyampi “visesamadhigacchatī”ti padaṃ yojetvāva vuttaṃ. Taṃsaṃvaṇṇanāyañca “visesanti anekabhāvāpādanaṃ, tena ca sādhetabbaṃ payojanavisesa”nti attho vutto.

At the time of pulling the saw, proceeding towards the person, they are said to have “come”; at the time of pushing, having departed from there, they are said to have “gone.” And it is not that the saw’s teeth, whether coming or going, are unknown, because mindfulness is established everywhere and because of the absence of saw’s teeth that go and come without touching the place to be cut. “Striving” is the energy in cutting the tree. “Application” is the very act of cutting. In the simile, the phrase “attains distinction” is not in the Pāli; however, it should be supplied and shown. For that very reason, in the Visuddhimagga, even in the simile, the phrase “attains distinction” is stated only after having been supplied. And in its commentary, the meaning is stated: “‘Distinction’ is the production of manifold states, and by that, a special purpose is to be accomplished.”

Yathā rukkhotiādi upamāsaṃsandanaṃ. Upanibandhati ārammaṇe cittaṃ etāyāti sati upanibandhanā nāma, tassā assāsapassāsānaṃ sallakkhaṇassa nimittanti upanibandhanānimittaṃ, nāsikaggaṃ mukhanimittaṃ vā. Evamevanti yathā so puriso kakacena rukkhaṃ chindanto āgatagate kakacadante amanasikarontopi phuṭṭhaphuṭṭhaṭṭhāneyeva satiyā upaṭṭhapanena āgatagate kakacadante jānāti, suttapadañca avirajjhanto atthakiccaṃ sādheti, evamevaṃ. Nāsikagge mukhanimitteti dīghanāsiko nāsikagge, itaro mukhaṃ asanaṃ nimīyati chādīyati etenāti mukhanimittanti laddhanāme uttaroṭṭhe.

The passage beginning “Just as a tree…” is the comparison with the simile. Mindfulness is called “binding” (upanibandhanā) because by it one binds the mind to the object. The sign for the observation of the in-breaths and out-breaths by it is the “binding sign” (upanibandhanānimitta), which is the tip of the nose or the mouth-sign. In the same way: just as that person, while cutting a tree with a saw, although not attending to the coming and going of the saw’s teeth, knows the coming and going of the saw’s teeth by the establishment of mindfulness only at the place of contact, and accomplishes the required task without contradicting the Sutta passage; so too… “At the tip of the nose or the mouth-sign”: a person with a long nose establishes mindfulness at the tip of the nose; another, at the upper lip, which has received the name “mouth-sign” (mukhanimitta) because the mouth (mukha) is covered (chādīyati) by it.

Idaṃ padhānanti yena vīriyārambhena āraddhavīriyassa yogino kāyopi cittampi kammaniyaṃ bhāvanākammakkhamaṃ bhāvanākammayoggaṃ hoti, idaṃ vīriyaṃ padhānanti phalena hetuṃ dasseti. Upakkilesā pahīyantīti cittassa upakkilesabhūtāni nīvaraṇāni vikkhambhanavasena pahīyanti. Vitakkā vūpasammantīti tato eva kāmavitakkādayo micchāvitakkā upasamaṃ gacchanti, nīvaraṇappahānena vā paṭhamajjhānādhigamaṃ dassetvā vitakkavūpasamāpadesena dutiyajjhānādīnamadhigamamāha. Ayaṃ payogoti ayaṃ jhānādhigamassa hetubhūto kammaṭṭhānānuyogo payogo. Saṃyojanā pahīyantīti dasapi saṃyojanāni maggappaṭipāṭiyā samucchedavasena pahīyanti. Anusayā byantī hontīti tathā sattapi anusayā anuppattidhammatāpādanena bhaṅgamattassapi anavasesato vigatantā honti. Ettha ca saṃyojanappahānaṃ nāma anusayanirodheneva [M 2.0216] hoti, pahīnesu ca saṃyojanesu anusayānaṃ lesopi na bhavissatīti ca dassanatthaṃ “saṃyojanā pahīyanti, anusayā byantī hontī”ti vuttaṃ. Ayaṃ visesoti imaṃ samādhiṃ nissāya anukkamena labbhamāno ayaṃ saṃyojanappahānādiko imassa samādhissa visesoti attho.

“This is striving”: By the initiation of effort, the body and mind of a yogi who has aroused energy become workable, fit for the work of development, and suitable for the work of development. This energy is called “striving”; he shows the cause by the result. “Defilements are abandoned”: The hindrances, which are defilements of the mind, are abandoned by way of suppression. “Thoughts subside”: From that very state, wrong thoughts such as sensual thoughts, etc., subside. Or, having shown the attainment of the first jhāna through the abandoning of hindrances, he speaks of the attainment of the second jhāna and so on by way of the subsiding of thoughts. “This is the practice”: This application to the meditation subject, which is the cause for attaining jhāna, is the practice. “Fetters are abandoned”: The ten fetters are abandoned by way of cutting off, in the sequence of the paths. “Latent tendencies are eradicated”: Likewise, the seven latent tendencies become eradicated without remainder by bringing about their nature of non-arising, leaving not even a trace of their breaking. And here, the abandonment of fetters occurs only through the cessation of latent tendencies. And to show that when the fetters are abandoned, not even a trace of the latent tendencies will remain, it is said: “Fetters are abandoned, latent tendencies are eradicated.” “This is the distinction”: This distinction, beginning with the abandonment of fetters, which is attained successively by relying on this concentration, is the distinction of this concentration.

Yassāti yena. Anupubbanti anukkamena. Paricitāti pariciṇṇā. Ayañhettha saṅkhepattho – ānāpānassati yathā buddhena bhagavatā desitā, tathā yena dīgharassapajaānanādividhinā [V 2.0192] anupubbaṃ paricitā suṭṭhu bhāvitā, tato eva paripuṇṇā soḷasannaṃ vatthūnaṃ pāripūriyā sabbaso puṇṇā, so bhikkhu imaṃ attano khandhādilokaṃ paññobhāsena pabhāseti. Yathā kiṃ? Abbhā muttova candimā abbhādiupakkilesavimutto candimā tārakarājā viyāti. “Abbhā muttova candimā”ti hi padassa niddese mahikādīnampi vuttattā ettha ādi-saddalopo katoti veditabbo.

“Yassa” means “by whom.” “Anupubbaṃ” means “gradually.” “Paricitā” means “cultivated.” Here, in brief, is the meaning: The mindfulness of breathing, as taught by the Blessed One, the Buddha, is gradually cultivated and well developed by someone through the method of discerning long and short breaths, etc.; and therefore, through the completion of the sixteen objects, it becomes complete and wholly fulfilled. That monk illuminates this world of his own aggregates and so forth with the light of wisdom. Like what? Like the moon freed from clouds; like the moon, the king of stars, freed from defilements such as clouds. For in the explanation of the phrase “like the moon freed from clouds,” since mist, etc., are also mentioned, it should be understood that the word “ādi” (etc.) has been elided here.

Idhāti kakacūpamāya. Assāti yogino. Idhāti vā imasmiṃ ṭhāne. Assāti upamābhūtassa kakacassa. Āgatagatavasena yathā tassa purisassa amanasikāro, evaṃ assāsapassāsānaṃ āgatagatavasena amanasikāramattameva ānayanappayojanaṃ. Na cirenevāti idaṃ katādhikāraṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Nimittanti paṭibhāganimittaṃ. Avasesajjhānaṅgapaṭimaṇḍitāti vitakkādiavasesajjhānaṅgapaṭimaṇḍitāti vadanti, vicārādīti pana vattabbaṃ nippariyāyena vitakkassa appanābhāvato. So hi pāḷiyaṃ “appanā byappanā”ti niddiṭṭho, taṃsampayogato vā yasmā jhānaṃ appanāti aṭṭhakathāvohāro, jhānaṅgesu ca samādhi padhānaṃ, tasmā taṃ appanāti dassento “avasesajjhānaṅgapaṭimaṇḍitā appanāsaṅkhātā ṭhapanā ca sampajjatī”ti āha. Kassaci pana gaṇanāvaseneva manasikārakālato pabhutīti ettha “anukkamato…pe… pattaṃ viya hotī”ti ettakova gantho parihīno, purāṇapotthakesu pana katthaci so gantho likhitoyeva tiṭṭhati.

“Here” (idha) refers to the simile of the saw. “Assā” refers to the yogi. Or “here” means in this place. “Assā” refers to the saw that serves as the simile. Just as that man has non-attention regarding the coming and going of the saw, so too, regarding the coming and going of the in-and-out breaths, the only purpose is to bring about non-attention. “Not long after” is said with reference to one who has made the necessary preparations. “Sign” means the counterpart sign. “Adorned with the remaining jhāna factors”: They say this means adorned with the remaining jhāna factors starting with initial thought (vitakka). But it should be said to start with sustained thought (vicāra), because initial thought, in the strict sense, does not have the nature of absorption (appanā). For it is pointed out in the Pāḷi as “application, initial application” (appanā byappanā). Or, because of its association with it, the commentarial usage is that jhāna is called absorption. And since concentration is primary among the jhāna factors, therefore, to show that it is absorption, he said, “Adorned with the remaining jhāna factors, the stabilization called absorption is accomplished.” However, for some, in the phrase “from the time of attention by way of counting,” this much of the text is missing: “gradually…pe… it is as if attained.” But in some old manuscripts, that text remains written.

Sāraddhakāyassa [M 2.0217] kassaci puggalassa. Onamati vatthikādipalambanena. Vikūjatīti saddaṃ karoti. Valiṃ gaṇhātīti. Tattha tattha valinaṃ hoti. Kasmā? Yasmā sāraddhakāyo garuko hotīti. Kāyadarathavūpasamena saddhiṃ sijjhamāno oḷārikaassāsapassāsanirodho byatirekamukhena tassa sādhanaṃ viya vutto. Oḷārikaassāsapassāsanirodhavasenāti anvayavasena tadatthassa sādhanaṃ. Kāyadarathe vūpasanteti cittajarūpānaṃ lahumudukammaññabhāvena yo sesatisantatirūpānampi lahuādibhāvo, so idha kāyassa lahubhāvoti adhippeto. Svāyaṃ yasmā cittassa lahuādibhāvena vinā natthi, tasmā vuttaṃ “kāyopi cittampi lahukaṃ hotī”ti.

Of some person whose body is agitated. It bends due to the hanging down of the bladder and so on. “It creaks” means it makes a sound. “It forms wrinkles” means here and there it becomes wrinkled. Why? Because an agitated body is heavy. The cessation of coarse in-and-out breathing, which is accomplished together with the calming of bodily distress, is spoken of as if it were the means for it by way of the negative method. “By way of the cessation of coarse in-and-out breathing” means: by way of the positive method, it is the means for accomplishing that purpose. “When bodily distress is calmed”: The lightness, etc., of even the remaining continuity of matter, which is due to the lightness, softness, and wieldiness of mind-born matter—this is what is meant here by the lightness of the body. Since this does not exist without the lightness, etc., of the mind, therefore it is said: “Both the body and the mind become light.”

Oḷārike assāsapassāse niruddhetiādi heṭṭhā vuttanayamhi vicetabbākārappattassa kāyasaṅkhārassa vicayanavidhiṃ dassetuṃ ānītaṃ.

The phrase “When the coarse in-and-out breaths have ceased,” etc., is adduced to show the method for investigating the bodily formation that has reached the state where it should be investigated, in accordance with the method stated below.

Uparūpari [V 2.0193] vibhūtānīti bhāvanābalena uddhaṃ uddhaṃ pākaṭāni honti. Desatoti pakatiyā phusanadesato, pubbe attano phusanavasena upadhāritaṭṭhānato.

“Higher and higher they become manifest” means they become manifest higher and higher through the power of development. “From the place” means from the natural place of contact, and from the location previously determined by one’s own act of contact.

“Kattha natthī”ti ṭhānavasena “kassa natthī”ti puggalavasena ca vīmaṃsiyamānamatthaṃ ekajjhaṃ katvā vibhāvetuṃ “antomātukucchiya”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha “yathā udake nimuggassa niruddhokāsatāya assāsapassāsā na pavattanti, evaṃ antomātukucchiyaṃ. Yathā matānaṃ samuṭṭhāpakacittābhāvato, evaṃ asaññībhūtānaṃ mucchāparetānaṃ asaññīsu vā jātānaṃ, tathā nirodhasamāpannāna”nti ācariyadhammapālattherena vuttaṃ. Mahāgaṇṭhipade pana “mucchāparetānaṃ cittappavattiyā dubbalabhāvato”ti kāraṇaṃ vuttaṃ. Catutthajjhānasamāpannānaṃ dhammatāvaseneva nesaṃ anuppajjanaṃ, tathā rūpārūpabhavasamaṅgīnaṃ. Keci pana “anupubbato sukhumabhāvappattiyā catutthajjhānasamāpannassa, rūpabhave rūpānaṃ bhavaṅgassa ca sukhumabhāvato rūpabhavasamaṅgīnaṃ natthī”ti kāraṇaṃ vadanti. Atthiyeva te assāsapassāsā pārisesatoti adhippāyo yathāvuttasattaṭṭhānavinimuttassa assāsapassāsānaṃ anuppajjanaṭṭhānassa abhāvato. Pakatiphuṭṭhavasenāti pakatiyā phusanaṭṭhānavasena. Nimittaṃ ṭhapetabbanti satiyā tattha sukhappavattanatthaṃ [M 2.0218] thirataraṃ saññāṇaṃ pavattetabbaṃ. Thirasaññāpadaṭṭhānā hi sati. Imamevāti imaṃ eva anupaṭṭhahantassa kāyasaṅkhārassa kaṇṭakuṭṭhāpanañāyena upaṭṭhāpanavidhimeva. Atthavasanti hetuṃ. Attho hi phalaṃ. So yassa vasena pavattati, so atthavasoti. Muṭṭhassatissāti vinaṭṭhassatissa. Asampajānassāti sampajaññavirahitassa, bhāventassa anukkamena anupaṭṭhahante assāsapassāse vīmaṃsitvā “ime te”ti upadhāretuṃ sammadeva jānituñca samatthāhi satipaññāhi virahitassāti adhippāyo. Ito aññaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ. Garukanti bhāriyaṃ. Sā cassa garukatā bhāvanāya sudukkarabhāvenāti āha “garukabhāvana”nti.

To clarify the meaning that is to be investigated, combining “Where is it not?” by way of location and “For whom is it not?” by way of person, the phrase “inside the mother’s womb,” etc., is stated. Therein, “Just as for one submerged in water, in-breaths and out-breaths do not occur due to the obstruction of space, so too inside the mother’s womb. Just as for the dead, due to the absence of the mind that generates them, so too for those who have become unconscious, for those overcome by fainting, for those born in unconscious realms, or for those who have attained cessation,” as stated by the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla. In the Mahāgaṇṭhipada, however, the reason given is, “For those overcome by fainting, it is due to the weakness of the mind's activity.” For those who have attained the fourth jhāna, their non-arising is simply by the force of nature, and likewise for those endowed with form and formless existence. Some, however, state the reason thus: “For one who has attained the fourth jhāna, due to the gradual attainment of a subtle state, and for those endowed with form existence, due to the subtlety of material form and the life-continuum in the form realm, it does not exist.” The intention is that those in-breaths and out-breaths do indeed exist by way of remainder, because there is no place of non-arising for in-breaths and out-breaths for one who is free from the seven aforementioned places. “By way of natural contact” means by way of the place of natural contact. “The sign should be established” means that a firmer perception should be made to occur there by means of mindfulness for the sake of its smooth progression. For mindfulness has firm perception as its proximate cause. “Just this” means just this method of establishing the bodily formation for one who does not attend to it, in the manner of removing a thorn. The phrase 'for the sake of purpose' refers to the cause. For purpose is the result. That by the power of which it proceeds is 'the power of purpose'. “For one of muddled mindfulness” means for one whose mindfulness is lost. “For one lacking clear comprehension” means for one devoid of clear comprehension; the intention is: for one who, while meditating, is devoid of the mindfulness and wisdom capable of investigating the in-and-out breaths when they do not appear in sequence, so as to ascertain 'these are they' and to know them properly. Another meditation subject than this. “Serious” means weighty. And its seriousness is due to the difficulty of its cultivation; thus it is called a 'weighty cultivation'.

Uparūpari santasukhumabhāvāpattito “balavatī suvisadā sūrā ca sati paññā ca icchitabbā”ti vatvā sukhumassa nāma atthassa sādhanenapi sukhumeneva bhavitabbanti dassetuṃ “yathā hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Idāni anupaṭṭhahantānaṃ assāsapassāsānaṃ pariyesanupāyaṃ dassento “tāhi ca panā”tiādimāha. Tattha anupadanti padānupadaṃ. Caritvāti gocaraṃ gahetvā. Tasmiṃyeva ṭhāneti upanibandhananimittasaññite ṭhāne. Yojetvāti manasikārena yojetvā. “Satirasmiyā bandhitvā”ti vā vuttamevatthamāha “tasmiṃyeva ṭhāne yojetvā”ti. Na hi upameyye bandhanayojanaṭṭhānāni visuṃ labbhanti. Nimittanti uggahanimittaṃ paṭibhāganimittaṃ vā. Ubhayampi hi [V 2.0194] idha ekajjhaṃ vuttaṃ. Tathā hi tūlapicuādi upamattayaṃ uggahe yujjati, sesaṃ ubhayattha. Ekacceti eke ācariyā.

Due to the attainment of a progressively peaceful and subtle state, having said, “Strong, very clear, and heroic mindfulness and wisdom should be desired,” and to show that even the means of achieving a so-called subtle goal must be subtle, the phrase “just as…” etc., is stated. Now, showing the method of searching for the in-breaths and out-breaths for those to whom they do not yet appear, he said, “And by these, moreover…” etc. Therein, “following” means step by step. “Having wandered” means having taken the range. “In that very place” means in the place designated as the sign of binding. “Having applied” means having applied through attention. Or, “having bound with the rein of mindfulness,” he states the very same meaning with “having applied in that very place.” For in the object of comparison, the places of binding and applying are not found separately. “Sign” refers to either the learning sign or the counterpart sign. For both are mentioned here together. For indeed, the three similes beginning with the cotton tuft are applicable to the learning sign; the rest to both. “Some” means some teachers.

Tārakarūpaṃ viyāti tārakāya pabhārūpaṃ viya. Maṇiguḷikādiupamā paṭibhāge vaṭṭanti. Kathaṃ panetaṃ ekaṃyeva kammaṭṭhānaṃ anekākārato upaṭṭhātīti āha “tañca paneta”ntiādi. Suttantanti ekaṃ suttaṃ. Paguṇappavattibhāvena avicchedaṃ mahāvisayatañca sandhāyāha “mahatī pabbateyyā nadī viyā”ti. Tattha byañjanasampattiyā samantabhaddakaṃ suttaṃ sabbabhāgamanoharā sabbapāliphullā vanaghaṭā viyāti āha “ekā vanarāji viyā”ti. Tenāha bhagavā “vanappagumbe yatha phussitagge”ti (khu. pā. 6.13; su. ni. 236) nānānusandhiyaṃ nānāpeyyālaṃ vividhanayanipuṇaṃ bahuvidhakammaṭṭhānamukhaṃ suttantaṃ atthikehi sakkaccaṃ samupapajjitabbanti āha – “sītacchāyo…pe… rukkho [M 2.0219] viyā”ti. Saññānānatāyāti nimittupaṭṭhānato pubbe pavattasaññānaṃ nānāvidhabhāvato. Saññajanti bhāvanāsaññājanitaṃ bhāvanāsaññāya sañjānanamattaṃ. Na hi asabhāvassa kutoci samuṭṭhānaṃ atthi. Tenāha – “nānato upaṭṭhātī”ti, upaṭṭhānākāramattanti vuttaṃ hoti.

“Like the form of a star” means like the form of the radiance of a star. The similes beginning with a gem bead are applicable to the counterpart sign. “But how does this one single meditation subject appear in many forms?”—thus he said “And that…” etc. “Suttanta” means a single sutta. Referring to its fluent progression, its uninterruptedness, and its vast scope, he said, “like a great mountain river.” Herein, due to the excellence of its phrasing, the sutta is beautiful all around, like a forest grove delightful in all its parts, with all its lines of trees in full bloom; thus he said, “like a single forest-line.” Therefore the Blessed One said, “As in a forest thicket with blossomed tops.” A suttanta with various connections, various repetitions, skilled in various methods, a gateway to many kinds of meditation subjects, should be carefully approached by those who have a need for it—thus he said, “like a tree with cool shade… etc.” “Due to the diversity of perception” means due to the diverse nature of the perceptions that occurred before the arising of the sign. “Born of perception” means generated by the perception of development; it is merely the perceiving by means of the perception of development. For that which has no intrinsic nature, there is no arising from anywhere. Therefore he said, “it appears as diverse.” This means it is merely the mode of appearance.

Ime tayo dhammāti assāso passāso nimittanti ime tayo dhammā. Natthīti kammaṭṭhānavasena manasikātabbabhāvena natthi na upalabbhati. Na upacāranti upacārampi na pāpuṇāti, pageva appananti adhippāyo. Yassa panāti vijjamānapakkho vuttanayānusāreneva veditabbo.

“These three things” are the in-breath, the out-breath, and the sign—these are the three things. “There is not” means it does not exist and is not found as something to be attended to by way of a meditation subject. “It does not reach access” means it does not even attain access concentration, how much more so absorption—this is the intention. “But for whom” refers to the existing side, which should be understood in accordance with the method already stated.

Idāni vuttasseva atthassa samatthanatthaṃ kakacūpamāyaṃ āgatā “nimitta”ntiādikā gāthā paccānītā. Nimitteti yathāvutte paṭibhāganimitte. Evaṃ hotīti bhāvanamanuyuttassa evaṃ hoti, tasmā “punappunaṃ evaṃ manasi karohī”ti vattabbo. Vosānaṃ āpajjeyyāti “nimittaṃ nāma dukkaraṃ uppādetuṃ, tayidaṃ laddhaṃ, handāhaṃ dāni yadā vā tadā vā visesaṃ nibbattessāmī”ti saṅkocaṃ āpajjeyya. Visīdeyyāti “ettakaṃ kālaṃ bhāvanamanuyuttassa nimittampi na uppannaṃ, abhabbo maññe visesassā”ti visādaṃ āpajjeyya. “Imāya paṭipadāya jarāmaraṇato muccissāmīti paṭipannassa nimitta”nti vutte kathaṃ saṅkocāpatti, bhiyyoso mattāya ussāhameva kareyyāti “nimittamidaṃ…pe… vattabbo”ti majjhimabhāṇakā āhu. Evanti vuttappakārena paṭibhāganimitteyeva bhāvanācittassa ṭhapanena. Ito pabhutīti ito paṭibhāganimittuppattito paṭṭhāya. Pubbe yaṃ vuttaṃ “anubandhanāya phusanāya ṭhapanāya ca manasi karotī”ti (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.ānāpānassatisamādhikathā), tattha [V 2.0195] anubandhanaṃ phusanañca vissajjetvā ṭhapanāvaseneva bhāvetabbanti āha “ṭhapanāvasena bhāvanā hotī”ti.

Now, to substantiate the meaning just stated, the verse beginning with “nimitta” that appears in the Kakacūpama Sutta has been brought forward. “Nimitta” refers to the counterpart sign as previously described. “Thus it happens” means it happens thus for one devoted to development; therefore, it should be said, “Again and again, attend to it in this way.” One might fall into slackness—thinking, “It is difficult to produce the sign, but now it has been attained. Now, whenever the time comes, I will achieve distinction”—one might fall into slackness. One might fall into despondency—thinking, “After spending so much time devoted to development, not even a sign has arisen. Surely, I am incapable of distinction”—one might fall into despondency. When it is said, “The sign arises for one practicing with the thought, ‘By this practice I will be freed from aging and death,’” how could there be slackness? Instead, one should exert even more effort—thus, the Majjhimabhāṇakas say, “This sign... should be spoken of.” “Thus”—in the manner described—by establishing the developing mind in the counterpart sign itself. “From here onward” means from the arising of the counterpart sign onward. Previously, it was said, “One attends to it for the sake of following, touching, and stabilizing.” There, having relinquished following and touching, it is said that one should develop it solely by way of stabilizing: “Development occurs by way of stabilizing.”

Porāṇehi vuttovāyamatthoti dassento “nimitte”ti gāthamāha. Tattha nimitteti paṭibhāganimitte. Ṭhapayaṃ cittanti bhāvanācittaṃ ṭhapento, ṭhapanāvasena manasikarontoti attho. Nānākāranti “cattāro vaṇṇā”ti evaṃ vuttaṃ nānākāraṃ. Ākārasāmaññavasena hetaṃ ekavacanaṃ. Vibhāvayanti vibhāvento antaradhāpento. Nimittuppattito paṭṭhāya hi te ākārā amanasikārato antarahitā viya honti. Assāsapassāseti [M 2.0220] assāsapassāse yo nānākāro, taṃ vibhāvayaṃ, assāsapassāsasambhūte vā nimitte. Sakaṃ cittaṃ nibandhatīti tāya eva ṭhapanāya attano cittaṃ upanibandhati, appetīti attho. Keci pana “vibhāvayanti vibhāvento, viditaṃ pākaṭaṃ karonto”ti atthaṃ vadanti, taṃ pubbabhāgavasena yujjeyya. Ayañhettha attho – dhitisampannattā dhīro yogī assāsapassāse nānākāraṃ vibhāvento nānākārato te pajānanto vidite pākaṭe karonto nānākāraṃ vā oḷārikoḷārike passambhento vūpasamento tattha yaṃ laddhaṃ nimittaṃ, tasmiṃ cittaṃ ṭhapento anukkamena sakaṃ cittaṃ nibandhati appetīti.

To show that this is the meaning stated by the ancients, he speaks the verse beginning with “nimitte.” Herein, “nimitte” refers to the counterpart sign. “Establishing the mind” means establishing the mind of development, meaning attending by way of stabilization. “Various aspects” refers to the various aspects spoken of as “the four colors.” This is a singular form by way of generalizing characteristics. “Discerning” means discerning, making them disappear. For from the arising of the sign, those aspects seem to vanish due to lack of attention. “In-breaths and out-breaths” means discerning the various aspects in the in-breaths and out-breaths, or in the sign arisen from the in-breaths and out-breaths. “He binds his own mind” means he binds his own mind through that very stabilization, he applies it—this is the meaning. Some, however, explain the meaning as “discerning, making it known and evident.” That would fit the preliminary stage. Here, the meaning is this: Being endowed with steadfastness, the wise yogi, discerning the various aspects in the in-breaths and out-breaths, knowing them distinctly, making them known and evident, or calming and pacifying the gross and subtle aspects, establishes the mind upon the sign that has been attained there, and gradually binds his own mind, applying it.

Yadā saddhādīni indriyāni suvisadāni tikkhāni pavattanti, tadā assaddhiyādīnaṃ dūrībhāvena sātisayaṃ thāmappattehi sattahi balehi laddhupatthambhāni vitakkādīni kāmāvacarāneva jhānaṅgāni bahūni hutvā pātubhavanti. Tato eva tesaṃ ujuvipaccanīkabhūtā kāmacchandādayo saddhiṃ tadekaṭṭhehi pāpadhammehi vidūrī bhavanti paṭibhāganimittuppattiyā saddhiṃ, taṃ ārabbha upacārajjhānaṃ uppajjati. Tena vuttaṃ “nimittupaṭṭhānato pabhuti nīvaraṇāni vikkhambhitāneva hontī”tiādi. Tattha sannisinnāvāti sammadeva nisīdiṃsu eva, upasantāyevāti attho. Vikkhambhitāneva sannisinnāvāti avadhāraṇena pana tadatthaṃ ussāho kātabboti dasseti. Dvīhākārehīti jhānadhammānaṃ paṭipakkhadūrībhāvo thirabhāvappatti cāti imehi dvīhi kāraṇehi. Idāni tāni kāraṇāni avatthāmukhena dassetuṃ “upacārabhūmiyaṃ vā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha upacārabhūmiyanti upacārāvatthāyaṃ. Yadipi hi tadā jhānaṅgāni paṭutarāni mahaggatabhāvappattāni nuppajjanti, tesaṃ pana paṭipakkhadhammānaṃ vikkhambhanena cittaṃ samādhiyati. Tenāha “nīvaraṇappahānenā”ti. Paṭilābhabhūmiyanti jhānassa adhigamāvatthāyaṃ. Tadā hi appanāppattānaṃ jhānadhammānaṃ uppattiyā cittaṃ samādhiyati. Tenāha “aṅgapātubhāvenā”ti.

When the faculties of faith and so on are very clear, sharp, and active, then, due to the removal of lack of faith and so on, and supported by the seven powers that have attained superior strength, thoughts and other factors—though still belonging to the sensual realm—become numerous and manifest as jhāna factors. From that very point, their direct opposites—such as sensual desire—along with other unwholesome states associated with them, become far removed along with the arising of the counterpart sign. Access concentration arises based on that. Therefore, it is said: “From the time the sign appears, the hindrances are already suppressed,” and so on. Here, “well-settled” means they have indeed settled properly, meaning they are well-calmed. The emphasis in “suppressed and well-settled” indicates that effort should be made to achieve that state. In two ways—by the removal of the opposing states of the jhāna factors and by the attainment of stability—these two causes are indicated. Now, to explain these causes by showing their respective states, it is said: “either in the stage of access...” Here, “in the stage of access” refers to the stage of access. For even though the jhāna factors have not yet arisen distinctly or reached the level of the sublime at that time, the mind becomes concentrated through the suppression of opposing states. Hence it is said: “by abandoning the hindrances.” “In the stage of attainment” refers to the stage of achieving jhāna. At that time, the mind becomes concentrated through the arising of the jhāna factors, which have reached full absorption. Hence it is said: “by the manifestation of the factors.”

Upacāre [V 2.0196] aṅgāni na thāmajātāni honti aṅgānaṃ athāmajātattā. Yathā nāma daharo kumārako ukkhipitvā ṭhapiyamāno punappunaṃ bhūmiyaṃ patati, evameva upacāre uppanne cittaṃ kālena nimittaṃ ārammaṇaṃ karoti, kālena bhavaṅgaṃ otarati. Tena vuttaṃ “upacārasamādhi kusalavīthiyaṃ javitvā bhavaṅgaṃ otaratī”ti. Appanāyaṃ pana aṅgāni thāmajātāni honti [M 2.0221] tesaṃ thāmajātattā. Yathā nāma balavā puriso āsanā vuṭṭhāya divasampi tiṭṭheyya, evameva appanāsamādhimhi uppanne cittaṃ sakiṃ bhavaṅgavāraṃ chinditvā kevalampi rattiṃ kevalampi divasaṃ tiṭṭhati, kusalajavanapaṭipāṭivaseneva pavattati. Tenāha – “appanāsamādhi…pe… na bhavaṅgaṃ otaratī”ti. Vaṇṇatoti picupiṇḍatārakarūpādīsu viya upaṭṭhitavaṇṇato. Lakkhaṇatoti kharabhāvādisabhāvato aniccādisabhāvato vā. Rakkhitabbaṃ taṃ nimittanti sambandho.

In access concentration, the factors are not strong because the factors are not strong. Just as a young boy, when lifted up and placed on his feet, repeatedly falls to the ground, so too, when access concentration arises, the mind sometimes takes the sign as its object and sometimes sinks into the life-continuum. Therefore, it is said: “Access concentration, after running its course in the wholesome cognitive process, sinks into the life-continuum.” But in absorption, the factors are strong because they are strong. Just as a strong man, having risen from his seat, could stand all day, so too, when absorption concentration arises, the mind, having cut off the life-continuum once, can remain for the entire night or the entire day, proceeding solely in the sequence of wholesome impulses. Therefore, it is said: “Absorption concentration... does not sink into the life-continuum.” “As to appearance” means from the appearance that presents itself, as in a lump of cotton, a star, or form, etc. “As to characteristic” means from the nature of hardness, etc., or from the nature of impermanence, etc. “That sign should be guarded”—this is the connection.

Laddhaparihānīti laddhaupacārajjhānaparihāni. Nimitte avinassante tadārammaṇaṃ jhānaṃ aparihīnameva hoti, nimitte pana ārakkhābhāvena vinaṭṭhe laddhaṃ laddhaṃ jhānampi vinassati tadāyattavuttito. Tenāha “ārakkhamhī”tiādi.

“The loss of what has been gained” means the loss of the access jhāna that has been gained. When the sign does not disappear, the jhāna that has that as its object does not decline. But when the sign is lost due to lack of protection, the jhāna that was gained also perishes because its occurrence depends on that sign. Hence, he said, “in protection,” etc.

Idāni tatrāyaṃ rakkhaṇūpāyotiādinā –

Now, by the words beginning with, “Herein, this is the means of protection…”

“Āvāso gocaro bhassaṃ, puggalo bhojanaṃ utu;

Iriyāpathoti sattete, asappāye vivajjaye.

“Dwelling, alms-range, talk, person, food, season, and posture—these seven unsuitable things one should avoid.”

“Sappāye satta sevetha, evañhi paṭipajjato;

Na cireneva kālena, hoti kassaci appanā”ti. (visuddhi. 1.59) –

“One should cultivate the seven suitable things; for one who practices thus, absorption occurs for someone before long.” (Visuddhimagga 1.59)

Evaṃ vuttaṃ rakkhaṇavidhiṃ saṅkhepato vibhāveti. Tatrāyaṃ vitthāro – yasmiṃ āvāse vasantassa anuppannaṃ vā nimittaṃ nuppajjati, uppannaṃ vā vinassati, anupaṭṭhitā ca sati na upaṭṭhāti, asamāhitañca cittaṃ na samādhiyati, ayaṃ asappāyo. Yattha nimittaṃ uppajjati ceva thāvarañca hoti, sati upaṭṭhāti, cittaṃ samādhiyati, ayaṃ sappāyo. Tasmā yasmiṃ vihāre bahū āvāsā honti, tattha ekamekasmiṃ tīṇi tīṇi divasāni vasitvā yatthassa cittaṃ ekaggaṃ hoti, tattha vasitabbaṃ.

He explains briefly the method of protection thus stated. Herein is the detailed explanation: A dwelling where, for one staying there, an unarisen sign does not arise, or an arisen one vanishes, where unestablished mindfulness is not established, and an unconcentrated mind does not become concentrated—this is unsuitable. Where a sign arises and is stable, mindfulness is established, and the mind becomes concentrated—this is suitable. Therefore, in a monastery where there are many dwellings, one should stay in each one for three days and then reside where one's mind becomes one-pointed.

Gocaragāmo [V 2.0197] pana yo senāsanato uttarena vā dakkhiṇena vā nātidūre diyaḍḍhakosabbhantare hoti sulabhasampannabhikkho, so sappāyo, viparīto asappāyo.

As for the alms-round village, one that is not too far from the monastery—within one and a half kosas to the north or to the south—and where alms-food is easily obtained, is suitable. The opposite is unsuitable.

Bhassanti [M 2.0222] dvattiṃsatiracchānakathāpariyāpannaṃ asappāyaṃ. Tañhissa nimittantaradhānāya saṃvattati. Dasakathāvatthunissitaṃ sappāyaṃ, tampimattāya bhāsitabbaṃ.

As for talk, that which is included in the thirty-two kinds of animal talk is unsuitable. For that leads to the disappearance of the sign. Talk based on the ten topics of discourse is suitable, but even that should be spoken in moderation.

Puggalopi atiracchānakathiko sīlādiguṇasampanno, yaṃ nissāya asamāhitaṃ vā cittaṃ samādhiyati, samāhitaṃ vā cittaṃ thirataraṃ hoti, evarūpo sappāyo. Kāyadaḷhībahulo pana tiracchānakathiko asappāyo. So hi taṃ kaddamodakamiva acchaṃ udakaṃ malīnameva karoti, tādisañca āgamma koṭapabbatavāsīdaharasseva samāpatti vinassati, pageva nimittaṃ.

A person who does not engage in animal talk, who is endowed with virtues such as morality, and by relying on whom an unconcentrated mind becomes concentrated, or a concentrated mind becomes steadier—such a person is suitable. But one who is much given to physical robustness and engages in animal talk is unsuitable. For he makes clear water soiled, just like muddy water; and by associating with such a person, even the attainment of a young bhikkhu dwelling on Mount Koṭa perishes, how much more so the sign.

Bhojanaṃ pana kassaci madhuraṃ, kassaci ambilaṃ sappāyaṃ hoti. Utupi kassaci sīto, kassaci uṇho sappāyo hoti. Tasmā yaṃ bhojanaṃ vā utuṃ vā sevantassa phāsu hoti, asamāhitaṃ vā cittaṃ samādhiyati, samāhitaṃ vā thirataraṃ hoti. Taṃ bhojanaṃ, so ca utu sappāyo. Itaraṃ bhojanaṃ, itaro ca utu asappāyo.

As for food, for some, sweet is suitable; for others, sour is suitable. As for the season, for some, cold is suitable; for others, hot is suitable. Therefore, whatever food or season one partakes of that brings comfort, or makes an unconcentrated mind become concentrated, or a concentrated mind become steadier—that food and that season are suitable. The other food and the other season are unsuitable.

Iriyāpathesupi kassaci caṅkamo sappāyo hoti, kassaci sayanaṭṭhānanisajjānaṃ aññataro. Tasmā taṃ āvāsaṃ viya tīṇi divasāni upaparikkhitvā yasmiṃ iriyāpathe asamāhitaṃ cittaṃ samādhiyati, samāhitaṃ vā thirataraṃ hoti, so sappāyo, itaro asappāyoti veditabbo. Iti imaṃ sattavidhaṃ asappāyaṃ vajjetvā sappāyaṃ sevitabbaṃ. Evaṃ paṭipannassa hi nimittāsevanabahulassa na cireneva kālena hoti kassaci appanā.

In the postures as well, walking is suitable for some; for others, one among lying down, standing, and sitting is suitable. Therefore, having tested for three days as one would with a dwelling, whichever posture causes the unconcentrated mind to become concentrated, or the concentrated mind to become steadier, is suitable; the other should be understood as unsuitable. Thus, having avoided this sevenfold unsuitability, what is suitable should be cultivated. For one who practices thus and is much engaged in cultivating the sign, absorption occurs for someone before long.

Yassa pana evampi paṭipajjato na hoti, tena dasavidhaṃ appanākosallaṃ sampādetabbanti dassetuṃ “vatthuvisadakiriyā”tiādimāha. Tattha (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.385; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.118; saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 3.5.232; a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.418) vitthuvisadakiriyā nāma ajjhattikabāhirānaṃ vatthūnaṃ visadabhāvakaraṇaṃ. Yadā hissa kesanakhalomāni dīghāni honti, sarīraṃ vā sedamalaggahitaṃ, tadā ajjhattikaṃ vatthu avisadaṃ hoti aparisuddhaṃ. Yadā panassa cīvaraṃ jiṇṇaṃ kiliṭṭhaṃ duggandhaṃ hoti, senāsanaṃ vā uklāpaṃ, tadā bāhiraṃ vatthu avisadaṃ hoti aparisuddhaṃ. Ajjhattikabāhire hi vatthumhi avisade [M 2.0223] uppannesu cittacetasikesu ñāṇampi aparisuddhaṃ hoti aparisuddhāni dīpakapallikavaṭṭitelāni [V 2.0198] nissāya uppannadīpasikhāya obhāso viya. Aparisuddhena ca ñāṇena saṅkhāre sammasato saṅkhārāpi avibhūtā honti, kammaṭṭhānamanuyuñjato kammaṭṭhānampi vuddhiṃ viruḷhiṃ vepullaṃ na gacchati. Visade pana ajjhattikabāhire vatthumhi uppannesu cittacetasikesu ñāṇampi visadaṃ hoti parisuddhāni dīpakapallikavaṭṭitelāni nissāya uppannadīpasikhāya obhāso viya. Parisuddhena ca ñāṇena saṅkhāre sammasato saṅkhārāpi vibhūtāhonti, kammaṭṭhānamanuyuñjato kammaṭṭhānampi vuddhiṃ viruḷhiṃ vepullaṃ gacchati.

But for one for whom it does not occur even when practicing thus, to show that the tenfold skill in absorption must be developed, he said, “making the basis clear,” and so on. Herein, “making the basis clear” means making internal and external bases clear. For when one’s hair, nails, or body hair is long, or the body is covered with sweat and dirt, then the internal basis is unclear and impure. When one’s robe is worn out, soiled, or foul-smelling, or the lodging is untidy, then the external basis is unclear and impure. When internal and external bases are unclear, the knowledge that arises in the consciousness and mental factors is also impure—like the light of a lamp flame arising in dependence on an impure lamp bowl, wick, and oil. With impure knowledge, when contemplating formations, the formations are also not distinct, and for one applying oneself to the meditation subject, the meditation subject does not go to growth, increase, and expansion. But when internal and external bases are clear, the knowledge that arises in the consciousness and mental factors is also clear—like the light of a lamp flame arising in dependence on a pure lamp bowl, wick, and oil. With pure knowledge, when contemplating formations, the formations also become distinct, and for one applying oneself to the meditation subject, the meditation subject goes to growth, increase, and expansion.

Indriyasamattapaṭipādanatā nāma saddhādīnaṃ indriyānaṃ samabhāvakaraṇaṃ.
