Sace hissa saddhindriyaṃ balavaṃ hoti, itarāni mandāni, tato vīriyindriyaṃ paggahakiccaṃ, satindriyaṃ upaṭṭhānakiccaṃ, samādhindriyaṃ avikkhepakiccaṃ, paññindriyaṃ dassanakiccaṃ kātuṃ na sakkoti. Tasmā taṃ dhammasabhāvapaccavekkhaṇena vā yathā vā manasikaroto balavaṃ jātaṃ, tathā amanasikārena hāpetabbaṃ. Vakkalittheravatthu cettha nidassanaṃ. Sace pana vīriyindriyaṃ balavaṃ hoti, atha neva saddhindriyaṃ adhimokkhakiccaṃ kātuṃ sakkoti, na itarāni itarakiccabhedaṃ. Tasmā taṃ passaddhādibhāvanāya hāpetabbaṃ. Tatrāpi soṇattheravatthu dassetabbaṃ. Evaṃ sesesupi ekassa balavabhāve sati itaresaṃ attano kiccesu asamatthatā veditabbā.

Bringing the faculties into balance means making the faculties of faith and the others equal. For if one’s faculty of faith is strong while the others are weak, then the faculty of energy cannot perform its function of exertion, the faculty of mindfulness cannot perform its function of establishing, the faculty of concentration cannot perform its function of non-distraction, and the faculty of wisdom cannot perform its function of seeing. Therefore, that faculty which has become strong should be diminished either by reflecting on the nature of phenomena or by not attending to it in the way that it became strong. The story of Vakkali Thera is an example here. But if the faculty of energy is strong, then neither can the faculty of faith perform its function of conviction, nor can the others perform their respective functions. Therefore, that faculty should be diminished by cultivating tranquility and so on. In this case, the story of Soṇa Thera should be shown. Thus, in the remaining cases as well, when one faculty is strong, the inability of the others to perform their own functions should be understood.

Visesato panettha saddhāpaññānaṃ samādhivīriyānañca samataṃ pasaṃsanti. Balavasaddho hi mandapañño mudhappasanno hoti, avatthusmiṃ pasīdati. Balavapañño mandasaddho kerāṭikapakkhaṃ bhajati, bhesajjasamuṭṭhito viya rogo atekiccho hoti. Ubhinnaṃ samatāya vatthusmiṃyeva pasīdati. Balavasamādhiṃ pana mandavīriyaṃ samādhissa kosajjapakkhattā kosajjaṃ abhibhavati, balavavīriyaṃ mandasamādhiṃvīriyassa uddhaccapakkhattā uddhaccaṃ abhibhavati. Samādhi pana vīriyena saṃyojito kosajje patituṃ na labhati, vīriyaṃ samādhinā saṃyojitaṃ uddhacce patituṃ na labhati. Tasmā tadubhayaṃ samaṃ kātabbaṃ. Ubhayasamatāya hi appanā hoti. Apica samādhikammikassa balavatīpi saddhā vaṭṭati. Evañhi saddahanto okappento appanaṃ pāpuṇissati, samādhipaññāsu pana samādhikammikassa ekaggatā balavatī vaṭṭati. Evañhi so appanaṃ pāpuṇāti, vipassanākammikassa paññā balavatī vaṭṭati[M 2.0224]. Evañhi so lakkhaṇappaṭivedhaṃ pāpuṇāti, ubhinnaṃ pana samatāyapi appanā hotiyeva. Sati pana sabbattha balavatī vaṭṭati. Sati hi cittaṃ uddhaccapakkhikānaṃ saddhāvīriyapaññānaṃ vasena uddhaccapātato kosajjapakkhena ca samādhinā kosajjapātato rakkhati. Tasmā sā loṇadhūpanaṃ viya sabbabyañjanesu, sabbakammikaamacco viya ca sabbarājakiccesu sabbattha icchitabbā.

Especially here, they praise the balance of faith and wisdom, and of concentration and energy. For one with strong faith but weak wisdom has misplaced confidence and places confidence in an improper object. One with strong wisdom but weak faith tends toward craftiness and becomes as incurable as a disease caused by medicine. Through the balance of the two, one has confidence in a proper object only. But one with strong concentration and weak energy is overcome by laziness, since concentration is on the side of laziness. One with strong energy and weak concentration is overcome by restlessness, since energy is on the side of restlessness. But concentration, when yoked with energy, does not get to fall into laziness, and energy, when yoked with concentration, does not get to fall into restlessness. Therefore, those two should be made equal, for absorption occurs through their balance. Furthermore, for one whose work is concentration, even strong faith is suitable. For thus, believing and being convinced, one will attain absorption. But between concentration and wisdom, for one whose work is concentration, strong one-pointedness is suitable. Thus, one attains absorption. For one whose work is insight, strong wisdom is suitable. For thus, one attains the penetration of the characteristics. But through the balance of the two as well, absorption certainly occurs. Mindfulness, however, should be strong in all circumstances. For mindfulness protects the mind from falling into restlessness—by means of faith, energy, and wisdom, which are on the side of restlessness—and from falling into laziness—by means of concentration, which is on the side of laziness. Therefore, it is desirable everywhere, like salt and seasoning in all curries, and like an all-accomplishing minister in all the king's affairs.

Nimittakusalatā [V 2.0199] nāma pathavīkasiṇādikassa cittekaggatānimittassa akatassa karaṇakosallaṃ, katassa bhāvanākosallaṃ, bhāvanāya laddhassa rakkhaṇakosallañca, taṃ idha adhippetaṃ.

Skill in the sign means skill in making the sign of one-pointedness of mind with regard to the earth kasiṇa and so on when it has not been made, skill in developing it when it has been made, and skill in protecting it when it has been attained through development. This is what is intended here.

Kathaṃ yasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ niggahetabbaṃ, tasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ niggaṇhāti? Yadāssa accāraddhavīriyatādīhi uddhataṃ cittaṃ hoti, tadā dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgādayo tayo abhāvetvā passaddhisambojjhaṅgādayo bhāveti. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā (saṃ. ni. 5.234) –

How does one restrain the mind at the time when the mind should be restrained? When one's mind is agitated due to excessively aroused energy and so on, then, without developing the three enlightenment factors beginning with investigation-of-dhammas, one develops the enlightenment factors beginning with tranquility. For this was said by the Blessed One:

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso mahantaṃ aggikkhandhaṃ nibbāpetukāmo assa, so tattha sukkhāni ceva tiṇāni pakkhipeyya, sukkhāni ca gomayāni pakkhipeyya, sukkhāni ca kaṭṭhāni pakkhipeyya, mukhavātañca dadeyya, na ca paṃsukena okireyya, bhabbo nu kho so puriso taṃ mahantaṃ aggikkhandhaṃ nibbāpetunti. No hetaṃ, bhante. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, yasmiṃ samaye uddhataṃ cittaṃ hoti, akālo tasmiṃ samaye dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya. Akālo vīriya…pe… akālo pītisambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya. Taṃ kissa hetu? Uddhataṃ, bhikkhave, cittaṃ, taṃ etehi dhammehi duvūpasamayaṃ hoti.

“Suppose, bhikkhus, a man wanted to extinguish a great mass of fire. If he were to throw dry grass into it, dry cow dung, and dry sticks, blow on it with his mouth, and not sprinkle it with dust, would that man be able to extinguish that great mass of fire?” “No, venerable sir.” “In the same way, bhikkhus, when the mind is agitated, it is not the time to develop the enlightenment factor of investigation of dhammas; it is not the time for the enlightenment factor of energy... it is not the time for the enlightenment factor of rapture. For what reason? Because, bhikkhus, an agitated mind is difficult to pacify with these dhammas.”

“Yasmiṃ kho, bhikkhave, samaye uddhataṃ cittaṃ hoti, kālo tasmiṃ samaye passaddhisambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya. Kālo samādhi…pe… kālo upekkhāsambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya. Taṃ kissa hetu? Uddhataṃ, bhikkhave, cittaṃ, taṃ etehi dhammehi suvūpasamayaṃ hoti. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso mahantaṃ aggikkhandhaṃ nibbāpetukāmo assa, so tattha allāni ceva tiṇāni pakkhipeyya, allāni ca gomayāni pakkhipeyya, allāni ca [M 2.0225] kaṭṭhāni pakkhipeyya, udakavātañca dadeyya, paṃsukena ca okireyya, bhabbo nu kho so puriso taṃ mahantaṃ aggikkhandhaṃ nibbāpetunti. Evaṃ, bhante”ti.

“But, bhikkhus, when the mind is agitated, that is the time to develop the enlightenment factor of tranquility. That is the time for the enlightenment factor of concentration... that is the time for the enlightenment factor of equanimity. For what reason? Because, bhikkhus, an agitated mind is easily pacified by these dhammas. Suppose, bhikkhus, a man wanted to extinguish a great mass of fire. If he were to throw wet grass into it, wet cow dung, and wet sticks, spray it with water, and cover it with dust, would that man be able to extinguish that great mass of fire?” “Yes, venerable sir.”

Ettha ca yathāsakaṃ āhāravasena passaddhisambojjhaṅgādīnaṃ bhāvanā veditabbā. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

Here, the development of the enlightenment factors beginning with tranquility should be understood by way of their respective nutriments. For this was said by the Blessed One:

“Atthi, bhikkhave, kāyappassaddhi cittappassaddhi, tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā passaddhisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya[V 2.0200], uppannassa vā passaddhisambojjhaṅgassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā saṃvattati. Tathā atthi, bhikkhave, samathanimittaṃ abyagganimittaṃ, tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā samādhisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya, uppannassa vā samādhisambojjhaṅgassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā saṃvattati…pe… tathā atthi, bhikkhave, upekkhāsambojjhaṅgaṭṭhānīyā dhammā, tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā upekkhāsambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya, uppannassa vā upekkhāsambojjhaṅgassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā saṃvattatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232).

“Bhikkhus, there is tranquility of body and tranquility of mind. Frequent wise attention to that is the nutriment for the arising of the enlightenment factor of tranquility that has not yet arisen, and for the increase, growth, development, and fulfillment of the enlightenment factor of tranquility that has already arisen. Similarly, bhikkhus, there is the sign of serenity and the sign of non-agitation. Frequent wise attention to that is the nutriment for the arising of the enlightenment factor of concentration that has not yet arisen, and for the increase, growth, development, and fulfillment of the enlightenment factor of concentration that has already arisen... Likewise, bhikkhus, there are states that are grounds for the enlightenment factor of equanimity. Frequent wise attention to that is the nutriment for the arising of the enlightenment factor of equanimity that has not yet arisen, and for the increase, growth, development, and fulfillment of the enlightenment factor of equanimity that has already arisen.”

Tattha yathāssa passaddhiādayo uppannapubbā, taṃ ākāraṃ sallakkhetvā tesaṃ uppādanavasena pavattamanasikārova tīsu padesupi yonisomanasikāro nāma. Samathanimittanti ca samathassevetaṃ adhivacanaṃ, avikkhepaṭṭhena ca tasseva abyagganimittanti.

Herein, having discerned the manner in which tranquility and other factors had previously arisen for him, the very attention that proceeds by way of generating them in all three instances is called ‘wise attention.’ And ‘sign of serenity’ is a designation for serenity itself, and in the sense of non-distraction, it is the ‘sign of non-agitation’ for that very serenity.

Apica satta dhammā passaddhisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattanti – paṇītabhojanasevanatā, utusukhasevanatā, iriyāpathasukhasevanatā, majjhattappayogatā, sāraddhakāyapuggalaparivajjanatā, passaddhakāyapuggalasevanatā, tadadhimuttatāti.

Furthermore, seven states conduce to the arising of the enlightenment factor of tranquility: partaking of choice food, partaking of pleasant weather, partaking of comfortable postures, application of neutrality, avoiding individuals with agitated bodies, associating with individuals with tranquil bodies, and inclination towards that.

Ekādasa dhammā samādhisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattanti – vatthuvisadatā, nimittakusalatā, indriyasamattapaṭipādanatā, samaye cittassa niggahaṇatā, samaye cittassa paggahaṇatā, nirassādassa cittassa saddhāsaṃvegavasena [M 2.0226] sampahaṃsanatā, samappavattassa ajjhupekkhanatā, asamāhitapuggalaparivajjanatā, samāhitapuggalasevanatā, jhānavimokkhapaccavekkhaṇatā, tadadhimuttatāti.

Eleven states conduce to the arising of the enlightenment factor of concentration: clarity of the basis, skill in the sign, balancing the faculties, restraining the mind at the right time, exerting the mind at the right time, gladdening the dispirited mind by means of faith and a sense of urgency, maintaining equanimity towards the mind that is proceeding evenly, avoiding individuals who are not concentrated, associating with individuals who are concentrated, reviewing the jhānas and liberations, and inclination towards that.

Pañca dhammā upekkhāsambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattanti – sattamajjhattatā, saṅkhāramajjhattatā, sattasaṅkhārakelāyanapuggalaparivajjanatā, sattasaṅkhāramajjhattapuggalasevanatā, tadadhimuttatāti. Iti imehi ākārehi ete dhamme uppādento passaddhisambojjhaṅgādayo bhāveti nāma. Evaṃ yasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ niggahetabbaṃ, tasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ niggaṇhāti.

Five states conduce to the arising of the enlightenment factor of equanimity: impartiality towards beings, impartiality towards formations, avoiding individuals who delight in beings and formations, associating with individuals who are impartial towards beings and formations, and inclination towards that. Thus, by these modes, one who arouses these states is said to develop the enlightenment factors beginning with tranquility. In this way, when the mind should be restrained, at that time one restrains the mind.

Kathañca yasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ paggahetabbaṃ, tasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ paggaṇhāti? Yadāssa atisithilavīriyatādīhi [V 2.0201] cittaṃ līnaṃ hoti, tadā passaddhisambojjhaṅgādayo tayo abhāvetvā dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgādayo bhāveti. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā (saṃ. ni. 5.234) –

And how, when the mind should be exerted, does one exert the mind? When one’s mind is sluggish due to excessive slackness of energy and so forth, then, without developing the three enlightenment factors beginning with tranquility, one develops the enlightenment factors beginning with investigation of dhammas. For this was said by the Blessed One:

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso parittaṃ aggiṃ ujjāletukāmo assa, so tattha allāni ceva tiṇāni pakkhipeyya…pe… paṃsukena ca okireyya, bhabbo nu kho so puriso taṃ parittaṃ aggiṃ ujjāletunti. No hetaṃ, bhante. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, yasmiṃ samaye līnaṃ cittaṃ hoti. Akālo tasmiṃ samaye passaddhisambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya. Akālo samādhi…pe… akālo upekkhāsambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya. Taṃ kissa hetu? Līnaṃ, bhikkhave, cittaṃ, taṃ etehi dhammehi dusamuṭṭhāpayaṃ hoti.

“Suppose, bhikkhus, a man wanted to kindle a small fire. If he were to throw wet grass into it... and cover it with dust, would that man be able to kindle that small fire?” “No, venerable sir.” “In the same way, bhikkhus, when the mind is sluggish, that is not the time to develop the enlightenment factor of tranquility. It is not the time for the enlightenment factor of concentration... it is not the time for the enlightenment factor of equanimity. For what reason? Because, bhikkhus, a sluggish mind is hard to arouse with these states.”

“Yasmiñca kho, bhikkhave, samaye līnaṃ cittaṃ hoti, kālo tasmiṃ samaye dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya, kālo vīriya…pe… kālo pītisambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya. Taṃ kissa hetu? Līnaṃ, bhikkhave, cittaṃ, taṃ etehi dhammehi susamuṭṭhāpayaṃ hoti. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso parittaṃ aggiṃ ujjāletukāmo assa, so tattha sukkhāni ceva tiṇāni pakkhipeyya…pe… na ca paṃsukena okireyya, bhabbo nu kho so puriso taṃ parittaṃ aggiṃ ujjāletunti. Evaṃ, bhante”ti.

“But, bhikkhus, at the time when the mind is sluggish, that is the time for developing the enlightenment factor of investigation of states, the enlightenment factor of energy... the enlightenment factor of rapture. For what reason? Because, bhikkhus, a sluggish mind is easily aroused by these states. Just as, bhikkhus, if a man wanted to kindle a small fire, he would throw dry grass into it... and would not cover it with dust, would that man be able to kindle that small fire?” “Yes, Bhante.”

Etthāpi [M 2.0227] yathāsakaṃ āhāravasena dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgādīnaṃ bhāvanā veditabbā. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā (saṃ. ni. 5.232) –

Here too, the development of the enlightenment factor of investigation of states and the others should be understood in terms of their respective nutriment. For this was said by the Blessed One (SN 5.232):

“Atthi, bhikkhave, kusalākusalā dhammā sāvajjānavajjā dhammā hīnappaṇītā dhammā kaṇhasukkasappaṭibhāgā dhammā, tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya, uppannassa vā dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā saṃvattati. Tathā atthi, bhikkhave, ārambhadhātu nikkamadhātu parakkamadhātu, tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā vīriyasambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya, uppannassa vā vīriyasambojjhaṅgassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā saṃvattati. Tathā atthi, bhikkhave, pītisambojjhaṅgaṭṭhānīyā dhammā, tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro ayamāhāro [V 2.0202] anuppannassa vā pītisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya, uppannassa vā pītisambojjhaṅgassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā saṃvattatī”ti.

“Bhikkhus, there are wholesome and unwholesome states, blameworthy and blameless states, inferior and superior states, dark and bright states with their counterparts. Therein, frequent wise attention is the nutriment for the arising of the enlightenment factor of investigation of states that has not yet arisen, and for the increase, growth, development, and fulfillment of the enlightenment factor of investigation of states that has already arisen. So too, bhikkhus, there are the element of initiative, the element of endeavor, and the element of exertion. Therein, frequent wise attention is the nutriment for the arising of the enlightenment factor of energy that has not yet arisen, and for the increase, growth, development, and fulfillment of the enlightenment factor of energy that has already arisen. So too, bhikkhus, there are states that are grounds for the enlightenment factor of rapture. Therein, frequent wise attention is the nutriment for the arising of the enlightenment factor of rapture that has not yet arisen, and for the increase, growth, development, and fulfillment of the enlightenment factor of rapture that has already arisen.”

Tattha sabhāvasāmaññalakkhaṇappaṭivedhavasena pavattamanasikāro kusalādīsu yonisomanasikāro nāma. Ārambhadhātuādīnaṃ uppādavasena pavattamanasikāro ārambhadhātuādīsu yonisomanasikāro nāma. Tattha ārambhadhātūti paṭhamavīriyaṃ vuccati. Nikkamadhātūti kosajjato nikkhantattā tato balavataraṃ. Parakkamadhātūti paraṃ paraṃ ṭhānaṃ akkamanato tatopi balavataraṃ. Pītisambojjhaṅgaṭṭhānīyā dhammāti pana pītiyā evetaṃ nāmaṃ, tassāpi uppādakamanasikāro yonisomanasikāro nāma.

Herein, wise attention in regard to wholesome states and so forth is the attention that proceeds by means of penetrating the individual and general characteristics. Wise attention in regard to the element of initiative and so forth is the attention that proceeds by means of generating the element of initiative and so forth. Herein, ‘the element of initiative’ is said to be the initial energy. ‘The element of endeavor’ is stronger than that, since it has emerged from sloth. ‘The element of exertion’ is even stronger than that, since it advances further and further. As for ‘states that are grounds for the enlightenment factor of rapture,’ this is just a name for rapture itself, and the attention that generates it is also called wise attention.

Apica satta dhammā dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattanti – paripucchakatā, vatthuvisadakiriyā, indriyasamattapaṭipādanā, duppaññapuggalaparivajjanā, paññavantapuggalasevanā, gambhīrañāṇacariyapaccavekkhaṇā, tadadhimuttatāti.

Furthermore, seven states conduce to the arising of the enlightenment factor of investigation of states: being one who questions, clarifying the basis, balancing the faculties, avoiding individuals of poor wisdom, associating with individuals of wisdom, reviewing the practice of profound knowledge, and inclination towards that.

Ekādasa dhammā vīriyasambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattanti – apāyādibhayapaccavekkhaṇatā, vīriyāyattalokiyalokuttaravisesādhigamānisaṃsadassitā, “buddhapaccekabuddhamahaāsāvakehi gatamaggo mayā gantabbo, so [M 2.0228] ca na sakkā kusītena gantu”nti evaṃ gamanavīthipaccavekkhaṇatā, dāyakānaṃ mahapphalatākaraṇena piṇḍāpacāyanatā, “vīriyārambhassa vaṇṇavādī me satthā, so ca anatikkamanīyasāsano, amhākañca bahūpakāro, paṭipattiyā ca pūjiyamāno pūjito hoti, na itarathā”ti evaṃ satthu mahattapaccavekkhaṇatā, “saddhammasaṅkhātaṃ me mahādāyajjaṃ gahetabbaṃ, tañca na sakkā kusītena gahetu”nti evaṃ dāyajjamahattapaccavekkhaṇatā, ālokasaññāmanasikārairiyāpathaparivattanaabbhokāsasevanādīhi thinamiddhavinodanatā, kusītapuggalaparivajjanatā, āraddhavīriyapuggalasevanatā, sammappadhānapaccavekkhaṇatā, tadadhimuttatāti.

Eleven states conduce to the arising of the enlightenment factor of energy: reflection on the fear of the states of deprivation, etc.; seeing the benefit of attaining worldly and supramundane distinction dependent on energy; reflection on the path of progress, thus: ‘The path traversed by the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and great disciples is to be traversed by me, and that cannot be traversed by the lazy’; reverence for almsfood by causing it to be of great fruit for the donors; reflection on the greatness of the Teacher, thus: ‘My Teacher praises the undertaking of energy, his teaching is not to be transgressed, he is of great help to us, and he is honored by practice and not otherwise’; reflection on the greatness of the inheritance, thus: ‘The great inheritance, namely the True Dhamma, is to be received by me, and that cannot be received by the lazy’; dispelling sloth and torpor through attention to the perception of light, changing posture, resorting to open spaces, and so forth; avoiding lazy individuals; associating with energetic individuals; reflection on the right exertions; and inclination towards that.

Ekādasa dhammā pītisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattanti – buddhānussati, dhammasaṅghasīlacāgadevatānussati, upasamānussati, lūkhapuggalaparivajjanatā, siniddhapuggalasevanatā, pasādanīyasuttantapaccavekkhaṇatā, tadadhimuttatāti. Iti imehi ākārehi ete dhamme uppādento dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgādayo bhāveti nāma. Evaṃ yasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ paggahetabbaṃ, tasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ paggaṇhāti.

Eleven states conduce to the arising of the enlightenment factor of rapture: recollection of the Buddha, Dhamma, Sangha, virtue, generosity, and deities; recollection of peace; avoiding coarse individuals; associating with gentle individuals; reflection on inspiring discourses; and inclination towards that. In these ways, by arousing these states, one develops the enlightenment factor of investigation of states and the others. Thus, at the time when the mind should be uplifted, one uplifts the mind.

Kathaṃ [V 2.0203] yasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ sampahaṃsetabbaṃ, tasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ sampahaṃseti? Yadāssa paññāpayogamandatāya vā upasamasukhānadhigamena vā nirassādaṃ cittaṃ hoti, tadā naṃ aṭṭhasaṃvegavatthupaccavekkhaṇena saṃvejeti. Aṭṭha saṃvegavatthūni nāma jātijarābyādhimaraṇāni cattāri, apāyadukkhaṃ pañcamaṃ, atīte vaṭṭamūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ, anāgate vaṭṭamūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ, paccuppanne āhārapariyeṭṭhimūlakaṃ dukkhanti. Buddhadhammasaṅghaguṇānussaraṇena cassa pasādaṃ janeti. Evaṃ yasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ sampahaṃsetabbaṃ, tasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ sampahaṃseti.

How, at the time when the mind should be gladdened, does one gladden the mind? When one’s mind is insipid due to weak application of wisdom or due to not attaining the bliss of serenity, one stirs it by reflecting on the eight grounds for spiritual urgency. The eight grounds for spiritual urgency are: birth, aging, sickness, and death (these four); suffering in the woeful states (the fifth); suffering rooted in the round of existence in the past; suffering rooted in the round of existence in the future; and suffering rooted in the search for food in the present. And one generates serene confidence by recollecting the qualities of the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha. Thus, at the time when the mind should be gladdened, one gladdens the mind.

Kathaṃ yasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ ajjhupekkhitabbaṃ, tasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ ajjhupekkhati? Yadāssa evaṃ paṭipajjato alīnaṃ anuddhataṃ anirassādaṃ ārammaṇe samappavattaṃ samathavīthippaṭipannaṃ cittaṃ hoti, tadā tassa paggahaniggahasampahaṃsanesu abyāpāraṃ āpajjati sārathi viya ca samappavattesu assesu. Evaṃ yasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ ajjhupekkhitabbaṃ, tasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ ajjhupekkhati.

How, at the time when the mind should be regarded with equanimity, does one regard the mind with equanimity? When, for one practicing thus, the mind is neither sluggish nor agitated, nor without savor, but proceeds evenly in its object, having entered upon the path of tranquility, then one becomes non-active in regard to uplifting, restraining, or gladdening it, like a charioteer regarding horses proceeding evenly. Thus, at the time when the mind should be regarded with equanimity, one regards the mind with equanimity.

Asamāhitapuggalaparivajjanā [M 2.0229] nāma nekkhammapaṭipadaṃ anāruḷhapubbānaṃ anekakiccappasutānaṃ vikkhittahadayānaṃ puggalānaṃ ārakā pariccāgo. Samāhitapuggalasevanā nāma nekkhammapaṭipadaṃ paṭipannānaṃ samādhilābhīnaṃ puggalānaṃ kālena kālaṃ upasaṅkamanaṃ. Tadadhimuttatā nāma samādhimuttatā, samādhigarusamādhininnasamādhipoṇasamādhipabbhāratāti attho. Evametaṃ dasavidhaṃ appanākosallaṃ sampādetabbaṃ. Tenāha – “imāni dasa appanākosallāni avijahantenā”ti. Tattha yena vidhinā appanāya kusalo hoti, so dasavidhopi vidhi appanākosallaṃ tannibbattaṃ vā ñāṇaṃ, evametaṃ dasavidhaṃ appanākosallaṃ sampādentassa paṭiladdhanimittasmiṃ appanā uppajjati. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Avoiding uncomposed individuals means keeping far away from people who have not previously embarked on the path of renunciation, who are engaged in many duties, and whose hearts are scattered. Associating with composed individuals means approaching from time to time those who have attained concentration and are practicing the path of renunciation. Being resolved upon that means being resolved upon concentration—that is, having respect for concentration, leaning towards concentration, inclined towards concentration, and sloping towards concentration. Thus, these ten skills in absorption should be accomplished. Therefore it is said: 'Without abandoning these ten skills in absorption...' Therein, by whatever method one becomes skilled in absorption, that ten-fold method is skill in absorption, or the knowledge produced thereby. Thus, for one developing these ten skills in absorption, absorption arises in the sign that has been attained. For it has been said:

“Evañhi sampādayato, appanākosallaṃ imaṃ;

Paṭiladdhe nimittasmiṃ, appanā sampavattatī”ti. (visuddhi. 1.67);

“For one thus accomplishing this skill in absorption, when the sign has been attained, absorption duly occurs.”

Yogo karaṇīyoti appanākosallaṃ sampādentassapi yadi appanā na hoti, tena kammaṭṭhānānuyogaṃ avijahitvā reṇuādīsu madhukarādīnaṃ pavatti ākāraṃ sallakkhetvā līnuddhatabhāvehi mānasaṃ mocetvā vīriyasamataṃ yojentena punappunaṃ yogo kātabbo. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Effort is to be made: If absorption does not occur even for one developing the skill in absorption, then that person, without abandoning engagement with the meditation subject, having observed the manner of behavior of bees and the like among pollen, etc., having freed the mind from states of sluggishness and agitation, and applying balanced energy, should make effort again and again. For it has been said:

“Evañhi [V 2.0204] paṭipannassa, sace sā nappavattati;

Tathāpi na jahe yogaṃ, vāyametheva paṇḍito.

“For one practicing thus, if that absorption does not occur, even so, one should not abandon the practice; a wise person should indeed strive.

“Hitvā hi sammavāyāmaṃ, visesaṃ nāma māṇavo;

Adhigacche parittampi, ṭhānametaṃ na vijjati.

“Indeed, for a person who has abandoned right effort to attain even a little distinction—such a possibility does not exist.

“Cittappavattiākāraṃ, tasmā sallakkhayaṃ budho;

Samataṃ vīriyasseva, yojayetha punappunaṃ.

“Therefore, a wise person, discerning the manner of the mind’s activity, should again and again apply evenness to energy.

“Īsakampi layaṃ yantaṃ, paggaṇhetheva mānasaṃ;

Accāraddhaṃ nisedhetvā, samameva pavattaye.

“Even if the mind goes slightly slack, one should indeed uplift it; and having restrained that which is over-exerted, one should make it proceed evenly.

“Reṇumhi uppaladale, sutte nāvāya nāḷiyā;

Yathā madhukarādīnaṃ, pavatti sammavaṇṇitā.

“Just as the conduct of bees and the like on pollen, on a lotus petal, on a thread, in a boat, or in a tube, has been well described.

“Līnauddhatabhāvehi, mocayitvāna sabbaso;

Evaṃ nimittābhimukhaṃ, mānasaṃ paṭipādaye”ti. (visuddhi. 1.67);

“Having entirely freed the mind from states of sluggishness and agitation, one should thus direct it towards the sign.”

Yathā [M 2.0230] hi acheko madhukaro “asukasmiṃ rukkhe pupphaṃ pupphita”nti ñatvā tikkhena vegena pakkhando taṃ atikkamitvā paṭinivattento khīṇe reṇumhi sampāpuṇāti, aparo acheko mandena javena pakkhando khīṇeyeva sampāpuṇāti, cheko pana samena javena pakkhando sukhena puppharāsiṃ sampatvā yāvadicchakaṃ reṇuṃ ādāya madhuṃ sampādetvā madhuṃ anubhavati, yathā ca sallakattaantevāsikesu udakathālagate uppalapatte satthakammaṃ sikkhantesu eko acheko vegena satthaṃ pātento uppalapattaṃ dvidhā vā chindati, udake vā paveseti, aparo acheko chijjanapavesanabhayā satthakena phusitumpi na visahati, cheko pana samena payogena tattha satthapadaṃ dassetvā pariyodātasippo hutvā tathārūpesu ṭhānesu kammaṃ katvā lābhaṃ labhati, yathā ca “yo catubyāmappamāṇaṃ makkaṭakasuttaṃ āharati, so cattāri sahassāni labhatī”ti raññā vutte eko achekapuriso vegena makkaṭakasuttaṃ ākaḍḍhanto tahiṃ tahiṃ chindatiyeva, aparo acheko chedanabhayā hatthena phusitumpi na visahati, cheko pana koṭito paṭṭhāya samena payogena daṇḍake veṭhetvā āharitvā lābhaṃ labhati, yathā ca acheko niyāmako balavavāte laṅkāraṃ [V 2.0205] pūrento nāvaṃ videsaṃ pakkhandāpeti, aparo acheko mandavāte laṅkāraṃ oropento nāvaṃ tattheva ṭhapeti, cheko pana mandavāte pūretvā balavavāte aḍḍhalaṅkāraṃ katvā sotthinā icchitaṭṭhānaṃ pāpuṇāti, yathā ca “yo telena achaḍḍento nāḷiṃ pūreti, so lābhaṃ labhatī”ti ācariyena antevāsikānaṃ vutte eko acheko lābhaluddho vegena pūrento telaṃ chaḍḍeti, aparo acheko telachaḍḍanabhayā āsiñcitumpi na visahati, cheko pana samena payogena pūretvā lābhaṃ labhati, evameva eko bhikkhu uppanne nimitte “sīghameva appanaṃ pāpuṇissāmī”ti gāḷhaṃ vīriyaṃ karoti, tassa cittaṃ accāraddhavīriyattā uddhacce patati, so na sakkoti appanaṃ pāpuṇituṃ. Eko accāraddhavīriyatāya dosaṃ disvā “kiṃ dāni me appanāyā”ti vīriyaṃ hāpeti, tassa cittaṃ atilīnavīriyattā kosajje patati, sopi na sakkoti appanaṃ pāpuṇituṃ. Yo pana īsakampi [M 2.0231] līnaṃ līnabhāvato, uddhataṃ uddhaccato mocetvā samena payogena nimittābhimukhaṃ pavatteti, so appanaṃ pāpuṇāti, tādisena bhavitabbaṃ.

Just as an unskilled honeybee, knowing that “a flower has bloomed on such-and-such a tree,” flying with swift speed, overshoots it and, turning back, arrives when the pollen is exhausted. Another unskilled honeybee, flying with slow speed, also arrives when it is exhausted. But a skilled bee, flying at a moderate speed, easily reaches the cluster of flowers, takes as much pollen as desired, produces honey, and enjoys it. And just as when surgery students are practicing knife-work on a lotus leaf placed in a water vessel, one unskilled student, letting the knife fall swiftly, either cuts the lotus leaf in two or sinks it into the water. Another unskilled student, fearing to cut or sink it, does not dare even to touch it with the scalpel. But the skilled student, applying moderate effort, demonstrates the knife-mark there, becomes one whose skill is purified, and having done the work in such situations, obtains a reward. And just as when a king declares, “Whoever brings a spider’s thread four fathoms long will receive four thousand,” one unskilled man, pulling the spider’s thread hastily, breaks it here and there. Another unskilled man, fearing to break it, does not dare even to touch it with his hand. But the skilled man, starting from the end, with moderate effort winds it on a stick, brings it, and receives the reward. And just as an unskilled helmsman, filling the sail in a strong wind, sends the ship off course to a foreign region. Another unskilled helmsman, lowering the sail in a gentle wind, keeps the ship right there. But the skilled helmsman, filling the sail in a gentle wind and making it a half-sail in a strong wind, safely reaches the desired destination. And just as when a teacher tells his students, “Whoever fills a measure with oil without spilling it will receive a reward,” one unskilled student, greedy for the reward, filling it hastily, spills the oil. Another unskilled student, fearing to spill the oil, does not dare even to pour it. But the skilled student, filling it with moderate effort, receives the reward. In the same way, one monk, when a sign arises, thinks, “I will quickly attain absorption,” and makes strong effort. His mind, due to over-exerted energy, falls into agitation, and he cannot attain absorption. Another monk, seeing the fault in over-exerted energy, thinks, “What use is absorption to me now?” and slackens his effort. His mind, due to excessively lax energy, falls into laziness, and he too cannot attain absorption. But the one who, having freed even a slightly sluggish mind from its state of sluggishness, and an agitated mind from its state of agitation, directs it towards the sign with moderate effort—he attains absorption. One should be like that.

Idāni evaṃ paṭipannassa appanāpavattiṃ dassento “tassevaṃ anuyuttassā”tiādimāha. Tattha paṭhamaṃ parikammantiādi aggahitaggahaṇena vuttaṃ, gahitaggahaṇena pana avisesena sabbesaṃ sabbā samaññā. Sabbānipi hi appanāya parikammattā paṭisaṅkhārakattā “parikammānī”tipi, yathā gāmādīnaṃ āsannappadeso “gāmūpacāro gharūpacāro”ti vuccati, evaṃ appanāya āsannattā samīpacārittā vā “upacārānī”tipi, ito pubbe parikammānaṃ upari appanāya ca anulomanato “anulomānī”tipi vuccanti. Yañcettha sabbantimaṃ, taṃ parittagottābhibhavanato mahaggatagottabhāvanato ca “gotrabhū”tipi vuccati. Gaṃ tāyatīti hi gottaṃ, parittanti pavattamānaṃ abhidhānaṃ buddhiñca ekaṃsikavisayatāya rakkhatīti parittagottaṃ. Yathā hi buddhi ārammaṇabhūtena atthena vinā na vattati, evaṃ abhidhānaṃ abhidheyyabhūtena, tasmā so tāni tāyati rakkhatīti vuccati. Taṃ pana mahaggatānuttaravidhuraṃ kāmataṇhāya gocarabhūtaṃ kāmāvacaradhammānaṃ āveṇikarūpaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Mahaggatagottepi iminā nayena attho veditabbo. Iti evarūpassa parittagottassa abhibhavanato mahaggatagottassa ca bhāvanato uppādanato antimaṃ “gotrabhū”tipi vuccati. Catutthameva hi pañcamaṃ vāti khippābhiññadandhābhiññānaṃ vasena vuttaṃ. Khippābhiññassa hi catutthaṃ appeti, dandhābhiññassa pañcamaṃ. Kasmā pana catutthaṃ pañcamaṃ vā appeti, na chaṭṭhaṃ vā sattamaṃ vāti āha “āsannabhavaṅgapātattā”ti. Yathā hi puriso chinnapapātābhimukho dhāvanto ṭhātukāmopi pariyante pādaṃ katvā ṭhātuṃ na sakkoti, papāte eva patati, evaṃ chaṭṭhaṃ vā sattamaṃ vā appetuṃ na sakkoti bhavaṅgassa āsannattā. Tasmā catutthapañcamesuyeva appanā hotīti veditabbā.

Now, to show the occurrence of absorption for one who has practiced thus, he said, 'For one thus devoted,' and so on. Herein, 'the first, preparatory,' and so on, is stated by way of specific application; but by way of general application, all designations apply to all without distinction. For all are also called 'preparations' (parikammāni) because they are a preparation for absorption and because they perform the act of preparing. Just as the vicinity of a village or house is called 'village-access' or 'house-access', so too, because of their nearness to absorption or because they move in proximity to it, they are also called 'accesses' (upacārāni). And because they conform to the preceding preparations and the subsequent absorption, they are also called 'conformity' (anulomāni). And what is the very last one here is also called 'change-of-lineage' (gotrabhū) because it overcomes the limited lineage and develops the sublime lineage. For 'lineage' (gotta) is that which protects the course. 'Limited lineage' (parittagotta) is so-called because it protects the presently occurring designation and cognition by way of having a definite object. Just as cognition does not occur without an object that is its resort, so too a designation does not occur without that which is to be designated; therefore, it is said that it protects them. That (limited lineage) should be understood as the unique nature of sense-sphere phenomena, which is destitute of the sublime and supramundane and is the domain of sensual craving. The meaning of 'sublime lineage' (mahaggatagotta) should also be understood in this way. Thus, because it overcomes such a limited lineage and develops or produces the sublime lineage, the final moment is also called 'change-of-lineage'. That it is the fourth or the fifth is stated according to whether one has swift or slow direct-knowledge. For one with swift direct-knowledge, the fourth attains absorption; for one with slow direct-knowledge, the fifth. But why does the fourth or fifth attain absorption, and not the sixth or seventh? He said, 'Because of the proximity to falling into the life-continuum.' Just as a man running toward a precipice, though wishing to stop, cannot place his foot at the edge and halt, but falls into the precipice itself, so too one cannot attain absorption at the sixth or seventh because of the proximity of the life-continuum. Therefore, it should be understood that absorption occurs only at the fourth or fifth.

“Purimā [V 2.0206] purimā kusalā dhammā pacchimānaṃ pacchimānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ āsevanapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.12) vuttattā “āsevanapaccayena kusalā dhammā balavanto hontī”ti āha. Yathā aladdhāsevanaṃ paṭhamaṃ javanaṃ dubbalattā gotrabhuṃ na uppādeti, laddhāsevanaṃ pana [M 2.0232] balavabhāvato dutiyaṃ vā tatiyaṃ vā gotrabhuṃ uppādeti, evaṃ laddhāsevanatāya balavabhāvato chaṭṭhampi sattamampi appetīti therassa adhippāyo. Tenāha – “tasmā chaṭṭhaṃ sattamaṃ vā appetī”ti. Tanti therassa vacanaṃ. Paṭikkhittanti suttasuttānulomaācariyavādehi anupatthambhitattā “attanomatimattaṃ therasseta”nti vatvā paṭikkhittaṃ. “Purimā purimā kusalā dhammā”ti pana suttapadamakāraṇaṃ āsevanapaccayalābhassa balavabhāve anekantikattā. Tathā hi aladdhāsevanāpi paṭhamacetanā diṭṭhadhammavedanīyā hoti, laddhāsevanā dutiyacetanā yāva chaṭṭhacetanā aparāpariyavedanīyā. Yadi chaṭṭhaṃ sattamañca parikkhīṇajavattā dubbalaṃ, na āsevanapaccayena balavaṃ, kathaṃ sattamajavanacetanā upapajjavedanīyā ānantariyā ca hotīti? Nāyaṃ viseso āsevanapaccayalābhena balavappattiyā kiñcarahi kiriyāvatthāvisesato. Kiriyāvatthā hi ādimajjhapariyosānavasena tividhā. Tattha pariyosānāvatthāya sanniṭṭhāpakacetanābhāvena upapajjavedanīyāditā hoti, na balavabhāvenāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Paṭisandhiyā anantarapaccayabhāvino vipākasantānassa anantarapaccayabhāvena tathā abhisaṅkhatattā”ti ca vadanti, tasmā chaṭṭhasattamānaṃ papātābhimukhatāya parikkhīṇajavatā na sakkā nivāretuṃ. Pubbabhāgacittānīti tīṇi cattāri vā cittāni.

Because it is said, 'Preceding wholesome states are a condition, by way of repetition, for subsequent wholesome states' (Paṭṭhāna 1.1.12), he says, 'Wholesome states become strong through the repetition condition.' The Elder's intention is this: Just as the first impulsion, not having gained repetition and thus being weak, does not produce change-of-lineage, but having gained repetition and thus become strong, it produces a second or a third change-of-lineage; so too, due to the strength from having gained repetition, the sixth or even the seventh attains absorption. Therefore, he says: 'Thus, the sixth or the seventh attains absorption.' That is the Elder's statement. It is rejected. It is rejected by stating, 'This is merely the Elder's personal opinion,' because it is unsupported by the Suttas and by the views of teachers that conform to the Suttas. Furthermore, the Sutta passage 'Preceding wholesome states...' is not a reason, because the attainment of strength through the repetition condition is not invariable. For the first volition, even without having gained repetition, is to be experienced in this very life, while the second volition up to the sixth volition, having gained repetition, are to be experienced in subsequent lives. If the sixth and seventh are weak due to being exhausted impulsion, and not strong through the repetition condition, how can the volition of the seventh impulsion be that which is to be experienced in the next life and be an immediately effective kamma? This distinction does not come from attaining strength through the repetition condition; rather, it comes from the specific functional stage of the action. For the functional stage of an action is threefold: initial, intermediate, and final. It should be understood that herein, in the final stage, its being that which is to be experienced in the next life, etc., is due to its being the concluding volition, not due to its strength. And some say, 'Because it is so formed by way of being a proximity condition for the resultant continuum which is to become the proximity condition for rebirth-linking.' Therefore, the exhausted-impulsion nature of the sixth and seventh, due to their facing towards falling, cannot be prevented. 'Preliminary-part consciousnesses' means three or four consciousnesses.

Etthāti etissaṃ kāyānupassanāyaṃ. Pārisuddhiṃ pattukāmoti adhigantukāmo samāpajjitukāmo ca. Tattha sallakkhaṇāvivaṭṭanāvasena adhigantukāmo, sallakkhaṇavasena samāpajjitukāmoti yojetabbaṃ. Āvajjanasamāpajjana…pe… vasippattanti ettha evaṃ tāva pañca vasiyo veditabbā – paṭhamajjhānato vuṭṭhāya paṭhamaṃ vitakkaṃ āvajjayato bhavaṅgaṃ upacchinditvā uppannāvajjanānantaraṃ vitakkārammaṇāneva cattāri pañca javanāni javanti, tato dve bhavaṅgāni, tato pana vicārārammaṇaṃ āvajjanaṃ vuttanayeneva javanānīti evaṃ pañcasu jhānaṅgesu yadā nirantaraṃ cittaṃ pesetuṃ sakkoti, athassa āvajjanavasī siddhā hoti. Ayaṃ pana bhavaṅgadvayantaritā matthakappattā vasī bhagavato yamakapāṭihāriye labbhati, aññesaṃ vā dhammasenāpatiādīnaṃ evarūpe uṭṭhāya samuṭṭhāya lahutaraṃ āvajjanavasīnibbattanakāle. Sā ca kho ittarā parittakālā, na satthu yamakapāṭihāriye [M 2.0233] viya ciratarappabandhavatī. Tathā hi taṃ sāvakehi asādhāraṇaṃ vuttaṃ. Ito paraṃ sīghatarā āvajjanavasī nāma natthi.

Here means: in this contemplation of the body. Desiring to attain purity means wishing to attain and wishing to enter. Therein, the wish to attain should be connected with discerning and unfolding, while the wish to enter should be connected with discernment. Regarding adverting, entering... up to mastery—here, indeed, five masteries should be understood as follows: Emerging from the first jhāna, when one adverts to initial thought, having cut off the life-continuum, immediately after the adverting that has arisen, four or five impulsions run with initial thought itself as their object. Then two life-continuum moments follow, after which adverting arises with sustained thought as its object, and impulsions proceed in the same manner as described. Thus, when one is able to direct the mind uninterruptedly among the five jhāna factors, then mastery of adverting is accomplished for that person. This mastery, however, which is interrupted by two life-continuum moments and has reached its peak, is obtained by the Blessed One during the Twin Miracle, or by others, such as the General of the Dhamma and so on, at the time of generating the mastery of adverting very swiftly, having completely arisen in such a case. And that mastery is temporary, of short duration; it is not of such a long-lasting continuity as the Teacher's during the Twin Miracle. Thus, it is said to be uncommon to the disciples. Beyond this, there is no swifter mastery of adverting.

Āyasmato [V 2.0207] pana mahāmoggallānassa nandopanandanāgarājadamane viya sīghaṃ samāpajjanasamatthatā samāpajjanavasī nāma. Ettha ca samāpajjitukāmatānantaraṃ dvīsu bhavaṅgesu uppannesu bhavaṅgaṃ upacchinditvā uppannāvajjanānantaraṃ samāpajjanaṃ sīghaṃ samāpajjanasamatthatā. Ayañca matthakappattā samāpajjanavasī satthu dhammadesanāyaṃ labbhati, taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “so kho ahaṃ, aggivessana, tassāyeva kathāya pariyosāne tasmiṃyeva purimasmiṃ samādhinimitte ajjhattameva cittaṃ saṇṭhapemi sannisādemi ekodiṃ karomi samādahāmi, yena sudaṃ niccakappaṃ viharāmī”ti (ma. ni. 1.387). Ito sīghatarā hi samāpajjanavasī nāma natthi.

The ability to enter absorption swiftly, like that of the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna in the taming of the nāga king Nandopananda, is called the mastery of entering. Here, the ability to enter absorption swiftly is this: immediately after the desire to enter, when two life-continuum moments have arisen, having cut off the life-continuum, immediately after the adverting that has arisen, one enters absorption. And this mastery of entering, which has reached its peak, is obtained by the Teacher during a Dhamma discourse. It is said in reference to this: “Then, Aggivessana, at the conclusion of that very talk, right there in that same preliminary sign of concentration, I steadied my mind internally, settled it, unified it, and concentrated it—by which I dwell perpetually.” Beyond this, there is no swifter mastery of entering.

Accharāmattaṃ vā dasaccharāmattaṃ vā khaṇaṃ jhānaṃ ṭhapetuṃ samatthatā adhiṭṭhānavasī nāma. Tatheva accharāmattaṃ vā dasaccharāmattaṃ vā lahukaṃ khaṇaṃ jhānasamaṅgī hutvā jhānato vuṭṭhātuṃ samatthatā vuṭṭhānavasī nāma. Bhavaṅgacittappavattiyeva hettha jhānato vuṭṭhānaṃ nāma. Ettha ca yathā “ettakameva khaṇaṃ jhānaṃ ṭhapessāmī”ti pubbaparikammavasena adhiṭṭhānasamatthatā adhiṭṭhānavasī, evaṃ “ettakameva khaṇaṃ jhānasamaṅgī hutvā jhānato vuṭṭhahissāmī”ti pubbaparikammavasena vuṭṭhānasamatthatā vuṭṭhānavasīti veditabbā, yā samāpattivuṭṭhānakusalatāti vuccati. Paccavekkhaṇavasī pana āvajjanavasiyā eva vuttā. Paccavekkhaṇajavanāneva hi tattha āvajjanānantarāni. Yadaggena hi āvajjanavasīsiddhi, tadaggena paccavekkhaṇavasīsiddhi veditabbā.

The ability to sustain the jhāna for a moment the length of a finger-snap or ten finger-snaps is called the mastery of resolve. Likewise, the ability to emerge from jhāna, having been endowed with jhāna for a brief moment the length of a finger-snap or ten finger-snaps, is called the mastery of emergence. Here, the very occurrence of the life-continuum consciousness is called emergence from jhāna. And here, just as the ability to resolve by means of prior preparation, ‘I will sustain the jhāna for just this long,’ is the mastery of resolve, so the ability to emerge by means of prior preparation, ‘Having been endowed with jhāna for just this long, I will emerge from jhāna,’ should be understood as the mastery of emergence. This is what is called skill in attainment and emergence. The mastery of reviewing, however, is explained by way of the mastery of adverting itself. For there, the reviewing impulsions are immediately after the adverting. By the same token that mastery of adverting is accomplished, mastery of reviewing should be understood to be accomplished.

Arūpapubbaṅgamaṃ vā…pe… vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetīti saṅkhepato vuttamatthaṃ vitthārato dassetuṃ “katha”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha jhānaṅgāni pariggahetvāti vitakkādīni jhānaṅgāni taṃsampayutte ca dhamme salakkhaṇarasādivasena pariggahetvā. “Jhānaṅgānī”ti hi idaṃ nidassanamattaṃ, jhānaṅgāni pana passanto taṃsampayutte ca dhamme passati. Tesaṃ nissayaṃ hadayavatthunti yathā nāma puriso antogehe sappaṃ disvā anubandhamāno tassa āsayaṃ passati, evameva kho ayampi yogāvacaro te arūpadhamme upaparikkhanto “ime dhammā kiṃ nissāya pavattantī”ti pariyesamāno tesaṃ nissayaṃ [M 2.0234] hadayavatthuṃ passati. Jhānaṅgāni arūpanti ettha taṃsampayuttadhammānampi gahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ.

To show in detail the meaning stated in brief as ‘…establishes insight preceded by the immaterial…,’ the passage beginning with ‘How?’ was stated. Therein, ‘having grasped the jhāna factors’ means having grasped the jhāna factors such as initial thought and so on, and the states associated with them, by way of their characteristic, function, and so on. For the phrase ‘jhāna factors’ is merely an indication; one who sees the jhāna factors also sees the states associated with them. Regarding the phrase ‘Their support is the heart-base’: just as a person, seeing a snake inside a house and pursuing it, sees its lair, so too this yogī, examining those immaterial phenomena and seeking, ‘On what do these phenomena depend for their occurrence?’, sees their support, the heart-base. Here, in the phrase ‘the jhāna factors are immaterial,’ it should be understood that the states associated with them are also included.

Arūpapubbaṅgamaṃ rūpapariggahaṃ dassetvā idāni rūpapubbaṅgamaṃ arūpapariggahaṃ dassento “atha vā”tiādimāha. Kesādīsu koṭṭhāsesu…pe… taṃnissitarūpāni ca pariggahetvāti ettha pana kese tāva thaddhalakkhaṇaṃ pathavīdhātūti pariggahetabbaṃ, tattheva ābandhanalakkhaṇaṃ āpodhātūti, paripācanalakkhaṇaṃ [V 2.0208] tejodhātūti, vitthambhanalakkhaṇaṃ vāyodhātūti evaṃ sabbakoṭṭhāsesu ekekasmiṃ koṭṭhāse cattāri cattāri mahābhūtāni pariggahetabbāni. Athānena yāthāvato sarasalakkhaṇato āvibhūtāsu dhātūsu kammasamuṭṭhānamhi tāva kese vuttalakkhaṇā tā catasso ca dhātuyo taṃnissito ca vaṇṇo gandho raso ojā jīvitaṃ kāyapasādoti evaṃ kāyadasakavasena dasa rūpāni, tattheva bhāvassa atthitāya bhāvadasakavasena dasa rūpāni, āhārasamuṭṭhānaṃ ojaṭṭhamakaṃ, utusamuṭṭhānaṃ cittasamuṭṭhānanti aparānipi catuvīsatīti evaṃ catusamuṭṭhānesu catuvīsatikoṭṭhāsesu catucattālīsa rūpāni pariggahetabbāni. Sedo assu kheḷo siṅghāṇikāti ime pana catūsu utucittasamuṭṭhānesu dvinnaṃ ojaṭṭhamakānaṃ vasena soḷasa soḷasa rūpāni. Udariyaṃ karīsaṃ pubbaṃ muttanti imesu catūsu utusamuṭṭhānesu utusamuṭṭhānasseva ojaṭṭhamakassa vasena aṭṭha aṭṭha rūpāni pariggahetabbāni. Esa tāva dvattiṃsākāre nayo.

Having shown the comprehension of form preceded by formlessness, he now states 'or alternatively' and so on, showing the comprehension of formlessness preceded by form. In the parts such as the hair... and having grasped the forms dependent on that. Here, however, first in the hair, the characteristic of hardness should be grasped as the earth element; right there, the characteristic of cohesion as the water element; the characteristic of ripening as the fire element; the characteristic of supporting as the air element. Thus, in each and every part, the four great elements should be grasped. Then, by this person, in the elements that are not manifest according to their true individual characteristics, first in the hair, in what is originated by kamma, the four elements with the aforementioned characteristics and the forms dependent on them—color, odor, taste, nutritive essence, life faculty, and body sensitivity—thus, by way of the body decad, ten forms; and right there, due to the existence of sex, by way of the sex decad, ten forms; the nutriment-originated octad with nutritive essence as the eighth, the temperature-originated octad, and the mind-originated octad—these being another twenty-four forms. Thus, in the twenty-four parts that arise from four origins, forty-four forms are to be grasped. As for sweat, tears, saliva, and nasal mucus, in these four, which are originated by temperature and mind, by way of two octads with nutritive essence as the eighth, there are sixteen forms each. In these four—stomach contents, feces, pus, and urine—which are originated only by temperature, by way of the temperature-originated octad with nutritive essence as the eighth, eight forms each are to be grasped. This, indeed, is the method in the thirty-two aspects.

Ye pana imasmiṃ dvattiṃsākāre āvibhūte apare cattāro tejokoṭṭhāsā, cha vāyokoṭṭhāsāti dasa ākārā āvi bhavanti, tattha asitādiparipācake tāva kammajatejokoṭṭhāsamhi ojaṭṭhamakañceva jīvitañcāti nava rūpāni, tathā cittaje assāsapassāsakoṭṭhāse ojaṭṭhamakañceva saddo cāti nava, sesesu catusamuṭṭhānesu aṭṭhasu jīvitanavakañceva tīṇi ca ojaṭṭhamakānīti tettiṃsa tettiṃsa rūpāni pariggahetabbāni. Evaṃ vitthārato dvācattālīsākāravasena imesu bhūtupādāyarūpesu pākaṭesu jātesu vatthudvāravasena pañca cakkhudasakādayo hadayavatthudasakañcāti aparānipi saṭṭhi rūpāni pariggahetabbāni. Sace panassa tena tena mukhena rūpaṃ pariggahetvā arūpaṃ pariggaṇhato sukhumattā arūpaṃ na upaṭṭhāti, tena dhuranikkhepaṃ akatvā rūpameva [M 2.0235] punappunaṃ sammasitabbaṃ manasi kātabbaṃ pariggahetabbaṃ vavatthapetabbaṃ. Yathā yathā hissa rūpaṃ suvikkhālitaṃ hoti nijjaṭaṃ suparisuddhaṃ, tathā tathā tadārammaṇā arūpadhammā sayameva pākaṭā honti.

But, when these thirty-two aspects have become manifest, the other four fire-parts and six air-parts—these ten aspects do not become manifest. Therein, first, in the kamma-originated fire-part which ripens what is eaten and so on, there are nine forms: the octad with nutritive essence as the eighth and the life faculty. Similarly, in the mind-originated in-breath and out-breath part, there are nine: the octad with nutritive essence as the eighth and sound. In the remaining eight parts, which are originated by the four origins, the life nonad and three octads with nutritive essence as the eighth, thus thirty-three forms each should be grasped. Thus, in detail, by way of the forty-two aspects, when these primary and derived material forms have become manifest, another sixty forms should be grasped by way of base and door: the five beginning with the eye decad, and the heart-base decad. But if, for one who has grasped form by this or that method, formlessness does not appear while trying to grasp it, due to its subtlety, he should not give up the burden; form itself should be repeatedly examined, attended to, grasped, and determined. For, in whatever way his form becomes well-washed, free of entanglement, and well-purified, in that same way the formless states having that as their object become manifest by themselves.

Yathā hi cakkhumato purisassa aparisuddhe ādāse mukhanimittaṃ olokentassa nimittaṃ na paññāyatīti na ādāsaṃ chaḍḍeti, atha kho naṃ punappunaṃ parimajjati, tassa parisuddhe ādāse nimittaṃ sayameva pākaṭaṃ hoti, evameva tena bhikkhunā dhuranikkhepaṃ akatvā rūpameva punappunaṃ sammasitabbaṃ manasi kātabbaṃ pariggahetabbaṃ vavatthapetabbaṃ. Yathā yathā hissa rūpaṃ suvikkhālitaṃ hoti nijjaṭaṃ suparisuddhaṃ, tathā tathā tadārammaṇā arūpadhammā sayameva pākaṭā honti. Evaṃ suvisuddharūpapariggahassa panassa arūpadhammā tīhākārehi upaṭṭhahanti phassavasena vā vedanāvasena vā viññāṇavasena vā.

For, just as for a man with sight looking at the reflection of his face in an unclean mirror, the reflection is not perceived, yet he does not discard the mirror, thinking, 'The reflection is not perceived.' Rather, he cleans it again and again. When the mirror is clean, the reflection becomes manifest for him by itself. In the very same way, that monk, not giving up the burden, should repeatedly examine, attend to, grasp, and determine form itself. For, in whatever way his form becomes well-washed, free of entanglement, and well-purified, in that same way the formless states having that as their object become manifest by themselves. Thus, for one who has a well-purified comprehension of form, the formless states present themselves in three ways: by way of contact, by way of feeling, or by way of consciousness.

Kathaṃ[V 2.0209]? Ekassa tāva “kese pathavīdhātu kakkhaḷalakkhaṇā…pe… assāsapassāse pathavīdhātu kakkhaḷalakkhaṇā”tiādinā nayena dhātuyo pariggaṇhantassa paṭhamābhinipāto phasso, taṃsampayuttā vedanā vedanākkhandho, saññā saññākkhandho, saddhiṃ phassena cetanā saṅkhārakkhandho, cittaṃ viññāṇakkhandhoti upaṭṭhāti. Evaṃ arūpadhammā phassavasena upaṭṭhahanti. Ekassa “kese pathavīdhātu kakkhaḷalakkhaṇā…pe… assāsapassāse pathavīdhātu kakkhaḷalakkhaṇā”ti tadārammaṇarasānubhavanakavedanā vedanākkhandho, taṃsampayuttā saññā saññākkhandho, taṃsampayutto phasso ca cetanā ca saṅkhārakkhandho, taṃsampayuttaṃ cittaṃ viññāṇakkhandhoti upaṭṭhāti. Evaṃ vedanāvasena arūpadhammā upaṭṭhahanti. Aparassa “kese pathavīdhātu kakkhaḷalakkhaṇā…pe… assāsapassāse pathavīdhātu kakkhaḷalakkhaṇā”ti ārammaṇapaṭivijānanaṃ viññāṇakkhandho, taṃsampayuttā vedanā vedanākkhandho, saññā saññākkhandho, phasso ca cetanā ca saṅkhārakkhandhoti upaṭṭhāti. Evaṃ viññāṇavasena arūpadhammā upaṭṭhahanti. Etenevupāyena “kammasamuṭṭhāne kese pathavīdhātu kakkhaḷalakkhaṇā”tiādinā nayena dvācattālīsāya dhātukoṭṭhāsesu catunnaṃ catunnaṃ dhātūnaṃ vasena sesesupi vatthu cakkhādīsu dasakesu manodhātumanoviññāṇadhātūnaṃ nissayalakkhaṇaṃ hadayavatthu rūpābhighātārahabhūtappasādalakkhaṇaṃ cakkhūtiādinā vatthudvāravasena pariggaṇhantassa paṭhamābhinipāto phasso, taṃsampayuttā vedanā vedanākkhandhotiādinā [M 2.0236] phassādivasena tīhi ākārehi arūpadhammā upaṭṭhahanti. Tena vuttaṃ “yathāpariggahitarūpārammaṇaṃ yathāpariggahitarūpavatthudvārārammaṇaṃ vā sasampayuttadhammaṃ viññāṇañca passatī”ti.

How? For one person, while comprehending the elements by the method beginning, “In the hair, the earth element has the characteristic of hardness… (and so on)... in the in-and-out-breaths, the earth element has the characteristic of hardness,” the first impact is contact; the feeling associated with it is the feeling aggregate; the perception is the perception aggregate; volition together with contact is the formations aggregate; and the mind is the consciousness aggregate. Thus it becomes manifest. In this way, the immaterial phenomena become manifest by way of contact. For another person, with “In the hair, the earth element has the characteristic of hardness… (and so on)... in the in-and-out-breaths, the earth element has the characteristic of hardness,” the feeling that is the experiencing of the flavor of that object is the feeling aggregate; the perception associated with it is the perception aggregate; the associated contact and volition are the formations aggregate; and the associated mind is the consciousness aggregate. Thus it becomes manifest. In this way, the immaterial phenomena become manifest by way of feeling. For yet another person, with “In the hair, the earth element has the characteristic of hardness… (and so on)... in the in-and-out-breaths, the earth element has the characteristic of hardness,” the distinct knowing of the object is the consciousness aggregate; the feeling associated with it is the feeling aggregate; the perception is the perception aggregate; and contact and volition are the formations aggregate. Thus it becomes manifest. In this way, the immaterial phenomena become manifest by way of consciousness. By this very method, for one who comprehends by way of the four elements in each of the forty-two elemental portions, by the method beginning, “In the kamma-born hair, the earth element has the characteristic of hardness,” and also in the remaining bases, the decads of the eye and so on, by way of the base and door—the heart-base having the characteristic of support for the mind-element and mind-consciousness-element, and the eye and so on having the characteristic of sensitive matter of the primary elements capable of being impacted by form—the first impact is contact, the feeling associated with it is the feeling aggregate, and so on. The immaterial phenomena become manifest in three ways by way of contact and so on. Therefore it was said: “One sees consciousness and its associated phenomena, which have as their object the material form as comprehended, or which have as their object the material base and door as comprehended.”

Idāni aññathāpi rūpapubbaṅgamaṃ arūpapariggahaṃ dassento “atha vā”tiādimāha. Tattha yathā hītiādi kāyassa cittassa ca assāsapassāsānaṃ samudayabhāvadassanaṃ. Kammāragaggarīti kammārānaṃ ukkāya aggidhamanabhastā. Dhamamānāyāti dhūmāyantiyā, vātaṃ gāhāpentiyāti attho. Tajjanti tadanurūpaṃ. Evamevanti ettha kammāragaggarī viya karajakāyo, vāyāmo viya cittaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kiñcāpi assāsapassāsā cittasamuṭṭhānā, karajakāyaṃ pana vinā tesaṃ appavattanato “kāyañca cittañca paṭicca assāsapassāsā”ti vuttaṃ.

Now, showing in another way the comprehension of the immaterial preceded by the material, he said, “Or else…” and so on. Therein, “Just as…” and so on is the showing of the state of arising of the in-and-out-breaths from the body and mind. ‘A blacksmith’s bellows’ means the bellows of blacksmiths for blowing on a fire. ‘Being blown’ means emitting smoke and causing wind to be taken in. ‘Corresponding’ means corresponding to that. In the phrase ‘Just so…,’ here the physical body should be seen as like the blacksmith’s bellows, and the mind as like the effort. Although the in-and-out-breaths are mind-originated, because they do not occur without the physical body, it was said, “Dependent on the body and the mind, the in-and-out-breaths arise.”

Tassāti nāmarūpassa. Paccayaṃ pariyesatīti “avijjāsamudayā rūpasamudayo”tiādinā avijjādikaṃ paccayaṃ pariyesati vīmaṃsati pariggaṇhāti. Kaṅkhaṃ vitaratīti “ahosiṃ nu kho ahaṃ atītamaddhāna”ntiādinayappavattaṃ soḷasavatthukaṃ vicikicchaṃ atikkamati pajahati. “Yaṃ kiñci rūpaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppanna”ntiādinayappavattaṃ kalāpasammasanaṃ. Pubbabhāgeti paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhipariyāpannāya [V 2.0210] udayabbayānupassanāya pubbabhāge uppanne. Obhāsādayoti obhāso ñāṇaṃ pīti passaddhi sukhaṃ adhimokkho paggaho upekkhā upaṭṭhānaṃ nikantīti ime obhāsādayo dasa.

‘Of that’ means of name-and-form. ‘He seeks the condition’ means he seeks, investigates, and comprehends the condition of ignorance and so on, by the method beginning, “With the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of form.” ‘He overcomes doubt’ means he transcends and abandons the doubt with sixteen bases that proceeds by the method beginning, “Was I indeed in the past?” The passage beginning, “Whatever material form, whether past, future, or present…” is the comprehension of groups. ‘In the preliminary stage’ means arisen in the preliminary stage of the insight into arising and passing away, which is included in the Purification by Knowledge and Vision of the Path. ‘Luminosity and so on’ means these ten: luminosity, knowledge, rapture, tranquility, bliss, resolution, exertion, equanimity, mindfulness, and attachment.

Tattha (visuddhi. 2.733; paṭi. ma. aṭṭha. 2.2.6) obhāsoti vipassanobhāso, so ca vipassanācittasamuṭṭhitaṃ santatipatitaṃ utusamuṭṭhānañca pabhassararūpaṃ. Tattha vipassanācittasamuṭṭhitaṃ yogino sarīraṭṭhameva pabhassaraṃ hutvā tiṭṭhati cittajarūpānaṃ sarīraṃ muñcitvā bahi appavattanato, itaraṃ sarīraṃ muñcitvā ñāṇānubhāvānurūpaṃ samantato pattharati, taṃ tasseva paññāyati. Tena phuṭṭhokāse rūpagatampi passati, passanto ca cakkhuviññāṇena passati, udāhu manoviññāṇenāti vīmaṃsitabbanti vadanti. Dibbacakkhulābhino viya taṃ manoviññāṇaviññeyyamevāti vattuṃ yuttaṃ viya dissati. So kho panāyaṃ obhāso kassaci bhikkhuno pallaṅkaṭṭhānamattameva obhāsento [M 2.0237] uppajjati, kassaci antogabbhaṃ, kassaci bahigabbhampi, kassaci sakalavihāraṃ, gāvutaṃ, aḍḍhayojanaṃ, yojanaṃ, dviyojanaṃ, tiyojanaṃ, kassaci pathavītalato yāva akaniṭṭhabrahmalokā ekālokaṃ kurumāno. Bhagavato pana dasasahassilokadhātuṃ obhāsento udapādi. Tasmiṃ pana uppanne yogāvacaro “na vata me ito pubbe evarūpo obhāso uppannapubbo, addhā maggappattosmi phalappattosmī”ti amaggameva “maggo”ti, aphalameva ca “phala”nti gaṇhāti. Tassa amaggaṃ “maggo”ti aphalaṃ vā “phala”nti gaṇhato vipassanāvīthi ukkantā nāma hoti. So attano mūlakammaṭṭhānaṃ vissajjetvā obhāsameva assādento nisīdati.

Therein, ‘luminosity’ means the luminosity of insight. And that is the radiant form originated from the insight-mind and continuously occurring, and also that which is originated from temperature. Therein, for the yogi, that which is originated from the insight-mind, having become luminous, remains only within the body, because mind-born materiality does not proceed outside after leaving the body. The other, after leaving the body, spreads all around in accordance with the power of knowledge, and it appears only to that one. In the space touched by it, one also sees forms. And while seeing, does one see with eye-consciousness, or with mind-consciousness? Thus, they say, it should be investigated. It seems fitting to say that, like one who has obtained the divine eye, it is to be known only by mind-consciousness. Now, this luminosity arises for a certain monk illuminating only the space of his cross-legged seat; for another, the interior of his chamber; for another, the exterior of the chamber as well; for another, the entire monastery; a gāvuta; half a yojana; a yojana; two yojanas; three yojanas; and for another, it arises making a single light from the surface of the earth up to the Akaniṭṭha Brahma world. For the Blessed One, however, it arose illuminating the ten-thousandfold world-system. When that luminosity has arisen, the yogi thinks, “Indeed, such a luminosity has never before arisen for me. Surely I have attained the path; I have attained the fruit!” Thus, he takes what is not the path as ‘the path,’ and what is not the fruit as ‘the fruit.’ For him who takes what is not the path as ‘the path’ or what is not the fruit as ‘the fruit,’ the course of insight is said to be derailed. He, having abandoned his original meditation subject, sits savoring only the luminosity.

Ñāṇanti vipassanāñāṇaṃ. Tassa kira rūpārūpadhamme tulayantassa tīrayantassa vissaṭṭhaindavajiramiva avihatavegaṃ tikhiṇaṃ sūraṃ ativisadaṃ ñāṇaṃ uppajjati.

Knowledge means insight-knowledge. It is said that for one weighing and judging material and immaterial phenomena, knowledge arises—with unimpeded momentum like a released thunderbolt of Indra, sharp, valiant, and exceedingly clear.

Pītīti vipassanāpīti. Tassa kira tasmiṃ samaye khuddikā pīti khaṇikā pīti okkantikā pīti ubbegā pīti pharaṇā pītīti ayaṃ pañcavidhā pīti sakalasarīraṃ pūrayamānā uppajjati.

Rapture means insight-rapture. It is said that for him, at that time, these five kinds of rapture arise, filling the whole body: minor rapture, momentary rapture, showering rapture, uplifting rapture, and all-pervading rapture.

Passaddhīti vipassanāpassaddhi. Tassa kira tasmiṃ samaye rattiṭṭhāne vā divāṭṭhāne vā nisinnassa kāyacittānaṃ neva daratho, na gāravaṃ, na kakkhaḷatā, na akammaññatā, na gelaññaṃ, na vaṅkatā hoti, atha kho panassa kāyacittāni passaddhāni lahūni mudūni kammaññāni [V 2.0211] suvisadāni ujukāniyeva honti. So imehi passaddhādīhi anuggahitakāyacitto tasmiṃ samaye amānusiṃ nāma ratiṃ anubhavati. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ –

Tranquility means insight-tranquility. It is said that for him, at that time, whether sitting during the night or day, there is no distress, no heaviness, no rigidity, no unworkability, no sickliness, nor crookedness of body and mind. Instead, his body and mind become tranquil, light, soft, workable, very clear, and straight. With his body and mind thus supported by these qualities of tranquility and so on, he at that time experiences a delight that is non-human. With reference to this, it is said:

“Suññāgāraṃ paviṭṭhassa, santacittassa bhikkhuno;

Amānusī ratī hoti, sammā dhammaṃ vipassato.

For a monk who has entered an empty dwelling, whose mind is peaceful, there is a non-human delight as he rightly sees the Dhamma with insight.

“Yato yato sammasati, khandhānaṃ udayabbayaṃ;

Labhatī pītipāmojjaṃ, amataṃ taṃ vijānata”nti. (dha. pa. 373-374);

Whenever he comprehends the rise and fall of the aggregates, he obtains joy and gladness; that is the Deathless for those who know.

Evamassa imaṃ amānusiṃ ratiṃ sādhayamānā lahutādisampayuttā passaddhi uppajjati.

Thus, for him, while bringing about this non-human delight, tranquility associated with lightness and so on arises.

Sukhanti [M 2.0238] vipassanāsukhaṃ. Tassa kira tasmiṃ samaye sakalasarīraṃ abhisandayamānaṃ atipaṇītaṃ sukhamuppajjati.

Happiness means insight-happiness. It is said that at that time, for him, an exceedingly refined happiness arises, suffusing his entire body.

Adhimokkhoti saddhā. Vipassanāsampayuttāyeva hissa cittacetasikānaṃ atisayappasādabhūtā balavatī saddhā uppajjati.

Resolution means faith. Indeed, for him, a strong faith arises, associated with insight, which is an exceptional serenity for his mind and mental factors.

Paggahoti vīriyaṃ. Vipassanāsampayuttameva hissa asithilamanaccāraddhaṃ supaggahitaṃ vīriyaṃ uppajjati.

Exertion means energy. Indeed, for him, energy arises, associated with insight, that is not too lax, not over-exerted, and well-exerted.

Upaṭṭhānanti sati. Vipassanāsampayuttāyeva hissa sūpaṭṭhitā suppatiṭṭhitā nikhātā acalā pabbatarājasadisā sati uppajjati. So yaṃ yaṃ ṭhānaṃ āvajjati samannāharati manasi karoti paccavekkhati, taṃ taṃ ṭhānamassa okkantitvā pakkhanditvā dibbacakkhuno paraloko viya satiyā upaṭṭhāti.

Establishment means mindfulness. Indeed, for him, mindfulness arises, associated with insight, that is well-established, firmly grounded, implanted, unshakable, like a king of mountains. Whatever object he adverts to, directs his mind to, gives attention to, or reviews, that very object, having been descended upon and rushed into, appears to him through mindfulness, just as the other world appears to one with the divine eye.

Upekkhāti vipassanupekkhā ceva āvajjanupekkhā ca. Tasmiñhissa samaye sabbasaṅkhāresu majjhattabhūtā vipassanupekkhā balavatī uppajjati, manodvāre āvajjanupekkhāpi. Sā hissa taṃ taṃ ṭhānaṃ āvajjentassa vissaṭṭhaindavajiramiva pattapuṭe pakkhandatattanārāco viya ca sūrā tikhiṇā hutvā vahati.

Equanimity means both insight-equanimity and adverting-equanimity. Indeed, at that time, for him, a strong insight-equanimity arises, which is neutral towards all formations, and also adverting-equanimity at the mind-door. For him, as he adverts to this or that object, that adverting-equanimity proceeds, being valiant and sharp, like a released thunderbolt of Indra and like a heated arrow rushing into a leaf-container.

Nikantīti [V 2.0212] vipassanānikanti. Evaṃ obhāsādipaṭimaṇḍitāya hissa vipassanāya ālayaṃ kurumānā sukhumā santākārā nikanti uppajjati, yā “kileso”ti pariggahetumpi na sakkā hoti.

Delight means insight-delight. Thus, for him, taking a liking to his insight which is adorned with light and so forth, a subtle delight of peaceful appearance arises, which cannot even be grasped as a 'defilement'.

Yathā ca obhāse, evaṃ etesupi aññatarasmiṃ uppanne yogāvacaro “na vata me ito pubbe evarūpaṃ ñāṇaṃ uppannapubbaṃ, evarūpā pīti, passaddhi, sukhaṃ, adhimokkho, paggaho, upaṭṭhānaṃ, upekkhā, nikanti uppannapubbā, addhā maggappattosmi phalappattosmī”ti amaggameva “maggo”ti aphalameva ca “phala”nti gaṇhāti, tassa amaggaṃ “maggo”ti aphalaṃ “phala”nti gaṇhato vipassanāvīthi ukkantā nāma hoti. So attano mūlakammaṭṭhānaṃ vissajjetvā nikantimeva assādento nisīdati.

And just as in the case of light, so too when any of these other phenomena arises, the yogi thinks: 'Indeed, never before has such knowledge arisen in me, nor such rapture, tranquility, happiness, resolution, exertion, establishment, equanimity, or delight. Surely I have attained the path, I have attained the fruit!' Thus he takes what is not the path as 'the path' and what is not the fruit as 'the fruit'. For him, who takes the non-path as 'the path' and the non-fruit as 'the fruit', the course of insight is said to have gone astray. Abandoning his original meditation subject, he sits savoring only the delight.

Ettha ca obhāsādayo upakkilesavatthutāya “upakkilesā”ti vuttā, na akusalattā, nikanti pana upakkileso ceva upakkilesavatthu ca[M 2.0239]. Vatthuvaseneva cete dasa, gāhavasena pana samatiṃsa honti. Kathaṃ? “Mama obhāso uppanno”ti gaṇhato hi diṭṭhiggāho hoti, “manāpo vata obhāso uppanno”ti gaṇhato mānaggāho, obhāsaṃ assādayato taṇhāgāho. Iti obhāse diṭṭhimānataṇhāvasena tayo gāhā. Tathā sesesupīti evaṃ gāhavasena samatiṃsa upakkilesā honti. Tesaṃ vasena akusalo abyatto yogāvacaro obhāsādīsu kampati vikkhipati, obhāsādīsu ekekaṃ “etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā”ti samanupassati. Tenāhu porāṇā –

Herein, light and the others are called 'corruptions' because they are the basis for corruption, not because they are unwholesome in themselves. Delight, however, is both a corruption and a basis for corruption. By way of their basis, these are ten; but by way of grasping, they become thirty. How so? For one who grasps, 'My light has arisen,' there is grasping through wrong view. For one who grasps, 'How delightful, the light has arisen!' there is grasping through conceit. For one who savors the light, there is grasping through craving. Thus, in connection with light, there are three kinds of grasping: by way of wrong view, conceit, and craving. The same applies to the rest. In this way, by way of grasping, there are thirty corruptions. Due to them, the unskillful, inexpert yogi wavers and is distracted by light and the other phenomena, and he regards each one as: 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self.' Therefore the ancients have said:

“Obhāse ceva ñāṇe ca, pītiyā ca vikampati;

Passaddhiyā sukhe ceva, yehi cittaṃ pavedhati.

He wavers in light and in knowledge, and in rapture; and in tranquility and in happiness, by which the mind is shaken.

“Adhimokkhe ca paggāhe, upaṭṭhāne ca kampati;

Upekkhāvajjanāya ceva, upekkhāya ca nikantiyā”ti. (paṭi. ma. 2.7)

He wavers in resolution and in exertion, and in establishment; he wavers in equanimity and in delight.

Kusalo paṇḍito byatto buddhisampanno yogāvacaro obhāsādīsu uppannesu “ayaṃ kho me obhāso uppanno, so kho panāyaṃ anicco saṅkhato paṭiccasamuppanno khayadhammo vayadhammo virāgadhammo nirodhadhammo”ti iti vā taṃ paññāya paricchindati upaparikkhati. Atha vā panassa [V 2.0213] evaṃ hoti – sace obhāso attā bhaveyya, attāti gahetuṃ vaṭṭeyya, anattāva panāyaṃ “attā”ti gahito. Tasmā so avasavattanaṭṭhena anattā, hutvā abhāvaṭṭhena anicco, uppādavayapaṭipīḷanaṭṭhena dukkhoti upaparikkhati. Yathā ca obhāse, evaṃ sesesupi. So evaṃ upaparikkhitvā obhāsaṃ “netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā”ti samanupassati. Ñāṇaṃ…pe… nikantiṃ “netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā”ti samanupassati. Evaṃ samanupassanto obhāsādīsu na kampati na vedhati. Tenāhu porāṇā –

A skilled, wise, discerning, intelligent meditator, when light and other phenomena arise, investigates with wisdom: 'This light has arisen for me, but it is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to decay, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation.' Or else, it occurs to him: 'If this light were self, it would be proper to take it as "self." But this is indeed not-self, though grasped as "self." Therefore, it is not-self in the sense of being uncontrollable; it is impermanent in the sense of being non-existent after having been; and it is suffering in the sense of being oppressed by arising and passing away.' He investigates the remaining phenomena in the same way as the light. Having investigated thus, he regards the light: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.' He regards knowledge... delight: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.' Thus regarding, he does not tremble or waver in the face of light and other phenomena. Therefore, the ancients have said:

“Imāni dasa ṭhānāni, paññā yassa pariccitā;

Dhammuddhaccakusalo hoti, na ca vikkhepa gacchatī”ti. (paṭi. ma. 2.7);

He whose wisdom has mastered these ten grounds becomes skilled regarding restlessness about phenomena and does not fall into distraction.

So evaṃ vikkhepaṃ agacchanto taṃ samatiṃsavidhaṃ upakkilesajaṭaṃ vijaṭetvā “obhāsādayo dhammā na maggo, upakkilesavimuttaṃ pana vīthippaṭipannaṃ vipassanāñāṇaṃ [M 2.0240] maggo”ti amaggaṃ maggañca vavatthapeti. Yaṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ “obhāsādayo dasa vipassanupakkilese pahāya upakkilesavimuttaṃ paṭipadāñāṇaṃ maggoti vavatthapetvā”ti. Udayaṃ pahāyāti udayabbayānupassanāya gahitaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ udayaṃ vissajjetvā tesaṃ bhaṅgasseva anupassanato bhaṅgānupassanāñāṇaṃ patvā ādīnavānupassanāpubbaṅgamāya nibbidānupassanāya nibbindanto muñcitukamyatāpaṭisaṅkhānupassanāsaṅkhārupekkhānulomañāṇānaṃ ciṇṇapariyante uppannagotrabhuñāṇānantaraṃ uppannena maggañāṇena sabbasaṅkhāresu virajjanto vimuccanto. Maggakkhaṇe hi ariyo virajjati vimuccatīti ca vuccati. Tenāha – “yathākkamaṃ cattāro ariyamagge pāpuṇitvā”ti. Maggaphalanibbānapahīnāvasiṭṭhakilesasaṅkhātassa paccavekkhitabbassa pabhedena ekūnavīsatibhedassa. Arahato hi avasiṭṭhakilesābhāvena ekūnavīsati paccavekkhaṇañāṇāni. Assāti ānāpānassatikammaṭṭhānikassa.

Thus, not falling into distraction, he disentangles that thirty-fold tangle of corruptions and establishes what is the non-path and what is the path: 'Phenomena such as light are not the path, but insight-knowledge, free from corruptions and proceeding along the course, is the path.' This is in reference to what was said: 'Having abandoned the ten corruptions of insight, such as light, he establishes that the knowledge of the practice, free from corruptions, is the path.' 'Having abandoned arising' means relinquishing the arising of formations grasped by the contemplation of arising and passing away, and by contemplating only their dissolution, attaining the knowledge of the contemplation of dissolution. Then, with the contemplation of danger as a precursor, becoming disenchanted through the contemplation of disgust, and through the knowledges of desire for deliverance, reflection, equanimity towards formations, and conformity, at the culmination of these practices, after the change-of-lineage knowledge has arisen, by the path-knowledge that arises immediately thereafter, one becomes dispassionate towards and liberated from all formations. For at the moment of the path, the noble one is said to become dispassionate and liberated. Therefore, it is said: 'having attained the four noble paths in sequence.' This refers to the nineteen kinds of reviewing, classified according to what is to be reviewed: the defilements abandoned by the path, the fruit, Nibbāna, and the remaining defilements. For an Arahant, as there are no remaining defilements, there are nineteen reviewing knowledges. 'Of him' refers to one who practices the meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing.

Visuṃ kammaṭṭhānabhāvanānayo nāma natthīti paṭhamacatukkavasena adhigatajjhānassa vedanācittadhammānupassanāvasena desitattā vuttaṃ. Tesanti tiṇṇaṃ catukkānaṃ. Pītippaṭisaṃvedīti pītiyā paṭi paṭi sammadeva vedanasīlo, tassā vā paṭi paṭi sammadeva vedo etassa atthi, taṃ vā paṭi paṭi sammadeva vedayamāno. Tattha kāmaṃ saṃvedanaggahaṇeneva pītiyā sakkaccaṃ viditabhāvo bodhito hoti, yehi pana pakārehi tassā saṃvedanaṃ icchitaṃ, taṃ dassetuṃ paṭi-saddaggahaṇaṃ “paṭi paṭi saṃvedīti paṭisaṃvedī”ti. Tenāha “dvīhākārehī”tiādi.

It is said that there is no separate method of meditation development, because for one who has attained jhāna by way of the first tetrad, it is taught by way of the contemplation of feelings, mind, and phenomena. 'Of them' refers to the three tetrads. 'Experiencing joy' means one whose nature is to repeatedly and thoroughly experience joy; or one for whom there is a repeated and thorough experience of it; or one who is repeatedly and thoroughly experiencing it. Here, although the state of having carefully known joy is indeed indicated by the mere inclusion of the word 'experiencing,' the prefix 'paṭi' is included to show in what ways its experience is intended, thus 'paṭi-saṃvedī' (repeatedly-experiencing). Therefore, it is said, 'in two ways,' etc.

Tattha [V 2.0214] kathaṃ ārammaṇato pīti paṭisaṃviditā hotīti pucchāvacanaṃ. Sappītike dve jhāne samāpajjatī”ti pītisahagatāni dve paṭhamadutiyajjhānāni paṭipāṭiyā samāpajjati. Tassāti tena. “Paṭisaṃviditā”ti hi padaṃ apekkhitvā kattuatthe etaṃ sāmivacanaṃ. Samāpattikkhaṇeti samāpannakkhaṇe. Jhānapaṭilābhenāti jhānena samaṅgibhāvena.
