Ārammaṇatoti ārammaṇamukhena, tadārammaṇajjhānapariyāpannā pīti paṭisaṃviditā hoti ārammaṇassa paṭisaṃviditattā. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Yathā nāma sappapariyesanaṃ carantena tassa āsaye [M 2.0241] paṭisaṃvidite sopi paṭisaṃvidito eva hoti mantāgadabalena tassa gahaṇassa sukarattā, evaṃ pītiyā āsayabhūte ārammaṇe paṭisaṃvidite sā pīti paṭisaṃviditā eva hoti salakkhaṇato sāmaññalakkhaṇato ca tassā gahaṇassa sukarattāti.

Therein, 'How is joy experienced by way of the object?' is the question. 'He attains the two jhānas accompanied by joy' means he successively attains the two, the first and second jhānas, which are associated with joy. 'Of him' means by him. Considering the word 'experienced' (paṭisaṃviditā), this is a genitive case used in the sense of the agent. 'At the moment of attainment' means at the moment of having attained. 'By the acquisition of jhāna' means by being endowed with jhāna. 'By way of the object' means through the object; the joy included in the jhāna that has that object is experienced because the object is experienced. What is meant by this? Just as, for one searching for a snake, when its lair is known, the snake itself is as good as known, because its capture is made easy by the power of charms and antidotes; so too, when the object which is the basis for joy is experienced, that joy is indeed experienced, because its grasping is made easy by way of its specific and general characteristics.

Kathaṃ asammohato pīti paṭisaṃviditā hotīti ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ. Vipassanākkhaṇeti vipassanāpaññāya tikkhavisadappavattāya visayato dassanakkhaṇe. Lakkhaṇapaṭivedhenāti pītiyā salakkhaṇassa sāmaññalakkhaṇassa ca paṭivijjhanena. Yañhi yassa visesato sāmaññato ca lakkhaṇaṃ, tasmiṃ vidite so yāthāvato vidito eva hoti. Tenāha – “asammohato pīti paṭisaṃviditā hotī”ti.

How is joy experienced without delusion? This should be brought forward and connected. 'At the moment of insight' means at the moment of seeing by way of its object with insight-wisdom that proceeds sharply and clearly. 'By penetrating the characteristics' means by penetrating the specific characteristic and the general characteristics of joy. For when the characteristic of something—both its specific and its general aspect—is known, that thing is indeed truly known. Therefore, it is said: 'Joy is experienced without delusion.'

Idāni tamatthaṃ pāḷiyā eva vibhāvetuṃ “vuttañheta”ntiādimāha. Tattha dīghaṃassāsavasenātiādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva. Tattha pana satokāritādassanavasena pāḷi āgatā, idha pītippaṭisaṃviditāvasena. Pītippaṭisaṃviditā ca atthato vibhattā eva. Apica ayamettha saṅkhepattho – dīghaṃassāsavasenāti dīghassa assāsassa ārammaṇabhūtassa vasena pajānato sā pīti paṭisaṃviditā hotīti sambandho. Cittassa ekaggataṃ avikkhepaṃ pajānatoti jhānapariyāpannaṃ avikkhepoti laddhanāmaṃ cittassekaggataṃ taṃsampayuttāya paññāya pajānato. Yatheva hi ārammaṇamukhena pīti paṭisaṃviditā hoti, evaṃ taṃsampayuttadhammāpi ārammaṇamukhena paṭisaṃviditā eva hontīti. Sati upaṭṭhitā hotīti dīghaṃassāsavasena jhānasampayuttā sati tassa ārammaṇe upaṭṭhitā ārammaṇamukhena jhānepi upaṭṭhitā nāma hoti. Tāya satiyāti evaṃ upaṭṭhitāya tāya satiyā yathāvuttena tena ñāṇena suppaṭividitattā ārammaṇassa tassa vasena tadārammaṇā sā pīti paṭisaṃviditā hoti. Dīghaṃpassāsavasenātiādīsupi imināva nayena attho veditabbo.

Now, to clarify that meaning in the Pāḷi itself, he says, “For it is said,” and so on. Therein, regarding “by means of a long in-breath” and so on, what should be said has already been stated below. However, there the Pāḷi is presented by way of showing the state of acting with mindfulness, while here it is by way of experiencing joy. And the experience of joy is, in meaning, indeed distinguished. Furthermore, this is the concise meaning here: regarding “by means of a long in-breath,” the connection is that for one who knows by means of the long in-breath, which has become the object, that joy is experienced. “Knowing the unification of mind, the non-distraction” means for one who knows, by means of the wisdom associated with it, the unification of mind, which is included in jhāna and has received the name “non-distraction.” For just as joy is experienced by way of the object, so too are the states associated with it indeed experienced by way of the object. “Mindfulness is established” means that mindfulness associated with jhāna, by means of a long in-breath, is established on its object; by way of the object, it is said to be established in the jhāna as well. “By that mindfulness” means that by that mindfulness thus established, because its object is thoroughly penetrated by that aforementioned knowledge, that joy, which has that as its object, is experienced by means of that object. In the case of “by means of a long out-breath” and so on, too, the meaning should be understood by this same method.

Evaṃ paṭhamacatukkavasena dassitaṃ pītippaṭisaṃvedanaṃ ārammaṇato asammohato ca vibhāgaso [V 2.0215] dassetuṃ “āvajjato”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha āvajjatoti jhānaṃ āvajjentassa. Sā pītīti sā jhānapariyāpannā pīti. Jānatoti samāpannakkhaṇe ārammaṇamukhena jānato. Tassa sā pīti paṭisaṃviditā hotīti sambandho. Passatoti dassanabhūtena [M 2.0242] ñāṇena jhānato vuṭṭhāya passantassa. Paccavekkhatoti jhānaṃ paccavekkhantassa. Cittaṃ adhiṭṭhahatoti “ettakaṃ velaṃ jhānasamaṅgī bhavissāmī”ti jhānacittaṃ adhiṭṭhahantassa. Evaṃ pañcannaṃ vasībhāvānaṃ vasena jhānassa pajānanamukhena ārammaṇato pītiyā paṭisaṃvedanā dassitā.

Thus, to show the experience of joy presented by way of the first tetrad—distinguished by way of its object and non-delusion—the passage beginning with “while adverting” is stated. Therein, “while adverting” refers to one adverting to the jhāna. “That joy” is that joy included within the jhāna. “While knowing” refers to one knowing by way of the object at the moment of attainment. The connection is: “that joy is experienced by him.” “While seeing” refers to one who, having emerged from the jhāna, sees with the knowledge that has become seeing. “While reviewing” refers to one reviewing the jhāna. “While determining the mind” refers to one determining the jhāna-mind, thinking, “I will be endowed with jhāna for this long.” Thus, by way of these five masteries, the experience of joy by way of the object is shown through knowing the jhāna.

Idāni yehi dhammehi jhānaṃ vipassanā ca sijjhanti, tesaṃ jhānapariyāpannānaṃ vipassanāmaggapariyāpannānañca saddhādīnaṃ vasena pītippaṭisaṃvedanaṃ dassetuṃ “saddhāya adhimuccato”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha adhimuccatoti saddahantassa, samathavipassanāvasenāti adhippāyo. Vīriyaṃ paggaṇhatotiādīsupi eseva nayo. Abhiññeyyanti abhivisiṭṭhāya paññāya jānitabbaṃ. Abhijānatoti vipassanāpaññāpubbaṅgamāya maggapaññāya jānato. Pariññeyyanti dukkhasaccaṃ tīraṇapariññāya maggapaññāya ca parijānato. Pahātabbanti samudayasaccaṃ pahānapariññāya maggapaññāya ca pajahato. Bhāvayato sacchikaroto bhāvetabbaṃ maggasaccaṃ, sacchikātabbaṃ nirodhasaccaṃ. Keci panettha pītiyā eva vasena abhiññeyyādīni uddharanti, taṃ ayuttaṃ jhānādisamudāyaṃ uddharitvā tato pītiyā niddhāraṇassa adhippetattā.

Now, to show the experience of joy by way of faith and other factors—which are included in jhāna and in the path of insight, and by which both jhāna and insight are accomplished—the passage beginning with “one who is resolved through faith” is stated. Therein, “resolved” means one who has faith; the intention is by way of serenity and insight. In “one who exerts energy” and so on, too, this is the same method. “To be directly known” means it is to be known by superior wisdom. “One who directly knows” refers to one who knows with the wisdom of the path, which is preceded by the wisdom of insight. “To be fully understood” refers to one who fully understands the truth of suffering by means of the full understanding of discrimination and the wisdom of the path. “To be abandoned” refers to one who abandons the truth of the origin by means of the full understanding of abandoning and the wisdom of the path. For one who develops and realizes, the truth of the path is to be developed, and the truth of cessation is to be realized. Some, however, here extract “to be directly known” and so on solely by way of joy. That is incorrect, because the intention is to extract the collection of jhāna and other factors, and from that, to determine joy.

Ettha ca “dīghaṃassāsavasenā”tiādinā paṭhamacatukkavasena ārammaṇato pītippaṭisaṃvedanaṃ vuttaṃ, tathā “āvajjato”tiādīhi pañcahi padehi. “Abhiññeyyaṃ abhijānato”tiādīhi pana asammohato, “saddhāya adhimuccato”tiādīhi ubhayathāpi saṅkhepato samathavasena ārammaṇato vipassanāvasena asammohato pītippaṭisaṃvedanaṃ vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kasmā panettha vedanānupassanāyaṃ pītisīsena vedanā gahitā, na sarūpato evāti? Bhūmivibhāgādivasena vedanaṃ bhinditvā catudhā vedanānupassanaṃ dassetuṃ. Apica vedanākammaṭṭhānaṃ dassento bhagavā pītiyā oḷārikattā taṃsampayuttasukhaṃ sukhaggahaṇatthaṃ pītisīsena dasseti.

And here, the experience of joy by way of the object is stated by way of the first tetrad, beginning with “by means of a long in-breath,” and similarly by the five terms beginning with “while adverting.” It should be understood that by the terms beginning with “knowing what is to be directly known,” it is stated by way of non-delusion; and by the terms beginning with “being resolved through faith,” the experience of joy is stated concisely in both ways: by way of serenity in relation to the object, and by way of insight in relation to non-delusion. But why here, in the contemplation of feelings, is feeling taken with joy as the heading, and not just in its own nature? It is taken thus to show the fourfold contemplation of feelings by dividing feeling by way of the division of grounds and so on. Furthermore, while teaching the meditation subject of feeling, the Blessed One, because of the grossness of joy, teaches the pleasure associated with it with joy as the heading, for the sake of the easy grasping of pleasure.

Eteneva nayena avasesapadānīti sukhappaṭisaṃvedī cittasaṅkhārappaṭisaṃvedīti padāni pītippaṭisaṃvedī-pade āgatanayeneva atthato veditabbāni. Sakkā hi “dvīhākārehi sukhappaṭisaṃviditā hoti, cittasaṅkhārappaṭisaṃviditā hoti ārammaṇato”tiādinā pītiṭṭhāne sukhādipadāni [M 2.0243] pakkhipitvā “sukhasahagatāni tīṇi jhānāni cattāri vā jhānāni samāpajjatī”tiādinā atthaṃ viññātuṃ. Tenāha “tiṇṇaṃ jhānānaṃ vasenā”tiādi. Vedanādayoti [V 2.0216] ādi-saddena saññā gahitā. Tenāha “dve khandhā”ti. Vipassanābhūmidassanatthanti pakiṇṇakasaṅkhārasammasanavasena vipassanāya bhūmidassanatthaṃ “sukhanti dve sukhānī”tiādi vuttaṃ samathe kāyikasukhābhāvato. Soti so passambhanapariyāyena vutto nirodho. “Imassa hi bhikkhuno apariggahitakāle”tiādinā vitthārato kāyasaṅkhāre vutto, tasmā tattha vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Tattha kāyasaṅkhāravasena āgato, idha cittasaṅkhāravasenāti ayameva viseso.

“By this same method, the remaining terms”: the terms “experiencing pleasure” and “experiencing mental formations” should be understood in meaning by the very method that occurred in the term “experiencing joy.” For it is possible to understand the meaning by inserting the terms “pleasure” and so on in the place of joy, as in the statement, “By two modes, pleasure is experienced, mental formations are experienced, by way of the object,” and so on, and “one attains the three jhānas or four jhānas accompanied by pleasure,” and so on. Therefore, he said, “by way of the three jhānas,” and so on. “Feeling and so on”: by the word “and so on,” perception is included. Therefore, he said, “two aggregates.” “For the purpose of showing the ground for insight”: for the purpose of showing the ground for insight by way of comprehending the miscellaneous formations, the passage “pleasure means two pleasures” and so on was stated, because of the absence of bodily pleasure in serenity. “That”: that is cessation, spoken of by way of tranquillization. The bodily formation is spoken of in detail in the passage, “For this monk, at a time when it is not grasped,” and so on; therefore, it should be understood by the very method stated there. This alone is the difference: there it came by way of the bodily formation, while here it is by way of the mental formation.

Evaṃ cittasaṅkhārassa passambhanaṃ atidesena dassetvā yadaññaṃ imasmiṃ catukke vattabbaṃ, taṃ dassetuṃ “apicā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha pītipadeti “pītippaṭisaṃvedī”tiādinā desitakoṭṭhāse. Pītisīsena vedanā vuttāti pītiapadesena taṃsampayuttā vedanā vuttā, na pītīti adhippāyo. Tattha kāraṇaṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva. Dvīsu cittasaṅkhārapadesūti “cittasaṅkhārappaṭisaṃvedī passambhayaṃ cittasaṅkhāra”nti cittasaṅkhārapaṭisaṃyuttesu dvīsu padesu. “Viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpa”nti vacanato cittena paṭibaddhāti cittapaṭibaddhā. Tato eva kāmaṃ cittena saṅkharīyantīti cittasaṅkhārā, saññāvedanādayo, idha pana upalakkhaṇamattaṃ, saññāvedanāva adhippetāti āha “saññāsampayuttā vedanā”ti.

Having thus shown the calming of mental formations by way of extension, the passage beginning with “furthermore” is stated to show what else is to be said in this tetrad. Here, “in the term for joy” refers to the section taught with “experiencing joy,” and so on. “Feeling is stated under the heading of joy” means that feeling associated with it is stated by way of the designation of joy, not joy itself—this is the intention. The reason for that has already been stated below. “In the two terms for mental formations” refers to the two terms connected with mental formations, namely, “experiencing mental formations” and “calming mental formations.” According to the statement, “With consciousness as condition, name-and-form arises,” they are connected to consciousness. Therefore, precisely because they are conditioned by consciousness, they are called mental formations—perception, feeling, and so on. Here, however, this is merely an indication; only perception and feeling are intended, thus he says, “feeling associated with perception.”

Cittappaṭisaṃvedīti ettha dvīhākārehi cittapaṭisaṃviditā hoti ārammaṇato asammohato ca. Kathaṃ ārammaṇato? Cattāri jhānāni samāpajjati, tassa samāpattikkhaṇe jhānapaṭilābhenātiādinā vuttanayānusārena sabbaṃ suviññeyyanti āha – “catunnaṃ jhānānaṃ vasena cittapaṭisaṃviditā veditabbā”ti. Cittaṃ modentoti jhānasampayuttaṃ cittaṃ sampayuttāya pītiyā modayamāno, taṃ vā pītiṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā pavattaṃ vipassanācittaṃ tāya eva ārammaṇabhūtāya pītiyāmodayamāno. Pamodentotiādīni padāni tasseva vevacanāni pītipariyāyabhāvato.

“One who experiences the mind”—here, the experience of the mind occurs in two ways: by way of the object and by way of non-delusion. How by way of the object? One attains the four jhānas; at the moment of attainment, in accordance with the method stated beginning with “through the attainment of jhāna,” everything is easily known. Thus it is said: “The experience of the mind should be understood by way of the four jhānas.” “Gladdening the mind” means gladdening the mind associated with jhāna with the joy associated with it; or, gladdening the insight-consciousness, which proceeds by taking that very joy as its object, with that same joy which has become the object. The terms “delighting” and the like are synonyms for that, being equivalent to joy.

Sampayuttāya pītiyā cittaṃ āmodetīti jhānacittasampayuttāya pītisambojjhaṅgabhūtāya odagyalakkhaṇāya jhānapītiyā tameva jhānacittaṃ sahajātādipaccayavasena [M 2.0244] ceva jhānapaccayavasena ca paribrūhento haṭṭhappahaṭṭhākāraṃ pāpento āmodeti pamodeti ca. Ārammaṇaṃ katvāti uḷāraṃ jhānasampayuttaṃ pītiṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā pavattamānaṃ vipassanācittaṃ tāya eva ārammaṇabhūtāya pītiyā yogāvacaro haṭṭhappahaṭṭhākāraṃ pāpento “āmodeti pamodetī”ti vuccati.

“He gladdens the mind with associated joy” means that by means of the jhāna-joy—which is associated with the jhāna-consciousness, has become the enlightenment factor of joy, and is characterized by uplift—he gladdens and delights that very jhāna-consciousness, augmenting it and bringing it to a state of elation and delight by way of co-nascence and other conditions, and by way of jhāna conditions. “Taking as object” means that when a meditator, having taken the sublime joy associated with jhāna as an object, brings the proceeding insight-consciousness to a state of elation and delight by means of that very joy which has become the object, he is said to “gladden and delight.”

Samaṃ [V 2.0217] ṭhapentoti yathā īsakampi līnapakkhaṃ uddhaccapakkhañca anupaggamma anonataṃ anunnataṃ yathā indriyānaṃ samattapaṭipattiyā avisamaṃ, samādhissa vā ukkaṃsagamanena āneñjappattiyā sammadeva ṭhitaṃ hoti, evaṃ appanāvasena ṭhapento. Lakkhaṇappaṭivedhenāti aniccādikassa lakkhaṇassa paṭi paṭi vijjhanena khaṇe khaṇe avabodhena. Khaṇikacittekaggatāti khaṇamattaṭṭhitiko samādhi. Sopi hi ārammaṇe nirantaraṃ ekākārena pavattamāno paṭipakkhena anabhibhūto appito viya cittaṃ niccalaṃ ṭhapeti. Tena vuttaṃ “evaṃ uppannāyā”tiādi.

“He establishes it evenly” means that he establishes it by way of absorption, so that it does not incline even slightly towards the side of sluggishness or the side of restlessness, being neither depressed nor elated, and being even in accordance with the balanced practice of the faculties; or, by the concentration's advance to excellence, through the attainment of imperturbability, it stands perfectly steady. “By penetration of the characteristics” means by repeatedly piercing through the characteristics of impermanence and so forth, by understanding them moment by moment. “Momentary one-pointedness of mind” is concentration that lasts only for a moment. For even that, when occurring uninterruptedly in a single mode upon the object, undisturbed by opposition, fixes the mind immovably as if it were planted. Therefore, it is said, “Thus arisen,” and so on.

Mocentoti vikkhambhanavimuttivasena vivecento visuṃ karonto, nīvaraṇāni pajahantoti attho. Vipassanākkhaṇeti bhaṅgānupassanākkhaṇe. Bhaṅgo hi nāma aniccatāya paramā koṭi, tasmā tāya bhaṅgānupassako yogāvacaro cittamukhena sabbaṃ saṅkhāragataṃ aniccato passati, no niccato, aniccassa dukkhattā dukkhassa ca anattattā tadeva dukkhato anupassati, no sukhato, anattato anupassati, no attato. Yasmā pana yaṃ aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ anattā, na taṃ abhinanditabbaṃ, yañca na abhinanditabbaṃ, na taṃ rañjitabbaṃ, tasmā bhaṅgadassanānusārena “aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ anattā”ti saṅkhāragate diṭṭhe tasmiṃ nibbindati, no nandati, virajjati, no rajjati, so evaṃ nibbindanto virajjanto lokiyeneva tāva ñāṇena rāgaṃ nirodheti no samudeti, nāssa samudayaṃ karotīti attho. Atha vā so evaṃ viratto yathā diṭṭhaṃ saṅkhāragataṃ, taṃ tathā diṭṭhaṃ attano ñāṇena nirodheti no samudeti, nirodhamevassa manasi karoti, no samudayanti attho, so evaṃ paṭipanno paṭinissajjati, no ādiyatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Ayañhi aniccādianupassanā saddhiṃ khandhābhisaṅkhārehi kilesānaṃ pariccajanato saṅkhatadosadassanena tabbiparīte nibbāne tanninnatāya pakkhandanato ca pariccāgapaṭinissaggo ceva pakkhandanapaṭinissaggo [M 2.0245] cāti vuccati. Tasmā tāya samannāgato yogāvacaro vuttanayena kilese ca pariccajati, nibbāne ca pakkhandati. Tena vuttaṃ “so vipassanākkhaṇe aniccānupassanāya niccasaññāto cittaṃ mocento vimocento…pe… paṭinissaggānupassanāya ādānato cittaṃ mocento vimocento assasati ceva passasati cā”ti.

“He releases” means separating, making distinct, by way of release through suppression; that is, abandoning the hindrances. “The moment of insight” refers to the moment of contemplating dissolution. For dissolution is indeed the ultimate limit of impermanence. Therefore, by means of it, the meditator contemplating dissolution sees all conditioned phenomena as impermanent, not permanent, through the mind's eye. Because what is impermanent is suffering, and what is suffering is non-self, he contemplates it as suffering, not as happiness, and as non-self, not as self. Since whatever is impermanent, suffering, and non-self should not be delighted in, and what should not be delighted in should not be attached to, therefore, by following the observation of dissolution, when the conditioned is seen as “impermanent, suffering, non-self,” he becomes disenchanted with it, not delighted; he becomes dispassionate, not attached. Thus disenchanted and dispassionate, with mundane knowledge for the time being, he brings lust to cessation, he does not arouse it; that is, he does not cause its arising. Or, being thus dispassionate, with his own knowledge he brings to cessation the conditioned phenomena that he has seen in such a way; he does not cause them to arise. That is, he attends only to their cessation, not to their arising. Practicing thus, he relinquishes, he does not grasp—this is what is said. For this contemplation of impermanence and so on is called both “relinquishment by abandonment” and “relinquishment by leaping forth,” because of abandoning the defilements together with the aggregate-formations through seeing the faults of the conditioned, and because of inclining towards and leaping into Nibbāna, which is the opposite of that. Therefore, endowed with this, the meditator, in the manner described, both abandons defilements and leaps into Nibbāna. Hence it is said: “At the moment of insight, through the contemplation of impermanence, he releases and frees the mind from the perception of permanence… through the contemplation of relinquishment, he releases and frees the mind from grasping—he breathes in and breathes out.”

Tattha aniccassa, aniccanti vā anupassanā aniccānupassanā. Tebhūmakadhammānaṃ aniccataṃ gahetvā pavattāya vipassanāya etaṃ nāmaṃ. Niccasaññātoti saṅkhatadhamme “niccā sassatā”ti pavattāya micchāsaññāya. Saññāsīsena cittadiṭṭhīnampi gahaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Esa nayo sukhasaññādīsupi. Nibbidānupassanāyāti saṅkhāresu nibbindanākārena pavattāya anupassanāya[V 2.0218]. Nanditoti sappītikataṇhāto. Virāgānupassanāyāti tathā virajjanākārena pavattāya anupassanāya. Tena vuttaṃ “rāgato mocento”ti. Nirodhānupassanāyāti saṅkhārānaṃ nirodhassa anupassanāya. Yathā saṅkhārā nirujjhantiyeva āyatiṃ punabbhavavasena nuppajjanti, evaṃ vā anupassanā nirodhānupassanā. Muñcitukamyatā hi ayaṃ balappattā. Tenāha “samudayato mocento”ti. Paṭinissajjanākārena pavattā anupassanā paṭinissaggānupassanā. Ādānatoti niccādivasena gahaṇato, paṭisandhiggahaṇato vāti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

Therein, the contemplation of what is impermanent, or contemplating 'as impermanent', is the contemplation of impermanence. This is the name for the insight that proceeds by taking up the impermanence of the phenomena of the three planes. 'From the perception of permanence' refers to the wrong perception that proceeds regarding conditioned phenomena as 'permanent, eternal'. It should be understood that the grasping of consciousness and views is also included under the heading of perception. This is the method also in the case of the perceptions of pleasure and so on. 'By the contemplation of disenchantment' means by the contemplation that proceeds in the manner of being disenchanted with formations. 'Nandito' means from craving accompanied by delight. 'By the contemplation of dispassion' means by the contemplation that proceeds in the manner of becoming dispassionate. Therefore, it is said, 'releasing from lust'. 'By the contemplation of cessation' means by the contemplation of the cessation of formations. Or, the contemplation of how formations just cease and do not arise again in the future by way of a new existence is the contemplation of cessation. For this is a desire for release that has gained strength. Therefore, he said, 'releasing from the origin'. The contemplation that proceeds in the manner of relinquishing is the contemplation of relinquishment. 'From grasping' means from grasping by way of permanence and so forth, or from grasping rebirth-linking—thus the meaning should be understood here.

Aniccanti anupassī, aniccassa vā anupassanasīlo aniccānupassīti ettha kiṃ pana taṃ aniccaṃ, kathaṃ vā aniccaṃ, kā vā aniccānupassanā, kassa vā aniccānupassanāti catukkaṃ vibhāvetabbanti taṃ dassento “aniccaṃ veditabba”ntiādimāha. Tattha niccaṃ nāma dhuvaṃ sassataṃ yathā taṃ nibbānaṃ, na niccanti aniccaṃ, udayabbayavantaṃ, atthato saṅkhatā dhammāti āha aniccanti pañcakkhandhā. Kasmā? Uppādavayaññathattabhāvāti, uppādavayaññathattasabbhāvāti attho. Tattha saṅkhatadhammānaṃ hetupaccayehi uppajjanaṃ ahutvā sambhavo attalābho uppādo, uppannānaṃ tesaṃ khaṇanirodho vināso vayo, jarāya aññathābhāvo aññathattaṃ. Yathā hi uppādāvatthāya bhinnāya bhaṅgāvatthāyaṃ vatthubhedo natthi, evaṃ ṭhitisaṅkhātāyaṃ bhaṅgābhimukhāvatthāyampi vatthubhedo natthi. Yattha jarāvohāro, tasmā ekassapi dhammassa jarā yujjati, yā khaṇikajarāti [M 2.0246] vuccati. Ekaṃsena ca uppādabhaṅgāvatthāsu vatthuno abhedo icchitabbo, aññathā “añño uppajjati, añño bhijjatī”ti āpajjeyya. Tayidaṃ khaṇikajaraṃ sandhāyāha “aññathatta”nti.

One who contemplates 'as impermanent', or one whose nature is to contemplate what is impermanent, is 'one who contemplates impermanence'. Herein, what is that which is impermanent? How is it impermanent? What is the contemplation of impermanence? And for whom is the contemplation of impermanence? This tetrad should be clarified. Showing this, he said, 'Impermanence should be known,' and so on. Therein, what is called 'permanent' is stable, eternal, like Nibbāna. What is not permanent is 'impermanent', possessing arising and passing away. In meaning, it is conditioned phenomena; thus he said the five aggregates are 'impermanent'. Why? Because of the state of arising, passing away, and alteration; the meaning is: because of the existence of arising, passing away, and alteration. Therein, for conditioned phenomena, their arising through causes and conditions—their coming into being from not having been, their acquisition of selfhood—is 'arising'. For those that have arisen, their momentary cessation, their destruction, is 'passing away'. Alteration by way of aging is 'otherness'. For just as when the state of arising has broken up, there is no difference in substance in the state of dissolution, so too, in the state designated as 'duration', which is the state facing dissolution, there is no difference in substance. Wherein the term 'aging' is used, therefore, aging is applicable even to a single phenomenon, which is called 'momentary aging'. And it is to be accepted that there is absolutely no difference of substance in the states of arising and dissolution; otherwise, it would follow that 'one thing arises, another perishes'. Referring to this momentary aging, he said 'alteration'.

Yassa lakkhaṇattayassa bhāvā khandhesu aniccasamaññā, tasmiṃ lakkhaṇattaye aniccatā samaññāti “aniccatāti tesaṃyeva uppādavayaññathatta”nti vatvā visesato dhammānaṃ khaṇikanirodhe aniccatāvohāroti dassento “hutvā abhāvo vā”tiādimāha. Tattha uppādapubbakattā abhāvassa hutvā-gahaṇaṃ. Tena pākaṭabhāvapubbakattaṃ vināsabhāvassa dasseti. Tenevākārenāti nibbattanākārena. Khaṇabhaṅgenāti khaṇikanirodhena. Tassā aniccatāyāti khaṇikabhaṅgasaṅkhātāya aniccatāya. Tāya anupassanāyāti yathāvuttāya aniccānupassanāya. Samannāgatoti samaṅgibhūto yogāvacaro.

The designation 'impermanence' exists for the aggregates because of the presence of a triad of characteristics, and in that triad of characteristics, 'impermanence' is the designation. Thus, having said, 'Impermanence is just their arising, passing away, and alteration,' and showing that, specifically, the term 'impermanence' is used for the momentary cessation of phenomena, he said, 'or, having been, non-existence,' and so on. Therein, the taking of 'having been' for non-existence is because it is preceded by arising. By that, he shows that the state of destruction is preceded by a manifest state. 'In that very manner' means in the manner of production. 'By momentary dissolution' means by momentary cessation. 'Of that impermanence' means of the impermanence designated as momentary dissolution. 'By that contemplation' means by the contemplation of impermanence as stated above. 'Endowed' means the yogī who is furnished with it.

Khayoti saṅkhārānaṃ vināso. Virajjanaṃ tesaṃyeva vilujjanaṃ virāgo, khayo eva virāgo khayavirāgo, khaṇikanirodho. Accantamettha etasmiṃ adhigate saṅkhārā virajjanti nirujjhantīti accantavirāgo, [V 2.0219] nibbānaṃ. Tenāha “khayavirāgoti saṅkhārānaṃ khaṇabhaṅgo. Accantavirāgoti nibbāna”nti. Tadubhayadassanavasena pavattāti khayavirāgānupassanāvasena vipassanāya, accantavirāgānupassanāvasena maggassa pavatti yojetabbā. Ārammaṇato vā vipassanāya khayavirāgānupassanāvasena pavatti, tanninnabhāvato accantavirāgānupassanāvasena, maggassa pana asammohato khayavirāgānupassanāvasena, ārammaṇato accantavirāgānupassanāvasena pavatti veditabbā. Eseva nayoti iminā yasmā virāgānupassīpade vuttanayānusārena “dve nirodhā khayanirodho ca accantanirodho cā”ti evamādiatthavaṇṇanaṃ atidissati, tasmā virāgaṭṭhāne nirodhapadaṃ pakkhipitvā “khayo saṅkhārānaṃ vināso”tiādinā idha vuttanayena tassa atthavaṇṇanā veditabbā.

'Destruction' is the perishing of formations. Fading away, the breaking up of those very same things, is 'dispassion'. Destruction itself is dispassion, hence 'destruction-dispassion', which is momentary cessation. Herein, when this is ultimately attained, formations fade away and cease; this is 'ultimate dispassion', which is Nibbāna. Therefore, he said, ''Destruction-dispassion' is the momentary dissolution of formations. 'Ultimate dispassion' is Nibbāna.' By way of seeing both, the occurrence of insight should be connected with the contemplation of destruction-dispassion, and the occurrence of the path with the contemplation of ultimate dispassion. Or, the occurrence of insight should be known by way of the contemplation of destruction-dispassion from the standpoint of its object, and by way of the contemplation of ultimate dispassion due to its inclination towards that. But for the path, its occurrence should be known by way of the contemplation of destruction-dispassion due to non-delusion, and by way of the contemplation of ultimate dispassion from the standpoint of its object. 'This is the method': by this, since, in accordance with the method stated in the section on 'one who contemplates dispassion', the explanation of the meaning such as, 'There are two cessations: cessation by destruction and ultimate cessation,' is indicated, therefore, having inserted the word 'cessation' in the place of 'dispassion', the explanation of its meaning should be understood in the manner stated here, beginning with ''Destruction' is the perishing of formations.'

Paṭinissajjanaṃ pahātabbassa tadaṅgavasena vā samucchedavasena vā pariccajanaṃ pariccāgapaṭinissaggo. Tathā sabbupadhīnaṃ paṭinissaggabhūte visaṅkhāre attano nissajjanaṃ tanninnatāya vā tadārammaṇatāya vā tattha pakkhandanaṃ pakkhandanapaṭinissaggo. Tadaṅgavasenāti ettha aniccānupassanā tāva tadaṅgappahānavasena niccasaññaṃ pariccajati, pariccajantī ca tassā tathā appavattiyaṃ [M 2.0247] ye “nicca”nti gahaṇavasena kilesā tammūlakā ca abhisaṅkhārā tadubhayamūlakā ca vipākakkhandhā anāgate uppajjeyyuṃ, te sabbepi appavattikaraṇavasena pariccajati, tathā dukkhasaññādayo. Tenāha – “vipassanā hi tadaṅgavasena saddhiṃ khandhābhisaṅkhārehi kilese pariccajatī”ti. Saṅkhatadosadassanenāti saṅkhate tebhūmakasaṅkhāragate aniccatādidosadassanena. Niccādibhāvena tabbiparīte. Tanninnatāyāti tadadhimuttatāya. Pakkhandatīti anupavisati anupavisantaṃ viya hoti. Saddhiṃ khandhābhisaṅkhārehi kilese pariccajatīti maggena kilesesu pariccattesu avipākadhammatāpādanena abhisaṅkhārā tammūlakā ca khandhā anuppattirahabhāvena pariccattā nāma hontīti sabbepi te maggo pariccajatīti vuttaṃ. Ubhayanti vipassanāñāṇaṃ maggañāṇañca. Maggañāṇampi hi gotrabhuñāṇassa anu pacchā nibbānadassanato anupassanāti vuccati.

The relinquishment of what is to be abandoned is abandoning either by way of substitution or by way of cutting off—this is relinquishment by abandoning (pariccāgapaṭinissaggo). Similarly, relinquishment by plunging (pakkhandanapaṭinissaggo) is the casting off of oneself into the unconditioned (Nibbāna), which is the relinquishment of all substrates of existence, or plunging into that (Nibbāna) by way of inclination towards it or by making it the object. 'By way of substitution' here means that, for instance, the contemplation of impermanence first abandons the perception of permanence by way of temporary abandonment. In so doing, it also abandons all defilements rooted in grasping 'permanence,' as well as the formations rooted in them and the resultant aggregates rooted in both that might arise in the future—all of these it abandons by causing their non-occurrence. The same applies to perceptions of suffering, etc. Hence it is said: 'Insight, by way of substitution, relinquishes defilements together with the formations of the aggregates.' 'By seeing the faults in the conditioned' means seeing the faults such as impermanence in the conditioned, which pertains to the formations of the three realms, that are contrary to permanence, etc. 'Inclination towards that' means being resolved on that. 'Plunges' means entering—it is as if one is entering. 'Relinquishes defilements together with the formations of the aggregates' means that when defilements are abandoned by the path, the formations and the aggregates rooted in them are also indeed abandoned by being brought to a state of being non-resultant phenomena and by being rendered incapable of arising; thus, it is said that the path relinquishes all of them. 'Both' refers to insight knowledge and path knowledge. For even path knowledge, following immediately after the change-of-lineage knowledge, is called 'contemplation' (anupassanā) because it sees Nibbāna.

Idañca catutthacatukkaṃ suddhavipassanāvaseneva vuttaṃ, purimāni pana tīṇi samathavipassanāvasena. Evaṃ catunnaṃ catukkānaṃ vasena soḷasavatthukāya ānāpānassatiyā bhāvanā veditabbā. Evaṃ soḷasavatthuvasena ca ayaṃ ānāpānassati bhāvitā mahapphalā hoti mahānisaṃsāti veditabbā. “Evaṃ bhāvito kho, bhikkhave, ānāpānassatisamādhī”tiādinā pana santabhāvādivasena mahānisaṃsatā dassitā. Vitakkupacchedasamatthatāyapi cassa mahānisaṃsatā [V 2.0220] daṭṭhabbā. Ayañhi santapaṇītaasecanakasukhavihārattā samādhiantarāyakarānaṃ vitakkānaṃ vasena ito cito ca cittassa vidhāvanaṃ upacchinditvā ānāpānārammaṇābhimukhameva cittaṃ karoti. Teneva vuttaṃ – “ānāpānassati bhāvetabbā vitakkupacchedāyā”ti (a. ni. 9.1; udā. 31). Vijjāvimuttipāripūriyā mūlabhāvenapi cassā mahānisaṃsatā veditabbā. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

This fourth tetrad is spoken purely in terms of insight, while the previous three are in terms of serenity and insight. Thus, the development of mindfulness of breathing should be understood through these four tetrads, making sixteen aspects. When mindfulness of breathing is developed in this way through these sixteen aspects, it is of great fruit and great benefit. The great benefits are shown in terms of tranquility and so forth, as stated: "Thus developed, monks, concentration through mindfulness of breathing..." Moreover, its great benefit should be seen in its ability to cut off discursive thoughts. For this concentration, being peaceful, refined, a source of refreshment, and a dwelling of ease, severs the wandering of the mind here and there caused by thoughts that obstruct concentration, and directs the mind solely toward the object of the breath. Therefore, it is said: "Mindfulness of breathing should be developed for the cutting off of discursive thoughts" (A.N. 9.1; Ud. 31). Its great benefit should also be understood in that it serves as the root for the fulfillment of knowledge and liberation. For the Blessed One has said:

“Ānāpānassati, bhikkhave, bhāvitā bahulīkatā cattāro satipaṭṭhāne paripūreti, cattāro satipaṭṭhānā bhāvitā bahulīkatā satta bojjhaṅge paripūrenti, satta bojjhaṅgā bhāvitā bahulīkatā vijjāvimuttiṃ paripūrentī”ti (ma. ni. 3.147).

"Mindfulness of breathing, monks, when developed and cultivated, perfects the four foundations of mindfulness. The four foundations of mindfulness, when developed and cultivated, perfect the seven factors of enlightenment. The seven factors of enlightenment, when developed and cultivated, perfect true knowledge and liberation." (MN 3.147)

Apica carimakānaṃ assāsapassāsānaṃ viditabhāvakaraṇatopissā mahānisaṃsatā veditabbā. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

Furthermore, its great benefit should be understood from its causing the final in-breaths and out-breaths to be known. For this was said by the Blessed One:

“Evaṃ [M 2.0248] bhāvitāya, rāhula, ānāpānassatiyā evaṃ bahulīkatāya yepi te carimakā assāsapassāsā, tepi viditāva nirujjhanti, no aviditā”ti (ma. ni. 2.121).

"Rāhula, when mindfulness of breathing is developed and cultivated in this way, even those final in-breaths and out-breaths cease with awareness, not without awareness." (MN 2.121)

Tattha nirodhavasena tayo carimakā bhavacarimakā jhānacarimakā cuticarimakāti. Bhavesu hi kāmabhave assāsapassāsā pavattanti, rūpārūpabhavesu na pavattanti, tasmā te bhavacarimakā. Jhānesu purime jhānattaye pavattanti, catutthe nappavattanti, tasmā te jhānacarimakā. Ye pana cuticittassa purato soḷasamena cittena saddhiṃ uppajjitvā cuticittena saha nirujjhanti, ime cuticarimakā nāma. Ime idha carimakāti adhippetā.

Here, in terms of cessation, there are three kinds of final: the final of existence, the final of absorption, and the final of death. For in the existences, in the sensuous existence, in-breaths and out-breaths occur, but in the form and formless existences they do not occur; therefore, these are the final of existence. In the absorptions, they occur in the first three absorptions, but not in the fourth; therefore, these are the final of absorption. But those that, having arisen together with the sixteenth consciousness before the death consciousness, cease together with the death consciousness—these are called the final of death. These are what are meant here by 'final.'

Ime kira imaṃ kammaṭṭhānamanuyuttassa bhikkhuno pākaṭā honti ānāpānārammaṇassa suṭṭhu pariggahitattā. Cuticittassa hi purato soḷasamacittassa uppādakkhaṇe uppādaṃ āvajjayato uppādopi nesaṃ pākaṭo hoti, ṭhitiṃ āvajjayato ṭhitipi nesaṃ pākaṭā hoti, bhaṅgaṃ āvajjayato bhaṅgopi nesaṃ pākaṭo hoti. Ito aññaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ bhāvetvā arahattappattassa bhikkhuno hi āyuantaraṃ paricchinnaṃ vā hoti aparicchinnaṃ vā, imaṃ pana soḷasavatthukaṃ ānāpānassatiṃ bhāvetvā arahattappattassa āyuantaraṃ paricchinnameva hoti. So “ettakaṃ dāni me āyusaṅkhārā pavattissanti, na ito para”nti ñatvā attano dhammatāya eva sarīrapaṭijaggananivāsanapārupanādīni [V 2.0221] sabbakiccāni katvā akkhīni nimīleti koṭapabbatavihāravāsitissatthero viya, mahākarañjiyavihāravāsimahātissatthero viya, devaputtaraṭṭhe piṇḍapātikatthero viya, cittalapabbatavihāravāsino dvebhātikattherā viya ca.

Indeed, for a bhikkhu devoted to this meditation subject, these become evident because the mindfulness-of-breathing object has been well grasped. For one who reflects on the arising moment of the sixteenth consciousness preceding the death-consciousness, its arising becomes evident; for one who reflects on its duration, its duration becomes evident; for one who reflects on its dissolution, its dissolution becomes evident. For a bhikkhu who attains arahantship by developing any other meditation subject, the remainder of his lifespan may be either determined or undetermined; but for one who attains arahantship by developing this sixteenfold mindfulness of breathing, the remainder of his lifespan is definitely determined. Knowing, 'Now only this much of my life-sustaining forces will continue, no more than this,' he completes all his duties—such as caring for the body, putting on the undergarment and outer robe, and so on—according to his nature, and then closes his eyes, just like the Elder Tissa dwelling at Koṭapabbata Vihāra, the Elder Mahātissa dwelling at Mahākarañjiya Vihāra, the Elder Piṇḍapātika in Devaputtaraṭṭha, and the two Elder Brothers dwelling in Cittalapabbata Vihāra.

Tatridaṃ ekavatthuparidīpanaṃ – dvebhātikattherānaṃ kireko puṇṇamuposathadivase pātimokkhaṃ osāretvā bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā caṅkame ṭhito juṇhapakkhe padosavelāyaṃ candālokena samantato āsiñcamānakhīradhāraṃ viya gaganatalaṃ rajatapaṭṭasadisaṃ vālikāsanthatañca bhūmibhāgaṃ disvā “ramaṇīyo vatāyaṃ kālo, deso ca mama ajjhāsayasadiso, kīva ciraṃ nu kho ayaṃ dukkhabhāro [M 2.0249] vahitabbo”ti attano āyusaṅkhāre upadhāretvā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ āha – “tumhehi kathaṃ parinibbāyantā bhikkhū diṭṭhapubbā”ti. Tatra keci āhaṃsu – “amhehi āsane nisinnakāva parinibbāyantā diṭṭhapubbā”ti. Keci “amhehi ākāse pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā nisinnakā”ti. Thero āha – “ahaṃ dāni vo caṅkamantameva parinibbāyamānaṃ dassayissāmī”ti. Tato caṅkame tiriyaṃ lekhaṃ katvā “ahaṃ ito caṅkamakoṭito parakoṭiṃ gantvā nivattamāno imaṃ lekhaṃ patvā parinibbāyissāmī”ti vatvā caṅkamaṃ oruyha parabhāgaṃ gantvā nivattamāno ekena pādena lekhaṃ akkantakkhaṇeyeva parinibbāyīti.

Here is the illumination of a single event: It is said that on the full-moon observance day, one of the two elder brothers, having recited the Pātimokkha and surrounded by the community of bhikkhus, went to his dwelling place. Standing on the walking path during the bright fortnight at dusk, he saw the sky suffused with moonlight like a stream of milk being poured all around, resembling a silver plate, and the ground strewn with sand. He thought, 'How delightful this time is, and the place is just as I desire. How long indeed must this burden of suffering be borne?' Reflecting on his own life-formations, he addressed the community of bhikkhus: 'In what manner have you previously seen bhikkhus passing into final Nibbāna?' Some replied, 'We have previously seen them passing into final Nibbāna while seated.' Others said, 'We have seen them seated cross-legged in the air.' The Elder said, 'Now I will show you one passing into final Nibbāna while walking.' Then, having made a line across the walking path, he said, 'Having gone from this end of the walking path to the other end and returning, upon reaching this line, I will pass into final Nibbāna.' Then descending to the walking path, he went to the far end and, while returning, at the very moment he stepped on the line with one foot, he passed into final Nibbāna.

Ānāpānassatisamādhikathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Concentration of Mindfulness of Breathing is concluded.

Paṭhamapaññattikathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the First Regulation

167. Yadipi ariyā neva attanāva attānaṃ jīvitā voropesuṃ, nāññamaññampi jīvitā voropesuṃ, nāpi migalaṇḍikaṃ samaṇakuttakaṃ upasaṅkamitvā samādapesuṃ, tathāpi yathāvuttehi tīhi pakārehi matānaṃ antare ariyānampi sabbhāvato “ariyapuggalamissakattā”ti vuttaṃ. Na hi ariyā pāṇātipātaṃ kariṃsu na samādapesuṃ, nāpi samanuññā ahesuṃ. Atha vā puthujjanakāle attanāva attānaṃ ghātetvā maraṇasamaye vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā ariyamaggaṃ paṭilabhitvā matānampi ariyānaṃ sabbhāvato imināva nayena attanāva attānaṃ jīvitā voropanassa ariyānampi sabbhāvato ariyapuggalamissakattā “moghapurisā”ti na vuttaṃ. “Te bhikkhū”ti vuttanti “kathañhi nāma te, bhikkhave, bhikkhū attanāpi attānaṃ jīvitā voropessantī”ti ettha “moghapurisā”ti avatvā “te bhikkhū”ti vuttaṃ.

167. Although the noble ones neither took their own lives, nor took one another's lives, nor did they approach a hunter or a sham ascetic to incite them, nevertheless, because noble ones are also present among those who died by the three ways as stated, the term 'being mixed with noble individuals' is used. For the noble ones did not commit the destruction of life, did not incite it, nor did they approve of it. Alternatively, because of the existence of noble ones who, while they were ordinary persons, killed themselves but at the moment of death developed insight, attained the noble path, and then died; and by this same method, because of the existence of noble ones among those who deprive themselves of life, they are not called 'worthless men' on account of being mixed with noble individuals. The phrase 'those bhikkhus' is used. Thus, in the passage 'How indeed, bhikkhus, could those bhikkhus deprive themselves of life?', instead of saying 'worthless men', it is said 'those bhikkhus'.

Anupaññattikathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Subsequent Regulation

168. Itthīsu [V 2.0222] paṭibaddhacittatā nāma chandarāgena sārattatā sāpekkhabhāvoti āha “sārattā apekkhavanto”ti. Maraṇassa guṇakittanaṃ jīvite ādīnavadassanapubbaṅgamanti āha “jīvite ādīnavaṃ dassetvā”ti. “Kiṃ tuyhiminā pāpakena dujjīvitenā”ti idaṃ jīvite ādīnavadassanaṃ. “Mataṃ [M 2.0250] te jīvitā seyyo”tiādi pana maraṇaguṇakittananti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Lobhādīnaṃ ativiya ussannattā anupaparikkhitvā kataṃ sāhasikakammaṃ kibbisanti vuccatīti āha – “kibbisaṃ sāhasikakammaṃ lobhādikilesussada”nti. Kasmā idaṃ vuccatīti chabbaggiyānaṃyevedaṃ vacanaṃ. Mata-saddo “gata”ntiādīsu viya bhāvavacanoti āha “tava maraṇa”nti. Katakāloti katamaraṇakālo. Atha vā kāloti maraṇassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ, tasmā katakāloti katamaraṇoti attho. Tenevāha “kālaṃ katvā, maritvā”ti. Divi bhavā dibbāti āha “devaloke uppannehī”ti. Samappitoti yutto. Samaṅgībhūtoti sammadeva ekībhāvaṃ gato.

168. Being attached to women means being infatuated with desire and lust, being in a state of longing—as it is said, 'infatuated and longing.' Praising the virtues of death is preceded by showing the dangers in life—as it is said, 'having shown the dangers in life.' The phrase, 'What good is this wretched, miserable life to you?' illustrates showing the dangers in life. On the other hand, 'Better for you is death than life' and similar statements should be understood as praising the virtues of death. An act done rashly without proper examination, due to the extreme intensity of greed and other defilements, is called a sinful, reckless deed—as it is said, 'A sinful deed is reckless action, due to the excess of greed and other defilements.' Why is this said? Because this is the very saying of the group of six. The word 'mata' (dead) is a word expressing a state, like 'gata' (gone), hence it is said, 'your death.' 'Katakālo' means the time of death has been made. Alternatively, 'kāla' is a term for death, so 'katakālo' means death has been made. Therefore, it is said, 'having made his time, having died.' 'Divine' refers to what exists in the heavenly realm—as it is said, 'by those arisen in the deva world.' 'Samappito' means endowed. 'Samaṅgībhūto' means having truly attained oneness.

Padabhājanīyavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Analysis of Terms

172. Ussukkavacananti pubbakālakiriyāvacanaṃ. Ayañhi samānakattukesu pubbāparakālakiriyāvacanesu pubbakālakiriyāvacanassa niruttivohāro. Sañciccāti imassa padassa “jānitvā sañjānitvā cecca abhivitaritvā”ti evaṃ pubbakālakiriyāvasena byañjanānurūpaṃ katvā padabhājane vattabbe tathā avatvā “jānanto sañjānanto”ti puggalādhiṭṭhānaṃ katvā “cecca abhivitaritvā vītikkamo”ti jīvitā voropanassa ca tadatthavasena niddiṭṭhattā vuttaṃ “byañjane ādaraṃ akatvā”ti. “Jānanto”ti avisesena vuttepi “sañcicca manussaviggahaṃ jīvitā voropeyyā”ti vuttattā pāṇavisayamettha jānananti āha “pāṇoti jānanto”ti, satto ayanti jānantoti attho. Pāṇoti hi vohārato satto, paramatthato jīvitindriyaṃ vuccati. “Manussaviggahoti jānanto”ti avatvā “pāṇoti jānanto”ti vacanaṃ “manusso aya”nti ajānitvā kevalaṃ sattasaññāya ghātentassapi pārājikabhāvadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Teneva eḷakacatukke (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.174) eḷakasaññāya manussapāṇaṃ vadhantassa pārājikāpatti dassitā. Tasmā “manussaviggaho”ti avatvā “pāṇoti jānanto”ti avisesena vuttaṃ.

172. The term 'ussukkavacana' is a word denoting a prior action. Indeed, among words denoting prior and subsequent actions performed by the same agent, this is the grammatical usage for a word denoting a prior action. The word 'sañcicca' should be analyzed in the word-analysis section in a way that corresponds to the letters, as a prior action, thus: 'having known, having recognized, having intended, and having transgressed.' However, instead of stating it in this way, it is stated as 'knowing and recognizing,' making the person the basis; and because 'the transgression is having intended and having transgressed' and the taking of life are indicated by that meaning, it is said 'without paying respect to the letter.' Even though 'knowing' is stated without specification, since 'intentionally depriving a human being of life' is mentioned, here 'knowing' refers to the sphere of a living being, thus it is said 'knowing it is a living being,' meaning 'knowing this is a sentient being.' For in conventional speech, 'pāṇa' refers to a sentient being, but in ultimate terms, it is called the life faculty. Instead of saying 'knowing it is a human form,' the statement 'knowing it is a living being' is made to show that even one who kills with the mere perception of a being—without knowing 'this is a human'—incurs a pārājika offense. For this reason, in the 'four goats' case, it is shown that one who kills a human life with the perception of a goat incurs a pārājika offense. Therefore, instead of saying 'it is a human form,' it is stated without specification as 'knowing it is a living being.'

Sañjānantoti ettha saha-saddena samānattho saṃ-saddoti āha – “teneva pāṇajānanākārena saddhiṃ [V 2.0223] jānanto”ti, teneva pāṇajānanākārena [M 2.0251] saddhiṃ jīvitā voropemīti jānantoti attho. Yadipi ekasseva cittassa ubhayārammaṇabhāvāsambhavato pāṇoti jānanena saddhiṃ jīvitā voropemīti jānanaṃ ekakkhaṇe na sambhavati, pāṇotisaññaṃ pana avijahitvā māremīti jānanaṃ sandhāya “teneva…pe… saddhiṃ jānanto”ti vuttaṃ. Tasmā saddhinti avijahitvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Keci pana “ñātapariññāya diṭṭhasabhāvesu dhammesu tīraṇapariññāya tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā ‘rūpaṃ anicca’ntiādinā sabhāvena saddhiṃ ekakkhaṇe aniccādilakkhaṇajānanaṃ viya ‘imaṃ pāṇaṃ māremī’ti attano kiriyāya saddhiṃyeva jānātī”ti vadanti. Apare pana ācariyā tatthāpi evaṃ na kathenti.

Here, regarding 'Sañjānanto,' it is said that the prefix 'saṃ-' has the same meaning as the word 'saha' (together): 'knowing together with that very mode of knowing a living being.' That is, the meaning is knowing 'I will deprive of life' together with that very mode of knowing a living being. Although, due to the impossibility of a single consciousness having two objects, the knowing 'I will deprive of life' together with the knowing 'it is a living being' is not possible in a single moment, it is said 'knowing together with that...' with reference to the knowledge 'I will kill' without having abandoned the perception 'it is a living being.' Therefore, 'together with' means 'without having abandoned.' Some, however, say that just as, in the case of phenomena whose own-nature has been seen through the full understanding as the known, one knows the characteristics of impermanence and so forth in a single moment together with their own-nature by imposing the three characteristics through the full understanding as investigation—by way of 'form is impermanent,' and so on—so too one knows 'I will kill this living being' together with one's own action. But other teachers do not speak thus even in that case.

Vadhakacetanāvasena cetetvāti “imaṃ māremī”ti vadhakacetanāya cintetvā. Pakappetvāti “vadhāmi na”nti evaṃ cittena paricchinditvā. Abhivitaritvāti sanniṭṭhānaṃ katvā. Tenevāha “nirāsaṅkacittaṃ pesetvā”ti. Upakkamavasenāti sāhatthikādiupakkamavasena. Evaṃ pavattassāti evaṃ yathāvuttavidhinā pavattassa. Kiñcāpi “sañciccā”ti imassa vippakatavacanattā “jīvitā voropeyyā”ti imināva aparakālakiriyāvacanena sabbathā pariniṭṭhitavītikkamo vutto, tathāpi “sañciccā”ti iminā vuccamānaṃ apariyositavītikkamampi avasānaṃ pāpetvā dassetuṃ “vītikkamo”ti padabhājanaṃ vuttaṃ. Tenevāha “ayaṃ sañciccasaddassa sikhāppatto atthoti vuttaṃ hotī”ti.

'Having intended' by way of the intention to kill means having thought with the intention to kill, 'I will kill this one.' 'Having planned' means having determined with the mind thus: 'I will kill that being.' 'Having carried through' means having made a firm resolution. Therefore, it is said, 'having sent forth a mind free from doubt.' 'By means of effort' means by way of effort such as personal action and so on. 'Of one who proceeds thus' means of one who proceeds in the manner described. Although, because 'sañcicca' is a word for an incomplete action, the transgression is said to be fully completed in every way by the word for a future action, 'should deprive of life,' nevertheless, the word analysis 'vītikkamo' (transgression) is stated in order to show that even the incomplete transgression expressed by 'sañcicca' is brought to its conclusion. Therefore, it is said: 'This is the meaning of the word "sañcicca" having reached its peak.'

Ādito paṭṭhāyāti paṭisandhiviññāṇena saddhiṃ uppannakalalarūpato paṭṭhāya. Sayanti etthāti seyyā, mātukucchisaṅkhāto gabbho seyyā etesanti gabbhaseyyakā, aṇḍajā jalābujā ca. Tesaṃ gabbhaseyyakānaṃ vasena sabbasukhumattabhāvadassanatthaṃ “yaṃ mātukucchismi”ntiādi vuttaṃ, na pārājikavatthuniyamanatthaṃ. Opapātikasaṃsedajāpi hi manussā pārājikavatthumeva. Na cevimaṃ sabbapaṭhamaṃ manussaviggahaṃ jīvitā voropetuṃ sakkā. Paṭisandhicittena hi saddhiṃ tiṃsa kammajarūpāni nibbattanti, tesu pana ṭhitesuyeva soḷasa bhavaṅgacittāni uppajjitvā nirujjhanti. Etasmiṃ antare gahitapaṭisandhikassa dārakassa vā mātuyā vā panassa antarāyo natthi. Ayañhi maraṇassa anokāso nāma. Ekasmiñhi soḷasacittakkhaṇe kāle dārakassa maraṇaṃ natthi tadā cuticittassa asambhavato, mātuyāpi [M 2.0252] tattakaṃ kālaṃ anatikkamitvā tadanantareyeva cavanadhammāya gabbhaggahaṇasseva asambhavato. Cittaggahaṇeneva avinābhāvato sesaarūpadhammānampi gahitattā rūpakāyupatthambhitasseva ca nāmakāyassa pañcavokāre pavattisabbhāvato vuttaṃ “sakalāpi pañcavokārapaṭisandhi dassitā hotī”ti. Tattha sakalāpi [V 2.0224] pañcavokārapaṭisandhīti paripuṇṇā anūnā rūpādipañcakkhandhānaṃ paṭisandhīti evamattho gahetabbo, na pana sakalāpi pañcavokārabhave paṭisandhīti. Tenevāha “tasmā tañca paṭhamaṃ cittaṃ…pe… kalalarūpanti ayaṃ sabbapaṭhamo manussaviggaho”ti. “Tadahujātassa eḷakassa lomaṃ jātiuṇṇā”ti keci. “Himavantappadese jātimantaeḷakalomaṃ jātiuṇṇā”ti apare. Sukhumajātilomā eva kira keci eḷakā himavante vijjanti. “Gabbhaṃ phāletvā gahitaeḷakalomaṃ jātiuṇṇā”ti aññe.

'From the beginning' means starting from the kalala-form that arises together with the rebirth-consciousness. They lie down herein, thus it is a 'seyyā' (lying-place); the womb, designated as the mother's belly, is a 'seyyā' for them, hence they are 'gabbhaseyyakā' (womb-lying ones), namely the egg-born and the womb-born. With reference to these womb-lying ones, the statement 'whatever is in the mother's womb' and so on was said to show the most subtle state of all, not to define the object of a pārājika offense. For spontaneously arisen and moisture-born humans are indeed objects of a pārājika offense. And it is not possible to deprive this very first human form of life. For together with the rebirth-consciousness, thirty kamma-born material phenomena are produced, and while these persist, sixteen life-continuum (bhavaṅga) mind-moments arise and cease. During this interval, there is no danger to either the child who has taken rebirth or to the mother. For this is called the 'non-opportunity for death.' For in the time of a single sixteen-mind-moment period, there is no death for the child, due to the impossibility of a death-consciousness then; nor for the mother, because conception itself is impossible for one who is of a nature to pass away immediately after that period. Since the remaining formless phenomena are also grasped due to their inseparability from the grasping of consciousness, and since the existence of the mental body in the five-constituent existence is supported by the physical body, it is said: 'The entire five-constituent rebirth is shown.' Here, 'the entire five-constituent rebirth' should be understood as a complete, non-deficient rebirth of the five aggregates beginning with form, not as rebirth in all five-constituent existences. Therefore, he said: 'Thus, that first consciousness... up to the kalala-form—this is the very first human form.' Some say: 'The wool of a lamb born that very day is the birth-wool (jātiuṇṇā).' Others say: 'The wool of a well-bred lamb from the Himalayan region is the birth-wool.' Indeed, it is said that some lambs with extremely fine birth-wool are found in the Himalayas. Still others say: 'The wool of a lamb taken by splitting open the womb is the birth-wool.'

Ekena aṃsunāti khuddakabhāṇakānaṃ matena vuttaṃ. Tathā hi “gabbhaseyyakasattānaṃ paṭisandhikkhaṇe pañcakkhandhā apacchā apure ekato pātubhavanti. Tasmiṃ khaṇe pātubhūtā kalalasaṅkhātā rūpasantati parittā hoti khuddakamakkhikāya ekavāyāmena pātabbamattā”ti vatvā puna “atibahuṃ etaṃ, saṇhasūciyā tele pakkhipitvā ukkhittāya paggharitvā agge ṭhitabindumatta”nti vuttaṃ. Tampi paṭikkhipitvā “ekakese telato uddharitvā gahite tassa paggharitvā agge ṭhitabindumatta”nti vuttaṃ. Tampi paṭikkhipitvā “imasmiṃ janapade manussānaṃ kese aṭṭhadhā phālite tato ekakoṭṭhāsappamāṇo uttarakurukānaṃ keso, tassa pasannatilatelato uddhaṭassa agge ṭhitabindumatta”nti vuttaṃ. Tampi paṭikkhipitvā “jātiuṇṇā nāma sukhumā, tassā ekaaṃsuno pasannatilatele pakkhipitvā uddhaṭassa paggharitvā agge ṭhitabindumatta”nti (vibha. aṭṭha. 26) khuddakabhāṇakehi vuttaṃ. Saṃyuttabhāṇakā pana “tīhi jātiuṇṇaṃsūhi katasuttagge saṇṭhitatelabinduppamāṇaṃ kalalaṃ hotī”ti (saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.235) vadanti. “Accha”nti vuttamatthaṃ pariyāyantarena vibhāveti “vippasanna”nti.

'By a single strand' is said according to the view of the reciters of the Khuddaka Nikāya. For thus it is stated: 'For womb-lying beings, at the moment of rebirth-linking, the five aggregates appear together, neither before nor after. At that moment, the continuity of matter that has appeared, designated as the kalala, is minute—the size of what can be drunk in one gulp by a small fly.' Having said this, they state further: 'This is too much; it is the size of a drop remaining at the tip of a fine needle that has been dipped in oil, lifted up, and allowed to drip.' Rejecting that too, they say: 'It is the size of a drop remaining at the tip of a single hair that has been drawn from oil and allowed to drip.' Rejecting that as well, they say: 'When a human hair in this country is split eightfold, one part is the size of a hair of the people of Uttarakuru; it is the size of a drop remaining at the tip of such a hair when it is drawn from clear sesame oil.' Rejecting that too, the reciters of the Khuddaka Nikāya say: 'Birth-wool (jātiuṇṇā) is fine. It is the size of a drop remaining at the tip of a single strand of it that has been dipped in clear sesame oil, drawn out, and allowed to drip.' The reciters of the Saṃyutta Nikāya, however, say: 'The kalala is the size of a drop of oil standing on the tip of a thread made from three strands of birth-wool.' The word 'accha' (clear) clarifies, by way of a different expression, the meaning stated as 'vippasanna' (very clear).

Sappimaṇḍoti pasannasappi. Yathāti idaṃ ānetvā etthāpi sambandhitabbaṃ, sappimaṇḍopi vuttabinduppamāṇova idha adhippeto. Evaṃvaṇṇappaṭibhāganti vuttappamāṇasaṇṭhānaparicchinnaṃ[M 2.0253]. Atha vā evaṃvaṇṇappaṭibhāganti evaṃvaṇṇaṃ evaṃsaṇṭhānañca. Paṭibhajanaṃ vā paṭibhāgo, sadisatābhajanaṃ sadisatāpattīti attho. Evaṃvidho vaṇṇappaṭibhāgo rūpato saṇṭhānato ca sadisatāpatti etassāti evaṃvaṇṇappaṭibhāgaṃ. Kalalanti pavuccatīti bhūtupādārūpasaṅkhāto santānavasena pavattamāno attabhāvo kalalaṃ nāmāti kathīyati. Vīsavassasatāyukassāti nidassanamattaṃ tato ūnādhikāyukamanussānampi sabbhāvato.

'Sappimaṇḍa' means clear ghee. The word 'yathā' (just as) should be brought in and connected here also; 'sappimaṇḍa' here is also intended to be of the size of the aforementioned drop. 'Evaṃvaṇṇappaṭibhāgaṃ' (of such an appearance) means defined by the aforementioned size and shape. Or, 'evaṃvaṇṇappaṭibhāgaṃ' means of such color and of such shape. Or, 'paṭibhāga' is 'paṭibhajana' (partaking); the meaning is that partaking of similarity is the attainment of similarity. It is 'evaṃvaṇṇappaṭibhāgaṃ' because for this being there is this kind of attainment of similarity in terms of color and shape. 'It is called kalala' means: the individual existence, designated as primary and derived matter, which proceeds by way of continuity, is called 'kalala'. 'Of one with a lifespan of one hundred and twenty years' is merely an illustration, because there also exist humans with lifespans shorter or longer than that.

Kalalakālepīti paṭhamasattāhabbhantare yaṃ santativasena pavattamānaṃ kalalasaṅkhātaṃ attabhāvaṃ jīvitā voropetuṃ sakkā, taṃ sandhāya vadati. Tato vā uddhanti dutiyasattāhādīsu abbudādibhāvappattaṃ [V 2.0225] sandhāya vuttaṃ. Nanu ca uppannānaṃ dhammānaṃ sarasanirodheneva nirujjhanato antarā upacchedo na sakkā kātuṃ, “tasmā…pe… jīvitindriyaṃ upacchindati uparodhetī”ti kasmā vuttanti āha – “jīvitindriyassa paveṇīghaṭanaṃ…pe… uparodhetīti vuccatī”ti. Kathañcāyamattho viññāyatīti āha “svāyamattho”tiādi.

'Even at the kalala stage' refers to that individual existence designated as the kalala, which proceeds by way of continuity within the first week, and which it is possible to deprive of life. 'Or from then onwards' is said with reference to having reached the state of abbuda and so on in the second week and thereafter. Is it not so that since arisen phenomena cease only with their own essential cessation, an interruption in between cannot be made? Why then was it said, 'Therefore... it cuts off, it obstructs the life-faculty'? He says: 'Because it disrupts the continuity of the life-faculty... it is called obstruction.' And how is this meaning to be understood? He says, 'This meaning is...', and so on.

Etthāha (sārattha. ṭī. 1.5; itivu. aṭṭha. 74) – khaṇe khaṇe nirujjhanasabhāvesu saṅkhāresu ko hanti, ko vā haññati, yadi cittacetasikasantāno, so arūpatāya na chedanabhedanādivasena vikopanasamattho, napi vikopanīyo. Atha rūpasantāno, so acetanatāya kaṭṭhakaliṅgarūpamoti na tattha chedanādinā pāṇātipāto labbhati yathā matasarīre. Payogopi pāṇātipātassa yathāvutto paharaṇappahārādiko atītesu vā saṅkhāresu bhaveyya anāgatesu vā paccuppannesu vā, tattha na tāva atītānāgatesu sambhavati tesaṃ abhāvato, paccuppannesu ca saṅkhārānaṃ khaṇikattā saraseneva nirujjhanasabhāvatāya vināsābhimukhesu nippayojano payogo siyā, vināsassa ca kāraṇarahitattā na paharaṇappahārādippayogahetukaṃ maraṇaṃ, nirīhakatāya ca saṅkhārānaṃ kassa so payogo, khaṇikattā vadhādhippāyasamakālabhijjanakassa kiriyāpariyosānakaālānavaṭṭhānato kassa vā pāṇātipātakammabaddhoti?

Here, an objector says: In conditioned phenomena that by their very nature cease moment by moment, who kills, or who is killed? If it is the continuum of mind and mental factors, being formless, it is not capable of being disrupted by cutting, breaking, or the like; nor can it be disrupted. But if it is the continuum of form, being insentient, it is like a piece of wood, so the killing of a living being is not accomplished there through cutting and so on, just as in a dead body. Furthermore, the application of killing—such as the aforementioned striking or blow—could occur in past, future, or present conditioned phenomena. Now, it cannot occur in past or future ones because they do not exist. As for present conditioned phenomena, due to their momentariness, they are ceasing by their own intrinsic nature and are facing destruction, so any application would be useless. And since destruction is without a cause, death is not caused by the application of striking, blows, and so on. Moreover, because conditioned phenomena are without volition, whose application is it? And due to their momentariness, since the time of the completion of the action does not coincide with the intention to kill which perishes in the same moment, to whom is the kamma of killing bound?

Vuccate [M 2.0254] – vadhakacetanāsahito saṅkhārānaṃ puñjo sattasaṅkhāto hanti. Tena pavattitavadhappayoganimittaṃ apagatusmāviññāṇajīvitindriyo matavohārappavattinibandhano yathāvuttavadhappayogākaraṇe uppajjanāraho rūpārūpadhammasamūho haññati, kevalo vā cittacetasikasantāno vadhappayogāvisayabhāvepi tassa pañcavokārabhave rūpasantānādhīnavuttitāya rūpasantāne parena payojitajīvitindriyupacchedakapayogavasena tannibbattivinibandhakavisadisarūpuppattiyā vihate vicchedo hotīti na pāṇātipātassa asambhavo, napi ahetuko pāṇātipāto, na ca payogo nippayojano paccuppannesu saṅkhāresu katappayogavasena tadanantaraṃ uppajjanārahassa saṅkhārakalāpassa tathā anuppattito. Khaṇikānaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ khaṇikamaraṇassa idha maraṇabhāvena anadhippetattā santatimaraṇassa ca yathāvuttanayena sahetukabhāvato na ahetukaṃ maraṇaṃ, na ca katturahito pāṇātipātappayogo nirīhakesupi saṅkhāresu sannihitatāmattena upakārakesu attano attano anurūpaphaluppādane niyatesu kāraṇesu kattuvohārasiddhito yathā “padīpo pakāseti, nisākaro candimā”ti. Na ca kevalassa vadhādhippāyasahabhuno cittacetasikakalāpassa pāṇātipāto icchito santānavasena avaṭṭhitasseva paṭijānanato, santānavasena [V 2.0226] pavattamānānañca padīpādīnaṃ atthakiriyāsiddhi dissatīti attheva pāṇātipātena kammunā baddho. Ayañca vicāro adinnādānādīsupi yathāsambhavaṃ vibhāvetabbo.

It is said: A collection of formations accompanied by the volition to kill, designated as a 'being', kills. By that volition, a collection of material and immaterial phenomena is killed. This collection, which would have been fit to arise had the aforementioned application of killing not been performed, becomes devoid of vitality, consciousness, and the life-faculty, and becomes the basis for the occurrence of the designation 'dead'—this being the result of the application of killing set in motion. Or, the mere continuum of mind and mental factors, even though it is not an object for the application of killing, undergoes severance. This is because in the five-aggregate existence its subsistence is dependent on the continuum of form; when that continuum of form is destroyed by means of an application employed by another that cuts off the life-faculty, and by the arising of a dissimilar form that obstructs its production, a severance occurs. Thus, the killing of a living being is not impossible. Nor is killing without a cause, nor is the application without purpose, because by means of the application made to present conditioned phenomena, a group of formations that was fit to arise immediately after does not arise in that way. Because the momentary death of momentary conditioned phenomena is not intended here in the sense of 'death', and because the death of the continuum has a cause in the way explained, death is not without a cause. Nor is the application of killing without an agent, since the conventional designation of 'agent' is established even for non-volitional conditioned phenomena which, as causes fixed in producing their own respective results, are helpful merely by their presence—just as it is said: 'The lamp illuminates,' and 'The moon is the night-maker.' Nor is 'killing' meant to apply to a mere group of mind and mental factors accompanied by the intention to kill, because it is acknowledged only for that which is established as a continuum. And since the accomplishment of a function is seen in the case of lamps and so on, which proceed by way of a continuum, one is indeed bound by the kamma of killing. This analysis should be applied to theft and other offenses as is appropriate.

Voropetuṃ na sakkāti upakkamena voropetuṃ na sakkā. Sattaṭṭhajavanavāramattanti khuddakabhāṇakānaṃ matena vuttaṃ. Saṃyuttabhāṇakā pana “rūpasantati arūpasantatī”ti dve santatiyo vatvā “udakaṃ akkamitvā gatassa yāva tīre akkantaudakalekhā na vippasīdati, addhānato āgatassa yāva kāye usumabhāvo na vūpasammati, ātapā āgantvā gabbhaṃ paviṭṭhassa yāva andhakārabhāvo na vigacchati, antogabbhe kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasi karitvā divā vātapānaṃ vivaritvā olokentassa yāva akkhīnaṃ phandanabhāvo na vūpasammati, ayaṃ rūpasantati nāma. Dve tayo javanavārā arūpasantati nāmā”ti vatvā “tadubhayampi santatipaccuppannaṃ nāmā”ti vadanti[M 2.0255]. Majjhimabhāṇakā pana vadanti “ekadvesantativārapariyāpannaṃ santatipaccuppannaṃ. Tattha andhakāre nisīditvā ālokaṭṭhānaṃ gatassa na ca tāva ārammaṇaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti. Yāva pana taṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti, etthantare pavattā rūpasantati arūpasantati vā ekadvesantativārā nāmāti veditabbā. Ālokaṭṭhāne caritvā ovarakaṃ paviṭṭhassapi na tāva sahasā rūpaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti. Yāva pana taṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti, etthantare pavattā rūpasantati arūpasantati vā ekadvesantativārā veditabbā. Dūre ṭhatvā pana rajakānaṃ hatthavikāraṃ ghaṇṭibheriākoṭanavikārañca disvāpi na tāva saddaṃ suṇāti. Yāva pana taṃ suṇāti, etasmimpi antare ekadvesantativārā veditabbā”ti. Ettha ca ālokaṭṭhānato ovarakaṃ paviṭṭhassa pageva tattha nisinnassa yāva rūpagataṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti, tattha upaḍḍhavelā avibhūtappāyā, upaḍḍhavelā vibhūtappāyā tadubhayaṃ gahetvā “dvesantativārā”ti vuttaṃ, tayidaṃ na sabbasādhāraṇaṃ, ekaccassa sīghampi pākaṭaṃ hotīti “ekadvesantativārā”ti ekaggahaṇampi kataṃ.

‘It cannot be stopped’ means it cannot be stopped by effort. ‘For only seven or eight javana-courses’ is said according to the view of the reciters of the Khuddaka Nikāya. The reciters of the Saṃyutta Nikāya, however, having stated that there are two continuities—the continuum of form and the continuum of non-form—say: ‘Just as, for one who has stepped into water and gone to the shore, the line of disturbed water does not clear; just as, for one who has come from a long journey, the heat in the body does not subside; just as, for one who, coming from the sunlight, has entered a room, the darkness does not disappear; just as, for one who, having focused on a meditation object inside a room, opens a window during the day and looks outside, the flickering of the eyes does not cease—this is called the continuum of form. Two or three javana-courses are called the continuum of non-form.’ And they say, ‘Both are called the “present of the continuum.”’ The reciters of the Majjhima Nikāya, however, say: ‘The “present of the continuum” is that which is included in one or two continuity-courses. Therein, for one who has been sitting in darkness and goes to a lighted place, the object does not immediately become clear. Until it becomes clear, the continuum of form or non-form that occurs in the meantime should be understood as one or two continuity-courses. For one who has been walking in a lighted place and enters a room, the form does not immediately become clear. Until it becomes clear, the continuum of form or non-form that occurs in the meantime should be understood as one or two continuity-courses. Moreover, standing at a distance, even after seeing the gestures of washermen’s hands and the striking of bells and drums, one does not immediately hear the sound. Until one hears it, the interval should be understood as one or two continuity-courses.’ And here, for one who enters a room from a lighted place—let alone one already sitting there—until the form becomes clear, half the time it is mostly indistinct, and half the time it is mostly distinct. Taking both together, it is called ‘two continuity-courses.’ But this is not universal, for in some cases it becomes clear quickly. Therefore, the inclusion of ‘one’ is also made, resulting in the term ‘one or two continuity-courses.’

Sabhāgasantativasenāti kusalākusalasomanassupekkhādinā sabhāgasantativasena. Iminā arūpasantati dassitā. Sattaṭṭhajavanavāramattanti ca kāmāvacarajavanavaseneva veditabbaṃ, na itarajavanavasena. Na hi te parimitakālā, antarā pavattabhavaṅgādayopi tadantogadhāti daṭṭhabbā. Yāva vā uṇhato āgantvātiādinā pana rūpasantatiṃ dasseti. Andhakāraṃ hotīti andhakāraṃ na vigacchati. Santatipaccuppannañcettha aṭṭhakathāsu āgataṃ, addhāpaccuppannaṃ sutte. Tathā hi bhaddekarattasutte addhāpaccuppannaṃ sandhāya “yo cāvuso mano, ye ca dhammā, ubhayametaṃ paccuppannaṃ, tasmiṃ ce paccuppanne chandarāgapaṭibaddhaṃ hoti viññāṇaṃ, chandarāgapaṭibaddhattā viññāṇassa [V 2.0227] tadabhinandati, tadabhinandanto paccuppannesu dhammesu saṃhīratī”ti (ma. ni. 3.284) vuttaṃ. Ettha hi manoti sasampayuttaṃ viññāṇamāha. Dhammāti ārammaṇadhammā. Manoti vā manāyatanaṃ. Dhammāti vedanādayo arūpakkhandhā. Ubhayametaṃ paccuppannanti addhāpaccuppannaṃ etaṃ ubhayaṃ hotīti attho. Viññāṇanti nikantiviññāṇaṃ. Tañhi tasmiṃ paccuppanne chandarāgavasena paṭibaddhaṃ hoti. Abhinandatīti taṇhādiṭṭhābhinandanāhi abhinandati[M 2.0256]. Tathābhūto ca vatthupariññāya abhāvato tesu paccuppannesu dhammesu saṃhīrati, taṇhādiṭṭhīhi ākaḍḍhīyatīti attho. Ettha ca “dvādasāyatanāni ekaṃ paccuppanna”nti āgatattā tattha pavatto chandarāgo addhāpaccuppannārammaṇo, na khaṇapaccuppannārammaṇoti viññāyati.

By way of the continuity of similar states means: by way of the continuity of similar states through wholesome, unwholesome, joy, equanimity, and so on. By this, the immaterial continuity is shown. And 'only seven or eight javana-courses' should be understood only by way of sense-sphere javanas, not by way of other javanas. For those are not of limited duration, and the life-continuum moments, etc., that occur in between should be seen as included within them. Or, by the phrase beginning with 'until coming from the heat,' it shows the material continuity. 'It is dark' means the darkness does not disappear. Here, the 'continuity-present' is found in the commentaries, while the 'duration-present' is found in the suttas. For so it is that in the Bhaddekaratta Sutta, with reference to the 'duration-present,' it is said: “Friend, the mind and the mental objects—both are present. If in that present, consciousness is bound by desire and lust, then because of the consciousness being bound by desire and lust, one delights in that. Delighting in that, one is carried away by present phenomena” (M. iii. 187). Herein, 'mind' refers to consciousness together with its associated states. 'Mental objects' refers to the objects of mind. Or, 'mind' is the mind-base. 'Mental objects' are the formless aggregates such as feeling and so on. 'Both are present' means both of these are the 'duration-present'. 'Consciousness' means craving-consciousness. For it is bound in that present by way of desire and lust. 'Delights' means one delights with the delights of craving and views. And being thus, due to the absence of full understanding of the basis, one is carried away by those present phenomena; the meaning is that one is dragged along by craving and views. And here, because it is stated that “the twelve sense-bases are one present,” it is understood that the desire and lust that occurs there has the 'duration-present' as its object, not the 'momentary-present' as its object.

Sattoti khandhasantāno. Tattha hi sattapaññatti. Jīvitindriyanti rūpārūpajīvitindriyaṃ. Rūpajīvitindriye hi vikopite itarampi taṃsambandhatāya vinassatīti. Taṃ vuttappakāramevāti taṃ jīvitindriyātipātanavidhānaṃ heṭṭhā vuttappakārameva. Saraseneva patanasabhāvassa antarā eva atīva pātanaṃ atipāto, saṇikaṃ patituṃ adatvā sīghapātananti attho. Atikkamma vā satthādīhi abhibhavitvā pātanaṃ atipāto, pāṇassa atipāto pāṇātipāto. Yāya cetanāya pavattamānassa jīvitindriyassa nissayabhūtesu mahābhūtesu upakkamakaraṇahetu taṃmahābhūtapaccayā uppajjanamahābhūtā nuppajjissanti, sā tādisappayogasamuṭṭhāpikā vadhakacetanā pāṇātipāto. Tenāha “yāya cetanāyā”tiādi.

A 'being' is a continuity of aggregates. For therein is the designation 'being'. The 'life faculty' is the material and immaterial life faculty. For when the material life faculty is destroyed, the other also perishes due to its connection with it. 'That is just as was said' means that the method of destroying the life faculty is just as was described below. Of that which has the nature of falling by its own momentum, causing it to fall excessively in between is 'atipāta' (transgressive falling); the meaning is, not allowing it to fall slowly but causing a swift fall. Or, having transgressed and overpowered with weapons and so on, causing it to fall is 'atipāta'. The 'atipāta' of life is 'pāṇātipāta' (taking life). That volition which, when it is occurring, because of the cause of making an effort upon the great elements which are the support for the life faculty, the great elements that would arise dependent on those great elements do not arise—that killer volition, which originates such an application, is 'pāṇātipāta'. Therefore, he said: “By which volition…” and so on.

Paharaṇanti kāyaviññattisahitāya vadhakacetanāya adhippetatthasādhanaṃ. Āṇāpananti vacīviññattisahitāya vadhakacetanāya adhippetatthasādhanaṃ. Teneva “sāvetukāmo na sāvetī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Upanikkhipananti asiādīnaṃ tassa upanikkhipanaṃ.

'Striking' is the accomplishment of the intended purpose by the killer volition accompanied by bodily intimation. 'Commanding' is the accomplishment of the intended purpose by the killer volition accompanied by verbal intimation. Therefore, it is said, “Wishing to make it heard, he does not make it heard,” and so on. 'Placing near' is the placing of a sword or other weapon near that person.

Aṭṭhakathāsu vuttamatthaṃ saṅkhipitvā dassento “saṅkhepato”tiādimāha. Tattha vijjāparijappananti mantaparijappanaṃ. Idāni aṭṭhakathāsu vitthāritamatthaṃ dassento āha “aṭṭhakathāsu panā”tiādi. Tattha āthabbaṇikāti āthabbaṇavedavedino. Āthabbaṇaṃ payojentīti āthabbaṇavedavihitaṃ mantaṃ tattha vuttavidhinā payojenti. Āthabbaṇikā hi sattāhaṃ aloṇakaṃ bhuñjitvā dabbe attharitvā pathaviyaṃ sayamānā tapaṃ caritvā sattame divase susānabhūmiṃ sajjetvā sattame pade ṭhatvā hatthaṃ vaṭṭetvā vaṭṭetvā mukhena vijjaṃ parijappanti, atha nesaṃ kammaṃ samijjhati. Paṭisenāyāti idaṃ heṭṭhā upari vā padadvayena sambandhamupagacchati. Ītiṃ [V 2.0228] uppādentīti ḍaṃsitvā māraṇatthāya vicchikādīnaṃ vissajjanavasena pīḷaṃ uppādenti[M 2.0257]. Etīti īti. Upaddavanti tato adhikatarapīḷaṃ. Pajjarakanti visamajjaraṃ. Sūcikanti aṅgapaccaṅgāni sūcīhi viya vijjhitvā pavattamānaṃ sūlaṃ. Visūcikanti sasūlaṃ āmātisāraṃ. Pakkhandiyanti rattātisāraṃ. Vijjaṃ parivattetvāti gandhāravijjādikaṃ attano vijjaṃ katupacāraṃ parijappitvā mantapaṭhanakkamena paṭhitvā. Tehīti tehi vatthūhi.

Summarizing and showing the meaning stated in the commentaries, he said, “In brief…” and so on. Therein, 'muttering of spells' means the muttering of mantras. Now, showing the meaning explained in detail in the commentaries, he said, “But in the commentaries…” and so on. Therein, 'practitioners of the Āthabbaṇa' are those who know the Āthabbaṇa Veda. 'They employ the Āthabbaṇa' means they employ the mantra prescribed in the Āthabbaṇa Veda according to the method stated therein. For the practitioners of the Āthabbaṇa, having eaten saltless food for seven days, having spread grass on the ground and lying down, having practiced austerities, on the seventh day, having prepared the charnel ground, standing on the seventh step, whirling their hand again and again, they mutter the spell with their mouth; then their work succeeds. The word 'paṭisenāya' connects with the two phrases above or below. 'They produce calamities' means they produce affliction by way of releasing scorpions and so on for the purpose of killing by biting. That which befalls is a 'calamity' (īti). An 'adversity' (upaddava) is an even greater affliction than that. 'Pajjaraka' is a violent fever. 'Sūcika' is a sharp pain that proceeds as if piercing the limbs and extremities with needles. 'Visūcika' is dysentery with sharp pain. 'Pakkhandiya' is bloody dysentery. 'Having recited the spell' means having muttered one's own spell, such as the Gandhāra spell, for which homage has been made, and having recited it in the sequence of mantra recitation. 'By them' means by those things.

Payojananti pavattamānaṃ. Disvātiādi diṭṭhavisādīnaṃ yathākkamena vuttaṃ. Dvattibyāmasatappamāṇanāguddharaṇeti dvattibyāmasatappamāṇe mahākāye nimminitvā ṭhitānaṃ nāgānaṃ uddharaṇe. Kumbhaṇḍānanti kumbhaṇḍadevānaṃ. Te kira devā mahodarā honti, rahassaṅgampi ca nesaṃ kumbho viya mahantaṃ hoti, tasmā “kumbhaṇḍā”ti vuccanti.
