Vessavaṇassa yakkhādhipatibhāvepi nayanāvudhena kumbhaṇḍānaṃ maraṇassa idha vuttattā tesupi tassa āṇāpavatti veditabbā.

'Application' is that which is occurring. The phrase beginning with 'having seen' is stated in due order with reference to seen poison and so on. 'The lifting of nāgas measuring two or three hundred fathoms' refers to the lifting of nāgas who have created and are standing in a great body measuring two or three hundred fathoms. 'Kumbhaṇḍas' means the Kumbhaṇḍa deities. It is said that these deities have large bellies, and their private parts are as large as a pot; therefore, they are called 'Kumbhaṇḍas.' Even though Vessavaṇa is the lord of yakkhas, since the death of Kumbhaṇḍas by the weapon of the eye is mentioned here, his command should be understood to extend to them as well.

Kecīti mahāsaṅghikā. “Aho vata yaṃ taṃ kucchigataṃ gabbhaṃ na sotthinā abhinikkhameyyā”ti pāṭho sundarataro. “Aho vatāyaṃ ta”ntipi pāṭho. “Ayaṃ itthī taṃ kucchigataṃ gabbhaṃ na sotthinā abhinikkhāmeyyā”ti vattabbaṃ. Kulumbassāti gabbhassa kulasseva vā, kuṭumbassāti vuttaṃ hoti. Bhāvanāmayiddhiyāti adhiṭṭhāniddhiṃ sandhāya vadanti. Ghaṭabhedanaṃ viya iddhivināso, agginibbāpanaṃ viya parūpaghātoti upamāsaṃsandanaṃ. Taṃ tesaṃ icchāmattamevāti etthāyaṃ vicāraṇā – tumhe iddhiyā parūpaghātaṃ vadetha, iddhi nāma cesā adhiṭṭhāniddhi vikubbaniddhi manomayiddhi ñāṇavipphāriddhi samādhivipphāriddhi ariyiddhi kammavipākajiddhi puññavatoiddhi vijjāmayiddhi tattha tattha sammāpayogapaccayā ijjhanaṭṭhena iddhīti dasavidhā. Tattha kataraṃ iddhiṃ vadethāti? Bhāvanāmayanti. Kiṃ pana bhāvanāmayiddhiyā parūpaghātakammaṃ hotīti? Āma ekavāraṃ hoti. Yathā hi ādittagharassa upari udakabharite ghaṭe khitte ghaṭopi bhijjati, aggipi nibbāyati, evameva bhāvanāmayiddhiyā ekavāraṃ parūpaghātakammaṃ hoti, tato paṭṭhāya pana sā nassatīti. Atha ne “bhāvanāmayiddhiyā neva ekavāraṃ, na dve vāre parūpaghātakammaṃ hotī”ti vatvā saññattiṃ āgacchantā pucchitabbā “bhāvanāmayiddhi kiṃ kusalā, akusalā, abyākatā, sukhāya vedanāya sampayuttā, dukkhāya[M 2.0258], adukkhamasukhāya, savitakkasavicārā, avitakkavicāramattā, avitakkaavicārā, kāmāvacarā, rūpāvacarā, arūpāvacarā”ti.

'Some' (keci) refers to the Mahāsaṅghikas. The reading, 'Oh, may that fetus in the womb not come forth safely' (aho vata yaṃ taṃ kucchigataṃ gabbhaṃ na sotthinā abhinikkhameyyā), is more elegant. There is also the reading, 'Oh, may this one...' (aho vatāyaṃ taṃ). It should be said, 'May this woman not safely deliver that fetus in her womb' (ayaṃ itthī taṃ kucchigataṃ gabbhaṃ na sotthinā abhinikkhāmeyyā). 'Of the family' (kulumbassa) refers either to the lineage of the fetus, or it is said to mean 'of the household' (kuṭumbassa). 'By the power of development' (bhāvanāmayiddhi) they speak referring to the power of resolve (adhiṭṭhāniddhi). The breaking of a pot is like the destruction of psychic power, and the extinguishing of fire is like harming others—this is the connection of the simile. That is merely their wish. Here is the consideration: You say that psychic power can harm others. But psychic power (iddhi) is of ten kinds: the power of resolve (adhiṭṭhāna-iddhi), the power of transformation (vikubbana-iddhi), the power of mind-made creation (manomaya-iddhi), the power of knowledge expansion (ñāṇavipphāra-iddhi), the power of concentration expansion (samādhivipphāra-iddhi), noble power (ariya-iddhi), the power of karmic result (kammavipākaja-iddhi), the power of the meritorious (puññavato-iddhi), the power of knowledge (vijjāmaya-iddhi), and the power that succeeds through the condition of proper application in various instances (tattha tattha sammāpayogapaccayā ijjhanaṭṭhena iddhi). Among these, which psychic power do you refer to? 'The power of development' (bhāvanāmayā). But does the power of development involve the act of harming others? Yes, it does once. Just as when a water-filled pot is thrown onto a burning house, the pot breaks and the fire is extinguished, so too, the power of development can harm others once, but thereafter it ceases. Then, if they say, 'By the power of development, the act of harming others does not occur even once or twice,' they should be questioned as they approach the declaration: 'Is the power of development wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate? Is it associated with pleasant feeling, painful feeling, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling? Does it involve initial and sustained thought, sustained thought only, or neither initial nor sustained thought? Does it pertain to the sense-sphere, the form-sphere, or the formless sphere?'

Imaṃ pana pañhaṃ ye jānanti, te evaṃ vakkhanti “bhāvanāmayiddhi kusalā vā hoti abyākatā [V 2.0229] vā, adukkhamasukhavedanīyā eva, avitakkaavicārā eva, rūpāvacarā evā”ti. Te vattabbā “pāṇātipātacetanā kusalākusalādīsu kataraṃ koṭṭhāsaṃ bhajatī”ti. Jānantā vakkhanti “pāṇātipātacetanā akusalāva, dukkhavedanīyāva, savitakkasavicārāva, kāmāvacarā evā”ti. Evaṃ sante “tumhākaṃ kathā neva kusalattikena sameti, na vedanāttikena, na vitakkattikena, na parittattikenā”ti. Kiṃ pana evaṃ mahantaṃ suttaṃ niratthakanti? No niratthakaṃ, tumhe panassa atthaṃ na jānātha. Iddhimā cetovasippattoti ettha hi na bhāvanāmayiddhi adhippetā, āthabbaṇiddhi pana adhippetā. Sā hi ettha labbhamānā labbhatīti.

But those who know this question will say thus: 'The power of development (bhāvanāmayiddhi) is either wholesome or indeterminate, is always accompanied by neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, is always without initial and sustained thought, and pertains only to the form realm.' They should then be asked: 'Under which category does the intention to kill living beings (pāṇātipātacetanā) fall—among the wholesome, unwholesome, and so on?' Those who know will say: 'The intention to kill living beings is always unwholesome, is always accompanied by painful feeling, is always with initial and sustained thought, and pertains only to the sense sphere.' Thus, if this is so, 'your statement does not fit with the threefold classification of the wholesome, nor with the threefold classification of feeling, nor with the threefold classification of thought, nor with the classification of the limited.' But is such a great discourse meaningless? No, it is not meaningless, but you do not understand its meaning. For here, in 'one who has attained mastery of mind through psychic power' (iddhimā cetovasippatto), it is not the power of development (bhāvanāmayiddhi) that is intended, but rather the power of the Atharva Veda (āthabbaṇa-iddhi). For that power, being obtainable here, is obtained.

Haritabbaṃ upanikkhipitabbanti hāraṃ, hārameva hārakanti āha “atha vā”tiādi. Jīvitaharaṇakaṃ upanikkhipitabbaṃ vā satthaṃ satthahārakanti vikappadvayenāha. “Hārakasattha”nti ca vattabbe satthahārakanti visesanassa paranipātaṃ katvā vuttaṃ. Yathā labhati, tathā kareyyāti adhippāyatthamāha. Upanikkhipeyyāti “pariyeseyyā”ti imassa sikhāppattamatthaṃ dasseti. Itarathāti “pariyeseyyā”ti imassa upanikkhipeyyāti evamatthaṃ aggahetvā yadi pariyesanamattameva adhippetaṃ siyāti attho. Pariyiṭṭhamattenāti pariyesitamattena. “Satthahārakaṃ vāssa pariyeseyyā”ti iminā vuccamānassa atthassa byañjanānurūpato paripuṇṇaṃ katvā avuttattā āha “byañjanaṃ anādiyitvā”ti. Sasati hiṃsatīti satthaṃ, sasanti hiṃsanti tenāti vā satthanti laguḷapāsāṇādīnampi satthasaṅgahitattā āha – “yaṃ ettha thāvarappayogasaṅgahitaṃ satthaṃ, tadeva dassetu”nti.

“That which should be brought or placed near” is a hāra; hāra itself is a hāraka, thus he says “or,” etc. He states with two alternatives that satthahāraka refers to a life-taking weapon or a weapon to be placed near. And when “hārakasattha” should be said, it is stated as “satthahāraka” by transposing the adjective. He states the intended meaning: “One should act according to how one obtains it.” “Should place near” indicates the ultimate meaning of “should seek.” “Otherwise” means: if, not taking the meaning of “should seek” as “should place near,” merely seeking were intended. “By merely having sought” means by that which has only been sought. Regarding the statement, “or one should seek a weapon-provider for him,” because the full meaning is not stated in accordance with the wording, he says, “disregarding the wording.” That which cuts or harms is a sattha, or that by which they cut or harm is a sattha. Because clubs, stones, and the like are also included under “weapon,” he says: “Here, that weapon which is included in a fixed application should be shown.”

Vuttāvasesanti vuttaasiādīhi avasiṭṭhaṃ. Laguḷanti muggarassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Satthasaṅgahoti mātikāyaṃ “satthahāraka”nti ettha vuttasatthasaṅgaho. Yasmā…pe… tasmā dvidhā bhinditvā padabhājanaṃ vuttanti īdisaṃ heṭṭhā vuttavibhaṅganayabhedadassananti veditabbaṃ. Narake vā papatātiādīti ettha ādi-saddena “papāte vā papatā”ti parato vuttaṃ avuttañca “rukkhato vā papatā”tiādi sabbaṃ maraṇūpāyaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Tenevāha [M 2.0259] “na hi sakkā sabbaṃ sarūpeneva vattu”nti. Parato vuttanayattāti parato nigamanavasena vuttassa dutiyapadassa padabhājane vuttanayattā. Atthato vuttamevāti maraṇūpāyassa bahuvidhatānidassanatthaṃ, tato ekadese dassite sabbaṃ vuttameva hotīti adhippāyo. Na hi sakkā…pe… vattunti “rukkhato vā papatā”tiādinā sarūpato sabbaṃ maraṇūpāyaṃ pariyosānaṃ pāpetvā na sakkā vattunti attho.

“The remainder of what is stated” is what is left after stating “sword,” etc. “A club” is a synonym for a cudgel. “The collection of weapons” refers to the collection of weapons mentioned in the matrix under “weapon-provider.” “Because… therefore, having split it in two, the division of words is stated” should be understood as showing such a distinction and division of the method explained below. “Or falls into hell,” etc. Here, the word “etc.” includes what is stated later, such as “or falls into an abyss,” and what is unstated, such as “or falls from a tree,” encompassing all means of death. Therefore, it is said, “For it is not possible to state everything in its exact form.” “Due to the method stated later” means due to the method stated later in the division of words for the second word, by way of conclusion. “In meaning, it is already stated” means that this is for the purpose of showing the manifold nature of the means of death. Thus, when a part is shown, all is effectively stated—this is the intention. “For it is not possible… to state” means that it is not possible to state all means of death in their exact form by bringing it to a conclusion with “or falls from a tree,” etc.—this is the meaning.

Mataṃ [V 2.0230] te jīvitā seyyoti ettha vuttamaraṇaṃ yasmā iti-saddo nidasseti, tasmā tattha vuttamaraṇaṃ iti-saddassa atthoti tampi gahetvā atthaṃ dassento āha – “maraṇacitto maraṇamanoti attho”ti. Cittassa atthadīpanatthaṃ vuttoti citta-saddassa vicittādianekatthavisayattā nāyaṃ citta-saddo idha aññasmiṃ atthe vattamāno daṭṭhabbo, api tu viññāṇasmiṃyeva vattamāno veditabboti tassa atthassa niyamanatthaṃ vutto. Iminā punaruttidosassapi idha anavakāsoti dasseti. Na tāva attho vuttoti “iti cittamano”ti uddharitvāpi iti-saddanidassitassa maraṇassa aparāmaṭṭhabhāvato vuttaṃ. Tāva-saddena pana parato “cittasaṅkappo”ti imassa padabhājane “maraṇasaññī”tiādinā itisaddatthassa vakkhamānataṃ vibhāveti. Tattha hi iti-saddanidassitaṃ maraṇasaṅkhātamatthaṃ gahetvā “maraṇasaññī maraṇacetano maraṇādhippāyo”ti vuttaṃ. Tenevāha – “cittasaṅkappoti imasmiṃ pade adhikāravasena itisaddo āharitabbo”ti. Kasmā āharitabboti āha “idañhī”tiādi. Kathaṃ panetaṃ viññāyatīti āha “tathā hissā”tiādi. Assāti iti-saddassa. Tameva atthanti maraṇasaṅkhātamatthaṃ. “Maraṇasaññī”tiādīsu hi maraṇaṃ iti-saddassa attho, “saññī”tiādi saṅkappasaddassa. Cittasaddassa panettha vicittavacanatā saṅkappasaddassa saññācetanādhippāyavasena tidhā atthaṃ dassentena vibhāvitāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tenevāha – “citto nānappakārako saṅkappo”tiādi. Adhippāyasaddena kimettha vuttanti āha – “adhippāyoti vitakko veditabbo”ti. Na idaṃ vitakkassa nāmanti idaṃ pana na kevalaṃ vitakkasseva nāmanti dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Pākaṭattā oḷārikattā ca uccākāratā veditabbā, apākaṭattā anoḷārikattā ca avacākāratā.

In “Death is better for you than life,” the death mentioned is indicated by the word iti; therefore, taking that mentioned death as the meaning of the word iti, he says: “The meaning is ‘death-minded, death-intending.’” As for the statement, “It is said to clarify the meaning of citta,” because the word citta has various meanings, such as “diverse,” this word citta should not be understood here as occurring in any other sense, but should be known as occurring only in the sense of “consciousness.” Thus, it is stated to restrict its meaning. By this, he also shows that there is no room for the fault of redundancy here. As for “The meaning is not yet stated,” this is said because even after extracting “iti cittamano,” the death indicated by the word iti has not been fully grasped. However, by the word tāva, he clarifies that the meaning of the word iti will be explained later in the word-analysis of “cittasaṅkappo” by means of “maraṇasaññī” (perceiving death), and so forth. For there, taking the meaning indicated by the word iti—that is, the concept of death—it is stated: “perceiving death, with volition for death, resolved on death.” Therefore, he says: “In this phrase ‘cittasaṅkappo,’ the word iti should be supplied by way of the governing context.” Why should it be supplied? He says, “Because this…,” and so forth. But how is this understood? He says, “Because it is thus…,” and so forth. Assa is for the word iti. “That very meaning” is the meaning designated as death. In phrases like “maraṇasaññī,” maraṇa (death) is the meaning of the word iti, and “saññī,” and so forth, is the meaning of the word saṅkappa. Here, it should be understood that the manifold nature of the word citta is clarified by the one explaining the word saṅkappa in three ways: in terms of perception (saññā), volition (cetanā), and resolve (adhippāya). Therefore, he says: “Citto (mind) is a saṅkappa (thought) of various kinds,” and so forth. What is meant here by the word adhippāya (resolve)? He says: “Adhippāya (resolve) should be understood as vitakka (thought).” As for “It is not a name for vitakka,” this is stated to show that it is not merely a name for vitakka alone. The state of being high should be understood from its being manifest and coarse; the state of being low, from its being unmanifest and subtle.

174. Kāyekadesepi [M 2.0260] kāya-saddo vattatīti āha “hatthena vā”tiādi. Paharaṇenāti satthena. Satthañhi paharanti etenāti paharaṇanti vuccati. Kammunā bajjhatīti pāṇātipātakammunā bajjhati, pāṇātipātakammassa siddhanti vuttaṃ hoti. Yo koci maratūti ettha yassa kassaci ekasseva jīvitindriyavisayā vadhakacetanā pavattati, na pahārapaccayā marantasseva jīvitindriyavisayā, nāpi samūhassāti veditabbā. Ubhayathāpīti uddesānuddesānaṃ vasena. Vadhakacittaṃ paccuppannārammaṇampi jīvitindriyaṃ pabandhavicchedanavasena ārammaṇaṃ katvā pavattatīti āha “pacchā vā teneva rogenā”tiādi. Yena hi pabandho vicchijjati, tādisaṃ payogaṃ nibbattentaṃ tadā vadhakacittaṃ pavattantaṃ paharitamatteyeva kammunā bajjhati. Manussaarahantassa ca puthujjanakāleyeva satthappahāre vā vise vā dinnepi yadi so arahattaṃ patvā teneva marati, arahantaghātako hotiyeva. Yaṃ pana puthujjanakāle dinnaṃ dānaṃ arahattaṃ patvā paribhuñjati, puthujjanasseva taṃ dinnaṃ hoti.

174. The word ‘kāya’ (body) also applies to a part of the body; thus he says ‘with the hand,’ and so forth. ‘With a striking instrument’ means with a weapon. For, ‘they strike with this,’ thus it is called a ‘striking instrument’ (paharaṇa). ‘One is bound by kamma’ means one is bound by the kamma of destroying life; this means that the accomplishment of the kamma of destroying life is stated. In ‘Let anyone die,’ it should be understood that the killing volition arises with the life faculty of any single being whatsoever as its object, not only with the life faculty of the one dying because of the blow as its object, nor of a group. ‘In both ways’ means by way of specifying and not specifying. The killing-consciousness, even when its object is present, operates by taking the life faculty as its object in the sense of severing its continuity; thus he says ‘or later by that very disease,’ and so forth. For, when one produces such an effort by which the continuity is severed, the killing-consciousness that arises at that time is bound by kamma at the very moment of striking. In the case of a human who is an arahant, even if a strike with a weapon or poison was given when he was an ordinary person, if he, having attained arahantship, dies by that very cause, the killer is indeed a killer of an arahant. However, a gift that was given when he was an ordinary person, which he enjoys after attaining arahantship, is considered a gift given only to an ordinary person.

Nanu [V 2.0231] ca yathā arahattaṃ patvā paribhuttampi puthujjanakāle dinnaṃ puthujjanadānameva hoti, evaṃ maraṇādhippāyena puthujjanakāle pahāre dinne arahattaṃ patvā teneva pahārena mate kasmā arahantaghātakoyeva hoti, na puthujjanaghātakoti? Visesasabbhāvato. Dānañhi deyyadhammassa pariccāgamattena hoti. Tathā hi dānacetanā cajitabbaṃ vatthuṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā cajanamattameva hoti, aññasantakakaraṇaṃva tassa cajanaṃ, tasmā yassa taṃ santakaṃ kataṃ, tasseva taṃ dinnaṃ hoti, na evaṃ vadho. So hi pāṇo pāṇasaññitā vadhakacetanā upakkamo tena maraṇanti imesaṃ pañcannaṃ aṅgānaṃ pāripūriyāva hoti, na apāripūriyā. Tasmā arahattaṃ pattasseva maraṇanti arahantaghātakoyeva hoti, na puthujjanaghātako. Yasmā pana “imaṃ māremī”ti yaṃ santānaṃ ārabbha māraṇicchā, tassa puthujjanakhīṇāsavabhāvena payogamaraṇakkhaṇānaṃ vasena satipi santānabhede abhedoyeva, yadā ca atthasiddhi, tadā khīṇāsavabhāvo, tasmā arahantaghātakoyeva hotīti niṭṭhamettha gantabbaṃ.

Is it not so that just as a gift given during one’s ordinary state, even if consumed after attaining arahantship, is still just a gift to an ordinary person, so too, when a blow is given with the intention of death during one’s ordinary state, and one dies from that very blow after attaining arahantship, why is the killer considered only a killer of an arahant and not a killer of an ordinary person? Because of the existence of a specific difference. For giving occurs merely through the relinquishing of the object to be given. Indeed, the volition of giving, having as its object the thing to be relinquished, is simply the act of relinquishing, like making something the possession of another. Therefore, to whomever it is made a possession, to that one it is given. Killing is not like this. For it occurs only through the fulfillment of these five factors: (1) a living being, (2) the perception of a living being, (3) the volition to kill, (4) the effort, and (5) death through that effort; it does not occur through their non-fulfillment. Therefore, since the death is of one who has attained arahantship, the killer is only a killer of an arahant, not a killer of an ordinary person. Furthermore, the desire to kill, ‘I will kill this one,’ is directed towards a particular life-continuum. Although there is a difference in the continuum—by way of the state of being an ordinary person and one with destroyed cankers at the moments of the effort and death respectively—it is in fact undivided. And when the goal is accomplished, the state is that of one with destroyed cankers. Therefore, the killer is indeed a killer of an arahant. This is the conclusion to be reached here.

Aññacittenāti avadhādhippāyena amāretukāmatācittena. Natthi pāṇātipātoti amāretukāmatācittena pahaṭattā. Kiñcāpi paṭhamappahāro [M 2.0261] na sayameva sakkoti māretuṃ, dutiyaṃ pana labhitvā sakkonto jīvitavināsanahetu hoti, tasmā “payogo tena ca maraṇa”nti iminā saṃsandanato paṭhamappahāreneva kammabaddho yutto, na dutiyena tassa aññacittena dinnattā. Tena vuttaṃ “ubhayehi matepi paṭhamappahāreneva kammunā baddho”ti.

‘With another mind’ means with no intention to kill, with a mind not desiring to kill. ‘There is no offense of destroying life’ is said because the blow was struck with a mind not desiring to kill. Although the first blow is not able to kill by itself, yet when a second is received from another, it becomes a contributing cause for the destruction of life. Therefore, by connecting this with the principle ‘the effort and the death resulting from it’, it is proper that one is bound by kamma for the first blow alone, not for the second, as his own was delivered with another mind. Hence, it is said: ‘Even when death results from both blows, one is bound by kamma due to the first blow alone.’

Kammāpattibyattibhāvatthanti ānantariyādikammavibhāgassa pārājikādiāpattivibhāgassa ca vibhāvanatthaṃ. “Eḷakaṃ māremī”ti pavattacetanāya pubbabhāgattā “imaṃ māremī”ti sanniṭṭhāpakacetanāya tadā sannihitattā yathāvatthukaṃ kammabaddho hotiyevāti āha “imaṃ vatthuṃ māremīti cetanāya atthibhāvato”tiādi. Sabbattha hi purimaṃ abhisandhicittaṃ appamāṇaṃ tena atthasiddhiyā abhāvato, vadhakacittaṃ pana tadārammaṇañca jīvitindriyaṃ anantariyādibhāve pamāṇanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ghātako ca hotīti pāṇaghātako hoti, pāṇātipātakammunāva baddho hotīti attho. Pubbe vuttanayeneva veditabbanti yathākkamaṃ pārājikathullaccayapācittiyāni veditabbāni. “Mātāpituarahantānaṃ aññataraṃ māremī”ti guṇamahantesu pavattapubbabhāgacetanāya dāruṇabhāvato tathāvidhapubbabhāgacetanāparivārā sanniṭṭhāpakacetanā dāruṇāva hotīti āha – “idha pana cetanā dāruṇā hotī”ti. Iminā ca “eḷakaṃ māressāmī”ti mātāpituādīnaṃ māraṇepi pubbabhāgacetanāya adāruṇattā aññathā pavattaānantariyakammato evaṃ pavattānantariyassa nātidāruṇatā vuttāva hotīti daṭṭhabbā.

‘For the purpose of making distinct the state of kamma and offense’ means: for the purpose of making clear the division of kamma, such as anantariya, and the division of offenses, such as pārājika. Because the volition that arises with the thought, ‘I will kill a goat,’ is the preliminary part, and the completing volition, ‘I will kill this one,’ is present at that time, the kamma is indeed bound according to the object. Thus, it is said, ‘because of the existence of the volition, “I will kill this being,”’ and so on. For in all cases, the prior intention (abhisandhicitta) is not the measure, because by it the purpose is not accomplished; but the killing mind and the life-faculty which is its object at that time are to be understood as the measure in being an anantariya kamma and so forth. ‘And he becomes a killer’ means he becomes a killer of a living being; the meaning is that he is bound by the kamma of taking life. ‘It should be understood by the method previously stated’ means the pārājika, thullaccaya, and pācittiya offenses should be understood in sequence. When one thinks, ‘I will kill one among my mother, father, or an arahant,’ due to the cruel nature of the preliminary volition directed towards those great in virtue, the completing volition, which is accompanied by such a preliminary volition, is indeed cruel. Thus, it is said: ‘Here, however, the volition is cruel.’ And by this, it should be understood that even in the killing of one’s mother, father, and so on, with the thought, ‘I will kill a goat,’ because of the non-cruel nature of the preliminary volition, the not-so-cruel nature of an anantariya kamma that has thus arisen, compared to an anantariya kamma that has arisen otherwise, is indeed stated.

Lohitakanti [V 2.0232] lohitamakkhitaṃ. Kammaṃ karonteti yuddhakammaṃ karonte. Yathādhippāyaṃ gateti yodhaṃ vijjhitvā pitari viddhe. Idañca yathādhippāyaṃ tena tathāviddhabhāvadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Ayathādhippāyaṃ pana ujukameva gantvā pitari viddhepi maraṇādhippāyena attanāva katappayogattā nevatthi visaṅketoti vadanti. Ānantariyaṃ pana natthīti pitaraṃ uddissa katappayogābhāvato.

‘Lohitaka’ means smeared with blood. ‘Kammaṃ karonte’ means while performing the act of battle. ‘Yathādhippāyaṃ gate’ means when it went according to the intention, that is, having pierced the warrior, the father was struck. And this is stated to show that it was struck in such a way by him, according to his intention. However, when it was not according to the intention, having gone straight and struck the father, they say that because the effort was made by oneself with the intention to cause death, there is no deviation. But there is no anantariya kamma, because of the absence of an effort made directed towards the father.

Adhiṭṭhāyāti mātikāvasena āṇattikapayogakathāvaṇṇanā

‘Adhiṭṭhāya’ is the explanation of the discourse on the application of a command, by way of the outline.

Evaṃ [M 2.0262] vijjhāti evaṃ dhanuṃ kaḍḍhetvā vijjha. Evaṃ paharāti evaṃ daḷhaṃ asiṃ gahetvā pahara. Evaṃ ghātehīti evaṃ kammakāraṇaṃ katvā mārehi. Majjheti hatthino piṭṭhimajjhe. Etenāti “adhiṭṭhahitvā āṇāpetī”tiādinā. Tatthāti āṇattikappayoge.

‘Evaṃ vijjha’ means: having drawn the bow in this way, pierce. ‘Evaṃ pahara’ means: having firmly grasped the sword in this way, strike. ‘Evaṃ ghātehi’ means: having performed the procedure in this way, kill. ‘Majjhe’ means: in the middle of the elephant’s back. ‘Etena’ refers to the text beginning with ‘having resolved, he commands.’ ‘Tattha’ means: in the application of a command.

Kiñcāpi kiriyaviseso aṭṭhakathāsu anāgato, pāḷiyaṃ pana “evaṃ vijjha, evaṃ pahara, evaṃ ghātehī”ti kiriyāvisesassa parāmaṭṭhattā ācariyaparamparāya ābhataṃ kiriyāvisesaṃ pāḷiyā saṃsandanato gahetvā dassento “aparo nayo”tiādimāha. Chedananti hatthādichedanaṃ. Bhedananti kucchiādiphālanaṃ. Atha vā usunā vijjhanaṃ, asinā chedanaṃ, muggarādīhi sīsādibhedananti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Saṅkhamuṇḍakanti saṅkhamuṇḍakammakāraṇaṃ. Taṃ karontā uttaroṭṭhaubhatokaṇṇacūḷikagalavāṭakaparicchedena cammaṃ chinditvā sabbakese ekato gaṇṭhiṃ katvā daṇḍakena paliveṭhetvā uppāṭenti, saha kesehi cammaṃ uṭṭhahati, tato sīsakaṭāhaṃ thūlasakkharāhi ghaṃsitvā dhovantā saṅkhavaṇṇaṃ karonti. Evamādīti ādi-saddena bilaṅgathālikaṃ rāhumukhaṃ jotimālikaṃ hatthapajjotikaṃ erakavattikaṃ cīrakavāsikaṃ eṇeyyakaṃ baḷisamaṃsikaṃ kahāpaṇikaṃ khārāpatacchikaṃ palighaparivattikaṃ palālapīṭhakanti evamādiṃ sabbaṃ kammakāraṇaṃ saṅgaṇhāti.

Although the particular action is not found in the commentaries, since the particular action is alluded to in the Pāḷi by ‘thus pierce, thus strike, thus kill,’ the author, taking the particular action handed down through the tradition of teachers and correlating it with the Pāḷi, shows it by saying, ‘another method,’ and so forth. ‘Chedana’ means the cutting of hands and so forth. ‘Bhedana’ means the splitting of the belly and so forth. Alternatively, the meaning here should be understood as: piercing with an arrow, cutting with a sword, and splitting the head and so forth with clubs and so forth. ‘Saṅkhamuṇḍaka’ means the act of making a conch-shell head. Those who perform this, after cutting the skin along the outline of the upper lip, both ear-tips, and the throat-circle, gather all the hair into a single knot, wrap it with a stick, and pull it up; the skin comes off with the hair. Then, scrubbing the skull with coarse gravel and washing it, they make it the color of a conch. ‘Evamādi’—by the word ‘ādi’ (and so forth), it includes all such acts as: bilaṅgathālika (the gruel-pot), rāhumukha (the Rāhu-mouth), jotimālika (the garland-of-lights), hatthapajjotika (the hand-torch), erakavattika (the eraka-wick), cīrakavāsika (the rag-garment), eṇeyyaka (the antelope), baḷisamaṃsika (the fish-hook flesh), kahāpaṇika (the coin-sized flesh removal), khārāpatacchika (the lye-scraping), palighaparivattika (the palisade-turning), and palālapīṭhaka (the straw-seat).

Tattha (a. ni. aṭṭha. 2.2.1) bilaṅgathālikanti kañjiyaukkhalikakammakāraṇaṃ. Taṃ kammaṃ karontā sīsakapālaṃ uppāṭetvā tattaṃ ayoguḷaṃ saṇḍāsena gahetvā tattha pakkhipanti, tena matthaluṅgaṃ pakkuthitvā upari uttarati. Rāhumukhanti rāhumukhakammakāraṇaṃ. Taṃ karonto saṅkunā mukhaṃ vivaritvā antomukhe dīpaṃ jālenti, kaṇṇacūḷikāhi vā paṭṭhāya mukhaṃ nikhādanena khaṇanti, lohitaṃ paggharitvā mukhaṃ pūreti. Jotimālikanti sakalasarīraṃ telapilotikāya veṭhetvā ālimpenti. Hatthapajjotikanti hatthe telapilotikāya veṭhetvā dīpaṃ viya pajjālenti. Erakavattikanti erakavattakammakāraṇaṃ. Taṃ karontā heṭṭhāgīvato paṭṭhāya cammavaṭṭe [V 2.0233] kantitvā gopphake [M 2.0263] pātenti, atha naṃ yottehi bandhitvā kaḍḍhanti, so attanova cammavaṭṭe akkamitvā patati. Cīrakavāsikanti cīrakavāsikakammakāraṇaṃ. Taṃ karontā tatheva cammavaṭṭe kantitvā kaṭiyaṃ ṭhapenti, kaṭito paṭṭhāya kantitvā gopphakesu ṭhapenti, uparimehi heṭṭhimasarīraṃ cīrakanivāsananivatthaṃ viya hoti. Eṇeyyakanti eṇeyyakammakāraṇaṃ. Taṃ karontā ubhosu kapparesu ca jaṇṇukesu ca ayavalayāni datvā ayasūlāni koṭṭenti, so catūhi ayasūlehi bhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhahati, atha naṃ parivāretvā aggiṃ karonti, taṃ kālena kālaṃ sandhito sūlāni apanetvā catūhi aṭṭhikoṭīhiyeva ṭhapenti.

Therein, ‘bilaṅgathālika’ refers to the act of making a gruel-pot. Those performing this act, having removed the skullcap, take a hot iron ball with tongs and place it therein; by that, the brain boils and rises to the top. ‘Rāhumukha’ refers to the act of making a Rāhu-mouth. One performing this pries open the mouth with a stake and lights a lamp inside the mouth; or, starting from the ear-tips, they dig into the mouth with a chisel, causing blood to gush out and fill the mouth. ‘Jotimālika’ refers to wrapping the entire body with oil-soaked cloth and setting it alight. ‘Hatthapajjotika’ refers to wrapping the hands with oil-soaked cloth and igniting them like lamps. ‘Erakavattika’ refers to the act of making an eraka-wick. Those performing this, starting from below the neck, flay a strip of skin and let it fall to the ankles; then they bind the person with straps and pull, causing the person to step on their own strip of skin and fall. ‘Cīrakavāsika’ refers to the act of making a rag-garment. Those performing this, in the same way, having flayed strips of skin, arrange them at the waist; and having flayed strips starting from the waist, they arrange them at the ankles, so that the lower body appears as if clad in a rag-garment. ‘Eṇeyyaka’ refers to the act of making like an antelope. Those performing this, having placed iron rings on both elbows and knees, hammer in iron stakes. The person stands on the ground on four iron stakes. Then, surrounding the person, they light a fire. From time to time, they remove the stakes from the joints and make the person stand only on the four bone-ends.

Baḷisamaṃsikanti ubhatomukhehi baḷisehi paharitvā cammamaṃsanahārūni uppāṭenti. Kahāpaṇikanti sakalasarīraṃ tikhiṇāhi vāsīhi koṭito paṭṭhāya kahāpaṇamattaṃ kahāpaṇamattaṃ pātentā koṭṭenti. Khārāpatacchikanti sarīraṃ tattha tattha āvudhehi paharitvā kocchehi khāraṃ ghaṃsanti, cammamaṃsanahārūni paggharitvā aṭṭhikasaṅkhalikāva tiṭṭhati. Palighaparivattikanti ekena passena nipajjāpetvā kaṇṇachidde ayasūlaṃ koṭṭetvā pathaviyā ekābaddhaṃ karonti, atha naṃ pāde gahetvā āviñchanti. Palālapīṭhakanti cheko kāraṇiko chavicammaṃ acchinditvā nisadapotehi aṭṭhīni bhinditvā kesesu gahetvā ukkhipati, maṃsarāsiyeva hoti, atha naṃ keseheva pariyonandhitvā gaṇhantā palālavaṭṭiṃ viya katvā paliveṭhenti.

‘Baḷisamaṃsika’ means they hook him with two-mouthed hooks and tear out skin, flesh, and sinews. ‘Kahāpaṇika’ means they chop the entire body with sharp adzes, starting from the top, causing pieces the size of a kahāpaṇa to fall, piece by piece. ‘Khārāpatacchika’ means they strike the body here and there with weapons and rub it with a caustic substance using brushes; skin, flesh, and sinews ooze out, until only a chain of bones remains. ‘Palighaparivattika’ means they make him lie on one side, hammer an iron stake through his ear-hole, fixing it to the ground as one piece; then, grasping his feet, they drag him around. ‘Palālapīṭhaka’ means a skilled executioner, without cutting the outer skin and hide, breaks the bones with stone pestles, then grasps him by the hair and lifts him up; he becomes just a heap of flesh. Then, wrapping him up completely with his own hair and taking hold of him, they make him like a bundle of straw and roll him up.

Vatthuṃ visaṃvādetvā tato aññaṃ māretīti sambandho. Purimapassādīnampi vatthusabhāgato vatthuggahaṇeneva gahaṇanti āha “purato paharitvā”tiādi. Cittena “purato vā”ti niyamaṃ katvā vā akatvā vā “purato paharitvā mārehī”ti vutte sace aññattha paharitvā māreti, lesaṃ oḍḍetvā avuttattā visaṅketova hoti. Cittena pana yattha katthaci paharitvā māraṇaṃ icchantopi sace “purato paharitvā mārehī”ti vadati, tassa lesaṃ oḍḍetvā tathā vuttamatthaṃ ṭhapetvā teneva cittena samuṭṭhāpitaviññattikattā manussaviggahapārājikato pariyāyena amuccanato “aññattha paharitvā māritepi nevatthi visaṅketo”ti vadanti, keci pana taṃ na icchanti. Vatthuvisesenāti mātuādivatthuvisesena[M 2.0264]. Kammavisesoti ānantariyādikammaviseso. Āpattivisesoti pārājikādiāpattiviseso.

Having miscommunicated about the object, he then kills another—this is the connection. Even in the case of the first sight and so on, due to the nature of the object, it is grasped by the taking of the object itself; thus he said, 'having struck in front,' etc. Whether or not one has made a mental specification, 'in front,' when it is said, 'Having struck in front, kill him,' if one then strikes elsewhere and kills, there is a discrepancy because a pretext was not stated. But if, while mentally intending to kill by striking anywhere, one says, 'Having struck in front, kill him,' some say that there is no discrepancy even if he is killed by being struck elsewhere. This is because the communication was initiated by that very intention—having set up a pretext for the agent and established the meaning as spoken—and because one is not indirectly freed from the pārājika offense for killing a human being. Some, however, do not accept this. 'By a specific object' means by a specific object such as one's mother. 'By a specific action' means a specific action such as an immediately effective kamma. 'By a specific offense' means a specific offense such as a pārājika.

“Etaṃ gāme ṭhita”nti gāmo puggalaniyamanatthaṃ vutto, na okāsaniyamanatthaṃ, tasmā okāsaṃ aniyametvā puggalasseva niyamitattā natthi visaṅketo. “Gāmeye vā”tiādīsu pana okāsassa niyamitattā aññattha mārite visaṅketo vutto.

Regarding 'This one staying in the village,' the village is mentioned for the purpose of specifying the person, not for specifying the place. Therefore, since the place is not specified and only the person is specified, there is no discrepancy. But in cases like 'or in the village,' since the place is specified, a discrepancy is spoken of if he is killed elsewhere.

Tuṇḍenāti [V 2.0234] khaggakoṭiyā. Tharunāti khaggamuṭṭhinā.

‘By the beak’ means by the tip of the sword. ‘By the hilt’ means by the hilt of the sword.

“Etaṃ gacchanta”nti gamanena puggalova niyamito, na iriyāpatho. Tenāha “natthi visaṅketo”ti. “Gacchantamevā”tiādinā iriyāpatho niyamito. Tenāha “visaṅketo hotī”ti.

Regarding 'this one going,' by 'going' only the person is specified, not the posture. For that reason, it is said, 'There is no discrepancy.' But by phrases such as 'the one who is actually going,' the posture is specified. For that reason, it is said, 'There is a discrepancy.'

“Dīghaṃ mārehī”ti vuttepi dīghasaṇṭhānānaṃ bahubhāvato itthannāmaṃ evarūpañca dīghanti aññesaṃ asādhāraṇalakkhaṇena aniddiṭṭhattā “aniyametvā āṇāpetī”ti vuttaṃ. Tenevāha “yaṃ kiñci tādisaṃ māretī”ti. Ettha ca “cittena bahūsu dīghasaṇṭhānesu ekaṃ niyametvā vuttepi vācāya aniyamitattā aññasmiṃ tādise mārite natthi visaṅketo”ti vadanti. Parapāṇimhi pāṇasaññitālakkhaṇassa aṅgassa abhāvato nevatthi pāṇātipātoti āha “āṇāpako muccatī”ti. Yadi evaṃ okāsaniyame sati kathaṃ pāṇātipātoti? Okāsaṃ niyamentassa tasmiṃ okāse nisinnassa jīvitindriyaṃ ārammaṇaṃ hotīti gahetabbaṃ. Okāsañhi niyametvā niddisanto tasmiṃ okāse nisinnaṃ mārāpetukāmo hoti, sayaṃ pana tadā tattha natthi, tasmā okāsena saha attano jīvitindriyaṃ ārammaṇaṃ na hotīti vadanti.

Even when it is said, 'Kill the tall one,' because there are many of a tall stature, and because a tall person of a specific name and appearance is not indicated by a characteristic not common to others, it is said that 'he commands without specifying.' For that very reason, it is said, 'he kills whatever such person.' And here they say: 'Even if one speaks having mentally specified one among many of a tall stature, because it was not specified by speech, if another such person is killed, there is no discrepancy.' Because the factor which is the characteristic of perceiving it as a living being is absent with respect to the life of another, there is no killing of a living being; thus it is said, 'the one who commands is freed.' If so, when there is specification of place, how is there killing of a living being? It should be understood that for one who specifies a place, the life-faculty of the one sitting in that place becomes the object. Indeed, one who indicates by specifying a place is desirous of having the one sitting in that place killed, but he himself is not there at that time. Therefore, they say, his own life-faculty together with the place does not become the object.

Adhiṭṭhāyāti mātikāvasena āṇattikapayogakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Regarding 'Adhiṭṭhāya' (having determined), the explanation of the discussion on the application of commands, according to the matrix, is finished.

Dūtakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discussion on Messengers

Evaṃ āṇāpentassa ācariyassa tāva dukkaṭanti sace sā āṇatti yathādhippāyaṃ na gacchati, ācariyassa āṇattikkhaṇe dukkaṭaṃ. Sace [M 2.0265] pana sā āṇatti yathādhippāyaṃ gacchati, yaṃ parato thullaccayaṃ vuttaṃ, āṇattikkhaṇe tadeva hoti. Atha so taṃ avassaṃ ghāteti, yaṃ parato “sabbesaṃ āpatti pārājikassā”ti vuttaṃ, tato imassa taṅkhaṇeyeva pārājikaṃ hotīti evamettha attho gahetabbo. Ācariyena pana heṭṭhā adinnādānakathāyaṃ (pārā. 121) vuttanayeneva ayamattho sakkā viññātunti idha na vutto. Vuttañhi tattha “āpatti dukkaṭassāti evaṃ āṇāpentassa ācariyassa tāva dukkaṭaṃ. Sace pana sā āṇatti yathādhippāyaṃ gacchati, yaṃ parato thullaccayaṃ vuttaṃ, āṇattikkhaṇe tadeva hoti. Atha taṃ bhaṇḍaṃ avassaṃ hāriyaṃ hoti, yaṃ parato ‘sabbesaṃ āpatti pārājikassā’ti vuttaṃ, tato imassa taṅkhaṇeyeva pārājikaṃ hotīti ayaṃ yutti sabbattha veditabbā”ti. Tesampi dukkaṭanti ārocanapaccayā dukkaṭaṃ. Paṭiggahitamatteti ettha avassaṃ ce paṭiggaṇhāti, tato pubbeva ācariyassa [V 2.0235] thullaccayaṃ, na pana paṭiggahiteti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kasmā panassa thullaccayanti āha “mahājano hi tena pāpe niyojito”ti.

When the teacher gives such an order, at first there is a dukkaṭa offense. If that instruction does not proceed according to its intended purpose, the teacher incurs a dukkaṭa at the moment of giving the instruction. However, if that instruction does proceed according to its intended purpose, then the thullaccaya that is spoken of as occurring later, occurs at that very moment of the instruction. Then, if that person inevitably kills the other, what was stated later as 'for all, the offense is a pārājika,' becomes a pārājika for this one at that very moment. This is how the meaning should be understood here. As for the teacher, this meaning can be understood by the very same method as explained previously in the section on taking what is not given, and so it is not stated here. For it was stated there: 'The offense is a dukkaṭa'—thus, for the teacher giving such an order, there is at first a dukkaṭa. But if that instruction proceeds according to its intended purpose, the thullaccaya that is spoken of as occurring later, occurs at that very moment of the instruction. Then, if that item is inevitably to be taken, what was stated later as 'for all, the offense is a pārājika,' becomes a pārājika for this one at that very moment. This principle should be understood everywhere. For them too, there is a dukkaṭa—a dukkaṭa due to the condition of informing. Here, regarding 'merely upon acceptance,' it should be understood that if one will inevitably accept the task, a thullaccaya occurs for the teacher even before that, and not only at the moment it is accepted. Why then is there a thullaccaya for him? He says: 'Because many people are engaged by him in evil.'

Mūlaṭṭhasseva dukkaṭanti idaṃ mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ āgatanayadassanamattaṃ, na pana taṃ ācariyassa adhippetaṃ. Tenāha “evaṃ sante”tiādi, evaṃ mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttanayena atthe satīti attho. Paṭiggahaṇe āpattiyeva na siyāti vadhakassa “sādhu suṭṭhū”ti māraṇapaṭiggahaṇe dukkaṭāpatti na siyā, evaṃ anoḷārikavisayepi tāva dukkaṭaṃ hoti, kimaṅgaṃ pana māraṇapaṭiggahaṇeti dassanatthaṃ sañcarittapaṭiggahaṇādi nidassitaṃ. “Aho vata itthannāmo hato assā”ti evaṃ maraṇābhinandanepi dukkaṭe sati pageva māraṇapaṭiggahaṇeti adhippāyo. Paṭiggaṇhantassevetaṃ dukkaṭanti avadhāraṇena visaṅketattā imassa paṭiggahaṇapaccayā mūlaṭṭhassa nattheva āpattīti dasseti. Keci pana “idha vuttadukkaṭaṃ paṭiggaṇhantassevāti ettakameva avadhāraṇena dassitaṃ, na pana mūlaṭṭhassa mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttadukkaṭaṃ paṭikkhitta”nti vadanti. Purimanayeti samanantarātīte avisakkiyadūtaniddese. Etanti dukkaṭaṃ. Yadi evaṃ kasmā pāḷiyaṃ na vuttanti āha “okāsābhāvenā”ti. Tattha mūlaṭṭhassa thullaccayavacanato paṭiggaṇhantassa dukkaṭaṃ vattuṃ okāso natthīti okāsābhāvena na vuttaṃ, na pana abhāvatoti adhippāyo.

'For the original instigator, there is only a dukkaṭa'—this is merely showing the method that has come down in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā; however, that is not the teacher's intended meaning. Therefore, he said, 'This being so,' etc. The meaning is: when there is a meaning according to the method stated in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā. If that were the case, there would be no offense at all in receiving—for the killer, in accepting the killing by saying 'Good, very good,' a dukkaṭa offense would not occur. Thus, even in a non-gross matter, there is at first a dukkaṭa; what then to say of accepting a killing? To show this, the acceptance of acting as a go-between, etc., was shown as an example. The intention is that when there is a dukkaṭa even for rejoicing in death, such as saying, 'Oh, that so-and-so might be killed!' what more for accepting a killing? 'This dukkaṭa is only for the one who receives'—by this emphasis, because the message has been dispatched, it shows that for the original instigator, there is no offense at all due to the condition of this receiving. Some, however, say, 'Here, the dukkaṭa mentioned is shown by the emphasis to apply only to the receiver; the dukkaṭa stated in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā for the original instigator is not, however, rejected.' 'In the previous method' refers to the immediately preceding explanation of the unwavering messenger. 'This' refers to the dukkaṭa. If so, why is it not stated in the Pāḷi? He said, 'Because of the lack of occasion.' There, because of the statement of a thullaccaya for the original instigator, there is no occasion to state the dukkaṭa for the one who receives. It was not stated because of the lack of occasion, and not, however, because of its absence. This is the intended meaning.

Āṇattikkhaṇe [M 2.0266] puthujjanoti ettha anāgate voropetabbajīvitindriyavasena atthasādhikacetanāya pavattattā arahantaghātako jātoti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Here, regarding 'a worldling at the moment of the command,' it should be understood that because the intention that accomplishes the purpose occurs with respect to the life faculty to be destroyed in the future, he becomes a killer of an arahant.

Dūtakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Discussion on Messengers is finished.

175. Sayaṃ saṅghattherattā “upaṭṭhānakāle”ti vuttaṃ. Vācāya vācāya dukkaṭanti “yo koci mama vacanaṃ sutvā imaṃ dhāretū”ti iminā adhippāyena avatvā kevalaṃ maraṇābhinandanavaseneva vuttattā “corāpi nāma taṃ na hanantī”tiādivācāsupi dukkaṭameva vuttaṃ. Ayamattho etena vuttoti yathā so jānātīti sambandho. Vākyabhedanti vacībhedaṃ. Dvinnaṃ uddissāti dve uddissa, dvinnaṃ vā maraṇaṃ uddissa. Ubho uddissa maraṇaṃ saṃvaṇṇentassa cetanāya ekattepi “dve pāṇātipātā”ti vattabbabhāvato balavabhāvaṃ āpajjitvā paṭisandhivipākasamanantaraṃ pavattiyaṃ anekāsupi jātīsu aparāpariyacetanāvasena dukkhuppādanato mahāvipākattā “akusalarāsī”ti vuttaṃ. Bahū uddissa maraṇasaṃvaṇṇanepi eseva nayo.

175. Because he himself was the elder of the Saṅgha, it was said, "at the time of attendance." For every utterance, it is a dukkaṭa offense. This is because it was said merely by way of rejoicing in death, without speaking with this intention: "Whoever, having heard my word, may he remember this." Even in statements like, "Indeed, even thieves do not kill him," etc., only a dukkaṭa offense was stated. "This meaning is spoken by this one" is connected as "so that he may know." 'Breaking of the sentence' means a breaking of speech. 'Intending two' means intending two people, or intending the death of two. For one who praises death intending both, even though the intention is single, because it must be called 'two acts of taking life,' it attains a strong nature, and since it produces suffering in many births in the course of existence immediately following the rebirth-linking resultant consciousness by way of subsequent intentions, it has a great result and is thus called a 'heap of the unwholesome.' The same method applies even in praising death intending many.

Evanti [V 2.0236] “sīsaṃ vā chinditvā papāte vā papatitvā”tiādinā. Ārocitamatteti vuttamatte. Yathā ariyamaggakkhaṇe cattāro satipaṭṭhānā cattāro sammappadhānā ca kiccavasena ijjhanti, evaṃ cetanāya ekattepi kiccavasena anekā pāṇātipātā ijjhantīti āha “tattakā pāṇātipātā”ti. Yathā hi attānaṃ sataṃ katvā dassetukāmassa “sataṃ homi sataṃ homī”ti kataparikammavasena laddhapaccuppannaparittārammaṇaṃ abhiññācittaṃ satantogadhānaṃ vaṇṇesu ekassa vaṇṇaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvāpi sataṃ nipphādeti, yathā ca ekassa maraṇe pavattamānāpi vadhakacetanā sakalasarīre uppajjamānaṃ nirujjhamānañca sakalampi jīvitindriyaṃ ekappahāreneva ālambitumasakkuṇeyyattā ṭhānappattaṃ ekadesappavattaṃ jīvitindriyaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā ārammaṇabhūtaṃ sakalampi jīvitindriyaṃ vināseti, evameva paccuppannaparittārammaṇāya vadhakacetanāya māretukāmatāya pariggahitasattesu ekasseva jīvitindriye ārammaṇe katepi kiccanipphattivasena sabbepi māritāva honti.

Thus, by such as 'having cut off the head or having fallen from a cliff.' 'Merely upon being informed' means 'merely upon being spoken.' Just as at the moment of the noble path, the four foundations of mindfulness and the four right efforts are accomplished by way of their function, so too, though the intention is one, many acts of taking life are accomplished by way of their function—thus he said, 'that many acts of taking life.' For example, just as for one who wishes to show himself as a hundred, having done preparatory work by thinking 'I will be a hundred, I will be a hundred,' the proficient supernormal consciousness, which has obtained a limited present object, accomplishes a hundred even by making the quality of one among a hundred its object; and just as the killing-intention, even when operating at the death of one, since it is unable to grasp with a single blow the entire life-faculty that is arising and ceasing throughout the whole body, makes the life-faculty that has reached a specific state and is operating in one part of the body its object, and thereby destroys the entire life-faculty that has become its object; in the very same way, with a killing-intention that has a limited present object and the desire to kill, even when the life-faculty of only one of the targeted beings is made the object, by way of the accomplishment of the function, all are indeed killed.

176. Yesaṃ [M 2.0267] hatthatoti yesaṃ ñātakapavāritānaṃ hatthato. Tesaṃ mūlaṃ datvā muccatīti idaṃ tena katapayogassa puna pākatikabhāvāpādanaṃ avasānaṃ pāpetvā dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. “Mūlena kītaṃ pana potthakaṃ potthakasāmikānaṃ datvā muccatiyevā”ti tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Kenaci pana “sace potthakaṃ sāmikānaṃ datvā mūlaṃ na gaṇhāti, na muccati attaniyabhāvato amocitattā”ti vatvā bahudhā papañcitaṃ, na taṃ sārato paccetabbaṃ. Potthakasāmikānañhi potthake dinne aññena kataṃ paṭilabhitvā attanā katapayogassa nāsitattā kathaṃ so na mucceyya, na ca pariccattassa attaniyabhāvo diṭṭhoti. Gaṇṭhipade pana “sace mūlena kīto hoti, potthakasāmikānaṃ potthakaṃ, yesaṃ hatthato mūlaṃ gahitaṃ, tesaṃ mūlaṃ datvā muccatīti kasmā vuttaṃ. Potthakanimittaṃ mūlassa gahitattā akappiyametaṃ. Yadi hi potthakasāmikassa potthakaṃ datvā sayameva mūlaṃ gaṇheyya, akappiyameva taṃ. Athāpi potthakasāmikassa santikā mūlaṃ aggahetvā sayameva taṃ potthakaṃ jhāpeyya, tathāpi aññā yena saddhādeyyavinipātane āpatti, tasmā evamāhā”ti vuttaṃ, tampi na sārato paccetabbaṃ. Tasmā gaṇṭhipadesu vuttanayovettha sārato daṭṭhabbo. “Maraṇavaṇṇaṃ likhissāmā”ti ekajjhāsayā hutvāti idaṃ tathā karonte sandhāya vuttaṃ, evaṃ pana asaṃvidahitvāpi maraṇādhippāyena tasmiṃ potthake vuttavidhiṃ karontassa pārājikameva.

176. 'Yesaṃ hatthatoti' means 'from the hands of those relatives who have been invited.' The statement 'he is freed by giving them the price' is made to show that the effort made by him is brought to an end by restoring it to its original state. It is stated in all three Gaṇṭhipadas that 'a book bought for a price, when given back to the owners of the book, indeed frees one.' However, some have elaborated extensively, saying: 'If, having given the book to its owners, one does not take the price, one is not freed because ownership has not been relinquished.' But this should not be accepted as the essential meaning. For when the book is given to its owners, and they recover what was done by another, since the effort made by oneself is nullified, how could he not be freed? Moreover, ownership is not seen to remain in what has been relinquished. In the Gaṇṭhipada, however, it is stated: 'If it was bought for a price, why is it said that one is freed by giving the book to the owners of the book, and giving the price to those from whose hands the price was taken? Because taking the price on account of the book is improper. For if, having given the book to its owner, one were to take the price for oneself, that would indeed be improper. Or even if, without receiving the price from the owner, one were to burn the book oneself, there would still be an offense of misusing what was given in faith. Therefore, it is stated thus.' But even this should not be accepted as the essential meaning. Therefore, in this matter, only the method stated in the Gaṇṭhipadas should be regarded as essential. The statement 'having formed a single intention: "We will write a description of death"' is made with reference to one who acts accordingly. However, even without such an explicit agreement, if one acts in the manner described in that book with the intention of causing death, it is a pārājika offense.

Pamāṇeti attanā sallakkhite pamāṇe. Tacchetvāti unnatappadesaṃ tacchetvā. Paṃsupacchinti sabbantimaṃ paṃsupacchiṃ. “Ettakaṃ ala”nti niṭṭhāpetukāmatāya sabbantimapayogasādhikā cetanā sanniṭṭhāpakacetanā[V 2.0237]. Suttantikattherāti vinaye apakataññuno suttantabhāṇakā. Mahāaṭṭhakathācariyatthereyeva sandhāya “vinayaṃ te na jānantīti upahāsavasena suttantikattherāti vutta”ntipi vadanti. Ettha ca mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “āvāṭe niṭṭhite patitvā marantu, aniṭṭhite mā marantū”ti iminā adhippāyena karontaṃ sandhāya sabbantimā sanniṭṭhāpakacetanā vuttā, mahāpaccarisaṅkhepaṭṭhakathāsu pana paṭhamappahārato paṭṭhāya “imasmiṃ āvāṭe patitvā marantū”ti iminā adhippāyena karontassa yasmiṃ yasmiṃ payoge kate tattha patitā maranti, taṃtaṃpayogasādhikaṃ sanniṭṭhāpakacetanaṃ [M 2.0268] sandhāya “ekasmimpi kudālappahāre dinne”tiādi vuttanti tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Tasmā tena tena pariyāyena aṭṭhakathāvādānaṃ aññamaññāvirodho yutto. Atha vā mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ ekasmiṃyeva divase avūpasanteneva payogena khaṇitvā niṭṭhāpentaṃ sandhāya sabbantimā sanniṭṭhāpakacetanā vuttā, itarāsu pana “imasmiṃ patitvā marantū”ti adhippāyena ekasmiṃ divase kiñci khaṇitvā aparasmimpi divase tatheva kiñci kiñci khaṇitvā niṭṭhāpentaṃ sandhāya vuttanti. Evampi aṭṭhakathānaṃ aññamaññāvirodho yuttoti amhākaṃ khanti.

'Pamāṇeti' means 'he measures' according to the measure he has determined. 'Tacchetvā' means 'having planed the elevated area.' 'Paṃsupacchi' means 'the very last basket of soil.' The statement 'Ettakaṃ alaṃ' (This is enough) refers to the finalizing intention (sanniṭṭhāpakacetanā), which is the intention that accomplishes the final application of effort with the desire to complete it. 'Suttantikatthera' refers to Suttanta reciters who are unskilled in the Vinaya. Some also say that it is said 'Suttanta elders' in a mocking way, with reference to the teachers of the Great Commentary, meaning 'they do not know the Vinaya.' Here, in the Great Commentary, the final finalizing intention is stated with reference to one who acts with this intention: 'Let them fall into the pit and die when it is finished, but not when it is unfinished.' In the Mahāpaccari and Saṅkhepa commentaries, however, it is stated in all three Gaṇṭhipadas that from the first strike onwards, with reference to one who acts with this intention: 'Let them fall into this pit and die,' for each application of effort made, they fall and die there, and thus the finalizing intention that accomplishes each such application of effort is referred to by phrases like 'even with a single strike of the spade,' and so on. Therefore, the non-contradiction of the commentarial views is appropriate through these various interpretations. Alternatively, in the Great Commentary, the final finalizing intention is stated with reference to one who digs and completes it in a single day with uninterrupted effort. In the other commentaries, however, it is stated with reference to one who, with the intention 'Let them fall into this and die,' digs a little on one day and then on another day digs a little more in the same way until completion. Thus, it is our acceptance that the commentaries do not contradict each other.

Attano dhammatāyāti ajānitvā pakkhalitvā vā. Arahantāpi saṅgahaṃ gacchantīti aññehi pātiyamānānaṃ amaritukāmānampi arahantānaṃ maraṇaṃ sambhavatīti vuttaṃ. Purimanayeti “maritukāmā idha marissantī”ti vuttanaye. Tattha patitaṃ bahi nīharitvāti ettha “imasmiṃ āvāṭeyeva marantūti niyamābhāvato bahi nīharitvā māritepi pārājikaṃ vuttaṃ. Āvāṭe patitvā thokaṃ cirāyitvā gacchantaṃ gahetvā mārite āvāṭasmiṃyeva aggahitattā pārājikaṃ na hotī”ti vadanti, taṃ pana aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “patitappayogena gahitattā”ti vuttahetussa idhāpi sambhavato vīmaṃsitvā gahetabbaṃ. Amaritukāmā vātipi adhippāyassa sambhavato opapātike uttarituṃ asakkuṇitvā matepi pārājikaṃ vuttaṃ. Nibbattitvāti vuttattā patanaṃ na dissatīti ce? Opapātikassa tattha nibbattiyeva patananti natthi virodho. Yasmā mātuyā patitvā parivattitaliṅgāya matāya so mātughātako hoti, na kevalaṃ manussapurisaghātako, tasmā patitasseva vasena āpattīti adhippāyena “patanarūpaṃ pamāṇa”nti vuttaṃ. Idaṃ pana akāraṇaṃ. “Manussabhūtaṃ mātaraṃ vā pitaraṃ vā api parivattaliṅgaṃ jīvitā voropentassa kammaṃ ānantariyaṃ hotī”ti ettakameva hi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ.

'By its own nature' means either through not knowing or through slipping. It is said that even Arahants are subject to death when they are caused to fall by others, even if they do not wish to die. 'In the former method' means in the method where it was said, 'Those who wish to die will die here.' Regarding 'having taken out one who has fallen there,' here, because there is no rule that 'they must die in this very pit,' a pārājika offense is stated even if they are killed after being taken out. Some say, 'If one who has fallen into the pit, lingered for a short while, and is leaving is seized and killed, since they were not seized in the pit itself, it is not a pārājika offense.' However, that statement should be investigated and accepted, since the reason stated in the commentary—'because they were seized by the effort of falling'—is also possible here. Since the intention 'even if they do not wish to die' is possible, a pārājika offense is stated even if a spontaneously reborn being dies, being unable to get out. If it is said, 'Since "having been reborn" is stated, falling is not seen'? For a spontaneously reborn being, the very rebirth there is the falling; there is no contradiction. Because when a mother, having fallen and with her gender changed, dies, he is a matricide, not merely a killer of a human male; therefore, with the intention that the offense is based on the one who has fallen, it is said, 'the measure is in accordance with the falling.' But this is not the reason. For in the commentary only this much is said: 'For one who deprives a human mother or father, even with changed gender, of life, the kamma is of immediate result.'

Tattha ca liṅge parivattepi so eva ekakammanibbatto bhavaṅgappabandho jīvitindriyappabandho ca, na aññoti “api parivattaliṅga”nti vuttaṃ. Yo hi liṅge aparivatte tasmiṃ attabhāve bhavaṅgajīvitindriyappabandho[V 2.0238], so eva parivattepi liṅge taṃyeva ca upādāya ekajātisamaññā. Na cettha bhāvakalāpagatajīvitindriyassa vasena codanā kātabbā tadaññasseva adhippetattā. Tañhi tattha avicchedavuttiyā pabandhavohāraṃ labhati, itarampi [M 2.0269] vā bhāvānupālatāsāmaññenāti anokāsāva codanā. Tasmā parivattepi liṅge tasseva ekakammanibbattassa santānassa jīvitā voropanato vohārabhedato so itthighātako vā hotu purisaghātako vā, ānantariyakammato na muccatīti ettakameva tattha vattabbaṃ. Idha pana yaṃyaṃjātikā sattā honti, te maraṇasamaye attano attano jātirūpeneva maranti, nāññarūpena, jātivaseneva ca pācittiyathullaccayapārājikehi bhavitabbaṃ. Tasmā nāgo vā supaṇṇo vā yakkharūpena vā petarūpena vā patitvā attano tiracchānarūpena marati, tattha pācittiyameva yuttaṃ, na thullaccayaṃ tiracchānagatasseva matattā. Teneva dutiyattheravāde maraṇarūpaṃ pamāṇaṃ, tasmā pācittiyanti vuttaṃ. Ayameva ca vādo yuttataro, teneva so pacchā vutto.

Even when the gender changes, it is the very same continuum of bhavaṅga and continuum of the life faculty, produced by a single kamma, and not another. Hence, it is said, 'even if the gender changes.' For the continuum of bhavaṅga and the life faculty that exists in a being when the gender has not changed is the very same when the gender changes, and based on that very continuum, it is designated as a single birth. Here, no objection should be raised on account of the life faculty belonging to the material group of gender, because something else is intended. For that obtains the designation of 'continuum' due to its unbroken persistence, or else by the commonality of sustaining existence; thus, the objection is out of place. Therefore, even when the gender changes, by depriving of life that same continuum produced by a single kamma—whether one becomes a slayer of a woman or a slayer of a man due to the difference in designation—one is not freed from an immediately resultant kamma. Only this much should be said there. But here, of whatever birth beings are, at the time of death, they die in the form of their own respective births, not in another form. And the offenses—pācittiya, thullaccaya, or pārājika—must be determined according to the birth. Thus, a nāga or a supaṇṇa, having fallen while in the form of a yakkha or a peta, dies in its own animal form. In that case, only a pācittiya is appropriate, not a thullaccaya, because it is one of the animal realm that has died. For this reason, in the second view of the elders, the form at death is the standard; hence it is said to be a pācittiya. This very view is more reasonable, and for that reason, it is stated later.

Imināva nayena manussaviggahe nāgasupaṇṇasadise tiracchānagate patitvā attano rūpena mate pācittiyena bhavitabbaṃ. Evaṃ sante pāḷiyaṃ “yakkho vā peto vā tiracchānagatamanussaviggaho vā tasmiṃ patati, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Patite dukkhā vedanā uppajjati, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Marati, āpatti thullaccayassā”ti kasmā vuttanti ce? Tattha keci vadanti – yakkho vā peto vāti paṭhamaṃ sakarūpeneva ṭhite yakkhapete dassetvā puna aññarūpenapi ṭhite teyeva yakkhapete dassetuṃ “tiracchānagatamanussaviggaho vā”ti vuttaṃ, na pana tādisaṃ tiracchānagataṃ visuṃ dassetuṃ. Tasmā tiracchānagataviggaho vā manussaviggaho vā yakkho vā peto vāti evamettha yojanā kātabbāti. Gaṇṭhipadesu pana tīsupi “pāḷiyaṃ manussaviggahena ṭhitatiracchānagatānaṃ āveṇikaṃ katvā thullaccayaṃ vuttaṃ viya dissatī”ti kathitaṃ. Yakkharūpapetarūpena matepi eseva nayoti iminā maraṇarūpasseva pamāṇattā thullaccayaṃ atidissati.

By this same method, if one falls upon an animal in human form, such as a nāga or supaṇṇa, and it dies in its own form, a pācittiya offense should be incurred. If this is so, why is it stated in the Pāli: 'If a yakkha, or a peta, or an animal in human form falls upon it, there is an offense of dukkaṭa. When it has fallen, a painful feeling arises, there is an offense of dukkaṭa. If it dies, there is an offense of thullaccaya'? There, some say: 'a yakkha or a peta'—first having shown yakkhas and petas abiding in their own forms, and then again, to show those very same yakkhas and petas abiding in another form, it is said 'or an animal in human form,' but not to show such an animal separately. Therefore, the construction here should be made thus: 'an animal in the form of a human, or a yakkha, or a peta.' But in all three Gaṇṭhipadas it is said: 'In the Pāli, it appears as if a thullaccaya is stated specifically for animals abiding in human form.' Even when one dies in the form of a yakkha or a peta, this is the same method; because the form at death itself is the standard, this indicates a thullaccaya.

Mudhāti amūlena, kiñci mūlaṃ aggahetvāti vuttaṃ hoti. So niddosoti tena tattha katapayogassa abhāvato. Yadi pana sopi tattha kiñci kiñci karoti, na muccatiyevāti dassento āha “evaṃ patitā”tiādi. Tattha evanti evaṃ mayā kateti attho. Na nassissantīti adassanaṃ na gamissanti, na palāyissantīti adhippāyo. Vippaṭisāre uppanneti mūlaṭṭhaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Yadi pana pacchimopi labhitvā tattha vuttappakāraṃ kiñci katvā puna vippaṭisāre uppanne evaṃ karoti, tassapi eseva nayo. Paṃsumhi patitvā maratīti [M 2.0270] abhinavapūrite [V 2.0239] paṃsumhi pāde pavesetvā uddharituṃ asakkonto tattheva patitvā marati. Jātapathavī jātāti idaṃ sabbathā matthakappattaṃ thirabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Paṃsunā pūrentena pana pādadaṇḍādīhi maddanatāḷanādinā suṭṭhutaraṃ thirabhāvaṃ āpādetvā pakatipathaviyā nibbisese kate jātapathavīlakkhaṇaṃ appattepi muccatiyeva. Opātaṃ haratīti ettha pokkharaṇīsadisattā muccati.

`Mudhā` means `amūlena`, without a cause; this means 'without taking any cause.' He is blameless because there was no effort made by him in that regard. But if even he does something there, he is not freed at all—showing this, it is said, 'thus fallen,' and so on. There, 'thus' means 'thus done by me.' 'They will not perish' means they will not go to disappearance, they will not flee—this is the intention. 'When remorse arises' is said with reference to the original person. But if even a later person, having obtained it, does something of the kind described there, and then when remorse arises again, acts thus, for him too this is the same method. 'He falls into the dust and dies' means: having put his feet into freshly piled dust, being unable to pull them out, he falls right there and dies. 'The earth has become established'—this is said to show the firmness that has reached the highest state in every way. But by one filling it with dust, having produced a very thorough firmness by pressing, beating, and so on with feet, sticks, and the like, and having made it indistinguishable from the natural ground, even if it has not reached the characteristic of 'established earth', one is indeed freed. 'He removes the pitfall'—here, one is freed because of its similarity to a lotus pond.

Hatthā muttamatteti oḍḍetvā hatthato muttamatte. Vatiṃ katvāti ettha yadi so pāse vuttappakāraṃ kañci visesaṃ na karoti, attanā katavatiyā viddhaṃsitāya muccati. Thaddhataraṃ vā pāsayaṭṭhiṃ ṭhapetīti thirabhāvatthaṃ aparāya pāsayaṭṭhiyā saddhiṃ bandhitvā vā tameva vā sithilabhūtaṃ thaddhataraṃ bandhitvā ṭhapeti. Daḷhataraṃ vā thirataraṃ vāti etthāpi eseva nayo. Khāṇukanti pāsayaṭṭhibandhanakhāṇukaṃ. Sabbattheva māraṇatthāya katappayogattā na muccati. Vippaṭisāre uppanneti mūlaṭṭhasseva vippaṭisāre uppanne.

'Hatthā muttamatta' means: having set it up, just upon being released from the hand. Regarding 'having made a fence,' here, if he does not make any special arrangement of the kind stated for the noose, he is freed when the fence made by himself is destroyed. 'He sets up a stiffer noose-stick' means for the sake of firmness, he sets it up either by binding it together with another noose-stick, or by binding that very one which has become loose more stiffly. The same principle applies here for 'stronger' or 'firmer.' 'The post' refers to the post for tying the noose-stick. In all cases, because the effort was made with the intention to kill, one is not freed. 'When remorse arises' refers to when remorse arises in the original person himself.

Tena alātena…pe… na muccatīti ettha “pubbe katappayogaṃ vināsetvā pacchā kusalacittena payoge katepi na muccatīti idaṃ sandhāya gantabba”nti tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Ayaṃ panettha adhippāyo yutto siyā – āditoyeva māraṇatthāya katappayogattā katapariyositāya pāsayaṭṭhiyā tappaccayā ye ye sattā marissanti, tesaṃ tesaṃ vasena paṭhamataraṃyeva pāṇātipātakammasiddhito pacchā kusalacittena aññathā katepi na muccatīti. Rajjuketi khuddakarajjuke. Sayaṃ vaṭṭitanti bahurajjuke ekato katvā attanā vaṭṭitaṃ. Ubbaṭṭetvāti te rajjuke visuṃ visuṃ katvā. Garukataraṃ karotīti atibhāriyaṃ karoti. Pariyesitvā katanti araññaṃ gantvā rukkhaṃ chinditvā tacchetvā kataṃ.

Regarding 'With that firebrand... he is not freed,' it is stated in all three Gaṇṭhipadas that this should be understood with reference to: 'Even if, after having destroyed the previously made application, an application is made later with a wholesome mind, he is not freed.' Herein, this intention would be appropriate: because the application was made from the very beginning for the purpose of killing, by means of the fully prepared snare-post, for whichever beings will die due to that cause, with respect to each of them, the kamma of destroying life is accomplished from the very first; therefore, even if something is done otherwise later with a wholesome mind, he is not freed. By 'cord' is meant a small rope. By 'twisted by himself' is meant twisted by himself, having put many ropes together as one. By 'untwisting' is meant having made those ropes separate. By 'makes it heavier' is meant he makes it very heavy. By 'made after searching' is meant having gone to the forest, cut a tree, and fashioned it.

177. Ālambanarukkho vāti tatthajātakaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tadatthamevāti māraṇatthameva. Visamaṇḍalanti mañcapīṭhādīsu ālittaṃ visamaṇḍalaṃ. Vatvā asiṃ upanikkhipatīti ettha mukhena avatvā vuttappakāraṃ manasā cintetvā upanikkhipanepi eseva nayo. Purimanayenāti “yesaṃ hatthato mūlaṃ gahita”ntiādinā. Sarīrassa virūpabhāvakaraṇato kuṭṭhādi visabhāgarogo nāma, jīvitappavattiyā vā asabhāgattā ananukūlattā gaṇḍapiḷakādi yo koci jīvitappavattipaccanīko visabhāgarogo.

177. By 'or a supporting tree,' it is said referring to one that has grown in that place. By 'for that very purpose' is meant for the purpose of killing. By 'a patch of poison' is meant a patch of poison smeared on a bed, chair, and so on. Regarding 'Having spoken, he places the sword,' this same method applies even when, without speaking with the mouth, he places it having thought with the mind in the manner described. By 'by the previous method' is meant by the text beginning, 'from whose hand the price was taken.' A disease of a dissimilar nature, such as leprosy, is so called because it causes disfigurement of the body; or, any disease of a dissimilar nature that is an impediment to the continuation of life, such as a boil or carbuncle, is so called because of its dissimilarity and its being unconducive to the continuation of life.

178. Paraṃ [M 2.0271] vā amanāparūpanti ettha amanāpaṃ rūpaṃ etassāti amanāparūpoti bāhiratthasamāso [V 2.0240] daṭṭhabbo. Manāpiyepi eseva nayoti etena manāpikaṃ rūpaṃ upasaṃharatīti ettha paraṃ vā manāparūpaṃ tassa samīpe ṭhapeti, attanā vā manāpiyena rūpena samannāgato tiṭṭhatītiādi yojetabbanti dasseti. Teneva aññatarasmiṃ gaṇṭhipade vuttaṃ –

178. Regarding 'or another displeasing form,' here the exocentric compound `amanāparūpa` should be seen as 'one for whom there is a displeasing form.' By 'this same method applies also to pleasing things,' it is shown that in the context of 'he presents a pleasing form,' it should be connected thus: 'he places another pleasing form near that person, or he himself stands endowed with a pleasing form,' and so on. For that reason, it is said in a certain Gaṇṭhipada:

“Mamālābhena esitthī, maratūti samīpago;

Duṭṭhacitto sace yāti, hoti so itthimārako.

“If one with a corrupted mind goes near and thinks, ‘May this woman die from not obtaining me,’ he becomes a killer of that woman.

“Bhikkhatthāya sace yāti, jānantopi na mārako;

Anatthiko hi so tassā, maraṇena upekkhako”ti.

“If he goes for the sake of alms, even though knowing, he is not a killer; for he has no interest in her death, being indifferent.”

Aparampi tattheva vuttaṃ –

Furthermore, it is said in that same place:

“Viyogena ca me jāyā, jananī ca na jīvati;

Iti jānaṃ viyuñjanto, tadatthī hoti mārako.

“‘My wife and my mother will not live through separation from me’; knowing this, one who causes separation for that purpose becomes a killer.

“Pabbajjādinimittañce, yāti jānaṃ na mārako;

Anatthiko hi so tesaṃ, maraṇena upekkhako”ti.

“If he goes for the sake of going forth and so on, though knowing, he is not a killer; for he has no interest in their death, being indifferent.”

Alaṅkaritvā upasaṃharatīti “alābhakena sussitvā maratū”ti iminā adhippāyena upasaṃharati. Teneva “sace uttasitvā marati, visaṅketo”ti vuttaṃ. Alābhakena sussitvā maratīti ettha ca pārājikanti pāṭhaseso daṭṭhabbo. Kuṇapagandhā cāti ahiādikuṇapānaṃ gandhā. Haṃsapupphanti haṃsādīnaṃ pakkhalomaṃ sandhāya vadati.

By 'having adorned, he presents it' is meant that he presents it with this intention: 'May she waste away and die from not obtaining it.' For that reason it is said: 'If she dies from being terrified, it is uncertain.' And regarding 'she wastes away and dies from not obtaining it,' the remainder of the text, 'it is a Pārājika,' should be understood. By 'and the stench of corpses' is meant the stench of the corpses of snakes and so on. By 'swan-down' he speaks referring to the wing and body feathers of swans and so on.

179. Asañciccāti idaṃ maraṇasaṃvattanikaupakkamassa asallakkhaṇaṃ sandhāya vuttanti āha “iminā upakkamenā”tiādi. Ajānantassāti idaṃ pana maraṇasaṃvattanikaupakkamakaraṇassa ajānanaṃ sandhāya vuttanti āha “iminā ayaṃ marissatī”tiādi. Namaraṇādhippāyassāti idaṃ upakkamaṃ jānantassapi maraṇādhippāyassa abhāvaṃ sandhāya vuttanti āha “maraṇaṃ anicchantassā”tiādi.

179. By 'unintentionally' is meant the non-observation of the undertaking connected with death, as stated: 'by this undertaking,' and so forth. By 'not knowing' is meant the not knowing of the undertaking causing death, as stated: 'by this, this one will die,' and so forth. By 'without intention of death' is meant the absence of intention of death even for one who knows the undertaking, as stated: 'not desiring death,' and so forth.

Padabhājanīyavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the analysis of terms is concluded.

Pakiṇṇakakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on Miscellaneous Topics

Domanassacitteneva [M 2.0272][V 2.0241] bhaṇatīti iminā sanniṭṭhāpakacetanā dukkhavedanāya sampayuttā evāti dasseti. Sukhabahulatāya hi rājāno hasamānāpi “ghātethā”ti vadanti, hāso pana nesaṃ anatthavūpasamādiaññavisayoti sanniṭṭhāpakacetanā dukkhavedanāya sampayuttā eva. Sati pana domanasse kathaṃ taṃ nappakāsatīti āha “sukhavokiṇṇattā”tiādi, pubbāpariyavasena ubhosu passesu uppajjanakasukhehi ākiṇṇattā uppannassa ca domanassassa anuppabandhanena pavattiyā abhāvato tadā uppannampi domanassaṃ nappakāsatīti attho.

“Speaking with a distressed mind”—by this, it is shown that the decisive volition is indeed associated with painful feeling. For kings, due to their abundance of pleasure, even while laughing, say, “Kill them!” But their laughter, being directed towards something other than the cessation of what is not beneficial, etc., the decisive volition is still associated with painful feeling. However, if there is distress, how does it not manifest? He says, “because it is interspersed with pleasure,” etc.—because, considering the sequence of before and after, it is interspersed with pleasures arising on both sides, and due to the lack of continuity in the occurrence of the arisen distress, even the distress that has arisen at that time does not manifest—this is the meaning.

Vinītavatthuvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Decided Cases

180. Maraṇatthikāva hutvāti imassa kāyassa bhedena saggapāpanādhippāyattā atthato maraṇatthikāva hutvā. Maraṇatthikabhāvaṃ ajānantāti evaṃ adhippāyino maraṇatthikā nāma hontīti attano maraṇatthikabhāvaṃ ajānantā. Na hi te attano cittappavattiṃ na jānanti. Vohāravasenāti pubbabhāgavohāravasena, maraṇādhippāyassa sanniṭṭhāpakacetanākkhaṇe karuṇāya abhāvato kāruññena pāse baddhasūkaramocanaṃ viya na hotīti adhippāyo. Yathāyunāti vuttamevatthaṃ yathānusandhināti pariyāyantarena vuttaṃ, yathānusandhinā yathāyuparicchedenāti vuttaṃ hoti. Atha vā yathānusandhināti yathānuppabandhena, yāva tasmiṃ bhave santānassa anuppabandho avicchinnappavatti hoti, tāva ṭhatvāti vuttaṃ hoti.

180. Being intent on death means being effectively intent on death, due to the intention of attaining heaven by the breaking up of this body. Not knowing their own state of being intent on death—those who are thus inclined are called 'intent on death,' not knowing their own state of being intent on death. For it is not that they do not know the workings of their own minds. By way of conventional speech—by way of the conventional usage of the initial stage, at the moment of the decisive volition aiming for death, there is no compassion, and thus, it is not like the release of a pig bound in a snare done out of compassion—this is the meaning. The meaning stated by 'as long as life lasts' is also stated by 'according to the connection' as an alternative expression; that is, by 'according to the connection,' 'according to the span of life' is meant. Or, 'according to the connection' means 'according to the unbroken sequence,' meaning that it lasts as long as the continuity of existence in that life remains unbroken.

Appaṭivekkhitvāti anupaparikkhitvā. Uddhaṃ vā adho vā saṅkamantīti pacchā āgatānaṃ okāsadānatthaṃ nisinnapāḷiyā uddhaṃ vā adho vā gacchanti. Paccavekkhaṇakiccaṃ natthīti pacchā āgatehi upaparikkhaṇakiccaṃ natthi. Heṭṭhā kismiñci vijjamāne sāṭakaṃ vali na gaṇhātīti āha “tasmiṃ vali na paññāyatī”ti. Paṭivekkhaṇañcedaṃ gihīnaṃ santakeyevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Without examining—without investigating. Moving up or down—they move up or down from the row of seated ones to give space to those who come afterward. There is no duty of reflection—there is no task of examination for those who come later. He says, 'in that, no wrinkle appears,' because if there is something underneath, the lower robe does not get wrinkled. This examination is indeed only for householders regarding their own property—this should be understood.

Pāḷiyaṃ musale ussiteti aññamaññaṃ upatthambhetvā dvīsu musalesu ussitesūti attho. Udukkhalabhaṇḍikanti udukkhalatthāya ānītaṃ dārubhaṇḍaṃ. Paṭibaddhanti bhojanapaṭibaddhaṃ, bhojanantarāyanti vuttaṃ hoti.

In the Pāḷi, 'the pestles being raised'—supporting each other, the two pestles are raised—this is the meaning. A mortar stand—the wooden stand brought for the mortar. Bound—bound to food, meaning an obstruction to food.

181. Aggakārikanti [M 2.0273][V 2.0242] ettha kārikā-saddassa bhāvavacanattā “aggakiriya”nti atthaṃ vatvāpi yasmā kiriyaṃ dātuṃ na sakkā, tasmā dānasaṅkhātāya aggakiriyāya yuttaṃ piṇḍapātameva idha upacāravuttiyā “aggakiriyā”ti gahetabbanti āha “paṭhamaṃ laddhapiṇḍapāta”ntiādi.

181. The foremost offering—here, because the word kārikā is a word denoting a state or action, even though the meaning is stated as “foremost action,” since an action cannot be given, therefore the alms-food associated with the foremost act of giving is figuratively taken here as “foremost action”—thus, he said, “the first alms-food obtained,” etc.

182-183. Daṇḍamuggaranti nikhādanamuggaraṃ. Vibhattibyattayenāti vibhattivipariṇāmena. Visesādhigamoti samādhi vipassanā ca ativiya pākaṭattā “hatthappatto viya dissatī”ti vuttaṃ. Upacchindatīti “visesādhigamassa vikkhepo mā hotū”ti āhāraṃ upacchindati. Visesādhigamanti lokuttaradhammapaṭilābhaṃ. Byākaritvāti ārocetvā. Upacchindati, na vaṭṭatīti yasmā sabhāgānaṃ lajjibhikkhūnaṃyeva ariyā attanā adhigatavisesaṃ tādise kāraṇe sati ārocenti, te ca bhikkhū appatirūpāya anesanāya paccayaṃ na pariyesanti, tasmā tehi pariyesitapaccaye kukkuccaṃ uppādetvā āhāraṃ upacchindituṃ na vaṭṭatīti attho. Sabhāgānañhi byākatattā upacchindituṃ na labhati. Te hi kappiyakhettaṃ. Teneva “sabhāgānañhi lajjibhikkhūnaṃ kathetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti idaṃ “upacchindati, na vaṭṭatī”ti imassa kāraṇaṃ dassentena vuttanti tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ.

A pestle and mallet—a mallet for driving in stakes. Through alteration of syntax—through a change of grammatical case. The attainment of distinction—concentration and insight are so extremely evident that it is said, “it appears as if it has come to hand.” He cuts it off—he cuts off food thinking, “May there be no disturbance to the attainment of distinction.” The attainment of distinction—the attainment of the supramundane Dhamma. Having declared—having announced. He cuts it off, but it is not proper—since noble ones, when there is such a reason, announce the distinction they have attained only to their fellows, the modest monks, and those monks do not seek requisites through an improper search, it is therefore not proper to cause them anxiety about the requisites they have sought and to cut off food—this is the meaning. For since it has been declared to his fellows, he is not permitted to cut it off. For they are a suitable field. For that reason, it was said by one showing the reason for “he cuts it off, but it is not proper” that “it is proper to tell one’s fellows, the modest monks.” This is stated in all three sub-commentaries.

Atha vā visesādhigamaṃ byākaritvāti idaṃ visesassa adhigatabhāvadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Adhigamantarāyaṃ asaṅkanteneva ca āhārupacchedo kātabboti anuññātattā adhigatena na kātabboti dassetuṃ “visesādhigamaṃ byākaritvā āhāraṃ upacchindati, na vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ. Kiṃ pana ariyā attanā adhigatavisesaṃ aññesaṃ ārocentīti imissā codanāya “sabhāgānañhi lajjibhikkhūnaṃ kathetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ. Ayamettha yuttataroti amhākaṃ khanti, gaṇṭhipadepi ayamattho dassitoyevāti. Bhaṇḍakaṃ dhovantāti cīvaraṃ dhovantā. Dhovanadaṇḍakanti bhaṇḍadhovanadaṇḍaṃ.

Alternatively, the phrase “having declared the attainment of distinction” is said to show the fact of having attained a distinction. Because cutting off food is permitted only for one who is wary of an obstruction to attainment, it is stated, “Having declared the attainment of distinction, he cuts off food; it is not fitting,” in order to show that this should not be done by one who has already attained. But do noble ones announce to others a distinction attained by themselves? In response to this objection, it is said, “For it is fitting to speak to fellow monks who are modest.” This is the more appropriate interpretation here, in our opinion; this meaning is shown in the sub-commentary as well. “Washing the requisite” means washing the robe. “A washing stick” means a stick for washing requisites.
