184. Ahaṃ kukkuccakoti “mama kiriyāya mareyya nu kho, no vā”ti evaṃ jātakukkuccako. Sabbatthāpi panettha evarūpesu vatthūsu amate thullaccayassa vuttattā tena katappayogena dukkhavedanā uppajjatu vā mā vā, pārājikāya abhāvato bhagavato vacanena thullaccayamevāti vadanti.

184. “I am anxious” means one in whom anxiety has arisen, thinking, “I wonder, will he die because of my action, or not?” In all such cases, since a serious offense is stated for these kinds of situations if the person does not die, they say that by the Blessed One’s word it is only a serious offense—whether or not painful feeling arises from the action performed by him—because there is no Pārājika offense.

185. Gabbho [M 2.0274] patati etenāti gabbhapātanaṃ, tādisaṃ bhesajjaṃ. Tenāha “yena paribhuttenā”tiādi[V 2.0243]. “Maraṇavaṇṇaṃ vā saṃvaṇṇeyyā”ti vuttattā pariyāyato āpattimokkho na hotīti āha “pariyāyo nāma natthī”ti.

185. An abortifacient (`gabbhapātanaṃ`) is that by which a fetus is expelled; it is that kind of medicine. Therefore, he said, “by which, when consumed,” and so on. Because it is said, “or one might praise death,” there is no escape from the offense by indirect means; thus, he said, “There is no such thing as an indirect way.”

Gabbhaṃ na gaṇhātīti gabbhaṃ na dhāreti. Vātena pāṇakehi vā gabbho vinassanto kammaṃ vinā na nassatīti adhippāyena “dvīhākārehī”ti vuttaṃ. Dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.26) pana “gabbho hi vātena pāṇakehi kammunā cāti tīhi kāraṇehi vinassatī”ti vatvā “kammunā vinassante pana buddhāpi paṭibāhituṃ na sakkontī”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha vātena pāṇakehi vā gabbhe vinassante na purimakammunā okāso kato, apica tappaccayā kammaṃ vipaccati, sayameva pana kammunā okāse kate na ekantena vāto pāṇakā vā apekkhitabbāti iminā adhippāyena kammassa visuṃ kāraṇabhāvo vuttoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Pāṇakā khāditvā antaradhāpentīti yojetabbaṃ. Avijāyanatthāya bhesajjaṃ dentassa kucchiyaṃ uppajjitvā vinassissantīti iminā adhippāyena dinne opātakkhaṇanādīsu viya kammabaddho, kucchiyaṃ na uppajjissantīti iminā pana adhippāyena dinne nevatthi kammabaddho.

“Does not take the womb” means “does not bear the conception.” The statement “by two means” is made with the intention that when an embryo perishes due to wind or creatures, it does not perish without kamma. In the Dīghanikāya commentary, however, after stating, “For an embryo perishes by three causes: wind, creatures, and kamma,” it is said, “But when it perishes due to kamma, even the Buddhas cannot prevent it.” In that context, when an embryo perishes due to wind or creatures, the opportunity is not created by past kamma; rather, kamma ripens on account of those causes. When, however, the opportunity is created by kamma itself, wind or creatures are not absolutely to be expected. It should be understood that with this intention, kamma is stated as a separate cause. “Creatures” should be construed as “they devour and make it disappear.” When medicine is given to prevent conception with the intention that “it will arise in the womb and then perish,” one is bound by kamma, as in the cases of pitfalls and so on. But when it is given with the intention that “it will not arise in the womb,” there is no bondage by kamma.

Sahadhammikānanti ekassa satthuno sāsane sahasikkhamānadhammānaṃ. Pañcannampi vivaṭṭanissitasīlattā “samasīlasaddhāpaññāna”nti vuttaṃ. Ñātakapavāritaṭṭhānatoti attano tesaṃ vā ñātakapavāritaṭṭhānato. Gilānassatthāya appavāritaṭṭhānatopi viññattiyā anuññātattā katāpi akatā viyāti akataviññatti, “vada, bhante, paccayenā”ti evaṃ akatapavāraṇaṭṭhāne ca viññatti akataviññatti.

“Fellow practitioners” means those who have the nature of training together in the dispensation of the one Teacher. Because all five possess virtue based on that which is free from the round of rebirth, it is said, “those of equal virtue, faith, and wisdom.” “From a place where relatives have made an invitation” means from a place where one's own or their relatives have made an invitation. For the sake of a sick person, since an intimation is permitted even from a place where one is not invited, even if it is made, it is as if it were not made; thus, it is an “unmade intimation.” And an intimation in a place where no invitation has been made—such as, “Speak, venerable sir, regarding a requisite”—is an “unmade intimation.”

Paṭiyādiyatīti sampādeti. Akātuṃ na vaṭṭatīti ettha dukkaṭaṃ vadanti. Sahadhammikesu vuttanayenevāti “imesampi pañcannaṃ akataviññattiyāpi bhesajjaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti kurundaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttattā kathitaṃ. Yāva ñātakā passantīti yāva tassa ñātakā passanti. Pitu bhaginī pitucchā. Mātu bhātā mātulo. Nappahontīti kātuṃ na sakkonti. Sacepi na yācantīti “yācituṃ dukkha”nti adhippāyena yadi na yācanti. Ābhogaṃ katvāti idaṃ kattabbatādassanavasena vuttaṃ, “ābhogaṃ pana akatvāpi [M 2.0275] dātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu likhitaṃ. Ete dasa ñātake ṭhapetvāti tesaṃ puttanattādayopi tappaṭibaddhattā ñātakā evāti tepi ettheva saṅgahitā. Tena aññesanti iminā aññātakānaṃ gahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tenevāha “etesaṃ puttaparamparāyā”tiādi. Kulaparivaṭṭoti kulānaṃ paṭipāṭi, kulaparamparāti vuttaṃ hoti. “Mayhaṃ dassanti karissantī”ti paccāsāya karontassapi yācitvāpi gahetabbaṭṭhānatāya ñātakesu [V 2.0244] vejjakammaṃ vā kuladūsakāpatti vā na hotīti vadanti. Sabbapadesupi vinicchayo veditabboti cūḷamātuyātiādīsu sabbapadesu “cūḷamātuyā sāmiko”tiādinā yojetvā heṭṭhā vuttanayena vinicchayo veditabbo.

“Prepares” means “makes ready.” Regarding “it is not permissible not to do it,” they say there is a dukkaṭa offense here. “In the same way as stated for fellow practitioners” is said because it is stated in the Kurundaṭṭhakathā: “For these five also, it is permissible to prepare medicine even with an unmade intimation.” “As long as relatives see” means as long as that person’s relatives see. The father’s sister is the paternal aunt. The mother’s brother is the maternal uncle. “They are not able” means “they cannot do it.” “Even if they do not request” means if they do not request with the intention that “it is difficult to ask.” “Having reflected”—this is said by way of showing what ought to be done. However, “it is permissible to give even without reflecting,” is written in all three sub-commentaries. Regarding “Setting aside these ten relatives”: their sons, grandsons, and so on, because of being connected to them, are indeed relatives, thus they too are included here. By this phrase “for others,” the inclusion of non-relatives should be understood. For that very reason, he said, “for their descendants,” and so on. “Family succession” means the order of families; this is to say, a family lineage. They say that even for one who acts with the expectation, “They will give to me, they will do for me,” because it is a situation where one may also request and receive, there is, with respect to relatives, no offense of medical practice or offense of corrupting families. “The judgment should be understood in all instances” means that in all instances, such as “of the younger mother,” the judgment should be understood according to the method stated below, by connecting it with phrases such as “the younger mother’s husband.”

Vuttanayena pariyesitvāti iminā “ñātisāmaṇerehi vā”tiādinā vuttamatthaṃ atidissati. Apaccāsīsantenāti “mayhaṃ dassanti karissantī”ti evaṃ attano atthāya apaccāsīsantena. Bhikkhusaṅghassa pana upakārakattaṃ paccāsīsantena kātuṃ vaṭṭati. “Bhesajjaṃ ācikkhathā”ti vuttepi yathā “aññamaññaṃ pana kathā kātabbā”ti idaṃ pariyāyattā vaṭṭati, evaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayena “idañcidañca gahetvā karontī”ti iminā pariyāyena kathentassapi nevatthi dosoti ācariyā.

By “having searched in the manner stated,” the meaning stated in the phrase beginning “with relatives or novices” is indicated. “Not expecting” means not expecting for one’s own benefit, thinking, “They will give to me, they will do for me.” It is, however, permissible to act while expecting to be a benefactor to the community of monks. The teachers say that even when one is told, “Prescribe a medicine,” just as this indirect approach is permissible—“they should, however, converse with one another”—so too, there is no fault for one who speaks with this indirect method, in the manner stated below: “taking this and that, they prepare it.”

Vinayalakkhaṇaṃ ajānantassa anācariyassa tadanurūpavohārāsambhavato īdisassa lābhassa uppatti nāma natthīti “ācariyabhāgo nāmāya”nti vuttaṃ, vinaye pakataññunā ācariyena labhitabbabhāgo ayanti vuttaṃ hoti. Pupphapūjanatthāya dinnepi akappiyavohārena vidhānassa ayuttattā “kappiyavasenā”ti vuttaṃ, “pupphaṃ āharathā”tiādinā kappiyavohāravasenāti attho.

For one who does not know the characteristic of the Vinaya, for one without a teacher, since a corresponding transaction is not possible, the arising of such a gain is nonexistent—thus it is said, “This is indeed the teacher’s share.” This means: this is the share to be obtained by a teacher skilled in the Vinaya. Even when given for the purpose of flower offerings, because the procedure with unallowable speech is inappropriate, it is said, “by way of what is allowable.” The meaning is: by way of allowable speech, such as, “Bring flowers.”

Yadi “parittaṃ karothā”ti vutte karonti, gihiveyyāvaccakaraṇaṭṭhāne tiṭṭhatīti “parittaṃ karotha, bhanteti vutte na kātabba”nti vuttaṃ, “bhaṇathā”ti vutte pana dhammakathāya ajjhesanaṭṭhāne ṭhitattā “kātabba”nti vuttaṃ. Dhammañhi anajjhiṭṭhenapi kathetuṃ vaṭṭati, pageva ajjhiṭṭhena. Cāletvā suttaṃ parimajjitvāti parittaṃ karontena kātabbavidhiṃ dasseti. Vihārato…pe… dukkaṭanti aññātakānaṃyeva dadato dukkaṭaṃ. No ce jānantīti yadi evaṃ vattuṃ na jānanti. Udakanti dakkhiṇodakaṃ. Pādesu apanītesu avamaṅgalasaññino hontīti āha “na pādā apanetabbā”ti[M 2.0276]. Gantuṃ vaṭṭatīti “parivāratthāya āgacchantū”ti vuttepi evaṃ sallakkhetvā gantuṃ vaṭṭati.

If, when told, “Perform the paritta,” they do so, it stands in the position of performing a service for laypeople. Therefore, it is said, “When told, ‘Perform the paritta, venerable sirs,’ it should not be done.” However, when told, “Recite,” since one stands in the position of being requested for a Dhamma talk, it is said, “It should be done.” For the Dhamma may be spoken even without being requested, how much more so when requested. “Having shaken the thread and wiped it” shows the procedure to be followed by one performing the paritta. “From the monastery… etc. … a dukkaṭa offense” means it is a dukkaṭa offense for one who gives only to non-relatives. “If they do not know” means if they do not know how to speak thus. “Water” means the water of dedication. When the feet are withdrawn, they have the perception of it being inauspicious; therefore, he says, “The feet should not be withdrawn.” “It is permissible to go” means even when told, “Let them come for the sake of the retinue,” having reflected thus, it is permissible to go.

Anāmaṭṭhapiṇḍapātoti apabbajitassa hatthato laddho attanā aññena vā pabbajitena aggahitaaggo piṇḍapāto. Thālaketi iminā pattopi gahitoyevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Dāmarikacorassāti rajjaṃ patthayamānassa pākaṭacorassa. Coranāgavatthūti ettha “coranāgassa kira āmaṭṭhaṃ dento kujjhissati, anāmaṭṭhaṃ na vaṭṭatīti thero pattaggahaṇahattheneva aggaṃ gahetvā patte bhattaṃ [V 2.0245] sabbamadāsi, so tena tussi. ‘Ettakaṃ mayha’nti bhattassa ekapasseyeva thokaṃ ṭhapetvāpi puna tena saddhiṃ sabbampi dātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cūḷagaṇṭhipade vuttaṃ.

‘Untouched almsfood’ is almsfood obtained from the hand of a non-renunciant, the top portion of which has not been taken by oneself or by another renunciant. By this word ‘with a bowl,’ it should be understood that what is in the bowl is also considered taken. Regarding the robber Dāmarika: he was a notorious robber aspiring for the kingdom. In the story of the robber Nāga, it is said in the Cūḷagaṇṭhipada: ‘It is said that the robber Nāga would get angry if given touched food; since it is not proper to give untouched food, the elder, with the very hand that was holding the bowl, took the top portion and gave all the food in the bowl. He was pleased by that. Even after setting aside a little on just one side of the food, thinking, “This much is for me,” it is proper to give all of it again along with that.’

Āmisassa dhammassa ca alābhena attano parassa ca antare sambhavantassa chiddassa vivarassa bhedassa paṭisantharaṇaṃ pidahanaṃ gaṇhanaṃ paṭisanthāro. Ayañhi lokasannivāso alabbhamānena āmisena ca dhammena cāti dvīhi chiddo, tassa taṃ chiddaṃ yathā na paññāyati, evaṃ pīṭhassa viya paccattharaṇena āmisena ca dhammena ca paṭisantharaṇaṃ āmisapaṭisanthāro dhammapaṭisanthāro cāti vuccati. Tattha dhammapaṭisanthāro kassaci na kātabbo natthi. Yassa kassaci hi gahaṭṭhassa vā pabbajitassa vā dhammena saṅgaho kātabboyeva. “Paṭisanthāro pana kassa kātabbo, kassa na kātabbo”ti idaṃ pana āmisapaṭisanthāraṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Ubbāsetvāti samantato tiyojanaṃ vilumpanto manusse palāpetvā aññesaṃ avāsaṃ katvā. Saṅghassatthāya āhaṭāti pākavaṭṭato taṃdivasassatthāya āhaṭā. Varapotthacittattharaṇanti anekappakārauttamarūpavicittattharaṇaṃ.

Reconciliation is the mending, covering, and closing of a gap, opening, or breach that arises between oneself and another due to not obtaining material things and the Dhamma. For this world of beings is flawed by two things: by not obtaining material things and the Dhamma. The reconciliation with material things and with the Dhamma, so that this flaw is not apparent—just as a seat is covered with a spread—is called material reconciliation and Dhamma reconciliation. Therein, Dhamma reconciliation is not to be withheld from anyone. Indeed, support with the Dhamma must be given to anyone whatsoever, whether a householder or a renunciant. But this statement, ‘For whom should reconciliation be done, and for whom should it not be done?’, was said referring to material reconciliation. ‘Having driven out’ means: plundering for three yojanas all around, having made the people flee, and having taken over the dwellings of others. ‘Brought for the sake of the Sangha’ means: brought from the regular alms-round for the sake of that day. ‘A splendid embroidered coverlet’ means: a spread adorned with many kinds of excellent and variegated forms.

187. Sattarasavaggiyesu pubbe ekassa aṅgulipatodena māritattā sesasoḷasajanesu udaraṃ āruhitvā nisinnamekaṃ ṭhapetvā “sesāpi pannarasa janā”ti vuttaṃ. Adūhalapāsāṇā viyāti adūhale āropitapāsāṇā viya. Kammādhippāyāti tajjanīyādikammakaraṇādhippāyā. Āvāhetvāti āvisāpetvā. Vāḷavihāranti caṇḍasattehi adhiṭṭhitavihāraṃ.

187. Among the group of seventeen, because one had been killed previously by a finger-poke, it was said, ‘the remaining fifteen persons,’ after setting aside one among the remaining sixteen persons who had climbed onto the belly and was sitting there. ‘Like stones on a smokeless surface’ means like stones placed on a smokeless surface. ‘With the intention of an act’ means with the intention of performing an act such as censure. ‘Having brought in’ means having caused to enter. ‘A fierce monastery’ means a monastery inhabited by fierce beings.

189. Yo [M 2.0277] rukkhena otthatopi na maratītiādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ bhūtagāmasikkhāpadaṭṭhakathāyaṃ sayameva vakkhati. Evañhi tattha vuttaṃ (pāci. aṭṭha. 92) –

189. Regarding what should be said in the passages such as, ‘One who does not die even when crushed by a tree,’ that will be explained in the commentary on the training rule concerning plant life itself. For thus it is said there (Pāci. Aṭṭha. 92):

“Manussaviggahapārājikavaṇṇanāyaṃ pana sabbaaṭṭhakathāsu ‘sace bhikkhu rukkhena vā ajjhotthato hoti opāte vā patito, sakkā ca hoti ekena passena rukkhaṃ chinditvā bhūmiṃ vā khaṇitvā nikkhamituṃ, jīvitahetupi attanā na kātabbaṃ, aññena pana bhikkhunā bhūmiṃ vā khaṇitvā rukkhaṃ vā chinditvā allarukkhato vā daṇḍakaṃ chinditvā taṃ rukkhaṃ pavaṭṭetvā nikkhamāpetuṃ vaṭṭati, anāpattī’ti vuttaṃ. Tattha kāraṇaṃ na dissati, ‘anujānāmi, bhikkhave, davaḍāhe ḍayhamāne paṭaggiṃ dātuṃ parittaṃ kātu’nti (cūḷava. 283) idaṃ pana ekameva suttaṃ dissati. Sace etassa anulomaṃ, attano na vaṭṭati, aññassa vaṭṭatīti idaṃ nānākaraṇaṃ na sakkā laddhuṃ. Attano atthāya [V 2.0246] karonto attasinehena akusalacitteneva karoti, paro pana kāruññena. Tasmā anāpattīti ce, etampi akāraṇaṃ. Kusalacittenapi hi imaṃ āpattiṃ āpajjati, sabbaṭṭhakathāsu pana vuttattā na sakkā paṭisedhetuṃ, gavesitabbā ettha yutti, aṭṭhakathācariyānaṃ vā saddhāya gantabba”nti.

“However, in the explanation of the Pārājika on human beings, it is stated in all the commentaries: ‘If a monk is crushed by a tree or has fallen into a pit, and it is possible to get out by cutting the tree on one side or by digging the ground, it should not be done by oneself, even for the sake of one’s life. But it is proper for another monk to have him get out by digging the ground or cutting the tree, or by cutting a stick from a green tree and levering that tree away; there is no offense.’ Therein, a reason is not seen. ‘I allow, monks, when a forest fire is blazing, to set a backfire or to make a protective enclosure’ (Cūḷavagga 283)—this one sutta alone is seen. If this is in accordance with that, this distinction—that it is not proper for oneself but proper for another—cannot be established. One who acts for one's own sake does so with self-love and an unwholesome mind, whereas another acts out of compassion. Therefore, if it is said there is no offense for this reason, this too is not a reason. For one incurs this offense even with a wholesome mind. But since it is stated in all the commentaries, it cannot be rejected. The logic herein should be sought, or one should proceed with faith in the commentary teachers.”

Tasmā yaṃ ettha ito aññathā kenaci papañcitaṃ, gaṇṭhipadesu ca kāraṇaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ na sārato paccetabbaṃ.

Therefore, whatever has been elaborated here otherwise than this by anyone, and the reason that has been stated in the knotty passages, should not be accepted as substantial.

190. Alla…pe… pācittiyanti sukkhaṭṭhānepi aggiṃ pātetvā iminā adhippāyena ālimpentassa pācittiyameva. Dukkaṭanti sukkhaṭṭhāne vā sukkhaṃ “asukkha”nti avavatthapetvā vā aggiṃ pātentassa dukkaṭaṃ. Kīḷādhippāyepi eseva nayo. Kīḷādhippāyo ca paṭapaṭāyamānasaddassādavaseneva veditabbo. Paṭipakkhabhūto aggi paṭaggi. Parittakaraṇanti ārakkhakaraṇaṃ. Sayaṃ vā uṭṭhitanti vāteritānaṃ veḷuādīnaṃ aññamaññasaṅghaṭṭanena samuṭṭhitaṃ. Nirupādānoti indhanarahito.

190. Wet… (etc.) …pācittiya: Even in a dry place, for one who kindles a fire with this intention, it is a pācittiya indeed. Dukkaṭa: It is a dukkaṭa offense for one who sets fire in a dry place, or to a dry thing without having determined it as ‘not dry’. With the intention of play, this is the same method. And the intention of play should be understood by way of enjoying the crackling sound. An opposing fire is a backfire. Making a protection means making a safeguard. ‘Or arisen by itself’ means: arisen from the mutual friction of bamboos, etc., stirred by the wind. ‘Without fuel’ means: devoid of fuel.

191-192. Khettameva otiṇṇattā pārājikanti “dvīhī”ti vutte dvīhipi pahārehi maraṇassa paccāsīsanato ekena vinā dvinnaṃ abhāvato [M 2.0278] ca pārājikaṃ. “Dvīhiyevāti niyamite pana ekena pahārena mārite natthi pārājika”nti vadanti. Paṭhamaṃ āhitabalavegassa pubbānuciṇṇavasena dhammānaṃ desantaruppattiyā gamanamattaṃ ṭhapetvā jīvitindriyassa tattha avijjamānattā “sīsacchedakassā”ti vuttaṃ. Imassa vatthussāti āghātanavatthussa. “Pānaparibhogenāti vuttattā loṇasovīrakaṃ yāmakālika”nti vadanti.

Because it has entered only the field, it is a pārājika. When it is said ‘by two,’ it is a pārājika because death is anticipated from both blows, and because without one there cannot be two. But when it is specified as ‘by two only,’ some say, ‘there is no pārājika if he is killed by one blow.’ Setting aside the mere movement of phenomena arising in another place by the power of past habituation of the first blow, which has applied force and momentum—because the life faculty is not present there—it is said, ‘of the one who cuts the head.’ ‘Of this case’ means of the case of striking. Because it is said, ‘by the consumption of a drink,’ they say, ‘salt-sour gruel is a yāmakālika.’

Vinītavatthuvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Decided Cases is completed.

Iti samantapāsādikāya vinayaṭṭhakathāya sāratthadīpaniyaṃ

Thus in the Sāratthadīpanī, a sub-commentary on the Samantapāsādikā, the commentary on the Vinaya—

Tatiyapārājikavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the third Pārājika is completed.

4. Catutthapārājikaṃ

4. The Fourth Pārājika

Catusaccavidūti [V 2.0247] cattāri saccāni samāhaṭāni catusaccaṃ, taṃ avedi paṭivijjhīti catusaccavidū. Satipi sāvakānaṃ paccekabuddhānañca catusaccavidubhāve anaññapubbakattā bhagavato catusaccadassanassa tattha ca sabbaññutāya balesu ca vasībhāvassa pattito parasantānesu pasāritabhāvena pākaṭattā ca bhagavāva visesena “catusaccavidū”ti thomanaṃ arahati.

‘Knower of the Four Truths’: The four truths, collected together, are the four truths; one who knew them, penetrated them, is called ‘Knower of the Four Truths.’ Even though disciples and Paccekabuddhas also possess the state of being knowers of the four truths, the Blessed One alone is especially worthy of the praise ‘Knower of the Four Truths’ because his vision of the four truths was not preceded by another, and because of his attainment of omniscience and mastery over the powers in that regard, and because it is evident through its dissemination in the mental continuums of others.

Vaggumudātīriyabhikkhuvatthuvaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Story of the Monks Dwelling on the Bank of the Vaggumudā

193. Adhiṭṭhemāti saṃvidahāma. Dūtakammanti gihīnaṃ paṇṇaṃ vā sāsanaṃ vā gahetvā tattha tattha gamanaṃ. Iriyāpathaṃ saṇṭhapetvāti padhānānurūpaṃ katvā. Pucchantānaṃ vāti “ayyā santairiyāpathā ativiya upasantā, kataraṃ visesamadhigacchiṃsū”ti pucchantānaṃ. Anāgatasambandhe pana asatīti “bhāsito bhavissatī”ti pāṭhasesaṃ katvā anāgatasambandhe asati. “Bhāsito”ti atītavacanaṃ kathaṃ anāgatavacanena sambandhamupagacchatīti āha “lakkhaṇaṃ pana saddasatthato pariyesitabba”nti. Īdise hi ṭhāne “dhātusambandhe paccayā”ti iminā lakkhaṇena dhātvatthasambandhe sati ayathākālavihitāpi paccayā sādhavo bhavantīti saddasatthavidū vadanti.

193. ‘Adhiṭṭhema’ means ‘we agree.’ ‘Dūtakamma’ is taking a letter or message from householders and going here and there. ‘Iriyāpathaṃ saṇṭhapetvā’ means having arranged it in accordance with one’s meditation effort. ‘Pucchantānaṃ vā’ refers to those who ask, “Venerable sirs, with calm deportment, they are exceedingly serene—what special attainment have they reached?” Regarding ‘Anāgatasambandhe pana asati’: having supplied the rest of the text as ‘bhāsito bhavissati,’ this means ‘when there is no future connection.’ How does ‘bhāsito,’ a past tense word, connect with a future tense word? He said, “The characteristic, however, must be sought from the science of grammar.” For in such a case, by the characteristic “in the connection of roots, there are suffixes,” when there is a connection of the root’s meaning, even suffixes applied not according to their proper time become valid—so say those who know the science of grammar.

194. Vaṇṇavāti [M 2.0279] iminā sakalasarīrānugatavaṇṇassa manāpatā vuttā. Pasannamukhavaṇṇāti iminā sakalasarīravaṇṇatopi adhikataraṃ mukhavaṇṇassa manāpatā vuttā. Vippasannachavivaṇṇāti iminā pana vijjamānasseva sarīravaṇṇassa ativiya pasannatā vuttā. Yasmā indriyānaṃ ūnattaṃ vā pūraṇattaṃ vā natthi, tasmā “abhiniviṭṭhokāsassa paripuṇṇattā”ti vuttaṃ. Chaṭṭhassa abhiniviṭṭhokāso hadayavatthu, pañcapasādānaṃ abhiniviṭṭhokāsassa paripuṇṇatāvacaneneva hadayavatthuādisakalasarīrassa paripuṇṇatā dassitāyeva hotīti āha – “manacchaṭṭhānaṃ [V 2.0248] indriyāna”nti. Yathā tanti ettha tanti nipātamattaṃ. Bhantamigappaṭibhāgāti kattabbākattabbassa ajānanato bhantamigasadisā. Catucakkanti catuiriyāpathaṃ. Iriyāpatho hi idha pavattanaṭṭhena “cakka”nti adhippeto. Navadvāranti navahi vaṇamukhehi navadvāraṃ. Dukkhanti sīsarogādidukkhaṃ. Sabbakiccesūti pattapacanacīvararajanayogaṭṭhānādikiccesu. Yāpetunti vahituṃ pavattetuṃ. Tenāha “gametu”nti.

194. By ‘vaṇṇavā’ is meant the pleasing appearance of the complexion pervading the entire body. By ‘pasannamukhavaṇṇā’ is meant that the facial complexion is even more pleasing than the complexion of the whole body. By ‘vippasannachavivaṇṇā,’ however, is meant the exceedingly clear and bright appearance of the already existing bodily complexion. Because there is no deficiency or excess in the faculties, it is said, “due to the completeness of the established domain.” The established domain of the sixth faculty is the heart-base. By the statement of the completeness of the established domains of the five sense faculties, the completeness of the entire body, including the heart-base, is indeed shown. Hence, he says, “the faculties including the mind as the sixth.” As for ‘tanti’ here, ‘tanti’ is merely a particle. By ‘bhantamigappaṭibhāgā’ is meant being like bewildered deer because of not knowing what should or should not be done. By ‘catucakka’ is meant the four modes of deportment. For ‘cakka’ here is intended in the sense of movement with regard to deportment. By ‘navadvāra’ is meant the nine openings through the nine wound-apertures. By ‘dukkha’ is meant suffering such as headaches and other pains. By ‘sabbakiccesu’ is meant in all duties such as cooking in the bowl, robe-dyeing, arranging the place for meditation, and so on. By ‘yāpetuṃ’ is meant to maintain or continue. Therefore, he says, ‘gametuṃ’.

195. Santoti iminā tesaṃ vijjamānataṃ dasseti, saṃvijjamānāti iminā pana tesaṃ upalabbhamānataṃ dasseti. Tenāha – “atthi ceva upalabbhanti cā”ti. Upalabbhantīti dissanti, ñāyantīti attho. Panthadūhanakammanti panthaghātanakammaṃ. Hanantoti mārento. Ghātentoti mārāpento. Atha vā hanantoti bandhanatāḷanādīhi hiṃsanto. Ghātentoti mārento. Chindantoti paresaṃ hatthādīni chindanto. Pacantoti daṇḍena uppīḷento. Pacanañhettha dahanaṃ vibādhanaṃ adhippetaṃ. Pacantoti vā tajjento tāsento. Atha vā pacantoti gāmesu aggipātanavasena gehādīni jhāpetvā tattha ajeḷakādīni pacanto.

195. By ‘santo’ is shown their existence, while by ‘saṃvijjamānā’ is shown their being obtainable. Hence it is said: “They exist and they are found.” By ‘upalabbhanti’ is meant they are seen or known. By ‘panthadūhanakamma’ is meant the act of highway robbery. By ‘hananto’ is meant killing. By ‘ghātento’ is meant causing to kill. Alternatively, by ‘hananto’ is meant harming through binding, beating, etc., while by ‘ghātento’ is meant killing. By ‘chindanto’ is meant cutting off others' hands, etc. By ‘pacanto’ is meant oppressing with a stick. Here, ‘pacana’ is intended to mean tormenting. Or, by ‘pacanto’ is meant threatening or terrifying. Alternatively, by ‘pacanto’ is meant setting fire to houses, etc., in villages and cooking goats, sheep, etc., there.

Ye sikkhāpadesu bahulagāravā na honti āpattivītikkamabahulā, te sikkhāpadesu atibbagāravā. Uddhateti akappiye kappiyasaññitāya kappiye akappiyasaññitāya avajje vajjasaññitāya vajje avajjasaññitāya ca uddhaccapakatike. Unnaḷeti uggatanaḷe, uṭṭhitatucchamāneti vuttaṃ hoti. Capaleti pattacīvaramaṇḍanādinā cāpallena yutte. Mukhareti mukhakhare[M 2.0280], kharavacaneti vuttaṃ hoti. Vikiṇṇavāceti asaṃyatavacane divasampi niratthakavacanappalāpine. Muṭṭhā naṭṭhā sati etesanti muṭṭhassatī, sativirahiteti vuttaṃ hoti. Asampajāneti nippaññe. Pākatindriyeti saṃvarābhāvena gihikāle viya vivaṭaindriye. Ācariyupajjhāyehi pariccattaketi dhammena āmisena ca asaṅgahetvā ācariyupajjhāyehi pariccatte anāthe appatiṭṭhe. Lābhagaruketi paccayagaruke.

Those who are not greatly reverential towards the training rules and are frequent transgressors of offenses are those lacking reverence towards the training rules. By ‘uddhatā’ is meant one who, due to agitation, perceives the improper as proper, the proper as improper, the blameworthy as blameless, and the blameless as blameworthy. By ‘unnaḷā’ is meant one with raised pride; it is said to be characterized by arisen, empty conceit. By ‘capalā’ is meant one who is endowed with frivolity, such as adorning the bowl and robes. By ‘mukharā’ is meant one with a harsh mouth; it is said to be characterized by harsh words. By ‘vikiṇṇavācā’ is meant one with unrestrained speech, indulging even during the day in meaningless chatter. By ‘muṭṭhassatī’ is meant one in whom mindfulness is lost and destroyed; it is said to be devoid of mindfulness. By ‘asampajāno’ is meant one lacking wisdom. By ‘pākatindriya’ is meant one with unguarded faculties, as in the time of a householder, due to an absence of restraint. By ‘ācariyupajjhāyehi pariccattaka’ is meant one abandoned by teachers and preceptors, unsupported by them through the Dhamma or material means, and thus being helpless and without support. By ‘lābhagaruka’ is meant one who is attached to the requisites.

Iriyāpathasaṇṭhapanādīnīti ādi-saddena paccayapaṭisevanasāmantajappānaṃ gahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Mahāniddese (mahāni. 87) hi iriyāpathasaṇṭhapanapaccayapaṭisevanasāmantajappanavasena tividhaṃ kuhakavatthu āgataṃ. Tattha pāpicchasseva sato sambhāvanādhippāyakatena iriyāpathena vimhāpanaṃ iriyāpathasaṇṭhapanasaṅkhātaṃ kuhakavatthu. Tathā cīvarādīhi nimantitassa tadatthikasseva sato pāpicchataṃ nissāya paṭikkhepanena te ca gahapatike attani suppatiṭṭhitasaddhe ñatvā puna tesaṃ “aho ayyo appiccho, na kiñci paṭiggaṇhituṃ icchati, suladdhaṃ vata no assa, sace appamattakampi [V 2.0249] kiñci paṭiggaṇheyyā”ti nānāvidhehi upāyehi paṇītāni cīvarādīni upanentānaṃ tadanuggahakāmataṃyeva āvikatvā paṭiggahaṇena ca tato pabhuti asītisakaṭabhārehi upanāmanahetubhūtaṃ vimhāpanaṃ paccayapaṭisevanasaṅkhātaṃ kuhakavatthūti veditabbaṃ. Pāpicchasseva pana sato uttarimanussadhammādhigamaparidīpanavācāya tathā tathā vimhāpanaṃ sāmantajappanasaṅkhātaṃ kuhakavatthūti veditabbaṃ. Cittalapabbatādivihāro lokasammatasenāsanaṃ nāma. Lokasammata …pe… upāyehi saṃvaṇṇiyamānaguṇoti sambandho. Paripācetunti pariṇāmetuṃ. Suddhacittena attano ganthadhurādikammaṃ katvā vicarantānaṃ tammūlakapaccayaparibhoge dosābhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “ye panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Bhikkhācāre asampajjamāneti gocaragāme bhikkhāya caritvā labhitabbapiṇḍapāte asampajjante. Te ca vattasīsena sabbampetaṃ karonti, na lābhanimittaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “tantipaveṇighaṭanakā sāsanajotakā”ti.

By ‘establishing postures, etc.’ (iriyāpathasaṇṭhapanādīni), the inclusion of the use of requisites and suggestive speech is to be understood by the word ‘etc.’ (ādi). Indeed, in the Mahāniddesa, three grounds of deceit are presented: through establishing posture, use of requisites, and suggestive speech. Therein, the ground of deceit known as ‘establishing posture’ is the deception by one with evil desires, who adopts a posture with the intention of being esteemed. Similarly, the ground of deceit known as ‘use of requisites’ should be understood as follows: when invited with robes and other requisites, such a person, being one who desires them, refuses them out of evil desire. Having come to know that the householders have well-established faith in him, he later accepts when they, through various means, bring fine robes and other items, saying, ‘Oh, the noble one is of few wishes! He does not want to accept anything. It would be a great gain for us if he would accept even some small thing!’ In accepting, he reveals only his desire to favor them. This deception, which from then on becomes the cause for them to bring eighty cartloads of goods, is the ground of deceit known as ‘use of requisites’. Furthermore, the ground of deceit called ‘suggestive speech’ is the deception by one with evil desires, who in various ways makes claims through speech that proclaims the attainment of superhuman states. A monastery such as Cittalapabbata is called a ‘world-approved dwelling.’ The connection is: ‘world-approved… having qualities that are praised by various means.’ ‘To ripen’ (paripācetun) means to transform. To show the absence of fault in the use of requisites originating from that source for those who wander about, having done their own work such as the burden of study with a pure mind, the passage beginning ‘But those who…’ was stated. ‘When the alms-round is unsuccessful’ (bhikkhācāre asampajjamāne) means when the almsfood to be obtained by wandering for alms in a resort village is not forthcoming. And they do all this with duty as their main concern, not for the sake of gain. Therefore it was said, ‘They are the upholders of the textual lineage, the illuminators of the Dispensation.’

Kicchenāti na dukkhāya paṭipadāya. Buddhānañhi cattāropi maggā sukhāpaṭipadāva honti, pāramīpūraṇakāle pana sarāgadosamohasseva sato āgatānaṃ yācakānaṃ alaṅkatappaṭiyattaṃ sīsaṃ kantitvā galalohitaṃ [M 2.0281] nīharitvā suañjitāni akkhīni uppāṭetvā kulavaṃsappatiṭṭhāpakaṃ puttaṃ manāpacāriniṃ bhariyanti evamādīni dentassa aññānipi khantivādīsadisesu attabhāvesu chejjabhejjādīni pāpuṇantassa āgamanīyapaṭipadaṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Kasirenāti tasseva vevacanaṃ.

‘With difficulty’ (kicchena) does not mean by a painful practice. For the Buddhas, all four paths are indeed of pleasant practice. However, this was said with reference to the practice to be undertaken during the time of fulfilling the perfections: when, while still possessed of greed, hatred, and delusion, one gives to beggars who have come such things as one's adorned and prepared head after cutting it off, blood from the throat after extracting it, well-anointed eyes after tearing them out, a son who establishes the family lineage, and a wife of pleasing conduct; and when, in other existences such as that of Khantivādī, one endures cutting, breaking, and so on. ‘With hardship’ (kasirena) is a synonym for that very term.

Ekasseva dātuṃ asakkuṇeyyatāya garubhāvato “garubhaṇḍānī”ti vuttaṃ, sabbesaṃ bhājetvāpi gahetuṃ asakkuṇeyyatāya “garuparikkhārānī”ti vuttaṃ. Sādhāraṇaparikkhārabhāvenāti saṅghikattā sabbabhikkhusādhāraṇaparikkhārabhāvena. Saṅgaṇhāti upalāpetīti idaṃ atheyyacittaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tenevāha – “tathābhāvato thenetvā”ti, avissajjiyaavebhaṅgiyabhāvato thenetvāti attho. Garubhaṇḍañhi kulasaṅgahatthāya vissajjento vibhajanto ca tassa avissajjiyaavaebhaṅgiyabhāvaṃ theneti. Kuladūsakadukkaṭaṃ āpajjatīti ettha “yo vissajjeyya, āpatti thullaccayassā”ti vuttattā vissajjanapaccayā thullaccayenapi na muccati.

Because it is a grave matter, in that it is not possible to give it to just one person, it is called ‘grave items’ (garubhaṇḍāni). Because it is not possible to take it even after dividing it among all, it is called ‘grave requisites’ (garuparikkhārāni). ‘By its nature as a common requisite’ means: because it belongs to the Sangha, by its nature as a requisite common to all monks. ‘He gathers, he cajoles’—this is said with reference to a mind intending to steal. Therefore it was said: ‘Because of that nature, having stolen it.’ The meaning is: having stolen it on account of its nature of being inalienable and indivisible. Indeed, one who relinquishes or divides a grave item for the sake of winning over a family steals its inalienable and indivisible nature. Regarding ‘he commits a dukkaṭa offense of corrupting a family,’ since it is said, ‘Whoever should relinquish it, there is a thullaccaya offense,’ he is not freed from a thullaccaya offense on account of relinquishing it.

Asantanti avijjamānaṃ. Abhūtanti anuppannaṃ. Anuppannattā hi tassa taṃ asantanti. Purimassa pacchimaṃ kāraṇavacanaṃ. Ullapatīti uggatāyuko lapati. Sīlañhi bhikkhuno āyu, taṃ tassa tathālapanasamakālameva vigacchati. Asantasambhāvanāyāti attano avijjamānaguṇehi sambhāvanāya. Evañhi gaṇhatā…pe… thenetvā gahitā hontīti ettha asantasambhāvanāya raṭṭhapiṇḍassa [V 2.0250] thenetvā gahitattā lokuttaradhammopi thenitoyeva hoti. Kitavassevāti kitavassa sakuṇaggahaṇamiva. Kerāṭikassāti saṭhassa. Gottaṃ vuccati sādhāraṇanāmaṃ, matta-saddo luttaniddiṭṭho, tasmā samaṇāti gottamattaṃ anubhavanti dhārentīti gotrabhuno, nāmamattasamaṇāti vuttaṃ hoti.

‘Non-existent’ (asantaṃ) means not present. ‘Unreal’ (abhūtaṃ) means not arisen. Indeed, because it has not arisen, for him it is non-existent. The latter is the reason-statement for the former. ‘He boasts’ (ullapati) means one of diminished lifespan speaks. For a monk, virtue is his life, and that life departs at the very moment he speaks thus. ‘By being esteemed for what is non-existent’ (asantasambhāvanāya) means by being esteemed for qualities one does not possess. Here, regarding ‘for one who takes thus... they are taken by stealing,’ because the country's almsfood has been taken by stealing through being esteemed for what is non-existent, even the supramundane Dhamma is thereby stolen. ‘Of a cheat’ (kitavassa) means like the bird-catching of a cheat. ‘Of a deceitful person’ (kerāṭikassa) means of a rogue. ‘Lineage’ (gotta) is called a common name; the word ‘mere’ (matta) is elided. Therefore, gotrabhuno means those who experience or bear merely the lineage-name ‘ascetic’; that is to say, ‘ascetics in name only’.

Vaggumudātīriyabhikkhuvatthuvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the story of the monks from the bank of the Vaggumudā River is concluded.

Adhimānavatthuvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Story of Conceit

196. Heṭṭhimamaggehi ñātamariyādāya eva jānanato aññā aggamaggapaññā, tassā phalabhāvato aggaphalapaññā taṃsahagatā sammāsaṅkappādayo ca aññāti vuttāti āha “aññaṃ byākariṃsūti arahattaṃ byākariṃsū”ti. Ariyasāvakassa tāva nuppajjatīti pahīnādhimānapaccayattā nuppajjati[M 2.0282]. Sīlavatopi…pe… nuppajjati akārakabhāvato. Tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvāti kalāpasammasanavasena tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā. Āraddhavipassakassāti udayabbayānupassanāya āraddhavipassakassa. Suddhasamathalābhī vipassanāya kammaṃ akatvāpi kilesasamudācāraṃ apassanto kevalaṃ aññāṇabalena “ariyohamasmī”ti maññatīti āha “suddhasamathalābhiṃ vā”ti. “Arahā aha”nti maññati uccavālaṅkavāsī mahānāgatthero viya.

196. The supreme path-knowledge is ‘other’ because it is known by the scope of what is known through the lower paths; the supreme fruit-knowledge is so because it is the fruit of that path; and the right resolve and so forth associated with it are also said to be ‘other’. Thus, he said: ‘“They declared another” means they declared arahantship.’ For a noble disciple, it does not arise; because the condition for conceit has been abandoned, it does not arise. Even for a virtuous one... it does not arise due to the absence of a cause. ‘Having imposed the three characteristics’ means having imposed the three characteristics by means of contemplating groups. ‘For one who has undertaken insight’ means for one who has begun insight with the contemplation of rise and fall. One who has only attained serenity, without having done the work of insight and not seeing the arising of defilements, may think, ‘I am a noble one,’ merely by the power of ignorance. Thus, he said: ‘or one who has only attained serenity.’ He thinks, ‘I am an arahant’—like the elder Mahānāga, who lived in Uccavālaṅka.

Talaṅgaravāsī dhammadinnatthero kira nāma eko pabhinnappaṭisambhido mahākhīṇāsavo mahato bhikkhusaṅghassa ovādadāyako ahosi. So ekadivasaṃ attano divāṭṭhāne nisīditvā “kinnu kho amhākaṃ ācariyassa uccavālaṅkavāsīmahānāgattherassa samaṇabhāvakiccaṃ matthakappattaṃ, no”ti āvajjento puthujjanabhāvamevassa disvā “mayi agacchante puthujjanakālakiriyameva karissatī”ti ca ñatvā iddhiyā vehāsaṃ uppatitvā divāṭṭhāne nisinnassa therassa samīpe orohitvā vanditvā vattaṃ dassetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. “Kiṃ, āvuso dhammadinna, akāle āgatosī”ti ca vutto “pañhaṃ, bhante, pucchituṃ āgatomhī”ti āha. Tato “pucchāvuso, jānamānā kathayissāmā”ti vutto pañhasahassaṃ pucchi. Thero pucchitaṃ pucchitaṃ pañhaṃ asajjamānova kathesi. Tato “atitikkhaṃ vo, bhante, ñāṇaṃ, kadā tumhehi ayaṃ dhammo adhigato”ti vutto “ito saṭṭhivassakāle, āvuso”ti āha. Samādhimhi, bhante, vaḷañjethāti. Na idaṃ, āvuso, bhāriyanti. Tena hi, bhante, ekaṃ hatthiṃ māpethāti. Thero sabbasetaṃ hatthiṃ māpesi. Idāni, bhante, yathā ayaṃ hatthī añjitakaṇṇo pasāritanaṅguṭṭho soṇḍaṃ [V 2.0251] mukhe pakkhipitvā bheravaṃ koñcanādaṃ karonto tumhākaṃ abhimukhaṃ āgacchati, tathā naṃ karothāti. Thero tathā katvā vegena āgacchato hatthissa bheravaṃ ākāraṃ disvā uṭṭhāya palāyituṃ āraddho. Tamenaṃ khīṇāsavatthero hatthaṃ pasāretvā cīvarakaṇṇe gahetvā “bhante, khīṇāsavassa sārajjaṃ nāma hotī”ti āha. So tasmiṃ kāle attano puthujjanabhāvaṃ ñatvā “avassayo me, āvuso, dhammadinna hohī”ti vatvā pādamūle ukkuṭikaṃ nisīdi. “Bhante, tumhākaṃ avassayo bhavissāmiccevāhaṃ āgato, mā cintayitthā”ti kammaṭṭhānaṃ [M 2.0283] kathesi. Thero kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā caṅkamaṃ oruyha tatiye padavāre aggaphalaṃ arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Thero kira dosacarito ahosi.

It is said that the elder Dhammadinna, who resided at Talaṅgara, was a great Arahant with the analytical knowledges, one who gave advice to a large community of monks. One day, while sitting in his daytime dwelling, he reflected, “I wonder if our teacher, the great elder Mahānāga, who resided in Uccavālaṅka, has brought the task of the ascetic’s life to its culmination or not.” Reflecting, he saw that he was still a worldling and knew, “If I do not go, he will die as a worldling.” So, rising into the air by psychic power, he descended near the elder who was seated in his daytime dwelling, paid respects, showed his duty, and sat to one side. When asked, “Friend Dhammadinna, why have you come at an untimely hour?” he replied, “Venerable sir, I have come to ask a question.” Then, being told, “Ask, friend, if we know, we will answer,” he posed a thousand questions. The elder answered each and every question without hesitation. Then Dhammadinna asked, “Venerable sir, your knowledge is exceedingly sharp. When did you attain this Dhamma?” The elder replied, “Sixty years ago, friend.” “Venerable sir, do you practice concentration?” “This is not difficult, friend.” “In that case, venerable sir, create an elephant.” The elder created an all-white elephant. “Now, venerable sir, make it so that this elephant approaches you with its ears raised, its tail outstretched, placing its trunk in its mouth, and making a terrifying trumpeting sound.” The elder did so, but upon seeing the terrifying appearance of the swiftly approaching elephant, he rose and began to flee. The Arahant elder stretched out his hand, grasped the corner of his robe, and said, “Venerable sir, is there such a thing as agitation for an Arahant?” At that moment, realizing his own state as a worldling, he said, “Friend Dhammadinna, be my refuge,” and sat squatting at his feet. “Venerable sir, I came precisely to be your refuge—do not worry.” He then taught him a meditation subject. The elder, having taken up the meditation subject, descended to the walking path and, at the third step, attained the supreme fruit, Arahantship. It is said that the elder was of an angry temperament.

Adhimānavatthuvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the subject of conceit is finished.

Savibhaṅgasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Training Rules with Analysis

197-198. Yasmā panātiādi “asantaṃ abhūtaṃ asaṃvijjamāna”nti etesaṃ kāraṇavacanaṃ. Tattha yanti yaṃ uttarimanussadhammaṃ. Anabhijānanti attani atthibhāvaṃ ajānanto. Samudācaratīti “atthi mayhaṃ esa dhammo”ti katheti jānāpeti vā. “Asantaṃ abhūta”nti imassa kāraṇavacanaṃ santāne anuppannoti. Ñāṇena ca asacchikatoti idaṃ pana “asaṃvijjamāna”nti etassa kāraṇavacanaṃ. Pakatimanussehi uttaritarānaṃ buddhādiuttamapurisānaṃ adhigamadhammo uttarimanussadhammoti āha “uttarimanussāna”ntiādi. Tanti uttarimanussadhammaṃ. Atha padabhājane bahuvacananiddeso kasmā katoti āha “padabhājane panā”tiādi. Kiñcāpi uttarimanussadhammo abyākatopi hoti, ārogyaṭṭhena pana bāhitikasutte viya “kusale dhamme”ti vuttaṃ. Assāti uttarimanussadhammassa. Khaṇalayamuhutta-saddā aññattha bhinnatthāpi honti, idha pana khaṇapariyāyavaseneva “taṃ khaṇaṃ taṃ layaṃ taṃ muhutta”nti pāḷiyaṃ vuttaṃ.

197-198. The phrase 'Yasmā pana' and so on is the causal explanation for 'not existing, not real, not present'. Therein, 'yaṃ' refers to 'which superhuman state'. 'Anabhijānanti' means not knowing its existence in oneself. 'Samudācarati' means he says or makes known, 'This state is mine'. The causal explanation for 'asantaṃ abhūtaṃ' is that it has not arisen in one's continuum. And 'not realized by knowledge' is the causal explanation for 'asaṃvijjamānaṃ'. The state to be attained by superior persons like the Buddhas, who are higher than ordinary humans, is called 'uttarimanussadhamma' (superhuman state); thus it is said 'of superhuman beings' and so on. 'Taṃ' refers to the superhuman state. Then, why is the plural designation made in the word-analysis? He says, 'In the word-analysis, however,' and so on. Although the superhuman state can also be indeterminate, it is called 'wholesome states' in the sense of health, as in the Bāhitika Sutta. 'Assa' refers to 'of the superhuman state'. The words 'khaṇa' (moment), 'laya' (instant), 'muhutta' (moment) have different meanings elsewhere, but here in the Pāḷi text, 'that moment, that instant, that muhutta' are stated by way of being synonyms for 'khaṇa'.

Adhigantabbato adhigamo, jhānādi, adhigamassa pucchā adhigamapucchā. Tenāha “jhānavimokkhādīsū”tiādi. Upāyapucchāti adhigamupāyapucchā. Kintīti kena pakārena, kena vidhināti attho. Katamesaṃ tvaṃ dhammānaṃ lābhīti idaṃ pana pubbe “kiṃ te adhigata”nti aniddhāritabhedā jhānādivisesā pucchitāti idāni tesaṃ niddhāretvā pucchanākāradassanaṃ.

Attainment (adhigama) is so called because it is to be attained (adhigantabbato), such as the jhānas and so on. The question about attainment is 'adhigamapucchā'. Therefore, he says, 'in jhānas, liberations, and so on'. 'Upāyapucchā' (question about the means) is the question about the means of attainment. 'Kintī' (how) means by what manner, by what method. As for the question 'Of which states are you a recipient?', this is showing the manner of questioning by now specifying them, since previously the particular states such as the jhānas were asked about without specifying their distinctions, as in 'What have you attained?'.

Tasmāti [V 2.0252] yasmā yathāvuttehi chahākārehi adhigamabyākaraṇaṃ sodhetabbaṃ, tasmā. Ettāvatāvāti ettakena byākaraṇamatteneva na sakkātabbo. Byākaraṇañhi ekaccassa ayāthāvatopi hotīti. Imesu pana chasu ṭhānesu sodhanatthaṃ vattabboti yathā nāma jātarūpapatirūpakampi [M 2.0284] jātarūpaṃ viya khāyatīti jātarūpaṃ nighaṃsanatāpanacchedanehi sodhetabbaṃ, evameva imesu idāneva vuttesu chasu ṭhānesu pakkhipitvā sodhanatthaṃ vattabbo. Vimokkhādīsūti ādi-saddena samādhisamāpattiñāṇadassanamaggabhāvanāphalasacchikiriyādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Pākaṭo hotīti adhigatavisesassa satisammosābhāvato. Sesapucchāsupi pākaṭo hotīti pade eseva nayo.

Therefore (tasmā): because the declaration of attainment should be purified by the six modes as stated, therefore. By so much (ettāvatā): he should not be honored by merely this much declaration. For the declaration of some can be untrue. However, he should be spoken to for the purpose of purification in these six instances. Just as counterfeit gold appears like gold, so gold should be purified by rubbing, heating, and cutting; even so, he should be spoken to for the purpose of purification by applying the test to these six instances just mentioned. In 'vimokkhādīsu' (in liberations and so on), by the word 'ādi' (and so on), it includes concentration, attainment, knowledge and vision, development of the path, and realization of the fruit. 'Pākaṭo hoti' (it becomes evident): because of the absence of confusion of mindfulness regarding the special attainment. In the other questions as well, this is the same method for the phrase 'pākaṭo hoti'.

Sabbesañhi attanā adhigatamaggena pahīnakilesā pākaṭā hontīti idaṃ yebhuyyavasena vuttaṃ. Kassaci hi attanā adhigatamaggavajjhakilesesu sandeho uppajjatiyeva mahānāmassa sakkassa viya. So hi sakadāgāmī samānopi “tassa mayhaṃ, bhante, evaṃ hoti ‘ko su nāma me dhammo ajjhattaṃ appahīno, yena me ekadā lobhadhammāpi cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhanti, dosadhammāpi cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhanti, mohadhammāpi cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhantī’”ti (ma. ni. 1.175) bhagavantaṃ pucchi. Ayaṃ kira rājā sakadāgāmimaggena lobhadosamohā niravasesā pahīyantīti saññī ahosi. Kiṃ ariyasāvakassa evaṃ sandeho uppajjatīti? Āma uppajjati. Kasmā? Paṇṇattiyaṃ akovidattā. “Ayaṃ kileso asukamaggavajjho”ti imissā paṇṇattiyā akovidassa hi ariyasāvakassa evaṃ hoti. Kiṃ tassa paccavekkhaṇā natthīti? Atthi, sā pana na sabbesaṃ paripuṇṇā hoti. Eko hi pahīnakilesameva paccavekkhati, eko avasiṭṭhakilesameva, eko maggameva, eko phalameva, eko nibbānameva. Imāsu pana pañcasu paccavekkhaṇāsu ekaṃ vā dve vā no laddhuṃ na vaṭṭati. Iti yassa paccavekkhaṇā na paripuṇṇā, tassa maggavajjhakilesapaṇṇattiyaṃ akovidattā evaṃ hoti. Uggahaparipucchākusalāti sajjhāyamaggasaṃvaṇṇanāsu nipuṇā.

For it is generally said that the defilements abandoned by the path one has attained become evident to all. Indeed, for some, doubt arises regarding the defilements to be abandoned by the path attained by oneself, as in the case of Mahānāma the Sakyan. Though he was a once-returner, he asked the Blessed One: 'Venerable sir, this thought occurs to me: "What quality remains unabandoned within me, due to which lustful thoughts may sometimes overwhelm my mind, hateful thoughts may overwhelm my mind, deluded thoughts may overwhelm my mind?"' This king, it seems, had the perception that greed, hatred, and delusion are abandoned without remainder by the path of a once-returner. Does such doubt arise for a noble disciple? Yes, it does arise. Why? Because of being unskilled in designation. For a noble disciple who is unskilled in this designation, 'This defilement is to be abandoned by such-and-such path,' it happens thus. If it is asked, 'Does he not have reflection?' He does, but that reflection is not complete for everyone. One reflects only on the abandoned defilements, another only on the remaining defilements, another only on the path, another only on the fruit, another only on Nibbāna. Among these five reflections, it is not that it is improper to have obtained one or two. Thus, for one whose reflection is not complete, because of being unskilled in the designation of defilements to be abandoned by the path, it happens thus. 'Skilled in learning and questioning' means they are skilled in recitation and in the exposition of the path.

Yāya paṭipadāya yassa ariyamaggo āgacchati, sā pubbabhāgapaṭipatti āgamanapaṭipadā. Sodhetabbāti suddhā udāhu na suddhāti vicāraṇavasena sodhetabbā. Na sujjhatīti tattha tattha pamādapaṭipattisabbhāvato. Apanetabboti attano paṭiññāya apanetabbo. “Sujjhatī”ti vatvā sujjhanākāraṃ dassetuṃ “dīgharatta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Paññāyatīti etthāpi “yadī”ti padaṃ ānetvā yadi so bhikkhu tāya paṭipadāya paññāyatīti sambandho[M 2.0285]. Catūsu paccayesu [V 2.0253] alaggattā “ākāse pāṇisamena cetasā”ti vuttaṃ. Vuttasadisanti tassa bhikkhuno byākaraṇaṃ imasmiṃ sutte vuttena sadisaṃ, samanti attho.

The practice by which the noble path comes to a noble one is the preliminary practice, the path of approach. 'It should be examined' (sodhetabbā): it should be examined by way of investigation as to whether it is pure or not pure. 'It is not pure' (na sujjhati): because of the possibility of heedless practice here and there. 'He should be dismissed' (apanetabbo): he should be dismissed by his own declaration. Having said, 'It is pure,' in order to show the manner of its purity, 'For a long time,' and so on was said. In 'It is discerned' (paññāyati), here too, bringing in the word 'if', the connection is: 'if that bhikkhu is discerned by that practice'. Because of non-attachment to the four requisites, it is said, 'with a mind like the palm of a hand in space'. 'Similar to what was said' (vuttasadisaṃ): the declaration of that bhikkhu is similar to what was said in this sutta; meaning, it is the same.

Khīṇāsavapaṭipattisadisā paṭipadā hotīti dīgharattaṃ suvikkhambhitakilesattā. Khīṇāsavassa nāma…pe… na hotīti pahīnavipallāsattā jīvitanikantiyā ca abhāvato na hoti. Puthujjanassa pana appahīnavipallāsattā jīvitanikantisabbhāvato ca appamattakenapi hoti.

The practice is similar to the practice of one whose taints are destroyed because the defilements have been thoroughly suppressed for a long time. For one whose taints are destroyed... it does not occur because distortions have been abandoned and because of the absence of craving for life. But for an ordinary person, because distortions have not been abandoned and because of the presence of craving for life, it occurs even with a slight cause.

Tatrimāni vatthūni – dīghabhāṇakaabhayatthero kira ekaṃ piṇḍapātikaṃ pariggahetuṃ asakkonto daharassa saññaṃ adāsi. So taṃ nahāyamānaṃ kalyāṇīnadīmukhadvāre nimujjitvā pāde aggahesi. Piṇḍapātiko “kumbhīlo”ti saññāya mahāsaddaṃ akāsi, tadā naṃ “puthujjano”ti jāniṃsu. Candamukhatissarājakāle pana mahāvihāre saṅghatthero khīṇāsavo dubbalacakkhuko vihāreyeva acchati. Taṃ rājā “theraṃ pariggaṇhissāmī”ti bhikkhūsu bhikkhācāraṃ gatesu appasaddo upasaṅkamitvā sappo viya pāde aggahesi. Thero silāthambho viya niccalo hutvā “ko etthā”ti āha. Ahaṃ, bhante, tissoti. Sugandhaṃ vāyasi no tissāti. Evaṃ khīṇāsavassa bhayaṃ nāma natthi. Ekacco pana puthujjanopi atisūro hoti nibbhayo, so rajanīyena ārammaṇena pariggaṇhitabbo. Vasabharājāpi hi ekaṃ theraṃ pariggaṇhamāno ghare nisīdāpetvā tassa santike badarasāḷavaṃ maddamāno nisīdi. Mahātherassa kheḷo calito, therassa puthujjanabhāvo āvibhūto. Khīṇāsavassa hi rasataṇhā nāma suppahīnā, dibbesupi rasesu nikanti nāma na hoti. Tasmā imehi upāyehi pariggahetvā sacassa bhayaṃ vā chambhitattaṃ vā rasataṇhā vā uppajjati, “na tvaṃ arahā”ti apanetabbo.

Here are these stories: It is said that the elder Abhaya the Dīghabhāṇaka, unable to test a certain alms-food monk, gave a signal to a young novice. While that monk was bathing at the mouth of the Kalyāṇī River, the novice submerged and grabbed his feet. The alms-food monk, perceiving it to be a crocodile, let out a loud cry, and thus they knew him to be an ordinary person. During the time of King Caṇḍamukha Tissa, the elder of the Saṅgha at the Mahāvihāra, an Arahant with weak eyesight, dwelt in the monastery itself. The king, thinking, 'I will test the elder,' approached quietly when the monks had gone on their alms-round and grabbed his feet like a snake. The elder, unmoving as a stone pillar, asked, 'Who is here?' 'It is I, venerable sir, Tissa.' 'You smell fragrant, Tissa.' Thus, for one whose cankers are destroyed, there is no such thing as fear. Yet, some ordinary people are very brave and fearless; they must be tested with a desirable object. For instance, King Vasabha, while testing an elder, had him sit in the house and then sat nearby crushing a jujube salad. The great elder's saliva flowed; the elder's nature as an ordinary person was revealed. For one whose cankers are destroyed, craving for tastes is well abandoned; there is no delight even in divine flavors. Therefore, having tested him by these means, if fear, terror, or craving for tastes arises in him, he should be dismissed with the words, 'You are not an Arahant'.

Asantaguṇasambhāvanalakkhaṇā pāpicchāti āha – “yā sā idhekacco…pe… ādinā nayenā”ti. Ādi-saddena “assaddho samāno ‘saddhoti maṃ jano jānātū’ti icchati, appassutova samāno ‘bahussutoti maṃ jano jānātū’ti icchati, saṅgaṇikārāmova samāno ‘pavivittoti maṃ jano jānātū’ti icchati, kusītova samāno [M 2.0286] ‘āraddhavīriyoti maṃ jano jānātū’ti icchati, muṭṭhassatīva samāno ‘upaṭṭhitassatīti maṃ jano jānātū’ti icchati, asamāhitova samāno ‘samāhitoti maṃ jano jānātū’ti icchati, duppaññova samāno ‘paññavāti maṃ jano jānātū’ti icchati, akhīṇāsavova samāno ‘khīṇāsavoti maṃ jano jānātū’ti icchati, yā evarūpā icchā icchāgatā pāpicchatā rāgo sārāgo cittassa sārāgo, ayaṃ vuccati pāpicchatā”ti (vibha. 851) evaṃ vuttaṃ pāḷipadesaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Pāpikāyāti [V 2.0254] lāmikāya icchāya. Apakatoti pāpikāya icchāya sammāājīvato apeto katoti icchāya apakato. Tathābhūto ca micchājīvena abhibhūto parājito nāma hotīti āha “abhibhūto parājito”ti.

Evil desire has the characteristic of conceiving of non-existent qualities; thus he says, 'Here, someone... and so on, by this method'. By the term 'and so on', it includes the passage from the Pāḷi which states: 'Though faithless, he wishes, "May people know me as faithful"; though with little learning, he wishes, "May people know me as very learned"; though fond of company, he wishes, "May people know me as one who delights in solitude"; though lazy, he wishes, "May people know me as one with aroused energy"; though with lapsed mindfulness, he wishes, "May people know me as one with mindfulness established"; though unconcentrated, he wishes, "May people know me as concentrated"; though of little wisdom, he wishes, "May people know me as wise"; though with cankers undestroyed, he wishes, "May people know me as one whose cankers are destroyed." Whatever such desire, being in a state of desire, evil desire, lust, passion, passion of the mind—this is called evil desire' (Vibh. 851). 'By evil' (pāpikāya) means by base desire. 'Led astray' (apakato) means: made removed from right livelihood by evil desire, thus he is 'led astray' by desire. And such a person is indeed overcome and defeated by wrong livelihood; thus he says, 'overcome, defeated'.

Sāmaññaṃ dupparāmaṭṭhaṃ nirayāyupakaḍḍhatīti yathā kuso yena duggahito, tassa hatthaṃ anukantati phāleti, evameva samaṇadhammasaṅkhātaṃ sāmaññampi khaṇḍasīlāditāya dupparāmaṭṭhaṃ nirayāya upakaḍḍhati, niraye nibbattāpetīti attho. Sithiloti olīyitvā karaṇena sithilaggāhena kato. Paribbājoti khaṇḍādibhāvappatto samaṇadhammo. Bhiyyo ākirate rajanti abbhantare vijjamānaṃ rāgarajādiṃ evarūpo samaṇadhammo apanetuṃ na sakkoti, atha kho tassa upari aparampi rāgarajādiṃ ākiratīti attho. Bhikkhubhāvoti pārājikaṃ āpajjitvā “samaṇo aha”nti paṭijānanato vohāramattasiddho bhikkhubhāvo. Ajānamevāti pāṭhe evāti avadhāraṇatthe nipāto. Ajānamevanti pāṭhe pana evaṃ jānāmi evaṃ passāmīti avacanti yojetabbaṃ.

“The state of a recluse, if wrongly handled, drags one to hell”—just as a blade of kusa grass, when wrongly grasped, cuts and splits the hand. Even so, the state of a recluse, also called the practice of a recluse, if wrongly handled on account of broken morality and the like, drags one to hell; the meaning is, it causes one to be reborn in hell. “Lax” (sithilo) means done by slacking off, with a loose grasp. “The wandering life” (paribbājo) refers to the practice of a recluse that has reached a state of being broken and the like. “It scatters more dust” (bhiyyo ākirate rajaṃ) means that such a practice of a recluse is not able to remove the dust of lust and the like existing within; but rather, it scatters even more dust of lust and the like over him; this is the meaning. “The state of a monk” (bhikkhubhāvo) refers to the state of a monk established merely by designation, on account of one who, having committed a pārājika offense, still professes, “I am a recluse.” In the reading “ajānameva,” the particle “eva” is for emphasis. In the reading “ajānamevaṃ,” however, it should be construed as the statement, “I know thus, I see thus.”

Padabhājanīyavaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Analysis of Terms

199. Asubhajjhānādīnīti ādi-saddena kāyagatāsatijjhānañca kasiṇajjhānañca saṅgaṇhāti. Tena “kāyagatāsatijjhānaṃ pathavīkasiṇajjhānaṃ samāpajji”ntiādiṃ vadantopi pārājikova hotīti veditabbaṃ. Vimokkhoti ettha vi-saddo visesattho vividhattho vāti dassento āha “suṭṭhu mutto”tiādi. Vimokkhoti cattāro ariyamaggā. Tassa saguṇato suññatādināmalābhaṃ dassento āha “so panāya” [M 2.0287] ntiādi. Maggo hi nāma pañcahi kāraṇehi nāmaṃ labhati sarasena vā paccanīkena vā saguṇena vā ārammaṇena vā āgamanena vā. Sace hi saṅkhārupekkhā aniccato saṅkhāre sammasitvā vuṭṭhāti, animittavimokkhena vimuccati, sace dukkhato sammasitvā vuṭṭhāti, appaṇihitavimokkhena vimuccati, sace anattato sammasitvā vuṭṭhāti, suññatavimokkhena vimuccati, idaṃ sarasato nāmaṃ nāma. Yasmā panesa aniccānupassanāya saṅkhārānaṃ ghanavinibbhogaṃ katvā niccanimittadhuvanimittasassatanimittāni pajahanto āgato, tasmā animitto. Dukkhānupassanāya pana sukhasaññaṃ pahāya paṇidhiṃ patthanaṃ sukkhāpetvā āgatattā appaṇihito. Anattānupassanāya attasattapuggalasaññaṃ pahāya saṅkhārānaṃ suññato diṭṭhattā suññatoti idaṃ paccanīkato nāmaṃ nāma.

199. “Meditations on the foul, etc.” (asubhajjhānādīni): by the word “etc.” (ādi), it includes the jhāna of mindfulness directed to the body and kasiṇa jhāna. Therefore, it should be known that even while saying such things as, “I have attained the jhāna of mindfulness directed to the body or the earth-kasiṇa jhāna,” he is one who has committed a pārājika offense. “Liberation” (vimokkho): here, showing that the prefix “vi-” has the meaning of 'special' or the meaning of 'various', he said, “thoroughly freed,” etc. “Liberation” refers to the four noble paths. To show its acquisition of names such as 'emptiness' on account of its own quality, he said, “But this…” etc. The path, indeed, obtains a name for five reasons: by its own nature, or by its opposite, or by its own quality, or by its object, or by its approach. For if equanimity towards formations, having contemplated formations as impermanent, arises, one is liberated by the signless liberation; if, having contemplated them as suffering, it arises, one is liberated by the desireless liberation; if, having contemplated them as non-self, it arises, one is liberated by the emptiness liberation—this is called naming by its own nature. And since this path, by means of the contemplation of impermanence, has effected the breaking up of the compactness of formations and has come while abandoning the signs of permanence, stability, and eternity, it is therefore 'signless.' By means of the contemplation of suffering, having abandoned the perception of pleasure and having dried up longing and aspiration, because it has come thus, it is 'desireless.' By means of the contemplation of non-self, having abandoned the perceptions of self, a being, and a person, and because formations are seen as empty, it is 'emptiness'—this is called naming by its opposite.

Rāgādīhi [V 2.0255] panesa suññatattā suññato. Rūpanimittādīnaṃ rāganimittādīnaṃyeva vā abhāvena animitto. Rāgādipaṇidhiādīnaṃ abhāvato appaṇihitoti idamassa saguṇato nāmaṃ. Svāyaṃ suññataṃ animittaṃ appaṇihitañca nibbānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ karotīti suññato animitto appaṇihitoti vuccati, idamassa ārammaṇato nāmaṃ. Āgamanaṃ pana duvidhaṃ vipassanāgamanaṃ maggāgamanañca. Tattha magge vipassanāgamanaṃ labbhati, phale maggāgamanaṃ. Anattānupassanā hi suññatā nāma, suññatavipassanāya maggo suññato. Aniccānupassanā animittā nāma, animittavipassanāya maggo animitto. Idaṃ pana nāmaṃ na abhidhammapariyāyena labbhati. Tathā hi taṃ saṅkhāranimittassa avijahanato na nippariyāyena animittaṃ, suttantapariyāyena pana labbhati. Tatra hi gotrabhuñāṇaṃ animittaṃ nibbānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā animittanāmakaṃ hutvā sayaṃ āgamaniyaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā maggassa nāmaṃ detīti vadanti, tena maggo animittoti vutto. Maggāgamanena pana phalaṃ animittanti yujjatiyeva. Dukkhānupassanā saṅkhāresu paṇidhiṃ sukkhāpetvā āgatattā appaṇihitā nāma, appaṇihitavipassanāya maggo appaṇihito, appaṇihitamaggassa phalaṃ appaṇihitaṃ. Evaṃ vipassanā attano nāmaṃ maggassa deti, maggo phalassāti idaṃ āgamanato nāmaṃ. Suññattāti vivittattā. Na hi magge rāgādayo santi, uparūpari uppajjanakarāgādīnaṃ kāraṇattā rāgādayo nimittanti āha “rāgadosamohanimittehī”ti. Saviggahānaṃ viya upaṭṭhānampettha nimittanti vadanti. Rāgādayova [M 2.0288] pavattiṭṭhānaṭṭhena paṇidhīti āha “rāgadosamohapaṇidhīna”nti.

Moreover, because it is empty of lust and so on, it is called 'empty.' Because of the absence of the sign of form and so on, or indeed of the sign of lust and so on, it is 'signless.' Because of the absence of aspiration for lust and so on, it is 'desireless.' This is its name according to its own qualities. Because this takes as its object Nibbāna, which is empty, signless, and desireless, it is called 'empty,' 'signless,' and 'desireless.' This is its name according to its object. The approach, however, is twofold: the approach of insight and the approach of the path. Therein, in the path, the approach of insight is obtained; in the fruition, the approach of the path is obtained. Indeed, the contemplation of non-self is called 'emptiness'; by means of the insight of emptiness, the path is 'empty.' The contemplation of impermanence is called 'signless'; by means of the insight of the signless, the path is 'signless.' This name, however, is not obtained by way of the Abhidhamma method. For in that method, because it does not abandon the sign of formations, it is not unconditionally signless. But it is obtained by way of the Suttanta method. There, they say that the change-of-lineage knowledge, having taken signless Nibbāna as its object and having become named 'signless,' stands in the position of approach and gives its name to the path. Therefore, the path is called 'signless.' By the approach of the path, however, it is indeed fitting that the fruition is 'signless.' The contemplation of suffering, because it has come having dried up aspiration in formations, is called 'desireless'; by means of the desireless insight, the path is 'desireless'; the fruition of the desireless path is 'desireless.' Thus, insight gives its own name to the path, and the path gives its name to the fruition. This is the name from the approach. 'Emptiness' is because of being secluded. For lust and so on do not exist in the path. Because they are the cause for lust and so on that arise again and again, lust and so on are a 'sign'; thus he said, 'by the signs of lust, hatred, and delusion.' Herein, they say that the appearance, like that of those with conflict, is a 'sign.' Lust and so on, because they are a standing-place for occurrence, are an 'aspiration'; thus he said, 'of the aspirations of lust, hatred, and delusion.'

Vatthuvijjādiṃ sandhāya avacanato “vijjānaṃ lābhīmhī”ti vuttepi hoti. Ekekakoṭṭhāsavasenāti satipaṭṭhānacatukkādiekekakoṭṭhāsavasena. Kiñcāpi mahāaṭṭhakathāyampi ekekakoṭṭhāsavaseneva dassitaṃ, tattha pana “lokuttarānaṃ satipaṭṭhānāna”ntiādinā paccekaṃ lokuttara-saddaṃ yojetvā ekekakoṭṭhāsavaseneva vuttaṃ, idha lokuttara-saddena vināti ayamettha viseso. Tatthāti tesu koṭṭhāsesu.

With reference to geomancy and so on, due to not specifying, even when one says, 'I am an obtainer of knowledges,' it occurs. 'Individually by each section' means individually by each section of the tetrads of the foundations of mindfulness, and so on. Although it is shown individually by each section even in the Great Commentary, there, however, by connecting the word 'supramundane' individually, such as 'of the supramundane foundations of mindfulness,' it is stated individually by each section. Here, the difference is that it is without the word 'supramundane.' 'There' means in those sections.

Nanu ca “kilesappahānamevā”ti kasmā vuttaṃ. Na hi kilesānaṃ pahānamattaṃ uttarimanussadhammo hotīti yo vadeyya, taṃ sandhāya kilesappahānassa maggakiccattā kiccavasena maggo dīpitoti dassetuṃ “taṃ panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Kāmarāgaṃ sandhāya “tatiyamaggena hi rāgadosānaṃ pahāna”nti vuttaṃ, na pana rūparāgaarūparāge sandhāya. Na hi te tena pahīyanti catutthamaggena pahātabbattā.

But why was it said, 'Only the abandoning of defilements'? With reference to one who might say that the mere abandoning of defilements is not a supramundane state, to show that the path is revealed by way of its function—because the abandoning of defilements is the function of the path—the phrase 'but that...' and so on was said. Concerning sensual desire, it was said, 'By the third path, lust and hatred are abandoned,' but not concerning desire for form and desire for the formless. For those are not abandoned by that path, since they are to be abandoned by the fourth path.

Rāgā [V 2.0256] cittaṃ vinīvaraṇatāti rāgā cittassa vinīvaraṇatāti vuttaṃ hoti. Rāgā vimuttassa cittassa tasseva rāganīvaraṇassa abhāvena vigatanīvaraṇattā vinīvaraṇatāti attho veditabbo. Esa nayo sesesupi.

'The mind is unhindered by lust' means it is said to be 'the mind's state of being unhindered by lust.' The meaning should be understood thus: for a mind freed from lust, because of the absence of that very hindrance of lust, it is called 'unhindered' due to its hindrances having departed. This is the method in the remaining cases as well.

Yā ca pañca vijjāti yojetabbaṃ. Nibbaṭṭitalokuttarattāti visuṃyeva lokato apagatalokuttarattā. Yathā vinā lokuttara-saddena “satipaṭṭhānādīnaṃ lābhīmhī”ti vuttepi pārājikaṃ hoti, evamidhāpi “atthapaṭisambhidāya lābhīmhīti vuttepi hotiyevā”ti vattuṃ yujjati. Kiñcāpi yujjati, atha kho mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vibhāgena vuttattā na sakkā evamidaṃ vattunti dassetuṃ “mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana…pe… na sakkā aññaṃ pamāṇaṃ kātu”nti vuttaṃ. Tampi tattheva paṭikkhittanti sambandho.

'And the five knowledges' should be connected. 'Because of its accomplished supramundane nature' means because its supramundane nature is distinctly departed from the world. Just as, without the word 'supramundane,' even when one says, 'I am an obtainer of the foundations of mindfulness, and so on,' a pārājika offense occurs, so too here it is fitting to say that 'even when one says, “I am an obtainer of the discrimination of meanings,” it still occurs.' Although it is fitting, because the Great Commentary explains it with distinctions, it is not possible to say it in this way. To show this, it was said, 'But in the Great Commentary…it is not possible to make another standard.' That too is rejected right there—this is the connection.

Suddhikavārakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discourse of the Purity Chapter

200. Ullapanākāranti [M 2.0289] samāpajjintiādiullapanākāraṃ. Āpattibhedanti “na paṭivijānantassa āpatti thullaccayassā”tiādiāpattibhedaṃ. Puna ānetvā paṭhamajjhānādīhi na yojitanti ettha “paṭhamajjhānenā”ti pāṭhoti gaṇṭhipade vuttaṃ, tadeva yuttaṃ.

200. 'The manner of proclamation' means the manner of proclaiming, such as 'I enter.' 'The distinction of offenses' means the distinction of offenses, such as, 'For one who does not recognize it, there is a grave offense.' Regarding the phrase 'Having brought it back, it is not connected with the first jhāna and so on,' herein, it is stated in the Gaṇṭhipada that the reading is 'by the first jhāna,' and that itself is correct.

Kattusādhanopi bhaṇita-saddo hotīti āha “atha vā”tiādi. Yena cittena musā bhaṇati, teneva cittena na sakkā “musā bhaṇāmī”ti jānituṃ, antarantarā pana aññena cittena “musā bhaṇāmī”ti jānātīti vuttaṃ “bhaṇantassa hoti musā bhaṇāmī”ti. Ayamettha attho dassitoti tīhi aṅgehi samannāgato musāvādoti ayamettha attho dassito. Na sakkā na bhavitunti pubbabhāgato paṭṭhāya ābhogaṃ katvā bhaṇitattā na sakkā na bhavituṃ. Āpattiyā na kāretabboti pubbabhāgakkhaṇe “musā bhaṇissāmī”ti ābhogaṃ vinā sahasā bhaṇantassa vacanakkhaṇe “musā eta”nti upaṭṭhitepi nivattetumasakkuṇeyyatāya avisayabhāvato āpattiyā na kāretabbo. Davāti sahasā. Ravāti aññaṃ vattukāmassa khalitvā aññabhaṇanaṃ.

The word 'bhaṇita' can also be an agent-noun; therefore, the text states, 'Or else...' and so on. With the same mind that one speaks falsely, it is not possible to know 'I am speaking falsely'; but intermittently, with another mind, one knows 'I am speaking falsely.' This is what is meant by the statement, 'While speaking, it occurs to him, "I am speaking falsely."' The meaning shown here is this: that false speech is endowed with three factors. 'It is not possible for it not to be': because it was spoken after making a preparation from the preliminary stage, it is not possible for it not to be. 'He should not be made to incur an offense': For one who speaks hastily without the prior intention 'I will speak falsely,' even if it occurs to him 'this is false' at the moment of speaking, he should not be made to incur an offense, due to his inability to retract it and because it is outside the scope of his intention. 'Davā' means hastily. 'Ravā' means slipping and saying something different when wishing to say something else.

Taṃ jānātīti taṃñāṇaṃ, tassa bhāvo taṃñāṇatā, ñāṇassa atthasaṃvedananti attho. Ñāṇasamodhānanti ñāṇassa bahubhāvo, ekacittuppāde anekañāṇatāti attho. Na hi sakkā…pe… jānitunti ārammaṇakaraṇassa abhāvato vuttaṃ. Asammohāvabodho ca īdisassa [V 2.0257] ñāṇassa natthi, “bhaṇissāmī”ti pavattacittaṃ “bhaṇāmī”ti pavattacittassa paccayo hutvā nirujjhati, tañca “bhaṇita”nti pavattacittassa paccayo hutvāti āha – “purimaṃ purimaṃ pana…pe… nirujjhatī”ti. Tasmiṃ pubbabhāge sati “sesadvayaṃ na hessatī”ti etaṃ natthi, avassaṃ hotiyevāti vuttaṃ hoti, bhaṇissāmīti pubbabhāge sati “bhaṇāmi bhaṇita”nti etaṃ dvayaṃ na na hoti, hotiyevāti adhippāyo. Ekaṃ viya pakāsatīti anekakkhaṇe uppannampi cittaṃ ekakkhaṇe uppannasadisaṃ hutvā pakāsati. Samāpajjintiādīnīti ādi-saddena samāpajjāmi, samāpannoti [M 2.0290] imāni dve saṅgaṇhāti. Tattha samāpajjiṃ, samāpannoti imesaṃ asatipi kālanānatte vacanavisesaṃ sandhāya visuṃ gahaṇaṃ.

'He knows that,' thus it is 'knowledge of that'; its state is 'the quality of that knowledge'; the meaning is the comprehension of the object by knowledge. 'Concurrence of knowledge' means the abundance of knowledge, that is, the multiplicity of knowledges in a single thought-moment. 'For it is not possible... to know' is said due to the absence of taking it as an object. And for such knowledge, there is no delusion-free understanding. The thought occurring as 'I will speak' ceases after serving as a condition for the thought occurring as 'I am speaking,' and that, in turn, serves as a condition for the thought occurring as 'it has been spoken.' Thus it is said: 'The former... ceases.' When that preliminary stage, 'I will speak,' is present, the thought 'the latter two will not be' does not exist; it is simply inevitable. The meaning is that when the preliminary stage 'I will speak' is present, the pair 'I am speaking' and 'it has been spoken' is not absent—it certainly arises. 'It appears as one' means that even though the mind arises over multiple moments, it appears as if arising in a single moment. Regarding 'I attained,' etc., by the word 'etc.,' it includes these two: 'I attain' and 'I have attained.' Therein, regarding 'I attained' and 'I have attained,' although there is no difference in time, they are taken separately with reference to the difference in expression.

207. Sakabhāvapariccajanavasenāti attano santakabhāvassa pariccajanavasena. Magguppattito pubbe viya “sarāgo sadoso”ti vattabbatābhāvato cattampi keci gaṇhanti, nayidamevanti dassanatthaṃ “vanto”ti vuttaṃ. Na hi yaṃ yena vantaṃ, so puna taṃ ādiyati. Tenāha “anādiyanabhāvadassanavasenā”ti. Vantampi kiñci santatilaggaṃ siyā, nayidamevanti dassanatthaṃ “mutto”ti vuttaṃ. Tenāha “santatito vimocanavasenā”ti. Muttampi kiñci muttabandhanaṃ viya phalaṃ kuhiñci tiṭṭhati, na evamidanti dassanatthaṃ “pahīno”ti vuttaṃ. Tenāha “kvaci anavaṭṭhānadassanavasenā”ti. Yathā kiñci dunnissaṭṭhaṃ puna ādāya sammadeva nissaṭṭhaṃ paṭinissaṭṭhanti vuccati, evaṃ vipassanāya nissaṭṭhaṃ ādinnasadisaṃ maggena pahīnaṃ paṭinissaṭṭhaṃ nāma hotīti dassanatthaṃ “paṭinissaṭṭho”ti vuttaṃ. Tenāha “ādinnapubbassa paṭinissaggadassanavasenā”ti. Ukkheṭitoti uttāsito, uttāsetvā palāpitoti vuttaṃ hoti. Yo ca uttāsetvā palāpito, na puna so taṃ ṭhānaṃ āgacchatīti āha “puna anallīyanabhāvadassanavasenā”ti, puna āgantvā santāne anuppattibhāvadassanavasenāti attho. Khiṭa-saddaṃ saddasatthavidū uttāsatthe paṭhantīti āha – “svāyamattho saddasatthato pariyesitabbo”ti. Aṇuyeva aṇusahagataṃ, atikhuddakanti vuttaṃ hoti.

207. 'By way of abandoning one's own state' means by way of relinquishing one's own property. Some hold that the defilements are abandoned because, as is the case before the arising of the path, one cannot be described as being 'with lust, with hatred'. To show that this is not so, 'vomited' is said. For what is vomited by someone is not taken up again by them. Therefore, it is said, 'by way of showing the state of non-appropriation.' Even something vomited might have a trace remaining. To show this is not so, 'freed' is said. Therefore, it is said, 'by way of showing release from the continuity.' Even something freed might remain somewhere, like a fruit freed from its bond. To show this is not so, 'abandoned' is said. Therefore, it is said, 'by way of showing non-establishment anywhere.' Just as something poorly discarded might be taken up again, but when properly discarded is called 'thoroughly discarded,' so too, what was discarded by insight but was like something still appropriated, when abandoned by the path, is called 'thoroughly abandoned.' To show this, 'thoroughly abandoned' is said. Therefore, it is said, 'by way of showing the thorough relinquishment of what was previously appropriated.' 'Frightened away' means terrified; it means driven off by terrifying. And what is driven off by terror does not return to that place. Thus it is said, 'by way of showing the state of not clinging again,' the meaning of which is 'by way of showing the state of not arising again in the mental continuum.' Experts in the science of sounds read the word 'khiṭa' in the sense of terror. Thus it is said, 'this meaning should be sought from the science of sounds.' 'Accompanied by the minute' means just minute; that is to say, exceedingly small.

Suddhikavārakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Chapter on Purity is concluded.

Vattukāmavārakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Section on the Desire to Speak

215. Kevalañhiyanti kevalañhi ayaṃ. “Vāro”ti ajjhāharitabbaṃ. Taṅkhaṇaññeva jānātīti “paṭhamajjhānaṃ samāpajji”ntiādimhi vutte tadatthassa pakatiyā vijānanalakkhaṇaṃ sandhāya [V 2.0258] vuttaṃ. Evaṃ pana vacībhedaṃ akatvā pakkamanādīsu aññataro bhikkhu “maṃ arahāti jānātū”ti tamhā āvāsā paṭhamaṃ pakkamatīti āgatavatthumhi viya tasmiṃ khaṇe aviditepi nikkhantamatte pārājikaṃ. Jānanalakkhaṇanti “taṅkhaṇe jānanaṃ nāma īdisa”nti vuttalakkhaṇaṃ[M 2.0291]. Viññattipatheti kāyavacīviññattīnaṃ gahaṇayogge padese, pakaticakkhunā pakatisotena ca daṭṭhuṃ sotuñca arahaṭṭhāneti vuttaṃ hoti. Tena viññattipathaṃ atikkamitvā ṭhito ce koci dibbena cakkhunā dibbāya ca sotadhātuyā disvā sutvā ca jānāti, na pārājikanti dīpeti. Assutapubbassa “kimidaṃ vutta”nti saṃsayuppattisabbhāvato “sutaṃ hotī”ti vuttaṃ. Paṭhamaṃ vacanamattaṃ assutapubbenapi “paṭhamajjhānaṃ samāpajji”nti vutte “kimida”nti sandehaṃ anuppādetvā “jhānaṃ nāma kiresa samāpajjī”ti ettakamattepi ñāte pārājikaṃ hotiyeva.

215. “Kevalañhi” means this “kevalañhi.” The word “vāro” (section) should be supplied. “He knows at that very moment”—thus, when it is said, “He attained the first jhāna,” etc., it is stated with reference to the characteristic of naturally knowing that meaning. However, without making any verbal distinction, in cases of departure and so on, if a certain bhikkhu, thinking, “Let him know me as an arahant,” is the first to leave that dwelling—just as in the case that has come down—even if it is not known at that moment, as soon as he has departed, it becomes a pārājika offense. The characteristic of knowing is the characteristic described as “knowing at that moment is of such a nature.” In the range of communication (viññattipathe): in a place suitable for grasping bodily and verbal communication; it is said to be a place suitable for seeing with the natural eye and hearing with the natural ear. By this, it is shown that if someone, having gone beyond the range of communication, stands and knows by means of the divine eye and the divine ear-element after seeing and hearing, it is not a pārājika offense.
