For one who has not heard it before, because of the possibility of the arising of doubt, “What is this that has been said?,” it is said, “It has been heard.” Even for one who has not previously heard just the first utterance, when it is said, “He attained the first jhāna,” if, without giving rise to the doubt, “What is this?,” it is known even to the extent, “He has, it seems, attained what is called jhāna,” it becomes a pārājika offense indeed.

Anāpattibhedakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Kinds of Non-Offenses

222. Anullapanādhippāyassāti atikkamitvā avattukāmassa, “uttarimanussadhammo aya”nti asallakkhentassāti adhippāyo. Sarūpato pana “anāpatti bhikkhu anullapanādhippāyassā”ti vinītavatthūsu tattha tattha āgatavatthuvasena veditabbo. “Uttarimanussadhammo aya”nti asallakkhetvā vadantopi vohārato aññaṃ byākaronto nāma hotīti vuttaṃ “aññaṃ byākarontassā”ti.

222. “For one not intending to boast” (anullapanādhippāyassa) means: for one who, having transgressed, does not wish to speak; for one not considering, “This is a superior human state”—this is the intention. In essence, however, “There is no offense for a bhikkhu not intending to boast” should be understood according to the cases that have come down here and there in the decided cases (vinītavatthūsu). Even while speaking without considering, “This is a superior human state,” one is, by convention, said to be declaring something else; thus it is said, “for one declaring something else.”

Padabhājanīyavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Padabhājanīya is concluded.

Bhāyantopīti “imassa mayi natthibhāvaṃ aññepi jānantā atthi nu kho”ti bhāyantopi.

“Even while fearing” (bhāyantopi) means: even while fearing, “Are there others who also know of the absence of this in me?”

Vinītavatthuvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Decided Cases

223. Sekkhabhūmiyanti iminā jhānabhūmimpi saṅgaṇhāti. Tiṇṇaṃ vivekānanti kāyacittaupadhivivekānaṃ.

223. By 'the stage of a learner,' this also includes the jhāna stage. By 'of the three seclusions,' it means of the seclusion of body, mind, and the substrates of existence.

Piṇḍāya caraṇassa bhojanapariyosānattā vuttaṃ “yāva bhojanapariyosāna”nti. Bhutvā āgacchantassapi [V 2.0259] puna vuttanayeneva sambhāvanicchāya cīvarasaṇṭhapanādīni karontassa dukkaṭameva.

Because the alms-round has the meal as its conclusion, it is said, 'until the end of the meal.' For one who returns after eating, if they again, in the manner already stated, perform actions such as arranging the robe, etc., with the desire for esteem, it is indeed a dukkaṭa offense.

225. Ārādhanīyo, āvuso, dhammo āraddhavīriyenāti vatthudvayaṃ ekasadisampi dvīhi bhikkhūhi visuṃ visuṃ ārocitattā bhagavatā vinicchinitaṃ sabbampi vinītavatthūsu āropetabbanti pāḷiyaṃ āropitaṃ.

225. “Friend, the Dhamma is to be accomplished by one with aroused energy.” Although the two cases are similar, because they were reported separately by two bhikkhus, they were decided by the Blessed One; and all of it is to be included among the decided cases. Thus, it is included in the Pāḷi.

226. Pasādabhaññanti [M 2.0292] kevalaṃ pasādamattena bhaṇanaṃ, na pana “sabhāvato ete arahantoyevā”ti cintetvā. Tenevettha anāpatti vuttā. Yadi pana “ete sabhāvato arahantoyevā”ti maññamāno “āyantu bhonto arahanto”tiādīni vadati, na sampaṭicchitabbaṃ.

226. “Speaking from confidence” means speaking merely out of confidence, and not from having thought, “These are arahants by nature.” For that reason, a non-offense is stated here. If, however, believing “These are arahants by nature,” one says, “Come, venerable arahants,” and so on, it should not be accepted.

227. Padasā gamanaṃ sandhāya katikāya katattā “yānena vā”tiādimāha. Tattha vijjāmayiddhiṃ sandhāya “iddhiyā”ti vuttaṃ. Aññamaññaṃ rakkhantīti “yo imamhā āvāsā paṭhamaṃ pakkamissati, taṃ mayaṃ ‘arahā’ti jānissāmā”ti evaṃ katikāya katattā apubbācarimaṃ asuddhacittena gacchantāpi saha nikkhantabhāvato aññamaññaṃ rakkhanti. Keci pana “hatthapāsaṃ avijahitvā aññamaññassa hatthaṃ gaṇhanto viya gacchantopi ‘uṭṭhetha gacchāma, etha gacchāmā’ti evaṃ saṃvidahitvā gamane pubbāparaṃ gacchantopi nāpajjatī”ti vadanti. Etaṃ pana adhammikaṃ katikavattanti “idha arahantoyeva vasantūti yadi bhikkhū katikaṃ karonti, etaṃ adhammikaṃ katikavatta”nti cūḷagaṇṭhipade vuttaṃ. Heṭṭhā vuttaṃ pana sabbampi katikavattaṃ sandhāya etaṃ vuttanti amhākaṃ khanti, vīmaṃsitvā gahetabbaṃ. Nānāverajjakāti nānājanapadavāsino. Saṅghalābhoti yathāvuḍḍhaṃ attano pāpuṇanakoṭṭhāso. Ayañca paṭikkhepo imināva nīhārena bahisīmaṭṭhānaṃ avisesena saṅghalābhassa sāmibhāvāpādanaṃ sandhāya kato. Visesato pana bahisīmaṭṭhānampi paricchinditvā ekekakoṭṭhāsato “ettakaṃ dātuṃ, īdisaṃ vā dātuṃ, ettakānaṃ vā dātuṃ, īdisassa vā dātuṃ ruccati saṅghassā”ti apalokanakammaṃ katvā dātuṃ vaṭṭati.

227. With reference to going on foot, because an agreement was made, it is said, “by vehicle or…” and so on. Therein, with reference to knowledge-based psychic power, it is said, “by psychic power.” “They protect one another” means that because the agreement was made thus: “Whoever departs from this residence first, we will know them as an arahant,” they protect one another due to having departed together, even while going with an impure mind and not one before the other. Some, however, say: “Even those who go without leaving arm’s reach, as if taking one another’s hand, and having arranged thus, ‘Arise, let us go; come, let us go,’ go one after the other in their departure, do not commit an offense.” But this is an unrighteous practice regarding an agreement, as it is said in the Cūḷagaṇṭhipada: “If bhikkhus make an agreement here, that ‘Only arahants should dwell here,’ this is an unrighteous practice regarding an agreement.” However, what was stated below was said with reference to all practices regarding agreements—this is our acceptance; it should be investigated and accepted. “Of various districts” means residents of various regions. “A gain for the Sangha” means one’s own portion to be received according to seniority. And this refusal is made, by this very method, with reference to causing the Sangha’s gains to become the property of those in a place outside the boundary without distinction. Specifically, however, having demarcated even a place outside the boundary, it is permissible to give after performing an act of announcement from each portion, saying: “It is approved by the Sangha to give this much, or to give such a thing, or to give to this many, or to give to such a one.”

228. Āyasmā ca lakkhaṇotiādīsu ko panāyasmā lakkhaṇo, kasmā cassa lakkhaṇoti nāmaṃ ahosi, ko cāyasmā mahāmoggallāno, kasmā ca sitaṃ pātvākāsīti taṃ sabbaṃ pakāsetuṃ “yvāya”ntiādi āraddhaṃ. Lakkhaṇasampannenāti purisalakkhaṇasampannena. Brahmasamenāti [V 2.0260] brahmattabhāvasamena. Īsakaṃ hasitaṃ sitanti vuccatīti āha “mandahasita”nti. Aṭṭhikasaṅkhalikanti nayidaṃ aviññāṇakaṃ aṭṭhisaṅkhalikamattaṃ, atha kho eko petoti āha “petaloke nibbattaṃ satta”nti. Ete attabhāvāti petattabhāvā. Na āpāthaṃ āgacchantīti devattabhāvā viya pakatiyā āpāthaṃ na āgacchanti. Tesaṃ pana [M 2.0293] ruciyā āpāthaṃ āgaccheyyuṃ. Manussānaṃ dukkhābhibhūtānaṃ anāthabhāvadassanapadaṭṭhānā karuṇāti āha “kāruññe kattabbe”ti. Attano ca sampattiṃ buddhañāṇassa ca sampattinti paccekaṃ sampatti-saddo yojetabbo. Tadubhayaṃ vibhāvetuṃ “tañhī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha “attano ca sampattiṃ anussaritvā sitaṃ pātvākāsī”ti padaṃ ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ. Dhammadhātūti sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ sandhāya vadati, dhammadhātūti vā dhammānaṃ sabhāvo. Upapattīti jāti. Upapattisīsena hi tathārūpaṃ attabhāvaṃ vadati. Dussaddhāpayā honti, tadassa tesaṃ dīgharattaṃ ahitāya dukkhāya. Dussaddhāpayāti idañca na lakkhaṇattheraṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, ye pana suṇanti “evaṃ kira vutta”nti, te sandhāya. Atha lakkhaṇatthero kasmā na addasa, kimassa dibbacakkhu natthīti? No natthi, mahāmoggallāno pana āvajjento addasa, itaro anāvajjanena na addasa.

228. In the passage beginning “And the Venerable Lakkhaṇa,” to explain all this—who the Venerable Lakkhaṇa was, why his name was Lakkhaṇa, who the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was, and why he manifested a smile—the passage beginning “yvāyaṃ” is introduced. By “endowed with marks” is meant endowed with the marks of a great man. By “equal to Brahmā” is meant equal to the state of being of Brahmā. A slight laugh is called a “sita,” thus it is said “a gentle smile.” By “a chain of bones” is meant not merely an inanimate chain of bones, but rather a peta; thus it is said “a being reborn in the peta-world.” By “these states of existence” is meant peta-states of existence. “They do not come into range” means that, like the states of existence of devas, they do not naturally come into range. They might, however, come into range by their own wish. For humans overwhelmed by suffering, compassion has as its proximate cause the seeing of their helplessness; thus it is said “when compassion is to be shown.” “His own attainment and the attainment of the Buddha’s knowledge”—the word “attainment” should be applied separately to each. To clarify both, the passage beginning “tañhi” is stated. There, the phrase “having recollected his own attainment, he manifested a smile” should be brought in and connected. By “the Dhamma-element,” he speaks with reference to omniscient knowledge; or, “the Dhamma-element” is the intrinsic nature of phenomena. By “rebirth” is meant birth. For by the heading of rebirth, he speaks of such a state of existence. They are difficult to inspire with faith, and that is for their long-term harm and suffering. And this “difficult to inspire with faith” is not said with reference to the Elder Lakkhaṇa, but with reference to those who hear, “So, it seems, it was said.” Then why did the Elder Lakkhaṇa not see? Does he not have the divine eye? It is not that he does not have it. But Mahāmoggallāna saw by directing his mind, while the other did not see through not directing his mind.

Vituḍentīti vinivijjhitvā ḍenti, asidhārūpamehi tikhiṇehi lohatuṇḍakehi vijjhitvā vijjhitvā ito cito ca gacchantīti attho. Tenāha “vinivijjhitvā gacchantī”ti. “Vitudantī”ti vā pāṭho. Phāsuḷantarikāhīti bhummatthe nissakkavacanaṃ. Lohatuṇḍakehīti lohasalākāsadisehi, kāḷalohamayeheva vā tuṇḍakehi. Pasādussadāti iminā aṭṭhisaṅghātamattaṃ hutvā paññāyamānānampi kāyappasādassa balavabhāvaṃ dasseti. Pakkagaṇḍasadisāti iminā pana ativiya mudusabhāvataṃ dasseti. Acchariyaṃ vatāti garahanacchariyaṃ nāmetaṃ.

“They peck” means they pierce through and fly; the meaning is that they go here and there, piercing again and again with sharp iron beaks like sword-blades. Therefore, he says, “having pierced through, they go.” Or the reading is “they torment.” “Between the ribs” is an ablative expression in the sense of the locative. “With iron beaks” means with things like iron rods, or with beaks made of black iron. By “abundant in clarity,” it shows the strength of the body’s clarity, even for those who appear as a mere collection of bones. By “like a ripe boil,” it shows an extremely soft nature. “Oh, how astonishing!”—this is what is called an astonishment of reproach.

Cakkhubhūtāti sampattadibbacakkhukā, lokassa cakkhubhūtāti evaṃ vā ettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Yatrāti hetuatthe nipātoti āha “yatrāti kāraṇavacana”nti. Appamāṇe sattanikāye, te ca kho vibhāgena kāmabhavādibhede bhave, nirayādibhedā gatiyo, nānattakāyanānattasaññīādiviññāṇaṭṭhitiyo, tathārūpe sattāvāse ca sabbaññutaññāṇañca me upanetuṃ paccakkhaṃ karontena.

“One who has become the eye” means one who possesses the perfected divine eye, or, “one who has become the eye of the world”—this is how the meaning should be understood here. “Yatra” is a particle in the sense of cause; thus he said, “‘yatra’ is a word expressing cause.” In the immeasurable multitude of beings, and indeed, by division, in those states of existence with distinctions such as the sensual realm, in destinations with distinctions such as hell, in the stations of consciousness such as those with diverse bodies and diverse perceptions, and in such abodes of beings—by making directly perceptible the truth in order to bring forth omniscience for me.

Goghātakoti gunnaṃ abhiṇhaṃ hananako. Tenāha “vadhitvā vadhitvā”ti. Tassāti gunnaṃ hananakammassa. Aparāpariyakammassāti aparāpariyavedanīyakammassa. Balavatā goghātakakammena vipāke [V 2.0261] dīyamāne [M 2.0294] aladdhokāsaṃ aparāpariyavedanīyaṃ, tasmiṃ vipakkavipāke idāni laddhokāsaṃ “avasesakamma”nti vuttaṃ. Kammasabhāgatāyāti kammassa sabhāgabhāvena sadisabhāvena. Ārammaṇasabhāgatāyāti ārammaṇassa sabhāgabhāvena sadisabhāvena. Yādise hi ārammaṇe pubbe taṃ kammaṃ tassa ca vipāko pavatto, tādiseyeva ārammaṇe idaṃ kammaṃ imassa vipāko ca pavattoti katvā vuttaṃ “tasseva kammassa vipākāvasesenā”ti. Bhavati hi taṃsadisepi tabbohāro yathā so eva tittiro, tāniyeva osadhānīti. Yasmā kammasarikkhakavisaye “kammaṃ vā kammanimittaṃ vā”ti dvayameva vuttaṃ, yasmā ca gatinimittaṃ viya kammaṃ kammanimittañca kammato bhinnaṃ visuṃ hutvā na tiṭṭhati, tasmā sarikkhakavipākadānassa kāraṇabhāvato yattha kammasarikkhakena vipākena bhavitabbaṃ, tattha kammaṃ vā kammanimittaṃ vā gahetvā paṭisandhi hotīti vadanti. Tenevāha – “tassa kira…pe… nimittaṃ ahosī”ti. Tattha nimittaṃ ahosīti pubbe katūpacitassa petūpapattinibbattanavasena katokāsassa tassa kammassa nimittabhūtaṃ idāni tathā upaṭṭhahantaṃ tassa vipākassa nimittaṃ ārammaṇaṃ ahosi. Soti goghātako. Aṭṭhikasaṅkhalikapeto jāto kammasarikkhakavipākavasena.

“Cattle-slaughterer” means one who frequently kills cattle. Hence it is said, “having killed and killed.” “Of his” refers to the kamma of killing cattle. “Of the kamma to be experienced in a subsequent existence” refers to the kamma whose result is to be experienced in a subsequent existence. When the result was being given by the powerful kamma of cattle-slaughter, the kamma to be experienced in a subsequent existence did not get an opportunity. Now, in that ripened result, the kamma which has obtained an opportunity is called “the remaining kamma.” “By the similarity of kamma” means by the similar nature of the kamma. “By the similarity of the object” means by the similar nature of the object. For just as in the past that kamma and its result occurred in relation to such an object, so too now this kamma and its result occur in relation to a similar object; therefore, it is said, “by the remainder of the result of that very kamma.” For indeed, such usage occurs even in similar cases, as when one says “that is the very partridge” or “those are the very medicinal herbs.” Since in the sphere of a result similar to the kamma only two things are mentioned—“the kamma or the sign of the kamma”—and since, like a sign of destiny, the kamma and the sign of the kamma do not stand separate and distinct from the kamma, therefore, because it is the cause for giving a result similar to the kamma, they say that wherever rebirth-linking is to occur with a result similar to the kamma, it takes either the kamma or the sign of the kamma as its object. Thus he said: “For him, indeed... the sign arose.” There, “the sign arose” means: the sign of that kamma—which had previously been accumulated and had created the opportunity by way of causing rebirth as a peta—now appeared in such a way, becoming the object, the sign, for that result. “He” was the cattle-slaughterer. He was born as a skeleton-peta by way of a result similar to the kamma.

229. Pesiyo katvāti gāviṃ vadhitvā vadhitvā gomaṃsaṃ phāletvā pesiyo katvā. Sukkhāpetvāti kālantaraṃ ṭhapanatthaṃ sukkhāpetvā. Sukkhāpitamaṃsapesīnañhi vallūrasamaññāti. Nippakkhacammeti vigatapakkhacamme. Urabbhe hantīti orabbhiko. Eḷaketi aje. Nivāpapuṭṭheti attanā dinnanivāpena posite asinā vadhitvā vadhitvā vikkiṇanto. Ekaṃ miganti dīpakamigaṃ. Kāraṇāhīti yātanāhi. Ñatvāti kammaṭṭhānaṃ ñatvā. Pesuññupasaṃhāravasena ito sutaṃ amutra, amutra vā sutaṃ idha sūcetīti sūcako. Anayabyasanaṃ pāpesi manusseti sambandho.

229. “Having made into strips” means having killed cows again and again, having cut up the beef, and having made it into strips. “Having dried” means having caused them to dry in order to keep them for a long time. For dried meat strips are indeed designated as ‘vallūra’. “On the hide without fur.” “One who kills sheep” is a sheep-slaughterer. “Eḷake” means goats. “Nourished by fodder” means: having nourished them with fodder given by himself, he kills them again and again with a sword and sells them. “One beast” means a leopard. “By means” means by torments. “Having known” means having known the meditation subject. “A slanderer” is one who, by way of slander, reports what was heard here to there, or what was heard there to here. The connection is: “He caused people to arrive at misfortune and disaster.”

Vinicchayāmaccoti raññā aḍḍakaraṇe ṭhapito vinicchayamahāmatto. So hi gāmajanakāyaṃ kūṭaṭṭhena vañcetīti “gāmakūṭo”ti vuccati. Keci “tādisoyeva gāmajeṭṭhako gāmakūṭo”ti vadanti. Samena bhavitabbaṃ [M 2.0295] dhammaṭṭhoti vattabbato. Rahassaṅge nisīdanavasena visamā nisajjā ahosi. Phusantoti theyyāya phusanto.

“Minister of justice” means a great minister of justice appointed by the king in the adjudication of cases. Indeed, he deceives the village folk with fraud, therefore he is called a “gāmakūṭa” (village-fraud). Some say that a village headman of such a nature is a “gāmakūṭa”. Because it should be said, “One must be impartial, standing in the Dhamma.” By way of sitting in a secluded place, the sitting was improper. “Touching” means touching with the intention to steal.

230. Anissaroti mātugāmo sasāmiko attano phasse anissaro. Dhaṃsitvāti bhassitvā [V 2.0262] apagantvā. Maṅganavasena ulatīti maṅguli, virūpabībhacchabhāvena pavattatīti attho. Tenāha “virūpaṃ duddasikaṃ bībhaccha”nti.

230. “Not her own master” means a woman who has a husband is not the master of her own physical contact. “Having destroyed” means having ruined and gone away. “Maṅguli” is so called because it is agitated by way of depravity; the meaning is that it proceeds with an ugly and repulsive nature. Therefore he said, “ugly, difficult to look at, and repulsive.”

Uddhaṃ uddhaṃ agginā pakkasarīratāya uppakkaṃ, heṭṭhato paggharaṇavasena kilinnasarīratāya okilinī, ito cito ca aṅgārasamparikiṇṇatāya okirinī. Tenāha “sā kirā”tiādi. Aṅgāracitaketi aṅgārasañcaye. Sarīrato paggharanti asuciduggandhajegucchāni sedagatāni. Tassa kira raññoti kāliṅgassa rañño. Nāṭakinīti naccanakicce adhigatā itthī. Sedanti sedanaṃ, tāpananti attho.

“Uppakkaṃ” means roasted, because the body is cooked by fire from above; “okilinī” means soiled, because the body is wet by way of oozing from below; “okirinī” means scattered, because it is strewn with embers from here and there. Therefore he said, “sā kirā,” and so on. “In a pyre of embers” means in a heap of embers. From the body ooze impure, foul-smelling, and disgusting sweats. “Of that king, indeed” refers to the king of Kāliṅga. “A female dancer” means a woman skilled in the art of dancing. “They sweat” means sweating, heating; this is the meaning.

Asīsakaṃ kabandhaṃ hutvā nibbatti kammāyūhanakāle tathā nimittaggahaṇaparicayato. Lāmakabhikkhūti hīnācāratāya lāmako, bhikkhuvesatāya bhikkhāhārena jīvanato ca bhikkhu. Cittakeḷinti cittaruciyaṃ taṃ taṃ kīḷanto. Ayamevāti bhikkhuvatthusmiṃ vuttanayo eva.

It was reborn as a headless trunk because of the familiarity with grasping such a sign at the time of the kamma's exertion. “A base monk” means: he is “lāmaka” (base) because of his low conduct, and he is a “bhikkhu” because he lives on alms-food in the guise of a monk. “Sporting according to the mind's pleasure” means sporting in this and that which is pleasing to the mind. “This very method” means just the method spoken of in the story of the monk.

231. Nissevālapaṇakakaddamoti tilabījakādibhedena sevālena nīlamaṇḍūkapiṭṭhivaṇṇena udakapiṭṭhaṃ chādetvā nibbattapaṇakena kaddamena ca virahito. Sundarehi titthehīti sukhāvagāhaṇaṭṭhānatāya kaddamādidosavirahato ca sundarehi titthehi. Tato udakadahato taṃhetu, taṃ upanissāyāti attho. Nāgabhavanagatopi hi so rahado tato uparimanussaloke jalāsayena sambandho hoti. Tena vuttaṃ “tato ayaṃ tapodā sandatī”ti. Atha vā tatoti nāgabhavane udakadahato ayaṃ tapodā sandati. Tañhi uparibhūmitalaṃ ārohati, uṇhabhāvena tapanato tapaṃ udakaṃ etissāti anvatthanāmavasena tapodāti vuccati. Petalokoti petānaṃ āvāsaṭṭhānaṃ. Keci pana “petalokoti lohakumbhīnirayā idhādhippetā”ti vadanti, nagarassa pana [M 2.0296] parito pabbatapādavanantaresu bahū petāvāsāpi santeva. Svāyamattho petavatthupāḷiyā lakkhaṇasaṃyuttena imāya ca vinītavatthupāḷiyā dīpetabbo.

231. “Free from algae, duckweed, and mud” means devoid of algae of various kinds like sesame seeds, which has the color of a blue frog's back, and of duckweed produced by covering the water's surface, and of mud. “With delightful fords” means with delightful fords because they are easy to enter and free from faults such as mud. “From that water-body” means because of that, or dependent on it. For that lake, even though in the Nāga realm, is connected to a water reservoir in the human world above. Hence it is said, “From there, this Tapodā flows.” Alternatively, “from that” means from the water-body in the Nāga realm, this Tapodā flows. For it rises to the upper ground level, and it is called Tapodā by way of its etymological meaning, because it has hot water (tapaṃ udakaṃ), being hot due to its heat. “The realm of Petas” means the dwelling place of the petas. Some, however, say, “‘The realm of Petas’ here refers to the Lohakumbhī hell,” but there are also many abodes of petas in the mountain foothills and forests surrounding the city. This meaning should be explained by the Petavatthu Pāḷi, the Lakkhaṇa Saṃyutta, and this Vinītavatthu Pāḷi.

Katahatthāti thirataraṃ lakkhesu avirajjhanasarakkhepā. Īdisā pana tattha vasībhūtā katahatthā nāma honti, tasmā yo sippameva uggaṇhāti, so katahattho nāma na hoti, ime pana katahatthā, ciṇṇavasībhāvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Sippadassanavasena kataṃ rājakulāni upecca asanaṃ sarakkhepo etehīti katupāsanā, rājakulādīsu dassitasippāti vuttaṃ hoti. Pabhaggoti parājito.

“Skilled hands” means very firm in their aim at targets, shooting arrows without missing. Such people, having mastery in that, are called “skilled hands.” Therefore, one who merely learns a craft is not called a “skilled hand,” but these are “skilled hands,” meaning they have practiced mastery. “Katupāsanā” means those who have secured a living by approaching royal families through the display of their craft; meaning they have displayed their craft in royal families and so on. “Pabhagga” means defeated.

232. Dosadassana [V 2.0263] pubbaka rūpa virāga bhāvanā saṅkhāta paṭipakkha bhāvanāvasena paṭighasaññānaṃ suppahīnattā mahatāpi saddena arūpasamāpattito na vuṭṭhāti, tathā pana na suppahīnattā sabbarūpāvacarasamāpattito vuṭṭhānaṃ siyāti idha āneñjasamādhīti catutthajjhānasamāpatti adhippetāti āha “anejaṃ acalaṃ kāyavācāvipphandavirahitaṃ catutthajjhānasamādhi”nti. Aññattha pana samādhipaccanīkānaṃ atidūratāya na iñjatīti āneñjoti arūpāvacarasamādhi vuccati. Samādhiparipanthake dhammeti vitakkavicārādike sandhāya vadati. Vitakkādīsu ādīnavasallakkhaṇassa na suṭṭhukatabhāvaṃ sandhāyāha “na suṭṭhu parisodhetvā”ti.

232. Because perceptions of aversion are thoroughly abandoned by means of the development of the antidote, which is called the development of dispassion towards form preceded by seeing faults, one does not emerge from the formless attainments even with a loud noise. However, if they are not so thoroughly abandoned, emergence from all form-sphere attainments would occur. Therefore, here, “imperturbable concentration” is intended to mean the fourth jhāna attainment; thus he said, “the fourth jhāna concentration, which is imperturbable, unwavering, and free from bodily and verbal agitation.” Elsewhere, however, “imperturbable” refers to the formless-sphere concentration because the hindrances to concentration are very far away, so it does not waver. “Obstacles to concentration” refers to factors like thought and examination. Pointing out the lack of thorough application in perceiving the dangers in thoughts, etc., it is said, “Not having fully purified.”

Nanu cāyamāyasmā mahāmoggallāno bhagavato paṭhamavasseva abhinavappattaarahatto, idañca uttarimanussadhammapārājikaṃ vīsatimavassato upari paññattaṃ, kathaṃ imassa vatthuno imasmiṃ pārājike bhagavatā vinicchitabhāvo vuttoti? Nāyaṃ doso. Ayañhettha ācariyānaṃ kathāmaggo – apaññattepi sikkhāpade therassa vacanaṃ sutvā “attano appatirūpaṃ uttarimanussadhammaṃ esa vadatī”ti maññamānā bhikkhū therassa dosaṃ āropentā ujjhāyiṃsu. Bhagavā ca therassa tathāvacane kāraṇaṃ dassetvā niddosabhāvaṃ karonto “anāpatti, bhikkhave, moggallānassā”ti āha. Saṅgītikārakā pana uttarimanussadhammādhikārattā tampi vatthuṃ ānetvā idha āropesunti.

But was not the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna a newly attained arahant in the very first year of the Blessed One? And this pārājika concerning superhuman states was laid down after the twentieth year. How, then, is it said that this matter was decided by the Blessed One under this pārājika? This is not a fault. For this is the teachers’ way of speaking: Even when the training rule had not yet been laid down, the bhikkhus, hearing the elder’s words and thinking, “He is declaring a superhuman state unbecoming of himself,” accused the elder and complained. The Blessed One, showing the reason for the elder’s statement and establishing his faultlessness, said, “There is no offense, bhikkhus, for Moggallāna.” But the compilers of the Saṅgīti, because it pertains to the subject of superhuman states, brought that incident and inserted it here.

Sāvakānaṃ uppaṭipāṭiyā anussaraṇaṃ natthīti dassetuṃ “na uppaṭipāṭiyā”ti āha. Asaññasamāpattinti saññāvirāgabhāvanāya vāyokasiṇanibbattitaṃ [M 2.0297] catutthajjhānasamāpattiṃ vadati. Pubbenivāsañāṇaṃ cutipaṭisandhiṃ gaṇhantampi anantarapaccayakkamavantānaṃ arūpadhammānaṃ vaseneva gaṇhātīti āha – “tatiye attabhāve cutimeva addasā”ti. Nayato sallakkhesīti vaṭṭe saṃsaraṇakasattānaṃ khandhānaṃ abhāvakālo nāma natthi, asaññabhave pana acittakā hutvā pañca kappasatāni pavattanti, iminā nayena sallakkhesi. Dukkaraṃ katanti khandhavikalassa pubbenivāsassa anussaraṇaṃ ṭhapetvā sammāsambuddhaṃ na sakkā aññehi kātunti nayato sallakkhentenapi dukkaraṃ katanti adhippāyo. Paṭividdhāti paṭividdhasadisā. Yathā nāma koci dhanusippe katahattho ekaṃ kesasaṅkhātaṃ vālaṃ satakkhattuṃ vidāletvā tato ekaṃ aṃsuṃ gahetvā vātiṅgaṇaphalassa majjhaṭṭhāne bandhitvā aparaṃ aṃsuṃ kaṇḍassa aggakoṭiyaṃ yathā tassa aṃsussa ūkāmattaṃ vā likkhāmattaṃ vā kaṇḍassa aggakoṭito adhikaṃ hutvā tiṭṭhati, evaṃ bandhitvā usabhamatte ṭhāne ṭhito kaṇḍabaddhāya vālakoṭiyā vātiṅgaṇabaddhaṃ vālassa koṭiṃ paṭivijjheyya[V 2.0264], evameva imināpi kataṃ dukkaranti vuttaṃ hoti. Etadagganti eso aggo. Yadidanti yo ayaṃ. Liṅgavipallāsavasenetaṃ vuttaṃ.

To show that there is no recalling in reverse order for disciples, he said, “not in reverse order.” “Unconscious attainment” refers to the attainment of the fourth jhāna produced by the air kasiṇa through the cultivation of dispassion toward perception. The knowledge of past lives, even when grasping death and rebirth-linking, grasps only by way of the formless phenomena which possess the sequence of immediate conditionality. Thus, he said, “He saw only the passing away in the third existence.” “He discerned by method” means that for beings wandering in the cycle, there is no time when the aggregates are non-existent. But in the unconscious realm, being without mind, they continue for five hundred eons. He discerned by this method. “He did what is hard to do” means that, apart from a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, no one else can recall past lives that are deficient in aggregates; thus, even when discerning by method, the meaning is that he did what is hard to do. “Penetrated” means similar to having penetrated. Just as someone skilled in archery might split a hair a hundred times, then take one fiber and fasten it in the middle of a vātiṅgaṇa fruit, and another fiber at the tip of the arrow shaft, so that the fiber’s size, no larger than a louse or a nit, stands out slightly from the arrow’s tip. Having fastened them in this way, and standing in a place the measure of an usabha, he would pierce the tip of the hair fastened to the vātiṅgaṇa with the tip of the arrow-bound hair. In the same way, it is said that he did what is hard to do. “Foremost” means this is the foremost. “That is” refers to this one. This is said by way of the interchange of gender.

Vinītavatthuvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Vinītavatthu is completed.

Nigamanavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Conclusion

233. Idhāti imasmiṃ bhikkhuvibhaṅge. Uddiṭṭhāti idha pātimokkhavasena anosāritattā cattāro pārājikāva uddiṭṭhā kathitāti attho gahetabbo. Yadi evaṃ heṭṭhā thullaccayadukkaṭānampi vuttattā pārājikāva uddiṭṭhāti kasmā vuttāti? Pārājikādhikārattā santesupi thullaccayadukkaṭesu idha pārājikāva vuttā. Yesaṃ…pe… asaṃvāsoti imamatthaṃ vā dīpetukāmo taṃsambandhena “uddiṭṭhā cattāro pārājikā”ti āha. Tatthāyasmantetiādikaṃ pana anuññātapātimokkhuddesakkamopi ayameva, nāññoti dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Bhikkhunīnaṃ asādhāraṇāni cattārīti ubbhajāṇumaṇḍalikā vajjapaṭicchādikā ukkhittānuvattikā aṭṭhavatthukāti imāni cattāri bhikkhunīnaṃ bhikkhūhi asādhāraṇāni nāma. Etesu ubbhajāṇumaṇḍalikā nāma yā kāyasaṃsaggarāgena avassutā teneva rāgena avassutassa manussapurisassa akkhakānaṃ adho jāṇumaṇḍalānaṃ [M 2.0298] kapparānañca upari yena kenaci sarīrāvayavena āmasanādiṃ sādiyati, tassā adhivacanaṃ. Yā pana bhikkhunī aññissā bhikkhuniyā pārājikasaṅkhātaṃ vajjaṃ jānaṃ paṭicchādeti, sā vajjapaṭicchādikā nāma. Samaggena pana saṅghena ukkhittaṃ bhikkhuṃ yā bhikkhunī yaṃdiṭṭhiko so hoti, tassā diṭṭhiyā gahaṇavasena anuvattati, sā ukkhittānuvattikā nāma. Yā pana kāyasaṃsaggarāgena tintā tathāvidhasseva purisassa hatthaggahaṇaṃ vā saṅghāṭikaṇṇaggahaṇaṃ vā sādiyati, kāyasaṃsaggasaṅkhātassa asaddhammassa paṭisevanatthāya purisassa hatthapāse santiṭṭhati vā, tattha ṭhatvā sallapati vā, saṅketaṃ vā gacchati, purisassa āgamanaṃ vā sādiyati, kenaci vā paṭicchannokāsaṃ pavisati, hatthapāse vā ṭhatvā kāyaṃ upasaṃharati, ayaṃ aṭṭhavatthukā nāmāti veditabbaṃ.

233. Here means in this Bhikkhuvibhaṅga. 'Set forth' means that here, by way of the Pātimokkha, because they are not omitted, the four pārājika offenses are set forth, meaning spoken; this is the meaning to be understood. If so, since thullaccaya and dukkaṭa offenses are also mentioned below, why is it said that only the pārājika offenses are 'set forth'? Because this is the section on the pārājikas. Even though thullaccaya and dukkaṭa offenses exist, here only the pārājika offenses are mentioned. Desiring to clarify this meaning, 'Of which…pe… no co-residence,' he said in connection with that, 'the four pārājikas are set forth.' The passage beginning 'Therein, venerable sirs...' is stated to show that this indeed is the authorized sequence of the Pātimokkha recitation, and not another. The four rules not shared by bhikkhunīs with bhikkhus are: ubbhajāṇumaṇḍalikā, vajjapaṭicchādikā, ukkhittānuvattikā, and aṭṭhavatthukā. These four are called 'not shared by bhikkhunīs with bhikkhus.' Among these, 'ubbhajāṇumaṇḍalikā' is the designation for a bhikkhunī who, impassioned with lust for bodily contact, consents to the touching, etc., by any bodily limb whatsoever, of a human male similarly impassioned with that same lust, in the area below the clavicles, below the kneecaps, and above the elbows. A bhikkhunī who knowingly conceals another bhikkhunī’s offense classified as pārājika is called a 'vajjapaṭicchādikā' (concealer of an offense). A bhikkhunī who follows a bhikkhu suspended by a unanimous Saṅgha by adopting whatever view he holds is called an 'ukkhittānuvattikā' (follower of one who is suspended). A bhikkhunī who, sullied by lust for bodily contact, consents to a man of the same disposition grasping her hand or the corner of her outer robe; or stands within arm’s reach of a man for the purpose of engaging in the unholy act of bodily contact; or stands there and converses with him; or goes to a rendezvous; or consents to a man’s approach; or enters a secluded place with him; or stands within arm’s reach and brings her body close to his—this is to be known as 'aṭṭhavatthukā' (one who commits the eight-fold offense).

Vatthuvipannāti pabbajjupasampadāya avatthubhāvato vatthuvipannā. Nesañhi “na, bhikkhave, paṇḍako pabbājetabbo, yo pabbājeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”tiādinā pabbajjā upasampadā ca paṭikkhittā. Tasmā te bhikkhubhāvāya abhabbattā pārājikāpannasadisatāya “pārājikā”ti [V 2.0265] vuttā. Tabbhāvabhāvitāya bhikkhubhāvo vasati etthāti vatthu, puggalānaṃ bhikkhubhāvārahatā. Sā pana pabbajjakkhandhakāgatasabbadosavirahitasampattiyuttatā. Taṃ vipannaṃ paṇḍakabhāvādiyogena yesaṃ te vatthuvipannā. Ahetukapaṭisandhikāti iminā tesaṃ vipākāvaraṇena samannāgatabhāvaṃ dassento maggāvaraṇe kāraṇamāha. Pārājikāpannasadisattā pārājikā. Theyyasaṃvāsakādikammaṃ mātughātādikaṃ viya ānantariyaṃ na hotīti āha “imesaṃ tiṇṇaṃ saggo avārito”ti.

'One whose basis is destroyed' means one whose basis is destroyed because of being without a basis for the going forth and higher ordination. For them, indeed, both the going forth and the higher ordination are prohibited by the text beginning, 'Bhikkhus, a paṇḍaka should not be given the going forth... an offense of wrong-doing.' Therefore, because they are incapable of the state of a bhikkhu and because of their similarity to one who has committed a pārājika offense, they are called 'pārājikā.' The basis (vatthu) is that wherein the state of a bhikkhu resides, due to being endowed with that nature; it is the suitability of persons for the state of a bhikkhu. That, in turn, is the endowment with the perfection of being free from all faults mentioned in the Chapter on the Going Forth. Those for whom that basis is destroyed through connection with being a paṇḍaka, etc., are 'ones whose basis is destroyed.' By the phrase 'those with a rootless rebirth-linking,' showing their state of being endowed with an obstruction by kamma-result, he states the reason for the obstruction to the path. Because of their similarity to one who has committed a pārājika offense, they are called 'pārājikā.' The act of co-residence by theft, etc., is not an immediately effective kamma like matricide, etc. Thus it is said: 'For these three, heaven is not barred.'

Dīghatāya lambamānaṃ aṅgajātametassāti lambī. So ettāvatā na pārājiko, atha kho yadā anabhiratiyā pīḷito attano aṅgajātaṃ mukhe vā vaccamagge vā paveseti, tadā pārājiko hoti. Mudu piṭṭhi etassāti mudupiṭṭhiko, kataparikammāya mudukāya piṭṭhiyā samannāgato. Sopi yadā anabhiratiyā pīḷito attano aṅgajātaṃ attano mukhavaccamaggesu aññataraṃ paveseti, tadā pārājiko hoti. Parassa aṅgajātaṃ attano mukhena gaṇhātīti yo anabhiratiyā pīḷito parassa suttassa vā pamattassa vā aṅgajātaṃ attano mukhena [M 2.0299] gaṇhāti. Parassa aṅgajāte abhinisīdatīti yo anabhiratiyā pīḷito parassa aṅgajātaṃ kammaniyaṃ disvā attano vaccamaggena tassūpari nisīdati, taṃ attano vaccamaggaṃ pavesetīti attho.

Because of its length, his sexual organ is dangling, hence he is a 'lambī' (one with a long organ). By that much, he is not a pārājika offender. But rather, when, oppressed by dissatisfaction, he inserts his own sexual organ into his mouth or anus, then he becomes a pārājika offender. He has a soft back, hence he is a 'mudupiṭṭhiko' (one with a soft back), endowed with a soft back that has been prepared. He too, when, oppressed by dissatisfaction, inserts his own sexual organ into one or the other of his own mouth or anus, then he becomes a pārājika offender. 'He takes another's sexual organ with his own mouth' means one who, oppressed by dissatisfaction, takes with his own mouth the sexual organ of another who is asleep or heedless. 'He sits down upon another's sexual organ' means one who, oppressed by dissatisfaction, seeing another's sexual organ is ready for the act, sits down upon it with his own anus; the meaning is that he makes it enter his own anus.

Etthāha – mātughātakapitughātakaarahantaghātakā tatiyapārājikaṃ āpannā, bhikkhunīdūsako lambīādayo cattāro paṭhamapārājikaṃ āpannā evāti kathaṃ catuvīsatīti? Vuccate – mātughātakādayo hi cattāro idha anupasampannā eva adhippetā, lambīādayo cattāro kiñcāpi paṭhamapārājikena saṅgahitā, yasmā pana etena pariyāyena methunaṃ dhammaṃ appaṭisevino honti, tasmā visuṃ vuttāti. Etena pariyāyenāti ubhinnaṃ rāgapariyuṭṭhānasaṅkhātena pariyāyena. Dutiyavikappe kaccitthāti ettha kacci atthāti padacchedo veditabbo.

Here it is said: The matricide, patricide, and arahant-killer have committed the third pārājika; the defiler of a bhikkhunī and the four beginning with the `lambī` have committed the first pārājika. How then are there twenty-four? The reply is stated: Here, the four beginning with the matricide are indeed intended as unordained persons. Although the four beginning with the `lambī` are included under the first pārājika, yet because by this method they are non-partakers of sexual intercourse, they are therefore mentioned separately. 'By this method' means by the method described as the overwhelming by lust of both parties. In the second alternative, in the word `kaccitthāti`, the word division should be known as `kacci atthāti`.

Nigamanavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Conclusion is completed.

Iti samantapāsādikāya vinayasaṃvaṇṇanāya sāratthadīpaniyaṃ

Thus in the Sāratthadīpanī, on the Samantapāsādikā, the Commentary on the Vinaya,

Catutthapārājikavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Fourth Pārājika is completed.

2. Saṅghādisesakaṇḍaṃ

2. The Chapter on Saṅghādisesa Offenses

1. Sukkavissaṭṭhisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

1. The Explanation of the Training Rule Concerning Emission of Semen

Idāni [M 2.0300][V 2.0266] pārājikasaṃvaṇṇanāsamanantarā yā terasakādisaṃvaṇṇanā samāraddhā, tassāpi –

Now, immediately following the explanation of the Pārājika offenses, the explanation of the thirteen and so on has been commenced. Of that also –

Anākulā asandehā, paripuṇṇavinicchayā;

Atthabyañjanasampannā, hoti sāratthadīpanī.

Unconfused, without doubt, of perfect ascertainment; endowed with meaning and phrasing, is the Sāratthadīpanī.

Terasakassāti terasa sikkhāpadāni parimāṇāni assa kaṇḍassāti terasakaṃ, tassa terasakassa kaṇḍassāti attho.

Regarding 'of the thirteenfold': 'Thirteen training rules are the measure of this section'; thus, it is called 'thirteenfold'. This is the meaning of 'of the thirteenfold section'.

234. Anabhiratoti aññattha gihibhāvaṃ patthayamāno vuccati, idha pana kāmarāgavasena ukkaṇṭhitatāya vikkhittacittatāya samannāgato adhippetoti āha vikkhittacittotiādi.

234. Regarding 'not delighting': elsewhere, this refers to one who longs for the state of a householder. Here, however, it is intended to mean one who, by the power of sensual lust, is agitated and possessed of a distracted mind. Therefore, the commentator said, 'with a distracted mind,' and so on.

236-237. Sañcetanikāti ettha saṃ-saddo vijjamānatthatāya sātthakoti dassento āha saṃvijjati cetanā assāti. Tattha cetanāti vītikkamavasappavattā pubbabhāgacetanā. Assāti sukkavissaṭṭhiyā. Imasmiṃ vikappe ika-saddassa visuṃ attho natthīti āha sañcetanāva sañcetanikāti. Idāni saṃ-saddassa atthaṃ anapekkhitvā ika-saddova assatthiatthaṃ pakāsetīti dassento sañcetanā vā assā atthīti sañcetanikāti dutiyavikappamāha. Saṃvijjati cetanā assāti padabhājane vattabbe byañjane ādaraṃ akatvā jānantotiādi vuttaṃ. Upakkamāmīti jānantoti mocanatthaṃ upakkamāmīti jānanto.

Here, regarding 'sañcetanikā,' to show that the prefix 'saṃ-' has the meaning of 'existence' and is thus significant, the commentator says: 'saṃvijjati cetanā assā' (there exists intention in it). Herein, 'cetanā' is the preliminary intention that occurs by the power of transgression. 'Assā' refers to the emission of semen. In this alternative, the suffix '-ika' has no separate meaning; hence, the commentator says: 'sañcetanā eva sañcetanikā' (intention itself is intentional). Now, to show that, without considering the meaning of the prefix 'saṃ-,' the suffix '-ika' alone expresses the meaning of possession, he states a second alternative: 'sañcetanā vā assā atthīti sañcetanikā' (or, it has intention, thus it is intentional). Although 'saṃvijjati cetanā assā' should have been stated in the word-analysis (padabhājana), the Blessed One, not being concerned with the exact phrasing, said 'jānanto' (knowing), and so on. The phrase 'upakkamāmīti jānanto' means 'knowing, "I am making an effort for the purpose of emission."'.

Āsayabhedatoti pittādiāsayabhedato. Buddhapaccekabuddhānampi hi raññopi cakkavattissa pittasemhapubbalohitāsayesu [V 2.0267] catūsu aññataro āsayo hotiyeva, mandapaññānaṃ pana cattāropi āsayā honti. Dhātunānattatoti pathavīdhātuādīnaṃ catunnaṃ dhātūnaṃ, cakkhādīnaṃ vā aṭṭhārasannaṃ dhātūnaṃ, rasasoṇitādīnaṃ vā dhātūnaṃ nānattato.

Due to the difference of disposition: this means due to the difference of disposition such as bile. For indeed, even for Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and wheel-turning kings, there is certainly one or another of the four dispositions—bile, phlegm, pus, and blood; but for those of dull wisdom, all four dispositions are present. Due to the diversity of elements: this means due to the diversity of the four elements beginning with earth, or of the eighteen elements beginning with the eye, or of the elements such as nutritive essence and blood.

Vatthisīsanti [M 2.0301] vatthipuṭassa abbhantare matthakapassaṃ. “Rāga…pe… asakkonto”ti rāgapariyuṭṭhānaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Rājā pana “sambhavassa sakalakāyo ṭhāna”nti sutapubbattā vīmaṃsanatthaṃ evamakāsīti vadanti. Dakasotanti muttamaggaṃ, aṅgajātappadesanti vuttaṃ hoti. Dakasotorohaṇato paṭṭhāya pana upādinnato vinimuttatāya sambhave utusamuṭṭhānameva rūpaṃ avasissati, sesaṃ tisamuṭṭhānaṃ natthīti veditabbaṃ. Āpodhātuyā santānavasena pavattamānāya avatthāviseso sambhavo, so catusamuṭṭhāniko aṭṭhakathāyaṃ catusamuṭṭhānikesu sambhavassa vuttattā. So pana soḷasavassakāle uppajjati, tassa rāgavasena ṭhānācāvanaṃ hotīti vadanti, tasmā yaṃ vuttaṃ kathāvatthuaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “sukkavissaṭṭhi nāma rāgasamuṭṭhānā hotī”ti, taṃ sambhavassa ṭhānācāvanaṃ sandhāya vuttanti veditabbaṃ, na pana sambhavo cittasamuṭṭhānoyevāti dīpetuṃ, teneva tattha vissaṭṭhiggahaṇaṃ kataṃ. “Khīṇāsavānaṃ pana brahmānañca sambhavo natthī”ti ācariyadhammapālattherena vuttaṃ, tasmā yaṃ vuttaṃ kathāvatthuaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (kathā. aṭṭha. 307) “tāsaṃ devatānaṃ sukkavissaṭṭhi nāma natthī”ti, tampi ṭhānācāvanaṃ sandhāya vuttanti gahetabbaṃ, na pana devatānaṃ sabbaso sambhavassa abhāvaṃ sandhāya. Channampi pana kāmāvacaradevatānaṃ kāmā pākatikāyeva. Manussā viya hi te dvayaṃdvayasamāpattivaseneva methunaṃ paṭisevanti, kevalaṃ pana nissandābhāvo tesaṃ vattabbo. Taṅkhaṇikapariḷāhavūpasamāvahaṃ samphassasukhameva hi tesaṃ kāmakiccaṃ. Keci pana “cātumahārājikatāvatiṃsānaṃyeva dvayaṃdvayasamāpattiyā kāmakiccaṃ ijjhati, yāmānaṃ aññamaññaṃ āliṅganamattena, tusitānaṃ hatthāmasanamattena, nimmānaratīnaṃ hasitamattena, paranimmitavasavattīnaṃ olokitamattena kāmakiccaṃ ijjhatī”ti vadanti, taṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ paṭikkhittaṃ tādisassa kāmesu virajjanassa tesu abhāvato kāmānañca uttaruttari paṇītatarapaṇītatamabhāvato.

The head of the bladder: this means the upper part inside the bladder-sac. 'Lust... unable...' is said in reference to being overwhelmed by lust. They say that the king, having previously heard that 'the entire body is the location of semen,' acted thus in order to investigate. The water channel: this means the urinary passage, that is, the region of the genitals. It should be understood that from the descent into the water channel onwards, because it is freed from what is clung to, only matter born of temperature remains in the semen; the remaining matter of three origins does not exist. Semen is a particular state of the water element proceeding by way of continuity; it is of fourfold origination because in the commentary, semen is mentioned among things of fourfold origination. They say that it arises at the age of sixteen, and due to lust, its dislodging from its place occurs. Therefore, what was said in the Kathāvatthu commentary, 'The emission of semen is born of lust,' should be understood as said in reference to the dislodging of the semen from its place, not to show that semen is born only of mind. For that very reason, the word 'vissaṭṭhi' (emission) was used there. The Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla said, 'For those with cankers destroyed and for Brahmās, there is no semen.' Therefore, what was said in the Kathāvatthu commentary, 'For those deities, there is no such thing as emission of semen,' that too should be taken as said in reference to the dislodging from its place, and not in reference to the complete absence of semen for deities. Moreover, for all six classes of sense-sphere deities, sensual pleasures are just natural. For like humans, they engage in sexual intercourse by means of pairwise union. However, it should be said that for them there is an absence of emission. For their sexual act is just the pleasure of contact which brings about the calming of the momentary burning. But some say, 'For the Cātumahārājika and Tāvatiṃsa deities, the sexual act is accomplished by pairwise union; for the Yāma deities, by a mere mutual embrace; for the Tusita deities, by a mere touching of hands; for the Nimmānaratī deities, by a mere smile; and for the Paranimmitavasavattī deities, by a mere glance.' That is refuted in the commentary because of the absence in them of such dispassion towards sensual pleasures, and because sensual pleasures become successively more and more sublime.

Tathevāti “mocanassādena nimitte upakkamato”tiādiṃ atidisati. “Vissaṭṭhīti ṭhānato cāvanā vuccatī”ti vuttattā dakasotaṃ otiṇṇamatteti kasmā vuttanti āha dakasotorohaṇañcetthātiādi. Etthāti tīsupi vādesu. Adhivāsetvāti nimitte upakkamitvā [M 2.0302] puna vippaṭisāre uppanne adhivāsetvā. Antarā nivāretunti ṭhānato cutaṃ dakasotaṃ otarituṃ adatvā antarā nivāretuṃ. Tenāha – ṭhānā cutañhi avassaṃ dakasotaṃ otaratīti[V 2.0268]. Ṭhānācāvanamattenevāti dakasotaṃ anotiṇṇepīti adhippāyo. Ettha ca “sakalo kāyo ṭhāna”nti vāde ṭhānācāvanaṃ vadantena sakalasarīrato cutassapi dakasotorohaṇato pubbe appamattakassa antarāḷassa sambhavato vuttaṃ. Sakalasarīre vā tasmiṃ tasmiṃ padese ṭhitassa ṭhānā cutaṃ sandhāya “ṭhānācāvanamattenevā”ti vuttaṃ. Nimitte upakkamantassevāti mocanassādena upakkamantassa. Hatthaparikammādīsu satipi mocanassāde nimitte upakkamābhāvato natthi āpattīti āha “hattaparikamma…pe… anāpattī”ti. Ayaṃ sabbācariyasādhāraṇavinicchayoti “dakasotorohaṇañcetthā”tiādinā vutto tiṇṇampi ācariyānaṃ sādhāraṇo vinicchayo.

Likewise: he extends by analogy beginning with, 'Because of applying oneself to the sign with the pleasure of release.' Because it was said, 'Discharge is said to be movement from the place,' why was it said, 'merely having entered the stream of water'? He says, beginning with, 'Here, entering the stream of water is meant.' 'Here' refers to all three views. 'Having tolerated' means having applied oneself to the sign and then, when remorse arises again, having tolerated it. 'Preventing in between' means not allowing what has moved from its place to descend into the stream of water, preventing it in between. Therefore, he said, 'For what has moved from its place inevitably descends into the stream of water.' 'Merely by movement from the place' means even without entering the stream of water—this is the meaning. And here, in the view that 'the entire body is the place,' by saying 'movement from the place,' it is said with reference to the possibility of a small intermediate amount existing before descending into the stream of water, even for that which has moved from the entire body. Alternatively, 'merely by movement from the place' is said with reference to the movement from the place where it is situated in this or that region of the entire body. 'Only for one who applies oneself to the sign' means for one who applies oneself with the pleasure of release. In hand-manipulation and so on, even though there is pleasure in release, there is no offense because there is no application to the sign. Therefore, he says, 'In hand-manipulation... no offense.' This is a judgment common to all teachers: the judgment stated by the passage beginning with 'here, entering the stream of water is meant,' is a judgment common to all three teachers.

Khobhakaraṇapaccayo nāma visabhāgabhesajjasenāsanāhārādipaccayo. Atthakāmatāya vā anatthakāmatāya vāti pasannā atthakāmatāya, kuddhā anatthakāmatāya. Atthāya vā anatthāya vāti sabhāvato bhavitabbāya atthāya vā anatthāya vā. Upasaṃharantīti attano devānubhāvena upanenti. Bodhisattamātā viya puttapaṭilābhanimittanti tadā kira pure puṇṇamāya sattamadivasato paṭṭhāya vigatasurāpānaṃ mālāgandhādivibhūtisampannaṃ nakkhattakīḷaṃ anubhavamānā bodhisattamātā sattame divase pātova uṭṭhāya gandhodakena nhāyitvā sabbālaṅkāravibhūsitā varabhojanaṃ bhuñjitvā uposathaṅgāni adhiṭṭhāya sirigabbhaṃ pavisitvā sirisayane nipannā niddaṃ okkamamānā imaṃ supinaṃ addasa – cattāro kira naṃ mahārājāno sayaneneva saddhiṃ ukkhipitvā anotattadahaṃ netvā nhāpetvā dibbavatthaṃ nivāsetvā dibbagandhehi vilimpetvā dibbapupphāni piḷandhitvā tato avidūre rajatapabbato, tassa anto kanakavimānaṃ atthi, tasmiṃ pācīnato sīsaṃ katvā nipajjāpesuṃ. Atha bodhisatto setavaravāraṇo hutvā tato avidūre eko suvaṇṇapabbato, tattha caritvā tato oruyha rajatapabbataṃ abhiruhitvā kanakavimānaṃ pavisitvā mātaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā dakkhiṇapassaṃ phāletvā kucchiṃ paviṭṭhasadiso ahosi. Imaṃ supinaṃ sandhāya etaṃ vuttaṃ “bodhisattamātā viya puttapaṭilābhanimitta”nti.

The condition called 'that which causes agitation' is a condition such as incompatible medicine, lodging, or food. Regarding the phrase 'either from the desire for benefit or from the desire for harm': pleased deities act out of a desire for benefit, while angry deities act out of a desire for harm. Regarding 'for benefit or for harm': this means for benefit or for harm that is to occur by its own nature. 'They bring it forth' means they present it through their own divine power. 'Like the Bodhisatta's mother, a sign of obtaining a son': it is said that at that time, starting from the seventh day before the full moon, the Bodhisatta's mother, abstaining from intoxicants and endowed with the splendor of garlands, perfumes, and so on, was enjoying the star festival. On the seventh day, rising early in the morning, she bathed in scented water, adorned herself with all ornaments, partook of excellent food, undertook the Uposatha precepts, entered her auspicious chamber, and lay down on her auspicious couch. As she was falling asleep, she saw this dream: it is said that the four great kings lifted her up along with her couch, took her to Lake Anotatta, bathed her, clothed her in divine garments, anointed her with divine perfumes, and adorned her with divine flowers. Not far from there is a silver mountain, and within it is a golden mansion. There they laid her down with her head to the east. Then the Bodhisatta, having become a magnificent white elephant, wandered on a golden mountain that was nearby. Descending from it and ascending the silver mountain, he entered the golden mansion, circumambulated his mother to the right, split open her right side, and seemed to enter her womb. This dream is referenced by the statement: 'Like the Bodhisatta's mother, a sign of obtaining a son.'

Pañca [M 2.0303] mahāsupineti (a. ni. aṭṭha. 3.5.196) mahantehi purisehi passitabbato mahantānañca atthānaṃ nimittabhāvato mahāsupine. Te pana pañca mahāsupine neva lokiyamahājano passati, na mahārājāno, na cakkavattirājāno, na aggasāvakā, na paccekabuddhā, na sammāsambuddhā, eko sabbaññubodhisattoyeva passati. Tena vuttaṃ “bodhisatto viya pañca mahāsupine”ti. Amhākañca pana bodhisatto kadā te supine passīti? “Sve buddho bhavissāmī”ti cātuddasiyaṃ pakkhassa rattivibhāyanakāle passi. Kālavasena hi divā diṭṭho [V 2.0269] supino na sameti, tathā paṭhamayāme majjhimayāme ca. Pacchimayāme balavapaccūse pana asitapītasāyite sammāpariṇāmagate kāyasmiṃ ojāya patiṭṭhitāya aruṇe uggacchamāne diṭṭhasupino sameti. Iṭṭhanimittaṃ supinaṃ passanto iṭṭhaṃ paṭilabhati, aniṭṭhanimittaṃ passanto aniṭṭhaṃ, tasmā bodhisattopi supinaṃ passanto rattivibhāyanakāle passi.

Regarding 'the five great dreams' (Aṅguttara Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā 3.5.196): they are called 'great dreams' because they are to be seen by great men and because they are signs of great benefits. But these five great dreams are not seen by ordinary worldly people, nor by great kings, nor by wheel-turning monarchs, nor by chief disciples, nor by paccekabuddhas, nor by perfectly enlightened Buddhas—only the one omniscient Bodhisatta sees them. Therefore, it is said, 'like the Bodhisatta, the five great dreams.' And when did our Bodhisatta see those dreams? He saw them at the time of night's dawning on the fourteenth day of the lunar fortnight, thinking, 'Tomorrow I shall become a Buddha.' For, due to the time, a dream seen during the day does not come true, and likewise one seen during the first or middle watch of the night. But a dream seen in the last watch, at strong dawn, after what has been eaten and drunk has been properly digested, when nutritive essence is established in the body, and as the morning light rises—such a dream comes true. One who sees a dream that is a desirable sign obtains a desirable result; one who sees an undesirable sign obtains an undesirable result. Therefore, the Bodhisatta also, when seeing a dream, saw it at the time of night’s dawning.

Ke pana te pañca mahāsupināti? Tathāgatassa arahato sammāsambuddhassa pubbeva sambodhā anabhisambuddhassa bodhisattasseva sato pañca mahāsupinā pāturahesuṃ (a. ni. 5.196) – ayaṃ mahāpathavī mahāsayanaṃ ahosi, himavā pabbatarājā bimbohanaṃ ahosi, puratthime samudde vāmahattho ohito ahosi, pacchime samudde dakkhiṇahattho ohito ahosi, dakkhiṇasamudde ubho pādā ohitā ahesuṃ, ayaṃ paṭhamo mahāsupino pāturahosi.

What, then, are those five great dreams? Before the enlightenment of the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, while he was still an unenlightened Bodhisatta, five great dreams appeared to him (Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.196): This great earth became his great bed; Himavā, king of mountains, became his pillow; his left hand was placed in the eastern ocean; his right hand was placed in the western ocean; and both his feet were placed in the southern ocean. This was the first great dream that appeared.

Puna caparaṃ dabbatiṇasaṅkhātā tiriyā nāma tiṇajāti naṅgalamattena rattadaṇḍena nābhito uggantvā tassa passantasseva vidatthimattaṃ ratanamattaṃ byāmamattaṃ yaṭṭhimattaṃ gāvutamattaṃ aḍḍhayojanamattaṃ yojanamattanti evaṃ uggantvā anekayojanasahassaṃ nabhaṃ āhacca ṭhitā ahosi, ayaṃ dutiyo mahāsupino pāturahosi.

Furthermore, a species of grass named Tiriya, also known as dabba grass, with a red stalk the size of a plough-pole, grew up from his navel. As he looked on, it grew to the size of a span, a cubit, a fathom, a staff-length, a gāvuta, half a yojana, and a yojana, and so on, rising up and up until it stood touching the sky for many thousands of yojanas. This was the second great dream that appeared.

Puna caparaṃ setā kimī kaṇhasīsā pādehi ussakkitvā yāva jāṇumaṇḍalā paṭicchādesuṃ, ayaṃ tatiyo mahāsupino pāturahosi.

Furthermore, white worms with black heads crawled up from his feet and covered him as far as his kneecaps. This was the third great dream that appeared.

Puna caparaṃ cattāro sakuṇā nānāvaṇṇā catūhi disāhi āgantvā pādamūle nipatitvā sabbasetā sampajjiṃsu, ayaṃ catuttho mahāsupino pāturahosi.

Furthermore, four birds of various colors came from the four directions, fell at his feet, and all became completely white. This was the fourth great dream that appeared.

Puna [M 2.0304] caparaṃ bodhisatto mahato mīḷhapabbatassa uparūpari caṅkamati alippamāno mīḷhena, ayaṃ pañcamo mahāsupino pāturahosi. Ime pañca mahāsupinā.

Furthermore, the Bodhisatta walked up and down on top of a great mountain of dung without being soiled by the dung. This was the fifth great dream that appeared. These are the five great dreams.

Tattha paṭhamo anuttarāya sammāsambodhiyā pubbanimittaṃ, dutiyo ariyassa aṭṭhaṅgikassa maggassa devamanussesu suppakāsitabhāvassa pubbanimittaṃ, tatiyo bahūnaṃ odātavasanānaṃ gihīnaṃ bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā saraṇagamanassa pubbanimittaṃ, catuttho khattiyādīnaṃ catunnaṃ vaṇṇānaṃ tathāgatappavedite dhammavinaye agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajitvā anuttaravimuttisacchikiriyāya pubbanimittaṃ, pañcamo catunnaṃ paccayānaṃ lābhitāya tesu ca anupalittabhāvassa pubbanimittaṃ.

Therein, the first was the precursor to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment; the second was the precursor to the Noble Eightfold Path being well proclaimed among gods and humans; the third was the precursor to many white-clad laypeople approaching the Blessed One and going for refuge; the fourth was the precursor to those of the four castes—khattiyas and others—going forth from the household life into homelessness in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, for the sake of realizing unsurpassed liberation; the fifth was the precursor to obtaining the four requisites and remaining unsoiled by them.

Apica [V 2.0270] yaṃ so cakkavāḷamahāpathaviṃ sirisayanabhūtaṃ addasa, taṃ buddhabhāvassa pubbanimittaṃ. Yaṃ himavantaṃ pabbatarājānaṃ bimbohanaṃ addasa, taṃ sabbaññutaññāṇabimbohanassa pubbanimittaṃ. Yaṃ cattāro hatthapāde samuddassa uparūparibhāgena gantvā cakkavāḷamatthake ṭhite addasa, taṃ dhammacakkassa appaṭivattiyabhāve pubbanimittaṃ. Yaṃ attānaṃ uttānakaṃ nipannaṃ addasa, taṃ tīsu bhavesu avakujjānaṃ sattānaṃ uttānamukhabhāvassa pubbanimittaṃ. Yaṃ akkhīni ummīletvā passanto viya ahosi, taṃ dibbacakkhupaṭilābhassa pubbanimittaṃ. Yaṃ yāva bhavaggā ekālokaṃ ahosi, taṃ anāvaraṇañāṇassa pubbanimittaṃ. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva. Iti taṃtaṃvisesādhigamanimittabhūte pañca mahāsupine passi. Tena vuttaṃ “bodhisatto viya pañca mahāsupine”ti.

Furthermore, that he saw the great earth of the world-system as a couch of glory was a preliminary sign of Buddhahood. That he saw the king of mountains, Himavanta, as a pillow was a preliminary sign of the pillow that is omniscient knowledge. That he saw his four hands and feet extending over the oceans and standing at the top of the world-system was a preliminary sign of the irreversible nature of the turning of the Dhamma-wheel. That he saw himself lying face-up was a preliminary sign of beings in the three realms, who were lying face down, becoming face-up. That it was as if he were opening his eyes and seeing was a preliminary sign of obtaining the divine eye. That there was a single light up to the peak of existence was a preliminary sign of obtaining unobstructed knowledge. The rest is as previously stated. Thus, he saw the five great dreams, which were signs of achieving those various distinctions. Therefore, it is said: "Like the Bodhisatta, the five great dreams."

Kosalarājā viya soḷasa supineti –

Like King Kosala, sixteen dreams—

“Usabhā rukkhā gāviyo gavā ca,

Asso kaṃso siṅgālī ca kumbho;

Pokkharaṇī ca apākacandanaṃ,

Lābūni sīdanti silā plavanti.

Bulls, trees, cows and oxen, a horse, a bowl, a female jackal and a pot, a lotus pond, and unripe sandalwood, gourds sink, stones float.

“Maṇḍūkiyo kaṇhasappe gilanti,

Kākaṃ suvaṇṇā parivārayanti;

Tasā vakā eḷakānaṃ bhayā hī”ti. (jā. 1.1.77) –

Female frogs swallow black snakes; golden swans surround a crow; timid wolves flee in fear of goats.

Ime soḷasa supine passanto kosalarājā viya.

Like King Kosala seeing these sixteen dreams.

1. Ekadivasaṃ [M 2.0305] kira kosalarājā rattiṃ niddūpagato pacchimayāme soḷasa supine passi (jā. aṭṭha. 1.1.mahāsupinajātakavaṇṇanā). Tattha cattāro añjanavaṇṇā kāḷausabhā “yujjhissāmā”ti catūhi disāhi rājaṅgaṇaṃ āgantvā “usabhayuddhaṃ passissāmā”ti mahājane sannipatite yujjhanākāraṃ dassetvā naditvā gajjitvā ayujjhitvāva paṭikkantā. Imaṃ paṭhamaṃ supinaṃ addasa.

1. It is said that one day, King Kosala, having fallen asleep at night, saw sixteen great dreams in the last watch. Therein, four jet-black bulls came from the four directions to the royal courtyard, intending to fight. And when a great crowd had gathered, thinking, 'We will see the bullfight,' they displayed a fighting posture, roared and bellowed, but turned back without actually fighting. This first dream he saw.

2. Khuddakā [V 2.0271] rukkhā ceva gacchā ca pathaviṃ bhinditvā vidatthimattampi ratanamattampi anuggantvāva pupphanti ceva phalanti ca. Imaṃ dutiyaṃ addasa.

2. Small trees and bushes, breaking through the earth and without growing even a span or a cubit, both flowered and bore fruit. This second one he saw.

3. Gāviyo tadahujātānaṃ vacchānaṃ khīraṃ pivantiyo addasa. Ayaṃ tatiyo supino.

3. He saw cows drinking the milk of their calves that were born that very day. This was the third dream.

4. Dhuravāhe ārohapariṇāhasampanne mahāgoṇe yugaparamparāya ayojetvā taruṇe godamme dhure yojente addasa, te dhuraṃ vahituṃ asakkontā chaḍḍetvā aṭṭhaṃsu, sakaṭāni nappavattiṃsu. Ayaṃ catuttho supino.

4. He saw that, instead of yoking the great oxen—strong and well-built, capable of pulling the load—they were yoking young bullocks to the yoke. These, unable to pull the load, cast it off and stood still, and the carts did not move. This was the fourth dream.

5. Ekaṃ ubhatomukhaṃ assaṃ addasa, tassa ubhosu passesu yavasīsaṃ denti, so dvīhipi mukhehi khādati. Ayaṃ pañcamo supino.

5. He saw a horse with two mouths. They gave it heads of barley on both sides, and it ate with both mouths. This was the fifth dream.

6. Mahājano satasahassagghanakaṃ suvaṇṇapātiṃ sammajjitvā “idha passāvaṃ karohī”ti ekassa jarasiṅgālassa upanāmesi, taṃ tattha passāvaṃ karontaṃ addasa. Ayaṃ chaṭṭho supino.

6. A great crowd, having polished a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand, offered it to an old jackal, saying, 'Urinate here.' He saw it urinating there. This was the sixth dream.

7. Eko puriso rajjuṃ vaṭṭetvā pādamūle nikkhipati, tena nisinnapīṭhassa heṭṭhā sayitā chātasiṅgālī tassa ajānantasseva taṃ khādati. Imaṃ sattamaṃ supinaṃ addasa.

7. A certain man was twisting a rope and placing it at his feet. A hungry female jackal, lying beneath the stool on which he sat, ate it without his knowing. This seventh dream he saw.

8. Rājadvāre bahūhi tucchakumbhehi parivāretvā ṭhapitaṃ ekaṃ mahantaṃ pūritakumbhaṃ addasa, cattāropi pana vaṇṇā catūhi disāhi catūhi anudisāhi ca ghaṭehi udakaṃ āharitvā pūritakumbhameva pūrenti, pūritapūritaṃ udakaṃ uttaritvā palāyati, tepi punappunaṃ tattheva udakaṃ āsiñcanti, tucchakumbhe olokentāpi natthi. Ayaṃ aṭṭhamo supino.

8. At the palace gate, he saw a single large, full pot placed there, surrounded by many empty pots. People of all four castes, from the four directions and the four intermediate directions, brought water in pots and filled only the full pot. The water, being filled again and again, overflowed and ran away, yet they repeatedly poured water into that very pot, while no one even looked at the empty pots. This was the eighth dream.

9. Ekaṃ [M 2.0306] pañcapadumasañchannaṃ gambhīraṃ sabbatotitthaṃ pokkharaṇiṃ addasa, samantato dvipadacatuppadā otaritvā tattha pānīyaṃ pivanti, tassā majjhe gambhīraṭṭhāne udakaṃ āvilaṃ, tīrappadese dvipadacatuppadānaṃ akkamanaṭṭhāne acchaṃ vippasannaṃ anāvilaṃ. Ayaṃ navamo supino.

9. He saw a deep pond covered with five kinds of lotuses, with bathing places on all sides. From all around, two-footed and four-footed creatures descended and drank water there. In its middle, in the deep part, the water was turbid, but near the bank, in the place where the two-footed and four-footed creatures stepped, it was clear, perfectly clear, and untroubled. This was the ninth dream.

10. Ekissāyeva ca kumbhiyā paccamānaṃ odanaṃ apākaṃ addasa, “apāka”nti vicāretvā vibhajitvā ṭhapitaṃ viya tīhākārehi paccamānaṃ ekasmiṃ passe atikilinno hoti, ekasmiṃ uttaṇḍulo, ekasmiṃ supakkoti. Ayaṃ dasamo supino.

10. He saw rice being cooked in a single pot that was unevenly cooked. It was as if it were divided, cooking in three ways: in one part it was very soft, in another part it was hard-grained, and in another part it was well-cooked. This was the tenth dream.

11. Satasahassagghanakaṃ [V 2.0272] candanasāraṃ pūtitakkena vikkiṇante addasa. Ayaṃ ekādasamo supino.

11. He saw heartwood of sandalwood worth a hundred thousand being sold for rotten buttermilk. This was the eleventh dream.

12. Tucchalābūni udake sīdantāni addasa. Ayaṃ dvādasamo supino.

12. He saw empty gourds sinking in the water. This was the twelfth dream.

13. Mahantamahantā kūṭāgārappamāṇā ghanasilā nāvā viya udake plavamānā addasa. Ayaṃ terasamo supino.

13. He saw massive, solid rocks the size of gabled mansions floating on the water like boats. This was the thirteenth dream.

14. Khuddakamadhukapupphappamāṇā maṇḍūkiyo mahante kaṇhasappe vegena anubandhitvā uppalanāḷe viya chinditvā maṃsaṃ khāditvā gilantiyo addasa. Ayaṃ cuddasamo supino.

14. He saw small frogs the size of tiny flowers swiftly pursuing large black cobras, cutting them up as if they were lotus stalks, eating their flesh, and swallowing them. This was the fourteenth dream.

15. Dasahi asaddhammehi samannāgataṃ gāmagocaraṃ kākaṃ kañcanavaṇṇavaṇṇatāya “suvaṇṇā”ti laddhanāme suvaṇṇarājahaṃse parivārente addasa. Ayaṃ pannarasamo supino.

15. He saw golden royal swans, which had acquired the name 'Golden' because of their golden-colored wings, attending upon a village-crow endowed with ten unwholesome qualities. This was the fifteenth dream.

16. Pubbe dīpino eḷake khādanti, te pana eḷake dīpino anubandhitvā murāmurāti khādante addasa, athaññe tasā vakā eḷake dūratova disvā tasitā tāsappattā hutvā eḷakānaṃ bhayā palāyitvā gumbagahanāni pavisitvā nilīyiṃsu. Ayaṃ soḷasamo supino.

16. Formerly, leopards ate goats. But he saw those goats pursuing the leopards and eating them with crunching sounds. Then other beasts of prey, such as lions and tigers, seeing the goats from afar, became terrified and frightened, and fled in fear of the goats, entering thickets and hiding. This was the sixteenth dream.

1. Tattha adhammikānaṃ rājūnaṃ adhammikānañca manussānaṃ kāle loke viparivattamāne kusale osanne akusale ussanne lokassa parihīnakāle [M 2.0307] devo na sammā vassissati, meghapādā chijjissanti, sassāni milāyissanti, dubbhikkhaṃ bhavissati, vassitukāmā viya catūhi disāhi meghā uṭṭhahitvā itthikāhi ātape patthaṭānaṃ vīhiādīnaṃ temanabhayena anto pavesitakāle purisesu kudālapiṭake ādāya āḷibandhanatthāya nikkhantesu vassanākāraṃ dassetvā gajjitvā vijjulatā nicchāretvā usabhā viya ayujjhitvā avassitvāva palāyissanti. Ayaṃ paṭhamassa vipāko.

1. At that time, during the age of unrighteous kings and unrighteous people, when the world is in upheaval, when the wholesome declines and the unwholesome flourishes, during the world's period of decay, the deva will not rain properly. The downpours will be cut off, the crops will wither, and there will be a famine. As if wishing to rain, clouds will rise from the four directions. At the time when women, fearing their paddy and other grains spread in the sun will get wet, are bringing them inside, and when men, taking hoes and baskets, have gone out to build embankments, the clouds, after showing the appearance of rain, thundering, and flashing lightning, will flee without raining, like bulls that flee without fighting. This is the result of the first dream.

2. Lokassa parihīnakāle manussānaṃ parittāyukakāle sattā tibbarāgā bhavissanti, asampattavayāva kumāriyo purisantaraṃ gantvā utuniyo ceva gabbhiniyo ca hutvā puttadhītāhi vaḍḍhissanti. Khuddakarukkhānaṃ pupphaṃ viya hi tāsaṃ utunibhāvo, phalaṃ viya ca puttadhītaro bhavissanti. Ayaṃ dutiyassa vipāko.

2. During the world's period of decay, when the lifespan of humans is short, beings will be intensely passionate. Young girls who have not yet reached maturity will go to other men, and becoming menstruous and pregnant, they will flourish with sons and daughters. For their menstruation will be like the flowers of small trees, and their sons and daughters will be like the fruit. This is the result of the second dream.

3. Manussānaṃ [V 2.0273] jeṭṭhāpacāyikakammassa naṭṭhakāle sattā mātāpitūsu vā sassusasuresu vā lajjaṃ anupaṭṭhapetvā sayameva kuṭumbaṃ saṃvidahantāva ghāsacchādanamattampi mahallakānaṃ dātukāmā dassanti, adātukāmā na dassanti, mahallakā anāthā hutvā asayaṃvasī dārake ārādhetvā jīvissanti tadahujātānaṃ vacchānaṃ khīraṃ pivantiyo mahāgāviyo viya. Ayaṃ tatiyassa vipāko.

3. When the practice of respecting elders is lost among humans, beings, showing no shame toward their parents or parents-in-law and arranging their households according to their own wishes, will give to the elderly just enough food and clothing if they wish to give, and will not give if they do not wish to give. The elderly, becoming helpless and not masters of themselves, will have to live by pleasing the young, just like great cows that drink the milk of calves born that very day. This is the result of the third dream.

4. Adhammikarājūnaṃ kāle adhammikarājāno paṇḍitānaṃ paveṇikusalānaṃ kammanittharaṇasamatthānaṃ mahāmattānaṃ yasaṃ na dassanti, dhammasabhāyaṃ vinicchayaṭṭhānepi paṇḍite vohārakusale mahallake amacce na ṭhapessanti. Tabbiparītānaṃ pana taruṇataruṇānaṃ yasaṃ dassanti, tathārūpe eva ca vinicchayaṭṭhāne ṭhapessanti, te rājakammāni ceva yuttāyuttañca ajānantā neva taṃ yasaṃ ukkhipituṃ sakkhissanti, na rājakammāni nittharituṃ, te asakkontā kammadhuraṃ chaḍḍessanti, mahallakāpi paṇḍitā amaccā yasaṃ alabhantā kiccāni nittharituṃ samatthāpi “kiṃ amhākaṃ etehi, mayaṃ bāhirakā jātā, abbhantarikā taruṇadārakā jānissantī”ti uppannāni kammāni na karissanti, evaṃ sabbathāpi tesaṃ rājūnaṃ hāniyeva bhavissati, dhuraṃ vahituṃ asamatthānaṃ vacchadammānaṃ dhure yojitakālo viya, dhuravāhānañca [M 2.0308] mahāgoṇānaṃ yugaparamparāya ayojitakālo viya bhavissati. Ayaṃ catutthassa vipāko.

4. In the time of unrighteous kings, unrighteous rulers will not grant high station to wise ministers who are skilled in tradition and capable of completing their work. In the court of justice and in positions of judgment, they will not appoint wise, elder ministers skilled in adjudication. Instead, they will grant high station to the very young, and will appoint only such persons to positions of judgment. Those young men, not knowing royal affairs nor what is proper and improper, will be unable to bear that high station, nor will they be able to complete the royal work. Being unable, they will cast off the yoke of their duties. The elder, wise ministers, though capable of completing their tasks, will not receive high station and, thinking, 'What are these matters to us? We have become outsiders. Let the young boys inside know,' they will not perform the duties that arise. Thus, in every way, there will be only decline for those kings. It will be like a time when trainable calves, unable to bear the yoke, are yoked to it, and like a time when great oxen, capable of bearing the yoke, are not yoked in their turn. This is the result of the fourth dream.

5. Adhammikarājakāleyeva adhammikabālarājāno adhammike lolamanusse vinicchaye ṭhapessanti, te pāpapuññesu anādarā bālā sabhāyaṃ nisīditvā vinicchayaṃ dentā ubhinnampi atthapaccatthikānaṃ hatthato lañjaṃ gahetvā khādissanti asso viya dvīhi mukhehi yavasīsaṃ. Ayaṃ pañcamassa vipāko.

5. In the very time of unrighteous kings, foolish and unrighteous rulers will appoint unrighteous and fickle men to positions of judgment. Those foolish men, having no respect for evil and meritorious deeds, sitting in the assembly and giving judgment, will take bribes from the hands of both litigants and devour them, like a horse eating an ear of barley with two mouths. This is the result of the fifth dream.

6. Adhammikāyeva vijātirājāno jātisampannānaṃ kulaputtānaṃ āsaṅkāya yasaṃ na dassanti, akulīne vaḍḍhessanti, evaṃ mahākulāni duggatāni bhavissanti, lāmakakulāni issarāni. Te ca kulīnā purisā jīvituṃ asakkontā “ime nissāya jīvissāmā”ti akulīnānaṃ dhītaro dassanti, iti tāsaṃ kuladhītānaṃ akulīnehi saddhiṃ saṃvāso jarasiṅgālassa suvaṇṇapātiyaṃ passāvakaraṇasadiso bhavissati. Ayaṃ chaṭṭhassa vipāko.

6. Unrighteous kings of low birth, being suspicious of sons of good family endowed with noble birth, will not grant them high station. They will promote the low-born. Thus, great families will become destitute, and lowly families will become powerful. And those men of good family, unable to make a living, thinking, 'We shall live by depending on these,' will give their daughters to the low-born. Thus, the cohabitation of those daughters of good family with low-born men will be like an old jackal urinating into a golden bowl. This is the result of the sixth dream.

7. Gacchante gacchante kāle itthiyo purisalolā surālolā alaṅkāralolā visikhālolā āmisalolā bhavissanti dussīlā durācārā. Tā sāmikehi kasigorakkhādīni kammāni katvā [V 2.0274] kicchena kasirena sambhataṃ dhanaṃ jārehi saddhiṃ suraṃ pivantiyo mālāgandhavilepanaṃ dhārayamānā antogehe accāyikampi kiccaṃ anoloketvā gehaparikkhepassa uparibhāgenapi chiddaṭṭhānehipi jāre upadhārayamānā sve vapitabbayuttakaṃ bījampi koṭṭetvā yāgubhattakhajjakāni sajjetvā khādamānā vilumpissanti heṭṭhāpīṭhakanipannakachātakasiṅgālī viya vaṭṭetvā vaṭṭetvā pādamūle nikkhittarajjuṃ. Ayaṃ sattamassa vipāko.

7. As time goes on, women will become lustful for men, fond of liquor, fond of adornments, fond of wandering the streets, and fond of material things; they will be immoral and of bad conduct. The wealth gathered with toil and trouble by their husbands through work such as ploughing and tending cattle, those women will squander. Drinking liquor with their lovers, wearing garlands, perfumes, and cosmetics, paying no attention to even urgent duties inside the house, and watching for their lovers through the upper parts of the house enclosure and through holes, they will pound even the seed grain that should be sown the next day, prepare gruel, rice, and savories, and, eating them, will waste everything. This will be like a hungry she-jackal lying under a bench, which eats the rope thrown at its feet again and again. This is the result of the seventh dream.

8. Gacchante gacchante kāle loko parihāyissati, raṭṭhaṃ nirojaṃ bhavissati, rājāno duggatā kapaṇā bhavissanti. Yo issaro bhavissati, tassa bhaṇḍāgāre satasahassamattā kahāpaṇā bhavissanti, te evaṃ duggatā sabbe janapade attano kammaṃ kārayissanti, upaddutā manussā sake kammante chaḍḍetvā rājūnaṃyeva atthāya pubbaṇṇāparaṇṇāni vapantā [M 2.0309] rakkhantā lāyantā maddantā pavesentā ucchukhettāni karontā yantāni vāhentā phāṇitādīni pacantā pupphārāme phalārāme ca karontā tattha tattha nipphannāni pupphaphalādīni āharitvā rañño koṭṭhāgārameva pūressanti, attano gehesu tucchakoṭṭhe olokentāpi na bhavissanti, tucchatucchakumbhe anoloketvā pūritakumbhapūraṇasadisameva bhavissati. Ayaṃ aṭṭhamassa vipāko.

8. As time goes on, the world will decline, kingdoms will become without essence, and kings will grow destitute and wretched. The ruler who remains will have only about a hundred thousand coins in his treasury. These impoverished rulers will force all the people in the land to work for them. Harassed, the people will abandon their own work and labor only for the kings’ benefit—sowing and guarding early and late crops, reaping, threshing, and bringing them in; making sugarcane fields, operating sugarcane presses, boiling molasses and so on; and making flower and fruit groves. Whatever flowers, fruits, and other things are produced there, they will gather and fill only the king’s storehouses. In their own homes, there will not even be anyone to look at their empty storehouses. It will be just like filling an already full pot while ignoring one's own utterly empty pots. This is the result of the eighth dream.

9. Gacchante gacchante kāle rājāno adhammikā bhavissanti, chandādivasena agatiṃ gacchantā rajjaṃ kāressanti, dhammena vinicchayaṃ nāma na dassanti, lañjavittakā bhavissanti dhanalolā, raṭṭhavāsikesu tesaṃ khantimettānuddayaṃ nāma na bhavissati, kakkhaḷā pharusā ucchuyante ucchugaṇṭhikā viya manusse pīḷentā nānappakāraṃ baliṃ uppādetvā dhanaṃ gaṇhissanti, manussā balipīḷitā kiñci dātuṃ asakkontā gāmanigamādayo chaḍḍetvā paccantaṃ gantvā vāsaṃ kappessanti, majjhimajanapado suñño bhavissati, paccanto ghanavāso seyyathāpi pokkharaṇiyā majjhe udakaṃ āvilaṃ pariyante vippasannaṃ. Ayaṃ navamassa vipāko.

9. As time goes on, kings will become unrighteous. Following the wrong course due to desire and so on, they will rule the kingdom. They will not give judgment according to the Dhamma. They will be desirous of bribes and greedy for wealth. Towards the inhabitants of the country, they will have no patience, loving-kindness, or compassion. Harsh and cruel, oppressing people like sugarcane joints in a sugarcane press, they will create various kinds of taxes and take their wealth. Oppressed by taxes and unable to give anything, people will abandon their villages and towns and go to the borderlands to make their dwelling. The central region will become empty, while the border region will be densely inhabited, just as in a pond the water in the middle is turbid while at the edge it is very clear. This is the result of the ninth.

10. Gacchante gacchante kāle rājāno adhammikā bhavissanti, tesu adhammikesu rājayuttāpi brāhmaṇagahapatikāpi negamajānapadāpīti samaṇabrāhmaṇe upādāya sabbe manussā adhammikā bhavissanti, tato tesaṃ ārakkhadevatā balipaṭiggāhikadevatā rukkhadevatā ākāsaṭṭhakadevatāti evaṃ devatāpi adhammikā bhavissanti, adhammikarājūnaṃ rajje vātā visamā kharā vāyissanti, te ākāsaṭṭhakavimānāni kampessanti, tesu kampitesu devatā kupitā devaṃ vassituṃ na dassanti, vassamānopi sakalaraṭṭhe ekappahāreneva na vassissati, vassamānopi sabbattha kasikammassa vā vappakammassa vā upakāro hutvā na vassissati. Yathā [V 2.0275] ca raṭṭhe, evaṃ janapadepi gāmepi ekataḷākassarepi ekappahāreneva na vassissati, taḷākassa uparibhāge vassanto heṭṭhābhāge na vassissati, heṭṭhā vassanto upari na vassissati, ekasmiṃ bhāge sassaṃ ativassena nassissati, ekasmiṃ avassanto milāyissati, ekasmiṃ sammā vassamāno sampādessati, evaṃ ekassa rañño rajje vuttā [M 2.0310] sassā tippakārā bhavissanti ekakumbhiyā odano viya. Ayaṃ dasamassa vipāko.

10. As time goes on, kings will become unrighteous. When those kings are unrighteous, their royal officials, brahmins and householders, and town and country folk—indeed, including ascetics and brahmins, all people will become unrighteous. Then their guardian deities, the deities who accept offerings, the tree deities, and the deities dwelling in the sky—thus, even the deities will become unrighteous. In the kingdom of unrighteous kings, the winds will blow unevenly and harshly, and they will shake the celestial mansions. When these are shaken, the angered deities will not allow the rain to fall. Even if it rains, it will not rain over the entire kingdom at once. Even when it rains, it will not rain everywhere so as to be a help to plowing or sowing. Just as in the kingdom, so too in the countryside, in a village, or even over a single lake or pond, it will not rain all at once. Raining on the upper part of a lake, it will not rain on the lower part. Raining on the lower part, it will not rain on the upper part. In one part, the crops will be destroyed by excessive rain; in another, they will wither from lack of rain; and in another, with proper rain, they will be brought to completion. Thus, in the kingdom of a single king, the sown crops will be of three kinds, like rice in a single pot. This is the result of the tenth.

11.
