Gacchante gacchante kāle sāsane parihāyante paccayalolā alajjikā bahū bhikkhū bhavissanti, te bhagavatā paccayaloluppaṃ nimmathetvā kathitadhammadesanaṃ cīvarādicatupaccayahetu paresaṃ desessanti, paccayehi mucchitvā niratthakapakkhe ṭhitā nibbānābhimukhaṃ katvā desetuṃ na sakkhissanti, kevalaṃ “padabyañjanasampattiñceva madhurasaddañca sutvā mahagghāni cīvarāni dassanti”iccevaṃ desessanti. Apare antaravīthicatukkarājadvārādīsu nisīditvā kahāpaṇaaḍḍhakahāpaṇapādamāsakarūpādīnipi nissāya desessanti. Iti bhagavatā nibbānagghanakaṃ katvā desitaṃ dhammaṃ catupaccayatthāya ceva kahāpaṇaaḍḍhakahāpaṇādiatthāya ca vikkiṇitvā desentā satasahassagghanakaṃ candanasāraṃ pūtitakkena vikkiṇantā viya bhavissanti. Ayaṃ ekādasamassa vipāko.

11. As time goes on, and the Dispensation declines, many shameless monks, greedy for requisites, will arise. They will teach to others the Dhamma discourse spoken by the Blessed One for crushing greed for requisites, but they will do so for the sake of robes and the other four requisites. Infatuated by requisites, they will be unable to teach while standing in the path of deliverance and making Nibbāna their aim. Instead, they will teach only with the thought, 'Having heard the perfection of words and phrases and a sweet voice, they will give us expensive robes.' Others, sitting in the middle of streets, at crossroads, royal gates, and such places, will teach dependent on coins, half-coins, quarter-coins, māsakas, rūpas, and the like. Thus, teaching by selling the Dhamma—which the Blessed One taught as having the value of Nibbāna—for the sake of the four requisites and for the sake of coins, half-coins, and the like, they will be like those who sell sandalwood core worth a hundred thousand for sour buttermilk. This is the result of the eleventh.

12. Adhammikarājakāle loke viparivattanteyeva rājāno jātisampannānaṃ kulaputtānaṃ yasaṃ na dassanti, akulīnānaññeva dassanti, te issarā bhavissanti, itare daliddā. Rājasammukhepi rājadvārepi amaccasammukhepi vinicchayaṭṭhānepi tucchalābusadisānaṃ akulīnānaṃyeva kathā osīditvā ṭhitā viya niccalā suppatiṭṭhitā bhavissati, saṅghasannipātepi saṅghakammagaṇakammaṭṭhānesu ceva pattacīvarapariveṇādivinicchayaṭṭhānesu ca dussīlānaṃ pāpapuggalānaṃyeva kathā niyyānikā bhavissati, na lajjibhikkhūnanti evaṃ sabbathāpi tucchalābūnaṃ sīdanakālo viya bhavissati. Ayaṃ dvādasamassa vipāko.

12. In the time of unrighteous kings, when the world is changing, kings will not bestow honor upon sons of good family endowed with noble birth, but will bestow it only upon the low-born. These will become powerful, while the others will be impoverished. Even in the presence of the king, at the royal gate, before ministers, or in places of judgment, the words of the low-born—who are like empty gourds—will be unshakable and well-established, as if they have sunk in and stood firm. In assemblies of the Sangha, in places for Sangha acts and group acts, and in places of judgment concerning bowls, robes, monasteries, and so forth, the words of the immoral and evil individuals alone will be decisive, not those of conscientious monks. Thus, in every way, it will be like a time when empty gourds sink. This is the result of the twelfth.

13. Tādiseyeva kāle adhammikarājāno akulīnānaṃ yasaṃ dassanti, te issarā bhavissanti, kulīnā duggatā. Tesu na keci gāravaṃ karissanti, itaresuyeva karissanti, rājasammukhe vā amaccasammukhe vā vinicchayaṭṭhāne vā vinicchayakusalānaṃ ghanasilāsadisānaṃ kulaputtānaṃ kathā na ogāhitvā patiṭṭhahissati. Tesu kathentesu “kiṃ ime kathentī”ti itare parihāsameva karissanti, bhikkhusannipātepi vuttappakāresu ṭhānesu neva pesale bhikkhū garukātabbe maññissanti, nāpi nesaṃ [M 2.0311][V 2.0276] kathā pariyogāhitvā patiṭṭhahissati, silānaṃ plavakālo viya bhavissati. Ayaṃ terasamassa vipāko.

13. In such a time, unrighteous kings will grant honor to the low-born; they will become rulers, while the high-born will be destitute. No one will show respect to the high-born; respect will be shown only to the low-born. In the presence of the king, or of ministers, or in the hall of justice, the words of noble scions skilled in judgment, who are like solid rock, will not penetrate and become established. When they speak, the others will only mock them, saying, “What are these men saying?” Even in a gathering of monks, in the aforementioned places, they will not consider the virtuous monks worthy of respect, nor will their words penetrate and become established. It will be like a time when rocks float. This is the result of the thirteenth dream.

14. Loke parihāyanteyeva manussā tibbarāgādijātikā kilesānuvattakā hutvā taruṇataruṇānaṃ attano bhariyānaṃ vase vattissanti, gehe dāsakammakarādayopi gomahiṃsādayopi hiraññasuvaṇṇampi sabbaṃ tāsaṃyeva āyattaṃ bhavissati, “asukahiraññasuvaṇṇaṃ vā paricchedādijātaṃ vā kaha”nti vutte “yattha vā tattha vā hotu, kiṃ tuyhiminā byāpārena, tvaṃ mayhaṃ ghare santaṃ vā asantaṃ vā jānitukāmo jāto”ti vatvā nānappakārehi akkositvā mukhasattīhi koṭṭetvā dāsaceṭakaṃ viya vase katvā attano issariyaṃ pavattessanti, evaṃ madhukapupphappamāṇamaṇḍūkapotikānaṃ āsīvise kaṇhasappe gilanakālo viya bhavissati. Ayaṃ cuddasamassa vipāko.

14. As the world declines, people will become of a nature of intense passion and so on, followers of the defilements. They will live under the power of their very young wives, and everything in the household—servants, workers, cattle, buffaloes, gold, and silver—will be entirely dependent on them. If asked, “Where is such-and-such gold or silver, or goods of a certain kind?” they will reply, “Let it be wherever it may be. What is this business to you? Have you become desirous of knowing what is or is not in my house?” And having spoken thus, they will revile them in various ways, striking them with mouth-daggers, and having brought them under their power like a slave or servant, they will exert their own authority. Thus, it will be like a time when venomous black snakes swallow young frogs the size of madhuka flowers. This is the result of the fourteenth dream.

15. Dubbalarājakāle rājāno hatthisippādīsu akusalā yuddhesu avisāradā bhavissanti, te attano rājādhipaccaṃ āsaṅkamānā samānajātikānaṃ kulaputtānaṃ issariyaṃ adatvā attano pādamūlikanhāpakakappakādīnaṃ dassanti, jātigottasampannā kulaputtā rājakule patiṭṭhaṃ alabhamānā jīvikaṃ kappetuṃ asamatthā hutvā issariyaṭṭhāne jātigottahīne akulīne upaṭṭhahantā vicarissanti, suvaṇṇarājahaṃsehi kākassa parivāritakālo viya bhavissati. Ayaṃ pannarasamassa vipāko.

15. In the time of weak kings, the rulers will be unskilled in the arts of elephants and so on, and lacking boldness in battle. Fearing for their own sovereignty, they will grant authority not to noble scions of equal birth but to their own foot-servants, bath-attendants, barbers, and the like. Noble scions endowed with birth and lineage, unable to find a position in the royal court and incapable of making a living, will wander about attending upon those of low birth and ignoble lineage in positions of authority. It will be like a time when a crow is surrounded by golden royal swans. This is the result of the fifteenth dream.

16. Adhammikarājakāleyeva ca akulīnāva rājavallabhā issarā bhavissanti, kulīnā appaññātā duggatā. Te rājavallabhā rājānaṃ attano kathaṃ gāhāpetvā vinicchayaṭṭhānādīsu balavanto hutvā dubbalānaṃ paveṇiāgatāni khettavatthuādīni “amhākaṃ santakāni etānī”ti abhiyuñjitvā te “na tumhākaṃ, amhāka”nti āgantvā vinicchayaṭṭhānādīsu vivadante vettalatādīhi pahārāpetvā gīvāyaṃ gahetvā apakaḍḍhāpetvā “attano pamāṇaṃ na jānātha, amhehi saddhiṃ vivadatha, idāni vo rañño kathetvā hatthapādacchedādīni kāressāmā”ti santajjessanti, te tesaṃ bhayena attano santakāni khettavatthūni “tumhākaṃyeva [M 2.0312] tāni, gaṇhathā”ti niyyātetvā attano gehāni pavisitvā bhītā nipajjissanti. Pāpabhikkhūpi pesale bhikkhū yathāruci viheṭhessanti, pesalā bhikkhū paṭisaraṇaṃ alabhamānā araññaṃ pavisitvā gahanaṭṭhānesu nilīyissanti, evaṃ hīnajaccehi ceva pāpabhikkhūhi ca upaddutānaṃ jātimantakulaputtānañceva pesalabhikkhūnañca eḷakānaṃ bhayena tasavakānaṃ palāyanakālo viya bhavissati[V 2.0277]. Ayaṃ soḷasamassa vipāko. Evaṃ tassa tassa atthassa pubbanimittabhūte soḷasa supine passi. Tena vuttaṃ – “kosalarājā viya soḷasa supine”ti. Ettha ca pubbanimittato attano atthānatthanimittaṃ supinaṃ passanto attano kammānubhāvena passati, kosalarājā viya lokassa atthānatthanimittaṃ supinaṃ passanto pana sabbasattasādhāraṇakammānubhāvena passatīti veditabbaṃ.

16. Moreover, in the time of unrighteous kings, only the low-born, the royal favorites, will be rulers, while the high-born will be unknown and destitute. Those royal favorites, having made the king accept their words, will become powerful in the halls of justice and so on. They will sue for the ancestral fields and lands of the weak, claiming, “These are our possessions!” When the owners come to the halls of justice and dispute, saying, “They are not yours, they are ours!” the favorites will have them beaten with canes and the like, seized by the neck, and dragged away. They will threaten them, saying, “You do not know your place, disputing with us! Now we will speak to the king and have your hands and feet cut off!” Terrified by them, the owners will relinquish their own fields and lands, saying, “They are yours indeed, take them!” and, entering their own homes, they will lie down in fear. Wicked monks, too, will harass virtuous monks as they please. The virtuous monks, finding no refuge, will enter the forest and hide in impenetrable places. Thus, for the high-born men of good family and the virtuous monks oppressed by the low-born and by wicked monks, it will be like a time of wild beasts fleeing in fear of goats. This is the result of the sixteenth dream. In this way, he saw the sixteen dreams that were portents of these various future events. Hence it is said: “like the Kosala king, sixteen dreams.” And here it should be understood that one who sees a dream that is a portent of one's own benefit or harm sees it through the power of one's own kamma; but one who, like the Kosala king, sees a dream that is a portent of the world's benefit or harm, sees it through the power of kamma common to all beings.

Kuddhā hi devatāti nāgamahāvihāre mahātherassa kuddhā devatā viya. Rohaṇe kira nāgamahāvihāre mahāthero bhikkhusaṅghaṃ anapaloketvāva ekaṃ nāgarukkhaṃ chindāpesi. Rukkhe adhivatthā devatā therassa kuddhā paṭhamameva naṃ saccasupinena palobhetvā pacchā “ito te sattadivasamatthake upaṭṭhāko rājā marissatī”ti supine ārocesi. Thero taṃ kathaṃ āharitvā rājorodhānaṃ ācikkhi. Tā ekappahāreneva mahāviravaṃ viraviṃsu. Rājā “kiṃ eta”nti pucchi. Tā ‘evaṃ therena vutta”nti ārocayiṃsu. Rājā divase gaṇāpetvā sattāhe vītivatte therassa hatthapāde chindāpesi. Ekantasaccameva hotīti phalassa saccabhāvato vuttaṃ, dassanaṃ pana vipallatthameva. Teneva pahīnavipallāsā pubbanimittabhūtampi supinaṃ na passanti, dvīhi tīhi vā kāraṇehi kadāci supinaṃ passantīti āha “saṃsaggabhedato”ti. “Asekkhā na passanti pahīnavipallāsattā”ti vacanato catunnampi kāraṇānaṃ vipallāso eva mūlakāraṇanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

The phrase 'the deity was angry' refers to an incident like that of the deity who was angry with the great elder at Nāgamahāvihāra. It is said that in Rohaṇa, at the Nāgamahāvihāra, a great elder, without consulting the Saṅgha of monks, had a certain nāga tree cut down. The deity dwelling in the tree became angry with the elder. First, she enticed him with a true dream, and later announced in another dream: “Seven days from now, the king who is your supporter will die.” The elder reported this matter to the royal women. They all raised a great wail at once. The king asked, “What is this?” They replied, “This is what the elder said.” The king had the days counted, and when seven days had passed, he had the elder’s hands and feet cut off. The dream is said to be 'absolutely true' because of the truth of the result, but the vision itself was distorted. For that reason, those who have abandoned perversions do not see even dreams that are portents. It is said that they may occasionally see a dream due to two or three causes, such as 'due to a disturbance of association.' From the saying, “Asekhas do not see dreams because they have abandoned perversions,” it should be understood that perversion itself is the root cause of all four causes.

Tanti supinakāle pavattaṃ bhavaṅgacittaṃ. Rūpanimittādiārammaṇanti kammanimittagatinimittato aññaṃ rūpanimittādiārammaṇaṃ na hoti. Īdisānīti paccakkhato anubhūtapubbaparikappitarūpādiārammaṇāni ceva rāgādisampayuttāni ca. Sabbohārikacittenāti pakaticittena. Dvīhi antehi muttoti [M 2.0313] kusalākusalasaṅkhātehi dvīhi antehi mutto. Āvajjanatadārammaṇakkhaṇeti idaṃ yāva tadārammaṇuppatti, tāva pavattaṃ cittavāraṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. “Supineneva diṭṭhaṃ viya me, sutaṃ viya meti kathanakāle pana abyākatoyeva āvajjanamattasseva uppajjanato”ti vadanti. Evaṃ vadantehi pañcadvāre dutiyamoghavāre viya manodvārepi āvajjanaṃ dvattikkhattuṃ uppajjitvā javanaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā bhavaṅgaṃ otaratīti adhippetanti daṭṭhabbaṃ ekacittakkhaṇikassa āvajjanassa uppattiyaṃ “diṭṭhaṃ viya me, sutaṃ viya me”ti kappanāya asambhavato.

That is the bhavaṅga-consciousness that occurs at the time of dreaming. As for 'an object such as a form-image': it is not an object such as a form-image that is other than a kamma-sign or a destiny-sign. Such things are: both objects such as form-images that have been previously experienced directly or imagined, and minds associated with lust, etc., arise. By 'unconventional consciousness' is meant the natural consciousness. 'Free from the two extremes' means free from the two extremes designated as wholesome and unwholesome. 'The moment of adverting and registering-consciousness'—this is said in reference to a thought-process that occurs for as long as there is the arising of registering-consciousness. They say: 'At the time of saying, “It was as if I saw in a dream, as if I heard,” it is only indeterminate because only adverting arises.' It should be understood that by those who say thus, it is intended that, just as in the second inoperative process at the five doors, so too at the mind door, adverting arises two or three times, stands in the place of javana, and sinks into bhavaṅga; because in the arising of an adverting that lasts for a single mind-moment, the conceiving, 'It was as if I saw, as if I heard,' is impossible.

Ettha ca “supinantepi tadārammaṇavacanato paccuppannavasena vā atītavasena vā sabhāvadhammāpi supinante ārammaṇaṃ hontī”ti vadanti. “Yadipi supinante vibhūtaṃ hutvā upaṭṭhite [V 2.0278] rūpādivatthumhi tadārammaṇaṃ vuttaṃ, tathāpi supinante upaṭṭhitanimittassa parikappavasena gahetabbatāya dubbalabhāvato dubbalavatthukattāti vutta”nti tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Keci pana “karajakāyassa nirussāhasantabhāvappattito tannissitaṃ hadayavatthu na suppasannaṃ hoti, tato tannissitāpi cittuppatti na suppasannā asuppasannavaṭṭinissitadīpappabhā viya, tasmā dubbalavatthukattāti ettha dubbalahadayavatthukattā”ti atthaṃ vadanti, vīmaṃsitvā yuttataraṃ gahetabbaṃ.

Here, they say, “Even in dreams, because of the statement regarding registering-consciousness, even intrinsic phenomena, whether by way of the present or by way of the past, become objects in dreams.” “Although in dreams, when an object such as a visible form appears vividly, registering-consciousness is said to occur, still, because the sign that has arisen in a dream must be grasped through conceptualization, it is said to have a weak basis due to its weakness.” This is stated in all three Ganthipadas. Some, however, say, “Because the kamma-born body has attained a state devoid of energy and tranquility, the heart-basis dependent on it is not very clear. Therefore, the arising of consciousness dependent on it is also not very clear, like the light of a lamp dependent on an unclear wick. Thus, ‘having a weak basis’ here means ‘having a weak heart-basis.’” Having investigated, the more suitable meaning should be accepted.

Supinantacetanāti manodvārikajavanavasena pavattā supinante cetanā. Supinañhi passanto manodvārikeneva javanena passati, na pañcadvārikena. Paṭibujjhanto ca manodvārikeneva paṭibujjhati, na pañcadvārikena. Niddāyantassa hi mahāvaṭṭiṃ jāletvā dīpe cakkhusamīpaṃ upanīte paṭhamaṃ cakkhudvārikaṃ āvajjanaṃ bhavaṅgaṃ na āvaṭṭeti, manodvārikameva āvaṭṭeti, atha javanaṃ javitvā bhavaṅgaṃ otarati. Dutiyavāre cakkhudvārikaṃ āvajjanaṃ bhavaṅgaṃ āvaṭṭeti, tato cakkhuviññāṇādīni javanapariyosānāni pavattanti, tadanantaraṃ bhavaṅgaṃ pavattati. Tatiyavāre manodvārikaāvajjanena bhavaṅge āvaṭṭite manodvārikajavanaṃ javati, tena cittena “kiṃ ayaṃ imasmiṃ ṭhāne āloko”ti jānāti. Tathā niddāyantassa kaṇṇasamīpe tūriyesu paggahitesu ghānasamīpe sugandhesu vā duggandhesu vā pupphesu upanītesu mukhe sappimhi vā phāṇite vā pakkhitte piṭṭhiyaṃ pāṇinā pahāre dinne paṭhamaṃ sotadvārikādīni āvajjanāni bhavaṅgaṃ na āvaṭṭenti[M 2.0314], manodvārikameva āvaṭṭeti, atha javanaṃ javitvā bhavaṅgaṃ otarati. Dutiyavāre sotadvārikādīni āvajjanāni bhavaṅgaṃ āvaṭṭenti, tato sotaghānajivhākāyaviññāṇādīni javanapariyosānāni pavattanti, tadanantaraṃ bhavaṅgaṃ pavattati. Tatiyavāre manodvārikaāvajjanena bhavaṅge āvaṭṭite manodvārikajavanaṃ javati, tena cittena ñatvā “kiṃ ayaṃ imasmiṃ ṭhāne saddo, saṅkhasaddo bherisaddo”ti vā “kiṃ ayaṃ imasmiṃ ṭhāne gandho, mūlagandho sāragandho”ti vā “kiṃ idaṃ mayhaṃ mukhe pakkhittaṃ, sappi phāṇita”nti vā “kenamhi piṭṭhiyaṃ pahaṭo, atithaddho me pahāro”ti vā vattā hoti, evaṃ manodvārikajavaneneva paṭibujjhati, na pañcadvārikena. Supinampi teneva passati, na pañcadvārikena.

‘Dream-volition’ is the volition in a dream that occurs by way of mind-door impulsion. For one who sees a dream sees it through the mind-door impulsion alone, not through the five-door impulsion. And when one awakens, it is through the mind-door impulsion alone that one awakens, not through the five-door impulsion. Indeed, for one who is sleeping, when a lamp with a large wick lit is brought near the eye, at first the eye-door adverting does not turn the life-continuum; only the mind-door adverting turns it. Then, after the impulsion has run, it sinks into the life-continuum. In the second process, the eye-door adverting turns the life-continuum, then eye-consciousness and the other processes ending in impulsion occur, after which the life-continuum occurs. In the third process, when the life-continuum has been turned by the mind-door adverting, the mind-door impulsion runs, and with that consciousness one knows, “What is this light in this place?” Similarly, for one who is sleeping, when musical instruments are played near the ear, or fragrant or foul-smelling flowers are brought near the nose, or ghee or molasses is placed in the mouth, or a blow is struck on the back with the hand, at first the advertings at the ear-door and other sense doors do not turn the life-continuum; only the mind-door adverting turns it. Then, after the impulsion has run, it sinks into the life-continuum. In the second process, the advertings at the ear-door and other sense doors turn the life-continuum, then ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and the other processes ending in impulsion occur, after which the life-continuum occurs. In the third process, when the life-continuum has been turned by the mind-door adverting, the mind-door impulsion runs, and having known with that consciousness, one is able to say, “What is this sound in this place? Is it the sound of a conch or the sound of a drum?” or “What is this smell in this place? Is it a root-smell or a heartwood-smell?” or “What is this placed in my mouth? Is it ghee or molasses?” or “By whom was I struck on the back? The blow to me is very hard.” Thus, one awakens only through the mind-door impulsion, not through the five-door impulsion. One also sees a dream only with that, not with the five-door impulsion.

Assāti assa āpattinikāyassa. Nanu ca ayuttoyaṃ niddeso “saṅgho ādimhi ceva sese ca icchitabbo assā”ti. Na hi āpattinikāyassa ādimhi ceva sese ca saṅgho icchito, kiñcarahi vuṭṭhānassāti imaṃ codanaṃ manasi sannidhāya yathā na virujjhati, tathā adhippāyaṃ vivaranto “kiṃ vuttaṃ hotī”tiādimāha. Āpattito vuṭṭhānassa ādimhi ceva sese [V 2.0279] ca icchito saṅgho āpattiyāva icchito nāma hotīti ayamettha adhippāyo. Āpattivuṭṭhānanti āpattito vuṭṭhānaṃ, anāpattikabhāvūpagamananti attho. Vacanakāraṇanti “saṅghādiseso”ti evaṃ vacane kāraṇaṃ. Samudāye niruḷho nikāya-saddo tadekadese pavattamānopi tāya eva ruḷhiyā pavattatīti āha ruḷīsaddenāti. Atha vā kiñci nimittaṃ gahetvā satipi aññasmiṃ taṃnimittayutte kismiñcideva visaye sammutiyā cirakālatāvasena nimittavirahepi pavattaniruḷho ruḷhī nāma. Yathā mahiyaṃ setīti mahiṃso, gacchatīti goti, evaṃ nikāya-saddassapi ruḷhibhāvo veditabbo. Ekasmimpi visiṭṭhe satipi sāmaññā viya samudāye pavattavohāro avayavepi pavattatīti āha avayave samūhavohārena vāti. Navamassa adhippāyassāti vīmaṃsādhippāyassa.

'Assa' means 'of that group of offenses.' Is not this directive inappropriate: 'The Saṅgha is required for it at the beginning and at the end'? For indeed, the Saṅgha is not required for the group of offenses at the beginning and at the end; rather, it is for the rehabilitation. Keeping this objection in mind, the commentator, explaining the intention in such a way that it does not conflict, said, beginning with 'What is meant?'. The intention here is this: the Saṅgha that is required at the beginning and at the end for rehabilitation from an offense is, in fact, called the Saṅgha required for the offense itself. 'Āpattivuṭṭhāna' means rehabilitation from an offense, that is, the attainment of a state of non-offense. 'The reason for the statement' means the reason for the statement 'saṅghādisesa.' The word 'nikāya,' established in the sense of a collection, even when it occurs in reference to a part of that collection, functions by that very established usage (ruḷhi); therefore, he said, 'by the established word (ruḷīsaddena).' Alternatively, 'ruḷhi' is the name for an established usage that, having taken some characteristic as a basis, continues to function by convention due to long duration, even when that characteristic is absent in some other context that possesses that characteristic. For example, 'mahiso' (buffalo) from 'mahiyaṃ seti' (it lies on the ground), and 'go' (cow) from 'gacchati' (it goes); similarly, the established nature of the word 'nikāya' should be understood. Even when there is a single distinguished item, the conventional term that applies to the collection as a general term also applies to a part; therefore, he said, 'or by the conventional term for the group applied to a part.' 'Of the ninth intention' means 'of the intention to investigate'.

238-239. Lomā etesaṃ santīti lomasā, bahulomāti vuttaṃ hoti. Arogo bhavissāmīti rāgapariḷāhavūpasamato nirogo bhavissāmi. Mocanenāti mocanatthāya upakkamakaraṇena. Upakkamakaraṇañhettha mocananti adhippetaṃ moceti etenāti katvā. Bījaṃ bhavissatīti coḷaggahaṇādikammaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ.

'Hairs (lomā) exist for them (etesaṃ), therefore (iti) they are lomasā (hairy)'; this means 'having many hairs.' 'I shall be free from disease' means: I shall be free from illness due to the subsiding of the fever of lust. 'By release' means by making an effort for the purpose of release. Here, making an effort is intended by 'release,' because one is released by means of this. 'There will be seed' is said with reference to the act of taking a cloth and so on.

240. Dve [M 2.0315] āpattisahassānīti khaṇḍacakkādibhedaṃ anāmasitvā vuttaṃ, icchantena pana khaṇḍacakkādibhedenapi āpattigaṇanā kātabbā. Missakacakkanti ubhatovaḍḍhanakaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Ettha ca nīlañca pītakañcātiādinā ekakkhaṇe anekavaṇṇānaṃ mocanādhippāyavacanaṃ yathādhippāyena mocanaṃ bhavatu vā mā vā, imināpi adhippāyena upakkamitvā mocentassa āpatti hotīti dassanatthaṃ. Na hi ekasmiṃ khaṇe nīlādīnaṃ sabbesampi mutti sambhavati. Aññaṃ vadatīti attano dosaṃ ujuṃ vattuṃ asakkonto puna puṭṭho aññaṃ bhaṇati.

240. 'Two thousand offenses' is said without considering the distinctions such as the broken wheel; but by one who wishes, the counting of offenses should also be done by means of the distinctions such as the broken wheel. 'Mixed wheel' is said with reference to the 'increasing-on-both-sides' wheel. And here, the statement of the intention to release threads of many colors in a single moment, beginning with 'blue and yellow,' is for the purpose of showing that an offense is incurred by one who, having made an effort, releases with such an intention, whether the release occurs according to the intention or not. For indeed, the release of all of them—blue and so on—is not possible in a single moment. 'He speaks of another matter' means: being unable to state his own fault directly, when questioned again, he says something else.

Mocanassādoti mocanassa pubbabhāge pavattaassādo. Teneva “mocetuṃ assādo mocanassādo”ti vuttaṃ. Gehassitapemanti ettha geha-saddena gehe ṭhitā mātubhaginīādayo ajjhattikañātakā gahitā. Tesu mātupemādivasena uppanno sineho gehassitapemaṃ, aññattha pana gehassitapemanti pañcakāmaguṇikarāgo vuccati. Sampayuttaassādasīsenāti rāgasampayuttasukhavedanāmukhena. Ekena padenāti gehassitapema-padena.

'Savoring of release' (mocanassādo) is the savoring that occurs in the preliminary stage of release. For that very reason, it is said, 'The savoring is in releasing, thus it is the savoring of release.' Here, in the phrase 'gehassitapema' (affection based on the household), by the word 'geha' (household), internal relatives who dwell in the home, such as mother, sister, and so on, are to be understood. The affection that arises towards them by way of a mother's love and so on is called 'gehassitapema.' Elsewhere, however, 'gehassitapema' refers to lust related to the five strands of sensual pleasure. 'With associated savoring as the head' means by way of pleasant feeling associated with lust. 'By one term' means by the term 'gehassitapema'.

Tathevāti mocanassādacetanāya eva. Pubbabhāge mocanassādavasena katappayogaṃ avijahitvāva sayitattā “sace pana…pe… saṅghādiseso”ti vuttaṃ. Puna suddhacitte uppanne tassa [V 2.0280] payogassa paṭippassaddhattā “suddhacitto…pe… anāpattī”ti vuttaṃ. Jagganatthāyāti dhovanatthāya. Anokāsanti aṅgajātappadesaṃ.

'Just so' means precisely by the volition of savoring release. Because of having fallen asleep without abandoning the effort made in the preliminary stage by way of savoring release, it is said, 'If, however... (etc.)... a saṅghādisesa offense.' Again, when a pure mind has arisen, because that effort has subsided, it is said, 'With a pure mind... (etc.)... no offense.' 'For the purpose of staying awake' means for the purpose of washing. 'An inappropriate place' means the region of the sexual organ.

263-264. Gehassitakāmavitakkanti pañcakāmaguṇasannissitaṃ kāmavitakkaṃ. Vatthiṃ daḷhaṃ gahetvāti aṅgajātassa agge passāvaniggamanaṭṭhāne cammaṃ daḷhaṃ gahetvā. Nimitte upakkamābhāvato “mocanassādādhippāyassapi mutte anāpattī”ti vuttaṃ.

'A thought of sensual desire based on the household' means a thought of sensual desire connected with the five strands of sensual pleasure. 'Having firmly grasped the penis-head' means having firmly grasped the skin at the tip of the sexual organ, at the place of urine's egress. Because of the absence of an effort at the sign, it is said, 'Even for one with the intention of savoring release, there is no offense if there is an emission'.

265. “Ehi me tvaṃ, āvuso, sāmaṇerāti āṇattiyā aññena katopi payogo attanāva kato nāma hotīti katvā āpatti vuttā. Yadi pana anāṇatto sayameva karoti, aṅgapāripūriyā abhāvato anāpattī”ti vadanti. Suttasāmaṇeravatthusmiṃ asucimhi muttepi aṅgajātassa gahaṇapaccayā dukkaṭaṃ vuttaṃ, na pana muttapaccayā.

265. Regarding 'Come, friend novice,' an offense is stated because an effort made by another through a command is considered as made by oneself. But if one who is not commanded does it of his own accord, there is no offense due to the non-fulfillment of the factors—so they say. In the story of the sleeping novice, even though impurity was emitted, a dukkaṭa offense is stated because of the condition of grasping the sexual organ, but not because of the condition of the emission.

266. Kāyatthambhanavatthusmiṃ [M 2.0316] calanavasena yathā aṅgajātepi upakkamo sambhavati, tathāpi vijambhitattā āpatti vuttā. “Pacchato vā”ti vacanato ubhosu passesu kaṭiyaṃ ūruppadesopi gahitoyevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ, tasmā ubhosupi passesu ṭhatvā imasmiṃ okāse nimittanti upanijjhāyantassapi āpattiyeva. “Aṅgajāta”nti vacanato nimittanti passāvamaggova vutto. Ummīlananimīlanavasena pana na kāretabboti ummīlananimīlanappayogavasaena āpattibhedo na kāretabboti attho. Anekakkhattumpi ummīletvā nimīletvā upanijjhāyantassa ekameva dukkaṭanti vuttaṃ hoti. Akkhīni avipphandetvā abhimukhaṃ sampattassa mātugāmassa nimittolokanepi āpattiyevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Dārudhītalikalepacittānaṃ aṅgajātupanijjhānepi dukkaṭa”nti vadanti.

266. In the story of stiffening the body, although an effort can occur in the sexual organ by way of movement, an offense is stated because of the stretching. From the words 'or from behind,' it should be understood that the region of the hips and thighs on both sides is also included. Therefore, for one who stands on both sides and gazes intently, thinking, 'This is the sign in this place,' there is indeed an offense. From the word 'sexual organ,' the sign is said to be the urinary passage itself. 'But a distinction should not be made by way of opening and closing the eyes' means that a distinction of offenses should not be made based on the effort of opening and closing the eyes. This means it is said that for one who gazes intently, opening and closing the eyes many times, there is only a single dukkaṭa offense. It should be understood that there is indeed an offense even in looking at the sign of a woman who has come directly in front, without moving the eyes. They say, 'There is a dukkaṭa offense even in gazing intently at the sexual organ of wooden dolls, clay figures, or paintings.'

267. Pupphāvalīti kīḷāvisesassādhivacanaṃ. Taṃ kīḷantā nadīādīsu chinnataṭaṃ udakena cikkhallaṃ katvā tattha ubho pāde pasāretvā nisinnā papatanti. “Pupphāvaliya”ntipi pāṭho. Pavesentassāti dvikammakattā vālikaṃ aṅgajātanti ubhayatthāpi upayogavacanaṃ kataṃ. Vālikanti vālikāyāti attho. Cetanā, upakkamo, muccananti imānettha tīṇi aṅgāni veditabbāni.

267. 'Pupphāvalī' is a name for a particular type of game. Those who play it, in rivers and so forth, having made a muddy place on a collapsed bank with water, sit there with both legs stretched out and slide down. There is also the reading 'Pupphāvaliyaṃ'. Because the verb 'paveseti' is transitive with two objects, the accusative case is used in both instances: 'vālikaṃ' and 'aṅgajātaṃ'. 'Vālikaṃ' means 'in the sand'. Herein, these three factors should be known: intention, undertaking, and release.

Sukkavissaṭṭhisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule concerning the emission of semen is concluded.

2. Kāyasaṃsaggasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

2. Explanation of the Training Rule Concerning Physical Contact

269. Dutiye [V 2.0281] yesu vivaṭesu andhakāro hoti, tāni vivarantoti brāhmaṇiyā saddhiṃ kāyasaṃsaggaṃ samāpajjitukāmo evamakāsi. Tena katassapi vippakārassa attani katattā “attano vippakāra”nti vuttaṃ. Uḷārattatāti uḷāracittatā, paṇītādhimuttatāti vuttaṃ hoti.

269. In the second training rule, desiring to engage in physical contact with the brahmin woman, he acted thus, opening those places which are dark when opened. Because the violation committed by him was committed against her, it is said, 'violation of herself'. 'Uḷārattatā' means 'the state of having a noble mind', 'the state of being inclined toward the sublime'; thus it is said.

270. Otiṇṇoti idaṃ kammasādhanaṃ kattusādhanaṃ vā hotīti tadubhayavasena atthaṃ dassento “yakkhādīhi viya sattā”tiādimāha. Asamapekkhitvāti yathāsabhāvaṃ anupaparikkhitvā, yathā te ratijanakā rūpādayo [M 2.0317] visayā aniccadukkhāsubhānattākārena avatthitā, tathā apassitvāti vuttaṃ hoti.

270. This word 'otiṇṇo' can be a derivation in the objective sense or a derivation in the agentive sense. Therefore, showing the meaning according to both of these, the Commentator said, 'beings as if possessed by yakkhas, etc.' 'Asamapekkhitvā' means not investigating their intrinsic nature; it means not seeing that those sense-objects which generate delight, such as visible forms, etc., are established in the mode of impermanence, suffering, foulness, and non-self.

271. Saññamavelanti sīlamariyādaṃ. Ācāroti ācaraṇaṃ hatthagahaṇādikiriyā. Assāti “kāyasaṃsaggaṃ samāpajjeyyā”ti padassa.

271. 'Saññamavelaṃ' means the boundary of virtue. 'Ācāro' means conduct, the act of taking the hand and so forth. 'Assa' refers to the word 'samāpajjeyya' in the phrase 'kāyasaṃsaggaṃ samāpajjeyya'.

273. Etesaṃ padānaṃ vasenāti āmasanādipadānaṃ vasena. Ito cito ca…pe… sañcopetīti attano hatthaṃ vā kāyaṃ vā tiriyaṃ ito cito ca sañcāreti. “Kāyato amocetvāvāti vacanato matthakato paṭṭhāya hatthaṃ otārentassa kāyato mocetvā nivatthasāṭakūpari omasantassa thullaccayaṃ, sāṭakato otāretvā jaṅghato paṭṭhāya kāyaṃ omasantassa puna saṅghādiseso”ti vadanti.

273. 'By means of these words' means by means of the words 'touching', etc. 'Moves... from here and there' means one moves one's hand or body sideways, from here and there. According to the phrase 'without releasing from the body', they say: 'For one lowering the hand starting from the head, if one releases it from the body and rubs over the worn lower garment, there is a thullaccaya offense. If one lowers it from the lower garment and rubs the body starting from the shin, there is again a saṅghādisesa offense.'

Dvādasasupi āmasanādippayogesu ekekasmiṃ payoge kāyato amocite ekekāva āpatti hotīti āha “mūlaggahaṇameva pamāṇa”nti. Idañca ekena hatthena kāyaṃ gahetvā itarena hatthena kāyaparāmasanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Ekena pana hatthena kāyapaṭibaddhaṃ gahetvā itarena tattha tattha kāyaṃ parāmasato payogagaṇanāya āpatti. Ayaṃ pana saṅghādiseso na kevalaṃ vatthuvaseneva, apica saññāvasenapīti āha “itthiyā itthisaññissa saṅghādiseso”ti. Pāḷiyaṃ tiracchānagato ca hotīti ettha tiracchānagatitthiyā tiracchānagatapurisassa ca gahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ.

In all twelve applications, such as touching, for each single application where the hand is not released from the body, there is only a single offense. Therefore, it is said, 'The initial grasp itself is the standard.' And this is said with reference to grasping the body with one hand and rubbing the body with the other hand. But for one who, having grasped something attached to the body with one hand, rubs the body here and there with the other, there is an offense for each count of application. This saṅghādisesa offense, however, is not based solely on the object, but also on perception. Therefore, it is said, 'For one who has the perception of "woman" with regard to a woman, there is a saṅghādisesa.' In the Pāḷi text, where it says 'and is an animal', the grasping of a female animal and a male animal should be understood.

Samasārāgoti kāyasaṃsaggarāgena ekasadisarāgo. Purimanayenevāti rajjuvatthādīhi parikkhipitvā gahaṇe vuttanayena. Puna purimanayenevāti samasārāgo vutto. Anantaranayenevāti kāyapaṭibaddhaāmasananayena[V 2.0282]. Veṇiggahaṇena lomānampi saṅgahitattā lomānaṃ phusanepi saṅghādiseso vutto. Idāni vuttamevatthaṃ pakāsetukāmo “upādinnakena hī”tiādimāha.

'Samasārāgo' means having a similar lust, that is, a lust similar to the lust for physical contact. 'Purimanayeneva' means by the method stated regarding grasping after encircling with ropes, cloths, etc. Again, 'by the previous method' refers to 'samasārāgo'. 'Anantaranayeneva' means by the immediately following method, that is, the method of rubbing what is attached to the body. Because hair is also included by the taking up of 'braid', a saṅghādisesa is stated even for touching hair. Now, desiring to clarify the meaning already stated, the Commentator said, 'For by what is appropriated...', etc.

Yathāniddiṭṭhaniddeseti yathāvuttakāyasaṃsagganiddese. Tenāti tena yathāvuttakāraṇena. Saññāya virāgitamhīti saññāya viraddhāya. Liṅgabyattayena “virāgitamhī”ti vuttaṃ. Imaṃ nāma vatthunti imasmiṃ sikkhāpade āgataṃ [M 2.0318] sandhāya vadati. Aññampi yaṃ kiñci vatthuṃ sandhāya vadatītipi keci. Sārattanti kāyasaṃsaggarāgena sārattaṃ. Virattanti kāyasaṃsaggarāgarahitaṃ mātubhaginīādiṃ sandhāya vadati. “Virattaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti virattaṃ gaṇhi, dukkaṭanti mātupemādivasena gahaṇe dukkaṭaṃ vuttaṃ.

'Yathāniddiṭṭhaniddese' means in the exposition of physical contact as stated. 'Tena' means by that reason as stated. 'Saññāya virāgitamhi' means when the perception is mistaken. 'Virāgitamhi' is said by way of a change of gender. 'This very object' refers to the object that comes in this training rule. Some say it also refers to any other object whatsoever. 'Sārattaṃ' means impassioned with the lust for physical contact. 'Virattaṃ' refers to one who is free from the lust for physical contact, such as a mother or sister. '"I will grasp one who is dispassionate"; he grasps one who is dispassionate; this is a dukkaṭa offense.' The dukkaṭa is stated for grasping by way of maternal affection, etc.

Imāya pāḷiyā sametīti sambandho. Kathaṃ sametīti ce? Yadi hi “itthiyā kāyapaṭibaddhaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti citte uppanne itthisaññā virāgitā bhaveyya, kāyapaṭibaddhaggahaṇe thullaccayaṃ vadantena bhagavatā “itthī ca hoti itthisaññī cā”ti na vattabbaṃ siyā, vuttañca, tasmā “itthiyā kāyapaṭibaddhaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti kāyaṃ gaṇhantassa itthisaññā virāgitā nāma na hotīti “kāyapaṭibaddhaṃ gaṇhissāmīti kāyaṃ gaṇhanto yathāvatthukameva āpajjatī”ti mahāsumattherena vuttavādo imāya pāḷiyā sameti. Yo panettha “satipi itthisaññāya kāyapaṭibaddhaṃ gaṇhantassa gahaṇasamaye ‘kāyapaṭibaddhaṃ gaṇhissāmī’ti saññaṃ ṭhapetvā ‘itthiṃ gaṇhāmī’ti saññāya abhāvato vatthusaññānaṃ bhinnattā ayutta”nti vadeyya, so pucchitabbo “kiṃ kāyapaṭibaddhaṃ vatthādiṃ gaṇhanto itthiyā rāgena gaṇhāti, udāhu vatthādīsu rāgenā”ti. Yadi “vatthādīsu rāgena gaṇhātī”ti vadeyya, itthiyā kāyapaṭibaddhaṃ ahutvā aññattha ṭhitaṃ vatthādiṃ gaṇhantassapi thullaccayaṃ siyā, tasmā itthī itthisaññā sārattabhāvo gahaṇañcāti aṅgapāripūrisabbhāvato mahāsumattheravādova yuttavādo. Aṭṭhakathāvinicchayehi ca sametīti etthāpi ayamadhippāyo – yadi saññāvirāgena virāgitaṃ nāma siyā, “sambahulā itthiyo bāhāhi parikkhipitvā gaṇhāmī”ti evaṃsaññissa “majjhagatitthiyo kāyapaṭibaddhena gaṇhāmī”ti evarūpāya saññāya abhāvato majjhagatānaṃ vasena thullaccayaṃ na siyā, evaṃ santepi aṭṭhakathāya thullaccayassa vuttattā saññāvirāgena virāgitaṃ nāma na hotīti ayamattho siddhoyevāti. Nīlena duviññeyyasabhāvato kāḷitthī vuttā.

The connection is that it aligns with this Pāḷi text. If it is asked, 'How does it align?' If, when the thought arises, 'I will take what is connected to a woman’s body,' the perception of a woman had faded, then the Blessed One, when speaking of a thullaccaya offense for taking what is connected to the body, would not have said, 'There is a woman and there is the perception of a woman.' But it was said. Therefore, for one who takes the body thinking, 'I will take what is connected to a woman’s body,' the perception of a woman is not considered to have faded. Thus, the statement made by the Great Elder Suma, 'One who takes the body thinking, "I will take what is connected to the body," incurs the offense according to the object,' aligns with this Pāḷi text. If someone here were to say, 'This is not right because, although there is the perception of a woman, for one who takes what is connected to a woman’s body, at the time of taking, having established the perception "I will take what is connected to the body," there is an absence of the perception "I am taking a woman," and thus the perceptions of the objects are different,' he should be asked, 'When taking cloth, etc., connected to the body, does one take it with lust for the woman, or with lust for the cloth, etc.?' If he were to say, 'One takes it with lust for the cloth, etc.,' then a thullaccaya offense would be incurred even for taking cloth, etc., that is not connected to a woman’s body but is located elsewhere. Therefore, because of the complete fulfillment of the factors—namely, the woman, the perception of a woman, the state of being impassioned, and the act of taking—the view of the Great Elder Suma is the correct view. And it aligns with the Commentaries and the Vinicchayas. Here too, this is the intention: if it were considered faded due to the fading of perception, then for one with the perception, 'I will take many women by embracing them with my arms,' there would be no thullaccaya offense with respect to the women in the middle, due to the absence of a perception of the kind, 'I am taking the women in the middle by what is connected to the body.' Even so, because a thullaccaya offense is stated in the Commentary, it is not considered faded due to the fading of perception. This meaning is indeed established. By 'dark' (nīla), a dark-skinned woman is meant, due to the nature of being difficult to discern.

279. Sevanādhippāyoti phassasukhasevanādhippāyo. Itthiyā kāyena bhikkhussa kāyapaṭibaddhāmasanavārepi [V 2.0283] phassaṃ paṭivijānātīti idaṃ attano kāyapaṭibaddhāmasanepi kāyasambandhasabhāvato vuttaṃ. Etthāti nissaggiyena nissaggiyavāre. Mokkhādhippāyoti ettha paṭhamaṃ kāyasaṃsaggarāge satipi pacchā mokkhādhippāyassa anāpatti.

279. 'The intention to indulge' means the intention to indulge in the pleasure of contact. The statement 'he is aware of the contact' even in the instance of a woman's body touching what is attached to a bhikkhu's body, is said because of the nature of bodily connection, even in the case of touching what is attached to his own body. 'Here' means in the section on what is to be forfeited, by means of what is to be forfeited. 'The intention for release': here, even if there is at first lust for bodily contact, there is no offense for one who afterwards has the intention for release.

281. Pāripanthikāti [M 2.0319] vilumpanikā, antarāyikāti vuttaṃ hoti. Nadīsotena vuyhamānaṃ mātaranti ukkaṭṭhaparicchedadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ, aññāsupi pana itthīsu kāruññādhippāyena mātari vuttanayena paṭipajjantassa nevatthi dosoti vadanti. “Mātara”nti vuttattā aññāsaṃ na vaṭṭatīti vadantāpi atthi. Tiṇaṇḍupakanti hirīverādimūlehi katacumbaṭakaṃ. Tālapaṇṇamuddikanti tālapaṇṇehi kataaṅgulimuddikaṃ. Parivattetvāti attano nivāsanapārupanabhāvato apanetvā, cīvaratthāya apanāmetvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Cīvaratthāya pādamūle ṭhapeti, vaṭṭatīti idaṃ nidassanamattaṃ, paccattharaṇavitānādiatthampi vaṭṭatiyeva, pūjādiatthaṃ tāvakālikampi gahetuṃ vaṭṭati.

281. 'Robbers' means plunderers; it means those who cause an obstacle. 'A mother being carried away by a river current' is said to show the highest limit. However, some say there is no fault for one who acts towards other women with an intention of compassion in the manner stated for a mother. There are also those who say that because 'mother' is specified, it is not allowable for others. 'A grass-ball' means a pad made from the roots of vetiver, etc. 'A palm-leaf ring' means a finger-ring made from palm leaves. 'Having exchanged' means having removed it from its state of being one's lower or upper garment; it means having set it aside for the purpose of a robe. 'He places it at his feet for the purpose of a robe; it is allowable'—this is merely an example; it is also allowable for the purpose of a ground-covering, a canopy, etc. It is allowable to take it temporarily for the purpose of an offering, etc.

Itthisaṇṭhānena katanti ettha heṭṭhimaparicchedato pārājikavatthubhūtatiracchānagatitthīnampi anāmāsabhāvato tādisaṃ itthisaṇṭhānena kataṃ tiracchānagatarūpampi anāmāsanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Bhikkhunīhi paṭimārūpaṃ āmasituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti ācariyā. Itthirūpāni dassetvā kataṃ vatthañca paccattharaṇañca bhittiñca itthirūpaṃ anāmasitvā gaṇhituṃ vaṭṭati. Bhinditvāti ettha hatthena aggahetvāva kenacideva daṇḍādinā bhinditabbaṃ. Ettha ca “anāmāsampi hatthena aparāmasitvā daṇḍādinā kenaci bhindituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti idha vuttattā “paṃsukūlaṃ gaṇhantena mātugāmasarīrepi satthādīhi vaṇaṃ katvā gahetabba”nti vuttattā ca gahitamaṇḍūkasappiniṃ daṇḍādīhi nippīḷetvā maṇḍūkaṃ vissajjāpetuṃ vaṭṭati.

Here, regarding 'made in the shape of a woman': because even female animals, which are the basis for a pārājika offense according to the lowest limit, are not to be touched, it should be understood that such an animal form made in the shape of a woman is also not to be touched. The teachers say, 'It is allowable for bhikkhunīs to touch a statue.' It is allowable to take cloth, a ground-covering, and a wall made displaying female forms, without touching the female form. Here, regarding 'having broken': it should be broken with something like a stick, without taking hold of it with the hand. And here, because it is said in this context, 'Even what is not to be touched, it is allowable to break with something like a stick without touching it with the hand,' and because it is said, 'When taking a rag-robe, it should be taken even by making a wound on a woman's body with a knife, etc.,' it is allowable to squeeze a female snake that has caught a frog with a stick, etc., and make it release the frog.

Maggaṃ adhiṭṭhāyāti magge gacchāmīti evaṃ maggasaññī hutvāti attho. Kīḷantenāti idaṃ gihisantakaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, bhikkhusantakaṃ pana yena kenaci adhippāyena anāmasitabbameva durupaciṇṇabhāvato. Tālapanasādīnīti cettha ādi-saddena nāḷikeralabujatipusaalābukumbhaṇḍapussaphalaeḷālukaphalānaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. “Yathāvuttaphalānaṃyeva cettha kīḷādhippāyena āmasanaṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti vuttattā pāsāṇasakkharādīni kīḷādhippāyenapi āmasituṃ vaṭṭati.

The meaning of 'having resolved on the path' is: having the perception of the path, thus, 'I will go on the path.' 'By one playing'—this is said with reference to the property of householders. But a bhikkhu's property is not to be touched with any intention whatsoever, because it is an improperly practiced act. Here, in 'palmyra, jackfruit, etc.,' by the word 'etc.' the inclusion of coconuts, breadfruits, cucumbers, bottle gourds, pumpkins, snake gourds, and muskmelons should be understood. Because it is said, 'Here, it is not allowable to touch only the aforementioned fruits with the intention of play,' it is allowable to touch stones, pebbles, etc., even with the intention of play.

Muttāti hatthikumbhajādikā aṭṭhavidhā muttā. Tathā hi hatthikumbhaṃ, varāhadāṭhaṃ, bhujaṅgasīsaṃ, valāhakaṃ, veḷu, macchasiro, saṅkho, sippīti aṭṭha muttāyoniyo. Tattha hatthikumbhajā [V 2.0284] pītavaṇṇā pabhāvihīnā. Varāhadāṭhajā [M 2.0320] varāhadāṭhavaṇṇāva. Bhujaṅgasīsajā nīlādivaṇṇā suvisuddhā vaṭṭalā. Valāhakajā ābhāsūrā dubbibhāgarūpā rattibhāge andhakāraṃ viddhamantiyo tiṭṭhanti, devūpabhogā eva ca honti. Veḷujā karakaphalasamānavaṇṇā na ābhāsūrā, te ca veḷū amanussagocare eva padese jāyanti. Macchasirajā pāṭhīnapiṭṭhisamaānavaṇṇā vaṭṭalā laghavo ca honti pabhāvihīnā ca, te ca macchā samuddamajjheyeva jāyanti. Saṅkhajā saṅkhaudaracchavivaṇṇā kolaphalappamāṇāpi honti pabhāvihīnāva. Sippijā pabhāvisesayuttā honti nānāsaṇṭhānā. Evaṃ jātito aṭṭhavidhāsu muttāsu yā macchasaṅkhasippijā, tā sāmuddikā. Bhujaṅgajāpi kāci sāmuddikā honti, itarā asāmuddikā. Yasmā bahulaṃ sāmuddikāva muttā loke dissanti, tatthāpi sappijāva, itarā kadāci kāci, tasmā sammohavinodaniyaṃ “muttāti sāmuddikā muttā”ti vuttaṃ.

Pearls are of eight kinds, such as those originating from an elephant's frontal globes. Indeed, there are eight sources of pearls: an elephant's frontal globe, a boar's tusk, a serpent's head, a cloud, bamboo, a fish's head, a conch, and an oyster. Among these, those from an elephant's frontal globe are yellow in color and lacking in radiance. Those from a boar's tusk are the very color of a boar's tusk. Those from a serpent's head are of blue and other colors, are very pure, and are round. Those from a cloud are radiant, have a form difficult to discern; at night, they stand dispelling the darkness, and are fit only for the enjoyment of deities. Those from bamboo are the color of a karaka fruit and are not radiant; and those bamboos grow only in a region that is not the resort of humans. Those from a fish's head are the color of a pāṭhīna fish's back, are round, light, and are lacking in radiance; and those fish are born only in the middle of the ocean. Those from a conch are the color of the inner surface of a conch, can be the size of a jujube fruit, and are also lacking in radiance. Those from an oyster are endowed with special radiance and are of various shapes. Thus, among the eight kinds of pearls by origin, those from fish, conches, and oysters are marine. Some from serpents are also marine, while the others are non-marine. Since marine pearls are mostly seen in the world, and among them, especially those from oysters, while the others are seen only sometimes, it is therefore stated in the Sammohavinodanī: 'Pearls are marine pearls.'

Maṇīti ṭhapetvā veḷuriyādike seso jotirasādibhedo sabbopi maṇi. Veḷuriyoti vaṃsavaṇṇamaṇi. Saṅkhoti sāmuddikasaṅkho. Silāti kāḷasilāpaṇḍusilāsetasilādibhedā sabbāpi silā. Rajatanti kahāpaṇādikaṃ vuttāvasesaṃ ratanasammataṃ. Jātarūpanti suvaṇṇaṃ. Lohitaṅkoti rattamaṇi. Masāragallanti kabaramaṇi. Bhaṇḍamūlatthāyāti pattacīvarādibhaṇḍamūlatthāya. Kuṭṭharogassāti nidassanamattaṃ, tāya vūpasametabbassa yassa kassaci rogassatthāyapi vaṭṭatiyeva. “Bhesajjatthañca adhiṭṭhāyeva muttā vaṭṭatī”ti tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Ākaramuttoti ākarato muttamatto. “Bhaṇḍamūlatthāya sampaṭicchituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti iminā ca āmasitumpi vaṭṭatīti dasseti. Pacitvā katoti kācakārehi pacitvā kato.

By 'gem' (maṇi) is meant any remaining gem of the kind such as jotirasa, etc., setting aside beryl and so on. By 'beryl' (veḷuriya) is meant a gem the color of bamboo. By 'conch' (saṅkho) is meant a marine conch. By 'crystal' (silā) is meant all crystal, of the kinds such as black crystal, pale crystal, white crystal, and so on. By 'silver' (rajata) is meant that which is considered a treasure, remaining from what has been said, such as the kahāpaṇa. By 'gold' (jātarūpa) is meant suvaṇṇa. By 'ruby' (lohitaṅko) is meant a red gem. By 'cat's eye' (masāragalla) is meant a variegated gem. By 'for the capital for goods' (bhaṇḍamūlatthāya) is meant for the capital for goods such as the bowl and robes. The phrase 'for leprosy' (kuṭṭharogassa) is just an example; it is indeed allowable for the sake of any disease whatsoever that is to be cured by it. 'And for medicinal purposes, an unpierced pearl is allowable'—this is stated in all three Gaṇṭhipada commentaries. By 'pearl from a mine' (ākaramutto) is meant a pearl extracted from a mine. By the phrase 'it is allowable to accept for the capital for goods,' he shows that it is also allowable to touch. By 'made by firing' (pacitvā kato) is meant that which is made by glassmakers by firing.

Dhotaviddho ca ratanamissoti alaṅkāratthaṃ kañcanalatādiṃ dassetvā kato ratanakhacito dhotaviddho anāmāso. Dhotaviddho ca ratanamisso cāti visuṃ vā padaṃ sambandhitabbaṃ. Pānīyasaṅkhoti iminā ca saṅkhena katapānīyabhājanapidhānādisamaṇaparikkhāropi āmasituṃ vaṭṭatīti siddhaṃ. Sesanti ratanamissaṃ ṭhapetvā avasesaṃ. Muggavaṇṇaṃyeva ratanasammissaṃ [M 2.0321] karonti, na aññanti āha “muggavaṇṇāvā”ti, muggavaṇṇā ratanamissāva na vaṭṭatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Sesāti ratanasammissaṃ ṭhapetvā avasesā muggavaṇṇā nīlasilā.

By 'polished, pierced, and mixed with gems' is meant a polished and pierced item set with gems, made for the purpose of ornamentation by displaying gold vines and so forth; it is not to be touched. Or, the words 'polished and pierced' and 'mixed with gems' should be connected separately. And by this phrase 'water conch' (pānīyasaṅkho), it is established that it is allowable to touch even the requisites of a monk, such as a drinking vessel, lid, etc., made from a conch. By 'the rest' is meant the remainder, setting aside that which is mixed with gems. He said 'or mung-bean colored' because they make only mung-bean colored items mixed with gems, not others. It comes to be said that mung-bean colored items mixed with gems are not allowable. By 'the rest' is meant the remaining mung-bean colored blue crystal, setting aside that which is mixed with gems.

Bījato paṭṭhāyāti dhātupāsāṇato paṭṭhāya. Suvaṇṇacetiyanti dhātukaraṇḍakaṃ. Paṭikkhipīti “dhātuṭṭhapanatthāya gaṇhathā”ti avatvā “tumhākaṃ gaṇhathā”ti pesitattā paṭikkhipi. Suvaṇṇabubbuḷakanti suvaṇṇatārakaṃ. “Keḷāpayitunti ito cito ca sañcārantehi āmasituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti [V 2.0285] mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Kacavarameva harituṃ vaṭṭatīti cetiyagopakā vā bhikkhū hontu aññe vā, hatthenapi puñchitvā kacavaraṃ apanetuṃ vaṭṭati, malampi pamajjituṃ vaṭṭatiyeva.

By 'from the seed' is meant from the ore-stone. By 'golden shrine' (suvaṇṇacetiya) is meant a relic casket. He refused because he was sent with the instruction 'You take it for yourselves,' without being told, 'Take it for the purpose of enshrining the relics.' By 'golden bubble' (suvaṇṇabubbuḷaka) is meant a golden star. In the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā it is said: 'It is allowable for monks who are moving it from here to there to touch it.' It is allowable to remove only the rubbish. Whether they are monks who are shrine-keepers or other monks, it is allowable to remove the rubbish by sweeping even with the hand, and it is indeed allowable to wipe away the dirt.

Ārakūṭalohanti kittimalohaṃ. Tīṇi hi kittimalohāni kaṃsalohaṃ, vaṭṭalohaṃ, ārakūṭanti. Tattha tiputambe missetvā kataṃ kaṃsalohaṃ, sīsatambe missetvā kataṃ vaṭṭalohaṃ, pakatirasatambe missetvā kataṃ ārakūṭaṃ. Teneva taṃkaraṇena nibbattattā “kittimaloha”nti vuccati. “Jātarūpagatikamevāti vuttattā ārakūṭaṃ suvaṇṇasadisameva āmasituṃ na vaṭṭati, aññaṃ pana vaṭṭatī”ti tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Keci pana “ārakūṭaṃ anāmasitabbato jātarūpagatikamevāti vuttaṃ, tasmā ubhayampi jātarūpaṃ viya āmasituṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti. Paṭhamaṃ vuttoyeva ca attho gaṇṭhipadakārehi adhippeto. Paṭijaggituṃ vaṭṭatīti senāsanapaṭibaddhattā vuttaṃ.

By 'ārakūṭa metal' (ārakūṭaloha) is meant artificial metal. Indeed, there are three kinds of artificial metal: bronze (kaṃsaloha), brass (vaṭṭaloha), and ārakūṭa. Among these, bronze is made by mixing tin and copper; brass is made by mixing lead and copper; and ārakūṭa is made by mixing natural mercury and copper. Because it is produced by that very process, it is called 'artificial metal.' 'Because it is said, "It is in the category of gold," ārakūṭa, being just like gold, is not to be touched, but the others are allowable'—this is stated in all three Gaṇṭhipada commentaries. But some say: 'Because ārakūṭa is not to be touched, it is said, "It is in the category of gold"; therefore, both bronze and brass are also not to be touched, like gold.' But the meaning stated first is the one intended by the authors of the Gaṇṭhipada. It is said that it is allowable to maintain because it is connected with the lodging.

Sāmikānaṃ pesetabbanti sāmikānaṃ sāsanaṃ pesetabbaṃ. Bhinditvāti hatthena aggahetvā aññena yena kenaci bhinditvā. Bherisaṅghāṭoti saṅghaṭitacammabherī. Vīṇāsaṅghāṭoti saṅghaṭitacammavīṇā. Cammavinaddhānaṃ bherivīṇānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tucchapokkharanti avinaddhacammaṃ bheripokkharaṃ vīṇāpokkharañca. Āropitacammanti bheriādīnaṃ vinaddhanatthāya mukhavaṭṭiyaṃ āropitacammaṃ tato uddharitvā visuṃ ṭhapitacammañca. Onahituṃ vāti bheripokkharādīni cammaṃ āropetvā vinandhituṃ. Onahāpetuṃ vāti tatheva aññehi vinandhāpetuṃ. Pārājikappahonakakāleti akuthitakāle.

By 'it should be sent to the owners' is meant a message should be sent to the owners. By 'having broken' is meant having broken it by some means or other, without taking hold of it with the hand. By 'drum-assembly' (bherisaṅghāṭa) is meant a drum with hide stretched over it. By 'lute-assembly' (vīṇāsaṅghāṭa) is meant a lute with hide stretched over it. This is a designation for drums and lutes that are bound with hide. By 'empty shell' (tucchapokkhara) is meant a drum-head and a lute-head that do not have hide stretched over them. By 'hide placed on' is meant hide placed on the rim of the mouth of a drum, etc., for the purpose of binding, and also hide that has been removed from there and set aside separately. By 'or to stretch' is meant to bind drum-heads, etc., after placing the hide on them. By 'or to have stretched' is meant to have others bind them in the same way. By 'at a time sufficient for a pārājika offense' is meant at a time when it is not seething.

282. Saṅkamādi [M 2.0322] bhūmigatikattā na kāyapaṭibaddhaṭṭhāniyanti dukkaṭaṃ vuttaṃ. Ekapadikasaṅkamoti khuddakasetu. Sakaṭamaggasaṅkamoti sakaṭamaggabhūto mahāsetu. Ṭhānā cāletunti rajjuṃ ṭhānā cāletuṃ. Paṭicchādetabbāti apanetabbā. Manussitthī, itthisaññitā, kāyasaṃsaggarāgo, tena rāgena vāyāmo, hatthaggāhādisamāpajjananti imānettha pañca aṅgāni.

282. Because a bridge and so forth are of the nature of the ground, they are not a place connected to the body; hence, a dukkaṭa offense is stated. By 'single-plank bridge' is meant a small bridge. By 'cart-path bridge' is meant a large bridge that has become a cart path. By 'to move from its place' is meant to move a rope from its place. By 'should be concealed' is meant it should be removed. Herein, these are the five factors: a human woman, the perception of her as a woman, lust for bodily contact, the effort due to that lust, and the engaging in such acts as holding the hand.

Kāyasaṃsaggasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule concerning bodily contact is concluded.

3. Duṭṭhullavācāsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

3. Explanation of the Training Rule on Coarse Speech

283. Tatiye [V 2.0286] uttarapadalopena chinnaottappā “chinnikā”ti vuttāti āha “chinnikāti chinnaotappā”ti.

283. In the third training rule, due to the elision of the latter word, women whose moral dread is cut off are called 'chinnikā'; therefore, he said, “'Chinnikā' means one whose moral dread is cut off.”

285. Yathā yuvā yuvatinti etena obhāsane nirāsaṅkabhāvaṃ dasseti. Methunupasañhitāhīti idaṃ duṭṭhullavācāya sikhāppattalakkhaṇadassanaṃ. Itthilakkhaṇenāti vuttamatthaṃ vivarituṃ “subhalakkhaṇenā”ti vuttaṃ. Na tāva sīsaṃ etīti “itthilakkhaṇena samannāgatāsī”tiādinā vaṇṇabhaṇanaṃ saṅghādisesāpattijanakaṃ hutvā matthakaṃ na pāpuṇāti. Vaṇṇabhaṇanañhi yenākārena bhaṇantassa saṅghādiseso hoti, tenākārena bhaṇantassa sikhāppattaṃ nāma hoti. “Itthilakkhaṇena samannāgatāsītiādikaṃ pana duṭṭhullavācassādarāgavasena bhaṇantassa dukkaṭa”nti gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ.

285. By 'just as a young man to a young woman,' it shows the absence of hesitation in addressing. The phrase 'connected with sexual intercourse' indicates the characteristic of reaching the peak of coarse speech. To explain the meaning of 'with the characteristics of a woman,' the phrase 'with beautiful characteristics' was stated. 'It does not yet reach the head' means that praising with words such as 'you are endowed with the characteristics of a woman,' while being capable of causing a saṅghādisesa offense, does not reach its culmination. For praising in the manner that constitutes a saṅghādisesa offense for the speaker is called 'reaching the peak.' However, it is stated in the glosses: 'For one who speaks such as "you are endowed with the characteristics of a woman" due to lustful delight in coarse speech, there is a dukkaṭa offense.'

Ekādasahi padehi aghaṭite sīsaṃ na etīti “animittāsī”tiādīhi ekādasahi padehi aghaṭite avaṇṇabhaṇanaṃ sīsaṃ na eti, avaṇṇabhaṇanaṃ nāma na hotīti vuttaṃ hoti. Ghaṭitepīti ekādasahi padehi avaṇṇabhaṇane ghaṭitepi. Imehi tīhi ghaṭiteyeva saṅghādisesoti “sikharaṇī”tiādīhi tīhiyeva padehi avaṇṇabhaṇane ghaṭiteyeva saṅghādiseso passāvamaggassa niyatavacanattā accoḷārikattā ca. Animittāsītiādīhi pana aṭṭhahi padehi ghaṭite kevalaṃ avaṇṇabhaṇanameva [M 2.0323] sampajjati, na saṅghādiseso, tasmā tāni thullaccayavatthūnīti keci. Akkosanamattattā dukkaṭavatthūnīti apare. Paribbājikāvatthusmiṃ viya thullaccayamevettha yuttataraṃ dissati. Kuñcikapaṇālimattanti kuñcikāchiddamattaṃ.

When not connected with the eleven phrases, it does not reach the head. This means that when dispraise is not connected with the eleven phrases beginning with 'you are without the sign,' it does not reach the head; that is to say, it is not called dispraise. 'Even when connected' means even when dispraise is connected with the eleven phrases. 'Only when connected with these three is it a saṅghādisesa' means that only when dispraise is connected with just the three phrases beginning with 'sikharaṇī' is it a saṅghādisesa offense, because it is a specific statement about the urinary passage and because of its extreme coarseness. However, when connected with the eight phrases beginning with 'you are without the sign,' only dispraise is accomplished, not a saṅghādisesa offense. Therefore, some say these are grounds for a thullaccaya offense. Others say they are grounds for a dukkaṭa offense because it is merely abuse. As in the case of the female wanderer, a thullaccaya offense seems more suitable here. 'The size of a key-spout' means the size of a keyhole.

286-287. Garukāpattinti bhikkhuniyā kāyasaṃsagge pārājikāpattiṃ sandhāya vadati. Hasanto hasantoti sabhāvadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Ahasantopi vācassādarāgena punappunaṃ vadati, āpattiyeva. Kāyacittatoti hatthamuddāya obhāsantassa kāyacittato samuṭṭhāti.

'A grave offense' refers to the pārājika offense for a bhikkhunī in the case of bodily contact. 'Laughing, laughing' is said to show the natural state. Even if not laughing, if one speaks repeatedly out of lustful delight in the speech, it is indeed an offense. 'From body and mind' means that for one who addresses with a hand gesture, the offense arises from the body and mind.

288. Tasmā dukkaṭanti appaṭivijānanahetu dukkaṭaṃ, paṭivijānantiyā pana akhettapadattā thullaccayena bhavitabbaṃ. Teneva paribbājikāvatthusmiṃ paṭivijānantiyā thullaccayaṃ vakkhati.

288. Therefore, it is a dukkaṭa offense due to her not understanding. However, for one who does understand, because it is not a 'field-term,' there should be a thullaccaya offense. For this very reason, in the case of the female wanderer, a thullaccaya offense will be stated for her understanding.

289. Asaddhammaṃ [V 2.0287] sandhāyāhāti “vāpita”nti imassa bījanikkhepavacanattā vuttaṃ. Saṃsīdatīti vahati pavattati. Atha vā saṃsīdatīti saṃsīdissati. Manussitthī, itthisaññitā, duṭṭhullavācassādarāgo, tena rāgena obhāsanaṃ, taṅkhaṇavijānananti imānettha pañca aṅgāni.

289. The phrase 'he says, referring to the wrong dhamma' is stated because this word 'sown' is a term for depositing seed. 'It sinks' means it carries on, it proceeds. Alternatively, 'it sinks' means it will sink. Herein, these are the five factors: a human woman, the perception of her as a woman, lustful delight in coarse speech, addressing with that lust, and her understanding at that moment.

Duṭṭhullavācāsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule concerning coarse speech is concluded.

4. Attakāmapāricariyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

4. Explanation of the Training Rule on Service for One's Own Desire

290. Catutthe cīvaranti nivāsanādi yaṃ kiñci cīvaraṃ. Piṇḍapātanti yo koci āhāro. So hi piṇḍolyena bhikkhuno patte patanato tattha tattha laddhabhikkhānaṃ piṇḍānaṃ pāto sannipātoti vā piṇḍapātoti vuccati. Senāsananti sayanañca āsanañca. Yattha hi vihārādike seti nipajjati āsati nisīdati, taṃ senāsanaṃ. Pati eti etasmāti paccayoti āha “patikaraṇaṭṭhena paccayo”ti. Rogassa patiayanaṭṭhena vā paccayo, paccanīkagamanaṭṭhenāti attho, vūpasamanatthenāti vuttaṃ hoti. Dhātukkhobhalakkhaṇassa hi taṃhetukadukkhavedanālakkhaṇassa vā rogassa paṭipakkhabhāvo patiayanaṭṭho. Yassa kassacīti sappiādīsu yassa kassaci. Sappāyassāti hitassa vikāravūpasamenāti [M 2.0324] adhippāyo. Bhisakkassa kammaṃ tena vidhātabbato, tenāha “anuññātattā”ti. Nagaraparikkhārehīti nagaraṃ parivāretvā rakkhaṇakehi. Āvāṭaparikkhepo parikhā uddāpo pākāro esikā paligho pākāramatthakamaṇḍalanti satta nagaraparikkhārāti vadanti. Setaparikkhāroti suvisuddhasīlālaṅkāro. Ariyamaggo hi idha “ratho”ti adhippeto. Tassa ca sammāvācādayo alaṅkāraṭṭhena “parikkhāro”ti vuttā. Cakkavīriyoti vīriyacakko. Jīvitaparikkhārāti jīvitassa pavattikāraṇāni. Samudānetabbāti sammā uddhaṃ uddhaṃ ānetabbā pariyesitabbā. Parivāropi hoti antarāyānaṃ parito vāraṇato, tenāha – “jīvita…pe… rakkhaṇato”ti. Tattha antaranti vivaraṃ, okāsoti attho. Rakkhaṇatoti verikānaṃ antaraṃ adatvā attano sāmīnaṃ parivāretvā ṭhitasevakā viya rakkhaṇato. Assāti jīvitassa. Kāraṇabhāvatoti cirappavattiyā kāraṇabhāvato. Rasāyanabhūtañhi bhesajjaṃ sucirampi kālaṃ jīvitaṃ pavattetiyeva.

290. In the fourth, 'robe' refers to any robe, such as a lower garment and so on. 'Almsfood' means any kind of food. It is called 'almsfood' because it is the falling of lumps of food into the monk's bowl by collection, or it is the falling and gathering of lumps of alms obtained here and there. 'Lodging' refers to both a bed and a seat. For wherever one lies down, reclines, sits, or dwells in a dwelling place like a monastery, that is lodging. 'Condition' (paccaya) means 'that from which one goes towards' (pati eti etasmā); hence, he said, 'it is a condition in the sense of causing to attain.' Or it is a condition in the sense of going against a disease, meaning, in the sense of going against what is contrary; it is said to be in the sense of appeasing. For the state of being an antagonist to a disease—which is characterized by the disturbance of elements or by painful feeling caused by that—is the sense of 'going against' (patiayana). 'Of whatever' means: of whatever among ghee and so on. 'Of what is suitable' means: of what is beneficial; the intended meaning is 'by appeasing disorders.' It is the work of a physician, to be administered by him; hence, he said, 'because it has been permitted.' 'City fortifications' refers to those protecting by surrounding a city. They say the seven city fortifications are: a surrounding trench, a moat, a rampart, a wall, a gate-post, a cross-bar, and a pavilion on top of the wall. 'Pure adornment' refers to the completely pure ornament of virtue. Here, the Noble Path is intended by 'chariot.' And right speech and other factors are called 'adornments' in the sense of embellishing it. 'Wheel of energy' means the wheel of energy. 'Necessities of life' are the causes for the continuation of life. They should be properly brought forth and sought. It is also 'protection' (parivāra) because it wards off dangers all around; hence, he said, 'for the protection of life…' There, 'gap' means an opening, an opportunity. 'By guarding' means by guarding like servants who, not giving enemies an opening, stand surrounding their masters. 'Its' refers to 'of life.' 'Because it is a cause' means because it is a cause for long continuation. For medicine that is an elixir indeed prolongs life for a very long time.

291. Upacāreti yattha ṭhito viññāpetuṃ sakkoti, tādise. Kāmo ceva hetu ca pāricariyā ca attho. Sesaṃ byañjanantiādīsu pāḷiyaṃ “attakāma”nti padaṃ uddharitvā attano [V 2.0288] kāmaṃ, attano hetuṃ, attano adhippāyaṃ, attano pāricariyanti cattāro atthā padabhājane vuttā. Tesu paṭhame atthavikappe kāmo ca hetu ca pāricariyā ca attho, sesaṃ adhippāyapadamekaṃ byañjanaṃ paṭhamaviggahe tadatthassa asambhavabhāvato niratthakattā. Dutiye pana atthavikappe adhippāyo ca pāricariyā ca attho, kāmo ca hetu cāti sesaṃ padadvayaṃ byañjanaṃ tesaṃ tattha atthābhāvatoti evaṃ cattāri padāni dvinnaṃ viggahānaṃ vasena yojitānīti keci vadanti. Gaṇṭhipade ca ayamevattho vutto. Cūḷamajjhimamahāgaṇṭhipadesu pana “paṭhamasmiṃ atthavikappe kāmo ca hetu ca pāricariyā ca adhippāyattho, sesaṃ methunadhammasaṅkhātena kāmenātiādi viggahavākyaṃ akkharavivaraṇamattato byañjanamattaṃ. Dutiye atthavikappe adhippāyo ca pāricariyā ca adhippāyattho, sesaṃ attanā kāmitā icchitātiādi viggahavākyaṃ akkharavivaraṇamattato byañjanamatta”nti evamattho vutto[M 2.0325]. “Byañjane ādaraṃ akatvā”ti vacanato ayamevattho idha yuttataroti viññāyati. Byañjane ādaraṃ akatvāti iminā hi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaviggahavasena byañjane ādaraṃ akatvāti ayamattho dīpito.

291. Upacāreti: In such a place where, standing, one is able to make something known. In passages such as, 'Desire, cause, and service are the meaning; the rest is the letter,' having extracted the word 'attakāma' from the Pāḷi, four meanings are stated in the word analysis: one's own desire, one's own cause, one's own intention, and one's own service. Among these, in the first interpretation of meaning, desire, cause, and service are the meaning, while the remaining single word 'intention' is the letter, because in the first analysis its meaning is not possible and is therefore meaningless. But in the second interpretation of meaning, intention and service are the meaning, while desire and cause, the remaining two words, are the letter because they lack meaning there. Thus, some say, these four words are applied by way of the two analyses. And this same meaning is stated in the Gaṇṭhipada. However, in the Cūḷa-, Majjhima-, and Mahā-Gaṇṭhipadas, the following meaning is stated: 'In the first interpretation of meaning, desire, cause, and service are the intended meaning; the rest—the analytical phrase such as "by desire, which is designated as the sexual act"—is merely the letter, being only an explanation of the letters. In the second interpretation of meaning, intention and service are the intended meaning; the rest—the analytical phrase such as "desired and wished for by oneself"—is merely the letter, being only an explanation of the letters.' In accordance with the saying 'not paying attention to the letter,' it is understood that this very meaning is more appropriate here. For by this phrase, 'not paying attention to the letter,' this meaning is explained: that one should not pay attention to the letter in accordance with the analysis stated in the commentary.

Idāni yathāvuttamevatthaṃ padabhājanena saṃsanditvā dassetuṃ “attano kāmaṃ attano hetuṃ attano pāricariyanti hi vutte jānissanti paṇḍitā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “attano hetu”nti vutte attano atthāyāti ayamattho viññāyati. “Attano kāmaṃ attano pāricariya”nti ca vutte kāmena pāricariyāti ayamattho viññāyati. Tasmā attano kāmaṃ attano hetuṃ attano pāricariyanti imehi tīhi padehi attano atthāya kāmena pāricariyā attakāmapāricariyāti ayamatthavikappo vuttoti viññū jānissanti. “Attano adhippāya”nti vutte pana adhippāyasaddassa kāmitasaddena samānatthabhāvato attano pāricariyanti imassa ca ubhayaviggahasāmaññato attano icchitakāmitaṭṭhena attakāmapāricariyāti ayamatthavikappo dvīhi padehi dassitoti viññū jānissantīti.

Now, to explain the meaning just as has been stated by connecting it with the word analysis, it begins with: 'For when it is said, "one's own desire, one's own cause, one's own service," the wise will understand,' and so on. This is what is said: When 'one's own cause' is said, this meaning, 'for one's own benefit,' is understood. And when 'one's own desire, one's own service' is said, this meaning, 'service through desire,' is understood. Therefore, the wise will understand that by these three terms—'one's own desire, one's own cause, one's own service'—this interpretation of meaning, 'attakāmapāricariyā' as 'service for one's own benefit through desire,' is stated here. But when 'one's own intention' is said, because the word 'intention' has a meaning similar to the word 'desired,' and due to the commonality of both analyses of 'one's own service,' the wise will understand that this interpretation of meaning, 'attakāmapāricariyā' as 'in the sense of what is desired and wished for by oneself,' is shown here by two terms.

Etadagganti esā aggā. Duṭṭhullavācāsikkhāpade kiñcāpi methunayācanaṃ āgataṃ, tathāpi taṃ duṭṭhullavācassādarāgavasena vuttaṃ, idha pana attano methunassādarāgavasenāti ayaṃ viseso. Vinītavatthūsu “tena hi bhagini aggadānaṃ dehī”ti idaṃ attano atthāya vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Manussitthī, itthisaññitā, attakāmapāricariyāya rāgo, tena rāgena vaṇṇabhaṇanaṃ, taṅkhaṇavijānananti imānettha pañca aṅgāni.

'This is the foremost' means this service is the highest. In the training rule on coarse speech, although a request for sexual intercourse is mentioned, that is stated by way of lust consisting of delight in coarse speech. Here, however, it is by way of lust consisting of delight in one's own sexual intercourse—this is the distinction. Regarding the Vinītavatthus, 'Then, sister, give the foremost offering'—this should be understood as spoken for one's own benefit. A human woman; perception of her as a woman; lust for service for one's own desire; praising her virtues because of that lust; and her understanding it at that moment—these are the five factors here.

Attakāmapāricariyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule on Service for One's Own Desire is concluded.

5. Sañcarittasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

5. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Acting as a Go-between

296. Pañcame [V 2.0289] paṇḍitassa bhāvo paṇḍiccaṃ, ñāṇassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Gatimantāti ñāṇagatiyā samannāgatā. Paṇḍitāti iminā sabhāvañāṇena samannāgatatā vuttā, byattāti iminā itthikattabbesu visāradapaññāya. Tenāha “upāyaññū visāradā”ti. Medhāvinīti ṭhānuppattipaññāsaṅkhātāya tasmiṃ tasmiṃ atthakicce upaṭṭhite ṭhānaso taṅkhaṇe eva [M 2.0326] uppajjanapaññāya samannāgatā. Tenāha “diṭṭhaṃ diṭṭhaṃ karotī”ti. Chekāti yāgubhattasampādanādīsu nipuṇā. Uṭṭhānavīriyasampannāti kāyikena vīriyena samannāgatā, yathā aññā kusītā nisinnaṭṭhāne nisinnāva honti, ṭhitaṭṭhāne ṭhitāva, evaṃ ahutvā vipphārikena cittena sabbakiccaṃ nipphādetīti vuttaṃ hoti. Kumārikāyāti nimittatthe bhummaṃ, hetumhi vā karaṇavacanaṃ. Tenāha “kumārikāya kāraṇā”ti. Āvahanaṃ āvāho, pariggahabhāvena dārikāya gaṇhāpanaṃ, tathā dāpanaṃ vivāho. Tenāha “dārakassā”tiādi.

296. In the fifth, the state of a wise person is wisdom; this is a designation for knowledge. 'Endowed with understanding' means endowed with the path of knowledge. By 'wise,' being endowed with natural knowledge is stated. By 'skillful,' being endowed with intrepid wisdom in matters to be done by a woman is stated. Therefore, he said, 'knowing the means, intrepid.' 'Intelligent' means endowed with intelligence known as situational wisdom, which is wisdom that arises in that very moment when this or that task presents itself. Therefore, he said, 'She does what is seen as it is seen.' 'Capable' means skilled in the preparation of rice-gruel, cooked rice, and so on. 'Endowed with energetic effort' means endowed with bodily energy; it is said that, unlike other lazy women who just remain seated in a place for sitting or remain standing in a place for standing, she is not like that and accomplishes every task with a pervasive mind. As for 'for a maiden,' it is the locative case in the sense of purpose, or it is the instrumental case in the sense of cause. Therefore, he said, 'for the reason of a maiden.' Bringing is `āvāha`, causing a girl to be taken in the sense of taking possession. Likewise, causing to be given is `vivāha`. Therefore, he said, 'for a boy,' and so on.

297-298. Bhattapācanaṃ sandhāya randhāpanaṃ vuttaṃ, yassa kassaci pācanaṃ sandhāya pacāpanaṃ vuttaṃ. Duṭṭhuṃ kulaṃ gatā duggatāti imamatthaṃ dassento “yattha vā gatā”tiādimāha. Āharaṇaṃ āhāro. Na upāhaṭanti na dinnaṃ. Kayo gahaṇaṃ, vikkayo dānaṃ. Tadubhayaṃ saṅgaṇhitvā “vohāro”ti vuttaṃ. Maṇḍitapasādhitoti ettha bāhirupakaraṇena alaṅkaraṇaṃ maṇḍanaṃ, ajjhattikānaṃ kesādīnaṃyeva saṇṭhapanaṃ pasādhanaṃ.

The term `randhāpana`, 'causing to be cooked,' is stated with reference to the cooking of cooked rice; the term `pacāpana`, 'causing to be cooked,' is stated with reference to the cooking of anything whatsoever. Wishing to show this meaning, '`duggatā` means one who has gone to a bad family,' the commentator said, 'or wherever she has gone,' and so on. `Āharaṇaṃ`: Bringing. `Na upāhaṭaṃ`: 'Not brought' means not given. `Kayo`, buying, is taking; `vikkayo`, selling, is giving. Having combined those two, it is called `vohāro`, 'a transaction.' Here, in `maṇḍitapasādhito`, 'adorned and beautified,' `maṇḍana`, adornment, is embellishment with external accessories; `pasādhana`, beautification, is the arranging of internal things, namely hair and so on.

300. “Abbhutaṃ kātuṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti iminā dukkaṭaṃ hotīti dīpeti. “Parājitena dātabba”nti vuttattā adento dhuranikkhepena kāretabbo. Acirakāle adhikāro etassa atthīti acirakālādhikārikaṃ, sañcarittaṃ. “Acirakālācārika”nti vā pāṭho, acirakāle ācāro ajjhācāro etassāti acirakālācārikaṃ.

300. By the phrase, 'It is not proper to perform a marvel,' it shows that there is an offense of wrong-doing. Because it was said, 'It must be given by the one who is defeated,' a monk who does not give should be made to do so through the laying down of the burden. The act of being a go-between is `acirakālādhikārika` because for this person there is authority for a short time. Or, there is the reading `acirakālācārika`; it is so called because for this person there is conduct or transgression in a short time.

Kiñcāpi ehibhikkhūpasampannā ceva saraṇagamanūpasampannā ca sañcarittādipaṇṇattivajjaṃ āpattiṃ āpajjanti, tesaṃ pana na sabbakālikattā te vajjetvā sabbakālānurūpaṃ tantiṃ ṭhapento bhagavā idhāpi ñatticatuttheneva kammena upasampannaṃ bhikkhuṃ dassetuṃ “tatra yvāyaṃ bhikkhu…pe… ayaṃ imasmiṃ atthe adhippeto bhikkhū”ti padabhājanaṃ āha, na pana nesaṃ sañcarittādiāpajjane abhabbabhāvato. Khīṇāsavāpi hi appassutā kiñcāpi lokavajjaṃ nāpajjanti, paṇṇattiyaṃ pana akovidattā vihārakāraṃ kuṭikāraṃ sahāgāraṃ sahaseyyanti evarūpā [V 2.0290] kāyadvāre āpattiyo āpajjanti, sañcarittaṃ padasodhammaṃ uttarichappañcavācaṃ bhūtārocananti evarūpā vacīdvāre [M 2.0327] āpattiyo āpajjanti, upanikkhittasādiyanavasena manodvāre rūpiyapaṭiggahaṇāpattiṃ āpajjanti.

Although monks ordained by the 'Come, monk' formula and those ordained by taking the refuges do commit offenses that are faults by enactment, such as acting as a go-between, yet because these types of ordination are not for all time, the Blessed One, excluding them and establishing a textual tradition suitable for all time, here also, in order to show a monk ordained by a formal act with a motion and three announcements, spoke the word-analysis: 'Therein, whichever monk... this is the monk intended in this meaning.' He did not, however, speak thus because of their being incapable of committing offenses such as acting as a go-between. For even Arahants with little learning, although they do not commit offenses that are blameworthy in the world, yet because of being unskilled in the enactments, they commit such offenses through the body-door as those concerning a large dwelling, a hut, a shared dwelling, and a shared sleeping place. They commit such offenses through the speech-door as acting as a go-between, reciting the Dhamma word-by-word, speaking more than five or six words, and reporting an actual superior human state. Through the mind-door, by way of delighting in what is placed nearby, they commit the offense of accepting gold and silver.

301. Sañcaraṇaṃ sañcaro, so etassa atthīti sañcarī, tassa bhāvo sañcarittaṃ. Tenāha “sañcaraṇabhāva”nti, itthipurisānaṃ antare sañcaraṇabhāvanti attho. Jāyattane jārattaneti ca nimittatthe bhummaṃ, jāyabhāvatthaṃ jārabhāvatthanti vuttaṃ hoti. Jāyabhāveti bhariyabhāvāya. Jārabhāveti sāmikabhāvāya. Kiñcāpi imassa padabhājane “jārī bhavissasī”ti itthiliṅgavasena padabhājanaṃ vuttaṃ, jārattaneti pana niddesassa ubhayaliṅgasādhāraṇattā purisaliṅgavasenapi yojetvā atthaṃ dassento “itthiyā matiṃ purisassa ārocento jārattane ārocetī”tiādimāha.
