Ettha hi “jāro bhavissasī”ti itthiyā matiṃ purisassa ārocento jārattane āroceti nāma. Pāḷiyaṃ pana itthiliṅgavaseneva yojanā katā, tadanusārena purisaliṅgavasenapi sakkā yojetunti.

301. Going about is `sañcara`; one who has that is a `sañcarī`; the state of that one is `sañcaritta`. Therefore, he said, 'the state of going about'; the meaning is the state of going about between women and men. And in 'for wifehood' (`jāyattane`) and 'for paramourhood' (`jārattane`), it is the locative case in the sense of purpose; it is said to mean 'for the sake of being a wife' and 'for the sake of being a paramour.' 'For the state of being a wife' (`jāyabhāve`) means for the sake of being a wife. 'For the state of being a paramour' (`jārabhāve`) means for the sake of being a husband. Although in the word-analysis of this rule, the phrase 'you will be a female paramour' (`jārī bhavissasi`) is stated in the feminine gender, because the term `jārattane` is common to both genders, the commentator, wishing to show the meaning by applying it in the masculine gender as well, said, 'When conveying the intention of a woman to a man, one conveys it "for paramourhood",' and so on. Here, indeed, when conveying the intention of a woman to a man by saying, 'You will be a paramour' (`jāro bhavissasi`), it is called conveying 'for paramourhood.' In the Pāḷi text, however, the application is made only in the feminine gender; following that, it is also possible to apply it in the masculine gender.

Idāni pāḷiyaṃ vuttanayenapi atthaṃ dassento “apicā”tiādimāha. Pati bhavissasīti vuttamevatthaṃ “sāmiko bhavissasī”ti pariyāyavacanena visesetvā dasseti. Idañca jārattaneti niddesassa ubhayaliṅgasādhāraṇattā vuttaṃ. Muhuttikā bhavissasīti asāmikaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, jārī bhavissasīti sasāmikaṃ sandhāya. Antamaso taṅkhaṇikāyapīti idaṃ nidassanamattanti āha “etenevupāyenā”tiādi.

Now, the commentator, wishing to show the meaning also by the method stated in the Pāḷi text, said, 'Furthermore,' and so on. He shows the very meaning already stated as 'you will be a husband' (`pati bhavissasi`), having specified it with the synonymous term 'you will be a master' (`sāmiko bhavissasi`). And this was said because the term `jārattane` is common to both genders. 'You will be for a moment' (`muhuttikā bhavissasi`) is said with reference to a woman without a husband; 'you will be a female paramour' (`jārī bhavissasi`) is said with reference to a woman with a husband. This, 'even for an instant,' is merely an example; therefore, he said, 'by this same method,' and so on.

303. Serivihāranti sacchandacāraṃ. Attano vasanti attano āṇaṃ. Gottanti gotamagottādikaṃ gottaṃ. Dhammoti paṇḍaraṅgaparibbājakādīnaṃ, tesaṃ tesaṃ vā kulānaṃ dhammo. Gottavantesu gottasaddo, dhammacārīsu ca dhammasaddo vattatīti āha “sagottehī”tiādi. Tattha sagottehīti samānagottehi, ekavaṃsajātehīti attho. Sahadhammikehīti ekassa satthusāsane sahacaritabbadhammehi, samānakuladhammehi vā. Tenevāha “ekaṃ satthāra”ntiādi. Tattha “ekaṃ satthāraṃ uddissa pabbajitehī”ti iminā paṇḍaraṅgaparibbājakādayo vuttā, ekagaṇapariyāpannehīti mālākārādiekagaṇapariyāpannehi.

303. `Serivihāra` means acting according to one's own wish. `Attano vasanti` means one's own authority (`attano āṇaṃ`). `Gotta` means a clan, such as the Gotama clan. `Dhamma` means the practice of the Paṇḍaraṅga wanderers and so on, or the custom of those various families. He said, 'with those of the same clan' (`sagottehi`), etc., because the word `gotta` applies to those who have a clan, and the word `dhamma` applies to those who follow a custom. Therein, 'with those of the same clan' (`sagottehi`) means with those of an equal clan, that is, those born of the same lineage. 'With those of the same custom' (`sahadhammikehi`) means with those who have a practice to be followed together in the teaching of one teacher, or with those who have the same family custom. Therefore, he said, 'one teacher,' and so on. Therein, by this, 'with those who have gone forth dedicating themselves to one teacher,' the Paṇḍaraṅga wanderers and so on are stated. 'With those included in one group' (`ekagaṇapariyāpannehi`) means with those included in one group, such as garland-makers.

Sasāmikā [M 2.0328] sārakkhā. Yassā gamane raññā daṇḍo ṭhapito, sā saparidaṇḍā. Pacchimānaṃ dvinnanti sārakkhasaparidaṇḍānaṃ micchācāro hoti tāsaṃ sasāmikabhāvato. Na itarāsanti itarāsaṃ [V 2.0291] māturakkhitādīnaṃ aṭṭhannaṃ purisantaragamane natthi micchācāro tāsaṃ asāmikabhāvato. Yā hi sāmikassa santakaṃ phassaṃ thenetvā paresaṃ abhiratiṃ uppādenti, tāsaṃ micchācāro, na ca mātādayo tāsaṃ phasse issarā. Mātādayo hi na attanā phassānubhavanatthaṃ tā rakkhanti, kevalaṃ anācāraṃ nisedhentā purisantaragamanaṃ tāsaṃ vārenti. Purisassa pana etāsu aṭṭhasupi hotiyeva micchācāro mātādīhi yathā purisena saddhiṃ saṃvāsaṃ na kappeti, tathā rakkhitattā paresaṃ rakkhitagopitaṃ phassaṃ thenetvā phuṭṭhabhāvato.

A woman with a husband is a `sārakkhā`. A woman for whose movement a penalty is imposed by the king is a `saparidaṇḍā`. For the last two, that is, for the `sārakkhā` and `saparidaṇḍā` women, there is sexual misconduct because of the fact that they have a husband. 'Not for the others' means that for the other eight, such as those protected by their mother, there is no sexual misconduct in going to another man, because of the fact that they do not have a husband. For those women who, having stolen the contact that is the property of the husband, arouse delight in others, for them there is sexual misconduct; and mothers and so on are not masters over their contact. Indeed, mothers and so on do not guard them for the sake of experiencing their contact themselves; merely wishing to prevent misconduct, they prevent their going to another man. For a man, however, with these eight women also, there is indeed sexual misconduct. This is because they are guarded by their mothers and so on in such a way that cohabitation with another man is not permitted, and because of having touched by stealing the contact that is guarded and protected by others.

Dhanena kītāti bhariyabhāvatthaṃ dhanena kītā. Tenāha “yasmā panā”tiādi. Bhogenāti bhogahetu. Bhogatthañhi vasantī “bhogavāsinī”ti vuccati. Labhitvāti yo naṃ vāseti, tassa hatthato labhitvā. Udakapattaṃ āmasitvā gahitā odapattakinī. Tenāha “ubhinna”ntiādi. Dhajena āhaṭāti ettha dhajayogato senāva dhajasaddena vuttā, ussitaddhajāya senāya āhaṭāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tenāha “ussitaddhajāyā”tiādi.

'Bought with wealth' means bought with wealth for the purpose of being a wife. Therefore, it is said, 'For which reason,' and so forth. 'Through enjoyment' means for the reason of enjoyment. For a woman who lives for the purpose of enjoyment is called a `bhogavāsinī`. 'Having obtained' means: he who makes her dwell with him has obtained her from her own hand. A woman taken after touching a water vessel is an `odapattakinī`. Therefore, it is said, 'Of both,' and so forth. 'Brought by a banner': here, due to the connection with a banner, the army itself is spoken of by the word 'banner'; it means she is brought by an army with a raised banner. Therefore, it is said, 'By an army with a raised banner,' and so forth.

305. Bahiddhā vimaṭṭhaṃ nāma hotīti aññattha ārocitaṃ nāma hoti. Taṃ kiriyaṃ sampādessatīti tassā ārocetvā taṃ kiccaṃ sampādetu vā mā vā, taṃkiriyāsampādane yogyataṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Dārakaṃ dārikañca ajānāpetvā tesaṃ mātāpituādīhi mātāpituādīnaṃyeva santikaṃ sāsane pesitepi haraṇavīmaṃsanapaccāharaṇasaṅkhātāya tivaṅgasampattiyā saṅghādiseso hotiyevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yaṃ uddissa sāsanaṃ pesitaṃ, taṃyeva sandhāya tassā mātuādīnaṃ ārocite vatthuno ekattā mātuādayopi khettamevāti khettameva otiṇṇabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “buddhaṃ paccakkhāmī”tiādi udāhaṭaṃ. Iminā sametīti etthāyamadhippāyo – yathā sayaṃ anārocetvā aññena antevāsiādinā ārocāpentassa visaṅketo natthi, evaṃ tassā sayaṃ [M 2.0329] anārocetvā ārocanatthaṃ mātuādīnaṃ vadantassapi natthi visaṅketoti. Gharaṃ nayatīti gharaṇī. Mūlaṭṭhānañca vasenāti ettha purisassa mātuādayo sāsanapesane mūlabhūtattā “mūlaṭṭhā”ti vuccanti. Māturakkhitāya mātā bhikkhuṃ pahiṇatīti ettha attano vā dhītu santikaṃ “itthannāmassa bhariyā hotū”ti bhikkhuṃ pahiṇati, purisassa vā santikaṃ “mama dhītā itthannāmassa bhariyā hotū”ti pahiṇatīti gahetabbaṃ. Esa nayo sesesupi. Pubbe vuttanayattāti paṭhamasaṅghādisese vuttanayattā.

305. 'It is called 'contacted outside'' means it is called 'informed in another place'. 'He will accomplish that action' is said with reference to the suitability for accomplishing that task, whether or not that task is accomplished after informing her. It should be understood that even when a message is sent by the parents and so on to the presence of the parents and so on, without letting the young man and young woman know, a saṅghādisesa offense indeed occurs through the completion of the three factors known as conveying, investigating, and conveying back. With reference to the very person for whom the message was sent, when her mother and so on are informed, because of the sameness of the matter, the mother and so on are indeed the 'field'. To show the fact of having entered the 'field', 'I renounce the Buddha,' and so forth, is cited. 'This is included by this' has the following meaning: just as for a monk who does not inform personally but has another, such as a pupil, inform, there is no discrepancy, so too, for a monk who, without informing her personally, speaks to her mother and so on for the purpose of informing, there is no discrepancy. 'She leads to the house' (gharaṃ nayati), therefore she is a housewife (gharaṇī). 'And by way of the root-place': here, in the sending of a message, the man's mother and so on are called the 'root-place' (mūlaṭṭhā) because they are the root cause. In the phrase, 'For a woman protected by her mother, the mother sends a monk,' it should be understood that she sends a monk either to her own daughter, saying, 'May you be the wife of so-and-so,' or she sends one to the man, saying, 'May my daughter be the wife of so-and-so.' This is the method in the remaining cases as well. 'Because of the method previously stated' means because of the method stated in the first saṅghādisesa.

338. Ettova pakkamatīti puna āgantvā āṇāpakassa anārocetvā tatoyeva pakkamati. Aññena karaṇīyenāti gamanahetuvisuddhidassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Teneva pana karaṇīyena gantvāpi [V 2.0292] kiñci anārocento na vīmaṃsati nāma. Anabhinanditvāti idaṃ tathā paṭipajjamānaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, satipi abhinandane sāsanaṃ anārocento pana na vīmaṃsati nāma. Tatiyapade vuttanayenāti “so tassā vacanaṃ anabhinanditvā”tiādinā vuttanayena. Vatthugaṇanāyāti sambahulānaṃ itthipurisānaṃ samabhāve sati dvinnaṃ dvinnaṃ itthipurisavatthūnaṃ gaṇanāya. Sace pana ekato adhikā honti, adhikānaṃ gaṇanāya āpattibhedo veditabbo.

338. 'He departs from that very place' means that without coming back and informing the one who gave the order, he departs from that very place. 'For some other business' is said to show the purity of the reason for going. However, even having gone for that very business, if he does not inform anyone, he is not called one who investigates. 'Without rejoicing' is said with reference to one who acts in such a way; however, even if there is rejoicing, one who does not convey the message is not called one who investigates. 'By the method stated in the third section' means by the method stated in 'He, without rejoicing in her words,' and so forth. 'By the count of the subjects' means by the count of pairs of male and female subjects when there is an equal number of many men and women. But if they are in excess on one side, the distinction of the offense should be known by the count of the excess subjects.

339-340. Pāḷiyaṃ catutthavāre asatipi “gacchanto na sampādeti, āgacchanto visaṃvādeti, anāpattī”ti idaṃ atthato āpannamevāti katvā vuttaṃ “catutthe anāpattī”ti. Kārukānanti vaḍḍhakīādīnaṃ. Tacchakaayokāratantavāyarajakanhāpitakā pañca kāravo “kārukā”ti vuccanti. Evarūpena…pe… anāpattīti tādisaṃ gihiveyyāvaccampi na hotīti katvā vuttaṃ.

Although in the Pāḷi the fourth instance is not present, this statement, 'Going, he does not accomplish; coming back, he deceives; there is no offense,' is indeed arrived at by way of meaning; having considered this, it was said, 'In the fourth, there is no offense.' 'Of artisans' means of carpenters and so on. The five artisans—the carpenter, blacksmith, weaver, washerman, and barber—are called kārukā. 'In such a case... there is no offense' was said because such a matter is not even considered lay service.

Kāyato samuṭṭhātīti paṇṇattiṃ vā alaṃvacanīyabhāvaṃ vā ajānantassa kāyato samuṭṭhāti. Vācato samuṭṭhātīti etthāpi eseva nayo. Kāyavācato samuṭṭhātīti paṇṇattiṃ jānitvā alaṃvacanīyabhāvaṃ ajānantassapi kāyavācato samuṭṭhātīti veditabbaṃ. Alaṃvacanīyā hontīti desacārittavasena paṇṇadānādinā pariccattā honti. Paṇṇattiṃ [M 2.0330] pana jānitvāti ettha alaṃvacanīyabhāvaṃ vāti ca daṭṭhabbaṃ. Teneva mātikāṭṭhakathāyaṃ (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. sañcarittasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) “tadubhayaṃ pana jānitvā eteheva tīhi nayehi samāpajjantassa tāneva tīṇi tadubhayajānanacittena sacittakāni hontī”ti vuttaṃ. Tasmā paṇṇattijānanacittenāti etthāpi tadubhayajānanaṃ vattabbaṃ. Bhikkhuṃ ajānāpetvā attano adhippāyaṃ paṇṇe likhitvā dinnaṃ harantassapi āpatti hoti, imassa sikkhāpadassa acittakattāti na gahetabbaṃ. Pāḷiyaṃ pana “ārocetī”ti vuttattā aṭṭhakathāyañca tattha tattha ārocanasseva dassitattā kāyena vā vācāya vā ārocentasseva āpatti hotīti gahetabbaṃ.

As for 'It arises from the body,' for one who does not know either the regulation or the state of being approachable, it arises from the body. As for 'It arises from speech,' here too the same method applies. As for 'It arises from body and speech,' it should be understood that it arises from body and speech even for one who knows the regulation but does not know the state of being approachable. 'They are approachable' means they are relinquished by way of local custom, through the giving of a leaf and so forth. Here, in 'But knowing the regulation,' 'or the state of being approachable' should also be understood. For that very reason, in the Mātikā Commentary it is said: 'But for one who, knowing both, transgresses through these three methods, those same three origins arise; with a mind that knows both, they are intentional.' Therefore, here in 'with a mind knowing the regulation,' the knowing of both should be stated. It should not be understood that 'an offense is incurred even by one who carries a message written on a leaf expressing one's own intention, given without informing the bhikkhu, on the grounds that this training rule is unintentional.' Rather, since it is said in the Pāḷi, 'he informs,' and since in the Commentary, in various places, only the act of informing is shown, it should be understood that an offense is incurred only by one who informs by body or by speech.

341. Duṭṭhullādīsupīti ādi-saddena sañcarittampi saṅgaṇhāti. Ettha pana kiñcāpi itthī nāma manussitthī, na yakkhī, na petī, na tiracchānagatā, puriso nāma manussapuriso, na yakkhotiādi na vuttaṃ, tathāpi manussajātikāva itthipurisā idha adhippetā. Tasmā yesu sañcarittaṃ samāpajjati, tesaṃ manussajātikatā, na nālaṃvacanīyatā, paṭiggaṇhanavīmaṃsanapaccāharaṇānīti imānettha pañcaṅgāni.

341. In 'In coarse offenses, etc.,' by the word 'etc.' matchmaking is also included. Here, however, although it is not stated that 'woman' means a human woman, not a female yakkha, not a female peta, not an animal, and 'man' means a human man, not a male yakkha, and so forth, nevertheless, only a woman and a man of human birth are intended here. Therefore, for those with whom matchmaking is undertaken, these are the five factors: their being of human birth, their state of being approachable, acceptance, investigation, and reporting back.

Sañcarittasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on matchmaking is finished.

6. Kuṭikārasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

6. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Building a Hut

342. Chaṭṭhe [V 2.0293] ettakenāti ettakena dāruādinā. Aparicchinnappamāṇāyoti aparicchinnadāruādippamāṇāyo. Mūlacchejjāya purisaṃ yācituṃ na vaṭṭatīti parasantakabhāvato mocetvā attanoyeva santakaṃ katvā yācituṃ na vaṭṭati. Evaṃ mūlacchejjāya aññātakaappavāritaṭṭhānato yācantassa aññātakaviññattiyā dukkaṭaṃ. Dāsaṃ attano atthāya sādiyantassapi dukkaṭameva “dāsidāsapaṭiggahaṇā paṭivirato hotī”ti (dī. ni. 1.10, 194) vacanato. Ñātakapavāritaṭṭhānato pana dāsaṃ mūlacchejjāya yācantassa sādiyanavasena dukkaṭaṃ. Sakakammaṃ na yācitabbāti pāṇātipātasikkhāpadarakkhaṇatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Aniyametvāpi na yācitabbāti manussānaṃ aññathā gāhassapi sambhavato vuttaṃ, suddhacittena pana hatthakammaṃ yācantassa āpatti nāma natthi.

342. In the sixth rule: 'with this much' means with this much wood and so forth. 'Of unspecified size' means of a size unspecified in terms of wood, etc. 'It is not allowable to ask a person for what is to be cut at the root' means it is not allowable to ask after having it released from being another's property and making it one's own. Thus, for one who asks for something by 'cutting at the root' from an unrelated, uninvited place, there is a dukkaṭa offense for requesting from an unrelated person. For one who accepts a slave for one's own benefit, there is also a dukkaṭa offense, because it is said: 'He abstains from accepting male and female slaves.' But for one who asks for a slave by 'cutting at the root' from a related or invited place, there is a dukkaṭa offense by way of acceptance. 'Work for oneself should not be requested' is said for the sake of protecting the training rule on destroying living beings. 'One should not ask without specifying' is said because it is possible for people to misunderstand. But for one who asks for manual labor with a pure mind, there is no offense.

Sabbakappiyabhāvadīpanatthanti [M 2.0331] sabbaso kappiyabhāvadīpanatthaṃ. Mūlaṃ dethāti vattuṃ vaṭṭatīti yasmā mūlaṃ dassāmāti tehi paṭhamaṃ vuttattā viññatti na hoti, yasmā ca mūlanti bhaṇitaṃ sāmaññavacanato akappiyavacanaṃ na hoti, tasmā mūlaṃ dethāti vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Anajjhāvutthakanti apariggahitaṃ. Akappiyakahāpaṇādi na dātabbanti kiñcāpi akappiyakahāpaṇādiṃ asādiyantena kappiyavohārato dātuṃ vaṭṭati, tathāpi sāruppaṃ na hoti. Manussā ca etassa santakaṃ kiñci atthīti viheṭhetabbaṃ maññantīti akappiyakahāpaṇādidānaṃ paṭikkhittaṃ. Tatheva pācetvāti hatthakammavaseneva pācetvā. “Kiṃ, bhante”ti ettakepi pucchite yadatthāya paviṭṭho, taṃ kathetuṃ vaṭṭati pucchitapañhattā.

As for 'to show the state of being allowable in all respects': for the purpose of showing the state of being allowable in every way. As for 'It is allowable to say, “Give the price”': because they first said, 'We will give the price,' it is not a request; and because 'price' is spoken as a general term, it is not an unallowable expression. Therefore, it is allowable to say, 'Give the price.' 'Uninhabited' means unowned. As for 'Unallowable kahāpaṇas and the like should not be given': although it is allowable for one who does not accept unallowable kahāpaṇas and the like to give them by way of allowable speech, it is nevertheless not suitable. And people, thinking, 'He has some property,' might consider him someone to be harassed. Therefore, the giving of unallowable kahāpaṇas and the like is rejected. 'Having had it done in the same way' means having had it done only by way of manual labor. When asked just this much, 'What is it, venerable sir?', it is allowable to state the purpose for which one has approached, because it is a declaration in response to a question.

Vattanti cārittaṃ, āpatti pana na hotīti adhippāyo. Kappiyaṃ kārāpetvā paṭiggahetabbānīti sākhāya laggarajasmiṃ patte patitepi sākhaṃ chinditvā khāditukāmatāyapi sati sukhaparibhogatthaṃ vuttaṃ. “Nadiṃ vā…pe… āharā”ti vatthuṃ vaṭṭatīti apariggahitattā vuttaṃ. Gehato…pe… paribhuñjitabbanti pariggahitaudakattā viññattiyā dukkaṭaṃ hotīti adhippāyo. Alajjīhi…pe… na kāretabbanti idaṃ uttaribhaṅgādhikārattā ajjhoharaṇīyaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Bāhiraparibhogesu pana alajjīhipi hatthakammaṃ kāretuṃ vaṭṭatīti.

As for 'They act': it is a custom, but there is no offense. This is the intention. As for 'Having had what is allowable made, it should be accepted': this is said for the sake of comfortable use, even when dust clinging to a branch has fallen into the bowl, and even when there is a desire to cut the branch and eat from it. The statement, 'It is allowable to say, “Bring from a river or…”' is said because it is unowned. As for 'From a house… it should not be used': because the water is owned, requesting it entails a dukkaṭa offense. This is the intention. This statement, 'Shameless ones… should not be made to do it,' is said in reference to something to be swallowed, because it is a matter concerning extra allowances. But in the case of external requisites, it is allowable to have even shameless ones perform manual labor.

Goṇaṃ pana…pe… āharāpetuṃ na vaṭṭatīti attano atthāya mūlacchejjavasena āharāpetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Āharāpentassa dukkaṭanti aññātakaviññattiyā dukkaṭaṃ. Attano atthāya sādiyanepi [V 2.0294] dukkaṭameva “hatthigavāssavaḷavapaṭiggahaṇā paṭivirato hotī”ti (dī. ni. 1.10, 194) vuttattā. Tenevāha “ñātakapavāritaṭṭhānatopi mūlacchejjāya yācituṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti. Rakkhitvāti yathā corā na haranti, evaṃ rakkhitvā. Jaggitvāti tiṇadānādīhi jaggitvā. Na sampaṭicchitabbanti attano atthāya goṇe sādiyanassa paṭikkhittattā vuttaṃ.

As for 'But an ox… it is not allowable to have it brought': it is not allowable to have it brought for one's own benefit by way of 'cutting at the root.' As for 'For one who has it brought, there is a dukkaṭa': there is a dukkaṭa for requesting from an unrelated person. Even in accepting it for one's own benefit, there is a dukkaṭa, because it is said, 'He abstains from accepting elephants, cattle, horses, and mares.' For that very reason, he said, 'It is not allowable to ask by “cutting at the root” even from a related or invited place.' 'Having guarded it' means having guarded it in such a way that thieves do not take it. 'Having tended to it' means having tended to it by giving grass and so forth. 'It should not be accepted' is said because accepting oxen for one's own benefit is rejected.

Sakaṭaṃ dethāti…pe… vaṭṭatīti mūlacchejjavasena sakaṭaṃ dethāti vattuṃ na vaṭṭati. Tāvakālikaṃ vaṭṭatīti tāvakālikaṃ katvā sabbattha yācituṃ vaṭṭati. Valliādīsu ca parapariggahitesu eseva nayoti yojetabbaṃ[M 2.0332]. Garubhaṇḍappahonakesuyeva ca valliādīsūti ettha ādi-saddena veḷumuñjapabbajatiṇamattikānaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Yaṃ pana vatthuvasena appaṃ hutvā agghavasena mahantaṃ haritālahiṅgulakādi, taṃ garubhaṇḍaṃ appahontampi yācituṃ na vaṭṭatīti vadanti.

As for '“Give a cart”… it is not allowable': it is not allowable to say, 'Give a cart,' by way of cutting at the root. 'Temporarily, it is allowable' means having made it temporary, it is allowable to ask in all cases. And in the case of creepers and the like, when they are possessed by others, this same method should be applied. And in the case of things sufficient for heavy goods, as well as creepers and the like—here, by the word 'and so on,' the inclusion of bamboo, muñja grass, pabbaja grass, and clay should be understood. But as for what is small in substance but great in value, such as orpiment, vermilion, and so on, even if it is not sufficient as heavy goods, it is not allowable to ask for it—so they say.

Sāti viññattiṃ parāmasati. Sā ca idha parikathādinā yena kenaci adhippāyaviññāpanaṃ viññattīti gahetabbā. Tenāha “sabbena sabba”nti, sabbappakārenāti attho. Tena “parikathādivasenapi viññāpanaṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti dīpeti. Parikathobhāsanimittakammampi hi cīvarapiṇḍapātesu dvīsu paccayesu na vaṭṭati. Idāni senāsanapaccaye adhippetaṃ viññattiṃ parikathādīhi visesetvā dassento “āhara dehīti viññattimattameva na vaṭṭatī”ti āha. Parikathobhāsanimittakammāni vaṭṭantīti ettha parikathā nāma pariyāyena kathanaṃ bhikkhusaṅghassa senāsanaṃ sambādhantiādivacanaṃ. Obhāso nāma ujukameva akathetvā yathā adhippāyo vibhūto hoti, evaṃ obhāsanaṃ, upāsakā, tumhe kuhiṃ vasathāti? Pāsāde, bhanteti. Bhikkhūnaṃ pana, upāsakā, pāsādo na vaṭṭatītiādivacanaṃ. Nimittakammaṃ nāma paccaye uddissa yathā adhippāyo viññāyati, evaṃ nimittakammaṃ, senāsanatthaṃ bhūmiparikammādīni karontassa “kiṃ, bhante, karosi, ko kārāpetī”ti vutte “na kocī”tiādivacanaṃ.

'Sā' refers to intimation. And here, 'intimation' should be understood as making one's intention known by any means whatsoever, such as by allusive talk. Therefore, he said, 'in every way,' the meaning of which is 'in all manners.' By this, he shows that making one's intention known even by way of allusive talk and so on is not allowable. For allusive talk, hinting, and making a sign are not allowable in regard to the two requisites: robes and alms-food. Now, wishing to show, by distinguishing with allusive talk and so on, the intended intimation regarding the requisite of lodging, he said, 'Merely the intimation “bring” or “give” is not allowable.' Here, regarding 'allusive talk, hinting, and making a sign are allowable': 'Allusive talk' means speaking indirectly, such as the statement, 'The lodging for the Sangha of monks is cramped.' 'Hinting' means not speaking directly, but in such a way that the intention becomes clear, such as saying, 'Lay devotees, where do you live?' When it is said, 'In a mansion, venerable sir,' it is a statement such as, 'But for monks, lay devotees, is a mansion not allowable?' 'Making a sign' means, with reference to a requisite, making a sign in such a way that the intention is understood; for one who is preparing the ground for a lodging, when asked, 'What are you doing, venerable sir? Who is having it done?' it is a statement such as, 'No one is having it done.'

Idāni gilānapaccaye viññattiādikaṃ sabbampi vaṭṭatīti dassento āha “gilānapaccaye panā”tiādi. Tathā uppannaṃ pana bhesajjaṃ roge vūpasante paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati, na vaṭṭatīti? Tattha vinayadharā “bhagavatā rogasīsena paribhogassa dvāraṃ dinnaṃ, tasmā arogakālepi paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati, āpatti na hotī”ti vadanti. Suttantikā pana “kiñcāpi [V 2.0295] āpatti na hoti, ājīvaṃ pana kopeti, tasmā sallekhappaṭipattiyaṃ ṭhitassa na vaṭṭati, sallekhaṃ kopetī”ti vadanti. Ukkamantīti apagacchanti.

Now, wishing to show that in the case of the requisite for the sick, everything, such as requesting, is allowable, he said, 'But in the case of the requisite for the sick,' and so on. But as for medicine so obtained, when the illness has subsided, is it allowable to use it, or is it not? Therein, the experts in the Vinaya say, 'The door for its use was given by the Blessed One with illness as the primary reason; therefore, it is allowable to use it even in a time of no illness, and there is no offense.' The Suttantikas, however, say, 'Although there is indeed no offense, it nevertheless corrupts one's livelihood. Therefore, for one established in the practice of effacement, it is not allowable; it corrupts effacement.' 'Ukkamanti' means they depart.

344. Maṇi kaṇṭhe assāti maṇikaṇṭho, maṇinā upalakkhito vā kaṇṭho assāti maṇikaṇṭhoti majjhapadalopīsamāso daṭṭhabbo. Devavaṇṇanti devattabhāvaṃ. Pasannākāranti pasannehi kātabbakiccaṃ, kāyaveyyāvaccasaṅkhātaṃ upaṭṭhānanti vuttaṃ hoti. Maṇiyācanāya tassa anāgamanena [M 2.0333] attano vaḍḍhi hotīti vuttaṃ “maṇinā me attho”ti, mantapadanīhārena vā tathā vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

344. 'Maṇikaṇṭha' means one on whose neck there is a jewel (maṇi kaṇṭhe assa), or one whose neck is marked by a jewel (maṇinā upalakkhito kaṇṭho assa)—this should be understood as a bahubbīhi compound with an elided middle term. 'Devavaṇṇaṃ' means the state of being a deva. 'Pasannākāraṃ' means the duty to be done by those who are pleased, that is, the attendance called 'bodily service,' so it is said. Because his own welfare comes about through that one's non-arrival due to the request for the jewel, it was said, 'I have need of the jewel.' Or, it should be understood that it was said thus by way of bringing out the words of the spell.

345. Vattamānasamīpeti vattamānassa samīpe atīte. Evaṃ vattuṃ labbhatīti “āgatosī”ti vattabbe vattamānasamīpattā “āgacchasī”ti evaṃ vattamānavohārena vattuṃ labbhati. Lakkhaṇaṃ panettha saddasatthānusārato veditabbaṃ. So eva nayoti “āgatomhī”ti vattabbe “āgacchāmī”ti ayampi vattamānasamīpe vattamānavohāroti dasseti.

345. 'Near the present' means in the past which is near the present. 'Thus it is possible to speak' means: when 'you have come' should be said, because of its nearness to the present, it is possible to speak with the present tense expression, 'you are coming.' Here, the grammatical rule should be known in accordance with the grammatical texts. 'This is the same method' shows that when 'I have come' should be said, this present tense expression 'I am coming' is also a present tense expression used for the near past.

348-349. Yasmā pana na sakkā kevalaṃ yācanāya kiñci kātuṃ, tasmā “sayaṃ yācitakehi upakaraṇehī”ti adhippāyattho vutto. Uddhaṃmukhaṃ littā ullittā, adhomukhaṃ littā avalittā. Yasmā pana uddhaṃmukhaṃ limpantā yebhuyyena anto limpanti, adhomukhaṃ limpantā ca bahi, tasmā vuttaṃ “ullittāti antolittā, avalittāti bahilittā”ti. Tattha ullittā nāma ṭhapetvā tulāpiṭṭhasaṅghātavātapānadhūmachiddādibhedaṃ alepokāsaṃ avasese lepokāse kuṭṭehi saddhiṃ ghaṭetvā chadanassa anto sudhāya vā mattikāya vā littā. Avalittā nāma vuttanayeneva chadanassa bahi littā. Ullittāvalittā nāma tatheva chadanassa anto ca bahi ca littā.

But since it is not possible to do anything by merely asking, therefore the intended meaning was stated as 'with implements requested by oneself.' Plastered facing upwards is `ullittā`; plastered facing downwards is `avalittā`. And since those who plaster facing upwards for the most part plaster the inside, and those who plaster facing downwards plaster the outside, therefore it was said: '`ullittā` means plastered inside, `avalittā` means plastered outside.' Therein, `ullittā` means plastered on the inside of the roof with lime-plaster or with clay, having joined it together with the walls in the remaining plasterable space, after setting aside the unplasterable space, which is differentiated as the joints of beams and planks, windows, smoke-holes, and so on. `Avalittā` means plastered on the outside of the roof in the same way as described. `Ullittāvalittā` means plastered in that same way both on the inside and the outside of the roof.

Byañjanaṃ sametīti “kārayamānenā”ti hetukattuvasena uddiṭṭhapadassa “kārāpentenā”ti hetukattuvaseneva niddesassa katattā byañjanaṃ sameti. Yadi evaṃ “karonto vā kārāpento vā”ti kasmā tassa padabhājanaṃ vuttanti āha “yasmā panā”tiādi. “Attanā vippakataṃ parehi pariyosāpetī”tiādivacanato “karontenapi idha vuttanayeneva paṭipajjitabba”nti vuttaṃ. Tattha idha vuttanayenevāti imasmiṃ sikkhāpade vuttanayeneva. Ubhopeteti kārakakārāpakā. Kārayamānenāti imināva padena saṅgahitāti kathaṃ saṅgahitā. Na hi kārayamāno karonto nāma hoti, evaṃ panettha adhippāyo veditabbo – yasmā karontenapi kārayamānenapi idha vuttanayeneva paṭipajjitabbaṃ, tasmā kārayamānena evaṃ paṭipajjitabbanti vutte pageva karontenāti idaṃ atthato [V 2.0296] āgatamevāti “kārayamānenā”ti bhagavatā vuttaṃ. Tato “kārayamānenā”ti vutte sāmatthiyato labbhamānopi attho teneva saṅgahito nāma hotīti. Byañjanaṃ [M 2.0334] vilomitaṃ bhaveyyāti yasmā “kārayamānenā”ti imassa “karontenā”ti idaṃ pariyāyavacanaṃ na hoti, tasmā karontena vā kārāpentena vāti padatthavasena niddese kate byañjanaṃ viruddhaṃ bhaveyyāti adhippāyo. Atthamattamevāti padatthato sāmatthiyato ca labbhamānaṃ atthamattameva.

"The wording is consistent" means: because the explanation of the indicated term "by one who is causing it to be made" (`kārayamānenā`), which is in the sense of the agent of the cause, was made as "by one who is causing it to be made" (`kārāpentenā`) in the very sense of the agent of the cause, the wording is consistent. If it is so, why was the analysis of its term given as "one who is doing or one who is causing it to be done"? To this, he says, "Because..." and so on. From the statement, "What was begun by oneself, one has completed by others," and so on, it is said, "Even by one who is doing, it must be practiced in the way stated here." Therein, "in the way stated here" means in the way stated in this training rule. "Both" means the doer and the one who causes it to be done. How are they included by this very term, "by one who is causing it to be done"? Indeed, one who is causing it to be done is not called a doer. The intention here should be understood thus: because it must be practiced in the way stated here by both one who is doing and one who is causing it to be done, therefore, when it is said, "It must be practiced thus by one who is causing it to be done," it is already arrived at in terms of meaning that this applies all the more so to one who is doing. Therefore, "by one who is causing it to be done" was said by the Blessed One. Hence, when "by one who is causing it to be done" is said, the meaning obtainable by implication is also included by that very term. "The wording would be contradictory" means: because "by one who is doing" is not a synonym for "by one who is causing it to be done," therefore, if the explanation were made in terms of the meaning of the words as "by one who is doing or by one who is causing it to be done," the wording would be contradictory; this is the intention. "Only the meaning" means just the meaning obtainable from the meaning of the words and by implication.

Uddesoti uddisitabbo. Abbohārikanti appamāṇaṃ. “Āyāmato ca vitthārato cā”ti avatvā vikappatthassa vā-saddassa vuttattā ekatobhāgena vaḍḍhitepi āpattiyevāti dassento “yo panā”tiādimāha. Tihatthāti vaḍḍhakīhatthena tihatthā. Pamāṇayutto mañcoti pakatividatthiyā navavidatthippamāṇo mañco. Pamāṇikā kāretabbāti ukkaṭṭhappamāṇaṃ sandhāya vuttattā ukkaṭṭhappamāṇayuttāva kuṭi adesitavatthukā na vaṭṭati, pamāṇato pana ūnatarā adesitavatthukāpi vaṭṭatīti kassaci sandeho siyāti taṃnivattanatthaṃ “pamāṇato ūnatarampī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha pamāṇato ūnataranti pāḷiyaṃ vuttappamāṇato ūnataraṃ. Pacchimena pamāṇena catuhatthato ūnatarā kuṭi nāma na hotīti catuhatthato paṭṭhāya kuṭilakkhaṇappattaṃ kuṭiṃ dassetuṃ “catuhatthaṃ pañcahatthampī”ti vuttaṃ. Kalalalepoti kenaci silesena katalepo, tambamattikādikalalalepo vā. Alepo evāti abbohārikāyevāti adhippāyo. Piṭṭhasaṅghāṭo dvārabāhā. Oloketvāpīti apaloketvāpi, apalokanakammavasenapi kātuṃ vaṭṭatīti adhippāyo.

An indication (`uddeso`) is what is to be indicated. 'Invalid' (`abbohārika`) means not meeting the measure (`appamāṇaṃ`). Without saying 'in length and in breadth,' because the word 'or' (`vā`), which has the meaning of an alternative, was stated, he said, 'Whatever bhikkhu...' (`yo pana`) and so on, to show that even if it is increased in one dimension, there is still an offense. 'Three cubits' (`tihatthā`) means three cubits by the carpenter's cubit. 'A bed of the proper measure' (`pamāṇayutto mañco`) means a bed measuring nine spans by the standard span. Because 'It should be made to measure' was said with reference to the maximum measure, a hut of the maximum measure on an unindicated site is not allowable; however, a hut smaller than the measure, even on an unindicated site, is allowable. Lest someone should have this doubt, to dispel it, 'even smaller than the measure...' and so on was said. Therein, 'smaller than the measure' means smaller than the measure stated in the Pāḷi. Because a so-called hut smaller than four cubits—the minimum measure—does not exist, 'four cubits or five cubits' was said to show a hut that has attained the characteristic of a hut, starting from four cubits. 'Mud plaster' (`kalalalepo`) means a plaster made with some adhesive, or a plaster of red clay and so on. It is considered as unplastered, and therefore it is invalid (`abbohārika`); this is the intention. The 'back-panel' (`piṭṭhasaṅghāṭo`) is the door-post. 'Having looked' (`oloketvāpi`) also means 'having announced' (`apaloketvāpi`); the intention is that it is allowable to do it by means of the formal act of announcement.

353. Yathā sīhādīnaṃ gocarāya pakkamantānaṃ nibaddhagamanamaggo na vaṭṭati, evaṃ hatthīnampi nibaddhagamanamaggo na vaṭṭati. Etesanti sīhādīnaṃ. Cāribhūmīti gocarabhūmi. Na gahitāti na vāritāti adhippāyo. Ārogyatthāyāti nirupaddavatthāya. Sesānīti pubbaṇṇanissitādīni. Pubbaṇṇanissitanti ettha pubbaṇṇaviruhanaṭṭhānaṃ pubbaṇṇa-saddena gahitaṃ. Tenāha – “sattannaṃ dhaññānaṃ…pe… ṭhita”nti. Abhihananti etthāti abbhāghātaṃ. “Verighara”nti vuttamevatthaṃ vibhāvetuṃ “corānaṃ māraṇatthāya kata”nti vuttaṃ. Dhammagandhikāti hatthapādādichindanagandhikā.

353. Just as the fixed path of lions and other animals going forth for food is not allowable, so too the fixed path of elephants is not allowable. 'Of these' (`etesaṃ`) means of lions and so on. 'Ranging ground' (`cāribhūmi`) means feeding ground. 'Not taken' (`na gahitā`) means not enclosed; this is the intention. 'For the sake of health' (`ārogyatthāya`) means for the sake of being free from danger. 'The remaining' (`sesāni`) means those dependent on early grain and so on. Here in 'dependent on early grain,' the place where early grain grows is taken by the word 'early grain.' Therefore he said, 'of the seven grains... standing...' 'A place of slaughter' (`abbhāghātaṃ`) is so called because 'they strike here.' To clarify the meaning already stated as a 'house of enmity' (`verighara`), it was said, 'made for the purpose of killing thieves.' A 'judicial block' (`dhammagandhikā`) is a block for the cutting off of hands, feet, and so on.

Āvijjituṃ [M 2.0335] na sakkā hotīti chindataṭādisambhavato na sakkā hoti āvijjituṃ. Pācinanti kuṭivatthusāmantā cinitabbaadhiṭṭhānaṃ. Kiñcāpi idha pubbapayogasahapayogānaṃ adinnādāne viya viseso natthi, tathāpi tesaṃ vibhāgena dassanaṃ chinditvā puna kātabbāti ettha [V 2.0297] kuṭiyā bhedanaparicchedadassanatthaṃ kataṃ. Tadatthāyāti tacchanatthāya. Evaṃ katanti adesitavatthuṃ pamāṇātikkantaṃ vā kataṃ. Dārunā kataṃ kuṭṭaṃ etthāti dārukuṭṭikā, kuṭi. Silākuṭṭikantiādīsupi eseva nayo. Paṇṇasālanti bahi paṇṇehi chādetabbaṃ ullittāvalittaṃ kuṭimeva vadati. Tenevāha “sabhitticchadanaṃ limpissāmī”ti.

'The surrounding area' (`pācinaṃ`) means the site to be built upon near the hut site. Although here there is no distinction between a prior effort and a concurrent effort as there is in the case of theft, nevertheless, showing them separately was done. Here, 'having demolished, it should be made again' was stated to show the division and boundary of the hut. 'For that purpose' (`tadatthāya`) means for the purpose of trimming. 'Thus made' (`evaṃ kataṃ`) means made on an unindicated site or exceeding the measure. 'A wooden-walled hut' (`dārukuṭṭikā`) is so called because 'here there is a wall made of wood'; it is a hut. In 'a stone-walled hut' and so on, this is the same method. A 'leaf-hut' (`paṇṇasālā`) refers to a hut that is plastered inside and out and is to be covered on the outside with leaves. Therefore he said, 'I will plaster the walls and roof.'

Antolepeneva niṭṭhāpetukāmaṃ sandhāya “antolepe vā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Bahilepe vāti etthāpi eseva nayo. Tasmiṃ dvārabaddhe vā vātapāne vā ṭhapiteti yojetabbaṃ. Tassokāsanti tassa dvārabaddhassa vā vātapānassa vā okāsaṃ. Puna vaḍḍhetvā vāti pubbeva ṭhapitokāsaṃ khuddakaṃ ce, bhedanena puna vaḍḍhetvā. Lepo na ghaṭiyatīti pubbe dinnalepo dvārabaddhena vā vātapānena vā saddhiṃ na ghaṭiyati, ekābaddhaṃ hutvā na tiṭṭhatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Tanti dvārabaddhaṃ vā vātapānaṃ vā. Paṭhamameva saṅghādisesoti lepakiccassa niṭṭhitattā dvārabaddhaṃ vā vātapānaṃ vā ṭhapanato pubbeyeva saṅghādiseso. Aṭṭhaṅgulamattena appattacchadanaṃ katvāti ettha evaṃ me āpatti na siyāti bhittiyaṃ vā chadane vā ekaṅgulamattampi okāsaṃ lepena aghaṭetvā ṭhapeti, vaṭṭatīti vadanti. Mattikākuṭṭameva mattikālepasaṅkhyaṃ gacchatīti āha – “sace mattikāya kuṭṭaṃ karoti, chadanalepena saddhiṃ ghaṭane āpattī”ti. Ubhinnaṃ anāpattīti purimassa lepassa aghaṭitattā dutiyassa attuddesikatāsambhavato ubhinnaṃ anāpatti, tasmā vināpi vattasīsena tena anāṇatto tassa karomīti karoti, ubhinnaṃ anāpattiyeva. Sace tena āṇatto karoti, mūlaṭṭhasseva āpatti.

With reference to the desire to finish it by plastering the interior, it is said, 'or on the interior plastering,' and so on. In the case of 'or on the exterior plastering' too, this is the same method. It should be connected as 'when it is placed on that door-frame or on that window.' 'Its opening' means the opening of that door-frame or of that window. 'Or having enlarged it again' means: if the opening previously established was small, having enlarged it again by breaking it. 'The plaster does not connect' means: the plaster previously applied does not connect with the door-frame or with the window; it is said that it does not stand having become a single bonded unit. 'That' means the door-frame or the window. 'A Saṅghādisesa offense from the very beginning' means: because the task of plastering is finished, the Saṅghādisesa offense is incurred even before the placing of the door-frame or the window. Regarding 'having made the roofing not reach by the measure of eight finger-breadths': here, some say that if one, thinking, 'In this way, there would be no offense for me,' leaves a space of even one finger-breadth on the wall or on the roof unconnected with plaster, it is allowable. He said, 'A clay wall itself goes into the category of clay plaster': 'If one makes a wall of clay, there is an offense upon its connection with the roof plaster.' 'No offense for both' means: because the first one's plaster was not connected, and because for the second one there is no possibility of it being for his own sake, there is no offense for both. Therefore, even without being at the head of the duty, being uninstructed by him, if one does it thinking, 'I will do it for him,' there is no offense for both. If one does it having been instructed by him, the offense is for the one at the root of the matter only.

354. Chattiṃsa catukkāni nāma “bhikkhu kuṭiṃ karotī”tiādimhi paṭhamavāre adesitavatthukacatukkaṃ desitavatthukacatukkaṃ pamāṇātikkantacatukkaṃ pamāṇikacatukkaṃ adesitavatthukappamāṇātikkantacatukkaṃ desitavatthukappamāṇikacatukkanti [M 2.0336] cha catukkāni, evaṃ samādisativārādīsupi pañcasūti chattiṃsa. Āpattibhedadassanatthaṃ vuttānīti “sārambhe ce bhikkhu vatthusmiṃ aparikkamane”ti avisesena mātikāya vuttattā sārambhaaparikkamanesupi saṅghādisesova siyāti micchāgāhanivattanatthaṃ sārambhe aparikkamane ca dukkaṭaṃ, adesitavatthukatāya pamāṇātikkantatāya ca saṅghādisesoti evaṃ āpattibhedadassanatthaṃ vuttāni.

354. The thirty-six tetrads are named thus: in the first section, beginning with 'a monk makes a hut,' there are six tetrads: the tetrad on an unindicated site, the tetrad on an indicated site, the tetrad on exceeding the measure, the tetrad on the correct measure, the tetrad on an unindicated site exceeding the measure, and the tetrad on an indicated site with the correct measure. Similarly, in the five sections beginning with 'one directs,' etc., there are thus thirty-six. 'They are stated to show the distinction in offenses' means: because it is stated generally in the Mātikā, 'If a monk, with an undertaking, on a site, without surveying,' a Saṅghādisesa offense might also be incurred in cases of an undertaking and not surveying. To avert this wrong grasp, it is stated thus to show the distinction in offenses: a Dukkaṭa offense for an undertaking and for not surveying, and a Saṅghādisesa offense for having an unindicated site and for exceeding the measure.

355-361. “Dvīhi saṅghādisesehī”ti vattabbe vibhattibyattayena ca vacanabyattayena ca dvinnaṃ saṅghādisesenāti vuttanti āha “dvīhi saṅghādisesehi…pe… attho veditabbo”ti. “Aññassa vā dātabbā”ti vuttattā vippakataṃ kuṭiṃ labhitvā attano atthāya karontassapi ādito [V 2.0298] paṭṭhāya akatattā anāpattiyevāti vadanti. Apacinitabbāti viddhaṃsetabbā. Bhūmisamaṃ katvāti kuṭivatthusamaṃ katvā.

When it should be said 'by two Saṅghādisesa offenses' (dvīhi saṅghādisesehi), it was said as 'of two, by a Saṅghādisesa offense' (dvinnaṃ saṅghādisesena) through an alteration of case and an alteration of number. Therefore, he said, 'the meaning of "by two Saṅghādisesa offenses... etc." should be understood.' Because it is said, 'or it should be given to another,' some say that for one who, having obtained an unfinished hut, makes it for his own sake, there is still no offense, because it was not made by him from the beginning. 'It should be taken down' means it should be demolished. 'Having made it level with the ground' means having made it level with the hut's site.

364. Na hettha lepo ghaṭiyatīti chadanalepassa abhāvato vuttaṃ, visuṃyeva anuññātattā pana sacepi leṇassa anto uparibhāge cittakammādikaraṇatthaṃ lepaṃ denti, vaṭṭatiyeva. Lepadānavasena akatā iṭṭhakādiguhā guhā nāmāti gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Tiṇehi vā paṇṇehi vā chāditakuṭikāva vuttāti “kukkuṭacchikagehaṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vatvā “chadanaṃ daṇḍakehī”tiādinā puna taṃ dassentehi tiṇapaṇṇacchadanā kuṭikāva vuttā. Chadanaṃ daṇḍakehi jālabandhaṃ katvāti chadanaṃ dīghato tiriyato ca ṭhapitadaṇḍakehi jālaṃ viya bandhitvā. Ogumphetvāti tiṇādiṃ viddhaṃsetvā. Bhittilepena saddhiṃ lepe ghaṭiteti ettha ullittāvalittabhāvassa chadanaṃ sandhāya vuttattā sacepi bhittilepena anatthiko hoti, chadanalepe samantato bhittiyā appamattakenapi ghaṭite bhittilepena vināpi āpattiyevāti vadanti. Upacikāmocanatthameva heṭṭhā pāsāṇakuṭṭaṃ katvā taṃ alimpitvā upari limpati, lepo na ghaṭiyati nāma, anāpattiyevāti iminā aṭṭhakathāvacanena taṃ na sameti. Tattha keci vadanti “bhittiṃ alimpitukāmatāya abhāvato chadanalepe pāsāṇakuṭṭena saddhiṃ ghaṭitepi tattha anāpatti vuttā”ti, tampi na yuttaṃ. “Upacikāmocanatthamevā”ti hi vuttattā pāsāṇakuṭṭe puna limpitukāmatāya abhāvoyeva viññāyati, teneva “taṃ alimpitvā”ti [M 2.0337] vuttaṃ. Tasmā “ullittādibhāvo…pe… chadanameva sandhāya vutto”ti idaṃ satipi bhittilepe chadanalepena vinā āpatti na hotīti chadanalepassa padhānabhāvadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ, na pana bhittilepena vināpi āpatti hotīti dassanatthanti vadanti, idameva cettha yuttataranti amhākaṃ khanti. Etthāti tiṇakuṭikāya.

364. 'Here plaster is not applied' is said because of the absence of roof plaster. However, because it is permitted separately, if they apply plaster inside a cave, in the upper part, for the purpose of making paintings and so on, it is indeed allowable. In the Ganthipada texts it is said: A cave made of bricks, etc., that is not made by way of applying plaster, is called a 'cave.' That only a hut covered with grass or with leaves is meant is shown by the commentators who, after saying, 'A chicken-coop style house is allowable,' again, when explaining that with 'a roof with sticks,' etc., spoke only of a hut covered with grass and leaves. 'Having made the roof a net-like binding with sticks' means: having bound the roof like a net with sticks placed lengthwise and crosswise. 'Ogumphetvā' means having shaken out the grass, etc. Regarding 'when the plaster is connected with the wall plaster': here, because the state of being plastered above and plastered below is said with reference to the roof, they say that even if one has no need for wall plaster, if the roof plaster is connected with the wall all around even by a small amount, there is still an offense even without wall plaster. That view does not agree with this statement of the commentary: 'If, solely for the purpose of being free from termites, one makes a stone wall below, and, without plastering it, plasters above, it is called "the plaster does not connect," and there is no offense.' Regarding that, some say, 'Because of the absence of the desire to plaster the wall, no offense is stated there even if the roof plaster connects with the stone wall.' That too is not correct. For, since it is said 'solely for the purpose of being free from termites,' it is understood that there is indeed an absence of desire to plaster the stone wall again; for that very reason it is said, 'without plastering it.' Therefore, they say that this statement, 'the state of being plastered above, etc. ... is said with reference to the roof only,' is said to show the primary importance of the roof plaster—that even if there is wall plaster, without roof plaster there is no offense. It is not, however, said to show that an offense occurs even without wall plaster. And this alone is more suitable here—this is our preference. 'Here' means: in the case of a grass hut.

Ettha ca tiṇakuṭikāya eva sabbathā anāpattibhāvassa dassanaṃ parivārapāḷiṃ ānetvā tiṇakuṭikāya sārambhādipaccayāpi anāpattibhāvo sukhena sakkā sādhetunti kataṃ. Tiṇakuṭikāya ca sabbathā anāpattibhāve sādhite teneva nayena leṇaguhādīsupi sārambhādipaccayāpi anāpattibhāvo sakkā viññātunti. Teneva “yaṃ panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tathā hi tiṇakuṭikāya sārambhādipaccayāpi anāpattibhāve sādhite teneva nayena aññassatthāya karontassapi sārambhādipaccayāpi anāpattibhāvo atthato dassitoyeva hoti. Evañca sati bhikkhu samādisitvā pakkamati “kuṭiṃ me karothā”ti, samādisati ca desitavatthukā ca hotu anārambhā ca saparikkamanā cāti, tassa kuṭiṃ karonti adesitavatthukaṃ sārambhaṃ aparikkamanaṃ. “Āpatti kārukānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ dukkaṭāna”nti pāḷiyaṃ aññassatthāya [V 2.0299] karontassapi sārambhādipaccayāpi dukkaṭaṃ kasmā vuttanti imaṃ codanaṃ manasi nidhāya “yaṃ pana…pe… akaraṇapaccayā vutta”nti idaṃ vuttaṃ. Ayañhettha adhippāyo – aññassatthāya karontassapi sārambhādipaccayāpi anāpattiyeva. “Āpatti kārukānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ dukkaṭāna”nti idaṃ pana aññassatthāya karontassa na sārambhādipaccayā āpattidassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ, kiñcarahi yathāsamādiṭṭhāya akaraṇapaccayā āpattidassanatthanti. Yasmā bahūsu potthakesu satasodhitasammate ca purāṇapotthake ayameva pāṭhakkamo dissati, tasmā yathādiṭṭhapāṭhānukkamenevettha attho pakāsito. Katthaci potthake pana “kuṭilakkhaṇappattampi kuṭiṃ…pe… anāpattī”ti imassānantaraṃ “yaṃ panā”tiādipāṭhaṃ likhanti, evañca sati tattha adhippāyo pākaṭoyeva. Anāpattīti vatvāti uposathāgārañca bhavissati, ahañca vasissāmītiādīsu vāsāgāratthāya eva aniyamitattā anāpattīti vatvā.

Here, the showing of the state of no offense in every way regarding a grass hut is done by bringing in the Parivāra Pāḷi, so that the state of no offense, even due to causes such as commencement, regarding a grass hut can be easily established. And when the state of no offense in every way regarding a grass hut is established, by that same method, the state of no offense, even due to causes such as commencement, in caves, grottoes, and so on, can be understood. For that reason, the passage beginning “Whatever…” was stated. For when the state of no offense, even due to causes such as commencement, regarding a grass hut is established, by that same method, the state of no offense, even due to causes such as commencement, for one who is making it for the sake of another is, by implication, indeed shown. This being so, a bhikkhu departs after instructing, “Make a hut for me,” and he instructs that it should be on a designated site, without commencement, and with a surrounding area; but they make the hut for him on an undesignated site, with commencement, and without a surrounding area. In the Pāḷi, it says, “There is an offense of three wrongdoings for the makers.” Keeping in mind the objection, “Why is a wrongdoing stated for one who is making it for the sake of another, even due to causes such as commencement?” this was said: “Whatever…pe… is stated due to the condition of not doing.” The intention here is this: for one who is making it for the sake of another, even due to causes such as commencement, there is indeed no offense. However, the statement, “There is an offense of three wrongdoings for the makers,” is not stated to show an offense due to causes such as commencement for one who is making it for the sake of another; but rather, it is to show an offense due to the condition of not doing as instructed. Because in many manuscripts, and in an ancient manuscript accepted as having been revised a hundred times, this very textual sequence is seen, the meaning here is explained according to the textual sequence as seen. In some manuscripts, however, they write the passage beginning “Whatever…” immediately after “even a hut that has attained the characteristics of a hut…pe… no offense.” And this being so, the intention there is quite clear. Having said “no offense”: having said that because it was not specified for the purpose of a dwelling place in cases such as, “It will be an Uposatha hall, and I will reside there,” there is no offense.

Pamāṇātikkantakuṭikaraṇalakkhaṇā [M 2.0338] kiriyāyeva, adesitavatthumūlikāyapi āpattiyā aṅgaṃ hoti pamāṇātikkantamūlikāyapi, tadubhayaṃ ekato katvā “kiriyākiriyato”ti vuttaṃ. Vatthuṃ adesāpetvā pamāṇayuttaṃ kuṭiṃ karontassapi vatthuṃ desāpetvā akiriyāya kuṭikaraṇakiriyāya ca samuṭṭhānato kiriyākiriyatova samuṭṭhātīti veditabbaṃ. Acittakanti paṇṇattiajānanacittena acittakaṃ. Ullittādīnaṃ aññataratā, heṭṭhimappamāṇasambhavo, adesitavatthutā, pamāṇātikkantatā, attuddesikatā, vāsāgāratā, lepaghaṭṭanāti imānettha cha vā satta vā aṅgāni.

The action itself, characterized by building a hut exceeding the measure, is a factor of an offense rooted in an undesignated site, and also of an offense rooted in exceeding the measure. Combining these two, it is said to arise 'from action and non-action'. It should be known that it arises from action and non-action because it originates from the action of building a hut and from non-action, both for one who builds a hut of proper measure without having the site designated, and also for one who has the site designated. 'Unconscious' means unconscious through a mind not knowing the regulation. Being one of the plastered types etc., the non-existence of a lesser measure, the site being undesignated, exceeding the measure, being intended for oneself, being a dwelling place, and the connection of plaster—these are the six or seven factors here.

Kuṭikārasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule concerning the making of a hut is concluded.

7. Vihārakārasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Making of a Dwelling

365. Sattame evaṃnāmake nagareti kosambīnāmake. Tassa kira nagarassa ārāmapokkharaṇīādīsu tesu tesu ṭhānesu kosambarukkhāva ussannā ahesuṃ, tasmā kosambīti saṅkhyaṃ agamāsi. Kusumbassa nāma isino assamato avidūre māpitattāti eke. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – kusumbassa isino nivāsabhūmi kosambī, tassa ca avidūre bhavattā nagaraṃ kosambīti saṅkhyaṃ gatanti. Ghositanāmakena kira seṭṭhinā so kāritoti ettha ko ghositaseṭṭhi, kathañcānena so ārāmo kāritoti? Pubbe kira addilaraṭṭhaṃ nāma ahosi. Tato kotūhalako nāma daliddo chātakabhayena saputtadāro subhikkhaṃ raṭṭhaṃ gacchanto puttaṃ [V 2.0300] vahituṃ asakkonto chaḍḍetvā agamāsi. Mātā nivattitvā taṃ gahetvā gatā. Te ekaṃ gopālakagāmaṃ pavisiṃsu. Gopālakānañca tadā bahupāyāso paṭiyatto hoti, tato pāyāsaṃ labhitvā bhuñjiṃsu. Atha so puriso bahutaraṃ pāyāsaṃ bhutto jīrāpetuṃ asakkonto rattibhāge kālaṃ katvā tattheva sunakhiyā kucchismiṃ paṭisandhiṃ gahetvā kukkuro jāto, so gopālakassa piyo ahosi. Gopālako ca paccekabuddhaṃ upaṭṭhāti. Paccekabuddhopi bhattakiccakāle kukkurassa ekaṃ piṇḍaṃ deti. So paccekabuddhe sinehaṃ uppādetvā gopālakena saddhiṃ paṇṇasālampi gacchati, gopālake [M 2.0339] asannihite bhattavelāyaṃ sayameva gantvā kālārocanatthaṃ paṇṇasāladvāre bhussati, antarāmaggepi caṇḍamige disvā bhussitvā palāpeti. So paccekabuddhe mudukena cittena kālaṃ katvā devaloke nibbatti. Tatrāssa “ghosakadevaputto”tveva nāmaṃ ahosi.

365. In the seventh: 'In a city of such a name' means in the city named Kosambī. It is said that in the parks, ponds, and other such places of that city, Kosamba trees were abundant; therefore, it came to be known by the name Kosambī. Some say it was so named because it was founded not far from the hermitage of the sage named Kusumba. This is what is said: the dwelling place of the sage Kusumba was Kosambī, and because the city was not far from it, it acquired the name Kosambī. 'It is said that it was built by a merchant named Ghosita.' Regarding this: who was this merchant Ghosita, and how was that park built by him? It is said that formerly, there was a country named Addilaraṭṭha. From there, a poor man named Kotūhalaka, fearing famine, was going to a prosperous country with his son and wife. Being unable to carry his son, he abandoned him and went on. The mother turned back, took the child, and proceeded. They entered a village of cowherds. At that time, the cowherds had much milk-rice prepared, and receiving milk-rice from them, they ate. Then that man, having eaten too much milk-rice and being unable to digest it, died during the night. Right there, he took rebirth-linking in the womb of a female dog and was born as a dog. He became dear to the cowherd. The cowherd attended upon a Paccekabuddha. The Paccekabuddha, at mealtime, would give one lump of food to the dog. The dog developed affection for the Paccekabuddha and would go with the cowherd to the leaf-hut. When the cowherd was not present at mealtime, the dog would go by itself to the door of the leaf-hut and bark to announce the time. On the path, if it saw fierce beasts, it would bark and make them flee. That dog, with a gentle mind towards the Paccekabuddha, died and was reborn in the deva-world. There, his name was indeed 'Ghosaka the devaputta'.

So devalokato cavitvā kosambiyaṃ ekasmiṃ kulaghare nibbatti. Taṃ aputtako kira seṭṭhi tassa mātāpitūnaṃ dhanaṃ datvā puttaṃ katvā aggahesi. Atha attano putte jāte sattakkhattuṃ ghātāpetuṃ upakkami. So puññavantatāya sattasupi ṭhānesu maraṇaṃ appatvā avasāne ekāya seṭṭhidhītāya veyyattiyena laddhajīviko aparabhāge pitu accayena seṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ patvā ghositaseṭṭhi nāma jāto. Aññepi kosambiyaṃ kukkuṭaseṭṭhi, pāvāriyaseṭṭhīti dve seṭṭhino atthi, iminā saddhiṃ tayo ahesuṃ.

Having passed away from the deva-world, he was reborn in a certain family home in Kosambī. It is said that a childless merchant, having given wealth to the child's parents, took him as a son. Then, when his own son was born, he attempted to have the child killed seven times. Due to his merit, he did not meet death in any of the seven instances, and in the end, his life was saved through the cleverness of a certain merchant's daughter. In a later part of his life, upon his father's passing, he attained the position of a merchant and became known as Ghositaseṭṭhi. There were also two other merchants in Kosambī—Kukkuṭaseṭṭhi and Pāvāriyaseṭṭhi; together with this one, there were three.

Tena ca samayena tesaṃ sahāyakānaṃ seṭṭhīnaṃ kulūpakā pañcasatā isayo pabbatapāde vasiṃsu. Te kālena kālaṃ loṇambilasevanatthaṃ manussapathaṃ āgacchanti. Athekasmiṃ vāre gimhasamaye manussapathaṃ āgacchantā nirudakaṃ mahākantāraṃ atikkamitvā kantārapariyosāne mahantaṃ nigrodharukkhaṃ disvā cintesuṃ “yādiso ayaṃ rukkho, addhā ettha mahesakkhāya devatāya bhavitabbaṃ, sādhu vatassa, sace no pānīyaṃ vā paribhojanīyaṃ vā dadeyyā”ti. Devatā isīnaṃ ajjhāsayaṃ viditvā “imesaṃ saṅgahaṃ karissāmī”ti attano ānubhāvena viṭapantarato naṅgalasīsamattaṃ udakadhāraṃ pavattesi. Isigaṇo rajatakkhandhasadisaṃ udakavaṭṭiṃ disvā attano bhājanehi udakaṃ gahetvā paribhogaṃ katvā cintesi “devatāya amhākaṃ paribhogudakaṃ dinnaṃ, idaṃ pana agāmakaṃ mahāraññaṃ, sādhu vatassa, sace no āhārampi dadeyyā”ti. Devatā isīnaṃ upakappanavasena dibbāni yāgukhajjakādīni datvā santappesi.

And at that time, five hundred ascetics, who were the teachers of those friendly merchants, lived at the foot of a mountain. From time to time, they would come to the region of humans to obtain salt and sour food. Then, on one occasion during the hot season, while coming to the region of humans, they crossed a great waterless wilderness. At the end of the wilderness, they saw a great banyan tree and thought, “Given the nature of this tree, there must surely be a deity of great power here. It would be excellent if she would give us drinking water or water for use.” The deity, knowing the ascetics’ intention, thought, “I will provide for them,” and by her own power, she caused a stream of water the size of a plough-head to flow from between the branches. The group of ascetics, seeing the torrent of water that resembled a silver bar, collected the water in their vessels, used it, and then thought, “The deity has given us water for use, but this is a great, uninhabited forest. It would be excellent if she would also give us food.” The deity, by way of providing for the ascetics, gave them divine rice-gruel, hard foods, and other such things, and satisfied them.

Isayo cintayiṃsu “devatāya amhākaṃ paribhogudakampi bhojanampi sabbaṃ dinnaṃ, sādhu vatassa[V 2.0301], sace no attānaṃ dasseyyā”ti. Devatā tesaṃ ajjhāsayaṃ viditvā upaḍḍhakāyaṃ dassesi. Devate mahatī te sampatti, kiṃ kammaṃ katvā imaṃ sampattiṃ adhigatāsīti. Nātimahantaṃ parittakaṃ kammaṃ katvāti. Upaḍḍhuposathakammaṃ nissāya hi devatāya sampatti laddhā. Anāthapiṇḍikassa [M 2.0340] kira gehe ayaṃ devaputto kammakāro ahosi. Seṭṭhissa hi gehe uposathadivasesu antamaso dāsakammakāre upādāya sabbo jano uposathiko hoti. Ekadivasaṃ ayaṃ kammakāro ekakova pāto uṭṭhāya kammantaṃ gato. Mahāseṭṭhi nivāpaṃ labhamānamanusse sallakkhento etassevekassa araññaṃ gatabhāvaṃ ñatvā assa sāyamāsatthāya nivāpaṃ adāsi. Bhattakāradāsī ekasseva bhattaṃ pacitvā araññato āgatassa bhattaṃ vaḍḍhetvā adāsi. Kammakāro cintayi “aññesu divasesu imasmiṃ kāle gehaṃ ekasaddaṃ ahosi, ajja ativiya sannisinnaṃ, kiṃ nu kho eta”nti. Tassa sā ācikkhi “ajja imasmiṃ gehe sabbe manussā uposathikā, mahāseṭṭhi tuyhevekassa nivāpaṃ adāsī”ti. Evaṃ ammāti. Āma sāmīti. “Imasmiṃ kāle uposathaṃ samādinnassa uposathakammaṃ hoti, na hotī”ti mahāseṭṭhiṃ puccha ammāti. Tāya gantvā pucchito mahāseṭṭhi āha – “sakalauposathakammaṃ na hoti, upaḍḍhakammaṃ pana hoti, uposathiko hotī”ti. Kammakāro bhattaṃ abhuñjitvā mukhaṃ vikkhāletvā uposathiko hutvā vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā nipajji. Tassa āhāraparikkhīṇakāyassa rattiṃ vāto kuppi. So paccūsasamaye kālaṃ katvā upaḍḍhuposathakammanissandena mahāvattaniaṭavidvāre nigrodharukkhadevaputto hutvā nibbatti.

The ascetics thought, “The deity has given us everything—water for use and food. It would be excellent if she would show herself to us.” The deity, knowing their intention, showed half of her body. They asked, “O deity, your prosperity is great. Having done what deed did you attain this prosperity?” She replied, “Having done a not-so-great, a small deed.” Indeed, the prosperity of a deity was obtained by relying on the deed of a half-Uposatha observance. It is said that in the house of Anāthapiṇḍika, this devaputta had been a workman. In the merchant's house, on Uposatha days, everyone, down to the slave-workers, would observe the Uposatha. One day, this workman, all alone, rose early and went to his work. The great merchant, while taking note of the people receiving their provisions, realized that this one man had gone to the forest and gave him provisions for his evening meal. The female slave who was the cook, having cooked rice for that one person, served a portion of rice to him when he returned from the forest. The workman thought, “On other days at this time, the house was full of noise, but today it is extremely quiet. What can be the reason for this?” She explained to him, “Today in this house, all the people are observing the Uposatha. The great merchant gave provisions only to you.” “Is that so, mother?” he asked. “Yes, master.” “For one who undertakes the Uposatha at this time, does the Uposatha-deed come to be or not? Please ask the great merchant, mother,” he said. The great merchant, having been asked by her, said: “The full Uposatha-deed does not come to be, but the half-deed does come to be; he becomes an observer of the Uposatha.” The workman, without eating the rice, rinsed his mouth, became an observer of the Uposatha, took his resting place, and lay down. For him, whose body was depleted from lack of food, a wind-illness arose during the night. At dawn, he passed away and, through the result of the half-Uposatha deed, was reborn as a devaputta of a banyan tree at the gate of the Mahāvaṭṭani forest.

So taṃ pavattiṃ isīnaṃ ārocesi. Isayo pucchiṃsu “tumhehi mayaṃ ‘buddho dhammo saṅgho’ti assutapubbaṃ sāvitā, uppanno nu kho loke buddho”ti. Āma, bhante, uppannoti. Idāni kuhiṃ vasatīti. Sāvatthiyaṃ nissāya jetavane, bhanteti. Isayo “tiṭṭhatha tumhe, mayaṃ satthāraṃ passissāmā”ti haṭṭhatuṭṭhā nikkhamitvā anupubbena kosambīnagaraṃ sampāpuṇiṃsu. Mahāseṭṭhino “isayo āgatā”ti paccuggamanaṃ katvā “sve amhākaṃ bhikkhaṃ gaṇhatha, bhante”ti nimantetvā punadivase isigaṇassa mahādānaṃ adaṃsu. Isayo “bhutvāva gacchāmā”ti āpucchiṃsu. Bhante, tumhe aññasmiṃ kāle ekampi māsaṃ dvepi tayopi cattāropi māse vasitvā gacchatha, imasmiṃ pana vāre hiyyo āgantvā “ajjeva gacchāmā”ti vadatha, kiṃ idanti. Āma gahapatayo buddho loke uppanno, na kho pana sakkā jīvitantarāyo jānituṃ, tena mayaṃ turitā gacchāmāti[M 2.0341]. Tena hi, bhante, mayampi āgacchāma, amhehi saddhiṃyeva gacchathāti. “Tumhe agāriyā nāma mahājaṭā, tiṭṭhatha tumhe, mayaṃ puretaraṃ gamissāmā”ti nikkhamitvā [V 2.0302] ekaṭṭhāne dve divasāni avasitvā turitagamanena sāvatthiṃ patvā jetavanavihāre satthu santikameva agamaṃsu. Tattha madhuradhammakathaṃ sutvā sabbeva pabbajitvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu.

He related that account to the ascetics. The ascetics asked, “By you, we have been made to hear what was never heard before: ‘Buddha, Dhamma, Saṅgha.’ Has a Buddha truly arisen in the world?” “Yes, venerable sirs, he has arisen.” “Where does he dwell now?” “Near Sāvatthī, in the Jeta Grove, venerable sirs.” The ascetics said, “You stay; we will see the Teacher.” Joyful and delighted, they set out and in due course reached the city of Kosambī. The great merchants, thinking, “The ascetics have come,” went out to meet them and invited them, saying, “Venerable sirs, tomorrow please accept our alms.” On the next day, they gave a great offering to the group of ascetics. The ascetics asked for leave, saying, “Having eaten, we will go.” The merchants asked, “Venerable sirs, at other times you stay for one, two, three, or even four months before you go. But on this occasion, having come yesterday, you say, ‘We will go today itself.’ What is the reason for this?” “Yes, householders, a Buddha has arisen in the world. But it is not possible to know the dangers to life. Therefore, we go in haste.” “Then, venerable sirs, we too will come. Please go together with us.” The ascetics replied, “You are householders, with great entanglements. You stay; we will go first.” They departed, and without staying in one place for two days, they reached Sāvatthī by swift travel and went right to the Teacher's presence at the Jetavana monastery. There, having heard the sweet Dhamma talk, all of them went forth and attained Arahantship.

Tepi tayo seṭṭhino pañcahi pañcahi sakaṭasatehi sappimadhuphāṇitādīni ceva paṭṭuṇṇadukūlādīni ca ādāya kosambito nikkhamitvā anupubbena sāvatthiṃ patvā jetavanasāmante khandhāvāraṃ bandhitvā satthu santikaṃ gantvā vanditvā paṭisanthāraṃ katvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Satthā tiṇṇampi sahāyānaṃ madhuradhammakathaṃ kathesi. Te balavasomanassajātā satthāraṃ nimantetvā punadivase mahādānaṃ adaṃsu, puna nimantetvā punadivaseti evaṃ aḍḍhamāsaṃ dānaṃ datvā “bhante, amhākaṃ janapadaṃ āgamanāya paṭiññaṃ dethā”ti pādamūle nipajjiṃsu. Bhagavā “suññāgāre kho gahapatayo tathāgatā abhiramantī”ti āha. “Ettāvatā paṭiññā dinnā nāma hotī”ti gahapatayo sallakkhetvā “dinnā no bhagavatā paṭiññā”ti pādamūle nipajjitvā dasabalaṃ vanditvā nikkhamitvā antarāmagge yojane yojane vihāraṃ kāretvā anupubbena kosambiṃ patvā “loke buddho uppanno”ti kathayiṃsu. Tayo janā attano attano ārāme mahantaṃ dhanapariccāgaṃ katvā bhagavato vihāre kārāpesuṃ. Tattha kukkuṭaseṭṭhinā kārito kukkuṭārāmo nāma ahosi. Pāvārikaseṭṭhinā ambavane kārito pāvārikambavanaṃ nāma. Ghositena kārito ghositārāmo nāma ahosi. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “ghositanāmakena kira seṭṭhinā so kārito”ti.

Those three merchants, taking five hundred carts each filled with ghee, honey, molasses, and other such things, as well as silk, woollen, and fine linen cloths, set out from Kosambī. Gradually, they reached Sāvatthī and, setting up camp near Jetavana, went to the presence of the Teacher. After paying homage and exchanging friendly greetings, they sat down to one side. The Teacher gave the three friends a sweet discourse on the Dhamma. Filled with great joy, they invited the Teacher and offered a great alms-giving the next day. Again, they invited him, and so on, offering alms for half a month. Then, they prostrated at his feet and said, "Venerable sir, please grant us your promise to come to our country." The Blessed One replied, "Householders, Tathāgatas delight in secluded dwellings." Understanding this, the householders considered, "By this much, a promise is given." Thinking, "A promise has been given to us by the Blessed One," they prostrated at his feet, paid homage to the Ten-Powered One, and departed. Along the way, they had a monastery built at every yojana and eventually returned to Kosambī, announcing, "A Buddha has arisen in the world!" The three men, each in their own park, made great expenditures of wealth and had monasteries built for the Blessed One. Therein, the monastery built by the merchant Kukkuṭa was called Kukkuṭārāma. The one built by the merchant Pāvārika in the mango grove was named Pāvārikambavana. The one built by Ghosita was called Ghositārāma. With reference to that, it was said: "It was built, it seems, by the merchant named Ghosita."

Yo abhinikkhamanakāle saddhiṃ nikkhanto, yassa ca satthārā parinibbānakāle brahmadaṇḍo āṇatto, taṃ sandhāyāha “bodhisattakāle upaṭṭhākachannassā”ti. Iminā ca yo majjhimanikāye channovādasutte (ma. ni. 3.389 ādayo) gilāno hutvā dhammasenāpatinā ovadiyamānopi māraṇantikavedanaṃ adhivāsetuṃ asakkonto tiṇhena satthena kaṇṭhanāḷiṃ chinditvā maraṇabhaye uppanne gatinimitte ca upaṭṭhite attano puthujjanabhāvaṃ ñatvā saṃviggo vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā saṅkhāre pariggaṇhanto arahattaṃ [M 2.0342] patvā samasīsī hutvā parinibbāyi, ayaṃ so na hotīti dasseti. Pūjāvacanappayoge kattari sāmivacanassapi icchitattā āha “gāmassa vā pūjita”nti. Lakkhaṇaṃ panettha saddasatthānusārato veditabbaṃ. Ekeko koṭṭhāsoti ekeko bhāgo.

He who went forth together with the Bodhisatta at the time of the Great Renunciation, and upon whom the brahmadaṇḍa was imposed by the Teacher at the time of his Parinibbāna—referring to him, it is said: 'of Channa, the attendant during the Bodhisatta's time.' And by this, it is shown that this is not the same person as the one who, in the Channovāda Sutta of the Majjhima Nikāya, being ill and, even when admonished by the General of the Dhamma, being unable to endure the pain leading to death, cut his own throat with a sharp knife; and who then, when the fear of death arose and the sign of his future destiny appeared, having realized his own status as a worldling, became agitated, established insight, and while comprehending the conditioned formations, attained Arahantship and passed into Parinibbāna as one who is blameless. In the usage of a word of veneration, since the genitive case is also desired for the agent, it is said, 'or honored by the village.' Herein, the grammatical rule should be understood in accordance with the grammatical texts. 'Ekeko koṭṭhāso' means 'each single part'.

366. Kiriyato samuṭṭhānabhāvoti kevalaṃ kiriyāmattato samuṭṭhānabhāvaṃ paṭikkhipati, vatthuno pana adesanāya kuṭikaraṇakiriyāya ca samuṭṭhānato kiriyākiriyato samuṭṭhātīti veditabbaṃ[V 2.0303]. Imasmiṃ sikkhāpade bhikkhū vā anabhineyyāti ettha vā-saddo “ayaṃ vā so mahānāgo”tiādīsu viya avadhāraṇatthoti daṭṭhabbo.

366. The phrase 'the state of arising from an action' rejects the state of arising as being from the mere action alone; rather, it should be understood that it arises from both action and non-action, that is, from the non-declaration of the site and from the action of making the hut. In this training rule, in the phrase 'bhikkhū vā anabhineyyā', the word 'vā' should be seen as being in the sense of emphasis, just as in such phrases as 'this indeed is that great nāga.'

Vihārakārasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule concerning the maker of a dwelling is concluded.

8. Paṭhamaduṭṭhadosasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

8. Explanation of the First Training Rule on Malicious Accusation

380. Aṭṭhame pākārena parikkhittanti sambandho. Gopuraṭṭālakayuttanti dvārapāsādena ca tattha tattha pākāramatthake patiṭṭhāpitaaṭṭālakehi ca yuttaṃ. Veḷūhi parikkhittattā abbhantare pupphūpagaphalūpagarukkhasañchannattā ca nīlobhāsaṃ. Chāyūdakasampattiyā bhūmibhāgasampattiyā ca manoramaṃ. Kāḷakavesenāti kalandakarūpena. Nivāpanti bhojanaṃ. Tanti uyyānaṃ. Dabboti tassa therassa nāmanti dabbatthambhe patitattā dabboti tassa therassa nāmaṃ ahosi.

8. In the eighth, the connection is with the phrase ‘enclosed by a wall’. ‘Endowed with a gatehouse and watchtowers’ means endowed with a gate-mansion and with watchtowers established here and there on top of the wall. Because it was enclosed with bamboos, and because the interior was covered with flowering and fruit-bearing trees, it had a dark-green lustre. It was delightful due to the abundance of shade and water, and the excellence of the grounds. ‘In the guise of a black squirrel’ means in the form of a squirrel. ‘Feeding ground’ means food. ‘That’ refers to the park. ‘Dabba is the name of that elder’: because he fell on a clump of Dabba grass, his name became Dabba.

Kassapadasabalassa sāsanosakkanakāle kira satta bhikkhū ekacittā hutvā aññe sāsane agāravaṃ karonte disvā “idha kiṃ karoma, ekamante samaṇadhammaṃ katvā dukkhassantaṃ karissāmā”ti nisseṇiṃ bandhitvā uccaṃ pabbatasikharaṃ abhiruhitvā attano cittabalaṃ jānantā “nisseṇiṃ pātentu, jīvite sālayā otarantu, mā pacchānutappino ahuvatthā”ti vatvā sabbe ekacittā hutvā nisseṇiṃ pātetvā “appamattā hotha, āvuso”ti aññamaññaṃ ovaditvā cittaruciyesu ṭhānesu nisīditvā samaṇadhammaṃ kātuṃ ārabhiṃsu.

380. During the time when the Dispensation of the Buddha Kassapa, the Ten-Powered One, was declining, it is said that seven monks, being of one mind, seeing others acting disrespectfully towards the Dispensation, thought, "What shall we do here? Let us practice the ascetic's life in seclusion and make an end of suffering." They fastened a ladder, climbed a high mountain peak, and, knowing the strength of their resolve, said, "Let them cast down the ladder! Let those with attachment to life descend! Do not be regretful afterwards!" All being of one mind, they cast down the ladder and, encouraging each other with, "Be diligent, friends," they sat in places of their liking and began to practice the ascetic's life.

Tatreko [M 2.0343] thero pañcame divase arahattaṃ patvā “mama kiccaṃ nipphannaṃ, ahaṃ imasmiṃ ṭhāne kiṃ karissāmī”ti iddhiyā uttarakuruto piṇḍapātaṃ āharitvā āha – “āvuso, imaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ paribhuñjatha, bhikkhācārakiccaṃ mamāyattaṃ hotu, tumhe attano kammaṃ karothā”ti. Kiṃ nu mayaṃ, āvuso, nisseṇiṃ pātentā evaṃ avacumha “yo paṭhamaṃ dhammaṃ sacchikaroti, so bhikkhaṃ āharatu, tenābhataṃ sesā paribhuñjitvā samaṇadhammaṃ karissantī”ti. Natthi, āvusoti. Tumhe attano pubbahetunāva labhittha, mayampi sakkontā vaṭṭassantaṃ karissāma, gacchatha tumheti. Thero te saññāpetuṃ asakkonto phāsukaṭṭhāne piṇḍapātaṃ paribhuñjitvā gato. Aparopi thero sattame divase anāgāmiphalaṃ patvā tato cuto suddhāvāsabrahmaloke nibbatto, itare therā ekaṃ buddhantaraṃ devamanussesu saṃsaritvā tesu tesu kulesu nibbattā. Eko gandhāraraṭṭhe takkasilanagare rājagehe nibbatto, eko paccantimaraṭṭhe [V 2.0304] paribbājikāya kucchimhi nibbatto, eko bāhiyaraṭṭhe kuṭumbiyagehe nibbatto, eko rājagahe kuṭumbiyagehe nibbatto.

Among them, one elder attained arahantship on the fifth day and thought, 'My task is accomplished. What shall I do in this place?' By means of psychic power, he brought almsfood from Uttarakuru and said, 'Friends, partake of this almsfood. Let the duty of the alms-round be my responsibility; you do your own work.' The others replied, 'Friend, when we were casting down the ladder, did we not say this: "Whoever first realizes the Dhamma, let him bring alms; the rest, having eaten what is brought by him, will practice the ascetic's life"?' 'Friend, there was no such statement,' he said. They replied, 'You have obtained this on account of your own past causes. We too, being able, shall make an end of the round of suffering. You may go.' The elder, being unable to convince them, consumed the almsfood in a comfortable place and departed. Another elder, on the seventh day, attained the fruit of non-returning and, passing away from there, was reborn in the Suddhāvāsa Brahma world. The other elders, having wandered through the realms of devas and humans for one Buddha-interval, were reborn in various families. One was reborn in a royal house in the city of Takkasilā in the Gandhāra country; one was reborn in a border country in the womb of a female wanderer; one was reborn in a householder's family in the Bāhiya country; and one was reborn in a householder's family in Rājagaha.

Ayaṃ pana dabbatthero mallaraṭṭhe anupiyanagare ekassa mallarañño gehe paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi. Tassa mātā upavijaññā kālamakāsi. Matasarīraṃ susānaṃ netvā dārucitakaṃ āropetvā aggiṃ adaṃsu. Aggivegasantattaṃ udarapaṭalaṃ dvedhā ahosi. Dārako attano puññabalena uppatitvā ekasmiṃ dabbatthambhe nipati, taṃ dārakaṃ gahetvā ayyikāya adaṃsu. Sā tassa nāmaṃ gaṇhantī dabbatthambhe patitvā laddhajīvikattā “dabbo”ti tassa nāmaṃ akāsi. Tena vuttaṃ “dabboti tassa therassa nāma”nti.

This Elder Dabba, however, in the Malla country, in the city of Anupiya, took conception in the house of a certain Malla king. His mother died when she was about to give birth. They took her corpse to the charnel ground, placed it on a pyre of wood, and set fire to it. Scorched by the force of the fire, her abdominal wall split in two. The child, by the power of his own merit, sprang up and landed on a certain clump of Dabba grass. They took that child and gave him to his grandmother. As she was giving him a name, because he had obtained his life by falling onto a clump of Dabba grass, she named him ‘Dabba’. Therefore, it was said, ‘Dabbo is the name of that elder.’

Tassa sattavassikakāle satthā bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto mallaraṭṭhe cārikaṃ caramāno anupiyanigamaṃ patvā anupiyambavane viharati. Dabbakumāro satthāraṃ disvā saha dassaneneva pasīditvā pabbajitukāmo hutvā “ahaṃ dasabalassa santike pabbajissāmī”ti ayyikaṃ āpucchi. Sā “sādhu tātā”ti dabbakumāraṃ ādāya satthu santikaṃ gantvā “bhante, imaṃ kumāraṃ pabbājethā”ti āha. Satthā aññatarassa bhikkhuno saññaṃ adāsi “bhikkhu imaṃ dārakaṃ pabbājehī”ti. So thero satthu vacanaṃ sutvā dabbakumāraṃ pabbājento tacapañcakakammaṭṭhānaṃ ācikkhi. Pubbahetusampanno katābhinīhāro [M 2.0344] paṭhamakesavaṭṭiyā voropanakkhaṇeyeva sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāsi, dutiyāya kesavaṭṭiyā oropiyamānāya sakadāgāmiphale, tatiyāya anāgāmiphale, sabbakesānaṃ pana oropanañca arahattaphalasacchikiriyā ca apacchā apure ahosi. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “thero kira sattavassikova saṃvegaṃ labhitvā pabbajito khuraggeyeva arahattaṃ pāpuṇīti veditabbo”ti.

When he was seven years old, the Teacher, surrounded by the community of monks, was traveling through the Malla country when he arrived at the market town of Anupiya and stayed in the Anupiya mango grove. The young Dabba, upon seeing the Teacher, was immediately filled with faith and desired to go forth. He said to his grandmother, 'I will go forth in the presence of the Ten-Powered One.' She replied, 'Very well, dear one,' and taking young Dabba, she went to the Teacher and said, 'Venerable Sir, please let this boy go forth.' The Teacher gave a sign to a certain monk, saying, 'Monk, let this boy go forth.'
