That elder, hearing the Teacher's words, while giving the going forth to young Dabba, taught him the meditation subject of the five parts ending with the skin. Endowed with past causes and having made his aspiration, at the very moment the first lock of hair was being removed, he became established in the fruit of stream-entry; when the second lock of hair was being removed, in the fruit of once-returning; and with the third, in the fruit of non-returning. The removal of all his hair and the realization of the fruit of arahantship occurred simultaneously, neither before nor after. Regarding this, it is said: 'It should be understood that the elder, it is said, having experienced spiritual urgency at the age of seven and gone forth, attained arahantship at the very tip of the razor.'

Sāvakena pattabbanti yathupanissayaṃ tena tena sāvakena pattabbaṃ. Tisso vijjātiādi yathāsambhavavasena vuttaṃ. Guṇajātanti “yañca kiñci sāvakena pattabba”nti napuṃsakaliṅgasambandhadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Catūsu saccesu catūhi maggehi soḷasavidhassa kiccassa katattāti dukkhasamudayanirodhamaggasaṅkhātesu catūsu saccesu dukkhapariññā samudayappahānaṃ nirodhasacchikiriyā maggabhāvanāti ekekassa maggassa catunnaṃ catunnaṃ kiccānaṃ vasena soḷasavidhassa kiccassa katattā. Tato tato paṭikkamitvāti tato tato kiccato ārammaṇato ca paṭivattitvā. Silāpaṭṭaketi pāsāṇaphalake. Terasāpīti bhattuddesakasenāsanaggāhāpakabhaṇḍāgārikacīvarapaṭiggāhakacīvarabhājanakayāgubhājanakaphalabhājanakakhajjabhājanakaappamattakavissajjakasāṭiyaggāhāpakapattaggāhāpakaārāmikapesakasāmaṇerapesakasammutīnaṃ [V 2.0305] vasena terasāpi sammutiyo dātuṃ vaṭṭanti.

"What is to be attained by a disciple" means: what is to be attained by each particular disciple according to their supporting conditions. "The three knowledges, etc." is stated in accordance with what is possible. "The collection of qualities" is stated to show the connection with the neuter gender in "whatever is to be attained by a disciple." "Because of having performed the sixteen-fold task in the four truths by means of the four paths" means: because in the four truths—designated as suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—the sixteen-fold task has been performed by way of the four functions for each respective path, namely: the full understanding of suffering, the abandoning of the origin, the realization of cessation, and the development of the path. "Having retreated from there" means: having turned back from that particular task and object. "On a stone slab" means: on a slab of stone. "Thirteen as well" means: by way of the appointments, it is permissible to grant thirteen appointments, namely: the appointer of food, the assigner of dwelling places, the storehouse keeper, the robe receiver, the robe divider, the gruel divider, the fruit divider, the snack divider, the distributor of minor requisites, the cloth receiver, the bowl receiver, the sender of monastery attendants, and the sender of novices.

382. Apisūti ettha sūti nipātamattaṃ, api-saddo aṭṭhānappayutto “vikāle”ti imassa anantaraṃ daṭṭhabbo, vikālepi āgacchantīti attho. Jānantāti dūrabhāvaṃ jānantā. Evaṃ sabbapadesūti ettha katikasaṇṭhānādīnaṃ nānappakārattā tasmiṃ tasmiṃ vihāre katikavattādīni visuṃ visuṃ kathāpetīti veditabbaṃ. Sabbavihāresu ca gamanamagge samappamāṇe katvā adhiṭṭhātīti vadanti. Ayañhi nimmitānaṃ dhammatāti aniyametvā nimmitānaṃ ayaṃ “ekasmiṃ bhāsamānasmi”ntiādi dhammatā. Tathā hi ye vaṇṇavayasarīrāvayavaparikkhārakiriyāvisesādīhi niyamaṃ akatvā nimmitā honti, te aniyametvā nimmitattā iddhimatā sadisāva honti. Ṭhānanisajjādīsu bhāsitatuṇhībhāvādīsu vā yaṃ yaṃ iddhimā karoti, taṃ tadeva karonti. Sace pana nānappakāre kātukāmo hoti, keci paṭhamavaye, keci majjhimavaye, keci pacchimavaye, tathā dīghakese, upaḍḍhamuṇḍe[M 2.0345], missakakese, upaḍḍharattacīvare, paṇḍukacīvare, padabhāṇadhammakathāsarabhaññapañhapucchanapañhavissajjanacīvarasibbanadhovanādīni karonte, aparepi vā nānappakārake kātukāmo hoti, tena pādakajjhānato vuṭṭhāya “ettakā bhikkhū paṭhamavayā hontū”tiādinā nayena parikammaṃ katvā puna samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya adhiṭṭhite adhiṭṭhānacittena saddhiṃ icchiticchitappakārāyeva honti. Avatthukavacanaṃ na hotīti nimmitānaṃ “ayaṃ mañco”tiādivacanaṃ avatthukaṃ na hoti sabbattha mañcapīṭhānaṃ sambhavato.

382. In "apisū", "sū" is merely a particle; the word "api" is used in the wrong place and should be understood immediately after "vikāle", with the meaning "they come even at an improper time." "Jānantā" means "knowing the farness." "Thus in all instances" means: here, because of the various kinds of agreements, arrangements, and so on, it should be understood that in each and every monastery, he had the rules of conduct and so on recited separately. And they say that in all monasteries, having made the paths for walking of equal measure, he determines it. "For this is the nature of the created" means: this is the nature of those created without being specified, such as "while one is speaking," etc. Indeed, those who are created without specifying distinctions such as complexion, age, bodily parts, requisites, activities, and so on, being created without specification, are just like the one with psychic power. In matters of standing, sitting, and so on, or in speaking, remaining silent, and so on, whatever the one with psychic power does, they do exactly that. But if one wishes to create various forms—some in the first stage of life, some in the middle stage, some in the last stage; likewise, with long hair, half-shaven heads, mixed-color hair; with half-dyed red robes, pale robes; or those engaging in reciting the text, teaching the Dhamma, chanting melodiously, asking questions, answering questions, sewing robes, washing them, and so on—or if one wishes to create other various forms, then that person, having emerged from the base jhāna, having made the preliminary preparation with the thought, "Let so many monks be in the first stage of life," and so on, and then re-entering jhāna and emerging, upon making the determination, they become exactly the kinds of forms that were wished for, together with the mind of determination. "It is not speech without a basis" means: for the created beings, speech such as "this is a couch" is not without a basis, because of the existence of couches and chairs everywhere.

383. Ekacārikabhattanti atimanāpattā visuṃ ṭhitikāya pāpetabbaṃ bhattaṃ. Taddhitavohārenāti cattāri parimāṇamassa catukkanti evaṃ taddhitavohārena. Odanassa pucchāya sādhakatamattā āha – “karaṇattheyeva karaṇavacana”nti, odanena karaṇabhūtena pucchantīti vuttaṃ hoti. Ye ca odanena karaṇabhūtena pucchanti, tesaṃ pucchanākāradassanatthaṃ “kiṃ, bhante, odanaṃ demāti pucchantī”ti vuttaṃ.

383. "Ekacārikabhatta" refers to a meal that, due to being excessively cherished, must be allotted separately. By derivative usage, it is said, "four is its measure, thus it is a 'catukka'", thus by derivative usage. Regarding the question about rice, to indicate the most effective means, it is said, "the term for instrument is used in the sense of instrument," meaning they ask using rice as an instrument. And to show the manner of questioning by those who ask using rice as the instrument, it is said, "'What, venerable sir, shall we give rice?' they ask."

Bhavoti bhavitabbo. Asamannāharitvāti ābhogaṃ akatvā. Rattiṃ sammantayamānāti kañci kālaṃ supitvā vuṭṭhāya sammantayamānā. Rattiyañhi paṭhamayāmamajjhimayāmesu supitvā pabuddhānaṃ ajjatanakālepi anajjatanābhimāno hoti, tasmā te “hiyyo”ti āhaṃsu. Ye pana rattiyaṃ kammappasutā jāgariyamanuyuttā honti, tesaṃ ajjatanābhimānoyeva, tasmā te “ajja”icceva voharanti, na “hiyyo”ti. Padhūpāyantāti punappunaṃ uppajjanakakodhavasena padhūpāyantā.

"Bhavo" means: that which is to be. "Asamannāharitvā" means: without directing the mind. "Deliberating at night" means: deliberating after having slept for some time and then arisen. For those who, having slept during the first or middle watch of the night, awaken, they have the perception of 'not-today' even in the present time; therefore, they said 'yesterday'. But for those who are engaged in work at night, devoted to wakefulness, they have only the perception of 'today'; therefore, they use the term 'today', not 'yesterday'. "Fuming" means: fuming because of anger that arises again and again.

384. Dabba [V 2.0306] dabbāti dutiyo dabba-saddo paṇḍitādhivacanoti āha “dabbā paṇḍitā”ti. Evaṃ na nibbeṭhentīti sambandho. Nibbeṭhentīti attānaṃ dosato mocenti. Vuṭṭhānalakkhaṇaṃ maññamānāti vuṭṭhānalakkhaṇanti maññamānā. Na ghaṭiyatīti therassa susīlapaṭiññāya tassā dussīlapaṭiññāvacanaṃ na ghaṭiyatīti adhippāyo. Ettha yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ parato āvi bhavissati. Nāsethāti setakaṃ datvā gihibhāvaṃ pāpethāti attho. Liṅganāsanā hettha adhippetā. Imameva ca dassetuṃ “tisso nāsanā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ekakammādisaṃvāsassa akaraṇaṃ saṃvāsanāsanā. Daṇḍakammanāsanā nāma vālukādīni okiritvā yāva khamāpeti, tāva daṇḍakammavasena [M 2.0346] nikkaḍḍhanaṃ. Cara pire vinassāti nikkaḍḍhanākāradassanaṃ. Tattha carāti gaccha, apehīti vuttaṃ hoti. Pireti para amāmaka, amhākaṃ anajjhattikabhūtāti attho. Pireti hi para-saddena samānatthaṃ sambodhanavacanaṃ. Atha vā pireti “parato”ti iminā samānatthaṃ nipātapadaṃ, tasmā cara pireti parato gaccha, mā idha tiṭṭhāti attho. Vinassāti adassanaṃ gaccha.

384. Regarding "dabbā": the second word "dabba" is a term for a wise person; therefore, he said, "Dabbā means the wise." The connection should be made thus: "they do not extricate themselves." "Nibbeṭhenti" means: they free themselves from the fault. "Thinking it has the characteristic of rising" means: thinking "it is the characteristic of rising." "It does not fit" means: the intention is that her declaration of being unvirtuous does not fit with the elder's claim of being virtuous. What should be said here will become clear later. "Nāsetha" means: the meaning is "having given white clothes, cause her to reach the state of a layperson." The destruction of the monastic characteristic is intended here. And to show this very point, "three kinds of destruction," etc., was said. Not performing the communal acts, etc., is the destruction of communion. The destruction by a disciplinary act is the expulsion by means of a disciplinary act—by scattering sand, etc.—until she asks for forgiveness. "Cara pire vinassa" shows the manner of expulsion. Therein, "cara" means "go, depart." "Pire" means "O other one, not dear, not ours, not belonging to us." For "pire" is a vocative term with the same meaning as the word "para." Alternatively, "pire" is a particle with the same meaning as "parato" (elsewhere). Therefore, "cara pire" means "go elsewhere, do not stand here." "Vinassa" means "go out of sight."

Yasmā te bhikkhū attānaṃ appakāsetvā ṭhitā, tasmā anuyuñjathāti imassa gavesatha jānāthāti attho vutto. Kārako hotīti “ayyenamhi dūsitā”ti paṭiññātattā tāya paṭiññāya yadi nāsitā, thero kārako hoti, sadosoti attho. Akārako hotīti tāya katapaṭiññaṃ anapekkhitvā yadi bhagavatā pakatidussīlabhāvaṃyeva sandhāya sā nāsitā, thero akārako hotīti adhippāyo. “Sakāya paṭiññāya nāsethā”ti vutte “ayyenamhi dūsitā”ti tāya katapaṭiññāya bhūtatā āpajjatīti āha – “bhante, tumhākaṃ vāde thero kārako hoti sadoso”ti. Bhikkhuniṃ anuddhaṃseti, dukkaṭanti iminā mahāaṭṭhakathāvādo dassito. Musāvāde pācittiyanti vuttanti bhikkhuniṃ anuddhaṃsentassa musāvāde pācittiyanti vuttaṃ.

Since those monks remained without revealing themselves, therefore, for the phrase 'anuyuñjatha,' the meaning 'search, know' is stated. As for 'He is the doer': because she had admitted, 'I have been corrupted by the venerable one,' if she was expelled on account of that admission, the elder is the doer; the meaning is that he is at fault. As for 'He is not the doer': if, disregarding the admission she made, the Blessed One, considering only her naturally immoral character, expelled her, the elder is not the doer; this is the intention. When it was said, 'Expel her by her own admission,' the admission she made, 'I have been corrupted by the venerable one,' becomes a fact. Thus, the minister said, 'Venerable sir, in your argument, the elder is the doer and is at fault.' By the statement, 'He slanders a bhikkhunī, it is a dukkaṭa offense,' the view of the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā is shown. As for what was said, 'For false speech, it is a pācittiya offense,' it is said that for one who slanders a bhikkhunī, there is a pācittiya offense for false speech.

Tatrāti tesu dukkaṭapācittiyesu. Ito paṭṭhāya “tasmā pācittiyameva yujjatī”ti vacanapariyantaṃ dvīsupi aṭṭhakathāsu adhippāyavibhāvanaṃ. Tattha purimanayeti “bhikkhuniṃ anuddhaṃseti, dukkaṭa”nti vuttaaṭṭhakathānaye. Dukkaṭameva yujjatīti kasmā vuttanti ce? Tattha kāraṇaṃ dassento “yathā”tiādimāha. Bhikkhuno bhikkhusmiṃ saṅghādisesoti bhikkhuṃ amūlakena antimavatthunā anuddhaṃsentassa bhikkhuno saṅghādisesoti attho. Pacchimanayepi “bhikkhuniṃ anuddhaṃsentassa musāvāde pācittiya”nti vuttaṃ. Kurundīnayepi musāvādattā pācittiyameva yujjatīti visaṃvādapurekkhatāya pācittiyameva yujjatīti adhippāyo. Yadi evaṃ bhikkhuṃ amūlakena [V 2.0307] antimavatthunā anuddhaṃsentassa akkosantassa ca musāvādattā pācittiyeneva bhavitabbanti ce? Tattha satipi musāvāde vacanappamāṇato saṅghādisesaomasavādapācittiyeheva bhavitabbaṃ, na sampajānamusāvādapācittiyenāti dassetuṃ “vacanappamāṇato”tiādimāha. Tattha vacanappamāṇatoti [M 2.0347] bhagavatā vuttapāḷivacanappamāṇato. Idāni taṃ vacanaṃ dassetuṃ “anuddhaṃsanādhippāyenā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Bhikkhussa pana bhikkhuniyā dukkaṭanti vacanaṃ natthīti bhikkhuniyā anuddhaṃsane bhikkhuno dukkaṭanti vacanaṃ natthi tathā pāḷiyaṃ anāgatattā. Sampajānamusāvāde pācittiyanti vacanamatthīti sāmaññato vuttaṃ sampajānamusāvādasikkhāpadaṃ dasseti.

Herein, 'tatra' refers to those dukkaṭa and pācittiya offenses. From this point up to the end of the statement 'therefore only a pācittiya offense is suitable,' is a clarification of the intention in both commentaries. Therein, in the former method—that is, in the method of the commentary where it was said, 'If one slanders a bhikkhunī, it is a dukkaṭa offense'—if it is asked why it was said that only a dukkaṭa offense is suitable, the commentator, showing the reason, states what begins with 'just as.' 'For a bhikkhu, regarding a bhikkhu, it is a Saṅghādisesa offense' means that for a bhikkhu who groundlessly slanders another bhikkhu with a terminal offense, it is a Saṅghādisesa. Also in the latter method, it was said: "For one who slanders a bhikkhunī, there is a pācittiya offense for false speech." Also in the Kurundī method, the phrase "because it is false speech, only a pācittiya offense is suitable" means that the intention is that because it is preceded by deception, only a pācittiya offense is suitable. If that is so, should it not also be only a pācittiya offense for a bhikkhu who groundlessly slanders and abuses another bhikkhu with a terminal offense, because it is false speech? Therein, even though there is false speech, according to the authority of the statement, it should be only a Saṅghādisesa or a pācittiya offense for contemptuous speech—not a pācittiya offense for intentional false speech. To show this, he says what begins with 'according to the authority of the statement.' Therein, 'according to the authority of the statement' means according to the authority of the Pāli words spoken by the Blessed One. Now, to present that statement, what begins with 'with the intention of slander' is said. However, the statement 'For a bhikkhu, regarding a bhikkhunī, it is a dukkaṭa offense' does not exist; this means there is no statement that for a bhikkhu slandering a bhikkhunī it is a dukkaṭa offense, because it does not appear thus in the Pāli. The statement 'For intentional false speech, it is a pācittiya offense' exists; this shows the training rule on intentional false speech, which was stated in general.

Idāni dvīsupi aṭṭhakathāvādesu adhippāyaṃ vibhāvetvā tesu pacchimavāde dosaṃ dassetvā purimavādaṃ patiṭṭhapetukāmo ācariyo “tatra panā”tiādimāha. Tatrāti “pācittiyameva yujjatī”ti vuttavāde. Anuddhaṃsanādhippāye asati pācittiyanti iminā sampajānamusāvāde pācittiyassa okāsaṃ dasseti. Visuṃ pācittiyaṃ vuttanti sampajānamusāvāde pācittiyato visuṃ aññameva pācittiyaṃ vuttaṃ. Etehi nāsanā natthīti sāmaññato vuttaṃ, imissā pana dukkaṭena nāsanā natthīti adhippāyo. Yadi evaṃ kasmā naṃ bhagavā nāsetīti āha “yasmā panā”tiādi.

Now, having clarified the intention in both commentarial views and having shown the fault in the latter view, the teacher, wishing to establish the former view, says what begins with 'tatra pana.' 'Tatra' refers to the view where it was said, 'only a pācittiya offense is suitable.' By 'when there is no intention to slander, it is a pācittiya offense,' he shows the occasion for a pācittiya offense in the case of intentional false speech. 'A separate pācittiya offense is stated' means that a pācittiya offense separate from the pācittiya for intentional false speech is stated. 'There is no expulsion by these' is stated generally, but the intention is that for this bhikkhunī, there is no expulsion by a dukkaṭa offense. If that is so, why does the Blessed One expel her? To this, he says what begins with 'yasmā pana.'

385-386. Dūsitoti duṭṭhasaddassa kammasādhanataṃ dasseti. Dūsayati paraṃ vināsetīti dūsako. Iminā “dūsayatīti doso”ti dosasaddassa kattusādhanatā vuttā. Pakatibhāvaṃ jahāpitoti dusasaddassa vikatiyaṃ paṭhitattā vuttaṃ, pakatiyā sommabhāvaṃ jahāpitoti attho, vikāramāpāditoti vuttaṃ hoti. Ākāranānattenāti dūsitākārassa dūsakākārassa ca nānattena. Anabhiraddhoti atuṭṭho. Yo pana atuṭṭho, so sukhito nāma na hotīti āha “na sukhito”ti. “Ārādhito rājā”tiādīsu pasāditoti atthasambhavato “na vā pasādito”ti vuttaṃ. Khīlasaddo thaddhabhāvavacano kacavarapariyāyo ca hotīti āha – “cittathaddhabhāvacittakacavarasaṅkhātaṃ paṭighakhīla”nti. Khīlayati tena cittaṃ thaddhabhāvaṃ āpajjatīti khīlaṃ, cittassa thaddhabhāvo. So ca atthato paṭighoyeva. Cittassa thaddhabhāvalakkhaṇo hi paṭigho, tasmiñca uppanne cittaṃ uklāpajātaṭṭhānaṃ viya amanuññaṃ hoti, tasmā kacavarasadisattāpi paṭighova “khīla”nti vutto. Tenāha “paṭighakhīla”nti. Cittassa thaddhabhāvattā kacavarasadisattā ca paṭighoyeva khīlaṃ paṭighakhīlaṃ. Nappatītoti pītisukhādīhi na abhigato na anugato, na upetoti attho. Yo ca pītisukhādīhi anupagato, so tehi [V 2.0308] vajjito [M 2.0348] nāma hotīti āha “pītisukhādīhi vajjito”ti. Yo ca tehi vajjito, na so tena abhisaṭo nāma hotīti āha “na abhisaṭo”ti, pītisukhādīhi na patthaṭoti attho.

385-386. 'Dūsita' shows the passive construction of the word 'duṭṭha.' One who corrupts, that is, destroys another, is a 'dūsaka.' By this, the active construction of the word 'dosa' is stated: 'dosa is that which corrupts (dūsayati).' 'Caused to abandon its natural state' is said because the word 'dusa' is known to have the meaning of 'alteration'; the meaning is 'caused to abandon its natural gentleness.' This means 'brought to a state of alteration.' 'Due to the difference in characteristics' means due to the difference between the characteristic of being corrupted ('dūsita') and the characteristic of being a corruptor ('dūsaka'). 'Anabhiraddha' means displeased. Whoever is displeased is not called happy; thus, he said, 'na sukhito' (not happy). In phrases such as 'ārādhito rājā' (the king was pleased), since the meaning 'pasādito' (pleased/pacified) is possible, the phrase 'na vā pasādito' (or not pleased) is stated. The word 'khīla' denotes a state of rigidity and is also a synonym for refuse; thus, he said, 'the stake of aversion (paṭighakhīla), which is reckoned as mental rigidity and mental refuse.' It is 'khīla' because by it the mind becomes rigid; it is the rigidity of the mind. And that, in essence, is aversion itself. For aversion is characterized by the mind's rigidity, and when it has arisen, the mind becomes unpleasant, like a rubbish heap; therefore, also because of its similarity to refuse, aversion itself is called 'khīla.' Hence, he said, 'paṭighakhīla.' Because of the mind's rigidity and its similarity to refuse, aversion itself is the stake—the stake of aversion. 'Nappatīta' means not reached, not accompanied by, not endowed with joy, happiness, and so on. And whatever is unaccompanied by joy, happiness, and so on, is called 'bereft' of them; thus, he said, 'pītisukhādīhi vajjito' (bereft of joy, happiness, etc.). And whatever is bereft of them is not called 'pervaded' by them; thus, he said, 'na abhisaṭo' (not pervaded), meaning not suffused with joy, happiness, and so on.

Yenāti yena kopena. Duṭṭhoti mātikāya āgatapadaṃ dasseti, kupitoti padabhājane āgatapadaṃ. Atthato ekattepi ubhinnaṃ padānaṃ vasena “ubhayampī”ti vuttaṃ. Evaṃ “tena ca kopena tena ca dosenā”ti imesaṃ padānaṃ vasena “dvīhī”ti vuttaṃ, atthato pana dosoyeva. So ca saṅkhārakkhandhapariyāpannoti āha “imehi dvīhi saṅkhārakkhandhameva dassetī”ti. “Anattamanatā anabhiraddhī”ti vacanehi domanassavedanāva vuttāti āha “imehi dvīhi vedanākkhandhaṃ dassetī”ti.

'Yena' means 'by which anger.' 'Duṭṭha' shows the word that comes in the mātikā (matrix), while 'kupita' shows the word that comes in the padabhājana (word-analysis). Although they are one in meaning, on account of the two words, it is said 'both.' Similarly, on account of the words 'tena ca kopena tena ca dosena' (with that anger and with that aversion), it is said 'by these two,' but in terms of meaning, it is only aversion. And that is included in the aggregate of formations—thus it is said, 'by these two, he shows only the aggregate of formations.' By the words 'anattamanatā' (displeasure) and 'anabhiraddhī' (dissatisfaction), only the feeling of displeasure (domanassavedanā) is stated—thus it is said, 'by these two, he shows the aggregate of feeling.'

Yadā pana codakena adiṭṭhaṃ asutaṃ aparisaṅkitaṃ vā hoti, tadā amūlakaṃ nāma hotīti āha “taṃ panassa…pe… codakavasena adhippeta”nti. Yadi cuditakavasena adhippetaṃ siyā, amūlakaṃ nāma anajjhāpannanti padabhājanaṃ vadeyyāti adhippāyo. Yaṃ pārājikanti bhikkhuno anurūpesu ekūnavīsatiyā pārājikesu aññataraṃ. Padabhājane pana pāḷiyaṃ āgatāneva gahetvā “catunnaṃ aññatarenā”ti vuttaṃ. Etanti cuditakassa āpannānāpannattaṃ. Idhāti imasmiṃ sikkhāpade.

But when it is unseen, unheard, or unsuspected by the accuser, then it is called baseless—thus it is said: 'That, however... is intended by the accuser.' If it were intended by the accused, the word-analysis would state 'baseless means not having committed an offense'; this is the meaning. 'Which is a pārājika offense' means any one of the nineteen pārājika offenses suitable for a bhikkhu. In the word-analysis, however, taking only those that come in the Pāḷi, it is said, 'by any one of the four.' 'This' refers to the state of the accused having committed an offense or not. 'Here' means in this training rule.

Tathevāti pasādasotena dibbasotena vāti imamatthaṃ atidisati. Sutvāva jānitabbato “sutaṭṭhāneyeva tiṭṭhatī”ti vuttaṃ. Parisaṅkanaṃ parisaṅkitaṃ, diṭṭhānugataṃ parisaṅkitaṃ diṭṭhaparisaṅkitaṃ. Evaṃ sesesupi. Imesanti kattuatthe sāmivacanaṃ, imehīti attho. Karissanti vāti ettha vibhattipariṇāmaṃ katvā imeti yojetabbaṃ. Diṭṭhaṃ atthi samūlakaṃ, atthi amūlakanti idaṃ ajjhācārassa sabbhāvāsabbhāvaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Atthi saññāsamūlakaṃ, atthi saññāamūlakanti idaṃ pana diṭṭhasaññāya sabbhāvāsabbhāvaṃ sandhāya.

'Tatheva' (thus) refers to this meaning: 'with the sensitive ear-element or with the divine ear-element.' Because it is to be known only by hearing, it is said: 'it stands only in the place of the heard.' `Parisaṅkanaṃ` is `parisaṅkitaṃ` (suspicion). Suspicion that follows upon seeing is `diṭṭhaparisaṅkitaṃ` (suspicion based on seeing). Thus also in the remaining cases. 'Imesaṃ' (of these) is the genitive case in the sense of the agent; the meaning is 'imehi' (by these). In 'karissanti vā' (or they will do), having changed the case ending, it should be connected as 'imehi'. 'There is what is seen with a basis, there is what is without a basis'—this is stated with reference to the occurrence or non-occurrence of a transgression. 'There is perception with a basis, there is perception without a basis'—this, however, is stated with reference to the occurrence or non-occurrence of a perception of what is seen.

Samīpe ṭhatvāti dvādasahatthabbhantare samīpe ṭhatvāti vadantīti tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Parato pana “dūtaṃ vā paṇṇaṃ vā sāsanaṃ pesetvā codentassa sīsaṃ na etī”ti parammukhācodanāya eva anāpattiyā vuttattā “samīpe ṭhatvā”ti idaṃ sammukhabhāvamattadassanatthaṃ vuttanti amhākaṃ khanti[M 2.0349]. Teneva mātikāṭṭhakathāyaṃ (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. duṭṭhadosasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) aṅgaṃ dassentena “cāvanādhippāyena sammukhācodanā”ti vuttaṃ, na ca sammukhabhāvo dvādasahatthabbhantareyevāti [V 2.0309] niyamo sakkā vatthuṃ. Vinayavinicchayañca patvā garukeyeva ṭhātabbanti vuttaṃ, tasmā upaparikkhitvā yuttataraṃ gahetabbaṃ. Codāpakasseva vācāya vācāya saṅghādisesoti āṇattassa vācāya vācāya codāpakassa saṅghādiseso. Mayāpi diṭṭhaṃ sutaṃ atthīti idaṃ āṇattassapi codakabhāvadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ, evaṃ pana avatvāpi “pārājikaṃ dhammaṃ ajjhāpannosī”ti idameva vacanaṃ parassa vacanaṃ viya akatvā anuddhaṃsanādhippāyena vadantassa saṅghādisesoyeva. Satipi pana anuddhaṃsanādhippāye “asukena evaṃ vutta”nti dassetvā vadantassa natthi saṅghādisesoti vadanti.

'Standing nearby' means standing nearby within twelve cubits; so it is said in all three Gaṇṭhipadas. But later, because it is said, 'For one who accuses by sending a messenger, a leaf, or a message, it does not come to a head,' meaning there is no offense for an accusation made in absence, it is our view that 'standing nearby' is said merely to show the state of being face-to-face. For that very reason, in the Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā, when showing the factor, it is said, 'a face-to-face accusation with the intention of causing to fall away.' And it is not possible to state a rule that being face-to-face is only within twelve cubits. And having come to the Vinayavinicchaya, it is said that one should stand on what is weighty. Therefore, having investigated, what is more suitable should be taken. 'A Saṅghādisesa for the accuser for every word' means a Saṅghādisesa for the accuser for every word of the one who was commanded. The phrase 'By me also it has been seen, it has been heard' is said to show the status of the one commanded as an accuser as well. However, even without saying this, for one who says just this statement, 'You have committed a pārājika offense,' not making it like the statement of another, with the intention of denouncing, it is a Saṅghādisesa. However, even if there is an intention of denouncing, for one who points out, 'It was said thus by so-and-so,' there is no Saṅghādisesa offense; so they say.

Sambahulā sambahule sambahulehi vatthūhi codentīti ettha sambahuleti bahuttaniddese kāraṇaṃ na dissati. Vatthucodakānaṃyeva hi ekānekavasena idaṃ catukkamāgataṃ, na cuditakassapi ekānekavasena. Tathā hi ekasseva cuditakassa vasena ekavatthuekacodakaekavatthunānācodakanānāvatthuekacodakanānāvatthunānācodakappabhedaṃ idaṃ catukkamāgataṃ, teneva catutthacodanaṃ dassentenapi “imissā codanāya nānāvatthūni nānācodakā”ti vuttaṃ, na pana “nānācuditakā”ti, tasmā “sambahule”ti bahuttaniddese kāraṇaṃ na dissati. Atha vā paṭhamaṃ tīsupi codanāsu ekattena cuditakaṃ niddisitvāpi idha bahuttena niddeso “na kevalaṃ ekasmiṃyeva cuditake codanā sambhavati, atha kho sambahulesupī”ti imamatthaṃ dassetuṃ kato.

“Many (accusers) accuse many (accused) with many grounds”—here, in the plural designation ‘sambahule’ (many), a reason is not seen. For this fourfold classification has come about only by way of the grounds and the accusers being one or many, not by way of the accused being one or many. Thus, with respect to a single accused, this fourfold classification with the divisions of one ground-one accuser, one ground-many accusers, many grounds-one accuser, and many grounds-many accusers has come about. For that very reason, even when showing the fourth accusation, it is said, “In this accusation, there are many grounds and many accusers,” but not “many accused.” Therefore, in the plural designation ‘sambahule,’ a reason is not seen. Alternatively, although in the first three accusations the accused was designated in the singular, here the designation is made in the plural to show this meaning: “An accusation does not arise only with respect to a single accused, but indeed it also arises with respect to many.”

Codetuṃ pana ko labhati, ko na labhatītiādi anuddhaṃsanādhippāyaṃ vināpi codanālakkhaṇaṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Sīlasampannoti idaṃ dussīlassa vacanaṃ appamāṇanti adhippāyena vuttaṃ. Bhikkhunīnaṃ pana bhikkhuṃ codetuṃ anissarattā “bhikkhunimevā”ti vuttaṃ. Satipi bhikkhunīnaṃ bhikkhūsu anissarabhāve tāhi katacodanāpi codanāruhattā codanāyevāti adhippāyena “pañcapi sahadhammikā labhantī”ti vuttaṃ. Bhikkhussa sutvā codetītiādinā codako yesaṃ sutvā codeti, tesampi vacanaṃ pamāṇamevāti sampaṭicchitattā tesaṃ codanāpi ruhatevāti dassetuṃ thero suttaṃ nidassesi.

“But who is allowed to accuse, and who is not,” etc., was stated to show the characteristic of an accusation even without the intention of denouncing. “Endowed with virtue”—this was said with the meaning that the word of an immoral person is not authoritative. As for nuns, because they do not have authority to accuse a monk, it was said, “only a nun (can accuse a nun).” Even though nuns do not have authority over monks, an accusation made by them, because of its suitability as an accusation, is indeed an accusation. With this meaning, it was said, “five co-religionists are also allowed.” By “A monk accuses after hearing,” etc., the Elder showed a sutta to demonstrate that because it is accepted that the word of those whom the accuser heard when accusing is also authoritative, their accusation is also valid.

Dūtaṃ [M 2.0350] vā paṇṇaṃ vā sāsanaṃ vā pesetvāti “tvaṃyeva gantvā codehī”ti dūtaṃ vā pesetvā yo taṃ codetuṃ sakkoti, tassa mukhasāsanaṃ vā paṇṇaṃ vā pesetvā. Sīsaṃ na etīti saṅghādiseso na hotīti adhippāyo. Kiñcāpi pāḷiyaṃ “codeti vā codāpeti vā”ti sāmaññato vuttattā dūtasāsanādīhi codāpentassapi āpattiyevāti paññāyati, “sīsaṃ na etī”ti [V 2.0310] idaṃ pana aṭṭhakathācariyappamāṇena gahetabbaṃ. Samayenāti pakatiyā saddaṃ sutvā atthavijānanasamayena.

“Having sent a messenger, or a letter, or a message”—this means by sending a messenger with the message, “You yourself go and accuse him,” or by sending an oral message or a letter to one who is capable of accusing him. The phrase “the head does not come” means there is no Saṅghādisesa offense. Although in the Pāḷi it is generally stated as “accuses or causes to accuse,” and it is understood that for one who causes accusation by means of a messenger, message, and so on, there is indeed an offense, the phrase “the head does not come” should be taken according to the authority of the commentary teachers. By “at the time” is meant at the natural time of hearing the sound and understanding the meaning.

Garukānaṃ dvinnanti pārājikasaṅghādisesānaṃ. Avasesānaṃ vasenāti pañcalahukāpattīnaṃ vasena. “Natthi dinna”ntiādi dasavatthukā micchādiṭṭhi. “Antavā loko, anantavā loko”tiādinayappavattā diṭṭhi sassatucchedasaṅkhātaṃ antaṃ gaṇhātīti antaggāhikā. Ājīvahetu paññattānaṃ channaṃ sikkhāpadānaṃ vasenāti ājīvahetu ājīvakāraṇā pāpiccho icchāpakato asantaṃ abhūtaṃ uttarimanussadhammaṃ ullapati, āpatti pārājikassa, ājīvahetu ājīvakāraṇā sañcarittaṃ samāpajjati, āpatti saṅghādisesassa, ājīvahetu ājīvakāraṇā yo te vihāre vasati, so bhikkhu arahāti bhaṇati, paṭivijānantassa āpatti thullaccayassa, ājīvahetu ājīvakāraṇā bhikkhu paṇītabhojanāni agilāno attano atthāya viññāpetvā bhuñjati, āpatti pācittiyassa, ājīvahetu ājīvakāraṇā bhikkhunī paṇītabhojanāni agilānā attano atthāya viññāpetvā bhuñjati, āpatti pāṭidesanīyassa, ājīvahetu ājīvakāraṇā bhikkhu sūpaṃ vā odanaṃ vā agilāno attano atthāya viññāpetvā bhuñjati, āpatti dukkaṭassa, ājīvavipattipaccayā imā cha āpattiyo āpajjatīti evaṃ parivārapāḷiyaṃ (pari. 287) dassitānaṃ channaṃ sikkhāpadānaṃ vasena. Diṭṭhivipattiājīvavipattīhi codentopi tammūlikāya āpattiyā eva codeti.

“Of the two grave offenses” means of the Pārājika and Saṅghādisesa offenses. “By way of the remaining” means by way of the five light offenses. “There is nothing given,” and so on, is the ten-fold basis of wrong view. The view that arises in the manner of “The world is finite, the world is infinite,” and so on, grasps the extreme known as eternalism and annihilationism; thus, it is called “holding to extremes.” “By way of the six training rules laid down on account of livelihood” means: on account of livelihood, due to the cause of livelihood, one with evil wishes, overcome by desire, speaks of a superhuman state that is not present, that is not real—this is an offense of Pārājika; on account of livelihood, due to the cause of livelihood, one engages in acting as a go-between—this is an offense of Saṅghādisesa; on account of livelihood, due to the cause of livelihood, one says, “The monk who dwells in your monastery is an Arahant”—for one who acknowledges it, there is an offense of grave transgression; on account of livelihood, due to the cause of livelihood, a monk, not being ill, requests fine foods for himself and eats them—this is an offense of Pācittiya; on account of livelihood, due to the cause of livelihood, a nun, not being ill, requests fine foods for herself and eats them—this is an offense of Pāṭidesanīya; on account of livelihood, due to the cause of livelihood, a monk, not being ill, requests soup or rice for himself and eats it—this is an offense of Dukkaṭa. On account of failure in livelihood, one falls into these six offenses. Thus, it is by way of the six training rules shown in the Parivāra-pāḷi. Even when accusing by means of failure in view and failure in livelihood, one accuses only by means of an offense rooted in that.

“Kasmā maṃ na vandasī”ti pucchite “assamaṇosi asakyaputtiyosī”ti avandanakāraṇassa vuttattā antimavatthuṃ ajjhāpanno na vanditabboti vadanti. Codetukāmatāya eva avanditvā attanā vattabbassa vuttamatthaṃ ṭhapetvā avandiyabhāve taṃ kāraṇaṃ na hotīti cūḷagaṇṭhipade majjhimagaṇṭhipade [M 2.0351] ca vuttaṃ. Antimavatthuṃ ajjhāpannassa avandanīyesu avuttattā tena saddhiṃ sayantassa sahaseyyāpattiyā abhāvato tassa ca paṭiggahaṇassa ruhanato tadeva yuttataranti viññāyati. Kiñcāpi yāva so bhikkhubhāvaṃ paṭijānāti, tāva vanditabbo. Yadā pana “assamaṇomhī”ti paṭijānāti, tadā na vanditabboti ayamettha viseso veditabbo. Antimavatthuṃ ajjhāpannassa hi bhikkhubhāvaṃ paṭijānantasseva bhikkhubhāvo, na tato paraṃ. Bhikkhubhāvaṃ appaṭijānanto hi anupasampannapakkhaṃ bhajati. Yasmā āmisaṃ dento attano icchitaṭṭhāneyeva deti, tasmā paṭipāṭiyā nisinnānaṃ yāgubhattādīni dentena ekassa codetukāmatāya adinnepi codanā nāma na hotīti āha “na tāvatā codanā hotī”ti.

When asked, “Why do you not pay homage to me?” and the reason for not paying homage is stated as, “You are not an ascetic, you are not a son of the Sakyans,” they say that one who has committed the final offense should not be paid homage. It is stated in the Cūḷagaṇṭhipada and the Majjhimagaṇṭhipada that not paying homage solely out of a desire to accuse—setting aside the matter to be spoken of by oneself—is not a reason for someone to be considered unworthy of homage. Because one who has committed the final offense is not mentioned among those who are unworthy of homage, and because there is no offense of sharing a sleeping place with him, and because his acceptance of offerings is valid, that very view is understood to be more appropriate. Indeed, as long as he acknowledges his status as a monk, he should be paid homage. But when he acknowledges, “I am not an ascetic,” then he should not be paid homage. This distinction should be understood here. For one who has committed the final offense, his status as a monk exists only as long as he acknowledges his status as a monk, not beyond that. Indeed, one who does not acknowledge his status as a monk enters the side of the unordained. Because one who gives material things gives only where he wishes, therefore, when giving rice-porridge, meals, and so on, to those seated in order, even if one does not give to one person out of a desire to accuse, it is not called an accusation. Thus, it is said, “By that much, it is not an accusation.”

Tiṃsānīti [V 2.0311] tiṃsa etesamatthīti tiṃsāni, tiṃsavantānīti attho, tiṃsādhikānīti vuttaṃ hoti. Guṇavacanattā taddhitalopaṃ katvā “tiṃsānī”ti vuttaṃ. Atha vā tiṃsa codanā adhikā etesūti tiṃsāni. Tasmiṃ adhikamiti ḍakārapaccaye sati rūpamidaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Navutānīti etthāpi eseva nayo.

Regarding tiṃsāni: 'they have thirty,' therefore tiṃsāni; the meaning is 'possessing thirty.' It is said to mean 'more than thirty.' Because it is a qualitative word, it is said as tiṃsāni after eliding the taddhita suffix. Alternatively, 'in these there are thirty additional accusations,' therefore tiṃsāni. In that word, this form should be understood when there is the ḍa-suffix in the sense of 'more.' In the word navutāni also, this is the same method.

Ubbāhikāya taṃ adhikaraṇaṃ vinicchinitabbanti ubbāhikāya sammatehi taṃ adhikaraṇaṃ vinicchinitabbaṃ. Alajjussannāya hi parisāya dasahaṅgehi samannāgato bhikkhu ubbāhikāya sammannitabbo. “Sīlavā hoti pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuto viharati ācāragocarasampanno”tiādinā samathakkhandhake (cūḷava. 231) vuttadasaṅgasampattiyā samannāgatā dve tayo bhikkhū uccinitvā tattheva vuttāya ñattidutiyakammavācāya sammannitabbā. Evaṃ sammatehi pana tehi bhikkhūhi visuṃ vā nisīditvā tassāyeva vā parisāya “aññehi na kiñci kathetabba”nti sāvetvā taṃ adhikaraṇaṃ vinicchinitabbaṃ. Tumhākanti cuditakacodake sandhāya vuttaṃ.

“That legal question should be decided by the Ubbāhikā procedure” means that legal question should be decided by those appointed through the Ubbāhikā procedure. Indeed, in an assembly abounding in shameless monks, a monk endowed with ten factors should be appointed by the Ubbāhikā procedure. Having selected two or three monks endowed with the ten factors spoken of in the Samathakkhandhaka, beginning with, “He is virtuous, dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha restraint, is endowed with good conduct and resort,” they should be appointed by the formal act consisting of a motion and one announcement spoken of in that very place. Then, those monks thus appointed should decide that legal question, either by sitting separately or, in that very assembly, after having announced, “Nothing is to be said by others.” “Your” is said with reference to the accused and the accuser.

Kimhīti kismiṃ vatthusmiṃ. Kimhi nampi na jānāsīti kimhi nanti vacanampi na jānāsi. Nāssa anuyogo dātabboti nāssa pucchā paṭipucchā dātabbā. “Dummaṅkūnaṃ puggalānaṃ niggahāyā”tiādivacanato “alajjīniggahatthāya…pe… paññatta”nti vuttaṃ. Ehitīti āgamissati. Diṭṭhasantānenāti diṭṭhasambandhena, diṭṭhaniyāmenāti vuttaṃ hoti. Vivādavatthusaṅkhāte atthe [M 2.0352] paccatthikā atthappaccatthikā. Saññaṃ datvāti tesaṃ kathaṃ pacchinditvā attano vacanaṃ sādhetuṃ saññaṃ katvā. Asuddhasaññāya uppannattā “ananucchaviko”ti āha. Ekasambhogaparibhogāti idaṃ attano santikā tesaṃ mocanatthaṃ vuttaṃ, na pana tesaṃ aññamaññasambhoge yojanatthaṃ. Vinicchayo na kātabboti “amhākaṃ vacane aṭṭhātabbasabhāvā ete alajjino”ti jānantena vinicchayo na kātabbo.

‘What is it?’: in what matter. ‘You do not even know “kimhi naṃ”’: you do not even know the phrase ‘kimhi naṃ.’ ‘There should be no investigation of him’: no questioning or cross-questioning should be given to him. From the statement beginning ‘For the restraint of the dull-witted individuals,’ it is said, ‘It was prescribed for the purpose of restraining the shameless…etc.’ ‘He will come’: he will arrive. ‘Through a seen continuum’: by the seen connection, meaning by the seen arrangement, it is said. In the matter designated as a ground for dispute, opponents are opponents of the matter. ‘Having given a sign’: having cut off their speech and made a sign to establish one’s own statement. Because an impure perception has arisen, he says, ‘unsuitable.’ ‘Shared use and enjoyment in common’: this is said for the purpose of releasing them from one’s own vicinity, not for the purpose of connecting them to each other in shared use. ‘A judgment should not be made’: knowing that ‘these shameless ones are of a nature not to abide by our words,’ a judgment should not be made.

Viraddhaṃ hotīti attanā katadosappaṭicchādanatthaṃ kañci musāvādaṃ katvā viraddhaṃ hoti. Paṭiññaṃ na detīti sace mayā katadosaṃ vakkhāmi, mayhaṃ anuvattakā bhijjissantīti “kataṃ mayā”ti paṭiññaṃ na deti. Suddho hotūti tesaṃ vacanena suddho nāma hotu, tesaṃ vacanena ekadvevāramassa vinicchayo dātabboti adhippāyo. Ṭhāne na tiṭṭhatīti lajjiṭṭhāne na tiṭṭhati. Vinicchayo na dātabboti alajjibhāvamāpannattā na dātabbo.

‘It is wrong’: it becomes wrong when one tells some lie to conceal a fault one has committed. ‘He does not acknowledge’: thinking, ‘If I confess the fault I committed, my followers will break away,’ he does not acknowledge by saying, ‘I did it.’ ‘Let him be pure’: by their words, let him be pure by name; the intention is that by their words, a decision should be given to him once or twice. ‘He does not stand in his place’: he does not stand in the place of the conscientious. ‘A decision should not be given’: it should not be given because he has fallen into a state of shamelessness.

Amūlakampi samūlakampi mūlaṃ gahetvā vadantīti āha “dve mūlānī”ti. Kālena vakkhāmītiādīsu [V 2.0312] eko ekaṃ okāsaṃ kāretvā codento kālena vadati nāma. Saṅghamajjhe gaṇamajjhe salākaggayāguaggavitakkamāḷakabhikkhācāramaggaāsanasālādīsu upaṭṭhākehi parivāritakkhaṇe vā codento akālena vadati nāma. Tacchena vadanto bhūtena vadati nāma. “Ambho mahallaka-parisāvacara-paṃsukūlika-dhammakathika-patirūpaṃ tava ida”nti vadanto pharusena vadati nāma. Kāraṇanissitaṃ pana katvā “bhante mahallakāttha, parisāvacarā paṃsukūlikā dhammakathikāttha, patirūpaṃ tumhākaṃ ida”nti vadanto saṇhena vadati nāma. Kāraṇanissitaṃ katvā vadanto atthasañhitena vadati nāma. Mettacitto vakkhāmi, no dosantaroti mettacittaṃ upaṭṭhāpetvā vakkhāmi, na duṭṭhacitto hutvā. Pannarasasu dhammesūti parisuddhakāyasamācāratā, parisuddhavacīsamācāratā, sabrahmacārīsu mettacittatā, bahussutatā, ubhinnaṃ pātimokkhānaṃ vitthārena svāgatasuvibhattasuppavattasuvinicchitatā, “kālena vakkhāmī”tiādinā vuttapañcadhammā, kāruññatā, hitesitā, anukampatā, āpattivuṭṭhānatā, vinayapurekkhāratāti imesu pannarasasu dhammesu. Tattha kāruññatāti kāruṇikabhāvo. Iminā karuṇā ca karuṇāpubbabhāgo ca dassito. Hitesitāti hitagavesanatā. Anukampatāti tena [M 2.0353] hitena saṃyojanā. Dvīhipi mettā ca mettāpubbabhāgo ca dassito. Āpattivuṭṭhānatāti āpattito vuṭṭhāpetvā suddhante patiṭṭhāpanā. Vatthuṃ codetvā sāretvā paṭiññaṃ āropetvā yathāpaṭiññāya kammakaraṇaṃ vinayapurekkhāratā nāma. Sacce ca akuppe cāti vacīsacce ca akuppatāya ca. Cuditakena hi saccañca vattabbaṃ, kopo ca na kātabbo, neva attanā kujjhitabbo, na paro ghaṭṭetabboti attho.

Because they speak taking even a rootless or a rooted (accusation) as a basis, he said, ‘two roots.’ In cases such as ‘I will speak at the right time’: when one person, having created an opportunity, accuses another, this is called speaking at the right time. When one accuses in the midst of the Saṅgha, in the midst of a group, at the ticket-distribution place, at the gruel-distribution place, at the promenade, on the alms-round path, in the sitting hall, or at a time when one is surrounded by attendants, this is called speaking at an improper time. One who speaks truthfully is called one who speaks with what is factual. One who says, ‘Hey, old man, you who frequent assemblies, you rag-robe wearer, you Dhamma-preacher, is this fitting for you?’ is called one who speaks harshly. But one who, basing it on a reason, says, ‘Venerable sirs, you are elders, you frequent assemblies, you are rag-robe wearers, you are Dhamma-preachers, is this fitting for you?’ is called one who speaks gently. One who speaks having based it on a reason is called one who speaks what is connected to the goal. ‘I will speak with a mind of loving-kindness, not with inner hatred’ means: I will speak having established a mind of loving-kindness, not having become one with a hostile mind. In the fifteen qualities: purity in bodily conduct, purity in verbal conduct, a mind of loving-kindness toward fellow practitioners, being learned, mastery of both Pātimokkhas in detail—being well-versed, well-analyzed, well-practiced, and well-decided—the five qualities stated beginning with ‘I will speak at the right time,’ compassion, seeking what is beneficial, sympathy, causing one to rise from an offense, and prioritizing the Vinaya—in these fifteen qualities. Therein, compassion means the state of being compassionate. By this, both compassion and the preliminary stage of compassion are shown. Seeking what is beneficial means searching for benefit. Sympathy means connecting with that benefit. By these two, both loving-kindness and the preliminary stage of loving-kindness are shown. Causing one to rise from an offense means causing one to rise from an offense and establishing them in purity. Prioritizing the Vinaya means: having accused regarding the matter, having reminded, having brought to an acknowledgement, and performing the formal act according to the acknowledgement. In truth and in imperturbability means: in truth of speech and in imperturbability. For the accuser should speak the truth and should not be angry; one should neither become angry oneself nor provoke another—this is the meaning.

Bhummappattiyāti bhummavacane sampatte, bhummatthe idaṃ upayogavacananti vuttaṃ hoti. Adhikarīyanti etthāti adhikaraṇāni. Ke adhikarīyanti? Samathā. Kathaṃ adhikarīyanti? Samanavasena. Adhikaraṇaṃ samenti vūpasamentīti hi samathā. Atha vā samanatthāya pavattamānehi samathehi adhikātabbānīti adhikaraṇāni. Yathā hi samanavasena samathānaṃ vivādādīsu adhikattubhāvo, evaṃ vivādādīnaṃ tehi adhikattabbatāpi. Tenāha “samathehi adhikaraṇīyatā”ti. Iminā adhikaraṇasaddassa kammasādhanatā vuttā. Gāhanti “asukaṃ codessāmī”ti manasā codanāya gahaṇaṃ. Cetananti “codessāmī”ti uppannacetanaṃ. Akkhantinti cuditake uppannaṃ akkhantiṃ. Vohāranti codanāvasappattavacanaṃ. Paṇṇattinti codanāvasappavattanāmapaṇṇattiṃ. Attādānaṃ gahetvāti codanaṃ manasā gahetvā. Taṃ adhikaraṇanti taṃ gāhalakkhaṇaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ.

Regarding `Bhummappattiyā`: when the locative case is intended, this is a usage in the accusative case in the sense of the locative; thus it is said. ‘They are adjudicated herein, therefore they are cases (adhikaraṇa).’ What are adjudicated? Settlements (samatha). How are they adjudicated? By way of settlement. For settlements (samatha) are so called because they settle (samenti) and pacify (vūpasamenti) a case (adhikaraṇa). Or, they are cases (adhikaraṇa) because they are to be adjudicated (adhikātabbāni) by settlements that proceed for the sake of settlement. For just as settlements have the role of being the adjudicators in disputes and so on by way of settlement, so too disputes and so on have the role of being what is to be adjudicated by them. Therefore he said, ‘adjudicability by settlements.’ By this, the derivation of the term ‘adhikaraṇa’ in the passive sense is stated. `Gāha` (grasping) is the mental grasping of an accusation, thinking, ‘I will accuse so-and-so.’ `Cetanā` (intention) is the intention that has arisen, ‘I will accuse.’ `Akkhanti` (impatience) is the impatience that has arisen in the accused. `Vohāra` (expression) is the speech that has reached the state of an accusation. `Paṇṇatti` (designation) is the nominal designation that proceeds by way of accusation. ‘Having taken it up’: having mentally grasped the accusation. ‘That is a case’: that `adhikaraṇa` is the one characterized by grasping.

Tasmā [V 2.0313] paṇṇatti adhikaraṇanti aṭṭhakathāsu katasanniṭṭhānaṃ dassetvā idāni tampi na yuttanti dassetuṃ “taṃ paneta”ntiādimāha. Teti aṭṭhakathācariyā. Pārājikadhammoti pārājikāpatti. Accantaakusalattāti lokavajjabhāvato pārājikāpattiyā ekantaakusalattā. Yāya paṇṇattiyāti nāmapaṇṇattiṃ sandhāya vadati. Abhilāpenāti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Paññattoti vohāravasena kathito. Adhikaraṇe pavattattā ca adhikaraṇanti mañcaṭṭhesu mañcavohāro viya. Yasmā amūlakena codento cuditake puggale taṃ adhikaraṇaṃ natthīti sallakkheti, tasmā tassa vacanaṃ abhidheyyasuññanti āha “sabhāvato natthī”ti. Tañca kho idhevāti tañca yathāvuttapariyāyena paṇṇattiyā adhikaraṇabhāvo idheva imasmiṃyeva sikkhāpade. “Mātāpi puttena vivadatī”tiādinayappavattassa [M 2.0354] vivādassa adhikaraṇabhāvo na sambhavati samathehi anadhikaraṇīyattāti āha “idhekacco vivādo”ti.

Therefore, having shown the established conclusion in the commentaries that a designation is a legal issue, he now says, beginning with 'but this,' to show that even that is not appropriate. 'Te' means the commentary teachers. 'Pārājikadhammo' means a pārājika offense. 'Accantaakusalattā': because a pārājika offense is blameworthy in the world, it is entirely unwholesome. 'Yāya paṇṇattiyā' refers to a name-designation. 'Abhilāpena' is a synonym for that very term. 'Paññatto' means spoken of by way of conventional usage. And because it occurs in a legal issue, it is called a 'legal issue,' just as the term 'bed' is used for those on a bed. Since one who accuses groundlessly perceives that there is no such legal issue in the accused person, his statement is therefore devoid of meaning; hence, the Teacher said, 'by nature, it does not exist.' 'And that, too, right here' means: and that state of being a legal issue for a designation, according to the manner described, is only here, in this very training rule. For a dispute that has arisen in the manner of 'A mother disputes with her son,' etc., the state of being a legal issue is not possible, because it is not to be settled by the settlement procedures. Therefore, he said, 'here, a certain dispute.'

Aṭṭhārasabhedakaravatthūnīti lakkhaṇavacanametaṃ yathā “yadi me byādhitā daheyyuṃ, dātabbamidamosadha”nti, tasmā tesu aññataraññataraṃ nissāya uppanno vivādo “aṭṭhārasabhedakaravatthūni nissāya uppanno”ti vuccati. Anuvādoti upavadanā ceva codanā ca. Tattha upavadanā nāma akkoso. Pañcapi āpattikkhandhāti mātikāya āgatā pañca āpattikkhandhā. Sattāti teyeva pañca, vibhaṅge āgatā thullaccayadubbhāsitāpattiyo dveti satta. Kiccayatāti kattabbatā. Karaṇīyatāti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Ubhayenapi apalokanādisaṅghakammaṃyeva dasseti, tenāha “apalokanakamma”ntiādi.

‘The eighteen grounds for causing schism’: this is a statement of cause, just as in ‘This medicine should be given, should they provide it for me on account of illness.’ Therefore, a dispute that has arisen depending on any one of those is called ‘one that has arisen depending on the eighteen grounds for causing schism.’ ‘Anuvāda’ means both censure and accusation. Therein, ‘upavadanā’ means abuse. ‘The five aggregates of offenses’ means the five aggregates of offenses that come in the matrix. ‘Seven’ means those same five, plus the two offenses that come in the Vibhaṅga, namely the thullaccaya and dubbhāsita offenses, thus making seven. ‘Kiccayatā’ means what ought to be done. ‘Karaṇīyatā’ is a synonym for that very term. By both, he shows only the Saṅgha act beginning with announcement; therefore, he said ‘the act of announcement,’ and so on.

Āpattādhikaraṇaṃ ṭhapetvā sesādhikaraṇehi codanāyeva natthīti āha “imasmiṃ panatthe…pe… āpattādhikaraṇameva adhippeta”nti. Sapadānukkamaniddesassāti padānaṃ anukkamena niddeso padānukkamaniddeso, padabhājanassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tena saha vattamānaṃ sapadānukkamaniddesaṃ, sikkhāpadaṃ, tassa padānukkamaniddesasahitassa sikkhāpadassāti attho, padabhājanasahitassāti vuttaṃ hoti.

Setting aside the legal issue of an offense, with the remaining legal issues there is no accusation at all. Therefore, he said, 'But in this matter... only the legal issue of an offense is intended.' 'Of that with the sequential explanation of terms' means: the explanation of terms in sequence is a 'sequential explanation of terms'; this is a designation for the 'analysis of terms' (padabhājana). A training rule that is accompanied by this is called 'one with the sequential explanation of terms.' The meaning is 'of that training rule accompanied by the sequential explanation of terms,' which is to say, 'accompanied by the analysis of terms.'

Assāti kattuatthe sāmivacanaṃ, anenāti attho. Tenāha “etena codakenā”tiādi. Idhāgatesūti imasmiṃ sikkhāpade āgatesu. Aññatra āgatesūti ito aññatra omasavādādisikkhāpadapāḷiyaṃ āgatesu. Dussīloti nissīlo sīlavirahito. Pāpadhammoti dussīlattā eva hīnajjhāsayatāya lāmakasabhāvo. Asucisaṅkassarasamācāroti aparisuddhakāyakammāditāya asuci hutvā saṅkāya saritabbasamācāro. Dussīlo hi kiñcideva [V 2.0314] asāruppaṃ disvā “idaṃ asukena kataṃ bhavissatī”ti paresaṃ āsaṅkanīyo hoti, kenacideva vā karaṇīyena mantayante bhikkhū disvā “kacci nu kho ime mayā katakammaṃ jānitvā mantentī”ti attanoyeva saṅkāya saritabbasamācāro. Paṭicchannakammantoti lajjitabbatāya paṭicchādetabbakammanto. Assamaṇoti [M 2.0355] na samaṇo. Salākaggahaṇādīsu “ahampi samaṇo”ti micchāpaṭiññāya samaṇapaṭiñño. Aseṭṭhacāritāya abrahmacārī. Uposathādīsu “ahampi brahmacārī”ti micchāpaṭiññāya brahmacāripaṭiñño. Pūtinā kammena sīlavipattiyā anto anupaviṭṭhattā antopūti. Chadvārehi rāgādikilesānuvassanena tintattā avassuto. Sañjātarāgādikacavarattā sīlavantehi chaḍḍetabbattā ca kasambujāto.

‘Assa’ is the genitive case in the sense of the agent; the meaning is ‘by this one.’ Therefore, he said, ‘by this accuser,’ and so on. ‘Those that have come here’ means those that have come in this training rule. ‘Those that have come elsewhere’ means those that have come elsewhere than this, in the Pāḷi of the training rule on contemptuous speech and so on. ‘Dussīlo’ means without virtue, devoid of moral conduct. ‘Pāpadhammo’ means one of a base nature due to having inferior inclinations, precisely because of being immoral. ‘Asucisaṅkassarasamācāro’ means one whose conduct is to be remembered with suspicion, having become impure due to impure bodily actions and so on. For an immoral person, upon seeing some improper act, becomes an object of suspicion to others, who think, ‘This must have been done by so-and-so.’ Or, upon seeing monks discussing some matter, his conduct is to be remembered with suspicion by himself, thinking, ‘I wonder if they are discussing the deed I have done, having come to know of it.’ ‘Paṭicchannakammanto’ means one whose actions should be concealed because they are shameful. ‘Assamaṇo’ means not an ascetic; in matters like taking voting tickets, he pretends to be an ascetic with the false claim, ‘I too am an ascetic.’ ‘Abrahmacārī’ means not leading the holy life due to un-noble conduct; in matters like the Uposatha, he pretends to lead the holy life with the false claim, ‘I too lead the holy life.’ ‘Antopūti’ means internally rotten, because of having entered within through a rotten deed, through the corruption of virtue. ‘Avassuto’ means soaked, because of being drenched by the downpour of defilements such as lust through the six doors. ‘Kasambujāto’ means born of refuse, both because of having arisen defilements such as lust, which are like rubbish, and because of being fit to be discarded by the virtuous.

Idha pāḷiyanti imasmiṃ sikkhāpade pāḷiyaṃ. Jeṭṭhabbatikoti kalidevīvataniyutto. Kalidevī kira sirīdeviyā jeṭṭhā, tasmā tassā vatadharo “jeṭṭhabbatiko”ti vuccati. Taṃ pana vataṃ samādiyitvā pūrento sakalasarīre masiṃ makkhetvā kākapattāni muṭṭhiyaṃ katvā kalideviṃ phalake likhāpetvā taṃ kājakoṭiyaṃ bandhitvā thomento vicarati. Yadaggenāti yattakena. Tadaggenāti tattakena. No kappetītiādi vematikabhāvadīpanatthameva vuttanti mahāpadumattherassa adhippāyo. Dutiyatthero pana “no kappeti, nassarati, pamuṭṭho”ti etehi vematikabhāvāvatthāya adīpanato añño vematikabhāvo, aññāni no kappanādīnīti catunnampi vibhāgena atthaṃ dasseti, tasmā tassa vādo yuttataroti pacchā vutto. Dassane vematiko hotīti puggale ñātepi tassa kiriyāya sammā adiṭṭhabhāvato cirakālātikkamato vā taṃ kiriyaṃ karonto “esa mayā diṭṭho vā, na vā”ti dassane vematiko hoti. Puggale vematiko hotīti tena katakamme ñātepi taṃ kammaṃ karontassa sammā adiṭṭhabhāvato kālantarabhāvato vā “tassa kammassa kārako ayaṃ vā, no”ti puggale vematiko hoti.

'Here in the Pāḷi' means in the Pāḷi of this training rule. 'Jeṭṭhabbatiko' means one devoted to the vow of Kalidevī. Kalidevī, it is said, was the elder sister of Sirīdevī; therefore, one who upholds her vow is called 'Jeṭṭhabbatiko.' One who, however, having undertaken that vow and fulfilling it, smears his whole body with ink, makes a handful of crow feathers, has an image of Kalidevī drawn on a plank, ties it to the end of a carrying pole, and wanders about praising it. 'Yadaggena' means by as much as. 'Tadaggena' means by that much. 'No kappeti,' etc., is said only for the purpose of indicating the state of doubt—this is the intention of the Elder Mahāpaduma. The second elder, however, shows the meaning by way of division of the four, saying: since the state of doubt is not indicated by these terms 'does not approve, does not remember, is confused,' the state of doubt is something else, and 'not approving' and so on are other things. Therefore, his view is more appropriate, and so it is stated later. 'He is doubtful in seeing' means: even though the person is known, because his action was not properly seen or because of the long passage of time, he is doubtful in seeing, thinking, 'Was this person seen by me or not?' 'He is doubtful about the person' means: even though the deed done by him is known, because the one doing that deed was not properly seen or because of an interval of time, he is doubtful about the person, thinking, 'Is this the doer of that deed or not?'

389. “Tajjanīyakammādisattavidhampi kammaṃ karissāmā”ti āpattiyā codentassa adhippāyo kammādhippāyo. “Āpattito vuṭṭhāpessāmī”ti adhippāyo vuṭṭhānādhippāyo. Anuddhaṃsentassāti iminā cāvanādhippāyaṃ dasseti. Akkosādhippāyena vadantassa pācittiyanti akkosādhippāyena sattahipi āpattikkhandhehi sammukhā vadantassa pācittiyaṃ. Dukkaṭanti akkosādhippāyena vadantassa dukkaṭaṃ.

389. 'I will perform the seven kinds of formal acts, beginning with the Tajjaniya act'—this intention of one who accuses another of an offense is the intention for a formal act (kammādhippāya). 'I will have him rehabilitated from the offense'—this intention is the intention for rehabilitation (vuṭṭhānādhippāya). By the phrase 'for one disparaging,' it shows the intention to depose (cāvanādhippāya). 'For one speaking with the intention to insult, it is a pācittiya offense' means: for one who, with the intention to insult, speaks face-to-face concerning any of the seven groups of offenses, it is a pācittiya offense. 'A dukkaṭa offense' means: for one who speaks with the intention to insult in the other's absence, it is a dukkaṭa offense.

“Evaṃ saṃvaddhā hi tassa bhagavato parisā yadidaṃ aññamaññavacanena aññamaññavuṭṭhāpanenā”ti vacanato kurundaṭṭhakathānayaṃ patiṭṭhapento “kurundiyaṃ [M 2.0356] panā”tiādimāha[V 2.0315]. Sabbatthevāti sabbaaṭṭhakathāsu. Yya-kāre sampatte re-kāro atikkanto nāma hotīti āha “re-kāre anatikkante”ti. Uposathassa ñattikammabhāvato ñattiyā samattāya uposatho kato nāma hotīti āha “yya-kāre sampatte na labbhatī”ti.

'Thus indeed was the assembly of the Blessed One increased, that is, by mutual instruction and mutual rehabilitation.' Because of this statement, while establishing the method of the Kurundī commentary, he said, 'But in the Kurundī…' and so on. 'In all instances' means in all the commentaries. When the 'yya' syllable is present, the 're' syllable is said to be passed over; therefore, he said, 'when the 're' syllable is not passed over.' Because the Uposatha is a formal act by declaration, when the declaration is complete, the Uposatha is said to have been performed; therefore, he said, 'when the 'yya' syllable is present, it is not obtained.'

Idañcidañcāti “pāṇātipātaṃ adinnādāna”ntiādiṃ. “Asuko ca asuko ca assamaṇo anupāsako”ti akkosādhippāyena parammukhā vadantassa dukkaṭaṃ, sammukhā vadantassa pana pācittiyameva. Yathā “asūriyaṃ passati kaññā”ti ettha “sūriyaṃ na passati kaññā”ti ayamattho labbhati, evaṃ “anokāsaṃ kārāpetvā”ti etthāpi “okāsaṃ akārāpetvā”ti ayamattho labbhatīti āha “yaṃ panā”tiādi. Yaṃ codeti, tassa upasampannoti saṅkhyūpagamanaṃ, tasmiṃ suddhasaññitā, yena pārājikena codeti, tassa diṭṭhādivasena amūlakatā, cāvanādhippāyena sammukhā codanā, tassa taṅkhaṇavijānananti imānettha pañca aṅgāni.

'This and that' refers to 'killing living beings, taking what is not given,' and so on. For one who, with the intention to insult, says behind another's back, 'So-and-so is not a recluse, not a lay follower,' it is a dukkaṭa offense; but for one who says it face-to-face, it is indeed a pācittiya offense. Just as in the phrase 'asūriyaṃ passati kaññā' (the girl sees no-sun), the meaning 'sūriyaṃ na passati kaññā' (the girl does not see the sun) is obtained, so too in 'anokāsaṃ kārāpetvā' (having caused no-opportunity to be made), the meaning 'okāsaṃ akārāpetvā' (not having caused an opportunity to be made) is obtained; therefore, he said, 'But as for what…' and so on. Herein, these are the five factors: (1) the person who is accused has attained the designation 'ordained'; (2) the perception of him as pure; (3) the groundlessness, by way of what was seen, etc., of the pārājika offense with which one accuses; (4) the accusation face-to-face with the intention to depose; and (5) that person's knowing at that very moment.

Paṭhamaduṭṭhadosasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the first training rule on the fault of malice is completed.

9. Dutiyaduṭṭhadosasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

9. Explanation of the Second Training Rule on the Fault of Malice

391. Navame disvāti ajikāya vippaṭipajjantaṃ chagalakaṃ disvā. Mettiyaṃ bhikkhuninti tassā bhikkhunikālaṃ gahetvā bhūtapubbavohārena voharanti. Veḷuvaneyevāti therassa bhikkhācāravelaṃ aggahetvā tehi vuttabhattuddesavelaṃyeva sandhāya vuttaṃ. Kacci noti kacci nu. Etamatthaṃ ārocesunti aññabhāgiyassa adhikaraṇassa kañcidesaṃ lesamattaṃ upādāya pārājikena dhammena anuddhaṃsitabhāvaṃ ārocesuṃ.

391. In the ninth rule, 'having seen' means: having seen the male goat misbehaving with the she-goat. 'The nun Mettiyā' means: they speak using a term for what has been in the past, referring to the time before she became a nun. 'In the Bamboo Grove' was said with reference only to the time for the apportionment of food spoken of by them, not taking the elder's time for going on almsround. 'Kacci no' means 'kacci nu.' 'They informed him of this matter' means: taking as a pretext a mere hint of a matter belonging to another part, they reported the fact of his being disparaged with a pārājika offense.

Aññabhāgassāti aññakoṭṭhāsassa, therassa manussajātibhikkhubhāvato aññassa tiracchānajātichagalakabhāvasaṅkhātassa koṭṭhāsassāti vuttaṃ hoti. Idanti sāmaññato napuṃsakaniddesena chagalakaṃ niddisati, idaṃ chagalakajātanti attho, ayaṃ chagalakoti vuttaṃ hoti. Adhikaraṇasaddāpekkho vā napuṃsakaniddeso, idaṃ chagalakasaṅkhātaṃ [M 2.0357] adhikaraṇanti vuttaṃ hoti. Aññabhāgoti yathāvuttatiracchānajātichagalakabhāvasaṅkhāto aññabhāgo, aññakoṭṭhāsoti attho. Assāti chagalakassa. “Aññabhāgasambandhī aññabhāgiya”nti paṭhamaviggahassa attho, “aññabhāgavantaṃ aññabhāgiya”nti dutiyaviggahassa. Dvīhipi viggahehi aññabhāgiyanti chagalakova [V 2.0316] vutto. Tiracchānajātichagalakabhāvañca ṭhapetvā paramatthato visuṃ chagalake asatipi “paṭimāya sarīra”ntiādīsu viya abhedepi bhedakappanāya pavattalokavohāravasena “aññabhāgassa idaṃ, aññabhāgo vā assa atthī”ti vuttaṃ.

'Of another part' means of another division; that is to say, of the division designated as the state of a goat of animal birth, which is other than the elder's state of being a monk of human birth. 'This' indicates the goat by a general neuter designation; the meaning is 'this is the goat species,' which is to say, 'this is the goat.' Alternatively, it is a neuter designation with reference to the word 'adhikaraṇa' (matter); which is to say, 'this matter is designated as the goat.' 'Another part' means the other part, the other division, designated as the state of a goat of animal birth, as described. 'Of it' means of the goat. The meaning of the first analysis is: 'related to another part, it is of another part (aññabhāgiya).' The meaning of the second analysis is: 'possessing another part, it is of another part (aññabhāgiya).' By both analyses, 'of another part' refers only to the goat. And although, in an ultimate sense, there is no goat separate from the state of being a goat of animal birth, just as in expressions like 'a body in an image,' where a distinction is made even though there is no separation, it is spoken of by way of worldly convention that 'this is of another part' or 'it has another part.'

Idāni dvīhipi viggahehi vuttamatthaṃ vitthāretvā dassento “yo hi so”tiādimāha. Soti so chagalako. Tassa “hotī”ti iminā sambandho. Tatoti tato manussajātito bhikkhubhāvato ca. So vā aññabhāgoti yathāvuttatiracchānajātichagalakabhāvasaṅkhāto aññabhāgo. Assāti chagalakassa. So chagalako aññabhāgiyasaṅkhātaṃ labhatīti yojetabbaṃ. “Adhikaraṇanti ādhāro, vatthu adhiṭṭhāna”nti heṭṭhā vuttamatthaṃ sarūpato dassetuṃ “yasmā cā”tiādimāha. Tesanti mettiyabhūmajakānaṃ. Imanti chagalakaṃ. Nāmakaraṇasaññāyāti nāmakaraṇasaṅkhātāya saññāya so chagalako adhikaraṇanti veditabboti yojetabbaṃ. Tañhi sandhāyāti “avassaṃ tumhehi leso oḍḍito, kiṃ vadatha, kiṃ passitthā”ti anuyuttehi tehi bhikkhūhi “chagalakassa vippaṭipattiṃ disvā dabbassa nāmaṃ tassa karimhā”ti vuttattā tassa nāmakaraṇasaññāya adhiṭṭhānabhūtaṃ taṃ chagalakaṃ sandhāya. Te bhikkhūti te anuyuñjakā bhikkhū. Āpattilesampi puggalasmiṃyeva āropetvā vuttattā “puggalānaṃyeva lesā”ti vuttaṃ. Padabhājane pana…pe… veditabbanti iminā nāmakaraṇasaññāya ādhārabhūtassa chagalakasaṅkhātassa adhikaraṇassa avacane kāraṇaṃ vuttaṃ.

Now, showing in detail the meaning stated by both analyses, he says, 'For whoever that is…' and so on. 'That' means that goat. Its connection is with the word 'is.' 'From that' means from that human birth and from the state of being a monk. 'Or that other part' means the other part designated as the state of a goat of animal birth, as described. 'Of it' means of the goat. It should be construed thus: that goat obtains the designation 'of another part.' To show in its own form the meaning stated below—'a matter (adhikaraṇa) is a basis, a subject, a foundation'—he says, 'And since…' and so on. 'Of them' means of Mettiya and Bhūmajaka. 'This' means this goat. 'By the perception of name-giving'—it should be construed that it is to be understood that that goat is the matter (adhikaraṇa) for the perception designated as name-giving. 'Referring to that' means: referring to that goat which is the foundation for the perception of name-giving, because when those monks were questioned, 'Surely a pretext was contrived by you! What do you say? What did you see?' they replied, 'Having seen the misconduct of the goat, we gave it Dabba's name.' 'Those monks' means those questioning monks. Because even a hint of an offense was attributed only to a person, it was said, 'The pretexts are only of persons.' But in the word-analysis… it should be understood—by this, the reason is stated for not mentioning the matter, designated as the goat, which is the basis for the perception of name-giving.

393. “Aññabhāgiyassa adhikaraṇassā”ti ettha pāḷiāgataadhikaraṇasaddapatirūpakaṃ aññaṃ adhikaraṇasaddaṃ pāḷiāgatatadaññasādhāraṇatāya ubhayapadatthaṃ uddharitvā “adhikaraṇaṃ nāma cattāri adhikaraṇānī”ti vuttaṃ. Atthuddhāravasena hi atthaṃ dassentena pāḷiyaṃ āgatasaddapatirūpako añño saddo ubhayapadattho uddharitabbo, na ca aññaṃ uddharitvā [M 2.0358] aññassa attho vattabbo, tasmā pāḷiāgataadhikaraṇasaddapatirūpako aññoyeva ubhayapadatthasādhāraṇo adhikaraṇasaddo uddhaṭoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tenevāha “adhikaraṇanti vacanasāmaññato atthuddhāravasena pavattāni cattāri adhikaraṇānī”ti. Yā ca sā avasāne…pe… codanā vuttāti bhikkhu saṅghādisesaṃ ajjhāpajjanto diṭṭho hoti, saṅghādisese saṅghādisesadiṭṭhī hoti, tañce pārājikena codetītiādicodanaṃ sandhāya vadati.

393. Here, regarding “of a case belonging to another category,” another word “adhikaraṇa,” which resembles the word “adhikaraṇa” found in the Pāli, is extracted—having a meaning common to both the term in the Pāli and this other term—and it is said, “Adhikaraṇa means the four adhikaraṇas.” For when showing the meaning by way of extracting the meaning, another word resembling the word found in the Pāli, having a meaning common to both terms, should be extracted; and one should not extract one word and explain the meaning of another. Therefore, it should be understood that another word “adhikaraṇa,” which resembles the word “adhikaraṇa” found in the Pāli and is common to the meaning of both terms, is the one extracted. For this very reason, he said, “Adhikaraṇa, by the commonality of the word and by way of extracting the meaning, refers to the four adhikaraṇas that occur.” And that accusation stated at the end... refers to an accusation such as: “a bhikkhu is seen committing a saṅghādisesa offense, he has the view that it is a saṅghādisesa, and if one accuses him of a pārājika offense,” etc.

Methunavītikkamāpattiyo vatthuto sabhāgā, itarāsaṃ pana adinnādānādiāpattīnaṃ samānepi pārājikāpattibhāve vatthuto visabhāgāti āha “sabhāgavisabhāgavatthuto”ti. Sabhāvasarikkhāsarikkhatoti [V 2.0317] sabhāvena sadisāsadisabhāvato. Paṭhamapārājikañhi paṭhamapārājikāpattiyā methunarāgena sabhāvato sadisaṃ, dosasampayuttamanussaviggahena asadisaṃ. Nanu ca “āpattādhikaraṇaṃ āpattādhikaraṇassa siyā tabbhāgiyaṃ, siyā aññabhāgiya”nti vuttattā uddesānukkamena tabbhāgiyataṃ aniddisitvā aññabhāgiyatā paṭhamaṃ kasmā niddiṭṭhāti āha “ādito paṭṭhāyā”tiādi. Vuttanayenevāti “sabhāgavisabhāgavatthuto”tiādinā vuttanayena.

Offenses of sexual transgression are of the same kind in terms of their object (vatthu), but other offenses, such as taking what is not given, etc., although they are the same in being pārājika offenses, are of a different kind in terms of their object. Therefore, he said, “in terms of similar and dissimilar object.” “Similar and dissimilar in nature” means because of being similar and dissimilar in nature. For the first pārājika offense is similar in nature to the first pārājika offense through sexual passion, but it is dissimilar to the offense of killing a human being, which is connected with aversion. But since it was said, “A case concerning an offense may be of the same category as a case concerning an offense, or it may be of another category,” why was the state of being of another category indicated first, without indicating the state of being of the same category according to the order of enumeration? Because of this objection, he said, “starting from the beginning,” etc. “In the same manner as stated” means in the manner stated by “in terms of similar and dissimilar object,” etc.

“Saṅghakammāni nissāya uppanna”nti vuttattā saṅghakammato kiccādhikaraṇaṃ visuṃ viya dissatīti āha “kiṃ panā”tiādi. “Kiccameva kiccādhikaraṇa”nti vuttattā “saṅghakammānamevetaṃ adhivacana”nti vuttaṃ. Yadi evaṃ “saṅghakammāni nissāya uppanna”nti kasmā vuttanti āha “evaṃ santepī”tiādi. Tassa tassa saṅghakammassa bhagavatā vuttaṃ itikattabbatālakkhaṇaṃyeva tato saṅghakammassa nipphajjanato phalūpacārena saṅghakammanti vattabbataṃ arahatīti āha “yaṃ kammalakkhaṇaṃ manasi karoti, taṃ nissāya uppajjanato”ti. Parivāsādisaṅghakammaṃ nissāya mānattādīnaṃ uppajjanato ukkhepanīyakammasīmāsammutikammādīni issāya osāraṇasīmāsamūhananādikammānaṃ uppajjanato ca “purimaṃ purimaṃ saṅghakamma”ntiādi vuttaṃ.

Because it is said, “arisen in dependence on Sangha acts,” the issue concerning a duty (kiccādhikaraṇa) appears as if separate from the Sangha act. Therefore, he said, “But what...” etc. Because it is said, “The duty itself is the issue concerning a duty,” it was stated, “This is merely a designation for Sangha acts.” If so, why was it said, “arisen in dependence on Sangha acts”? Because of this objection, he said, “Even so...” etc. For each and every Sangha act, the Blessed One has stated its characteristic as 'what ought to be done.' Because the accomplishment of a Sangha act arises from that, it is fit to be called a “Sangha act” by a figurative expression based on the result. Therefore, he said, “Because it arises in dependence on that characteristic of the act that one bears in mind.” Because mānatta, etc., arise in dependence on Sangha acts such as probation (parivāsa); and because acts such as reinstatement (osāraṇa), dissolution of a boundary (sīmāsamūhana), etc., arise in dependence on acts such as suspension (ukkhepanīya), designation of a boundary (sīmāsammuti), etc., it was said, “the preceding Sangha act...” etc.

395-400. Savatthukaṃ katvāti puggalādhiṭṭhānaṃ katvā. Dīghādinoti dīgharassakāḷaodātādino. Diṭṭhādinoti diṭṭhasutādino. Lohapattasadisoti [M 2.0359] ayopattasadiso. Aṅgāni paṭhamaduṭṭhadose vuttasadisāni, idha pana kañcidesaṃ lesamattaṃ upādiyanā adhikā.

“Having made it have an object” means having made the individual the basis. “Long, etc.” means long, short, black, white, etc. “Seen, etc.” means seen, heard, etc. “Like a metal sheet” means like an iron sheet. The factors are similar to those stated in the first training rule on malicious accusation; here, however, the clinging to some mere trifle is additional.

Dutiyaduṭṭhadosasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the second training rule on malicious accusation is finished.

10. Paṭhamasaṅghabhedasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

10. Explanation of the First Training Rule on Schism in the Sangha

410. Dasame ye dubbalā honti appathāmā, na sakkonti araññakādīni sevantā dukkhassantaṃ kātuṃ, te sandhāyāha “bahūnaṃ kulaputtānaṃ maggantarāyāya saṃvattantī”ti. Adhivāsanakhantisampannoti “khamo hoti sītassā”tiādinā vuttasītuṇhādisahanalakkhaṇāya khantiyā samannāgato. Byañjanapadameva paramaṃ assāti padaparamo. Yassa hi puggalassa bahumpi suṇato bahumpi bhaṇato bahumpi dhārayato bahumpi vācayato na tāya jātiyā dhammābhisamayo hoti[V 2.0318], ayaṃ “padaparamo”ti vuccati. Abhisambhuṇitvāti nipphādetvā. Nābhisambhuṇātīti na sampādeti, araññavāsaṃ sampādetuṃ na sakkotīti vuttaṃ hoti. Dhammato apetaṃ uddhammaṃ. Asabbaññū assāti tesaṃ anurūpassa ajānanato asabbaññū bhaveyya. “Na, bhikkhave, asenāsanikena vassaṃ upagantabba”nti (mahāva. 204) vacanato “cattāro pana…pe… paṭikkhittamevā”ti vuttaṃ. Idameva vacanaṃ sandhāya pāḷiyampi “aṭṭha māse kho mayā devadatta rukkhamūlasenāsanaṃ anuññāta”nti vuttaṃ.

410. In the tenth, those who are weak and lacking in strength, unable to frequent forest dwellings and other such places to make an end of suffering—this is said with reference to them: “For many clansmen, they become an obstacle on the path.” Endowed with the patience of endurance: this refers to being possessed of the patience that has the characteristic of bearing cold, heat, and so on, as described in the phrase, “he is tolerant of cold,” etc. One for whom the letter and word alone is the highest is a 'padaparamo' (one devoted to words). For a person who, despite hearing much, speaking much, retaining much, and reciting much, does not attain penetration of the Dhamma in that very life—such a one is called a 'padaparamo'. `Abhisambhuṇitvā` means having accomplished. `Nābhisambhuṇāti` means one does not accomplish; that is to say, it is said that one is unable to accomplish the forest-dwelling life. That which is devoid of the Dhamma is 'against the Dhamma' (uddhamma). He would be not all-knowing: because he does not know what is suitable for them, he would be not all-knowing. “Monks, one should not enter the rains residence without a dwelling place”—in accordance with this statement (Mahāvagga 204), it is said, “But four… indeed, it is prohibited.” Referring to this very statement, it is also said in the Pāli: “For eight months, Devadatta, I have allowed the root-of-a-tree dwelling.”

Tīhi koṭīhīti tīhi ākārehi, tīhi kāraṇehīti attho. Tadubhayavimuttaparisaṅkitanti diṭṭhaṃ sutanti idaṃ ubhayaṃ anissāya “kiṃ nu kho idaṃ bhikkhuṃ uddissa vadhitvā sampādita”nti kevalameva parisaṅkitaṃ. Macchabandhanaṃ jālaṃ, vāgurā migabandhanī. Kappatīti yadi tesaṃ vacanena āsaṅkā upacchinnā hoti, vaṭṭati. Pavattamaṃsanti vikkāyikamaṃsaṃ. Maṅgalādīnanti ādi-saddena āhunapāhunādike saṅgaṇhāti. Bhikkhūnaṃyeva atthāyāti ettha aṭṭhānappayutto eva-saddo, bhikkhūnaṃ atthāya akatamevāti sambandhitabbaṃ. Tasmā “bhikkhūnañca dassāma, maṅgalādīnañca atthāya bhavissatī”ti missetvā katampi na vaṭṭatīti veditabbaṃ. Keci pana “bhikkhūnaṃyevāti [M 2.0360] avadhāraṇena bhikkhūnañca aññesañca atthāya kataṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti, taṃ na sundaraṃ. Yattha ca nibbematiko hotīti bhikkhūnaṃ atthāya katepi sabbena sabbaṃ parisaṅkitābhāvamāha. Tamevatthaṃ āvikātuṃ “sace panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Itaresaṃ vaṭṭatīti ajānantānaṃ vaṭṭati, jānato evettha āpatti hotīti. Teyevāti ye uddissa kataṃ, teyeva. Uddisakatamaṃsaparibhogato akappiyamaṃsaparibhogassa visesaṃ dassetuṃ “akappiyamaṃsaṃ panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Purimasmiṃ sacittakā āpatti, itarasmiṃ acittakā. Tenāha “akappiyamaṃsaṃ ajānitvā bhuñjantassapi āpattiyevā”ti. “Paribhogakāle pucchitvā paribhuñjissāmīti vā gahetvā pucchitvā paribhuñjitabba”nti vacanato akappiyamaṃsaṃ ajānitvā gaṇhantassa paṭiggahaṇena anāpatti siyā. Ajānitvāpi bhuñjantasseva hi āpatti vuttā. Vattanti vadantīti iminā āpatti natthīti dasseti.

“By three points” means by three aspects, by three reasons. “Suspected, though free from both (seen and heard)”: this means that without relying on those two, namely what is seen and what is heard, it is merely suspected, thinking, 'I wonder, was this prepared by killing it for a monk?' A device for catching fish is a net (jāla); a snare (vāgurā) is a device for catching wild animals. “It is allowable”: if the suspicion is cut off by their word, it is allowable. “Readily available meat” means meat available for sale. “Auspicious occasions, etc.”: by the word “etc.,” he includes offerings, gifts for guests, and the like. Regarding 'only for the benefit of the monks': here the word 'eva' is used in a non-standard position; it should be construed as 'it was indeed not made for the benefit of the monks.' Therefore, it should be understood that even meat prepared with the mixed intention, “We will give to the monks, and it will also be for auspicious occasions, etc.,” is not allowable. Some, however, say, “By the restrictive sense of 'only for the monks,' meat prepared for the benefit of both monks and others is allowable,” but that is not sound. “And where one is free from doubt”: this shows the complete absence of suspicion even when it is made for the benefit of monks. To make that very meaning clear, the passage beginning “But if…” was stated. “It is allowable for others” means it is allowable for those who do not know; for one who knows, there is an offense here. “Those very ones” means those for whom it was made. To show the distinction between consuming meat specifically prepared for one and consuming unallowable meat, the passage beginning “But unallowable meat…” was stated. In the former case, the offense involves intention; in the latter, it does not. Therefore, he said, “There is indeed an offense even for one who eats unallowable meat without knowing.” In accordance with the statement, “At the time of consumption, one should ask and then consume; or having taken it with the thought, ‘I will ask and then consume,’ one should ask and then consume,” there may be no offense in the receiving for one who accepts unallowable meat without knowing. For an offense is stated only for one who eats it, even without knowing. By saying 'they say', he shows that (in their opinion) there is no offense.
