Sallekhā vutti etesanti sallekhavuttino. Bāhulikoti ekassa la-kārassa lopaṃ katvā vuttaṃ. Kappanti āyukappaṃ. Saṅghabhedako hi ekaṃ kappaṃ asītibhāge katvā tato ekabhāgamattaṃ kālaṃ niraye tiṭṭheyyāti āyukappaṃ sandhāya “kappaṃ nirayamhi paccatī”ti vuttaṃ. Kappaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (vibha. aṭṭha. 809) pana “saṇṭhahante hi kappe kappavemajjhe vā saṅghabhedaṃ katvā kappavināseyeva muccati. Sacepi hi sve kappo vinassissatīti ajja saṅghabhedaṃ karoti, sveva [V 2.0319] muccati, ekadivasameva niraye paccatī”ti vuttaṃ. Tatthāpi kappavināseyevāti āyukappavināseyevāti atthe sati natthi virodho. Saṇṭhahanteti idampi “sve vinassissatī”ti viya abhūtaparikappanavasena vuttaṃ. “Ekadivasameva niraye paccatī”ti etthāpi tato paraṃ kappābhāve āyukappassapi abhāvatoti avirodhato atthayojanā daṭṭhabbā. Brahmaṃ puññanti seṭṭhaṃ puññaṃ. Kappaṃ saggamhi modatīti etthāpi āyukappameva.

Those whose practice is effacement are sallekhavuttino. Bāhulika is stated by eliding one 'la' syllable (from bāhullika). Kappa means a life-span aeon. A schismatic, indeed, would remain in hell for a period of time equal to one of eighty parts of an aeon; it is with reference to this life-span aeon that it is said, 'he is tormented in hell for an aeon.' In the commentary on the Kappa (Vibhaṅga Aṭṭhakathā 809), however, it is stated: “When an aeon is established, one who causes a schism in the middle of the aeon is freed only at the destruction of the aeon. Even if, thinking, ‘The aeon will be destroyed tomorrow,’ one causes a schism today, he is freed the very next day—he is tormented in hell for only a single day.” There too, if the meaning of 'only at the destruction of the aeon' is taken as 'only at the destruction of the life-span aeon,' there is no contradiction. This phrase 'when it is established' is also stated by way of an unreal supposition, like 'it will be destroyed tomorrow.' In the phrase 'he is tormented in hell for only a single day,' the application of the meaning should also be seen as being without contradiction, on the grounds that because there is no aeon after that, there is also no life-span aeon. Brahmaṃ puññaṃ means supreme merit. In the phrase 'he rejoices in heaven for an aeon,' here too, it refers only to the life-span aeon.

411. Laddhinānāsaṃvāsakenāti bhāvappadhānoyaṃ niddeso, laddhinānāsaṃvāsakabhāvenāti attho. Kammanānāsaṃvāsakenāti etthāpi eseva nayo. Aññathā nānāsaṃvāsakena sahitassa samānasaṃvāsakassapi [M 2.0361] saṅghassa asamānasaṃvāsakattaṃ āpajjeyya. Tattha laddhinānāsaṃvāsako nāma ukkhittānuvattako. So hi attano laddhiyā nānāsaṃvāsako jātoti “laddhinānāsaṃvāsako”ti vuccati. Kammanānāsaṃvāsako nāma ukkhepanīyakammakato. So hi ukkhepanīyakammavasena nānāsaṃvāsako hotīti “kammanānāsaṃvāsako”ti vuccati. Virahitoti vimutto. Kāyasāmaggīdānaṃ tesu tesu saṅghakammesu hatthapāsūpagamanavasena veditabbaṃ.

411. “By one not in communion due to view”: this is an explanation where the state is primary; the meaning is “because of the state of being not in communion due to view.” “By one not in communion due to a formal act”: here too, the same principle applies. Otherwise, a Sangha of those in communion, by being associated with one who is not in communion, would fall into a state of non-communion. In this context, “one not in communion due to view” is a follower of one who has been suspended. He is called “one not in communion due to view” because he has become not in communion due to his own view. “One not in communion due to a formal act” is one upon whom an act of suspension has been performed. He is called “one not in communion due to a formal act” because he becomes not in communion by means of the act of suspension. “Separated” means freed. The giving of bodily unity, in those various acts of the Sangha, should be understood as approaching within arm’s reach.

“Bhedāya parakkameyyā”ti visuṃ vuttattā bhedanasaṃvattanikassa adhikaraṇassa samādāya paggaṇhato pubbepi pakkhapariyesanādivasena saṅghabhedāya parakkamantassa samanubhāsanakammaṃ kātabbanti veditabbaṃ. Imāni vatthūnīti aṭṭhārasa bhedakaravatthūni. Kammenāti apalokanādīsu catūsu kammesu aññatarena kammena. Uddesenāti pañcasu pātimokkhuddesesu aññatarena uddesena. Vohārenāti tāhi tāhi upapattīhi “adhammaṃ dhammo”tiādiaṭṭhārasabhedakaravatthudīpakena vohārena. Anussāvanāyāti “nanu tumhe jānātha mayhaṃ uccākulā pabbajitabhāvaṃ bahussutabhāvañca, mādiso nāma uddhammaṃ ubbinayaṃ satthusāsanaṃ gāheyyāti cittampi uppādetuṃ tumhākaṃ yuttaṃ, kiṃ mayhaṃ avīci nīluppalavanaṃ viya sītalo, kimahaṃ apāyato na bhāyāmī”tiādinā nayena kaṇṇamūle vacībhedaṃ katvā anussāvanena. Salākaggāhenāti evaṃ anussāvetvā tesaṃ cittaṃ upatthambhetvā anivattidhamme katvā “gaṇhatha imaṃ salāka”nti salākaggāhena. Pañcahi kāraṇehi saṅghabhedo hotīti ettha kammameva uddeso vā saṅghabhede padhānakāraṇanti veditabbaṃ. Vohārānussāvanasalākaggāhā pana pubbabhāgā. Aṭṭhārasavatthudīpanavasaena hi voharantena tattha rucijananatthaṃ anussāvetvā salākāya gahitāyapi abhinnova hoti saṅgho. Yadā pana evaṃ cattāro vā atirekā vā salākaṃ gahetvā āveṇikakammaṃ vā uddesaṃ vā karonti, tadā saṅgho bhinno nāma hoti. Abbhussitanti abbhuggataṃ. Accheyyāti vihareyya, pavatteyyāti attho.

“One should strive for schism”—because it is stated separately, it should be understood that the act of admonition is to be performed for one who, striving for schism, takes up and upholds a dispute that leads to division, even beforehand, by means of seeking a faction and so on. These are the grounds—the eighteen grounds for causing schism. By act—by any one of the four acts, starting with seeking approval. By recitation—by any one of the five Pātimokkha recitations. By speech—by such and such modes, declaring “what is not Dhamma as Dhamma,” etc., illuminating the eighteen grounds for causing schism. By proclamation—by making a verbal distinction near the ear, proclaiming in such a way as, “Do you not know my high birth and my being a renunciant and learned? Is it fitting for you to even conceive the thought that one like me would take up the Teacher's Dispensation as being without Dhamma and without Vinaya? Is Avīci cool for me, like a blue lotus grove? Do I not fear the states of deprivation?” By having the voting slip taken—after thus proclaiming, supporting their resolve, and making them adhere to irreversible principles, saying, “Take this voting slip,” by having the voting slip taken. Regarding the statement, 'Schism occurs due to five factors,' here it should be understood that the act or the recitation is the primary cause in schism. Speech, proclamation, and the taking of the voting slip, however, are preliminary actions. For even if one speaks by illuminating the eighteen grounds, proclaims to generate interest there, and the voting slip is taken, the Saṅgha remains unbroken. But when four or more take the voting slip and perform a separate act or recitation, then the Saṅgha is said to be divided. “Has arisen”—has arisen. “Should remain”—should continue, should proceed—this is the meaning.

“Lajjī [V 2.0320] rakkhissatī”ti vacanato āpattibhayena ārocanaṃ lajjīnaṃyeva bhāroti āha “lajjīhi bhikkhūhī”ti. Alajjissapi anārocentassa āpattiyeva “ye passanti, ye suṇantī”ti vacanato. Samāgacchatūti ekī [M 2.0362] bhavatu. Ekībhāvo ca samānaladdhivasena hotīti āha “ekaladdhiko hotū”ti. Sampattiyāti sīlādisampattiyā. Paṭinissajjantassa anāpattibhāvato “sotthibhāvo tassa bhikkhuno”ti vuttaṃ. Appaṭinissajjato dukkaṭanti visuṃ visuṃ vadantānaṃ gaṇanāya dukkaṭaṃ. Pahontenāti gantuṃ samatthena agilānena. Saṅghabhedassa garukabhāvato avassaṃ kattabbatādassanatthaṃ “dūrepi bhāroyevā”ti vuttaṃ, āpatti pana addhayojanabbhantare gantuṃ samatthassa agilānasseva veditabbā.

From the statement, “The conscientious one will protect (himself),” the duty of reporting out of fear of an offense falls only on the conscientious,” thus it is said, “by the conscientious monks.” Even for the shameless one who does not report, there is indeed an offense, as stated by the words, “those who see, those who hear.” “Let them come together” means let them be united. And unity is achieved by way of having the same view, thus it is said, “let him be of one view.” “Through attainment” refers to attainment in virtue, etc. Since there is no offense for one who relinquishes (the view), it is said, “well-being for that monk.” For one who does not relinquish (the view), there is a dukkaṭa—a dukkaṭa according to the count of those who speak separately. “Able” refers to one who is capable of going, not ill. Due to the gravity of schism in the Saṅgha, to emphasize the necessity of action, it is said, “even from afar, it is indeed a burden.” However, the offense should be understood as applicable only to one who is capable of going within half a yojana and is not ill.

416. Asamanubhāsantassāti kammakārake kattuniddesoti āha “asamanubhāsiyamānassā”ti. Tatiyakammavācāya paṭinissajjanto ñattiyā dukkaṭaṃ dvīhi kammavācāhi thullaccaye ca āpajjatiyevāti āha “paṭinissajjantassa saṅghādisesena anāpattī”ti. Assāti devadattassa. Katena bhavitabbanti samanubhāsanakammena katena bhavitabbaṃ. Attano rucimattena vadeyyātiādikammikattā appaṭinissajjantassapi anāpattīti adhippāyena vadeyya. Apaññatte sikkhāpade samanubhāsanakammasseva abhāvato “na hi paññattaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ vītikkamantassā”ti vuttaṃ. Sikkhāpadaṃ paññapenteneva hi samanubhāsanakammaṃ anuññātaṃ. Uddissa anuññātatoti “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, romanthakassa romanthana”ntiādiṃ (cūḷava. 273) uddissa anuññātaṃ sandhāya vadanti. Anāpattiyanti anāpattivāre. Āpattiṃ ropetabboti anissajjanapaccayā āpannapācittiyāpattiṃ ukkhepanīyakammakaraṇatthaṃ āropetabboti attho.

416. The expression 'asamanubhāsantassa' (of one not admonishing) is a designation of the agent in the sense of the object of the action, thus it is said 'asamanubhāsiyamānassa' (of one not being admonished). One who relinquishes at the third formal pronouncement incurs a dukkaṭa for the motion and thullaccayas for the two formal pronouncements, therefore it is said, 'for one who relinquishes, there is no Saṅghādisesa offense.' “Assa” refers to Devadatta. “Should be dealt with by action” means it should be dealt with by the act of admonition. Regarding 'He may speak according to his own preference,' one might say this with the intention that even for one who does not relinquish there is no offense, because he is the instigator of the action. Because the act of admonition itself does not exist for an unpromulgated training rule, it is said: “not for one who transgresses a promulgated training rule.” Indeed, the act of admonition was permitted by the very one who promulgated the training rule. Regarding 'authorized with reference to,' they say this referring to what was authorized for a specific case, such as, “I allow, monks, rumination for a ruminant,” etc. (Cūḷavagga 273). “Non-offense” refers to the non-offense section. “An offense should be charged” means that, in order to perform the act of suspension, a Pācittiya offense resulting from the failure to relinquish should be charged; this is the meaning.

Āpattiyeva na jātāti saṅghādisesāpatti na jātāyevāti attho. Sā panesāti sā pana esā anāpatti. Tivaṅgikanti kāyavācācittavasena tivaṅgikaṃ, kāyavācācittato samuṭṭhātīti vuttaṃ hoti. “Nappaṭinissajjāmī”ti saññāya abhāvena muccanato saññāvimokkhaṃ. Sacittakanti “nappaṭinissajjāmī”ti jānanacittena sacittakaṃ. Bhedāya parakkamanaṃ, dhammakammena samanubhāsanaṃ, kammavācāpariyosānaṃ, appaṭinissajjananti imānettha cattāri aṅgāni.

“Indeed, no offense has been committed” means that no Saṅghādisesa offense has been committed; this is the meaning. “But this” refers to this non-offense. “Threefold” means threefold in terms of body, speech, and mind; it is said to arise from body, speech, and mind. It is 'release through perception' because one is freed due to the absence of the perception, “I will not relinquish.” “With intention” means with the knowing mind, with the thought, “I will not relinquish,” thus it is with intention. Striving for schism, admonishment by a lawful act, completion of the formal pronouncement, and non-relinquishment—these are the four factors here.

Paṭhamasaṅghabhedasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the first training rule on schism in the Saṅgha is finished.

11. Dutiyasaṅghabhedasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

11. Explanation of the Second Training Rule on Schism in the Sangha

417-418. Ekādasame [M 2.0363][V 2.0321] yaṃ vacanaṃ samaggepi vagge avayavabhūte karoti bhindati, taṃ kalahakārakavacanaṃ idha vagganti vuccatīti āha “vaggaṃ asāmaggipakkhiyavacanaṃ vadantī”ti. Asāmaggipakkhe bhavā asāmaggipakkhiyā, kalahakā. Tesaṃ vacanaṃ asāmaggipakkhiyavacanaṃ, asāmaggipakkhe vā bhavaṃ vacanaṃ asāmaggipakkhiyavacanaṃ. Yasmā ubbāhikādikammaṃ bahūnampi kātuṃ vaṭṭati, tasmā “na hi saṅgho saṅghassa kammaṃ karotī”ti idaṃ niggahavasena kattabbakammaṃ sandhāya vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Aṅgāni panettha bhedāya parakkamanaṃ pahāya anuvattanaṃ pakkhipitvā heṭṭhā vuttasadisāneva.

In the eleventh, that speech which, even in a united group, makes it into separate parts and breaks it, that quarrel-causing speech is here called 'vagga'. Therefore, it is said: 'They call "vagga" speech that belongs to the faction of disunity.' Those who are in the faction of disunity are `asāmaggipakkhiyā`, the quarrelsome ones. Their speech is `asāmaggipakkhiyavacanaṃ`; or, speech that arises in the faction of disunity is `asāmaggipakkhiyavacanaṃ`. Because it is allowable for even many to perform an act such as `ubbāhika`, therefore, this statement, 'the Sangha does not perform an act for the Sangha,' should be understood as being said in reference to an act that should be done by way of censure. As for the factors here, having excluded 'striving for division' and included 'following along', they are just the same as those stated previously.

Dutiyasaṅghabhedasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Second Training Rule on Schism in the Sangha is concluded.

12. Dubbacasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

12. Explanation of the Training Rule on Being Difficult to Correct

424. Dvādasame vambhanavacananti garahavacanaṃ. Apasādetukāmoti khipitukāmo, tajjetukāmo vā, ghaṭṭetukāmoti vuttaṃ hoti. Saṭasaddo patitasaddena samānattho. Visesanassa ca paranipātaṃ katvā tiṇakaṭṭhapaṇṇasaṭanti vuttanti āha “tattha tattha patitaṃ tiṇakaṭṭhapaṇṇa”nti. Kenāpīti vātasadisena nadīsadisena ca kenāpi.

424. In the twelfth, `vambhanavacana` means speech of reproach. `Apasādetukāmo` means desiring to scold, or desiring to threaten, or desiring to provoke; so it is said. The word `saṭa` has the same meaning as the word `patita` (fallen). And having placed the adjective after, it is said `tiṇakaṭṭhapaṇṇasaṭa`; thus, he said: 'grass, wood, and leaves fallen here and there.' `Kenāpi` means: by something similar to the wind and similar to a river's current.

425-426. Vattuṃ asakkuṇeyyoti kismiñci vuccamāne asahanato ovadituṃ asakkuṇeyyo. Dukkhaṃ vaco etasmiṃ vippaṭikūlaggāhe vipaccanīkavāde anādare puggaleti dubbaco. Tenāha “dukkhena kicchena vaditabbo”tiādi. Dubbacabhāvakaraṇīyehīti dubbacabhāvakārakehi. Kattuatthe anīyasaddo daṭṭhabbo. Tenevāha “ye dhammā dubbacaṃ puggalaṃ karontī”tiādi. Pāpikā icchā etassāti pāpiccho, tassa bhāvo pāpicchatā, asantaguṇasambhāvanatā paṭiggahaṇe ca amattaññutā pāpicchatāti veditabbā. Attukkaṃsakā ca te paravambhakā cāti attukkaṃsakaparavambhakā. Ye attānaṃ ukkaṃsanti ukkhipanti ucce ṭhāne ṭhapenti, parañca vambhenti garahanti nīce ṭhāne ṭhapenti, tesametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tesaṃ bhāvo attukkaṃsakaparavambhakatā. Kujjhanasīlo kodhano, tassa bhāvo kodhanatā. Kujjhanalakkhaṇassa kodhassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ.

'Unable to be spoken to' means: one would be unable to advise due to intolerance when something is being said. A person for whom speech is difficult, who has a perverse view, speaks oppositionally, and is disrespectful, is `dubbaco` (difficult to correct). Therefore, he said: 'He should be spoken to with difficulty and with trouble,' and so on. `Dubbacabhāvakaraṇīyehi` means: by things that cause the state of being difficult to correct. The suffix `anīya` should be understood in the sense of the agent. For that very reason, he said: 'those qualities that make a person difficult to correct,' and so on. One for whom there is an evil wish is a `pāpiccho`; his state is `pāpicchatā`. `Pāpicchatā` should be known as the extolling of non-existent virtues and immoderation in receiving. And they are self-exalters and disparagers of others, thus they are `attukkaṃsakaparavambhakā`. Those who exalt themselves, lift themselves up, and place themselves in a high position, and who disparage and censure others, placing them in a low position—this is a designation for them. Their state is `attukkaṃsakaparavambhakatā`. One whose nature is to be angry is `kodhano`; his state is `kodhanatā`. This is a designation for anger, which has the characteristic of being prone to anger.

Pubbakāle [M 2.0364][V 2.0322] kodho, aparakāle upanāhoti āha “kodhahetu upanāhitā”ti. Tattha upanahanasīlo, upanāho vā etassa atthīti upanāhī, tassa bhāvo upanāhitā. Punappunaṃ cittapariyonaddhalakkhaṇassa kodhassevetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Sakiñhi uppanno kodho kodhoyeva, tatuttari upanāho. Abhisaṅgoti dummocanīyo balavaupanāho. So assa atthīti abhisaṅgī, tassa bhāvo abhisaṅgitā. Dummocanīyassa balavaupanāhassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Codakaṃ paṭippharaṇatāti codakassa paṭiviruddhena paccanīkena hutvā avaṭṭhānaṃ. Codakaṃ apasādanatāti “kiṃ nu kho tuyhaṃ bālassa abyattassa bhaṇitena, tvampi nāma bhaṇitabbaṃ maññissasī”ti evaṃ codakassa ghaṭṭanā. Codakassa paccāropanatāti “tvampi khosi itthannāmaṃ āpattiṃ āpanno, taṃ tāva paṭikarohī”ti evaṃ codakassa upari paṭiāropanatā.

In a former time, it is anger; in a later time, it is resentment. Thus it is said: 'Resentfulness has anger as its cause.' Therein, one whose nature is to bear a grudge, or one for whom there is resentment, is an `upanāhī`; his state is `upanāhitā`. This is a designation for anger which has the characteristic of repeatedly enveloping the mind. For anger that has arisen once is just anger; further than that is resentment. `Abhisaṅga` is a strong resentment that is difficult to release. One for whom that exists is an `abhisaṅgī`; his state is `abhisaṅgitā`. This is a designation for a strong resentment that is difficult to release. `Codakaṃ paṭippharaṇatā` is standing in opposition to the accuser, being hostile and contrary. `Codakaṃ apasādanatā` is provoking the accuser, saying: 'What indeed is there in the speech of a foolish, inept person like you? Do you really think you should speak?' `Codakassa paccāropanatā` is laying blame back upon the accuser, saying: 'You too have committed such-and-such an offense; first, you should deal with that!'

Aññena aññaṃ paṭicaraṇatāti aññena kāraṇena, vacanena vā aññassa kāraṇassa, vacanassa vā paṭicchādanavasena caraṇatā. Paṭicchādanattho eva vā carasaddo anekatthattā dhātūnanti paṭicchādanatāti attho. Tāya samannāgato hi puggalo yaṃ codakena dosavibhāvanakāraṇaṃ, vacanaṃ vā vuttaṃ, taṃ tato aññeneva codanāya amūlikabhāvadīpanena kāraṇena, tadatthabodhakena vacanena vā paṭicchādeti. “Āpattiṃ āpannosī”ti vutte “ko āpanno, kiṃ āpanno, kismiṃ āpanno, kaṃ bhaṇatha, kiṃ bhaṇathā”ti vā vatvā “evarūpaṃ kiñci tayā diṭṭha”nti vutte “na suṇāmī”ti sotaṃ vā upanāmetvā vikkhepaṃ karontopi aññenaññaṃ paṭicchādeti. “Itthannāmaṃ āpattiṃ āpannosī”ti puṭṭhe “pāṭaliputtaṃ gatomhī”ti vatvā puna “na tava pāṭaliputtagamanaṃ pucchāma, āpattiṃ pucchāmā”ti vutte tato “rājagahaṃ gatomhī”ti vatvā “rājagahaṃ vā yāhi brāhmaṇagahaṃ vā, āpattiṃ āpannosī”ti vutte “tattha me sūkaramaṃsaṃ laddha”ntiādīni vatvā bahiddhā kathāvikkhipanampi atthato aññenaññaṃ paṭicaraṇamevāti visuṃ na gahitaṃ.

`Aññena aññaṃ paṭicaraṇatā` means the act of behaving by way of concealing another reason or statement with a different reason or statement. Or, because verbal roots have multiple meanings, the word `cara` simply has the meaning of 'concealing'; thus, the meaning is 'concealment'. For a person endowed with this, when a reason or statement revealing a fault is stated by an accuser, he conceals it with a different reason that shows the accusation to be baseless, or with a statement that makes its meaning known. When told, 'You have committed an offense,' he might say, 'Who has committed an offense? What offense? In what case? Whom are you addressing? What are you saying?' Or, when told, 'Was anything of this sort seen by you?' he says, 'I do not hear,' or, having turned his ear, he creates a distraction, thus concealing one thing with another. When asked, 'Have you committed such-and-such an offense?' he says, 'I went to Pāṭaliputta.' When told again, 'We are not asking about your going to Pāṭaliputta, we are asking about the offense,' he then says, 'From there I went to Rājagaha.' When told, 'Go to Rājagaha or go to a Brahmin's house, have you committed the offense?' he says, 'There I obtained pork,' and so on. Even the distraction of the conversation to outside matters is, in meaning, just `aññenaññaṃ paṭicaraṇa`, and so it is not taken up separately.

Apadānenāti attano cariyāya. Apadīyanti hi dosā etena dakkhīyanti, luyanti chijjantīti vā apadānaṃ, sattānaṃ sammā micchā vā vattappayogo. Na sampāyanatāti “āvuso, tvaṃ kuhiṃ vasasi, kaṃ nissāya vasasī”ti vā “yaṃ tvaṃ vadesi ‘mayā esa āpattiṃ āpajjanto diṭṭho’ti, tvaṃ [M 2.0365] tasmiṃ samaye kiṃ karosi, ayaṃ kiṃ karoti, kattha ca tvaṃ ahosi, kattha aya”nti vā ādinā nayena cariyaṃ puṭṭhena sampādetvā akathanaṃ.

`Apadānena` means: by one's own story or conduct. For by this, faults are taken up and seen, or they are cut and severed, thus it is `apadāna`; it is the application of speech by beings, either rightly or wrongly. `Na sampāyanatā` is not telling the story completely when asked about one's conduct in a manner such as: 'Friend, where do you reside? Depending on whom do you reside?' or, 'Regarding what you say, "I saw this one committing an offense"—at that time, what were you doing? What was he doing? And where were you? Where was he?' and so on.

Makkhipaḷāsitāti ettha paraguṇamakkhanalakkhaṇo makkho, so etassa atthīti makkhī. Tādiso [V 2.0323] puggalo agāriyo anagāriyo vā samāno paresaṃ sukatakaraṇaṃ vināseti. Agāriyopi hi kenaci anukampakena daliddo samāno uccaṭṭhāne ṭhapito, aparena samayena “kiṃ tayā mayhaṃ kata”nti tassa sukatakaraṇaṃ vināseti. Anagāriyopi sāmaṇerakālato pabhuti ācariyena vā upajjhāyena vā catūhi paccayehi uddesaparipucchādīhi ca anuggahetvā dhammakathānayapakaraṇakosallādīni sikkhāpito, aparena samayena rājarājamahāmattādīhi sakkato garukato ācariyupajjhāyesu acittīkato caramāno “ayaṃ amhehi daharakāle eva anuggahito saṃvaddhito ca, atha ca panidāni nissineho jāto”ti vuccamāno “kiṃ mayhaṃ tumhehi kata”nti tesaṃ sukatakaraṇaṃ vināseti.

In the term 'Makkhipaḷāsitā' (disparagement and rivalry), 'makkha' (disparagement) has the characteristic of disparaging the virtues of others; one who has this is 'makkhī' (a disparager). Such a person, whether a householder or one gone forth, destroys the good deeds done for them by others. Indeed, a householder, though poor, might be placed in a high position by some compassionate person. At a later time, he might say, 'What have you done for me?' and thus destroy the good deed done for him. Or one gone forth, from the time he was a novice, may have been supported by a teacher or a preceptor with the four requisites and trained in recitation, questioning, skill in the method of Dhamma exposition, and the scriptures. At a later time, when honored and respected by kings, royal ministers, and others, while behaving disrespectfully towards his teachers and preceptors, he might be told, 'This person was supported and brought up by us from a young age, but now he has become ungrateful.' He might then say, 'What have you done for me?' and thus destroy the good deeds they have done.

“Bahussutepi puggale ajjhottharitvā īdisassa ceva bahussutassa aniyatā gati, tava vā mama vā ko viseso”tiādinā nayena uppajjamāno yugaggāhalakkhaṇo paḷāso. So paraguṇehi attano guṇānaṃ samakaraṇaraso. Tathā hesa paresaṃ guṇe ḍaṃsitvā viya attano guṇehi same karotīti paḷāsoti vuccati, so etassa atthīti paḷāsī. Makkhī ca paḷāsī ca makkhipaḷāsino, tesaṃ bhāvo makkhipaḷāsitā. Atthato pana makkho ceva paḷāso ca.

Paḷāsa (rivalry) has the characteristic of competitiveness, arising by way of overpowering even learned persons and thinking, “The destination of such a learned person is uncertain; what difference is there between you and me?” and so on. It has the function of making one's own qualities equal to the qualities of others. Indeed, because this one makes his own qualities equal to those of others, as if biting at their qualities, it is called 'paḷāsa'; one who has this is a 'paḷāsī' (a rivalrous person). A 'makkhī' (disparager) and a 'paḷāsī' (rivalrous person) are 'makkhipaḷāsino' (disparagers and rivalrous persons); their state is 'makkhipaḷāsitā' (disparagement and rivalry). In terms of meaning, however, it is both 'makkha' (disparagement) and 'paḷāsa' (rivalry).

Issati parasampattiṃ na sahatīti issukī. Maccharāyati attano sampattiṃ nigūhati, paresaṃ sādhāraṇabhāvaṃ na sahati, maccheraṃ vā etassa atthīti maccharī. Saṭhayati na sammā bhāsatīti saṭho, attano avijjamānaguṇappakāsanalakkhaṇena sāṭheyyena samannāgato kerāṭikapuggalo. Kerāṭiko ca ānandamaccho viya hoti. Ānandamaccho nāma kira macchānaṃ naṅguṭṭhaṃ dasseti, sappānaṃ sīsaṃ “tumhehi sadiso aha”nti jānāpetuṃ, evameva kerāṭiko puggalo yaṃ yaṃ suttantikaṃ vā ābhidhammikaṃ [M 2.0366] vā upasaṅkamati, taṃ taṃ evaṃ vadati “ahaṃ tumhākaṃ antevāsī, tumhe mayhaṃ anukampakā, nāhaṃ tumhe muñcāmī”ti “evamete ‘sagāravo ayaṃ amhesu sappatisso’ti maññissantī”ti. Sāṭheyyena hi samannāgatassa puggalassa asantaguṇasambhāvanena cittānurūpakiriyāviharato “evaṃcitto evaṃkiriyo”ti duviññeyyattā kucchiṃ vā piṭṭhiṃ vā jānituṃ na sakkā. Yato so –

He envies (issati) and cannot bear the success of others, thus he is envious (issukī). He is stingy (maccharāyati) in that he conceals his own success and cannot bear it being common to others, or because stinginess (maccheraṃ) exists in him, thus he is stingy (maccharī). He is fraudulent (saṭhayati) and does not speak correctly, thus he is a fraud (saṭho); he is a roguish person (kerāṭikapuggalo) endowed with fraudulence (sāṭheyya), which has the characteristic of displaying non-existent virtues. And the roguish person is like the Ānanda fish. The Ānanda fish, it is said, shows its tail to fish and its head to snakes to make it known, “I am like you.” Similarly, a roguish person approaches whichever Suttantika or Ābhidhammika teacher and says, “I am your resident pupil, you are compassionate towards me, I will not leave you,” thinking, “In this way, they will think, ‘This person is respectful and deferential towards us.’” Indeed, for a person endowed with fraudulence, because of displaying non-existent virtues and being devoid of conduct that corresponds to his mind, it is difficult to know, “his mind is thus, his action is thus,” so it is not possible to know his belly or his back. Because he is—

“Vāmena sūkaro hoti, dakkhiṇena ajāmigo;

Sarena nelako hoti, visāṇena jaraggavo”ti. (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.296; vibha. aṭṭha. 894; mahāni. aṭṭha. 166) –

“On the left, he is a boar; on the right, a wild goat; by voice, he is a young bull; by horn, an old ox.”

Evaṃ [V 2.0324] vuttayakkhasūkarasadiso hoti. Katapāpapaṭicchādanalakkhaṇā māyā, sā assa atthīti māyāvī.

Thus, he is like the aforementioned yaksha-boar. Deceit (māyā) has the characteristic of concealing evil that has been done; he has that, therefore he is deceitful (māyāvī).

Thambhasamaṅgitāya thaddho. Vātabharitabhastāsadisathaddhabhāvapaggahitasiraanivātavuttikārakaroti thambho. Yena samannāgato puggalo gilitanaṅgalasadiso viya ajagaro, vātabharitabhastā viya ca thaddho hutvā garuṭṭhāniye disvā onamitumpi na icchati, pariyanteneva carati. Abbhunnatilakkhaṇo atimāno, so etassa atthīti atimānī.

He is stiff (thaddho) through being endowed with stubbornness (thambha). Stubbornness (thambho) causes one to act with stiffness like a leather bag filled with wind, with head held high and with unbending conduct. A person endowed with this, like a python that has swallowed a ploughshare or like a leather bag filled with wind, becomes stiff and, upon seeing those worthy of respect, does not wish even to bow; he keeps to the periphery. Conceit (atimāno) has the characteristic of self-exaltation; he has that, therefore he is conceited (atimānī).

Saṃ attano diṭṭhiṃ parāmasati sabhāvaṃ atikkamitvā parato āmasatīti sandiṭṭhiparāmāsī. Ādhānaṃ gaṇhātīti ādhānaggāhī. “Ādhāna”nti daḷhaṃ vuccati, daḷhaggāhīti attho. Yuttaṃ kāraṇaṃ disvāva laddhiṃ paṭinissajjatīti paṭinissaggī, dukkhena kicchena kasirena bahumpi kāraṇaṃ dassetvā na sakkā paṭinissaggiṃ kātunti duppaṭinissaggī, yo attano diṭṭhiṃ “idameva sacca”nti daḷhaṃ gaṇhitvā api buddhādīhi kāraṇaṃ dassetvā vuccamāno na paṭinissajjati, tassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tādiso hi puggalo yaṃ yadeva dhammaṃ vā adhammaṃ vā suṇāti, taṃ sabbaṃ “evaṃ amhākaṃ ācariyehi kathitaṃ, evaṃ amhehi suta”nti kummova aṅgāni sake kapāle antoyeva samodahati. Yathā hi kacchapo attano pādādike aṅge kenaci ghaṭṭite sabbāni aṅgāni attano kapāleyeva samodahati, na bahi nīharati, evamayampi “na sundaro tava gāho, chaḍḍehi na”nti vutto taṃ na vissajjeti, antoyeva attano hadaye eva ṭhapetvā vicarati. Yathā kumbhīlā gahitaṃ na paṭinissajjanti, evaṃ kumbhīlaggāhaṃ gaṇhāti, na vissajjeti. Makkhipaḷāsitādiyugaḷattayena [M 2.0367] dassite makkhapaḷāsādayo cha dhamme visuṃ visuṃ gahetvā “ekūnavīsati dhammā”ti vuttaṃ. Anumānasuttaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.181) pana makkhapaḷāsādayopi yugaḷavasena ekaṃ katvā “soḷasa dhammā”ti vuttaṃ.

He wrongly grasps (parāmasati) his own view (saṃ diṭṭhiṃ), transgressing its true nature and grasping it wrongly, thus he is one who wrongly grasps his own view (sandiṭṭhiparāmāsī). He grasps firmly (ādhānaṃ gaṇhāti), thus he is one who grasps firmly (ādhānaggāhī). 'Ādhāna' means 'firm'; the meaning is 'one who grasps firmly.' One who, upon seeing a suitable reason, will relinquish (paṭinissajjissati) his belief is one who is able to relinquish (paṭinissaggī). One whom it is not possible to make relinquish his view, even after being shown many reasons with difficulty, trouble, and hardship, is one who is difficult to make relinquish (duppaṭinissaggī). This is the designation for one who, having firmly grasped his own view as “this alone is true,” does not relinquish it even when being told and shown reasons by the Buddha and others. Indeed, such a person, whatever Dhamma or non-Dhamma he hears, says of it all, “Thus it was taught by our teachers, thus we have heard it,” just as a tortoise draws its limbs into its own shell. For just as a tortoise, when any of its limbs such as its feet are touched by someone, draws all its limbs into its own shell and does not extend them outward, so too this person, when told, “Your view is not good, abandon it,” does not release it but keeps it within his own heart and goes about his way. Just as crocodiles do not release what they have seized, so he seizes with a crocodile's grip and does not let go. By the three pairs shown, beginning with 'disparagement and rivalry,' taking the six qualities—disparagement, rivalry, and so on—separately, it is said there are 'nineteen qualities.' But in the commentary on the Anumāna Sutta, disparagement, rivalry, and so on are also taken as pairs, making one, and it is said there are 'sixteen qualities.'

Pakārehi āvahanaṃ padakkhiṇaṃ, tato padakkhiṇato gahaṇasīlo padakkhiṇaggāhī, na padakkhiṇaggāhī appadakkhiṇaggāhī. Yo vuccamāno “tumhe maṃ kasmā vadatha, ahaṃ attano kappiyākappiyaṃ sāvajjānavajjaṃ atthānatthaṃ jānāmī”ti vadati, ayaṃ anusāsaniṃ padakkhiṇato na gaṇhāti, vāmatova gaṇhāti, tasmā “appadakkhiṇaggāhī”ti vuccati, tenāha “yathānusiṭṭha”ntiādi.

To bring forth in various ways is 'padakkhiṇa'. From that, one whose habit is to receive respectfully is a 'padakkhiṇaggāhī'. One who is not a 'padakkhiṇaggāhī' is an 'appadakkhiṇaggāhī'. Whoever, when being instructed, says, “Why do you speak to me? I know for myself what is allowable and unallowable, blameworthy and blameless, beneficial and not beneficial,” this person does not accept the instruction respectfully; he takes it perversely. Therefore, he is called an 'appadakkhiṇaggāhī'. For that reason, the Teacher said, “as instructed,” and so on.

Uddeseti [V 2.0325] pātimokkhuddese. Atha sabbāneva sikkhāpadāni kathaṃ pātimokkhuddesapariyāpannānīti āha “yassa siyā āpatti, so āvikareyyāti evaṃ saṅgahitattā”ti. “Yassa siyā āpattī”ti hi iminā sabbāpi āpattiyo nidānuddese saṅgahitāyeva honti. Pañcahi sahadhammikehi sikkhitabbattāti labbhamānavasena vuttaṃ. Sahadhammikena sahakāraṇenātipi attho daṭṭhabbo. “Vacanāyā”ti nissakke sampadānavacananti āha “tato mama vacanato”ti. Aṅgāni cettha paṭhamasaṅghabhedasadisāni. Ayaṃ pana viseso – yathā tattha bhedāya parakkamanaṃ, evaṃ idha avacanīyakaraṇatā daṭṭhabbā.

In the Pātimokkha recitation, 'uddeseti' (he recites). Then, how are all the training rules included in the Pātimokkha recitation? The Teacher said: “Because they are included thus: ‘If there should be an offense for anyone, he should declare it.’” Indeed, by this phrase, “If there should be an offense for anyone,” all offenses are included in the introductory recitation. “It should be trained in by five co-religionists” is said in the sense of what is obtainable. The meaning should also be understood as “with a co-religionist, with a cause.” Regarding 'vacanāya', it is a dative in the sense of the ablative, so the Teacher said, “then from my word.” And the factors here are similar to the first training rule on causing a schism in the Sangha. But this is the difference: just as there, there is striving for a schism, so here, the act of making oneself unadmonishable should be understood.

Dubbacasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on being difficult to admonish is concluded.

13. Kuladūsakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

13. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Corrupting Families

431. Terasame kīṭāgirīti tassa nigamassa nāmaṃ. Tañhi sandhāya parato “na assajipunabbasukehi bhikkhūhi kīṭāgirismiṃ vatthabba”nti vuttaṃ. Tena pana yogato so janapadopi “kīṭāgiri”icceva saṅkhyaṃ gatoti āha “evaṃnāmake janapade”ti. Āvāse niyuttā āvāsikā, nibaddhavāsino. Te akataṃ senāsanaṃ karonti, jiṇṇaṃ paṭisaṅkharonti, kate issarā honti. Tenāha “so yesaṃ āyatto…pe… te āvāsikā”ti[M 2.0368]. Nivāso nivāsamattaṃ etesaṃ atthīti nevāsikāti āha “ye pana kevala”ntiādi. Teti assajipunabbasukā. Cha janāti paṇḍuko lohitako mettiyo bhūmajako assaji punabbasukoti ime cha janā. Sammāti ālapanavacanametaṃ. Āyamukhabhūtāti āyassa mukhabhūtā. Dhuraṭṭhāneti sāvatthiyā avidūre ṭhāne. Vassāne hemante cāti dvīsu utūsu vassanato “dvīhi meghehī”ti vuttaṃ. Diyaḍḍhabhikkhusahassato gaṇācariyānaṃ channaṃ janānaṃ adhikattā “samadhika”nti vuttaṃ, sādhikanti attho. Ma-kāro padasandhivasena āgato. Akatavatthunti akatapubbaṃ abhinavavatthuṃ.

431. In the thirteenth, 'Kīṭāgiri' is the name of that market town. For, referring to that, it was said later, 'The Assaji-Punabbasu monks should not live in Kīṭāgiri.' And due to connection with that, that country also came to be known as 'Kīṭāgiri'; therefore it is said 'in a country with such a name.' Those appointed in a residence are 'āvāsikā' (residents), permanent dwellers. They prepare an unprepared lodging, repair a dilapidated one, and are masters over the prepared one. Therefore it is said, 'that which is dependent on them... (etc.) ... they are the residents.' Because they have a mere dwelling, they are 'nevāsikā' (mere dwellers); so it is said, 'but those who are merely...' etc. 'Te' (they) are the Assaji-Punabbasu monks. 'Six persons' means: Paṇḍuka, Lohitaka, Mettiya, Bhūmajaka, Assaji, and Punabbasu—these six persons. 'Āyasmā' is a term of address. 'Āyamukhabhūtā' means they became an entrance for income. 'Dhuraṭṭhāne' means in a place not far from Sāvatthī. Because it rains in two seasons, the rainy season and winter, it was said 'with two clouds.' Because the six group-teachers were in addition to the one and a half thousand monks, it was said 'samadhikaṃ' (with an excess), the meaning is 'sādhikaṃ' (with an addition). The letter 'ma' has come by way of word-conjunction. 'Akatavatthuṃ' means a new item, not made before.

Kaṇikārādayo puppharukkhā, jātisumanādayo pupphagacchā. Koṭṭananti sayaṃ chindanaṃ. Koṭṭāpananti “imaṃ chinda bhindā”ti aññehi chedāpanaṃ. Āḷiyā bandhananti yathā gacchamūle udakaṃ santiṭṭhati, tathā samantato bandhanaṃ. Udakassāti akappiyaudakassa. Kappiyaudakasiñcananti imināva siñcāpanampi saṅgahitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Nanu “udakassa secanaṃ secāpana”nti imināva sāmaññato kappiyākappiyaudakasiñcanādiṃ sakkā saṅgahetuṃ, tasmā kappiyaudakasiñcanādi [V 2.0326] kasmā visuṃ vuttanti? “Ārāmādiatthaṃ ropite akappiyavohāresupi kappiyaudakasiñcanādi vaṭṭatī”ti vakkhamānattā idhāpi vibhāgaṃ katvā kappiyaudakasiñcanādi visuṃ dassitaṃ. Hatthamukhapādadhovananhānodakasiñcananti imināpi pakārantarena kappiyaudakasiñcanameva dasseti. “Akappiyavohāro”ti koṭṭanakhaṇanādivasena sayaṃ karaṇassapi kathaṃ saṅgahoti? Akappiyanti voharīyatīti akappiyavohāroti akappiyabhūtaṃ karaṇakārāpanādi sabbameva saṅgahitaṃ, na pana akappiyavacanamattanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kappiyavohārepi eseva nayo. Sukkhamātikāya ujukaraṇanti iminā purāṇapaṇṇādiharaṇampi saṅgahitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kudālādīni bhūmiyaṃ ṭhapetvā ṭhānato hatthena gahetvā ṭhānameva pākaṭataranti “obhāso”ti vuttaṃ.

Kaṇikāra and so on are flowering trees; Jātisumanā and so on are flowering shrubs. 'Koṭṭana' is cutting oneself. 'Koṭṭāpana' is causing others to cut by saying, 'Cut this, break this.' 'Āḷiyā bandhana' is making a basin all around so that water stands at the root of a shrub. 'Of water' means of unsuitable water. It should be understood that by 'sprinkling suitable water', causing others to sprinkle is also included. Is it not possible to include the sprinkling of both suitable and unsuitable water generally by the phrase 'the sprinkling of water and causing to sprinkle'? So why is 'sprinkling suitable water' stated separately? Because it will be said, 'When something is planted for the purpose of a monastery, etc., even in unsuitable transactions, sprinkling suitable water, etc., is allowable,' a distinction is made here also, and 'sprinkling suitable water', etc., is shown separately. And by 'sprinkling water for washing hands, face, and feet, and for bathing', he shows just the sprinkling of suitable water in another way. Regarding 'unsuitable transaction': how is even doing it oneself by way of cutting, digging, etc., included? It is called 'unsuitable', thus it is an 'unsuitable transaction'; in this term, everything that has become unsuitable, such as doing and causing to do, is included, but it should be understood that the mere speaking of what is unsuitable is not. This same method applies also to 'suitable transaction'. By 'straightening a dry water-channel', it should be understood that removing old leaves, etc., is also included. Than placing tools like hoes on the ground and standing, taking them by hand and standing is itself clearer; therefore it is called 'obhāso' (a showing).

Mahāpaccarivādamhi patiṭṭhapetukāmo pacchā vadati. Vanatthāyāti idaṃ keci “vatatthāyā”ti paṭhanti, tesaṃ vatiatthāyāti attho. Akappiyavohārepi ekaccaṃ vaṭṭatīti dassetuṃ “na kevalañca sesa”ntiādimāha. Yaṃ kiñci mātikanti sukkhamātikaṃ vā asukkhamātikaṃ vā. “Kappiyaudakaṃ [M 2.0369] siñcitu”nti iminā “kappiyaudakaṃ siñcathāti vattumpi vaṭṭatī”ti dasseti. Sayaṃ ropetumpi vaṭṭatīti iminā “ropehīti vattuṃ vaṭṭatī”tipi siddhaṃ. Aññatthāya vā karontassāti vatthupūjādiatthaṃ karontassa. Kasmā na anāpattīti vatthupūjanatthāya ganthanādīsu kasmā na anāpatti. Anāpattiyevāti paṭivacanaṃ datvā idāni tameva anāpattibhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “yathāhī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tatthāti ārāmādiatthāya rukkharopane. Tathā vatthupūjanatthāyapi anāpattiyevāti ratanattayapūjanatthāyapi kappiyavohārena pariyāyādīhi ca ganthāpane anāpattiyevāti attho.

Wishing to establish his view in the Mahāpaccarī commentary, he speaks later. This 'vanatthāya' (for the sake of a grove), some read as 'vatatthāya'; for them, the meaning is 'for the purpose of a fence.' To show that a certain action is allowable even in an unsuitable transaction, he said, 'not only the remaining...' and so on. 'Whatever water-channel' means a dry water-channel or a wet one. By 'to sprinkle suitable water', he shows that it is also allowable to say, 'Sprinkle suitable water.' By 'it is allowable even to plant oneself', it is also established that 'it is allowable to say, "Plant!"' 'Or for one doing it for another purpose' means for one doing it for the purpose of venerating a sacred object, etc. 'Why is it not a case of no-offense?' means why is there not no-offense in tying, etc., for the purpose of venerating a sacred object? Having given the reply, 'It is indeed no-offense,' he now says 'just as...' etc., to show that very state of no-offense. 'There' means in the planting of a tree for the sake of a monastery, etc. 'Likewise, for the purpose of venerating a sacred object also, it is indeed no-offense' means that for the purpose of venerating the Three Jewels also, in causing to tie by means of suitable transaction, circumlocution, etc., there is indeed no-offense.

“Tathā vatthupūjanatthāyā”ti hi sāmaññato vuttepi “yathā hi tattha kappiyavohārena pariyāyādīhi cā”ti vuttattā kappiyavohārādīhi ganthāpane eva anāpatti viññāyati, na sayaṃ ganthane, teneva paro sayaṃ ganthanampi kasmā na vaṭṭatīti codento “nanu cā”tiādimāha. Yathā ārāmādiatthaṃ kappiyapathaviyaṃ sayaṃ ropetumpi vaṭṭati, tathā vatthupūjanatthāya sayaṃ ganthanepi kasmā na vaṭṭatīti codakassa adhippāyo. Vuttantiādi ācariyassa parihāro. Atha “na pana mahāaṭṭhakathāya”nti kasmā vadati. Mahāpaccariādīsu vuttampi hi pamāṇamevāti nāyaṃ virodho, mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ avuttampi tattheva vuttena saṃsanditvā pamāṇamevāti patiṭṭhāpetuṃ vuttattā. Taṃ kathanti maññeyyāsīti sambandho. Mahāaṭṭhakathāyañca kappiyaudakasecanaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ kathanti etthāyamadhippāyo. Kiñcāpi mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ ārāmādiatthāya [V 2.0327] kappiyapathaviyaṃ sayaṃ ropanaṃ na vuttaṃ, kappiyaudakassa pana sayaṃ siñcanaṃ vuttameva, tasmā yathā ārāmādiatthāya kappiyaudakaṃ sayaṃ siñcitumpi vaṭṭati, tathā vatthupūjanatthāya sayaṃ ganthanampi kasmā na vaṭṭatīti. Tampi na virujjhatīti yadetaṃ ārāmādiatthāya sayaṃ ropanaṃ kappiyaudakasiñcanañca vuttaṃ, tampi na virujjhati. Kathaṃ taṃ na virujjhatīti āha “tatrahī”tiādi. Etaṃ vuttanti mālāvacchaṃ ropentipi ropāpentipi siñcantipi siñcāpentipīti etaṃ vuttaṃ. Aññatra pana pariyāyo atthīti “mālāvacchaṃ ropentipi ropāpentipi siñcantipi siñcāpentipī”ti kulasaṅgahatthāya ropanasiñcanaṃ sandhāya vuttattā tato aññatra ārāmādiatthāya mālāvaccharopane pariyāyo atthi. Tattha pariyāyaṃ idha [M 2.0370] ca pariyāyābhāvaṃ ñatvāti tattha “mālāvacchaṃ ropentī”tiādīsu “mālāvaccha”nti visesavacanasabbhāvato pariyāyaṃ, idha “ganthentī”tiādīsu tathāvidhavisesavacanābhāvato pariyāyābhāvañca ñatvā.

Even though it is generally said, 'Likewise for the purpose of making offerings to the objects of veneration,' since it is stated, 'Just as there, by means of allowable speech, indirect methods, and so on,' it is understood that there is no offense only in having them strung by means of allowable speech, etc., but not in stringing them oneself. Therefore, an objector, asking, 'Why is it not allowable to string them oneself?' says, 'Is it not so?' and so on. The objector's intention is: 'Just as it is allowable to plant oneself on allowable ground for the sake of a monastery, etc., why is it not allowable to string them oneself for the purpose of making offerings to the objects of veneration?' The passage beginning with 'It is said' is the Teacher's refutation. Then, why does he say, 'But not in the Great Commentary'? For what is said in the Mahāpaccari, etc., is indeed authoritative, so this is no contradiction, since it is said in order to establish that even what is not stated in the Great Commentary is authoritative when compared with what is stated there. The connection should be understood as, 'How is that?' Moreover, in the Great Commentary, the sprinkling of allowable water is mentioned. Here, the intention is, 'How is that?' Although the Great Commentary does not mention planting oneself on allowable ground for the sake of a monastery, etc., it does mention sprinkling allowable water oneself. Therefore, just as it is allowable to sprinkle allowable water oneself for the sake of a monastery, etc., why is it not allowable to string them oneself for the purpose of making offerings to the objects of veneration? Regarding the statement, 'That too is not contradictory': that which is mentioned—namely, planting oneself for the sake of a monastery, etc., and the sprinkling of allowable water—that too is not contradictory. To the question, 'How is that not contradictory?' he replies with 'For there,' etc. This is said: 'They plant the flower-plot, have it planted, water it, or have it watered.' The phrase 'Apart from that, however, there is an alternative method' means: since 'They plant the flower-plot... or have it watered' is said in reference to planting and watering for the sake of supporting lay families, apart from that, there is an alternative method for planting a flower-plot for the sake of a monastery, etc. The phrase 'Having known the existence of an alternative method there and the absence of an alternative method here' refers to knowing that there, in 'They plant the flower-plot,' etc., an alternative method exists due to the presence of the specific term 'flower-plot,' whereas here, in 'stringing,' etc., there is an absence of an alternative method due to the absence of such a specific term.

Nanu ca yathā “ganthentī”ti sāmaññato vuttattā pariyāyo na labbhatīti yassa kassaci atthāya sayaṃ ganthanaṃ na vaṭṭati, evaṃ “ganthāpentī”ti sāmaññato vuttattā pariyāyena ganthāpanampi na vaṭṭatīti āpajjati. Evañca sati parato “evaṃ jāna, evaṃ kate sobheyya, yathā etāni pupphāni na vikiriyanti, tathā karohītiādinā kappiyavacanena kāretuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti idaṃ virujjhatīti? Na virujjhati, pariyāyena hi kārāpanaṃ ganthāpanameva na hoti, tasmā yathāvuttanayena pariyāyato kārāpanaṃ vaṭṭati. Sabbaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbanti heṭṭhā vuttaṃ vinicchayameva saṅkhepato nigameti. Haraṇādīsu kasmā anāpattīti vatthupūjanatthāya haraṇādīsu kasmā anāpatti. Kulitthiādīnaṃ atthāya haraṇatoti kulitthiādīnaṃ haraṇassa tattha vuttattāti adhippāyo. Tenevāha “haraṇādhikāre hī”tiādi. Mālanti pupphadāmaṃ. Mañjarī viyāti kusumamañjarī viya. Hārasadisanti muttāhārasadisaṃ.

Is it not so that, just as stringing them oneself is not allowable for any purpose whatsoever because 'they string' is stated generally and thus no alternative method is found, so too it would follow that having them strung by an alternative method is also not allowable because 'they have them strung' is also stated generally? And if this is so, does it not contradict the later statement: 'It is allowable to have it done with allowable words, such as, “Know this; it would be beautiful if done this way; do it in such a way that these flowers are not scattered,” and so on'? It does not contradict, for causing it to be done by an alternative method is not the same as having it strung. Therefore, causing it to be done by an alternative method, according to the aforesaid manner, is allowable. The phrase 'Everything should be understood according to the manner stated' briefly concludes the decision stated above. 'Why is there no offense in carrying and so on?' means: why is there no offense in carrying and so on for the purpose of making offerings to the objects of veneration? The intention is that this is because carrying for the sake of women of good family and so on is mentioned there. For that very reason, he said the phrase beginning with, 'For in the section on carrying.' 'A garland' means a string of flowers. 'Like a spray' means like a spray of blossoms. 'Like a necklace' means like a pearl necklace.

Pācittiyañceva dukkaṭañcāti pathavīkhaṇanapaccayā pācittiyaṃ, kulasaṅgahapaccayā dukkaṭaṃ. Akappiyavohārenāti “idaṃ khaṇa, idaṃ ropehī”tiādiakappiyavohārena. Dukkaṭamevāti kulasaṅgahapaccayā dukkaṭaṃ. Ubhayatthāti kappiyākappiyapathaviyaṃ. Sabbatthāti kulasaṅgahaparibhogaārāmādiatthāya ropite. Dukkaṭampīti na kevalaṃ pācittiyameva. Kappiyenāti kappiyena udakena. Tesaṃyeva dvinnanti kuladūsanaparibhogānaṃ. Dukkaṭanti kulasaṅgahatthāya sayaṃ siñcane kappiyavohārena akappiyavohārena vā siñcāpane ca dukkaṭaṃ, paribhogatthāya pana sayaṃ siñcane akappiyavohārena siñcāpane ca dukkaṭaṃ. Āpattibahulatā veditabbāti ettha sayaṃ siñcane [V 2.0328] dhārāpacchedagaṇanāya āpattigaṇanā veditabbā. Siñcāpane pana punappunaṃ āṇāpentassa vācāya vācāya āpatti, sakiṃ āṇattassa bahūnaṃ siñcanepi ekāva.

'Both a pācittiya and a dukkaṭa' means: a pācittiya on account of digging the earth, and a dukkaṭa on account of supporting a lay family. 'By unallowable speech' means: by unallowable speech such as, 'Dig this, plant this,' and so on. 'Only a dukkaṭa' means: a dukkaṭa on account of supporting a lay family. 'In both cases' means: on allowable and unallowable ground. 'In all cases' means: when planted for the purpose of supporting a lay family, for personal use, for a monastery, and so on. 'Also a dukkaṭa' means: it is not merely a pācittiya. 'With allowable' means: with allowable water. 'For those same two' means: for corrupting a family and for personal use. 'A dukkaṭa' means: there is a dukkaṭa for watering oneself for the purpose of supporting a lay family, and for causing it to be watered by either allowable or unallowable speech. For the purpose of personal use, however, there is a dukkaṭa for watering oneself and for causing it to be watered by unallowable speech. 'The multiplicity of offenses should be understood' means: herein, when watering oneself, the number of offenses should be understood by counting the interruptions of the stream. When causing it to be watered, however, for one who commands repeatedly, there is an offense for each utterance. For one who commands once, even if many things are watered, there is only one offense.

Dukkaṭapācittiyānīti kulasaṅgahapaccayā dukkaṭaṃ, bhūtagāmapātabyatāya pācittiyaṃ. Aññatthāti vatthupūjādiatthāya ocinane. Sakiṃ āṇattoti akappiyavohārena āṇatto. Pācittiyamevāti akappiyavacanena [M 2.0371] āṇattattā pācittiyaṃ. Kappiyavacanena pana vatthupūjādiatthāya ocināpentassa anāpattiyeva.

'Dukkaṭa and pācittiya offenses' means: a dukkaṭa on account of supporting a lay family, and a pācittiya on account of destroying vegetation. 'In another case' means: when plucking for the purpose of making offerings to the objects of veneration, etc. 'Commanded once' means: one who is commanded with unallowable speech. 'Only a pācittiya' means: it is a pācittiya because the command was given with unallowable words. However, for one who causes them to be plucked with allowable words for the purpose of making offerings to the objects of veneration, etc., there is no offense at all.

Ganthanena nibbattaṃ gantimaṃ. Esa nayo sesesupi. Na vaṭṭatīti kulasaṅgahatthāya vatthupūjādiatthāya vā vuttanayena karontassa ca kārāpentassa ca dukkaṭanti attho. Purimanayenevāti “bhikkhussa vā”tiādinā vuttanayena. Dhammāsanavitāne baddhakaṇṭakesu pupphāni vijjhitvā ṭhapentīti sambandho. Uparūpari vijjhitvā chattasadisaṃ katvā āvuṇanato “chattātichattaṃ viyā”ti vuttaṃ. “Kadalikkhandhamhī”tiādinā vuttaṃ sabbameva sandhāya “taṃ atioḷārikamevā”ti vuttaṃ, sayaṃ karontassa akappiyavacaneneva kārāpentassa ca dukkaṭamevāti attho. Pupphavijjhanatthanti vuttattā pupphāni vijjhituṃyeva kaṇṭakaṃ bandhituṃ na vaṭṭati, pupphadāmādibandhanatthaṃ pana vaṭṭati. Kaṇṭakampi bandhituṃ na vaṭṭatīti ca idaṃ aṭṭhakathācariyappamāṇena gahetabbaṃ. Pavesetuṃ na vaṭṭatīti vuttattā pupphacchidde apavesetvā uparūpari ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭati. Jālamayaṃ vitānaṃ jālavitānaṃ. Nāgadantakampi sacchiddakaṃyeva gahetabbaṃ. Pupphapaṭicchakaṃ daṇḍādīhi katapupphādhāraṇaṃ, tampi sacchiddameva idha vuttaṃ. Asokapiṇḍiyāti asokapupphamañjarikāya. “Dhammarajju nāma cetiyaṃ vā bodhiṃ vā pupphapavesanatthaṃ āvijjhitvā baddharajjū”ti mahāgaṇṭhipade majjhimagaṇṭhipade ca vuttaṃ, tasmā tathābaddhāya rajjuyā cetiyassa ca antare pupphāni pavesetuṃ vaṭṭatīti viññāyati. Gaṇṭhipade pana “dhammarajjunti sithilaṃ vaṭṭikaṃ rajjuṃ katvā bodhiṃ vā cetiyaṃ vā parikkhipitvā dhammāsane vā lambitvā tattha pupphāni pavesentī”ti vuttaṃ, tasmā sithilavaṭṭikāya rajjuyā antarepi pupphāni pavesetuṃ vaṭṭatīti viññāyati, vīmaṃsitvā yuttataraṃ gahetabbaṃ. Ubhayatthāpi panettha nevatthi virodhoti amhākaṃ khanti.

That which is produced by tying is called 'tied' (gantimaṃ). This method applies to the rest as well. 'It is not allowable' means that for one who does or causes to be done in the manner stated, for the purpose of gaining favor with a family or for honoring objects, etc., it is a dukkaṭa offense. By the previous method: by the method stated beginning with 'for a bhikkhu,' and so on. The connection is that they pierce and place flowers on the fastened thorns of the Dharma seat canopy. Because they are pierced layer by layer and made like an umbrella, and suspended, it is said, 'like an umbrella upon an umbrella.' Referring to all that is stated beginning with 'on a banana trunk,' etc., it is said, 'that is indeed exceedingly coarse.' The meaning is that for one who does it oneself, it is unallowable by the very word itself, and for one who causes it to be done, it is indeed a dukkaṭa offense. Since it is said, 'for the purpose of piercing flowers,' it is not allowable to fasten thorns merely to pierce flowers, but it is allowable for the purpose of fastening flower garlands, etc. And that it is not allowable to fasten thorns should be understood according to the authority of the commentary teachers. Since it is said, 'it is not allowable to insert,' it is allowable to place them layer by layer without inserting them into the flower-stalk holes. A net-like canopy is a 'net canopy' (jālavitānaṃ). Even a 'nāgadantaka' (elephant-tusk decoration) should be understood as having a hole. A 'pupphapaṭicchakaṃ' (flower receptacle) is a flower holder made with sticks, etc.; that too is said here to have a hole. 'Asoka clusters' (asokapiṇḍiyā) means an asoka flower cluster. In the Mahāgaṇṭhipada and Majjhimagaṇṭhipada, it is stated: 'A 'dhammarajju' (Dhamma cord) is a cord tied after encircling a shrine or a Bodhi tree for the purpose of inserting flowers.' Therefore, it is understood that it is allowable to insert flowers into the space between such a tied cord and the shrine. However, in the Gaṇṭhipada, it is stated: ''Dhammarajju' means making a loose, coiled cord, encircling a Bodhi tree or shrine, or hanging it over the Dharma seat, and then inserting flowers there.' Therefore, it is understood that it is allowable to insert flowers even into the space of a loosely coiled cord. Having investigated, the more appropriate interpretation should be adopted. In both cases, however, there is no contradiction here—this is our acceptance.

Matthakadāmanti dhammāsanādimatthake lambakadāmaṃ. Pupphehi veṭhentīti pupphadāmena veṭhenti. Tesaṃyevāti uppalādīnaṃyeva. Vākena vā daṇḍakena vāti visuṃ acchinnena pupphasahiteneva vākena vā daṇḍakena vā. Khandhe ṭhapitakāsāvassāti khandhe ṭhapitasaṅghāṭiṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tañhi tathā bandhituṃ [V 2.0329] sakkā bhaveyya. Imināva aññampi tādisaṃ kāsāvaṃ vā vatthaṃ vā vuttanayena bandhitvā tattha pupphāni pakkhipituṃ vaṭṭatīti siddhaṃ. Aṃsabhaṇḍikaṃ pasibbake pakkhittasadisattā veṭhimaṃ nāma na jātaṃ, tasmā sithilabandhassa antarantarā pakkhipituṃ vaṭṭatīti vadanti.

'Matthakadāma' means a hanging garland at the head of the Dharma seat, and so on. 'They wrap with flowers' means they wrap with flower garlands. 'Of those very ones' means only of lotuses, and so on. 'With a bark-strip or a stalk' means with a bark-strip or a stalk that is not cut off separately, but is together with the flower. 'Of the saffron robe placed on the shoulder' is said referring to the outer robe placed on the shoulder. For it could indeed be tied in that way. By this very statement, it is established that it is allowable to tie another such saffron robe or cloth in the stated manner and place flowers therein. Because it is like something placed in a shoulder bag, it does not become what is called a 'wrapping' (veṭhimaṃ). Therefore, they say that it is allowable to place flowers in the gaps of a loose binding.

Pupphapaṭe [M 2.0372] ca daṭṭhabbanti pupphapaṭaṃ karontassa dīghato pupphadāmassa haraṇapaccāharaṇavasena pūraṇaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tiriyato haraṇaṃ pana vāyimaṃ nāma hoti, na pūrimaṃ. Purimaṭṭhānaṃ atikkāmetīti ettha “aphusāpetvāpi atikkāmentassa āpattiyevā”ti tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. “Purimaṭṭhānaṃ atikkāmetī”ti avisesena vuttattā taṃ yuttaṃ. Keci pana “aññamaññaṃ aphusāpetvā anekakkhattuṃ parikkhipituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vadantīti vuttaṃ, tattha kāraṇaṃ na dissati. Bandhituṃ vaṭṭatīti puppharahitāya suttakoṭiyā vākakoṭiyā vā bandhituṃ vaṭṭati. Ekavāraṃ haritvā vā parikkhipitvā vāti idaṃ pubbe vuttacetiyādiparikkhepaṃ pupphapaṭakaraṇañca sandhāya vuttaṃ, tasmā cetiyaṃ vā bodhiṃ vā parikkhipantena ekavāraṃ parikkhipitvā purimaṭṭhānaṃ sampatte aññassa dātabbaṃ, tenapi ekavāraṃ parikkhipitvā tatheva kātabbaṃ. Pupphapaṭaṃ karontena ca ekavāraṃ haritvā aññassa dātabbaṃ, tenapi tatheva kātabbaṃ. Sacepi dveyeva bhikkhū ubhosu passesu ṭhatvā pariyāyena haranti, vaṭṭatiyevāti vadanti.

'And in the case of a flower-cloth, it should be seen'—this is said with reference to filling the cloth lengthwise by means of bringing and bringing back the flower garland, for one making a flower-cloth. Bringing it widthwise, however, is called 'weaving' (vāyimaṃ), not 'filling' (pūrimaṃ). Regarding 'passing beyond the original position,' it is stated in all three Gaṇṭhipada texts: 'Even for one who passes beyond without making it touch, there is an offense.' Since 'passing beyond the original position' is stated generally, that is fitting. It is said that some say, 'It is permissible to wrap around multiple times without them touching each other,' but no reason for this is seen. 'It is permissible to tie' means it is permissible to tie with the end of a thread or fiber that is without flowers. 'Having carried once or wrapped once'—this is said with reference to the previously mentioned encircling of shrines and the like, and the making of flower-cloths. Therefore, when encircling a shrine or the Bodhi tree, one should wrap around once and, upon reaching the original position, give it to another, who should then do likewise. And one making a flower-cloth, having carried it once, should give it to another, who should also do likewise. They say that if just two monks, standing on both sides, carry it in turn, it is indeed permissible.

Pūritanti dīghato pasāraṇavasena pūritaṃ. Vāyituṃ na labhatīti dīghato pasārite tiriyato haraṇaṃ vāyanaṃ nāma hotīti ekavārampi pupphaguṇaṃ tiriyato harituṃ na vaṭṭati. Pupphāni ṭhapentenāti aganthitāni pākatikapupphāni ṭhapentena. Pupphadāmaṃ pana pūjanatthāya bhūmiyaṃ ṭhapentena phusāpetvā vā aphusāpetvā vā diguṇaṃ katvā ṭhapetuṃ na vaṭṭatīti vadanti. Ghaṭikadāmaolambakoti ante ghaṭikākārayutto yamakadāmaolambako. Ekekaṃ pana dāmaṃ nikkhantasuttakoṭiyāva bandhitvā olambituṃ vaṭṭati, pupphadāmadvayaṃ saṅghaṭitukāmenapi nikkhantasuttakoṭiyāva suttakoṭiṃ saṅghaṭituṃ vaṭṭati. Aḍḍhacandākārena mālāguṇaparikkhepoti aḍḍhacandākārena mālāguṇassa punappunaṃ haraṇapaccāharaṇavasena pūretvā parikkhipanaṃ. Teneva taṃ pūrime paviṭṭhaṃ, tasmā etampi aḍḍhacandākāraṃ punappunaṃ haraṇapaccāharaṇavasena pūritaṃ na vaṭṭati. Ekavāraṃ pana aḍḍhacandākārena mālāguṇaṃ harituṃ vaṭṭatīti vadanti. Pupphadāmakaraṇanti ettha suttakoṭiyaṃ gahetvāpi ekato kātuṃ na vaṭṭatīti vadanti. Geṇḍukakharapattadāmānaṃ paṭikkhittattā celādīhi katadāmampi na vaṭṭati akappiyānulomattāti vadanti.

“Filled” (pūritaṃ) means filled by extending lengthwise. “Not being able to weave” (vāyituṃ na labhati) means that when extended lengthwise, the horizontal movement is called weaving—thus, it is not permissible to move the flower garland horizontally even once. “Placing flowers” (pupphāni ṭhapentena) means placing unbound, natural flowers. However, when placing a flower garland on the ground for worship, whether touching or not touching, they say it is not permissible to place it folded double. “A hanging garland with a pot-shaped end” (ghaṭikadāmaolambako) means a double garland hanging with a pot-shaped end. It is permissible to tie and hang each garland only at the end of the thread. Even if one wishes to join two flower garlands, it is permissible to join them thread end to thread end. “Arranging the flower garland in a half-moon shape” (aḍḍhacandākārena mālāguṇaparikkhepo) means encompassing it by filling it through repeatedly moving it back and forth in a half-moon pattern. Therefore, since that is included in the aforementioned filling, this too, being filled by repeated back-and-forth movement in a half-moon shape, is not permissible. However, they say it is permissible to move the flower garland once in a half-moon shape. Regarding the making of flower garlands, they say that even gathering them on one side by holding the end of the thread is not permissible. Since garlands made of balls and rough leaves are prohibited, garlands made of cloth and the like are also not permissible, as they are similar to what is unsuitable, they say.

“Lāsiyanāṭakaṃ [V 2.0330][M 2.0373] nāṭentī”ti vatvā tameva pariyāyantarena dassetuṃ “recakaṃ dentī”ti vuttaṃ, abhinayaṃ dassentīti attho, attano adhippāyaṃ pakāsetvā “evaṃ naccitabba”nti paṭhamaṃ uṭṭhahitvā naccanākāraṃ dassentīti vuttaṃ hoti. Keci pana “mukhe aṅguliyo pakkhipitvā saddaṃ karontā cakkamiva attānaṃ bhamayamānā recakaṃ denti nāmā”ti vadanti. Ekekāya pantiyā aṭṭha aṭṭha padāni assāti aṭṭhapadaṃ. “Aṭṭhāpada”ntipi paṭhanti. Dasapadepi eseva nayo. Padānīti ca sāriādīnaṃ patiṭṭhānaṭṭhānāni. Dasapadaṃ nāma dvīhi pantīhi vīsatiyā padehi kīḷanajūtaṃ. Ākāseyeva kīḷantīti “ayaṃ sārī asukapadaṃ mayā nītā, ayaṃ asukapada”nti kevalaṃ mukheneva vadantā ākāseyeva jūtaṃ kīḷanti. Jūtaphalaketi jūtamaṇḍale. Pāsakakīḷāya kīḷantīti pāsakaṃ vuccati chasu passesu ekekaṃ yāva chakkaṃ dassetvā katakīḷanaṃ, taṃ vaḍḍhetvā yathāladdhaekakādivasena sāriyo apanentā upanentā ca kīḷanti. Ghaṭena kīḷā ghaṭikāti eke.

Having said, ‘They perform the Lāsya dance’ (Lāsiyanāṭakaṃ nāṭentī), to show that very thing in another way, it is stated, ‘They give recaka’ (recakaṃ dentī). The meaning is that they display the art of acting. It is said that having expressed their own intention, they first rise and show the manner of dancing, saying, ‘Thus one should dance.’ Some, however, say: ‘Making a sound by inserting fingers into the mouth and spinning oneself like a wheel is called giving recaka.’ Because it has eight by eight spaces, it is called aṭṭhapada. Some also read it as aṭṭhāpada. The same method applies to dasapada. And ‘spaces’ (padāni) are the places for the game pieces to stand. Dasapada is a game played with two rows and twenty spaces. ‘They play in the air itself’ (ākāseyeva kīḷanti) means that they play the game in the air itself, merely by speaking, saying, ‘This piece has been moved by me to such-and-such a space, this one to such-and-such a space.’ ‘On a game board’ (jūtaphalake) means on the gambling ground. ‘They play the dice game’ (pāsakakīḷāya kīḷanti) means: pāsaka is the name for a game played with a die that shows from one up to six on its six sides. Rolling it, they play by moving the pieces off and on according to the number obtained, such as one and so on. A game with a stick is called ghaṭikā, say some.

Mañjaṭṭhiyā vāti mañjaṭṭhirukkhasāraṃ gahetvā pakkakasāvaṃ sandhāya vadati. Salākahatthanti tālahīrādīnaṃ kalāpassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Bahūsu salākāsu visesarahitaṃ ekaṃ salākaṃ gahetvā tāsu pakkhipitvā puna taṃyeva uddharantā salākahatthena kīḷantīti keci. Paṇṇena vaṃsākārena katā nāḷikā paṇṇanāḷikā. Tenevāha “taṃ dhamantā”ti. Pucchantassa mukhāgataṃ akkharaṃ gahetvā naṭṭhamuṭṭhilābhālābhādijānanakīḷā akkharikātipi vadanti. Hatthisminti nimittatthe bhummaṃ, hatthinimittasippeti attho. Assasmintiādīsupi eseva nayo. “Usseḷenti apphoṭentī”ti dvinnaṃ padānaṃ attho pākaṭoyevāti na vutto. Tattha usseḷentīti mukhena usseḷanasaddaṃ pamuñcanti, mahantaṃ katvā abyattasaddaṃ pavattentīti attho. “Ajānaṃ saññaṃ dentā ajapālakā viya mukhena vātaṃ nicchārentā sukhumaṃ abyattanādaṃ pavattentī”tipi vadanti. Apphoṭentīti bhujahatthasaṅghaṭṭanasaddaṃ pavattenti, vāmahatthaṃ ure ṭhapetvā dakkhiṇena pāṇinā tattha tāḷanena saddaṃ karontīti attho. Mukhaḍiṇḍimanti mukhabheriyā etaṃ adhivacanaṃ.

‘Or with mañjaṭṭhi’ (Mañjaṭṭhiyā vā) is said with reference to taking the heartwood of the mañjaṭṭhi tree and its ripe, astringent juice. ‘A handful of sticks’ (Salākahattha) is a designation for a bunch of tāla-hīra and the like. Some say that they play with a handful of sticks by taking one undifferentiated stick from among many, placing it among them, and then drawing out that very one again. A tube made from a leaf in the shape of a bamboo is a paṇṇanāḷikā. For that reason it says, ‘blowing that.’ They also say that akkharikā is the game of knowing the gain, loss, etc., of a lost fistful by taking a letter that comes from the mouth of one who asks. In ‘hatthismiṃ,’ the locative case is used in the sense of a sign; the meaning is ‘the art of elephant signs.’ The same method applies to ‘assasmiṃ’ and so on. The meaning of the two words ‘usseḷenti’ and ‘apphoṭentī’ is quite clear, so it is not stated. Therein, ‘usseḷenti’ means they emit a cheering sound with their mouths; the meaning is that they produce a loud, indistinct sound. They also say: ‘Like goatherds giving a signal to goats, they emit wind from the mouth and produce a subtle, indistinct sound.’ ‘Apphoṭentī’ means they produce the sound of striking the arm and hand together; the meaning is that they place the left hand on the chest and make a sound by striking it there with the right hand. ‘Mukhaḍiṇḍima’ is a designation for a mouth-drum.

432. Pasādāvahenāti [M 2.0374] pasādajananakena. Abhikkamanaṃ abhikkantanti āha “gamanenā”ti. Paṭikkamanaṃ paṭikkantaṃ. Nivattanenāti nivattimattaṃ dasseti. Nivattetvā pana gamanaṃ gamanameva. Abhimukhaṃ lokitaṃ ālokitanti āha “purato dassanenā”ti. Ito cito ca dassanenāti anudisāpekkhanaṃ dasseti. Yaṃdisābhimukho gacchati tiṭṭhati nisīdati, tadabhimukhaṃ pekkhanaṃ ālokitaṃ, tadanugatadisālokanaṃ “vilokita”nti hi vuccati. Aññānipi heṭṭhā upari pacchato pekkhanavasena olokitaullokitāpalokitāni nāma honti. Tāni [V 2.0331] pana na samaṇasāruppāni appasādāvahāni, tenevettha ālokitavilokitāneva gahitāni. Tesanti samāse guṇībhūtānipi pabbāni parāmasati. “Pabbasaṅkocanenā”ti hi vuttattā pabbāni tattha guṇībhūtāni saṅkocanassa padhānattā. Satisampajaññehīti sātthakatādipariggāhikāya satiyā tathāpavattasampajaññena ca samantato pakārehi, pakaṭṭhaṃ vā savisesaṃ jānātīti sampajāno, tassa bhāvo sampajaññaṃ. Tathāpavattañāṇassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Abhisaṅkhatattāti sammā pavattitattā. Heṭṭhākhittacakkhūti khandhaṃ anāmetvāva adhokhittacakkhu. Khandhaṃ nāmetvā hi heṭṭhāvalokanaṃ na samaṇasāruppaṃ. “Okkhittacakkhū”ti ca iminā yugamattadassitā vuttā.

432. `Pasādāvahena` means: by that which generates confidence. `Abhikkamanaṃ abhikkantaṃ`: He said that this means 'by going forward.' `Paṭikkamanaṃ` is `paṭikkantaṃ` (going back). By `nivattanena`, it indicates merely turning back. However, having turned back, going is simply going. `Abhimukhaṃ lokitaṃ ālokitaṃ`: He said that this means 'by seeing in front.' By `ito cito ca dassanena`, it indicates looking towards one side and the other. When one goes, stands, or sits facing a certain direction, looking towards that direction is `ālokitaṃ`; and looking in the direction one is following is called `vilokitaṃ`. Other ways of looking—by way of looking down, up, and behind—are also called `olokita`, `ullokita`, and `apalokita`. But these are not suitable for a recluse and do not inspire confidence; therefore, only `ālokita` and `vilokita` are included here. With `tesaṃ`, it refers to the limbs (`pabbāni`), even though they are subordinate in the compound. For since it is said 'by the bending of the limbs' (`pabbasaṅkocanena`), the limbs are subordinate there, because the bending is primary. By `satisampajaññehi`: with mindfulness that comprehends what is beneficial, etc., and with clear comprehension that proceeds accordingly. Or, one who knows (`jānāti`) in all ways, or excellently and specifically, is `sampajāno` (one with clear comprehension). The state of that is `sampajaññaṃ` (clear comprehension). This is a designation for knowledge that has arisen in such a way. `Abhisaṅkhatattā` means: because of being well-performed. `Heṭṭhākhittacakkhu` means: having the eyes cast downwards without bending the shoulders. For looking down by bending the shoulders is not suitable for a recluse. And by this term 'with eyes cast down' (`okkhittacakkhu`), it is said that seeing for the distance of a yoke's length is indicated.

Bondoti lolo mandadhātukoti attho. Bhakuṭiṃ katvāti bhamukabhedaṃ katvā. Sākhalyena yuttāti “tattha katamaṃ sākhalyaṃ? Yā sā vācā nelā kaṇṇasukhā”tiādinā (dha. sa. 1350) nayena vuttasākhalyena samannāgatā, muduvacanāti attho. Nelāti elaṃ vuccati doso, nāssā elanti nelā, niddosāti attho. Kaṇṇasukhāti byañjanamadhuratāya kaṇṇānaṃ sukhā, sūcinā vijjhanaṃ viya kaṇṇasūlaṃ na janeti. Dānanibaddhānīti nibaddhadānāni.

`Bondo` means: he is fickle, of dull nature. `Bhakuṭiṃ katvā` means: having made a frown, making a furrow on the brow. `Sākhalyena yuttā` means: endowed with agreeableness, as explained by the method beginning, "Therein, what is agreeableness? It is speech that is flawless (`nelā`), pleasant to the ear (`kaṇṇasukhā`)" (Dhs §1350); the meaning is gentle speech. `Nelā`: a fault is called `elaṃ`; for this speech, there is no fault, therefore it is `nelā`; the meaning is flawless. `Kaṇṇasukhā` means: pleasant to the ears due to the sweetness of the syllables; it does not produce an ear-ache like being pierced with a needle. `Dānanibaddhāni` means: constant gifts.

“Sāriputtamoggallāne āmantesī”ti vatvā “gacchatha tumhe sāriputtā”ti vacanato “sāriputtā”ti idaṃ ekasesanayena vuttanti ayamattho pākaṭoyevāti na vutto. “Sāriputtā”ti hi idaṃ ekasesanayena vuttaṃ virūpekasesassapi icchitattā, tenevettha bahuvacananiddeso katoti. Saddhassa pasannassāti ratanattayassa saddhāya [M 2.0375] samannāgatassa tatoyeva ca pasannassa, kammaphalasaddhāya vā samannāgatattā saddhassa ratanattayappasādabahulatāya pasannassa.

Having said, 'He addressed Sāriputta and Moggallāna,' and because it is said, 'Go, you Sāriputtas,' the meaning that this word 'Sāriputtas' is spoken by the method of `ekasesa` (ellipsis) is perfectly clear, and therefore was not stated by the commentator. Indeed, this 'Sāriputtas' is spoken by the method of `ekasesa` because even a heterogeneous `ekasesa` (`virūpekasesa`) is intended. Therefore, the plural designation is made here; thus it should be understood. Of one who is faithful and confident (`saddhassa pasannassa`): of one endowed with faith in the Triple Gem and therefore confident; or, of one who is faithful because of being endowed with faith in the fruit of kamma, and confident because of an abundance of serene confidence in the Triple Gem.

433. Āpattiṃ ropetabbāti kuladūsakakammena āpannāpattiṃ ropetabbā. Tasmiṃ vihāreti bahigāme vihāraṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Antogāme vihāro pana “tasmiṃ gāme na vasitabba”nti imināva saṅgahito gāmaggahaṇeneva gahitattā. “Tasmiṃ vihāre”ti vacanato tassa gāmassa sāmantā aññasmiṃ vihāre vasituṃ vaṭṭati. Sāmantagāme piṇḍāya na caritabbanti tasmiṃ vihāre vāsassa paṭikkhittattā yadi tattha vasati, tena sāmantagāmepi piṇḍāya na caritabbanti adhippāyo. Tasmiṃ gāme piṇḍāya na caritabbanti yasmiṃ gāme kuladūsakakammaṃ kataṃ, tasmiṃ gāme na caritabbaṃ. Yasmiñhi gāme vā nigame vā kuladūsakakammaṃ kataṃ, yasmiñca vihāre vasati, neva tasmiṃ gāme vā nigame vā carituṃ labbhati, na vihāre vasituṃ. Sāmantavihāre vasantena pana sāmantagāme carituṃ vaṭṭati tattha vāsassa appaṭikkhittattā.

433. The offense should be imputed: the offense incurred through the act of corrupting families should be imputed. 'In that monastery' is said with reference to a monastery outside the village. A monastery inside the village, however, is included by this very phrase, 'one should not dwell in that village,' because it is encompassed by the term 'village.' Because it says, 'in that monastery,' it is permissible to dwell in another monastery near that village. 'One should not go for alms in a neighboring village': because dwelling in that monastery is forbidden, the intention is that if one dwells there, one should not go for alms even in a neighboring village. 'One should not go for alms in that village': in whichever village the act of corrupting families was done, in that village one should not go for alms. Indeed, in whichever village or town the act of corrupting families was done, if one dwells in the monastery there, one is permitted neither to go for alms in that village or town, nor to dwell in that monastery. But for one dwelling in a neighboring monastery, it is permissible to go for alms in a neighboring village, because dwelling there is not forbidden.

435. Aṭṭhārasa [V 2.0332] vattānīti “na upasampādetabbaṃ, na nissayo dātabbo, na sāmaṇero upaṭṭhāpetabbo, na bhikkhunovādakasammuti sāditabbā, sammatena bhikkhuniyo na ovaditabbā, yāya āpattiyā saṅghena pabbājanīyakammaṃ kataṃ hoti, na sā āpatti āpajjitabbā aññā vā tādisikā tato vā pāpiṭṭhatarā, kammaṃ na garahitabbaṃ, kammikā na garahitabbā, na pakatattassa bhikkhuno uposatho ṭhapetabbo, na pavāraṇā ṭhapetabbā, na savacanīyaṃ kātabbaṃ, na anuvādo ṭhapetabbo, na okāso kāretabbo, na codetabbo, na sāretabbo, na bhikkhūhi sampayojetabba”nti evamāgatāni aṭṭhārasa vattāni.

435. The eighteen duties: 'One should not give higher ordination; one should not give dependence; one should not have a novice attend upon oneself; one should not consent to the authorization to be an instructor of bhikkhunīs; even if authorized, one should not instruct bhikkhunīs; one should not commit that offense for which the Sangha performed the act of banishment, nor any other similar to it, nor one worse than that; the act should not be criticized; those who performed the act should not be criticized; the Uposatha of a regular bhikkhu should not be suspended; the Pavāraṇā should not be suspended; the `savacanīya` act should not be performed; a formal charge should not be suspended; an opportunity should not be made; one should not accuse another; one should not remind another of an offense; one should not set bhikkhus at variance with each other'—these are the eighteen duties that have come down.

Assajipunabbasukappadhānā assajipunabbasukāti vuttā sahacaraṇañāyena. Anulomapaṭipadaṃ appaṭipajjanatāyāti yathāpaññattasammāvattasaṅkhātaṃ anulomapaṭipadaṃ appaṭipajjanatāya, yena vattena ciṇṇena saṅgho anulomiko hoti, tasmiṃ avattanatoti vuttaṃ hoti. Na pannalomā hontīti patitalomā na honti, anukūlavuttino na hontīti [M 2.0376] attho. Nittharaṇamaggaṃ na paṭipajjantīti anulomavattasaṅkhātaṃ nittharaṇūpāyaṃ na paṭipajjanti, yena vattena ciṇṇena sāpattikabhāvato nittiṇṇā honti, tasmiṃ nittharaṇakavattasmiṃ na vattanti, āpattivuṭṭhānatthaṃ turitaturitā chandajātā na hontīti vuttaṃ hoti. Dasahi akkosavatthūhīti jātināmagottakammasippaābādhaliṅgakilesaāpattihīnasaṅkhātehidasahi akkosakāraṇehi. Chandagāmitā pāpentītiādīsu ya-kāro “sayaṃ abhiññā”tiādīsu viya luttaniddiṭṭhoti āha “chandagāmitāyapi pāpentī”tiādi. Tesanti assajipunabbasukānaṃ gaṇapāmokkhānaṃ.

Assaji and Punabbasuka, the leaders, were called Assaji-Punabbasuka by way of their shared conduct. ‘By not practicing the proper course of conduct’ means by not practicing the proper course of conduct, which is known as the rightly prescribed good conduct, by which conduct, having been practiced, the Sangha becomes harmonious; this is what is meant by not acting in accordance with that. ‘They are not with lowered hair’ means their hair is not lowered; the meaning is that they are not of compliant behavior. ‘They do not follow the path of escape’ means they do not practice the means of escape, which is known as proper conduct, by which conduct, having been practiced, they are freed from the state of being under an offense. They do not engage in that conduct which is a means of escape; this is what is meant by their not being eager and zealous for rising from an offense. With the ten grounds for abuse: namely, birth, name, clan, occupation, skill, ailment, sign, defilement, offense, and being considered inferior—these are the ten reasons for abuse. In phrases like ‘they lead to partiality,’ etc., the ya-sound is elided, as in ‘having directly known for oneself,’ thus he says ‘they lead to partiality as well,’ etc. ‘Of them’ means of Assaji and Punabbasuka, the leaders of the group.

436-437. Nigamassa apākaṭattā taṃ dassetuṃ “tatthā”tiādimāha. Parasantakaṃ deti, dukkaṭamevāti vissāsaggāhena parasantakaṃ gahetvā dentaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tañca kho vatthupūjanatthāyāti mātāpitūnampi dentena vatthupūjanatthāya eva dātabbanti dasseti. “Maṇḍanatthāya pana sivaliṅgādipūjanatthāyāti ettakameva vuttattā imaṃ vikkiṇitvā jīvikampi kappessantīti mātuādīnaṃ dātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti. Kassacipīti ñātakassa aññātakassa vā kassacipi. Ñātisāmaṇerehevāti anucchavikattā vuttaṃ. Sampattānaṃ sāmaṇerānaṃ upaḍḍhabhāgaṃ dātuṃ vaṭṭatīti saṅghikassa lābhassa upacārasīmagatānaṃ sāmaṇerānampi santakattā tesampi upaḍḍhabhāgo labbhatevāti katvā vuttaṃ. Cūḷakanti upaḍḍhabhāgatopi upaḍḍhaṃ. Catutthabhāgassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ.

Because the conclusion was not clear, he began with ‘there,’ etc., in order to show it. ‘Giving another’s property incurs a dukkaṭa offense’ is said with reference to one who takes another’s property by way of trust and then gives it. And ‘it should only be given for the purpose of honoring the Three Jewels’ shows that even when giving to one’s parents, it should only be given for the purpose of honoring the Three Jewels. Some say, ‘Since only this much is said: “For the purpose of adornment or for worshiping a Sīvalī image, etc.,” one may sell this and make a living; therefore, it is proper to give it to one’s mother and others.’ ‘To anyone’ means to any person, whether a relative or not a relative. ‘By novice relatives only’ is said because it is fitting. ‘It is permissible to give half a share to novices who have arrived’ is said on the grounds that novices who have come within the precincts of the boundary also have ownership of the Sangha’s gains, and thus they too are certainly entitled to a half share. ‘A small portion’ means half of a half share. This is a term for a fourth part.

“Sāmaṇerā…pe… ṭhapentī”ti idaṃ vassaggena abhājiyaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tattha tatthāti magge [V 2.0333] vā cetiyaṅgaṇe vā. Dāpetuṃ na labhantīti sāmaṇerehi dāpetuṃ ananucchavikattā vuttaṃ. Na hi taṃ pupphadānaṃ nāma siyā. Yadi hi tathā āgatānaṃ tesaṃ dānaṃ pupphadānaṃ bhaveyya, sāmaṇerehipi dātuṃ na labbheyya. Sayamevāti sāmaṇerā sayameva. Yāgubhattādīni ādāyāti idaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ atthāya yāgubhattādisampādanaṃ sandhāya vuttattā “na vaṭṭatī”ti avisesena vuttaṃ.

‘The novices… (etc.) … they set aside’—this was said with reference to what is not to be divided according to seniority. ‘Here and there’ means on the road or in the cetiya courtyard. ‘It is not allowable to have them give’ is said because it is unsuitable to have novices give. Indeed, that would not be called an offering of flowers.
