An ‘ovaraka’, they say, is another chamber inside a chamber. A ‘muṇḍacchadanapāsāda’ (flat-roofed palace) is a palace endowed with a moon-terrace.

489. Satthoti jaṅghasattho sakaṭasattho vā. Pariyādiyitvāti vinivijjhitvā. Vuttamevatthaṃ vibhāveti “antopaviṭṭhena…pe… ṭhito hotī”ti. Tattha antopaviṭṭhenāti gāmassa nadiyā vā antopaviṭṭhena. Nadīparihāro ca labbhatīti ettha “visuṃ nadīparihārassa avuttattā gāmādīhi aññattha viya cīvarahatthapāsoyeva nadīparihāro”ti tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Vihārasīmanti avippavāsasīmaṃ sandhāyāha. Vihāraṃ gantvā vasitabbanti antosīmāya yattha katthaci vasitabbaṃ. Satthasamīpeyevāti idaṃ yathāvuttaabbhantaraparicchedavasena [M 2.0395] vuttaṃ. Pāḷiyaṃ nānākulassa [V 2.0349] sattho hoti, satthe cīvaraṃ nikkhipitvā hatthapāsā na vijahitabbanti ettha hatthapāso nāma satthassa hatthapāsoti veditabbaṃ.

489. ‘Sattha’ (caravan) means a caravan on foot or a cart caravan. ‘Pariyādiyitvā’ (having encompassed) means having discerned. He clarifies the very meaning that was stated: ‘antopaviṭṭhena…pe… ṭhito hoti’ (having entered inside… he stands). There, ‘antopaviṭṭhena’ (having entered inside) means having entered inside a village or a river. Regarding ‘nadīparihāro ca labbhati’ (and a river boundary is obtained), here it is said in all three Gaṇṭhipadas: ‘Since a river boundary is not stated separately, the river boundary is just the hand's reach for the robe, as in places other than a village, etc.’ Regarding ‘vihārasīma’ (monastery boundary), he speaks with reference to the non-separation boundary. Regarding ‘vihāraṃ gantvā vasitabbaṃ’ (one should go to the monastery and dwell), it means one must dwell anywhere within the boundary. Regarding ‘satthasamīpeyeva’ (only near the caravan), this is said according to the demarcation of the interior as stated. In the Pāḷi, regarding ‘nānākulassa sattho hoti, satthe cīvaraṃ nikkhipitvā hatthapāsā na vijahitabbaṃ’ (there is a caravan of various families; having placed a robe in the caravan, one should not abandon the hand's reach), here ‘hatthapāso’ should be understood as the hand's reach of the caravan.

490. Ekakulassa khetteti aparikkhittaṃ sandhāya vadati. Yasmā “nānākulassa parikkhitte khette cīvaraṃ nikkhipitvā khettadvāramūle vā tassa hatthapāse vā vatthabba”nti vuttaṃ, tasmā dvāramūlato aññattha antokhettepi vasantena cīvaraṃ hatthapāse katvāyeva vasitabbaṃ.

490. Regarding ‘ekakulassa khette’ (in the field of one family), he speaks with reference to an unenclosed field. Because it is said, ‘In an enclosed field of various families, having placed a robe, one should dwell at the field-gate or within its hand's reach,’ therefore, one dwelling elsewhere than the gate-foot, even inside the field, must dwell only after bringing the robe within hand's reach.

491-494. “Vihāro nāma saparikkhitto vā aparikkhitto vā sakalo āvāso”ti vadanti. Yasmiṃ vihāreti ettha pana ekaṃ gehameva vuttaṃ. Ekakulanānākulasantakatā cettha kārāpakānaṃ vasena veditabbā. Chāyāya phuṭṭhokāsassa anto evāti yadā mahāvīthiyaṃ ujukameva gacchantaṃ sūriyamaṇḍalaṃ majjhanhikaṃ pāpuṇāti, tadā yaṃ okāsaṃ chāyā pharati, taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Agamanapatheti yaṃ tadaheva gantvā puna āgantuṃ sakkā na hoti, tādisaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ.

They say: ‘A vihāra is the entire residence, whether enclosed or unenclosed.’ But here, regarding ‘yasmiṃ vihāre’ (in which monastery), only a single building is meant. And here, whether it belongs to one family or various families should be understood according to the donors. Regarding ‘chāyāya phuṭṭhokāsassa anto eva’ (only within the space touched by the shadow), this is said with reference to the space the shadow covers when the solar disc, going straight along the great path, reaches the meridian. Regarding ‘agamanapathe’ (on a path of no return), this is said with reference to such a place that it is not possible to go and return on that very day.

495. Nadiṃ otaratīti hatthapāsaṃ muñcitvā otarati. Na āpajjatīti paribhogapaccayā dukkaṭaṃ nāpajjati. Tenāha “so hī”tiādi. Aparibhogārahattāti imināva nissaggiyacīvaraṃ anissajjetvā paribhuñjantassa dukkaṭaṃ acittakanti siddhaṃ. Ekaṃ pārupitvā ekaṃ aṃsakūṭe ṭhapetvā gantabbanti idaṃ bahūnaṃ sañcāraṭṭhāne evaṃ akatvā gamanaṃ na sāruppanti katvā vuttaṃ. Bahigāme ṭhapetvā…pe… vinayakammaṃ kātabbanti vuttattā adhiṭṭhāne viya parammukhā ṭhitampi nissaggiyaṃ cīvaraṃ nissajjituṃ nissaṭṭhacīvarañca dātuṃ vaṭṭatīti veditabbaṃ.

495. Regarding ‘nadiṃ otarati’ (he descends into the river), it means he descends having released the hand's reach. Regarding ‘na āpajjati’ (he does not incur an offense), it means he does not incur a dukkaṭa offense on account of use. Therefore, he says, ‘so hi’ (for he), and so on. By this very statement ‘aparibhogārahattā’ (because it is not fit for use), it is established that for one who uses a robe to be forfeited without having forfeited it, the dukkaṭa offense is an acittaka one. Regarding ‘ekaṃ pārupitvā ekaṃ aṃsakūṭe ṭhapetvā gantabbaṃ’ (having worn one, placing one on the shoulder, one should go), this is said because it is not proper to go without doing so in a place where many people move about. Because it is said, ‘Having placed it outside the village… a Vinaya act should be done,’ it should be understood that, just as in the case of determination, it is allowable to forfeit a robe that is to be forfeited and to give a forfeited robe, even if it is out of sight.

Gamane saussāhattā “nissayo pana na paṭippassambhatī”ti vuttaṃ. Muhuttaṃ sayitvā…pe… nissayo ca paṭippassambhatīti ettha “ussāhe apariccattepi gamanassa upacchinnattā puna uṭṭhāya saussāhaṃ gacchantānampi antarā aruṇe uṭṭhite nissayo paṭippassambhatiyevā”ti vadanti. Parato muhuttaṃ ṭhatvāti etthāpi eseva nayo. Aññamaññassa vacanaṃ aggahetvā gatāti ettha sace evaṃ gacchantā “purāruṇā aññamaññaṃ passissāmā”ti ussāhaṃ vināva gatā honti, aruṇuggamane nissayapaṭippassaddhi na vattabbā paṭhamataraṃyeva paṭippassambhanato. Atha “purāruṇā passissāmā”ti saussāhāva [M 2.0396] gacchanti, nissayapaṭippassaddhiyeva na vattabbā. Evañca sati “saha aruṇuggamanā nissayo paṭippassambhatī”ti kasmā vuttaṃ? Vuccate – saussahattā paṭhamataraṃ paṭippassaddhi na vuttā. Satipi [V 2.0350] ca ussāhabhāve ekato gamanassa upacchinnattā “muhuttaṃ ṭhatvā”ti ettha viya saha aruṇuggamanā paṭippassaddhiyeva vuttā.

Because of exertion in going, it is said: ‘However, the dependence does not subside.’ Regarding ‘muhuttaṃ sayitvā…pe… nissayo ca paṭippassambhati’ (having slept for a moment… and the dependence subsides), here they say: ‘Even when exertion is not relinquished, because the going is interrupted, even for those rising again and going with exertion, if dawn arises in between, the dependence indeed subsides.’ Regarding ‘parato muhuttaṃ ṭhatvā’ (having stood for a moment afterwards), here too the same principle applies. Regarding ‘aññamaññassa vacanaṃ aggahetvā gatā’ (having gone without taking each other's words), here, if they go thus without exertion, thinking, ‘We will see each other before dawn,’ then at the rising of dawn, the subsiding of dependence should not be stated, because it has already subsided earlier. But if they go with exertion, thinking, ‘We will see each other before dawn,’ then the subsiding of dependence itself should not be stated. If this is the case, why is it said: ‘With the rising of dawn, the dependence subsides’? It is said: Because of exertion, the subsiding was not stated to occur earlier. And even when there is a state of exertion, because the going together is interrupted, just as in the case of ‘having stood for a moment,’ the subsiding is stated to occur precisely with the rising of dawn.

Antosīmāyaṃ gāmanti avippavāsasīmāsammutiyā pacchā patiṭṭhāpitagāmaṃ sandhāya vadati gāmaṃ anto katvā avippavāsasīmāsammutiyā abhāvato. Neva cīvarāni nissaggiyāni hontīti avippavāsasīmābhāvato vuttaṃ, na nissayo paṭippassambhatīti saussāhabhāvato. Antarāmaggeyeva ca nesaṃ aruṇaṃ uggacchatīti dhammaṃ sutvā āgacchantānaṃ aruṇaṃ uggacchati. Assatiyā gacchatīti assatiyā attano cīvaraṃ apaccuddharitvā therassa cīvaraṃ apaccuddharāpetvā gacchati. Evaṃ gate tasmiṃ pacchā therena saritvā paṭipajjitabbavidhiṃ dasseti “attano cīvaraṃ paccuddharitvā daharassa cīvaraṃ vissāsena gahetvā ṭhapetabba”nti. Gantvā vattabboti āgatakiccaṃ niṭṭhapetvā vihāraṃ gatena paṭipajjitabbavidhiṃ dasseti. Anadhiṭṭhitacīvaratā, anatthatakathinatā, aladdhasammutitā, rattivippavāsoti imānettha cattāri aṅgāni.

Regarding ‘the village within the boundary,’ this is said in reference to a village established after the declaration of a non-separation boundary, because there is no declaration of a non-separation boundary that includes a village within it. ‘The robes are not liable to forfeiture’—this is stated because of the non-separation boundary. ‘The dependence does not subside’—this is stated because of the state of having exertion. ‘And dawn breaks for them while still on the road’—this means dawn rises for those who are coming after having heard the Dhamma. ‘He goes unmindfully’—this means he goes unmindfully, without having withdrawn his own robe and without causing the elder’s robe to be withdrawn. When he has gone thus, the elder, having remembered afterwards, shows the procedure to be followed: ‘One should withdraw one’s own robe and, with trust, take the junior monk’s robe and set it aside.’ Regarding the phrase ‘Having gone, it should be said,’ it shows the procedure to be followed by one who has gone to the monastery after having completed the business for which one came. The state of the robe being undetermined, the state of the Kathina not being spread, the state of permission not being obtained, and being away for the night—these are the four factors here.

Udositasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule concerning the Udosita is concluded.

3. Tatiyakathinasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

3. The explanation of the third training rule concerning the Kathina.

497-499. Tatiye pāḷiyaṃ cīvarapaccāsā nikkhipitunti ettha cīvarapaccāsāya satiyā nikkhipitunti evamattho gahetabbo. Bhaṇḍikābaddhāni bhaṇḍikabaddhānītipi paṭhanti, bhaṇḍikaṃ katvā baddhānīti attho. Niṭṭhitacīvarasmiṃ bhikkhunāti ettha purimasikkhāpade viya sāmivaseneva karaṇavacanassa attho veditabbo.

In the third, regarding the Pāḷi phrase ‘cīvarapaccāsā nikkhipituṃ’ (to put aside with expectation for a robe), the meaning should be understood thus: ‘to put it aside when there is an expectation for a robe.’ Some also recite `bhaṇḍikābaddhāni` or `bhaṇḍikabaddhāni`; the meaning is ‘tied after making a bundle.’ Regarding ‘niṭṭhitacīvarasmiṃ bhikkhunā’ (by a bhikkhu whose robe-work is finished), here, as in the previous training rule, the meaning of the instrumental word should be understood in the sense of the owner.

500. Anatthate kathine cīvaramāse bhikkhuno uppannacīvaraṃ anadhiṭṭhitaṃ avikappitaṃ tasmiṃ māse ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭatīti āha “ekaṃ pacchimakattikamāsaṃ ṭhapetvā”ti. Keci pana “kālepi ādissa dinnaṃ, etaṃ akālacīvaranti [M 2.0397] vacanato anatthate kathine pacchimakattikamāsasaṅkhāte cīvaramāse uppannacīvarassapi paccāsācīvare asati dasāhaparihāroyeva, tato paraṃ ṭhapetuṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti, taṃ aṭṭhakathāya na sameti. Tathā hi accekacīvarasikkhāpadaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.646-649 ādayo) “pavāraṇamāsassa juṇhapakkhapañcamiyaṃ uppannassa accekacīvarassa anatthate kathine ekādasadivasādhiko māso, atthate kathine ekādasadivasādhikā pañca māsā parihāro”ti vuttaṃ. Tameva ca parihāraṃ sandhāya [V 2.0351] “chaṭṭhito paṭṭhāya pana uppannaṃ anaccekacīvarampi paccuddharitvā ṭhapitacīvarampi etaṃ parihāraṃ labhatiyevā”ti (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.646-649) vuttaṃ. Tasmā cīvaramāse dasāhato parampi anadhiṭṭhitaṃ avikappitampi ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭati.

500. When the Kathina is not spread, during the robe-month, it is permissible for a bhikkhu to keep for that month a robe that has arisen for him—one that is undetermined and not shared; therefore, it is said: ‘…except for the last month of Kattika.’ Some, however, say: ‘Because of the saying, “Even if given by designation at the proper time, this is an out-of-season robe,” when the Kathina is not spread, even for a robe that arises during the robe-month, which is reckoned as the last month of Kattika—if there is no expected robe—only a ten-day allowance is obtained; beyond that, it is not permissible to keep it.’ That does not agree with the Commentary. For in the commentary on the training rule concerning the emergency robe, it is stated: ‘For an emergency robe that arises on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the Pavāraṇā month, when the Kathina is not spread, the allowance is a month and eleven days; when the Kathina is spread, the allowance is five months and eleven days.’ And referring to that same allowance, it is said: ‘From the sixth day onward, even a non-emergency robe that arises, and a robe that has been withdrawn and stored, certainly obtains this allowance.’ Therefore, in the robe-month, it is permissible to keep a robe that is undetermined and not shared even beyond ten days.

Yadi evaṃ “kālepi ādissa dinnaṃ, etaṃ akālacīvara”nti idaṃ kasmā vuttanti ce? Akālacīvarasāmaññato atthuddhāravasena vuttaṃ paṭhamāniyate sotassa raho viya. Ekādasamāse sattamāse ca uppannañhi cīvaraṃ vutthavassehi sesehi ca sammukhībhūtehi bhājetuṃ labbhatīti akālacīvaraṃ nāma jātaṃ. Kāle pana “saṅghassa idaṃ akālacīvaraṃ dammī”ti anuddisitvā “saṅghassa dammī”ti dinnaṃ vutthavassehiyeva bhājetabbaṃ, na aññehīti kālacīvaranti vuccati. Ādissa dinnaṃ pana sammukhībhūtehi sabbehiyeva bhājetabbanti akālacīvaraṃ, tasmā kālepi ādissa dinnassa vutthavassehi sesehi ca sampattehi bhājanīyattā akālacīvarasāmaññato “kālepi ādissa dinnaṃ, etaṃ akālacīvara”nti atthuddhāravasena vuttaṃ. Yadi evaṃ “ekapuggalassa vā idaṃ tuyhaṃ dammīti dinna”nti kasmā vuttaṃ. Na hi puggalassa ādissa dinnaṃ kenaci bhājanīyaṃ hotīti? Nāyaṃ virodho ādissa vacanasāmaññato labbhamānamatthaṃ dassetuṃ tathā vuttattā.

If it is asked why it is said, ‘Even if given by designation at the proper time, this is an out-of-season robe,’ the answer is: It is stated by way of extracting the meaning from the general characteristic of an out-of-season robe, just as in the case of ‘sotassa raho’ in the first Aniyata rule. For a robe that has arisen during the eleventh or seventh month can be distributed by those who have completed the rains-residence and by the others who are present—thus it has come to be called an ‘out-of-season robe.’ But at the proper time, if something is given by saying, ‘I give this to the Saṅgha,’ without specifying, ‘I give this out-of-season robe to the Saṅgha,’ it should be distributed only by those who have completed the rains-residence, not by others—this is called an ‘in-season robe.’ However, what is given with a designation must be distributed by all who are present—hence it is an ‘out-of-season robe.’ Therefore, because what is given with a designation even at the proper time is to be distributed by those who have completed the rains-residence and by the others who have arrived, it is stated by way of the general characteristic of an out-of-season robe and by extracting the meaning: ‘Even if given by designation at the proper time, this is an out-of-season robe.’ If so, why is it said, ‘…or given to a single individual, “I give this to you”’? For what is given with a designation to an individual is not to be shared by anyone. This is not a contradiction, because it was said in that way to show the meaning that is obtainable from the general characteristic of the word ‘designation.’

Evaṃ pana avatvāti “tato ce uttari”nti imassa “māsaparamato uttari”nti padabhājanaṃ avatvā. Tāva uppannaṃ paccāsācīvaranti paccattavacanaṃ “attano gatikaṃ karotī”ti karaṇakiriyāya kattubhāvato. Antarā uppannañhi paccāsācīvaraṃ māsaparamaṃ mūlacīvaraṃ ṭhapetuṃ adatvā attano dasāhaparamatāya eva paricchindatīti attano gatikaṃ karoti. Tato uddhaṃ mūlacīvaranti ettha pana mūlacīvaranti paccattavacanaṃ. Vīsatimadivasato uddhañhi uppannaṃ [M 2.0398] paccāsācīvaraṃ dasāhaparamaṃ gantuṃ adatvā mūlacīvaraṃ attanā saddhiṃ karaṇasambandhatāmattena sakakālavasena paricchindatīti attano gatikaṃ karoti. Paccāsācīvare pana labhitvā visuṃ ṭhapentassa dasāhaṃ anatikkante natthi tappaccayā āpatti. Pāḷiyaṃ dasāhā kāretabbanti ettha dasāhāti karaṇatthe nissakkavacanaṃ, dasāhenāti attho. Pañcāhuppannetiādiṃ rassaṃ katvāpi paṭhanti. Ekavīse uppanne…pe… navāhā kāretabbantiādi paccāsācīvarassa uppannadivasaṃ ṭhapetvā vuttaṃ.

However, 'without saying' means: without stating the word analysis of 'tato ce uttari' as 'māsaparamato uttari'. Here, 'uppannaṃ paccāsācīvaraṃ' (an arisen expectancy-robe) is in the nominative case, due to its being the agent of the action in 'attano gatikaṃ karoti' (he makes it of the same kind as his own). For an expectancy-robe that has arisen in the interim, without allowing the original robe to be kept for a maximum of one month, one limits it to one's own maximum of ten days—thus one makes it of the same kind as his own. In the phrase 'tato uddhaṃ mūlacīvaraṃ' (beyond that, the original robe), the word 'mūlacīvaraṃ' is in the nominative case. For an expectancy-robe that has arisen beyond twenty days, without allowing it to go for a maximum of ten days, one limits the original robe merely by its connection of being done together with oneself, according to its own time—thus one makes it of the same kind as his own. However, regarding an expectancy-robe, for one who, having obtained it, keeps it separately, if ten days have not been exceeded, there is no offense on that account. In the Pāli text, regarding 'dasāhā kāretabbaṃ' (it should be made within ten days), here 'dasāhā' is in the ablative case used in the sense of the instrumental; the meaning is 'by ten days.' Some also recite 'pañcāhuppannaṃ,' etc., by making it short. The statement 'Having arisen on the twenty-first… up to 'it should be made within nine days'' etc., is stated having set aside the day the expectancy-robe arose.

Aññaṃ paccāsācīvaraṃ…pe… kāretabbanti idaṃ satiyā eva paccāsāya vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Sace pana “ito paṭṭhāya cīvaraṃ na labhissāmī”ti paccāsā upacchinnā, mūlacīvarampi [V 2.0352] dasāhaṃ ce sampattaṃ, tadaheva adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ. Paccāsācīvarampi parikkhāracoḷaṃ adhiṭṭhātabbanti paṭhamataraṃ uppannaṃ visabhāgapaccāsācīvaraṃ sandhāya vadati. Aññamaññanti aññaṃ aññaṃ, ayameva vā pāṭho. Aṅgaṃ panettha paṭhamakathine vuttasadisameva. Kevalañhi tattha dasāhātikkamo, idha māsātikkamoti ayaṃ viseso.

"Another expectancy-robe… it should be made"—this should be understood as stated only when there is an expectation. If, however, the expectation is cut off with the thought, "From now on, I will not receive a robe," and if the original robe has also reached ten days, it should be determined on that very day. The statement "An expectancy-robe should also be determined as a requisite-cloth" is said in reference to an expectancy-robe of a dissimilar nature that arose earlier. "Aññamaññaṃ" means "aññaṃ aññaṃ"; or this itself is the reading. The factor here is just like that stated in the first Kathina rule. The only difference is that there it is the exceeding of ten days, whereas here it is the exceeding of a month.

Tatiyakathinasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the third training rule concerning the Kathina is concluded.

4. Purāṇacīvarasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

4. The Explanation of the Training Rule Concerning Old Robes

503. Catutthe bhattavissagganti pāḷipadassa bhattakiccanti attho veditabbo, “bhattasaṃvidhāna”ntipi keci. Tattha nāma tvanti imassapi so nāma tvanti attho veditabbo, “tāya nāma tva”nti keci.

4. In the fourth, of the Pāli word 'bhattavissagga', the meaning should be understood as 'bhattakicca' (the task of the meal); some also say 'bhattasaṃvidhāna' (the arranging of the meal). Herein, of this phrase 'nāma tvaṃ', the meaning should be understood as 'so nāma tvaṃ' (you are that one by name); some say 'tāya nāma tvaṃ' (you are by that name).

505. Pitā ca mātā ca pitaro, pitūnaṃ pitaro pitāmahā, tesaṃyeva yugo pitāmahayugo, tasmā yāva sattamā pitāmahayugā pitāmahadvandāti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Evañhi pitāmahaggahaṇeneva mātāmahopi gahitoti. “Yāva sattamā pitāmahayugā”ti vacanato heṭṭhā ca uddhañca aṭṭhamayugo ñāti nāma na hoti. Desanāmukhameva cetanti pitāmahayugāti pitāmaha-ggahaṇaṃ desanāmukhaṃ pitāmahīmātāmahīādīnampi adhippetattā. Pitu mātā pitāmahī. Mātu pitā mātāmaho[M 2.0399]. Mātu mātā mātāmahī. Ettha kiñcāpi pañcasatasākiyānīnaṃ vasena bhikkhubhāve ṭhatvā parivattaliṅgāya bhikkhuniyā ca vasena ekatoupasampannā bhikkhunī labbhati, tathāpi pakatiniyāmeneva dassetuṃ “bhikkhunī nāma ubhatosaṅghe upasampannā”ti vuttaṃ. “Kappaṃ katvāti vacanato dinnakappameva pācittiyaṃ janetī”ti vadanti. “Purāṇacīvaraṃ nāma sakiṃ nivatthampi sakiṃ pārutampī”ti idaṃ nidassanamattanti āha “antamaso paribhogasīsenā”tiādi. “Kāyena phusitvā paribhogoyeva paribhogo nāmā”ti kurundiyaṃ adhippāyo.

503. Father and mother are parents; the fathers of the fathers are paternal grandfathers. Their pair is the paternal grandfather-pair. Therefore, up to the seventh paternal grandfather-pair, the pair of paternal grandfathers—thus the meaning should be understood here. For thus, by the taking up of 'paternal grandfather,' the maternal grandfather is also taken up. Because of the statement 'up to the seventh paternal grandfather-pair,' the eighth pair below and above is not called a relative. This is merely an introductory expression; the taking up of 'paternal grandfather' is an introductory expression because paternal grandmothers, maternal grandmothers, and so on are also intended. The father’s mother is the paternal grandmother. The mother’s father is the maternal grandfather. The mother’s mother is the maternal grandmother. Here, although a bhikkhunī ordained on one side is found—by way of the five hundred Sakyan ladies, or by way of a bhikkhunī who, having been in the state of a bhikkhu, changed gender—nevertheless, to show the normal rule, it is stated: 'A bhikkhunī is one who is ordained in both Saṅghas.' Because of the phrase 'having made it allowable,' they say that only a robe that has been made allowable generates a pācittiya offense. The statement 'An old robe is one that has been worn even once or put on even once' is merely an example; therefore, he said, 'at least by way of use,' etc. The intention in the Kurundī is: 'Use is only the use consisting of touching with the body.'

506. Kāyavikāraṃ katvāti idaṃ yāva “orato ṭhapetī”ti padaṃ, tāva sabbapadesu sambandhitabbaṃ. Yathā sā “dhovāpetukāmo aya”nti jānāti, evaṃ kāyavikāraṃ katvāti attho. “Kāyavikāraṃ katvā”ti vacanato kāyavācāhi kañci vikāraṃ akatvā hatthena hatthe dentassapi anāpatti. Antodvādasahatthe okāseti idaṃ visesanaṃ yathāsambhavaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Tathā [V 2.0353] hi hatthena hatthe dentassa pādamūle ca ṭhapetvā dentassa “antodvādasahatthe okāse”ti idaṃ vattabbanti natthi aññathā asambhavato. Sati hi sambhave byabhicāre ca visesanaṃ sātthakaṃ hoti. Upari “khipatī”tiādīni pana sandhāya idaṃ visesanaṃ vuttaṃ, tasmā antodvādasahatthe okāse ṭhatvā upari khipantassa aññassa hatthe pesentassa ca āpatti. Upacāraṃ pana muñcitvā kāyavācāhi vikāraṃ katvā āṇāpentassapi anāpatti. Upacāreti antodvādasahatthameva okāsaṃ vadati. Upacāraṃ muñcitvāti dvādasahatthūpacāraṃ muñcitvā.

505. This phrase 'having made a bodily gesture' should be connected with all phrases up to the phrase 'places it on this side.' The meaning is: having made a bodily gesture in such a way that she knows, 'This one wants it washed.' Because of the statement 'having made a bodily gesture,' there is no offense even for one who gives from hand to hand without making any gesture with body or speech. This qualification 'in a place within twelve cubits' should be applied as is possible. For thus, for one who gives from hand to hand and for one who gives by placing it at the feet, this statement 'in a place within twelve cubits' is not to be said, because it is otherwise impossible. For a qualification is meaningful when there is possibility and deviation. However, this qualification was stated in reference to 'throws it upwards,' etc. Therefore, there is an offense for one who, standing in a place within twelve cubits, throws it upwards or sends it into another's hand. However, having gone beyond the vicinity, there is no offense even for one who gives a command by making a gesture with body or speech. 'Vicinity' means a place just within twelve cubits. 'Having gone beyond the vicinity' means having gone beyond the vicinity of twelve cubits.

Ekena vatthunāti paṭhamaṃ katvā niṭṭhāpitaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Rajane anāpattīti rajanaṃ paccāsīsantassapi “dhovitvā ānehī”ti vuttattā anāpatti anāṇattiyā katattā. “Avuttā dhovatī”ti iminā “avuttā rajati, avuttā ākoṭetī”ti idampi vuttameva hotīti āha – “avuttā dhovatīti iminā lakkhaṇena anāpattī”ti. Sambahulā āpattiyo āpajjatīti pācittiyena saddhiṃ dve dukkaṭāni āpajjati. Yathāvatthukamevāti nissaggiyamevāti attho. Pañca satāni parimāṇametāsanti pañcasatā.

506. "With one item" is said in reference to a task that was first undertaken and completed. "No offense in dyeing": even for one who is expecting the dyeing, because it was said, "Having washed it, bring it," there is no offense, because it was done without being commanded. By this phrase "washes without being told," this is also said: "dyes without being told, beats without being told." Therefore, he said: "There is no offense by the characteristic expressed in 'washes without being told'." "He incurs many offenses" means: he incurs two offenses of wrong-doing along with a pācittiya offense. "Just according to the item" means it is simply a nissaggiya offense. "Five hundred is their measure"; therefore, they are the "five hundred."

507. Cīvaraṃ [M 2.0400] dhovāti…pe… āṇāpentassāti ettha tāya dhovanaṃ paccāsīsantassapi anāpatti. Purāṇacīvaratā, upacāre ṭhatvā aññātikāya bhikkhuniyā āṇāpanaṃ, tassā dhovanādīni cāti imānettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

507. He washes the robe… up to 'for one who gives an order.' Here, there is no offense even for one who expects her to do the washing. The three factors here are: the state of being an old robe, standing in the vicinity and giving an order to an unrelated bhikkhunī, and her washing, etc.

Purāṇacīvarasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on old robes is concluded.

5. Cīvarapaṭiggahaṇasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

5. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Receiving a Robe

508. Pañcame apaññatte sikkhāpadeti gaṇamhā ohīyanasikkhāpade apaññatte. Vihāravāranti vihārapaṭijagganavāraṃ. Koṭṭhāsasampattīti sakalā aṅgapaccaṅgasampatti. Sabbapariyantanti chaṭṭhassa aññacīvarassa abhāvā pañcannaṃ cīvarānaṃ ekamekaṃ sabbesaṃ pariyantanti sabbapariyantaṃ. Antaravāsakādīsu hi pañcasu ekamekaṃ aññassa chaṭṭhassa abhāvā pañcannaṃ antameva hoti. Athavā pañcasu cīvaresu ekamekaṃ attano aññassa dutiyassa abhāvā antameva hotīti sabbameva pariyantanti sabbapariyantaṃ, sabbaso vā pariyantanti sabbapariyantaṃ. Tenāha – “aññaṃ…pe… natthī”ti. Yathā tassa manoratho na pūratīti “sarīrapāripūriṃ [V 2.0354] passissāmī”ti tassa uppanno manoratho yathā na pūrati. Evaṃ hatthataleyeva dassetvāti sarīraṃ adassetvāva dātabbacīvaraṃ hatthatale “handā”ti dassetvā.

508. In the fifth, 'when the training rule was not laid down' means when the training rule on falling away from the group was not laid down. 'The turn for the monastery' means the turn for maintaining the monastery. 'Perfection of the parts' means the complete perfection of the major and minor parts. 'The very end of all' means that due to the absence of another, a sixth robe, each one of the five robes is the end of all; hence, 'the very end of all.' For among the five—the inner robe and so on—each one, in the absence of another, a sixth, is indeed the end of the five. Alternatively, among the five robes, each one, in the absence of another, a second of its kind, is indeed the end; thus, every single one is the end, hence 'the very end of all.' Or, it is the end in every way, hence 'the very end of all.' Therefore, he said: 'another… and so on… there is not.' 'Just as his wish is not fulfilled' means: the wish that arose in him, 'I will see the perfection of the body,' is not fulfilled. Thus, 'having shown it only on the palm of the hand' means, without showing the body, having shown the robe to be given on the palm of the hand, saying, 'Here you are.'

510. Vihatthatāyāti vihatahatthatāya, agaṇatāya appaccayatāya appaṭisaraṇatāyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Samabhitunnattāti pīḷitattā. Parivattetabbaṃ parivattaṃ, parivattameva pārivattakaṃ, parivattetvā dīyamānanti attho.

510. 'Due to helplessness' means due to having a ruined hand; it is said to mean due to being without reliance, without refuge. 'Due to being afflicted' means due to being oppressed. 'What is to be exchanged' is an 'exchange item' (parivatta). The exchange item itself is an 'item for exchange' (pārivattaka). The meaning is 'that which is given after having been exchanged.'

512. Upacāreti dvādasahatthūpacāraṃ sandhāya vadati. Upacāraṃ vā muñcitvā khipantīti dvādasahatthaṃ muñcitvā orato ṭhapenti, na purimasikkhāpade viya dvādasahatthabbhantareyevāti adhippāyo. Aññatra pārivattakāti yaṃ antamaso harītakakhaṇḍampi datvā vā dassāmīti ābhogaṃ katvā vā pārivattakaṃ gaṇhāti, taṃ ṭhapetvā. Acittakabhāvena na sametīti yathā aññātikāya ñātikasaññissa vematikassa ca gaṇhato acittakattā āpatti[M 2.0401], evamidhāpi “bhikkhuniyā santakaṃ ida”nti ajānitvā gaṇhatopi āpattiyevāti adhippāyo. Vassāvāsikaṃ detīti puggalikaṃ katvā deti. Paṃsukūlaṃ attano atthāya ṭhapitabhāvaṃ jānitvā gaṇhantenapi aññassa santakaṃ gahitaṃ nāma na hotīti āha – “sace pana saṅkārakūṭādīsū”tiādi. Asāmikañhi paṃsukūlanti vuccati. Paṃsukūlaṃ adhiṭṭhahitvāti “asāmikaṃ ida”nti saññaṃ uppādetvā. Evaṃ pana paṃsukūlasaññaṃ anuppādetvā gaṇhituṃ na vaṭṭati.

512. 'In the vicinity' refers to the twelve-cubit vicinity. 'Or having thrown it outside the vicinity' means having placed it outside the twelve cubits, not within the twelve cubits as in the previous training rule; this is the intention. 'Apart from an exchange item' means excluding that which one receives as an exchange item, having given at least a piece of myrobalan or having made the resolution, 'I will give it.' 'It does not meet the case due to lack of intention' means: just as there is an offense for one who, perceiving a non-relative as a relative, or for one who is doubtful, takes something, because the act is unintentional in that respect, so too here, there is an offense even for one who takes it without knowing, 'This belongs to a bhikkhunī'; this is the intention. 'She gives the rains-residence robe' means she gives it, having made it personal property. Since for one who takes a rag-robe, knowing it has been set aside for his own use, it is not called taking what belongs to another, he said: 'But if from a rubbish heap, etc.' For a rag-robe is called 'ownerless.' 'Having determined it as a rag-robe' means having generated the perception, 'This is ownerless.' However, it is not allowable to take it without generating this perception of it as a rag-robe.

513. Aññātikāya aññātikasaññīti tikapācittiyanti ettha iti-saddo ādiattho. Tīṇi parimāṇamassāti tikaṃ, tikañca taṃ pācittiyañcāti tikapācittiyaṃ, tīṇi pācittiyānīti attho.

513. In the phrase 'for one who perceives a non-relative as a non-relative, it is a threefold pācittiya,' the word 'iti' has the meaning of 'etcetera.' That which has three as its measure is a 'triad' (tika). A pācittiya that is a triad is a 'threefold pācittiya' (tikapācittiya); the meaning is 'three pācittiya offenses.'

514. Pattatthavikādiṃ yaṃkiñcīti anadhiṭṭhānupagaṃ sandhāya vadati. “Cīvaraṃ nāma channaṃ cīvarānaṃ aññataraṃ cīvaraṃ vikappanupagaṃ pacchima”nti hi vuttattā adhiṭṭhānupagaṃ yaṃkiñci na vaṭṭati. Tenevāha – “vikappanupagapacchimacīvarappamāṇa”ntiādi. Yasmā bhisicchavi mahantāpi senāsanasaṅgahitattā cīvarasaṅkhyaṃ na gacchatīti neva adhiṭṭhānupagā na vikappanupagā ca, tasmā anadhiṭṭhānupagasāmaññato vuttaṃ. Sacepi mañcappamāṇā bhisicchavi hoti, vaṭṭatiyevāti. Ko pana vādo pattatthavikādīsūti mahatiyāpi tāva bhisicchaviyā anadhiṭṭhānupagattā anāpatti, tato khuddakataresu anadhiṭṭhānupagesu pattatthavikādīsu kimeva vattabbanti adhippāyo. Paṭiggahaṇaṃ kiriyā, [V 2.0355] aparivattanaṃ akiriyā. Vikappanupagacīvaratā, pārivattakābhāvo, aññātikāya hatthato gahaṇanti imānettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

514. 'Whatever things such as a bag for a bowl'—this is said with reference to what is not subject to determination (adhiṭṭhāna). For since it is said, 'A robe means any one of the six kinds of robes, the last of which is suitable for alienation (vikappana),' anything whatsoever that is subject to determination is not allowable. Therefore, it is said: 'the measure of the last robe suitable for alienation,' etc. Because even a large leather hide, being included under lodging, does not count as a robe, it is neither subject to determination nor suitable for alienation. Therefore, it is spoken of generally as not being subject to determination. Even if a leather hide is the size of a bed, it is allowable. 'What then is to be said of things like a bag for a bowl?' The intention is this: since there is no offense even with a large leather hide because it is not subject to determination, what need be said of smaller things not subject to determination, such as a bag for a bowl? Receiving is an action; not exchanging is a non-action. The three factors here are: the state of being a robe suitable for alienation, the absence of an exchange, and taking it from the hand of an unrelated woman.

Cīvarapaṭiggahaṇasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule on Receiving a Robe is Concluded.

6. Aññātakaviññattisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

6. The Explanation of the Training Rule Concerning Requesting from a Non-relative

515. Chaṭṭhe patikiṭṭhoti nihīno, lāmakoti attho. Lolajātikoti lolasabhāvo. Paṭuyeva paṭṭo. Tenāha “cheko”tiādi. Kismiṃ viyāti ettha “kismiṃ viyā”ti nipātavasena samānatthaṃ “kiṃsu viyā”ti nipātapadanti āha “kiṃsu viyā”ti, kiṃ viyāti [M 2.0402] attho, dukkhaṃ viyāti adhippāyo. Tenāha “kileso viyā”tiādi. Dhammavasena upacāravasena nimantanā dhammanimantanāti pāḷipadassa attho veditabbo. Sace pana “vadeyyātha, bhante, yenattho”ti idaṃ saccameva vuttaṃ siyā, pavāritoyeva hoti. Yasmā pana pavāretvāpi adātukāmo appavāritaṭṭhāneyeva tiṭṭhati, tasmā bhagavā pavāritāpavāritabhāvaṃ avicāretvā “ñātako te, upananda, aññātako”ti ñātakaaññātakabhāvaṃyeva vicāresi. Musiṃsūti vilumpiṃsu.

515. In the sixth, ‘patikiṭṭha’ means low, inferior; the meaning is worthless. ‘Lolajātika’ means having a fickle nature. ‘Paṭṭa’ is just ‘paṭu’ (clever). Therefore, it is said, ‘clever,’ etc. Regarding ‘kismiṃ viyā,’ here ‘kismiṃ viyā’ as a particle is synonymous with the particle ‘kiṃsu viyā’; thus it is said ‘kiṃsu viyā.’ The meaning is ‘like what?’ The intention is ‘like suffering.’ Therefore, it is said, ‘like a defilement,’ etc. The meaning of the Pali term ‘dhammanimantanā’ should be understood as an invitation by way of the Dhamma, that is, by way of metaphor. However, if this statement, ‘Venerable sir, you should speak of what is needed,’ were indeed truly spoken, then one would be considered as having been invited. But because, even after having invited, one is unwilling to give and stands in the position of not having invited, therefore the Blessed One, without considering the state of having been invited or not, considered only the state of being a relative or a non-relative, saying, ‘Upānanda, is he your relative or a non-relative?’ ‘Musiṃsu’ means they plundered.

517. Anupubbakathāti anupubbena vinicchayakathā. Sesaparikkhārānaṃ saddhivihārikehi gahitattā nivāsanapārupanamattameva avasiṭṭhanti āha “nivāsanapārupanamattaṃyeva haritvā”ti. Saddhivihārikānaṃ tāva āgamanassa vā anāgamanassa vā ajānanatāya vuttaṃ “therehi neva tāva…pe… bhañjitabba”nti. Paresampi atthāya labhantīti attano cīvaraṃ dadamānā sayaṃ sākhābhaṅgena paṭicchādentīti tesaṃ atthāyapi bhañjituṃ labhanti. “Tiṇena vā paṇṇena vā paṭicchādetvā āgantabba”nti vacanato īdisesu bhūtagāmapātabyatāpi anuññātāyeva hotīti āha – “neva bhūtagāmapātabyatāya pācittiyaṃ hotī”ti. Na tesaṃ dhāraṇe dukkaṭanti tesaṃ titthiyaddhajānaṃ dhāraṇepi dukkaṭaṃ natthi.

517. ‘Anupubbakathā’ means a discourse of investigation in sequence. Because the other requisites had been taken by the co-residents, only the lower and upper robes remained. Therefore, it is said, ‘having taken only the lower and upper robes.’ Because it was not yet known whether the co-residents would come or not, it was said, ‘the elders should not yet… distribute it.’ They also obtain for the sake of others, meaning that while giving away their own robes, they cover themselves with broken branches; thus, they are also permitted to break them for the sake of others. From the statement, ‘one should return after covering with grass or leaves,’ it is clear that the felling of plants is also allowed in such cases. Therefore, it is said, ‘there is no offense of pācittiya for the felling of plants.’ ‘There is no offense of wrong-doing in wearing them’ means that even in wearing those banners of the sectarians, there is no wrong-doing.

Yāni ca nesaṃ vatthāni dentīti sambandho. Therānaṃ sayameva dinnattā vuttaṃ “acchinnacīvaraṭṭhāne ṭhitattā”ti. Yadi laddhiṃ gaṇhāti, titthiyapakkantako nāma hoti, tasmā vuttaṃ “laddhiṃ aggahetvā”ti. “No ce hoti saṅghassa vihāracīvaraṃ vā…pe… āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti iminā antarāmagge paviṭṭhavihārato nikkhamitvā aññattha attano abhirucitaṭṭhānaṃ [V 2.0356] gacchantassa dukkaṭaṃ vuttaṃ. Iminā ca “yaṃ āvāsaṃ paṭhamaṃ upagacchatī”ti vuttaṃ antarāmagge ṭhitavihārampi sace naggo hutvā gacchati, dukkaṭamevāti veditabbaṃ. Yadi evaṃ tattha kasmā na vuttanti ce? Anokāsattā. Tattha hi “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, acchinnacīvarassa vā…pe… cīvaraṃ viññāpetu”nti iminā sambandhena saṅghikampi cīvaraṃ nivāsetuṃ pārupituñca anujānanto “yaṃ āvāsaṃ paṭhamaṃ…pe… gahetvā pārupitu”nti āha, tasmā tattha anokāsattā dukkaṭaṃ na vuttaṃ.

The connection is: ‘and whatever robes they give to them.’ Because it was given by the elders themselves, it is said, ‘because of standing in the position of one whose robe has been taken away.’ If one accepts the view, one is called one who has gone over to the sectarians; therefore, it is said, ‘without accepting the view.’ By the statement, ‘If there is no monastery robe of the Sangha… there is an offense of wrong-doing,’ an offense of wrong-doing is stated for one who, having entered a monastery along the way, leaves it and goes elsewhere to a place of one’s own liking. And by this, it should be understood that even if one goes naked to a monastery situated along the way, which is referred to by ‘whichever monastery one first approaches,’ there is indeed an offense of wrong-doing. If so, why was it not stated there? Because there was no occasion for it. For there, in connection with this, ‘Monks, I allow one whose robe has been taken away… to request a robe,’ while allowing even a Sangha robe to be worn as a lower garment and an upper garment, he said, ‘whichever monastery one first approaches… having taken it, to cover oneself.’ Therefore, because there was no occasion there, an offense of wrong-doing was not stated.

Vihāracīvaranti [M 2.0403] senāsanacīvaraṃ. Cimilikāhīti paṭapilotikāhi. Tassa uparīti bhūmattharaṇassa upari. Videsagatenāti aññaṃ cīvaraṃ alabhitvā videsagatena. Ekasmiṃ…pe… ṭhapetabbanti ettha “lesena gahetvā agatattā ṭhapentena ca saṅghikaparibhogeneva ṭhapitattā aññasmiṃ senāsane niyamitampi aññattha ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti. Paribhogenevāti aññaṃ cīvaraṃ alabhitvā paribhuñjanena.

‘A monastery robe’ means a lodging robe. ‘With rags’ means with scraps of cloth. ‘On top of it’ means on top of the ground covering. ‘Having gone to another region’ means by one who has gone to another region without obtaining another robe. Regarding ‘in one… should be placed,’ here they say, ‘because it was taken by a pretext and brought away, and because when placing it, it was placed for the use of the Sangha, it is permissible to place it elsewhere even if it was designated for another lodging.’ ‘Only by using’ means by using it, not having obtained another robe.

519-521. Paribhogajiṇṇanti yathā tena cīvarena sarīraṃ paṭicchādetuṃ na sakkā, evaṃ jiṇṇaṃ. Kappiyavohārenāti kayavikkayāpattito mocanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. “Viññāpentassā”ti imasseva atthaṃ vibhāveti “cetāpentassa parivattāpentassā”ti. Attano dhanena hi viññāpanaṃ nāma parivattanamevāti adhippāyo. Saṅghavasena pavāritānaṃ viññāpane vattaṃ dasseti “pamāṇameva vaṭṭatī”ti. Saṅghavasena hi pavārite sabbesaṃ sādhāraṇattā adhikaṃ viññāpetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Yaṃ yaṃ pavāretīti yaṃ yaṃ cīvarādiṃ dassāmīti pavāreti. Viññāpanakiccaṃ natthīti vinā viññattiyā dīyamānattā viññāpetvā kiṃ karissatīti adhippāyo. Aññassatthāyāti etthāpi “ñātakānaṃ pavāritāna”nti idaṃ anuvattatiyevāti āha “attano ñātakapavārite”tiādi. Vikappanupagacīvaratā, samayābhāvo, aññātakaviññatti, tāya ca paṭilābhoti imānettha cattāri aṅgāni.

519-521. ‘Worn out through use’ means it is so worn that the body can no longer be covered with that robe. ‘Through an allowable transaction’ is said for the purpose of being exempted from the offense concerning buying and selling. The phrase ‘for one who is requesting’ clarifies its meaning with ‘for one who is causing to be purchased, for one who is causing to be exchanged.’ The intention is that a request made with one’s own wealth is indeed an exchange. He shows the proper practice in requesting from those invited by way of the Sangha: ‘only the proper amount is allowable.’ For when invited by way of the Sangha, since it is common to all, it is not permitted to request more. ‘Whatever one invites with’ means one invites by saying, ‘I will give such and such a robe, etc.’ ‘There is no need for a request’—the intention is, since it is given without a request, what would one do by requesting? ‘For the sake of another’—here too, ‘for relatives who have invited’ applies accordingly, thus it is said: ‘for one’s own relatives who have been invited,’ etc. Here, there are four factors: the robe not having undergone determination, the absence of the proper occasion, a request to a non-relative, and acquisition through that.

Aññātakaviññattisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule Concerning Requesting from a Non-relative is concluded.

7. Tatuttarisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

7. The Explanation of the Training Rule on What is Further

522. Sattame pāḷiyaṃ paggāhikasālanti dussavāṇijakānaṃ āpaṇaṃ. “Paggāhitasāla”ntipi paṭhanti.

522. In the seventh, in the Pāḷi, `paggāhikasāla` means a shop of cloth merchants. Some also read it as `paggāhitasāla`.

523-524. Abhīti [V 2.0357] upasaggoti tassa visesatthābhāvaṃ dasseti. Tenāha “haritunti attho”ti. Vara-saddassa icchāyaṃ vattamānattā āha “icchāpeyyā”ti. Daṭṭhu khematoti ettha gāthābandhavasena anunāsikalopo daṭṭhabbo. Saantaranti antaravāsakasahitaṃ. Uttaranti uttarāsaṅgaṃ. Assa cīvarassāti sāditabbacīvarassa. Acchinnasabbacīvarenāti acchinnāni [M 2.0404] sabbāni tīṇi cīvarāni assāti acchinnasabbacīvaro, tenāti attho. Yassa hi acchindanasamaye tīṇi cīvarāni sannihitāni honti, tāni sabbāni acchinnānīti so “acchinnasabbacīvaro”ti vuccati. Teneva “acchinnasabbacīvarena ticīvarakenā”ti vuttaṃ. Ticīvarakenāti hi acchindanasamaye ticīvarassa sannihitabhāvaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, na pana vinayatecīvarikabhāvaṃ dhutaṅgatecīvarikabhāvaṃ vā sandhāya. Evaṃ paṭipajjitabbanti “santaruttaraparamaṃ tena bhikkhunā tato cīvaraṃ sāditabba”nti vuttavidhinā paṭipajjitabbaṃ. Aññenāti acchinnaasabbacīvarena. Yassa tīsu cīvaresu ekaṃ vā dve vā cīvarāni acchinnāni honti, tenāti attho. Aññathāpīti “santaruttaraparama”nti vuttavidhānato aññathāpi. Yassa hi tīsu dve cīvarāni acchinnāni honti, ekaṃ sāditabbaṃ. Ekasmiṃ acchinne na sāditabbanti na tassa santaruttaraparamasādiyanaṃ sambhavati, ayameva ca attho padabhājanena vibhāvito. Tenāha “taṃ vibhāgaṃ dassetu”nti.

523-524. By `abhīti upasaggo` (the prefix `abhi`), he shows its lack of special meaning. Therefore, he said, 'the meaning is `haritun`.' Because the word `vara` occurs in the sense of desire, he said, `icchāpeyyā`. Here in `daṭṭhu khemato`, the elision of the nasal should be understood by the power of the verse structure. `Saantara` means together with the inner robe. `Uttara` means the upper robe. `Assa cīvarassa` means of the robe to be accepted. By `acchinnasabbacīvarena` is meant: he for whom all three robes are robbed is an `acchinnasabbacīvaro`; `tena` means 'by him'. For a monk for whom, at the time of the robbery, the three robes are present, and all of them are robbed, he is called an `acchinnasabbacīvaro` ('one whose all robes are robbed'). Therefore it is said, `acchinnasabbacīvarena ticīvarakenā` ('by one whose all robes are robbed, who has three robes'). For `ticīvarikena` is said referring to the state of the three robes being present at the time of the robbery, but it is not said referring to the state of being a three-robe-wearer according to the Vinaya or according to the ascetic practices. `Evaṃ paṭipajjitabbaṃ` means one should practice according to the method that was taught: 'a robe up to the maximum of the inner and outer robes should be accepted by that monk from that'. `Aññena` means by one who is not an `acchinnasabbacīvaro`. The meaning is: by him for whom, among the three robes, one or two robes are robbed. `Aññathāpi` means also otherwise than the method taught as `santaruttaraparama`. For a monk for whom, of the three robes, two are robbed, one may be accepted. When one [robe] is robbed, it is not to be accepted [in that manner]; therefore for him, the acceptance up to the maximum of the inner and outer robes is not possible. And this very meaning has been made clear by the word-analysis. Therefore, he said, 'to show that distinction'.

Keci pana “ticīvarakenāti vuttattā ticīvaraṃ parikkhāracoḷavasena adhiṭṭhahitvā paribhuñjato tasmiṃ naṭṭhe bahūnipi gahetuṃ labhatī”ti vadanti, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ. Padabhājanassa hi adhippāyaṃ dassentena yasmā pana “acchinnasabbacīvarena…pe… taṃ vibhāgaṃ dassetu”nti vuttaṃ, padabhājane ca na tādiso attho upalabbhati, tasmā taṃ na gahetabbameva. Yampi mātikāṭṭhakathāyaṃ (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. tatuttarisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) vuttaṃ “yassa adhiṭṭhitacīvarassa tīṇi naṭṭhānī”ti, tatthāpi adhiṭṭhitaggahaṇaṃ sarūpakathanamattanti gahetabbaṃ, na pana ticīvarādhiṭṭhānena adhiṭṭhitacīvarassevāti evamattho gahetabbo pāḷiyaṃ aṭṭhakathāyañca tathā atthassa asambhavato. Na hi ticīvarādhiṭṭhānena adhiṭṭhitacīvarasseva idaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññattanti sakkā viññātuṃ. Purimasikkhāpadena hi acchinnacīvarassa aññātakaviññattiyā anuññātattā pamāṇaṃ ajānitvā viññāpanavatthusmiṃ pamāṇato sādiyanaṃ anujānantena bhagavatā idaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññattaṃ, tasmā “parikkhāracoḷikassa bahumpi sādituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti ayamattho neva pāḷiyā sameti, na ca bhagavato adhippāyaṃ anulometi.

Some, however, say: 'Because it is said `ticīvarikena`, for one who, having determined the three robes as requisite cloths, uses them, when they are lost, he is allowed to take even many.' This should not be accepted. For, because the commentator, showing the intention of the word-analysis, said, `acchinnasabbacīvarena…pe… taṃ vibhāgaṃ dassetu`, and in the word-analysis such a meaning is not found, therefore that [view] should not be accepted at all. And as to what was said in the Mātikā-commentary: `yassa adhiṭṭhitacīvarassa tīṇi naṭṭhāni` ('for whom three designated robes are lost'), there also, the term `adhiṭṭhita` should be taken as a mere statement of its nature. The meaning should not be taken as 'only of a robe determined by the determination of the three robes,' because of the impossibility of such a meaning in the Pāḷi and in the commentary. For it is not possible to understand that this training rule was laid down only for a robe determined by the determination of the three robes. For, since by the previous training rule requesting from an unknown person was permitted for one whose robe was robbed, this training rule was laid down by the Blessed One permitting acceptance according to the measure in a case of requesting, when the measure is not known. Therefore, this meaning that 'for one who uses [robes as] requisite cloths, it is permissible to accept many' neither agrees with the Pāḷi, nor does it conform to the intention of the Blessed One.

Yassa tīṇi naṭṭhāni, tena dve sāditabbānīti ettha yassa ticīvarato adhikampi cīvaraṃ aññattha [V 2.0358] ṭhitaṃ atthi, tadātassa cīvarassa alabbhanīyabhāvato tenapi [M 2.0405] sādituṃ vaṭṭatīti veditabbaṃ. Pakatiyāva santaruttarena caratīti sāsaṅkasikkhāpadavasena vā avippavāsasammutivasena vā tatiyassa alābhena vā carati. “Dve naṭṭhānī”ti adhikārattā vuttaṃ “dve sāditabbānī”ti. Ekaṃ sādiyanteneva samo bhavissatīti tiṇṇaṃ cīvarānaṃ dvīsu naṭṭhesu ekaṃ sādiyantena samo bhavissati ubhinnampi santaruttaraparamatāya avaṭṭhānato. Yassa ekaṃyeva hotīti aññena kenaci kāraṇena vinaṭṭhasesacīvaraṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ.

Here, regarding the statement, 'For whom three [robes] are lost, two should be accepted by him,' it should be understood that if a monk has an extra robe beyond the three robes located elsewhere, then because that robe is unobtainable, it is permissible for him also to accept [new robes]. 'One who by nature goes about with an inner and outer robe' means one who does so either on account of the training rule concerning a dangerous place, or on account of the authorization for non-separation [from the robes], or from not obtaining a third. Because 'two are lost' is the topic, it is said, 'two should be accepted.' 'By accepting just one, he will become complete' means that when two of the three robes are lost, by accepting one he will become complete, because both situations result in the state of having the maximum of an inner and outer robe. 'For whom there is only one' is said with reference to a remaining robe, the others having been lost due to some other reason.

526. “Sesakaṃ tuyheva hotūti dentī”ti vuttattā “pamāṇayuttaṃ gaṇhissāma, sesakaṃ āharissāmā”ti vatvā gahetvā gamanasamayepi “sesakampi tumhākaññeva hotū”ti vadanti, laddhakappiyameva. Pavāritānanti acchinnakālato pubbeyeva pavāritānaṃ. Pāḷiyā na sametīti santaruttaraparamato uttari sādiyane anāpattidassanatthaṃ “anāpatti ñātakānaṃ pavāritāna”nti vuttattā na sameti. Santaruttaraparamaṃ sādiyantassa hi āpattippasaṅgoyeva natthi, sati ca sikkhāpadena āpattippasaṅge anāpatti yuttā dassetunti adhippāyo. Keci pana “pamāṇameva vaṭṭatīti idaṃ sallekhadassanatthaṃ vutta”nti vadanti.

526. Because it is said, 'They give saying, "Let the remainder be yours,"' [the following occurs]: having said, 'We will take a suitable amount and bring the remainder,' and having taken it, even at the time of departure they say, 'Let the remainder also be yours.' This is indeed something made allowable (`laddhakappiya`). `Pavāritānaṃ` refers to those who have been invited even before the time of the robbery. 'It does not agree with the Pāḷi' means that it does not agree because it was said, 'There is no offense for relatives and for those who have been invited,' in order to show there is no offense in accepting more than the maximum of the inner and outer robes. For one who accepts the maximum of the inner and outer robes, there is no occasion for an offense at all. The intention is that if there were an occasion for an offense through the training rule, it would be proper to show [the case of] no offense. Some, however, say, 'This was said to show the practice of effacement (`sallekha`), that only the [proper] measure is allowable.'

Yasmā panidaṃ…pe… na vuttanti etthāyamadhippāyo – “aññassatthāyā”ti vuccamāne aññesaṃ atthāya pamāṇaṃ atikkamitvāpi gaṇhituṃ vaṭṭatīti āpajjati, tañca aññassatthāya viññāpanavatthusmiṃ paññattattā vatthunā saṃsandiyamānaṃ na sameti. Na hi yaṃ vatthuṃ nissāya sikkhāpadaṃ paññattaṃ, tasmiṃyeva anāpattivacanaṃ yuttanti. Gaṇṭhipadesu pana tīsupi “imassa sikkhāpadassa attano sādiyanapaṭibaddhatāvasena pavattattā ‘aññassatthāyā’ti vattuṃ okāsoyeva natthi, tasmā na vutta”nti kathitaṃ. Idha “aññassatthāyā”ti avuttattā aññesaṃ atthāya ñātakapavāritesu adhikaṃ viññāpentassa āpattīti ce? Na, tattha purimasikkhāpadeneva anāpattisiddhito. Tatuttaritā, acchinnādikāraṇatā, aññātakaviññatti, tāya ca paṭilābhoti imānettha cattāri aṅgāni.

Herein, this is the intention regarding why 'for the benefit of another' is not stated: if it were stated, the fault would arise that it would be permissible to receive even by exceeding the measure for the benefit of others. And that, because it was laid down regarding the matter of requesting for the benefit of another, does not accord when compared with the subject matter. Indeed, it is not appropriate to have a statement of no-offense regarding the very subject matter based on which the training rule was laid down. However, in all three Gaṇṭhipadas, it is said: 'Since this training rule proceeds by way of being connected with one's own acceptance, there is no occasion at all to say 'for the benefit of another'; therefore, it is not stated.' Here, if it is said: 'Because 'for the benefit of another' is not stated, is there an offense for a monk who requests in excess for the benefit of others from relatives or those who have invited?' No, because in that case the establishment of no-offense is already accomplished by the previous training rule. Here, these are the four factors: exceeding that, having a reason such as being robbed by thieves, requesting from a non-relative, and receiving it thereby.

Tatuttarisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Tatuttari Training Rule is finished.

8. Paṭhamaupakkhaṭasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

8. Explanation of the First Training Rule Concerning What Has Been Prepared

527. Aṭṭhame [M 2.0406][V 2.0359] api mayyāti pāṭhepi soyevattho. Ayyāti pana bahuvacanena āmantanaṃ kataṃ.

527. In the eighth, even in the reading 'api ayyā,' the meaning is the same. But the word 'ayyā' is an address made in the plural.

528-529. Apadissāti “itthannāmassa bhikkhuno dassāmī”ti evaṃ apadisitvā. Paccayaṃ katvāti kāraṇaṃ katvā. Uddissāti ettha yo kattāti “uddissā”ti iminā vuttauddisanakiriyāya yo kattā. Cīvaraṃ cetāpenti parivattenti etenāti cīvaracetāpannaṃ. Na-kārāgamaṃ katvā cīvaracetāpannanti vuttaṃ, “cīvaracetāpana”ntipi paṭhanti. Pacuravohāravasenāti yebhuyyavohāravasena. Yebhuyyavasena hi gharasāmikaṃ daṭṭhukāmā tassa gharaṃ gacchantīti tatheva bahulaṃ vohāro. Byañjanamattamevāti attho netabbo natthīti adhippāyo.

528-529. 'Apadissati' means having thus indicated, 'I will give to the monk of such-and-such a name.' 'Paccayaṃ katvā' means having made a reason. 'Uddissāti': here, the agent is the agent of the act of designating stated by 'uddissā.' 'Cīvaraṃ cetāpenti parivattenti etenāti cīvaracetāpanaṃ' means that by which they procure or exchange a robe is 'cīvaracetāpanaṃ.' Having made the augment 'na,' it is said as 'cīvaracetāpannaṃ'; they also recite it as 'cīvaracetāpanaṃ.' 'Pacuravohāravasenāti' means by way of common usage. For, generally, those who wish to see the householder go to his house, thus the usage is common in that way. 'Byañjanamattamevāti': the intention is that this is merely the expression; there is no meaning to be taken.

531. Samakepi pana anāpattīti yadagghanakaṃ so dātukāmo hoti, tadagghanake anāpatti mūlaṃ vaḍḍhetvā adhikavidhānaṃ anāpannattā. Ettha ca “dātukāmomhī”ti attano santike avuttepi dātukāmataṃ sutvā yadagghanakaṃ so dātukāmo hoti, tadagghanakaṃ āharāpetuṃ vaṭṭati. Agghavaḍḍhanakañhi idaṃ sikkhāpadanti ettha agghavaḍḍhanaṃ etassa atthīti agghavaḍḍhanakaṃ, agghavaḍḍhanaṃ sandhāya idaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññattanti adhippāyo. Cīvaraṃ dehīti saṅghāṭiādīsu yaṃkiñci cīvaraṃ sandhāya vadati. Cīvare bhiyyokamyatā, aññātakaviññatti, tāya ca paṭilābhoti imānettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

531. Regarding 'But no offense even for an equal value': for an item of the value that the donor wishes to give, there is no offense, because one has not arrived at making an excessive arrangement by increasing the base price. And here, even if 'I wish to give' is not said in one's presence, upon hearing of the wish to give, it is permissible to have an item brought of the value that he wishes to give. Regarding 'Indeed, this is the training rule concerning increasing the value': here, the analysis is: 'it has an increase of value,' thus it is 'agghavaḍḍhanakaṃ' (concerning increasing the value); the intention is that this training rule was laid down concerning an increase of value. 'Give a robe' means one speaks referring to any kind of robe, such as the double-robe and so on. Here, these are the three factors: desire for more with respect to a robe, requesting from a non-relative, and receiving it thereby.

Paṭhamaupakkhaṭasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the First Training Rule Concerning What Has Been Prepared is finished.

532. Dutiyaupakkhaṭe vattabbaṃ natthi.

532. In the Second (Rule) Concerning What Has Been Prepared, there is nothing to be said.

10. Rājasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

10. Explanation of the Training Rule Concerning Kings

537-539. Rājasikkhāpade pana “ajjaṇho”ti pāṭhe “ajjuṇho”tipi paṭhanti. Bhogoti bhuñjitabbo. Yaṃ vuttaṃ mātikāṭṭhakathāyaṃ “iminā [M 2.0407] cīvaracetāpannena cīvaraṃ cetāpetvā itthannāmaṃ bhikkhuṃ cīvarena acchādehīti idaṃ āgamanasuddhiṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Sace hi ‘idaṃ itthannāmassa bhikkhuno dehī’ti peseyya, āgamanassa asuddhattā akappiyavatthuṃ ārabbha bhikkhunā [V 2.0360] kappiyakārakopi niddisitabbo na bhaveyyā”ti, tattha āgamanassa suddhiyā vā asuddhiyā vā visesappayojanaṃ na dissati. Satipi hi āgamanassa asuddhabhāve dūto attano kusalatāya kappiyavohārena vadati, “kappiyakārako na niddisitabbo”ti idaṃ natthi, na ca dūtena kappiyavohāravasena vutte dāyakena idaṃ kathaṃ pesitanti īdisī vicāraṇā upalabbhati, avicāretvā ca taṃ na sakkā jānituṃ, yadi pana āgamanassa asuddhattā kappiyakārako niddisitabbo na bhaveyya, cīvarānaṃ atthāya dūtassa hatthe akappiyavatthusmiṃ pesite sabbattha dāyakena kathaṃ pesitanti pucchitvāva kappiyakārako niddisitabbo bhaveyya. Tasmā asatipi āgamanasuddhiyaṃ sace so dūto attano kusalatāya kappiyavohāravasena vadati, dūtasseva vacanaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Yadi hi āgamanasuddhiyevettha pamāṇaṃ, mūlasāmikena kappiyavohāravasena pesitassa dūtassa akappiyavohāravasena vadatopi kappiyakārako niddisitabbo bhaveyya, tasmā sabbattha dūtavacanameva pamāṇanti gahetabbaṃ.

537-539. In the Training Rule Concerning Kings, where the text reads 'ajjaṇho,' some also recite it as 'ajjuṇho.' 'Bhogo' means what is to be consumed. What was stated in the Mātikāṭṭhakathā—'By means of this robe-fund, have a robe procured and clothe such-and-such a monk'—was said to indicate the purity of the source. For if one were to send it saying, 'Give this to such-and-such a monk,' due to the impurity of the source, a steward could not be appointed by the monk concerning an unallowable item. In this matter, no special purpose is seen regarding whether the source is pure or impure. For even if the source is impure, the messenger, out of his own skillfulness, speaks in terms of what is allowable. The statement that 'a steward should not be appointed' is not the case. Nor is any such consideration found on the part of the donor as to how this was sent when the messenger speaks in terms of what is allowable. And without such consideration, it cannot be known. But if, due to the impurity of the source, a steward could not be appointed, then when an unallowable item is sent in the messenger’s hands for the sake of robes, a steward could be appointed only after asking the donor in every case how it was sent. Therefore, even if the source is impure, if that messenger, out of his own skillfulness, speaks in terms of what is allowable, the messenger’s words alone should be accepted. If purity of the source were the sole standard here, then even when a messenger, sent by the original owner with words that are allowable, speaks in terms of what is unallowable, a steward would have to be appointed. Hence, in all cases, the messenger’s words alone should be taken as the standard.

Iminā cīvaracetāpannenātiādinā pana imamatthaṃ dasseti – kappiya vasena āgatampi cīvaramūlaṃ īdisena dūtavacanena akappiyaṃ hoti, tasmā taṃ paṭikkhipitabbanti. Tenevāha – “tena bhikkhunā so dūto evamassa vacanīyo”tiādi. Suvaṇṇaṃ, rajataṃ, kahāpaṇo, māsakoti imāni hi cattāri nissaggiyavatthūni, muttā, maṇi, veḷuriyo, saṅkho, silā, pavāḷaṃ, lohitaṅko, masāragallaṃ, satta dhaññāni, dāsidāsaṃ, khettaṃ, vatthu, pupphārāmaphalārāmādayoti imāni dukkaṭavatthūni ca attano vā cetiyasaṅghagaṇapuggalānaṃ vā atthāya sampaṭicchituṃ na vaṭṭanti, tasmā taṃ sādituṃ na vaṭṭatīti dassanatthaṃ “na kho mayaṃ, āvuso, cīvaracetāpannaṃ paṭiggaṇhāmā”ti vuttaṃ, “cīvarañca kho mayaṃ paṭiggaṇhāmā”ti idaṃ pana attānaṃ uddissa ābhatattā vattuṃ vaṭṭati, tasmā vuttaṃ. “Veyyāvaccakaro niddisitabbo”ti idaṃ “atthi panāyasmato koci veyyāvaccakaro”ti kappiyavacanena vuttattā anuññātaṃ. Sace pana dūto “ko imaṃ gaṇhātī”ti vā [M 2.0408] “kassa demī”ti vā vadati, na niddisitabbo. “Ārāmiko vā upāsako vā”ti idaṃ sāruppatāya vuttaṃ, ṭhapetvā pana pañca sahadhammike yo koci kappiyakārako vaṭṭati. “Eso kho, āvuso, bhikkhūnaṃ veyyāvaccakaro”ti idaṃ bhikkhussa kappiyavacanadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Evameva hi vattabbaṃ, “etassa dehī”tiādi na vattabbaṃ. So vā cetāpessati vāti ettha eko vā-saddo padapūraṇo, “saññatto so mayā”tiādi pana dūtena evaṃ ārociteyeva taṃ codetuṃ vaṭṭati, nevāssa hatthe datvā gatamattakāraṇenāti dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ.

By the phrase 'Iminā cīvaracetāpannenāti,' etc., this meaning is shown: even a robe-fund that has come in an allowable manner becomes unallowable through such words of a messenger; therefore, it should be rejected. For that reason, it is said: 'That monk should speak to that messenger thus,' etc. Gold, silver, kahāpaṇa coins, and māsaka coins—these are the four grounds for offenses entailing relinquishment. Pearls, gems, beryl, conch shells, stone, coral, rubies, cat's-eye, the seven kinds of grain, male and female slaves, fields, land, flower gardens, and fruit orchards—these are grounds for offenses of wrong-doing. They are not to be accepted for oneself or for the benefit of a shrine, the Saṅgha, a group, or individuals. Therefore, to show that it is not allowable to consent to them, it was said: 'We do not, friend, accept a robe-fund.' But as for 'we do accept a robe,' it is allowable to say this because it has been brought having been designated for oneself; therefore, it was said. 'A steward should be appointed'—this is permitted because it was said with allowable words: 'Is there, venerable sir, any steward?' But if the messenger says, 'Who will take this?' or 'To whom shall I give it?' then a steward should not be appointed. 'A monastery attendant or a lay follower'—this was said for the sake of suitability. But setting aside the five co-residents, any steward is allowable. 'This, friend, is the steward for the monks'—this was said to show the monk's allowable speech. It should be said in just this way; one should not say, 'Give it to this one,' etc. In the phrase 'So vā cetāpessati vā,' one 'vā' is a mere expletive. As for the phrase 'He has been instructed by me,' etc., this was said to show that it is allowable to prompt the steward only when the messenger has reported back in this way, and not for the mere reason that the messenger has placed it in the steward's hands and departed.

Etāni [V 2.0361] hi vacanāni…pe… na vattabboti ettha “evaṃ vadanto paṭikkhittassa katattā vattabhede dukkaṭaṃ āpajjati, codanā pana hotiyevā”ti mahāgaṇṭhipade majjhimagaṇṭhipade ca vuttaṃ. Uddiṭṭhacodanāparicchedaṃ dassetvāti “dutiyampi vattabbo”tiādinā dassetvā. Pucchiyamānoti ettha pucchiyamānenāti attho gahetabboti āha “karaṇatthe paccattavacana”nti. Āgatakāraṇaṃ bhañjatīti āgatakāraṇaṃ vināseti.

Regarding the phrase 'These words... etc. ...should not be said': here, it is stated in the Mahāgaṇṭhipada and the Majjhimagaṇṭhipada that 'by speaking thus, because of having done what was rejected, one incurs a dukkaṭa for a breach of the rule, but the prompting still occurs.' Having shown the scope of the designated prompting, it is indicated by the phrase beginning 'it should be spoken a second time.' Regarding 'pucchiyamāno': here, the meaning 'by the one being questioned' is to be understood. Thus it is said: 'the personal ending is in the instrumental sense.' 'Āgatakāraṇaṃ bhañjatīti' means one nullifies the reason for its coming.

Ettha keci vadanti “āgatakāraṇaṃ nāma cīvaraggahaṇaṃ, taṃ bhañjatīti vuttattā puna taṃ cīvaraṃ yena kenaci ākārena gahetuṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti. Keci pana “āgatakāraṇaṃ nāma kāyavācāhi codanā, taṃ bhañjatīti vuttattā puna taṃ yena kenaci ākārena codetuṃ na labhati. Sace sayameva deti, mūlasāmiko vā dāpeti, gahetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti. Apare pana “āgatakāraṇaṃ nāma ṭhānaṃ, taṃ bhañjatīti vuttattā yathā ‘attho me, āvuso, cīvarenā’ti ekāya codanāya dve ṭhānāni bhañjati, evamidhāpi sace āsane nisīdati, ekāya nisajjāya dve ṭhānāni bhañjati. Āmisaṃ ce paṭiggaṇhāti, ekena paṭiggahaṇena dve ṭhānāni bhañjati. Dhammaṃ ce bhāsati, dhammadesanāsikkhāpade vuttaparicchedāya ekāya vācāya dve ṭhānāni bhañjatī”ti vadanti. Imesaṃ pana sabbesampi vādaṃ “ayutta”nti paṭikkhipitvā tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu idaṃ vuttaṃ “āgatakāraṇaṃ nāma ṭhānameva, tasmā ‘na kattabba’nti vāritassa katattā nisajjādīsu katesu chasu ṭhānesu ekaṃ ṭhānaṃ bhañjatī”ti.

Here, some say: 'The reason for coming is the taking of the robe; since it is said that one "breaks" it, it is not proper to take that robe again by any means.' Others, however, say: 'The reason for coming is a request by body or speech; since it is said that one "breaks" it, one does not get to make a request again by any means. If one gives of one's own accord, or the original owner has it given, it is proper to take it.' Still others say: 'The reason for coming is a position; since it is said that one "breaks" it, just as by one request, saying, "Friend, I have need of a robe," one breaks two positions, so too here—if one sits on a seat, one breaks two positions with one sitting. If one accepts a material offering, one breaks two positions with one acceptance. If one speaks the Dhamma, one breaks two positions with one utterance within the limit stated in the training rule on teaching the Dhamma.' However, having rejected the views of all these as 'unsuitable,' it is said in all three Ganthipadas: 'The reason for coming is only a position. Therefore, because of having done what was forbidden with "it should not be done," when actions such as sitting are performed, one breaks one position among the six positions.'

Tatra [M 2.0409] tatra ṭhāne tiṭṭhatīti idaṃ codakassa ṭhitaṭṭhānato apakkamma tatra tatra uddissa ṭhānaṃyeva sandhāya vuttaṃ. “Sāmaṃ vā gantabbaṃ, dūto vā pāhetabbo”ti idaṃ sabhāvato codetuṃ anicchantenapi kātabbamevāti vadanti. Mukhaṃ vivaritvā sayameva kappiyakārakattaṃ upagatoti mukhavevaṭikakappiyakārako. Avicāretukāmatāyāti imasmiṃ pakkhe “natthamhākaṃ kappiyakārako”ti idaṃ “tādisaṃ karonto kappiyakārako natthī”ti iminā adhippāyena vuttaṃ.

The statement, 'He stands in this and that place,' was said with reference only to the act of standing, having moved away from the requesting bhikkhu's standing place and having singled out this and that place. Regarding, 'One should go oneself, or a messenger should be sent,' they say this must be done even by one who is by nature unwilling to request. 'Having opened his mouth, he himself has undertaken the role of a kappiyakāraka'—thus he is a mukhavevaṭikakappiyakāraka. In the view of 'due to unwillingness to investigate,' the statement, 'We have no kappiyakāraka,' was said with this intention: 'There is no kappiyakāraka who does such a thing.'

“Meṇḍakasikkhāpade vuttanayena paṭipajjitabba”nti vatvā idāni taṃ meṇḍakasikkhāpadaṃ dassento “vuttañheta”ntiādimāha. Idameva hi “santi, bhikkhave, saddhā pasannā”tiādivacanaṃ bhesajjakkhandhake meṇḍakavatthusmiṃ (mahāva. 299) vuttattā “meṇḍakasikkhāpada”nti vuttaṃ. Tattha hi meṇḍakena nāma seṭṭhinā –

Having said, 'One should proceed according to the method stated in the Meṇḍaka training rule,' now, wishing to show that Meṇḍaka training rule, he says, 'For it has been said,' and so forth. Indeed, this very statement, 'There are, bhikkhus, faithful, devoted ones,' and so forth, is called the 'Meṇḍaka training rule' because it was spoken in the Bhesajjakkhandhaka in the story of Meṇḍaka. There, indeed, the treasurer named Meṇḍaka said:

“Santi[V 2.0362], bhante, maggā kantārā appodakā appabhakkhā, na sukarā apātheyyena gantuṃ, sādhu, bhante, bhagavā bhikkhūnaṃ pātheyyaṃ anujānātū”ti –

‘Venerable sir, there are paths that are wildernesses, with little water and little food, not easy to travel without provisions. It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would permit provisions for the bhikkhus.’

Yācitena bhagavatā –

The Blessed One, having been requested,

“Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, pātheyyaṃ pariyesituṃ. Taṇḍulo taṇḍulatthikena, muggo muggatthikena, māso māsatthikena, loṇaṃ loṇatthikena, guḷo guḷatthikena, telaṃ telatthikena, sappi sappitthikenā”ti –

‘I permit, bhikkhus, that you seek provisions. Rice for one who needs rice, green gram for one who needs green gram, black gram for one who needs black gram, salt for one who needs salt, molasses for one who needs molasses, oil for one who needs oil, and ghee for one who needs ghee.’

Vatvā idaṃ vuttaṃ –

Having said this, this was said:

“Santi, bhikkhave, manussā saddhā pasannā, te kappiyakārakānaṃ hatthe hiraññaṃ upanikkhipanti ‘iminā ayyassa yaṃ kappiyaṃ, taṃ dethā’ti. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, yaṃ tato kappiyaṃ, taṃ sādituṃ, na tvevāhaṃ bhikkhave kenaci pariyāyena jātarūparajataṃ sāditabbaṃ pariyesitabbanti vadāmī”ti.

‘There are, bhikkhus, people who are faithful and devoted; they deposit gold and silver in the hands of stewards, saying, “With this, give the venerable one what is allowable.” I permit, bhikkhus, that you consent to what is allowable from that. But, bhikkhus, I do not say in any way at all that gold and silver should be consented to or sought.’

Hiraññaṃ [M 2.0410] upanikkhipantīti etthāpi bhikkhussa ārocanaṃ atthiyevāti gahetabbaṃ. Aññathā aniddiṭṭhakappiyakārakattaṃ bhajatīti na codetabbo siyā. Yadi mūlaṃ sandhāya codeti, taṃ sāditameva siyāti āha “mūlaṃ asādiyantenā”ti.

Here too, regarding 'they deposit gold and silver,' it should be understood that there is indeed an informing of the bhikkhu. Otherwise, it would fall into the state of being from an undesignated steward, and thus he would not be subject to being requested. If one makes a request with reference to the principal amount, that would indeed be a consenting to it; therefore, he said, 'by one not consenting to the principal.'

“Aññātakaappavāritesu viya paṭipajjitabbanti idaṃ attanā codanāṭhānañca na kātabbanti dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Aññaṃ pana kappiyakārakaṃ pesetvā lokacārittavasena anuyuñjitvāpi kappiyavatthuṃ āharāpetuṃ vaṭṭati attānaṃ uddissa nikkhittassa attano santakattā”ti keci vadanti, taṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “aññātakaappavāritesu viya paṭipajjitabbaṃ. Sace sayameva cīvaraṃ ānetvā denti, gahetabbaṃ. No ce, kiñci na vattabbā”ti daḷhaṃ katvā vuttattā na gahetabbanti amhākaṃ khanti. Na hi aññātakaappavāritaṃ sayaṃ aviññāpetvā aññena viññāpetuṃ vaṭṭati, na ca yattha aññaṃ pesetvā āharāpetuṃ vaṭṭati, tattha sayaṃ gantvā na āharāpetabbanti sakkā vatthuṃ. Yadi cettha aññena āharāpetuṃ vaṭṭati, “aññātakaappavāritesu viya paṭipajjitabba”ntiādivacanameva niratthakaṃ siyā. “Dūtenā”ti imassa byabhicāraṃ dasseti “sayaṃ āharitvāpī”ti. Dadantesūti iminā sambandho[V 2.0363]. Piṇḍapātādīnaṃ atthāyāti iminā pana “cīvaracetāpanna”nti imassa byabhicāraṃ dasseti. “Eseva nayo”ti vuttattā piṇḍapātādīnaṃ atthāya dinnepi ṭhānacodanādi sabbaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva kātabbaṃ.

The statement, 'One should act as toward non-relatives who are uninvited,' was said to show that one should not oneself perform the requesting or the standing. Some say: 'However, by sending another steward, and by inquiring according to worldly custom, it is proper to have an allowable item brought, because what was deposited for oneself is one's own property.' That is not to be accepted, because it is stated firmly in the commentary: 'One should act as toward non-relatives who are uninvited. If they themselves bring a robe and give it, it should be taken. If not, nothing should be said.' This is our opinion. For it is not proper, without making the request oneself, to have another make the request from a non-relative who is uninvited. Nor can it be said that where it is proper to send another to have something brought, one should not go oneself and have it brought. If it were proper here to have it brought by another, the statement beginning with 'one should act as toward non-relatives who are uninvited' would be meaningless. With 'even having brought it oneself,' he shows the exception to 'by a messenger'; there is a connection with 'when they give.' However, with 'for the sake of alms-food, etc.,' he shows the exception to 'robe-fund.' Because it is said, 'This is the method,' even when something is given for the sake of alms-food, etc., everything—such as the standing, requesting, etc.—should be done according to the method previously stated.

Paṭiggahaṇepi paribhogepi āpattīti paṭiggahaṇe pācittiyaṃ, paribhoge dukkaṭaṃ. Sveva sāpattikoti dukkaṭāpattiṃ sandhāya vadati. Idañca aṭṭhakathāpamāṇeneva gahetabbaṃ. “Parassa niddosabhāvadassanatthaṃ sveva sāpattiko sadosoti vuttaṃ hotī”tipi vadanti. “Codetīti vuttattā pana āpattiyā codetīti katvā sveva sāpattikoti idaṃ dukkaṭaṃyeva sandhāya vattuṃ yutta”nti tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Paṭiggahaṇepi paribhogepi āpattiyevāti dukkaṭameva sandhāya vuttaṃ. Taḷākassapi khettasaṅgahitattā tassa paṭiggahaṇepi āpatti vuttā. Cattāro paccaye saṅgho paribhuñjatūti detīti ettha “bhikkhusaṅgho cattāro paccaye paribhuñcatu, taḷākaṃ dammī”ti vā “catupaccayaparibhogatthaṃ taḷākaṃ [M 2.0411] dammī”ti vā vadati, vaṭṭatiyeva. “Ito taḷākato uppanne cattāro paccaye dammī”ti vutte pana vattabbameva natthi.

In both receiving and making use of, there is an offense: in receiving, it is a pācittiya offense; in making use of, a dukkaṭa offense. ‘He himself is an offender’ refers to the dukkaṭa offense. This should be understood only according to the commentary. Some also say, ‘To show the faultless nature of another, it is said, “he himself is an offender, with fault.”’ However, since it is said ‘he accuses,’ taking it to mean ‘he accuses of an offense,’ it is appropriate to state ‘he himself is an offender’ only with reference to the dukkaṭa offense. This is stated in all three gaṇṭhipadas. ‘In both receiving and making use of, there is an offense’ refers only to the dukkaṭa offense. Regarding the pond, because it is included as part of a field, an offense is stated even for receiving it. When, in this case, one gives, saying, ‘May the Saṅgha make use of the four requisites,’ here one may say, ‘May the Saṅgha of bhikkhus make use of the four requisites; I give the pond,’ or ‘I give the pond for the purpose of making use of the four requisites’—this is permissible. But if one says, ‘From the produce of this pond, I give the four requisites,’ then there is nothing further to be said.

Amhākaṃ ekaṃ kappiyakārakaṃ ṭhapethāti vutteti idaṃ īdisaṃyeva sandhāya vuttaṃ. Kappiyakkamena sampaṭicchitesu khettataḷākādīsu pana avuttepi kappiyakārakaṃ ṭhapetuṃ labbhatiyeva. Yasmā parasantakaṃ nāsetuṃ bhikkhūnaṃ na vaṭṭati, tasmā “na sassakāle”ti vuttaṃ. “Janapadassa sāmikoti imināva yo taṃ janapadaṃ vicāreti, tenapi acchinditvā dinnaṃ vaṭṭatiyevā”ti vadanti. Udakavāhakanti udakamātikaṃ. Kappiyavohārepīti ettha “vidhānaṃ vakkhāmā”ti pāṭhaseso. Udakavasenāti udakaparibhogatthaṃ. Suddhacittānanti kevalaṃ udakaparibhogatthamevāti adhippāyo. Alajjinā kārāpite vattabbameva natthīti āha “lajjībhikkhunā”ti. Pakatibhāgo nāma imasmiṃ raṭṭhe catuambaṇamattaṃ. Akaṭṭhapubbaṃ navasassaṃ nāma. Aparicchinnabhāgeti “ettake bhūmibhāge ettako bhāgo dātabbo”ti evaṃ aparicchinnabhāge.

‘Appoint one steward for us’—this was said with reference to just such a case. However, regarding fields, ponds, and the like received through an allowable procedure, it is indeed permissible to appoint a steward even if it is not explicitly stated. Since it is not proper for bhikkhus to destroy what belongs to others, therefore it was said, ‘not at the time of harvest.’ ‘The owner of the district’—by this, they say that for whatever person administers that district, a gift from him without it having been seized is indeed permissible. ‘Water-carrier’ means a water-channel. Regarding ‘in an allowable transaction,’ here the rest of the reading is ‘we will explain the method.’ ‘By means of water’ means for the purpose of using water. ‘With pure intent’—the meaning is solely for the purpose of using water. There is nothing to be said about something caused to be done by a shameless one—thus it is said, ‘by a conscientious bhikkhu.’ A standard share in this country is about four ambaṇas in measure. ‘New grain’ means grain not previously ploughed. ‘An unapportioned share’—meaning, in a share not demarcated thus: ‘in such a portion of land, such a share should be given.’

Rajjuyā vā daṇḍena vāti ettha “pādehipi minituṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti. Khale vā ṭhatvā rakkhatīti ettha pana thenetvā gaṇhante disvā “mā gaṇhathā”ti nivārento rakkhati nāma. Sace pana avicāretvā kevalaṃ tuṇhībhūtova rakkhaṇatthāya olokento tiṭṭhati, vaṭṭati. Sacepi tasmiṃ tuṇhībhūte corikāya haranti, “mayaṃ bhikkhusaṅghassa ārocessāmā”ti evaṃ vattuṃ vaṭṭatīti vadanti. Nīharāpeti paṭisāmetīti etthāpi “sace pariyāyena vadati, vaṭṭatī”ti [V 2.0364] vadanti. Apubbassa anuppāditattā aññesaṃ vaṭṭatīti āha “tasseva taṃ akappiya”nti.

‘By a rope or by a stick’—here, they say, ‘It is not proper to measure even with the feet.’ ‘Or standing in the threshing floor, he protects’—here, however, seeing those who are taking by stealing and preventing them by saying, ‘Do not take,’ he is called one who protects. But if, without administering, he merely stands silent, looking on for the sake of protecting, it is allowable. Even if, while he is silent, they carry it off by theft, they say it is proper to say, ‘We will inform the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.’ ‘He has it removed, he has it restored’—here too, they say, ‘If he speaks indirectly, it is allowable.’ Because a new revenue was not generated, it is allowable for others; thus he said, ‘That is unallowable for him alone.’

Nanu ca dubbicāritamattena tasseva taṃ akappiyaṃ, na sabbesaṃ rūpiyasaṃvohāre catutthapatto viya. Vuttañhi tattha (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.589) “yo pana rūpiyaṃ asampaṭicchitvā ‘therassa pattaṃ kiṇitvā dehī’ti pahitakappiyakārakena saddhiṃ kammārakulaṃ gantvā pattaṃ disvā ‘ime kahāpaṇe gahetvā imaṃ dehī’ti kahāpaṇe dāpetvā gahito, ayaṃ patto etasseva bhikkhuno na vaṭṭati dubbicāritattā, aññesaṃ pana vaṭṭati mūlassa asampaṭicchitattā”ti. Tasmā [M 2.0412] yaṃ te āharanti, sabbesaṃ akappiyaṃ. Kasmā? Kahāpaṇānaṃ vicāritattāti idaṃ kasmā vuttanti? Ettha keci vadanti “kahāpaṇe sādiyitvā vicāritaṃ sandhāya evaṃ vutta”nti. Saṅghikattā ca nissajjituṃ na sakkā, tasmā sabbesaṃ na kappatīti tesaṃ adhippāyo. Keci pana “asādiyitvāpi kahāpaṇānaṃ vicāritattā rūpiyasaṃvohāro kato hoti, saṅghikattā ca nissajjituṃ na sakkā, tasmā sabbesaṃ na kappatī”ti vadanti. Gaṇṭhipadesu pana tīsupi idaṃ vuttaṃ “catutthapatto gihisantakānaṃyeva kahāpaṇānaṃ vicāritattā aññesaṃ kappati, idha pana saṅghikānaṃ vicāritattā sabbesaṃ na kappatī”ti. Sabbesampi vādo tena tena pariyāyena yujjatiyeva.

But is it not so that because of mere mismanagement, it is unallowable for him alone, not for all, as in the case of the fourth bowl regarding monetary transactions?
