For it is said there: 'But if a bhikkhu, without himself accepting money, goes with a designated steward to the craftsman's house after saying, "Buy a bowl for the elder and give it to him," and seeing the bowl, says, "Take these kahāpaṇas and give this," and the bowl is obtained after having caused the kahāpaṇas to be given—this bowl is not allowable for that very bhikkhu due to his mismanagement, but it is allowable for others because the principal was not accepted by them.' Therefore, what they bring is unallowable for all. Why? 'Because the kahāpaṇas were managed.' Why was this said? Here, some say, 'This was stated with reference to managing the kahāpaṇas after consenting to them.' And because it is Saṅgha property, it cannot be forfeited; therefore, it is not allowable for all—this is their intention. Others, however, say, 'Even without consenting, because the kahāpaṇas were managed, a monetary transaction has been done; and because it is Saṅgha property, it cannot be forfeited; therefore, it is not allowable for all.' But in all three Gaṇṭhipadas, this is stated: 'The fourth bowl is allowable for others because only kahāpaṇas belonging to householders were managed, but here, because Saṅgha property was managed, it is not allowable for all.' The arguments of all are indeed justifiable in one way or another.

Catusāladvāreti bhojanasālaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Pariyāyena kathitattāti “gaṇhā”ti avatvā “sīmā gatā”ti pariyāyena kathitattā. Pakatibhūmikaraṇatthaṃ “heṭṭhā gahitaṃ paṃsu”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Dāsaṃ dammīti ettha “manussaṃ dammīti vutte vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti. Kukkuṭasūkarā…pe… vaṭṭatīti ettha kukkuṭasūkaresu dīyamānesu “imehi amhākaṃ attho natthi, sukhaṃ jīvantu, araññe vissajjethā”ti vattuṃ vaṭṭati. “Khettavatthupaṭiggahaṇā paṭivirato hotī”tiādivacanato (dī. ni. 1.10, 194) khettādīnaṃ paṭiggahaṇe ayaṃ sabbo vinicchayo vutto. Kappiyakārakassa bhikkhunā niddiṭṭhabhāvo, dūtena appitatā, tatuttari vāyāmo, tena vāyāmena paṭilābhoti imānettha cattāri aṅgāni.

'At the four-halled gate' is said with reference to the dining hall. 'Because it was spoken of indirectly' means because, without saying 'take,' it was spoken of indirectly as 'the boundary has been reached.' For the purpose of restoring the natural ground, it is said, 'earth taken from below,' and so on. Regarding 'I give a slave,' they say, 'it is allowable when it is said as "I give a person."' Concerning 'chickens and pigs... it is allowable,' here, when chickens and pigs are being given, it is proper to say, 'We have no use for these; may they live happily; release them in the forest.' From the statement, 'He abstains from accepting fields and land,' and so on, this entire legal decision concerning the acceptance of fields and the like is stated. The state of having been indicated to the steward by the bhikkhu, the state of being offered by a messenger, effort beyond that, and acquisition through that effort—these are the four factors here.

Rājasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule concerning a king is concluded.

Niṭṭhito cīvaravaggo paṭhamo.

The first chapter on robes is concluded.

2. Kosiyavaggo

2. The Chapter on Silk

1. Kosiyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Training Rule on Silk

542. Pāḷiyaṃ [V 2.0365] “kosiyakārake”ti ettha kosaṃ karontīti kosakārakāti laddhavohārānaṃ pāṇakānaṃ kosato nibbattaṃ kosiyaṃ, taṃ karontīti kosiyakārakā, tantavāyā. Saṃhananaṃ saṅghāto[M 2.0413], vināsoti attho. Kosiyamissakanti kosiyatantunā missaṃ. “Avāyima”nti vuttattā vāyitvā ce karonti, anāpatti. Anāpatti vitānaṃ vātiādinā vitānādīnaṃ atthāya karaṇepi tenākārena paribhogepi anāpatti vuttā.

2. In the Pāḷi, regarding 'kosiyakārake' here: 'They make a cocoon (kosaṃ), thus they are kosakārakā'—of creatures that have received this designation, kosiyaṃ is that which is produced from the cocoon. 'They make that, thus they are kosiyakārakā'—weavers are to be understood. Saṃhananaṃ, saṅghāto, and vināso mean destruction. Kosiyamissakaṃ means mixed with silk thread. Because 'avāyima' (unwoven) is stated, if they make it by weaving, there is no offense. By the text beginning with 'anāpatti vitānaṃ vā,' it is stated that there is no offense even in making for the purpose of canopies and so on, and also in using them in that manner.

Evampi missetvā katameva hotīti iminā vātena āharitvā pātitepi acittakattā āpattiyevāti dasseti. Kosiyamissakatā, attano atthāya santhatassa karaṇaṃ kārāpanaṃ, paṭilābho cāti imānettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

1. By the text, 'Even thus mixed, it is indeed made,' it is shown that even if it is brought by the wind and made to fall, because this is an acittaka training rule, it is indeed an offense. The three factors here are: the state of being mixed with silk; for one's own sake, the making or causing to be made of a spread; and the acquisition.

Kosiyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

542. The explanation of the training rule on silk is concluded.

547. Suddhakāḷakasikkhāpadaṃ uttānatthameva.

The training rule concerning pure black wool has an obvious meaning.

3. Dvebhāgasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

3. Explanation of the Training Rule Concerning Two Parts

552. Dvebhāgasikkhāpade pana dve bhāgāti ukkaṭṭhaparicchedo kāḷakānaṃ adhikaggahaṇassa paṭikkhepavasena sikkhāpadassa paññattattā. Tatiyaṃ odātānaṃ catutthaṃ gocariyānanti ayaṃ heṭṭhimaparicchedo tesaṃ adhikaggahaṇe paṭikkhepābhāvato, tasmā kāḷakānaṃ bhāgadvayato adhikaṃ na vaṭṭati, sesānaṃ pana vuttappamāṇato adhikampi vaṭṭati. “Kāḷakānaṃyeva ca adhikaggahaṇassa paṭikkhittattā kāḷakānaṃ upaḍḍhaṃ odātānaṃ vā gocariyānaṃ vā upaḍḍhaṃ gahetvāpi kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti, “anāpatti bahutaraṃ odātānaṃ bahutaraṃ gocariyānaṃ ādiyitvā karoti, suddhaṃ odātānaṃ suddhaṃ gocariyānaṃ ādiyitvā karotī”ti iminā taṃ sameti. “Kāḷake odāte ca ṭhapetvā sesā gocariyesuyeva saṅgahaṃ gacchantī”ti vadanti. Dve [V 2.0366] koṭṭhāsā kāḷakānanti ettha pana “ekassapi kāḷakalomassa atirekabhāve nissaggiyaṃ hotī”ti mātikāṭṭhakathāyaṃ (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. dvebhāgasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) ttaṃ, taṃ “dhārayitvā dve tulā ādātabbā”ti vacanato tulādhāraṇāya na sameti[M 2.0414]. Na hi lome gaṇetvā tulādhāraṇā karīyati, atha gaṇetvāva dhārayitabbaṃ siyā, kiṃ tulādhāraṇāya, tasmā evamettha adhippāyo yutto siyā – acittakattā sikkhāpadassa pubbe tulāya dhārayitvā ṭhapitesu ekampi lomaṃ tattha pateyya, nissaggiyanti. Aññathā dubbiññeyyabhāvato dve tulā nādātabbā, ūnakatarāva ādātabbā siyuṃ.

In the training rule concerning two portions, the term 'two portions' is the upper limit, because the training rule was laid down by way of prohibiting the taking of an excess of black wool. The phrase 'a third of white, a fourth of tawny' is the lower limit, because there is no prohibition on taking an excess of these. Therefore, for black wool, more than two portions is not allowable, but for the others, even more than the stated amount is allowable. They say: 'Because the taking of an excess of only black wool is prohibited, it is allowable to make it by taking half of black wool and half of white wool or tawny wool.' That accords with this: 'There is no offense if one makes it taking more white wool or more tawny wool, or if one makes it taking pure white wool or pure tawny wool.' They also say: 'Having set aside black and white wool, the remaining types are included only under tawny wool.' But here, regarding 'two parts of black wool,' it is said in the Mātikāṭṭhakathā: 'If there is an excess of even one black wool fiber, it is to be forfeited.' That does not accord with weighing by a balance, for weighing by a balance is not done by counting the fibers. If it were to be held only after counting, what would be the use of weighing by a balance? Therefore, this intention is suitable here: because the training rule is an acittaka one, among those previously weighed by a balance and set aside, if even one fiber were to fall there, it is to be forfeited. Otherwise, because it would be difficult to know, two portions by weight should not be taken; only a lesser amount should be taken.

Dvebhāgasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

547. The explanation of the training rule concerning two portions is concluded.

4. Chabbassasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Six Years

557. Chabbassasikkhāpade pana “yesaṃ no santhate dārakā uhadantipi ummihantipi, yesaṃ no santhatā undūrehipi khajjantī”ti evaṃ pāḷipadānaṃ sambandho veditabbo. Hada karīsossagge, miha secaneti panimassatthaṃ sandhāyāha “vaccampi passāvampi karontī”ti. Pavāraṇāuposathapāṭipadadivasesu santhataṃ karitvā puna chaṭṭhe vasse paripuṇṇe pavāraṇāuposathapāṭipadadivasesu karonto “chabbassāni karotī”ti vuccati. Dutiyadivasato paṭṭhāya karonto pana atirekachabbassāni karoti nāma.

557. In the training rule concerning six years, however, the connection of the Pāḷi words should be understood thus: 'on whose felt mat children defecate and urinate, and whose felt mat is gnawed by rats.' Having considered the meaning of the root hada in the sense of 'excreting feces' and miha in the sense of 'discharging,' the Teacher said, 'they produce feces and urine.' One who, having made a felt mat on the Pavāraṇā, Uposatha, or Pāṭipadā days, and again, when the sixth year is complete, makes it on the Pavāraṇā, Uposatha, or Pāṭipadā days, is said to 'make it for six years.' However, one who makes it starting from the second day onwards is said to make it for more than six years.

Chabbassasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Six Years is concluded.

5. Nisīdanasanthatasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Sitting-Mat

565-6. Nisīdanasanthatasikkhāpade pana paññāyissatīti sace sā katikā manāpā bhavissati, manāpatāya bhikkhusaṅgho sandississati. Sace amanāpā, amanāpatāya sandississatīti adhippāyo, āraññakaṅgādīni tīṇi pāḷiyaṃ padhānaṅgavasena vuttāni, sesānipi te samādiyiṃsuyevāti veditabbaṃ. Tenevāha “santhate catutthacīvarasaññitāyā”ti. Ujjhitvāti vissajjetvā.

In the training rule concerning the sitting-mat, however, the intention of 'it will be apparent' is this: if that stipulation is pleasing, it will be apparent to the Bhikkhusaṅgha by its pleasing nature. If it is unpleasing, it will be apparent by its unpleasing nature. The three ascetic practices beginning with the forest-dweller's practice are spoken of in the Pāḷi as primary factors; it should be known that they undertook the remaining ascetic practices as well. Therefore, he said, 'with the perception of the felt mat as a fourth robe.' 'Having discarded' means having abandoned.

567. Nisīdanasanthatattā [M 2.0415] nivāsanapārupanakiccaṃ natthīti āha “sakiṃ nisinnañceva nipannañcā”ti[V 2.0367]. Vidatthimattanti sugatavidatthiṃ sandhāya vadati. Idañca heṭṭhimaparicchedadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. “Vitānādīnaṃyeva atthāya karaṇe anāpattivacanato sace nipajjanatthāya karonti, āpattiyevā”ti tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Akappiyattā pana “paribhuñjituṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ. Idañca nisīdanasanthataṃ nāma nisīdanacīvarameva, nāññanti vadanti. Nisīdanasikkhāpadepi nisīdanaṃ nāma sadasaṃ vuccatīti ca aṭṭhakathāyañcassa “santhatasadisaṃ santharitvā ekasmiṃ ante sugatavidatthiyā vidatthimatte padese dvīsu ṭhānesu phāletvā tisso dasā karīyanti, tāhi dasāhi sadasaṃ nāma vuccatī”ti (pāci. aṭṭha. 531) vacanato idhāpi “nisīdanaṃ nāma sadasaṃ vuccatī”ti ca “santhate catutthacīvarasaññitāyā”ti ca vacanato taṃ yuttaṃ viya dissati. Keci pana “nisīdanasanthataṃ eḷakalomāni santharitvā santhataṃ viya karonti, taṃ avāyimaṃ anadhiṭṭhānupagaṃ, nisīdanacīvaraṃ pana channaṃ cīvarānaṃ aññatarena karoti adhiṭṭhānupagaṃ, taṃ karontā ca nantakāni santharitvā santhatasadisaṃ karontī”ti vadanti, vīmaṃsitvā yuttataraṃ gahetabbaṃ.

567. Because it is a sitting-mat, it does not have the function of an undergarment or an outer robe; therefore, he said, 'it is only for sitting and lying upon.' The phrase 'a span in measure' is said in reference to the Sugata's span. And this is said to show the lower limit. In all three Gaṇṭhipadas it is said: 'Because no-offense is stated for making it for the purpose of canopies and so on, if they make it for the purpose of lying down, it is indeed an offense.' However, because it is unsuitable, it is said: 'it is not allowable to use.' Some say that this so-called sitting-mat is just a sitting-cloth, nothing else. And in the training rule on the sitting-cloth, what is called a 'sitting-cloth' is said to be 'that which has a fringe'; and in its commentary it is said: 'Having spread it like a felt mat, at one end, in a space the measure of a Sugata's span, one should split it in two places and make three fringes. Because of these fringes, it is called "that which has a fringe"' (Pāc. Aṭṭha. 531). Therefore, because it is said here too, 'what is called a sitting-cloth is said to be "that which has a fringe,"' and 'with the perception of the felt mat as a fourth robe,' this seems appropriate. However, some say: 'They make a sitting-mat by spreading goat's wool, like a felt mat. That is unwoven and not suitable for formal determination. A sitting-cloth, however, is made from one of the six kinds of robe-cloth and is suitable for formal determination. And when making it, they spread out rags and make it resemble a felt mat.' Having investigated, the more suitable view should be adopted.

Nisīdanasanthatasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Sitting-Mat is concluded.

6. Eḷakalomasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Goat-Hair Wool

571. Eḷalomasikkhāpade pana āsumbhīti ettha “asumbhī”ti paṭhanti. Kilantāti iminā kilantatāya te onamitvā pātetuṃ na sakkontīti dasseti. Addhānamaggappaṭipannassāti idaṃ vatthumattadīpanavasena pāḷiyaṃ vuttaṃ. Yattha katthaci pana dhammena labhitvā gaṇhituṃ vaṭṭatiyeva. Tiyojanaparamanti ca gahitaṭṭhānato tiyojanappamāṇaṃ desanti evamattho gahetabbo.

571. In the training rule concerning goat-hair wool, in the phrase `āsumbhīti`, some read `asumbhī`ti. By the word `kilantāti`, it is shown that due to exhaustion, they were unable to bend down and drop them. The phrase `addhānamaggappaṭipannassāti` is stated in the Pāḷi merely by way of explaining the situation. However, it is indeed allowable to take something acquired lawfully wherever it may be. And by `tiyojanaparamanti`, the meaning to be understood is a distance measuring three yojanas from the place where it was taken.

572. Sahatthāti karaṇatthe nissakkavacananti āha “sahatthenā”ti. Asante hāraketi pāḷiyaṃ bhikkhuno anurūpatādassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ, na pana hārake vijjamāne tiyojanabbhantare sahatthā harantassa āpattidassanatthaṃ. Tiyojanato bahi bahitiyojananti āha “tiyojanato bahi pātetī”ti. Tena haritepi āpattiyevāti saussāhattā anāṇattiyā haṭattā ca. Satipi hi saussāhabhāve āṇattiyā [M 2.0416] ce harati, anāpatti “aññaṃ harāpetī”ti vacanato. Añño harissatīti adhippāyābhāvato “suddhacittena ṭhapita”nti vuttaṃ. Saussāhattāti tiyojanātikkamane saussāhattā. Idañca “añño harissatī”ti asuddhacittena ṭhapitaṃ sandhāya [V 2.0368] vuttaṃ, acittakattāti idaṃ pana suddhacittena ṭhapitaṃ sandhāya. Anāpatti pāḷiyā na sametīti “tiyojanaṃ haratī”tiādipāḷiyā, visesato “aññaṃ harāpetī”ti pāḷiyā ca na sameti.

572. `Sahatthāti` is an ablative case ending in the sense of instrument; hence he said, `sahatthenā`ti. The phrase `asante hārake`ti in the Pāḷi is stated to show what is appropriate for a bhikkhu, not to show an offense for one who carries it with his own hand within three yojanas when a carrier is present. Regarding `Tiyojanato bahi`, which means 'outside the three yojanas,' he said, `tiyojanato bahi pātetī`ti. Therefore, even when carried by him, there is still an offense, because of his own effort and because it was carried without being commanded. For even if there is one's own effort, if one carries it having been commanded, there is no offense, according to the text `aññaṃ harāpetī`ti. Because there is no intention that 'another will carry it,' it is said, `suddhacittena ṭhapita`nti. `Saussāhattā`ti means because of one's own effort in transgressing three yojanas. And this is said in reference to it being placed with an impure mind, thinking 'another will carry it,' whereas `acittakattā`ti is said in reference to it being placed with a pure mind. The no-offense does not accord with the Pāḷi; that is, it does not accord with the Pāḷi beginning `tiyojanaṃ haratī`ti, and especially with the Pāḷi `aññaṃ harāpetī`ti.

Sace sāmikaṃ jānāpetvā ṭhapeti, āṇattiyā harāpeti nāmāti āha “sāmikassa ajānantassevā”ti. Agacchantepīti gamanaṃ upacchinditvā ṭhitayānepi. Heṭṭhā vā gacchantoti bhūmiyaṃ gacchanto. Aññaṃ harāpetīti ettha añña-ggahaṇena sāmaññato tiracchānagatāpi saṅgahitāti āha – “aññaṃ harāpetīti vacanato anāpattī”ti. Suṅkaghāte āpatti hotīti aññaṃ harāpentassa āpatti. Tattha anāpattīti aññavihitassa theyyacittābhāvato anāpatti.

If one places it after informing the owner, it is called 'causing it to be carried by command'; it is for this reason that he said, `sāmikassa ajānantassevā`ti (only when the owner is unaware), specifying the condition for an offense. `Agacchantepī`ti means even in a vehicle that has stopped its movement. `Heṭṭhā vā gacchanto`ti means one going on the ground. In `aññaṃ harāpetī`ti, by the word `añña`, even animals are generally included; hence he said, 'according to the text `aññaṃ harāpetī`ti, there is no offense.' `Suṅkaghāte āpatti hotī`ti means the offense is for one who causes another to carry it. There, there is no offense for one who has forgotten, due to the absence of a thieving mind.

575. “Taṃ harantassāti puna tiyojanaṃ harantassā”ti mahāgaṇṭhipade vuttaṃ. Taṃ pana mātikāṭṭhakathāyaṃ aṅgesu “paṭhamappaṭilābho sati iminā vacanena na sameti. “Paṭhamappaṭilābho”ti hi idaṃ dutiyappaṭilābho āpattiyā aṅgaṃ na hotīti dīpeti, tasmā pāḷiyaṃ aṭṭhakathāyañca visesābhāvato acchinnaṃ paṭilabhitvā harantassa puna tiyojanātikkamepi anāpatti vuttāti amhākaṃ khanti. Aññathā acchinnaṃ paṭilabhitvā puna tiyojanaṃ haratīti vadeyya. Vīmaṃsitvā yuttataraṃ gahetabbaṃ. Anāpatti katabhaṇḍanti ettha “kambalakojavādikatabhaṇḍampi. Pakaticīvare laggalomāni āpattiṃ janentiyevā”ti vadanti. Tanukapattatthavikantare aghaṭṭanatthaṃ pakkhipanti. Pakkhittanti kaṇṇacchidde pakkhittaṃ. Nidhānamukhaṃ nāmāti iminā katabhaṇḍasaṅkhyaṃ na gacchatīti dasseti. Eḷakalomānaṃ akatabhaṇḍatā, paṭhamappaṭilābho, attanā ādāya vā aññassa ajānantassa yāne pakkhipitvā vā tiyojanātikkamanaṃ, āharaṇapaccāharaṇaṃ, avāsādhippāyatāti imānettha pañca aṅgāni.

575. “‘Taṃ harantassā’ti means ‘puna tiyojanaṃ harantassā’ti (for one who carries it again for three yojanas)”; so it is said in the Mahāgaṇṭhipada. But that does not accord with this statement in the Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā regarding the factors: ‘paṭhamappaṭilābho’ (the first acquisition). For this phrase ‘paṭhamappaṭilābho’ti indicates that a second acquisition is not a factor for the offense. Therefore, because there is no distinction in the Pāḷi and in the commentary, our view is that for one who, having recovered what was stolen (‘acchinnaṃ’), carries it, no offense is stated even in transgressing three yojanas again. Otherwise, one would have to say: “Having recovered what was stolen, one carries it again for three yojanas.” Having investigated, the more suitable interpretation should be adopted. Regarding ‘anāpatti katabhaṇḍan’ti, they say: “Hairs attached to a regular robe generate an offense, even in the case of made goods such as blankets and rugs.” They place them inside a thin bowl-bag to prevent rubbing. ‘Pakkhittan’ti means placed in an ear-hole. By the phrase ‘nidhānamukhaṃ nāmā’ti, it is shown that it does not come into the category of ‘made goods’. The five factors here are: the state of the goat-hair wool as unmade goods, the first acquisition, transgressing three yojanas by taking it oneself or by placing it in the vehicle of another who is unaware, carrying it away and bringing it back, and the intention to depart from the residence.

Eḷakalomasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule Concerning Goat-Hair Wool is concluded.

576. Eḷakalomadhovāpanasikkhāpadaṃ [M 2.0417] uttānatthameva.

576. The training rule concerning having goat-hair wool washed is of clear meaning indeed.

8. Rūpiyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

8. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Money

583-584. Rūpiyasikkhāpade pana satthuvaṇṇoti satthunā samānavaṇṇo. Satthuno vaṇṇo satthuvaṇṇo, satthuvaṇṇo viya vaṇṇo assāti satthuvaṇṇoti majjhapadalopīsamāso daṭṭhabbo. Pākatiko [V 2.0369] nāma etarahi pakatikahāpaṇo. Rukkhaphalabījamayoti tintiṇikādirukkhānaṃ phalabījena kato. Iccetaṃ sabbampīti yathāvuttabhedaṃ sabbampi catubbidhaṃ nissaggiyavatthu hotīti sambandho. Jātarūpamāsakoti suvaṇṇakahāpaṇo.

In the training rule on money, ‘resembling the Teacher’ (satthuvaṇṇo) means ‘of a similar color to the Teacher’ (satthunā samānavaṇṇo). The Teacher's color is ‘teacher-color’ (satthuvaṇṇo); one whose color is like the Teacher's color is ‘teacher-color’ (satthuvaṇṇo)—this should be understood as a compound with the middle term elided. ‘Common’ (pākatiko) refers to the current common coin (pakatikahāpaṇo). ‘Made from the seed of the fruit of a tree’ (rukkhaphalabījamayo) means made from the seed of the fruit of trees like the tamarind. ‘All this’ (iccetaṃ sabbampi) has the connection that all four types, with the distinctions as stated, are objects for relinquishment. ‘A gold māsaka’ (jātarūpamāsako) means a gold coin (suvaṇṇakahāpaṇo).

Gaṇheyyāti attano atthāya dīyamānaṃ vā katthaci ṭhitaṃ vā nippariggahaṃ disvā sayaṃ gaṇheyya. “Idaṃ ayyassa hotū”ti evaṃ sammukhā vā “asukasmiṃ nāma ṭhāne mama hiraññasuvaṇṇaṃ atthi, taṃ tuyhaṃ hotū”ti evaṃ parammukhā ṭhitaṃ vā kevalaṃ vācāya vā hatthamuddāya vā “tuyha”nti vatvā pariccattassa kāyavācāhi appaṭikkhipitvā cittena sādiyanaṃ upanikkhittasādiyanaṃ nāma. “Sādiyatī”ti vuttamevatthaṃ vibhāveti “gaṇhitukāmo hotī”ti. “Idaṃ guttaṭṭhāna”nti ācikkhitabbanti paccayaparibhogaṃyeva sandhāya ācikkhitabbaṃ. “Idha nikkhipāhī”ti vutte “uggaṇhāpeyya vā”ti vuttalakkhaṇena nissaggiyaṃ hotīti āha – “idha nikkhipāhīti na vattabba”nti. Parato “imaṃ gaṇhā”ti na vattabbanti etthāpi eseva nayo. Kappiyañca akappiyañca nissāya ṭhitameva hotīti yasmā tato uppannapaccayaparibhogo kappati, tasmā kappiyaṃ nissāya ṭhitaṃ. Yasmā pana dubbicāraṇāya tato uppannapaccayaparibhogopi na kappati, tasmā akappiyaṃ nissāya ṭhitanti veditabbaṃ.

“He might take” (gaṇheyya) means he might take for his own benefit what is being given, or having seen unowned wealth placed somewhere, he might take it himself. When something relinquished is not rejected by body or speech but is consented to with the mind—whether it is said in one's presence, “Let this be for the venerable one”; or from a distance, “In such-and-such a place there is my gold and silver, let it be yours”; or by saying “It is yours” merely by word or by a hand gesture—this is called “consenting to what is placed nearby” (upanikkhittasādiyanaṃ). “He consents” (sādiyati) clarifies this same meaning as “he wishes to take”. “This is a protected place” (idaṃ guttaṭṭhānaṃ)—this should be declared only with reference to the use of requisites. When it is said, “Place it here” (idha nikkhipāhi), it becomes an item for relinquishment according to the stated characteristic “or he might have it taken up” (uggaṇhāpeyya vā); therefore, he said, “One should not say, ‘Place it here.’” Further on, “One should not say, ‘Take this’”—here too, this is the same method. It is established as depending on what is allowable and what is unallowable. In this regard, because the use of requisites arisen from that is allowable, it is therefore established as depending on what is allowable. But because, due to difficulty in investigation, the use of requisites arisen from that is also not allowable, it should therefore be understood as established as depending on what is unallowable.

Na tena kiñci kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ cetāpitanti ettha cetāpitaṃ ce, natthi paribhogupāyo, tasmā evaṃ vuttaṃ. Akappiyañhi nissaggiyaṃ vatthuṃ uggaṇhitvā taṃ anissajjitvāva cetāpitaṃ kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ saṅghassa nissaṭṭhampi sabbesaṃ na kappati. Keci pana “yasmā nissaggiyaṃ vatthuṃ paṭiggahetvā cetāpitaṃ kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ saṅghassa nissajjāmīti nissaṭṭhaṃ vināva upāyaṃ paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati, tasmā [M 2.0418] ‘na tena kiñci kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ cetāpita’nti vutta”nti vadanti. “Ārāmikānaṃ vā pattabhāganti idaṃ gihīnaṃ hatthagatopi soyeva bhāgoti katvā vuttaṃ. Sace pana tena aññaṃ parivattetvā ārāmikā denti, paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti majjhimagaṇṭhipade cūḷagaṇṭhipade ca vuttaṃ. Tato haritvāti aññesaṃ pattabhāgato haritvā. Kasiṇaparikammanti ālokakasiṇaparikammaṃ. Mañcapīṭhādīni vāti ettha “tato gahitamañcapīṭhādīni parivattetvā aññaṃ ce gahitaṃ, vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti. Chāyāpīti bhojanasālādīnaṃ chāyāpi. Paricchedātikkantāti gehaparicchedaṃ atikkantā, chāyāya gatagataṭṭhānaṃ gehaṃ nāma na hotīti adhippāyo. Maggenapīti ettha “sace añño maggo natthi, maggaṃ adhiṭṭhahitvā gantuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti. Kītāyāti tena vatthunā kītāya. Upanikkhepaṃ ṭhapetvā saṅgho paccaye paribhuñjatīti sace upāsako “atibahu etaṃ hiraññaṃ, idaṃ, bhante, ajjeva na vināsetabba”nti vatvā sayaṃ [V 2.0370] upanikkhepaṃ ṭhapeti, aññena vā ṭhapāpeti, etaṃ upanikkhepaṃ ṭhapetvā tato udayaṃ paribhuñjanto saṅgho paccaye paribhuñjati, tena vatthunā gahitattā “akappiya”nti vuttaṃ.

“No allowable item is to be purchased with that” (na tena kiñci kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ cetāpitanti). Here, if an allowable item is purchased, there is no means of using it; therefore, it is said thus. For, having received an unallowable object that is for relinquishment, and without having relinquished it, an allowable item purchased with it, even if relinquished to the Saṅgha, is not allowable for anyone. Some, however, say: “Because, having received an object for relinquishment, an allowable item purchased with it, when relinquished to the Saṅgha with the words, ‘I relinquish,’ is allowable to be used without any other means, therefore it is said, ‘No allowable item is to be purchased with that.’” “Or the share that has come to the monastery attendants” (ārāmikānaṃ vā pattabhāganti)—this is said on the grounds that even if it has come into the hands of laypeople, it is that same share. “But if the monastery attendants, having exchanged it for something else, give it, it is allowable to use it”; this is stated in the Majjhimagaṇṭhipada and the Cūḷagaṇṭhipada. “Having taken from that” (tato haritvā) means having taken it from the share that has come to others. “Preliminary work for the kasiṇa” (kasiṇaparikammanti) means the preliminary work for the light kasiṇa. “Or beds, chairs, etc.” (mañcapīṭhādīni vāti)—here they say: “If beds, chairs, etc., taken from that share are exchanged and something else is received, it is allowable.” “Even the shade” (chāyāpīti) means the shade of dining halls and so on. “Having gone beyond the boundary” (paricchedātikkantāti) means having gone beyond the boundary of the dwelling; the intention is that a place one has gone to in the shade is not called a dwelling. “Even by the path” (maggenapīti)—here they say: “If there is no other path, it is allowable to go, having determined upon the path.” “Purchased” (kītāyāti) means purchased with that object. “Having set aside the deposit, the Saṅgha uses the requisites” (upanikkhepaṃ ṭhapetvā saṅgho paccaye paribhuñjatīti)—if a lay follower says, “This gold and silver is too much, venerable sir, it should not be wasted today,” and he himself sets aside a deposit or has another set it aside, then having set aside this deposit, the Saṅgha uses the requisites by using the proceeds from it. Because it was received by means of that object, it is called “unallowable” (akappiyaṃ).

585. Patitokāsaṃ asamannāharantena pātetabbanti idaṃ nirapekkhabhāvadassanaparanti veditabbaṃ, tasmā patitaṭṭhāne ñātepissa gūthaṃ chaḍḍentassa viya nirapekkhabhāvoyevettha pamāṇanti veditabbaṃ. Asantasambhāvanāyāti attani avijjamānauttarimanussadhammārocanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Theyyaparibhogo nāma anarahassa paribhogo. Bhagavatā hi attano sāsane sīlavato paccayā anuññātā, na dussīlassa. Dāyakānampi sīlavato eva pariccāgo, na dussīlassa attano kārānaṃ mahapphalabhāvassa paccāsīsanato. Iti satthārā ananuññātattā dāyakehi ca apariccattattā dussīlassa paribhogo theyyaparibhogo. Iṇavasena paribhogo iṇaparibhogo, paṭiggāhakato dakkhiṇāvisuddhiyā abhāvato iṇaṃ gahetvā paribhogo viyāti attho. Tasmāti “sīlavato”tiādinā vuttamevatthaṃ kāraṇabhāvena paccāmasati. Cīvaraṃ paribhoge paribhogeti kāyato mocetvā mocetvā paribhoge. Purebhatta…pe… pacchimayāmesu paccavekkhitabbanti sambandho. Tathā asakkontena yathāvuttakālavisesavasena ekasmiṃ divase catukkhattuṃ tikkhattuṃ dvikkhattuṃ sakiṃyeva vā paccavekkhitabbaṃ.

585. 'It should be dropped without paying attention to the place where it has fallen'—this should be understood as a phrase showing a state of non-attachment. Therefore, even if the place where it fell is known, the standard here is simply a state of non-attachment, like one discarding feces. 'By imagining what is not real' is said with reference to announcing a superhuman state that is not present in oneself. 'Use as theft' is the use by one who is unworthy. For by the Blessed One, in his dispensation, requisites are permitted for the virtuous, not for the unvirtuous. For donors too, the relinquishment is only for the virtuous, not for the unvirtuous, because they hope for their own deeds to be of great fruit. Thus, because it is not permitted by the Teacher and not relinquished by the donors, the use by an unvirtuous person is 'use as theft.' 'Use as debt' is use in the manner of a debt. The meaning is that it is like using something after taking a loan, because of the absence of the purity of the offering on account of the recipient. 'Therefore' refers back to the meaning already stated, beginning with 'for the virtuous,' as the reason. 'Using the robe...' means using it after repeatedly removing it from the body. The connection is that it should be reflected upon 'before the meal... and in the last watches of the night.' Similarly, one who is unable to do so should reflect four times, three times, twice, or just once in a single day, according to the specific times mentioned.

Sacassa [M 2.0419] apaccavekkhatova aruṇo uggacchati, iṇaparibhogaṭṭhāne tiṭṭhatīti ettha “hiyyo yaṃ mayā cīvaraṃ paribhuttaṃ, taṃ yāvadeva sītassa paṭighātāya…pe… hirikopīnappaṭicchādanatthaṃ, hiyyo yo mayā piṇḍapāto paribhutto, so neva davāyātiādinā sace atītaparibhogapaccavekkhaṇaṃ na kareyya, iṇaparibhogaṭṭhāne tiṭṭhatī”ti vadanti, vīmaṃsitabbaṃ. Senāsanampi paribhoge paribhogeti pavese pavese. Evaṃ pana asakkontena purebhattādīsu paccavekkhitabbaṃ. Taṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva sakkā viññātunti idha visuṃ na vuttaṃ. Satipaccayatāti satiyā paccayabhāvo, paṭiggahaṇassa paribhogassa ca paccavekkhaṇasatiyā paccayabhāvo yujjati, paccavekkhitvāva paṭiggahetabbaṃ paribhuñjitabbañcāti attho. Tenevāha “satiṃ katvā”tiādi. Evaṃ santepīti yadipi dvīsupi ṭhānesu paccavekkhaṇā yuttā, evaṃ santepi. Apare panāhu “satipaccayatāti satibhesajjaparibhogassa paccayabhāve paccayeti attho. Evaṃ santepīti paccaye satipī”ti, taṃ tesaṃ matimattaṃ. Tathā hi paccayasannissitasīlaṃ paccavekkhaṇāya visujjhati, na paccayasabbhāvamattena.

If dawn arises for him while he has not reflected, he stands in the position of one who consumes a debt. Herein, some say: 'If one were not to perform the reflection on past consumption, saying, "Yesterday, the robe I used was solely for warding off cold... and for covering the parts that cause shame and fear; yesterday, the almsfood I consumed was not for amusement," and so on, one stands in the position of one who consumes a debt.' This should be investigated. And as for lodging, 'in using, in using' means each time one enters. However, by one who is unable to do so, it should be reflected upon before the meal and so on. That can be known by the method stated above, so it is not stated separately here. As for 'mindfulness as a condition' (satipaccayatā), it is the state of mindfulness being a condition; it is fitting that the mindfulness of reflection is a condition for both receiving and using. The meaning is that one should receive and use only after having reflected. Therefore, he said, 'having established mindfulness,' etc. As for 'even so' (evaṃ santepi): although reflection is appropriate in both instances, even so... Other teachers, however, say: 'As for satipaccayatā, the meaning is: when there is a condition (sati paccaye), that is, when there is a condition for the use of medicine.' And 'even so' (evaṃ santepi) means 'even when there is a condition' (paccaye satipi). That is merely their opinion. For it is true that morality dependent on requisites is purified by reflection, not by the mere existence of the requisites.

Nanu ca “paribhoge karontassa anāpattī”ti iminā pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlaṃ vuttaṃ, tasmā [V 2.0371] paccayasannissitasīlassa pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlassa ca ko visesoti? Vuccate – purimesu tāva tīsu paccayesu viseso pākaṭoyeva, gilānapaccaye pana yathā vatiṃ katvā rukkhamūle gopite tassa phalānipi rakkhitāniyeva honti, evameva paccavekkhaṇāya paccayasannissitasīle rakkhite tappaṭibaddhaṃ pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlampi nipphannaṃ nāma hoti. Gilānapaccayaṃ apaccavekkhitvā paribhuñjantassa sīlaṃ bhijjamānaṃ pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlameva bhijjati, paccayasannissitasīlaṃ pana pacchābhattapurimayāmādīsu yāva aruṇuggamanā apaccavekkhantasseva bhijjati. Purebhattañhi apaccavekkhitvāpi gilānapaccayaṃ paribhuñjantassa anāpatti, idametesaṃ nānākaraṇaṃ.

Is it not so that by this statement, 'There is no offense for one who is using a requisite,' the morality of Pātimokkha restraint is stated? Therefore, what is the difference between the morality dependent on requisites and the morality of Pātimokkha restraint? It is said: First, in the former three requisites, the difference is quite evident. But regarding the requisite for the sick, just as when the root of a tree is protected by making a fence, its fruits are also protected, even so, when the morality dependent on requisites is protected by reflection, the morality of Pātimokkha restraint connected to it is also accomplished. For one who uses the requisite for the sick without reflecting, when his morality is broken, it is only the morality of Pātimokkha restraint that is broken. But the morality dependent on requisites is broken only for one who does not reflect from after the meal, during the first watch of the night, and so on, until the rising of the dawn. For there is no offense for one who uses the requisite for the sick before the meal, even without reflecting. This is the distinction between them.

Evaṃ paccayasannissitasīlassa visuddhiṃ dassetvā teneva pasaṅgena sabbāpi suddhiyo dassetuṃ “catubbidhā hi suddhī”tiādimāha. Tattha sujjhati etāyāti suddhi, yathādhammaṃ desanāva suddhi desanāsuddhi. Vuṭṭhānassapi cettha desanāya eva saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Chinnamūlāpattīnaṃ pana abhikkhutāpaṭiññāva desanā. Adhiṭṭhānavisiṭṭho saṃvarova suddhi saṃvarasuddhi. Dhammena samena [M 2.0420] paccayānaṃ pariyeṭṭhi eva suddhi pariyeṭṭhisuddhi. Catūsu paccayesu vuttavidhinā paccavekkhaṇāva suddhi paccavekkhaṇasuddhi. Esa tāva suddhīsu samāsanayo. Suddhimantesu sīlesu desanā suddhi etassāti desanāsuddhi. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Na puna evaṃ karissāmīti ettha evanti saṃvarabhedaṃ sandhāyāha. Pahāyāti vajjetvā, akatvāti attho. Dātabbaṭṭhena dāyaṃ, taṃ ādiyantīti dāyādā, ananuññātesu sabbena sabbaṃ paribhogābhāvato anuññātesuyeva ca paribhogasabbhāvabhāvato bhikkhūhi paribhuñjitabbapaccayā bhagavato santakā. Dhammadāyādasuttañcettha sādhakanti –

Thus, having shown the purity of the morality dependent on requisites, by that same connection, in order to show all the purities, he said, 'For purity is fourfold,' and so on. Herein, 'one is purified by this,' thus it is 'purity'; the teaching according to the Dhamma itself is purity—this is 'purity of teaching.' And here, emergence from an offense should be understood as included in 'teaching' itself. For those with offenses cut off at the root, however, the declaration of no longer being a bhikkhu is itself the 'teaching.' Restraint distinguished by determination is purity—this is 'purity of restraint.' The search for requisites in accordance with the Dhamma and with equity is purity—this is 'purity of search.' Reflection on the four requisites according to the stated method is purity—this is 'purity of reflection.' This, first, is the concise method regarding the purities. Among the moralities that possess purity, 'teaching is the purity of this one,' thus it is 'purity of teaching.' This same method applies to the rest as well. In the phrase 'I will not do so again,' the word 'so' is said in reference to the breach of restraint. 'Having abandoned' means having avoided, that is, not doing. An inheritance is so called in the sense of 'that which is to be given'; 'they receive that,' thus they are 'heirs.' Because there is absolutely no use of what is not permitted, and because use is possible only for what is permitted, the requisites to be used by the bhikkhus are the property of the Blessed One. And the Dhammadāyāda Sutta is evidence for this:

“Dhammadāyādā me, bhikkhave, bhavatha, mā āmisadāyādā. Atthi me tumhesu anukampā, ‘kinti me sāvakā dhammadāyādā bhaveyyuṃ, no āmisadāyādā’”ti (ma. ni. 1.29) –

“Be my heirs in the Dhamma, bhikkhus, not heirs in material things. I have compassion for you, thinking, ‘How may my disciples be heirs in the Dhamma, not heirs in material things?’”

Evaṃ pavattaṃ dhammadāyādasuttañca ettha etasmiṃ atthe sādhakaṃ.

Thus, the Dhammadāyāda Sutta, which proceeds in this way, is evidence for this meaning here.

Avītarāgānaṃ taṇhāparavasatāya paccayaparibhoge sāmibhāvo natthi, tadabhāvena vītarāgānaṃ tattha sāmibhāvo yathāruci paribhogasabbhāvato. Tathā hi te paṭikūlampi appaṭikūlākārena appaṭikūlampi paṭikūlākārena tadubhayampi vajjetvā ajjhupekkhanākārena paccaye [V 2.0372] paribhuñjanti, dāyakānañca manorathaṃ paripūrenti. Tenāha – “te hi taṇhāya dāsabyaṃ atītattā sāmino hutvā paribhuñjantī”ti. Yo panāyaṃ sīlavato paccavekkhitaparibhogo, so iṇaparibhogassa paccanīkattā āṇaṇyaparibhogo nāma hoti. Yathā hi iṇāyiko attano ruciyā icchitadesaṃ gantuṃ na labhati, evaṃ iṇaparibhogayutto lokato nissarituṃ na labhatīti tappaṭipakkhattā sīlavato paccavekkhitaparibhogo āṇaṇyaparibhogoti vuccati, tasmā nippariyāyato catuparibhogavinimutto visuṃyevāyaṃ paribhogoti veditabbo. So idha visuṃ na vutto, dāyajjaparibhogeyeva vā saṅgahaṃ gacchatīti. Sīlavāpi hi imāya sikkhāya samannāgatattā sekkhotveva vuccati. Sabbesanti ariyānaṃ puthujjanānañca.

For those not free from lust, because of their subservience to craving, there is no mastery in the use of requisites. Due to the absence of that subservience, for those free from lust, there is mastery in that use, because it is possible for them to use requisites as they wish. Indeed, they use requisites by regarding the disagreeable as agreeable, the agreeable as disagreeable, or, having avoided both, by regarding them with equanimity, and they fulfill the wishes of the donors. Therefore, it is said: 'For they, having transcended slavery to craving, use requisites having become masters.' Now, this use with reflection by a virtuous one is called 'use free from debt' because it is the opposite of 'use as a debt.' For just as a debtor is not able to go to a desired place according to his own wish, so too one who engages in use as a debt is not able to escape from the world. Because it is the opposite of that, the use with reflection by a virtuous one is called 'use free from debt.' Therefore, it should be known that this use is absolutely distinct, being liberated from the four kinds of use. It is not stated separately here, or it is included in the 'use as an inheritance.' For even a virtuous one, because of being endowed with this training, is called a 'learner.' 'Of all' means of both noble ones and worldlings.

Kathaṃ [M 2.0421] puthujjanānaṃ ime paribhogā sambhavantīti? Upacāravasena. Yo hi puthujjanassapi sallekhappaṭipattiyaṃ ṭhitassa paccayagedhaṃ pahāya tattha anupalittena cittena paribhogo, so sāmiparibhogo viya hoti. Sīlavato pana paccavekkhitaparibhogo dāyajjaparibhogo viya hoti dāyakānaṃ manorathassa avirādhanato. Teneva vuttaṃ “dāyajjaparibhogeyeva vā saṅgahaṃ gacchatī”ti. Kalyāṇaputhujjanassa paribhoge vattabbameva natthi tassa sekkhasaṅgahato. Sekkhasuttañhetassa atthassa sādhakaṃ.

How do these uses come to be for worldlings? By way of figurative speech. For the use by even a worldling who is established in the practice of effacement—having abandoned greed for requisites and using them with an unstained mind—is like the use of a master. For a virtuous person, however, use with reflection is like the use as an inheritance, because it does not frustrate the wishes of the donors. Therefore, it is said: “Or it is included in the use as an inheritance.” Regarding the use by a virtuous worldling, there is nothing to be said, because he is included among the learners. The Sekkha Sutta is indeed proof of this meaning.

Lajjinā saddhiṃ paribhogo nāma lajjissa santakaṃ gahetvā paribhogo. Alajjinā saddhinti etthāpi eseva nayo. Ādito paṭṭhāya hi alajjī nāma natthīti iminā diṭṭhadiṭṭhesuyeva āsaṅkā na kātabbāti dasseti. Attano bhārabhūtā saddhivihārikādayo. Sopi nivāretabboti yo passati, tena nivāretabbo. Yasmā alajjīparibhogo nāma lajjino vuccati, tasmā āpatti nāma natthi ubhinnampi alajjībhāvato, “alajjīparibhogo”ti idaṃ nāmamattameva na labbhatīti vuttaṃ hoti. “Āpatti pana atthiyevāti vadantī”ti tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ.

'Use with a conscientious person' means taking and using what belongs to a conscientious person. Regarding 'with a shameless person,' here too the same method applies. By the phrase 'from the outset there is no such thing as a shameless person,' it is shown that suspicion should not be entertained in every single thing that is seen. One's own burdensome co-residents and others—he who sees should prevent them. Because 'use with a shameless one' is said of a conscientious one, therefore there is no offense for either, due to their being shameless. Thus it is said that this term 'use with a shameless one' is a mere name and is not applicable. 'But an offense does indeed exist, they say'—this is stated in all three knot-passages.

Adhammiyoti anesanādīhi uppanno. Dhammiyoti bhikkhācariyādīhi uppanno. Saṅghasseva detīti bhattaṃ aggahetvā attanā laddhasalākaṃyeva deti. Sace pana lajjī alajjiṃ paggaṇhāti…pe… antaradhāpetīti ettha kevalaṃ paggaṇhitukāmatāya evaṃ kātuṃ na vaṭṭati, dhammassa pana sāsanassa sotūnañca anuggahatthāya vaṭṭatīti veditabbaṃ. Purimanayena “so āpattiyā kāretabbo”ti vuttattā imassa āpattiyevāti vadanti. Uddesaggahaṇādinā dhammassa paribhogo dhammaparibhogo. Dhammānuggahena gaṇhantassa āpattiyā abhāvepi thero tassa alajjibhāvaṃyeva [V 2.0373] sandhāya “pāpo kirāya”ntiādimāha. Tassa pana santiketi mahārakkhitattherassa santike.

'Unrighteous' means that which is obtained through improper seeking and so on. 'Righteous' means that which is obtained through the alms-round and so on. 'He gives only to the Sangha' means that, not taking the food portion, he gives only the ticket he himself has received. Regarding 'But if a conscientious one supports a shameless one... causes it to disappear,' here it is not proper to act thus merely out of a desire to support. It should be understood, however, that it is proper for the sake of benefiting the Dhamma, the Dispensation, and the listeners. Because it was said according to the previous method, 'He should be dealt with for the offense,' they say that for this one there is indeed an offense. The use of the Dhamma by means of learning the text and so on is 'use of the Dhamma.' Even though there is no offense for one who accepts for the benefit of the Dhamma, the Elder, referring only to that one's shamelessness, said, 'He is indeed wicked,' and so on. 'Near him' means near the Elder Mahārakkhita.

586. Rājorodhādayotiādi “idaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti cetanāmattasambhavato vuttaṃ. Assatiyā dinnanti ettha assatiyā dinnaṃ nāma apariccattaṃ hoti, tasmā dasante baddhakahāpaṇādi assatiyā dinnaṃ bhikkhunā [M 2.0422] vatthasaññāya paṭiggahitañca, tato neva rūpiyaṃ dinnaṃ, nāpi paṭiggahitañca hotīti ettha āpattidesanākiccaṃ natthi, taṃ pana dāyakānameva paṭidātabbaṃ. Tena akappiyavatthunā te ce dāyakā sappiādīni kiṇitvāna saṅghassa tassa ca bhikkhuno denti, sabbesaṃ kappati dāyakānaṃyeva santakattā. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana puññakāmehi pariccajitvā dinnameva sandhāya “puññakāmā…pe… rūpiye arūpiyasaññī rūpiyaṃ paṭiggaṇhātīti veditabbo”ti vuttaṃ, tasmā pariccajitvā dinnaṃ vatthasaññāya gaṇhatopi nissaggiyameva. Tena yadi te dāyakā no āgantvā gaṇhanti, dāyake pucchitvā attano atthāya ce pariccattaṃ, saṅghe nissajjitvā āpatti desetabbā. Tava coḷakaṃ passāhīhi iminā gihisantakepi “idaṃ gaṇhathā”tiādiakappiyavohārena vidhānaṃ bhikkhuno na kappatīti dīpeti. Ekaparicchedānīti kiriyākiriyabhāvato ekaparicchedāni. Jātarūparajatabhāvo, attuddesikatā, kahāpaṇādīsu aññatarabhāvoti imānettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

586. The phrase 'the king's harem, etc.' is stated because of the mere arising of the intention, 'I will take this.' Regarding the phrase 'given unmindfully,' what is given unmindfully is un-relinquished. Therefore, if coins, etc., tied in the corner of a robe are given unmindfully and a bhikkhu accepts them with the perception of them being cloth, then gold and silver are neither given nor accepted. In this case, there is no duty to confess an offense; it should be returned to the donors themselves. If those donors, with that unallowable item, buy ghee, etc., and give it to the Sangha and to that bhikkhu, it is allowable for all, because it is the property of the donors themselves. In the Commentary, however, referring to what is given by merit-seekers after having relinquished it, it is said: 'Merit-seekers...pe... one who, perceiving it as not being gold and silver, accepts gold and silver, it should be known...' Therefore, for one who accepts what was given after relinquishment with the perception of it being cloth, it is indeed an offense of forfeiture. For that reason, if those donors do not come and take it, after asking the donors, if it was relinquished for one's own benefit, one must forfeit it in the midst of the Sangha and confess the offense. By the phrase 'Look at your rag!', it is shown that it is not allowable for a bhikkhu to make arrangements concerning a layperson's property with unallowable speech such as 'Take this.' 'Of a single determination' means they are of a single determination because of being an action or non-action. The state of being gold and silver, being designated for oneself, and being one or another among coins, etc.—these are the three factors here.

Rūpiyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule concerning gold and silver is concluded.

9. Rūpiyasaṃvohārasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

9. Explanation of the Training Rule on Transactions involving Gold and Silver

587. Rūpiyasaṃvohārasikkhāpade jātarūpādicatubbidhampi nissaggiyavatthu idha rūpiyaggahaṇeneva gahitanti āha “jātarūparajataparivattana”nti. Paṭiggahitaparivattaneti sāditarūpiyassa parivattane, asādiyitvā vā kappiyena gāhena paṭiggahitarūpiyaparivattane.

587. In the training rule on transactions involving gold and silver, it is said that the four kinds of forfeitable items, beginning with gold, are included here by the term for gold and silver (`rūpiya`), as in 'exchange of gold and silver'. 'Regarding the exchange of what is received' means: in the exchange of gold and silver (`rūpiya`) that has been consented to, or in the exchange of gold and silver (`rūpiya`) received through an allowable procedure without having consented to it.

589. Ga-kārassa ka-kāraṃ katvā “sīsūpaka”nti likhitaṃ, padabhājane ghanakatanti piṇḍaṃ kataṃ. Satthuvaṇṇotiādīsu “satthuvaṇṇo ca kahāpaṇo ca…pe… ye ca vohāraṃ gacchantī”ti evaṃ sabbattha samuccayo veditabbo. Rūpiye rūpiyasaññīti sakasantakaṃ vadati. Rūpiyaṃ cetāpetīti parasantakaṃ vadati. “Nissaggiyavatthunā dukkaṭavatthuṃ vā kappiyavatthuṃ vā cetāpentassapi eseva nayo”ti idaṃ kasmā vuttaṃ. Na [M 2.0423] hi “rūpiye rūpiyasaññī arūpiyaṃ cetāpeti[V 2.0374], nissaggiyaṃ pācittiya”ntiādittiko pāḷiyaṃ vuttoti āha “yo hī”tiādi. Tassānulomattāti etthāyamadhippāyo – rūpiyasaṃvohāro nāma na kevalaṃ rūpiyena rūpiyaparivattanameva, atha kho “arūpiye rūpiyasaññī rūpiyaṃ cetāpetī”ti vuttattā arūpiyena rūpiyacetāpanampi rūpiyasaṃvohāro nāma hotīti etasmiṃ pakkhepi rūpiye sati rūpiyasaṃvohāroyeva hotīti ayamattho avuttopi viññāyatīti. Arūpiyaṃ nāma dukkaṭavatthukappiyavatthūni. Ekantena rūpiyapakkheti ekena antena rūpiyapakkheti ayaṃ attho gahetabbo. “Ekato rūpiyapakkhe”ti vā pāṭho veditabbo. “Ekarūpiyapakkhe”tipi paṭhanti, tatthāpi ekato rūpiyapakkheti ayamevattho gahetabbo.

589. By changing the letter 'ga' to 'ka', it is written as 'sīsūpaka'. In the word-analysis, 'ghanakataṃ' means 'made into a lump'. In phrases like 'satthuvaṇṇo', it should be understood that everywhere there is a conjunction, such as: 'the color similar to the Teacher's complexion and the kahāpaṇa coin… and those who engage in trade'. 'Perceiving it as 'rūpiya' when it is 'rūpiya'' refers to one's own property. 'Causes 'rūpiya' to be exchanged' refers to another's property. Why was it said, 'For one who causes a `dukkaṭa` item or an allowable item to be exchanged with a forfeitable item, this same principle applies'? Because the triad beginning with, 'If, perceiving it as 'rūpiya' when it is 'rūpiya', one causes what is not 'rūpiya' to be exchanged, it is a forfeitable offense of expiation' is not stated in the Pāḷi. Therefore, it says 'yo hi', and so on. Herein, in 'Because it is in accordance with that', this is the intention: a 'monetary transaction' is not merely the exchange of 'rūpiya' with 'rūpiya'. Rather, because it is said, 'perceiving what is not 'rūpiya' as 'rūpiya', one causes 'rūpiya' to be exchanged', causing 'rūpiya' to be exchanged with what is not 'rūpiya' is also called a 'monetary transaction'. Thus, in this case as well, when 'rūpiya' is present, it is indeed a 'monetary transaction'. This meaning is understood even if unstated. 'What is not 'rūpiya'' refers to items that are a `dukkaṭa` offense and allowable items. 'Ekantena rūpiyapakkhe' should be taken to mean 'exclusively on the side of 'rūpiya''. Alternatively, the reading should be understood as 'ekato rūpiyapakkhe'. Some also read it as 'ekarūpiyapakkhe'; there too, this same meaning should be taken: 'on one side, in the case of 'rūpiya''.

Kappiyavatthunā kappiyavatthuno kayavikkayepi tāva nissaggiyaṃ hoti, dukkaṭavatthunā dukkaṭavatthuno kayavikkaye kasmā na hotīti andhakaṭṭhakathāya adhippāyo. Idaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ…pe… arūpiyena ca rūpiyacetāpanaṃ sandhāya vuttanti sambandho. Idhāti imasmiṃ rūpiyasaṃvohārasikkhāpade. Tatthāti kayavikkayasikkhāpade. Tenevāti kappiyavatthunāyeva.

The intention of the Andhaka commentary is: 'In the buying and selling of an allowable item with an allowable item, a `nissaggiya` offense occurs; but why does it not occur in the buying and selling of an item entailing a `dukkaṭa` offense with an item entailing a `dukkaṭa` offense?' This training rule… was stated with reference to causing 'rūpiya' to be exchanged with what is not 'rūpiya'; thus the connection should be made. 'Here' means in this training rule on monetary transactions. 'There' means in the training rule on buying and selling. 'By that very thing' means by an allowable item itself.

Puna kappiyabhāvaṃ netuṃ asakkuṇeyyattā “mahāakappiyo nāmā”ti vuttaṃ. “Na sakkā kenaci upāyena kappiyo kātunti idaṃ pañcannaṃyeva sahadhammikānaṃ antare parivattanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, gihīhi pana gahetvā attano santakaṃ katvā dinnaṃ sabbesaṃ kappatī”ti vadanti. “Na sakkā kenaci upāyena kappiyo kātu”nti pana imināva paṭiggahitarūpiyaṃ anissajjitvāva tena cetāpitaṃ kappiyabhaṇḍampi saṅghassa nissaṭṭhaṃ paribhuñjituṃ na vaṭṭatīti siddhaṃ.

Furthermore, because it was impossible to lead it back to an allowable state, it was said, 'It is called greatly unallowable.' The statement, 'It cannot be made allowable by any means,' was said with reference to exchange among only the five co-religionists. However, they say, 'What is given by laypeople, after they have taken it and made it their own property, is allowable for all.' But by this very statement, 'It cannot be made allowable by any means,' it is established that an allowable requisite purchased with that received 'rūpiya'—without having relinquished it—is not fit to be used, even if relinquished to the Saṅgha.

Ye pana “paṭiggahitarūpiyaṃ anissajjitvāpi tena parivattitaṃ kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ saṅghassa nissaṭṭhaṃ paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti, tesaṃ “na sakkā kenaci upāyena kappiyo kātu”nti idaṃ na yujjati. Te panettha evaṃ vadanti “yasmā nissajjitabbavatthuṃ anissajjitvāva uparūpari aññaṃ aññaṃyeva kataṃ, tasmā paricchedābhāvato idha nissajjituṃ avatvā ‘na sakkā kenaci upāyena kappiyo kātu’nti vuttaṃ, paricchedābhāvatoyeva ‘mūle mūlasāmikānaṃ[M 2.0424], patte ca pattasāmikānaṃ dinne kappiyo hotī’ti ca na vutta”nti. Yadi paṭiggahitarūpiyaṃ anissajjitvā cetāpitaṃ kappiyabhaṇḍampi saṅghassa nissaṭṭhaṃ paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati, evaṃ sante idhāpi avasānavatthuṃ gahetvā saṅghassa nissaṭṭhaṃ kasmā na vaṭṭati, “yo pana rūpiyaṃ uggaṇhitvā…pe… patte ca pattasāmikānaṃ dinne kappiyo hotī”ti imināpi paṭiggahitarūpiyaṃ [V 2.0375] anissajjitvā cetāpitaṃ kappiyabhaṇḍampi saṅghassa nissaṭṭhaṃ paribhuñjituṃ na vaṭṭatīti siddhaṃ. Yadi taṃ nissaṭṭhaṃ paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭeyya, “mūle mūlasāmikānaṃ, patte ca pattasāmikānaṃ dinne kappiyo hotī”ti na vadeyya. Apare panettha evaṃ vadanti “yadi saṅghassa nissaṭṭhaṃ hoti, rūpiyapaṭiggāhakassa na vaṭṭati, tasmā tassapi yathā vaṭṭati, tathā dassanatthaṃ ‘mūle mūlasāmikāna’ntiādi vutta”nti.

As for those who say, 'Even without relinquishing the received 'rūpiya', it is allowable to use an allowable requisite exchanged with it, after it has been relinquished to the Saṅgha,' for them, this statement, 'It cannot be made allowable by any means,' is not tenable. Herein, those teachers say thus: 'Because, without relinquishing the item that should be relinquished, one new thing after another has been made, therefore, due to the lack of a demarcation, without speaking of relinquishing it here, it was said, 'It cannot be made allowable by any means.' And it is because of this lack of demarcation that it was also not said, 'It becomes allowable when the root item is given to the original owners, and the bowl to the owners of the bowl.' If it were allowable to use an allowable requisite procured without relinquishing the received 'rūpiya', after it has been relinquished to the Saṅgha, this being the case, why would it not be allowable here also to take the final item and relinquish it to the Saṅgha? By this text, 'But whoever, having accepted 'rūpiya'… it becomes allowable when the bowl is given to the owners of the bowl,' it is established that an allowable requisite procured without relinquishing the received 'rūpiya' is not allowable to be used, even if relinquished to the Saṅgha. If it were allowable to use that relinquished item, it would not have been said, 'It becomes allowable when the root item is given to the original owners, and the bowl to the owners of the bowl.' Herein, other teachers say thus: 'If it is relinquished to the Saṅgha, it is not allowable for the one who accepted the 'rūpiya'. Therefore, in order to show how it becomes allowable for that person also, it was said, 'The root item to the original owners,' and so on.'

Dutiyapattasadisoyevāti iminā pañcannampi sahadhammikānaṃ na kappatīti dasseti. Tattha kāraṇamāha “mūlassa sampaṭicchitattā”ti. Atha mūlassa sampaṭicchitattā rūpiyapaṭiggāhakassa tāva akappiyo hotu, sesānaṃ pana kasmā na kappatīti maññamāno pucchati “kasmā sesānaṃ na kappatī”ti. Kāraṇamāha “mūlassa anissaṭṭhattā”ti. Pattassa kappiyabhāvepi sampaṭicchitamūlassa nissajjitabbassa anissaṭṭhattā tena gahitapatto sesānampi na kappati. Yadi hi tena sampaṭicchitamūlaṃ saṅghamajjhe nissaṭṭhaṃ siyā, tena kappiyena kammena ārāmikādīhi gahetvā dinnapatto rūpiyapaṭiggāhakaṃ ṭhapetvā sesānaṃ vaṭṭati. Apare pana “mūlaṃ sampaṭicchitvā gahitapattopi yadi saṅghassa nissaṭṭho, sesānaṃ kappatī”ti vadanti. Evaṃ sante “mūlassa anissaṭṭhattā”ti na vattabbaṃ, “saṅghassa anissaṭṭhattā”ti evameva vattabbaṃ.

By 'just like the second bowl,' it is shown that it is not allowable for any of the five co-religionists. Here, the reason is stated: 'because the price was accepted.' Now, granted that because the price was accepted, it is unallowable for the one who received the money, but thinking thus, why is it not allowable for the others? One asks, 'Why is it not allowable for the others?' The reason is stated: 'because the price was not relinquished.' Even if the bowl itself is an allowable object, since the accepted price, which should have been relinquished, was not relinquished, the bowl taken by him is not allowable for the others either. For if that accepted price had been relinquished in the midst of the Saṅgha, then the bowl, taken by the monastery attendants and others through an allowable act and given, would be allowable for the others, except for the one who received the money. Others, however, say: 'Even if the bowl was taken after accepting the price, if it has been relinquished to the Saṅgha, it is allowable for the others.' If this is the case, then it should not be said, 'because the price was not relinquished,' but rather, 'because it was not relinquished to the Saṅgha.' This is what should be said.

Dubbicāritattāti iminā rūpiyasaṃvohāro anena katoti dasseti. Aññesaṃ pana vaṭṭatīti yasmānena rūpiyasaṃvohāramattameva kataṃ, na mūlaṃ sampaṭicchitaṃ, tasmā vinayakammavasena saṅghassa nissaṭṭhakālato paṭṭhāya aññesaṃ vaṭṭati. Imasmiṃyeva ca atthe pamāṇaṃ dassento “mahāsumattherassa kirā”tiādimāha. Apare pana “dubbicāritattāti iminā kevalaṃ gihisantakabhāvena ṭhite dubbicāritamattaṃ vuttaṃ, na rūpiyasaṃvohārāpajjanaṃ, tasmā rūpiyasaṃvohārābhāvato so patto nissajjituṃ na sakkāti tassa na kappati, anissaṭṭhopi aññesaṃ [M 2.0425] kappati. Anissaṭṭhasseva ca aññesaṃ kappiyabhāvadassanatthaṃ ‘mahāsumattherassa kirā’tiādivatthūni udāhaṭāni. Saṅghassa nissajjīti idañca aññesaṃ kappiyattā kevalaṃ saṅghassa pariccattabhāvaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, na pana vinayakammavasena saṅghassa nissaṭṭhabhāvaṃ. Imassa ca atthassa sappissa pūretvāti idaṃ vacanaṃ sādhaka”nti vadanti.

By 'due to misconduct,' it is shown that he engaged in a monetary transaction. But it is allowable for others because he only engaged in the monetary transaction and did not accept the principal; therefore, from the time it was relinquished to the Sangha by means of a formal act of the Vinaya, it is allowable for others. And in this very matter, wishing to show the authority, he says, 'It is said of the Elder Mahāsumana,' and so on. Others, however, say: 'By "due to misconduct," merely the misconduct while it remained the property of a layperson is stated, not the incurring of a monetary transaction. Therefore, due to the absence of a monetary transaction, that bowl cannot be relinquished, so it is not allowable for him, but even if un-relinquished, it is allowable for others.' And in order to show the state of being allowable for others even when it is un-relinquished, the stories beginning with 'It is said of the Elder Mahāsumana' are cited. And this phrase 'relinquished to the Sangha' is said with reference merely to the state of being surrendered to the Sangha, because of its allowability for others, and not with reference to the state of being relinquished to the Sangha by means of a formal act of the Vinaya. And the statement 'having filled it with ghee' is proof of this meaning,' they say.

591. Rūpiyapaṭiggahaṇarūpiyasaṃvohāresu yena ekekameva kataṃ, tena tattha tattha vuttanayeneva nissajjitabbaṃ. Yena pana paṭiggahitarūpiyeneva saṃvohāro kato, tena kathaṃ nissajjitabbanti? Nayidaṃ dukkaraṃ, “ahaṃ, bhante, nānappakārakaṃ rūpiyasaṃvohāraṃ samāpajji”nti evameva [V 2.0376] nissajjitabbaṃ. “Imasmiṃ sikkhāpadepi ‘arūpiye rūpiyasaññī, āpatti dukkaṭassā’tiādittikassa avasānapade anāpattiyā vuttattā kappiyavatthuvaseneva idaṃ tikaṃ vutta”nti tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Keci pana “arūpiyaggahaṇena kappiyavatthudukkaṭavatthūnaṃ saṅgahoti purimapadadvayaṃ kappiyavatthudukkaṭavatthūnaṃ vasena vuttaṃ, avasānapadameva kappiyavatthuvasena vutta”nti vadanti, taṃ na yujjati anāpattimissite avasānattike saññānānattaṃ ṭhapetvā vatthunānattassa abhāvato. Dukkaṭavatthunā pana dukkaṭavatthuno cetāpanaṃ neva idha, na tattha pāḷiyaṃ vuttanti vacanamettha sādhakaṃ. Yaṃ attano dhanena parivattati, tassa vā dhanassa vā rūpiyabhāvo ceva, parivattanañcāti imānettha dve aṅgāni.

591. In the cases of accepting money and monetary transactions, when only one or the other was done, it should be relinquished in the manner stated in each respective case. But when a transaction was done with the very money that was accepted, how should it be relinquished by that monk? This is not difficult; it should be relinquished just by saying, 'Venerable sir, I have engaged in various kinds of monetary transactions.' In this training rule, it is stated in all three commentaries that this triad is spoken only by way of an allowable object, because in the final clause of the triad beginning with 'perceiving what is not money as money, there is an offense of wrong conduct,' 'no offense' is stated. Some, however, say: 'By the term "non-money," allowable objects and objects of wrong conduct are included; thus the first two clauses are stated with reference to allowable objects and objects of wrong conduct, and only the final clause is stated with reference to an allowable object.' That is not tenable, because in the final triad, which is mixed with a 'no offense' ruling, there is no difference in the object, setting aside the difference in perception. The statement that the exchange of an object of wrong conduct by means of an object of wrong conduct is stated neither here, nor there in the Pāḷi, is proof in this matter. When one exchanges with one's own property, there are two factors here: both the state of that property as money, and the exchange itself.

Rūpiyasaṃvohārasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule concerning monetary transactions is concluded.

10. Kayavikkayasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

10. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Buying and Selling

593. Kayavikkayasikkhāpade pāḷiyaṃ jānāhīti ettha upadhārehīti attho, suṭṭhu upadhāretvā gaṇha, idaṃ na manāpanti puna dātuṃ na sakkhissasīti adhippāyo.

593. In the Pāḷi of the training rule on buying and selling, herein, in the word 'jānāhi', the meaning is 'upadhārehi' (pay attention). Take it after considering it well. The intention is: 'This is not pleasing; you will not be able to give it back again.'

594-595. Kayanti parabhaṇḍassa gahaṇaṃ. Vikkayanti attano bhaṇḍassa dānaṃ. Tenāha “iminā imaṃ dehī”tiādi. Yasmā kayitaṃ nāma parassa [M 2.0426] hatthato gahitaṃ vuccati, vikkītañca parassa hatthe dinnaṃ, tasmā “kayitañca hoti parabhaṇḍaṃ attano hatthagataṃ karontena, vikkītañca attano bhaṇḍaṃ parahatthagataṃ karontenā”ti vuttaṃ. Yadi evaṃ pāḷiyaṃ parato “kayitañca hoti vikkayitañcā”ti vatvā “attano bhaṇḍaṃ parahatthagataṃ parabhaṇḍaṃ attano hatthagata”nti kasmā vuttanti āha “iminā imantiādivacanānurūpato panā”tiādi. Imināti hi sakasantakaṃ vuttaṃ. Tadanurūpato pāḷiyaṃ paṭhamaṃ attano bhaṇḍaṃ dassitaṃ, na kayavikkayapadānurūpato. Tañhi viparītato parasantakaggahaṇaṃ purakkhatvā ṭhitaṃ.

'Buying' is the taking of another's goods. 'Selling' is the giving of one's own goods. Therefore, he said, 'Give me this for that,' etc. Because what is called 'bought' is said to be what is taken from another's hand, and what is 'sold' is said to be what is given into another's hand, therefore it is said, 'There is buying by one who makes another's goods come into one's own hand, and there is selling by one who makes one's own goods go into another's hand.' If this is so, then why, after stating in the Pāḷi, 'there is buying and there is selling,' is it further said, 'one's own goods going into another's hand, and another's goods coming into one's own hand'? He said: 'But it is in accordance with the statement "Give me this for that," etc.' For by 'iminā' (by this), one's own possession is meant. Accordingly, in the Pāḷi, one's own goods are shown first, not in accordance with the order of the words 'buying and selling.' For that stands in reverse, giving priority to the taking of another's possession.

Kāmaṃ sesañātakepi “imaṃ dehī”ti vadato viññatti na hoti, saddhādeyyavinipātanassapi pana abhāvaṃ dassetukāmo “mātaraṃ pana pitaraṃ vā”ti āha. Viññatti na hotīti idaṃ visuṃ viññāpanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Aññaṃ kiñci avatvā evaṃ vadanto aññātakaṃ viññāpeti nāmāti āha – “aññātakaṃ ‘imaṃ dehī’ti vadato viññattī”ti. [V 2.0377] Aññaṃ kiñci avatvā “imaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti dinnaṃ aññātakassa dinnaṃ nāma hotīti vuttaṃ “saddhādeyyavinipātana”nti. Tisso āpattiyoti aññātakaviññattisaddhādeyyavinipātanakayavikkayāpattisaṅkhātā tisso āpattiyo.

Granted, even in the case of other relatives, for one who says, 'Give this,' there is no solicitation. However, wishing to show also the absence of squandering what is given in faith, he said, 'but a mother or a father.' The statement 'There is no solicitation' was said referring to a distinct act of soliciting. Without saying anything else, one who speaks thus indeed solicits a non-relative; thus he says: 'For one who says to a non-relative, "Give this," there is solicitation.' Without saying anything else, what is given with the words, 'Take this,' is indeed what is given to a non-relative; this is called 'squandering what is given in faith.' As to 'three offenses': these are the three offenses reckoned as soliciting a non-relative, squandering what is given in faith, and buying and selling.

Imaṃ nāma karohīti vadati, vaṭṭatīti ettha bhuttosi, idāni kasmā na karosīti vatthumpi vaṭṭati. “Nissaggiyaṃ pācittiya”nti kiñcāpi satiyeva nissaggiyavatthumhi pācittiyaṃ vuttaṃ, asatipi pana tasmiṃ pācittiyanti idaṃ aṭṭhakathāpamāṇena gahetabbanti dassetuṃ “kiñcāpī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Paribhutteti sappiādiṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Yaṃ attano dhanena parivatteti, yena ca parivatteti, tesaṃ kappiyavatthutā, asahadhammikatā, kayavikkayāpajjanañcāti imānettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

He says, 'Do this thing.' Herein, it is allowable; it is also allowable to say, 'You have eaten, now why do you not do it?' Although an offense entailing expiation is stated only when there is an item to be relinquished, in order to show that there is an offense of expiation even when that item is not present—and that this should be understood according to the authority of the commentary—it is said, 'although,' etc. The word 'used' is said referring to things like ghee. That which one exchanges with one's own wealth, and that with which one exchanges it—their being allowable items, their not belonging to a co-religionist, and the incurring of the offense of buying and selling: these are the three factors here.

Kayavikkayasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on buying and selling is finished.

Niṭṭhito kosiyavaggo dutiyo.

The second chapter, the Kosiyavagga, is completed.

3. Pattavaggo

3. The Chapter on the Bowl

1. Pattasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

1. The Explanation of the Training Rule on the Bowl

598-602. Pattavaggassa [M 2.0427] paṭhame bhaṇḍanti vikketabbabhaṇḍaṃ. Yasmā vaṇṇasaddo saṇṭhānajātirūpāyatanakāraṇapamāṇaguṇapasaṃsādīsu dissati. “Mahantaṃ sapparājavaṇṇaṃ abhinimminitvā”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.142) hi saṇṭhānaṃ vuccati. “Brāhmaṇova seṭṭho vaṇṇo, hīno añño vaṇṇo”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.402) jāti. “Paramāya vaṇṇapokkharatāya samannāgato”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.303) rūpāyatanaṃ.

598-602. In the first [rule] of the Chapter on the Bowl, 'goods' (bhaṇḍa) means goods to be sold. The word 'appearance' (vaṇṇa) is seen in the sense of shape, caste, the form-as-sense-base, cause, measure, quality, praise, and so on. For in 'Having created a great serpent king's appearance,' etc. (SN 1.142), it is called shape. In 'The brahmin is the superior caste (vaṇṇa), other castes are inferior,' etc. (MN 2.402), [it means] caste. In 'Endowed with the utmost excellence of complexion (vaṇṇa),' etc. (DN 1.303), [it means] the form-as-sense-base.

“Na harāmi na bhañjāmi, ārā siṅghāmi vārijaṃ;

Atha kena nu vaṇṇena, gandhatthenoti vuccatī”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.234; jā. 1.6.116) –

In 'I do not take, I do not break, I smell the water-born [lotus] from afar; by what reason (vaṇṇa), then, am I called a “fragrance thief”?' etc. (SN 1.234; Ja 1.6.116),

Ādīsu [V 2.0378] kāraṇaṃ. “Tayo pattassa vaṇṇā”tiādīsu (pārā. 602) pamāṇaṃ. “Kadā saññuḷhā pana te gahapati ime samaṇassa gotamassa vaṇṇā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.77) guṇo. “Vaṇṇārahassa vaṇṇaṃ bhāsatī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 4.3) pasaṃsā. Tasmā vuttaṃ “tayo pattassa vaṇṇāti tīṇi pattassa pamāṇānī”ti.

in such [passages, it means] cause. In 'Three vaṇṇā of the bowl,' etc. (Pārā. 602), [it means] measure. In 'When, householder, were these praises (vaṇṇā) of the ascetic Gotama compiled?' etc. (MN 2.77), [it means] quality. In 'He speaks praise (vaṇṇa) of one worthy of praise,' etc. (AN 4.3), [it means] praise. Therefore, it is said: '“The three vaṇṇā of the bowl” means the three measures of the bowl.'

Aḍḍhaterasapalā hotīti ettha “māsānaṃ aḍḍhaterasapalāni gaṇhātī”ti vadanti. “Magadhanāḷi nāma chapasatā nāḷī”ti keci. “Aṭṭhapasatā”ti apare. Tattha purimānaṃ matena tipasatāya nāḷiyā dve nāḷiyo ekā magadhanāḷi hoti, pacchimānaṃ catupasatāya nāḷiyā dve nāḷiyo ekā magadhanāḷi. Ācariyadhammapālattherena pana “pakatiyā catumuṭṭhikaṃ kuḍuvaṃ, catukuḍuvaṃ nāḷikaṃ, tāya nāḷiyā soḷasa nāḷiyo doṇaṃ, taṃ pana magadhanāḷiyā dvādasa nāḷiyo hontī”ti vuttaṃ, tasmā tena nayena “magadhanāḷi nāma pañca kuḍuvāni ekañca muṭṭhiṃ ekāya muṭṭhiyā tatiyañca bhāgaṃ gaṇhātī”ti veditabbaṃ.

Here, regarding 'it is twelve and a half palas,' some say, 'It takes twelve and a half palas of beans (māsa).' Some say, 'A Magadhan nāḷi is a nāḷi of six pasata.' Others say, 'of eight pasata.' Therein, according to the view of the former, with a nāḷi of three pasata, two nāḷi make one Magadhan nāḷi. According to the latter, with a nāḷi of four pasata, two nāḷi make one Magadhan nāḷi. However, the elder Ācariya Dhammapāla has said: 'By the standard measure, four handfuls (muṭṭhi) are a kuḍuva; four kuḍuva are a nāḷika; sixteen of those nāḷi are a doṇa; and that [doṇa] is twelve nāḷi by the Magadhan measure.' Therefore, by that method, it should be understood that 'a Magadhan nāḷi comprises five kuḍuva, one handful, and a third part of a handful.'

Sabbasambhārasaṅkhatoti jīrakādisabbasambhārehi saṅkhato. Ālopassa ālopassa anurūpanti ettha “byañjanassa mattā nāma odanacatuttho bhāgo”ti brahmāyusuttassa aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 2.387) vuttattā ālopassa catutthabhāgappamāṇaṃ byañjanaṃ ālopassa anurūpanti gahetabbaṃ. Idha pana sūpasseva odanacatutthabhāgappamāṇataṃ [M 2.0428] dassetvā etassa lakkhaṇe dassite itarassapi dassitameva hotīti byañjanassa tathā visesetvā pamāṇaṃ na dassitaṃ.

'Prepared with all ingredients' means prepared with all ingredients such as cumin. Regarding 'suitable for each morsel,' here, because it is said in the commentary to the Brahmāyusutta (MN-a 2.387), 'The measure of relish is a fourth part of the rice,' it should be understood that relish in the measure of a fourth part of a morsel is suitable for the morsel. Here, however, having shown the measure of the soup itself to be a fourth part of the rice, when this characteristic is shown, that of the other [relishes] is also shown. Therefore, the measure of relish is not shown separately in that way.

Magadhanāḷiyā upaḍḍhappamāṇo idha patthoti āha “patthodananti magadhanāḷiyā upaḍḍhanāḷikodana”nti. Iminā ca “patthadvayaṃ magadhanāḷī”ti dassitaṃ hoti. Pattho ca “catupalo kuḍuvo, catukuḍuvo pattho”ti iminā lokiyavohārena veditabbo. Bhājanaparibhogenāti udakāharaṇādinā bhājanaparibhogena.

Half the measure of a Magadhan nāḷi is here a pattha; thus he said, 'a pattha of rice means half a nāḷi of rice by the Magadhan nāḷi [measure].' And by this, it is shown that 'two pattha are a Magadhan nāḷi.' And a pattha should be understood by this worldly usage: 'four pala are a kuḍuva; four kuḍuva are a pattha.' 'By use of the vessel' means by the use of the vessel, such as for carrying water.

607. Dhoteti paribhogāvasānadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ, na pana dhoteyeva dukkaṭaṃ āpajjati tato puretaraṃ paribhogakāleyeva āpajjanato.

607. 'Having washed' is said to show the end of the use; one does not, however, incur a dukkaṭa offense only upon washing, because it is incurred earlier, at the very time of use.

608. Pañcahi dvīhīti idaṃ “ettāvatā kāḷavaṇṇatā sampajjatī”ti dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. “Yadi pana ekenapi pākena kāḷavaṇṇo hoti, adhiṭṭhānupagoyevā”ti vadanti. Hatthānāgatassapi adhiṭṭhātabbabhāvadassanatthaṃ “yadihī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Iminā ca dūre ṭhitampi adhiṭṭhātuṃ [V 2.0379] vikappetuñca labhati, ṭhapitaṭṭhānasallakkhaṇañca na pamāṇanti veditabbaṃ. Sutvā vāti pattakārakena pesitabhikkhunā anāṇatto kevalaṃ tassa kathentassa vacanamattaṃ sutvā. Na pamāṇanti tena apesitattā. Sāmantavihāreti idaṃ upacāramattaṃ, tato dūre ṭhitampi adhiṭṭhātuṃ vaṭṭatiyeva. Ṭhapitaṭṭhānaṃ sallakkhetvāti idampi upacāramattaṃ, pattasallakkhaṇamevettha pamāṇaṃ. Patte vā chiddaṃ hotīti mukhavaṭṭito heṭṭhā dvaṅgulamattokāsato paṭṭhāya yattha katthaci chiddaṃ hoti. Sesamettha paṭhamakathine vuttanayameva.

608. 'With five or two' is said to show that 'by this much the black color is achieved.' But some say, 'If, however, it becomes black with even one firing, it is fit for determination.' The phrase beginning 'if indeed' is stated to show that even something not in hand can be determined. And by this, it should be understood that one may determine and perform vikappana on something even when it is at a distance, and that identifying the place where it was put is not the standard. 'Or having heard' means having heard merely the words of someone speaking, being a monk not commissioned and sent by the bowl-maker. 'It is not the standard' because he was not sent by that person. 'In a nearby monastery' is a figurative expression; it is indeed permissible to determine a bowl even when it is far from there. 'Having identified the place where it was put' is also a figurative expression; here, identifying the bowl itself is the standard. 'Or if there is a hole in the bowl' means there is a hole anywhere starting from a space of about two finger-widths below the rim of the mouth. The rest here is just according to the method stated in the first kathina [section].

Pattasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on the bowl is finished.

2. Ūnapañcabandhanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Fewer Than Five Fastenings

610. Dutiyasikkhāpade hatthesu piṇḍāya caratīti pāḷipadassa hatthesu labhitabbapiṇḍatthāya caratīti attho veditabbo.

610. In the second training rule, the meaning of the Pali phrase 'goes for alms in the hands' should be understood as 'goes for the purpose of alms to be received in the hands.'

612-613. “Tassa [M 2.0429] so apattoti vacanato so patto adhiṭṭhānampi vijahati apattattā. Apattabhāvatoyeva hi ‘pañcabandhanaṃ pattaṃ cetāpetī’ti pāḷiyaṃ na vutta”nti tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Keci pana “apattoti idaṃ ‘aññaṃ pattaṃ viññāpetuṃ vaṭṭatī’ti dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ, so pana patto adhiṭṭhānaṃ na vijahatī”ti vadanti, taṃ yuttaṃ viya dissati “yassa pañca ekāyeva vā dasaṅgulā, so baddhopi abaddhopi apattoyevā”ti vakkhamānattā. Na hi mukhavaṭṭiyā pañcasu ṭhānesu dvaṅgulamattāhi rājīhi adhiṭṭhānaṃ vijahatīti sakkā vattuṃ, ekāya pana rājiyā dasaṅgulāya sace tattha vuttappamāṇo chiddo paññāyati, chiddeneva adhiṭṭhānavijahanaṃ siyāti yuttaṃ vattuṃ. Bandhanokāse sati asati vā bandhanavirahito patto abandhanoti vutto, bandhanokāsavirahitoyeva pana abandhanokāsoti vutto.

612-613. Because it is said, ‘That is not a bowl for him,’ that bowl relinquishes its determination on account of being not a bowl. Indeed, precisely because it is not a bowl, the phrase ‘causes a bowl with five fastenings to be obtained’ is not stated in the Pali,” so it is said in all three knot passages. But some say, “This ‘not a bowl’ is stated to show that ‘it is permissible to request another bowl,’ but that bowl does not relinquish its determination.” This seems reasonable, because it will be said, “For which [bowl] there are five [cracks], or even one of ten finger-breadths, whether bound or unbound, it is indeed not a bowl.” For it cannot be said that the determination is relinquished by lines of two finger-breadths in five places on the rim; but with one line of ten finger-breadths, if a hole of the size mentioned there appears, it is reasonable to say that the relinquishing of the determination would be by the hole itself. A bowl lacking a fastening, whether there is a place for a fastening or not, is called ‘unbound.’ But one that is lacking a place for a fastening is called ‘one without a place for a fastening.’

Tipusuttakena vā bandhitvāti ettha “bandhitabbo”ti pāṭho gahetabbo. Purāṇapotthakepi hi ayameva pāṭho dissati. Suddhehi…pe… na vaṭṭatīti idaṃ uṇhabhojane pakkhitte vilīyamānattā vuttaṃ. Phāṇitaṃ jhāpetvā pāsāṇacuṇṇena bandhituṃ vaṭṭatīti pāsāṇacuṇṇena saddhiṃ phāṇitaṃ pacitvā tathāpakkena pāsāṇacuṇṇena bandhituṃ vaṭṭati.

Regarding 'or by tying with a lead string,' here the reading 'should be tied' should be taken. For this very reading is found even in old manuscripts. The text abbreviated as `Suddhehi…pe… na vaṭṭati` is stated because it dissolves when hot food is placed in it. Regarding 'it is allowable to heat molasses and bind with stone powder,' this means it is allowable to bind with stone powder that has been cooked together with molasses.

615. Anukampāya na gaṇhantassa dukkaṭanti vuttattā yassa so patto na ruccati, tassapi [V 2.0380] agaṇhantassa anāpatti. Teneva mātikāṭṭhakathāyaṃ (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. ūnapañcabandhanasīkkhāpadavaṇṇanā) vuttaṃ “sace therassa patto na ruccati, appicchatāya vā na gaṇhāti, vaṭṭatī”ti. Pattapariyantoti pariyantapatto, avasānapattoti attho. “Saṅghamajjhe pattaṃ gāhāpentena alajjiṃ agāhāpetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti. “Anujānāmi bhikkhave ādhārakanti vuttattā pīṭhādīsu yattha katthaci ādhāraṃ ṭhapetvā tattha pattaṃ ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭati ādhāraṭhapanokāsassa aniyamitattā”ti vadanti. Aparibhogenāti ayuttaparibhogena.

615. Because it was said, 'For one who does not accept it out of compassion, it is a dukkaṭa offense,' even for one to whom that bowl is not agreeable, there is no offense in not accepting it. Therefore, in the Mātikāṭṭhakathā (Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī Aṭṭhakathā, Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Fewer Than Five Fastenings), it is stated: 'If the bowl is not agreeable to the elder, or if he does not accept it out of contentment, it is allowable.' 'Pattapariyanta' means a bowl at its limit, that is, a final bowl. They say, 'When causing a bowl to be taken in the midst of the Saṅgha, it is allowable not to cause a shameless person to take it.' Because it was said, 'I allow, O bhikkhus, a stand,' they say, 'It is allowable to place a stand on a stool or the like anywhere whatsoever and place the bowl on it, because the place for setting the stand is not restricted.' 'Aparibhogena' means by unsuitable use.

616. Pāḷiyaṃ “abandhanena pattena abandhanaṃ pattaṃ. Ekabandhanaṃ pattaṃ… dvibandhanaṃ pattaṃ… tibandhanaṃ… catubandhanaṃ… abandhanokāsaṃ… eka… dvi… ti… catubandhanokāsaṃ pattaṃ cetāpetī”ti evaṃ ekekena pattena dasadhā dasavidhaṃ pattaṃ cetāpanavasena [M 2.0430] ekanissaggiyapācittiyasataṃ vuttaṃ. Imasmiṃ sikkhāpade pamāṇayuttaṃ aggahitakāḷavaṇṇampi pattaṃ viññāpentassa āpattiyevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Adhiṭṭhānupagapattassa ūnapañcabandhanatā, attuddesikatā, akataviññatti, tāya ca paṭilābhoti imānettha cattāri aṅgāni.

616.
