In the Pāli, it is said: 'A bowl without a fastening... a bowl with one fastening... two... three... four... a bowl with allowance for no fastening... one... two... three... four fastenings—if one causes [such a] bowl to be acquired.' Thus, by way of causing each of the ten types of bowls to be acquired, one hundred nissaggiya pācittiya offenses are stated. In this training rule, it should be understood that there is an offense even for one who requests a bowl that is of suitable measure and of an unaccepted black color. Here, these are the four factors: (1) the bowl being one suitable for determination and having fewer than five fastenings; (2) its being intended for oneself; (3) an improper request having been made; (4) and the obtaining of it through that request.

Ūnapañcabandhanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Fewer Than Five Fastenings is concluded.

3. Bhesajjasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

3. Explanation of the Training Rule on Medicine

622. Tatiyasikkhāpade yesaṃ maṃsaṃ kappatīti idaṃ nissaggiyavatthudassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ, na pana yesaṃ maṃsaṃ na kappati, tesaṃ sappiādīni na kappantīti dassanatthaṃ. Manussakhīrādīnipi hi no na kappanti, kuto sasassa sappīti āha “yesañhi khīraṃ atthi, sappipi tesaṃ atthiyevā”ti. “Idañca yebhuyyena vutta”nti vadanti. Uggahitakaṃ katvā nikkhittanti appaṭiggahitaṃ sayameva gahetvā nikkhittaṃ. Sayaṃkataṃ nirāmisameva vaṭṭatīti tadahupurebhattameva sandhāya vuttaṃ. Atha sayaṃkataṃ nirāmisaṃ bhuñjantassa kasmā sāmaṃpāko na hotīti āha – “navanītaṃ tāpentassa hi sāmaṃpāko na hotī”ti. Savatthukapaṭiggahitassa vatthugatikattā āha – “savatthukassa paṭiggahitattā”ti. Pacchābhattaṃ paṭiggahitehīti pacchābhattaṃ paṭiggahitakhīradadhīhi. Purebhattampi ca uggahitakehi kataṃ abbhañjanādīsu upanetabbanti sambandho. Ubhayesampīti pacchābhattaṃ paṭiggahitakhīradadhīhi ca purebhattaṃ uggahitakehi ca katānaṃ. Eseva nayoti nissaggiyaṃ hotīti attho. Akappiyamaṃsasappimhīti akappiyamaṃsasattānaṃ [V 2.0381] sappimhi. Kāraṇapatirūpakaṃ vatvāti sajātiyānaṃ sappibhāvatoti kāraṇapatirūpakaṃ vatvā.

3. In the third training rule, this phrase, ‘for whom meat is allowable,’ is stated to show the object to be relinquished; it is not, however, stated to show that for those beings whose meat is not allowable, their ghee and so on are not allowable. For indeed, human milk and the like are not unallowable; from where is there ghee of a rabbit? Therefore, he said, ‘For whom there is milk, for them there is also ghee.’ They say, ‘And this is stated by way of generalization.’ ‘Having taken it up and set it aside’ means what was not formally received, having taken it by oneself, is set aside. ‘What is self-made and without material food-object is allowable’ is stated with reference only to the forenoon of that day. Then, for one consuming what is self-made and without material food-object, why is there no sāmaṃpāka offense? He said, ‘For one heating fresh butter, there is no sāmaṃpāka offense.’ Because of its being similar to the object for what was received together with its object, he said, ‘because of its being received with its object.’ ‘By what was received after the meal’ means by milk and curd received after the meal. And also in the forenoon, what is made from what was taken up should be used for anointing and so on; this is the connection. ‘Of both’ means of what is made from milk and curd received after the meal and from what was taken up in the forenoon. ‘This is the very method’ means it becomes something to be relinquished. ‘In the ghee of unallowable meat’ means in the ghee of beings of unallowable meat. ‘Having stated a corresponding reason’ means having stated a corresponding reason, saying, ‘because it is of the nature of ghee of those of a similar species.’

Sappinayeneva veditabbanti nirāmisameva sattāhaṃ vaṭṭatīti attho. Etthāti navanīte. Dhotaṃ vaṭṭatīti adhotaṃ ce, savatthukapaṭiggahitaṃ hoti, tasmā dhotaṃ paṭiggahetvā sattāhaṃ nikkhipituṃ vaṭṭatīti therānaṃ adhippāyo. Takkato uddhaṭamattameva khādiṃsūti ettha takkato uddhaṭamattaṃ adhotampi paṭiggahetvā paribhuñjantā dhovitvā pacitvā [M 2.0431] vā paribhuñjiṃsūti evamattho gahetabbo. Therassa hi dadhiguḷikādisahitampi paṭiggahitaṃ pacchā dhovitvā pacitvā vā paribhuñjantassa savatthukapaṭiggahaṇe doso natthīti adhippāyo, teneva therassa adhippāyaṃ dassentena “tasmā navanītaṃ paribhuñjantena…pe… ayamettha adhippāyo”ti vuttaṃ. Keci pana “takkato uddhaṭamattameva khādiṃsū”ti vacanassa adhippāyaṃ ajānantā “takkato uddhaṭamattaṃ adhotampi dadhiguḷikādisahitaṃ vikālepi paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ. Na hi dadhiguḷikādiāmisena saṃsaṭṭharasaṃ navanītaṃ paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭatīti sakkā vattuṃ. Navanītaṃ paribhuñjantenāti adhovitvā paṭiggahitanavanītaṃ paribhuñjantena. Dadhi eva dadhigataṃ yathā “gūthagataṃ muttagata”nti (ma. ni. 2.119). Khayaṃ gamissatīti vacanato khīraṃ pakkhipitvā pakkasappiādipi vikāle kappatīti veditabbaṃ. Kukkuccāyanti kukkuccakāti iminā attanāpi tattha kukkuccasabbhāvaṃ dīpeti. Teneva mātikāṭṭhakathāyaṃ (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. bhesajjasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) “nibbaṭṭitasappi vā navanītaṃ vā pacituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ. Tāni paṭiggahetvāti tāni khīradadhīni paṭiggahetvā.

622. ‘It should be known by the method for ghee’ means that what is without material food-object is allowable for seven days. ‘Here’ means in the case of fresh butter. ‘Washed is allowable’ means that if it is unwashed, it is a receiving with its object; therefore, the intention of the elders is that it is allowable to receive it washed and to store it for seven days. Here, in ‘They ate only what was lifted from the buttermilk,’ this is the meaning to be understood: having received what was just lifted from the buttermilk, even if unwashed, those who consumed it, consumed it after washing or cooking it. For the elder, indeed, there is no fault in the receiving with its object when consuming what was received together with curd lumps, etc., after washing or cooking it later; this is the intention. For that reason, showing the elder’s intention, it was said, ‘Therefore, by one consuming fresh butter… this is the intention here.’ Some, however, not knowing the intention of the statement, ‘They ate only what was lifted from the buttermilk,’ say, ‘It is allowable to consume what was just lifted from the buttermilk, even if unwashed and together with curd lumps, etc., even at the wrong time.’ That should not be accepted. For it is not possible to say that it is allowable to consume fresh butter whose taste is mixed with a material food-object such as curd lumps. ‘By one consuming fresh butter’ means by one consuming fresh butter received without washing. Curd itself is what is inherent in curd, just as in ‘what is inherent in excrement, what is inherent in urine.’ Because of the statement, ‘it will go to destruction,’ it should be known that boiled ghee, etc., into which milk has been put, is also allowable at the wrong time. By this, ‘the scrupulous are scrupulous,’ he reveals his own state of scrupulousness in that matter. Therefore, in the Mātikā Aṭṭhakathā it is said, ‘It is allowable to cook extracted ghee or fresh butter.’ ‘Having received them’ means having received that milk and curd.

Paṭiggahetvā ṭhapitabhesajjehīti paṭiggahetvā ṭhapitayāvajīvikabhesajjehi. Vuttanayena yathā taṇḍulādīni na paccanti, tathā lajjīyeva sampādetvā detīti lajjīsāmaṇeraggahaṇaṃ, apica alajjinā ajjhoharitabbaṃ yaṃ kiñci abhisaṅkharāpetuṃ na vaṭṭati, tasmāpi evamāha. Tile paṭiggahetvā katatelanti attanā bhajjanādīni akatvā gahitatelaṃ. Teneva “sāmisampi vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ. Nibbaṭṭitattāti yāvakālikavatthuto vivecitattā. Ubhayampīti attanā ca parena ca kataṃ. Yāva aruṇassa uggamanā tiṭṭhati, nissaggiyanti sattamadivase katatelaṃ sace yāva aruṇuggamanā tiṭṭhati, nissaggiyaṃ.

‘By medicines received and stored’ means by life-long medicines received and stored. Just as, by the method stated, rice and so on are not cooked, so too, a conscientious one prepares and gives; therefore, the term ‘conscientious novice’ is used. Furthermore, it is not allowable to have any kind of material food-object that is to be consumed by a shameless one prepared; for this reason, too, he said this. ‘Oil made after receiving sesame’ means oil that was received without oneself having done the roasting and so on. Therefore it is said, ‘Even with a material food-object it is allowable.’ ‘Because it is produced’ means because it is separated from an object allowable for the forenoon. ‘Both’ means made by oneself and by another. ‘If it remains until the rising of the dawn, it is to be relinquished’ means if oil made on the seventh day remains until the rising of the dawn, it is to be relinquished.

623. Acchavasanti dukkaṭavatthuno vasāya anuññātattā taṃsadisānaṃ dukkaṭavatthūnaṃyeva akappiyamaṃsasattānaṃ vasā anuññātā, na thullaccayavatthūnaṃ manussānaṃ vasāti āha “ṭhapetvā manussavasa”nti[V 2.0382]. Saṃsaṭṭhanti parissāvitaṃ. “Kāle paṭiggahitaṃ vikāle anupasampannenapi nippakkaṃ saṃsaṭṭhañca paribhuñjantassa dvepi dukkaṭāni hontiyevā”ti vadanti. Yasmā khīradadhiādīni pakkhipitvā telaṃ pacanti, tasmā kasaṭaṃ na vaṭṭati, telameva [M 2.0432] vaṭṭati. Tena vuttaṃ “pakkatelakasaṭe viya kukkuccāyatī”ti. “Sace vasāya saddhiṃ pakkattā na vaṭṭati, idaṃ kasmā vaṭṭatī”ti pucchantā “bhante”tiādimāhaṃsu. Etaṃ vaṭṭatīti nanu etaṃ dadhiguḷikādīhi pakkaṃ navanītaṃ vaṭṭatīti attho.

623. ‘Bear fat’: Because the fat of a `dukkaṭa` object was permitted, the fat of similar beings of unallowable meat, which are also `dukkaṭa` objects, is permitted, but not the fat of humans, which are `thullaccaya` objects; therefore, he said, ‘excluding human fat.’ ‘Mixed’ means strained. They say: ‘For one not fully ordained who consumes at the wrong time what was received at the proper time, both what is cooked and what is mixed, there are two `dukkaṭa` offenses.’ Because they cook oil by adding milk, curd, and so on, the dregs are not allowable; only the oil is allowable. Therefore it is said, ‘He is scrupulous as if about the dregs of cooked oil.’ Asking, ‘If it is not allowable because of being cooked together with fat, why is this allowable?’ they said, ‘Venerable sir,’ and so on. ‘This is allowable’ means: Is this fresh butter cooked with curd lumps and so on allowable?

“Madhukarīhi nāma madhumakkhikāhīti ayaṃ khuddakamakkhikānaṃ bhamaramakkhikānañca sāmaññaniddeso”ti tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Keci pana “daṇḍakesu madhukarā madhukarī makkhikā nāmā”ti vatvā “tāhi madhukarīādīhi tīhi makkhikāhi kataṃ madhu nāmā”ti vadanti. Bhamaramakkhikāhīti mahābhamaramakkhikāhi. Silesasadisanti ghanapakkaṃ vuttaṃ. Itaranti tanukamadhu. Madhupaṭalanti madhurahitaṃ kevalaṃ madhupaṭalaṃ. “Sace madhusahitaṃ paṭalaṃ paṭiggahetvā nikkhipanti, paṭalassa bhājanaṭṭhāniyattā madhuno vasena sattāhātikkame nissaggiyaṃ hotī”ti vadanti, “madhumakkhitaṃ pana madhugatikamevā”ti iminā taṃ na sameti.

In all three glosses, it is stated: 'By "madhukarī" are meant honeybees; this is a general designation for small bees and bumblebees.' Some, however, say, 'In the reeds, "madhukara," "madhukarī," and "makkhikā" are names,' and then declare, 'Honey made by these three types of bees—madhukarī and others—is called honey.' By 'bhamaramakkhikā' are meant large bumblebees. 'Silesasadisa' (like gum): this is said of that which is thickly ripened. 'Itara' (the other): this refers to thin honey. 'Madhupaṭala' (honeycomb): this means honeycomb devoid of honey, just the honeycomb alone. Some say, 'If they receive a honeycomb containing honey and set it aside, because the comb serves as a container, on account of the honey it becomes an item to be forfeited after the passing of seven days.' This, however, does not agree with the text, 'but that which is smeared with honey is just like honey.'

“Phāṇitaṃ nāma ucchumhā nibbatta”nti pāḷiyaṃ avisesena vuttattā aṭṭhakathāyañca “ucchurasaṃ upādāya…pe… avatthukā ucchuvikati ‘phāṇita’nti veditabbā”ti vacanato ucchurasopi nikkasaṭo sattāhakālikoti veditabbo. Kenaci pana “madhumhi cattāro kālikā yathāsambhavaṃ yojetabbā, ucchumhi cā”ti vatvā “samakkhikaṇḍaseḷakaṃ yāvakālikaṃ, aneḷakaṃ udakasambhinnaṃ yāmakālikaṃ, asambhinnaṃ sattāhakālikaṃ, madhusitthaṃ parisuddhaṃ yāvajīvikaṃ, tathā ucchu vā raso vā sakasaṭo yāvakāliko, nikkasaṭo udakasambhinno yāmakāliko, asambhinno sattāhakāliko, suddhakasaṭaṃ yāvajīvika”nti ca vatvā uttaripi bahudhā papañcitaṃ. Tattha “udakasambhinnaṃ madhu vā ucchuraso vā udakasambhinno yāmakāliko”ti idaṃ neva pāḷiyaṃ, na aṭṭhakathāyaṃ dissati. “Yāvakālikaṃ samānaṃ garutarampi muddikājātirasaṃ attanā saṃsaṭṭhaṃ lahukaṃ yāmakālikabhāvaṃ upanentaṃ udakaṃ lahutaraṃ sattāhakālikaṃ attanā saṃsaṭṭhaṃ garutaraṃ yāmakālikabhāvaṃ upanetī”ti ettha kāraṇaṃ soyeva pucchitabbo, sabbattha pāḷiyaṃ aṭṭhakathāyañca udakasambhedena garutarassapi lahubhāvopagamanaṃyeva dassitaṃ. Pāḷiyampi hi “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, gilānassa guḷaṃ, agilānassa guḷodaka”nti (mahāva. 284) vadantena [M 2.0433] agilānena paribhuñjituṃ ayuttopi guḷo udakasambhinno agilānassapi vaṭṭatīti anuññāto.

‘Phāṇita is produced from sugarcane,’ as stated generally in the Pāli, and as it is said in the commentary, ‘...what is derived from sugarcane juice... without solid residue is to be understood as phāṇita,’ therefore even sugarcane juice without dregs is to be understood as a sattāhakālika (permissible for seven days). Some, however, having said, ‘In honey, the four time-periods should be applied as is possible, and in sugarcane also,’ have elaborated extensively, saying: ‘Honey with bees and comb pieces is a yāvakālika (permissible for the forenoon); honey without comb pieces mixed with water is a yāmakālika (permissible for a watch); unmixed honey is a sattāhakālika; purified beeswax is a yāvajīvika (permissible for life). Similarly, sugarcane or its juice with dregs is a yāvakālika; without dregs and mixed with water, it is a yāmakālika; unmixed, it is a sattāhakālika; the pure dregs are a yāvajīvika.’ Therein, the statement, ‘Honey or sugarcane juice mixed with water is a yāmakālika,’ is found neither in the Pāli nor in the commentary. Regarding this point—that water, which leads even a substance of a more restrictive time-period like grape juice (a yāvakālika) when mixed with it to the state of a less restrictive time-period (a yāmakālika), leads a substance of a less restrictive time-period (a sattāhakālika) when mixed with it to the state of a more restrictive time-period (a yāmakālika)—the reason for this should be asked of that very person. For everywhere in the Pāli and the commentary, it is shown only that even a substance of a more restrictive time-period comes to a less restrictive state through being mixed with water. Indeed, in the Pāli as well, by the one who said, ‘I allow, monks, jaggery for the sick, and jaggery-water for one who is not sick,’ it was permitted that jaggery, though unsuitable for one who is not sick to consume, is allowable even for one who is not sick when it is mixed with water.

Yampi [V 2.0383] ca “ucchu ce yāvakāliko, ucchuraso ce yāmakāliko, phāṇitaṃ ce sattāhakālikaṃ, taco ce yāvajīviko”ti aṭṭhakathāvacanaṃ dassetvā “ucchuraso udakasambhinno yāmakāliko”ti aññena kenaci vuttaṃ, tampi tathāvidhassa aṭṭhakathāvacanassa imissā samantapāsādikāya vinayaṭṭhakathāya abhāvato na sārato paccetabbaṃ. Tatoyeva ca “ucchuraso udakena sambhinnopi asambhinnopi sattāhakālikoyevā”ti keci ācariyā vadanti. Bhesajjakkhandhake ca “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, ucchurasa”nti (mahāva. 300) ettha tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu avisesena vuttaṃ “ucchuraso sattāhakāliko”ti.

And as for the commentary statement that has been shown—'If it is sugarcane, it is a yāvakālika; if sugarcane juice, a yāmakālika; if molasses, a sattāhakālika; if the peel, a yāvajīvika'—and the statement made by some other person, 'Sugarcane juice mixed with water is a yāmakālika,' that too should not be taken as authoritative, because a commentary statement of that kind is absent in this Samantapāsādikā, the Vinaya commentary. Therefore, some teachers say: 'Sugarcane juice, whether mixed with water or not, is indeed a sattāhakālika.' And in the Chapter on Medicines, regarding the text 'I allow, monks, sugarcane juice,' it is stated without distinction in all three glosses: 'Sugarcane juice is a sattāhakālika.'

Sayaṃkataṃ nirāmisameva vaṭṭatīti ettha aparissāvitaṃ paṭiggahitampi karaṇasamaye parissāvetvā kasaṭaṃ apanetvāva attanā katanti gahetabbaṃ. Jhāmaucchuphāṇitanti agginā daḍḍhe ucchukhette jhāmaucchunā kataphāṇitaṃ. Koṭṭitaucchuphāṇitanti khuddānukhuddakaṃ chinditvā koṭṭetvā nippīḷetvā pakkaṃ yebhuyyena ca sakasaṭaṃ phāṇitaṃ. Tādisassa ca kasaṭassa abbohārikattā “taṃ yutta”nti vuttaṃ. Sītudakena katanti madhukapupphāni sītodake pakkhipitvā madditvā puppharase udakagate sati taṃ udakaṃ gahetvā pacitvā kataphāṇitaṃ. Khīraṃ pakkhipitvā kataṃ madhukaphāṇitaṃ yāvakālikanti ettha khīraṃ pakkhipitvā pakkatelaṃ kasmā vikāle vaṭṭatīti ce? Tele pakkhittakhīraṃ telameva hoti, aññaṃ pana khīraṃ pakkhipitvā kataṃ khīrabhāvaṃ gaṇhātīti idamettha kāraṇaṃ. Yadi evaṃ khaṇḍasakkharampi khīraṃ pakkhipitvā karonti, taṃ kasmā vaṭṭatīti āha “khaṇḍasakkharaṃ panā”tiādi. Tattha khīrajallikanti khīrapheṇaṃ.

Regarding 'Self-made and unadulterated is allowable': here, even what was received unstrained should be understood as 'made by oneself' only after it is strained at the time of preparation and the dregs are removed. 'Molasses from burnt sugarcane' is molasses made from sugarcane in a sugarcane field that was burnt by fire. 'Molasses from crushed sugarcane' is molasses, usually with dregs, made by cutting sugarcane into very small pieces, crushing, pressing, and cooking it. And because such dregs are not for consumption, it is said, 'That is suitable.' 'Made with cold water' is molasses made by placing madhuka flowers in cold water, crushing them, and when the flower essence has entered the water, taking that water and cooking it. Regarding 'Molasses from the madhuka flower made by adding milk is a yāvakālika': here, if it is asked why oil cooked with milk added is allowable at the wrong time, the reason here is this: milk added to oil becomes just oil, but another substance made with milk added takes on the nature of milk. If so, since they also make lump sugar by adding milk, why is that allowable? To this, he said, 'But lump sugar...' and so on. Therein, 'khīrajallika' means milk foam.

Bhesajjodissaṃ dassentena “sattavidhañhi odissaṃ nāmā”tiādinā itarānipi atthuddhāravasena vuttāni. Vikaṭānīti apakatibhesajjattā vikaṭāni, virūpānīti attho. Dukkaṭavatthūnampi akappiyamaṃsānaṃ vasāya anuññātattā “vasodissa”nti vuttaṃ. Oḷārikānampi āhāratthaṃ pharituṃ samatthānaṃ sappiādīnaṃ bhesajjanāmena anuññātattā “bhesajjodissa”nti vuttaṃ[M 2.0434]. “Pacchābhattato paṭṭhāya sati paccayeti vuttattā paṭiggahitabhesajjāni dutiyadivasato paṭṭhāya purebhattampi sati paccaye paribhuñjitabbāni, na āhāratthaṃ bhesajjatthāya paṭiggahitattā”ti vadanti.

While explaining the 'designation of medicine,' the commentator, by way of the text beginning 'Indeed, there are seven kinds of designations,' also stated the others by way of explaining their meaning. 'Vikaṭāni' (altered): because they are medicines not in their natural state, they are 'altered'; the meaning is 'altered in form.' Because the fat of unallowable meats—which are objects entailing a dukkaṭa offense—was permitted, it is called 'designation of fat.' Because even substantial things like ghee, which are able to suffice for the purpose of food, were permitted under the name of 'medicine,' it is called 'designation of medicine.' Some say: 'Because it was said, "From after the meal onwards, if there is a reason," medicines that have been received should be consumed from the second day onwards, even before the meal, if there is a reason—not for the purpose of food, because they were received for the purpose of medicine.'

624. Dvāravātapānakavāṭesūti mahādvārassa vātapānānañca kavāṭaphalakesu. Kasāve pakkhittāni tāni attano sabhāvaṃ pariccajanti, tasmā “makkhetabbānī”ti vuttaṃ, ghuṇapāṇakādiparihāratthaṃ makkhetabbānīti attho. Adhiṭṭhetīti “idāni mayhaṃ ajjhoharaṇīyaṃ na bhavissati[V 2.0384], bāhiraparibhogatthāya gamissatī”ti cittaṃ uppādetīti attho. Tenevāha – “sappiñca telañca vasañca muddhani telaṃ vā abbhañjanaṃ vā”tiādi. “Evaṃ adhiṭṭhitañca paṭiggahaṇaṃ vijahatī”ti vadanti.

624. “On the door and window panels” refers to the panels of the main gate and the windows. When astringent substances are applied to them, they abandon their own nature; therefore, it is said, “they should be smeared.” The meaning is that they should be smeared to prevent wood-boring insects and other creatures. “One determines” means one arouses the thought, “Now this will not be for my consumption but will be for external use.” Therefore, he said: “Ghee, oil, and fat, or oil for the head, or ointment,” and so on. And they say that a determination made thus relinquishes the receiving.

625. Sace dvinnaṃ santakaṃ ekena paṭiggahitaṃ avibhattaṃ hoti, paribhuñjituṃ pana na vaṭṭatīti ettha majjhe pāṭho parihīno, evaṃ panettha pāṭho veditabbo “sace dvinnaṃ santakaṃ ekena paṭiggahitaṃ avibhattaṃ hoti, sattāhātikkame dvinnampi anāpatti, paribhuñjituṃ pana na vaṭṭatī”ti. Aññathā pana saddappayogopi na saṅgacchati. Gaṇṭhipadepi ca ayameva pāṭho dassito. Tattha dvinnampi anāpattīti yathā aññassa santakaṃ ekena paṭiggahitaṃ sattāhātikkamena nissaggiyaṃ na hoti parasantakabhāvato, evamidampi avibhattattā ubhayasādhāraṇampi avinibbhogabhāvato nissaggiyaṃ na hotīti adhippāyo. Paribhuñjituṃ pana na vaṭṭatīti bhikkhunā paṭiggahitattā sattāhātikkame yassa kassaci bhikkhuno paribhuñjituṃ na vaṭṭati paṭiggahitasappiādīnaṃ paribhogassa sattāheneva paricchinnattā. “Tāni paṭiggahetvā sattāhaparamaṃ sannidhikārakaṃ paribhuñjitabbānī”ti hi vuttaṃ. Gaṇṭhipadesu pana tīsupi idha pāṭhassa parihīnabhāvaṃ asallakkhetvā “paribhuñjituṃ pana na vaṭṭatīti idaṃ antosattāhe paribhogaṃ sandhāya vuttanti saññāya vissāsaggāhābhāvato paribhuñjituṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti evamattho vutto, so na gahetabbo.

625. Regarding the text, 'If something belonging to two monks is received by one and is not divided, it is not allowable to use it,' here the middle part of the text is missing. The text here should be understood thus: 'If something belonging to two monks is received by one and is not divided, upon exceeding seven days, there is no offense for either of them, but it is not allowable to use it.' Otherwise, the grammatical construction does not fit. And in the glosses, this very text is shown. There, 'no offense for either of them' means that just as something belonging to another, when received by one monk, does not become subject to forfeiture by exceeding seven days because it is another's property, so too this item, because it is undivided and common to both, does not become subject to forfeiture due to its indivisible nature—this is the intended meaning. 'But it is not allowable to use it' means that because it was received by a monk, upon exceeding seven days, it is not allowable for any monk whatsoever to use it, since the use of received ghee and so on is limited by just seven days. For it is said: “Having received them, they should be used for a maximum of seven days as a stored item.” However, in all three glosses, not noticing that the text here is missing, it is said: '“But it is not allowable to use it”—this is said in reference to its use within seven days,' with the idea that 'due to the absence of taking it with confidence, it is not allowable to use it.' This meaning should not be accepted.

Āvuso, imaṃ telaṃ sattāhamattaṃ paribhuñja tvanti iminā yena paṭiggahitaṃ, tena antosattāheyeva parassa vissajjitabhāvaṃ dasseti. Kassa āpattīti paṭhamaṃ tāva ubhinnaṃ sādhāraṇattā anāpatti vuttā. Idāni [M 2.0435] pana ekena itarassa vissaṭṭhabhāvato ubhayasādhāraṇatā natthīti vibhattasadisaṃ hutvā ṭhitaṃ, tasmā ettha paṭiggahitassa sattāhātikkame ekassa āpattiyā bhavitabbanti maññamāno “kiṃ paṭiggahaṇapaccayā paṭiggāhakassa āpatti, udāhu yassa santakaṃ jātaṃ, tassā”ti pucchati. Nissaṭṭhabhāvatoyeva ca idha “avibhattabhāvato”ti kāraṇaṃ avatvā “yena paṭiggahitaṃ, tena vissajjitattā”ti vuttaṃ. Idañca vissaṭṭhabhāvato ubhayasādhāraṇataṃ pahāya ekassa santakaṃ hontampi yena paṭiggahitaṃ, tato aññassa santakaṃ jātaṃ, tasmā parasantakapaṭiggahaṇe viya paṭiggāhakassa paṭiggahaṇapaccayā natthi āpattīti dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ, na pana “yena paṭiggahitaṃ, tena vissajjitattā”ti vacanato avissajjite sati avibhattepi sattāhātikkame āpattīti dassanatthaṃ avissajjite avibhattabhāvatoyeva anāpattiyā siddhattā. Sace pana itaro yena paṭiggahitaṃ, tasseva antosattāhe attano bhāgampi [V 2.0385] vissajjeti, sattāhātikkame siyā āpatti yena paṭiggahitaṃ, tasseva santakabhāvamāpannattā itarassa appaṭiggahitattā. Iminā tassa santakabhāvepi aññena paṭiggahitasakasantake viya tena appaṭiggahitabhāvato anāpattīti dīpeti. Idaṃ pana adhippāyaṃ ajānitvā ito aññathā gaṇṭhipadakārādīhi papañcitaṃ, na taṃ sārato paccetabbaṃ.

By the words, 'Friend, use this oil for just seven days,' it is shown that the one by whom it was received relinquished it to the other within seven days. As for 'Whose offense is it?': first, it was stated that there is no offense because it is common to both. But now, since one has relinquished it to the other, the state of being common to both no longer exists, and it stands as if divided. Therefore, thinking that in this case, upon exceeding seven days, an offense should occur for one of them, he asks: 'Is the offense for the receiver on account of the receiving, or is it for the one whose property it has become?' And here, precisely because of the relinquishment, the reason is not stated as 'due to being undivided'; rather, it is said, 'because it was relinquished by the one who received it.' This was stated to show that although, due to the relinquishment, it ceases to be common to both and becomes the property of one, it has become the property of someone other than the one who received it. Therefore, just as in the case of receiving another's property, there is no offense for the receiver on account of the receiving. It was not, however, stated in order to show that if it is not relinquished, even though it is undivided, there is an offense upon exceeding seven days; for when it is not relinquished, the absence of an offense is already established precisely because of its being undivided. If, however, the other monk also relinquishes his share within seven days to the very one by whom it was received, then upon exceeding seven days, an offense would occur for the one by whom it was received, since it has become his sole property, whereas the other has not received it. By this, it is shown that even when it becomes the other's property, there is no offense for him because it was not received by him, just as in the case of one's own property that has been received by another. But not understanding this intended meaning, it has been elaborated upon otherwise by the writers of the glosses and others; that should not be accepted as authoritative.

Aparibhogaṃ hotīti kassaci amanuññassa patitattā paribhogārahaṃ na hoti. Yena cittenāti yena pariccajitukāmatācittena. “Antosattāhe”ti adhikārattā “antosattāhe anapekkho datvā paṭilabhitvā paribhuñjatī”ti imaṃ sambandhaṃ sandhāya mahāsumattherena “evaṃ antosattāhe datvā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Mahāpadumatthero pana yadi evaṃ “vissajjetī”ti imināva taṃ siddhaṃ, sattāhātikkantaṃ pana nissaṭṭhaṃ paṭilabhitvā paribhuñjituṃ na vaṭṭati, tasmā tassa paribhogamukhadassanamidanti āha – “nayidaṃ yācitabba”ntiādi. Aññena bhikkhunāti ettha suddhacittena dinnattā sayampi āharāpetvā paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭatiyeva. Sappiādīnaṃ paṭiggahitabhāvo, attano santakatā, sattāhātikkamoti imānettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

“It is not for use” means that because it has fallen to someone disagreeable, it is not fit for use. “With what mind” means with a mind desiring to relinquish. Because “within seven days” is the governing topic, in reference to the connection, “within seven days, having given it without attachment, and having received it back, one may use it,” the Great Elder Sumati said, “Thus, having given it within seven days,” and so on. The Great Elder Paduma, however, said that if this is so, then “he relinquishes” alone would suffice; but it is not allowable to receive back and use a relinquished item that has exceeded seven days. Therefore, this demonstrates the method of its use, as in the statement, “This should not be requested,” and so on. Regarding “by another monk”: here, because it was given with a pure mind, it is indeed allowable for oneself to have it brought and use it. The state of having been received of ghee and so on, its being one's own property, and the exceeding of seven days—these are the three factors here.

Bhesajjasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Training Rule on Medicine is concluded.

4. Vassikasāṭikasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

4. Explanation of the Training Rule on the Rains-Cloth

627. Catutthe [M 2.0436] sibbanarajanakappapariyosānena niṭṭhāpetvāti sūcikammaniṭṭhānena sakimpi vaṇṇabhedamattarajanena kappabindukaraṇena ca niṭṭhāpetvā. Samayeti vassānasamaye.

627. In the fourth, 'having completed it by the end of the process of sewing and dyeing' means having completed it by the finishing of needlework, even just once, by dyeing it merely enough to break the color, and by making the `kappabindu` mark. 'At the proper time' means during the rainy season.

628. Kucchisamayoti antosamayo. “Ayameko aḍḍhamāso pariyesanakkhettañceva karaṇakkhettañca. Etasmiñhi antare vassikasāṭikaṃ aladdhaṃ pariyesituṃ laddhaṃ kātuñca vaṭṭati, nivāsetuṃ adhiṭṭhātuñca na vaṭṭatī”ti potthakesu pāṭho dissati, so apāṭho. Evaṃ panettha pāṭhena bhavitabbaṃ “ayameko aḍḍhamāso pariyesanakkhettaṃ. Etasmiñhi antare vassikasāṭikaṃ aladdhaṃ pariyesituṃ vaṭṭati, laddhaṃ kātuṃ nivāsetuṃ adhiṭṭhātuñca na vaṭṭatī”ti. Na hi gimhānaṃ pacchimamāsassa paṭhamo aḍḍhamāso karaṇakkhettaṃ hoti. “Aḍḍhamāso seso gimhānanti katvā nivāsetabba”nti vacanato pana gimhānaṃ pacchimamāsassa pacchimo aḍḍhamāso karaṇakkhettañceva nivāsanakkhettañca hoti. Teneva mātikāṭṭhakathāyaṃ (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. vahisakasāṭikasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) “gimhānaṃ pacchimo māso pariyesanakkhettaṃ, pacchimo aḍḍhamāso [V 2.0386] karaṇanivāsanakkhettampī”ti vuttaṃ. Tasmā pāḷiyā mātikāṭṭhakathāya ca avirodhaṃ icchantena vuttanayeneva pāṭho gahetabbo.

628. `Kucchisamayo` means the time within. 'This is one half-month, both a period for searching and a period for making. For within this time, if a rainy-season robe has not been obtained, it is permissible to search for it, and having obtained it, it is permissible to make it; but it is not permissible to wear it or to determine it'—this reading is found in the texts, but it is not the correct reading. Instead, the reading here should be: 'This is one half-month, a period for searching. For within this time, if a rainy-season robe has not been obtained, it is permissible to search for it, but having obtained it, it is not permissible to make it, wear it, or to determine it.' For the first half of the last month of the hot season is not a period for making. However, based on the statement, 'There being a half-month left of the hot season, it should be made and worn,' the latter half of the last month of the hot season is both a period for making and a period for wearing. Therefore, in the Mātikāṭṭhakathā it is said: 'The last month of the hot season is a period for searching, and the latter half-month is also a period for making and wearing.' Thus, one who wishes for non-contradiction with the Pāḷi and the Mātikāṭṭhakathā should accept the reading in the manner stated.

“Viññattiṃ katvā nipphādentassa aññātakaviññattisikkhāpadena anāpattī”ti vadantena “piṭṭhisamayattā iminā sikkhāpadena āpattī”ti dīpitā hoti. Na hi ñātakapavāritaṭṭhānato piṭṭhisamaye satuppādakaraṇamattenapi sambhavantī āpatti tato garukatarāya viññattiyā na hotīti sakkā vattuṃ. Teneva bhadantabuddhadattācariyena vuttaṃ –

By the one who says, 'For one who makes a request and has it completed, there is no offense under the training rule concerning requesting from non-relatives,' it is shown that 'there is an offense under this training rule because it is the `piṭṭhisamaya` (post-period).' For it cannot be said that an offense, which occurs even by merely giving a hint during the `piṭṭhisamaya` from relatives or those who have extended an invitation, would not occur through a request, which is more serious than that. Therefore, it was said by the venerable teacher Buddhadatta:

“Katvā pana satuppādaṃ, vassikasāṭicīvaraṃ;

Nipphādentassa bhikkhussa, samaye piṭṭhisammate.

However, for a monk who, having given a hint, is having a rains-cloth completed in the time designated as the `piṭṭhisamaya` (post-period),

“Hoti nissaggiyāpatti, ñātakāñātakādino;

Tesuyeva ca viññattiṃ, katvā nipphādane tathā”ti.

there is a `nissaggiya` (entailing forfeiture) offense, from relatives, non-relatives, and so on; and likewise, when one makes a request to them and has it completed.

Kenassa [M 2.0437] hoti āpattīti assa mātaraṃ cīvaraṃ yācantassa kena sikkhāpadena āpattīti pucchati. “Pariṇataṃ viññāpentassa pariṇāmanasikkhāpadena āpattī”ti codanābhāvaṃ dasseti no ca saṅghe pariṇatanti. Atha aññātakaviññattisikkhāpadenāti ce, etampi natthīti āha “anāpatti ca ñātake”ti. “Ñātake viññāpentassā”ti pāṭhaseso. Imamatthaṃ sandhāyāti piṭṭhisamaye vassikasāṭikatthaṃ ñātakapavāritaṭṭhāne satuppādakaraṇena āpattiṃ, aññātakaviññattisikkhāpadena anāpattiñca sandhāya.

As to 'By what is there an offense for him?': he asks, 'For a monk who asks his mother for a robe, by which training rule is there an offense?' He shows that the objection, 'For one who requests what has been designated for the Sangha, there is an offense by the training rule on appropriation,' does not apply, with the words 'and it was not designated for the Sangha.' Then, if one were to ask, 'Is it by the training rule concerning requesting from a non-relative?'—this too is not the case, for he said, 'and no offense in the case of a relative.' The remainder of the text, 'for one requesting from a relative,' is to be supplied. 'Referring to this meaning' means: referring to the offense through giving a hint in the `piṭṭhisamaya` at a place of invited relatives for the purpose of a rains-cloth, and to the non-offense under the training rule concerning requesting from a non-relative.

Aññātakaappavāritaṭṭhānato…pe… dukkaṭanti idaṃ vassikasāṭikaṃ adinnapubbe sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tenevettha vattabhede dukkaṭaṃ vuttaṃ, dinnapubbesu pana vattabhedo natthi. Tenevāha – “ye manussā…pe… vattabhedo natthī”ti. Idanti yathāvuttanissaggiyapācittiyaṃ. Viññattiṃ katvā nipphādentassāti aññātakaappavāritaṭṭhānato viññattiṃ katvā nipphādentassa. Pakatiyā vassikasāṭikadāyakā nāma saṅghavasena vā puggalavasena vā apavāretvā anusaṃvaccharaṃ vassikasāṭikānaṃ dāyakā. Aññātakaviññattisikkhāpadena anāpattīti ettha imināpi sikkhāpadena anāpattīti veditabbaṃ. Kucchisamaye hi attano ñātakapavāritaṭṭhānato “detha me vassikasāṭika”ntiādinā viññāpentassapi anāpatti. Tenevāha – “na vattabbā detha meti idañhi pariyesanakāle aññātakaappavārite eva sandhāya vutta”nti. Mātikāṭṭhakathāyañhi (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. vassikasāṭikasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) vuttaṃ [V 2.0387] “attano ñātakapavāritaṭṭhānato pana ‘detha me vassikasāṭikacīvara’ntiādikāya viññattiyāpi pariyesitabba”nti.

The statement 'From a place of uninvited non-relatives… (and so on)… a `dukkaṭa` offense' was said in reference to those who have not previously given a rains-cloth. Therefore, a `dukkaṭa` for a different case (`vattabheda`) is mentioned here; but for those who have given previously, there is no `dukkaṭa` for a different case. Therefore, he said: 'Those people… (and so on)… there is no `dukkaṭa` for a different case.' 'This' refers to the `nissaggiya pācittiya` offense as stated. 'For one who makes a request and has it completed' means for one who makes a request from a place of uninvited non-relatives and has it completed. By nature, donors of rains-cloths are those who, without being invited, give rains-cloths annually, either on behalf of the Sangha or on behalf of an individual. Regarding 'no offense by the training rule concerning requesting from non-relatives,' it should be understood here that there is no offense by this training rule either. For during the proper time, there is no offense even for one who requests from their own place of invited relatives, saying, 'Give me a rains-cloth,' and so on. Therefore, he said: 'The words, "You should not say, ‘Give it to me,’” were said referring only to seeking from uninvited non-relatives during the search period.' Indeed, in the Mātikāṭṭhakathā it is said: 'But from one’s own place of invited relatives, one may also search by means of a request such as, “Give me a rains-cloth robe.”'

629. “Ākāsato patitaudakenevāti vacanato chadanakoṭiyā patitaudakena nahāyantassa anāpattī”ti tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ.

629. Because of the Pāḷi text, 'only with water fallen from the sky,' it is said in all three `gaṇṭhipada`s that 'there is no offense for one bathing with water that has fallen from the edge of a roof.'

630. Cha māse parihāraṃ labhatīti etena antovassepi yāva vassānassa pacchimadivasā akatā parihāraṃ labhatīti dīpitaṃ hoti. Yasmā mūlacīvaraṃ karontena hemantassa pacchimuposathadivaseyeva kātabbaṃ, tasmā gimhānato ekūnatiṃsadivase parihāraṃ labhati, evaṃ santepi [M 2.0438] appakaṃ ūnamadhikaṃ vā gaṇanūpagaṃ na hotīti katvā “tato parampi…pe… ekamāsa”nti vuttaṃ. Ekāhadvīhādivasena…pe… laddhā ceva niṭṭhitā cāti iminā ekāhānāgatāya vassūpanāyikāya laddhā ceva niṭṭhitā ca, dvīhānāgatāya…pe… dasāhānāgatāya vassūpanāyikāya laddhā ceva niṭṭhitā ca, antovasse vā laddhā ceva niṭṭhitā cāti ayamattho dassito. Tattha āsāḷhimāsassa juṇhapakkhapuṇṇamiyaṃ laddhā ceva niṭṭhitā ca vassikasāṭikā “ekāhānāgatāya vassūpanāyikāya laddhā ceva niṭṭhitā cā”ti vuccati. Eteneva nayena juṇhapakkhassa chaṭṭhiyaṃ laddhā ceva niṭṭhitā ca “dasāhānāgatāya vassūpanāyikāya laddhā ceva niṭṭhitā cā”ti vuccati. Yāva paṭhamakattikatemāsapuṇṇamī, tāva antotemāse laddhā ceva niṭṭhitā ca “antovasse laddhā ceva niṭṭhitā cā”ti vuccati. Paṭhamakattikatemāsapuṇṇamito parañhi laddhā ceva niṭṭhitā ca yāva cīvarakālo nātikkamati, tāva anadhiṭṭhahitvā ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭatīti na tatrāyaṃ vicāraṇā sambhavati.

630. “He obtains a dispensation for six months”—by this, it is shown that even within the rains-residence, if it is not made by the last day of the rainy season, a dispensation is obtained. Because the basic robe must be made by a monk on the very last Uposatha day of the winter season, he therefore obtains a dispensation on the twenty-ninth day from the hot season. Even so, a small amount, whether less or more, is not included in the count; having considered this, it was said, “Beyond that... up to one month.” By this phrase, “obtained and completed for one day, two days, etc.”: the meaning shown is that for the entering of the rains-residence approaching in one day, it is both obtained and completed; for that approaching in two days... for that approaching in ten days, it is both obtained and completed; or, it is both obtained and completed within the rains-residence. Therein, a rains-bathing cloth that is both obtained and completed on the full-moon day of the waxing fortnight of the month of Āsāḷha is called “obtained and completed for the entering of the rains-residence approaching in one day.” By this same method, one that is both obtained and completed on the sixth day of the waxing fortnight is called “obtained and completed for the entering of the rains-residence approaching in ten days.” As long as it is before the full-moon day of the first Kattika month, a robe obtained and completed within that three-month period is called “obtained and completed within the rains-residence.” Indeed, after the full-moon day of the first Kattika month, as long as the robe-season has not passed, it is permissible to keep what is both obtained and completed without having made a formal determination. Therefore, this investigation does not arise in that case.

Tasmiṃyeva antodasāhe adhiṭṭhātabbāti avisesena vuttepi vassānato pubbe ekāhadvīhādivasena anāgatāya vassūpanāyikāya laddhā tehi divasehi saddhiṃ dasāhaṃ anatikkamantena vassūpanāyikadivasato paṭṭhāya adhiṭṭhānakkhettaṃ sampattāyeva adhiṭṭhātabbā, na tato pubbe adhiṭṭhānassa akhettattā. Antovasse pana laddhā tasmiṃyeva antovasse laddhadivasato paṭṭhāya dasāhaṃ anatikkāmetvā adhiṭṭhātabbā.

Even though it is said without specification, “It should be determined within that very ten-day period,” if a robe is obtained before the rainy season for the entering of the rains-residence that is one, two, or more days away, it should be determined only upon reaching the proper period for determination. This begins from the day of entering the rains-residence, and the determination must be made without exceeding ten days when counted together with those previous days. It should not be determined before that, because it is not the proper period for determination. However, if a robe is obtained within the rains-residence, it should be determined starting from the day it was obtained within that very rains-residence, without letting ten days be exceeded.

Nanu ca vassānato pubbe anadhiṭṭhahitvā dasāhaṃ atikkāmetuṃ vaṭṭatiyeva, tasmā adhiṭṭhānassa akhettabhūtepi divase gahetvā “antodasāhe adhiṭṭhātabba”nti kasmā vuttaṃ? Yathā “antovasse laddhāpi yāva na niṭṭhāti, tāva anadhiṭṭhahitvā dasāhaṃ atikkāmetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti akatāya [V 2.0388] anadhiṭṭhānakkhettasadisāpi atikkantadivasā dasāhaṃ atikkāmetvā niṭṭhitāya gaṇanūpagā hontīti niṭṭhitadivaseyeva adhiṭṭhātabbā, evamidhāpi vassānato pubbe anadhiṭṭhānakkhettabhūtāpi divasā laddhadivasato paṭṭhāya gaṇanūpagā hontīti dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Yadi evaṃ “tasmiṃyeva antodasāhe”ti avisesena vuttattā dasāhānāgatāya vassūpanāyikāya [M 2.0439] chaṭṭhiyaṃ laddhā puṇṇamiyaṃ adhiṭṭhātabbāti āpajjatīti? Nāpajjati “cātumāsaṃ adhiṭṭhātu”nti vacaneneva paṭikkhittattā. Evaṃ sante “dasāhānāgatāyā”ti iminā kiṃ payojananti ce? Vassānato pubbeyeva dasāhe atikkante vassūpanāyikadivase niṭṭhitā tadaheva adhiṭṭhātabbāti dassanatthaṃ vuttanti idamettha payojanaṃ. Tenevāha – “dasāhātikkame niṭṭhitā tadaheva adhiṭṭhātabbā”ti.

Is it not the case that before the rainy season, it is indeed permissible to let ten days pass without making a formal determination? Therefore, having obtained it on a day that is not a proper period for determination, why was it said, “It should be determined within ten days”? Just as it is said, “Even if a robe is obtained within the rains-residence, as long as it is not completed, it is permissible to let ten days pass without making a formal determination,” so for an unmade robe, the days that have passed—although they are like a period not for determination—are included in the count for a robe that is completed after ten days have passed, and thus it should be determined on the very day of completion. Similarly here too, it was said in order to show that even the days before the rainy season, which are not a proper period for determination, are included in the count starting from the day the robe was obtained. If so, because it was stated without specification as “within that very ten-day period,” does it not follow that a robe obtained on the sixth day, when the commencement of the rains-residence is less than ten days away, should be determined on the full-moon day? It does not follow, because it is rejected by the very words, “to determine for four months.” If that is the case, what is the purpose of this phrase, “when it is less than ten days away”? It was said in order to show that if ten days have already passed before the rainy season, a robe completed on the day of the commencement of the rains-residence should be determined on that very day. This is the purpose here. Therefore, he said: “If completed after the passing of ten days, it should be determined on that very day.”

Dasāhe appahonte cīvarakālaṃ nātikkametabbāti temāsabbhantare dasāhe appahonte laddhā ceva niṭṭhitā ca cīvarakālaṃ nātikkametabbāti attho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti “paṭhamakattikatemāsapuṇṇamito pubbe sattamito paṭṭhāya laddhā ceva niṭṭhitā ca vassikasāṭikā dasāhe anatikkanteyeva cīvarakālaṃ otiṇṇattā tattha anadhiṭṭhahitvāpi ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Iminā ca imaṃ dīpeti – akatā ce vassikasāṭikā, vassānaṃ cātumāsaṃ akatattāyeva parihāraṃ labhati, katāya pana dasāhaparamasikkhāpadaṃ avikopetvā parihāro vattabboti.

“When ten days are not sufficient, the robe-season should not be exceeded” means that within the three-month period, when ten days are not sufficient, for a robe that is both obtained and completed, the robe-season should not be exceeded. This is what is said: “For a rains-bathing cloth that is both obtained and completed starting from the seventh day before the first Kattika full-moon, because it has entered the robe-season while the ten days have not yet been exceeded, it is permissible to keep it in that case even without having made a formal determination.” And by this, he clarifies the following: If the rains-bathing cloth is unmade, one obtains the dispensation for the four months of the rainy season simply because of it being unmade. But for a made one, the dispensation should be stated without violating the training rule with a maximum of ten days.

Yadā vā tadā vā adhiṭṭhātuṃ vaṭṭatīti cātumāsabbhantare dasāhe atikkantepi natthi dosoti adhippāyo. “Kadā adhiṭṭhātabbā…pe… yadi nappahoti, yāva kattikapuṇṇamā parihāraṃ labhatī”ti imināpi kurundivacanena akatāya vassikasāṭikāya cātumāsaṃ parihāro, katāya dasāhameva parihāroti ayamattho dīpitoyevāti āha “apicā”tiādi.

“It is permissible to determine it at some time or other” means that even if ten days are exceeded within the four-month period, there is no fault. By this statement from the Kurundi commentary as well—“When should it be determined? … If it is not sufficient, one obtains the dispensation up until the Kattika full-moon day”—this meaning is indeed shown: for an unmade rains-bathing cloth, the dispensation is for four months; for a made one, the dispensation is for only ten days. Therefore, he said, “Moreover,” and so on.

Pāḷiyaṃ acchinnacīvarassa naṭṭhacīvarassātiādinā nissaggiyena anāpatti vuttā, udāhu naggassa nahāyato dukkaṭena anāpatti vuttāti? Kimettha pucchitabbaṃ. Sabbasikkhāpadesu hi yattha yattha mūlasikkhāpadena āpattippasaṅgo, tattha tattha anāpattidassanatthaṃ anāpattivāro ārabhīyatīti idhāpi nissaggiyena anāpattidassanatthanti yuttaṃ vattuṃ. Na hi mūlāpattiyā anāpattiṃ adassetvā antarā vuttāya eva āpattiyā anāpattidassanatthaṃ anāpattivāro ārabhīyatīti. Teneva tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu idaṃ vuttaṃ “acchinnacīvarassa naṭṭhacīvarassa cāti ettha acchinnasesacīvarassa naṭṭhasesacīvarassa ca asamaye nivāsentassa pariyesantassa ca anāpatti[V 2.0389]. Āpadāsūti ettha anivatthaṃ corā [M 2.0440] harantīti asamaye nivāsentassa anāpattī”ti. Mātikāṭṭhakathāyampi (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. vassikasāṭikasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) vuttaṃ “acchinnacīvarassa vā naṭṭhacīvarassa vā anivatthaṃ corā harantīti evaṃ āpadāsu vā nivāsayato ummattakādīnañca anāpattī”ti. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana naggassa nahāyato dukkaṭeneva anāpattiṃ sandhāya “acchinnacīvarassāti etaṃ vassikasāṭikameva sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tesañhi naggānaṃ kāyovassāpane anāpatti. Ettha ca mahagghavassikasāṭikaṃ nivāsetvā nahāyantassa corupaddavo āpadā nāmā”ti yaṃ vuttaṃ, tattha kāraṇaṃ pariyesitabbaṃ.

In the Pāḷi, is non-offense declared by means of an offense entailing forfeiture for one whose robe is robbed or lost, and so on, or is non-offense declared by means of an offense of wrong conduct for one bathing naked? What should be asked here? Indeed, in all training precepts, wherever there is an occasion for an offense by the root training precept, there the non-offense section is begun in order to show non-offense. Therefore, it is proper to say that here too, it is to show non-offense by means of an offense entailing forfeiture. For the non-offense section is not begun to show non-offense for an offense mentioned in between, without having shown non-offense for the root offense. For this very reason, in all three gaṇṭhipadas, this is said: ‘Regarding “for one whose robe is robbed or whose robe is lost”—here, for one whose remaining robe is robbed or whose remaining robe is lost, there is no offense for wearing it or searching at the improper time. Regarding “in dangers”—here, because thieves take the unworn robe, there is no offense for wearing it at the improper time.’ In the Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā as well, it is stated: ‘For one whose robe is robbed or whose robe is lost, or because thieves take the unworn robe—thus in dangers, there is no offense for one who wears it, nor for the insane, and so on.’ In the Commentary, however, with reference to the non-offense by means of an offense of wrong conduct for one bathing naked, it is said: ‘The phrase “for one whose robe is robbed” is said referring only to the rainy-season robe. For those naked ones, there is no offense in letting the body be rained upon. And here, for one who bathes having worn an expensive rainy-season robe, the danger from thieves is called a “danger”.’ The reason for what was said thus should be investigated.

Atha ubhayenapi anāpattidassanatthaṃ “acchinnacīvarassā”tiādi āraddhanti evamadhippāyo siyā, evampi “acchinnacīvarassāti etaṃ vassikasāṭikameva sandhāya vutta”ntiādinā visesetvā na vattabbaṃ. Evañhi vattabbaṃ siyā “acchinnasesacīvarassa naṭṭhasesacīvarassa vā asamaye nivāsentassa pariyesantassa ca nissaggiyena anāpatti, acchinnavassikasāṭikassa naṭṭhavassikasāṭikassa vā naggassa nahāyato dukkaṭena anāpatti, āpadāsu anivatthaṃ corā harantīti asamaye nivāsayato nissaggiyena anāpatti, mahagghavassikasāṭikaṃ nivāsetvā nahāyantassa corā haranti, naggassa nahāyato dukkaṭena anāpattī”ti. Sesamettha uttānameva.

Now, if the intention were that ‘for one whose robe is robbed,’ and so on, is begun in order to show non-offense by means of both, even so, it should not be specified by saying, ‘the phrase “for one whose robe is robbed” is said referring only to the rainy-season robe,’ and so on. For it should be said thus: ‘For one whose remaining robe is robbed or whose remaining robe is lost, there is no offense entailing forfeiture for wearing it or searching at the improper time; for one whose rainy-season robe is robbed or whose rainy-season robe is lost, there is no offense of wrong conduct for bathing naked. In dangers, because thieves take the unworn robe, there is no offense entailing forfeiture for wearing it at the improper time. When thieves take an expensive rainy-season robe from one who is bathing having worn it, there is no offense of wrong conduct for bathing naked.’ The rest here is self-evident.

Aṅgesu pana vassikasāṭikāya attuddesikatā, asamaye pariyesanatā, tāya ca paṭilābhoti imāni tāva pariyesanāpattiyā tīṇi aṅgāni. Sacīvaratā, āpadābhāvo, vassikasāṭikāya sakabhāvo, asamaye nivāsananti imāni nivāsanāpattiyā cattāri aṅgāni.

As for the factors, first, for the offense of searching, there are these three factors: the rainy-season robe being intended for oneself, searching at the improper time, and obtaining it thereby. For the offense of wearing, there are these four factors: possessing a robe, the absence of danger, the rainy-season robe being one's own property, and wearing it at the improper time.

Vassikasāṭikasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training precept on the rainy-season robe is finished.

5. Cīvaraacchindanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

5. The Explanation of the Training Precept on Snatching a Robe.

631. Pañcame yampi tyāhanti ettha yanti kāraṇavacanaṃ, tasmā evamettha sambandho veditabbo – mayā saddhiṃ janapadacārikaṃ pakkamissatīti yaṃ kāraṇaṃ nissāya ahaṃ te, āvuso, cīvaraṃ adāsiṃ, taṃ na karosīti kupito [M 2.0441] anattamano acchindīti. Yanti vā cīvaraṃ [V 2.0390] parāmasati, tattha “mayā saddhiṃ janapadacārikaṃ pakkamissatīti yampi te ahaṃ cīvaraṃ adāsiṃ, taṃ cīvaraṃ gaṇhissāmīti kupito anattamano acchindī”ti sambandhitabbaṃ.

631. In the fifth, regarding `yampi tyāhaṃ`, here `yaṃ` is a word expressing cause. Therefore, the connection here should be understood thus: Angry and displeased, he snatched it, thinking, 'Friend, I gave you the robe for the reason that “You will depart on a journey through the countryside with me,” but you do not do so.' Alternatively, `yaṃ` refers to the robe. In that case, the connection should be made thus: Angry and displeased, he snatched it, thinking, 'I will take back the robe which I gave you with the thought, “He will depart on a journey through the countryside with me.”'

633. Āṇatto bahūni gaṇhāti, ekaṃ pācittiyanti “cīvaraṃ gaṇhā”ti āṇattiyā ekacīvaravisayattā ekameva pācittiyaṃ. Vācāya vācāya dukkaṭanti ettha acchinnesu vatthugaṇanāya pācittiyāni. Ekavācāya sambahulā āpattiyoti idaṃ acchinnesu vatthugaṇanāya āpajjitabbaṃ pācittiyāpattiṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Āṇattiyā āpajjitabbaṃ pana dukkaṭaṃ ekameva.

633. “Being ordered, one takes many, but it is one pācittiya” means: because the order, “Take the robe,” has a single robe as its object, it is only one pācittiya. Regarding “For each utterance, a dukkaṭa”: here, with regard to the snatched items, there are pācittiyas according to the count of the items. This statement, “With one utterance, multiple offenses,” was said referring to the pācittiya offense to be incurred according to the count of the snatched items. However, the dukkaṭa to be incurred due to the order is only one.

634. Evanti iminā “vatthugaṇanāya dukkaṭānī”ti idaṃ parāmasati. Eseva nayoti sithilaṃ gāḷhañca pakkhittāsu āpattiyā bahuttaṃ ekattañca atidissati.

634. By `evaṃ` (thus), this refers to the statement, “There are dukkaṭas according to the count of the items.” `Eseva nayo` (This is the very method) indicates the multiplicity and singularity of the offense in cases applied loosely and tightly.

635. Āvuso, mayantiādīsu gaṇhitukāmatāya evaṃ vuttepi teneva dinnattā anāpatti. Amhākaṃ santike upajjhaṃ gaṇhissatīti idaṃ sāmaṇerassapi dānaṃ dīpeti. Tasmā kiñcāpi pāḷiyaṃ “bhikkhussa sāmaṃ cīvaraṃ datvā”ti vuttaṃ, tathāpi anupasampannakāle datvāpi upasampannakāle acchindantassa pācittiyamevāti veditabbaṃ. Acchindanasamaye upasampannabhāvoyeva hettha pamāṇaṃ. Detīti tuṭṭho vā kupito vā deti. Rundhathāti nivāretha. Evaṃ pana dātuṃ na vaṭṭatīti ettha evaṃ dinnaṃ na tāva tassa santakanti anadhiṭṭhahitvāva paribhuñjitabbanti veditabbaṃ. Āharāpetuṃ pana vaṭṭatīti evaṃ dinnaṃ bhatisadisattā āharāpetuṃ vaṭṭati. Cajitvā dinnanti vuttanayena adatvā anapekkhena hutvā tasseva dinnaṃ. Bhaṇḍagghena kāretabboti sakasaññāya vinā gaṇhanto bhaṇḍaṃ agghāpetvā āpattiyā kāretabbo. Vikappanupagapacchimacīvaratā, sāmaṃ dinnatā, sakasaññitā, upasampannatā, kodhavasena acchindanaṃ acchindāpanaṃ vāti imānettha pañca aṅgāni.

635. In phrases like `Āvuso, mayaṃ` (“Friend, we...”), even if it is said with a desire to take, there is no offense because it is given back by that same person. The phrase “He will take the preceptor in our presence” indicates that giving to a novice is also included. Therefore, although the Pāli states, “Having given a robe by oneself to a monk,” it should be understood that even if given when the recipient is not yet fully ordained, for one who snatches it back when the recipient is fully ordained, it is indeed a pācittiya. Here, the state of being fully ordained at the time of snatching is the standard. `Deti` (gives) means one gives either pleased or angry. `Rundhatha` means “you should prevent.” Regarding “However, it is not proper to give in this way,” it should be understood that what is given thus is not yet the recipient's property, and it should be used only without having been determined. However, it is proper to have it brought back; because what is given in this way is like wages, it is proper to have it brought back. `Cajitvā dinnaṃ` (given having relinquished) means it was given to that very person without expectation, not in the way previously mentioned. `Bhaṇḍagghena kāretabbo` (he should be made to pay the value of the goods) means that one who takes without the perception of it being his own should be made to pay the value of the goods and be dealt with for the offense. Here, these are the five factors: (1) the state of being a robe that is at least suitable for sharing (`vikappana`), (2) it being given by oneself, (3) the perception of it being one's own property, (4) the recipient being fully ordained, and (5) snatching or causing to snatch out of anger.

Cīvaraacchindanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule on Snatching a Robe is concluded.

6. Suttaviññattisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

6. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Requesting Thread.

636. Chaṭṭhe [M 2.0442] pāḷiyaṃ cīvarakārasamayeti iminā vassaṃvutthabhikkhūnaṃ cīvarakammasamayattā cīvaramāso vutto, athaññopi pana cīvarakammakālo cīvarakārasamayoti vattuṃ vaṭṭati.

636. In the sixth, 'the time for making robes' in the Pāli refers to the robe month, because it is the time for robe-making activities for monks who have completed the rains residence; however, another period for robe-making activities can also be called the time for making robes.

638. Pañcahipi [V 2.0391] missetvāti khomādīhi pañcahi missetvā. Vītavītaṭṭhānaṃ yattha saṃharitvā ṭhapenti, tassa turīti adhivacanaṃ. Suttaṃ pavesetvā yena ākoṭentā ghanabhāvaṃ sampādenti, taṃ vemanti vuccati. Yaṃ yanti yaṃ yaṃ payogaṃ. Tantūnaṃ attano santakattā vītavītaṭṭhānaṃ paṭiladdhameva hotīti āha “dīghato…pe… vīte nissaggiyaṃ pācittiya”nti. Pāḷiyampi hi imināva adhippāyena “paṭilābhena nissaggiya”nti vuttaṃ, tasmā yāva cīvaraṃ vaḍḍhati, tāva iminā pamāṇena āpattiyo vaḍḍhanti.

638. 'Mixing with five' means mixing with the five kinds of thread beginning with linen. The object on which they roll up and place the woven cloth is called a 'turī'. The shuttle with which they insert the thread and strike it to produce firmness is called a 'vema'. 'Yaṃ yaṃ' means whatever effort. Because the threads are one's own property, the woven portion is considered already obtained; hence, it is said, 'If it is long... when woven, it is a nissaggiya pācittiya.' Indeed, in the Pāli also, it is said with this very intention, 'nissaggiya upon acquisition.' Therefore, as much as the robe-cloth increases, the offenses increase according to this measure.

Seso kappiyoti ettha hatthakammayācanavasena. Pubbe vuttanayena nissaggiyanti dīghaso vidatthimatte tiriyaṃ hatthamatte ca vīte nissaggiyaṃ. Tenevāti akappiyatantavāyena. Tatheva dukkaṭanti paricchede paricchede dukkaṭaṃ. Kedārabaddhādīhīti ādi-saddena acchimaṇḍalabaddhādi gahitaṃ. Tante ṭhitaṃyeva adhiṭṭhātabbanti ettha “pacchā vītaṭṭhānaṃ adhiṭṭhitagatikameva hoti, puna adhiṭṭhānakiccaṃ natthi. Sace pana paricchedaṃ dassetvā antarantarā avītaṃ hoti, puna adhiṭṭhātabba”nti vadanti. Eseva nayoti vikappanupagappamāṇamatte vīte tante ṭhitaṃyeva adhiṭṭhātabbanti attho. Cīvaratthāya viññāpitasuttaṃ, attuddesikatā, akappiyatantavāyena vāyāpananti imānettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

Here, 'the rest is permissible' is in the sense of requesting hand-work. As previously explained, it is a nissaggiya: when a span in length and a cubit in width is woven, it is a nissaggiya. 'By that very one' means by an improper weaver. 'Likewise a dukkaṭa' means a dukkaṭa for each section. In 'bound like a rice-paddy field, etc.', by the word 'etc.', 'bound like an elephant's eye-socket', etc., is included. Here, regarding 'it should be determined while still on the loom', some say: 'Afterwards, the woven portion is as if already determined; there is no further need for an act of determination. But if, after indicating the sections, there are unwoven gaps in between, it must be determined again.' This is the method: the meaning is that when a measure of cloth suitable for vikappana has been woven, it should be determined while it is still on the loom. Thread requested for the sake of a robe, being intended for oneself, and having it woven by an improper weaver—these are the three factors here.

Mātikāṭṭhakathāyaṃ (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. suttaviññattisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) pana vāyāpeyyāti ettha “cīvaraṃ me, āvuso, vāyathāti akappiyaviññattiyā vāyāpeyyā”ti atthaṃ vatvā aṅgesupi “akappiyatantavāyena akappiyaviññattiyā vāyāpana”nti visesetvā vuttaṃ, tathāvidhaṃ pana visesavacanaṃ neva pāḷiyaṃ, na aṭṭhakathāyaṃ upalabbhati. Pāḷiyampi “ñātakānaṃ pavāritāna”nti ettakameva anāpattivāre vuttaṃ, aṭṭhakathāyañca suttatantavāyānameva kappiyākappiyabhāvena bahudhā nayo dassito[M 2.0443], na kappiyākappiyaviññattivasenāti. “Akappiyaviññattiyā vāyāpeyyā”ti ca visesetvā vadantena ayaṃ nāma kappiyaviññattīti visuṃ na dassitaṃ, tasmā vīmaṃsitvā gahetabbaṃ.

However, in the Mātikā Commentary (Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī Aṭṭhakathā, Suttaviññatti Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā), regarding 'one should have it woven,' having stated the meaning as 'one should have it woven through an improper request, saying, “Friend, weave a robe for me,”' it is also stated specifically regarding the factors as 'having it woven by an improper weaver through an improper request.' But such a specific statement is found neither in the Pāli nor in the commentary. In the Pāli also, only 'of relatives who have invited' is stated in the section on non-offenses. And in the commentary, the method is shown in many ways with regard to the permissibility and impermissibility of only the thread and the weaver, not by way of a proper or improper request. And by the one who, specifying, says 'one should have it woven through an improper request,' what is called a 'proper request' is not shown separately. Therefore, this should be investigated and then accepted.

Suttaviññattisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule on Requesting Thread is concluded.

7. Mahāpesakārasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

7. The Explanation of the Training Rule Concerning Great Weavers.

642. Sattame kiñcimattaṃ anupadajjeyyāti idaṃ tassa kattabbākāramattadassanaṃ, dānaṃ panettha [V 2.0392] aṅgaṃ na hoti suttavaḍḍhanavaseneva āpajjitabbattā. Teneva padabhājanepi “tassa vacanena āyataṃ vā vitthataṃ vā appitaṃ vā karoti, payoge dukkaṭaṃ, paṭilābhena nissaggiya”nti suttavaḍḍhanākārameva dassetvā āpatti vuttā. Mātikāṭṭhakathāyampi (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. mahāpesakārasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) vuttaṃ “na bhikkhuno piṇḍapātadānamattena taṃ nissaggiyaṃ hoti. Sace pana te tassa vacanena cīvarasāmikānaṃ hatthato suttaṃ gahetvā īsakampi āyataṃ vā vitthataṃ vā appitaṃ vā karonti, atha tesaṃ payoge bhikkhuno dukkaṭaṃ, paṭilābhena nissaggiyaṃ hotī”ti. Āyatādīsu sattasu ākāresu ādimhi tayo ākāre suttavaḍḍhanena vinā na sakkā kātunti āha “suttavaḍḍhanaākārameva dassetī”ti. Suvītādayo hi ākāre vināpi suttavaḍḍhanena sakkā kātuṃ. Sesamettha uttānameva. Aññātakaappavāritānaṃ tantavāye upasaṅkamitvā vikappamāpajjanatā, cīvarassa attuddesikatā, tassa vacanena suttavaḍḍhanaṃ, cīvarassa paṭilābhoti imānettha cattāri aṅgāni.

642. In the seventh rule, the phrase 'should contribute even a little' indicates merely showing the manner of what is to be done by him. Here, giving is not a factor, as the offense is to be incurred solely by means of increasing the thread. Therefore, even in the word-analysis, the offense is stated by showing only the aspect of increasing the thread: 'At his instruction, if one makes it long, or wide, or dense, there is an offense of wrong-doing in the effort, and it becomes subject to forfeiture upon acquisition.' In the Commentary to the Mātikā, it is also said: 'A robe does not become subject to forfeiture for a monk merely by the giving of almsfood. But if, at his instruction, they take thread from the hands of the robe's owners and make it even slightly long, or wide, or dense, then in their effort, there is an offense of wrong-doing for the monk, and it becomes subject to forfeiture upon acquisition.' Among the seven aspects, such as length and so on, because the first three aspects cannot be done without increasing the thread, he said, 'it shows only the aspect of increasing the thread.' Indeed, aspects such as 'well-woven' can be done even without increasing the thread. The rest here is self-evident. Herein, these are the four factors: (1) approaching weavers who are unrelated and uninvited and making a stipulation; (2) the robe being intended for oneself; (3) the increasing of the thread at his instruction; and (4) the acquisition of the robe.

Mahāpesakārasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule Concerning Great Weavers is concluded.

8. Accekacīvarasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

8. The Explanation of the Training Rule Concerning an Urgent Robe

646. Aṭṭhame asammohatthanti dasāhānāgatapade asammohatthaṃ. Paṭhamapadassāti dasāhānāgatapadassa. Tāni divasānīti tesu divasesu. Uppajjeyyāti saṅghato vā gaṇato vā ujukaṃ attanoyeva vā uppajjeyya. Pañcamitoti ettha vassaṃ vasantassa saṅghassa pañcamito pubbe uppannaṃ [M 2.0444] accekacīvaraṃ pañcamiyaṃ vibhajitvā gahitaṃ accekacīvaraparihārameva labhati. Ujukaṃ attanoyeva uppannaṃ ce, pañcamiyaṃ uppannameva accekacīvaraparihāraṃ labhati, na tato pubbeti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

646. In the eighth rule, 'for the purpose of non-confusion' means for the purpose of non-confusion regarding the phrase 'when ten days have not yet come.' 'The first phrase' means the phrase 'when ten days have not yet come.' 'Those days' means 'in those days.' 'Might arise' means it might arise from the Saṅgha, or from a group, or directly for oneself. 'From the fifth': here, an urgent robe that has arisen for the Saṅgha dwelling for the rains-retreat before the fifth day, if it is divided and received on the fifth day, obtains only the allowance for an urgent robe. If it arises directly for oneself, it should be understood that one obtains the allowance for an urgent robe only if it arose on the fifth day, not before that.

Saddhāmattakanti dhammassavanādīhi taṅkhaṇuppannaṃ saddhāmattakaṃ. Ārocitaṃ cīvaranti ārocetvā dinnacīvaraṃ. Chaṭṭhiyaṃ uppannacīvarassa ekādasamo aruṇo cīvarakāle uṭṭhātīti āha “chaṭṭhito paṭṭhāyā”tiādi. Ṭhapitacīvarampīti padhānacīvaradassanamukhena sabbampi atirekacīvaraṃ vuttaṃ. Atha “cīvaramāsepi atirekacīvaraṃ nikkhipituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti idaṃ kuto laddhanti ce? “Visuṃ ananuññātepi imasmiṃ sikkhāpade ‘cīvarakālasamayo nāma anatthate kathine vassānassa pacchimo māso, atthate kathine pañca māsā’ti vadantena tatiyakathinasikkhāpade ‘akālacīvaraṃ nāma anatthate kathine ekādasamāse uppannaṃ, atthate kathine sattamāse uppanna’nti [V 2.0393] vadantena ca anuññātameva hotī”ti vadanti. “Aṭṭhakathāvacanappamāṇena gahetabba”nti ca keci.

'Mere faith' refers to the mere faith that arises at that moment from hearing the Dhamma and so on. 'An announced robe' means a robe given after it has been announced. He says, 'beginning from the sixth day,' and so on, because the eleventh dawn for a robe that arose on the sixth day rises within the robe season. 'Even a stored robe': by way of showing the principal robe, every kind of extra robe is meant. Then, if it is asked, 'From where is it derived that "it is permissible to keep an extra robe even in the robe month"?', some say: 'Although not separately permitted in this training rule, it is indeed permitted by the one who says, "The robe-season time is the last month of the rains-retreat when the Kathina is not spread, and five months when the Kathina is spread," and by the one who says in the third Kathina training rule, "An out-of-season robe is one that arose in the eleventh month when the Kathina is not spread, and in the seventh month when it is spread."' And some say, 'It should be taken on the authority of the commentary's statement.'

650. Idāni paṭhamakathinādisikkhāpadehi tassa tassa cīvarassa labbhamānaṃ parihāraṃ idheva upasaṃharitvā dassento “iti atirekacīvarassa dasāhaṃ parihāro”tiādimāha. “Anatthate kathine ekādasadivasādhiko māso, atthate kathine ekādasadivasādhikā pañca māsā”ti ayameva pāṭho gahetabbo. Keci panettha “kāmañcesa ‘dasāhaparamaṃ atirekacīvaraṃ dhāretabba’nti imināva siddho, aṭṭhuppattivasena pana apubbaṃ viya atthaṃ dassetvā sikkhāpadaṃ ṭhapita”nti pāṭhaṃ vatvā “dasadivasādhiko māso, dasadivasādhikā pañca māsāti pāṭhena bhavitabba”nti vadanti, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ tassa pamādapāṭhattā. Na hi dasāhena asampattāya kattikatemāsikapuṇṇamāya cīvarakālato pubbe dasa divasā adhikā honti. Evañhi sati “navāhānāgataṃ kattikatemāsikapuṇṇama”nti vattabbaṃ.

650. Now, showing the allowance obtainable for each respective robe through the first Kathina training rule and others, having gathered it right here, he said, 'Thus, the allowance for an extra robe is ten days,' and so on. 'When the Kathina is not spread, a month plus eleven days; when the Kathina is spread, five months plus eleven days'—this very reading should be taken. Some here, however, having stated the reading, 'Although this is already established by the phrase, "An extra robe may be kept for a maximum of ten days," the training rule was laid down by showing a meaning as if it were new by means of the origin story,' say, 'The reading should be "a month plus ten days, five months plus ten days."' That should not be accepted, because it is a careless reading. For indeed, when the Kattika full-moon of the three-month period has not been reached by ten days, ten days are not extra before the robe season. If this were so, it would have to be said, 'The Kattika full-moon of the three-month period has not yet come by nine days.'

Mātikāṭṭhakathāyampi (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. accekacīvarasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) “pavāraṇamāsassa juṇhapakkhapañcamito paṭṭhāya uppannassa cīvarassa nidhānakālo dassito hotī”ti vatvā “kāmañcesa ‘dasāhaparamaṃ atirekacīvaraṃ dhāretabba’nti imināva siddho, aṭṭhuppattivasena pana apubbaṃ viya atthaṃ dassetvā sikkhāpadaṃ ṭhapita”nti pāṭho [M 2.0445] dassito, sopi pamādapāṭhoyeva. “Juṇhapakkhapañcamito paṭṭhāyā”ti ca vuttattā tattheva pubbāparavirodhopi siyā, chaṭṭhito paṭṭhāyāti vattabbaṃ. Evañhi sati “dasāhaparamasikkhāpadeneva siddha”nti sakkā vattuṃ. Imameva ca pamādapāṭhaṃ gahetvā bhadantabuddhadattācariyena ca –

In the Commentary to the Mātikā as well, having said, 'The time for keeping a robe that arose beginning from the fifth day of the waxing moon of the Pavāraṇā month is shown,' the reading, 'Although this is already established by the phrase, "An extra robe may be kept for a maximum of ten days," the training rule was laid down by showing a meaning as if it were new by means of the origin story,' is presented. That, too, is just a careless reading. And because it is said, 'beginning from the fifth day of the waxing moon,' there could also be a contradiction between earlier and later statements right there; it should be said, 'beginning from the sixth day.' For if this is so, it can be said, 'It is established by the training rule of the ten-day maximum itself.' And taking this very careless reading, the venerable teacher Buddhadatta also—

“Tassāccāyikavatthassa, kathine tu anatthate;

Parihārekamāsova, dasāhaparamo mato.

'For that urgent cloth, when the Kathina is not spread, the allowance is held to be one month plus ten days.

“Atthate kathine tassa, pañca māsā pakāsitā;

Parihāro munindena, dasāhaparamā panā”ti. –

'When the Kathina is spread, for that cloth, five months plus ten days have been declared as the allowance by the Sage-King.'–

Vuttaṃ.

It has been said.

Accekacīvarakāle uppannattā “accekacīvarasadise”ti vuttaṃ. “Pañcamiyaṃ uppannaṃ anaccekacīvaraṃ [V 2.0394] dasāhaṃ atikkāmayato cīvarakālato pubbeyeva āpatti hoti, na cīvarakālātikkame, tasmā cīvarakālātikkame puna āpajjitabbāya āpattiyā abhāvaṃ sandhāya ‘anaccekacīvare anaccekacīvarasaññī anāpattī’ti vutta”nti tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Vikappanupagapacchimappamāṇassa accekacīvarassa attano santakatā, dasāhānāgatāya kattikatemāsikapuṇṇamāya uppannabhāvo, anadhiṭṭhitaavikappitatā, cīvarakālātikkamoti imānettha cattāri aṅgāni.

Because it arose at the time of an emergency robe, it is called 'like an emergency robe.' It is stated in all three glosses: 'For one who exceeds ten days with a non-emergency robe that arose on the fifth day, an offense occurs even before the robe-season, not at the exceeding of the robe-season. Therefore, with reference to the absence of a further offense to be incurred at the exceeding of the robe-season, it is said, “In the case of a non-emergency robe, for one who perceives it as a non-emergency robe, there is no offense.”' Herein, these are the four factors: an emergency robe of the final measure suitable for vikappanā being one's own property; its arising on the full-moon day of the three-month Kattika period, before ten days have arrived; its not being determined or made subject to vikappanā; and the exceeding of the robe-season.

Accekacīvarasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule on the Emergency Robe is completed.

9. Sāsaṅkasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

9. The Explanation of the Training Rule on What is Fraught with Danger

652. Navame antaraghareti antare gharāni ettha, etassāti vā antaragharanti laddhavohāre gocaragāme. Tenāha “antogāme”ti. Pāḷiyaṃ vippavasantīti idaṃ yasmiṃ vihāre vasantā antaraghare cīvaraṃ nikkhipiṃsu, tato aññattha vasante sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tasmiñhi vihāre antaraghare cīvaraṃ nikkhipitvā vasituṃ anuññātattā tattha vāso vippavāso nāma na hoti. Dubbalacoḷā duccoḷā virūpacoḷā vā, duccoḷattā eva lūkhacīvarā.

652. In the ninth rule, 'antaraghare' (within the houses) means 'antare gharāni' (within the houses) here, or it refers to a village for alms-round, which is commonly called 'antaraghara'. Therefore, it is said, 'antogāme' (within the village). In the Pāḷi, 'vippavasanti' (dwelling apart) is said with reference to those who, while dwelling in a certain monastery, deposited a robe within the houses and then dwelt elsewhere. For, since it was permitted to deposit a robe within the houses and dwell in that monastery, dwelling there is not called 'dwelling apart'. 'Dubbalacoḷā' (robes of poor quality) means 'duccoḷā' (inferior robes) or 'virūpacoḷā' (ugly robes); or, due to their inferiority, they are 'lūkhacīvarā' (rough robes).

653. “Paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharatī”ti imassa vibhaṅge “upasampajjā”ti uddharitabbe “upasampajja”nti uddharitvā “yo paṭhamassa jhānassa lābho paṭilābho”tiādi [M 2.0446] vuttaṃ, taṃ sandhāyāha “upasampajjantiādīsu viyā”ti. Ādi-saddena “anāpucchaṃ vā pakkameyyā”tiādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Upagantvāti upa-saddassa atthamāha. Vasitvāti akhaṇḍaṃ vasitvā. “Yena yassa hi sambandho, dūraṭṭhampi ca tassa ta”nti vacanato “imassa…pe… iminā sambandho”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha imassāti “upavassa”nti padassa. Nikkhipeyyāti ṭhapeyya.

653. In the analysis of 'he dwells, having attained the first jhāna' (paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati), where 'upasampajjā' (attainment) should have been extracted, 'upasampajja' (having attained) was extracted, and it was said, 'the gain, the attainment of the first jhāna,' and so forth. Referring to this, it is stated, 'as in the case of "upasampajja," and so forth'. By the word 'and so forth,' the inclusion of 'or he may depart without asking,' and so forth, should be understood. 'Upagantvā' (having approached)—this states the meaning of the prefix 'upa-'. 'Vasitvā' (having stayed) means having stayed without interruption. In accordance with the saying, 'Whatever connection one has with something, even if it is far away, that belongs to him,' it is said, 'this... has a connection with this'. Therein, 'imassa' (of this) refers to the word 'upavassa'. 'Nikkhipeyya' (he may place) means 'ṭhapeyya' (he may set down).

Ettāvatā ca purimikāya upagantvā akhaṇḍaṃ katvā vutthavassena āraññakesu senāsanesu viharantena sakalaṃ kattikamāsaṃ ticīvarena vippavasituṃ anuññātaṃ hoti. Anatthatakathinassa hi cīvaramāse vippavāso na vaṭṭati atthatakathinānaṃyeva asamādānacārassa anuññātattā. Keci pana “anatthatakathinānaṃ cīvaramāsepi asamādānacāro labbhatī”ti vatvā bahudhā papañcenti, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ. Byañjanavicāraṇanti “upavassa upavassitvā”tiādivicāraṇaṃ[V 2.0395]. Tassapīti “vutthavassāna”nti vibhaṅgapadassa. Vutthavassānanti ca niddhāraṇe sāmivacanaṃ. Tenāha – “evarūpānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ abbhantare”ti. Senāsanesūti ettha tathārūpesūti sambandhitabbaṃ.

By this much, it is permitted for one who has completed the rains-residence—having gone and stayed for the preceding period without a break, and dwelling in forest lodgings—to dwell apart from the three robes for the entire month of Kattika. For a monk for whom the kaṭhina has not been spread, dwelling apart during the robe-month is not allowable, because the practice of travelling without taking the robes was permitted only for those for whom the kaṭhina has been spread. Some, however, saying, 'Even for those for whom the kaṭhina has not been spread, the practice of travelling without taking the robes is allowable during the robe-month,' elaborate in various ways; that should not be accepted. 'Examination of the letter' means the examination of 'upavassa upavassitvā' ('having resided, having resided'), and so on. 'Of that too' refers to the analysis-word 'vutthavassānaṃ'. And 'vutthavassānaṃ' ('of those who have completed the rains-residence') is the genitive of specification. Therefore, it is said: 'among such bhikkhus'. Here, in 'in lodgings' (senāsanesu), it should be connected with 'of such a kind' (tathārūpesu).

Parikkhepārahaṭṭhānatoti ettha “parikkhepārahaṭṭhānaṃ nāma dve leḍḍupātā”ti vadanti, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ. Aparikkhittassa pana gāmassa pariyante ṭhitagharūpacārato paṭṭhāya eko leḍḍupāto parikkhepārahaṭṭhānanti idamettha sanniṭṭhānaṃ. Teneva visuddhimaggepi (visuddhi. 1.31) vuttaṃ “aparikkhittassa paṭhamaleḍḍupātato paṭṭhāyā”ti. Sabbapaṭhamanti gāmābhimukhadisābhāgato sabbapaṭhamaṃ. Taṃ paricchedaṃ katvāti taṃ paṭhamasenāsanādiṃ paricchedaṃ katvā. Idañca vinayadharānaṃ matena vuttaṃ, majjhimabhāṇakānaṃ matena pana “senāsanādīnaṃ upacāre ṭhitassa ekaleḍḍupātaṃ muñcitvā minitabba”nti majjhimabhāṇakā vadanti. Teneva majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “vihārassapi gāmasseva upacāraṃ nīharitvā ubhinnaṃ leḍḍupātānaṃ antarā minitabba”nti vuttaṃ. Pañcadhanusatikanti āropitena ācariyadhanunā pañcadhanusatappamāṇaṃ. Tato tato maggaṃ pidahatīti tattha tattha khuddakamaggaṃ pidahati. Dhutaṅgacoroti iminā imassapi sikkhāpadassa aṅgasampattiyā abhāvaṃ dīpeti.

Regarding 'from a place suitable for enclosure' (parikkhepārahaṭṭhānato), herein some say, 'A place suitable for enclosure is two clod-throws,' but that should not be accepted. For an unenclosed village, however, starting from the vicinity of the houses situated at the edge, one clod-throw is the place suitable for enclosure; this is the conclusion here. For that very reason, it is also said in the Visuddhimagga: 'for an unenclosed village, starting from the first clod-throw.' 'The very first' (sabbapaṭhamaṃ) means the very first from the part in the direction facing the village. 'Having made that the boundary' (taṃ paricchedaṃ katvā) means having made a boundary of that first lodging, and so on. And this is stated according to the opinion of the Vinaya-experts. But according to the opinion of the Majjhima-reciters, the Majjhima-reciters say: 'One should measure by leaving aside one clod-throw in the vicinity where the lodging, and so on, is situated.' For that very reason, it is said in the Majjhima Nikāya commentary: 'Having excluded the vicinity of both the monastery and the village, one should measure in between the two clod-throws.' 'Five hundred bow-lengths' (pañcadhanusatikaṃ) means a measure of five hundred bow-lengths with the teacher's strung bow. 'It blocks the path from here and there' (tato tato maggaṃ pidahati) means it blocks a small path in various places. By 'a thief regarding the ascetic practices' (dhutaṅgacoro), it shows the absence of the fulfillment of the factors of this training rule as well.

“Sāsaṅkānī”ti sammatānīti corānaṃ niviṭṭhokāsādidassanena “sāsaṅkānī”ti sammatāni.
